Sheriff Manimbayan Abas
Sheriff Manimbayan Abas (born May 5, 1979) is a Filipino
lawyer, election administrator, and regional politician from
Cotabato City.
He served as Chairperson of the Commission on Elections
(COMELEC) from November 2017 to February 2022, becoming the
first Muslim Filipino, the first Mindanaoan, and the youngest person
to hold that office in Philippine history.
He was also the first sitting COMELEC commissioner ever to be
elevated to the chairpersonship, a distinction that set him apart not
just as a symbolic milestone but as someone who already
understood the commission's mechanics from the inside before
leading it.
Among his most consequential acts in office was presiding over the
2019 Bangsamoro Autonomy Plebiscite, the historic popular vote
that ratified Republic Act No. 11054 (the Bangsamoro Organic
Law) and formally established the Bangsamoro Autonomous
Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM) in place of the old
Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (ARMM).
Following his retirement from national service, Abas pivoted back
to his home region. In 2026, he filed his Certificate of Candidacy
for the 1st Parliamentary District of Cotabato City, running under
the United Bangsamoro Justice Party (UBJP) in the inaugural
Bangsamoro Parliamentary Elections.

EARLY LIFE AND BACKGROUND
Sheriff Manimbayan Abas was born on May 5, 1979, in Cotabato
City, the beating heart of the Bangsamoro homeland in the
Philippines.
He grew up in a family with deep roots in the Moro movement,
which shaped his political and legal consciousness from early on.
His uncle is Mohagher Iqbal, one of the most consequential figures
in the Bangsamoro peace process and longtime chief negotiator and
Minister of Education of the Moro Islamic Liberation Front (MILF).
That family connection to the peace negotiations would later
become a point of scrutiny when Abas rose to lead COMELEC, but
it also speaks to the broader ecosystem of Bangsamoro public
service that Abas came from: a world where law, governance, and
community advocacy are deeply intertwined.
He completed his primary and secondary schooling in Mindanao
before heading to higher education, first in Cotabato City and later
in Davao.
EDUCATION
Abas built his academic foundation with a strong grounding in the
humanities and the law, both of which would prove useful in a
career that required sharp analytical thinking and the ability to
communicate clearly with the public.
He earned a Bachelor of Arts in Philosophy from Notre Dame
University in Cotabato City in 1999.
He then pursued his law degree at Ateneo de Davao University,
completing his Bachelor of Laws (LL.B.) in 2004.
In 2005, he passed the Philippine Bar Examination, officially entering the legal profession.
The combination of philosophical training and legal education gave Abas a particular style: he tended to reason
carefully and speak plainly, two traits that served him well both in the classroom and later in the glare of national
media attention.

PAGE 3
EARLY LEGAL AND GOVERNMENT CAREER
Before his name became associated with national elections, Abas quietly built a reputation as a legal officer and
public servant in Muslim Mindanao.
He worked as a law professor, sharing what he had learned in Davao with the next generation of Bangsamoro
lawyers.
In government, he devoted eight years to the Civil Service Commission (CSC), the agency that manages the
professional standards and conduct of Philippine bureaucrats.
From June 2007 to April 2015, Abas served the CSC's regional office for the Autonomous Region in Muslim
Mindanao (ARMM), rising through the ranks from legal officer to Acting Assistant Regional Director.
That role, unglamorous by most measures but deeply practical, gave Abas a ground-level understanding of how
government systems actually work, or fail to work, in a region that had seen decades of underinvestment and
conflict.
It was the kind of foundation that would make him a credible voice not just on election procedures but on
governance more broadly.
COMMISSION ON ELECTIONS
Appointment as Commissioner (2015–2017)
On April 28, 2015, President Benigno S. Aquino III appointed Abas as a COMELEC commissioner to fill a
vacancy created by the retirement of incumbent members.
He joined the commission alongside Chairperson Andres Bautista and Commissioner Rowena Guanzon, two
figures who would each, in very different ways, leave their own marks on Philippine electoral history.
At 35 years old, Abas was already one of the youngest commissioners ever to sit on the poll body.
His first major test came in the 2016 national and local elections.
Abas was designated head of the Packing and Shipping Committee, the team responsible for deploying the
enormous logistics operation that a nationwide automated election demands.
Under his watch, the committee coordinated the deployment of over 92,000 vote-counting machines (VCMs) and
approximately 56 million official ballots to precincts across the Philippine archipelago, from the mountain
provinces of the Cordillera to the farthest islands of the Sulu Sea.
Senator Cynthia Villar, who sponsored his later confirmation as chairperson, would note that the 2016 elections
were widely regarded as one of the most transparent and efficient in Philippine history, with 96 percent of precinct
results reported within 12 hours, a record at the time.
Abas's role in that logistical success did not go unnoticed.

PAGE 4
Promotion to Chairperson (2017–2022)
The path to the chairpersonship opened abruptly when Andres Bautista resigned on October 11, 2017, amid
mounting personal and legal controversies involving allegations of hidden wealth.
President Rodrigo R. Duterte designated Abas as the new COMELEC Chairperson on November 22, 2017.
The appointment was not without controversy.
Critics pointed to Abas's kinship with Mohagher Iqbal of the MILF, raising questions about potential conflicts of
interest at a time when the commission was preparing to administer plebiscites on the Bangsamoro Basic Law
(BBL) and the proposed Bangsamoro political entity.
Abas addressed this directly and formally: he inhibited himself from all official proceedings related to the
Bangsamoro Basic Law, removing himself entirely from deliberations where his family ties could create even the
appearance of partiality.
The Commission on Appointments (CA) officially confirmed his appointment on May 23, 2018.
At 38 years old, Abas had broken a set of institutional records that had stood for the poll body's entire history:
First chairperson from Mindanao
First Muslim Filipino to lead the commission
First sitting commissioner promoted to the chairpersonship
Youngest chairperson in COMELEC history
His term was set to run until February 2, 2022, the end of his original seven-year constitutional appointment.
KEY ELECTIONS AND MILESTONES
2018 Barangay and Sangguniang Kabataan Elections
Among the first tests of Abas's leadership were the 2018 Philippine barangay and Sangguniang Kabataan
elections, which involved coordinating localized polling across tens of thousands of barangays and engaging the
youth electorate through the Sangguniang Kabataan (SK) electoral process.
The elections provided early proof that Abas could manage the operational complexity of nationwide polling while
keeping the commission's credibility intact.
2019 Bangsamoro Autonomy Plebiscite
The most historically significant exercise of Abas's tenure was his oversight of the 2019 Bangsamoro autonomy
plebiscite.
Held in January and February 2019, the plebiscite asked voters in Muslim Mindanao to ratify Republic Act No.
11054, more commonly known as the Bangsamoro Organic Law (BOL).
The affirmative vote formally established the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM)
and replaced the long-troubled ARMM, which had existed since 1989 but had never quite delivered the degree of
genuine self-governance it promised.

PAGE 5
The plebiscite was the culmination of decades of peace negotiations, including those led by Abas's own uncle
Mohagher Iqbal, and its successful administration under a Bangsamoro Muslim chairperson carried its own
symbolic weight.
Abas's inhibition from the BBL proceedings had, by this point, helped insulate the commission from accusations of
bias, and the plebiscite proceeded without major procedural challenge to its integrity.
2019 Midterm General Elections
The 2019 midterm elections were the other major national test during Abas's tenure.
The automated election system registered a 72 percent voter turnout, a strong showing by Philippine standards.
There were isolated technical problems: some vote-counting machines (VCMs) experienced glitches, and a number
of secure digital (SD) cards had to be replaced at affected precincts.
But Abas was quick to note what did not happen: there were zero nationwide election failures, and the winning
candidates in most races were proclaimed with a speed that had rarely been seen in previous election cycles.
The 2019 midterms also demonstrated COMELEC's capacity to handle both national and local elections
simultaneously at scale, without systemic collapse.
Retirement and End of Tenure
Abas completed his full constitutional term and retired from COMELEC on February 2, 2022, just months
before the May 2022 presidential election that brought Ferdinand Marcos Jr. to the presidency.
He stepped down alongside veteran commissioners Rowena Guanzon and Antonio Kho Jr., who also concluded
their tenures on the same date.
His successor as acting chair was Socorro B. Inting.
POST-COMELEC CAREER
Abas Law Firm
Following his retirement from government service, Abas returned to private practice and established the Abas Law
Firm, a legal practice specializing in election law advisory and litigation.
Given his seven years at the helm of the Philippines' electoral body, his expertise in election law was, by this point,
arguably unmatched in the country.
The firm positioned itself to advise on the increasingly complex intersection of election administration, political
party law, and the evolving legal landscape of the BARMM.
Bangsamoro Parliamentary Politics
In late 2024, Abas made a public pivot back to regional governance.

PAGE 6
With the Bangsamoro Parliament's inaugural elections drawing near, he formalized his intent to run for a seat
representing the 1st Parliamentary District of Cotabato City under the United Bangsamoro Justice Party
(UBJP), the political arm of the MILF and the dominant force within the interim Bangsamoro Transition Authority
(BTA).
His initial Certificate of Candidacy filing in November 2024 came at a moment of considerable uncertainty: the
Supreme Court had recently ruled to exclude Sulu province from the BARMM, which necessitated legislative and
administrative adjustments to the electoral framework.
Congressional bills were filed in late 2024 to defer the elections, and Abas acknowledged at the time that the
timing was uncertain, with roughly equal odds that the elections would proceed as scheduled or be pushed back.
Ultimately, under Republic Act No. 12317, signed into law by President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. on March 25, 2026,
the first regular Bangsamoro Parliamentary Elections were officially rescheduled to September 14, 2026.
Abas filed his finalized Certificate of Candidacy on May 6, 2026, joining other UBJP candidates including
Mansoor Ebrahim, son of MILF Chairman Ahod "Al Haj Murad" Ebrahim.
If elected, Abas would make history once more: he would become the first former COMELEC chairperson to
serve as a member of the Bangsamoro Parliament.
In his own words, shared with reporters at the time of his initial filing, the motivation was straightforward: after
years of serving the national government, he wanted to bring that experience home to serve his own community
directly.
LEGACY AND SIGNIFICANCE
The record Abas built at COMELEC is, in many ways, a Bangsamoro story embedded inside a national institution.
His appointment and confirmation broke barriers that had stood since the poll body's founding, not through
confrontation, but through competence and careful navigation of an institution that had never before been led by
someone from Muslim Mindanao.
His handling of the 2019 plebiscite, the democratic exercise that gave the Bangsamoro people a formal political
home, remains the most symbolically resonant chapter of his public career.
The fact that it was administered cleanly, under a Muslim chairperson who voluntarily stepped aside from related
proceedings to preserve impartiality, is a point of pride for Bangsamoro advocates of democratic governance.
His return to regional politics in 2026 represents a third act: not just a former official seeking a new platform, but a
person with deep technical knowledge of how elections work choosing to put that knowledge in the service of the
very community whose rights he spent years protecting from the other side of the ballot.

Macapanton "Jun" Y. Abbas Jr
Atty. Macapanton "Jun" Y. Abbas Jr. was a Filipino jurist, legal
strategist, diplomat, and intellectual leader at the heart of the
Bangsamoro self-determination movement.
A man who carried both constitutional law and Islamic
jurisprudence with equal confidence, Abbas spent decades
navigating the intersections of Philippine state politics, international
Islamic diplomacy, and Muslim civil society during the latter half of
the 20th century and the early years of the 21st.
He's historically recognized for co-founding the Bangsamoro
Liberation Organization (BMLO), for making the legal and moral
case for federalism as a peaceful alternative to outright secession,
and for building early institutional structures that protected Muslim
legal rights in a Republic that too often ignored them.

Notability

co-founder of the Bangsamoro

pioneer of constitutional and
international law advocacy for
Bangsamoro self-determination

Islam; leading legal challenges against

juristic framework behind the 1976
Tripoli Agreement; championing

to secession
EARLY LIFE AND FAMILY
Macapanton Abbas Jr. was born into an aristocratic Maranao
Muslim family belonging to the traditional royal lineages, the pat a
pangampong sa ranao, of Lanao del Sur.
The household he grew up in wasn't simply prestigious by name. It
was built on a foundation of legal excellence and civic duty, a
standard set by his father.
His father, Judge Macapanton Abbas Sr., was a towering figure in
Philippine judicial history. The elder Abbas holds the distinction of
being the nation's first Muslim bar topnotcher (finishing 2nd place
in the pre-war era), the first Muslim Provincial Fiscal, and later the
first Muslim District Court Judge in the country. That combination
of firsts says everything about the world Jun Abbas Jr. was shaped
by: a household where the law wasn't just a profession but a form of
public service and, in many ways, a form of resistance.
His brother, Atty. Firdausi Y. Abbas, walked a parallel path. Firdausi
became known in his own right as a human rights lawyer, political activist, and academic. Together, the Abbas
brothers formed one of the most formidable intellectual partnerships in Moro politics, consistently pushing for
constitutional reform and the protection of minority rights. They weren't always in the same room, but they were
almost always on the same side.
EDUCATION
Abbas's education reflects the dual world he inhabited: elite secular law training on one hand, and serious
engagement with Islamic scholarship on the other.
He pursued his legal studies at the University of the Philippines College of Law, one of the most prestigious law
schools in the country. At UP, he distinguished himself not just in the classroom but as a charismatic leader of the
Sigma Rho Fraternity, the kind of figure who commands a room and knows how to build alliances within it.
He was formally admitted to the Philippine Bar in 1969, establishing his formal credentials in constitutional
frameworks and administrative law.
But Abbas didn't stop at domestic legal training. He spent years immersing himself in Middle Eastern political
models, Shari'ah jurisprudence, and international treaty law. That breadth gave him something rare: the ability to
communicate fluently with foreign diplomats and national policy architects at the same time, in the same
conversation.
CAREER AND INSTITUTIONAL CONTRIBUTIONS
Abbas's multi-decade career was never confined to a single lane. He moved between grassroots resistance,
academic analysis, formal diplomacy, and constitutional governance, sometimes all at once.

PAGE 3
The Jabidah Massacre and the Birth of the BMLO (1968)
The 1968 Jabidah Massacre, the cold-blooded execution of Moro military recruits on Corregidor Island, was a
turning point for an entire generation of Muslim Filipino leaders.
In its aftermath, Abbas joined senior figures including Rashid Lucman, Domocao Alonto, and Salipada Pendatun to
establish the Bangsamoro Liberation Organization (BMLO). Abbas served as the organization's youthful strategist
and legal counsel, the person tasked with translating raw, localized grievances into structured political demands
that could be articulated in legal and diplomatic language. It was the role he was born and trained for.
Ansar el Islam and Intellectual Mobilization (1969)
A year later, in 1969, Abbas co-founded Ansar el Islam, a mass religious-intellectual movement designed to
preserve and cultivate Islam within the Philippines.
What made Ansar el Islam significant wasn't just its religious dimension. The organizational structure Abbas helped
build became a genuine incubator for the next generation of Moro student activists. The intellectual groundwork
laid there directly informed the early ideological framework of what would later emerge as both the Moro National
Liberation Front (MNLF) and the Moro Islamic Liberation Front (MILF). In that sense, Abbas's influence on the
Bangsamoro movement runs much deeper than most public accounts acknowledge.
Moderate Factional Leadership within the MNLF
As armed conflict escalated under Martial Law, Abbas aligned with the MNLF but consistently pushed for
diplomatic and legal avenues over the barrel of a gun.
Recognizing deep ideological differences with Nur Misuari's centralized command style, Abbas, alongside figures
like Dimas Pendato, helped spearhead a moderate faction within the MNLF. This faction prioritized political self-
determination, regional autonomy, and structural alignment with international bodies over continuous, destructive
secessionist warfare. It was a position that required both courage and strategic clarity: courage because it meant
resisting pressure from more militant voices, and clarity because it meant articulating a vision of what Bangsamoro
political life could actually look like.
Chairman of the Islamic Directorate of the Philippines
Abbas also served as Chairman of the Islamic Directorate of the Philippines (IDP), where he managed localized
socioeconomic development funds and represented the cultural and religious interests of Filipino Muslims to
international partners, particularly in the Middle East.
The IDP chairmanship placed him at the interface between domestic Muslim civil society and the broader Islamic
world, a position he used to build the kind of diplomatic credibility that would prove invaluable during his years
abroad.
CLASHES WITH THE MARCOS REGIME
During the 1970s, Abbas transformed from elite intellectual into one of the Marcos administration's most
formidable legal and political opponents. His resistance wasn't just principled; it was methodical, strategic, and
sustained.

PAGE 4
The 1971 Constitutional Convention Crisis
Before Martial Law was even declared, Abbas was already in the fight.
During the 1971 Constitutional Convention, he engaged in aggressive legal battles against the Marcos
administration's attempts to manipulate political representation in Mindanao. He formally challenged election
returns in Lanao del Sur, arguing before the courts that the Marcos-controlled Commission on Elections
(COMELEC) was deliberately disenfranchising the Moro electorate, specifically to install state-sanctioned
delegates who would rubber-stamp Marcos's drive toward centralized power. The legal fight went to the courts
(documented in the case Bashier v. Commission on Elections, G.R. No. L-33692), and it placed Abbas squarely in
the crosshairs of an administration that did not take legal challenges lightly.
Exile and the International Stage
When Marcos declared Martial Law in September 1972, the regime moved quickly against anyone with influence
over Moro youth and intellectual circles. The Abbas brothers were among those targeted.
Refusing military arrest, Abbas went underground and eventually fled into political exile, moving through
sanctuaries in Malaysia, Saudi Arabia, and Libya. From abroad, he didn't go quiet. He partnered with prominent
anti-Marcos figures, including the dissident Alex Psinakis, to expose state-sponsored atrocities to the international
press, most notably the burning of Jolo, which he helped bring to the attention of the global media.
The PTFRDM and a Final Break with Marcos (1975)
In 1975, reading a shift in the political climate, Abbas briefly returned to the Philippines under a tactical amnesty to
participate in the Presidential Task Force for the Reconstruction and Development of Mindanao (PTFRDM).
It didn't last.
Abbas quickly concluded that the administration had no genuine interest in structural autonomy. He publicly
accused the Marcos government of using the development fund as a tokenistic public-relations exercise, a
smokescreen designed to mask ongoing military pacification and the continued displacement of Maranao
communities. Having said as much out loud and in public, he severed ties with the administration entirely,
cementing his status as a permanent exile and a persistent diplomatic thorn in Malacañang's side until Marcos was
ousted in 1986.
LEGAL ARGUMENTS REGARDING THE 1976 TRIPOLI
AGREEMENT
The 1976 Tripoli Agreement, co-signed by the Philippine government, the MNLF, and the Organization of Islamic
Cooperation (OIC), was one of the most consequential diplomatic instruments in the history of the Moro peace
process. And when Ferdinand Marcos moved to systematically dilute it, Abbas produced the legal
counterarguments that would frame Moro negotiating strategy for the next thirty years.

PAGE 5
Pacta Sunt Servanda vs. the Plebiscite Maneuver
The central fracture point of the Agreement came from Article 16, which gave the government room to use
"constitutional processes" to implement autonomy. Marcos exploited this language to hold a localized plebiscite in
1977, deliberately splitting the agreed-upon 13 provinces into two weak, separate administrative regions where
Christian majorities outnumbered Muslims.
Abbas attacked this maneuver through international law, invoking pacta sunt servanda, the foundational treaty
doctrine that agreements must be kept in good faith.
His argument rested on two pillars. First, the Tripoli Agreement was a binding international treaty brokered by a
multilateral body (the OIC), and as such it stood above unilateral domestic manipulation. Second, and crucially, a
state cannot invoke its own domestic municipal law, or a manufactured plebiscite, as lawful justification for failing
to honor an international treaty obligation. It was a rigorous, principled argument, and it resonated far beyond the
Philippines.
Asymmetric Federalism and Genuine Devolution
Abbas was equally forceful in rejecting what Marcos called "administrative decentralization," a model that kept
local governance financially and operationally beholden to Manila.
His counter-proposal was asymmetric federalism: a structural arrangement where the Bangsamoro region would
possess inherent, non-negotiable legislative authority over local taxation, ancestral domains, and natural resources.
Not powers granted by Manila's goodwill, but powers built into the architecture of the state itself. This wasn't just a
legal argument; it was a vision of what genuine self-determination actually looks like in practice.
The Security Force Integration Clause
The Tripoli Agreement also included provisions for special regional security forces. Marcos attempted to limit the
Moro contingent to 3,000 men placed under strict Armed Forces of the Philippines command.
Abbas countered with a constitutional defense of a 15,000-man regional security force, grounding his argument in a
simple but powerful point: an autonomous state cannot be genuinely autonomous if its security is controlled by an
external military. A centralized military occupation, he argued, is inherently incompatible with the legal definition
of an autonomous region.
MAJOR WORKS AND POLICY POSITIONS
Abbas was prolific in the way that scholars embedded in active political struggles tend to be: his output took the
form of legal petitions, position papers, and monographs delivered to international forums rather than neatly bound
academic volumes.
His federalism treatises made the sustained case that federalism is the ultimate peaceful antidote to separatism.
Partition and military suppression, he argued, were both inherently flawed responses to the Moro question. What
was needed instead was an autonomous Bangsamoro state within a wider Federal Republic of the Philippines, one
that respected indigenous Moro identity without requiring the dismemberment of the Philippine state.

PAGE 6
Injustice to the Bangsa Moro was perhaps his most powerful written work, a landmark essay and monograph that
systematically documented the land-grabbing, economic marginalization, and legal erasure of Islamic civilization
that had been written out of the dominant Christianized historical narrative of the Philippine Republic. It was the
kind of document that doesn't just make an argument; it assembles the evidence so thoroughly that the argument
becomes difficult to ignore.
He also regularly compiled detailed OIC Treaty Compliance Audits, briefs submitted to the Organization of
Islamic Cooperation that evaluated the Philippine government's implementation of peace protocols. Abbas
positioned himself as a rigorous, ongoing monitor of international treaty adherence, ensuring that Manila's
commitments couldn't simply be forgotten once international attention moved elsewhere.
PERSONAL LIFE AND CULTURAL SIGNIFICANCE
Abbas's personal life was a study in navigating multiple worlds simultaneously: the traditional royal courts of the
Lanao sultanates, the elite legal circles of Metro Manila, and the diplomatic corridors of Kuala Lumpur, Jeddah,
and Tripoli.
His years of exile, which might have diminished a lesser figure, transformed him into something more: an
international diplomat who built alliances for the Bangsamoro across the Islamic world. He was notably effective at
securing diplomatic leverage from Middle Eastern states, keeping the Moro struggle on the permanent agenda of
the OIC during years when it might otherwise have been marginalized.
Within Maranao society, Abbas was revered as an exemplary Aga Khan in the cultural sense of the term: an
educated nobleman who chose to weaponize the law rather than a rifle. He was known for his sharp wit, his
sophisticated oratorical style, and a deep personal commitment to preserving Maranao cultural heritage alongside
Islamic principles. People who knew him describe someone who was formidable in a legal brief and equally at ease
in a traditional Maranao gathering.
AWARDS, RECOGNITION, AND LEGACY
Abbas was repeatedly honored by the Bangsamoro Transition Commission (BTC) and by various Moro non-
governmental organizations as a foundational architect of modern Moro autonomy.
His most enduring legacy, though, isn't an award. It's traceable in the legislative history of Mindanao itself. The
legal concepts he developed, and the critiques he leveled at the Tripoli Agreement, can be tracked across the
successive organic acts of the region, influencing the evolution from the flawed Autonomous Region in Muslim
Mindanao (ARMM) all the way through to the current Bangsamoro Organic Law (BOL).
Abbas is remembered for something that matters profoundly in the history of the Bangsamoro: he shifted the
paradigm of the Moro struggle from purely armed conflict to constitutional diplomacy. He proved, through decades
of work, that minority rights and regional self-preservation can be systematically articulated through international
law and structural state reform rather than through the violence that so often defines this chapter of Philippine
history.
His life's work stands as evidence that the most durable form of resistance is sometimes not a weapon but an
argument, made precisely, made persistently, and made in the right rooms.

Hasmin M. Abdulhalim
Dr. Hasmin M. Abdulhalim, RL, MLIS, is the Director of the
University Library at Mindanao State University (MSU) Main
Campus in Marawi City, a position she assumed in February 2026
through Special Order No. 119-OP, Series of 2026, after more than
two decades of teaching and administrative service within the
university system.
A Registered Librarian with a PhD in Educational Administration
and Supervision, she spent over twenty years as a full time faculty
member in the Department of Library and Information Science
before rising through the university's governance structures,
including the University System Curriculum Committee, the Campus
Quality Assurance Board, and the University Research Ethics
Committee.
She is widely recognized for steering the University Library's post
Marawi Siege transformation into a culturally inclusive, community
centered space, complete with prayer and ablution rooms, and for
championing library systems aligned with the United Nations
Sustainable Development Goals, particularly in support of
individuals with psychosocial disabilities.
Beyond MSU, she served as President of the Philippine Librarians
Association, Inc. (PLAI), BARMM Regional Council, from 2022 to
2023, advancing professional development and advocacy for
librarians across the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim
Mindanao.
Contents
1 Overview
2 History of the MSU Main Campus Library
2.1 A Sanctuary Amidst Crisis
2.2 Space Reimagining and Cultural Integration
2.3 Post Pandemic Upgrades and Partnership Era
3 Education
4 Career and Public Service
5 Leadership Roles
6 Contributions, Achievements, and Legacy
7 References
Overview
Dr. Hasmin M. Abdulhalim, RL, MLIS, is a prominent academic
administrator and educator at Mindanao State University (MSU) Main Campus in Marawi City.

PAGE 2
Serving as the University Library Director, she is a central figure in advancing the institution's academic
ecosystem, knowledge preservation, and administrative systems.
Before ascending to her institutional leadership role, Dr. Abdulhalim spent over two decades as a full time faculty
member in the Department of Library and Information Science under the College of Social Sciences and
Humanities (CSSH).
Beyond her campus contributions, she has served as a regional leader in the Philippine library community, driving
modernization and professional growth in library sciences across the region.
History of the MSU Main Campus Library
The history of the University Library is deeply intertwined with the evolution of Mindanao State University, which
was established in 1961 through Republic Act 1387 to serve the educational and cultural needs of Southern
Philippines.
Since its inception, the main campus library in Marawi City has functioned as the intellectual heart of the campus.
A Sanctuary Amidst Crisis
Over the decades, the library transitioned from a traditional repository of books into a vital community hub.
During the devastating Marawi Siege of 2017, when much of the surrounding city faced destruction, the MSU
Main Campus became a haven of institutional resilience.
In the post conflict recovery period, students famously dubbed the University Library their "happy place." It was
one of the few vibrant spaces where students from diverse cultural backgrounds gathered not just to study, but to
find a sense of normalcy, safety, and community.
Space Reimagining and Cultural Integration
In April 2019, the library administration launched an ambitious modernization initiative themed "Transforming
Lives: Re imagining, Re tooling, and Re creating the University Library."
This project fundamentally adapted the facility to serve its predominantly Muslim student body and the local
community more holistically.
Key historical upgrades included the Banggolo Reading Room, the transformation of the second floor into a
spacious, high capacity study area to accommodate the dense population of student researchers.
Ablution and prayer rooms were also introduced: the building became uniquely inclusive by installing dedicated
male and female ablution spaces alongside separate prayer rooms, directly supporting the religious and daily
routines of its users.
Infrastructure improvements followed as well, including a dedicated water pump system, integrated to maintain
sanitation standards independent of the city's wider municipal struggles.

PAGE 3
Post Pandemic Upgrades and Partnership Era
Following years of hybrid operations and structural adjustments, the library officially resumed full regular
operations and centralized research assistance services on July 13, 2026.
To overcome the physical limitations of its geographic location, the university entered into a landmark resource
sharing partnership with the University of the Philippines (UP) in late 2025.
Facilitated by the MSU Board of Regents, this collaboration systematically links MSU's academic community with
UP's digital databases and specialized catalogs.
Today, alongside its physical main building, the university operates a separate Digital Library and Institutional
Repository located adjacent to the Aga Khan Museum.
This division is tasked with digitizing permanent university publications, multimedia collections, and historical
artifacts that trace the institutional history of the region.
Education
Dr. Abdulhalim possesses an extensive academic background that bridges library sciences and educational
leadership.
Her Master in Library and Information Science (MLIS) provided the theoretical foundations and technical skills
necessary for her lifelong career in modern information systems and cataloging management.
Her Doctor of Philosophy (PhD) in Educational Administration and Supervision equipped her with the
organizational governance capabilities required to steer complex, university wide academic units.
She holds professional credentialing as a Registered Librarian (RL) in the Philippines, having passed the national
licensure examination mandated by the Professional Regulation Commission.
Career and Public Service
Dr. Abdulhalim's professional tenure at Mindanao State University spans more than twenty years, reflecting a
steady rise from classroom teaching to university wide governance.
As an Associate Professor V within CSSH, she has trained generations of Filipino library professionals.
Her service portfolio demonstrates deep involvement in institutional quality control and academic integrity, and she
has lent her regulatory and development expertise to several of the university's high level governing bodies.
Within the University System Curriculum Committee (USCC), she evaluated and refined academic programs
across the university network.
As part of the Campus Quality Assurance Board, she served as the College Coordinator for Quality Assurance,
aligning local curricula with international institutional benchmarks.
Through the University Research Ethics Committee, she helped ensure that academic and scientific inquiries
conducted under the university's banner meet rigorous ethical and human subject protection protocols.

PAGE 4
At the department level, she served as Chairperson of the Department of Library and Information Science, where
she directly managed recruitment, program standards, and faculty development.
Leadership Roles
Dr. Abdulhalim reached a major career milestone in February 2026.
Through Special Order No. 119-OP, Series of 2026, issued by the MSU System President, Atty. Paisalin P.D. Tago,
CPA, she was officially designated as the Director of the University Library for the MSU Main Campus.
On February 16, 2026, she officially took over the administrative reins from outgoing director Zaalica B. Edres
during an official turnover ceremony witnessed by Executive Vice President Dr. Abdulcader M. Ayo.
Her leadership also extends significantly beyond campus borders. She served as the President of the Philippine
Librarians Association, Inc. (PLAI), BARMM Regional Council, for the 2022 to 2023 term.
In this capacity, she spearheaded professional development programs and advocacy networks for librarians
operating throughout the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao.
Contributions, Achievements, and Legacy
At the core of Dr. Abdulhalim's legacy is her dedication to making information spaces socio culturally inclusive
and aligned with global standards.
Her modern administrative strategies directly connect local library resources to broader developmental metrics.
On community inclusivity, Dr. Abdulhalim initiated a public access framework allowing local Marawi City
residents free entry to university library services every Friday, breaking down institutional barriers between the
campus and the public.
On sustainability and SDG alignment, she has championed institutional data collection tailored to the United
Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), specifically targeting SDG 10 (Reduced Inequalities) by adapting
library tracking systems to capture support structures for individuals with psychosocial disabilities, such as ADHD.
On institutional stewardship, by bridging the gap between historical print archives and modern digital repositories,
she continues to direct the preservation of fragile documentation reflecting the rich cultural heritage of the
Meranaw people and the broader Mindanao frontier.

Jashim A. Abdulrahman
Prof. Atty. Jashim A. Abdulrahman, Sh.L., MAIS is a Shari'ah
lawyer, a member of the Integrated Bar of the Philippines, and the
Dean of the King Faisal Center for Islamic, Arabic and Asian Studies
(KFCIAAS) at Mindanao State University (MSU) in Marawi City.
An Associate Professor V, he also lectures at the MSU College of
Law and reviews bar takers in Shari'ah subjects.
His faculty profile carries a short motto: "Success is Doing not

His schooling started in Marawi City: Banggolo Elementary School
(1994), then Marawi City National High School (1998), where he
finished among the top seven.
At MSU, Fisheries Technology (2002) appears on his record, but
Islamic Studies became his road.
In 2005 he earned his Bachelor of Arts in Islamic Studies, major in

In November 2008 he sat for the Special Shari'ah Bar Examinations at the Court of Appeals in Manila (November 9

He then took the 2020/2021 Philippine Bar Examinations, held at MSU-IIT in Iligan City on February 4 and 6,

Teaching Career
He started teaching right after college. From 2005 to 2008 he was a college instructor at Lanao Islamic Paramedical

At the Philippine Muslim Teachers' College, he was a college instructor (2008 to 2012) and a professional lecturer

He also taught in the College Bound Program of the former Pre-University Center from 2009 to 2014.
At KFCIAAS, he began as Instructor III on June 7, 2010. He became Assistant Professor IV in February 2019 and

College Secretary, KFCIAAS (2011 to 2014)

Research Coordinator, KFCIAAS (Academic Years 2018 to 2019 and 2019 to 2020)

Shari'ah Bar Review and Writings
Since 2009 he has been a regular Shari'ah Bar training lecturer and reviewer at the Shari'ah Training Center of the
National Commission on Muslim Filipinos.

title: Abdurahim, Sabuddin N.
text:
PAGE 1
Sabuddin N. Abdurahim
Sabuddin N. Abdurahim is a Filipino public servant and spiritual leader from Tawi-Tawi currently serving as the
Secretary of the National Commission on Muslim Filipinos (NCMF). A Tausug Muslim leader, he was
reappointed to this position by President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr. on March 6, 2026, for a two-year term.
Abdurahim is the first individual from Tawi-Tawi to lead the NCMF, bringing over three decades of experience in
healthcare, local governance, and national diplomatic affairs. His tenure has been marked by the modernization of
Hajj operations for Filipino pilgrims, the decentralization of NCMF regional offices, and strengthening of
community resilience programs across Muslim communities in the Philippines.
Contents
1 Early Life and Family
2 Education and Spiritual Background
3 Professional Career
3.1 Medical Technologist and Healthcare Service (Pre-2016)
3.2 Local Governance: Sangguniang Panlalawigan (2016-2024)
4 National Leadership: NCMF Tenure
4.1 Initial Appointment and Reappointment
4.2 Institutional Contributions
4.2.1 Hajj Operations Reform
4.2.2 Decentralization and Regional Empowerment
4.2.3 Community Resilience Programs

5.3 Qatar and South Korea: Business Mission (December 2025)
5.4 Halal Diplomacy and Tourism Positioning (2026)
6 Personal Values and Leadership Philosophy
7 Recognition and Awards
8 Challenges and Criticisms
9 Legacy and Future Directions
10 References
11 Further Reading
12 See Also
Early Life and Family
Abdurahim was born and raised in Tawi-Tawi, a province often referred to as the "Cradle of Islam" in the
Philippines. His deep roots in the ZAMBASULTA region (comprising Zamboanga, Basilan, Sulu, and Tawi-Tawi)
have shaped his identity as a Tausug Muslim leader and public servant. He is married to Dewy Sabuddin, who
serves as a Barangay Chairwoman in their home province, reflecting a shared commitment to community
leadership and governance.

PAGE 2

His early life in the maritime and predominantly Muslim
provinces of Mindanao instilled in him a deep understanding of
regional economic challenges, interreligious dynamics, and the
aspirations of Muslim Filipino communities. This background
became foundational to his later work in local and national
governance.
Education and Spiritual Background
Abdurahim's educational and spiritual formation reflects a
synthesis of technical expertise and Islamic scholarship. He
earned a Bachelor of Science degree in Medical Technology,
establishing a foundation in healthcare and scientific practice.
Recognizing the need for broader competency in public
administration, he pursued a Master's degree in Public
Administration (MPA), equipping him with the tools to navigate
complex governance structures. He has completed all academic
requirements for a Doctor of Philosophy in Peace and
Development, signaling his commitment to the scholarly
dimensions of conflict resolution and regional stability.
Beyond formal education, Abdurahim is a respected Sheikh
within the Muslim Filipino community. He served as an accredited
Murshid (Spiritual Guide and Teacher) in the ZAMBASULTA
region from 1999 to 2023, a role that required deep knowledge of
Islamic theology, ethics, and community pastoral care. His status
as a Murshid elevated his standing as a trusted moral and spiritual
authority among Muslim Filipinos, particularly in Mindanao.
Professional Career
Medical Technologist and Healthcare Service (Pre-
2016)
Before entering electoral politics, Abdurahim devoted more than
two decades to healthcare. He worked as a Medical Technologist
at the Integrated Provincial Health Office in Bongao, Tawi-
Tawi, where he gained frontline experience in medical diagnostics
and patient care. This lengthy tenure in the healthcare sector
provided him with practical insight into the health infrastructure
challenges facing remote island communities and informed his
later advocacy for improved medical facilities in the
ZAMBASULTA region.

PAGE 3
Local Governance: Sangguniang Panlalawigan (2016-2024)
In 2016, Abdurahim transitioned from healthcare to electoral politics, serving as a member of the Sangguniang
Panlalawigan of Tawi-Tawi for three consecutive terms (2016-2024). During this period, he held strategic
committee chairmanships that shaped provincial policy and resource allocation.
As Chair of the Committee on Budget and Appropriation, Abdurahim oversaw the fiscal stewardship of
provincial funds, ensuring that development projects aligned with regional priorities. Concurrently, he chaired the
Committee on Infrastructure, positioning himself at the center of decisions regarding public works,
transportation networks, and the connectivity challenges unique to an archipelago province.
His chairmanship of the Committee on Business, Trade, and Investment reflected his commitment to economic
diversification. Tawi-Tawi's strategic location within the BIMP-EAGA (Brunei-Indonesia-Malaysia-Philippines
East ASEAN Growth Area) corridor made this committee work particularly crucial. Abdurahim authored and
supported legislative measures designed to attract external investment, facilitate cross-border commerce, and
leverage the province's maritime advantages.
Reflecting his medical background, he also served as Vice Chair of the Committees on Health and Education,
where he championed healthcare access and educational equity in a province historically underserved by national
infrastructure investment.
National Leadership: NCMF Tenure
Initial Appointment and Reappointment
Abdurahim was appointed Secretary of the National Commission on Muslim Filipinos (NCMF) in March 2024.
His appointment carried symbolic and substantive weight: he became the first individual from Tawi-Tawi to lead
the commission at the national level. The appointment was formally endorsed by all six governors of the
Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM), reflecting broad regional support and
confidence in his leadership credentials.
In March 2026, President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr. reappointed him for an additional two-year term, affirming the
success of his tenure. He also serves as a member of the Mindanao Development Authority (MinDA) Board of
Directors, expanding his influence over regional economic policy beyond Muslim affairs.
Institutional Contributions
Hajj Operations Reform
Among Abdurahim's most visible contributions is the modernization and efficiency of Hajj operations for Filipino
Muslim pilgrims. Serving as Amirul Hajj (Leader of Pilgrims) for three consecutive years (2024, 2025, and 2026),
he implemented operational reforms that resulted in the most delay-free and efficiently organized pilgrimages in
recent history.
His strategy involved streamlining communications with the Saudi government and the Philippine diplomatic
missions in Jeddah and Madinah, reducing bureaucratic bottlenecks that had plagued earlier Hajj seasons. These
reforms had immediate practical benefits: Filipino pilgrims experienced shorter processing times, faster hotel

PAGE 4
accommodations, and more reliable transportation arrangements. The success of these operations enhanced the
reputation of the Philippines in the eyes of the Saudi authorities and affirmed the NCMF's capacity to manage
complex international religious logistics.
Decentralization and Regional Empowerment
Abdurahim spearheaded a major institutional restructuring: the decentralization of NCMF regional offices.
Rather than concentrating decision-making authority in the national office, he devolved significant operational and
policy responsibilities to regional offices, positioning them as primary implementing units. This shift recognized
the diverse cultural and economic contexts across the ZAMBASULTA, Davao, Caraga, and other Muslim-majority
areas. Decentralization enabled faster response to local needs and strengthened the community accountability of
NCMF programs.
Community Resilience Programs
Under his leadership, the NCMF strengthened programs related to Bagong Pilipinas Community Resilience, with
particular focus on peacebuilding and social cohesion in Muslim communities. These initiatives addressed
grassroots conflict prevention, interfaith dialogue, and economic empowerment of women and youth in Muslim-
majority barangays. His work here drew on both his spiritual authority as a Murshid and his administrative
experience in provincial governance.
International Diplomacy and Engagement
Saudi Arabia: Hajj Diplomacy (Annual, 2024-2026)
As Amirul Hajj, Abdurahim led annual diplomatic missions to Saudi Arabia, meeting with officials at the Ministry
of Hajj and Umrah, the Philippine embassies, and senior representatives of the Saudi government. These missions
yielded operational breakthroughs and strengthened bilateral relations on matters of religious and cultural
significance. His personal engagement signaled to Saudi Arabia that the Philippines treats Hajj coordination as a
matter of executive priority.
Indonesia: Benchmarking Mission (February 2025)
In February 2025, Abdurahim dispatched and personally oversaw a high-level benchmarking mission to Jakarta,
targeting the most advanced Islamic governance institutions in Southeast Asia. The delegation engaged with the
Hajj Organizing Agency and the Halal Product Assurance Organizing Agency, studying best practices in Halal
certification standards, Madrasah education frameworks, and Islamic finance mechanisms.
This engagement reflected Abdurahim's vision of positioning the Philippines not merely as a consumer of Islamic
institutional expertise, but as a potential contributor to regional standards. The Indonesian models offered valuable
lessons for upgrading the NCMF's regulatory and educational capacity.
Qatar and South Korea: Business Mission (December 2025)
Representing the Mindanao Development Authority (MinDA), Abdurahim joined an outbound business mission
to Doha and Seoul in December 2025. The delegation sought international investor interest in Mindanao
infrastructure and agricultural projects. This mission positioned Muslim Mindanao as an investment destination

PAGE 5
within broader regional development corridors, potentially unlocking capital for ports, agribusiness, and renewable
energy projects aligned with national development goals.
Halal Diplomacy and Tourism Positioning (2026)
Most recently, Abdurahim has focused on positioning the Philippines as a global player in Halal Tourism. He has
hosted international summits in Manila aimed at building partnerships with foreign industry advocates and private
sector collaborators in Halal food, hospitality, and cultural tourism. This initiative recognizes that the Philippines'
Muslim communities represent a unique cultural and religious asset that can be leveraged for economic benefit
while maintaining spiritual authenticity.
Personal Values and Leadership Philosophy
Abdurahim's public service is guided by a philosophy of ethical leadership and the integration of Islamic values
with democratic governance. He has consistently advocated for the principle that public office is a trust, not a
privilege, and that Muslim leaders bear a responsibility to serve both their faith communities and the broader
nation.
His spiritual background as a Murshid informs his approach to consensus-building and conflict resolution. In
provincial legislative debates, colleagues noted his tendency to seek common ground and frame divisive issues in
terms of community welfare rather than partisan advantage. This approach reflects the Islamic emphasis on shura
(consultation) and adl (justice).
Recognition and Awards
Abdurahim has received numerous accolades for his public service contributions. He was honored with the Dangal
ng Pinas Award for Outstanding Public Service, recognizing his dedication to national advancement. He also
received a Governance Excellence Award, affirming his institutional leadership and administrative competence.
These recognitions validate his track record across healthcare, local governance, and national diplomacy.
Challenges and Criticisms
As is typical for public figures, Abdurahim has faced scrutiny regarding certain policy decisions. Some regional
observers have questioned the pace of NCMF decentralization, particularly regarding the adequacy of funding and
technical support provided to regional offices. Others have debated the emphasis on international diplomacy
relative to domestic grassroots programming. These critiques, while substantive, remain within normal bounds of
democratic discourse and do not diminish his overall reputation as an effective administrator.
Legacy and Future Directions
Abdurahim's appointment as NCMF Secretary represents a broader shift in Muslim Filipino leadership: the
emergence of provincial figures from maritime and peripheral regions into national roles. His tenure suggests that
the future of Muslim Filipino affairs will increasingly be shaped by leaders with deep community roots, rather than
exclusively by personalities based in Manila or major urban centers.

PAGE 6
Looking forward, his work on Halal standards, interfaith dialogue, and regional development positions him to
influence not only national Muslim policy, but also the Philippines' standing in the broader Islamic world and
Southeast Asian regional frameworks.

title: Abdurahman, Nagder J.
text:
PAGE 1
Nagder J. Abdurahman
Dr. Nagder J. Abdurahman, Ed.D. is a Tausug educator, researcher, and academic administrator who serves as
the Chancellor of Mindanao State University–Sulu (MSU-Sulu) in Jolo, Sulu, Philippines.
A son of the Suluk heartland, he is widely recognized as the first truly "homegrown" chancellor of MSU-Sulu,
having studied, taught, and built his career within the very institution he now leads.
His leadership, which began around September 2019, has been defined by a practical and people-centered
approach: expanding access to higher education in one of the country's most historically underserved regions,
modernizing campus infrastructure, and keeping Tausug culture and indigenous knowledge at the center of the
university's identity.
In a region where education has long been intertwined with questions of peace, community resilience, and cultural
survival, Dr. Abdurahman represents something meaningful: a local son steering a major state university toward
greater relevance, inclusivity, and excellence.
Contents

2 Education
3 Career
3.1 Early Academic Career
3.2 Appointment as Chancellor
3.3 Key Institutional Priorities
3.4 Community and Regional Engagement
4 Leadership Style and Values

11 External Links
Background
Dr. Nagder J. Abdurahman was born and raised in the Sulu province of the southern Philippines, deep in the Tausug
heartland.
He belongs to the Tausug people, one of the major ethnolinguistic groups of the Sulu Archipelago and a
cornerstone of the broader Bangsamoro identity.
The Tausug have a long history of asserting their political autonomy, preserving their Islamic traditions, and
navigating complex relationships with the Philippine state, all of which forms the cultural backdrop of Dr.
Abdurahman's personal and professional life.

PAGE 2

Details about his exact birthdate and early childhood remain
relatively private, which is consistent with many public figures
from the region who tend to let their work speak rather than their
personal biography.
What is clear from his career and advocacy is that he carries a
deep sense of responsibility toward the Tausug community and a
genuine commitment to improving the lives of people in Sulu
through education and research.
Education
Dr. Abdurahman is an alumnus of MSU-Sulu itself, which makes
his rise to its chancellorship particularly meaningful within the
institution's history.
He earned a Doctor of Education (Ed.D.), with expertise
spanning educational leadership, institutional management,
language studies, professional education, and peace and
development studies.
His academic interests have always leaned toward practical
application: how do you actually run a university better, and how
do you connect formal higher education with the realities of a
complex, multicultural community?
One of his notable contributions to educational scholarship is the
book Management Effective and Job Motivation: A Simple Guide
for Higher Education, which reflects his commitment to making
academic administration accessible and useful for practitioners.
His research profile, maintained on platforms like ResearchGate
and Google Scholar, shows a dual focus: modern leadership theory
applied to higher education, and indigenous knowledge systems,
particularly affiliative leadership among Taumaas (traditional
Tausug headmen) in Suluk communities.
That second thread is notable because it signals a scholar who
doesn't treat Western management frameworks as the only valid
lens. He actively works to understand and document how
leadership has always functioned in Tausug society.
Career
Early Academic Career
Dr. Abdurahman built his career as a professor and administrator
within the MSU system, steadily gaining experience in teaching,
research, and institutional governance.

PAGE 3
Before his appointment as chancellor, he served in various academic and administrative capacities that gave him
firsthand knowledge of how the university operates at multiple levels.
His trajectory from student to faculty to the top administrative post of MSU-Sulu reflects the kind of institutional
loyalty and deep contextual knowledge that shaped his leadership philosophy.
Appointment as Chancellor
He was appointed Chancellor of MSU-Sulu around September 2019, stepping into one of the most demanding
leadership roles in the Bangsamoro region.
As chancellor, he oversees an institution that serves students from Sulu, Tawi-Tawi, and surrounding communities,
many of whom come from areas with limited access to quality secondary and tertiary education.
He has served multiple terms in the role, with reappointments from the MSU Board of Regents reflecting strong
performance reviews from the MSU system.
By 2025, a formal five-year evaluation of his chancellorship was conducted, and the assessment affirmed the
direction and quality of his leadership.
Key Institutional Priorities
Under his watch, MSU-Sulu has pursued several concrete development tracks:
Dr. Abdurahman rolled out flexible learning options during and after the COVID-19 pandemic, ensuring students
in remote or conflict-affected areas could continue their education without being physically present on campus.
He championed significant infrastructure development across the campus, including new academic buildings,
dormitory facilities, a nursing building, and upgrades to the university's information and communications
technology (ICT) systems.
He strengthened MSU-Sulu's research and extension services, pushing the university to become more active in
knowledge production and community engagement beyond the classroom.
He pursued collaborations with other campuses within the MSU system, with other institutions in the BARMM,
and with international partners, to widen opportunities for students and faculty.
Community and Regional Engagement
Beyond the campus, Dr. Abdurahman has been an active presence in regional academic and civic life.
He has delivered commencement addresses not only at MSU-Sulu but also as a guest speaker at nearby institutions
such as Lapak Agricultural College, where he consistently ties themes of inspiration to the call for community
service.
He has been involved in discussions around expanding academic programs, including exploratory conversations
about establishing a College of Law at MSU-Sulu, which would address a significant gap in professional legal
education in the province.
He has also supported cultural preservation initiatives and regional forums on peace, governance, and development,
positioning MSU-Sulu as a contributor to the broader Bangsamoro conversation.

PAGE 4
Educational outreach efforts in communities like Siasi reflect his conviction that the university's responsibility
doesn't end at the campus gate.
Leadership Style and Values
Those who work alongside Dr. Abdurahman consistently describe him as approachable, grounded, and genuinely
committed to the institution and the people it serves.
His leadership philosophy leans on what he and his colleagues have described as "internal integration and external
adaptation": modernizing the university's systems and programs while staying firmly rooted in the social and
cultural realities of Sulu.
He doesn't treat the Western academic model as a template to be copied wholesale. Instead, he looks for approaches
that work within the specific context of a university operating in a region with its own history, challenges, and
strengths.
His values, as expressed through both his public statements and his research interests, center on service, resilience,
education as empowerment, and cultural pride.
In a setting where the intersection of faith, culture, and governance is constant, he approaches leadership with the
kind of patience and cultural fluency that the job demands.
He remains, at heart, a professor, staying connected to the classroom and the scholarly life even while carrying the
administrative weight of a chancellorship.
Family life stays largely outside public discourse, which is consistent with the Tausug cultural preference for
communal rather than individual focus in public leadership.
Cultural Significance
MSU-Sulu was established in 1974 to bring higher education closer to the communities of the Sulu Archipelago.
Decades later, having a Tausug educator at the helm of the institution carries real symbolic and practical weight.
Dr. Abdurahman's chancellorship represents something the institution hadn't quite seen before: a leader who grew
up in the same cultural world as the students he serves, who speaks from lived experience rather than outside
observation, and who sees the university's mission through a Suluk lens.
His contributions to scholarship on indigenous Tausug leadership traditions, particularly his work on affiliative
leadership among Taumaas, are a reminder that the knowledge and governance systems of the Tausug people are
worth studying and documenting, not as historical curiosities but as living frameworks with continuing relevance.
In the broader landscape of Muslim Mindanao, his presence adds a Sulu voice to conversations often dominated by
perspectives from Cotabato or other parts of the BARMM, ensuring that the distinct experience of the Sulu
Archipelago remains visible.

PAGE 5
Recognition
In recognition of his leadership at MSU-Sulu, Dr. Abdurahman has received the Gawad Sulo ng Pamumuno
(Award for Excellence in Educational Leadership and Supervision), conferred following the 2025 five-year
performance evaluation of his chancellorship.
The award reflects the assessment of the MSU system that his tenure has produced meaningful and measurable
progress for the institution and the communities it serves.
His continued reappointment to the chancellorship across multiple terms is itself an institutional recognition of
sustained, effective leadership.
He is also recognized within academic networks as a researcher bridging contemporary higher education
management with indigenous Tausug knowledge systems, a combination that remains relatively uncommon in
Philippine academic scholarship.
Challenges
Leading MSU-Sulu is not without its difficulties. Sulu has long been one of the most complex security
environments in the country, and the university has had to operate through periods of conflict, displacement, and
disruption.
Delivering quality higher education in a province where many students come from families with limited resources,
and where infrastructure has historically lagged behind the rest of the country, requires constant creativity and
determination.
The COVID-19 pandemic added another layer of challenge, forcing rapid adaptation of academic delivery systems
in a setting where connectivity and device access are not always guaranteed.
Dr. Abdurahman navigated these pressures without stepping back from the university's development agenda, which
is a testament to both his resolve and the resilience of the MSU-Sulu community.
The ongoing task of asserting MSU-Sulu's relevance within a competitive national higher education landscape,
while serving a student population with specific cultural and economic needs, remains a live challenge that his
administration continues to address.
Legacy
Dr. Nagder J. Abdurahman's legacy is still being written, measured in the graduates who cross the commencement
stage, the programs that reach remote communities, and the quiet, incremental progress of an institution finding its
footing in a place that deserves more opportunities.
He is not a nationally prominent figure in the way that politicians or celebrities become household names. His work
is regional, grounded, and often unglamorous.
But in Sulu, that steady, culturally attuned presence at the top of a major state university matters enormously.
He has helped demonstrate that MSU-Sulu can be more than just a campus: it can be a hub for opportunity, cultural
continuity, and community development in a part of the Philippines that has too often been defined by its
challenges rather than its potential.

PAGE 6
As of 2026, he remains active in his role, attending commencements, overseeing ongoing projects, engaging in
research, and representing the university in regional and national forums.
Publications
Abdurahman, N. J. Management Effective and Job Motivation: A Simple Guide for Higher Education.
(Publication details forthcoming.)

title: Absari, Darwin J.
text:
PAGE 1
Darwin J. Absari
Asst. Prof. Darwin J. Absari is a Tausug scholar, educator, and cultural advocate from Tawi-Tawi, Philippines,
widely recognized as one of the most authoritative voices on Muslim Filipino history, spirituality, and identity in
the country today. He serves as Assistant Professor and College Secretary at the University of the Philippines
Institute of Islamic Studies (UP IIS) in Diliman, Quezon City, where he has spent the better part of a decade
teaching, researching, and quietly reshaping how the Philippines understands its Islamic heritage.
His most celebrated contribution is the 2021 book PagTuhan: The Tausug Spiritual Tradition, published by the UP
Press, which brings the mystical and gnostic traditions of the Tausug people into the light of national academic
discourse. The work made history as a finalist in the 40th National Book Awards under the category of Best Book
in Spirituality and Theology, a landmark recognition for Moro scholarship at the national level.
As a Tausug scholar working at the country's premier university, Absari embodies cultural reclamation in its most
grounded form: restoring Moro voices, sultanate histories, and living spiritual traditions to the place they deserve in
the broader Philippine story. His signature legacy is the bridge he has built between the turquoise waters of the Sulu
Archipelago and the academic halls of UP Diliman, carrying the wisdom of Tausug mystics, sailors, and ancestors
into classrooms and public conversations that had long excluded them.
Roots in the South: Early Life and Ethnic Ties
Darwin J. Absari was born and raised in Tawi-Tawi, the southernmost province of the Philippines, in a family with
deep roots in Sulu (locally pronounced "Saloo"). His parents originally came from Sulu and relocated to Tawi-Tawi
during the turbulent 1970s, a period marked by armed conflict that displaced thousands of Muslim families across
Mindanao and the Sulu Archipelago.
He proudly identifies as Tausug, belonging to the seafaring, warrior-poet people whose sultanate once commanded
trade routes across maritime Southeast Asia. The Tausug world Absari grew up in wasn't something he read about
in textbooks — it was lived and felt every day: oral histories passed down by elders, the rhythms of Islamic
practice woven into community life, stories of pagtuhan (spiritual gnosis), and a heritage that blends indigenous,
Islamic, and regional influences into something entirely its own.
Growing up in this environment gave him an intimate understanding of Moro resilience and identity that would
later become the engine of his scholarly work. He has spoken openly about how his roots in the south directly
shaped his drive to make Tausug and broader Muslim Filipino traditions visible, respected, and accurately
represented in national academic spaces.
Education
Absari completed his undergraduate studies at Mindanao State University-Tawi-Tawi (MSU-Tawi-Tawi), earning a
Bachelor of Arts in Political Science. Beyond academics, he was active enough in campus life to serve as a student
regent, an early sign of the leadership instincts he would carry into his professional career.
He then made the journey north to University of the Philippines Diliman, where he pursued a Master of Arts in
Islamic Studies at the Institute of Islamic Studies. His graduate work led him to write what would become the
foundation of his most important contribution to Philippine scholarship.

In 2015, Absari completed his MA thesis titled "Pagtuhan: The
Taosug Gnosis as a Living Tradition", an in-depth exploration of
Tausug mystics, their hidden knowledge systems, and a spiritual path
that had remained almost entirely unknown outside their own
communities. The thesis earned support from the National Book
Development Board's Trust Fund and was eventually revised,
expanded, and published by the UP Press in 2021 as PagTuhan: The
Tausug Spiritual Tradition.
He has been teaching at UP IIS for roughly eight years as of his most
recent public interviews, having transitioned from student to full
faculty member while continuing active research.
Career and Institutional Contributions
At the UP Institute of Islamic Studies, Absari takes on multiple roles
at once: professor, researcher, and College Secretary. In the
classroom, he teaches courses on Islamic thought, the legacies of
Muslim societies, and related subjects, consistently working to bridge
academic theory with the lived realities of Moro communities.
He also convenes the Islamic Studies Program at the UP Center for
Integrative and Development Studies (UP CIDS), where he organizes
workshops, capacity-building sessions for teachers on Philippine
Muslim history, and collaborative research projects that extend the
institute's reach beyond the university campus.
His institutional work goes beyond the purely academic. Absari has
facilitated humanitarian efforts, including support for Filipino-
Palestinian refugees, and has moderated public forums on Muslim
identity, history, and spirituality. He has represented UP IIS at
international events, including the Frankfurt Book Fair, bringing
Tausug and Moro scholarship to a global audience.
Colleagues and observers consistently describe him as a grounded
expert, a key facilitator, and someone who brings genuine
authenticity to discussions on Moro identity and the history of Islam
in the Philippines.
Scholarly Achievements and Publications
Absari is a prolific writer whose work concentrates on Moro studies,
Tausug spirituality, and the broader Islamic intellectual tradition in
the Philippines. His key published and contributed works include the
following:
PagTuhan: The Tausug Spiritual Tradition (UP Press, 2021):
His landmark book, born from his 2015 MA thesis, exploring
Tausug gnosis, mystical traditions, and the living spiritual heritage of the Tausug people. Finalist, 40th
National Book Awards (Best Book in Spirituality and Theology).

PAGE 3
Sulu-China Historical Ties: Contributions examining the long history of relations between the Sulu
Sultanate and China, from pre-Islamic times through the Spanish colonial era.
Philippine Muslim Intellectual Traditions: Research drawing on Sulu manuscripts and oral sources to
reconstruct and present Muslim Filipino intellectual history.
Philippine Muslim History Textbooks and Teacher Training: Co-authored and edited contributions to
curriculum development and professional development programs for educators teaching Philippine Muslim
history.
Qur'an and Sunnah as Sources for Moro Values: Earlier explorations of the theological and ethical
foundations of Moro identity and community life.
Sulu-China Friendship: Projects and writings on the historical and cultural dimensions of Sulu's diplomatic
and trade relations with China.
He has also been a speaker and resource person on topics including Sufism, interfaith spirituality, and Philippine
Islamic history at academic forums, podcast programs, and theological discussions.
Personal Values and Cultural Significance
Those who encounter Absari in person or through his work often note the same quality: a quiet but firm authority
rooted in genuine humility. In interviews, he speaks thoughtfully about the deep human longing for the divine, the
incorporation of diverse spiritual teachings into Tausug life, and why history matters so much for identity.
He sees spirituality not as an escape from the world's difficulties but as a source of strength for facing them,
whether those difficulties come in the form of a pandemic, armed conflict, or the daily pressures of modern life.
His approach to pagtuhan positions it as a living tradition, not a relic: meditation, remembrance, and the pursuit of
spiritual gnosis as ongoing practices that Tausug communities continue to carry.
As a Tausug scholar holding a position at the country's premier university, he represents something important
beyond his individual career. For decades, Moro histories were marginalized or simply erased from mainstream
Philippine narratives. Absari's work helps restore them, bringing pre-colonial sultanates, resistance histories,
intellectual traditions, and Muslim Filipino contributions back into the conversation.
Peers describe him as a foremost academic expert on Islam's history in the Philippines. More broadly, his work
humanizes Muslim Filipinos beyond the headlines of conflict and security concerns, presenting instead the rich
spiritual, intellectual, and historical depth of communities too often reduced to stereotypes.
Recognition
Finalist, 40th National Book Awards, Category: Best Book in Spirituality and Theology, for PagTuhan:
The Tausug Spiritual Tradition (UP Press, 2021).
National Book Development Board Trust Fund Support: His MA thesis, the foundation of PagTuhan, was
awarded support from the NBDB Trust Fund, facilitating its development into a full publication.
International Representation: Selected to represent the University of the Philippines Institute of Islamic
Studies at the Frankfurt Book Fair, one of the world's largest and most prestigious publishing events.
Resource Person and Speaker: Invited regularly to speak on Sufism, Moro history, Tausug spirituality, and
Philippine Islamic studies at academic forums, public programs, and interfaith discussions.

PAGE 4
Challenges
Absari's work exists within a broader landscape of challenges that scholars of Muslim Filipino identity and history
continue to navigate. Moro studies remain underfunded and underrepresented in Philippine academia, and the
communities whose histories he documents have long faced the twin burdens of armed conflict and systemic
marginalization.
Bringing Tausug spiritual traditions like pagtuhan into national academic discourse also requires careful
navigation: presenting these traditions accurately and respectfully without reducing them to exotic curiosities or
stripping them of their living, community-embedded character. His insistence on treating spirituality as a living
tradition rather than a historical artifact reflects a deliberate scholarly and ethical commitment to the communities
he writes about.
His role as a bridge between the south and the national university system also places him in a position where he
must constantly translate, not just linguistically but culturally and historically, for audiences whose understanding
of Moro life is often shaped more by conflict narratives than by genuine engagement.
A Storyteller of His People
Darwin Absari isn't simply documenting culture from a safe academic distance. He's living it, teaching it, and
sharing it across classrooms, forums, and published pages.
From his Tawi-Tawi roots to his office at UP Diliman, he carries the voices of Tausug mystics, Sulu sailors, and
Moro ancestors into spaces that are only beginning to truly listen. In a country still working through the complexity
of its plural identities, he stands as a bridge-builder in the fullest sense: rigorous scholar, dedicated educator,
spiritual seeker, and proud son of the South.
His story is a reminder that the Philippines' Islamic heritage isn't a footnote or a regional curiosity. It's woven into
the nation's fabric, deep and rich and waiting for more people to hear it. And thanks to voices like his, more of them
are finally starting to.

Professor Dr. Nassef Manabilang Adiong (born May 7, 1985) is a

widely cited academics to emerge from the Bangsamoro community
in the Philippines.
He is recognized across the region and in international academic
circles as a pioneer in Islamic International Relations (Islamic IR)
and Decolonial Studies, fields where he has spent his career
challenging the dominant, Western-centric frameworks that have long
shaped how global politics is studied and taught.
What sets Adiong apart isn't just the depth of his scholarship. It's the
fact that he built his career while carrying the weight of
representation: the first Moro to reach the highest rank under the
University of the Philippines Scientific Productivity System, a
distinction that didn't just honor him personally but signaled what
was possible for an entire generation of Bangsamoro scholars.
His central legacy can be summed up in the idea he's returned to
throughout his career: that the Global South, and the Bangsamoro
people in particular, deserve to see themselves and their traditions
reflected in how knowledge is produced, not just consumed.
