Early Life and Background
Nassef Manabilang Adiong was born on May 7, 1985, in Iligan City, Lanao del Norte, in the southern Philippines.
<ref name="wiki">Wikipedia, "Nassef Manabilang Adiong," accessed March 2026.</ref>
Growing up in Iligan, a city with a mixed Christian and Muslim population sitting at the edge of the historically
Maranao heartland, gave Adiong an early and visceral education in the realities of religious pluralism, cultural
coexistence, and the tensions that sometimes accompany both.
His formative years were shaped in no small part by his mother, whose teachings gave him the spiritual and ethical
bearings that would later anchor his most distinctive ideas about governance, scholarship, and public service.<ref
name="nassef">Nassef Manabilang Adiong Official Website, "About Nassef," nassef.info.</ref>
His early schooling took place at the Trinity University of Asia (then known as Trinity College of Quezon City), a
multi-faith institution whose environment, almost certainly, reinforced his instinct to engage across religious and
cultural divides rather than retreat from them.<ref name="wiki"/>
Education
Bachelor of Arts in International Studies
Adiong pursued his undergraduate studies at the University of the East in Manila, graduating in 2006 with a degree
in International Studies and the distinction of Magna Cum Laude.<ref name="wiki"/> It was a strong start that
pointed toward both the rigor and the global orientation his academic career would embody.
Master in International Studies
He completed his graduate studies at the University of the Philippines Diliman in 2009, earning a Master in
International Studies with the support of the UP Presidential Scholarship and the Willy Keng Scholarship.<ref
name="nassef"/> UP Diliman's Institute of Islamic Studies and its broader academic community gave him both the
intellectual environment and the institutional backing to develop what would become a distinctly Bangsamoro
scholarly perspective.
Doctor of Philosophy in International Relations
Adiong earned his doctorate from Middle East Technical University (METU) in Ankara, Turkey, in 2014. His
doctoral work was funded by the prestigious Erasmus Mundus Mobility with Asia scholarship alongside a
fellowship from TÜBİTAK, Turkey's premier research funding body.<ref name="wiki"/>
Pursuing a PhD in Turkey rather than in a conventional Western capital was itself a meaningful choice. METU's
location in Ankara, at the crossroads of European and Islamic intellectual traditions, gave Adiong exposure to
debates about sovereignty, authority, and the nation-state from outside the typical Anglo-American framing of
international relations.

PAGE 3
Advanced Studies
Beyond his doctorate, Adiong completed coursework toward a second PhD in Civilization Studies at the Alliance
of Civilizations Institute under Ibn Haldun University in Turkey, supported by a TÜRGEV scholarship.<ref
name="nassef"/> This pursuit reflects a genuine intellectual curiosity about how civilizations interact, build, and
sometimes clash, questions that sit at the very heart of his life's work.
Career
Early Academic Work and the University of the Philippines
After completing his studies, Adiong returned to the Philippines and built his academic home within the University
of the Philippines system. At UP, he developed his core research programs in Islamic IR and decolonial thought,
becoming one of the more distinctive voices in Philippine political science precisely because he was willing to
challenge foundational assumptions rather than simply apply them.
His association with the UP Center for Integrative and Development Studies (UP CIDS) became one of the more
consequential chapters in his career. There, he established the Decolonial Studies Program (DSP), an institutional
home for scholars and students interested in dismantling the "Western colonization of knowledge" in the Global
South academy.<ref name="dsp">UP CIDS Decolonial Studies Program, Institutional Overview.</ref>
Director, Policy Research and Legal Services, Bangsamoro Parliament
In more recent years, Adiong has taken on a directly consequential role in governance: serving as the Director of
the Policy Research and Legal Services (PRLS) for the Bangsamoro Parliament.<ref name="bta">Bangsamoro
Parliament Press Release, "Parliament commends Director Adiong's stellar career," November 2021.</ref>
This isn't just an academic position. In this role, he oversees policy review and legislative drafting for the
Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM), bringing his scholarship to bear on the very
real and urgent business of building a self-governing Bangsamoro polity.
It's a fitting culmination of a career that has always insisted on the connection between ideas and action, between
how we think about governance and how we actually practice it.
Scholarly Contributions
Islamic International Relations
Adiong has dedicated a significant portion of his career to articulating a coherent framework for Islamic
International Relations: how Islamic principles of sovereignty, authority, and territorial organization interact with,
and sometimes resist, the assumptions baked into the modern nation-state system.
In his work, Islam is not treated as a problem for international relations theory or as a disruptive force to be
explained away. Instead, Adiong presents Islam as a fully formed, non-alien participant in global political
discourse, one with its own rich tradition of thinking about order, justice, and the obligations of states and peoples
toward one another.<ref name="oxford">Adiong, N. M., "Muslim Views of the Polity," Oxford Research
Encyclopedia of International Studies, 2019.</ref>

PAGE 4
His edited volume Islam in International Relations: Politics and Paradigms (Routledge, 2018), co-edited with
international scholars, is considered a landmark contribution to the field, bringing together perspectives that had
rarely been assembled in a single, accessible academic work.
Decolonial Studies
Perhaps Adiong's most enduring intellectual contribution is his introduction of decoloniality as a sustained
framework within Philippine social science. He has argued, consistently and forcefully, that the dominant canons of
political science and international relations have been shaped by the intellectual preferences of the colonizing West,
and that scholars from the Global South must actively reclaim their own epistemological traditions.
The colonization of knowledge in the Global South academy is as real and as damaging as the
colonization of land. Decoloniality asks us to name that reality, and then to build something in its
place.
Through the Decolonial Studies Program at UP CIDS, he created institutional space for this reckoning, mentoring
students and collaborating with scholars who are developing non-Western intellectual frameworks across the
humanities and social sciences.
Moral Governance
One of the more distinctive ideas Adiong has developed is his philosophy of Moral Governance, which he has
applied specifically to the Bangsamoro context. He organizes this concept around five interconnected principles:
Faith, Freedom, Moral Authority, Common Good, and Social Justice.<ref name="moral">Adiong, N. M.,
"Principles and Practice of Moral Governance," 2021.</ref>
His 2021 book Principles and Practice of Moral Governance in the Bangsamoro represents his most sustained
attempt to translate this philosophy into a practical framework for governance, one that draws from Islamic ethics
and Bangsamoro tradition rather than simply importing governance models developed elsewhere.
Institutional Building
Adiong's contributions aren't limited to ideas on paper. He's also been a builder, someone who creates organizations
and networks through which other scholars can work.
In 2015, he founded the Philippine International Studies Organization (PHISO), now the premier professional
association for international studies scholars in the country, offering a critical platform for engaging with global
theories from a distinctly Filipino vantage point.<ref name="phiso">PHISO, "History and Mission," phiso.org.
</ref>
In 2012, he formed the International Relations and Islamic Studies Research Cohort (Co-IRIS) to connect scholars
working at the intersection of faith and geopolitics across different countries and traditions.<ref name="nassef"/>
In 2022, he established the Bangsamoro Research and Legal Network (BRLN), providing a dedicated platform for
Bangsamoro studies and legal research at a critical moment in the region's political development.<ref
name="brln">BRLN, "Founding and Mandate," nassef.info/brln.</ref>

PAGE 5
Published Works
Adiong has authored, co-authored, and edited a substantial body of work across political science, Islamic studies,
and decolonial theory. His most significant publications include:
Adiong, N. M. (2023). The Contemporary World.
Adiong, N. M. (2021). Principles and Practice of Moral Governance in the Bangsamoro.
Adiong, N. M. (2021). The Irony of Systemic Racism in the Global South Academy.
Adiong, N. M., et al. (Eds.). (2018). Islam in International Relations: Politics and Paradigms. Routledge.
Cruz, F. A., & Adiong, N. M. (Eds.). (2020). International Studies in the Philippines: Mapping New
Frontiers. Routledge.
Adiong, N. M. (2019). "Muslim Views of the Polity." Oxford Research Encyclopedia of International
Studies.
Honors and Recognition
The recognition Adiong has received over the course of his career reflects both the quality of his scholarship and its
broader significance to communities and institutions beyond the university.
In 2018, he was named one of the Outstanding Young Men (TOYM) of the Philippines, honored specifically for his
contributions to the field of International Relations.<ref name="toym">JCI Philippines, "TOYM 2018 Honorees."
</ref>
In 2021, he reached the highest rank under the University of the Philippines Scientific Productivity System,
becoming a UP Scientist III. This made him the first Moro scholar in the history of the university to achieve this
distinction, a milestone that resonated far beyond the walls of any single institution.<ref name="upiis">UP Institute
of Islamic Studies, "Congratulations to Dr. Nassef Manabilang Adiong, UP Scientist III," November 2021.</ref>
Also in 2021, the Bangsamoro Transition Authority passed a legislative resolution commending Adiong for his
"stellar career" and citing him as an inspiration to the youth of the Bangsamoro.<ref name="bta"/>
In 2022, he received the A. Noam Chomsky Global Connections Award in the category of "Rising Star Emerging
Scholar" from the STAR Scholars Network, a recognition of his growing international influence in critical and
global IR studies.<ref name="star">STAR Scholars Network, "2022 Global Connections Award Recipients."</ref>
Legacy and Cultural Significance
What makes Adiong's career worth examining closely, especially for those in the Bangsamoro community, is not
simply the list of awards or the volume of his publications. It's what his career represents.
He pursued his doctorate in Turkey, built organizations in Manila, mentored students across the country, and then
returned to serve the Bangsamoro Parliament. At every step, he carried the question of what it means to be
Bangsamoro in a world whose dominant intellectual frameworks were built without them in mind.
His insistence on decoloniality is not abstract. It's a direct response to the experience of communities like his own,
whose history, culture, and faith have too often been treated as objects of study rather than sources of knowledge.
Through the organizations he founded, the books he edited, and the students he mentored, Adiong has helped create
an infrastructure for Bangsamoro intellectual life that will outlast any single career. That, perhaps more than any
individual award, is his most significant contribution.

PAGE 6
Challenges and Context
Building a career in Islamic IR and decolonial studies in the Philippine academy has not been without its
difficulties. These are fields that challenge established disciplinary norms and power structures, and Adiong has
been candid about the resistance that this kind of work can encounter.
His 2021 work The Irony of Systemic Racism in the Global South Academy addresses this directly, naming the
structural biases that shape what kinds of scholarship are recognized, funded, and published in institutions that
claim to operate on merit alone.
For a Moro scholar working in a country where the Muslim Mindanao region has long been peripheralized in
national political life, the challenge of making Bangsamoro perspectives visible and credible within mainstream
Philippine academia carries personal as well as intellectual stakes.

title: Aguam, Abdul
text:
PAGE 1
Atty. Abdul "Dabs" Aguam
Personal Information
Full Name: Abdul Aguam
Nickname: "Dabs"
Ethnicity: Meranaw
Religion: Islam
Region: Lanao, Mindanao, Philippines
Education

(Passed)

Director for Legal Services, MSU System
Abdul Aguam
Atty. Abdul "Dabs" Aguam was a Filipino attorney, academic
administrator, and institutional builder from the Lanao region of
Mindanao, best known as the founder and inaugural Dean of the
Mindanao State University (MSU) College of Law.
Warmly referred to as "Dabs" by colleagues and students alike, he
spent the heart of his professional life at MSU in Marawi City,
where he wore two hats simultaneously: shaping the college that
would train generations of Bangsamoro lawyers, and serving as the
university system's chief legal counsel.
His legacy goes beyond administrative titles. Before Aguam came
along, a young Muslim from Lanao who wanted to become a lawyer
essentially had one path forward: pack up and head to Manila.
Aguam's decision to anchor a rigorous law school in Marawi City
changed that equation permanently.
Contents
1 BACKGROUND
2 EDUCATION
3 CAREER
3.1 Private Practice and Litigation
3.2 Director for Legal Services, MSU System
3.3 Founder and First Dean, MSU College of Law
4 INSTITUTIONAL CONTRIBUTIONS
4.1 College Seal and Visual Identity
4.2 Integration of Shari'ah into Legal Education
5 LEGACY
6 RECOGNITION
7 CHALLENGES
8 SEE ALSO
9 CATEGORIES
BACKGROUND
Abdul Aguam was born and raised in the Lanao region of
Mindanao, deeply embedded in the Meranaw cultural world that has
long defined the social and intellectual character of the Lake Lanao
basin.

PAGE 2
Member, Integrated Bar of the Philippines
(IBP)
Affiliation
Mindanao State University
Integrated Bar of the Philippines
Notability
Founder and inaugural Dean of the Mindanao
State University College of Law; pioneered
legal education in the Bangsamoro heartland
Known For
Establishing MSU College of Law; designing
the original institutional seal incorporating
Meranaw cultural symbols; democratizing
access to the legal profession in Muslim
Mindanao
Pull Quote
Remembered as the "servant-lawyer" who built
a school from the ground up so that
Bangsamoro youth would never again have to
travel to Manila just to pursue justice.
He came from an established family whose public-service
orientation was woven into its identity, blending customary
leadership traditions with a commitment to civic welfare that was, at
the time, quietly radical in its ambitions.
Growing up in a Mindanao navigating profound socio-political
shifts, Aguam developed an early conviction that the rule of law was
not an abstraction reserved for Manila courtrooms. It was a living
tool, and it belonged in the south. That conviction would become
the animating force of his entire career.
He practiced the Islamic faith with devout and quiet conviction, and
it shaped how he understood his professional responsibilities: not as
titles to accumulate, but as service to render.
EDUCATION
Aguam pursued higher education during an era when opportunities
for formal legal training in Muslim Mindanao were extremely
limited, with most law schools concentrated in Manila and the
northern Visayas.
He completed his tertiary and legal studies with academic
distinction, earning his Bachelor of Laws (LL.B.) degree and
building a strong grounding in Philippine jurisprudence,
constitutional frameworks, and the local legal systems that governed
Mindanao communities.
He subsequently passed the Philippine Bar Examination, formally
entering the legal profession as a licensed attorney and member of the Integrated Bar of the Philippines (IBP).
CAREER
Private Practice and Litigation
Aguam maintained an active private legal practice throughout his career, appearing as counsel in regional civil
litigations and administrative proceedings of significant local consequence.
As an IBP member, he was known for engaging seriously with the communities he represented, at times extending
pro bono guidance to individuals and families navigating public systems without the resources to pay for legal
help.
His courtroom experience gave him something that purely academic lawyers often lack: a granular, street-level
understanding of what the law actually looks like when it meets real people in Mindanao.

PAGE 3
Director for Legal Services, MSU System
Before or alongside his deanship, Aguam served as the Director for Legal Services of the Mindanao State
University System, functioning as the primary legal counsel for the broader MSU network.
In this executive role, he defended institutional interests, interpreted complex public administration frameworks,
and advised university leadership on policy, governance, and structural matters. It was demanding, unglamorous
work, but it gave him an unusually complete picture of how a major state university actually runs, knowledge he
would later channel into building the College of Law with institutional realism.
Founder and First Dean, MSU College of Law
This is where Atty. Aguam's mark on history is most enduring.
The MSU College of Law was formally constituted through Board of Regents Resolution No. 12, dated January
8, 1981, and began offering the Bachelor of Laws degree in Academic Year 1987-88. Aguam stepped into its
leadership at the very beginning, tasked with turning a BOR resolution into a functioning, credible, and competitive
law school.
What he inherited was essentially a blank page.
He designed the curriculum from scratch, benchmarking it against national standards while deliberately weaving in
the specific socio-legal realities of Mindanao, including Shari'ah law and jurisprudence, which MSU Law
incorporated into its academic mission in a way no Manila school could replicate with the same authenticity.
Under his guidance, the college built the academic infrastructure that would sustain it for decades. He established
the instructional frameworks that eventually allowed MSU Law to open extension campuses in Iligan City and
General Santos City, bringing legal education to a wider swath of Mindanao than any single campus could reach.
The school he left behind has produced judges, prosecutors, civil rights advocates, regional ministers, and
lawmakers, many of them from Bangsamoro communities that had historically been locked out of the legal
profession.
INSTITUTIONAL CONTRIBUTIONS
College Seal and Visual Identity
Beyond curriculum and administration, Aguam made a contribution to MSU Law's identity that persists to this day
in visual form.
He was one of the primary designers of the original MSU College of Law seal, an iconographic work that
embedded Meranaw cultural symbolism directly into the institution's public face.
His design incorporated the Panolong, the elaborately carved house beam that functions in Meranaw architecture
as a symbol of royalty, protection, and cultural pride. It also featured the crescent as an affirmation of the school's
Islamic heritage, and the outline of the Mindanao landmass, grounding the institution geographically and
politically in the south.

PAGE 4
That design heritage was not forgotten. When the MSU Board of Regents approved a modernized institutional logo
in a subsequent era, it formally integrated Aguam's foundational concepts into the new design, giving his visual
legacy a kind of quiet immortality inside the institution he built.
Integration of Shari'ah into Legal Education
Under Aguam's deanship, MSU College of Law was among the earliest Philippine law schools to treat Islamic law
and jurisprudence not as an exotic elective but as a substantive pillar of the curriculum.
This was consistent with the school's broader vision: that MSU Law existed not merely to produce lawyers who
could practice in Manila, but to develop legal professionals who could serve Muslim Filipino communities with
cultural competence and genuine understanding of the legal systems those communities actually live under.
LEGACY
When Atty. Abdul "Dabs" Aguam passed away, the Bangsamoro legal community lost one of its most
consequential architects.
His most lasting legacy is straightforward: he built a law school where there was none. Before the MSU College of
Law existed, a Muslim youth from Marawi or Maguindanao who wanted to become a lawyer faced costs,
distances, and cultural dislocation that effectively functioned as a barrier to entry. Aguam's work dismantled that
barrier.
In the decades since he served as founding dean, MSU Law graduates have spread through the Philippine justice
system, rising to positions in the judiciary, public prosecution, the Public Attorney's Office, the Bangsamoro
Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM), and private practice across Mindanao.
Within the informal lore of Bangsamoro legal culture, Aguam's name carries the weight of a founding figure: the
"servant-lawyer" who understood that his degree was not a credential to hoard but a tool to share.
His integration of Meranaw cultural symbolism into the college's institutional identity was equally significant. It
established a precedent that the south's legal institutions did not need to look northward for their sense of self.
RECOGNITION
Atty. Aguam's contributions were recognized across both the academic and legal communities of Mindanao:
Pillar of Legal Education: Commemorated by the MSU College of Law community as its institutional
founder, the figure who built the school from a Board of Regents resolution into a functioning, accredited
institution of legal learning.
IBP Recognition: Acknowledged by regional chapters of the Integrated Bar of the Philippines for his dual
contribution as an active practitioner and as the educator who enlarged the Philippine Bar's ranks with
Bangsamoro lawyers.
Design Legacy: His foundational iconographic work for the college seal was formally acknowledged when
the Board of Regents preserved and integrated his original design concepts into the MSU College of Law's
modernized, BOR-approved institutional logo.

PAGE 5
CHALLENGES
The work Atty. Aguam undertook was not without its difficulties.
Founding a law school in Marawi City during a period of political volatility and uneven resource allocation
required sustained advocacy for funding, faculty, and facilities that institutions in Manila took for granted.
Convincing the broader Philippine legal establishment to take a law school in Mindanao seriously demanded
sustained excellence and consistency in Bar examination performance, year after year. Establishing that credibility
from zero was the daily challenge of his deanship.
The socio-political tensions of Mindanao during the post-Martial Law period also meant that the institution he led
operated in conditions that demanded both institutional resilience and personal steadiness. On both counts, by all
accounts, Aguam delivered.

title: Al-Raschid-Arsad, Nefertari
text:
PAGE 1
Nefertari Al-Raschid-Arsad
Prof. Nefertari Al-Raschid-Arsad, Ph.D. is a Filipino scholar, educator, and cultural advocate specializing in
Philippine Muslim studies, Muslim education policy, and Tausug leadership traditions.
She serves as an Associate Professor at the University of the Philippines Institute of Islamic Studies (UP IIS) in
Diliman, where she has built a body of work that sits at the crossroads of classical Islamic knowledge and the lived
realities of Muslim communities in the Philippines.
Deeply rooted in the Tausug (or Suluk) community of the Sulu archipelago, she brings both scholarly discipline
and cultural authenticity to her research, particularly in her explorations of how Islamic leadership models are
understood and practiced at the community level.
Her signature legacy is best captured in one thread running through all her work: education as a tool for
empowerment, justice, and genuine cultural flourishing among Filipino Muslims.
She's known for championing the integration of madrasah education into national curricula, for producing nuanced
scholarship on Tausug constructs of leadership, and for helping sustain the intellectual legacy of foundational
Philippine Islamic scholars like Cesar Adib Majul.
As a quality assurance officer, a project leader, a researcher, and a teacher, she represents a generation of Muslim
Filipino academics who insist that Islamic perspectives belong squarely in the national conversation on education,
governance, and peacebuilding.

Background
The full details of Prof. Arsad's early life remain largely private, as is common among academics who center their
scholarship rather than personal biography.
What her research and writing reveal, though, is a scholar deeply formed by the Tausug community of the Sulu
archipelago.

Her explorations of Tausug constructs of leadership go beyond
textual sources. She draws from oral accounts and lived traditions
within Tausug communities, which points strongly to personal or
familial ties that give her work an authenticity that purely academic
distance rarely achieves.
She belongs to a generation of Muslim Filipino intellectuals who
came of age navigating two worlds: the rigorous, secular academic
tradition of the University of the Philippines, and the rich, faith-
grounded culture of the Bangsamoro communities they came from
and continue to serve.
That dual formation is visible in everything she does, from the
questions she asks in her research to the frameworks she builds for
Muslim education policy.
Education
Prof. Arsad completed her undergraduate studies at the very
institution she now serves, earning a Bachelor of Arts in Islamic
Studies from the University of the Philippines Institute of Islamic
Studies.
She pursued advanced graduate studies with a clear and consistent
focus: education policy and Islamic thought in the Philippine
context.
Her master's-level work included the development of a framework
for integrating madrasah education into the basic education
curriculum, an early and telling sign of her commitment to practical,
bridge-building solutions rather than purely theoretical inquiry.
She eventually earned a Doctor of Philosophy (Ph.D.), deepening
her expertise in Muslim educational systems, curriculum
development, and the intersections of Islamic values with national
educational frameworks.
Her academic formation at UP IIS also immersed her in the
intellectual legacy of pioneering Philippine Islamic scholars, an
engagement she has carried forward in her professional career.
Career
Prof. Arsad's career has unfolded entirely within the University of
the Philippines system, where she has grown from student to faculty
member and institutional leader at the UP Institute of Islamic
Studies.

contributions to Philippine
Islamic studies
As an Associate Professor, she teaches and mentors students in the
field of Islamic studies, bringing her research interests in education,
leadership, and Muslim community development directly into the
classroom.
Beyond teaching, she serves as the Quality Assurance Officer of UP
IIS, a role in which she has been recognized for championing QA efforts and completing external reviewer training,
contributing to the institutional development of one of the country's most important centers for Islamic scholarship.
She has also taken on a leadership role in the UP Center for Integrative and Development Studies (CIDS) Islamic
Studies Program, serving as research coordinator and project leader for initiatives that address real-world
challenges in Muslim education and community development.
Her career has taken her to webinars, roundtables, and conferences where she has presented and spoken on topics
ranging from classical Islamic curricula to contemporary issues in Muslim education in the Bangsamoro context.
She has organized and participated in academic forums that bring together scholars, policymakers, and community
leaders to tackle the practical questions of how Muslim education in the Philippines can be made more inclusive,
more effective, and more culturally grounded.
Institutional Contributions
One of Prof. Arsad's most consistent contributions is her work on madrasah mainstreaming. Through UP CIDS
discussion papers and related publications, she has helped shape policy conversations around how madrasah
schools can be integrated into the Philippines' K-12 framework without sacrificing their religious and cultural
integrity.
Her work on the Arabic Language and Islamic Values Education (ALIVE) program reflects the same impulse:
finding ways to bring Islamic values education into national curricula in a manner that is both rigorous and
contextually appropriate for Muslim Filipino students.
She has contributed introductory essays to collections of the posthumous writings of Cesar Adib Majul, the
foremost historian of Philippine Islam. This contribution reflects her role not just as a researcher but as a keeper
and transmitter of the intellectual tradition she belongs to.
As Quality Assurance Officer, she has worked to strengthen the institutional foundations of UP IIS, ensuring that
academic standards and review processes keep pace with the growing demands placed on the institute.
Her project leadership under UP CIDS has produced discussion papers and policy frameworks that speak directly
to government bodies, educators, and community stakeholders working on Muslim education reform.
Scholarship and Research
Prof. Arsad's most distinctive scholarly contribution is her work on Tausug Constructs of Leadership, a study that
challenges oversimplified and often politically charged representations of Islamic leadership in mainstream
Philippine media and discourse.
Rather than framing Islamic leadership through the lens of conflict or extremism, which has become all too
common in discussions involving groups like ISIS, she returns to the source: Qur'anic principles, Prophetic
example, and local Tausug expressions of what it means to lead well.

PAGE 4
In her framework, leaders emerge in figurative and symbolic terms: as nurturers, as stewards (khalifah), and as
embodiments of moral responsibility toward their communities and toward God.
This scholarship is both a corrective and a contribution. It reorients the conversation away from fear-based
narratives and toward the rich, internally coherent traditions of Islamic leadership that Tausug communities have
actually lived by.
Her publications also tackle the relationship between madrasah education and the Sustainable Development Goals,
arguing that well-integrated Islamic education is not in tension with modern development frameworks but can
actively support them.
Across her body of work, a consistent argument emerges: that Muslim Filipino education, when done well,
produces global citizens who are grounded in faith, equipped for the modern world, and committed to justice and
service.
Cultural Significance
Prof. Arsad represents a generation of Muslim Filipino academics who assert the relevance of Islamic perspectives
in national discourse without compromising scholarly rigor.
Her emphasis on khalifah as stewardship, on education as a form of worship and social responsibility, and on
bridging traditional madrasah systems with modern educational frameworks carries significance that goes well
beyond academic publishing.
In a country where Muslim communities have long navigated between marginalization and assertion, her work
offers a model of engagement that is constructive, grounded, and unafraid to claim space in national conversations
about education, governance, and cultural identity.
She embodies the values she studies: ethical leadership, service to community, knowledge-seeking for the benefit
of others, and a balanced integration of sacred and beneficial learning.
Her cultural contribution is also representational. As a Tausug woman scholar at one of the Philippines' most
prestigious universities, she demonstrates that Muslim Filipinas can and do occupy positions of intellectual
leadership, producing scholarship that matters to both academic and community audiences.
Recognition
Prof. Arsad has been recognized within the University of the Philippines system for her contributions to quality
assurance, having completed external reviewer training and been cited for her efforts in championing QA initiatives
at UP IIS.
Her scholarship has been published through UP CIDS discussion papers, a platform that gives her research
visibility among policymakers, educators, and development practitioners working on Muslim education in the
Philippines.
Her contributions to Cesar Adib Majul's posthumous publications mark a form of peer recognition within the field
of Philippine Islamic studies, acknowledging her as a scholar capable of contextualizing and introducing the work
of a foundational figure in the discipline.

PAGE 5
Her active presence in academic conferences, webinars, and roundtables on Muslim education and Bangsamoro
development reflects the professional community's recognition of her as a credible and valuable voice in these
conversations.
Challenges
Like many scholars working at the intersection of religion, culture, and public policy in the Philippines, Prof. Arsad
navigates a landscape shaped by persistent misrepresentations of Islam and Muslim communities in mainstream
discourse.
Her scholarship on Tausug constructs of leadership is itself a direct response to this challenge: the need to reclaim
and articulate authentic Islamic leadership traditions in a media environment that too often reduces Islamic identity
to conflict and extremism.
The work of integrating madrasah education into national curricula also comes with structural challenges, including
questions of funding, accreditation, teacher training, and the delicate negotiation of religious content within a
secular public education system.
Muslim scholars in the Philippines also face the broader challenge of building and sustaining institutional capacity
in a context where Islamic studies programs remain relatively under-resourced compared to other academic fields.
Prof. Arsad's career can be read, in part, as a sustained response to these challenges: doing the patient, painstaking
work of building frameworks, producing evidence, and training the next generation of Muslim Filipino scholars.
A Storyteller's Reflection
Encountering Prof. Nefertari Al-Raschid-Arsad through her writings feels like sitting down with a thoughtful
mentor who has stories stretching from Sulu to Diliman, always circling back to the same core questions: What
does it mean to lead as a Muslim? How do we educate our children so they thrive as both Filipinos and people of
faith?
Her approach isn't flashy or self-promotional. It's steady, rooted, and constructive, exactly the kind of voice that
builds understanding across divides and across generations.
In the broader tapestry of Philippine Islamic studies, she continues the work of integration and critical engagement
that scholars like Cesar Adib Majul began, while staying grounded in the community realities that give that work
its purpose and its urgency.
She is, in many ways, a bridge: between the classical and the contemporary, between the madrasah and the
university, between the Tausug communities of Sulu and the national conversations happening in Diliman.

title: Alauya, Ameladin Masacal Basman
text:

Ameladin Masacal Basman Alauya
Ameladin Masacal Basman Alauya (also written as Ameladin
M.B. Alauya) was a Maranao jurist, scholar, and legal author
from Lanao del Sur, Philippines, widely regarded as one of the
founding architects of procedural clarity in the Philippine Shari'ah
court system.
He served as a judge in the Shari'ah Circuit Courts within the
region then governed by the Autonomous Region in Muslim
Mindanao (ARMM), today the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region
in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM).
His most enduring contribution to Philippine legal history is the
Shari'ah Remedial Law Compendium, a landmark reference work
that bridged the gap between the substantive law under
Presidential Decree No. 1083 (the Code of Muslim Personal
Laws) and the practical procedural rules governing Shari'ah
litigation.
In the legal community, Judge Alauya has come to be remembered
as The Architect of Procedure: the man who turned a patchwork
of Islamic jurisprudence and Philippine statutory law into a
coherent, usable system that ordinary lawyers, judges, and
litigants could actually follow.
That legacy was not just academic. For Muslim Filipinos
navigating courts of marriage, inheritance, and family law, his
work meant the difference between justice delayed by procedural
chaos and justice delivered with dignity.
Contents
1 Background and Early Life
2 Education and Academic Formation
3 Career in the Shari'ah Judiciary
3.1 The Challenge of Dual Legal Systems
4 The Shari'ah Remedial Law Compendium
4.1 Structure and Contribution
5 Personal Values and Philosophy
6 Legacy
7 Recognition
8 Challenges and Institutional Context
9 Death
10 Further Reading
11 See Also

PAGE 2
Background and Early Life
Judge Alauya was born into the Alauya family of Lanao del Sur, one of the most storied lineages in Maranao
society.
The name "Alauya" carries generations of weight in the Lake Lanao basin, associated with the noble heritage of the
Confederate States of Lanao and the broader tradition of Maranao leadership that has shaped Muslim Mindanao's
political and cultural identity for centuries.<ref name="LanaoRoyalty">Sultan Alauya Alonto, a prominent figure
of the Ramain sultanate and the first Muslim senator of the Philippine Commonwealth, is among the most
celebrated bearers of the Alauya name. See: "List of Political Families in the Philippines," Wikipedia, retrieved
2025; and "Marawi Royal Lineage," Sultanates of Marawi Blog, http://sultanatesofmarawi.blogspot.com/</ref>
Growing up in this environment, young Ameladin was steeped in two things simultaneously: the deep Islamic
scholarship of his community and the very real expectation that intellectual service was a form of duty.
His upbringing, like that of many children of the Bangsamoro elite of his generation, followed a "dual-curriculum"
model, meaning he received both a formal secular Philippine education and intensive Islamic studies, likely
including foundational instruction in Arabic, Qur'anic recitation, and the basics of fiqh (Islamic jurisprudence).<ref
name="SourceDoc">Research profile on Judge Ameladin Masacal Basman Alauya synthesized from provided
records, judicial archives, and academic bibliographies. On file with BangsamoroPedia editorial records.</ref>
This early combination of two intellectual worlds would define everything he would later do in the law.
Education and Academic Formation
Judge Alauya's educational path gravitated early toward Shari'ah law and its intersection with modern Philippine
judicial institutions.
He was part of a cohort of Bangsamoro legal scholars who came of age after the promulgation of Presidential
Decree No. 1083 on February 4, 1977, the landmark decree that formally established the Shari'ah court system in
the Philippines as a state-recognized judicial structure.<ref name="PD1083">Presidential Decree No. 1083, "A
Decree to Ordain and Promulgate a Code Recognizing the System of Filipino Muslim Laws, Codifying Muslim
Personal Laws, and Providing for its Administration and for Other Purposes," signed February 4, 1977.</ref>
PD 1083 was, in the words of one legal scholar, "undoubtedly a progressive step," making the Philippines the only
Catholic-majority country in the world to formally recognize Islamic law as part of its national legal framework.
<ref name="UMelb">Stephens, M. "Islam, Syari'ah and Governance Background Paper." ARC Federation
Fellowship Research Series. University of Melbourne Law School, retrieved via https://law.unimelb.edu.au/</ref>
But the law's promise and its practical delivery were two different things, and Alauya recognized this early.
He specialized in the technical dimensions of PD 1083 with a focus on procedure: how cases actually moved
through the Shari'ah courts, what the rules of evidence looked like in practice, how filings were structured, and how
the Islamic jurisprudential schools (particularly the Hanafi and Shafi'i schools recognized in Philippine practice)
interacted with the secular Rules of Court.<ref name="SourceDoc"/>
His academic formation gave him both the Arabic-language conceptual tools to navigate classical Islamic
jurisprudence and the English-based legal training to translate those tools into documents that could function within
the Philippine court system.

PAGE 3
Career in the Shari'ah Judiciary
Judge Alauya served as a judge in the Shari'ah Circuit Courts of the Philippines, the courts that function at the
grassroots level of the Shari'ah judicial system.
Under PD 1083, the Shari'ah Circuit Courts (SHCCs) handle cases involving marriage, divorce, breach of contract
to marry, dower, maintenance, and restitution of conjugal rights, making them the most directly accessible point of
contact between ordinary Muslim Filipinos and the formal justice system.<ref name="PD1083"/><ref
name="UMelb"/>
His territory of service centered on Lanao del Sur and the surrounding ARMM region, an area where the
intersection of Adat (customary Maranao law, also known as taritib and igma) and Shari'ah created some of the
most legally complex family and property disputes in the country.<ref name="LanaoAdat">On Maranao adat law
and its intersection with Shari'ah, see: "Confederate States of Lanao," Wikipedia, retrieved 2025.</ref>
His courtroom philosophy was defined by what colleagues and sources describe as a commitment to "procedural
clarity." He believed that the Shari'ah court system in the Philippines should not be a "hidden law," accessible only
to those already initiated into Islamic jurisprudence, but a transparent, navigable system that any Muslim Filipino
could engage with in confidence.<ref name="SourceDoc"/>
This conviction shaped how he ran his courtroom and, eventually, how he picked up his pen.
The Challenge of Dual Legal Systems
One of the defining tensions of Judge Alauya's judicial career was the constant negotiation between two
overlapping but distinct legal systems.
On one side sat the Shari'ah, rooted in the Qur'an, Hadith, and centuries of classical Islamic jurisprudential
reasoning, drawing particularly from the Hanafi and Shafi'i schools within the Philippine context.
On the other sat the ordinary Philippine Rules of Court and the Special Rules of Procedure Governing Shari'ah
Courts (formally, the Ijra'at Mahakim al-Shari'a), promulgated by the Supreme Court of the Philippines on
September 20, 1983.<ref name="SharihaProcedure">Scribd document: "Shariah Court Procedure and Evidence,"
citing the 13th Shari'ah Law Training Seminar conducted by the National Commission on Muslim Filipinos, Lanao
del Sur, November-December 2012.</ref>
These two systems differed in significant ways. The Special Rules of Procedure are summary in nature while the
Rules of Court are not. Pleadings and motions allowed under the Rules of Court may be prohibited under the
Special Rules. The terminology itself could shift: a plaintiff became a mudda'i; their counsel became a wakil.<ref
name="SharihaProcedure"/>
Navigating this terrain demanded fluency in two legal languages simultaneously, and that is precisely the skill
Judge Alauya carried to the bench every day.
The Shari'ah Remedial Law Compendium
Judge Alauya's most defining achievement, and the work that secured his place in the history of Philippine Islamic
law, is the Shari'ah Remedial Law Compendium.

PAGE 4
This book emerged from a gap that practitioners felt keenly: while PD 1083 provided the substantive law of
Muslim personal relations in the Philippines (marriage, divorce, inheritance, and property), the procedural
dimension of Shari'ah litigation remained scattered, murky, and inconsistently applied.<ref name="SourceDoc"/>
How do you file a motion in a Shari'ah court? What are the timelines? How does evidence work when classical
Islamic rules of testimony meet Philippine procedural norms? What happens when the Special Rules are silent on
an issue and you need to borrow from the Rules of Court in a suppletory capacity?
These questions had answers, technically, but those answers were spread across PD 1083 itself, the Supreme
Court's 1983 Special Rules, scattered administrative orders, and classical fiqh texts that most practitioners simply
didn't have easy access to.
The Shari'ah Remedial Law Compendium pulled all of this together.
Structure and Contribution
The compendium accomplished three things that no previous Philippine legal publication had done in combination.
First, it aligned the Special Rules of Procedure Governing Shari'ah Courts with the broader Rules of Court of the
Philippines, clarifying where the two systems overlapped, where one deferred to the other, and where genuine
conflict required a principled resolution.<ref name="SourceDoc"/>
Second, it served as the standard preparatory reference for candidates taking the Shari'ah Bar Examinations, the
specialized bar exam system established under PD 1083 and administered through the Office of the Bar Confidant
of the Supreme Court in coordination with the National Commission on Muslim Filipinos (NCMF).<ref
name="SharihBar">Requirements for Filing Shari'ah Bar Examinations, NCMF (National Commission on Muslim
Filipinos), https://ncmf.gov.ph/</ref>
Third, and perhaps most importantly for the ordinary Muslim litigant, it provided a practical "roadmap" for what
due process actually looked like in a Shari'ah court: a system where being Muslim and being a rights-bearing
Philippine citizen were not contradictory but complementary.<ref name="SourceDoc"/>
The compendium is cited as a primary source in the Shari'ah law curricula of Philippine law schools, including the
Mindanao State University system, and remains a standard reference in the preparation of practitioners seeking
admission to the Shari'ah Bar.<ref name="MSUSyll">Macadindang, J.C. (instructor). Shariah Law II (JD 113)
course syllabus. College of Law, Mindanao State University-Gensan Extension. Retrieved via CliffsNotes Study
Notes platform, https://www.cliffsnotes.com/study-notes/28214418</ref>
In this sense, every examination candidate who opens the compendium to study for the Shari'ah Bar is, in some
quiet way, continuing Judge Alauya's work.
Personal Values and Philosophy
Those who knew or studied Judge Alauya describe a man guided by what might be called the principle of
Intellectual Jihad (understood in its classical, non-military sense): the conviction that the liberation and dignity of
the Bangsamoro people depended not on political theater, but on mastery of knowledge and the tools of the law.
<ref name="SourceDoc"/>
For him, the Shari'ah court system was not a concession granted by the Philippine state. It was a recognition of a
sovereign Islamic legal tradition that had governed Muslim Mindanao for centuries before Manila was even a
political entity. Strengthening that system through rigorous scholarship was a form of cultural preservation.

PAGE 5
He belonged to a generation that came of age amid the post-independence tensions of Muslim Mindanao, watched
the establishment of the MNLF and later the MILF, lived through Martial Law, and saw PD 1083 emerge from that
turbulent period as a hard-won acknowledgment of Muslim Filipino legal identity. He chose to respond not with a
gun but with a pen and a procedural manual.
This orientation toward maratabat (Maranao pride, honor, and dignity) expressed through intellectual excellence
rather than armed resistance was a thread that ran through everything he did in his legal career.
He also appears to have been a committed family man who placed multi-disciplinary achievement at the center of
his household values. His children pursued careers in law, healthcare, and education, fields that collectively reflect
his belief that service to the community required many kinds of knowledge working together.<ref
name="SourceDoc"/>
Legacy
Judge Ameladin Masacal Basman Alauya did not hold the highest judicial office in the land. He was not a politician
or a senator. He did not lead a peace negotiation.
But the work he left behind sits at the foundation of every Shari'ah court proceeding that has been conducted with
procedural integrity in the Philippines since his compendium was published.
His legacy is most visible in three places.
The first is in the hands of every Shari'ah Bar examiner who uses his compendium to frame questions, and every
examinee who uses it to find answers.
The second is in the Shari'ah courtrooms of Lanao, Maguindanao, Cotabato, Zamboanga, and Basilan, where the
procedural architecture he helped build makes it possible for a Muslim Filipino to file a case, understand what's
happening, and receive a decision that reflects both their faith and their rights as citizens.
The third is in his children, who represent what he modeled: the idea that service to the Bangsamoro community
takes many forms, and all of them matter.
The empowerment of the Bangsamoro people lay in the mastery of the law and the pen.
That sentence, drawn from those who knew him and studied his work, is as good a summary of his life as any
epitaph.<ref name="SourceDoc"/>
Recognition
Judge Alauya's recognition came largely through the practical adoption of his scholarship rather than through
formal state honors.
The Shari'ah Remedial Law Compendium achieved institutional recognition as a standard reference text in Shari'ah
legal education in the Philippines, cited in law school syllabi and bar review programs across the MSU system and
other institutions offering Shari'ah law courses.<ref name="MSUSyll"/>
His service as a Shari'ah Circuit Court judge placed him among the pioneering generation of jurists who gave
credibility and structure to a court system that, at its establishment, was more of a promise than a functioning
institution.

PAGE 6
Template:Editorial note
Challenges and Institutional Context
Judge Alauya's career unfolded against the backdrop of a Shari'ah judicial system that faced (and in many ways still
faces) severe structural challenges.
At the time of his service, a significant number of Shari'ah court positions across the Philippines remained vacant,
leaving existing judges stretched across cases and jurisdictions far beyond what any single court officer could
reasonably handle.<ref name="JBCList">List of Shari'ah Courts and Judges as of June 2021, Judicial and Bar
Council (JBC), sourced from NCMF: https://ncmf.gov.ph/wp-content/uploads/2022/12/UPDATED-SHARIAH-
COURTS-AND-JUDGES-1.pdf</ref>
The Shari'ah Appellate Court, provided for under Republic Act No. 6734, was never actually established, meaning
that Shari'ah District Court decisions had no specialized appellate body to review them, a structural gap that
persisted for decades.<ref name="ShariahWiki">Sharia in the Philippines. Wikipedia, retrieved February 2026.
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sharia_in_the_Philippines</ref>
Members of the Shari'ah Bar (those who passed the Shari'ah Bar Examination) occupied a legally ambiguous
position: they were "special members" of the Integrated Bar of the Philippines rather than full members, and could
practice law only before Shari'ah courts, not in the regular court system.<ref name="AlawivAlauya">Sophia Alawi
v. Ashary M. Alauya, A.M. No. SDC-97-2-P, Supreme Court of the Philippines, February 24, 1997. Note: This case
involves a different Alauya (Ashary M. Alauya, Executive Clerk of Court, 4th Judicial Shari'ah District, Marawi
City) but illustrates the broader institutional and professional challenges faced by Shari'ah judicial officers of the
same era and community.</ref>
In this environment, producing a rigorous, usable procedural reference was not just a scholarly exercise. It was an
act of institutional repair.
Death
The exact date and circumstances of Judge Alauya's death are not confirmed in available public records as of this
writing.
His passing is described in source materials as "untimely," suggesting he died before reaching a conventional
retirement age, though specific details await verification from official records or family sources.
Template:Editorial note
Further Reading

edition details pending bibliographic verification.)

February 4, 1977. Available at: https://lawphil.net/statutes/presdecs/pd1977/pd_1083_1977.html

al-Shari'a). September 20, 1983.

(2022 Edition).

PAGE 7

Saaduddin M. Alauya Jr.
Atty. Saaduddin M. Alauya Jr., CPA is a Bangsamoro lawyer,
certified public accountant, and academic administrator known for his
work in Mindanao State University (MSU), regional governance in the
Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (ARMM), and the
development of Islamic finance education in Mindanao.
Academic and Administrative Career
Alauya has long been associated with Mindanao State University,
where he served as Legal Director of the Legal Services Division.
In that role, he handled legal matters involving the university,
supporting institutional governance and ensuring compliance with
applicable laws and policies.
He later assumed the position of Vice Chancellor for Administration
and Finance of MSU, a role that involves oversight of:
Administrative systems
Financial management
Institutional operations
This position places him within the core leadership of the university.
Role in Islamic Finance Education
Alauya was part of the group that worked toward the establishment of academic offerings in Islamic Banking and
Finance at Mindanao State University.
This initiative reflects a growing interest in integrating Islamic finance into formal education in the Philippines,
particularly in the Bangsamoro context.
He has also served as a lecturer on:

PAGE 2
Islamic capital
Islamic contracts
These areas are rooted in principles of Shari'ah and are central to the development of Islamic financial systems.
Legislative Experience
Alauya also served as an Assemblyman in the Regional Legislative Assembly of the Autonomous Region in
Muslim Mindanao (ARMM).
As a member of the regional legislature, he took part in:
Regional lawmaking
Policy discussions
Governance within the autonomous framework
This role connects his academic and administrative work with direct experience in public governance.
Professional Profile
Alauya’s career combines multiple fields:
Law
Accounting
Academic administration
Regional governance
This combination reflects a practical approach to leadership, grounded in both technical expertise and institutional
work.
Place in the Bangsamoro Narrative
Atty. Saaduddin M. Alauya Jr. represents a development-oriented strand of Bangsamoro leadership.
His work shows how education, law, and governance intersect, especially in institutions like Mindanao State
University that serve as key centers of learning in the region.
His involvement in Islamic finance education also reflects a continuing effort to align academic programs with the
cultural and economic context of the Bangsamoro.

Arifa Alauya-Ala
Arifa A. Ala is a Filipino career central banker, lawyer, and Certified
Public Accountant who serves as the Senior Assistant Governor of
the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP), heading the Financial
Supervision Sub-Sector (FSSS) III. Over a career spanning more than
25 years at the BSP, she has become the Philippines' most
consequential advocate for Islamic banking and Shari'ah-compliant
finance—earning her an international reputation and the informal title
of the country's foremost architect of Islamic finance.
Ala was the BSP's lead point person for the landmark Republic Act
No. 11439, signed into law in 2019, which opened the Philippine
banking sector to a genuine dual banking system for the first time in
modern history. More than just a regulator, she has also been a
relentless champion of financial inclusion for the Bangsamoro region
—a community that, for decades, found itself shut out of the formal
financial system because conventional banking products conflicted
with the Islamic prohibition on riba (interest). Her life's work is
captured in a simple but powerful idea: that choice, dignity, and
belonging in the financial system are not privileges—they're rights.

Background and Early Life
Ala grew up in Mindanao, and that upbringing gave her something that no classroom could teach: a firsthand
understanding of what financial exclusion actually looks like. She saw communities that worked hard, saved what
they could, and built small enterprises—but remained disconnected from banks that couldn't, or wouldn't, serve
them in a way that aligned with their faith and values. That lived context would later shape every policy she drafted
and every forum she chaired.
Her family background, while not extensively documented in public records, placed her firmly within the fabric of
Mindanao society—a region defined by its cultural plurality, its deep Islamic heritage, and the economic
marginalization that has historically accompanied both. These roots never left her, even as her career took her from
the streets of Mindanao to the boardrooms of Kuala Lumpur and Dubai.
Education
Ala's academic path is genuinely unusual—and that's precisely what makes her so effective in her work.
She started with a Bachelor of Science in Business Administration, major in Accounting, from Mindanao State
University. That degree gave her the quantitative backbone that bank supervision demands: reading financial
statements, assessing credit risk, and understanding the economic substance of transactions rather than just their

PAGE 3
surface form.
From there, she moved to Manila for law school, earning a Juris Doctor from San Beda College and passing the
Philippine Bar Examinations. That combination—CPA and lawyer—is rare anywhere, and within the BSP, it made
her uniquely suited to tackle Islamic financial instruments, which are structurally complex precisely because they
avoid interest while still creating economic value.
She didn't stop there. Ala completed a Master of Business Administration at the Ateneo de Manila University,
sharpening her strategic and management lens. Then came arguably her most elite academic credential: a Master
in Public Management through a joint program between the Lee Kuan Yew School of Public Policy at the
National University of Singapore and the John F. Kennedy School of Government at Harvard University. That
program placed her in a global cohort of senior civil servants and gave her a framework for thinking about policy
design that reaches well beyond the BSP's walls.
Career at the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas
Ala started at the BSP at the ground floor—literally—as a Bank Officer I. That's the entry level. What followed
was a 25-year climb that wasn't accidental; it was the product of sustained mastery of the Financial Supervision
Sector (FSS) and a growing reputation as the person you brought in when something was legally and technically
complicated.
She eventually rose to lead the Financial Supervision Sub-Sector III, where she now oversees the supervision of
banks and non-bank financial institutions. It's a broad mandate, covering everything from routine prudential
oversight to the cutting-edge regulatory work on Islamic banking.
Inside the institution, Ala has also built the next generation of regulators. She chaired the committees that
developed the BSP's Problem Bank Resolution and Supervisory Writing courses under the Professional
Enhancement Program for Supervisors—a quiet but meaningful contribution to institutional memory. That kind of
mentorship work rarely gets headlines, but it shapes the culture of a central bank for decades.
Pioneering Islamic Finance in the Philippines
The Single-Bank Era and Its Limits
To understand what Ala built, you first have to understand what came before. For roughly 50 years—from 1973 to
2019—the entirety of the Philippines' Islamic banking sector consisted of a single institution: the Al-Amanah
Islamic Investment Bank, a state-run entity operating under a 1973 mandate. It was isolated, undercapitalized, and
unable to serve the full breadth of the Muslim community's financial needs. There was no regulatory framework to
invite new players, no tax structure designed for Shari'ah-compliant transactions, and no inter-agency coordination
to make the ecosystem function.
That was the landscape Ala inherited—and decided to change.
Republic Act No. 11439: The Islamic Banking Law
In August 2019, President Rodrigo Duterte signed Republic Act No. 11439, the Islamic Banking Law. Ala was
the BSP's lead point person throughout the bill's deliberations and eventual passage. The law did several things that
hadn't been done before in Philippine financial regulation:<ref name="ra11439">Republic of the Philippines.

PAGE 4
(2019). Republic Act No. 11439: An Act Providing for the Regulation and Organization of Islamic Banks. Official
Gazette of the Republic of the Philippines.</ref>
It formally established a dual banking system, allowing new full Islamic banks and Islamic Banking Units
(IBUs) within conventional banks to operate side by side.
It gave the BSP explicit authority to issue prudential standards—covering capital adequacy, liquidity, and
risk management—tailored specifically for Shari'ah-compliant operations.
It required all Islamic banks to establish Shari'ah Advisory Councils staffed by scholars qualified in
banking, finance, and Islamic jurisprudence.
The law moved Islamic banking from a legacy relic into a living, scalable system.
BSP Circular No. 1070: The Shari'ah Governance Framework
A law is only as strong as its implementing rules. Ala understood that, which is why one of her most consequential
contributions was her leadership in drafting BSP Circular No. 1070—the Shari'ah Governance Framework.<ref
name="circ1070">Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas. (2019). BSP Circular No. 1070: Guidelines on the Establishment
and Operation of Islamic Banks and Islamic Banking Units. BSP Media and Research Portal.</ref>
This framework spelled out exactly how Shari'ah Advisory Councils work, what qualifications their members need,
how they interact with a bank's board and management, and how their decisions get documented and reviewed. It
made sure that the "interest-free" promise of Islamic banking wasn't just a marketing claim—it was an
operationally enforced reality.
Key Policy Innovations
The Islamic Finance Coordination Forum (IFCF)
Ala recognized early that no central bank, working alone, could build a financial ecosystem. Accounting rules, tax
regulations, securities laws, insurance frameworks—all of these touch Islamic finance, and they're all governed by
different agencies. So she championed the creation of the Islamic Finance Coordination Forum (IFCF), which
she chairs, bringing together the Bureau of Internal Revenue (BIR), the Securities and Exchange Commission
(SEC), the Insurance Commission (IC), the Bangsamoro Government, and other key stakeholders under one
coordinating roof.<ref name="ifcf">Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas. (2023). Islamic Finance Coordination Forum:
Overview and Mandate. BSP Media and Research Portal.</ref>
The IFCF is the institutional expression of her "whole-of-government" philosophy: the idea that Islamic finance
can't flourish through the BSP alone but only through a coordinated national strategy.
Tax Neutrality: Solving the Double Taxation Problem
One of the most stubborn obstacles to Islamic finance in the Philippines has been the risk of double taxation.
Islamic contracts often involve multiple asset transfers—in a Murabaha transaction, for example, a bank buys an
asset and then sells it to a client at a markup. Under the conventional tax code, that could trigger multiple rounds of
Value Added Tax (VAT) and Documentary Stamp Tax (DST), making Islamic products more expensive than their
conventional counterparts—which defeats the purpose.

PAGE 5
Ala worked closely with the BIR to solve this. The result was Revenue Regulations No. 17-2020 and, more
recently, Revenue Memorandum Circular No. 81-2024—regulations that institutionalize tax neutrality, meaning
Islamic banking transactions are assessed based on their economic substance, not their legal form.<ref
name="bir2020">Bureau of Internal Revenue. (2020). Revenue Regulations No. 17-2020: Implementing the Tax
Provisions of Republic Act No. 11439. BIR Official Website.</ref>
These policy wins have conveyed to the global market that the Philippines fosters an open and
competitive financial system, ready for the entry of local and international investors.
— Ashary Tamano, The Architect of Shari'ah-Compliant Finance (2026)
Impact and Legacy
Financial Inclusion in the Bangsamoro
The numbers behind Ala's work are striking. As of late 2020, over 92% of municipalities in the BARMM were
unbanked—meaning most families had no access to formal financial services at all.<ref
name="barmm_data">Asian Development Bank. (2024). Islamic Finance – Philippines Industry Opportunity
Study. ADB Publications.</ref> Her work directly attacked that gap, licensing institutions like Card Bank, Inc.—
the first microfinance-oriented rural bank with an IBU—and Maybank Philippines—the first commercial bank
IBU in the country.
Programs like the CARD MRI Paglambo Project and ASA Philippines have demonstrated that Shari'ah-
compliant microfinance isn't just ethically sound—it's commercially viable. Thousands of families in the region
have gained access to ethical capital for small businesses, on terms that don't require them to compromise their
faith.
Cultural and Spiritual Dimension
Ala often points out something that gets lost in the policy language: for many Filipino Muslims, being shut out of
conventional banking isn't just an economic problem—it's a spiritual one. Accessing a loan that charges riba
creates a moral conflict that many observant Muslims would rather avoid altogether, even at significant personal
cost.
By building a Shari'ah-compliant space, she gave those communities back something beyond a bank account. She
restored, in her own words, choice, dignity, and belonging to people who had long been invisible to the financial
system.
Peace Through Prosperity
The Bangsamoro has endured decades of conflict, and poverty and exclusion have been among its root causes.
Ala's work connects economic empowerment to peacebuilding in a way that goes beyond rhetoric. When families
have access to fair, ethical capital—and can grow small businesses, send children to school, and build assets—the
conditions that fuel resentment and instability start to shift. Islamic finance, in her framework, is a peace dividend
as much as it is a financial product.

PAGE 6
International Recognition
Ala's work hasn't gone unnoticed beyond the Philippines. She has been recognized by some of the most respected
names in global Islamic finance:
WOMANi Most Influential Women in Islamic Business and Finance — Named by the Cambridge
Institute of Islamic Finance (IFA) for three consecutive years: 2022, 2023, and 2024. She was also
designated a WOMANi Five-Star Alumni and Influencer at the 5th Annual WOMANi Symposium in
Dubai.<ref name="womani">Cambridge Institute of Islamic Finance. (2024). WOMANi Annual Report
2024. IFA Publications.</ref>
WOMANi Professional Award — Conferred in Jakarta in 2022 for her leadership of the IFCF.
Woman Influencer in Financial Services Industry — Received at the 2025 World Financial Innovation
Series (WFIS) in Pasay City, recognizing her role in making Islamic finance a pillar of inclusive growth.
On the international policy stage, Ala has represented the Philippines at the Global Forum on Islamic Economics
and Finance (GFIEF) in Kuala Lumpur (May 2024), where she spoke alongside representatives from Bank
Negara Malaysia and Moody's Ratings. She has been actively engaged with the Islamic Financial Services Board
(IFSB) and the Accounting and Auditing Organization for Islamic Financial Institutions (AAOIFI)—ensuring
that Philippine regulations benchmark against global standards. Her participation in the 22nd Islamic Financial
Stability Forum in 2024 further cemented her standing as a serious voice in global financial governance.<ref
name="ifsb2024">Islamic Financial Services Board. (2024). 22nd Islamic Financial Stability Forum: Proceedings
and Outcomes. IFSB Publications.</ref>
Comparative Context
Breaking from the Amanah Bank Model
What Ala built is fundamentally different from what came before. The Amanah Bank model was a state monopoly
—a single institution carrying an impossible burden with limited tools. Ala's approach democratized Islamic
finance: any bank, conventional or otherwise, can participate in the system as long as it meets Shari'ah and
prudential standards. That shift—from a single isolated player to a systemic, pluralistic framework—is the
structural legacy that will outlast any individual award or recognition.
Among Her Regional Contemporaries
Ala's work is often discussed alongside leaders from Indonesia and Malaysia, countries with far larger Muslim
populations and more mature Islamic finance markets. Indonesian Finance Minister Sri Mulyani Indrawati's Green
Sukuk program is a frequently cited comparison. The difference is context: Indonesia and Malaysia were working
with existing ecosystems. Ala built hers from scratch, in a predominantly non-Christian country with a complex tax
environment and a political backdrop defined by decades of conflict. Her achievement in securing tax neutrality
under those conditions is considered a regional benchmark.
Challenges and Open Questions
For all the progress, Ala has been candid about what remains undone.

PAGE 7
The shortage of qualified Shari'ah scholars—particularly those who also understand modern financial
instruments—remains a genuine bottleneck. The BSP allows foreign consultants, but local capacity is thin, and the
long-term sustainability of the industry depends on developing homegrown expertise.
Public awareness and literacy around Islamic finance is still low, and the misconception that it's exclusively a
religious product for Muslims continues to slow adoption. Ala has led capacity-building initiatives to counter this,
but diffusion into the mainstream takes time.
The Al-Amanah Islamic Investment Bank itself continues to face operational challenges—governance issues,
undercapitalization, limited market reach. It's a reminder that good laws don't automatically produce viable
institutions, and that the regulatory framework Ala built is only as strong as the players that operate within it.
The COVID-19 pandemic also set back early momentum. Exploratory discussions with foreign investors were
stalled, and the economic disruption complicated efforts to expand the IBU network during the critical early years
of RA 11439's implementation.

Aslama M. Alauya-Lamping
Dr. Aslama Masacal Alauya-Lamping, MD, FPCP, FPCCP, FCCP,
is a Maranao physician, pulmonologist, and internal medicine
specialist based in Marawi City, Lanao del Sur, Philippines.
She is the youngest child of Justice Saaduddin A. Alauya Sr., the first
Jurisconsult in Islamic Law of the Philippines, and the first doctor in
a family that has otherwise distinguished itself almost entirely
through the law.
Her story is one of quiet, persistent firsts: first Maranao lady
valedictorian of the MSU College of Medicine, first Maranao
pulmonologist, first Maranao doctor to earn the Distinguished Public
Servant Award from the Philippine College of Chest Physicians, first
Maranao doctor and pulmonologist to receive the Pride of Ranaw
Award, first Maranao elected president of the Iligan Society of
Internists, and the first Maranao woman to graduate with distinction
from a Harvard Medical School certificate program.
She stands not only as a pride of Ranaw in her own right, but as the
medical pillar of a family that has, across two generations, broken
barriers in law, banking, Islamic jurisprudence, and Philippine
governance.
