Background and Family
The Alauya family of Bacolod Grande, Lanao del Sur, is one of the most accomplished Bangsamoro families in
modern Philippine public life.
At the center of it all is Justice Saaduddin A. Alauya Sr., a Maranao lawyer and Aleem (Islamic scholar) who served
as Vice Governor of Lanao del Sur in 1989, as Acting Governor from 1992 to 1995, and as Chairman of the Code
Commission on Muslim Laws in the Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao in 1994.
In August 1996, President Fidel V. Ramos appointed him as Jurisconsult in Islamic Law of the Philippines,
making him the first person to hold that office under the Supreme Court of the Philippines.<ref
name="wiki_alauya">Template:Cite web</ref>
The Jurisconsult, created under Presidential Decree 1083 or the Code of Muslim Personal Laws, functions as an
expert advisor to the Supreme Court on matters of Islamic law.<ref name="wiki_alauya" />
He is also a prolific legal author, having written foundational texts on Muslim inheritance law, fundamentals of
Islamic jurisprudence, Islamic penal law, and procedure and evidence under the Muslim Code.<ref
name="wiki_alauya" />
During part of his career, Justice Alauya served as a professor at Umm Al-Qura University in Makkah, Saudi
Arabia, a tenure that would shape the early education and worldview of his youngest daughter.
His children have matched his legacy, each staking out their own "firsts."
Atty. Arifa Alauya-Ala, a Certified Public Accountant and lawyer, is the first Maranao woman to serve as Senior
Assistant Governor of the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP), the country's central bank.<ref
name="bsp_ala">Template:Cite web</ref>
She is the BSP's lead advocate for Islamic banking and finance, chairing the Inter-Agency Working Group on
Islamic Banking and Finance, and was a key figure in the passage of the Islamic Banking Law (Republic Act No.
11439) in 2019.<ref name="context_ala">Template:Cite web</ref>
In September 2025, she was recognized as a "Woman Influencer in Financial Services Industry" by the World
Financial Innovation Series.<ref name="context_ala" />
Atty. Asma Alauya also serves in the legal services sector of the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas. [Note: The specific
title of General Legal Counsel attributed to Atty. Asma Alauya could not be independently verified through
available public records at the time of writing. This detail is sourced from family accounts and is subject to
verification.]
Atty. Saaduddin M. Alauya Jr., a lawyer and Certified Public Accountant, currently serves as Vice Chancellor for
Administration and Finance of Mindanao State University Main Campus in Marawi City.<ref
name="msu_alauya">Template:Cite web</ref>
Into this family of pioneering lawyers, administrators, and jurists, Dr. Aslama stepped not with a bar examination
but with a stethoscope.

PAGE 3
She became the first doctor in the family and, in doing so, opened an entirely new frontier for the Alauya legacy.
Early Life and Education Abroad
Dr. Aslama spent a significant portion of her early years and formative schooling in Makkah, Saudi Arabia, during
the period when her father was serving as a professor at Umm Al-Qura University.
Growing up between the spiritual heart of the Islamic world and the cultural heartbeat of Marawi City gave her
something few Maranao children of her generation had: a genuinely global perspective, paired with an unshakeable
sense of who she was and where she came from.
From her earliest years in school through college, she was consistently at the top of her class.
She graduated as Valedictorian at every level of her academic journey, from grade school all the way to the College
of Medicine.
Medical Education
Dr. Aslama completed her medical degree at the Mindanao State University College of Medicine, where she made
history as the first Maranao lady Valedictorian of the college.
That achievement alone would have been remarkable, but it was only the opening chapter of a much longer record.
After earning her medical degree from MSU, she pursued residency training at the National Kidney and Transplant
Institute (NKTI) in Metro Manila, then went on to complete fellowship training in pulmonary medicine at the
University of the Philippines.<ref name="hms_feature">Template:Cite web</ref>
She holds the credentials MD, FPCP (Fellow of the Philippine College of Physicians), FPCCP (Fellow of the
Philippine College of Chest Physicians), and FCCP (Fellow of the American College of Chest Physicians).
Medical Career
Clinical Work
Dr. Aslama is a pulmonologist and internal medicine specialist who has built her practice in Iligan City and the
broader Lanao region.
She serves as one of the consultants at Amai Pakpak Medical Center, the only tertiary hospital in Marawi City
serving Lanao del Sur and its neighboring cities and provinces.<ref name="hms_feature" />
She also holds a private pulmonology practice at Mercy Community Hospital and other hospitals in Iligan City.
During the COVID-19 pandemic, Dr. Aslama worked on the frontlines as a clinician in the respiratory unit of the
internal medicine department at Amai Pakpak Medical Center, treating patients at the height of the health crisis
while simultaneously training resident physicians.
Following her graduation from Harvard Medical School in 2024, she was assigned as medical specialist supervisor
of Station 8 at Amai Pakpak Medical Center, a general medicine ward that routinely handles more patients than its
official capacity, including critical cases when the intensive care unit is full.<ref name="hms_feature" />

PAGE 4
She has been implementing lean management principles in that ward, applying the capstone work she developed at
Harvard to improve patient outcomes and care efficiency at the hospital level.
First Maranao Pulmonologist
Among Dr. Aslama's most significant achievements is a straightforward but historically weighty fact: she is the
first Maranao pulmonologist in the Philippines.
In a region where respiratory diseases, tuberculosis, and pulmonary complications from COVID-19 have placed
enormous pressure on healthcare capacity, having the first Maranao specialist in pulmonary medicine based in the
heart of Lanao is more than a milestone. It's a public health breakthrough.
Leadership in Medicine
Dr. Aslama made history as the first Maranao woman elected President of the Iligan Society of Internists, a
distinction that reflects her standing not just as a clinician but as a recognized leader among her peers in the
medical community.
She currently serves as Vice President of the Philippine College of Chest Physicians, Northern Mindanao Chapter,
continuing to expand Maranao representation in the country's medical leadership landscape.
Harvard Medical School and International Recognition
Between managing her clinical responsibilities and training resident physicians at Amai Pakpak Medical Center,
Dr. Aslama applied to the Harvard Medical School Postgraduate Medical Education's Leadership in Medicine:
Southeast Asia certificate program (now expanded as the Leadership in Medicine: Asia Pacific program).<ref
name="hms_sea">Template:Cite web</ref>
She was accepted.
"I realized that aside from being a clinician, I wanted to learn about leadership, solving problems, and
managing teams." (Dr. Aslama Alauya-Lamping, as cited by Harvard Medical School, 2024)
The one-year blended certificate program, developed in partnership with Sunway University in Malaysia, combines
in-person workshops (in Bandar Sunway, Selangor and Boston, Massachusetts), pre-recorded lectures, and live
webinars, covering leadership, health care finance, human resource management, quality management, and
organizational change.<ref name="hms_sea" />
In February 2024, Dr. Aslama traveled to Boston for the final in-person workshop and graduation ceremony.
She graduated with distinction.
Harvard Medical School faculty recognized her as one of the top three capstone project proposal authors in her
cohort.
She also received the Excellence Award for her team assignment, an honor recognizing standout performance in
the program's collaborative finance component.<ref name="hms_feature" />

PAGE 5
Her capstone proposal focused on implementing lean management principles to improve cardiopulmonary
resuscitation outcomes in the general medicine ward of Amai Pakpak Medical Center, a practical and immediately
applicable contribution to her home hospital.<ref name="hms_feature" />
"The process of developing this capstone proposal made me realize the many ways in which we can
improve processes in any institution. Starting with a small scope, we can gradually expand until we
cover a larger dimension by integrating all the smaller scopes." (Dr. Aslama Alauya-Lamping, Harvard
Medical School, 2024)
She is the first Maranao woman to graduate with distinction from a Harvard Medical School postgraduate
certificate program, and the first from her community to earn recognition at that institution's level.
Awards and Distinctions
Dr. Aslama's record of "firsts" spans local, national, and international scales.
Pride of Ranaw Award
The Provincial Government of Lanao del Sur bestows the Pride of Ranaw Award on individuals whose
achievements, integrity, and service bring distinction and honor to the Maranao people.
Dr. Aslama is the first Maranao doctor and pulmonologist to receive this recognition, which she accepted after
completing her Harvard Medical School program.<ref name="hms_feature" />
"I am so happy and grateful for my experience at Harvard Medical School, and my community is so
thankful that I received this training." (Dr. Aslama Alauya-Lamping, Harvard Medical School, 2024)
Distinguished Public Servant Award (Philippine College of Chest Physicians)
The Philippine College of Chest Physicians (PCCP) confers its Distinguished Public Servant Award on members
who have demonstrated exemplary service, leadership, and significant contributions to the advancement of
pulmonary medicine in the Philippines.
Dr. Aslama is the first Maranao recipient of this award, recognizing her record of clinical service, community
engagement, and healthcare leadership in a medically underserved region.
Valedictorian, MSU College of Medicine
Her distinction as the first Maranao lady Valedictorian of the MSU College of Medicine placed her at the top of
one of Mindanao's most competitive professional schools, a milestone that set the tone for everything that
followed.

Leadership in Medicine program marks her as the first Maranao woman honored in that capacity by one of the

Aslama M. Alauya-Lamping
Dr. Aslama Masacal Alauya-Lamping, MD, FPCP, FPCCP, FCCP,
is a Maranao physician, pulmonologist, and internal medicine
specialist based in Marawi City, Lanao del Sur, Philippines.
She is the youngest child of Justice Saaduddin A. Alauya Sr., the first
Jurisconsult in Islamic Law of the Philippines, and the first doctor in
a family that has otherwise distinguished itself almost entirely
through the law.
Her story is one of quiet, persistent firsts: first Maranao lady
valedictorian of the MSU College of Medicine, first Maranao
pulmonologist, first Maranao doctor to earn the Distinguished Public
Servant Award from the Philippine College of Chest Physicians, first
Maranao doctor and pulmonologist to receive the Pride of Ranaw
Award, first Maranao elected president of the Iligan Society of
Internists, and the first Maranao woman to graduate with distinction
from a Harvard Medical School certificate program.
She stands not only as a pride of Ranaw in her own right, but as the
medical pillar of a family that has, across two generations, broken
barriers in law, banking, Islamic jurisprudence, and Philippine
governance.

Background and Family
The Alauya family of Bacolod Grande, Lanao del Sur, is one of the most accomplished Bangsamoro families in
modern Philippine public life.
At the center of it all is Justice Saaduddin A. Alauya Sr., a Maranao lawyer and Aleem (Islamic scholar) who served
as Vice Governor of Lanao del Sur in 1989, as Acting Governor from 1992 to 1995, and as Chairman of the Code
Commission on Muslim Laws in the Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao in 1994.
In August 1996, President Fidel V. Ramos appointed him as Jurisconsult in Islamic Law of the Philippines,
making him the first person to hold that office under the Supreme Court of the Philippines.<ref
name="wiki_alauya">Template:Cite web</ref>
The Jurisconsult, created under Presidential Decree 1083 or the Code of Muslim Personal Laws, functions as an
expert advisor to the Supreme Court on matters of Islamic law.<ref name="wiki_alauya" />
He is also a prolific legal author, having written foundational texts on Muslim inheritance law, fundamentals of
Islamic jurisprudence, Islamic penal law, and procedure and evidence under the Muslim Code.<ref
name="wiki_alauya" />
During part of his career, Justice Alauya served as a professor at Umm Al-Qura University in Makkah, Saudi
Arabia, a tenure that would shape the early education and worldview of his youngest daughter.
His children have matched his legacy, each staking out their own "firsts."
Atty. Arifa Alauya-Ala, a Certified Public Accountant and lawyer, is the first Maranao woman to serve as Senior
Assistant Governor of the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP), the country's central bank.<ref
name="bsp_ala">Template:Cite web</ref>
She is the BSP's lead advocate for Islamic banking and finance, chairing the Inter-Agency Working Group on
Islamic Banking and Finance, and was a key figure in the passage of the Islamic Banking Law (Republic Act No.
11439) in 2019.<ref name="context_ala">Template:Cite web</ref>
In September 2025, she was recognized as a "Woman Influencer in Financial Services Industry" by the World
Financial Innovation Series.<ref name="context_ala" />
Atty. Asma Alauya also serves in the legal services sector of the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas. [Note: The specific
title of General Legal Counsel attributed to Atty. Asma Alauya could not be independently verified through
available public records at the time of writing. This detail is sourced from family accounts and is subject to
verification.]
Atty. Saaduddin M. Alauya Jr., a lawyer and Certified Public Accountant, currently serves as Vice Chancellor for
Administration and Finance of Mindanao State University Main Campus in Marawi City.<ref
name="msu_alauya">Template:Cite web</ref>
Into this family of pioneering lawyers, administrators, and jurists, Dr. Aslama stepped not with a bar examination
but with a stethoscope.

PAGE 3
She became the first doctor in the family and, in doing so, opened an entirely new frontier for the Alauya legacy.
Early Life and Education Abroad
Dr. Aslama spent a significant portion of her early years and formative schooling in Makkah, Saudi Arabia, during
the period when her father was serving as a professor at Umm Al-Qura University.
Growing up between the spiritual heart of the Islamic world and the cultural heartbeat of Marawi City gave her
something few Maranao children of her generation had: a genuinely global perspective, paired with an unshakeable
sense of who she was and where she came from.
From her earliest years in school through college, she was consistently at the top of her class.
She graduated as Valedictorian at every level of her academic journey, from grade school all the way to the College
of Medicine.
Medical Education
Dr. Aslama completed her medical degree at the Mindanao State University College of Medicine, where she made
history as the first Maranao lady Valedictorian of the college.
That achievement alone would have been remarkable, but it was only the opening chapter of a much longer record.
After earning her medical degree from MSU, she pursued residency training at the National Kidney and Transplant
Institute (NKTI) in Metro Manila, then went on to complete fellowship training in pulmonary medicine at the
University of the Philippines.<ref name="hms_feature">Template:Cite web</ref>
She holds the credentials MD, FPCP (Fellow of the Philippine College of Physicians), FPCCP (Fellow of the
Philippine College of Chest Physicians), and FCCP (Fellow of the American College of Chest Physicians).
Medical Career
Clinical Work
Dr. Aslama is a pulmonologist and internal medicine specialist who has built her practice in Iligan City and the
broader Lanao region.
She serves as one of the consultants at Amai Pakpak Medical Center, the only tertiary hospital in Marawi City
serving Lanao del Sur and its neighboring cities and provinces.<ref name="hms_feature" />
She also holds a private pulmonology practice at Mercy Community Hospital and other hospitals in Iligan City.
During the COVID-19 pandemic, Dr. Aslama worked on the frontlines as a clinician in the respiratory unit of the
internal medicine department at Amai Pakpak Medical Center, treating patients at the height of the health crisis
while simultaneously training resident physicians.
Following her graduation from Harvard Medical School in 2024, she was assigned as medical specialist supervisor
of Station 8 at Amai Pakpak Medical Center, a general medicine ward that routinely handles more patients than its
official capacity, including critical cases when the intensive care unit is full.<ref name="hms_feature" />

PAGE 4
She has been implementing lean management principles in that ward, applying the capstone work she developed at
Harvard to improve patient outcomes and care efficiency at the hospital level.
First Maranao Pulmonologist
Among Dr. Aslama's most significant achievements is a straightforward but historically weighty fact: she is the
first Maranao pulmonologist in the Philippines.
In a region where respiratory diseases, tuberculosis, and pulmonary complications from COVID-19 have placed
enormous pressure on healthcare capacity, having the first Maranao specialist in pulmonary medicine based in the
heart of Lanao is more than a milestone. It's a public health breakthrough.
Leadership in Medicine
Dr. Aslama made history as the first Maranao woman elected President of the Iligan Society of Internists, a
distinction that reflects her standing not just as a clinician but as a recognized leader among her peers in the
medical community.
She currently serves as Vice President of the Philippine College of Chest Physicians, Northern Mindanao Chapter,
continuing to expand Maranao representation in the country's medical leadership landscape.
Harvard Medical School and International Recognition
Between managing her clinical responsibilities and training resident physicians at Amai Pakpak Medical Center,
Dr. Aslama applied to the Harvard Medical School Postgraduate Medical Education's Leadership in Medicine:
Southeast Asia certificate program (now expanded as the Leadership in Medicine: Asia Pacific program).<ref
name="hms_sea">Template:Cite web</ref>
She was accepted.
"I realized that aside from being a clinician, I wanted to learn about leadership, solving problems, and
managing teams." (Dr. Aslama Alauya-Lamping, as cited by Harvard Medical School, 2024)
The one-year blended certificate program, developed in partnership with Sunway University in Malaysia, combines
in-person workshops (in Bandar Sunway, Selangor and Boston, Massachusetts), pre-recorded lectures, and live
webinars, covering leadership, health care finance, human resource management, quality management, and
organizational change.<ref name="hms_sea" />
In February 2024, Dr. Aslama traveled to Boston for the final in-person workshop and graduation ceremony.
She graduated with distinction.
Harvard Medical School faculty recognized her as one of the top three capstone project proposal authors in her
cohort.
She also received the Excellence Award for her team assignment, an honor recognizing standout performance in
the program's collaborative finance component.<ref name="hms_feature" />

PAGE 5
Her capstone proposal focused on implementing lean management principles to improve cardiopulmonary
resuscitation outcomes in the general medicine ward of Amai Pakpak Medical Center, a practical and immediately
applicable contribution to her home hospital.<ref name="hms_feature" />
"The process of developing this capstone proposal made me realize the many ways in which we can
improve processes in any institution. Starting with a small scope, we can gradually expand until we
cover a larger dimension by integrating all the smaller scopes." (Dr. Aslama Alauya-Lamping, Harvard
Medical School, 2024)
She is the first Maranao woman to graduate with distinction from a Harvard Medical School postgraduate
certificate program, and the first from her community to earn recognition at that institution's level.
Awards and Distinctions
Dr. Aslama's record of "firsts" spans local, national, and international scales.
Pride of Ranaw Award
The Provincial Government of Lanao del Sur bestows the Pride of Ranaw Award on individuals whose
achievements, integrity, and service bring distinction and honor to the Maranao people.
Dr. Aslama is the first Maranao doctor and pulmonologist to receive this recognition, which she accepted after
completing her Harvard Medical School program.<ref name="hms_feature" />
"I am so happy and grateful for my experience at Harvard Medical School, and my community is so
thankful that I received this training." (Dr. Aslama Alauya-Lamping, Harvard Medical School, 2024)
Distinguished Public Servant Award (Philippine College of Chest Physicians)
The Philippine College of Chest Physicians (PCCP) confers its Distinguished Public Servant Award on members
who have demonstrated exemplary service, leadership, and significant contributions to the advancement of
pulmonary medicine in the Philippines.
Dr. Aslama is the first Maranao recipient of this award, recognizing her record of clinical service, community
engagement, and healthcare leadership in a medically underserved region.
Valedictorian, MSU College of Medicine
Her distinction as the first Maranao lady Valedictorian of the MSU College of Medicine placed her at the top of
one of Mindanao's most competitive professional schools, a milestone that set the tone for everything that
followed.
Harvard Excellence Award

world's foremost medical institutions.

Anshari P. Ali
Dr. Anshari P. Ali was a distinguished Filipino Islamic scholar,
Shari'ah lawyer, and academic administrator who served as the 6th
Chancellor of Mindanao State University - General Santos (MSU-
GSC) from 2018 to 2021. A visionary leader committed to
transforming MSU-GSC into a globally competitive institution and
national peace university, Dr. Ali's tenure was marked by
groundbreaking initiatives including the establishment of Region
XII's first College of Medicine, expanded international partnerships
across Asia and the Middle East, and the modernization of
university systems during the COVID-19 pandemic. As a
Maguindanaoan scholar deeply rooted in Islamic jurisprudence and
education, he dedicated his career to advancing quality education
and improving the living conditions of Moro and Indigenous
Peoples in Mindanao.
Contents
1 Background and Education
2 Academic Career
3 Chancellorship (2018–2021)
3.1 Vision and Administrative Framework
3.2 International Partnerships
3.3 Modernization and Innovation
3.4 College of Medicine Establishment
3.5 COVID-19 Response

5 Recognition and Awards
6 Legacy
7 See Also
8 External Links
Background and Education
Dr. Anshari P. Ali pursued his doctoral studies at the International
Islamic University Malaysia's International Institute of Islamic
Thought and Civilization (ISTAC), where he earned his Doctor of
Philosophy in Islamic Civilization. This advanced training in Islamic thought and civilization provided the
intellectual foundation for his later work as both a legal practitioner and educational administrator. Beyond his
academic credentials, Dr. Ali was a practicing Shari'ah lawyer and a certified member of the Shari'ah Bar in the
Philippines, positioning him uniquely at the intersection of Islamic scholarship, legal practice, and higher education
administration.

PAGE 2
Academic Career
Dr. Ali began his academic journey at MSU-General Santos in 1992 as a faculty member, eventually rising to the
rank of Full Professor VI. For nearly three decades, he taught Shari'ah courses in the College of Law Extension and
Islamic Studies courses in the College of Social Sciences and Humanities' Islamic Studies Department. His
classroom expertise spanned Islamic jurisprudence, family law, and the philosophical foundations of Islamic
education. Before his election as Chancellor, he served as the Assistant Dean of the College of Law Extension,
where he gained administrative experience that would prove valuable in his later leadership role.
Chancellorship (2018–2021)
Vision and Administrative Framework
Upon assuming the chancellorship in 2018, Dr. Ali articulated a dual vision for MSU-GSC: to become a globally
competitive university while simultaneously fulfilling its mission as a national peace university. This framework
guided his strategic initiatives throughout his three-year tenure, balancing academic excellence with social
responsibility to the Bangsamoro region and Mindanao's Indigenous communities.
International Partnerships
During his first year in office, Dr. Ali aggressively pursued international collaborations, signing Memoranda of
Understanding with universities and institutions across Asia that shared MSU-GSC's commitment to Islamic values
and regional peace. Strategic partnerships were established with institutions in Brunei, Singapore, Indonesia, and
the United Arab Emirates. To institutionalize and expand these global engagements, he created the Office of
International Affairs, providing the university with dedicated capacity for managing international partnerships and
student exchanges.
Dr. Ali also strengthened MSU-GSC's relationship with the Office of the Presidential Adviser on the Peace Process,
working through the Campus Institute of Peace and Development in Mindanao to advance the university's role in
peacebuilding efforts across the region.
Modernization and Innovation
Recognizing the imperative of technological advancement, Dr. Ali championed the creation of the Information and
Communications Technology Office to modernize instructional modalities and administrative processes throughout
the university. This initiative proved particularly critical as the institution navigated the challenges of the COVID-
19 pandemic and the transition to remote learning environments. His vision of MSU-GSC as a "SMART
University" reflected his understanding that technological integration was essential to remaining competitive in
21st-century higher education.
College of Medicine Establishment
One of Dr. Ali's most significant achievements was serving as the driving force behind the establishment of MSU-
GSC's College of Medicine—the first medical college in Region XII (SOCCSKSARGEN). This milestone
represented a transformative moment in the university's history, expanding MSU-GSC's academic portfolio into
medical education and addressing critical healthcare workforce needs in Mindanao. The college's creation
demonstrated Dr. Ali's ability to translate institutional vision into concrete structural achievements.

PAGE 3
COVID-19 Response
Under Dr. Ali's leadership, MSU-Gensan distinguished itself through its exemplary response to the COVID-19
pandemic. The university received a Special Citation from the General Santos City Local Government Unit for
displaying exceptional practices and making significant contributions to the battle against COVID-19 in the
Philippines. Additionally, the General Santos Chamber of Commerce and Industries Inc. recognized MSU-Gensan
as a "true entrepreneurial hero" for its pandemic-era efforts, highlighting the institution's role in supporting
community resilience during unprecedented challenges.
Publications and Scholarship
Dr. Ali was a prolific scholar whose written work contributed significantly to the discourse on Islamic law and
education in the Philippines. He authored two seminal books published by MSU-GSC: The Evolution of Islamic
Law in the Philippines: History, Texts and Analysis (2009) and The Muslim Educational Needs: An Exposition on
the Fundamental Elements and Objectives of Islamic Education (2012). Both works remain important references
for understanding the development of Islamic legal systems and educational frameworks in the Philippine context.
Additionally, Dr. Ali published three articles in international academic journals addressing critical issues in Islamic
Family Law, secularism in the application of Islamic Family Law, and legal impediments to implementing Islamic
Family Law in the Philippines. These scholarly contributions reflected his expertise in navigating the complex
intersections of religious law, secular legal systems, and Philippine jurisprudence.
Recognition and Awards
Dr. Ali's contributions to education and community service earned him significant recognition both nationally and
internationally. In 2019, he was honored as one of UNESCO's Most Outstanding Educators in the Philippines,
acknowledging his exceptional impact on educational development and his innovative approaches to university
administration. He was also accorded the Mindanao Governance and Leadership Excellence Award, recognizing his
exemplary leadership in advancing governance standards and institutional effectiveness in the Mindanao region.
Legacy
Chancellor Ali's academic accomplishments were prodigious, but his enduring legacy lies in his unwavering
commitment to helping others and advancing the welfare of marginalized communities. His leadership vision
encompassed not merely institutional excellence but a deeper social purpose: positioning MSU-GSC as a strong
partner in improving the living conditions of Moro and Indigenous Peoples in Mindanao. He consistently fulfilled
the university's mandate to provide quality education and administrative services to all stakeholders, demonstrating
that academic leadership could be both intellectually rigorous and deeply humane.
The MSU-Gensan community remembers Chancellor Ali as a transformative leader whose work created lasting
institutional structures—the College of Medicine, the Office of International Affairs, the ICT Office—that will
continue serving students and communities for generations. His integration of Islamic scholarship with modern
educational administration, his commitment to peace and development, and his visionary approach to university
leadership established a standard of excellence that continues to inspire the institution he served with dedication
and distinction.

title: Ali, Bato R. Sr
text:
PAGE 1
Bato R. Ali Sr
Sultan Bato R. Ali Sr. was a prominent Filipino politician, traditional Maranao leader, and one of the most
foundational figures in the cultural and religious life of Marawi City.
He served both in local governance and national legislation during the mid-20th century, navigating a period when
the formal institutions of the Republic of the Philippines and the age-old structures of the Maranao sultanate had to
find a way to coexist.
Today, Sultan Bato R. Ali Sr. is widely remembered as a pillar of Maranao heritage, most directly because of two
institutions that bear his mark: the Dansalan Bato Ali Mosque and the Marawi Sultanate League.
Contents
1 PUBLIC SERVICE AND POLITICAL CAREER
1.1 National Assembly Representation
1.2 Mayor of Dansalan
2 STRUCTURAL AND CULTURAL PILLARS
2.1 The Dansalan Bato Ali Mosque
2.2 The Marawi Sultanate League
3 LEGACY
4 SEE ALSO
5 REFERENCES
6 CATEGORIES
PUBLIC SERVICE AND POLITICAL CAREER
Sultan Bato Ali Sr. spent much of his public life at the intersection of two worlds: the traditional Maranao sultanate
and the formal legal system of the Philippine Republic.
That balancing act was not always easy, but it reflected something consistent about who he was; a leader who
refused to treat cultural identity and civic obligation as mutually exclusive.
National Assembly Representation
During the Second World War, Sultan Ali stepped into the national arena.
He represented the undivided province of Lanao at the National Assembly of the Philippines, serving from
September 25, 1943 to February 2, 1944.
His tenure was brief, as were most legislative careers during that turbulent wartime period, but it established him as
a recognized voice for the Maranao people in national affairs.
Mayor of Dansalan
After the war, Sultan Ali returned to serve his community directly.

PAGE 2
Sultan Bato R. Ali Sr.
Full Name
Sultan Bato R. Ali Sr.
Other Titles
Sultan; Mayor of Dansalan
Ethnicity
Maranao
Region
Lanao del Sur, Mindanao
Political Office
Member, National Assembly of the Philippines
(1943–1944); Mayor of Dansalan / Marawi City
(1948–1953)
Traditional Office
Sultan; Founder, Marawi Sultanate League (est.
1954)
He served as the Mayor of the City of Dansalan, the lakeside
settlement that would officially be renamed Marawi City in 1956.
His mayoral tenure ran from 1948 until March 9, 1953, years in
which the city was still finding its footing as a formal
municipality while its residents remained deeply rooted in
centuries-old Maranao customs and ways of life.
That tension between the modern and the traditional was, in many
ways, the defining challenge of Sultan Ali's career, and it shaped
every institutional decision he made.
STRUCTURAL AND CULTURAL
PILLARS
Sultan Bato Ali Sr.'s most enduring contributions are not
measured in legislation or executive orders.
They are measured in structures and institutions that his
community still turns to, even now, decades after his time.
The Dansalan Bato Ali Mosque
In the 1950s, Sultan Ali founded what was then known simply as
the Bato Ali Mosque, built at a commanding location overlooking
Lake Lanao in what is today the heart of Marawi City's Ground
Zero.
The mosque was not just a place of worship. In the Maranao
tradition, a mosque anchors a community's spiritual and social
identity, and this one did exactly that.
Its history, however, has been anything but peaceful.
The original structure was burned to the ground during the
Martial Law period under President Ferdinand Marcos Sr.
The lot was briefly repurposed as a cemetery before the
community came together to fund a full reconstruction,
completing it by 1980.
Decades later, in May 2017, the mosque was captured by ISIS-
affiliated Maute group militants during the Marawi Siege.
The structure served as a heavily fortified stronghold where
hostages were held, making it one of the siege's most haunting
landmarks.

PAGE 3
Religion
Islam (Sunni)
Notability
Maranao statesman, traditional sultan, and
foundational figure in the cultural and religious
heritage of Marawi City
Known For
Founding the Dansalan Bato Ali Mosque and
establishing the Marawi Sultanate League in
1954
Pull Quote
"His ancestral lineages and institutional
frameworks remain deeply embedded in
Marawi's modern civil society."
After the city's liberation, the building was assessed as structurally
unsafe and was demolished with the formal authorization of
traditional leaders.
The community rebuilt it once again, and on May 17, 2023, the
reconstructed mosque was inaugurated as Masjid Dansalan.
It stands today as a symbol of Maranao resilience, directly tied to
the family and vision of Sultan Bato R. Ali Sr.
The Marawi Sultanate League
On August 14, 1954, Sultan Ali founded the Marawi Sultanate
League (MSL), an organization born from a clear-eyed
recognition that traditional Maranao governance needed a formal
home within an increasingly Westernized political landscape.
The league brought together the traditional royal leaders and
Datus representing the Lima Pumagsopa sa Marawi, the Five
Emirates of Marawi, which include historic socio-political
realms such as Buadi Ibango.
What Sultan Ali built was not a ceremonial body. The MSL functions as a living customary council.
It upholds Maranao ancestral law (Adat), mediates clan feuds (Rido), and acts as the official custodian and
administering body of heritage sites, including Masjid Dansalan.
In the post-conflict era, the league has taken on an even wider role, guiding community-led rehabilitation efforts
and keeping Maranao cultural identity alive in the face of displacement and loss.
LEGACY
Sultan Bato R. Ali Sr. left behind something harder to quantify than a political record: a framework of leadership
that wove traditional aristocracy together with civic responsibility.
He showed that a sultan could sit in a municipal hall or a legislative chamber without abandoning the values that
gave his title meaning.
His ancestral lineages and the institutional frameworks he built remain deeply embedded in Marawi's modern civil
society.
Successive generations of sultans have continued to lead the Marawi Sultanate League, steering community-driven
urban rehabilitation, identity preservation, and interfaith dialogue in the years since the siege.
In a city that has survived war, martial law, and one of the most destructive urban battles in recent Philippine
history, Sultan Bato R. Ali Sr.'s legacy endures not as nostalgia, but as active foundation.

title: Ali, Omar Mohammad Solitario
text:
PAGE 1
Omar Mohammad Solitario Ali
Omar Mohammad Solitario Ali (c. 1950s, Marawi City — April 8, 2022, Cagayan de Oro) was one of the most
consequential figures in the modern history of Maranao political leadership. A former commander of the Moro National
Liberation Front (MNLF), two-term Mayor of Marawi City, federalism advocate, government peace emissary, and counter-
extremism campaigner, he lived a life that traced the entire arc of the Bangsamoro struggle, from jungle insurgency to
institutional governance.
His name, "Solitario" (The Solitary One), wasn't just a moniker. It described how he lived his convictions: often standing
alone, often misunderstood, but never veering from what he believed was right for his people and for Islam. He is remembered
today as the man who gave birth to the concept of "Moral Governance" in Marawi City, a framework that continues to shape
how the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM) imagines the relationship between Islamic ethics
and modern public administration.
Contents
1 Background and Lineage
2 The Revolutionary Years: MNLF and the Birth of "Solitario"
3 Education and Intellectual Formation
4 Mayoral Tenure (2001–2007): Building Moral Governance
4.1 The Moral Governance Framework
4.2 Development, Tourism, and Rido Resolution
5 Political Evolution: Federalism and the PDP-Laban Years
6 The 2017 Marawi Siege: The Emissary in the Crossfire
6.1 The Peace Emissary Role
6.2 Arrest Orders, Clearance, and Revocation
7 Drug Accusations and Political Persecution
8 Counter-Extremism Work and Theological Moderation
9 Legacy
9.1 Architect of Moral Governance
9.2 Bridge Between Generations
9.3 The Legend of Solitario
10 Death
11 Recognition
12 References
13 Further Reading
14 See Also
Background and Lineage
To understand Omar Ali, you have to understand the Maranao world he came from. The Lanao provinces are governed by one
of the oldest and most structured traditional political systems in the Philippines: the Pat a Pangampong sa Ranao, or the four
principalities of Masiu, Unayan, Balo-i, and Bayabao.<ref name="familysearch">Lanao del Sur Province, Philippines
Genealogy. FamilySearch. Accessed March 17, 2026.
https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Lanao_del_Sur_Province,_Philippines_Genealogy</ref> In this world, political power
has always followed lineage, and lineage is validated by an unwritten but deeply felt code called Igma Ago Taritib (Order and
Consensus).<ref name="familysearch" />

PAGE 2
Ali was born into a family that sat at a high point within this traditional hierarchy. His connections, both through his father and
his mother, tied him to original datuships in Marawi.<ref name="mindanews2022a">PAGDARO SA KALINAW: Dureza's
Betrayal and Duterte's Hypocrisy in Marawi. MindaNews. Accessed March 17, 2026.
https://mindanews.com/mindaviews/2017/09/pagdaro-sa-kalinaw-durezas-betrayal-and-dutertes-hypocrisy-in-marawi/</ref>
The move to carry his mother's surname, "Ali," rather than his father's "Salic" (the name used by his half-brother, Fahad "Pre"
Salic) was deliberate and strategic. He adopted "Ali" as both his revolutionary identity and his political brand, connecting him
directly to the clans of Marawi and Baloi, and specifically to the datuships of Guimba and Buadi Sacayo.<ref
name="mindanews2022a" />
This wasn't just a name change. It was a political statement, one that allowed him to command loyalty across multiple sub-
clans and to speak with authority not just as one man but as the embodiment of an entire kinship network.
Central to that network was the concept of maratabat: the Maranao ethos of honor, rank, and the preservation of family
prestige. For the Ali-Salic family, maratabat was the engine behind their dominance of the Marawi executive office for nearly
two decades. During the 2016 elections, Maguindanaon datus with Maranaw ancestry crossed provincial borders to campaign
for the family, a demonstration that their influence had never been limited by administrative lines but was rooted in a centuries-
old genealogical bond.<ref name="philstar2016b">Maguindanaon datus back Lanao del Sur gubernatorial bet. Philstar.com.
April 7, 2016. https://www.philstar.com/nation/2016/04/07/1570412/maguindanaon-datus-back-lanao-del-sur-gubernatorial-
bet</ref>
The Revolutionary Years: MNLF and the Birth of "Solitario"
Omar Ali came of age during the most violent chapter of modern Moro history. The Jabidah Massacre of 1968 and the
declaration of Martial Law by Ferdinand Marcos in 1972 sent a generation of Moro youth into the hills.<ref
name="academiadoc">DEMOCRACY AT GUNPOINT: Election-related Violence in the Philippines. Academia.edu. Accessed
March 17, 2026.
https://www.academia.edu/33693019/DEMOCRACY_AT_GUNPOINT_Election_related_Violence_in_the_Philippines_</ref>
The Moro National Liberation Front, founded by Nur Misuari, became the vehicle for a people who had decided that they
would no longer wait for justice to arrive through institutions that had never treated them as equals.<ref name="academiadoc"
/>
Ali joined the MNLF and rose to become a commander in the Lanao sector. In the jungle, he earned the name "Solitario"
because he was precisely that: a fighter who could hold the line alone, who kept his cool when others panicked, and whose
loyalty to the cause never wavered even when it cost him everything.<ref name="mindanews2022a" /> He was part of the
revolutionary vanguard that ultimately forced the Philippine government to the negotiating table, a process that led to the 1976
Tripoli Agreement, which specifically named Lanao del Sur and Marawi City as central to the proposed autonomous region.
<ref name="pcid">VIOLENCE IN POLITICS AND THE POLITICS OF VIOLENCE. Philippine Center for Islam and
Democracy. Accessed March 17, 2026. https://www.pcid.com.ph/wp-content/uploads/2017/03/Violence-in-Politics.pdf</ref>
More than a military period, the revolutionary years gave Ali something most politicians can never buy: what his colleagues
would later call "revolutionary legitimacy." He wasn't just a datu who got elected. He was an "elder brother of the struggle," a
title that carried genuine moral weight in Maranao society.<ref name="mindanews2022b">BANGSAMORO SPEAKS: On the
Marawi Siege and the people unjustly implicated. MindaNews. April 2022.
https://mindanews.com/mindaviews/2022/04/bangsamoro-speaks-on-the-marawi-siege-and-the-people-unjustly-
implicated/</ref> When the 1996 Final Peace Agreement was signed, Ali was among those who crossed from the jungle into
the government, joining fellow MNLF leaders like Gerry Salapuddin in the work of translating military influence into
something that could actually govern a people.<ref name="academiadoc" />
Education and Intellectual Formation
What separated Omar Ali from many of his contemporaries was his refusal to let the revolution be his only credential. He
pursued formal education with the same seriousness he brought to the battlefield.

PAGE 3
He completed his studies in law, which gave him the language and tools to challenge the state within its own framework,
something he would do repeatedly in the final years of his life when defending himself and his family against criminal
accusations.<ref name="mindanews2022b" /> He argued for due process in an environment that often relied on what he
bluntly called "raw intelligence," and he knew enough about the law to name exactly what was being violated.<ref
name="mindanews2022b" />
He also earned a Master in Development Management (MDM) from the Asian Institute of Management (AIM), an
institution known for training public and private sector leaders across Asia.<ref name="mindanews2022b" /> His time at AIM
fundamentally changed how he saw Marawi City, not just as a religious center or a symbol of Moro resistance, but as a city
that could plan for itself, attract investment, and manage its own socioeconomic development with competence and
confidence.<ref name="philstar2016a">Ex-Marawi mayor to focus on preserving local cultures, arts. Philstar.com. April 1,
2016. https://www.philstar.com/nation/2016/04/01/1568318/ex-marawi-mayor-focus-preserving-local-cultures-arts</ref>
Alongside his legal and managerial training, Ali held the rank of Major in the Reserved Command of the Philippine Army. It
was a rank that puzzled many outsiders: why would a former rebel hold a commission in the national military? For Ali, it was a
deliberate statement of philosophy. A Moro leader could work within the state without surrendering to it.<ref
name="mindanews2022b" />
Mayoral Tenure (2001–2007): Building Moral Governance
Omar Ali served two terms as Mayor of Marawi City, from 2001 to 2007. The era is still talked about in the city today, and not
always quietly.
The Moral Governance Framework
His entire approach to running Marawi was built on a single conviction: that a city's administration should reflect the values of
its people, and that for a majority-Muslim city, those values were Islamic. He called it "Moral Governance," and he meant it
literally.
Under his administration, gambling was banned outright. Video karera machines were destroyed. Billiard halls were shut
down. The distribution of alcohol and pornography was prohibited.<ref name="philstar2006">Marawi City cracks down on
criminality. Philstar.com. April 1, 2006. https://www.philstar.com/nation/2006/04/01/329222/marawi-city-cracks-down-
criminality</ref> These weren't symbolic moves. They were enforced.
He also implemented dress codes and ordinances regulating public conduct, including strict rules on the public behavior of
men who dressed or presented as women, and guidelines on modest attire for Muslim women.<ref name="philstar2006" />
Human rights organizations outside Marawi raised concerns about some of these policies. Inside the city, many residents saw
them as an honest effort to preserve what Marawi was, against what they felt it was slowly being pressured to become.
Development, Tourism, and Rido Resolution
Ali wasn't only interested in moral enforcement. His AIM training showed up in his push to develop Marawi City as an eco-
tourism hub, emphasizing the preservation of Maranaw arts, crafts, and traditions as the city's most sustainable economic asset.
<ref name="philstar2016a" /> He frequently invoked the Dansalan Declaration of 1935, the historic appeal of Maranao sultans
to the United States for a separate independence, positioning his governance as the living continuation of that centuries-old
claim to self-determination.<ref name="philstar2016a" />
He also tackled rido, the clan feuds that had long drained Lanao of energy and investment. Using his own standing in the
Sultanate system, he personally brokered settlements between families, creating a more stable environment for growth.<ref
name="philstar2016a" /> This was governance through relationship, the Maranao way, made effective by the credibility of the
man doing it.

PAGE 4
Political Evolution: Federalism and the PDP-Laban Years
When Rodrigo Duterte rose to national prominence in 2016, Omar Ali saw an opportunity he couldn't pass up. He became the
Regional President of PDP-Laban and played a central role in delivering the Duterte vote in Lanao del Sur.<ref
name="mindanews2022b" />
His support for Duterte wasn't just political calculation. He genuinely believed in federalism as, in his own words, the "antidote
to extremism." The logic was straightforward: when Moro communities can govern themselves, implement Islamic principles
in their own territories, and manage their own resources, the recruitment pitches of radical groups lose their power.<ref
name="mindanews2022b" /> He had been watching "imperial Manila" run the Muslim south for decades, and he was
convinced the model had failed everyone.
He attempted to reclaim the Marawi mayoralty in both 2016 and 2019 but lost both times to Majul Gandamra.<ref
name="mindanewsmain">Omar Solitario Ali: "I cannot be and I will not be a terrorist." MindaNews. April 2022.
https://mindanews.com/top-stories/2022/04/omar-solitario-ali-i-cannot-be-and-i-will-not-be-a-terrorist/</ref> The electoral
defeats stung. But his influence as a unifying voice across the MNLF-MILF divide, and his standing as a "kingmaker" in
Lanao politics, remained very much alive.<ref name="mindanews2022b" />
The 2017 Marawi Siege: The Emissary in the Crossfire
The most painful and most defining chapter of Omar Ali's life began on May 23, 2017, when the ISIS-inspired Maute group
launched the siege that would leave Marawi City in ruins.
Ali's position was uniquely complicated. His half-brother Fahad Salic was related by marriage to the Maute family, a
connection made 35 years earlier that had nothing to do with ideology.<ref name="mindanews2022a" /> But in the climate of
Martial Law and military intelligence reports, "related to" became "in league with," and Ali found himself caught in a trap he
had not built.
The Peace Emissary Role
Months before the siege broke out, Ali had been working as a consultant for the Office of the Presidential Adviser on the Peace
Process (OPAPP). He had personally contacted Secretary Jesus Dureza to warn about the growing radicalization of the Maute
brothers.<ref name="mindanews2022a" /> He was then sent to Butig to meet with the Maute group directly, using his status as
a revolutionary elder to make one last argument for a different path.<ref name="mindanews2022b" />
He described those conversations as "very confrontational." He argued with Abdullah Maute directly about the meaning of
Islam, about social change, and about where the path they were on would lead.
"I told them their path leads only to the destruction of Lanao. This is not the Islam we inherited. This is not what
our fathers fought for." (Omar Solitario Ali, as recounted in his later interviews)
When the siege finally erupted, Ali was in Cagayan de Oro, meeting with other Moro leaders on containment strategies.<ref
name="mindanews2022b" />
Arrest Orders, Clearance, and Revocation
Despite his documented role as a government emissary, Ali's name was included in the arrest orders issued under Martial Law.
<ref name="mindanewsmain" /> The Department of National Defense alleged links between Ali, his sons (including Vice
Mayor Arafat Salic), and the Maute group. Ali rejected these charges entirely, calling the family marriage connection "a
coincidence of 35 years ago" that implied no political alignment.<ref name="mindanews2022b" />
What followed was a disorienting sequence of bureaucratic reversals:
August 16, 2017: Defense Secretary Delfin Lorenzana issued a "conditional clearance" for Ali and his sons, acting on
the representation of Secretary Dureza.<ref name="oppap">Statement of Presidential Peace Adviser on Martial Law

PAGE 5
Clearance. peace.gov.ph. August 2017. https://peace.gov.ph/2017/08/statement-presidential-peace-adviser-martial-law-
clearance-former-marawi-mayor-omar-solitario/</ref>
August 22, 2017: The clearance was revoked following what were described as "vehement objections" from the military
and from local political rivals in Marawi who claimed Ali was shielding the terrorists.<ref name="mindanews2022a" />
Ali spent several years in what he called a "safe sanctuary," unable to return to Marawi City, even as he continued to offer the
government ideas on how to end the siege and begin the recovery.<ref name="oppap" /> For his supporters, this episode was a
textbook case of state intelligence weaponized by local political rivalry.
Drug Accusations and Political Persecution
On top of the rebellion charges, Ali's name appeared in President Duterte's "narco-list" in August 2016. Government
intelligence reports alleged that the drug trade in Lanao del Sur was controlled by the Ali and Salic brothers, including claims
about the liquidation of rival drug operators.<ref name="politiko">Duterte drug matrix: Salic brothers control all drug trade in
Lanao del Sur. Politiko. September 23, 2017. https://politiko.com.ph/2017/09/23/duterte-drug-matrix-salic-brothers-control-
drug-trade-lanao-del-sur-sent-kill-orders-rival-drug-lords-dealers/</ref>
Ali's response was consistent and direct: he called the allegations the product of "dirty local politics," a coordinated effort to
neutralize the Ali-Salic clan's electoral power. He pointed out that a man running a drug empire would not be living in the
circumstances he lived in, and that the shabu allegedly recovered from his home during a raid had been planted by enemies.
<ref name="mindanewsmain" />
He died in 2022 without ever having faced those charges in a courtroom, without ever having his day to answer formally or be
formally cleared.
Counter-Extremism Work and Theological Moderation
Throughout the controversy and the years of living away from home, Omar Ali never stopped doing the one thing he
considered his most important work: arguing against extremism in the Maranao language, in the Maranao voice, from a
Maranao perspective.
For four years, he was the lead speaker on DXSR Radio Salam, a program funded through an OPAPP grant specifically
designed to counter the spread of radical ideology in Lanao.<ref name="mindanews2022b" /> He also wrote and distributed a
small book laying out practical strategies for communities to resist radicalization.<ref name="oppap" />
His theology was one of deliberate, studied moderation. He described himself as a "strong pillar of moderation in religion," a
man who had spent decades studying what he called "Authentic Islam" and who could tell, chapter by verse, why the Maute
group's ideology was a deviation from the Quran, not a fulfillment of it.<ref name="mindanews2022b" /> He once said
plainly: if he had been the leader of Marawi City when the siege happened, he would have either talked the terrorists out or
died fighting them. The destruction of his birthplace was, for him, the worst possible outcome, and one he had tried everything
in his power to prevent.
Legacy
Omar Mohammad Solitario Ali passed away on April 8, 2022, in a hospital in Cagayan de Oro, from a brain tumor. He was in
the middle of preparing for yet another run for the Marawi mayorship, still carrying the same vision he'd had since his days in
the MNLF: a Marawi City that was modern, self-governing, morally grounded, and finally at peace.<ref
name="inquirer">Former Marawi mayor Omar Ali passes away. Inquirer.net. 2022.
https://newsinfo.inquirer.net/1580659/former-marawi-mayor-omar-ali-passes-away</ref>

PAGE 6
Architect of Moral Governance
His two terms as mayor remain the most studied period of Marawi's civic history. The policies he put in place during 2001 to
2007 are now recognized as an early and locally developed model of what the BARMM has since formalized under the "Moral
Governance" framework. He showed that Islamic ethics weren't incompatible with local government functions. They could be
the foundation of them.<ref name="mindanews2022b" />
Bridge Between Generations
Ali was one of the few leaders in the history of the Bangsamoro struggle who could genuinely speak to both the MNLF and the
MILF, to the datus of the old sultanate and to the youth who knew him from the radio. His role in gathering MNLF and MILF
leaders in 2015 to align their efforts toward the peace process is considered a turning point in Moro intra-group diplomacy.<ref
name="mindanews2022b" />
To the youth leaders and women's groups of Marawi, he was "Ama" (Father), a mentor who took the democratic process
seriously even when it failed him, and who believed that self-determination had to be won through elections and institutions,
not just through the barrel of a gun.<ref name="mindanews2022b" />
The Legend of Solitario
He died carrying unresolved charges he believed were fabricated. His supporters call this a symbol of the "selective justice"
that has defined the state's relationship with Moro leaders for generations. For them, the fact that he never had his day in court
is not a footnote but a central part of his story: a man who served his people, served the government that distrusted him, stood
against the extremists who wanted his city, and was never given a fair hearing for any of it.<ref name="mindanews2022b" />
His name, Solitario, carries its meaning into history: a leader who stood alone in his convictions, more often than not, but who
never stopped standing.
Death
Omar Mohammad Solitario Ali passed away on April 8, 2022, in Cagayan de Oro City, Philippines, after a prolonged illness
caused by a brain tumor. He had been living away from Marawi City for years due to the unresolved legal situation stemming
from the 2017 siege, and his health had deteriorated during that period of displacement. He was reportedly in the process of
filing his candidacy for the Marawi mayorship when he died, a final act that speaks to the kind of leader he was: still running,
still believing, until the very end.<ref name="mindanewsmain" /><ref name="inquirer" />
Recognition
Served as Mayor of Marawi City for two consecutive terms (2001–2007), among the longest sustained periods of
reformist governance in the city's modern history.
Acknowledged by Bangsamoro civic and political leaders as a pioneer of Moral Governance in local Muslim
administration.<ref name="mindanews2022b" />
Recognized as a key architect of the 2015 MNLF-MILF unity effort that contributed to the foundation of the
BARMM peace framework.<ref name="mindanews2022b" />
Honored posthumously by colleagues in the Moro peace movement as an elder of the struggle whose revolutionary
legitimacy and theological moderation distinguished him from most of his contemporaries.

title: Ali-Gutoc, Bai Tomanina
text:
PAGE 1
Bai Tomanina Ali-Gutoc

Bai Tomanina Ali-Gutoc
Bai Tomanina Ali-Gutoc was a prominent Maranao noblewoman, educator, and real property developer who
played a defining role in establishing Filipino educational and cultural institutions in Saudi Arabia during the
1980s. As the first Directress of the International Philippine School of Jeddah, she helped create what would
become the largest Philippine international school worldwide, leaving an enduring legacy within both the Maranao
diaspora and the broader Filipino expatriate community. A matriarch of the influential Ali clan of Lanao, Bai
Tomanina embodied the traditional Maranao values of maratabat, communal solidarity, and Islamic faith, while
pioneering modern pathways for Filipinos abroad.
Contents
1 Early Life and Family
2 Education and Institutional Leadership
2.1 International Philippine School of Jeddah
2.2 Philippine Islamic Center
3 Career and Achievements
3.1 Community and Cultural Leadership
3.2 Values and Cultural Significance
4 Legacy
5 See Also
6 Further Reading
Early Life and Family
Bai Tomanina was born into the Maranao ethnic group,
native to the region surrounding Lake Lanao in Mindanao.
She belonged to the influential Ali clan of Balo-i, Lanao
del Norte, a lineage deeply rooted in the traditional socio-
political structures of the Sultanate of Lanao. The title
"Bai," which she carried, is a noble designation for
Maranao women reflecting their status within traditional
governance and community leadership.
Her marriage to Ambassador Candidato B. Gutoc, a
distinguished diplomat who served as Ambassador to
Bahrain and later as Consul General in Jeddah, connected
her to both diplomatic service and international Muslim
affairs. The union produced two notable children: Samira Ali Gutoc, a prominent civic leader and politician who
continued her mother's legacy of public service, and Dr. Alexis A. Gutoc.
Education and Institutional Leadership
While specific details of her formal schooling remain part of private family records, Bai Tomanina's professional
life was distinguished by a commitment to educational institution-building and cultural preservation.

PAGE 2
International Philippine School of Jeddah
In the early 1980s, Bai Tomanina worked alongside her husband and community leaders, including the diplomat
Ambassador Mauyag Tamano, to establish the Philippine School in Jeddah, serving the growing Filipino expatriate
population in Saudi Arabia. She served as the institution's first Directress, laying the institutional foundations that
would allow it to expand into the largest Philippine international school worldwide.
Her leadership during these formative years was critical to establishing curricula, hiring faculty, and building
relationships with both the Philippine government and the Saudi Arabian authorities. The school became a vital
anchor for Filipino family life abroad, providing not only academic education but also cultural continuity for
children of overseas workers.
Philippine Islamic Center
Bai Tomanina was instrumental in establishing the Philippine Islamic Center at the Philippine Embassy premises in
Jeddah. The center served as a cultural and religious anchor for Muslim Filipinos in the region, providing spaces
for Islamic observance, Quranic study, and community gathering. This work reflected her deeper mission to
preserve Maranao and Filipino Muslim identity within the diaspora.
Career and Achievements
Beyond her institutional leadership, Bai Tomanina established herself as a successful real property developer,
operating across both public service and private sectors. Her professional accomplishments reflected multiple
dimensions of leadership.
Community and Cultural Leadership
As a "Bae," a traditional Maranao noble title, she exercised leadership that extended beyond business into cultural
stewardship. She advocated for the welfare of Muslim women and the broader Filipino community abroad,
ensuring that traditional values and governance structures remained relevant in international settings. She was
known for raising awareness about Maranao heritage among the diaspora population, particularly ensuring that
younger generations maintained connection to their Moro cultural roots.
Values and Cultural Significance
Bai Tomanina's life reflected the core values of the Maranao people: maratabat, which encompasses honor, self-
esteem, and dignity; communal solidarity; and deep faith in Islam. Her family, friends, and colleagues remembered
her for emphasizing humility, care for others, and excellence in all endeavors. Her cultural significance lies in her
role as a bridge between traditional Maranao nobility and the modern, globalized Filipino identity, demonstrating
how indigenous leadership structures could adapt to and lead effectively in international contexts.
She was a primary figure in maintaining Maranao traditions and values within her family and the
expatriate community, ensuring that younger generations remained connected to their heritage.

PAGE 3
Legacy
Bai Tomanina Ali-Gutoc passed away in early 2025, concluding a life dedicated to education, cultural preservation,
and community service. Her legacy is sustained through the International Philippine School of Jeddah, which
continues to serve thousands of Filipino families worldwide, and through the ongoing public service of her
daughter Samira Ali Gutoc. The institutions she helped establish remain testaments to her vision of maintaining
Filipino and Maranao cultural identity while advancing educational opportunity in the global diaspora.
Her work demonstrated that traditional cultural leadership, when grounded in education and institutional vision,
could transcend geographic boundaries and create lasting impact for future generations.

Abul Khayr D. Alonto
Abul Khayr Dangcal Alonto (1945–2019), also known as Datu
Abul Khayr, was a Maranao political leader, revolutionary
commander, diplomat, and development administrator whose career
traced one of the most dramatic arcs in the modern political history
of Mindanao. He was among the original "Top 90" cadres trained by
the Moro National Liberation Front (MNLF), eventually rising to
Vice Chairman of the organization during its most volatile early
years. Yet he would go on to serve as Vice Mayor and Acting Mayor
of Marawi City, a Philippine Ambassador to Nigeria, Speaker of a
regional legislative body, and finally as Cabinet-rank Chairperson of
the Mindanao Development Authority (MinDA) under President
Rodrigo Duterte. Across five decades of public life, he embodied the
transformation of the Bangsamoro struggle from armed rebellion to
institutional governance, earning a place as one of the most complex
and consequential figures in Bangsamoro political history.
His life's work came down to a single, hard-won conviction: that
peace cannot outlast poverty, and that development is not merely an
economic goal but a political one.<ref
name="tamano2024">Tamano, Ashary. Datu Abul Khayr Dangcal
Alonto: From MNLF Commander to Architect of Mindanao
Development. Unpublished research document, 2024.</ref>
Contents
1 Family Background and Early Life
1.1 The Jabidah Massacre and Youth Organizing
2 Entry into the Moro National Liberation Front
2.1 The "Top 90" Training
3 Armed Struggle and Field Command in Lanao
4 Vice Mayor, Acting Mayor, and the Turn Underground
5 Internal MNLF Fractures and Realignment
6 From Revolutionary to Autonomy Institution-Builder
7 Diplomatic Career and the Nigerian Ambassadorship
8 Re-emergence in MNLF Leadership and Peace Advocacy

10 Leadership Style and Political Philosophy
11 Death
12 Legacy
