Corporate and Commercial Law;
Islamic Finance; Public Finance
Management; PPP; Civil and Family
Law; Tax Law; Real Estate; Labor Law;
Intellectual Property
Notable Affiliations
For Atty. Angkaya-Kuhutan, this heritage isn't just a biographical
footnote. It's the lens through which she approaches her legal work,
especially her research and advocacy focused on Moro Muslim
women, their rights under both civil and Islamic law, and the legal
structures that shape their lives.
EDUCATION
She pursued her legal education at the University of the
Philippines College of Law in Diliman, one of the most rigorous
and prestigious law schools in the country, and she didn't just pass
through quietly.
During her time there, she earned the Best Pleading Award from
the UP Office of Legal Aid, was recognized as an awardee of the
Roberto Sabido Prize for Best Legal Paper, and received the
Bienvenido C. Ambion Prize for Best Paper in Private
International Law.
She also represented UP Law in the Philip C. Jessup International
Moot Court Competition, one of the most demanding and
prestigious legal competitions in the world, earning a citation for
her participation.
Before law school, she completed her undergraduate degree in
Business Administration at the UP College of Business
Administration, graduating cum laude.
She also holds a degree in Real Estate Management from Lyceum
of Alabang, rounding out a professional formation that is unusual
even by the standards of Manila's top legal practitioners: business-
trained, academically decorated, and grounded in the practical
worlds of property, commerce, and governance.
LEGAL CAREER
Early Career in Top-Tier Law Firms
After passing the bar, Atty. Angkaya-Kuhutan began her legal career
at some of the most respected law firms in the country.
She worked with Castillo Laman Tan Pantaleon & San Jose Law
Offices, Puyat Jacinto & Santos Law Offices, and Poblador
Bautista & Reyes Law Offices, handling the kind of complex,
high-stakes work that defines elite commercial practice in the
Philippines: mergers and acquisitions, investment structuring,
public-private partnerships, privatization, project finance, banking,
insurance, and capital markets transactions.

PAGE 3
World Bank; Asian Development Bank;
PPP Center (Philippines); Department
of Finance (Philippines); BARMM
Ministry of Finance and Budget and
Management; Islamic Relief Worldwide
(Philippines Branch); HealthJustice
Philippines; Oxfam Pilipinas; Philippine
Chamber of Commerce and Industry
(Parañaque City)
Notability
One of a very small number of Tausug
Muslim women to hold a Juris Doctor
from the University of the Philippines
and to practice at the intersection of
Philippine law, Islamic finance, and
public financial management at both
the national and Bangsamoro regional
level.
Known For
Legal research on Moro Muslim
women's rights; Islamic finance
consultancy for BARMM; property tax
reform advocacy; establishment of the
Philippine branch of Islamic Relief
Worldwide; academic scholarship
recognized by the Philippine Law
Journal and the Roberto Sabido Prize.
She also handled corporate housekeeping and regulatory
compliance, and reviewed contracts and commercial agreements
across a remarkably wide range of sectors, from energy and mining
to healthcare, tourism, and fintech.
General Practice and Consultancy
Today, she manages her own general law practice while serving as
legal counsel, corporate secretary, and consultant for a diverse
portfolio of clients: government agencies, multilateral development
banks, non-government organizations, and private entities in real
estate, construction, manufacturing, and financial technology.
Her practice covers corporate and commercial law, civil and family
law, labor disputes, and property matters, and she has represented
SMEs, families, and individuals in a wide range of legal situations.
She has also taught business courses at the UP School of
Economics and the UP College of Business Administration,
bringing her practitioner's perspective into the classroom while
completing her law degree.
PUBLIC FINANCE AND
GOVERNMENT WORK
One of the most distinctive threads in Atty. Angkaya-Kuhutan's
career is her deep engagement with public financial management
and government reform, work that has taken her from Manila's
central government offices to development bank corridors and,
ultimately, to the Bangsamoro itself.
She was part of the legal team advising the PPP Center and project
sponsors on feasibility studies, project structuring, and legal
documentation for public-private partnerships.
At the Department of Finance, she worked on internal revenue, customs, and local treasury operations.
She held key consultancy positions with the World Bank and the Asian Development Bank, contributing to
significant tax policy reforms and public financial management frameworks.
Her work with the Bureau of Local Government Finance supported property tax reforms and local revenue
generation, including providing assistance in the passage of the Real Property Valuation and Assessment
Reform Act, a landmark piece of legislation that modernized property valuation across the country.
BANGSAMORO AND ISLAMIC FINANCE WORK
Perhaps the most personally resonant dimension of her career is her work as an Islamic finance consultant to the
Ministry of Finance and Budget and Management of the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim
Mindanao (BARMM).

PAGE 4
This role puts her at the intersection of two worlds she knows deeply: the technical machinery of Philippine public
finance law and the distinct legal and ethical framework of Islamic finance.
Islamic finance operates on principles derived from Shari'ah, prohibiting interest (riba) and emphasizing equity,
risk-sharing, and ethical investment. Integrating these principles into the governance and budget structures of the
Bangsamoro is not a simple legal exercise. It requires someone who can read both systems fluently and help bridge
them in a way that is legally sound and culturally grounded.
She brings formal credentials to this work. She is a Fellow and Certified Shari'ah Advisor and Auditor (CSAA)
of the Accounting and Auditing Organization for Islamic Financial Institutions (AAOIFI), the leading international
standard-setting body for Islamic finance. She is also an Honorary Fellow and Certified Islamic Arbitrator and
Expert of the International Islamic Centre for Reconciliation and Arbitration (IICRA).
ACADEMIC SCHOLARSHIP
Atty. Angkaya-Kuhutan has also contributed to legal scholarship, with work published in the Philippine Law
Journal, one of the oldest and most prestigious law reviews in the country, and recognized by institutions
including the Randwick Research International Social Science Journal.
Her academic writing engages directly with the legal position of Moro Muslim women, examining the protections,
gaps, and possibilities within both the Philippine legal framework and Islamic law.
This scholarship reflects a larger commitment: to make visible the legal realities of a community that has often
been underrepresented in both legal academia and formal governance.
HUMANITARIAN AND NGO WORK
Beyond her legal and consultancy practice, she has contributed meaningfully to the humanitarian sector.
She was instrumental in establishing the Philippine branch of Islamic Relief Worldwide in the aftermath of
Typhoon Yolanda (Haiyan) in 2013, one of the strongest typhoons ever recorded, which devastated communities
across the Visayas and parts of Mindanao.
Islamic Relief is one of the world's largest Muslim humanitarian organizations, and bringing its Philippine
operations to life in the immediate aftermath of a catastrophic disaster required not just legal skill but genuine
dedication to community service.
She has also provided consultancy services to HealthJustice Philippines and Oxfam Pilipinas, organizations
working at the intersection of public health, social justice, and development in the Philippines.

title: Angnie, Ansary Abu Anas Abdulmalik
text:

Ansary "Abu Anas" Abdulmalik Angnie
Sheikh Ansary "Abu Anas" Abdulmalik Angnie is a pretty big
deal in the world of Islamic scholarship in the Philippines. He's
not just a religious leader; he's also an educator who has spent
years trying to bridge the gap between traditional religious
teaching and modern education. People often call him "Abu
Anas," and he’s widely respected as a primary authority on Hadith
—the traditions and sayings of the Prophet Muhammad—within
the region.
Contents
1 A Pioneer in Education
2 Leadership and Institutional Impact
3 Reforming the Madrasah System
4 Community Service and Local Leadership
5 Religious Guidance and Hajj
A Pioneer in Education
Sheikh Ansary actually made history by becoming the very first
Filipino to graduate from the College of Hadith (Kolliyatul
Hadith) at the prestigious Islamic University of Madinah in Saudi
Arabia. After he finished his studies there, he didn't just stay
abroad; he came back home to serve as an official missionary, or
Da'ee, for the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia. His main mission was to
share Islamic knowledge and give some much-needed guidance to
the Muslim community back in the Philippines.
Leadership and Institutional Impact
Over the years, Sheikh Ansary has worn a lot of different hats. He served as the President of the Integrated Sharif
Kabunsuan Islamic Foundation (ISISF) and was the Director, or Mudhir, at Jamiatu Janoub al-Filibiniyyah (JJF),
which many people know as Ma'hadul Kuwait. One of his most influential roles was serving as the President of the
League of Pilot Madaris in the Philippines. In that position, he worked hard to make sure Madrasah education
across the country was meeting higher standards.
Reforming the Madrasah System
One of the coolest things Sheikh Ansary has done is push for the Refined Standard Madrasah Curriculum (RSMC).
The idea behind this was to make sure that private Madaris (Islamic schools) were actually recognized as part of
the national education system. Because of this work, students can now transfer between public schools and private
Madaris without losing their academic credits. The curriculum he advocates for is a mix of both worlds—students
study the Qur'an and Islamic history alongside regular subjects like Math, English, and Filipino, so they're ready
for both their spiritual lives and their future careers.

PAGE 2
Community Service and Local Leadership
Right now, Sheikh Ansary is the Chairman of the Provincial Ulama Council of Lanao del Sur. This makes him a
key link between the religious community and the local government. He's the one who leads the council in making
big calls, like spotting the moon to start Ramadan or declaring the date for Eid’l Fitr. During the COVID-19
pandemic, he even used his platform to help with public health, giving lectures to explain why vaccinations were
important for the community's safety.
Religious Guidance and Hajj
Every year during the Hajj pilgrimage to Mecca, Sheikh Ansary serves as a Sheikh for Filipino pilgrims. He helps
them through the spiritual and logistical parts of the journey, making sure everything goes smoothly. As a Maranao
scholar, he's also famous for his "Wasyat" or lectures. He has this unique talent for taking really deep, complex
theological ideas and explaining them in the Maranao language so that everyone can understand and relate to them.
His journey from being a pioneering student in Madinah to a foundational leader at home has left a lasting mark on
the Bangsamoro region and the Philippines as a whole.
Profile provided by Hanif A. Nasroden (https://www.facebook.com/almaarif.nasroden)

Abdulmajeed D. Ansano
Aleem Abdulmajeed D. Ansano (1943, 2008), more widely known
among the Maranao people as Aleem Majeed Ansano or Aleem
Majeed Diguro Ansano, was a Filipino Islamic scholar, educator,
author, and political leader from Lanao who became one of the
defining figures of 20th century Maranao intellectual and religious
life. Recognized as one of the pioneer Ulama of Lanao Province, he
served as Professor of the King Faisal Center for Islamic, Arabic,
and Asian Studies and later as Secretary of the Department of
Education, Culture and Sports of the Autonomous Region in
Muslim Mindanao (DECS-ARMM) in 1996, the agency that would
eventually evolve into today's BARMM Ministry of Education and
Higher Education. He was also a co-founder of the Ompia Party,
one of the most influential political movements in Lanao's history,
and a co-developer of the standardized Maranao orthography that is
still used to write the Maranao language today.
Though he sought the governorship of Lanao twice and did not win
either bid, Aleem Majeed's legacy rests less on electoral office and
more on the institutions he built, the students he taught, and the
written Maranao language he helped preserve for future generations.
Contents
1 EARLY LIFE AND EDUCATION
2 RELIGIOUS AND EDUCATIONAL LEADERSHIP
3 POLITICAL CAREER AND THE OMPIA PARTY
4 LITERARY WORK AND THE MARANAO
ORTHOGRAPHY
5 PERSONAL LIFE
6 DEATH AND LEGACY
7 QUOTE
8 SEE ALSO
9 REFERENCES
EARLY LIFE AND EDUCATION
Aleem Abdulmajeed Ansano pursued an academic and religious
formation that took him well beyond the borders of Lanao. He
began his theological studies at the Theology University in Bagasi,
Tripoli, Libya, where he immersed himself in the study of Islamic
theology. He went on to study at the University of the Philippines,
where he earned a Master's degree in Islamic Philosophy. He later
completed two more Master's degrees, one in Education and another
in Public Administration, both from Mindanao State University in Marawi.

PAGE 2
This combination of foreign Islamic education and Philippine graduate study placed him among a small circle of
Maranao scholars in his generation who moved fluently between the world of the madrasa and the world of the
secular university, a duality that would come to define much of his public life.
RELIGIOUS AND EDUCATIONAL LEADERSHIP
Aleem Majeed was counted among the pioneer Ulama of Lanao Province, the religious scholars whose teachings
shaped the moral and spiritual direction of the Maranao community in the years following Philippine
independence. His voice carried weight both from the minbar and inside the classroom, and he was known for
treating Islamic scholarship and secular education not as competing pursuits but as two halves of the same calling.
He served as Director of the King Faisal Center for Islamic, Arabic, and Asian Studies, an institution dedicated to
the study and propagation of Islamic learning in the region. In 1996, he was appointed Secretary of the Department
of Education, Culture and Sports of the Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (DECS-ARMM), the
predecessor agency of what is now the BARMM Ministry of Education and Higher Education. In this capacity, he
helped shape education policy for Muslim Mindanao at a formative period in the region's history, working to
ensure that young Maranao learners could grow up grounded in both the teachings of the Qur'an and the sciences of
the modern world.
POLITICAL CAREER AND THE OMPIA PARTY
Aleem Majeed twice sought the governorship of Lanao but did not secure the post in either attempt. His more
lasting political contribution came through his partnership with his close friend and contemporary, Dr. Mahid
Mutilan, with whom he co-founded the Ompia Party. The party became one of the dominant political forces in
Lanao, and the bond between its two founders became something of a local legend. As people in Lanao were fond
of saying, there was no Mahid Mutilan without Aleem Majeed Diguro Ansano, and no Ompia Party without Aleem
Majeed Ansano. Together, the two envisioned a Lanao that was united, educated, and rooted in faith.
LITERARY WORK AND THE MARANAO ORTHOGRAPHY
Beyond his roles in government and religious leadership, Aleem Majeed devoted much of his intellectual energy to
preserving Maranao language and culture in written form. He authored a number of books in both Maranao and
Arabic, among them the well known work Gonanao ko masa.
His most enduring scholarly contribution, however, may be his work on the Maranao orthography, the standardized
writing system he helped develop alongside Senator Ahmad Domocao "Domie" Alonto and Shaiekh Abdul Azis
Guroalim Saromantang. This orthography would later be referenced in Lobel's 2009 linguistic study and remains
foundational to how the Maranao language is written today, helping ensure that the language would continue to be
passed down through written as well as spoken tradition.
PERSONAL LIFE
Aleem Majeed was married to Dra. Intan Zainab Baguan Dimakuta, a Doctor of Education from Wato Balindong,
whose own scholarly accomplishments matched his. Together they raised a family grounded in faith and public
service.

PAGE 3
Their son, Atty. Khalid Dimakuta Ansano, has continued the family's tradition of service. Atty. Ansano is a lawyer
who currently serves as Provincial Director of the Ministry of Agriculture, Fisheries and Agrarian Reform
(MAFAR), where he has worked on behalf of Maranao farmers, fisherfolk, and landowners. Before his work at
MAFAR, he was a founder of the Development Assistance Team, a civil society organization in Lanao known for
advocating on behalf of victims of the Marawi Siege.
DEATH AND LEGACY
Aleem Abdulmajeed Ansano died in 2008, but his name continues to be spoken with reverence across Lanao and
the wider BARMM region. He is remembered as a politician who, in many ways, served his people most
effectively outside the halls of power, a scholar who taught from the dusty roads of his homeland rather than from
an ivory tower, and a leader who, by all accounts, never stopped seeing himself as a student.
His influence persists wherever a Maranao child learns to read in their own mother tongue, wherever a farmer
works their land with dignity, and wherever a student recites both the Qur'an and algebra in the same breath.
Through the continued work of his son and the institutions he helped build, the spirit of Aleem Majeed Ansano
remains woven into the foundations of Lanao's religious and educational life.
QUOTE
"Verily, with hardship comes ease." (Qur'an 94:5)

Ivy Sarah Mae Berowa Arimao
Dr. Ivy Sarah Mae Berowa Arimao, RSW is a Filipino social
worker, educator, and public administration scholar based at
Mindanao State University (MSU) in Marawi City. She currently
serves as Professor VI in the Department of Public Administration,
College of Public Affairs, a permanent post she has held since
October 2024, and she also carries the title of Special Assistant to the
Office of the Vice President for Academic Affairs within the MSU
System.
Born on April 1, 1985 in Marawi City, Ivy grew up in the Dimaluna
area near the MSU campus, where she still resides today. She is
married to Jehanoddin Carim Arimao, an administrative employee at
MSU, and the couple has four children. Her father, the late Pasayod
Patarandang Berowa, and her mother, Alma Eliot Elape, raised her
in Marawi City before she went on to build a career that stretched
from frontline social work to the halls of academia.
Contents
1 Early Life and Education
2 Early Career and Field Work
3 Academic Career
4 Research and International Engagement
5 Professional Affiliations and Civic Involvement
6 See Also
7 References
Early Life and Education
Ivy studied elementary education at the Integrated Laboratory School
in Marawi City, graduating in 1998 as a Bronze Medalist. She
completed secondary school at the Science Training Center/ICNHS
in 2002, before enrolling at Mindanao State University for her
Bachelor of Science in Social Work, which she completed in 2006.
She went on to earn her Master in Public Administration at MSU in
2018, then her Doctor of Public Administration in 2023, both from
the same university where she now teaches. She holds a Professional
Regulation Commission license as a Registered Social Worker
(RSW) under RA 1080, having passed the licensure examination in
Cagayan de Oro City in June 2006.

PAGE 2
scholarship at international conferences
across Asia and Europe.
Pull Quote
"From the evacuation centers of Iligan to
the lecture halls of Lisbon, her work never
strayed far from the people it was meant to
serve."
Early Career and Field Work
Ivy's first professional role came in August 2006, when she worked
as a Community Organizer for the Community Empowerment
Program in Balindong, Lanao del Sur, a project of the Davao Medical
School Foundation's Institute of Primary Health Care in partnership
with the Japan International Cooperation Agency. From January 2007
to February 2008, she served as Municipal Facilitator for the ARMM
Social Fund Project under the Department of Social Welfare and Development, ARMM.
Her work then took her to Agusan del Sur, where from January to December 2010 she served as Project
Development Officer IV for a special project against gender-based violence under DSWD CARAGA. She followed
this with two years as City Link/Team Leader for the Pantawid Pamilyang Pilipino Program in Iligan City
(December 2010 to August 2012), then two more years as Cluster Grievance Redress System Officer for the same
program in Lanao del Sur (August 2012 to November 2014).
In between these postings, she took on short-term assignments that reflected her willingness to respond wherever
she was needed, including a stint as Camp Manager at a DSWD evacuation center in Pala-o, Iligan City in late
2011, and a brief posting as Field Supervisor for a gender, peace, and security project under the Office of the
Presidential Adviser on the Peace Process in October 2010.
Academic Career
Ivy's move into teaching began in September 2008, when she joined Iligan Medical Center College as an Instructor
in the Social Work Department. In November 2014, she transitioned into MSU's academic ranks as Assistant
Professor I at the College of Social Sciences and Humanities, first on a contractual basis and later, from 2016 to
2019, as a probationary appointee.
By August 2019 she had moved to the College of Public Affairs as Associate Professor V, this time on a permanent
appointment, and in October 2024 she was promoted to Professor VI, the rank she holds today. In April and May of
that year, she also served as Exchange Faculty at ISCTE, the Instituto Universitario de Lisboa in Portugal, under
the Erasmus+ Mobility Program, bringing Mindanao's governance experience into conversation with European
academic circles.
Research and International Engagement
Much of Ivy's scholarship centers on the Conditional Cash Transfer (CCT) Program and its implementation
challenges in Balindong, Lanao del Sur, a subject she carried into international academic spaces. Her paper on this
topic was presented at the 3rd International Social Development Conference in Kedah, Malaysia in 2018, and later
published in the International Journal of Advanced Science and Technology in 2020.
She has also brought her research on governance during the COVID-19 pandemic to conferences in Indonesia and
Nepal, including the International Conference India and Southeast Asia (ICISA) in Makassar in 2021 and the
EROPA Virtual Conference in 2022, where she spoke on Philippine government responses to the pandemic and
their implications for policy. As a speaker, she has covered topics ranging from generalist social work practice to
leadership in the BARMM government context, often lecturing to graduate students and civic groups at MSU's
College of Public Affairs.

PAGE 3
Professional Affiliations and Civic Involvement
Ivy holds memberships in several professional and alumni organizations, including the Philippine Society for
Public Administration (PSPA), the Philippine Association of Social Workers Incorporated (PASWI), the JSPS
Alumni Association of the Philippines, the MSU Alumni Association, and Alpha Phi Omega. She has also
completed numerous learning and development programs over the years, covering outcomes-based education,
records management, curriculum development, and disaster and pandemic response, among other topics.
Her technical skill set spans teaching, counseling, project management, facilitating, training needs assessment,
gender and development work, computer literacy, process documentation, case study writing, and community
organizing.

title: Arpa, Pulong
text:
PAGE 1
PULONG ARPA
Full Name
Pulong Arpa (also spelled Pullong)
Born
1900s, Sulu Archipelago, Philippines
Died
1980s
Ethnic Group
Sama (Sulu Archipelago)
Pulong Arpa
Pulong Arpa (1900s–1980s), also spelled Pullong, was a
Filipino military officer, diplomat, and public servant from
the Sulu Archipelago. He is best remembered as the First
Filipino and First Bangsamoro Ambassador to Egypt,
serving from 1957 to 1963. A Sama Muslim from Sulu, Arpa
broke new ground in a foreign service that had historically
been the preserve of Christian elites from Luzon and the
Visayas. His career spanned two starkly different worlds: the
brutal jungles of a World War II guerrilla campaign, and the
sophisticated chambers of Cold War-era Arab diplomacy.
Contents
1 BACKGROUND
2 EDUCATION
3 CAREER
3.1 Military Service and World War II
3.2 Diplomatic Career
4 INSTITUTIONAL CONTRIBUTIONS
5 LEGACY
6 RECOGNITION
7 SEE ALSO
8 REFERENCES
9 EXTERNAL LINKS
BACKGROUND
Arpa was born into the Sulu Archipelago, deep in the
maritime heartland of Muslim Mindanao. He came from the
Sama people, a seafaring ethnolinguistic group native to the
islands and coastal waters of Sulu, historically
underrepresented in national leadership. His rise to
prominence was a milestone not just for himself, but for an
entire community that had long lived on the margins of
Philippine state power.
His family roots ran deep into the region's ruling and religious
classes. His father, Imam Arpa of Siasi, Sulu, was a respected
religious leader and community figure. His mother, Tan Lu
Liyan (also known as Liyudayang), connected him through
the maternal line to Datu Piang, the legendary
Maguindanaoan chieftain who dominated the political
landscape of the late Spanish and early American colonial

PAGE 2
Parents
Imam Arpa of Siasi, Sulu; Tan Lu Liyan
(Liyudayang)
Notable Relative
Datu Piang of Maguindanao (grand-uncle,
maternal side)
Military Rank
Colonel (Retired), Armed Forces of the
Philippines
Military Education
Philippine Military Academy (PMA)
WWII Command
1st Battalion, 75th Provisional Infantry
Regiment, Negros Force
Diplomatic Posts
Minister Plenipotentiary to Egypt (1957);
Ambassador Extraordinary and
Plenipotentiary to Egypt and Syria (1960–
1963)
Appointed By
President Carlos P. Garcia
periods. Through her father, Tan Sing Lian, Arpa also
belonged to a prominent Chinese-Tausug merchant lineage
with trading networks stretching across the Sulu and Celebes
Seas.
EDUCATION
Arpa pursued a rigorous military education, eventually
graduating from the Philippine Military Academy (PMA). His
class included figures who would go on to define the early
Armed Forces of the Philippines, among them Colonel Edwin
Andrews, the decorated officer after whom Edwin Andrews
Air Base in Zamboanga City was later named.
CAREER
Military Service and World War II
When Japanese forces swept across the Philippine
archipelago in 1941, Arpa was already a commissioned
officer. Rather than surrender, he joined the armed resistance.
He commanded the 1st Battalion of the 75th Provisional
Infantry Regiment under the Negros Force, leading Filipino
guerrillas in the dense jungles of Negros Island in campaigns
to defend key positions and disrupt enemy supply lines.
His service came at a terrible cost. When organized
American-Filipino resistance collapsed, Arpa was captured.
He was interned at the notorious Camp O'Donnell in Capas,
Tarlac, the harrowing final destination of the Bataan Death
March survivors. He endured the brutal conditions of the
camp and survived. When the Philippines was liberated, he
returned to active military duty and eventually retired with the
rank of Colonel.
Diplomatic Career
After Philippine independence in 1946, the national
government sought capable, culturally credible
representatives for a young republic navigating the Cold War.
President Carlos P. Garcia looked beyond the usual circles of
the foreign service and found Pulong Arpa.
On April 12, 1957, President Garcia administered Arpa's oath
of office, appointing him Minister Plenipotentiary to Egypt.
It was a historic first: Arpa became the first Filipino Muslim
ever appointed to the foreign service with the rank of

PAGE 3
NOTABILITY
First Filipino and First Bangsamoro
Ambassador to Egypt; first Filipino Muslim to
hold the rank of Minister Plenipotentiary in
the Philippine foreign service
KNOWN FOR
Pioneering Philippine diplomacy in the Arab
world; establishing the only Philippine
diplomatic mission in the Arab and African
regions from 1957 to the mid-1970s; WWII
guerrilla service and POW survival at Camp
O'Donnell
PULL QUOTE
"By deploying a proud Sama Muslim officer
to Cairo, the Philippines built early bridges of
trust with the Arab and Islamic worlds that
would define its foreign policy for decades."
Minister. Cairo, the intellectual and cultural heart of the Arab
world, was where the Philippines would now plant its
diplomatic flag in the region.
As the geopolitical significance of the Middle East grew
through the late 1950s, so did the scope of Arpa's mission. In
1960, the Philippine government elevated the legation to a
full-scale embassy, and Arpa was promoted to the rank of
Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary. That
same year, President Garcia concurrently appointed him the
first official Philippine Ambassador to Syria, at a time
when Egypt and Syria had merged to form the United Arab
Republic (UAR). Even after Syria broke away from the UAR
following a 1961 coup, Arpa's Cairo mission retained
diplomatic jurisdiction over Syrian affairs, effectively laying
the institutional groundwork for the future Embassy of the
Philippines in Damascus.
INSTITUTIONAL
CONTRIBUTIONS
Arpa's mission in Cairo was not just a posting. It was the
foundation of Philippine diplomacy across an entire region.
From 1957 until the mid-1970s, the embassy he established
stood as the only Philippine diplomatic mission in the
entire Arab and African regions. The communication
channels, cultural exchanges, and early diplomatic treaties he
helped initiate shaped how the Philippine government would
relate to Islamic nations for generations, including how it
would eventually approach the question of Muslim Mindanao in its foreign policy.
His appointment was also a statement, made in policy rather than words, that the Philippines recognized its Muslim
citizens as part of its national identity, not just its internal affairs.
LEGACY
Arpa is remembered as a pioneer on two fronts. In the military, he was a combat soldier who survived one of the
war's most brutal prison camps and came out of it still committed to service. In diplomacy, he built something that
outlasted his tenure: a framework for Philippine engagement with the Arab world that his successors would inherit
and expand.
For the Bangsamoro people, his life represents an early proof of what was possible. A Sama Muslim from Sulu,
with no access to the inherited advantages that defined the Manila-centric foreign service, rose to represent the
Philippine republic at the highest diplomatic level in the Arab world. That story still carries weight.
Those who knew him described a man of many dimensions: a disciplined military officer, a skilled diplomat, an
avid swimmer and sports enthusiast in his younger years, and in his final decades, an elder statesman and
irreplaceable keeper of Sulu's history.

PAGE 4
RECOGNITION
First Filipino Muslim appointed to the foreign service with the rank of Minister (1957)
First Filipino and First Bangsamoro Ambassador to Egypt (1957–1963)
First Philippine Ambassador to Syria (1960)
Founding builder of the Philippine diplomatic presence in the Arab and African worlds

notes, and verified secondary accounts of Philippine diplomatic and military history.

text:

c. 1963

Abdulcader Maruhom Ayo
Dr. Abdulcader Maruhom Ayo (born c. 1963) is a Filipino
academic leader, legal scholar, and engineer who currently serves as
the Executive Vice President (EVP) of the Mindanao State
University (MSU) System, one of the Philippines' foremost
institutions for higher learning in Muslim Mindanao.
A Maranao polymath in the truest sense, Dr. Ayo built his career
across continents and disciplines, starting as a mining and safety
engineer in Manila and the oil fields of Saudi Arabia before
returning home to become one of the MSU System's most trusted
administrators.
He is perhaps best known as a topnotcher of the Special Shariah Bar
Examinations and as the longtime Dean of the King Faisal Center
for Islamic, Arabic and Asian Studies (KFCIAAS), where his seven-
year leadership was recognized for its depth and consistency.
His guiding legacy: bridging faith, law, and learning in service of
the Bangsamoro people.
Affectionately called "Dodong" or "Duds" by colleagues and
friends, he represents a model of Muslim Filipino excellence rooted
in both religious devotion and rigorous scholarship.
Contents
1 Early Life and Background
2 Education
3 Professional Career
3.1 Engineering and International Service
3.2 Return to Academia
3.3 Administrative Leadership at KFCIAAS
4 Institutional Contributions
4.1 Appointment as Executive Vice President
4.2 Service to the Supreme Court of the Philippines
5 Academic Achievements and Research
6 Personal Values and Cultural Significance
7 Legacy
8 Recognition
9 Challenges
10 References

PAGE 2
Early Life and Background
Dr. Ayo was born around 1963, and while the source materials do not detail his precise birthplace, his life and
career have been deeply intertwined with the Bangsamoro region and the broader Muslim Filipino community.
He grew up in a tradition that valued both faith and learning, a foundation that would later define how he
approached every professional role he took on, whether as an engineer in the Middle East or as a dean shaping the
next generation of Bangsamoro scholars.
His personal values, particularly his belief that "Family is Everything," have been a constant thread throughout a
career that took him far from home before bringing him back to serve the communities that shaped him.
Education
Dr. Ayo's academic credentials are wide-ranging and reflect a man who refused to be confined to a single
discipline.
His technical education began with a degree in Mining Engineering, which gave him the scientific grounding for
his early career in the extractive industries.
He later earned a Master of Arts in Islamic Studies, deepening his understanding of the religious and legal
traditions central to Bangsamoro identity.
He went on to earn a Juris Doctor (JD), and passed the Special Shariah Bar Examinations in Manila, where he
ranked among the topnotchers, a distinction that reflects both his legal acumen and his mastery of Islamic
jurisprudence.
He also holds a Shariah Licentiate (Sh.L.) and is a Civil Service Professional, underscoring the breadth of his
qualifications across religious, civil, and legal frameworks.
His academic journey culminated in a Doctor of Philosophy in Philippine Studies, a degree that brought together
his experiences in law, culture, governance, and the particular challenges facing Muslim Filipinos in a pluralist
society.
Professional Career
Engineering and International Service
Dr. Ayo's working life started in the technical sector.
In 1984, he served as a Safety Engineer at the Bureau of Mines Central Office in Manila, applying his mining
engineering background to regulatory and workplace safety work at the national level.
From 1986 to 1997, he spent over a decade working as a Senior Engineer for a petroleum company in Saudi
Arabia, gaining substantial international experience in one of the world's most demanding industrial environments.
This period abroad was not just a professional chapter; it also deepened his connection to the broader Islamic
world, an experience that would later enrich his scholarship and his approach to Islamic education at MSU.

PAGE 3
Return to Academia
After his stint overseas, Dr. Ayo transitioned into academic life, bringing both his technical background and his
deepening legal and religious scholarship into the classroom.
He began teaching at the College of Engineering at Adamson University in Manila, one of the Philippines' well-
regarded institutions, where he honed his skills as an educator.
Upon returning to Mindanao, he became a lecturer at the MSU College of Law, where he taught courses
intersecting Islamic jurisprudence and the Philippine legal system.
He subsequently joined the King Faisal Center for Islamic, Arabic and Asian Studies (KFCIAAS), which
would become the central theater for the most consequential chapter of his career.
Administrative Leadership at KFCIAAS
Dr. Ayo's leadership at KFCIAAS unfolded over two terms, totaling a seven-year tenure as its Dean, a period that
colleagues and the university administration have described as one of "exemplary leadership."
During his time as dean, he worked to strengthen KFCIAAS as an academic home for Islamic scholarship within
the MSU System, supporting research, faculty development, and programs that serve both Muslim Filipino students
and the wider Bangsamoro community.
His sustained leadership of the center stands as one of the defining contributions of his career, cementing his
reputation as a steady, principled steward of one of the university's most culturally significant units.
Institutional Contributions
Appointment as Executive Vice President
In August 2025, MSU System President Atty. Paisalin P. Tago appointed Dr. Ayo as the Executive Vice President
of the MSU System, formalized through Special Order No. 1142-OP.
The EVP role places him at the operational center of one of the Philippines' most important regional universities,
responsible for translating the university's vision into day-to-day institutional action.
In this capacity, Dr. Ayo is a key figure in implementing the university's 9-Point Agenda, a strategic framework
aimed at strengthening MSU's academic programs, research output, community engagement, and institutional
governance.
He has also been a consistent advocate for building an inclusive university environment, one that reflects the
cultural and religious diversity of the Bangsamoro region while upholding standards of academic excellence.
Service to the Supreme Court of the Philippines
Beyond the campus, Dr. Ayo has served as a Special Shariah Bar Examiner for the Supreme Court of the
Philippines, specifically handling the area of Islamic Law on Inheritance.

PAGE 4
This role places him among a small circle of Filipino legal scholars trusted by the country's highest court to
evaluate competence in Shariah law, a significant distinction that underscores his standing both within MSU and in
the broader Philippine legal community.
Academic Achievements and Research
Dr. Ayo's scholarly work sits at the crossroads of Islamic law, Philippine governance, and education, areas that are
especially critical to the ongoing development of the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao
(BARMM).
His research on Islamic Inheritance Law examines the perceptions of ulama and professionals regarding the law
as codified under Presidential Decree 1083 (the Code of Muslim Personal Laws of the Philippines), contributing
to ongoing conversations about how Shariah-based legal frameworks operate within the Philippine constitutional
system.
He has also written on the role of Information and Communications Technology (ICT) in teacher education
programs within the BARMM, addressing the practical challenges of modernizing education delivery in a region
still navigating decades of conflict and underdevelopment.
His teaching expertise covers Islamic Jurisprudence, Persons and Family Relations, and Islamic Court
Procedure, areas that are foundational to both the legal practice and the cultural fabric of Muslim Filipino
communities.
Personal Values and Cultural Significance
Dr. Ayo is the kind of person who leads as much by character as by title.
Known to friends and colleagues as "Dodong" or "Duds," he carries a warmth and accessibility that belies the
weight of his credentials, a quality that has made him a trusted figure not just within MSU but across the
Bangsamoro scholarly community.
He credits much of his success to his faith and to his family. His wife, Hadja Jannah Dayamala Macadindang
Disamburun-Ayo, and their two children are, by his own account, the anchor of everything he does.
His oft-repeated philosophy, "Family is Everything," reflects a deeply held conviction that personal integrity and
strong family bonds are inseparable from meaningful public service.
Within the Bangsamoro region, he's frequently cited as a living example of what it means to be an "ideal Muslim"
in public life: someone who takes faith seriously, pursues knowledge rigorously, and puts that knowledge in service
of the community.
Legacy
Dr. Ayo's career tells a story that's still being written, but its contours are already clear.
He's a man who crossed disciplines and continents, from the mining offices of Manila to the oil fields of Saudi
Arabia to the lecture halls of MSU, and brought everything he gathered back to serve the Bangsamoro people.

PAGE 5
As a Shariah Bar topnotcher, a long-serving dean, a Supreme Court examiner, and now the Executive Vice
President of the MSU System, he stands as a pillar of institutional continuity in a region where continuity is both
rare and vital.
His legacy is rooted in the idea that Islamic scholarship and secular academic excellence don't have to be in
tension. At their best, they strengthen each other, and Dr. Ayo has spent his career proving that.
Recognition
Topnotcher, Special Shariah Bar Examinations, Manila
Cited for "exemplary leadership" during his tenure as Dean of KFCIAAS, MSU
Appointed Executive Vice President of the MSU System, August 2025 (Special Order No. 1142-OP)
Commissioned as Special Shariah Bar Examiner, Supreme Court of the Philippines (Islamic Law on
Inheritance)
Recognized as a role model for the Bangsamoro academic community
Challenges
Dr. Ayo's work has not taken place in an easy environment.
The Bangsamoro region has long grappled with the legacy of armed conflict, political instability, and systemic
underdevelopment, realities that shape the context in which MSU operates and that make the university's mission
both more urgent and more difficult.
Leading within that context requires more than academic competence; it demands resilience, cultural fluency, and a
willingness to navigate institutional complexity without losing sight of the communities the university is meant to
serve.
His career trajectory, from technical worker to legal scholar to senior university administrator, reflects both the
opportunities that hard work and faith can open and the persistence required to pursue them in a region where such
paths are rarely smooth.

text:

Muammar Tomara M. Ayo
Dr. Muammar Tomara M. Ayo is a distinguished Maranao Shariah legal expert and diplomat whose career bridges
Islamic jurisprudence with humanitarian diplomacy in service of Overseas Filipino Workers (OFWs) in the Middle
East.
His work as a Shariah Legal Officer at the Philippine Embassy in Kuwait and Riyadh exemplifies the intersection
of faith-based legal scholarship and practical OFW protection, making him a vital figure in the Bangsamoro
representation within Philippine foreign service.
Contents
1 Early Life and Background
2 Education and Academic Achievement
3 Professional Career and Institutional Contributions
3.1 Philippine Embassy in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia
3.2 Philippine Embassy in Kuwait
4 Shariah Legal Expertise and OFW Protection
5 Oplan Kabataan and Humanitarian Advocacy
6 Legacy and Impact
7 References
8 Further Reading
9 See Also
Early Life and Background
Dr. Muammar Tomara M. Ayo hails from the Maranao people, a
major Muslim ethnolinguistic group native to the Lanao region of
Mindanao in the southern Philippines.
The Maranao identity deeply shaped his commitment to serving
the broader Bangsamoro community and to bridging Islamic legal
traditions with Philippine governance.
His family held a strong tradition of public service and religious
scholarship, which influenced his specialization in Shariah law
and eventually his dual role as both a diplomat and a jurist.
Education and Academic Achievement
Dr. Ayo's academic background merges traditional Islamic
scholarship with modern legal and administrative training.
He is a licensed Shariah Counselor in the Philippines, having
successfully passed the Special Shariah Bar Examinations, a
credential that demonstrates his mastery of Islamic jurisprudence
within the Philippine legal context.

PAGE 2
His doctoral degree reflects his expertise in Islamic studies and social sciences, equipping him to interpret complex
theological and legal concepts for OFW populations in the Middle East.
Throughout his career, Dr. Ayo underwent specialized diplomatic and legal training programs focused on
international labor laws, human rights protections, and consular administration.
Professional Career and Institutional Contributions
Dr. Ayo's institutional impact is most visible through his service with the Philippine Department of Foreign Affairs,
where he held key positions that allowed him to translate complex Islamic legal principles into actionable
protection for Filipino workers abroad.
His dual expertise as a Shariah jurist and a seasoned diplomat positioned him as a critical bridge between
Philippine legal systems and the Islamic legal frameworks of host countries.
The central theme of his career is leveraging Shariah law's emphasis on justice (Adl) and mercy (Rahmah) to
resolve humanitarian crises facing distressed Filipinos.
Philippine Embassy in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia
In Riyadh, Dr. Ayo served as a Legal Officer and ATN (Assistance-to-Nationals) Assistant within the embassy's
Assistance-to-Nationals section, a role that positioned him at the frontlines of crisis response.
He was a primary responder for Filipinos in distress, providing legal representation and administrative support for
workers detained or facing labor disputes in one of the world's most populous OFW destinations.
Dr. Ayo participated in Embassy-on-Wheels missions to remote regions such as Al Khobar and Dammam, ensuring
that consular and legal services reached workers outside the capital and extended the reach of Philippine protection
to isolated communities.
His presence in these outlying areas was particularly significant, as many OFWs in remote locations lacked easy
access to embassy services or legal counsel.
Philippine Embassy in Kuwait
Dr. Ayo's mission in Kuwait centered on administrative leadership, legal counsel, and crisis management within
one of the Philippine foreign service's busiest missions, given Kuwait's high concentration of OFWs.
He served as Administrative Officer while simultaneously functioning as the embassy's Shariah Legal Officer, a
dual role that reflected both his administrative competence and his specialized expertise.
As Shariah Legal Officer, Dr. Ayo was instrumental in navigating Kuwait's complex legal environment, where he
resolved disputes involving marriage, inheritance, and personal status for Muslim Filipinos, ensuring their rights
under Philippine law were recognized even while residing overseas.
His work included coordinating the repatriation of undocumented Filipinos, often negotiating with host-country
authorities to secure exit clearances for distressed citizens who might otherwise have faced legal penalties.

PAGE 3
Shariah Legal Expertise and OFW Protection
Dr. Ayo's professional contributions focus on the practical application of Islamic law to safeguard Filipino citizens
in Muslim-majority countries.
He authored a comprehensive series of Shariah Legal Notes for OFWs while serving at the Philippine Embassies in
both Kuwait and Riyadh, translating dense jurisprudence into accessible guidance.
These guides addressed critical topics for OFW populations, including the legal requirements for Muslim converts
to register their conversion at the Philippine Embassy or Consulate in accordance with Presidential Decree No.
1083 (the Code of Muslim Personal Laws of the Philippines).
The guides emphasized that while OFWs worked in Islamic legal jurisdictions, their rights under Philippine law
remained valid and enforceable, particularly for matters of personal status, marriage, and inheritance.
Dr. Ayo's notes on family and marriage law clarified the concept of mahram (legal guardianship) and explained
how Islamic principles of guardianship operated within Philippine legal protections for women travelers and
married individuals.
His labor relations guidance advocated for Islamic diplomacy in wage disputes, advising workers that under
Shariah law, employers bear a religious obligation to pay salaries promptly and fairly.
In a particularly important contribution, he clarified that Shariah law condemns beating, torture, and corporal
punishment, emphasizing both the presumption of innocence and the right to defense in local courts, thereby
protecting Filipino workers from abusive treatment under the guise of religious authority.
Dr. Ayo's notes also addressed the concept of hajj (pilgrimage to Mecca), inheritance rules under Islamic law, and
the spiritual and legal significance of conversion to Islam, ensuring OFWs understood their rights and
responsibilities in their adopted host countries.
Oplan Kabataan and Humanitarian Advocacy
Dr. Ayo served as a primary architect in Oplan Kabataan, a groundbreaking repatriation program designed to bring
home undocumented children of OFWs born in the Middle East without proper legal status.
The children targeted by the program, often described as those born "out of wedlock or without documentation,"
faced severe legal vulnerabilities in the Middle East, including potential denial of education, healthcare, and legal
protection.
As a Shariah Legal Officer, Dr. Ayo's expertise was essential in negotiating with host-country authorities, many of
whom applied strict interpretations of Islamic family law to these cases.
His representations leveraged his knowledge of Islamic jurisprudence to reach agreements with religious and
government officials, often convincing them to waive court-imposed fees and penalties at no cost to the Philippine
government.
These negotiations exemplified his commitment to the Islamic principles of rahmah (mercy) and adl (justice), using
religious understanding rather than protracted legal battles to resolve humanitarian crises.
Dr. Ayo facilitated the successful repatriation of hundreds of distressed Filipinos and their children through
complex legal negotiations, making a measurable humanitarian impact on vulnerable OFW families.

PAGE 4
Legacy and Impact
Dr. Muammar Tomara M. Ayo's career demonstrates that Islamic jurisprudence and Filipino citizenship are not
competing identities but complementary frameworks for justice and protection.
As a Maranao Muslim serving in the national government's diplomatic corps, he provided a living model of how
Bangsamoro identity strengthens rather than diminishes service to the broader Philippine nation.
His work established protocols and practices for handling Shariah-related cases within the Department of Foreign
Affairs, Office of the Undersecretary for Migrant Workers Affairs, creating institutional frameworks that outlasted
his personal tenure.
The Shariah Legal Notes he authored became foundational resources for OFWs navigating legal systems in the
Middle East, circulated through official embassy channels and OFW support networks.
His contributions to the development of diplomatic practices in Shariah legal matters advanced Philippine foreign
service competence in Muslim-majority countries and reinforced the Philippines' credibility as a nation committed
to protecting all its citizens, regardless of their faith.
Dr. Ayo's legacy is one of bridging worlds: the legal traditions of Islam and the Philippines, the spiritual
commitments of faith and the institutional demands of government, the individual vulnerabilities of OFWs and the
collective strength of diplomatic advocacy.

title: Baddiri, Edilwasif Tapsiril
text:
PAGE 1
Edilwasif Tapsiril Baddiri
Edilwasif Tapsiril Baddiri (born December 13, 1975) is a Filipino jurist, lawyer, and public servant of full Tausug
descent, currently serving as an Associate Justice of the Court of Appeals of the Philippines.
He was appointed to the appellate court by President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. on February 24, 2025, and took his oath
of office before Chief Justice Alexander G. Gesmundo on April 11, 2025, filling the seat left vacant by retired
Justice Edwin D. Sorongon.
A product of Ateneo de Manila's law faculty and Harvard University's Kennedy School of Government, Baddiri
brings to the bench not only elite academic credentials but also decades of ground-level legal work, from defending
indigent clients in Sulu to presiding over a busy Metro Manila trial court.
He is widely recognized within the Bangsamoro legal community as the fifth Tausug jurist to reach the Court of
Appeals, a milestone that carries deep symbolic weight for a people long underrepresented in the national judiciary.

2 EDUCATION
3 CAREER

3.3 The Judiciary: Trial Courts

BACKGROUND
Edilwasif Tapsiril Baddiri was born on December 13, 1975, and is a full-blooded Tausug, an indigenous ethnic
group native to the Sulu Archipelago in the southern Philippines.
The Tausug, whose name translates roughly to "people of the current," have long maintained a proud tradition of
political and legal autonomy rooted in the Sultanate of Sulu, one of the oldest Islamic polities in Southeast Asia.

PAGE 2
Edilwasif Tapsiril Baddiri
Associate Justice Edilwasif Tapsiril Baddiri
Personal Information
Born: December 13, 1975
Ethnicity
Tausug (Sulu Archipelago)
Education

(2015-2023)

Affiliations
Growing up in the cultural and socio-political landscape of Sulu
shaped Baddiri in ways that went well beyond the personal. He
came of age in a region grappling with armed conflict, political
marginalization, and the slow, uneven progress of the peace
process between Manila and the Bangsamoro people. These
realities became the invisible curriculum behind his formal
education.
His middle name, Tapsiril, reflects his maternal lineage, a quiet
but meaningful marker of family heritage in Tausug naming
tradition.
While the details of his immediate family life are kept private,
consistent with judicial security norms, those who know Baddiri
describe his personal life as a balanced synthesis of demanding
legal professionalism and steadfast Islamic faith. He is known in
legal circles for integrating his identity as a Muslim Filipino into
his practice not as a talking point but as a genuine orientation
toward justice.
EDUCATION
Baddiri pursued his undergraduate and legal studies in Manila,
and in 2000 he earned his Bachelor of Laws (Ll.B.) from the
Ateneo de Manila University School of Law, one of the
Philippines' most competitive and respected law programs.
At Ateneo Law, he was part of a rigorous academic culture known
for producing graduates who combine doctrinal mastery with a
commitment to public interest law. This formative experience
would later express itself in his early career work on human rights
cases and pro bono representation.
Four years after passing the bar, Baddiri was selected for the
highly competitive Fulbright Scholarship Program in 2004,
awarded through the Philippine-American Educational
Foundation (PAEF). The Fulbright brought him to the John F.
Kennedy School of Government at Harvard University, where he
completed a Master in Public Administration (MPA) in 2006.
The Harvard Kennedy School experience gave Baddiri fluency in
the intersection of governance, public policy, and institutional
reform, a toolkit he would draw on in his later work with the
National Commission on Muslim Filipinos and, eventually, his
judicial appointments.

PAGE 3
President, Philippine Muslim Judges Association
(PMJA)
Key Convener, Young Moro Professionals
Network (YMPN)
Appointed By
President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr. (February 24,
2025)
Oath Administered By
Chief Justice Alexander G. Gesmundo (April 11,
2025)
Notability
Fifth Tausug jurist to serve on the Philippine
Court of Appeals; Fulbright Scholar and Harvard
Kennedy School alumnus; leading advocate for
Shari'ah integration into the Philippine judicial
system.
Known For
Bangsamoro legal representation at the appellate
level; presidency of the Philippine Muslim
Judges Association; championing Shari'ah court
modernization; civic leadership through the
Young Moro Professionals Network.
Pull Quote
"A Tausug from the shores of Sulu, a jurist
shaped by Ateneo and Harvard, and a voice for
the Bangsamoro people at the highest levels of
Philippine law."
CAREER
Early Career
Baddiri began his professional life in the courts, working as a
legal assistant at a Regional Trial Court, learning the day-to-day
machinery of Philippine judicial procedure from the ground up.
He also stepped into the classroom early, teaching the Philippine
Constitution at Ateneo de Zamboanga University, an institution
with deep roots in the Muslim Mindanao region and a strong
connection to the communities he came from.
He then moved into local governance, serving as a legislator in the
province of Sulu, where he gained direct experience in the
legislative and political challenges unique to the Bangsamoro
south. Alongside this, he took on human rights cases and offered
pro bono legal counsel to indigent clients, work that grounded his
legal career in the lived realities of people who often had no one
else to turn to.
National Commission on Muslim Filipinos
From 2010 to 2015, Baddiri served as a Commissioner of the
National Commission on Muslim Filipinos (NCMF), representing
the youth and civic sectors. The NCMF is the primary government
agency mandated to preserve and develop the culture, tradition,
institutions, and well-being of Filipino Muslims.
His five-year tenure at the NCMF gave him a panoramic view of
Muslim Filipino affairs at the national level, and deepened his
understanding of how Muslim communities interface with the
Philippine state, from policy to practice.
The Judiciary: Trial Courts
Baddiri entered the judiciary in 2015, appointed as the Presiding
Judge of Branch 115 of the Regional Trial Court in Pasay City,
where he served until 2023.
He also handled judicial assignments in Catanauan, Quezon
(Branch 96) and served as acting presiding judge in Makati City
(Branch 142), demonstrating the kind of versatility and reliability
that the Judicial and Bar Council looks for when evaluating
judicial officers for elevation.
He was later designated as Executive Judge of the RTC in Pasay
City, a role that carries administrative responsibility for the court's
operations beyond his individual docket.

PAGE 4
Throughout his time on the trial bench, Baddiri was known for applying careful legal reasoning alongside a
sensitivity to the social dimensions of the cases before him, a quality rooted in his background in human rights
advocacy and public service.
Court of Appeals
On February 24, 2025, President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. appointed Baddiri as Associate Justice of the Court of
Appeals of the Philippines, filling the seat vacated by the retirement of Justice Edwin D. Sorongon.
He took his oath of office on April 11, 2025, in a ceremony before Chief Justice Alexander G. Gesmundo at the
Supreme Court, formalizing his elevation to the second-highest tier of the Philippine judicial hierarchy.
The appointment was met with celebration across the Bangsamoro legal community, who saw in it not just a
personal achievement but a recognition of Muslim Filipino competence and leadership at the national appellate
level.
INSTITUTIONAL CONTRIBUTIONS
Philippine Muslim Judges Association (PMJA)
Baddiri serves as President of the Philippine Muslim Judges Association (PMJA), an organization of Muslim
magistrates working within the Philippine justice system.
Under his leadership, the PMJA has worked closely with the Supreme Court's Strategic Plan for Judicial
Innovations (SPJI) 2022-2027 to bridge the longstanding gap between the regular civil court system and the
Shari'ah courts of Muslim Mindanao. He has consistently championed the modernization and broader integration of
Shari'ah justice into the Philippine legal framework, arguing that a just legal system must be one that Muslim
Filipinos can access in ways that respect their faith and legal traditions.
Young Moro Professionals Network (YMPN)
Baddiri is one of the key conveners of the Young Moro Professionals Network (YMPN), a civic initiative dedicated
to ethics, public service, and youth empowerment within the Bangsamoro community.
The YMPN reflects a generation of Muslim Filipino professionals who see civic leadership not as a departure from
their identity but as an expression of it. Baddiri's involvement signals his commitment to mentoring and building
pipelines for the next generation of Bangsamoro leaders in law, governance, and public life.
Legal Academia and Scholarship
Baddiri has served as a law professor, teaching Political Law, Criminal Procedure, and Public International Law at
Manuel S. Enverga University Foundation School of Law, among other institutions.
He has also written on the complex relationships between the Bangsamoro people, the national government, and
the evolving peace process, contributing to the scholarly conversation on how law can serve as a tool for inclusion
rather than a mechanism of exclusion.

PAGE 5
His scholarship reflects a consistent orientation: making the Philippine legal system more responsive to the realities
and rights of Muslim Filipino communities.
LEGACY
Justice Edilwasif Tapsiril Baddiri occupies a historically significant place in the Bangsamoro legal tradition as the
fifth Tausug jurist to reach the Court of Appeals, following in the footsteps of landmark Muslim magistrates
including Justices Assali S. Isnani, Jainal D. Rasul, Omar U. Amin, and Hakim Abdulwahid.
His career arc tells a compelling story about what is possible when an individual from a historically marginalized
community combines intellectual excellence with public service. From the shores of Sulu to the halls of Ateneo,
from Cambridge, Massachusetts to the Court of Appeals in Manila, Baddiri has navigated and mastered some of the
most demanding institutions the Philippines and the United States have to offer, while keeping his Tausug identity
and Islamic faith at the center of who he is.
For the Bangsamoro people, his presence on the appellate bench is more than symbolic. It signals a slow but
meaningful expansion of representation in the national justice system, the kind of institutional inclusion that shapes
how laws are interpreted and how justice is delivered to communities that have too often felt invisible within it.
RECOGNITION
Fulbright Scholarship recipient (2004), awarded through the Philippine-American Educational Foundation
(PAEF)
Formally recognized by the Muslim Lawyers of ZAMBASULTA for his integrity and swift progression
through the judicial hierarchy
Celebrated by the Fulbright Philippines Commission upon his oath-taking as Court of Appeals Associate
Justice (April 2025)
Honored by Manuel S. Enverga University Foundation as a distinguished faculty member and alumnus of the
School of Law
CHALLENGES
Baddiri's career has unfolded against the backdrop of a Philippine legal system that has historically
underrepresented Muslim Filipinos at the appellate level, whether in terms of numbers, institutional voice, or
cultural sensitivity in judicial decision-making.
Navigating that system as a full-blooded Tausug from Sulu required not only legal acumen but also a capacity for
bridging two worlds: the Bangsamoro south and the Metro Manila legal establishment. His work in the PMJA
reflects an ongoing effort to address structural gaps, particularly the disconnect between civil and Shari'ah courts
that affects Muslim litigants on a daily basis.
His elevation to the Court of Appeals places him in a position where his every decision will be watched with
particular interest, both by those who celebrate his appointment and by those who continue to ask whether the
Philippine judiciary is truly capable of meaningful reform in its approach to Muslim Filipino affairs.

title: Bahjin, Ishmael I.
text:
PAGE 1
Ishmael I. Bahjin
Atty. Ishmael I. Bahjin is a Filipino lawyer and senior government official who has made peacebuilding his life's
work, not just his job title.
As Director IV at the Office of the Presidential Adviser on Peace, Reconciliation and Unity (OPAPRU), he
leads the Social Healing and Peacebuilding Office (SHAPEO), a unit dedicated to addressing what most peace
frameworks ignore: the emotional, psychological, and social toll that decades of armed conflict leave behind.
Bahjin is one of the central figures in the implementation of the Comprehensive Agreement on the Bangsamoro
(CAB), the landmark peace deal between the Philippine government and the Moro Islamic Liberation Front
(MILF).
He works across both major tracks of the agreement: the Political Track, covering governance and legislation, and
the Normalization Track, which deals with the decommissioning of combatants and the rebuilding of communities.
As a Tausug lawyer operating at the national level, Bahjin serves as a living bridge between Manila's institutions
and the Muslim and indigenous communities of Mindanao that those institutions have historically struggled to
understand, let alone serve.
His signature contribution to Philippine peacebuilding is the reframing of civil registration, a basic administrative
process, as a genuine tool for peace. Without legal identities, former combatants cannot fully rejoin civilian life.
Bahjin has made fixing that gap a priority.

He is the son of Sulu Paramount Sultan Dr. Ibrahim Bahjin
and Nurse Radzma Bahjin. His ninang, Ambassador Corazon
Bahjin‑Yap, was the first Muslim‑Filipina to pass the Foreign
Service Officer exam. Public service, clearly, runs in the family.
His roots are in the Tausug culture of the Sulu Archipelago, one
of the region's oldest and most storied maritime communities.
That heritage isn't just biographical detail. It shapes how Bahjin
approaches his work, including his sustained attention to Sulu's
political future and his insistence that peace must be culturally
grounded, not just legislated from the center.
Education
Bahjin earned his law degree from the University of the
Philippines (UP) College of Law, one of the country's most
competitive legal programs.
He was admitted to the Philippine Bar in 2018, stepping into
professional life at a moment when the Bangsamoro peace
process was entering a critical new phase following the
ratification of the Bangsamoro Organic Law.
His legal training became foundational to his peacebuilding
career, particularly in understanding the institutional gaps that
prevent marginalized communities, especially former
combatants, from accessing basic rights and government
services.
Professional Career
OPAPRU and the Rise to Director IV
After passing the bar, Bahjin built his career within the structures
of the OPAPRU (formerly the Office of the Presidential Adviser
on the Peace Process, or OPAPP).
He rose through the ranks to reach the position of Director IV,
one of the agency's most senior technical and leadership roles.
His work spans multiple programs and bodies within the
OPAPRU ecosystem, making him one of the more versatile
officials in the country's peace architecture.

PAGE 3
Social Healing and Peacebuilding Office (SHAPEO)
As head of SHAPEO, Bahjin oversees programs that tackle what he describes as the "invisible" damage of war:
trauma, community distrust, social displacement, and the psychological burden carried by communities that have
lived through decades of conflict.
His approach to social healing is deliberate and long-term. He argues that peace agreements create a framework but
that actual reconciliation happens at the community level, through sustained human engagement and not just policy
rollouts.
National Government IGRB Secretariat
Bahjin also serves on the National Government Secretariat of the Intergovernmental Relations Body (IGRB),
a coordination mechanism designed to manage the relationship between the Philippine national government and the
Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM).
The IGRB is a technical body, but its work is politically delicate. It deals with the translation of peace
commitments into functional governance arrangements, which means navigating real tensions between Manila's
administrative culture and the Bangsamoro region's political aspirations.
Spokesperson and Technical Expert on the CAB
Bahjin regularly represents OPAPRU in public forums, media engagements, and inter-agency discussions on the
status of the Comprehensive Agreement on the Bangsamoro.
He speaks with authority on both the Political Track (legislation, governance, fiscal arrangements, and the
transition of BARMM institutions) and the Normalization Track (decommissioning of combatants, reintegration
programs, and socioeconomic interventions).
His role as a Tausug official giving voice to Bangsamoro concerns within a national government body is itself a
signal of the kind of inclusion the peace process is meant to produce.
Institutional Contributions
Civil Registration as a Peacebuilding Tool
One of Bahjin's most distinctive policy contributions is his framing of civil registration not as a bureaucratic
formality but as an act of peacebuilding.
Many former MILF and MNLF combatants have no official documentation. Without birth certificates, national
IDs, or legal identities, they cannot access government services, register their children in school, open bank
accounts, or fully participate in the economy of civilian life.
Bahjin has advocated for dedicated programs to bring undocumented former combatants into the civil registry
system, treating legal identity as a precondition for meaningful reintegration.

PAGE 4
National Action Plan on Youth, Peace, and Security (NAPYPS)
Bahjin is a lead proponent of the National Action Plan on Youth, Peace, and Security (NAPYPS), the
Philippines' framework for involving young people as genuine stakeholders in peacebuilding rather than simply as
beneficiaries of programs designed by adults.
He believes that lasting peace requires the active participation of the generation that will live longest with its
consequences, and he has worked to create institutional pathways for youth engagement in the Bangsamoro peace
process.
Prevention of Violent Extremism (PVE)
On the issue of violent extremism, Bahjin's position is grounded in the same structural logic that defines his
broader work.
He argues that successful implementation of peace agreements directly addresses the root causes of radicalization:
poor governance, political marginalization, economic exclusion, and the sense that the state is not just absent but
adversarial.
His approach to Prevention of Violent Extremism (PVE) is holistic, treating agreement implementation itself as the
most durable form of counter-extremism strategy available to the government.
Sulu's Functional Integration
Following the Supreme Court ruling that excluded Sulu from the BARMM, Bahjin has been one of the more vocal
government voices on the question of the province's future.
He has advocated for a concept he calls functional integration, the idea that Sulu does not need formal BARMM
membership to participate in the peace process and the region's development trajectory.
His vision draws on Sulu's historical identity as a maritime trading hub, suggesting that the province can reclaim
that role and serve as a bridge between the Philippine archipelago and its neighbors in maritime Southeast Asia, all
while remaining a meaningful partner in the Bangsamoro peace framework.
Values and Legacy
Bahjin's work is oriented around two ideas that he treats as inseparable: social healing and intergenerational
justice.
He consistently argues that peace is not simply the absence of armed conflict. It's the presence of conditions, legal,
economic, psychological, and cultural, that allow communities to recover, rebuild, and imagine a shared future.
His leadership style has been described as community-based and futures-oriented. He draws on "futures thinking"
and scenario planning to help peace institutions remain adaptable as political and social conditions evolve.
As a Tausug professional in a senior national government role, Bahjin represents the kind of Bangsamoro presence
in Manila's corridors of power that the peace process was designed to make possible.
His career is, in a sense, evidence of what meaningful inclusion looks like when it's given the conditions to
develop.

title: Baja, Noralyn Jubaira
text:
PAGE 1
Noralyn Jubaira Baja
Ambassador Noralyn Jubaira Baja is a career diplomat from the Philippines and a pioneering figure among
Muslim women in the Philippine Foreign Service. She currently serves as Ambassador Extraordinary and
Plenipotentiary to the Sultanate of Oman, a position she has held since early 2026 after presenting her
credentials to His Majesty Sultan Haitham bin Tarik on February 11 of that year.
Born into the proud intellectual tradition of the Tausug community of the Sulu Archipelago, she's the daughter of
the legendary Tausug Muslim writer Ibrahim A. Jubaira, who was the first Filipino to receive the Presidential
Medal of Merit for Literature. That literary and cultural heritage didn't just shape who she is; it shaped what she
stands for: a living bridge between Muslim Mindanao and the world.
With a career spanning nearly four decades in the Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA), Baja has built a record
that's both quietly historic and genuinely impressive. She served as the first female Philippine Ambassador to
South Africa, held senior headquarters roles overseeing multilateral and Middle East diplomacy, and has
represented the Philippines in postings across Europe, Africa, and now the Arabian Peninsula.
Her story is really about what it looks like when a Muslim Filipina from the Sulu Archipelago rises to the top of the
country's diplomatic service, and does so on her own terms.
