Early Life and Background
Noralyn Jubaira grew up with deep roots in the Tausug
community of the Sulu Archipelago, one of the oldest and most
storied Muslim communities in Southeast Asia. Her family
background wasn't just influential; it was, by any measure,
extraordinary.
Her father, Ibrahim A. Jubaira, earned a place in Philippine
literary history as a distinguished Tausug Muslim writer and the
first Filipino to be awarded the Presidential Medal of Merit for
Literature. He was celebrated for capturing the soul of the
Tausug people through his writing, and for putting the Muslim
Filipino experience on the national literary map at a time when
that kind of recognition was rare.
Growing up in that environment, surrounded by the intellectual
traditions and cultural pride of Muslim Mindanao, left a mark on
Noralyn. She would later describe her work in the Foreign
Service as a continuation of her father's mission: representing the
best of what the Philippines can offer to the world, and doing it
as a Muslim Filipina from the South.
Education
Baja pursued her higher education at the University of the
Philippines, one of the country's most prestigious academic
institutions, where she studied economics and public policy. She
graduated with distinction and was later recognized as an
outstanding alumna of the UP Diliman School of Economics, a
recognition that acknowledged her transition from high-
achieving student to leading figure in national public service.
Her academic background gave her the analytical grounding that
would later prove essential in the complex negotiations, policy
advocacy, and bilateral engagements that define a career
diplomat's daily life.
Diplomatic Career
Baja entered the Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA) in 1987
as a Staff Assistant at the Office of United Nations and
International Organizations (UNIO). It was an entry-level
position, but she didn't stay there long. Over the next four
decades, she climbed steadily through the ranks, earning
assignments and promotions that took her from Manila's Padre
Faura headquarters to postings across three continents.

PAGE 3
Distinguished Alumni Award
(2025)
Foreign Postings
Her overseas assignments have included diplomatic positions in:
Geneva, Switzerland (multilateral diplomacy hub, home to numerous UN agencies)
Berlin, Germany
Athens, Greece
Each posting gave her a different lens on international affairs, and collectively they built the kind of broad
diplomatic experience that's difficult to replicate.
Headquarters Leadership
Back in Manila, Baja served in senior executive roles that placed her at the center of Philippine foreign policy
formulation. She was appointed Assistant Secretary for two of the DFA's most consequential offices:
The Office of United Nations and International Organizations (UNIO), where she oversaw the
Philippines' engagement with multilateral bodies.
The Office of Middle East and African Affairs (OMEAA), a particularly critical portfolio given the
millions of Overseas Filipino Workers (OFWs) in the Gulf region and the African continent.
Ambassador to South Africa (2023–2025)
Baja made history as the first female Philippine Ambassador to South Africa, serving as the resident envoy in
Pretoria from 2023 to 2025.<ref>Template:Cite web</ref>
In addition to her primary assignment in South Africa, she held non-resident accreditation to
Zambia<ref>Template:Cite web</ref> and Eswatini, demonstrating the breadth of her diplomatic responsibilities
on the African continent.
During her Pretoria posting, she was formally commended for her dedication to OFW welfare and for expanding
the Philippines' diplomatic footprint through the establishment of new honorary consulates.
Ambassador to Oman (2026–Present)
In early 2026, Baja was appointed Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary to the Sultanate of Oman.
She officially presented her credentials to His Majesty Sultan Haitham bin Tarik on February 11, 2026,
marking the formal start of her current posting.<ref>Template:Cite web</ref>
The Oman assignment is a strategically important one. The Philippines maintains significant labor migration ties
with the Sultanate, and the post demands both economic diplomacy and active engagement with the Filipino
community in Oman. Baja's background in Middle East affairs from her time at OMEAA makes her well-suited for
the role.
Institutional Contributions
Across her career, Ambassador Baja has consistently advocated for causes that go beyond the standard portfolio of
a career diplomat.

PAGE 4
Overseas Filipino Workers (OFW) Welfare
Perhaps her most consistent priority has been the welfare of Overseas Filipino Workers. Whether in South Africa or
in Middle Eastern postings, she's known for making direct community engagement a core part of her ambassadorial
duties. She has actively pursued bilateral negotiations for improved labor agreements and has pushed for expanded
consular infrastructure, including the establishment of honorary consulates, to bring assistance closer to where
Filipinos live and work.
Bilateral Economic Cooperation
Baja has been actively involved in negotiating trade and labor agreements that protect and advance Philippine
interests. Her economics background has made her a credible voice in these negotiations, helping to anchor
discussions in data and analysis rather than just diplomatic pleasantries.
Professionalism and Mentorship
Within the DFA, she's known for living by the principle that "attitude determines altitude." Her career arc, from
entry-level staff assistant to resident ambassador in multiple countries, has made her an inspiration for younger
Foreign Service officers, particularly women and those from Muslim Mindanao communities.
Cultural Significance
Ambassador Baja's career carries cultural weight that goes beyond individual achievement. As a Tausug woman
holding one of the highest ranks in the Philippine Foreign Service, she represents the successful integration of a
distinctly Bangsamoro identity into national public life.
She continues the legacy of her father, Ibrahim A. Jubaira, who spent his literary career insisting that the Muslim
Filipino experience was an inseparable part of the Philippine story. In her own way, she makes the same argument
through diplomacy: that a Tausug woman from the Sulu Archipelago belongs in the highest offices of the Republic,
and belongs at the table with heads of state and foreign ministers.
Her postings in Muslim-majority countries, including the Sultanate of Oman, also carry a quiet but important
symbolic dimension. She's not just a Philippine representative in these countries; she's a Muslim Filipina
representative, and that matters to the communities she serves.
Personal Life
Ambassador Baja is married to Ambassador Leslie Baja, who is also a Philippine career diplomat serving in his
own posting abroad.<ref>Template:Cite web</ref>
Theirs is a genuinely uncommon arrangement: two ambassadors, two separate countries, one marriage. It's a life
that demands a particular kind of commitment and flexibility, and by all accounts, they've made it work. Their story
has become something of a quiet inspiration for younger Foreign Service officers who wonder whether it's possible
to pursue a demanding diplomatic career while building a meaningful personal life.

PAGE 5
Awards and Recognition
Over nearly four decades of service, Ambassador Baja has received several prestigious commendations that reflect
both the quality of her work and the esteem in which she's held by her peers and alma mater.
National Orders of Diplomatic Merit
Order of Sikatuna (Rank of Datu): One of the Philippines' highest diplomatic honors, conferred upon
career ambassadors for exceptionally meritorious service in international relations.<ref>Template:Cite
web</ref>
Gawad Mabini (Rank of Dakilang Kamanong): One of the highest honors for members of the Philippine
Foreign Service, awarded for distinguished foreign service and strategic promotion of Philippine interests
abroad.
Academic Recognition
UPAA Distinguished Alumni Award (2025): On August 16, 2025, she was honored by the University of
the Philippines Alumni Association (UPAA) for her exemplary achievements in the Foreign Service.
<ref>Template:Cite web</ref> The award goes to alumni whose lives and work embody the University's
core values of honor, excellence, and service.
Outstanding Alumna, UP Diliman School of Economics: She has been formally recognized by her home
college, with citations noting her journey from top student to leading public servant.<ref>Template:Cite
web</ref>
Community and Service Commendations
Recognition for OFW Welfare: During her tenures in South Africa and the Middle East, she received
citations from Filipino community organizations for her dedication to migrant worker welfare and her efforts
to expand diplomatic reach through new honorary consulates.
Diplomatic Milestone in South Africa: She was officially recognized for her historic role as the first
female Philippine Ambassador to South Africa, a milestone recorded in the institutional history of the
Department of Foreign Affairs.
Legacy
Ambassador Noralyn Jubaira Baja's legacy is still being written, and that's partly the point. She's still active, still in
the field, still presenting credentials and negotiating agreements and fighting for OFWs.
But even at this point in her career, a few things are already clear.
She proved that a Tausug Muslim woman from the Sulu Archipelago could rise to the very top of the Philippine
Foreign Service, not despite her identity but with it fully intact. She brought her father's legacy into a new domain,
carrying forward his insistence that Muslim Filipinos are not peripheral to the Philippine story but central to it. And
she built a career of nearly 40 years on a foundation of genuine professionalism, consistent advocacy for Filipinos
abroad, and the quiet belief that where you come from doesn't limit how far you can go.

PAGE 6
That combination, of historic firsts, sustained excellence, and deep cultural rootedness, is what makes her story
worth telling and remembering.

Mohammad Muariff Sumndad Balang
Mohammad Muariff Sumndad Balang is a Filipino lawyer and
certified public accountant of Meranao ethnicity who represents the
rise of the modern Bangsamoro professional class.
With a nationwide top-10 finish in the 2011 CPA licensure
examination and his distinction as Class Salutatorian at the
University of the Philippines College of Law in 2020, Balang
embodies the intellectual rigor and resilience that define the Meranao
contribution to Philippine governance and professional practice.
His rare dual qualification as both CPA and licensed lawyer makes
him uniquely positioned to navigate the complex intersection of
corporate finance, tax regulation, and the emerging legal frameworks
of the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region (BARMM).
Contents

2 Education

Early Life and Family Background
Mohammad Muariff Sumndad Balang was born into a Meranao family in Mindanao, the core homeland of the
Meranao people, often called the "People of the Lake" due to their historical settlement around Lake Lanao in
Lanao del Sur province.
While specific biographical details of his parents remain private, Balang's achievement is frequently cited as a
source of pride within Meranao intellectual circles.

PAGE 2
His family background reflects values central to Meranao culture: Islamic faith, commitment to education, and the
pursuit of maratabat (honor and dignity in Meranao tradition).
Education
Undergraduate Studies
Balang earned his Bachelor of Science in Accountancy from Mindanao State University (MSU) in Marawi City,
graduating Cum Laude.
His performance at MSU, the premier institution in the Mindanao region, established a foundation in financial
reporting, auditing principles, and accounting ethics that would later distinguish his CPA examination performance.
CPA Licensure
In October 2011, Balang placed ninth nationwide in the Professional Regulation Commission (PRC) Certified
Public Accountant Licensure Examination with a score of 92.29 percent.
His top-10 finish represented a significant achievement for MSU and the broader Meranao academic tradition,
demonstrating that students from regional institutions could compete at the highest levels of national professional
certification.
Legal Education
Balang pursued his Juris Doctor at the University of the Philippines (UP) College of Law, one of the Philippines'
premier law schools and a consistent producer of bar topnotchers.
He graduated as Class Salutatorian of the Class of 2020, one of the highest honors achievable at UP Law.
This honor reflected not only academic excellence but also his capacity for rigorous legal analysis and original
scholarship.
Career and Professional Contributions
Dual CPA-Lawyer Practice
Balang is one of a select group of professionals in the Philippines holding both active CPA and Bar licenses, a dual
qualification highly valued in corporate law, taxation, forensic accounting, and financial litigation.
This rare combination positions him at the intersection of accounting standards and legal doctrine, allowing him to
advise clients on complex matters where financial and legal considerations are inseparable.
Areas of Expertise
Balang's professional specialization centers on three interconnected fields:

PAGE 3
Taxation and Financial Law: Drawing on his ninth-place CPA ranking, his expertise encompasses tax planning,
Bureau of Internal Revenue (BIR) disputes, tax litigation, and financial restructuring for multinational and local
corporations.
Corporate Governance and Mergers & Acquisitions: His training at UP Law, particularly under the guidance of
faculty known for corporate practice, has positioned him to specialize in corporate governance compliance,
securities regulation, and M&A transactions involving complex cross-border or regulatory elements.
Bangsamoro Legal Frameworks: Given his Meranao heritage and professional background, Balang is uniquely
equipped to advise on the fiscal autonomy provisions of the Bangsamoro Organic Law (BOL), specifically the
integration of national tax regimes with emerging regional financial governance structures.
Professional Recognition
Balang's standing in the legal profession is evidenced by his receipt of the prestigious Violeta Calvo-Drilon
Scholarship from ACCRALAW during his final year at UP Law in November 2019.
The scholarship is awarded annually to UP Law students demonstrating exceptional academic performance and
commitment to legal excellence.
His receipt of this honor placed him among the most distinguished students of his law school cohort.
Contribution to Meranao Intellectual Tradition
Bridging Regional and National Excellence
Balang's educational trajectory, from MSU-Marawi to the University of the Philippines, exemplifies what some
scholars call the "MSU-to-UP pipeline" in Philippine legal and professional development.
By excelling at a regional institution and then achieving the rank of Class Salutatorian at the country's most
prestigious law school, he demonstrated the competitive quality of Mindanao-based education and challenged
historical narratives that positioned Manila institutions as the sole source of elite professional training.
Modern Meranao Professionalism
In the context of Meranao tradition, which has historically revered the Ulama (Islamic scholars) and Datu
(traditional leaders) as the primary sources of authority and wisdom, Balang represents the emergence of the
modern Meranao professional class.
He navigates secular legal systems while remaining rooted in values of maratabat (honor), intellectual rigor, and
service to community, demonstrating that traditional Meranao values are compatible with excellence in
contemporary professional practice.
Inspiration for the Bangsamoro
Within the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region, particularly during its ongoing transition to full autonomy, figures
like Balang serve as role models for younger Meranao and Bangsamoro students aspiring to advanced professional
credentials.

PAGE 4
His achievements, particularly his success in national competitions (the CPA board exam) and elite institutions (UP
Law), demonstrate that barriers to professional advancement are surmountable for students from the Bangsamoro
region.
Personal Values and Legacy
Balang's professional identity reflects the Meranao value of Mabuting Pakikitungo, often translated as "proper
conduct" or "wholesome interaction," though the concept encompasses professional ethics, integrity, and respect
for others in all dealings.
His emphasis on both technical expertise (evidenced by his CPA achievement) and advanced legal reasoning
(demonstrated by his law school honors) reflects a commitment to holistic professional development that honors
both intellectual disciplines.
Current Status
As of 2025, Balang maintains active status as a member of the Philippine Bar and holds a current Professional
Regulation Commission (PRC) certificate as a Certified Public Accountant.
He continues to practice law and consult on matters bridging corporate finance, tax regulation, and Bangsamoro
governance frameworks.

Maulana A. Balangi
Maulana A. Balangi, more widely known by his popular name Alan
Balangi-Amer (born in Tamparan, Lanao del Sur), is a Maranao
peace advocate, human rights defender, and civic leader who has
spent more than two decades in the thick of the struggle for
Bangsamoro self-determination and justice. He is the founder and
leader of the One Bangsamoro Movement (1BANGSA), a multi-
sectoral coalition of activists and community leaders that became one
of the most visible Bangsamoro civil society voices in Metro Manila
from the ill-fated Memorandum of Agreement on Ancestral Domain
(MOA-AD) crisis of 2008 all the way to the successful ratification of
the Bangsamoro Organic Law (BOL) in 2019. Where institutions
hesitated, Balangi-Amer showed up on the streets, at the negotiating
table's edge, and in front of cameras and microphones, carrying the
Bangsamoro cause to the heart of the Philippine capital. His story is,
at its core, the story of what one determined person from a small
town in Lanao can do when conscience refuses to be quiet.
Contents
1 Early Life and Background
2 Education and Student Activism
3 Founding of the One Bangsamoro Movement
4 The Long Road to the Bangsamoro Organic Law
4.1 Rebuilding After MOA-AD (2008-2012)
4.2 From FAB to the Comprehensive Agreement (2012-
2014)
4.3 The Mamasapano Setback and Interfaith Response
(2015)
4.4 The Duterte Era and the Bangsamoro Organic Law
(2016-2019)
5 Humanitarian Work and Crisis Response
5.1 Battle of Marawi (2017)
5.2 COVID-19 Pandemic Response (2020)
5.3 Jolo Cathedral Bombing (2019)
6 Advocacy Beyond the Peace Process
6.1 International Muslim Rights
6.2 Lake Lanao Development
7 Recognition and Legacy
8 See Also
9 Further Reading
10 References

PAGE 2
Early Life and Background
Balangi-Amer grew up in Tamparan, Lanao del Sur, a rural municipality nestled along the shores of Lake Lanao in
the highlands of Mindanao. Tamparan is the kind of place where mornings begin with mist rolling off the lake and
the call to prayer drifting across the water, and that environment, deeply Islamic and deeply rooted in Maranao
tradition, shaped the man he would become.<ref name="panimbang">Panimbang, G. (n.d.). Moro activist: 2
decades as frontliner for peace and justice for the Bangsamoro. REBUILD, Inc.</ref>
Coming from a community that lived with the consequences of the Moro conflict close at hand, Balangi-Amer
carried to Manila not just ambition but a clear sense of what he was fighting for. The contrast between the peaceful
beauty of his hometown and the decades of armed conflict and political neglect that had scarred the Bangsamoro
homeland gave his advocacy its emotional core, a thread he would weave through every rally, forum, and open
letter for the next twenty-plus years.
Education and Student Activism
Balangi-Amer's political education began in earnest during his college years in Metro Manila, where he found
himself in the middle of a historic opening in the Bangsamoro peace process. When MILF–Government of the
Republic of the Philippines (GRP) peace negotiations formally opened in January 1997, the young student from
Tamparan was already on the streets, making noise as a street parliamentarian.<ref name="panimbang" />
He rose to become President of the Integrated Muslim Student Association of the Philippines (IMUSTAPHIL),
one of the most prominent Muslim student organizations in the national capital region. That position gave him a
platform, but what he did with it went well beyond student council business. He was the prime mover behind the
founding of the Bangsamoro Youth Peace Advocate (BYPA), a formation built specifically to channel the voices
of Bangsamoro youth and students when President Joseph Estrada's declaration of All-Out War against the MILF in
March 2000 threatened to undo the fragile progress of the peace talks.<ref name="panimbang" />
He was also a founding convener of the Muslim Youth National Assembly (MYNA), a coalition that became a
significant force in the civil society movement that contributed to the ouster of President Estrada in 2001. During
this period, Balangi-Amer represented Muslim youth in conferences both in the Philippines and abroad, building a
network and a reputation that would serve him well in the harder years ahead.<ref name="panimbang" />
Founding of the One Bangsamoro Movement
The crisis that created 1BANGSA came suddenly. On August 5, 2008, the Supreme Court of the Philippines (http
s://sc.judiciary.gov.ph/) issued a Temporary Restraining Order (TRO) blocking the signing of the Memorandum of
Agreement on Ancestral Domain (MOA-AD), a landmark agreement that had been years in the making between
the MILF and the GRP. Three days later, on August 8, 2008, Balangi-Amer gathered together multi-sectoral leaders
and activists and formally established the One Bangsamoro Movement, or 1BANGSA.<ref name="panimbang"
/>
The timing was not accidental. The MOA-AD's collapse had sent shockwaves through Bangsamoro communities
and reignited armed clashes in Mindanao. Balangi-Amer's response was to build a civilian frontline presence in the
capital, a group that could lobby, rally, hold press conferences, and keep the peace process alive in public
consciousness when political momentum faltered. 1BANGSA was designed from the start not as a fringe protest
group but as a broad, credible coalition that could speak to multiple audiences, from government panels to ordinary
Filipino citizens.<ref name="panimbang" />

PAGE 3
The Long Road to the Bangsamoro Organic Law
Rebuilding After MOA-AD (2008-2012)
After the MOA-AD fell apart and violence flared in Mindanao, many feared the peace process was finished.
Balangi-Amer refused to accept that conclusion. As a street parliamentarian, he took on the role of a civilian
pressure point, lobbying both the MILF and the GRP to return to the negotiating table. He organized a sustained
program of rallies, conferences, fora, and symposiums in Metro Manila, creating what amounted to a continuous
public conversation about why the talks had to continue and what was at stake if they did not.<ref
name="panimbang" />
That sustained pressure, combined with formal diplomatic efforts, eventually bore fruit. On October 15, 2012,
under the administration of Benigno Aquino III, the Framework Agreement on the Bangsamoro (FAB) was signed,
giving the peace negotiation a new direction after it had been teetering on the edge of collapse. 1BANGSA and
Balangi-Amer had been part of the civilian current that helped keep the talks moving toward that outcome.<ref
name="panimbang" />
From FAB to the Comprehensive Agreement (2012-2014)
The FAB was a framework, not a finish line. Balangi-Amer kept 1BANGSA engaged through the years of detailed
negotiations that followed, continuing to hold public forums and push for a stronger, more comprehensive
agreement. On March 27, 2014, the Comprehensive Agreement on the Bangsamoro (CAB) was signed, a
document that went further than any previous agreement in defining the path toward Bangsamoro political
autonomy. The signing prompted the creation of the Bangsamoro Transition Commission (BTC) under the
leadership of Mohagher Iqbal, which was mandated to draft what would become the Bangsamoro Basic Law
(BBL).<ref name="panimbang" />
The Mamasapano Setback and Interfaith Response (2015)
The peace process hit one of its most painful moments in January 2015, when the Mamasapano clash killed 44
members of the Philippine National Police Special Action Force along with MILF fighters and civilians. The
tragedy poisoned the political atmosphere and threatened to kill the BBL before it could be enacted.
Balangi-Amer's response was to look for bridges across the divisions that the tragedy had deepened. He called for
an interfaith dialogue that led to an Interfaith Prayer Rally, bringing together the Catholic Bishops Conference of
the Philippines (CBCP), Iglesia ni Cristo, the Philippine National Police (PNP), and the Armed Forces of the
Philippines (AFP) on a shared platform calling for sustained peace in Mindanao. The rally was a signal that peace
had supporters who transcended religious and institutional lines, and it helped prevent the Mamasapano tragedy
from permanently derailing the legislative process.<ref name="panimbang" />
He also launched the 1 Million Signatures for Bangsamoro campaign, a signature drive in support of the
immediate passage of the BBL, bringing ordinary citizens into an advocacy that had often felt like the exclusive
territory of politicians and diplomats.<ref name="panimbang" />

PAGE 4
The Duterte Era and the Bangsamoro Organic Law (2016-2019)
When Rodrigo Duterte won the 2016 presidential election, he brought with him a stated commitment to correcting
historical injustices against the Bangsamoro. Duterte reconstituted the BTC, expanding it from 15 to 21
commissioners under the late Chairman Ghazali Jaffar, and the strengthened body eventually produced the
Bangsamoro Organic Law (BOL).<ref name="panimbang" />
For Balangi-Amer and 1BANGSA, the final push for the BOL meant more organizing. During the critical six-day
Bicameral Committee Conference on the BOL, he and his group closely monitored the congressional proceedings
and organized a motorcade in Metro Manila, staging a press conference alongside the Mindanao Alliance for Peace
(MAP) and other groups, calling on the Bicameral Committee to pass the BOL without further delay.<ref
name="panimbang" />
Once the BOL was ratified through a plebiscite on January 21, 2019, becoming Republic Act No. 11054,
1BANGSA moved quickly. On February 11, 2019, the organization sent an open letter to President Duterte calling
for "fair and equal" appointments to fill the 80 seats of the Bangsamoro Transition Authority (BTA), the interim
parliament that would govern the transition from the Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (ARMM) to the
new Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM).<ref name="panimbang" />
To prepare Bangsamoro communities for the plebiscite, Balangi-Amer led a campaign he called "Kampanya para
sa Kaalaman at Pagtalima ng BOL," a public information and advocacy drive to help communities understand the
BOL and make an informed choice. And on January 10, 2019, just days before the plebiscite, he convened the 1st
1BANGSA National Leaders Assembly at the Great Eastern Hotel in Quezon City, gathering 350 leaders from
Bangsamoro communities outside the proposed Bangsamoro territory. The assembly was graced by BTC Chairman
Ghazali Jaafar and Defense Secretary Delfin Lorenzana, and it sent a powerful signal that support for the BOL
extended far beyond Mindanao.<ref name="panimbang" />
Humanitarian Work and Crisis Response
Battle of Marawi (2017)
When the Siege of Marawi began in May 2017, Balangi-Amer joined other leaders in Metro Manila in appealing
directly to President Duterte to halt airstrikes, declare a ceasefire, and allow humanitarian groups to reach trapped
civilians. He specifically called on authorities not to target mosques (masajids) in the military operations.<ref
name="panimbang" />
Beyond appeals, he acted. Under the 1BANGSA program branded "1sang Tulong at Ayuda para sa Bangsamoro,"
he took an active role in distributing relief goods to Internally Displaced Persons (IDPs) from Marawi, channeling
financial assistance worth eight million pesos' worth of relief packages donated by the people of Bulacan.<ref
name="panimbang" />
COVID-19 Pandemic Response (2020)
When COVID-19 hit the Philippines, 1BANGSA and Balangi-Amer did not stand aside. In April 2020, the
organization wrote directly to President Duterte seeking an extension of the Enhanced Community Quarantine
(ECQ) to contain the spread of the pandemic. He and his members set up Hatid Ginhawa Kontra COVID-19:
Tulong at Ayuda para sa Bangsamoro, a program that provided medical support, psychosocial assistance, legal
guidance, and Islamic counselling to Bangsamoro communities, in addition to distributing relief goods.<ref
name="panimbang" />

PAGE 5
Balangi-Amer also initiated a radio program called 1BANGSA Tayo! over 94.1 University Radio, using the
airwaves to give Bangsamoro listeners accurate, accessible information about COVID-19 at a time when
misinformation was rampant.<ref name="panimbang" />
Jolo Cathedral Bombing (2019)
On February 3, 2019, 1BANGSA joined the National Commission on Muslim Filipinos (NCMF) and the PNP at a
prayer rally condemning the bombing of the Cathedral of Our Lady of Mount Carmel in Jolo, Sulu on January 27,
2019, which killed 22 people, and a subsequent blast at a mosque in Zamboanga City that left 2 dead. Balangi-
Amer's participation was a deliberate statement that opposition to terrorism was a Bangsamoro value, not just a
government talking point.<ref name="panimbang" />
Advocacy Beyond the Peace Process
International Muslim Rights
Balangi-Amer's sense of solidarity with Muslims under threat was never limited to the Philippines. He was vocal in
condemning the persecution of Rohingya Muslims in Myanmar, calling on the Myanmar government to provide
equal protection of law for Burmese Muslims and urging the international community to bring the mass killings
before the International Criminal Court.<ref name="panimbang" />
He also organized rallies and protests expressing solidarity with Muslims in the Middle East who, in his words,
were "unjustifiably maltreated and persecuted." That internationalism gave 1BANGSA a moral scope that went
beyond domestic politics and connected the Bangsamoro struggle to a broader conversation about justice for
Muslim minorities worldwide.<ref name="panimbang" />
Lake Lanao Development
Balangi-Amer's concern for his home region led him to champion the creation of a dedicated government body for
Lake Lanao, the massive freshwater lake that supplies an estimated 65 percent of Mindanao's electrical power. He
lobbied for the creation of a "Lake Lanao Development Office" under the Office of the President and actively
supported a bill creating the Lake Lanao Development Authority (LLDA), which was under discussion in the
18th Congress in 2019.<ref name="panimbang" />
His position was straightforward: a lake this critical to Mindanao's energy supply and the livelihoods of Maranao
communities around it deserved a dedicated, empowered government institution, not just ad hoc management from
multiple agencies.
Recognition and Legacy
The recognition that meant the most to Balangi-Amer came from within the Bangsamoro world itself. The
Bangsamoro Transition Commission (BTC), through its Chairman Ghazali Jaffar, formally acknowledged the
contributions of 1BANGSA and its leader to the passage of the Bangsamoro Organic Law. The MSU-Institute of
Peace and Development in Mindanao (MSU-IPDM) awarded him a Certificate of Recognition in November 2019,
during the Mindanao Week of Peace celebrations, for his "exemplary contributions to peacebuilding in Mindanao
and relentless pursuit of Human Rights for the Bangsamoro for more than two decades."<ref name="panimbang"
/> The certificate was signed by Dr. Akram Latiph, the IPDM's Executive Director at the time.

PAGE 6
That citation captures what those who have worked with him tend to say: what distinguishes Balangi-Amer is not
just what he achieved, but how long he stayed at it. Two decades is a long time to carry a cause, especially a cause
that spent much of those two decades looking like it might never succeed. The MOA-AD collapsed. Mamasapano
happened. The BBL stalled. And each time, he came back. Not with bitterness but with another rally, another open
letter, another forum, another reason to believe the next chapter would be different.
His story matters for Bangsamoro youth because it demonstrates that sustained civilian pressure, done creatively
and persistently, can actually move the needle on national policy. The BOL exists today as a law partly because of
street parliamentarians like Balangi-Amer who refused to let the conversation die in the years when it would have
been very easy for it to do so.
"As a man, he was real and religious; as a friend, he was indispensable and true; as a leader, he was
example; as a citizen, he was most patriotic; and as a personality, he was dynamic and virtuous." —
Prof. Gaphor Panimbang, Executive Director, REBUILD, Inc.<ref name="panimbang" />

Ali Marohomsalic Balindong
Judge Ali Marohomsalic Balindong is a Maranao lawyer, jurist,
educator, and public servant from Lanao del Sur, known for his
service across the judiciary, academia, and government in
Mindanao.
He holds the traditional title of Sultan through the Royal House of
Pagayawan, connecting his public career to a deep heritage of
Maranao customary leadership and cultural identity.
Contents
1 EARLY LIFE AND EDUCATION
2 LEGAL AND ACADEMIC CAREER
3 JUDICIAL CAREER
4 GOVERNMENT SERVICE
5 TRADITIONAL LEADERSHIP
6 LEGACY AND CONTRIBUTIONS
7 SEE ALSO
EARLY LIFE AND EDUCATION
Judge Balindong comes from Lanao del Sur, one of the provinces at
the heart of Maranao culture and the Bangsamoro homeland.
He pursued a career in law, establishing credentials as both a
practitioner and an educator, and built a professional profile that
spans the courtroom, the classroom, and the government service
sector.
Specific details on his birth date, educational institutions, and bar
admission year were not available in the submitted biography and
could not be independently verified at the time of writing.
LEGAL AND ACADEMIC CAREER
Judge Balindong served as a Professor of Law at Mindanao State
University (MSU), one of the premier state universities in Muslim
Mindanao and a major center for legal education in the region.
His time at MSU gave him the platform to mentor students who
would go on to careers in law, public service, and community
leadership throughout Mindanao.

PAGE 2

Notability

Known For

levels in Lanao del Sur; teaching law at
Mindanao State University; government
work advancing Muslim Filipino welfare
through OMA/NCMF Region X; and
traditional leadership through the Royal
House of Pagayawan.
He was a practitioner before the bench as well, building a reputation
as a respected legal professional in Lanao del Sur before his
appointment to the judiciary.
JUDICIAL CAREER
Judge Balindong's judicial career began at the Municipal Circuit
Trial Court (MCTC) level, where he presided over cases at the
local level in Lanao del Sur.
He was subsequently appointed as a Regional Trial Court (RTC)
Judge, a significant elevation that placed him among the senior
members of the Philippine judiciary handling a wider and more
complex docket.
His years on the bench were defined by a commitment to the fair
administration of justice, with particular importance given the
socio-political context of Lanao del Sur as part of the broader
Bangsamoro region.
GOVERNMENT SERVICE
Beyond the courts, Judge Balindong served as Regional Director of
Region X under the Office on Muslim Affairs (OMA), the national
government agency responsible for Muslim Filipino welfare,
representation, and development.
The OMA was later reorganized and transformed into the National
Commission on Muslim Filipinos (NCMF) through Republic Act
No. 9997, enacted in 2010.
In this executive role, he worked on programs aimed at the socio-
economic advancement of Muslim communities, fostering cultural
understanding and support for Muslim Filipinos within the
framework of national governance.
It is worth noting that Region X (Northern Mindanao) and the
predominantly Muslim Lanao del Sur are geographically adjacent,
and regional OMA/NCMF offices served Muslim communities
across regional boundaries.
TRADITIONAL LEADERSHIP
Judge Balindong carries the title of Sultan through the Royal
House of Pagayawan, one of the recognized royal houses of the
Maranao people under the traditional governance structure of
Lanao.

PAGE 3
The Pagayawan sultanate is part of the broader Taritib and Igma (customary law and code of conduct) of the
Maranao, which organizes the four major confederations (Pat a Pangampong a Ranao) and their corresponding
royal houses.
His dual identity as a career public servant and a traditional leader is, in many ways, a reflection of how many
Maranao leaders navigate modernity without abandoning their roots.
LEGACY AND CONTRIBUTIONS
Judge Balindong's legacy sits at the crossroads of law, education, public service, and tradition.
As a judge, he upheld rule of law in one of the country's most complex legal environments. As a law professor at
MSU, he contributed to building the next generation of Mindanao lawyers. As a government official, he worked for
the welfare of Muslim Filipinos through national institutions. And as a Sultan, he remained connected to the
cultural foundation that gives meaning to all of that work.
His career is a useful reference point for understanding how Muslim Filipino professionals have engaged with
Philippine national institutions while remaining rooted in Bangsamoro identity and heritage.

title: Balindong, Ali Pangalian Macaorao
text:
PAGE 1
Atty. Ali Pangalian M. Balindong
Full Name
Ali Pangalian Macaorao Balindong
Born
January 1, 1940 Lanao (present-day Dapao,
Pualas, Lanao del Sur), Philippine
Commonwealth
Ali Pangalian Macaorao Balindong
Ali Pangalian Macaorao Balindong (January 1, 1940 – October 2, 2025) was a Filipino lawyer, statesman, and
one of the most enduring voices in the long struggle for Bangsamoro self-determination.
Over a career spanning more than five decades, he served in nearly every chamber of Philippine governance: from
the 1971 Constitutional Convention, to the floors of the House of Representatives, to the historic halls of the first
Bangsamoro Parliament, where he served as Speaker until his death.
He was 85 years old.
Contents
1 BACKGROUND
2 EDUCATION
3 CAREER
3.1 Early Legal and Constitutional Work
3.2 ARMM Assemblyman and Regional Speaker
3.3 House of Representatives
3.4 Consultative Committee on Charter Change
3.5 Bangsamoro Parliament
4 INSTITUTIONAL CONTRIBUTIONS
5 LEGACY
6 RECOGNITION
7 SEE ALSO
8 REFERENCES
9 CATEGORIES
BACKGROUND
Pangalian Balindong came from a family that knew what public life
meant.
He was born on January 1, 1940, in Lanao, now the barangay of
Dapao in Pualas, Lanao del Sur. His father, Sultan Amer Macaorao
Balindong, served as mayor of Malabang, and the family belonged
to one of the influential clans of the region. His mother was
Maimona Marohom. As the eldest son of that household, Pangalian
carried both the weight and the opportunity that came with his
lineage.
He was, by most accounts, a man who took that seriously.
A Maranao through and through, Balindong would go on to spend
his adult life arguing, legislating, and negotiating on behalf of
Muslim Filipinos, from courtrooms and convention halls to the very
parliament his people had long fought to establish.

PAGE 2
Died
October 2, 2025 (aged 85) Quezon City,
Philippines
Ethnicity
Maranao
Clan

Education

University (1966) Graduate units in Public

2025) Deputy Speaker, House of

of Representatives, Lanao del Sur 2nd
District (1995–1998; 2007–2016) Speaker,
ARMM Regional Legislative Assembly
He married Jamela Malawani Alonto on April 28, 1968. They raised
eight children together.
EDUCATION
Balindong completed his primary schooling at the Malabang Central
Elementary School in 1954, then moved on to Our Lady of Peace
High School, finishing in 1958.
For higher education, he went to Manila and enrolled at Manuel L.
Quezon University. He earned a degree in Political Science in 1962,
then stayed on to pursue law, finishing his LL.B. in 1966. He passed
the bar examinations the following year, in 1967.
He later pursued graduate studies in public administration at the
Mindanao State University, taking up master's units that deepened
his grounding in governance.
He was also a member of the Mu Kappa Phi Exclusive Law
Fraternity.
CAREER
Early Legal and Constitutional Work
Before he ever held elective office, Balindong was already doing
meaningful work in the political trenches.
After passing the bar, he went into private legal practice and took on
a role that would define much of his early public life: legal counsel
for the Moro National Liberation Front (MNLF). This wasn't a
peripheral position. The MNLF was at the center of the Bangsamoro
struggle for self-governance, and Balindong's legal expertise was
part of how that movement engaged with the Philippine state.
In 1971, he joined the Philippine Constitutional Convention as a
delegate representing the Lone District of Lanao del Sur. He was
just over 30 years old. It was his first formal seat at a table where
the rules of the country were being written, and it wouldn't be his
last.
ARMM Assemblyman and Regional Speaker
Balindong began his electoral career through the Autonomous
Region in Muslim Mindanao.

PAGE 3
(1991–1993) Assemblyman, ARMM 2nd
District, Lanao del Sur (1990–1993)
Delegate, 1971 Philippine Constitutional
Convention
Spouse
Jamela Malawani Alonto (m. April 28, 1968)
Children

Fraternity
Mu Kappa Phi Exclusive Law Fraternity
Notability
First Speaker of the Bangsamoro Parliament;
author of the law creating the National
Commission on Muslim Filipinos; champion
of Bangsamoro political rights across five
decades of public service
Known For
Authoring Republic Act No. 9997 (National
Commission on Muslim Filipinos Act);
Republic Act No. 10908 (Integrated History
Act of 2016); advocacy for the Bangsamoro
Organic Law; legal counsel for the MNLF
Pull Quote
"A dreamer for peace, defender of
Bangsamoro."
From 1990 to 1993, he served as Assemblyman representing the 2nd
District of Lanao del Sur in the ARMM Regional Legislative
Assembly. During that same period, from 1991 to 1993, he rose to
become Speaker of that assembly. It was his first experience
presiding over a legislative body, and a preview of what he would
do again, decades later, in the Bangsamoro Parliament.
House of Representatives
Getting to Congress wasn't easy. Balindong ran for the House of
Representatives in the 1987 elections but lost to Mohammad Ali
Dimaporo.
He kept at it. In 1995, he won the seat for Lanao del Sur's 2nd
District, representing his constituency in the 10th Congress. He
served from June 30, 1995, to June 30, 1998, with Mohammad Ali
Dimaporo as his predecessor and Benasing Macarambon, Jr., as his
successor.
After a gap, he ran again in 2007 and won, this time serving across
three consecutive congresses: the 14th, 15th, and 16th. His second
run in Congress lasted from June 30, 2007, to June 30, 2016,
succeeding Benasing Macarambon, Jr., and followed by Mauyag
Papandayan, Jr.
In 2013, midway through his final congressional term, he was
elevated to Deputy Speaker of the House of Representatives, a
position he held under President Benigno Aquino III until 2016.
It was during these years in Congress that Balindong produced some
of his most lasting legislative work.
He authored Republic Act No. 9997, which established the National
Commission on Muslim Filipinos in 2009. The law gave Muslim
Filipinos a dedicated government body to address their welfare,
rights, and integration into national life.
He also authored the Integrated History Act of 2016, or Republic
Act No. 10908, which required the inclusion of Moro and
indigenous peoples' history in the national history curriculum. The
law was a direct challenge to the way Philippine education had long
sidelined or erased Bangsamoro perspectives from the national
story.
He filed House Bill 144, which proposed banning the use of
religious identifiers such as "Muslim" or "Christian" when
describing crime suspects in news reporting, arguing that such
labeling fed harmful stereotypes and deepened communal divisions.

PAGE 4
And throughout his time in Congress, he was one of the loudest voices pushing for the Bangsamoro Basic Law, the
legislative framework that would eventually take shape as the Bangsamoro Organic Law of 2018, establishing the
Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM).
Consultative Committee on Charter Change
In 2018, President Rodrigo Duterte appointed Balindong to the 25-member Consultative Committee to Review the
1987 Philippine Constitution, convened under Executive Order No. 10.
The committee was composed of former government officials, veteran lawyers, and academics, all tasked with
drafting a federal constitution. Balindong's inclusion reflected his standing as one of the country's most experienced
Muslim Filipino statesmen.
Bangsamoro Parliament
In 2019, Balindong joined the Bangsamoro Transition Authority (BTA), the interim body that constituted the first
Bangsamoro Parliament.
On March 29, 2019, he was elected Speaker of the BTA Parliament, having been nominated by Mohagher Iqbal. He
was nominated by the Bangsamoro Transition Authority itself and appointed under President Duterte, with Chief
Minister Murad Ebrahim heading the executive side of the new government.
In September 2022, he was reelected to the speakership, this time with Abdulraof Macacua serving as an additional
Chief Minister and under the appointment of President Bongbong Marcos.
He held the speakership until his death on October 2, 2025, having served in the role for over six years. He was
succeeded by Mohammad Yacob.
INSTITUTIONAL CONTRIBUTIONS
Balindong's contribution to Philippine institutions runs across three distinct levels.
At the national level, his landmark legislation gave Muslim Filipinos a formal government commission (the
NCMF), rewrote how Philippine history is taught, and pushed for constitutional and legislative reforms that
recognized Bangsamoro political identity.
At the regional level, he helped shape the governance architecture of the ARMM through his time as ARMM
Assemblyman and Regional Speaker, years before BARMM existed.
At the transitional level, he became the face of the Bangsamoro Parliament's opening chapter, presiding over its
earliest sessions as a body that represented the culmination of decades of peace negotiations.
His legal work for the MNLF in the earlier part of his career also placed him at the intersection of armed struggle
and peaceful advocacy, navigating a moment in Bangsamoro history when both were happening simultaneously.
LEGACY
Pangalian Balindong lived long enough to see the parliament his people had long demanded finally come to life,
and he got to preside over it.

PAGE 5
That alone would have been enough. But his legacy is also rooted in the quieter, harder work of legislation: the
education act, the Muslim Filipinos commission, the anti-stereotyping bill, the years of pushing for the
Bangsamoro Organic Law. These were not symbolic gestures. They were structural changes to how the Philippine
state related to its Muslim citizens.
He was described by the Bangsamoro Information Office as "a dreamer for peace, defender of Bangsamoro," and
that characterization held across the different chapters of his life, whether he was sitting as legal counsel for the
MNLF, arguing on the floor of Congress, or presiding over a parliament that represented the hopes of millions.
He died at St. Luke's Medical Center in Quezon City on October 2, 2025, after an undisclosed illness. He was 85.
RECOGNITION
Balindong's standing was recognized at multiple points in his career through appointments and elections to bodies
that carried significant national weight, including the 1971 Constitutional Convention, the position of Deputy
Speaker of the House, and the 25-member Consultative Committee on Charter Change in 2018.
His election and reelection as Speaker of the Bangsamoro Parliament is perhaps the clearest institutional
recognition of the trust placed in him by the Bangsamoro community and its political leadership.

title: Balindong, Amer Macaorao
text:
PAGE 1
Amer Macaorao Balindong
Sultan Amer Macaorao Balindong (1909–2009) was a Maranao statesman, traditional ruler, and educator from
Lanao del Sur in Mindanao, Philippines.
He served as the hereditary Sultan of Picong, a title rooted in both Maranao and Maguindanaon royal bloodlines,
and as the elected Municipal Mayor of Malabang for more than two decades (1953–1974), one of the longest
uninterrupted mayoral tenures in the province's history.<ref name="fb_amer">Facebook. Sultan Amer Macaorao
Balindong. Photo post. Retrieved from https://www.facebook.com/100046906275159/photos/sultan-amer-
macaorao-balindongmunicipal-mayor-of-malabang-lanao-del-sur1953-1974/2967584176593217/</ref>
Balindong is especially remembered for founding Mah'ad Lanao al-Islamia, the region's first formal Arabic and
Islamic university, and for maintaining Malabang as a zone of interfaith harmony during a period when violent
conflict was tearing through much of Mindanao.
His descendants continue to hold significant positions throughout Lanao del Sur and the Bangsamoro Autonomous
Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM), making the Balindong family one of the most enduring political
dynasties in the Bangsamoro region.
Contents
1 Lineage and Royal Authority
2 Political Career
2.1 Election and First Term (1953)
2.2 Governance and Interfaith Peace
3 Martial Law and the Partition of Greater Malabang
4 Educational and Religious Contributions
4.1 Mah'ad Lanao al-Islamia
4.2 Masjid Campu Muslim and Islamic Center
5 Death and Legacy
6 References
7 See Also
Lineage and Royal Authority
Sultan Amer was born in Barangay Dapao, Pualas, Lanao del Sur, into a family with deep royal credentials on both
Maranao and Maguindanaon sides.
On his paternal side, he was a direct descendant of Datu Nago, the 5th Noni (a formal noble rank) of Ranao Ragat,
and further traced his lineage to Datu Benito Balindong, a grandson of the founding ancestral figure Balindong,
also known as Aradi.<ref name="fb_amer" />
His Maguindanaon connection came through a forebear named Amatunding, who married Potri Gayang, the
sister of the 17th-century Moro hero and sultan Sultan Muhammad Dipatuan Kudarat.<ref
name="mindanews">MindaNews. (2021, August). Book review: Revolutionary Democrat — The Life and Times

PAGE 2
Sultan Amer Macaorao Balindong
Born
1909

Philippines
Died
2009 (aged approximately 100)
Lanao del Sur, Philippines
Ethnicity

Pikong

Notable Descendants

https://mindanews.com/mindaviews/2021/08/book-review-
revolutionary-democrat-the-life-and-times-of-pangalian-
balindong/</ref>
That marriage bound the Balindong lineage to one of the most
powerful sultanate networks in precolonial Muslim Mindanao,
lending Sultan Amer a legitimacy that stretched well beyond the
territorial boundaries of Picong.
He was formally recognized as the Radia Pangadapun sa Pikong
(the designated royal heir of Picong) before eventually being
enthroned as the traditional Sultan of Picong, the municipality now
officially known as Picong (formerly Sultan Gumander).<ref
name="philatlas">PhilAtlas. Picong, Lanao del Sur. Retrieved from
https://www.philatlas.com/mindanao/barmm/lanao-del-
sur/picong.html</ref>
Political Career
Election and First Term (1953)
In 1953, Sultan Amer entered the political arena and won the post of
Municipal Mayor of Malabang, defeating then-incumbent Datu
Kakae Delana in a closely watched race.<ref name="mindanews" />
At the time, Malabang was a sprawling territory: it encompassed
what are today the separate towns of Balabagan, Kapatagan, and
Picong (then still called Sultan Gumander).
Balindong would win reelection continuously, holding the
mayoralty without interruption until 1974, making his tenure one of
the longest in the recorded history of Lanao del Sur local
governance.
Governance and Interfaith Peace
His administration is widely remembered for two qualities: a sincere
commitment to Muslim-Christian integration, and a consistent
ability to keep sectarian violence out of his municipality even as
Mindanao was engulfed in armed conflict.
The late 1960s and early 1970s brought devastating communal
unrest across the region, with the Moro conflict claiming thousands
of lives throughout Mindanao.
Malabang, however, remained relatively stable under his watch.

PAGE 3
Atty. Ali Pangalian M. Balindong (son;
inaugural Speaker of the Bangsamoro
Parliament)
Notability
Traditional Sultan of Picong and one of the
longest-serving Municipal Mayors of
Malabang, Lanao del Sur, governing a unified
Greater Malabang for over two decades
(1953–1974)
Known For
Founding Mah'ad Lanao al-Islamia;
sustaining interfaith peace in Malabang
during the Mindanao conflict; building the
Masjid Campu Muslim and an adjacent
Islamic Center for women and youth
Pull Quote
"He built schools where others built fences,
and kept the peace when Mindanao was at
war with itself."
Contemporary accounts describe Malabang as having maintained
relative interfaith stability during Sultan Balindong's administration,
though the municipality, like much of Lanao del Sur, was not
without its history of clan feuding and civil unrest.
Martial Law and the Partition of Greater
Malabang
Sultan Amer's political strength was substantial enough to attract the
attention of the Marcos administration.
During the Martial Law period under President Ferdinand Marcos
Sr., the national government pursued a policy of fragmenting
territories controlled by politically dominant clans in Muslim
Mindanao.
Greater Malabang was split into four distinct municipalities through
executive and presidential decrees: Malabang, Balabagan,
Kapatagan, and Sultan Gumander (later officially renamed
Picong in 2006).<ref name="wiki_picong">Wikipedia. Picong,
Lanao del Sur. Retrieved from
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Picong,_Lanao_del_Sur</ref>
The intent was to dilute the family's localized political authority.
In practice, the partition had the opposite effect: rather than shrinking Balindong influence, it spread family
members across more electoral units.
Consecutive generations secured mayorships and legislative seats in multiple partitioned towns, ultimately
expanding the dynasty's geographic reach across the restructured political landscape of southern Lanao del Sur.
Educational and Religious Contributions
Mah'ad Lanao al-Islamia
Sultan Amer's most enduring contribution to the region is not political at all: it's educational.
He founded the Mah'ad Lanao al-Islamia in Malabang, the first formal institution for Arabic and Islamic higher
learning in the area.
In the institution's early years, he personally funded operations and paid faculty salaries from his own pocket, so
that local youth could access quality Islamic education at no cost.
The investment produced generational returns.
The university has since produced thousands of Islamic scholars (Ulamas) and religious teachers (Ustadz), many of
whom secured international scholarships in the Middle East and returned to serve communities across Lanao and
beyond.

PAGE 4
Mah'ad Lanao al-Islamia eventually gained formal recognition from the Philippine Department of Education
(DepEd) and was selected as a flagship pilot institution under the Basic Education Assistance for Mindanao
(BEAM) project, which aimed to bridge traditional Islamic instruction with the national standard curriculum.<ref
name="fb_amer" />
Masjid Campu Muslim and Islamic Center
Sultan Amer also directed the construction and funding of the Masjid Campu Muslim, which became one of the
earliest and most architecturally distinctive mosques along the coastal Lanao region.
Adjacent to the mosque, he built an Islamic Center dedicated to the religious education and civic development of
women and youth in the broader Malabang community.
Together, the two facilities formed a hub of faith, learning, and public service that remains a landmark of his
governance.
Death and Legacy
Sultan Amer Macaorao Balindong passed away in 2009 at approximately 100 years of age, leaving behind a
political and cultural legacy that remains visible across Lanao del Sur and the BARMM today.<ref
name="fb_amer" /><ref name="mindanews" />
His eldest son, Atty. Ali Pangalian M. Balindong (1940–2025), carried the family's tradition of public service into
some of the most consequential chapters in Bangsamoro history.
Pangalian served as a delegate to the 1971 Philippine Constitutional Convention, acted as legal counsel to the Moro
National Liberation Front (MNLF) during the landmark 1976 Tripoli Agreement, won multiple terms as
Representative of Lanao del Sur's 2nd District, and rose to Deputy Speaker of the Philippine House of
Representatives.<ref name="bangsamoro_gov">Bangsamoro Government. Speaker Pangalian Balindong: A
dreamer for peace, defender of Bangsamoro. Retrieved from https://bangsamoro.gov.ph/news/latest-news/speaker-
pangalian-balindong-a-dreamer-for-peace-defender-of-bangsamoro/</ref>
Most notably, Pangalian became the inaugural Speaker of the Bangsamoro Parliament, a post he held until his
passing in October 2025, cementing the Balindong name at the highest level of Bangsamoro governance.<ref
name="wiki_pangalian">Wikipedia. Pangalian Balindong. Retrieved from
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pangalian_Balindong</ref>
Other descendants continue to serve across the region: former Malabang Mayor Amir "Gary" Balindong, Mayor
Amin D. Balindong, Picong Mayor Mesron D. Balindong, and Bangsamoro Member of Parliament Ahmad Amir A.
Balindong all hold or have held executive and legislative positions within Lanao del Sur and the BARMM.<ref
name="lanaodelsur">Lanao del Sur Official Website. Oath-taking of Malabang and Picong officials. Retrieved
from https://lanaodelsur.gov.ph/oath-taking-of-malabang-and-picong-officials/</ref><ref
name="barmm_parliament">BARMM Parliament. Member of Parliament: Balindong, Ahmad Amir A. Retrieved
from https://parliament.bangsamoro.gov.ph/member-parliament/balindong-ahmad-amir-a/</ref>
Sultan Amer built his legacy on three pillars: the traditional authority of a sultan who commanded deep communal
respect, the political resolve of a mayor who chose peace over partisanship, and the educational foresight of a
founder who invested in Bangsamoro youth before the state ever did.
Across all three, he delivered.

Atty. Bayan G. Balt
Bayan G. Balt (born December 23, 1953) is a lawyer and civic leader from Bayang, Lanao del Sur. He is the great-
grandson of the Sultan of Bayang and Sultan Pandapatan, the two Maranao Muslim leaders who commanded forces
in the May 2, 1902 Battle of Bayang against United States military forces. Since 1995, Balt has served as legal
counsel on the environment for the Moro National Liberation Front (MNLF). His professional roles have included
regional appointments in labor, legal practice, leadership of multiple civil society organizations, and participation
in international peace agreement reviews and conferences.
Early Life and Family Background
Bayan G. Balt was born on December 23, 1953, in Barangay Bairan, Bayang, Lanao del Sur, to parents Abdullah
A. Balt, a former Municipal Vice Mayor, and Za-alika G. Goling-Balt. He is the great-grandson of the Sultan of
Bayang and Sultan Pandapatan, the two Maranao Muslim leaders who led the Filipino Muslims in the May 2, 1902
Battle of Bayang (also known as the Battle of Padang Karbala). This battle was fought against the United States
32nd cavalry forces under Colonel Frank Baldwin and General John "Black Jack" Pershing. According to the
profile, this battle was recorded in U.S. history as the fiercest battle in the history of the entire Philippine
insurrection.
Balt is married to Mrs. Annamilly Pangarungan Alug-Balt. They have five children: Atty. Anzarullah Zhadradi A.
Abdullah, Atty. Princess Shanihar A. Abdullah, Atty. Shayma A. Abdullah, Dra. Arabecca Shania A. Abdullah, and
Mr. Abdulbayan Shevardnadze A. Abdullah.

Education and Legal Training
Balt earned a Bachelor of Arts in Political Science from MLQ University
in Manila between 1970 and 1973 as a consistent National Intellectual
Scholarship Program (NISGP) Scholar. He then earned a Bachelor of
Laws from the same institution between 1974 and 1977, also as a NISGP
Scholar. He was a graduate of the Philippine Shari'a Training Institute at
Mindanao State University (MSU Marawi City) from 1981 to 1982.
On April 8, 1978, Balt was admitted to the Philippine Bar by the Supreme
Court to practice law in the Philippines. His Roll of Attorney number is
28131.
Legal Career and Law Practice
Balt worked as a Senior Lawyer at the Department of Agrarian Reform,
Marawi City District Office from 1978 to 1980. He was a Senior Partner
at the Pangadapun, Mamondiong, Balt, Barambangan and Madum Law
Firm in Marawi City from 1980 to 1986. In 2000, he became a Senior
Partner of the Balt, Abdullah, Abdullah and Abdullah Law Offices at 122
Quezon Avenue in Marawi City, a position he has held to the present.
Since 1982, Balt has served as Provincial Coordinator of the Free Legal
Assistance Group (FLAG), described in the source as a group of lawyers
that assist the poor, weak and defenseless in Lanao del Sur.
He filed four environmental suits against corporations: National Power
Corporation, TRANSCO, and PSALM. These cases (Civil Cases No.
1918-03, 1546-05, 1619-06, and ERC case No. 221-2002, EIA case No.
2004-001) involved issues of electricity pricing, damages, non-payment of
taxes, and protections of consumers and people living around Lake Lanao.
According to the source, these cases are terminated and for resolutions by
courts.
Balt has hosted the "Lawyer's Forum, Views and Interviews" on Local
Television Channel 13 (simulcast on Channel 1 Marawi Cable and radio
DXKC in Marawi City) from 2013 to the present.
Political and Civic Leadership
Balt was appointed Regional Assemblyman (Lupong Tagapagpagapanap
ng Pook, or LTP) of the Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao
(ARMM) by former Senator Nene Q. Pimentel Jr., then Minister of Local
Government, from 1986 to 1988.
He was appointed Regional Cabinet Secretary of the Department of Labor
and Employment (DOLE-ARMM) in Cotabato City by former Governor
Nur P. Misuari from 1997 to 1999. From 1998 to 1999, he was awarded "Most Outstanding Public Official" while
serving in this position, sponsored by the Manila Bulletin and the Newsmen Association of the Philippines.

PAGE 3
Balt has held positions of leadership in several organizations:
Ranao Movement Against Corruptions & Crime (RMACC) - Chairman/led Convenor. The source describes it
as a group of NGOs and Civil Society dedicated to eradicate corruptions in Mindanao.
Integrated Bar of the Philippines (IBP), Marawi City & Lanao Del Sur Chapter - President from 2013 to
2015.
Ranao Federal State Movement (RFSM) - Chairman, Iligan City, from 2017 to the present.
PDP-LABAN, Lanao Del Sur Chapter - Provincial Chairman (on leave), under former Senate President Aquilino
"Nene" Q. Pimentel Jr., since 1982 to the present.
Mindanao Council, Bansang Nagkaisa sa Diwa at Layunin (BANDILA) - Chairman.
Christians And Muslims for Peace (CAMP), Philippine Chapter - National President from 2002 to the present.
The source states that CAMP was founded at the Crystal Cathedral Church in Garden Grove, California, and aims
to promote peace and better understanding including interfaith dialogue between Muslims and Christians.
Alliance of Regional Coalitions Against People's Poverty (ARCAPP) - National Chairman from 2005 to the
present. The source describes it as a coalition of 32 NGOs and Civil Society Organizations located in Cagayan de
Oro City.
Diplomatic and International Engagement
As Regional Secretary of Labor and Employment in ARMM (1997–1999), Balt undertook diplomatic missions
regarding labor and worker issues.
In 1998, he was sent to Sabah, Malaysia to prevent the untimely deportation of some 450,000 undocumented
Filipino workers. According to the source, he held meetings with Abu Talib Harun, Officer In-charge of
Immigration at the Ministry of Home Affairs. Upon his request, the deportation of undocumented workers was
deferred for at least three years.
In 1999, he was sent to Riyadh, Saudi Arabia to negotiate for the return of 64 Filipino workers stranded at the
Philippine Embassy in Riyadh who could not return to the Philippines due to refusal of their employers to issue exit
visas. He held a meeting with Mohammad Al-Shanani, then Saudi Arabia's Minister of Labor and Social Affairs,
who granted the issuance of exit visas to the 64 stranded Filipino workers, thus paving the way for their return to
the Philippines.
Also in 1999, he launched the "Job for Peace 2000" to request from Arab and Muslim Ministers of Labor to
allocate at least ten percent of their jobs order for Muslim Mindanao. The source states that he held meetings with
Minister Matar Humaid Al Tair of the Arab Emirates, Mohammad Al-Shanani of Saudi Arabia, and Sheikh Fallah
Al-Thani of Qatar. These officials granted his request to hire workers from Muslim Mindanao.
From 1998 to 1999, as ARMM Labor Chief, he led a Labor and Investment mission to Southeast Asia and the
Middle East. In Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia, he conferred with officials of the Malaysian Manufacturers Association.
In Jeddah, Saudi Arabia, he held meetings with the Jeddah Chamber of Commerce and Industry. In Riyadh, Saudi
Arabia, he met with the Chairman of the Saudi Recruitment Agency. In Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates, he held
talks with top officials of the Abu Dhabi Chamber of Commerce and Industry. In Doha, Qatar, he met with top
major recruitment and employers agencies. The source states that the mission brought investment awareness and
improved ARMM's rating as an investment haven in these countries.

PAGE 4
Between 1998 and 1999, while chairman of the Regional Tripartite Wage and Productivity Board (RTWPB) in the
Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao, Balt increased the wages of ARMM workers twice, for the first time
during this period.
Peace Process and Legal Counsel
Since 1995, Balt has served as Legal Counsel on Environment for the Moro National Liberation Front (MNLF). He
participated as counsel and member of the Tripartite Review Process in 2007 that reviewed the 1996 Final Peace
Agreement between the Government of the Philippines (GPH), the MNLF, and the Organization of Islamic
Cooperation (OIC). He also served as counsel and member of the final Tripartite Review Process of the 1996 Final
Peace Agreement held in Jeddah, Saudi Arabia, from January 25 to 27, 2016.
In May 2016, during the national and local elections, Balt served as Coalition Chief Legal Counsel of all
supporters, movements and organizations of Duterte in ARMM, including the PPRD, Hugpong Federalismo,
MRRD-NECC, and NUIMD.
Balt attended the 4th World Peace Forum held in Bogor, West Java, Indonesia, from November 23 to 25, 2012, as
an official delegate of the MNLF delegation. He was also a participant in the GRP-MNLF-OIC review of the 1996
Final Peace Agreement held in Bandung, Republic of Indonesia, in March 2012.
International Advocacy and Speaking Engagements
Balt has participated in several international conferences. In October 2000, he was a keynote speaker at the 3rd
International Conference on Peace and Understanding held at the Campus of the Crystal Cathedral Ministry in
Garden Grove, California.
In July 2004, he delivered a paper entitled "The Environmental Case of Lake Lanao" during the 10th World
Environmental Conference held at the Boston Towers Plaza Hotel in Boston, Massachusetts.
In March 2005, he was a speaker at the 9th Cairo International Conference on Energy and Environment held at the
Pyramisa Resort Hotel in Sharm El-Sheik, Egypt, on the topic "The Agus hydroelectric power plants and the
Environment of Lake Lanao."
In June 2005, he served as a resource speaker at the 32nd annual meeting of the Council of Foreign Ministers of the
Organization of Islamic Cooperation (OIC) held in Sana'a, Republic of Yemen, speaking on the topic "Lake Lanao,
a nature's gift to the Maranaos."
Balt was an official delegate to the 33rd meeting of the Council of Foreign Ministers of the Organization of Islamic
Cooperation held in Baku, Republic of Azerbaijan, from June 23 to 26, 2007. He also attended the Council's 41st
meeting held in Kuwait City from May 26 to 28, 2015.
International Travel
According to his profile, Balt has visited Saudi Arabia, Egypt, Kuwait, Bahrain, United Arab Emirates, Qatar,
Republic of Yemen, Republic of Azerbaijan, India, Thailand, People's Republic of China, Taiwan, Hong Kong,
South Korea, Japan, Singapore, Indonesia, Malaysia, and San Francisco, Los Angeles, and New York in the United
States.

PAGE 5
Academic and Professional Affiliations
Balt is a member of the Beta Sigma Lambda Exclusive Law Fraternity since 1974.
Recognition and Awards
Balt was awarded "Most Outstanding Public Official" in 1998-1999 while serving as Regional Secretary of the
Department of Labor and Employment in ARMM, an award sponsored by the Manila Bulletin and the Newsmen
Association of the Philippines.
Roles and Positions
Balt's career has included simultaneous leadership of multiple organizations. Since 1995, he has served as Legal
Counsel on Environment for the MNLF. He has held the position of Provincial Coordinator of FLAG since 1982,
and served as President of the IBP Marawi City & Lanao Del Sur Chapter from 2013 to 2015. He has been a senior
partner in private law practice since 2000 and has hosted a legal affairs television program since 2013.
Further Reading

Amilpasa "Caloy" Bandaying
Amilpasa "Caloy" Bandaying (born c. 1944) is a Moro
leader, former Moro National Liberation Front (MNLF)
cadre, military officer, and public servant from the
Zamboanga area in the Philippines.
He is best known as one of the surviving members of the
MNLF Top 90, the elite founding batch of MNLF guerrillas
trained in Pangkor Laut Island, Malaysia in 1969.
Over the course of several decades, Bandaying moved from
armed revolutionary to institutional builder, serving in
military, legislative, and civic roles while staying committed
to peace, indigenous peoples' rights, and an accurate telling of
Bangsamoro history.
Contents
1 BACKGROUND AND EARLY LIFE
2 EDUCATION AND THE TURNING POINT
3 MNLF TOP 90 AND REVOLUTIONARY YEARS
4 MILITARY AND GOVERNMENT CAREER
5 MAJOR CONTRIBUTIONS
6 PERSONAL LIFE AND FAMILY
7 LEGACY AND SIGNIFICANCE
8 SEE ALSO
BACKGROUND AND EARLY LIFE
Caloy Bandaying grew up in the Zamboanga area during a
period of deepening unrest across Mindanao.
He was born around the mid-1940s, with accounts placing his
81st birthday in late 2025.
The details of his exact birthplace and parents remain
relatively private in public records, but his roots tie him
firmly to Muslim Mindanao and its indigenous heritage.
He has long been recognized for his close ties to indigenous
peoples (IPs) in and around Zamboanga City, including the
Subanen, Sama, and related groups. That dual identity, as
both a Moro leader and an advocate for IP communities,
would shape much of his later public work.

PAGE 2
Government Region IX (RAG-
9)
Notability
Surviving member of the MNLF's legendary
Top 90; intellectual cadre of the early Moro
nationalist movement; Regional
Assemblyman and peace advocate
Known For
MNLF Top 90 founding cadre; Zone III
Propaganda and Intelligence Officer; Regional
Assemblyman of RAG-9; contribution to the
Organic Act for the ARMM (RA 6734);
advocacy for indigenous peoples in
Zamboanga City
Pull Quote
"Revolutions involve not just battlefield
courage but the harder work of
reconciliation, institution-building, and
mentoring the next generation."
EDUCATION AND THE TURNING
POINT
Bandaying earned a Bachelor of Arts in Political Science
from Zamboanga A.E. Colleges (now Universidad de
Zamboanga) in 1967.
He then headed to Manila to study law, first at the University
of Manila, where he was among the top students in his batch,
before transferring to Ateneo Law School after one semester.
His legal career, however, never got off the ground.
The Jabidah Massacre of 1968 changed everything. Like
many young Moro intellectuals of his generation, Bandaying
was radicalized by the event. He left his law studies behind
and joined the emerging Moro nationalist movement, a
decision that would define the next several decades of his life.
MNLF TOP 90 AND
REVOLUTIONARY YEARS
In 1969, Bandaying became part of the original Top 90, the
founding batch of MNLF cadres who underwent guerrilla
warfare training on Pangkor Laut Island in Malaysia.
This group formed the organizational backbone of the MNLF:
its early command structure, its ideological core, and its
leadership pool. Fellow members of this cohort include names
central to Bangsamoro history, among them Nur Misuari,
Abul Khayr Alonto, and Jamil Lucman.
Within the organization, Bandaying served as Zone III Propaganda and Intelligence Officer in Zamboanga del Sur.
He has been consistent in interviews and public statements on one important point: the Top 90 did not formally
surrender or seek amnesty. Government peace initiatives, particularly those led by Rear Admiral Romulo
Espaldon, opened paths for reconciliation, but on terms that did not require the cadres to abandon their dignity or
their identity as revolutionary fighters.
MILITARY AND GOVERNMENT CAREER
By 1974, Bandaying had entered the Officer Training program at Fort Bonifacio Army School Center.
He graduated at the top of his class, posting a general average of 89.51%.
Espaldon, recognizing his ability, brought him on as an aide and close staff officer, even as some within the
military establishment remained skeptical about a man who had come out of the MNLF. Bandaying rose to the rank
of First Lieutenant, took on sensitive roles within the Southern Command (SOUTHCOM), and served as military
liaison to the Regional Autonomous Government, Region IX (RAG-9).

PAGE 3
In 1979, he was appointed Secretary of the Admiral's Unified Staff Office.
His transition to civilian governance followed naturally. In 1982, he was appointed Regional Assemblyman of
RAG-9 and elected Speaker Pro Tempore of that body.
Under President Corazon Aquino in 1987, he joined the Regional Consultative Commission, contributing to the
drafting of the Organic Act for the Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (Republic Act 6734).
He later served as City Hall Executive Assistant on Muslim Affairs in Zamboanga City, and remained active in
advocacy work covering peace, good governance, and federalism.
MAJOR CONTRIBUTIONS
Bandaying's contributions have come through both direct action and careful reflection.
As one of the few surviving members of the Top 90, he is a primary witness to the MNLF's formative years, and
has been consulted in academic research on Bangsamoro history, peace processes, and political transitions.
He has spoken publicly on topics including indigenous peoples' rights, national heroes, and the complexities of the
Moro struggle, consistently emphasizing dignity, historical integrity, and the importance of truth.
He has also taken steps to correct the historical record where he felt it had been distorted. Bandaying has distanced
himself from unauthorized online versions of texts attributed to him, including certain circulating versions of "The
Bangsamoro Story," noting factual inaccuracies in those texts and working toward corrections. His own writings
and oral accounts stress reconciliation, the difficulty of institution-building after conflict, and the need for inclusive
development across Mindanao.
As a member of the Council of Elders and an IP leader, he has worked to preserve the customs and traditions of
Muslim tribes and to support government programs for indigenous communities, while continuing to bridge divides
between Moro groups and the wider population of Zamboanga.
PERSONAL LIFE AND FAMILY
Bandaying is married to Kah Hadji Nene Bandaying, who is frequently mentioned alongside him in tributes from
friends and colleagues.
Those who know him personally describe him as kind, eloquent, and steadfast. He is a proud grandfather, including
to healthy triplets, and his faith and commitment to community come through in both his public appearances and
private life.
LEGACY AND SIGNIFICANCE
What makes Caloy Bandaying's story compelling is the arc of it: a young man radicalized by injustice who spent
decades afterward building the institutions he once fought against from the outside.
He fought for Moro self-determination in his youth. Later, he invested those same energies into making autonomy
actually work, through military service, legislation, local governance, and civil society engagement.
He represents a generation that navigated the turn from armed struggle to political participation, and did so without
abandoning the principles that drove them to resistance in the first place.

PAGE 4
In Zamboanga and in broader Bangsamoro discourse, he remains a respected voice on peace, indigenous rights, and
historical accuracy. His story is a reminder that revolutions require not just courage on the battlefield but the much
harder work of reconciliation, institution-building, and passing something meaningful on to the next generation.
As a surviving Top 90 member and Moro intellectual, Bandaying's legacy continues through consultations,
advocacy, and a quiet but firm insistence on getting the historical record right.
