Early Life and Education
Bansao's formative years were shaped by his pursuit of a
multidisciplinary educational foundation spanning the
humanities, law, and administration.
In 1984, he earned his Bachelor of Arts from Saint Michael's
College in Iligan City, where he distinguished himself as an
Outstanding Student Leader recognized by the institution's
student body and faculty for his commitment to educational
welfare and community service.
He pursued legal studies at the University of the East, earning his
Bachelor of Laws degree in 1996, equipping him with
foundational expertise in corporate law, constitutional
interpretation, and regulatory frameworks.
His advanced studies in public administration followed at
Mindanao State University (MSU-Maguindanao campus), where
he completed a Master's degree in Public Administration in 2004.
The culmination of his formal education came through his
doctoral research at Bulacan State University, where he earned a
Doctorate in Public Administration on June 1, 2013, recognized
with a Leadership Award from the Graduate School in grateful
acknowledgment of his steadfast institutional stewardship across
multiple organizations.
Scholarly Contributions
Bansao has authored three major works that synthesize his
expertise in governance, constitutional design, and corporate law:
Politics and Governance with the Postulate of the 1987
Constitution examines the normative foundations and structural
innovations embedded in the Philippine Constitution, with
particular attention to federalism and subsidiary governance
frameworks relevant to the BARMM context.
The Corporation Code of the Philippines, 2013 Edition
provides a comprehensive treatment of corporate formation,
management accountability, and regulatory compliance under
Batas Pambansa Bilang 68, aimed at practitioners and
institutional leaders navigating Philippine corporate structures.
PNP's Commitment on Crime Investigation: Input to Police
Force Capability Building addresses organizational
modernization and investigative capacity within the Philippine National Police, particularly relevant to law
enforcement development in autonomous regions.

PAGE 3
These works demonstrate Bansao's commitment to bridging theory and practice in governance, making complex
legal frameworks accessible to policymakers and institutional leaders.
Academic Career
Bansao has established himself as a committed educator across multiple institutions throughout the Muslim
Mindanao region and beyond, reflecting his belief in cultivating the next generation of governance practitioners.
He currently serves as a part-time Associate Professor and Instructor at the School of Graduate Studies at
Mindanao State University, General Santos City, teaching advanced courses in public administration and
governance.
His faculty appointments extend to several other higher education institutions, including Notre Dame of
Dadiangas University (NDDU, Graduate Studies), Marvelous College of Technology (MCTI), Ramon
Magsaysay Memorial Colleges (RMMC) in Koronadal City, South Cotabato, Gen Santos Foundation College,
Inc. (GFI) in General Santos City, and the Southeast Asian Institute of Technology (SEAIT) in Tupi, South
Cotabato.
At Ramon Magsaysay Memorial Colleges, he was commended by students and fellow educators as an Excellent
Instructor in the College of Criminal Justice, demonstrating his ability to engage diverse audiences on complex
institutional topics.
His teaching approach emphasizes the connection between historical institutional development, constitutional
frameworks, and practical governance challenges facing decentralized regions.
Speaking Engagements and Public Advocacy
Bansao has been invited to serve as a resource person and keynote speaker at numerous forums addressing
governance, criminal justice, gender awareness, and human rights.
In January 2020, he served as Resource Person on Career Guidance at Immaculate Conception International,
addressing students about pathways in public service and governance careers.
He delivered keynote remarks on Criminal Justice Education at the Philippine National Police headquarters in
Malolos City on May 22 and 25, 2017, discussing contemporary challenges in law enforcement capacity building
and investigative standards.
During the July 25, 2016 State of the Nation Address (SONA) broadcast coverage by Channel 36 (CLTV36) from
San Fernando City, Pampanga, Bansao served as Keynote Speaker, offering commentary on national governance
priorities and the role of regional leadership in the Marcos administration's federalism agenda.
On August 10, 2015, he delivered keynote remarks on Gender Awareness and Human Rights at Bulacan State
University's Hiyas Convention Center in Malolos City, engaging with faculty and students on the intersection of
constitutional rights and institutional accountability in protecting vulnerable populations.
He has served as Guest Lecturer at several institutions, including the College of Saint Lawrence, Jesus Is Lord
Colleges Foundation, and Bulacan State University, where he has instructed on topics ranging from
constitutional law to organizational management.

PAGE 4
Government and Institutional Service
Bansao's career encompasses extensive service across multiple levels of government and statutory institutions,
reflecting a pattern of deepening engagement with institutional modernization and capacity building.
Senate and Legislative Staff
In 1997, Bansao served as a Staff Consultant to the late Senate President Ernesto Maceda, focusing on Muslim
Affairs at the Philippine Senate. This role placed him at the center of national-level discussions on Muslim Filipino
representation and regional autonomy during a transitional period in Philippine governance.
He also served as Secretary and Chief of Staff to his late brother, Assemblyman Atty. Rakil Dagalangit, during the
Marcos regime's final years (1982-1987), representing Lanao Del Sur in the defunct Batasang Pampook regional
legislative body.
Autonomous Region Administration
Following the establishment of the Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (ARMM), Bansao held several
senior legal and administrative positions:
He served as a Legislative Staff Officer V and Chief of Staff to Assemblyman Samer M. Salic of the defunct
Regional Legislative Assembly-ARMM, exercising supervisory functions and management over legislative
operations.
As Planning Officer III, he headed the Project Development Division of the Department of Education during the
tenure of late Undersecretary Macapanton Y. Abbas, Jr., commencing September 1, 2003. In this role, he oversaw
long-term institutional planning and development initiatives.
Bansao also served as Legal Officer V and as Director for Maguindanao province of the National Police
Commission (NAPOLCOM), exercising legal authority over police accountability and standards within the
autonomous region's law enforcement apparatus.
Transportation, Land, and Law Enforcement
Beyond the ARMM administrative apparatus, Bansao worked as an Attorney II with the Department of
Transportation and Communication (DOTr) in the Caraga Region, based in Butuan City, advising on regulatory and
contractual matters.
On May 28, 2002, he assumed the position of Legal Officer II at the Land Transportation Office, Region 12 (LTO-
12), managing licensing, regulatory, and dispute resolution functions for land-based transportation.
He was also engaged as a Confidential Agent with the National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) in a civilian
capacity, supporting investigative and intelligence operations.
Barangay-Level Leadership
From 1980 to 1984, Bansao was elected Kabataang Barangay Federation President in the Municipality of Lumba-
Bayabao, Lanao Del Sur, holding the equivalent rank of Councilor. During his tenure, he received the Multi-
Awards Recognition from the Councilors' League of the Philippines in 1984, cited as one of the most outstanding

PAGE 5
Councilors for his outstanding contributions to peace, progress, and development in the Philippines.
Present-Day Leadership Positions
Business and Professional Leadership
Bansao currently serves as Chief Executive Officer and President of Bansao Consultancy Services, offering
advisory services on governance, public administration, and institutional development to public and private sector
clients.
Chamber of Commerce Advocacy
As the incumbent National Chairman of the Filipino Muslim Chamber of Commerce and Industry, Bansao
leads advocacy efforts on behalf of Muslim Filipino entrepreneurs and business interests, focusing on inclusive
economic development, capacity building, and market access across the BARMM region and national marketplace.
Political Party Leadership
He holds the position of Vice President of the Partido Federal ng Pilipinas (PFP) representing the provinces of
Lanao del Sur, Maguindanao del Norte, and Maguindanao del Sur within the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region.
The PFP, whose National Chairman is President Ferdinand R. Marcos, Jr., advocates federalism and decentralized
governance as mechanisms for ensuring regional autonomy and local development.
Professional Associations
Bansao previously served as President of the Professional Public Administration Society (PRO-PAS), an
association of government administrators and public management professionals.
He served as Vice-President of the Graduate Studies Student Council (GSSC) at the Graduate Studies division
of Bulacan State University during his doctoral studies, representing student interests in institutional governance.
Legacy and Impact
Throughout his multifaceted career, Bansao has consistently advocated for institutional modernization, legal
literacy, and inclusive dialogue as pathways to sustainable governance in conflict-affected regions.
His scholarship emphasizes the binding relationship between constitutional design, institutional capacity, and
development outcomes, particularly in federal or autonomous systems where power is distributed across multiple
governance levels.
As a practitioner-scholar, he bridges academic rigor and practical policymaking, mentoring the next generation of
governance professionals while contributing directly to institutional reform initiatives at local, regional, and
national levels.
His work through the Filipino Muslim Chamber of Commerce reflects a sustained commitment to ensuring that
economic development and business growth are equitably distributed across Muslim Filipino communities and that
institutional barriers to entrepreneurship are systematically dismantled.

PAGE 6
Through his political engagement with the Partido Federal ng Pilipinas, he advocates decentralization and
federalism as institutional mechanisms capable of addressing longstanding regional grievances while strengthening
democratic participation and local accountability.
Personal Life
Bansao is widely known by the affectionate nickname Bruce among students, colleagues, and friends, reflecting
his approachable and personable leadership style despite his formal institutional roles.

Hamid Aminoddin Barra
Atty. Hamid Aminoddin D. Barra (born October 9, 1953, Marinaut, Marawi City) is a Meranao lawyer, Islamic
scholar, educator, peace negotiator, and public servant who has spent more than five decades at the intersection of
law, faith, and governance in Muslim Mindanao. He currently serves as the inaugural Minister of the Ministry of
Human Settlements and Development (MHSD) of the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao
(BARMM). A product of both Philippine civil law and Malaysian Islamic legal scholarship, Barra is widely
regarded as one of the principal architects of the Bangsamoro's legal and institutional framework, and a central
figure in translating the aspirations of the Moro people into workable, durable governance structures.
Contents
1 EARLY LIFE AND FORMATION
2 LEGAL EDUCATION AND THE MALAYSIAN

EARLY LIFE AND FORMATION
Hamid Aminoddin D. Barra grew up in Marinaut, one of the oldest
and most historically layered districts of Marawi City. Marinaut was
not just a neighborhood, it was a living expression of the Meranao
way of life, organized around what locals describe as the "isa ka
masjid, isa ka sulutan, isa ka agama" principle: one mosque, one
sultan, one religion. In that environment, the mosque was not
simply a place of prayer but the beating heart of community
governance, dispute resolution, and social organization.
The Marawi of Barra's childhood was in the middle of a significant
transition. The city, still commonly known by its colonial name
Dansalan in earlier decades, was steadily reclaiming its identity as
an Islamic center. Traders from Manila and Cebu rubbed shoulders
with international residents in the markets around Lake Lanao,
giving young Hamid an early exposure to the kind of cosmopolitan
exchange that would later define his diplomatic career. But this era

also had its tensions. The steady migration of Christian settlers into
Mindanao brought land disputes and the gradual erosion of ancestral
domains, realities that quietly shaped Barra's later commitment to
housing rights and land justice.
His early schooling followed a deliberate dual-track path. He
attended Marinaut Elementary School before moving on to
Dansalan College for both his secondary and undergraduate
education. Dansalan College had a well-established reputation for
inter-religious dialogue and literary culture, and Barra graduated in
1973 with a Bachelor of Arts in English. For Barra, learning English
and engaging with Western academic traditions was not a departure
from his identity as a Meranao Muslim. It was, as he has framed it
throughout his career, the strategic acquisition of the tools necessary
to make Meranao and Bangsamoro aspirations legible to the broader
world.
The destruction of Masjid Marinaut during the 2017 Marawi Siege,
and its subsequent reconstruction as a historical landmark under
Barra's own ministerial supervision decades later, gives his life story
a striking circular quality. The mosque that anchored his childhood
values would eventually become a project he helped restore, full
circle.
LEGAL EDUCATION AND THE
MALAYSIAN INFLUENCE
Barra's formal legal education began at Mindanao State University's
College of Law, where he enrolled in 1981 as an academic scholar.
He passed the Philippine Bar examinations in 1985 and was
admitted to the Bar on June 2, 1986, giving him the credentials to
navigate the country's civil law system. But Barra's intellectual
ambitions did not stop at the Philippine Civil Code.
His deeper interest was in how Islamic law could be systematically
woven into national legal frameworks, a question that led him to the
International Islamic University Malaysia (IIUM) in Kuala Lumpur.
Malaysia was then at the forefront of what scholars called the
"Islamization of Knowledge" movement, an effort to harmonize
classical Islamic scholarship with modern social, legal, and
scientific disciplines. IIUM was one of its institutional flagships.
Supported by grants from the Asia Foundation and IIUM itself,
Barra completed his Master of Comparative Laws in 1987. His
thesis, "The Code of Muslim Personal Laws: A Study of Islamic
Law in the Philippines," became one of the foundational texts for
practitioners trying to understand Presidential Decree No. 1083, the law that formally recognized Shari'ah in
Philippine jurisprudence. The significance of that work was not just academic. By treating PD 1083 as statutory
law rather than mere religious custom, Barra gave Muslim legal practitioners a legitimate framework to work
within the national court system.

PAGE 3
He returned to IIUM for his doctorate, completing his Doctor of Philosophy in Laws in 1994. His dissertation,
"The Shari'ah Court System: A Study in Comparative Procedural Law," tackled a very practical problem: Philippine
Shari'ah courts lacked standardized procedures that could hold up alongside the mainstream Rules of Court. Barra's
PhD essentially provided the operational blueprint that these courts needed to function as genuine, recognized
components of the national judiciary rather than as parallel informal venues.
INSTITUTION-BUILDING AT MSU MARAWI
Returning to the Philippines after his years in Malaysia, Barra devoted more than three decades to the King Faisal
Center for Islamic, Arabic, and Asian Studies (KFCIAAS) at Mindanao State University Marawi. He served two
terms as Dean (1988 to 1990, and again from 2000 to 2006) and spent over two decades on the faculty as Professor
of Muslim Laws (1995 to 2018). His core pedagogical mission was to produce what he called "Moro intellectuals":
graduates equally fluent in Islamic jurisprudence and Philippine civil law, capable of working within the system
while remaining grounded in their faith and cultural identity.
His classroom became something of a training ground for a generation of Bangsamoro professionals. Students he
mentored went on to serve as Shari'ah judges, members of the Bangsamoro Parliament, and senior officials across
the BARMM government. For Barra, Islam was never just a system of ritual observance. He consistently taught it
as a complete civilization, encompassing governance, economics, family law, and social relations.
From 2001 to 2006, Barra also served as MSU's Resident Ombudsman, a role that put him at the center of
institutional accountability within one of Mindanao's most important universities. His experience navigating
questions of oversight, transparency, and institutional integrity in a conflict-affected region was, in retrospect,
direct preparation for the "Moral Governance" framework he would later champion as a government minister.
SCHOLARLY CONTRIBUTIONS
Barra's publications do real work in the world. His 1988 book, The Code of Muslim Personal Laws: A Study of
Islamic Law in the Philippines, published with support from the Asia Foundation, remains a standard reference for
practitioners in both the Shari'ah Bar and the regular judiciary. It is regularly cited in Southeast Asian legal
scholarship on the subject of legal pluralism.
In 2004, he published A Primer on the Code of Muslim Personal Laws of the Philippines, a more accessible
companion text aimed at community leaders and organizers who needed to understand their rights under PD 1083
without wading through dense legal prose. Then in 2007, he co-authored The Code of Muslim Personal Laws in
Practice: What Influential Muslims and Shari'ah Lawyers Think with the Social Weather Stations, an empirical
survey that mapped the gap between what the law said on paper and what actually happened in practice. That study
identified specific cultural and institutional barriers blocking effective implementation of Shari'ah in the
Philippines, the kind of evidence-based research that tends to outlast any particular administration.
Barra has also been a consistent advocate for Meranao and Bangsamoro legal scholarship more broadly. In his
foreword to a published legal text by a fellow Meranao attorney, he observed that publications by Muslim legal
scholars are still rare, and that the growth of a local legal literature grounded in Shari'ah is essential to building
what he calls "lasting peace through a regime of law."

PAGE 4
THE PEACE PROCESS
The years 2011 and 2012 marked Barra's move from the academy to the negotiating table. President Benigno
Aquino III appointed him as a member of the Government of the Philippines (GPH) Peace Negotiating Panel,
tasked with reviving talks with the Moro Islamic Liberation Front (MILF) after years of stalled progress. It was
high-stakes work. Previous agreements had failed constitutional scrutiny, and there was deep skepticism on all
sides about whether a durable settlement was possible.
Barra's contribution to those negotiations drew directly from his expertise in comparative law. He helped articulate
the concept of an "asymmetric relationship" between the central government and the Bangsamoro political entity, a
framework that would later be embedded in the Bangsamoro Organic Law. His skill was in framing the Moro
conflict not as a religious or sectarian war but as a legal and historical grievance with a constitutional remedy. He
argued persistently that the tensions in Mindanao would only begin to unravel through a legal architecture that
honestly acknowledged the distinct identity and history of the Moro people.
Following the signing of the Comprehensive Agreement on the Bangsamoro (CAB) in 2014, Barra transitioned into
consultancy roles with the Asian Development Bank and The Asia Foundation, focusing on Islamic culture and
transitional justice. These engagements kept him in the process and gave him a platform to ensure that the Shari'ah
dimension of the transition was not sidelined by international development partners more comfortable with secular
governance models.
MINISTER OF HUMAN SETTLEMENTS AND DEVELOPMENT
When BARMM was formally inaugurated in 2019, Barra was appointed as the inaugural Minister of the Ministry
of Human Settlements and Development. It was a fitting assignment. His career had long circled around questions
of land, identity, and the right of a people to live on their own terms in their own home. The MHSD's mandate
covers housing, human settlements, and urban and rural development, with particular focus on the Bangsamoro's
post-conflict context.
Under Barra's leadership, the ministry has concentrated on three areas: housing for displaced persons and former
combatants, the rehabilitation of Marawi City, and the establishment of ethical standards, what he calls "Moral
Governance," in land administration.
The Marawi Rehabilitation Program has been the most emotionally charged of these responsibilities. Barra
oversaw the construction of 200 housing units in Barangay Matampay Kormatan and the installation of solar-
powered street lights in internally displaced persons (IDP) shelters throughout the city. He has been deliberate
about the quality of these interventions. The solar lights, for instance, use monocrystalline technology chosen for
its 20% performance advantage and five-year lifespan, a detail that reflects Barra's consistent "sustainability first"
disposition. Under his watch, the MHSD has been recognized in published BARMM key milestones for its
achievements in housing development, disaster response, and environmental protection.
Barra has also guided the MHSD in partnerships with Islamic financial institutions. During the signing of a
memorandum of agreement with Al-Amanah Bank, he reminded participants that the ministry answers not only to
taxpayers and government but, as he put it, to "Allah SWT above all." That framing is not rhetorical ornamentation
for Barra. It is the theological foundation of his approach to public accountability.
By the close of his first ministerial term, the MHSD had completed 1,107 housing units under his watch, each one
representing, in his view, a concrete fulfillment of the government's commitment to the people it serves.

PAGE 5
LEGISLATIVE WORK
During his term as a Member of Parliament from 2019 to 2022, Barra authored several bills and resolutions aimed
at consolidating the legal gains of the peace process. His most consequential legislative effort is Parliament Bill
No. 146, "An Act Providing for the Bangsamoro Code of Muslim Personal Laws," a direct outgrowth of the
research he began at IIUM in the 1980s. The bill seeks to update or replace Presidential Decree No. 1083 with a
code better suited to the autonomous powers of the BARMM. As of late 2021, the bill remained at the First
Reading stage, a reminder of how slowly institutional change moves even in favorable political conditions.
Barra also took a principled and publicly visible stand on Proposed Resolution No. 569, which called on the
President to veto a national law prohibiting child marriage. His argument was jurisdictional rather than an
endorsement of the practice: that the Bangsamoro government should be empowered to address sensitive matters of
family and personal relations through its own Islamized legal codes, rather than having uniform national laws
imposed on communities with distinct religious traditions and governance frameworks.
His committee assignments, covering Human Settlements and Development, the Special Committee on Marawi,
and Basic, Higher, and Technical Education, reflect the full range of his expertise and his commitment to applying
it where it is most needed.
MORAL GOVERNANCE AND THE ULAMA
A theme that runs through every phase of Barra's career is the relationship between faith and public administration.
He has been a prominent leader within the National Ulama Conference of the Philippines (NUCP), consistently
arguing that religious scholars must serve as the moral compass of any genuinely Islamic governance project.
In his messages to the NUCP, Barra describes the Ulama as the inheritors of prophetic responsibility, the people
most obligated to model integrity in public life. He believes their unity is not merely desirable but an
"indispensable requisite" for the Bangsamoro experiment to succeed. This is not abstract theology for him. It
shapes the way he runs his ministry, from the language he uses at contract signings, where he is known to cite
Qur'anic verses on the importance of written agreements, to the values he invokes when public funds are at stake.
INTERNATIONAL ENGAGEMENT
Barra has represented the Bangsamoro at forums and conferences around the world, consistently framing the Moro
experience as a case study in resolving sub-national conflicts through law rather than force. In 2009, he participated
in both the Parliament of the World's Religions in Melbourne and the Asia-Europe Meeting on Interfaith Dialogue
in Seoul. In 2011, he presented a paper on "Peace and Reconciliation: the Case of Muslim Mindanao" at the World
Peace Conference in Hiroshima.
In May 2024, during commemorations of the 60th anniversary of diplomatic relations between the Philippines and
Malaysia, Barra delivered a presentation at the Islamic Arts Museum in Kuala Lumpur tracing the history of Islam
in the Philippines from pre-colonial times through the establishment of BARMM. His intent was to reframe
international perceptions of the Moro conflict: not a sectarian war, but a centuries-long struggle for legal and
cultural recognition by a people with a distinct identity predating the Philippine Republic.
Through the Bishops-Ulama Conference (BUC), Barra has also spent decades building relationships with Christian
leaders, grounding interfaith dialogue in shared human values rather than theological debate.

PAGE 6
MEDIA AND PUBLIC COMMUNICATION
Long before his career in government, Barra was a familiar public voice in Marawi and surrounding provinces.
From 1979 to 2007, he was a regular lecturer on DXSO Radio ng Bayan and Marawi Cable TV, particularly during
Ramadhan, offering legal and spiritual guidance to the community in accessible, conversational language.
In the 1970s and 1980s, he also worked as an editor for community publications including SINAR and SINDAO.
These were not simply newspapers. In communities where literacy was a political act and local issues rarely found
coverage in national media, these papers gave Meranao readers a platform in their own language, on their own
terms. That early grounding in grassroots communication has stayed with Barra throughout his ministerial work.
He emphasizes post-distribution monitoring and house-to-house visits at MHSD projects, the same instinct to
check whether the work is actually reaching people.
LEGACY
Hamid Aminoddin D. Barra's life work is, at its core, about making the Bangsamoro home real: legally, physically,
morally. He has done this through academic research that gave Shari'ah practitioners a workable roadmap, through
peace negotiations that helped build the constitutional architecture for regional autonomy, through legislation that
seeks to anchor Bangsamoro identity in law, and through a ministry that has put thousands of families under a roof
they can call their own.
His approach to public service has always been defined by a "rule of law with a heart," the insistence that legal
rigor and human compassion are not opposites but necessary partners. As BARMM moves toward its first regular
parliamentary elections, the institutions Barra helped build, the court procedures, the legal codes, the housing
frameworks, will face the test of durability that outlasts any individual administration. His career suggests those
foundations are built to last.

Jamaloden Basar
Atty. Jamaloden A. Basar is a Bangsamoro lawyer, educator, and
academic administrator who currently serves as
Superintendent/Chancellor of the Mindanao State University Maigo
College of Education, Science and Technology (MSU-MCEST) in
Maigo, Lanao del Norte, Philippines.
He brings more than three decades of combined legal and
administrative experience to the role, having served in various
capacities across the MSU System, from campus-level publication
work all the way up to the system-wide vice presidency for
administration and finance.
Basar is perhaps best known for leading the historic transformation of
the MSU Maigo School of Arts and Trades (MSU-MSAT) into a full
college, a milestone that had never been achieved in that campus's
history, and for building a culture of academic excellence that has
produced some of the country's top-performing teachers in the
Licensure Examination for Teachers (LET).

PAGE 2
Early Life and Background
Jamaloden A. Basar was born and raised in Madalum, a municipality in the interior of Lanao del Sur, the heartland
of the Maranao people and one of the predominantly Muslim provinces in Mindanao.
Growing up in Madalum instilled in him the values that would define his career: a grounded sense of community, a
drive to prove that young people from rural Bangsamoro areas could compete and excel on the national stage, and a
practical understanding of what inclusive public service really means.
He completed his elementary education at Madalum Central Elementary School (MCES) in Madalum, Lanao del
Sur, from 1976 to 1982, graduating with honors.
Education
Secondary
Basar pursued his secondary education at the MSU University Training Center (MSU-UTC) in Marawi City,
completing the course from 1982 to 1986.
He distinguished himself early, earning recognition as an Outstanding Student and Leadership Awardee, a fitting
preview of the institutional leadership roles he would eventually take on.
Tertiary
For his undergraduate degree, he stayed within the MSU ecosystem, enrolling at MSU Main Campus in Marawi
City, where he pursued a Bachelor of Arts in Political Science from 1986 to 1990.
He graduated as a consistent academic scholar, a recognition reserved for students who maintained strong academic
standing across all semesters.
The political science foundation proved especially useful later in his career, giving him a solid grounding in
governance theory, public administration, and legal philosophy that complemented his eventual legal training.
Juris Doctor
After finishing his undergraduate degree, Basar took up law at the MSU Main College of Law in Marawi City,
completing the Juris Doctor program from 1991 to 1994.
He graduated as a Dean's Lister, placing him among the top students in his law class.
He later passed the Philippine Bar Examinations administered by the Supreme Court of the Philippines in October
2009, earning the right to practice law and subsequently becoming a member of the Integrated Bar of the
Philippines (IBP).

PAGE 3
Career
Early Career: Publications and Administration at MSU (1994--2012)
Basar's professional life began not in the courtroom but in the newsroom, or at least the campus publication office.
From 1994 to 2004, he served as Information Officer II and Head of the Official Publication at the Office of the
President of Mindanao State University in Marawi City.
This decade-long stint was formative. Managing a university's official publication required not just writing skills
but institutional awareness, diplomatic communication, and a nose for what matters in academic governance. It
was, in many ways, an extended apprenticeship in understanding how a complex university system actually works
from the inside.
From 2004 to 2012, he moved into administrative work, serving as Administrative Officer IV at the same MSU
Office of the President.
In this role, he handled executive-level administrative tasks under the university's top leadership, gaining direct
exposure to how major institutional decisions were made, how budgets were managed, and how the MSU System
as a whole was run.
Private Practice and Legal Work (2012--2016)
Between 2012 and 2016, Basar transitioned into a period of parallel engagements that combined private law
practice with institutional legal work.
He managed the Basar Law Office, based in New Capitol, Bangon, Marawi City, where he handled cases and legal
matters as a practicing attorney.
Simultaneously, he served as Legal Counsel and Member of the Board of Directors at the Philippine Integrated
School in Marawi City, and as Head Legal Counsel at the Masiricampo Abantas Memorial Islamic and Science
Academy, also in Marawi City.
These concurrent roles allowed him to build a reputation as a reliable legal mind within the Marawi and
Bangsamoro institutional community, particularly in the education sector.
University Legal Counsel, MSU Main Campus (2016--2017)
In 2016, Basar rejoined the MSU System in a formal capacity, this time as University Legal Counsel and Director
of the Legal Services Division at the MSU Main Campus Legal Office in Marawi City.
In this role, he successfully defended the university in various legal cases, protecting the institution's interests at a
time when higher education governance in the Philippines was increasingly subject to legal scrutiny and
accountability demands.
His tenure as legal counsel was brief, running only until 2017, but it solidified his standing within the MSU
hierarchy as both a capable lawyer and a trustworthy institutional insider.

PAGE 4
MSU System Vice President for Administration and Finance (2017--2021)
Basar's most senior executive role before his current assignment came when he was appointed SUC Vice-President
IV, serving as the MSU System's Vice President for Administration and Finance from 2017 to 2021.
At this level, he was responsible for overseeing the fiscal and administrative operations of the entire MSU System,
a sprawling network of constituent universities and colleges spread across Mindanao, Sulu, and Palawan.
One of his signature initiatives during this period was the conceptualization and launch of the Annual University
System-wide Finance Summit, a regular convening designed to promote sound fiscal management and operational
efficiency across all MSU campuses.
The Finance Summit was more than a meeting. It created a shared culture of fiscal accountability and best practices
among the diverse units of the MSU System, helping to standardize how resources were managed and reported
across campuses that often operated in very different local contexts.
During this period, he also served concurrently as Assistant Dean of the College of Law at the MSU-General
Santos Extension (2018--2020), and took on the chairmanship of the MSU System Athletic Association (MSU
SAA) beginning in 2018, a position he continues to hold.
Law Professor, MSU Main College of Law (2021--2022)
Following his tenure as VP for Administration and Finance, Basar served as a Law Professor at the MSU Main
College of Law in Marawi City from 2021 to 2022.
Teaching law at the institution where he himself had been a Dean's Lister completed a meaningful circle in his
professional story, one that moved from student to executive administrator to teacher.
Superintendent/Chancellor, MSU-MCEST (2024--Present)
In 2024, Basar was designated as Superintendent/Chancellor of what was then known as the MSU Maigo School of
Arts and Trades (MSU-MSAT), a constituent college of the MSU System located in Maigo, Lanao del Norte in
Northern Mindanao.
He inherited a campus with a solid tradition of technical and vocational education and the aspiration to grow into
something more comprehensive.
Under his leadership, the campus undertook a historic institutional transformation: MSU-MSAT was formally
renamed the MSU Maigo College of Education, Science and Technology (MSU-MCEST), reflecting a major
expansion of its academic identity, programs, and ambitions.
This was a first in the campus's history. The new name signaled a shift away from the institution's original arts-and-
trades focus toward a broader mandate that now includes education programs, science disciplines, and technology-
oriented courses.
"MSU-MCEST is a globally recognized institution in education, science, and technology, committed to
advancing instruction, research, innovations, peace and development."
The transformation was not merely cosmetic. It involved a rethinking of what the campus could offer to the
communities of Northern Mindanao and the broader Bangsamoro region, and what kind of graduates it wanted to
produce for an increasingly complex world.

PAGE 5
Academic Excellence and the LET Topnotchers
One of the most visible markers of MSU-MCEST's rise under Basar's stewardship is its consistent production of
national topnotchers in the Licensure Examination for Teachers (LET).
Since his involvement with the campus, MSU-MCEST has placed graduates in the Top 10 of the LET multiple
times: Top 1 in 2025, Top 4 in 2024, Top 2 in 2022, and Top 7 in 2017, all national rankings across the entire
Philippines.
For a campus the size and relative remoteness of MSU-MCEST, these results are extraordinary. They reflect not
just strong individual students, but the kind of systematic investment in instruction quality, faculty development,
and student preparation that takes years to build.
The Commission on Higher Education (CHED) formally recognized the campus's achievement in 2022, awarding a
Certificate of Recognition for excellence in instruction and training that resulted in a graduate placing in the Top 10
of the June 2022 LET (Elementary). This recognition is part of the broader track record Basar has been building at
the campus level since his connection to it.
International Engagements
Beyond campus administration, Basar has represented the MSU System and MSU-MCEST on several international
platforms.
He led a delegation to Malaysia in 2018 for the establishment of academic linkages in Malacca, and represented
Mindanao State University at Universiti Sains Malaysia in Penang in 2017.
As Superintendent of MSU-MCEST, he has delivered official remarks during Memorandum of Understanding
(MOU) signing ceremonies at Universitas Tanjungpura in Malaysia and at Tan Trao University in Vietnam,
expanding the campus's network of international academic partnerships.
He has also served as a keynote speaker at various international academic institutions, positioning MSU-MCEST as
a credible participant in regional higher education dialogue.
Research and Publications
Basar has pursued scholarly work alongside his administrative responsibilities.
He authored a research study entitled "Digital Marketing and Islamic Financing Among Muslim Women Micro-
entrepreneurs for Sustainable Peace and Development," a work that sits at the intersection of economic
empowerment, Islamic finance principles, and the ongoing peace-and-development agenda in Mindanao.
He also presented this research paper at an academic forum and received a Certificate of Appreciation for the
presentation, signaling peer recognition of the study's contribution to the field.
He has participated in the 12th ASEAN Universities International Conference on Islamic Finance (AICIF), among
other academic and professional convening, further deepening his engagement with Islamic finance as both a
scholarly and practical domain.

PAGE 6
Legal Practice and Professional Membership
Basar is a member of the Integrated Bar of the Philippines (IBP), having successfully passed the Bar Examinations
given by the Supreme Court of the Philippines in October 2009.
He is also a member of the Mu Kappa Phi National Exclusive Law Fraternity, a brotherhood of legal professionals
dedicated to excellence, integrity, and service in the legal profession.
Recognition and Awards
Over the course of his career, Basar has received a wide range of formal recognitions from government agencies,
academic institutions, and community organizations.
He was issued a Certificate of Commendation of Merit by Mindanao State University (MSU) for his service as part
of the MSU Crisis Team during the Marawi Siege, a particularly significant recognition given the gravity of that
conflict and the extraordinary demands placed on MSU personnel during and after the siege.
The Commission on Higher Education (CHED) awarded him a Certificate of Recognition for excellence in
instruction and training in connection with the 2022 LET topnotcher produced by MSU-MCEST.
The Local Government Unit of Maigo honored him with both a Plaque of Recognition for lifetime achievement
and the Most Outstanding Maigohanon Award for exemplary service, lasting accomplishments, and dedication to
public welfare, recognitions that reflect how deeply his work has been felt in the local community of Maigo.
The National Intelligence Coordinating Agency (NICA) awarded him a Certificate of Commendation for his
contribution to an Information Drive on Preventing Violent Extremism and CTG Awareness, underscoring his
engagement with national security and counter-radicalization efforts.
He received a Plaque of Recognition from the MSU System for participation in the Rawaten Cultural Gala during
the 63rd System Foundation Celebration, and a Plaque of Appreciation for support during the 60th Founding
Anniversary of MSU.
The Department of Health (DOH) recognized him for his support of the Voluntary Blood Donation program, and
the Department of Information and Communications Technology (DICT) recognized MSU-MCEST under his
leadership as an institutional partner of the ICT Literacy and Competency Development Bureau (ILCDB).
TESDA Region X acknowledged the campus's participation in the 2023 Regional Skills Competition in Northern
Mindanao, and MSU-IIT NMPC honored him for collaboration in support of inclusive financial services aligned
with the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs).
The MSU-MSAT Faculty Union awarded him a Plaque of Appreciation for exceptional leadership and
contributions to the campus's academic and physical development, and MSU-MSAT itself issued multiple Plaques
of Commendation recognizing his stewardship from his earliest days as campus head.
Regional recognition also came when Basar was identified by the Regional Development Council of Region X as
one of the Outstanding Young Leaders in Northern Mindanao in 2021.<ref name="msumsat-officials">Campus
Officials. MSU Maigo. Retrieved from https://msumsat.edu.ph/home/campus-officials.php</ref>
In 2022, he was reportedly conferred the prestigious Ten Outstanding Young Men (TOYM) award, which
recognizes Filipinos who have made significant contributions in their respective fields and communities.<ref
name="msumsat-officials" />

PAGE 7
Community and Institutional Service
Basar's record of service extends beyond the walls of academia.
He has served as a guest speaker at the MSU University Training Center's (MSU-UTC) 10th Completion Exercise,
connecting with the secondary-level institution that shaped his own early formation.
He has been involved in the ASEAN 2022 Commemorative Event and Cultural Showcase, participating in regional
cultural and diplomatic engagement.
His campus has also partnered with multiple agencies for skills training, blood donation drives, anti-extremism
information campaigns, and ICT literacy programs, reflecting a philosophy that a university's responsibility doesn't
end at the campus gate.
Legacy
Atty. Jamaloden A. Basar's career is a study in institutional loyalty and steady, earned advancement.
He didn't arrive at the chancellorship of MSU-MCEST from the outside. He grew up within the MSU System,
learned its rhythms as a publications officer, mastered its administrative mechanics, defended it in court, managed
its finances at the system level, and taught in its law school. By the time he was entrusted with transforming one of
its campuses, he already knew the institution from nearly every angle possible.
The transformation of MSU-MSAT into MSU-MCEST, the first such institutional elevation in that campus's
history, stands as his most visible legacy to date. But the LET topnotchers, the international partnerships, the
community recognitions, and the faculty tributes paint a fuller picture: a leader who understands that transforming
an institution means transforming the people inside it, and that the most durable measure of a campus leader's work
is what his graduates go on to do.
His story also carries meaning within the Bangsamoro context. A Maranao from Madalum, Lanao del Sur, who rose
through the MSU System to become its VP for Finance and then a campus chancellor, Basar represents the kind of
upward trajectory that the MSU System was originally designed to make possible for young Muslims in Mindanao.

Yassin Guro Hadji Basher
Yassin Guro Hadji Basher (born September 29, 1995) is a Filipino
public servant, educator, and writer from Lumba-Bayabao, Lanao
del Sur. He is recognized for his research on Maranao folk wisdom
and native healing practices, his contributions to local literature, and
his service to the community.
Contents
1 Early Life and Education
2 Career
3 Cultural and Literary Contributions
4 Community Service
5 Legacy
Early Life and Education
Basher was born in Lumba-Bayabao, Lanao del Sur. He studied at
Mindanao State University in Marawi City, where he completed his
undergraduate thesis on the folk wisdom (katunungan-bayan) of his
hometown. He later earned his Master’s degree with the thesis
Lakam at Tawar: A Native Healing Practice, which won the Best
Thesis award. He became a licensed professional teacher in 2019
and taught at Kakai Dayagun Dagalangit National High School. He
is currently pursuing his Doctor of Philosophy (PhD) at the same
university.
Career
Basher serves as a Barangay Kagawad in Bacolod II, Lumba-
Bayabao. He was also recognized as the Community Head of a
Learning Hub during the COVID-19 pandemic, the only hub in Lanao supported by the Angat Buhay program of
former Vice President Leni Robredo. His advocacy centers on ensuring that no child is left behind in education,
emphasizing both academic learning and character development.
Cultural and Literary Contributions
In 2021, Basher joined the Datu a Bantogen sa Ranao competition, where he was named 3rd runner-up and
received the “Best History Award.” His team was also nominated for Best in Advocacy, Editing, and Direction. He
has published works including the essay UPUAN (Chair) through Lakbay-Diwa Publishing and the poem PARA
SAYO (For You) through Pinagpala Publishing Services. He continues to write poems, haikus, short stories, and
essays, believing that Maranao literature is the heartbeat of history and the pillar of identity.

PAGE 2
Community Service
Basher emphasizes patience, compassion, and conviction in public service. He believes that true leadership is
shown in listening to people, addressing local problems, and raising the standard of living despite limited
resources. His projects and initiatives in the barangay reflect his commitment to grassroots change, rooted in
culture and community solidarity.
Legacy
Basher aspires to highlight the cultural richness of Lumba-Bayabao and share Maranao heritage with the wider
world. His work in education, literature, and public service reflects his dedication to preserving identity and
fostering community growth.

Atty. Amoran Mai Batara
Atty. Amoran Mai Batara is a Filipino lawyer, retired Assistant
Regional Prosecutor, businessman, public servant, and traditional
Maranao leader known for his work in law, governance,
entrepreneurship, and the preservation of Maranao culture. He
served for years at the Department of Justice and is widely
respected in the Bangsamoro region for his stand against corruption,
having built a long career without compromising his integrity for
personal gain.
He carries the traditional title of Raja Muda of Madaya, a position
tied to Maranao customary governance, through which he continues
to promote unity and the preservation of cultural heritage among
Maranao communities.
Contents
1 Early Life and Education
2 Bar Examination and Legal Career
3 Business and Entrepreneurship
4 Integrity and Anti-Corruption Advocacy
5 Public Service and National Involvement
6 Traditional Leadership and Cultural Stewardship
7 Family
8 Legacy
9 See Also
Early Life and Education
Atty. Batara was born into a family already known for leadership
and public service in the Lanao region. He is the nephew of former
Marawi City Mayor Sheikh Macapado Batara, and grew up
surrounded by examples of civic responsibility. He was a consistent
honor student from an early age, and that early discipline carried
him through the rest of his academic life.
He completed his undergraduate studies at the Philippine School of
Business Administration (PSBA), where he picked up the
foundations that would later serve him just as well in business as
they did in law. Pursuing a legal education afterward wasn't easy for
him: he was juggling business responsibilities and family life at the
same time, but he pushed through and eventually graduated Cum
Laude from law school, a result that reflected both his intellect and
his sheer persistence.

PAGE 2
Integrity in public office, legal advocacy,
business leadership, and Maranao
cultural stewardship as Raja Muda of
Madaya
Bar Examination and Legal Career
Atty. Batara passed the Philippine Bar Examination during what's
remembered as one of the toughest periods in the exam's history, a
stretch when passing rates were unusually low. He is recognized as
the first Maranao graduate of the Western Mindanao State University (WMSU) College of Law to pass the Bar, a
milestone that meant a great deal to the institution at a time when confidence in its law program needed exactly that
kind of boost. His success is still pointed to as an inspiration for law students from Mindanao who came after him.
Once admitted to the Bar, he built a reputation as a fair and capable lawyer. He served as a Notary Public in
Marawi City, assisting individuals, families, and organizations with their legal needs. His practice eventually
extended to Zamboanga City, where he represented traders and business groups, helping them navigate legal
matters and protect their interests.
He later joined the Department of Justice, serving as an Assistant Regional Prosecutor until his retirement.
Throughout his time there, colleagues knew him for handling cases with independence and fairness, the kind of
prosecutor who didn't bend to outside pressure. His retirement closed out a career spent largely in service of a
stronger, more accountable justice system.
Business and Entrepreneurship
Alongside his legal career, Atty. Batara built and managed his own business ventures, doing so while raising a
family and studying law at the same time. That balancing act is part of what people in his community point to when
describing him: someone who didn't choose between his ambitions, but pursued all of them together. His business
success, paired with the way he conducted himself ethically while building it, earned him recognition as one of the
respected businessmen in his community.
Integrity and Anti-Corruption Advocacy
If there's one thing people consistently bring up about Atty. Batara, it's his refusal to take shortcuts. He has long
held the view that success and public service don't require compromising one's integrity, and he's known for turning
down gifts, favors, commissions, or any benefit that might call his judgment into question.
That reputation followed him through both his legal practice and his time in government, where colleagues and
community members alike came to see him as someone whose decisions were guided by principle rather than
convenience. For Atty. Batara, leadership has never been about wealth or influence: it's about character, plain and
simple.
Public Service and National Involvement
Atty. Batara was also known as a trusted associate and supporter of the late Fernando Poe Jr. (FPJ), sharing his
vision for honest governance and a government that actually serves ordinary Filipinos. He was identified among
the nominees associated with FPJPM, reflecting a broader commitment to nation-building and public welfare that
went beyond his work in the courtroom.

PAGE 3
Traditional Leadership and Cultural Stewardship
As Raja Muda of Madaya, Atty. Batara holds a customary leadership role centered on preserving Maranao
traditions and cultural heritage. In this capacity, he works to promote peace, unity, and cooperation among families
and communities, often serving as a bridge between traditional governance structures and the demands of modern
public life.
Family
Atty. Batara is married to Bae Hadja Naderah Sampaco Ali-Batara, daughter of Sultan Bato R. Ali Sr., the former
Mayor of Dansalan (now Marawi City) and founder of the Marawi Sultanate League. Their marriage joined two
families with deep roots in Maranao leadership, education, and public service.
Together, they have eight children and several grandchildren, many of whom remain active in community work,
education, and cultural preservation, carrying forward the values their parents and grandparents instilled in them.
Legacy
Atty. Amoran Mai Batara's life reflects a rare combination of legal excellence, business acumen, ethical conviction,
and cultural commitment. From his historic Bar Examination achievement to his decades of service at the
Department of Justice, and from his business ventures to his role as Raja Muda of Madaya, his story is often cited
as proof that one can rise through hard work and education without ever giving up one's principles.
His example continues to resonate, particularly with young Filipinos from Mindanao, as a reminder that
perseverance, faith, and integrity can carry someone a long way.

title: Benito, Pangadapun
text:
PAGE 1
Pangadapun Benito
Sultan Pangadapun Benito is one of Mindanao's most compelling bridge figures: a man who wore the crown of
royal lineage and the badge of public office with equal commitment. Recognized as the first Meranao sultan of the
Maguindanao Sultanate and counted among the Top 50 Model Sultans of the Iranun people, he left his mark not
through conquest but through the quieter, harder work of peacemaking, political statecraft, and community
building.
He's the founding mayor of Balabagan in Lanao del Sur, a municipality that literally came into being because he
and a rival chose governance over conflict. His story is a case study in how royal tradition and democratic politics
can work together instead of pulling in opposite directions.
Contents
1 Background and Royal Lineage
2 Early Life
3 Political Career and the Founding of Balabagan
4 Peacemaking and Governance
5 Enthronement as Sultan
6 Family and Continuing Legacy
7 Recognition
8 External Links
Background and Royal Lineage
Sultan Pangadapun Benito came from deep roots. He was born and raised in Upper Unayan, a region in what is
now Lanao del Sur, and his genealogy drew from some of the most prominent royal houses in the area: Pagayawan,
Picong, Tubok, and Ganassi.
His father, Macabalang (known affectionately as "Amai Pangadapun"), was himself descended from local rulers of
west Unayan. His mother, often identified as Bae P'ki or from the Maguindanao royal line, connected him directly
to an even older chain of sultans.
Genealogical accounts trace him as a descendant of the 16th Sultan of Maguindanao, Kibad Sahriyal Benito,
through Sultan Alamansa Dolkarnain and Sultan Qudratullah Untong, the 18th Sultan. This lineage blended Iranun-
Meranao and Maguindanaon traditions, reflecting the historical reality that coastal Lanao areas once fell under the
broader Maguindanao Sultanate before distinct local sultanates took shape.
In short, his royal blood wasn't just one thing. It was a living record of the region's interconnected histories.
Early Life
The historical record on his formal schooling is sparse, but accounts consistently describe him as someone who
grew up grounded in the principles of taritib (customary law) and igma (consensus-based decision-making). These
weren't just cultural accessories. They were the practical tools of leadership in his community, and he developed
them early.

PAGE 2
Sultan Pangadapun Benito

Described as diligent and humble, he carried himself less like a man
born to privilege and more like someone who understood that lineage
comes with responsibility. That sense of duty shaped everything that
followed.
Political Career and the Founding of
Balabagan
Sultan Pangadapun's entry into electoral politics came in the post-war
period, when he ran for mayor of the then-undivided municipality of
Malabang in Lanao del Sur. His opponent wasn't a stranger. It was his
own cousin and childhood friend, Amer "Macaorao" Balindong, who
would later become Sultan of Picong.
The two had actually fought side by side as guerrilla allies during the
Japanese occupation, which made their political rivalry both deeply
personal and historically layered.
After Sultan Pangadapun lost the initial race, the situation risked
becoming something much darker. In Mindanao, political contests
between influential clans can tip quickly into rido (clan feud). Two
senior statesmen stepped in: Congressman Rashid Lucman and
Senator Domocao Alonto. Their solution was pragmatic and creative.
Instead of forcing one man to lose, they worked to carve out a new
municipality and give both leaders their own ground to govern.
Republic Act No. 5978 was passed on July 5, 1969, officially
establishing Balabagan as a separate municipality, with its effectivity
recognized retroactively from March 16, 1960. Sultan Pangadapun
Benito was appointed its first mayor.
He served unopposed in subsequent elections and eventually retired,
having built Balabagan from the ground up during some of the most
turbulent years in Mindanao's modern history.
Peacemaking and Governance
Being mayor of a newly carved municipality wasn't just an
administrative role. Balabagan was dealing with its own internal
tensions, including a serious rido that had already claimed lives and
fractured the community.
Sultan Pangadapun didn't sidestep the problem. Working alongside
Senator Alonto and other respected datus, he helped broker a
reconciliation that brought the feuding parties back to the table. This
was the kind of leadership his community needed most: someone
who could speak the language of adat (tradition) and the language of
governance at the same time.

PAGE 3
1960)
Distinctions
Top 50 Model Sultans of the Iranun People;
Recognized by royal houses of Sulu, Brunei,
and Johor
Notability

Maguindanao Sultanate; founding and first
mayor of Balabagan, Lanao del Sur;
peacemaker who resolved deadly clan
conflict through dialogue and customary
mediation
Known For
Founding Balabagan through political
statesmanship; brokering peace during a life-
claiming rido; embodying unity across
Meranao, Iranun, and Maguindanaon
communities; passing a legacy of public
service to his descendants
Pull Quote
"He turned rivalry into opportunity and
conflict into covenant — a royal who led not
by title alone, but by the steadiness of his
character."
He used dialogue, customary mediation, and the weight of his
political and royal standing to restore peace. It wasn't glamorous
work, but it held.
Enthronement as Sultan
Around 1960, Sultan Pangadapun Benito was formally enthroned as
Sultan of Maguindanao, referenced in some accounts as the 24th in
certain lines of succession. His recognition came not just from within
Lanao del Sur but from royal houses in Sulu, Brunei, and Johor, as
well as from broader Philippine leadership circles.
His title carried real weight because it represented unity across three
historically connected communities: the Meranao, the Iranun, and the
Maguindanaon. He was acknowledged as the first Meranao sultan
within the Maguindanao Sultanate, a distinction that reflected not just
his bloodline but the respect he had earned through decades of
service, humility, and principled leadership.
Family and Continuing Legacy
Sultan Pangadapun and his wife, Hadji Mariam Dari-Benito, raised a
family that carried the tradition of public service into the next
generation. Their son, Engr. Macapado M. Benito Sr., born in 1953 in
Pagayawan, followed a strikingly parallel path: he served as mayor of
Calanogas and was himself later crowned Sultan of Maguindanao.
The sultanate didn't end with one generation.
Today, descendants and local historians remember Sultan Pangadapun with warmth and admiration. He's held up as
proof that royal lineage in Mindanao isn't ceremonial nostalgia. It's a living framework for responsibility, for
mediation, and for keeping communities intact through transition and conflict.
Recognition
Sultan Pangadapun Benito was recognized among the Top 50 Model Sultans of the Iranun people, an
acknowledgment of both his character and his contributions to peace and governance in the Bangsamoro region.
His enthronement earned recognition from royal houses in Sulu, Brunei, and Johor, affirming the cross-cultural and
transnational respect he commanded among the region's royal institutions. These weren't honorary gestures. They
reflected a consensus, built over decades, that he embodied what the sultanate was always meant to be: a force for
unity, not division.

biographical data

text:

Nazh-Far Mariwa Berganio
Nazh-Far Mariwa Berganio is a Filipino humanitarian leader
and human rights advocate who has emerged as one of the most
prominent voices for internally displaced persons (IDPs) in the
Philippines and globally. He serves as the co-founder and
president of Ako Bakwit, Inc., a groundbreaking advocacy
organization dedicated to protecting the rights of families
displaced by conflict and disasters. In March 2026, he was
appointed to the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees
(UNHCR) Global IDP Advisory Group, making him one of only
12 global leaders tasked with shaping the UN's strategy on internal
displacement.
Berganio's signature advocacy philosophy centers on "dignity over
charity," pushing for systemic solutions that grant IDPs the same
rights and access to services as settled citizens rather than treating
displacement as a charity case. His Tausug heritage and personal
journey from Jolo, Sulu to becoming a globally recognized
humanitarian exemplify the resilience of displaced communities
and their fight for institutional recognition.
His most notable achievements include spearheading the
campaign for the IDP Rights Act in the Philippine Congress and
representing Filipino IDPs on the international stage through his
UNHCR appointment—a milestone celebrated by the Philippine
Commission on Human Rights (CHR) as a significant
breakthrough for Filipino representation in global humanitarian
governance.

2 Education and Professional Development
3 Career and Professional Expertise
3.1 Land Acquisition and Political Consultancy
3.2 Transition to Humanitarian Leadership

4.1 Ako Bakwit, Inc.
4.2 UNHCR Global IDP Advisory Group

PAGE 2

Early Life and Background
Berganio was born and raised in Jolo, Sulu, a municipality in the Bangsamoro region of the Philippines that has
long been affected by armed conflict and displacement. He belongs to the Tausug ethnic group, whose name means
"people of the current," indigenous to the Sulu Archipelago. Growing up in this conflict-affected region shaped his
understanding of the systemic challenges faced by displaced communities.
In 2006, seeking better opportunities beyond the limited prospects in his homeland, Berganio made a pivotal
decision to relocate to Manila. He arrived in the capital with only 10,000 pesos—a modest sum that underscored
the financial vulnerability common among internal migrants from conflict zones. This migration experience
became formative; he encountered urban discrimination and navigated the barriers that many IDPs face when
attempting to integrate into metropolitan areas. These early struggles with marginalization and limited resources
would later inform his advocacy work, giving him firsthand insight into the "invisible displacement" that occurs
when conflict-affected populations move to cities without formal support systems.
Education and Professional Development
Before dedicating himself full-time to humanitarian work, Berganio built a diverse professional career that
combined practical expertise with leadership development. His professional background includes extensive
experience in land acquisition and political consultancy, where he advised various local and national elected
officials across the Philippines. This work gave him valuable insights into governance structures, policy-making
processes, and the mechanics of political advocacy—skills that would prove essential in his later work advocating
for IDP rights legislation.
Berganio is an active member of JCI Philippines (Junior Chamber International), a global leadership development
organization focused on creating positive change through civic engagement. Within this network, he has earned the
distinguished title of JCI Senator (membership number #84363), a recognition given to individuals who have
demonstrated exceptional leadership and commitment to community service. His involvement in JCI Philippines
has expanded his network of civic leaders and provided him with platforms to amplify his advocacy on national
and regional stages.
While the available records do not specify formal tertiary education credentials, Berganio's professional trajectory
demonstrates a commitment to continuous learning through practical experience, mentorship networks, and
participation in leadership organizations that emphasize skill-building in areas such as public speaking, project
management, and social entrepreneurship.
Career and Professional Expertise
Berganio's career arc represents a deliberate transition from conventional professional work to dedicated
humanitarian service, though his earlier roles provided essential foundations for his advocacy work.

PAGE 3
Land Acquisition and Political Consultancy
Prior to founding Ako Bakwit, Berganio worked extensively in the field of land acquisition, navigating the complex
legal and bureaucratic processes involved in property rights and territorial disputes. This expertise proved
particularly relevant given that land tenure insecurity is a major issue for many IDP communities, especially those
living in informal settlements after displacement.
His work as a political consultant involved advising elected officials at both local government unit (LGU) and
national levels. This role required deep knowledge of Philippine governance structures, legislative processes, and
the art of coalition-building—competencies he would later deploy in his advocacy for the IDP Rights Act. Through
this work, he developed relationships with policymakers and gained credibility within political circles, positioning
him to effectively lobby for legislative reforms.
Transition to Humanitarian Leadership
The catalytic moment for Berganio's full-time shift to humanitarian work came during the COVID-19 pandemic,
when he recognized that existing government response mechanisms were failing to reach IDP communities. Many
families displaced by the Marawi siege of 2017 had resettled in the National Capital Region (NCR) and
CALABARZON, surviving through informal vending in areas like Quiapo and Baclaran. When pandemic
lockdowns disrupted their livelihoods, these families faced compounded vulnerabilities—lacking both the
economic safety nets available to formal workers and the community support systems they had left behind in
Mindanao.
Seeing this gap, Berganio co-founded Ako Bakwit with Samira Gutoc in 2020, transforming his professional skills
in political consultancy and advocacy into a focused mission to serve displaced populations.
Institutional Contributions
Ako Bakwit, Inc.
In 2020, Berganio co-founded Ako Bakwit, Inc. (literal translation: "I am an evacuee/displaced person") alongside
Samira Ali Gutoc, a prominent civic leader and former member of the Bangsamoro Transition Commission. The
organization was legally incorporated during the height of the COVID-19 pandemic to address the specific
vulnerabilities of IDP families, particularly those from the Marawi siege who had relocated to Metro Manila.
The founding partnership combined Gutoc's policy influence and national political platform with Berganio's
operational leadership and lived experience as a displaced person. While Gutoc serves as Chairperson and primary
public advocate, Berganio manages executive operations as President. This division of labor allowed the
organization to operate on two fronts simultaneously: Gutoc focused on media engagement and legislative
lobbying, while Berganio coordinated on-the-ground relief operations and built community organizing structures
among IDP populations.
Ako Bakwit gained rapid prominence for its work during the pandemic, when it:
Distributed emergency relief supplies to IDP families who were excluded from government aid programs due
to lack of proper documentation
Provided legal assistance to families facing eviction from informal settlements
Documented cases of discrimination against Muslim IDPs in accessing healthcare and social services
Advocated for the inclusion of IDPs in COVID-19 vaccination rollouts

PAGE 4
The organization operates through a network of "convenors" and regional coordinators, collaborating with groups
such as Kazalimbago and the Bangsamoro Watch Initiative to coordinate relief missions and legal aid for
displaced families across Mindanao and Metro Manila.
What distinguishes Ako Bakwit from traditional humanitarian organizations is its advocacy model, which
emphasizes rights-based approaches over charity-based relief. Rather than simply distributing aid, the
organization focuses on systemic advocacy: pushing for policy reforms, legal frameworks, and institutional
changes that address the root causes of IDP vulnerability.
UNHCR Global IDP Advisory Group
In March 2026, Berganio was appointed to the UNHCR Global IDP Advisory Group for the 2026–2027 term,
becoming one of only 12 global leaders selected to advise the United Nations on its strategy for addressing internal
displacement worldwide. This appointment represents a watershed moment both for Berganio personally and for
Filipino representation in international humanitarian governance.
The Advisory Group's mandate includes:
Providing strategic counsel to UNHCR on protection frameworks for IDPs
Identifying gaps in current international response mechanisms
Amplifying the voices of displaced communities in global policy discussions
Sharing best practices and innovative approaches from different regional contexts
Berganio's selection was based on his demonstrated leadership in grassroots advocacy, his ability to bridge
community organizing with policy influence, and his credibility as someone who brings lived experience of
displacement to international forums. The Philippine Commission on Human Rights (CHR) publicly celebrated his
appointment as a significant milestone for the country's participation in shaping global humanitarian norms.
In this role, Berganio brings a distinctly Asian and Filipino perspective to conversations often dominated by
African and Middle Eastern displacement contexts. He has emphasized the need for international frameworks to
better address "urban displacement"—when IDPs relocate to cities rather than refugee camps—and the unique
challenges of protracted displacement in contexts where armed conflict is localized rather than nationwide.
Achievements and Recognition
Policy Advocacy and Legislative Impact
Berganio is a principal advocate for the IDP Rights Act, a proposed legislation in the Philippine Congress that
would establish a comprehensive national framework for the protection and assistance of internally displaced
persons. The bill seeks to:
Define legal rights and entitlements for IDPs
Establish coordination mechanisms across government agencies
Create dedicated funding streams for displacement response
Mandate data collection on displacement to inform policy
His advocacy strategy has involved coalition-building across religious, ethnic, and political lines—bringing
together Muslim, Christian, and Indigenous leaders to present a unified front. He has testified before congressional
committees, organized community consultations to gather testimonies from displaced families, and worked with
legal experts to refine the bill's language.

PAGE 5
Cultural and National Significance
As a Tausug professional who has achieved international recognition, Berganio represents an important counter-
narrative to prevailing stereotypes about Muslim Mindanao communities. His success challenges reductive
portrayals of the Bangsamoro region and demonstrates the leadership potential of individuals from conflict-affected
areas when given platforms and resources.
The Philippine Commission on Human Rights has highlighted his UNHCR appointment as evidence that Filipino
civil society leaders can compete at the highest levels of global governance, particularly in specialized fields like
humanitarian protection.
Philosophy of "Dignity Over Charity"
Central to Berganio's advocacy is the principle of dignity over charity—a framework that rejects paternalistic
approaches to humanitarian aid in favor of rights-based empowerment. This philosophy manifests in several key
positions:
Legal recognition: IDPs should have formal legal status that entitles them to services, not discretionary
assistance
Political participation: Displaced communities should have voice in decisions affecting their lives,
including participation in peace processes and development planning
Economic integration: Rather than perpetual dependence on relief aid, IDPs need access to livelihood
programs, skills training, and formal employment
Social dignity: Humanitarian interventions should preserve the cultural identity and social cohesion of
displaced communities rather than imposing assimilationist models
This philosophy has influenced Ako Bakwit's programmatic approach, which prioritizes community organizing,
legal empowerment, and advocacy over traditional relief distribution.
Challenges and Criticisms
Like many advocacy organizations, Ako Bakwit and Berganio's leadership have faced various challenges and
criticisms:
Funding and Sustainability
As a relatively young organization founded during a global pandemic, Ako Bakwit has navigated significant
resource constraints. Unlike large international NGOs with stable institutional funding, the organization relies
heavily on individual donations, small grants, and volunteer labor. This financial precarity limits its ability to scale
operations and provide sustained support to displaced communities.
Political Sensitivities
Advocacy work on displacement in the Philippines inevitably intersects with contentious political issues—armed
conflict in Mindanao, the peace process with Moro groups, military operations, and government resettlement
programs. Berganio's work requires careful navigation of these sensitivities, particularly when critiquing
government policies while also seeking to collaborate with state agencies on legislative reforms.

PAGE 6
Some critics have questioned whether rights-based advocacy adequately addresses the immediate survival needs of
displaced families, arguing that legislative campaigns may not translate quickly enough into tangible improvements
in people's lives.
Representation Questions
While Berganio's Tausug identity and personal displacement experience lend authenticity to his advocacy, some
observers note that the IDP population in the Philippines is extremely diverse—including not just Muslim
Mindanao communities but also Indigenous peoples, Christian communities affected by natural disasters, and
urban poor populations displaced by development projects. There are ongoing discussions about ensuring that
advocacy organizations adequately represent this diversity rather than centering primarily on conflict-related
displacement in Muslim areas.

Dr. Alma Elape Berowa: From Scholar of Psychology
to Steward of a University System in Times of Crisis
Introduction: A Life Shaped by Place and Purpose
In Philippine higher education, attention often centers on institutions in Metro Manila, where resources and policy
converge. However, in Mindanao, a different kind of leadership has quietly emerged—one built on endurance,
cultural understanding, and crisis navigation.
Dr. Alma Elape Berowa exemplifies this leadership. Her career spans over four decades within the Mindanao State
University (https://www.msumain.edu.ph/) (MSU) System, where she progressed from a young instructor in 1980
to the longest-serving Vice President for Academic Affairs, a role she held from 2011 until her retirement in 2025¹.
Her journey is intertwined with MSU's mission to bridge cultures, educate marginalized communities, and provide
stability in a diverse and conflict-prone region.
Understanding Dr. Berowa means recognizing how academic leadership can transcend classrooms and
administrative roles, becoming a service that directly addresses societal realities.
Early Life: Foundations of Excellence in Gigaquit
Dr. Berowa was born on September 16, 1960, in Gigaquit, Surigao del Norte. Her upbringing in the Caraga region
shaped her early experiences and ambitions. Even as a child, she demonstrated academic discipline, graduating as
salutatorian in elementary school and valedictorian in high school.
These achievements reflected her commitment and focus. In a provincial setting with limited opportunities,
academic distinction required intelligence, persistence, and clarity of purpose.

PAGE 2
