Her transition to Mindanao State University marked a turning
point. MSU, established to integrate the country's diverse cultural
communities, became the institutional home where her intellectual
and professional identity took shape.
Education: The Making of a Social
Psychologist
Dr. Berowa entered MSU as a full scholar and completed her
Bachelor of Arts in Psychology, graduating cum laude in 1980.
Her undergraduate training, which included a minor in sociology,
provided her with an interdisciplinary perspective that became
central to her work. Rather than viewing human behavior in
isolation, she approached it as something deeply embedded in
social structures, cultural practices, and lived experiences.
She pursued graduate studies in education, beginning at the
University of the Philippines (https://up.edu.ph) Diliman before
completing her Master of Arts in Education, major in Guidance
and Counseling, at MSU. This combination of psychology and
education reflected a dual commitment: understanding human
behavior and applying that understanding in institutional and
community contexts.
Her academic journey culminated with a Doctor of Philosophy in
Psychology, major in Social Psychology, from Ateneo de Manila
University between 1990 and 1996. This period of advanced study
deepened her engagement with questions of identity, conflict, and
social interaction—issues that would later become central to her
research and leadership, especially within the context of
Mindanao.
Her education was a deliberate shaping of a scholar whose work
would intersect with pressing social issues in the region.
Academic Career: Rising Through the
Ranks
Dr. Berowa began her academic career in 1980 as an Instructor I
in the Department of Psychology at MSU. Over four decades, she
advanced through the academic ranks, becoming Full Professor
VI in 2000 and attaining the distinction of University Professor in
2022.
Her rise was cumulative, built on years of teaching, research, and
service. Her long tenure allowed her to develop familiarity with
the institution's culture and challenges. She was shaped by the
system and, in turn, shaped it.

PAGE 3
Position
Vice President for Academic
Affairs, MSU System
Tenure
2011 to 2025
Her work extended beyond the classroom. She contributed to
curriculum development, mentored students and junior faculty,
and participated in academic governance. Her role expanded from
teacher to steward of the university's intellectual direction.
Leadership: From Department to System
Before ascending to system-wide leadership, Dr. Berowa held several key administrative positions within MSU-
Marawi, including Department Chair of Psychology, Guidance Coordinator, College Secretary, Assistant Dean, and
Dean of the College of Social Sciences and Humanities. Each role enhanced her understanding of academic
institutions, from departmental operations to college administration.
When she became Vice President for Academic Affairs in 2011, she brought decades of institutional experience.
Her tenure, lasting until 2025, is the longest in the history of the MSU System. During this time, she oversaw
critical aspects of academic governance, including curriculum development, faculty promotion, admissions,
scholarship programs, and accreditation processes.
Her leadership style emphasized continuity and system-building. Rather than pursuing short-term reforms, she
focused on institutionalizing enduring processes. She chaired key bodies, including the University System
Curriculum Committee, the Academic Promotion Panel, and the Quality Assurance Board, all vital for maintaining
and improving academic standards.
The results of her efforts became evident in the university's performance. Under her guidance, MSU achieved top
national rankings in accredited programs, particularly in 2023 and 2024. These achievements reflect both
administrative efficiency and a commitment to academic excellence.
Crisis Leadership: The Marawi Siege
If her administrative work demonstrated her capacity for system-building, the events of 2017 revealed her
leadership under pressure.
When armed conflict erupted in Marawi City on May 23, 2017, the MSU campus became the center of a
humanitarian crisis. Many fled for safety, but Dr. Berowa chose to remain on campus. From the first day of the
siege until the city's liberation in October, she stayed alongside a small group of university officials.
During this period, her responsibilities extended far beyond academic administration. She helped organize the
evacuation of vulnerable faculty and students, assisted in the distribution of food and essential supplies to those
remaining on campus and in surrounding communities, and drew on her training as a psychologist to lead
psychosocial interventions for individuals coping with trauma and displacement.
One of the most symbolic moments was the "Bakwit Graduation" held in Iligan City, allowing displaced students to
complete an important milestone in their lives. This act underscored a central principle of her leadership: education
must continue, even amid disruption.
Her presence during the siege transformed her role. She became not just an academic administrator, but a crisis
leader, humanitarian worker, and a source of stability for a community in turmoil.

PAGE 4
Scholarship and Advocacy: Gender, Peace, and Society
Parallel to her administrative work, Dr. Berowa actively engaged in research and advocacy focused on reproductive
health, gender dynamics, and the experiences of conflict-affected communities.
Her publications explored the reproductive health perspectives of Maranao youth, the experiences of women in
conflict settings, and the ethical challenges of researching marginalized communities. These works connect
academic inquiry with real-world concerns.
She was a founding member of the Al-Mujadilah Development Foundation, focusing on women's rights and
development in Muslim communities, and worked with organizations like BIRTHDEV, which supports women and
children affected by conflict and disasters.
Through these efforts, she bridged the gap between research and practice, ensuring her work had tangible impact
beyond academic publications.
Gender and Institutional Reform
As Chair of Gender and Development from 2015 to 2023, Dr. Berowa integrated gender perspectives into
university policies and programs. She mainstreamed gender sensitivity in the curriculum and promoted awareness
of issues like violence against women and reproductive health.
Her efforts aligned with national and international frameworks on gender equality, positioning MSU as a
responsive institution. She also participated in policy discussions at the national level through her involvement with
the Commission on Higher Education and other bodies.
Global Engagement and Academic Exchange
Dr. Berowa's work extended internationally through conferences, research collaborations, and academic exchanges.
She participated in Erasmus exchange programs in Portugal and Türkiye.
These experiences enriched the MSU System's internationalization and allowed her to share the challenges of
Mindanao with a broader audience.
Personal Life and Values
Behind her professional accomplishments lies a life shaped by personal commitments. She is a mother of five,
many of whom have pursued careers in academia and public service. Her role as a parent and her experiences as a
widow reflect a balance between personal resilience and public duty.
Her values—service, empathy, and commitment to community—are evident in both her professional and personal
life.
A Legacy of Continuity and Care
Dr. Alma Elape Berowa's career exemplifies the achievements of academic leadership grounded in intellectual rigor
and human concern. Her work strengthened institutional systems, advanced scholarship, and ensured educational
continuity during a challenging period in MSU's history.

PAGE 5
Her legacy is defined not just by her positions, but by her impact on students, colleagues, and the broader
community. In a region often marked by challenges, she showed that leadership rooted in knowledge, compassion,
and resilience can create lasting change.

in both intellectual rigor and genuine human concern.

most difficult periods in MSU's history.

community.

knowledge, compassion, and resilience can produce change that actually lasts.

Abdulwahid A. Bidin
Abdulwahid A. Bidin (April 7, 1925 – February 2, 1999) was a Filipino jurist, former guerrilla fighter, and public
servant who made history on January 12, 1987, when President Corazon C. Aquino appointed him as the 117th
Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the Philippines, making him the first Filipino Muslim ever to sit on the
Court since it was formally established on June 11, 1901.<ref name="wiki_bidin">Template:Cite web</ref><ref
name="philstar2009">Template:Cite web</ref> That was nearly nine decades of constitutional crises, landmark
rulings, and a court interpreting laws that affected millions of Muslim Filipinos, without a single Muslim voice
among the magistrates.
Born in the stilt-house community of Sitangkai in the southernmost Sulu Archipelago, Bidin grew up navigating
the complex intersection of maritime Sama culture, Islamic tradition, and the American colonial education system,
a navigation that would define his entire professional life. He fought as a guerrilla against the Japanese occupation,
earned a law degree from the University of the Philippines, served as an elected provincial board member, rose
through the judiciary as a trial judge and appellate court justice, and eventually took a seat on the country's highest
bench. Along the way, he built a record of principled, independent jurisprudence that continues to shape Philippine
constitutional law today.
His most cited opinion, People v. Marti (G.R. No. 81561, 1991), remains the definitive Philippine authority on the
private search doctrine. His dissent in Marcos v. Manglapus (G.R. No. 88220, 1989) stands as a principled defense
of constitutional rights against executive overreach. And his work in Board of Commissioners (CID) v. Dela Rosa
(G.R. Nos. 95122-23, 1991) reinforced due process protections in citizenship disputes. Beyond the written
opinions, Bidin spent his career as a living proof that a devout Muslim from the Philippine south could serve at the
very apex of a secular state, without compromising his faith, his community, or his judicial integrity. He retired in
1995 and passed away on February 2, 1999, but the standard he set, for excellence, independence, and principled
engagement with the law, continues to resonate in Philippine legal circles.

Early Life and the Sulu Archipelago
Abdulwahid A. Bidin was born on April 7, 1925, in Sitangkai, a
municipality now part of Tawi-Tawi Province in the southernmost
reaches of the Sulu Archipelago.<ref name="wiki_bidin"/>
Sitangkai sits geographically closer to Sabah, Malaysia, than to
Manila, and much of it is built on stilts above the shallow, coral-rich
waters of the Celebes Sea. The place is often called "the Venice of
the South" for how thoroughly its life revolves around the sea. Its
people, the Sama Dilaut and neighboring island communities, had
long looked outward to the broader Malay world and inward to the
Islamic faith for their cultural and spiritual identity.
By the time Bidin was born, the Sulu Archipelago was under the full
weight of American colonial administration. The "Moro Province"
policy brought public schools, secular governance, and a deliberate
cultural integration program to communities whose social and legal
lives had been governed for generations by Shari'ah and by adat
(customary law rooted in Islamic principles and local tradition).
Growing up at this intersection, Bidin received his elementary
education in Tawi-Tawi before moving to the provincial capital of
Jolo for secondary schooling.<ref name="wiki_bidin"/>
Jolo was the commercial and intellectual heart of the southern
Philippines: a city layered with Spanish and American colonial
history, Malay trade connections, and the deep heritage of the
Tausug Sultanate. For the young Bidin, relocating there was an early
lesson in navigating cultural plurality. He learned to move between
Sama and Tausug communities, between Muslim and non-Muslim
peers, between customary authority and national regulation. That
capacity to hold multiple frameworks simultaneously without being
captured by any single one would become one of the most
consistent features of his eventual legal career.
World War II and the Anti-Japanese
Resistance
Like virtually every young Filipino of his generation, Bidin's youth
was irrevocably shaped by the Japanese invasion and occupation,
which began in late 1941. In the Southern Philippines, the
occupation was met with fierce, organized guerrilla resistance, and
Bidin chose to join it.<ref name="wiki_bidin"/> That choice was
not a small one. In 1941, the relationship between the Bangsamoro
people and the Philippine state was already complicated and

PAGE 3
contested. Questions of Muslim self-determination, land rights, and cultural recognition were longstanding fault
lines in Philippine politics. Yet Bidin fought for the Philippine nation, fighting alongside Christian and Muslim
guerrillas against the same occupier and for the same soil.
The war years left a lasting mark on his worldview. Having lived through the collapse of legal order, the brutality
of occupation, and the moral imperatives of organized resistance, he emerged with a hard-won understanding of
what the rule of law is designed to protect, and what happens to human society when it fails. That wartime
experience would later inform a judicial temperament that was notably attentive to the fragility of rights and
skeptical of any state tendency to accumulate power at the individual's expense. After Philippine independence was
restored in 1946, Bidin's status as a veteran and his demonstrated intellectual promise made him eligible for a
government scholarship to the University of the Philippines.<ref name="wiki_bidin"/>
Education at the University of the Philippines
The University of the Philippines College of Law in the late 1940s was a world unlike anything Bidin had grown
up in. It was urban, predominantly Christian, shaped by American legal pedagogy, and populated largely by the
children of established Luzon and Visayas families who would go on to dominate Philippine public life for
decades. As a government scholar from the Muslim south, Bidin was, in the most direct sense, an outsider.<ref
name="wiki_bidin"/>
He navigated this environment with the intellectual composure that would become characteristic of his entire
career. During his time at UP, he became a member of Alpha Phi Beta, one of the university's most distinguished
fraternities, which cultivated a deliberate culture of intellectual rigor and produced multiple Supreme Court justices
and prominent figures in national public life.<ref name="apb">Template:Cite web</ref> Membership gave him
entry into the networks of mentorship and professional connection that shaped Philippine law from the inside, a
kind of integration that was both deliberate and demanding.
The legal curriculum Bidin mastered was grounded in the 1935 Constitution, explicitly modeled on American
constitutionalism and layered over a civil law tradition inherited from Spanish colonial rule.<ref
name="malacanang_journal">Template:Cite web</ref> He did not succeed in this environment by erasing who he
was. He succeeded on his own terms, maintaining his religious and cultural identity as a Muslim from the southern
Philippines while excelling in a legal tradition built around very different assumptions. Upon earning his Bachelor
of Laws degree and passing the Philippine Bar Examination, he made a decision that set him apart from many of
his contemporaries: he returned to Sulu.
Private Practice and Provincial Politics
Back in Sulu, Bidin's private legal practice brought him face to face, on a daily basis, with the friction between the
national legal code and the customary systems of adat and Shari'ah that still governed land, marriage, inheritance,
and commercial relations in the Muslim south.<ref name="wiki_bidin"/> This was not a theoretical exposure to
legal pluralism. It was the lived texture of it: disputes where the applicable law was genuinely contested, where
customary authority and state authority made competing claims, and where the lawyer had to be a translator as
much as an advocate.
His growing reputation as a principled and effective advocate drew him into provincial governance. From 1956 to
1959, he served as an elected member of the Sulu Provincial Board, running under the banner of the Grand
Alliance affiliated with the Progressive Party of the Philippines.<ref name="wiki_bidin"/> His three years on the
Board gave him direct experience in local legislation and a close-up view of the socio-economic drivers fueling
growing tensions in the Muslim south. The seeds of what would eventually become the Moro National Liberation

PAGE 4
Front and its armed campaign for Bangsamoro self-determination were being planted in communities experiencing
land dispossession, political neglect, and cultural erasure during this period. Bidin saw this not as an outside
observer but as an elected official with a direct responsibility to the affected people.
The Judicial Career: From Zamboanga to the Court of Appeals
In 1968, Bidin received his appointment as a trial judge in Zamboanga City, one of Mindanao's major commercial
and administrative hubs.<ref name="wiki_bidin"/> It was no minor posting: Zamboanga carried a large,
commercially active docket reflecting the full range of human conflict, from petty criminal matters to contested
land titles involving competing traditional and statutory claims. Beyond his primary assignment at Regional Trial
Court Branch 12, he also served as pairing judge at RTC Branch 13 (a special drug court), and at various points
served as assisting judge in Basilan Province and acting presiding judge at the RTC of Bongao, Tawi-Tawi.
The national recognition he earned during these years reflected the quality of what he was doing with that
workload. In 1979, the Integrated Bar of the Philippines awarded him the distinction of Most Outstanding Trial
Court Judge, a peer-assessed honor evaluated on integrity, legal acumen, and case management.<ref
name="wiki_bidin"/> Receiving that distinction while operating in a high-volume, high-pressure jurisdiction
during the martial law era, when the judiciary was under sustained political pressure from the Marcos
administration, speaks to something more than technical competence. It speaks to character.
In 1983, he was elevated to the Intermediate Appellate Court (now the Court of Appeals), bringing him to Manila
in an official judicial capacity for the first time.<ref name="wiki_bidin"/> The appellate work allowed him to
develop the broader jurisprudential perspective that would characterize his Supreme Court tenure: carefully
researched, clearly written opinions attentive to both the doctrine at stake and the real-world implications for the
parties before the bench.
The 1987 Appointment: Making History on the High Bench
The People Power Revolution of February 1986 was more than a change of government. It was a mandate for
institutional renewal. The Philippine judiciary had been systematically subordinated to executive will during the
martial law years, and President Aquino moved deliberately to rebuild the Supreme Court's integrity, appointing
jurists distinguished by their credentials, their independence from the old regime, and their diversity of
background.<ref name="aquino_presidency">Template:Cite web</ref>
On January 12, 1987, Abdulwahid A. Bidin was appointed the 117th Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the
Philippines, replacing Associate Justice Lino Patajo.<ref name="wiki_bidin"/> He was sixty-one years old. His
mandatory retirement in 1995 would create the vacancy eventually filled by Regino C. Hermosisima Jr.<ref
name="hermosisima">Template:Cite web</ref>
The historical significance of the appointment was immediately and widely recognized. For the first time in the
Court's eighty-six-year history, a Filipino Muslim would sit among the fifteen magistrates charged with interpreting
the nation's fundamental law.<ref name="philstar2009"/> That fact alone merited commemoration. But Bidin was
not appointed to be a symbol. On any objective measure, he was among the country's most qualified jurists.
The Court he joined was operating at an extraordinary historical juncture. The 1987 Constitution, drafted by a
commission convened by President Aquino and ratified by the Filipino people in February 1987, was a direct
response to the Marcos era: an expanded Bill of Rights, stronger provisions for judicial independence, explicit
recognition of the rights of cultural communities, and a substantially broader mandate for judicial review.<ref

PAGE 5
name="aquino_presidency"/> The Bidin Court was tasked with giving this new constitutional text its authoritative
interpretation at the very moment when the entire democratic architecture of the Philippines was being rebuilt from
the foundations.
For the Bangsamoro community, the appointment carried a weight that transcended institutional representation.<ref
name="bangsamoro_gazette_dimaampao">Template:Cite web</ref> The twentieth-century Muslim Filipino
experience had been marked by armed conflict, cultural suppression, and a well-founded sense of exclusion from
the national project. Against that backdrop, a Tausug Muslim from Tawi-Tawi sitting on the country's highest bench
was not a small thing. It signaled, for the first time at the very apex of the Philippine state, that Muslim Filipinos
were full members of the republic: not subjects to be administered or problems to be managed, but citizens whose
perspectives were essential to the interpretive work that a constitutional democracy requires.
Landmark Decisions and Judicial Philosophy
A justice's legacy ultimately rests on the written opinions they leave behind. By this measure, Bidin's eight-year
tenure on the High Tribunal left a substantial and enduring mark.
People v. Andre Marti (G.R. No. 81561, 1991): The Private Search Doctrine
Of all the opinions Justice Bidin authored, People v. Andre Marti is the most frequently cited in Philippine law
schools today.<ref name="marti">People of the Philippines v. Andre Marti, G.R. No. 81561, January 18, 1991. Full
text at Template:Cite web</ref> The case arose in August 1987 when a man named Andre Marti brought four gift-
wrapped packages to a forwarding agency in Ermita, Manila, declaring the contents as books, cigars, and gloves
destined for Zurich. The agency's proprietor, Job Reyes, opened the packages before forwarding them to the Bureau
of Customs, as was standard procedure, and found them packed with marijuana. Reyes reported the discovery to
the National Bureau of Investigation, and Marti was charged under the Dangerous Drugs Act.
The defense argument was predictable: the search was unconstitutional. Article III, Section 2 of the 1987
Constitution guarantees the right of the people to be secure in their persons, papers, and effects against
unreasonable searches and seizures. Marti argued that the evidence should be excluded.
Writing for the Court, Justice Bidin disposed of this argument with characteristic economy and precision. The
constitutional protection against unreasonable searches and seizures, he held, is a restraint directed exclusively at
the government, not at private individuals acting on their own initiative without government direction. Since the
search had been conducted by Reyes, a private person, and not by a government agent, the evidence was perfectly
admissible. The subsequent presence of NBI agents did not retroactively convert Reyes's independent action into a
state-conducted search.
The constitutional proscription against unlawful searches and seizures applies as a restraint directed
only against the government and its agencies tasked with the enforcement of the law. It is not meant to
be invoked against acts of private individuals.
The "state action" doctrine established by this decision had deep roots in American jurisprudence, but Bidin's
ponencia gave it clear, authoritative, and accessible articulation in the Philippine context for the first time. Three
and a half decades later, People v. Marti remains the go-to Philippine authority on this doctrine, cited in virtually
every subsequent case involving searches conducted by private parties.<ref name="marti"/>

PAGE 6
Marcos v. Manglapus (G.R. No. 88220, 1989): A Dissent for Civil Liberties
The constitutional drama of Marcos v. Manglapus unfolded against one of the most politically charged backdrops
in Philippine history: the effort by Ferdinand Marcos and his family, then living in exile in Hawaii following the
1986 Revolution, to return to the Philippines. The Aquino government, citing national security concerns, refused to
allow the return. The Supreme Court was asked whether the President had the power to bar a former head of state
from returning to his own country.
The majority upheld the government's position, relying on the theory of "residual powers," executive powers not
explicitly enumerated in the Constitution but implied by the functional demands of effective governance.<ref
name="marcos_manglapus">Template:Cite web</ref> The majority reasoning was sophisticated, even persuasive
in its policy logic. But it had a structural weakness: the explicit text of the Bill of Rights guarantees the right to
travel, and overriding that textually grounded guarantee through unenumerated residual powers was, for the
dissenters, a step the Constitution simply did not authorize.
Justice Bidin voted to grant the petition and allow the Marcoses to return. His position was rooted in strict
constitutionalism: fundamental rights explicitly protected by the Bill of Rights cannot be curtailed without a
specific, duly enacted law authorizing that curtailment, and no such law existed.<ref name="marcos_manglapus"/>
Voting as he did required Bidin to prioritize his reading of the Constitution over both political prudence and
institutional loyalty to his appointing authority. It was an act of genuine judicial independence, the kind that is easy
to celebrate in the abstract and much harder to perform in practice.
Board of Commissioners (CID) v. Dela Rosa (G.R. Nos. 95122-23, 1991): Due Process and
Citizenship
In Board of Commissioners (CID) v. Dela Rosa, Justice Bidin addressed the constitutionally sensitive intersection
of citizenship claims, administrative jurisdiction, and the procedural guarantees of due process.<ref
name="dela_rosa">Board of Commissioners (CID) v. Dela Rosa, G.R. Nos. 95122-23, May 31, 1991. Full text at
Template:Cite web</ref> The case involved William Gatchalian, whose Filipino citizenship was challenged by the
Commission on Immigration and Deportation, which sought to have him deported as an alien. The central question:
could an administrative agency, rather than a court of law, have the final say over a substantive dispute about a
person's citizenship?
Bidin's decision established a principle of lasting importance: when citizenship itself is at stake, the state is
obligated to apply the highest standards of procedural due process, and the courts, not executive bodies, must serve
as the ultimate arbiters of genuine citizenship disputes. An individual who has established a prima facie case of
being a Filipino national cannot have that question finally resolved against him by an administrative body
operating without full judicial process. The ruling provided meaningful protection against arbitrary administrative
action and reinforced the post-1987 constitutional order's fundamental commitment to ensuring that no person is
subjected to arbitrary deprivation of so fundamental a status as national citizenship.<ref name="dela_rosa"/>
Expertise in Shari'ah and the Sarah Balabagan Mission
One of the less-examined dimensions of Bidin's career is the depth and practical utility of his expertise in Islamic
law, and the dramatic use to which that expertise was put almost immediately after his mandatory retirement from
the Supreme Court on April 7, 1995. His mastery of Shari'ah was not peripheral to his professional identity; it was
integral to it.

PAGE 7
Presidential Decree No. 1083, the Code of Muslim Personal Laws of the Philippines, promulgated by President
Marcos in 1977, had created a specialized legal framework for the Muslim community, governing matters of family
law, inheritance, and personal status according to Shari'ah principles.<ref
name="code_muslim_laws">Template:Cite web</ref> Bidin's fluency in both secular Philippine legal tradition and
Islamic jurisprudence made him a uniquely valuable institutional asset, not just domestically but in the conduct of
Philippine foreign policy with Muslim-majority nations.
That value became dramatically apparent in 1995, in the case of Sarah Balabagan: a young Filipina domestic
worker in the United Arab Emirates who had been sentenced to death for killing her employer, whom she claimed
had raped her.<ref name="kasama">Template:Cite web</ref> President Fidel V. Ramos, recognizing the need for a
legal expert who could engage with UAE authorities on their own terms, sent Bidin to the UAE.
His ability to engage with UAE religious and legal officials on the technical merits of Islamic jurisprudence, on the
doctrines of qisas (retributive justice), diyya (blood money), and pardon under Shari'ah, gave the Philippine
government a set of diplomatic tools that a purely secular envoy simply would not have possessed. His
involvement, as part of a broader diplomatic effort, contributed to Balabagan's eventual release, and cemented his
reputation as a diplomat-jurist: a rare figure who could speak the language of international law and the language of
Shari'ah with equal fluency and authority.<ref name="kasama"/>
The Cultural Weight of Being 'First'
There is a reasonable objection sometimes raised about "first" titles: that they can become substitutes for
substantive progress, a way of celebrating inclusion without actually achieving it. Bidin's case challenges this
objection on multiple levels. The barrier he broke had stood for nearly nine decades. The quality of his
contributions to Philippine law was objectively substantial. And the community his appointment represented had
been seeking recognition at this level for a very long time.
For the Bangsamoro people, Bidin's presence on the Supreme Court carried a significance that is difficult to convey
from the outside.<ref name="bangsamoro_gazette_dimaampao"/> The Bangsamoro experience in the twentieth
century had been marked by armed conflict, displacement, cultural marginalization, and a persistent sense of
exclusion from the institutions of the Philippine state. Against this history, the appointment of a Muslim jurist from
Tawi-Tawi to one of the fifteen seats on the country's highest bench was an institutional statement, imperfect and
overdue, but real: that Muslim Filipinos belonged to the republic whose laws they were asked to obey.
Bidin understood and embraced this responsibility. He mentored a generation of Muslim lawyers, encouraging
them to pursue careers in the national judiciary and at the Shari'ah bar.<ref
name="bangsamoro_gazette_ar161">Template:Cite web</ref> He demonstrated, by sustained example, that a
devout Muslim could serve at the highest level of a secular state without compromising either his faith or his
professional integrity. His presence on the Court helped dismantle the stereotypes that had too long associated
Muslim Filipinos primarily with armed conflict rather than legal excellence and civic participation.
The Twenty-Six-Year Gap: From Bidin to Dimaampao
When Bidin retired in April 1995, the expectation among Bangsamoro leaders and legal advocates was that his
departure would prompt a renewed institutional commitment to Muslim representation on the Court. That
expectation went largely unfulfilled for an extraordinary length of time. Twenty-six years passed before a second
Muslim jurist would sit on the Supreme Court of the Philippines.<ref name="philstar2009"/>

PAGE 8
The interim was not silent. Bangsamoro leaders, Muslim lawyers' organizations, and civil society actors repeatedly
raised the issue, citing the 1996 Final Peace Agreement between the government and the MNLF and Republic Act
No. 9054 as the legal bases for a policy of meaningful inclusion.<ref name="bangsamoro_gazette_dimaampao"/>
A 2009 opinion piece in the Philippine Star, written in the context of upcoming Supreme Court vacancies, captured
the accumulated frustration of that period: fourteen years after Bidin's death, still no Muslim had sat in the High
Tribunal, despite explicit policy commitments and a growing pool of qualified Muslim jurists at the Court of
Appeals level.<ref name="philstar2009"/>
The appointment of Japar B. Dimaampao as the 191st Associate Justice of the Supreme Court by President Rodrigo
R. Duterte in September 2021 finally ended the twenty-six-year drought.<ref
name="dimaampao_wiki">Template:Cite web</ref><ref name="gma_dimaampao">Template:Cite web</ref>
Dimaampao, a Maranao jurist from Marawi City, Lanao del Sur, is a distinguished expert in taxation law and
Shari'ah who became the Court of Appeals' youngest associate justice at forty years old, and served at the appellate
level for seventeen years before his elevation to the High Court.<ref
name="mindanews_dimaampao">Template:Cite web</ref> He has spoken publicly about the precedent set by
Bidin, describing his predecessor as the pioneer who made his own appointment conceivable and whose example
motivated him through the fourteen unsuccessful Judicial and Bar Council applications that preceded his eventual
selection.<ref name="bangsamoro_gazette_ar161"/>
Together, Bidin and Dimaampao represent the entire total of Muslim justices in the history of a fifteen-member
court adjudicating the affairs of a nation that includes a substantial Muslim minority population. The statistic
remains a source of legitimate advocacy for Bangsamoro communities who continue to push for institutional
representation commensurate with their historical presence in the Philippine nation.
Commemoration and Academic Legacy
The formal institutional recognition of Bidin's contributions is still being developed, but what exists is meaningful.
The Mindanao State University College of Law, Tawi-Tawi Extension Campus, situated in his home province, has
launched the "Justice Abdulwahid Bidin Lecture Series," a program that brings together legal scholars and
practitioners to discuss Shari'ah, Bangsamoro law, and constitutional jurisprudence in his honor.<ref
name="msu_tcto">Template:Cite web</ref> Anchored in Tawi-Tawi, his birthplace, the lecture series is a fitting
tribute: a sustained academic initiative dedicated to the very intersection of legal traditions that Bidin spent his
career navigating.
Beyond formal programs, Bidin's judicial record is increasingly invoked in policy discussions about strengthening
the Philippine Shari'ah court system and establishing a Shari'ah Appellate Court, a reform that legal scholars and
Bangsamoro legal advocates have pursued for decades.<ref name="sc_shariah_summit">Template:Cite web</ref>
The Supreme Court's announcement of its first National Shari'ah Summit reflects a broader institutional movement
to bring the Islamic legal dimension of the Philippine state more fully into mainstream judicial discourse, a project
that Bidin's career both anticipated and legitimized.
His written decisions endure in the most practical of ways: they are taught in every Philippine law school, cited in
legal briefs, and discussed in every advanced course on constitutional law and administrative law in the country.
People v. Marti appears in constitutional law syllabi as the definitive Philippine case on the private search doctrine;
the Marcos v. Manglapus dissent is regularly assigned to students studying the boundaries of executive power; the
Dela Rosa decision surfaces in administrative law courses on citizenship and due process.<ref name="marti"/><ref
name="marcos_manglapus"/><ref name="dela_rosa"/> That kind of intellectual persistence, the ongoing daily
invocation of a man's reasoning by thousands of students and practitioners, is not a minor legacy. It is, in the
deepest sense, legal immortality.

PAGE 9
Death
Justice Abdulwahid A. Bidin passed away on February 2, 1999, four years after his retirement from the Supreme
Court, at the age of seventy-three.<ref name="biographies_net">Template:Cite web</ref> He left behind a body of
jurisprudence that continues to shape Philippine law, a generation of Muslim legal professionals he helped
encourage into the profession, and a precedent, honored imperfectly and belatedly, but eventually renewed, that the
nation's highest bench must be broad enough to accommodate the nation's full plurality.
The Jurist of the Crescent was not simply a milestone. He was a standard. And the standard he set, for excellence,
for independence, for principled engagement with the law, remains worth building on as the Philippines continues
the long, unfinished work of becoming a truly inclusive democracy.

H. Farouk/Pantawagas Maruhom Anggol Capalan Biston
(rahimahullah; June 16, 1932 – November 23, 2010) was a Filipino
educator and public servant from Bacolod-Kalawi, Lanao del Sur,
best remembered for a public service career built on quiet discipline
and an untarnished reputation. A Dansalan College scholar and honor
student who studied Political Science at Silliman University before
pursuing law at the University of Manila, he taught at LNCAT (now
MSU LNCAT), managed government finances at the Philippine
Pilgrimage Authority and the Bureau of Internal Revenue, served as
OIC Mayor of his hometown, and later lent his expertise as a
consultant to Governor Zacaria Candao, the first Governor of the
Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (ARMM). To this day, he
is remembered as the patriarch of the Biston family and as a man
whose name, in his own words, was never allowed to be tarnished.

3.2 A Lifetime of Trusted Leadership

Early Life
Pantawagas Biston was born on June 16, 1932, in Bacolod-Kalawi,
Lanao del Sur. He would go on to become one of the town's most
respected sons, a quiet man whose life eventually became a kind of
blueprint for how to live with integrity in public service.
Education
Biston pursued his college education at Silliman University in
Dumaguete City, where he took up AB Political Science as a
Dansalan College (DC) Scholar, a distinction he earned for being an
honor student. He later moved on to study law at the University of
Manila, though he did not complete his law degree, choosing instead
to carry his political science training and disciplined mindset directly
into teaching and public service.

PAGE 2
Governor of the Autonomous Region in
Muslim Mindanao (ARMM)
Spouse / Family
Patriarch of the Biston family
Notability
Regarded as a model of incorruptible public
service in Lanao del Sur, having managed
government funds across several agencies
without a single stain on his name.
Known For
His decades-long career spanning education
and government finance, and the family
principle he lived by: "Do not tarnish my
name."
Career
A Teacher Who Pushed for Greatness
Long before he entered public office, Biston was already shaping
young minds as a professor and teacher at LNCAT, the institution
now known as MSU LNCAT. He was known around campus for
holding his students to incredibly rigorous standards. Former
students still tell stories of him tossing chalk or erasers across the
room just to snap a distracted classmate back to attention, a habit that
became something of a legend among those who sat in his class.
Underneath that strict exterior, though, was a mentor who genuinely
cared about pushing every young person in front of him toward their
full potential. It says something about the kind of teacher he was that
several of his former students went on to become well-known names
in their own right.
A Lifetime of Trusted Leadership
Biston's commitment to public development eventually carried him into vital financial and government roles. He
served as Chief, Director, and Fiscal Comptroller of the Finance Division for the Philippine Pilgrimage Authority
(PHILPA), an agency that operated under Secretary Lininding Pangandaman at the time. PHILPA has since evolved
into today's Bureau of Pilgrimage and Endowment under the National Commission on Muslim Filipinos (NCMF),
continuing the same mission of protecting the rights and welfare of Muslim Filipinos.
From there, he brought his financial expertise to the Bureau of Internal Revenue (BIR), where he served as a Chief
Revenue Officer. He performed so well in that role that he was already being lined up for a promotion to Regional
Director. But duty called him back home instead: then Governor Saidamen Balt Pangarungan appointed him OIC
Mayor of Bacolod-Kalawi, Lanao del Sur, the very town where he was born and raised.
A Trusted Voice in the New ARMM
Biston's reputation for sound judgment and financial discipline followed him well into the region's political
development. When the Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (ARMM) was established, he was tapped as a
consultant by its first Governor, Zacaria Candao. It was a fitting role for a man who had already spent decades
helping build trustworthy institutions across Muslim Mindanao, and it placed him right at the center of one of the
most significant political milestones in the region's history.
Character and Legacy
By nature, Biston was a quiet, reserved man who rarely offered an opinion unless asked. He preferred to let his
everyday actions speak louder than his words ever could. Across the region, he was known for his generosity and
his readiness to help anyone who needed it, regardless of who they were. Those who knew him say that in his
entire lifetime, no one could point to a single bad word about his character.

PAGE 3
Handling public funds across so many financial and government posts is the kind of responsibility that tests
anybody's integrity, but Biston held himself to an uncompromising standard throughout. He never once engaged in
corruption, cheating, or misuse of public resources. Instead, he lived and governed by a simple principle that he
impressed deeply upon his children: "Do not tarnish my name."
He carried that principle all the way to his final days on November 23, 2010, leaving behind a name that remains
entirely untarnished and a memory that continues to inspire the Biston family and the community of Bacolod-
Kalawi.

text:

Kamar M. Boloto
Atty. Kamar M. Boloto, CPA was a Filipino lawyer, certified
public accountant, and institutional leader from Malabang, Lanao
del Sur whose historic academic achievements made him one of the
most celebrated figures in Bangsamoro history.
He is best remembered for a feat no Muslim Filipino had
accomplished before him: topping the Certified Public Accountant
(CPA) Board Examinations outright, and then going on to place 2nd
in the 1970 Philippine Bar Examinations with a remarkable average
of 86.75%.
Together, these two milestones earned him what his community calls
the "Double Crown of Excellence," a legacy that continues to inspire
generations of Maranao and Muslim Filipino professionals long
after his time.
Beyond the examination halls, Boloto gave the rest of his career to
building institutions. He served as Director of the Finance Division
at Mindanao State University (MSU-Marawi), and he was among
the key proponents who pushed for the establishment of MSU-
Malabang, bringing higher education to his own hometown on the
Lanao coast.
His story is not just about individual brilliance. It's about what that
brilliance meant to a community still fighting for its place in the
Philippine professional mainstream.
Contents
1 Early Life and Heritage
2 Education
2.1 Law: University of the East College of Law
2.2 Accountancy: The First Muslim CPA Topnotcher
3 Career
3.1 Finance Division Director, Mindanao State University
3.2 Establishing MSU-Malabang
4 Cultural Significance
5 Legacy and Recognition
6 See Also
7 Further Reading

PAGE 2
Early Life and Heritage
Atty. Boloto was born and raised in Malabang, Lanao del Sur, a coastal municipality with deep historical roots as a
former seat of power linked to both the Sultanate of Maguindanao and the princely states of Lanao.<ref
name="malabang_history">Malabang is recognized as one of the oldest municipalities in Mindanao, historically
associated with the spread of Islam in the Lake Lanao region.</ref>
He was a proud member of the Maranao tribe, whose name means "People of the Lake," referring to their ancestral
homeland surrounding Lake Lanao.<ref name="maranao_identity">The Maranao are one of the major Muslim
ethnolinguistic groups in Mindanao, known for their elaborate artistic traditions, oral literature, and the concept of
Maratabat (honor and self-worth).</ref>
Growing up in Malabang meant growing up at the intersection of Islamic tradition and the practical demands of
mid-20th century Philippine society. The values instilled in him early, particularly Maratabat (a deep sense of
honor and personal worth) and Kanggiginawai (mutual respect and dignity in one's conduct), were not just cultural
ornaments. They became the internal compass that drove his extraordinary discipline in academia and public
service.
His hometown was no stranger to leadership. Malabang had produced local officials, religious scholars, and
community figures, but no one from its ranks had yet broken into the national topnotcher lists of the country's most
prestigious professional examinations. Boloto would change that.
Education
Law: University of the East College of Law
Atty. Boloto pursued his legal education at the University of the East (UE) College of Law in Manila, an institution
that had built a reputation as a "cradle of topnotchers" in Philippine bar history.<ref
name="ue_college_of_law">The University of the East College of Law has produced numerous bar topnotchers
and prominent legal practitioners throughout the 20th century.</ref>
In 1970, he sat for the Philippine Bar Examinations, the country's most demanding professional licensure test for
aspiring lawyers. He placed 2nd nationwide, with an average of 86.75%, a score that placed him firmly among the
country's brightest legal minds of his generation.<ref name="1970_bar_results">Philippine Bar Examination
results for 1970, as administered by the Supreme Court of the Philippines.</ref>
His achievement was particularly significant in context. He was the first Filipino Muslim to break into the Top 10
of the Bar Examinations since the post-war period, following the pioneering example of Macapanton Abbas Sr.,
who had placed 2nd in the Bar in the 1940s.<ref name="macapanton_reference">Macapanton Abbas Sr. is
recognized as one of the earliest Muslim Filipino topnotchers in the Philippine Bar Examinations.</ref>
Accountancy: The First Muslim CPA Topnotcher
Before his legal triumph, Boloto had already made history in the field of accountancy.
He became the first Muslim Filipino to top the CPA Board Examinations outright, taking the Rank 1 position
and earning the title of Certified Public Accountant.<ref name="cpa_topnotcher">Boloto's achievement in the CPA
Board Examinations marked a historic first for Muslim Filipino representation among national board topnotchers in
the Philippines.</ref>

PAGE 3
This dual mastery of Law and Accountancy was rare then as it is now. It gave him a professional profile that was
uniquely suited for institutional leadership, combining legal acumen with fiscal rigor in a single person.
Career
Finance Division Director, Mindanao State University
After his licensure examinations, Atty. Boloto dedicated a significant portion of his professional life to Mindanao
State University (MSU), the flagship state university serving the Muslim and indigenous communities of
Mindanao.
He served as the Director of the Finance Division at MSU-Marawi, overseeing the university's budgetary and
fiscal operations during one of its most critical expansion phases in the 1970s.<ref name="msu_code_1976">MSU
Code of 1976, BOR Resolution No. 1280, Mindanao State University Board of Regents. His role in the Finance
Division is documented within the university's official governance records of the period.</ref>
His contributions during this period are formally acknowledged in the MSU Code of 1976 (BOR Resolution No.
1280), which structured the university's fiscal governance policies at a time when MSU was rapidly growing to
serve a larger student population across Mindanao.
Managing the finances of a regional state university in the 1970s was no small feat. The period coincided with the
Marcos martial law era and the escalating conflict in Mindanao, both of which created fiscal pressures that
demanded careful, principled administration. Boloto navigated these challenges with the same discipline that had
defined his academic career.
Establishing MSU-Malabang
Perhaps the most enduring mark Atty. Boloto left on his community was his role in bringing the Mindanao State
University system to his own hometown.
Driven by a genuine desire to democratize access to higher education in the Lanao coastal area, he became one of
the primary proponents of establishing an MSU branch in Malabang, Lanao del Sur.
Working closely with MSU President Ali Dimaporo, Boloto formally submitted the municipal resolution that
called for the creation of MSU-Malabang.<ref name="bor_1589">Board of Regents Resolution No. 1589, Series of
1978, Mindanao State University. Signed on August 1, 1978. This resolution formally authorized the establishment
of MSU-Malabang.</ref>
BOR Resolution No. 1589 was signed on August 1, 1978, officially authorizing the establishment of MSU-
Malabang. That date marks a milestone not just for Malabang but for the entire Lanao coastal corridor, where
young people now had access to affordable tertiary education without having to travel to Marawi or Manila.
MSU-Malabang continues to operate today, and its founding story carries Boloto's name as one of the men who
made it happen.
Cultural Significance
Atty. Boloto's legacy cannot be fully understood outside of its social and historical context.

PAGE 4
In 1970, when he placed 2nd in the Bar, Muslim-Christian tensions in Mindanao were already escalating toward
what would become the armed conflict of the early 1970s and the imposition of martial law. Against this backdrop,
a young Maranao man from a small coastal town standing near the top of the country's most prestigious
professional examination was more than a personal achievement. It was a statement.
He showed that the Bangsamoro people belong not just on the battlefield of political struggle, but in
the highest halls of Philippine intellectual and professional life.
His success challenged stereotypes about Muslim Filipinos that had long been used to marginalize the community.
He did it not through protest or politics, but through extraordinary academic performance, a form of assertion that
was peaceful, undeniable, and impossible to dismiss.
Decades later, the Bangsamoro Parliament and the National Commission on Muslim Filipinos (NCMF)
continue to cite Atty. Boloto as a foundational inspiration for current Muslim bar and board topnotchers.<ref
name="ncmf_reference">National Commission on Muslim Filipinos (NCMF), documentation on Bangsamoro
professional achievers cited in institutional advocacy materials.</ref>
His name is invoked not as nostalgia, but as a living benchmark: what is possible when a Bangsamoro Filipino is
given the opportunity, and takes it.
Legacy and Recognition
The "Double Crown of Excellence" is the phrase most associated with Atty. Boloto's legacy: the rare combination
of topping the CPA Board and placing 2nd in the Philippine Bar, two of the most competitive professional
examinations in the country.
He established a high-water mark for Maranao and Muslim Filipino academic achievement at the national level,
one that stood as an aspirational reference point for the community for generations.
His generational influence is reflected in the Boloto family name's continuing presence in academia. His son,
Kamar V. Boloto Jr., followed his path as an educator and professional at MSU, carrying forward a family
tradition of service to the same institution his father helped shape.<ref name="boloto_family">Details of Kamar V.
Boloto Jr.'s professional association with Mindanao State University are noted in community records relating to the
Boloto family's contributions to the MSU system.</ref>
The establishment of MSU-Malabang, formalized through BOR Resolution No. 1589 in 1978, stands as his most
concrete and lasting institutional contribution: a campus that continues to educate the sons and daughters of the
Lanao coast, long after his own career had passed.

text:

Lindao Macarambon Boransing
Atty. Lindao Macarambon Boransing (also written as Bae Lindao Macarambon-Boransing) was a Filipino
lawyer from Iligan City, Lanao del Norte, and is historically recognized as the first Maranao woman to pass the
Philippine Bar Examinations, having been admitted to the practice of law in 1961. Her milestone came during a
decade when very few Muslim women from Mindanao dared to pursue higher education beyond regional
boundaries, let alone take on the national bar. She is also widely remembered as the life partner and steadfast
support of Prof. Manaros B. Boransing, the founding Dean and Vice President for the Mindanao State University-
Iligan Institute of Technology (MSU-IIT), known across the Lanao region as the "Father of IIT." Together, the two
formed one of the most consequential intellectual and civic partnerships in Bangsamoro history, placing the rule of
law and the power of education side by side as twin pillars of community transformation.
Contents
1 Early Life
2 Education
3 Career
3.1 Legal Practice
3.2 Civic and Community Contributions
4 The Boransing Partnership
5 Cultural Significance
6 Faith and Personal Values
7 Legacy and Recognition
8 Notes on Sources and Research Gaps
9 Further Reading
10 See Also
Early Life
Lindao Macarambon was born and raised in Iligan City, a city that
sits at a cultural and geographic crossroads between the
predominantly Christian Northern Mindanao and the heartland of
the Maranao people along the shores of Lake Lanao. She grew up
as part of the Macarambon clan, a family embedded in the social
fabric of Maranao society, where lineage, faith, and community
standing mattered enormously. The mid-20th century Philippines
was a complex place for Muslim women. Prevailing social norms
in many Maranao communities still steered young women toward
early domestic roles, and the idea of a woman traveling to Manila
alone to pursue a law degree was, frankly, not something most
families encouraged. That Lindao chose to do exactly that says
something meaningful about both her personal determination and the openness of her family to support a different
kind of path.
She grew up speaking Maranao and came of age during the Commonwealth and early post-independence era of the
Philippines, a time when the Muslim Filipinos of Mindanao were navigating shifting political landscapes while
holding fast to their Islamic identity and adat (customary traditions). Her early formation, grounded in that dual

PAGE 2
loyalty to faith and civic life, would define the arc of her entire professional career.
Education
Atty. Lindao pursued her legal education in Manila, joining a small but determined cohort of Muslim students who
made the journey to the capital in the 1950s for higher studies. The exact institution where she completed her
Bachelor of Laws (LL.B.) degree has not been definitively confirmed in available public records, and primary
verification through university archives or the Supreme Court Roll of Attorneys is recommended. What is firmly
documented, however, is that she successfully hurdled the 1961 Philippine Bar Examinations, making her the
first woman of Maranao heritage to earn admission to the Philippine Bar.<ref name="wiki-asia">Template:Cite
web</ref>
Some accounts describe her more broadly as the first Muslim woman in the Philippines to have been admitted to
the Bar. While this broader claim is widely cited in oral tradition and community memory across the Lanao region,
it has not yet been conclusively verified against primary records such as the Supreme Court Roll of Attorneys for
the period. Researchers and those expanding this article are encouraged to consult the Supreme Court's official rolls
for 1961 to confirm or refine this scope.<ref name="wiki-asia" />
Passing the bar in 1961 was no small feat for anyone. For a Maranao woman doing it in that era, it was
extraordinary, and it did not go unnoticed in the communities of Lanao del Norte and Lanao del Sur.
Career
Legal Practice
After her bar admission, Atty. Lindao returned to her roots in the Iligan-Lanao corridor, where she established
herself as a practicing lawyer. Her professional work was characterized by a quiet, principled approach to justice,
and she often found herself bridging two different legal frameworks that intersected in the lives of her community:
the civil law system of the Philippine Republic, and the Shari'ah-rooted customary norms that governed personal
and family matters among Muslims. This was not merely a professional challenge. It required cultural sensitivity, a
deep understanding of Islamic jurisprudence, and the kind of trust that only comes from being genuinely embedded
in the community you serve.
She was, by most accounts from those who knew her, a practitioner who took cases seriously and who understood
that the law was only as meaningful as its application in people's daily lives. Her presence as a female Maranao
lawyer gave many families from the region a point of access to the formal legal system that they might not
otherwise have sought out.
Civic and Community Contributions
Beyond her legal work, Atty. Lindao was deeply involved in the civic life of Iligan City. She served informally as a
legal resource and adviser for community initiatives, organizations, and individuals who needed guidance but could
not easily navigate the formal legal system on their own. This kind of behind-the-scenes, sustained public service is
often underdocumented but critically important in communities where formal institutions are not always accessible
or trusted.

PAGE 3
She was also present, alongside her husband, in the early and formative years of MSU-IIT's development. While
Prof. Manaros Boransing was the institutional face of that era, Atty. Lindao provided what the source documents
describe as "the legal and emotional anchor" for the family's deep involvement in shaping a university that would
go on to become one of the country's leading science and technology institutions.<ref name="msuiit-
history">Template:Cite web</ref>
The Boransing Partnership
The story of Atty. Lindao is inseparable from that of her husband, Prof. Manaros B. Boransing, though it is
important to recognize her as a person of individual distinction, not merely as a spouse.
Prof. Boransing was appointed Dean of IIT on July 9, 1973, and later became the Vice President for MSU-IIT
when the campus was granted autonomous status in 1975 under the Mindanao State University Board of Regents.
<ref name="msuiit-history" /><ref name="msuiit-50">Template:Cite web</ref> He served in that capacity until
1988, and is affectionately known throughout the institution as the Father of IIT, a moniker that reflects his role in
transforming the institution into a financially independent, academically robust campus.<ref name="father-
iit">Template:Cite web</ref>
Note: Some accounts, including the source document accompanying this article, describe Prof. Boransing as the
"Founding Chancellor" of MSU-IIT. This is inconsistent with official MSU-IIT records, which identify Dr. Camar
A. Umpa as the first Chancellor of MSU-IIT, having succeeded Boransing in that leadership transition.
Researchers should consult the MSU-IIT Board of Regents records to confirm titles and succession.
The home the two built together in Iligan became what their contemporaries describe as a gathering place for
intellectual exchange, community deliberation, and civic planning. Atty. Lindao's legal training and Prof.
Boransing's educational leadership fed each other. They shared the belief, common to the best minds of their
generation in Mindanao, that the so-called "Mindanao problem" could not be solved by arms or politics alone, but
required world-class education and the consistent application of the rule of law.
"Her success was a message to every Maranao girl: The courtrooms and chambers of justice are as
much your home as the traditional torogan."
This sentiment, preserved in the oral tradition of those who knew her, captures why her legacy endures not just as a
historical footnote but as a living reference point for Bangsamoro women in law, governance, and public life.
Cultural Significance
Atty. Lindao's achievement must be understood in its full cultural context. The Maranao people place enormous
social value on family, lineage, and the role of women within the domestic sphere. In many traditional families, a
woman pursuing a law degree in Manila in the 1950s would have been seen as an unusual, even transgressive,
choice. The fact that Lindao did it, and did it successfully, was a quiet but powerful argument that the traditional
Maranao identity and modern professional life were not in conflict.
She demonstrated that a devout Muslim woman could sit for and pass one of the most rigorous national
examinations in the Philippines, earn the respect of the formal legal system, and still remain rooted in the culture
and community that raised her. She did not migrate to Manila or transform into a Manila-based professional. She
came home, and she served.

PAGE 4
For the Bangsamoro women who came after her, whether in law, medicine, education, government, or the arts,
Atty. Lindao is part of the foundation. She belongs in the same conversation as other pioneering Bangsamoro
women like Tarhata Alonto-Lucman, the first woman governor of Lanao del Sur, as figures who showed what was
possible when a Maranao woman was given, or claimed for herself, the space to lead.
Faith and Personal Values
Atty. Lindao's Islamic faith was central to how she understood her role as a lawyer and as a public figure. For her,
the pursuit of justice was not simply a professional obligation but a moral and spiritual one. Islam places the
concept of 'adl, or justice, among its highest values, and that framework appears to have shaped both the cases she
chose to take and the manner in which she practiced.
Her commitment to her roots, to remaining in the Lanao region rather than chasing higher status or more lucrative
work in major urban centers, also reflects a set of personal values consistent with Islamic notions of community
responsibility and service. She didn't practice law for recognition. She practiced it because the people around her
needed what she could offer.
Legacy and Recognition
Atty. Lindao Macarambon Boransing is formally recognized in the Wikipedia List of First Women Lawyers and
Judges in Asia as the first female Maranao lawyer, alongside other pioneering women who broke legal barriers
across the continent.<ref name="wiki-asia" />
Her legacy lives on in multiple ways. Every Maranao woman who has passed the bar since 1961 has, in some
sense, walked through a door she opened. Every family in the Lanao region that has ever sought legal advice from
a Muslim woman lawyer has benefited, even if unknowingly, from the credibility she established for that kind of
professional relationship.
The MSU-IIT community, whose founding she witnessed and quietly shaped alongside her husband, also carries
traces of her influence. The institution she helped anchor in its early years has gone on to become a Centre of
Excellence in Science and Technology, one of the Philippines' premier higher education institutions, and one of the
few in Mindanao to break into international university rankings.<ref name="msuiit-history" />
Her story, however, is still incompletely documented. Much of what is known about her comes from oral histories,
community memory, and the records associated with her husband's career. A dedicated effort to recover her
individual story, through interviews with surviving contemporaries, family members, archival research at the
Supreme Court, and documentation from Iligan City's civic history, would be a meaningful contribution to
Bangsamoro women's history.
Notes on Sources and Research Gaps
The following source pathways are recommended for those seeking to expand or verify this article:
Supreme Court Roll of Attorneys (1961): The official record for confirming her bar admission year, roll
number, and the scope of her "first" designation among Muslim women.
MSU-IIT Archives: Records from the 1973 to 1988 period of Prof. Boransing's leadership may contain
references to Atty. Lindao's legal and advisory roles.
Oral Histories of Iligan City: Community elders and historians in Iligan and the Lanao region maintain
accounts of her presence and influence. These should be recorded and preserved systematically.

PAGE 5
National Commission on Muslim Filipinos (NCMF) Archives: May contain biographical or reference
materials related to pioneering Bangsamoro professionals.
Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM) Historical Records: May document
her as part of broader narratives on Bangsamoro women in law and public service.

title: Busran-Lao, Yasmin
text:
PAGE 1
Yasmin Busran-Lao
Yasmin Busran-Lao is one of the most quietly consequential figures in Philippine peacebuilding, a woman whose
fingerprints are on landmark agreements, grassroots organizations, and national policy shifts that have reshaped
how the country understands both peace and Muslim womanhood.
Over more than 25 years, she has championed women's rights, gender justice, and sustainable peace in Muslim
Mindanao, doing so not as a bystander or commentator but as a practitioner, a negotiator, and an organizer who
worked from barangay halls to national peace panels.
She is perhaps best known for her role as a member of the Government Peace Negotiating Panel during talks
with the Moro Islamic Liberation Front (MILF), a position that placed her at the heart of one of the Philippines'
most complex and historic diplomatic processes.
Her contributions directly fed into the 2014 Comprehensive Agreement on the Bangsamoro (CAB), a peace
treaty celebrated internationally for its unusually strong, gender-sensitive provisions.

Early Life and Background
Yasmin Busran-Lao grew up in Muslim Mindanao at a time when the region was anything but peaceful.
During the 1970s siege of Marawi City under Martial Law, her family was among the thousands forced to flee
their homes, becoming bakwit, the local term for internally displaced persons caught between government troops
and Moro rebels.
To escape the crossfire, her family crossed Lanao Lake by pump boat, seeking refuge among her father's relatives.
That experience of sudden displacement, of leaving behind everything familiar in the middle of the night, stayed
with her.

Growing up amid structural poverty and recurring armed conflict
gave Busran-Lao something that no classroom could fully teach: a
visceral understanding of what conflict does to ordinary people, and
in particular to women and children who rarely appear in the
headlines but bear the heaviest burden of war.
Later in life, witnessing the "all-out-war" of 2000 and its wave of
displacement would further sharpen her resolve to advocate for the
most vulnerable in her community.
Education
Busran-Lao built an academic foundation that was, from the
beginning, deliberately cross-disciplinary.
She earned a Bachelor of Arts in Psychology from Far Eastern
University, graduating magna cum laude, a distinction that reflected
not just academic ability but the kind of focused, disciplined
thinking she would later bring to policy and advocacy work.
She then pursued a Master's degree in Clinical Counselling
Psychology at the Ateneo de Manila University, developing a
framework for understanding trauma, community behavior, and the
psychological dimensions of conflict.
Knowing that culture and religion would be central to any
meaningful work in Muslim Mindanao, she also undertook
specialized coursework in Islamic Studies at the University of the
Philippines Diliman, and in Muslim Personal Laws at Mindanao
State University.
That combination, behavioral science layered with deep knowledge
of Islamic jurisprudence and cultural context, is precisely what
made her effective in spaces where most outsiders struggled to
connect.
Career and Institutional Contributions
Grassroots and Civil Society Leadership
Long before she sat at government negotiating tables, Busran-Lao
was building institutions from the ground up.
She founded the Al-Mujadilah Development Foundation, Inc.
(AMDF), based in Marawi City, naming it after the 58th Surah of
the Qur'an, Al-Mujadila, which translates roughly as "The Woman
Who Pleads" or "She Who Disputes."
The name was not accidental.

PAGE 3

Public Service; Marie
Claire "Women of

AMDF was deliberately designed as a space where Muslim
women's voices could be amplified in discussions about social
justice, community peacebuilding, and reproductive health.
Under her leadership, AMDF produced pioneering educational
materials that are still referenced today, including a Primer on the
Code of Muslim Personal Laws and a CEDAW Primer translated
into four Moro dialects, making international human rights
frameworks accessible to communities that had long been excluded
from those conversations.
She also co-founded Nisa Ul-Haqq Fi Bangsamoro (Women for Truth and Justice in the Bangsamoro), a network
of Muslim women leaders that conducts community-based research to push for policies that align the core
teachings of the Qur'an with modern human rights principles.
Both organizations represent her conviction that lasting change doesn't come from the top down; it grows from
within communities, when people are given the tools to advocate for themselves.
Government Peace Negotiations
Busran-Lao's most internationally recognized contribution came through her appointment to the Government
Peace Negotiating Panel for the talks with the Moro Islamic Liberation Front (MILF).
Working alongside Chief Negotiator Miriam Coronel-Ferrer, she made it her mission to ensure that the resulting
peace framework wasn't just a political document but one that explicitly recognized women's security needs and
guaranteed their meaningful participation in the Bangsamoro transition.
That work bore fruit in the 2014 Comprehensive Agreement on the Bangsamoro, a treaty that drew international
attention for its gender-sensitive provisions, widely regarded as a model for inclusive peacebuilding.
National Commission on Muslim Filipinos
She also served as the Cabinet-level Secretary of the National Commission on Muslim Filipinos (NCMF) and
as Presidential Assistant for Muslim Affairs under President Benigno Aquino III.
In those roles, she oversaw cultural, social, and economic policies affecting Muslim minorities across the country,
bridging the gap between Malacañang and communities that had long felt disconnected from the machinery of
national government.
National Politics
In 2010, Busran-Lao was selected by the Liberal Party to join its national senatorial slate.
Her campaign carried a clear and deliberate message: that politics could be practiced differently, without the
traditional machinery of money, dynasty, or patronage, and that ordinary citizens deserved to be the spokespersons
of their own political futures.
While her Senate bid did not succeed, it reflected her broader belief that political reform requires new kinds of
voices and new modes of participation.

PAGE 4
Personal Philosophy
At the core of everything Busran-Lao does is a conviction that social justice and women's rights are not foreign
concepts imposed on Muslim communities, but principles already present in Islam itself.
She has consistently refused the framing that pits Islamic tradition against international human rights frameworks,
arguing instead that the Qur'an, read carefully and honestly, already calls for equity, fairness, and the protection of
the vulnerable.
For her, the challenge has never been to convince Muslim communities to adopt "outside" values. The challenge
has been to help those communities rediscover and articulate values they already hold.
She is also a firm believer in grassroots-driven democracy, insisting that real political reform only happens when
ordinary people have platforms to name their own needs and lead their own solutions.
Recognition and Awards
Recognition
Details

internationally praised as a landmark treaty for gender-inclusive peacebuilding.

Fellowship Award for Public
Service
Awarded by the Benigno S. Aquino Foundation and the U.S. Embassy in recognition of her
work with marginalized communities.
Marie Claire "Women of
Substance" Top 25
Named among the top 25 women of substance in the Philippines for her pioneering
contributions to Muslim women's rights.
Policy Network Collaboration
Collaborated with the Change Politics Movement, the Human Development Network, and
INCITEGov to advance inclusive democratic governance.
Legacy
Yasmin Busran-Lao's most enduring contribution may be a shift in narrative.
For too long, Moro women were cast in Philippine public discourse as passive figures, victims of conflict, silent
presences in a story dominated by men with guns or men at desks.
She helped dismantle that framing systematically, through organizations she built, agreements she shaped,
educational materials she produced, and coalitions she formed.
She showed that Muslim women could be architects of peace rather than simply its beneficiaries, and that faith, far
from being an obstacle to gender justice, could be its most powerful foundation.
Her legacy lives in the gender provisions of the CAB, in the women's networks she helped establish across
Mindanao, and in the countless advocates she mentored who continue her work in communities she once
organized.

Usopay Hamdag Cadar
Dr. Usopay Hamdag Cadar (born October 24, 1945) is a Filipino
Maranao ethnomusicologist, master musician, and cultural scholar
known for his foundational work on kulintang music and his efforts
to document and preserve the musical traditions of the Lanao region.
A holder of the traditional title of Dato, Cadar stands as a key figure
in bridging indigenous Maranao knowledge with global academic
discourse. His work reframed Maranao music not as “folk
expression,” but as a structured and sophisticated classical system
rooted in cultural identity and social practice.
