Early Life and Background
Usopay Hamdag Cadar was born on October 24, 1945 in the
Philippines and is of Maranao descent, an indigenous Muslim
ethnolinguistic group from the Lanao provinces of Mindanao.
:contentReference[oaicite:1]{index=1}
He traces his lineage to the royal house of the Sultanate of Bayang in
Lanao del Sur, a background that gave him early exposure to courtly
musical traditions and ceremonial practices.
This environment provided him direct access to the cultural forms he
would later document and analyze in academic settings.
Education
Cadar’s academic path reflects a transition from scientific training to cultural scholarship.

PAGE 2
He earned his Bachelor of Science in Fisheries from Mindanao State University in 1968.
:contentReference[oaicite:2]{index=2}
He later pursued ethnomusicology at the University of Washington, where he completed his Master of Arts in
1971. His thesis, The Maranao Kolintang Music, became one of the earliest formal studies of the tradition.
In 1980, he earned his Doctor of Philosophy in Ethnomusicology from the same institution under the mentorship
of Dr. Robert Garfias. :contentReference[oaicite:3]{index=3}
Career and Scholarly Work
Cadar’s career is defined by both academic research and performance.
His 1985 publication, Context and Style in the Vocal Music of the Muranao in Mindanao, Philippines, is widely
regarded as a definitive study of Maranao vocal traditions. :contentReference[oaicite:4]{index=4}
As a musician, he is recognized as a virtuoso of the kulintang (locally termed kolintang), performing
internationally to demonstrate the depth and structure of Southeast Asian gong-chime traditions.
His work consistently emphasizes insider knowledge, drawing from lived cultural experience rather than purely
external observation.
Institutional Contributions
Cadar played a key role in institutionalizing the study of Maranao music in academic settings.
At the University of Washington, he helped establish a Kulintang Ensemble that preserved authentic performance
practices and transmitted them to new generations of students. :contentReference[oaicite:5]{index=5}
His extensive field recordings and performances are preserved in the University of Washington Ethnomusicology
Archives, forming a major resource for scholars of Philippine music.
He also collaborated with Mindanao State University - Iligan Institute of Technology (MSU-IIT), supporting local
publication efforts and encouraging Filipino scholars to document their own cultural traditions.
Music Theory and Ethnomusicology
Cadar’s research provided an “insider” framework for understanding Maranao music.
He described kulintang music as a topographic system, where musicians conceptualize patterns based on the
physical arrangement of gongs rather than abstract pitch systems. :contentReference[oaicite:6]{index=6}
He identified three primary compositional forms:
Song-based compositions derived from vocal traditions
Abstract instrumental forms
Imitative patterns reflecting environmental or social sounds
He also emphasized that kulintang tuning does not follow a universal pitch standard, with each set maintaining its
own tonal identity while preserving a consistent structural contour.

PAGE 3
The Kulintang Ensemble
Cadar documented the traditional Maranao ensemble known as the Lima ka Daradiyat (five-instrument
ensemble).
Its components include:
Kolintang – the melodic leader composed of eight graduated gongs
Agong – two large hanging gongs producing interlocking rhythms
Dabakan – a goblet-shaped drum establishing the core beat
Babndir – a timekeeping gong that maintains rhythmic cohesion
He highlighted the role of improvisation, particularly among master performers, as a defining feature of Maranao
musical expression.
Cultural Significance
Cadar’s work centers on cultural reclamation and representation.
He argued for the use of indigenous terminology, such as kolintang, to challenge colonial interpretations of
Southeast Asian music. :contentReference[oaicite:7]{index=7}
As a Dato, he views his scholarship as part of a broader responsibility to safeguard Maranao heritage, where music
is inseparable from identity, social order, and traditional governance.
His efforts contributed to the emergence of a “kulintang movement” among the Filipino diaspora, using music as a
means of cultural continuity and identity formation.
Legacy
Dr. Usopay H. Cadar’s legacy lies in both preservation and reinterpretation.
He established frameworks that allowed Maranao music to be studied on its own terms while making it accessible
to global audiences.
His work continues to influence ethnomusicology, cultural studies, and heritage preservation, particularly in the
context of indigenous knowledge systems.
Challenges
Cadar’s work required navigating the gap between indigenous knowledge and Western academic frameworks.
Presenting Maranao music within formal institutions often involved correcting misconceptions and resisting
oversimplified classifications of the tradition.
He addressed these challenges by grounding his work in lived experience and cultural authority.

PAGE 4
Recognition
Cadar is widely recognized in academic and cultural circles for his contributions to ethnomusicology and Southeast
Asian music studies.
His recordings, writings, and performances continue to serve as reference points for scholars, musicians, and
cultural practitioners.

Aliah Pacalna Cali-Pascan
Aliah Pacalna Cali-Pascan, JD, DPA, Sh.C. is a Filipino
academic executive, legal practitioner, and peace strategist based
in Marawi City, Philippines.
She holds the position of Assistant Vice Chancellor for
Academic Affairs at Mindanao State University (MSU) Main
Campus, where she holds the rank of Chancellor 1.
Her career sits at the intersection of public administration, Islamic
jurisprudence, and community-based peacebuilding, making her
one of the more distinctive academic leaders in the Bangsamoro
region.
Dr. Cali-Pascan is widely recognized for her leadership during two
of Marawi's most difficult chapters: the 2017 Marawi Siege and
the COVID-19 pandemic lockdowns of 2020.
Beyond crisis management, she has built a sustained body of work
around institutional reform, women's advocacy, transitional justice,
and the push to officially designate MSU as a "National Peace
University."

PAGE 2
Background and Credentials
Dr. Cali-Pascan brings together a rare mix of qualifications that span three distinct but complementary fields.
Her Juris Doctor (JD) grounds her firmly in Philippine statutory and constitutional law, giving her the legal
vocabulary to engage policy, institutional governance, and conflict resolution with precision.
The Doctor of Public Administration (DPA) feeds directly into her reform-oriented work inside MSU's
administrative structure, where systems thinking and institutional efficiency aren't just concepts but daily practice.
What sets her apart further is the Shari'ah Counselor (Sh.C.) designation, which qualifies her to practice and
consult within the Philippines' Shari'ah court system.
This credential puts her at the crossroads of alternative dispute resolution (ADR), Islamic arbitration, and
community mediation, areas that are especially consequential in Muslim Mindanao where formal and customary
legal systems often overlap.
Together, these credentials reflect a career built not just on academic achievement but on the practical need to serve
a community where law, faith, and governance are deeply intertwined.
Career at Mindanao State University
Early Administrative Work
Before her elevation to a senior executive role, Dr. Cali-Pascan served as Executive Assistant III under the MSU
Office of the President.
It was in this capacity that she drove some of the university's most important modernization initiatives.
She oversaw MSU's compliance with the Anti-Red Tape Act (ARTA), the national legislation designed to cut
bureaucratic delays in public services, ensuring that students, faculty, and the general public could access university
services without unnecessary friction.
She also led the implementation of MSU's Strategic Performance Management System (SPMS) and
championed the adoption of a university-wide Quality Management System (QMS), bringing MSU's
administrative processes into alignment with recognized quality standards.
These weren't flashy reforms, but they were consequential: the kind of structural groundwork that makes an
institution more resilient, more accountable, and more responsive to the people it serves.
Assistant Vice Chancellor for Academic Affairs
In December 2022, Dr. Cali-Pascan was designated to the permanent position of Assistant Vice Chancellor for
Academic Affairs at MSU Main Campus, carrying the rank of Chancellor 1.
In this role, she oversees academic policy development, faculty development programs, and the alignment of the
university's various academic systems.
The position places her at the center of MSU's long-term institutional direction, particularly as the university
continues to define its role in post-conflict Marawi.

PAGE 3
Crisis Leadership
The 2017 Marawi Siege
When the Marawi Siege erupted in May 2017, Dr. Cali-Pascan was serving as Director of the MSU-Marawi
Presidential Management Staff (PMS).
The siege placed MSU in an extraordinarily difficult position: a civilian academic institution suddenly surrounded
by active armed conflict, with students and personnel caught in the middle.
Her role as liaison between the university and external security forces required careful, high-stakes negotiation on a
near-daily basis.
She defended the temporary military presence on campus as a necessary measure for student safety, while
simultaneously working to ensure that soldiers remained out of academic buildings so that students wouldn't feel
intimidated or surveilled in their own learning spaces.
She also arranged for female soldiers to assist during post-siege enrollment periods, a practical and sensitive
measure aimed at making female students feel safer returning to campus.
It was a difficult position to navigate publicly, but her decisions during that period reflected a consistent priority:
protect the students, keep the academic mission alive, and maintain the university's integrity as a civilian space.
COVID-19 and the 2020 Lockdown
The pandemic brought a different kind of crisis to MSU.
When Marawi entered Enhanced Community Quarantine (ECQ) in 2020, more than 1,500 students were suddenly
stranded on campus with no clear path home.
Dr. Cali-Pascan coordinated the massive logistical effort to manage, feed, and safely repatriate all of them, a task
that required careful coordination across multiple agencies and barangays under strict lockdown conditions.
Her handling of this situation demonstrated the same quality that defined her work during the Marawi Siege: a
calm, practical focus on the welfare of students even under institutional pressure.
Peace Advocacy
The National Peace University Campaign
As a designated Peace Action Officer for MSU's Institute for Peace and Development in Mindanao (IPDM),
Dr. Cali-Pascan has become one of the leading voices behind the campaign to officially recognize and legally
certify MSU as a National Peace University.
This isn't a symbolic gesture. The campaign is a strategic initiative backed by the university's Board of Regents,
aiming to institutionalize MSU's peace-oriented mission and give it national standing.
She is one of the primary authors of this initiative, which frames MSU's entire existence, especially its persistence
through conflict and recovery, as proof of the university's unique qualification for the designation.

PAGE 4
Radio Advocacy: #ShuaraMSU
To reach beyond the campus and into the community, Dr. Cali-Pascan hosts #ShuaraMSU (which translates to
"The Voice of MSU"), a radio program broadcast over Radyo Pilipinas Marawi (97.5 FM).
The program covers stories of local peacebuilders, Bangsamoro heritage and culture, and discussions on the
region's historical narrative.
She has used the platform to feature cultural programming as well, including film screenings of Dekada '70,
reflecting her belief that cultural memory is part of the peace process.
Grassroots Mediation Training
Through partnerships with international organizations like World Vision, Dr. Cali-Pascan conducts hands-on
mediation training for members of the Lupon Tagapamayapa (local village justice councils) in Marawi barangays.
The goal is practical: give grassroots community leaders formal mediation frameworks they can actually use to
resolve disputes before they escalate.
In a city where clan-based conflict (rido) has historically led to cycles of violence, this kind of community-level
capacity building is seen as one of the most effective long-term interventions available.
Women's Leadership and Transitional Justice
Bae a Tomanor (B'TARA)
Dr. Cali-Pascan is an active and prominent member of Bae a Tomanor (B'TARA), an organization that brings
together women royalty, officials, and academic leaders in Lanao del Sur.
Through B'TARA, she advocates for women to serve as "Third Siders" in community conflicts, that is, as trusted,
neutral parties who can enter volatile situations and help de-escalate tensions without being seen as aligned with
any one clan or faction.
In the context of Maranao society, where rido (clan feuds) can persist for generations, having women from
respected families and institutions take on this mediating role carries real cultural weight.
Transitional Justice and Cultural Repatriation
Dr. Cali-Pascan is also a vocal advocate for cultural repatriation, arguing that the return of historical artifacts to
Muslim Mindanao is not simply a cultural issue but a matter of collective dignity and historical justice for the
Bangsamoro people.
She frames transitional justice in this broader sense: healing a community means addressing not only the physical
destruction of war but also the erasure of cultural memory and the displacement of heritage.

PAGE 5
International Dialogue
She represents MSU in international academic and diplomatic spaces, including dialogues with global delegations
such as Indonesia's Leimena Group.
These engagements are aimed at building cross-border networks across Southeast Asia around themes of religious
freedom, interfaith dialogue, and moderate Islamic education, areas where MSU can position itself as a regional
thought leader.
Legacy and Significance
Dr. Cali-Pascan's career is a study in what it looks like to hold institutional and community roles simultaneously
without losing sight of either.
She's a university administrator who also sits in village mediation sessions. She's a Shari'ah counselor who designs
university quality management systems. She's a peace strategist who runs a radio program.
What connects all of it is a consistent orientation toward the people of Marawi and the Bangsamoro region:
keeping them educated, keeping them safe, and working to make sure their culture, history, and dignity are part of
any post-conflict future.
Her push to name MSU a National Peace University is perhaps the clearest expression of that vision: not just
rebuilding an institution, but insisting that what MSU has lived through gives it a specific and permanent role in the
national peace narrative.
Recognition
Dr. Cali-Pascan's work has been recognized within MSU's institutional framework through her designation as
Peace Action Officer under IPDM and her permanent appointment as Assistant Vice Chancellor for Academic
Affairs.
Her advocacy through the National Peace University campaign and her crisis leadership during the Marawi Siege
and the COVID-19 pandemic have positioned her as one of the more visible academic peace advocates in Muslim
Mindanao.
Personal Life
Dr. Cali-Pascan is married to Walid Bacaraman Pascan and is a mother to their son, Faris Sufyan Cali Pascan.

Al-Hussein Caluang
Hadji Al-Hussein Caluang (born May 16, 1947, in Kambing,
Kalingalan Caluang, Sulu), widely known by his epithet "The Lion
of Mindanao," was one of the most significant military figures in
the history of the Bangsamoro armed struggle.
He is recognized as the only Field Marshal of the Moro National
Liberation Front (MNLF), a distinction conferred by the late
MNLF Chairman Abul Khayr Alonto, and his life traces the full arc
of the Bangsamoro experience: from the jungles of Sulu to
international training grounds in Malaysia, Cuba, and Angola, and
eventually into the halls of local governance and peace advocacy.

BACKGROUND AND HERITAGE
Hadji Al-Hussein Caluang was born on May 16, 1947, in Kambing,
Kalingalan Caluang, Sulu, as recorded in his Certificate of Live
Birth issued by the Office of the Civil Registrar General.
He was the firstborn child of his parents, delivered by a hilot
(traditional midwife), and weighed 3,175 grams at birth.
His father, Sayyid Captain Kalingalan Caluang, was the chief
police officer of the area, while his mother, Lucia Ismael Jaudinez,
was a housewife. His parents were married in 1945 in Kambing,
Kalingalan Caluang, Sulu, with his father at 23 and his mother at 20
years of age at the time of his birth. Both parents were Filipino
citizens of the Islamic faith.
Caluang came from a lineage rooted deeply in the political and
spiritual traditions of the Sulu Archipelago. He was a descendant of
the sultans who governed Sulu until the arrival of the Americans in

PAGE 2
Moro National Liberation Front
(MNLF)
Rank
Field Marshal (MNLF, sole holder of the
rank)
Political Offices
Municipal Mayor, Kalingalan Caluang,
Sulu; Member, Regional Autonomous
Government Assembly of Region IX
Notability
The only Field Marshal of the Moro
National Liberation Front (MNLF);
Tausug military commander and
statesman from Sulu; member of the
historic Top 90 founding cadre
Known For
Armed resistance leadership during the
Bangsamoro struggle; attendance at the
1976 Tripoli Agreement negotiations;
transition from guerrilla commander to
peace advocate and elected official
the late 19th century, placing him squarely within the long
continuum of Moro resistance to foreign domination, from the
Spanish and American colonial periods through the post-war era.
This heritage shaped his sense of identity and duty from an early
age, making his later path into armed struggle less a departure from
his roots than a continuation of them.
THE MNLF AND THE TOP 90
Caluang is one of the original members of the celebrated "Top 90,"
also called Batch 90, the pioneering group of volunteers who
underwent intensive military training in Pangkor Island, Sabah,
Malaysia, and formed the core command structure of the Moro
National Liberation Front.
As part of the broader Third World liberation movement of that era,
the MNLF drew support from Arab and Muslim countries, including
Libya, which provided financial backing through zakat and
international solidarity networks.
Following his training in Malaysia, Caluang was sent to Cuba in
1971, where he spent three months receiving specialized training in
mass communication, recruitment, and both rural and urban warfare. This training was conducted under a general
operating in close proximity to Fidel Castro's command.
He subsequently volunteered for deployment to Angola, where he and fellow dissidents from Asia, Europe, the
Middle East, and Africa put their guerrilla training into practice against opposing military units.
Upon returning to Mindanao, Caluang applied everything he had learned and helped develop the MNLF's
operational capacity in the field.
His reputation grew formidable. The late MNLF Chairman Abul Khayr Alonto would later describe him as the only
Field Marshal of the MNLF, a singular distinction that earned him the enduring epithet "Lion of Mindanao." He
was not only respected within the MNLF's ranks but was also, by many accounts, feared by the Armed Forces of
the Philippines.
MARTIAL LAW AND RETURN TO THE FOLD OF THE LAW
Following the declaration of Martial Law under President Ferdinand Marcos, Al-Hussein Caluang was reportedly
placed on a military blacklist, a reflection of how central his role had become in the armed resistance in Sulu.
As the political and security landscape shifted, senior MNLF leaders and commanders engaged in deliberations
about the movement's future direction.
Acting upon the collective recommendations of MNLF leadership, including then Secretary-General Bakrin
Lukman and other senior commanders, Caluang made the decision to voluntarily return to the fold of the law.
President Marcos had reportedly expressed a strong personal desire for Caluang's return, recognizing his singular
importance as a field leader during the conflict in Sulu.

PAGE 3
This decision was not a military surrender. It was, rather, a deliberate and negotiated step toward political
engagement, marking an important turning point both in Caluang's personal journey and in the broader evolution of
Bangsamoro conflict-to-peace efforts.
THE 1976 TRIPOLI AGREEMENT AND POLITICAL SERVICE
Caluang was present at the historic negotiations brokered by Libyan leader Muammar Gaddafi in the mid-1970s,
which culminated in the 1976 Tripoli Agreement, the landmark accord signed between the MNLF and the
government of Ferdinand Marcos.
During this period, President Marcos reportedly asked Caluang to serve as his bodyguard during an official visit to
the United States in the late 1970s.
After the Tripoli Agreement collapsed, Caluang and many of his contemporaries returned to the jungle to continue
the armed struggle.
In August 1975, Caluang was appointed Commander of the Paramilitary Force for Southern Luuk, Sulu.
A few months later, Presidential Decree No. 838 divided the Municipality of Luuk, Sulu into two municipalities to
accelerate economic development in the area. The newly created municipality was named Kalingalan Caluang, in
honor of his father, Sayyid Captain Kalingalan Caluang. Presidential Decree No. 838 was signed on December 6,
1975, by President Marcos.
Al-Hussein Caluang subsequently served as Municipal Mayor of Kalingalan Caluang, Sulu, bringing his
family's name and legacy directly into the formal governance of the community that bore it.
He later served as a member of the Assembly of the Regional Autonomous Government of Region IX, marking
his continued engagement in formal political institutions and cementing his transition from armed resistance to
political participation.
LATER LIFE AND LEGACY
In his later years, Caluang became a vocal supporter of the peace process and expressed disagreement with
certain approaches taken by former MNLF Chairman Nur Misuari, including the 2013 Zamboanga City siege.
While acknowledging Misuari's continued following, particularly in Sulu and Zamboanga del Norte, Caluang
consistently advocated for dialogue and reconciliation within the MNLF.
He was among the MNLF pioneers who supported the reorganization of the MNLF under Chairman Alonto, a
move endorsed by the 57-member Organization of Islamic Cooperation (OIC).
Despite his age, Caluang retained an aura of authority and near-mythic reverence among the region's Muslims.
Many held him in extraordinary regard, with some even believing him to be impervious to bullets, a testament to
the kind of legendary status he had accumulated over decades of service and sacrifice.
The life and contributions of Hadji Al-Hussein Caluang continue to be studied in the fields of Bangsamoro history,
peace and conflict studies, and political history. He stands as a compelling example of the intersection between
traditional Islamic leadership, mass revolutionary struggle, and the long, difficult process of peace-building in
Mindanao.

PAGE 4
A tribute poem, "But Lion's Name!" was written by Prof. Neldy Jolo in his honor following his passing. It reflects
the depth of reverence accorded to him within the Bangsamoro community.
THE CALUANG FAMILY
The Caluang family has played a sustained role in the political, spiritual, and cultural life of Sulu across multiple
generations.
Sayyid Captain Kalingalan Caluang, father of Hadji Al-Hussein, was a distinguished statesman and community
leader remembered as one of the "Fighting 21 of Sulu" and as the founder of Ansarul Islam. He served as OIC
Governor of Sulu and is traditionally credited as the Magbabangun, the figure responsible for the continuation and
organization of the Giba tradition during the enthronement of the Sultan of Sulu. He played a pivotal role in
facilitating the enthronement of Sultan Jainal Abirin, following the reign of Sultan Jamalul Kiram II.
Hadji Al Hassan Caluang, grandson of Captain Kalingalan Caluang, served as OIC Governor of Sulu and played
a quiet but significant role in the efforts that contributed to the 1996 Jakarta Peace Agreement between the
MNLF and the Philippine government. A Sunni Imam, he holds ijazah (authorization and certification) in the
Science of Ihsan (Tasawwuf), including a rare comprehensive ijazah encompassing forty Sunni Sufi turuq (spiritual
orders), a distinction seldom granted to a single individual and particularly unique within the Philippines.
Dr. Calingalan Hussin Caluang, son of Hadji Al Hassan Caluang, is recognized as the Naqib al-Sadat al-Ashraf
of the Philippines. He is regarded as the first individual in the country since the arrival of Islam in the Philippine
archipelago in the 13th century to formally hold this office with an authenticated ijazah in the Science of Nasab
(Islamic Genealogy). He received this authorization from the Naqib al-Sadat al-Ashraf of Algeria and the Naqib al-
Sadat al-Ashraf of Turkey, empowering him in the preservation, verification, and transmission of noble
genealogical lineages. A dedicated student of the Islamic sciences, he has received multiple ijazat across various
disciplines from respected scholars (ulama) in several countries, and continues to pursue advanced studies across
the various madhahib (schools of Islamic jurisprudence).

2014. https://old.pcij.org/blog/2014/03/28/of-warriors-and-peacemakers

https://newsinfo.inquirer.net/586928/pioneers-of-mnlf-oust-nur-misuari

https://southeastasiaglobe.com/philippines-mindanao-southeast-asia-globe/

PAGE 5
4. Revolutionary Contemporary Writings Asia (RCW-Asia). "Interview with Al Caluang." Oral history archive.
https://rcw-asia.com/browsearchives/interview-with-al-caluang
5. Rear Admiral Romulo Espaldon Memorial Facebook Page. Condolence tribute and photograph caption
identifying Caluang. https://www.facebook.com/AdmiralEspaldon

Province of Sulu, into Two Municipalities." Signed December 6, 1975, by President Ferdinand E. Marcos.

title: Camlian, Abdulla U.
text:
PAGE 1
Hadji Abdulla "Al" U. Camlian
Born
Zamboanga City, Philippines
Ethnicity
Sama-Bangingi, Tausug
Education
Cairo Military Academy (1965)
Known
for
Chairman, MILF Technical
Committee; MILF Peace Panel
Member; Bangsamoro Transition
Commission Commissioner
Roles
Executive Assistant, Southern
Philippine Development
Administration;
Deputy Executive Director, Office
on Muslim Affairs
Movement
Bangsamoro liberation and peace
process
Religion
Islam
Abdulla U. Camlian
Hadji Abdulla "Al" U. Camlian was a Bangsamoro leader, peace
process technician, and one of the Moro Islamic Liberation Front's
(MILF) most consequential behind-the-scenes figures in the long
negotiation with the Government of the Republic of the Philippines
(GRP). He wasn't the kind of leader who made the headlines on
signing day, though he was there for that too. His real work happened
in rooms most people never read about: technical committees,
wealth-sharing working groups, law-drafting sessions, and the
grinding consultation processes that turn peace agreements into
actual governing structures. If the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region
in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM) has a fiscal architecture that is
meaningful rather than merely ceremonial, part of that has to do with
the kind of careful, persistent work that people like Al Camlian put
into the decades-long process of making it real.<ref
name="spf">Sasakawa Peace Foundation. Asia Pacific Broadband
Institute. Profile of Hadji Abdulla "Al" U. Camlian. Retrieved from
https://www.spf.org/apbi/news_en/p_160113.html</ref>
His signature contribution to the Bangsamoro struggle was what you
could call "technical peacemaking," the patient, often unglamorous
work of translating political aspirations into legal text, fiscal rules,
and institutional design. He embodied a generation of non-combatant
Bangsamoro leaders whose weapons were drafts, position papers, and
cross-table negotiations rather than arms, and whose legacy is written
less in monuments than in clauses, annexes, and the functioning
machinery of autonomy.
Contents
1 Early Life and Background
2 Education
3 Government Service
4 The Peace Process: Technical Leadership
4.1 MILF Technical Working Group
4.2 Chairman of the MILF Technical Committee
5 Wealth-Sharing Negotiations
5.1 Why the Money Track Mattered Most
5.2 Camlian as Wealth-Sharing Adviser
5.3 Fiscal Governance During the Transition
6 The Bangsamoro Transition Commission
6.1 From Agreement to Law
6.2 Signing the Comprehensive Agreement
7 Implementation and Continuing Role
8 Legacy
9 Further Reading

PAGE 2
10 See Also
Early Life and Background
Al Camlian came from the Zamboanga City–Basilan corridor, a crossroads of Bangsamoro identity where Sama-
Bangingi and Tausug communities have long lived alongside each other.<ref name="milf_reconstitution">GMA
News. "MILF Forms New Peace Panel." 2010. Retrieved from
https://www.gmanetwork.com/news/topstories/nation/200880/milf-forms-new-peace-panel/story/</ref> That
background mattered more than it might seem. The MILF's legitimacy as a representative body rested partly on its
ability to bring together the diverse peoples of Muslim Mindanao under one platform, and a leader with Camlian's
ethnolinguistic roots helped demonstrate that the movement was broader than any single community or geography.
Public records describe him as "one of the leaders of the liberation movement of the Moro people in the 1970s,"
which places his political formation during the most turbulent decade in modern Bangsamoro history: the
declaration of martial law, the eruption of armed conflict in Mindanao and Sulu, and the forging of the first major
political consciousness among Moro youth.<ref name="spf" /> He entered the struggle not through a single
dramatic moment but through the accumulation of commitments that defined his generation.
Education
Camlian is a graduate of the Cairo Military Academy, having completed his studies there in 1965.<ref name="spf"
/><ref name="cab">Comprehensive Agreement on the Bangsamoro. 2014. Retrieved from
https://www.peaceagreements.org/view/881/</ref> That single biographical detail is easy to skip over, but it says a
lot about his formation. A generation of Moro students who went to Cairo in the 1960s returned shaped by
something bigger than military training: they came back with exposure to post-colonial thought, pan-Islamic
political consciousness, and the debates about statehood and self-determination that were alive across the Muslim
world at that time.
Cairo in those years was a hub. Students from across Asia and Africa were there, wrestling with questions about
identity, liberation, and governance. For Camlian, that environment helped build the intellectual and institutional
vocabulary he would later deploy in the peace process, not as ideology loudly proclaimed, but as the kind of
structured thinking that disciplines a movement toward what is actually achievable in a negotiating room.
His military academy formation also shaped his instinct for structure and planning. His later career pattern
consistently shows a preference for roles that require institutional architecture, process design, and the disciplined
conversion of political goals into operational plans, all things that an academy environment tends to develop.
Government Service
Before he became a central figure in the MILF's negotiating machinery, Camlian had a stretch of government
service that would prove strategically important. Public records identify him as having served as an executive
assistant at the Southern Philippine Development Administration and later as Deputy Executive Director of the
Office on Muslim Affairs (now the National Commission on Muslim Filipinos).<ref name="spf" /><ref
name="lawphil">Executive Order No. 120 (2012). Retrieved from
https://lawphil.net/executive/execord/eo2012/pdf/eo_120_2012.pdf</ref>

PAGE 3
Those aren't just résumé entries. The Mindanao peace process was always complicated by a credibility problem on
both sides: communities who had lived through displacement and marginalization were skeptical of Manila's
promises, and state institutions were often skeptical of insurgent commitments. People who had walked on both
sides of that divide, without being dismissed as mere government collaborators, were genuinely hard to find and
enormously valuable when found.
Camlian is consistently described in the documentary record as a figure "standing between the Philippine
Government and Moro people," which is the language of interface work rather than battlefield command.<ref
name="spf" /> His government service gave him something that pure movement figures often lacked: fluency in
the state's grammar. He understood how agencies process decisions, how appropriations flow (and stall), and how
bureaucratic "technicalities" can become political weapons in the hands of those who want to slow or block an
agreement. That knowledge later made him a more effective advocate for the Bangsamoro's fiscal and
administrative interests precisely because he could see the obstacles coming.
The Peace Process: Technical Leadership
MILF Technical Working Group
The public documentary trail around Camlian's formal roles in the peace process begins to get specific around
2008. A peace advocacy forum document from that year identifies him explicitly as "MILF-TWG Chairman" and
records him participating as a technical resource person.<ref name="kas">Konrad Adenauer Stiftung. Peace Forum
Document, 2008. Retrieved from https://www.kas.de/c/document_library/get_file?
groupId=252038&uuid=19ee2b46-2ec6-44f2-8dee-964aff9abe93</ref> What makes that documentation interesting
is that he was not purely playing a technical role: the forum shows him engaging historical and identity arguments,
which is a reminder that technical leadership in the Bangsamoro peace process was never value-neutral. You
brought your people's history and memory into the room with the draft texts.
The technical working groups were the peace process' real engine. While the public watched signings and
handshakes, the TWGs were the bodies where dense questions, including revenue authority, policing arrangements,
and demobilization frameworks, were hammered into actual language.<ref name="mindanews">Mindanews.
"GPH-MILF Talks Post-FAB Signing: The Devils and Angels in the Details." 2012. Retrieved from
https://mindanews.com/peace-process/2012/11/gph-milf-talks-post-fab-signing-the-devils-and-angels-in-the-
details/</ref> Chairing one of those groups was a position of real institutional authority, not a ceremonial
appointment.
Chairman of the MILF Technical Committee
By 2010, when the MILF reconstituted its peace panel, public reporting describes Camlian as "erstwhile member
and later chairman of the MILF Technical Committee," with additional note that he had served in the MILF
Technical Working Group.<ref name="milf_reconstitution" /> That progression, from TWG member to TWG
chairman to Technical Committee chair, traces a clear arc of growing institutional authority within the MILF's
negotiating architecture.
The Technical Committee sat above the individual working groups, coordinating across tracks and ensuring the
MILF's positions on power-sharing, wealth-sharing, and normalization were internally consistent. It was, in other
words, the body that had to hold everything together when the devil was in the details of multiple simultaneous
negotiations. The person chairing it needed to be trusted by the panel, knowledgeable across portfolios, and steady
enough to keep the internal machinery from fragmenting under pressure.

PAGE 4
Wealth-Sharing Negotiations
Why the Money Track Mattered Most
Experienced negotiators will often tell you that the real fight in any autonomy arrangement is not the name or the
flag. It is who controls the revenue, who sets the rules for resource extraction, and how predictable the fiscal
pipeline is when the political wind shifts. The Annex on Revenue Generation and Wealth-Sharing negotiated under
the Framework Agreement on the Bangsamoro (FAB) addressed exactly those questions: a block grant for the
Bangsamoro, special development funding, revenue-raising powers, and explicit sharing rules between the central
government and the new region.<ref name="wealth_sharing">Annex on Revenue Generation and Wealth-Sharing.
Retrieved from https://www.peaceagreements.org/view/869/</ref>
Among the specific provisions embedded in the text: certain central government collections within the Bangsamoro
would be shared 75% to the Bangsamoro and 25% to the central government, with a provision that the central
government's 25% share could be remitted back to the Bangsamoro for a transitional period. The block grant could
not fall below the last budget the Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (ARMM) received before the
transition authority took over.<ref name="wealth_sharing" /> These were not symbolic gestures. They were fiscal
floors that determined whether autonomy would be real or performative.
Camlian as Wealth-Sharing Adviser
A contemporaneous account of post-Framework Agreement negotiations specifically identifies Camlian as the
MILF panel adviser for the Wealth-Sharing Technical Working Group, paired with his government counterpart on
the same track.<ref name="mindanews" /> Being an adviser at that level is not a background role: advisers are the
principals' first line when a text choice can move billions, alter regulatory sovereignty, or expose the agreement to
constitutional attack.
During 2013, as negotiations on the annexes faced friction and delays, Camlian appears in news reports as an
active MILF peace panel member commenting publicly on the pace of the process, including the stalling of the
wealth-sharing annex signing.<ref name="gma_2013">GMA News. "Govt Working as Fast as Possible on Peace,
Palace Assures MILF." 2013. Retrieved from https://www.gmanetwork.com/news/topstories/nation/303804/govt-
working-as-fast-as-possible-on-peace-palace-assures-milf/story/</ref> He was not waiting quietly on the sidelines.
He was engaged, visible, and willing to push.
The wealth-sharing mandate required a particular kind of leader: someone who could translate the moral weight of
the Bangsamoro's historical grievance into concrete fiscal rules that would survive legal scrutiny, convince skeptics
in Manila, and still be tangible enough to justify continued commitment to the peace process among communities
who had been promised so much before. Camlian's documented role in that track puts him at exactly that
intersection.
Fiscal Governance During the Transition
Camlian's concern for fiscal architecture did not stop when the agreements were signed. In Bangsamoro Transition
Commission consultations on transitioning the bureaucracy from ARMM to the new Bangsamoro government, he
is quoted pressing that national government funding flowing into the region, including local government shares,
should be routed through the Bangsamoro government rather than being channeled separately.<ref
name="iag_bureaucracy">Institute for Autonomy and Governance. "Policy Report: Transitioning Bureaucracy

PAGE 5
from ARMM to Bangsamoro." Retrieved from https://iag.org.ph/think/1206-policy-report-transitioning-
bureaucracy-from-armm-to-bangsamoro</ref> That is a sovereignty argument expressed in fiscal language: if the
money doesn't pass through the regional government's hands, the regional government doesn't actually govern.
He also consistently advocated for competence and integrity in the civil service as a structural safeguard against
repeating ARMM's failures. In his reading, which the documentary record supports, the old arrangement had been
delegitimized in the eyes of many Bangsamoro communities not only because of the structural limits of its
autonomy but also because governance had often been poor. Building the new region on integrity was not a nice-to-
have; it was a strategic necessity for long-term credibility.<ref name="iag_bureaucracy" />
The Bangsamoro Transition Commission
From Agreement to Law
The pivot from a negotiated peace agreement to an actual new government required law-making, and that meant a
different kind of work. The Bangsamoro Transition Commission (BTC/TransCom) was the body tasked with
drafting the proposed Bangsamoro Basic Law, recommending constitutional amendments where needed,
coordinating development programs, and conducting consultations across the region.<ref name="lawphil" />
Camlian is named among the MILF-side commissioners appointed to this body in 2012.<ref
name="transcom">Institute for Autonomy and Governance. "TransCom Members Named; MILF Peace Panel
Chair Iqbal is TransCom Chair." Retrieved from https://www.iag.org.ph/news/827-transcom-members-named-milf-
peace-panel-chair-iqbal-is-transcom-chair</ref><ref name="parliament">Bangsamoro Parliament. "Historical
Development of the Bangsamoro Transition Authority Parliament." Retrieved from
https://parliament.bangsamoro.gov.ph/historical-development-of-the-bangsamoro-transition-authority-
parliament/</ref>
The BTC's enabling order (Executive Order No. 120) explicitly authorized the commission to create technical
committees, designate their members, and engage outside experts and professional advisers.<ref name="lawphil"
/> That authority was built into the design because the drafters understood that law-making of this scope, covering
fiscal architecture, parliamentary form, intergovernmental relations, and fundamental rights, was impossible
without sustained technical expertise. It was, in effect, an institutional acknowledgment of what figures like
Camlian represented: that peace-to-governance transitions don't happen without the people who can sit in a room
for months and get the clauses right.
Signing the Comprehensive Agreement
Camlian is listed as an MILF peace panel member among the signatories of the Comprehensive Agreement on the
Bangsamoro (CAB).<ref name="cab" /> That formal position meant he carried shared institutional responsibility
not only for the text of the agreements but for the claim that the MILF's negotiating team had produced something
worth implementing. It was a commitment made in public, on paper, with names attached.
The CAB itself built on years of annex negotiations across the power-sharing, wealth-sharing, and normalization
tracks, and the fact that Camlian's name is on it is consistent with the documentary picture of someone who was
present at, and instrumental in, multiple phases of the process that produced it.

PAGE 6
Implementation and Continuing Role
After the signing, the peace process moved into its most test-prone phase: implementation. Agreements that look
clean on paper often fragment when they meet budget cycles, bureaucratic resistance, political turnover, and the
competing interests of local power holders. The Third Party Monitoring Team (TPMT), the independent body
tasked with monitoring compliance with the CAB, publicly identifies Camlian as a member of the MILF
Implementing Panel (chaired by Mohagher Iqbal) during the mid-2010s implementation phase.<ref
name="tpmt">Third Party Monitoring Team. Public Report 4, 2017. Retrieved from https://peace.gov.ph/wp-
content/uploads/2017/07/170728-TPMT-PR-4-f.pdf</ref>
That detail matters because it confirms something the broader record already suggests: he was not a figure who
showed up for the symbolic moments and disappeared during the difficult work. He stayed. He moved from
technical committee work to panel advisory roles to implementation monitoring, tracking the agreement through its
most vulnerable stages. That kind of institutional continuity, carrying memory and accountability across phases, is
rare and genuinely important.
The road to BARMM itself was long after the agreements were signed. The Bangsamoro Organic Law was enacted
in 2018, and plebiscites in January and February 2019 ratified the region's territorial extent and formal
establishment.<ref name="sc">Supreme Court of the Philippines. "SC Upholds Validity of Bangsamoro Organic
Law, Declares Sulu Not Part of Bangsamoro Region." Retrieved from https://sc.judiciary.gov.ph/sc-upholds-
validity-of-bangsamoro-organic-law-declares-sulu-not-part-of-bangsamoro-region/</ref> The Bangsamoro
Transition Authority (BTA) assumed office in February 2019, beginning the work of actually running the new
region as it transitioned from ARMM.<ref name="bta">Institute for Autonomy and Governance. "Bangsamoro
Transition Authority: A Transition Beyond Bridging ARMM to BARMM." Retrieved from
https://www.iag.org.ph/think/1831-bangsamoro-transition-authority-a-transition-beyond-bridging-armm-to-
barmm</ref> The institutional groundwork Camlian helped lay through years of technical committee work, wealth-
sharing negotiations, and BTC drafting is part of what made those milestones possible to reach at all.
Legacy
Al Camlian's story illustrates something that gets overlooked in the standard telling of the Bangsamoro peace
process: the indispensable role of what might be called "technical mujahideen," people whose contribution to the
struggle was not measured in battles but in the quality of the governance architecture they helped design.
His documentary footprint clusters at the hinge points where autonomy becomes real or collapses: the fiscal rules
that determine whether a regional government can actually deliver, the civil service standards that determine
whether a new government earns or squanders public trust, the legal texts that determine whether agreements
survive courts and legislatures. He didn't just show up at those moments; he often helped shape what was possible
at them.
A peace agreement is not an end. It is a design for governance that must still survive courts,
legislatures, budgets, and public trust. The people who do the technical work make the difference
between a design that holds and one that doesn't.
Three qualities stand out from the composite picture the public record provides. First, he was willing to do the
unglamorous work, the committee sessions, the consultation marathons, the definitional arguments over clauses
that most people will never read, because he understood that the unglamorous work is where the agreement lives or
dies. Second, he stayed. He is traceable across the arc from TWG chairmanship through panel reconstitution, annex
negotiation, BTC law-drafting, agreement signing, and implementation monitoring, which means he was carrying

PAGE 7
institutional memory and continuity across decades. Third, he brought both movement legitimacy and governance
fluency to the table, a combination that was genuinely hard to find and genuinely necessary for the Bangsamoro
peace process to move from conflict to constitutional governance.
His legacy is not a single monument or a single moment. It is woven into the fiscal architecture of BARMM, the
organic law that established it, and the transition processes that brought it to life.
Further Reading
Comprehensive Agreement on the Bangsamoro (2014). Full text available at the Peace Agreements Database.
Framework Agreement on the Bangsamoro (2012). Philippine Official Gazette.
Annex on Revenue Generation and Wealth-Sharing (2013). Peace Agreements Database.
Executive Order No. 120 (2012). Establishing the Bangsamoro Transition Commission. Available at LawPhil
Project.
Institute for Autonomy and Governance. "Policy Report: Transitioning Bureaucracy from ARMM to
Bangsamoro."
Third Party Monitoring Team. Public Report No. 4 (2017). Office of the Presidential Adviser on the Peace
Process.
Sakili, Abraham P. "The Bangsamoro Framework Agreement: Historical, Cultural, and Social Facts in

title: Carim Panumpang, Sr.
text:
PAGE 1
Carim Panumpang, Sr.
Atty. Carim L. Panumpang, Sr. (also known as Atty. Rex Panumpang) was a prominently influential Filipino
lawyer and government official whose career spanned public service, civil society leadership, and interfaith
advocacy.
He is best remembered for his groundbreaking work bridging Islamic law with Philippine national jurisprudence,
empowering Muslim Filipinos through legal protections, and advancing the Halal industry as a framework for
religiously authentic entrepreneurship and economic inclusion.
As the Undersecretary for Special Concerns at the Department of Agrarian Reform (DAR), Panumpang
championed inclusive rural development and placed Muslim and women farmer voices at the center of land reform
policy.
Through his leadership of the Halal International Chamber of Commerce and Industries of the Philippines
(HICCIP) and the Muslim Legal Aid Foundation Inc., he established institutional pathways for Muslim Filipinos
to access culturally grounded legal services and participate in the global Halal economy.
His legacy is inseparable from his conviction that justice and prosperity for Muslim Filipinos must remain
anchored in Shari'ah principles, national legal frameworks, and collaborative governance structures.

Early Life and Education
Little is publicly documented about Panumpang's early life, family
background, or formal education.
However, his professional trajectory reveals a lawyer deeply
committed to public service and Muslim community advocacy from
his formative years onward.
His work across government, civil society, and religious institutions
suggests he completed law school and undertook specialized training in agrarian law and Islamic jurisprudence,
though specific details remain unverified in publicly available sources.

PAGE 3
Government Service at the Department of Agrarian Reform
Appointment and Mandate
Panumpang served as Undersecretary for Special Concerns at the Department of Agrarian Reform during the
administration of President Rodrigo Duterte.
His office was tasked with identifying and addressing systemic barriers affecting agrarian reform beneficiaries
(ARBs), particularly marginalized and underserved populations including women farmers, Muslim communities in
BARMM, and vulnerable rural families.
Agrarian Justice and CLOA Validation
One of his most visible initiatives was spearheading nationwide CLOA (Certificate of Land Ownership Award)
Validation activities.
This multi-year program systematically verified whether emancipation patents (EPs) and CLOAs issued under the
Comprehensive Agrarian Reform Program (CARP) remained in the possession of their original beneficiaries and
continued to be productively farmed.
Panumpang was explicit about the purpose: "The real objective of CARP is to develop agriculture. We award lots
to beneficiaries and the colatilla [conditions] carried under this CLOA is for them to make the land productive."
He warned farmer-beneficiaries against selling their awarded lots and threatened blacklisting from future programs
and repossession proceedings against lot buyers, emphasizing that agrarian parcels were meant to lift families out
of poverty, not to be treated as tradeable assets.
Women Farmer Empowerment
Throughout his tenure, Panumpang consistently advocated for the recognition of women as central actors in
agrarian reform, not peripheral beneficiaries.
Speaking before over 600 participants during Women's Month celebrations, he highlighted DAR's initiatives in
gender awareness and the inclusion of rural women in departmental services.
He repeatedly emphasized that women farmers possessed "enormous potential to improve food production" and
were vital partners in nation-building.
This advocacy reflected his broader belief that inclusive development rooted in Shari'ah principles required
centering women's agency and rights, consistent with Islamic teachings on women's economic participation and
inheritance protections.
Support Services and Infrastructure
Panumpang oversaw initiatives that moved beyond land distribution to comprehensive support services.
He championed the Tulay ng Pangulo para sa Kaunlarang Pang-Agraryo (President's Bridge Program), which
constructed prefabricated steel bridges connecting farmlands to markets, addressing logistical barriers that
prevented ARBs from reaching buyers.

PAGE 4
He also supported programs designed to attract youth into agriculture, organizing "Stakeholders' Engagement with
the Youth" and sponsoring film competitions like "PelikulAgraryo" to counter the Philippines' aging farming
population and inspire younger generations to embrace agricultural careers.
Marawi Relief and BARMM Collaboration
In 2021, Panumpang's Special Concerns Office served as lead convener for consultative meetings aimed at
distributing government-owned lands in war-ravaged Marawi City to qualified farmer-beneficiaries.
He articulated a powerful vision of this work as "legitimizing the ownership of Marawi farmers over lands that they
deserve to own a long time ago as part of their rights to their ancestral domain."
This statement encapsulated his philosophy: agrarian justice was inseparable from recognizing indigenous and
ancestral claims rooted in Bangsamoro history and identity.
Legal Advocacy and Shari'ah-Based Legal Pluralism
Muslim Legal Aid Foundation Inc.
As President of the Muslim Legal Aid Foundation Inc. (commonly abbreviated as MUSLAID), Panumpang
established an institutional mechanism for providing pro bono legal services to Muslim Filipinos facing systemic
discrimination and marginalization.
The foundation's work centered on human rights cases and legal protections under Philippine and Islamic law,
particularly addressing cases of mistaken identity in which innocent Muslims were arrested or detained due to
profiling or shared names with suspects in high-profile crimes such as the Maguindanao Massacre.
His vision for MUSLAID transcended reactive defense; he saw it as a bridge institution that could educate Muslim
Filipinos about their rights under both Presidential Decree No. 1083 (the Code of Muslim Personal Laws) and the
Philippine Constitution, while simultaneously educating the broader legal system about Islamic jurisprudence and
Muslim-specific vulnerabilities.
Code of Muslim Personal Laws Advocacy
Panumpang was a vocal champion of Presidential Decree No. 1083 (PDCL), which established the legal
framework for Muslim Filipino autonomy in matters of marriage, divorce, inheritance, and family relations.
He consistently advocated for the PDCL as the primary legal resource for Muslim Filipinos in these domains,
arguing that respect for religious self-determination was both a constitutional right and a practical necessity.
His legal work underscored the concept of legal pluralism (the coexistence of multiple legal systems within a
single state) as a feature rather than a flaw of the Philippine legal order.
This placed him among a small cohort of Muslim Filipino legal scholars pushing for institutional recognition that
justice for Muslim communities required honoring Shari'ah alongside civil law.

PAGE 5
Support for Shari'ah Bar and Legal Hybridity
Panumpang advocated for the establishment of a Shari'ah Bar in the Philippines, envisioning a cadre of lawyers
trained in both Islamic jurisprudence and Philippine law who could represent Muslim clients with cultural and
religious fluency.
He promoted the concept of legal hybridity, encouraging dialogue between the Supreme Court and Islamic
scholars to harmonize Islamic law with Philippine national law in ways that honored both systems' integrity.
Through his partnerships with the National Commission on Muslim Filipinos (NCMF), he supported the
development of executive education programs in Halal Industry and Islamic Banking, creating a pipeline of locally
trained technical personnel capable of implementing Shari'ah-based economic models.
Halal Industry Development and Shari'ah-Based Entrepreneurship
Leadership of HICCIP
Panumpang served as Chairman of the Halal International Chamber of Commerce and Industries of the
Philippines (HICCIP), the premier government-recognized Halal certification body in the Philippines.
HICCIP was established on June 26, 2013, with the mission of encouraging investments and partnerships in Halal-
based businesses while ensuring the authenticity and credibility of Philippine Halal-certified products for local and
international Muslim consumers.
Under Panumpang's leadership, HICCIP became accredited by the National Commission on Muslim Filipinos
(NCMF) and gained international recognition from Halal authorities in Malaysia (JAKIM), Singapore (MUIS), and
Thailand (CICOT).
Certification and Institutional Integrity
Central to Panumpang's vision was the institutionalization of strict Halal certification processes that involved
physical inspections, product analysis, laboratory testing, and consultation with the Ulama Council (Muslim
scholars) to ensure compliance with both Shari'ah Law and the Philippine National Standard on Halal.
He believed that Halal certification was not merely a compliance mechanism but a spiritual and institutional
commitment to protect the integrity of Muslim economic life.
This work reflected his conviction that justice for Muslim Filipinos required creating parallel institutions
(chambers of commerce, certification bodies, legal aid foundations) that could operate according to Shari'ah
principles while interfacing with Philippine government and civil society.
Global Market Integration and Inclusive Entrepreneurship
Panumpang actively pursued international recognition for Filipino Halal products, positioning the Philippines as a
credible actor in the multi-trillion-dollar global Islamic economy.
He promoted Halal not as a niche market but as a "way of life" and economic model that benefited everyone,
including non-Muslim business partners and consumers.

PAGE 6
He championed programs to upskill Micro, Small, and Medium Enterprises (MSMEs) in Halal standards, helping
Filipino businesses tap into international Halal supply chains and markets.
This entrepreneurial vision was inseparable from his legal advocacy; he saw Halal economic development as a
pathway to Muslim Filipino empowerment that required both institutional (HICCIP) and legal (PDCL, MUSLAID)
scaffolding.
Institutional Innovation and Community Organizing
Networks and Diaspora Engagement
Panumpang was instrumental in organizing Muslim Filipino community associations abroad, particularly in
Malaysia, to support the diaspora and maintain ties between overseas Filipinos and their home communities.
This work reflected a transnational vision of Muslim Filipino identity and collective welfare that transcended
national borders.
Professional Training and Capacity Building
Through NCMF partnerships and academic collaborations, Panumpang supported the development of professional
training modules in Halal Industry and Islamic Banking.
These programs were designed not merely to produce technicians but to cultivate a corps of Muslim Filipino
professionals equipped with both Shari'ah and contemporary business knowledge, capable of leading institutions
that honored both systems.
Legacy and Vision
Atty. Carim L. Panumpang, Sr.'s career embodied a distinctive philosophy of justice and development rooted in two
core principles.
First, that Muslim Filipinos' rights and prosperity were inseparable from institutional recognition of Shari'ah
principles and Islamic law.
Second, that this institutional recognition did not require separatism or conflict with Philippine national law, but
rather creative legal pluralism, dialogue, and hybrid governance structures that honored both systems' integrity.
His work across agrarian reform, legal aid, and Halal industry development demonstrates that the pursuit of justice,
economic inclusion, and cultural integrity for Muslim Filipinos is not a series of isolated challenges but an
integrated vision of development.
A farmer's right to productive land, a widow's right to inherit under Shari'ah law, a Muslim entrepreneur's right to
participate in the global economy according to Islamic principles, these were not separate struggles but expressions
of a single commitment: ensuring that Muslim Filipinos could flourish as full participants in Philippine society
without compromising their religious identity or values.
His legacy invites ongoing reflection on how the Philippine state and civil society can continue expanding
institutional space for legal pluralism, Shari'ah-based development, and the kind of inclusive governance that
honors both national law and religious tradition.

PAGE 7
Death
Atty. Carim L. Panumpang, Sr. passed away in August 2023.
His specific contributions during the transition to the Marcos administration (which began in June 2022) and the
circumstances of his death remain publicly undocumented.
Recognition
While Panumpang did not achieve widespread national prominence comparable to major political figures or
celebrities, he commanded respect within Muslim Filipino legal and business circles.
His visibility was concentrated in specialized communities (agrarian reform beneficiaries, legal professionals,
Halal industry practitioners, Muslim civil society organizations) rather than the general public.

title: Casib, Mohammad Nur
text:
PAGE 1
Mohammad Nur Casib
Mohammad Nur Gumaos Casib (born June 9, 2006, Cagayan de Oro City), known by the nickname Iman, is a
Filipino-Meranaw STEM scholar widely recognized as one of the most accomplished student competitors in
Philippine academic history.<ref name="minda2025">Arguillas, Carolyn O. "Moro Whiz Kid in Math, Physics,
Chemistry and Statistics Off to MIT for College." MindaNews, March 2025. https://mindanews.com/top-
stories/2025/03/moro-whiz-kid-in-math-physics-chemistry-and-statistics-off-to-mit-for-college/</ref> A product of
the Philippine Science High School – Central Mindanao Campus (PSHS-CMC), he has accumulated medals across
six distinct scientific disciplines—mathematics, physics, chemistry, statistics, astronomy/astrophysics, and nuclear
science—at both national and international levels.<ref name="dostpost">Reyes, Renante. "The Rise of Pisay
Prodigy: Mohammad Nur Casib's Historic Journey in STEM." DOST S&T Post, 2025.
http://sntpost.dost.gov.ph/dost/the-rise-of-pisay-prodigy-mohamad-nur-casibs-historic-journey-in-stem</ref> He
holds several historic firsts for the Philippines and the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao
(BARMM): the first Filipino to win gold at the International Olympiad on Astronomy and Astrophysics (IOAA);
the first Philippine student to be named Nuclear Ambassador at the inaugural International Nuclear Science
Olympiad (INSO); and the first Bangsamoro, as well as the first student from PSHS-Central Mindanao Campus, to
be admitted to the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT).<ref name="manstd">Manila Standard Staff.
"Marawi Math Prodigy Bound for MIT after Dominating Academics." Manila Standard, April 1, 2025.
https://manilastandard.net/news/314574880/marawi-math-prodigy-bound-for-mit-after-dominating-
academics.html</ref><ref name="barmm2024">Usop, Kasan Jr. "Young Bangsamoro Puts PH on Map with Gold
Win at Astronomy Olympiad." BARMM Official Website, September 2024. https://bangsamoro.gov.ph/news/latest-
news/young-bangsamoro-puts-ph-on-map-with-gold-win-at-astronomy-olympiad/</ref>

Early Life
Mohammad Nur Gumaos Casib was born in Cagayan de Oro City
but grew up in Marawi City, Lanao del Sur, the provincial capital
of the predominantly Meranaw heartland of mainland Mindanao.
He is the eldest of four children in a household of distinguished
medical professionals: his father, Dr. Norodin S. Casib, is a
general surgeon, and his mother, Dr. Sittienor M. Gumaos-Casib,
is an obstetrics-gynecologist; both serve at the Amai Pakpak
Medical Center, the primary government hospital in Marawi City.
<ref name="minda2025"/> His parents noted a pronounced
aptitude for numbers from his earliest years, describing a child for
whom quantitative reasoning came naturally and with evident
pleasure.<ref name="dostpost"/>
The formative period of his childhood was dramatically altered by
the 2017 Marawi Siege, a five-month military conflict between
Philippine government forces and Islamist militants of the Maute
Group and Abu Sayyaf, which resulted in the near-total
destruction of Marawi's central districts and the displacement of
an estimated 360,000 residents.<ref
name="minda_nuclear">Arguillas, Carolyn O. "Moro Student
Wins Gold in 1st Int'l Nuclear Science Olympiad; Is Hailed as
'Nuclear Ambassador'." MindaNews, August 10, 2024.
https://mindanews.com/top-stories/2024/08/moro-student-wins-
gold-in-1st-intl-nuclear-science-olympiad-is-hailed-as-nuclear-
ambassador/</ref> The Casib family was among the displaced. In
the shadow of the siege, where adversity sought to confine him,
Nur Casib instead broke free—discovered himself and unleashed
brilliance that would echo his name in the portals of greatness. An
eventual return to Marawi City in January 2019, following a
period of resettlement, coincided with Casib's emergence on the
national competition circuit.<ref name="minda_nuclear"/> His
parents have emphasized that the disruption of the siege, while
traumatic, indirectly expanded his educational horizon by
accelerating the family's engagement with specialized schooling
opportunities outside the conflict zone.

Early Competition Record
Casib's competitive career began when he was grade 5 in My
Precious Child Learning Center in Marawi City. In his upper
primary years from 2018-2019, he qualified to represent the
country in three (3) international mathematics competitions
through the Mathematics Trainers' Guild (MTG)-Philippines, a
highly renowned center specialized to train students for different
academic circles most especially Mathematics. In 2018, he won a
gold medal at the 15th International Mathematics and Science
Olympiad (IMSO) held in Zhuji City, Zhejiang Province, China,
and a bronze medal at the 21st Po Leung Kuk Primary
Mathematics World Contest (PMWC) in Hong Kong.<ref
name="minda_nuclear"/>. In August 2019, he clenched a silver
medal at the South Africa International Mathematics Competition
(SAIMC) in Durban, South Africa. In April 2019, few months
prior to South Africa's math tilt, he was the National Champion in
the prestigious grade 6 Metrobank-MTAP-DepEd Mathematics
Challenge (MMC)-individual category, publicly stating at the time
that his goal was "to bring the banner of the Bangsamoro region to
the competition."<ref name="minda_nuclear"/> During the covid
pandemic, he continued to qualify in several high-ground
international math tilts conducted online winning gold in the 25th
Junior Balkan Mathematical Olympiad & silver in the Indonesia
International Mathematics Competition all in 2021. The following
year in 2022, he won another gold in one of China's hardest math
competition, the China North Mathematical Olympiad. These
early achievements established the scope and character of what
would become a record-breaking scholastic career.
Education
Philippine Science High School – Central Mindanao
Campus
Casib enrolled at the Philippine Science High School – Central Mindanao Campus (PSHS-CMC), located in Balo-i,
Lanao del Norte, a specialized secondary institution under the Department of Science and Technology (DOST).<ref
name="manstd"/> The PSHS system, commonly known as "Pisay," operates a national network of campuses with a
mandate to identify and cultivate talent in the sciences and mathematics, preparing scholars for both national
Olympiad teams and international competition.<ref name="dostpost"/> The CMC, one of the regional campuses,
admitted Casib as part of its highly selective intake, where students are assessed through a rigorous national
competitive examination.
Within the PSHS-CMC, Casib distinguished himself not only through his academic record but also through an
extraordinary breadth of competitive participation. Where most Pisay scholars concentrate on one or two
disciplines, Casib competed—and excelled—simultaneously across mathematics, physics, chemistry, statistics,
astronomy and astrophysics, and nuclear science, a feat described by faculty and competition administrators as
without precedent in the system's history.<ref name="dostpost"/> His training for international Olympiads involved

PAGE 4
extended periods in Metro Manila, where he studied under specialists at the University of the Philippines Diliman
Institute of Mathematics, the Ateneo de Manila University's Philippine Institute of Pure and Applied Chemistry, the
PSHS Main Campus, and the PAGASA Observatory.<ref name="barmm2024"/>
Massachusetts Institute of Technology
On March 14, 2025—coinciding with International Pi Day—Casib accessed his online admissions portal and
confirmed acceptance to the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) in Cambridge, Massachusetts, as a
member of the MIT Class of 2029.<ref name="minda2025"/> The formal notification letter, dated March 18, 2025,
was signed by Stuart Schmill, MIT's Dean of Admissions and Student Financial Services, who stated that Casib
"stood out as one of the most talented and promising students in an incredibly competitive applicant pool."<ref
name="mindanao2025">Arguillas, Carolyn O. "MINDANAO 2025: Mindanawon Students Shine in Yale, MIT,
Leuven and International Competitions." MindaNews, January 6, 2026. https://mindanews.com/top-
stories/2026/01/mindanao-2025-mindanawon-students-shine-in-yale-mit-leuven-and-international-
competitions/</ref>
He is the first student from PSHS-CMC, and the first known individual from the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region
in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM), to enter MIT at the undergraduate level.<ref name="minda2025"/> He was
awarded a full scholarship and is pursuing a double major in Artificial Intelligence and Chemistry, with a minor in
Physics—a combination that positions him at the intersection of computational science and molecular engineering.
<ref name="mindanao2025"/>
Career and Competitive Achievements
Mathematics
Philippine Mathematical Olympiad
The Philippine Mathematical Olympiad (PMO) is the national qualifying examination for the Philippine team to
the International Mathematical Olympiad (IMO). Casib competed in the PMO from 2023 through 2025, showing a
consistent upward trajectory: he placed First Runner-up at the 25th PMO in 2023; Second Runner-up at the 26th
PMO in 2024; and Overall Champion at the 27th PMO, held at Far Eastern University in Manila on March 8–9,
2025, where he bested a field that included multiple IMO veterans.<ref name="minda2025"/>
International Mathematical Olympiad
Casib represented the Philippines at the International Mathematical Olympiad (IMO) on three occasions. At the
63rd IMO held in Oslo, Norway, in 2022, he won a bronze medal.<ref name="ph63imo">Philippine Graphic Staff.
"PH Wins 2 Bronzes, 4 Honorable Mentions at 63rd International Mathematical Olympiad." Philippine Graphic,
July 27, 2022. https://philippinesgraphic.com.ph/2022/07/27/ph-wins-2-bronzes-4-honorable-mentions-at-63rd-
international-mathematical-olympiad/</ref> At the 64th IMO in Chiba, Japan, in 2023, he again secured a bronze
medal, making him the first Bangsamoro student to receive multiple IMO distinctions.<ref
name="minda_nuclear"/> At the 65th IMO in Bath, United Kingdom, in July 2024, he received an Honorable
Mention.<ref name="mb65imo">Manila Bulletin Staff. "Filipino Students Win at 65th International Mathematical
Olympiad in UK." Manila Bulletin, July 20, 2024. https://mb.com.ph/2024/7/20/filipino-students-win-at-65th-
international-mathematical-olympiad-in-uk</ref>

PAGE 5
Asian Pacific Mathematics Olympiad
Casib won a silver medal at the 35th Asian Pacific Mathematics Olympiad (APMO) in 2023.<ref
name="minda_nuclear"/> In 2024, he secured a gold medal at the 36th APMO—only the fourth gold medal the
Philippines had ever won in the competition's history, representing a landmark achievement for Philippine
mathematics on the regional stage.<ref name="dostpost"/>
Statistics
In February 2025, Casib led the PSHS-CMC team to the championship of the 24th National Statistical Challenge,
held at the University of the Philippines Diliman School of Statistics. Beyond the team victory, he was personally
awarded the competition's inaugural Most Valuable Pearson (MVP) distinction—a title created specifically to
recognize the individual with the highest score on the written examination—the first time in the competition's
history that such an individual award was conferred.<ref name="minda2025"/>. They were the defending
champion after winning the the 23rd National Statistical Challenge in 2024.
Physics
At the 2025 Philippine Physics Olympiad (PPO), held at the University of the Philippines Los Baños on March 15–
16, 2025, Casib was declared the "Absolute Winner and Gold Medalist," a designation indicating the single highest
individual score among all participants nationwide—a distinction that separates the top scorer from the broader
cohort of gold medalists.<ref name="minda2025"/><ref name="pshs_ppo">Philippine Science High School.
"Pisay Pride in Math & Physics!" PSHS Official Website, 2025. https://pshs.edu.ph/pisay-pride-in-math-
physics/</ref>
Astronomy and Astrophysics
The International Olympiad on Astronomy and Astrophysics (IOAA) tests mastery of theoretical astrophysics,
observational astronomy, complex data analysis, and practical night-sky navigation. Casib's IOAA career
constitutes two consecutive historic milestones for the Philippines.
At the 16th IOAA in Poland in August 2023, he won a silver medal—the first medal of any kind the Philippines
had received in the competition since the country began participating in 2010.<ref
name="luwaran_nuclear">Luwaran Staff. "Moro Student Hailed as 'Nuclear Ambassador' in Olympiad Held in
New Clark City." Luwaran, August 2024. https://www.luwaran.com/news/article/2738/moro-student-hailed-as----
nuclear-ambassador----in-olympiad-held-in-new-clark-city</ref>
At the 17th IOAA held in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, from August 17–27, 2024, he surpassed that achievement by
winning the country's first-ever gold medal at the competition—in an event that drew participants from over fifty
countries.<ref name="barmm2024"/> The Philippine Senate formally recognized this achievement through the
adoption of Senate Resolution No. 214, commending Casib for elevating the Philippines' standing in the
international academic community.<ref name="senres214">Senate of the Philippines. Resolution No. 214:
Commending Mohammad Nur Casib for Winning the First-Ever Gold Medal for the Philippines at the 17th
International Olympiad on Astronomy and Astrophysics. 19th Congress.
https://legacy.senate.gov.ph/19th_congress/resolutions/resno214.pdf</ref> His achievement was additionally
recognized by the Philippine government through a separate commendatory document from the Office of the
President.<ref name="senph4">Senate of the Philippines. Resolution from the 19th Congress.
https://legacy.senate.gov.ph/lisdata/4517541056!.pdf</ref>

Nuclear Science
The inaugural International Nuclear Science Olympiad (INSO) was held at New Clark City, Pampanga, from
August 1–6, 2024, organized by the Philippine Nuclear Science Institute in collaboration with the DOST, DepEd,
and the National Research Council of the Philippines, with support from the International Atomic Energy Agency
(IAEA).<ref name="iaea_inso">International Atomic Energy Agency. "First Ever International Nuclear Science
Olympiad Held in Run Up to International Youth Day." IAEA Newscenter, August 2024.
https://www.iaea.org/newscenter/news/first-ever-international-nuclear-science-olympiad-held-in-run-up-to-
international-youth-day</ref> The competition drew 55 participants from 14 countries across the Asia-Pacific
region and assessed mastery of topics ranging from atomic structure and radiation physics to nuclear medicine and
environmental radioactivity, over examinations totaling 8.5 hours.<ref name="minda_nuclear"/>
Among all 55 competitors, Casib achieved the highest aggregate score in both the theoretical and experimental
components of the competition, winning a gold medal and the top-scorer award for the written examination.<ref
name="rappler_inso">Rappler Staff. "Filipino Students Win 2 Golds, 1 Silver at International Nuclear Science
Competition." Rappler, August 9, 2024. https://www.rappler.com/bulletin-board/contests-awards/filipino-students-
win-golds-silver-medals-international-nuclear-science-competition-august-2024/</ref> On the basis of this
performance, he was conferred the title of "Nuclear Science Olympiad Ambassador" for the 2024–2025 period—an
honorary designation created for the inaugural edition of the competition to recognize its highest-achieving
participant—tasked with promoting nuclear science education and mentoring future INSO competitors.<ref
name="minda_nuclear"/><ref name="pshs_inso">Philippine Science High School. "PSHS Celebrates Gold and
Silver Victories at 1st International Nuclear Science Olympiad." PSHS Official Website, 2024.
https://pshs.edu.ph/</ref>
Chemistry
International Chemistry Olympiad
Casib represented the Philippines at the International Chemistry Olympiad (IChO) twice. At the 55th IChO held in
Zurich, Switzerland, in 2023, he won a bronze medal.<ref name="barmmp_zurich">Parliament of the Bangsamoro
Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao. Resolution Congratulating Mohammad Nur Guma-os Casib for
Winning the Bronze Medal in the International Chemistry Olympiad Held in Zurich, Switzerland.
https://parliament.bangsamoro.gov.ph/adopted-resolution/resolution-congratulating-mohammad-nur-guma-os-
casib-a-native-of-lanao-del-sur-for-winning-the-bronze-medal-in-the-international-chemistry-olympiad-held-in-
zurich-switzerland-thereby-giving-pride/</ref>
At the 57th IChO held in Dubai, United Arab Emirates, in July 2025, he won a silver medal—the highest-scoring
silver for the Philippines at that edition and the fourth silver the country had ever won in the IChO's history, with
reports noting his score fell remarkably close to the threshold for a gold medal.<ref
name="pshs_icho25">Philippine Science High School. "Mabuhay, Team Philippines! 1 Silver and 3 Bronze
Medals for PH at the 2025 International Chemistry Olympiad." PSHS Official Website, July 2025.
https://pshs.edu.ph/mabuhay-team-philippines/</ref><ref name="filipinotimes">Filipino Times Staff. "Filipino

https://filipinotimes.net/latest-news/2025/07/16/filipino-scholars-bag-4-medals-at-international-chemistry-
olympiad-in-dubai/</ref>
National Chemistry Olympiad
In March 2025, coinciding with the national competition season, Casib and his PSHS-CMC teammates won gold at
the 24th Philippine National Chemistry Olympiad (PNCO), held at the University of the Philippines Manila
College of Arts and Sciences on March 22.<ref name="minda2025"/> Gold awardees at the PNCO earn eligibility
to represent the Philippines at the IChO, consistent with the pathway he subsequently fulfilled at the 57th IChO in
Dubai.
