Historic Significance
Mohammad Nur Casib's career carries significance at multiple intersecting levels—national, regional, and cultural.
Within the Philippine educational system, he is the first known student to have simultaneously held the titles of
National Statistical Champion MVP, Physics Olympiad Absolute Winner, and Mathematics Olympiad Overall
Champion within a single calendar year (2025), constituting what observers have described as an unprecedented
"Triple Crown" or, more expansively, a "Sextuple Crown" when accounting for his concurrent national-level
chemistry and earlier international achievements.<ref name="dostpost"/>
Within the PSHS system, he is the first student from the Central Mindanao Campus to be admitted to MIT and the
first in the system's history to have competed at the highest international level across six distinct disciplines
simultaneously.<ref name="minda2025"/>
For the Philippines in the specific arena of astronomy and astrophysics, his 2024 IOAA gold is the country's first in
fourteen years of IOAA participation—a milestone formally recognized by the Senate of the Philippines.<ref
name="senres214"/>
Within the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM), Casib is celebrated as the first
Bangsamoro individual to have achieved admission to MIT, the first Moro student to win multiple IMO
distinctions, and a cultural reference point for what his community's institutions of governance have termed a "New
Moro" identity grounded in scientific excellence.<ref name="barmm2024"/>
Public Reception
Casib's achievements have generated formal institutional recognition at multiple levels of Philippine governance.

PAGE 8
The Philippine Senate adopted Resolution No. 214 commending him for his gold medal at the 17th IOAA in 2024.
<ref name="senres214"/> A second Senate resolution further recognized his broader contributions to Philippine
STEM.<ref name="senph4"/>
The Bangsamoro Parliament (formerly the Bangsamoro Transition Authority) has adopted multiple resolutions in
his honor. Resolution No. 389 congratulated him upon winning the bronze medal at the 55th IChO in Zurich.<ref
name="barmmp_zurich"/> Resolution No. 485, adopted in August 2024, specifically recognized his gold medal
and Nuclear Ambassador designation at the inaugural INSO, with parliamentary members framing his
achievements as a "collective triumph" for the Bangsamoro people rather than merely an individual
accomplishment.<ref name="barmmp_inso">Parliament of the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim
Mindanao. Resolution No. 485: Resolution Congratulating and Commending the 1st International Nuclear Science
Olympiad Gold Medalist and Highest Scorer Awardee and Named Nuclear Ambassador, Mohammad Nur Casib, of
PSHS-CMC. https://parliament.bangsamoro.gov.ph/adopted-resolution/resolution-congratulating-and-commending-
the-1st-international-nuclear-science-olympiad-gold-medalist-and-highest-scorer-awardee-and-named-nuclear-
ambassador-mohammad-nur-casib-of-philippine-science-h/</ref>
Regional political figures, including former Maguindanao Governor and Representative Esmael "Toto"
Mangudadatu, publicly commended Casib's achievements on social media as models of Bangsamoro youth
aspiration.<ref name="rappler_inso"/> The Bangsamoro Youth Commission (BYC) similarly issued a statement
declaring that his accomplishments "inspire fellow Bangsamoro youths."<ref name="barmm2024"/>
Civil society and media coverage across the Philippine archipelago—from national broadsheets including the
Manila Bulletin and Manila Standard to the Mindanao-based analytical outlet MindaNews—consistently framed
his story within a counter-narrative to the historical association of the Bangsamoro region with conflict and
political instability, emphasizing instead the region's capacity for educational excellence when supported by
appropriate institutional infrastructure.<ref name="manstd"/><ref name="dostpost"/>
Contributions
Beyond his own competitive record, Casib's most durable structural contribution to Philippine STEM is his role as
the inaugural Nuclear Science Olympiad Ambassador. In this capacity, conferred for the 2024–2025 period, he is
formally tasked with promoting nuclear science literacy among secondary students across the Asia-Pacific region,
mentoring candidates preparing for future editions of the INSO, and serving as a public face for the IAEA's
educational outreach initiatives in the Philippines.<ref name="minda_nuclear"/><ref name="iaea_inso"/> This role
is directly relevant to the Philippines' current national discussions around nuclear energy as a potential component
of the country's long-term energy transition strategy.
His choice of academic concentration at MIT—a double major in Artificial Intelligence and Chemistry with a
minor in Physics—positions him for eventual contributions in computational chemistry, a discipline with
significant applications in pharmaceutical design, materials science, and sustainable development. His training
under multiple national and international academic specialists, alongside sustained engagement with the PSHS
mentorship network, has prepared him for advanced research in these intersecting domains.<ref
name="mindanao2025"/>
Legacy
Casib has materially altered the narrative frameworks through which the Bangsamoro region, the PSHS-CMC, and
Filipino youth from Mindanao are discussed within both domestic and international educational contexts. Before
his career, no student from BARMM had held multiple medals at the IMO; no Filipino had ever won gold at the

PAGE 9
IOAA; and no student from the PSHS-CMC had entered MIT.
Within Marawi City—a community still in active reconstruction following the 2017 siege—Casib's trajectory
serves as a tangible demonstration that conditions of displacement and material deprivation are not determinative
of intellectual potential when institutional support is adequate and familial investment in education is sustained.
<ref name="minda_nuclear"/> His story has been used by DOST and PSHS administrators as a model for
expanding STEM scholarship access to underrepresented regions, particularly Mindanao and the Bangsamoro.<ref
name="dostpost"/>
His personal motto, Plus Ultra (from the Latin: "Further Beyond"), reflects a philosophy of continuous self-
overcoming that has resonated widely as a public message for younger students across the Philippines and the
BARMM in particular.
Personal Life
Casib is a practicing Muslim and identifies strongly with his Meranaw cultural heritage. He frequently attributes
his academic achievements to divine will, regularly employing Islamic phrases of gratitude—Tabarakallah
(blessed be God) and Alhamdulillah (praise be to God)—in public communications and post-competition
statements.<ref name="minda2025"/>
A notable episode illustrating the intersection of his faith practice and competitive life occurred during the 2025
national competition season, which coincided with the Islamic month of Ramadan. Casib competed across multiple
Olympiads—including the 27th PMO, the PPO, and the PNCO—while observing the Ramadan fast. His father
described the period as "very tough," noting that Nur managed disrupted sleep schedules and reduced caloric intake
while simultaneously performing at peak level across disciplines.<ref name="minda2025"/>
On the morning of March 15, 2025—the day of the PPO—he accessed his MIT admissions portal before the
competition began, having decided that the certainty of a result, whether favorable or unfavorable, would allow
him greater mental composure than waiting. He has publicly noted that the combination of faith in his preparation
and trust in a higher power enabled him to proceed with the competition regardless of outcome.<ref
name="minda2025"/>
He lives with his family in Marawi City and Balo-i, Lanao del Norte. As of early 2026, he is enrolled at MIT in
Cambridge, Massachusetts.<ref name="mindanao2025"/>

Esnaen Macaumbang "Teng" Catong
Dr. Esnaen Macaumbang "Teng" Catong is a Filipino academic,
government official, athlete, and social entrepreneur from Pagadian
City, Zamboanga del Sur. He currently serves as Undersecretary
and Deputy Director-General (DDG) of the National Anti-Poverty
Commission (NAPC) under the Office of the President, a post he
has held since April 2024. He is a humble member of the Iranun
royal nobles of Illana Bay and the Moro Gulf, and his career spans
youth and student leadership, university administration, athletics,
defense and security advisory work, and national anti-poverty
governance.

Early Life
Catong was born and raised in Pagadian City, Zamboanga del Sur,
in southwestern Mindanao. His childhood was shaped by two
defining experiences of adversity in the 1970s.
During the height of the Moro conflict, Catong and his family lived
as bakwits, or internally displaced persons, fleeing volatile
crossfires in the region. That experience rooted his lifelong
dedication to marginalized communities.

PAGE 2

government official who rose from

Deputy Director-General, a WMSU dean

humanitarian relief work during the
2013 Zamboanga Siege, the COVID-19
pandemic, and Typhoon Odette
On August 17, 1976, an 8.1 magnitude earthquake struck the Moro
Gulf and triggered a catastrophic tsunami that devastated the
coastlines of Pagadian City. Catong survived the disaster, an ordeal
that permanently shaped his later focus on institutional crisis
management and humanitarian intervention.
To help his family recover from the economic toll of war and
disaster, Catong worked as a manual farmer, tilling the land while
making his way through school.
Education
Catong completed his early schooling at Pagadian City Pilot School
before moving on to the Zamboanga del Sur School of Arts and
Trades (ZSSAT). He pursued higher education at Western Mindanao
State University (WMSU), where he earned his Bachelor of Arts in
Political Science and later his Bachelor of Laws at the WMSU
College of Law, while also teaching political science, history, and
research and development courses.
He went on to complete advanced postgraduate and doctoral
coursework at the University of the Philippines. He earned a Master
of Arts in History, with a cognate in Political Science, and
completed all academic requirements for a PhD in History, cognate
in Political Science, short of the dissertation, in 2013. He has since
gone on to successfully pass the final examination, the dissertation
final defense, for his PhD in Development Studies, major in
Agrarian and Rural Development, with cognates in Strategic
Planning and Public Policy, and Sociology, at the UP Los Baños
College of Public Affairs and Development. His dissertation, titled
Implications of the Philippine Rice Trade Policy on the Political
and Socioeconomic Development in Western Mindanao,
Philippines, was successfully defended on April 28, 2026.
His academic footprint spans both UP Diliman and UP Los Baños, covering History, Political Science, Public
Policy, Strategic Planning, Sociology, and Development Studies.
Fellowships
Catong was awarded the DAP-EDPS-Dean Flagship Program and the Rockefeller Research Fellowship, tracking
international public policy, national policies on education and peace-building, and developmental socioeconomics.
He attended the first of two batches of the Executive Development Flagship Programme for SUCs Deans at the
Development Academy of the Philippines (DAP), where his institutional research paper focused on steering state
universities toward becoming Centers of Excellence in Conflict Resolution and Social Development, in 2014.
He also won the Asia Research Fellowship Programme for Young Muslim Scholars in Bangkok, Thailand, under
the auspices of the Asia Resource Foundation and the Rockefeller Foundation, based in New York. The initial
capitalization for his business ventures in Western Mindanao came from his research grants and fellowships, and
the profits from his garments and food businesses went on to sustain two decades of his humanitarian activities.

PAGE 3
Youth, Student, and Faculty Leadership
Grassroots and Student Governance
Catong's public service career began at the grassroots level. He served as the first Sangguniang Kabataan (SK)
Chairman of Barangay Tiguma in Pagadian City and an ex officio member of the Barangay Council, from 1992 to
1996, known for his clear stance on good governance and anti-corruption. During his term, he ran two notable
programs: the "Barangay Clean and Green Program," through which thousands of trees were planted by in-and-out-
of-school youth in vacant spaces, and the "Adopt a Farm for the Youth Program."
In 1991, Catong served as President of the Supreme Student Government at ZSSAT, the first Muslim student to
hold that position in the school's 45-year history at that time. He graduated with academic honors and received
several distinctions: the Oration and Elocution Award as National Champion, the Most Outstanding Leadership
Award as SSG President and three-term Senator, finalist status in the Search for the 10 Most Outstanding Boy
Scouts of the Philippines as National Awardee representing Region IX, and the Athletics Award as Table Tennis
Singles Division Champion in Pagadian City and Regional Player at WMRAA. His alma mater later honored him
with the Most Outstanding Alumnus Plaque of Recognition in 2022 and the Most Distinguished Alumni Award in
2026.
While studying at the WMSU College of Law, Catong was overwhelmingly elected President of the University
Student Council, where he successfully countered proposed tuition hikes through strategic diplomacy and helped
keep the university's main campus and external studies units peaceful throughout his term, from 1997 to 1998.
Following the passage of Republic Act No. 8292, the Higher Education Modernization Act, Catong made history as
the first Student Regent on the WMSU Board of Regents, embedding student rights directly into the university's
highest policymaking body during the same 1997 to 1998 period.
In 2004, he was an active member and co-editor of the CSSP-UP Diliman Graduate Students Association Editorial
Board, which served as a platform for further research engagements and fellowships at home and abroad.
Institutional Academic Leadership
Catong rose through the academic ranks at WMSU, from Instructor to Assistant Professor to Associate Professor,
eventually becoming a full-fledged, state-accredited Professor, while holding several high-level administrative
posts.
As Chairperson of the Department of Political Science, he revised the Political Science curriculum and grew the
department from a single section to three full sections. He positioned the department as a vibrant partner of the
university and of underprivileged communities through research and development programs across Western
Mindanao, leading a university research team that studied the region's socioeconomic development. The resulting
paper, the Multi-Stakeholder Profiling of the Socioeconomic Development of Western Mindanao, was presented to
foreign funding institutions, the Philippine Economic Team, and the Union of Local Authorities in the Philippines
at a national conference sponsored by SEAMEO-INNOTECH at UP Diliman in 2008.
As Chairperson of the Graduate School for Social Sciences, Catong helped grow enrollment in the graduate
program by supporting the university's vertical articulation policy. He authored the Faculty Development Program
(FDP) in the Board of Regents, which required professors to be capacitated and to teach within their fields of
specialization. He argued before the Academic Council and Board of Regents that educators need to be capacitated
and vertically articulated to properly serve the communities they work for, reasoning that educators cannot give
what they do not know, much less share something they do not know about.

PAGE 4
As Dean of the College of Social Sciences, Catong chaired the university's committee for conflict resolution and
social development during the 2013 Zamboanga Siege, which displaced five Muslim-dominated urban barangays
in Zamboanga City. He coordinated post-war trauma engagements and humanitarian extension services. He was
recalled to WMSU to become its youngest College of Social Sciences Dean, leaving UP Diliman before finishing
his History PhD dissertation in order to serve the victims of the siege. While serving as dean during the post-war
period, he attended the Development Academy of the Philippines as part of the Flagship Executive Development
Fellowship Program for SUCs from 2013 to 2014.
Elected President of the WMSU Faculty Union, Catong returned to the Board of Regents as the youngest Faculty
Regent in the Philippines, spending years advocating for institutional transparency, collective bargaining rights, and
the welfare of teachers and employees. Working with key stakeholders, he helped pioneer a scrap-and-build
mechanism at the Board of Regents, the highest policy and governing body of WMSU, the oldest academic
institution in Mindanao, founded by the Americans in 1904 as the old Normal School and later transformed into
Western Mindanao State University through Presidential Decree 1427 under President Ferdinand E. Marcos Sr.
This mechanism created hundreds of new plantilla items for the teaching force, in line with public policy and the
accounting and auditing rules of the Department of Budget and Management and the Commission on Audit, and
the model was eventually adopted across the Philippine bureaucracy nationwide, from 2008 to 2010. It was during
this period that Catong took his first leave of absence to perform Hajj and Umrah.
During his thirteen years at the College of Social Sciences of UP Diliman, Catong personally mentored students Ian
Dominic M. Oriño, Alvin Rex Magbanua Lucero, and Nicolo Mel Nich Carb Carballo, who became part of the
National Champion team in the SY 2009-2010 Quiz Bowl covering History, Geography, Economics, and Political
Science, held at the Philippine Normal University Social Hall. These three mentees went on to become a practicing
lawyer, the Zamboanga City Director of the Department of the Interior and Local Government (DILG), and a
Lingkod Bayan at the Department of Environment and Natural Resources of Region IX, respectively.
He also served as a Professorial Lecturer at the Philippine Public Safety College (PPSC), teaching strategic
governance, public policy, and national safety frameworks to senior law enforcement, jail, and fire safety
administrators through the Officers Senior Executive Course (OSEC) and the Master's in Public Safety
Administration (MPSA) programs.
Athletic Career
Catong is an accomplished and self-described "science-based" athlete with championship credentials in two
demanding sports.
In lawn tennis, he competed across regional and institutional athletic meets, earning a reputation as a strong
competitor and advocating for sports programs as a vehicle for youth development and community peace-building.
In golf, Catong is known for his strategic precision on the green and has used the sport as a networking platform
connecting academic, corporate, and government leaders. In 2022, he ranked first in the Qualifying Rounds for
admission and accreditation as a Teaching Golf Professional under the Games and Amusement Board (GAB) and
the PGA of the Philippines (PGAP).
He is also a Class A competitor in table tennis.

PAGE 5
Strategic Leadership in Peace, Security, and Regional Development
National Security and Defense Advisory Roles
Catong has served as a civilian advisor to the Philippine armed services. He was a key member of the Regional
Advisory Group for Police Transformation and Development (RAGPTD) in Police Regional Office 9 (Zamboanga
Peninsula), guiding structural reforms, transparency initiatives, and community-oriented policing under the PNP
P.A.T.R.O.L. Plan 2030.
He was also appointed to the Multi-Stakeholder Advisory Board of the Philippine Air Force's Air Combat
Command, where he served as Vice Chair for Command and Control and concurrently as Chairperson of the Policy
and Governance Committee from 2021 to 2025, working to align defense operations and air combat policy with
good governance and national security mandates.
Socio-Political Analysis and Regional Peace
Catong has served as a socio-political media analyst for ABS-CBN's TV Patrol Chavacano and the ABS-CBN
News Channel (ANC), offering analysis on national security, the National ID System, federalism, and the State of
the Nation Addresses of three Philippine presidents.
He pioneered academic research on using cultural paradigms for peace-building, particularly through his work on
optimizing Maratabat, the Maranao concept of pride and honor, as a localized framework for rebuilding community
resilience after the 2017 Marawi Siege.
His scholarship on Philippines-Saudi Arabia Relations, 1968-1998: A Diplomatic History, along with his advocacy
for an "Active Three-O Diplomacy," helped shape frameworks for labor migration, energy security, and human
rights. His peace paradigms have been shared across Southeast Asian academic and policy forums, aligning local
Mindanao peace initiatives with the broader goals of the ASEAN Socio-Cultural Community.
In 2005, he represented the Philippines and the NAPC-Office of the President at the 4th International Conference
on Governance and Development (ICGD4) in Bangkok, Thailand, presenting research on the Magna Carta of the
Poor as a policy framework for sustainable development.
National Anti-Poverty Governance
Catong served as Regional President of the Partido Federal ng Pilipinas (PFP) and as a campaign organizer and
strategist in the Zamboanga Peninsula during the 2022 national elections, which resulted in a 59.81 percent victory
for President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. Following this, he was appointed by President Marcos to the National Anti-
Poverty Commission (NAPC) as Deputy Director-General with the rank of Undersecretary in 2024, overseeing the
Local Affairs Coordinating and Monitoring Service (NAPC-LACMS) from April 22, 2024 to January 27, 2026.
Under his leadership, NAPC-LACMS conducted a nationwide orientation seminar rollout covering all
municipalities, cities, and provinces in the country for the full implementation of Republic Act No. 11291, the
Magna Carta of the Poor. This effort produced the South Cotabato Provincial Poverty Reduction Action Plan
(PPRAP), the first completed among the country's 82 provinces, developed under the leadership of League of
Provinces of the Philippines President and South Cotabato Governor Reynaldo Sucayan Tamayo Jr., who also
serves as NAPC Vice-Chairman for the Government Sector.

PAGE 6
As Undersecretary, Catong serves as a premiere Resource Speaker on Public Policy and Governance for the DILG
Local Government Academy (LGA), where he addresses newly elected and reelected local officials nationwide,
including governors, vice-governors, mayors, vice-mayors, and provincial, city, and municipal legislators. Through
this platform, he became the primary trailblazer of the Magna Carta of the Poor Local Poverty Reduction Action
Plan (MCP-LPRAP), conducting briefing sessions that guide local officials in designing, funding, and legally
executing local budgets that guarantee the five fundamental rights of the poor: food, work, education, housing, and
health.
Entrepreneurial and Humanitarian Work
Catong is the sole proprietor of Teng's Grill-Zamboanga and was formerly the proprietor of SKUL Garments &
Printing Specialist. He converted his business assets into humanitarian logistics during three major crises.
The Zamboanga Siege (2013)
When the 2013 Zamboanga Siege displaced over 100,000 residents, Catong converted his restaurant into an
emergency kitchen, becoming the largest private donor of freshly cooked hot meals delivered directly to evacuation
clusters. He was featured by former Vice-President and Magandang Gabi Bayan host Noli de Castro for delivering
28,000 halal food packs, twice daily and free of charge, over nine days. He went on to co-design an organized food
production and distribution system for the 21-day urban conflict together with then-DSWD Secretary Dinky
Soliman, with the support of Assistant Secretary Romo and Director Riduan of DSWD-IX, and his golfing buddies
who served as commanders across the PNP and AFP.
As sole proprietor of his garments and printing business, he donated all finished and unfinished school uniforms
intended for delivery to 17 schools across ZamPen-BaSulTa as sadakah to war victims. White cotton cloth
originally meant for school and sports uniforms was likewise given as sadakah, used for burial requirements for
Muslims who died during the war and in evacuation shelters, including the Zamboanga Sports Complex. He also
provided his two vehicles free of charge for burial transport for as long as they remained serviceable.
The remaining proceeds from his garments and printing business went toward rebuilding houses of worship,
masjids, Catholic churches, and Christian chapels destroyed at ground zero, a gesture meant to show that the
people of Zamboanga cared for humanity regardless of faith. He eventually retired SKUL Garments & Printing
Specialist after exhausting its resources in service of the relief effort. To sustain ongoing humanitarian work,
particularly a university-led food pantry, he personally donated about 50 sacks of rice through Teng's Grill-
Zamboanga as part of the "Building Back Better Zamboanga" effort.
The COVID-19 Pandemic (2020)
During the pandemic, Teng's Grill mobilized to feed medical and security frontliners. To protect rural livelihoods,
Catong bypassed failing commercial markets and bought food directly from isolated farmers and fisherfolk, using
the supplies to feed urban poor communities and support local community pantries. He worked alongside health
and social workers and several military officers based in Western Mindanao at the time.
Typhoon Odette in Dinagat Islands (2021)
Following the devastation of Super Typhoon Odette, Catong funded and organized, with a reliable friend, an
independent, cross-regional maritime relief operation from Zamboanga, delivering food and survival packs directly
to isolated coastal communities in the Dinagat Islands. At the time, the province was led by Governor Arlene

PAGE 7
"Kaka" Bag-ao, with Nilo P. Demerey Jr. serving as Vice-Governor before later becoming Governor himself. The
operation was the first to deliver potable water and food supplies from mainland Mindanao to the islands, and was
made possible with the cooperation of the Joint Task Force Sambisig and the support of a friend and fellow golfer
from the Philippine Navy.
Languages
Catong speaks and writes English, Spanish, Filipino, and Cebuano, and is also fluent in Tausug, Yakan, M'ranao,
Tausaraya, Maguindanaon, Iranun, Chavacano, and Hiligaynon-Karay-a/Ilonggo. He is currently learning Arabic
and Bahasa.
Awards and Recognition
During the 57th Founding Anniversary Celebration of Pagadian City (Araw ng Pagadian City), Catong received the
2026 Most Outstanding Pagadianon Award in Public Service, the highest accolade given to the city's distinguished
bona fide inhabitants.

title: Cayongcat-Nuska, Hadja Sittie Aisah Bani
text:
PAGE 1
Hadja Sittie Aisah "Baicon" Bani
Cayongcat-Nuska
Full Name
Hadja Sittie Aisah "Baicon" Bani
Cayongcat-Nuska
Ethnic Affiliation
Maranao (Meranaw)
Traditional Title
Bae a Labi
Birthplace
Marawi City, Lanao del Sur, Philippines
Secondary Education
Dansalan College, Marawi City (Batch
1988-1989)
Higher Education
Hadja Sittie Aisah Bani Cayongcat-Nuska
Hadja Sittie Aisah "Baicon" Bani Cayongcat-Nuska is a Filipino civic leader, peace advocate, social
entrepreneur, and national public official from Marawi City, Lanao del Sur. She currently serves as a Commissioner
of the National Commission on Muslim Filipinos (NCMF), appointed in May 2024 by President Ferdinand R.
Marcos Jr.
Before entering national government, she built a decade-long career in civil society, most notably as the co-founder
and Executive Director of the Raheemah Women's Organization (also known as the Raheemah Peace Weavers
Cooperative). Through that organization, she led a grassroots movement to rebuild livelihoods, revive Meranaw
cultural traditions, and restore the dignity of thousands of families displaced by the 2017 Marawi Siege. She also
holds the traditional customary title of Bae a Labi, a designation within the Maranao socio-political system that
recognizes a royal female leader in community mediation and governance.
Contents
1 BACKGROUND
2 EDUCATION
3 CAREER
3.1 Post-Marawi Siege Relief Work (2019)
3.2 Founding the Raheemah Women's Organization (2020)
3.3 The Raheemah Economic Hub and Youth Development
Center (2022)
3.4 Strategic Institutional Partnerships
4 INSTITUTIONAL CONTRIBUTIONS
4.1 Chairperson, Provincial Tourism, Culture, and Arts
Council of Lanao del Sur
4.2 Appointment as NCMF Commissioner (2024)
5 RECOGNITION
5.1 "Iconic Woman Creating a Better World" Award, WEF
Australia 2025
5.2 INACRAFT 2026 Panelist
5.3 The Peace Walking Movement
6 LEGACY
7 SEE ALSO
8 CATEGORIES
BACKGROUND
Cayongcat-Nuska is Maranao, a member of the "People of the
Lake," the Muslim ethno-linguistic community indigenous to the
Lanao region of Mindanao. The Maranao are renowned for their
rich artistic heritage, including the iconic Okir design tradition,
intricate weaving, and a well-developed system of customary law
and governance known as Adat.

PAGE 2
Public Administration (advanced
studies)
Occupation
Commissioner, National Commission
on Muslim Filipinos; Civic Leader;
Social Entrepreneur
Organization
Raheemah Women's Organization /
Raheemah Peace Weavers Cooperative
(co-founder and Executive Director)
Appointed
May 2024 (NCMF Commissioner, by
President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr.)
Religion
Islam
Region
Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in
Muslim Mindanao (BARMM)
Notability
NCMF Commissioner; co-founder of the
Raheemah Women's Organization;
pioneer of post-Marawi Siege grassroots
economic rehabilitation; Bae a Labi
traditional titleholder; international
peacebuilding advocate
Known For
Transforming post-conflict
humanitarian aid into culturally rooted
livelihood programs; reviving Meranaw
textile traditions (Inaul and Landap) as
economic tools; founding the Raheemah
Economic Hub and Youth Development
Center; receiving the "Iconic Woman
Creating a Better World" award at WEF
Australia 2025
Within this tradition, she carries the title of Bae a Labi, a customary
designation for a royal female leader who holds recognized
authority in community mediation, counseling, and local
governance. The title is not ceremonial in the passive sense. In
Maranao society, a Bae a Labi is expected to be an active voice,
someone communities turn to when disputes need resolving or when
collective decisions need to be made with cultural legitimacy behind
them.
This grounding in Maranao culture and Adat has defined her entire
approach to public service. Rather than treating traditional values
and modern governance as separate lanes, she has consistently
worked to run them together, using customary frameworks to build
trust at the grassroots level while engaging the mechanisms of the
Philippine national government to back it up.
EDUCATION
Cayongcat-Nuska completed her secondary education at Dansalan
College in Marawi City, graduating with the Batch of 1988-1989.
Dansalan College has long been recognized as one of the Lanao
region's most important educational institutions, with a strong
tradition of fostering interfaith dialogue, civic responsibility, and
community leadership.
She later pursued advanced studies in Public Administration, a field
that would directly inform her work in community development,
cooperative governance, and eventually, her role in the national
executive bureaucracy. Her appointment to national office was
formally celebrated by her colleagues at the Department of Public
Administration, a recognition of how deeply her academic
formation shaped her trajectory as a public servant.
CAREER
Post-Marawi Siege Relief Work (2019)
The 2017 Battle of Marawi was one of the most devastating urban conflicts in the Philippines' modern history. The
five-month siege reduced large portions of the city to rubble and displaced an estimated 300,000 to 400,000
residents, many of whom were still living in temporary shelters years after the fighting ended.
Cayongcat-Nuska launched her response in 2019, organizing a grassroots voluntary humanitarian initiative to reach
internally displaced persons (IDPs) who were still struggling well into the post-conflict period. This early volunteer
work was self-organized, unfunded, and built almost entirely on community trust and personal commitment. It was
also the seed of everything that came after.

PAGE 3
Founding the Raheemah Women's Organization (2020)
By 2020, she had come to a clear-eyed conclusion: emergency relief alone was not going to rebuild Marawi.
Distributing goods kept people from starving, but it didn't give them back agency, income, or dignity. With that in
mind, she transformed her volunteer group into a formal institution.
In the middle of the global COVID-19 pandemic, she co-founded and became Executive Director of the
Raheemah Women's Organization, which also operates as the Raheemah Peace Weavers Cooperative. The
name "Raheemah" draws from an Arabic root meaning mercy and compassion, a deliberate choice that reflects the
organization's ethos.
From the start, the cooperative's model was different from conventional post-conflict NGO work. Instead of
positioning beneficiaries as passive recipients, Cayongcat-Nuska built programs that turned affected women into
active economic participants, starting with what many of them already knew: traditional Meranaw craftsmanship.
The Raheemah Economic Hub and Youth Development Center (2022)
The cooperative's work culminated in a major milestone in October 2022, when Cayongcat-Nuska's team partner-
built and inaugurated the Raheemah Economic Hub and Youth Development Center. The Hub functions as a
structured economic space where livelihood programs, enterprise training, and cultural production converge under
one roof.
The Hub's programs specifically target demographics that are often the last to benefit from post-conflict
reconstruction:
Widows and solo parents who lost primary breadwinners to the conflict
Senior citizens who lacked the economic safety nets to recover without structured support
Marginalized former female combatants of the Islamic military, a population rarely acknowledged in
mainstream rehabilitation frameworks
The economic engine running through all of these programs is Meranaw cultural enterprise, particularly the revival
of traditional textile weaving. Under Cayongcat-Nuska's direction, weavers trained in producing Inaul (a
traditional handwoven cloth associated with Maranao royalty and ceremony) and Landap (another heritage
textile), and in creating intricate beadwork that is distinctly Meranaw in aesthetic. By connecting these heritage
crafts to actual markets, the cooperative turned cultural preservation into a practical income source.
Strategic Institutional Partnerships
The Raheemah Women's Organization did not work in isolation. Cayongcat-Nuska built a network of institutional
partnerships that brought in resources, expertise, and reach:
Save the Children Philippines: She partnered with the organization's Restoring Livelihoods and Learning
Project, which provided skills training and raw materials to hundreds of women affected by the siege across
Lanao del Sur.
#SafeBackToSchool Campaign: She directed Raheemah weavers to contribute localized artisanal trims to
backpacks distributed to children across the Bangsamoro region, integrating cultural production into a large-
scale education support campaign and giving weavers a reliable production contract.
Task Force Bangon Marawi (TFBM): She coordinated directly with the government's inter-agency
rehabilitation task force, aligning the cooperative's community-level livelihood activities with the state-led

PAGE 4
Marawi rehabilitation master plans.
INSTITUTIONAL CONTRIBUTIONS
Chairperson, Provincial Tourism, Culture, and Arts Council of Lanao del Sur
Prior to and alongside her work with the Raheemah cooperative, Cayongcat-Nuska served as Chairperson of the
Provincial Tourism, Culture, and Arts Council of Lanao del Sur. In that role, she focused on tourism data
optimization and the protection of regional cultural heritage assets. The position gave her experience operating at
the intersection of government policy and cultural advocacy, a rehearsal of sorts for the national responsibilities
that would follow.
Appointment as NCMF Commissioner (2024)
In May 2024, President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr. appointed Cayongcat-Nuska as a Commissioner of the National
Commission on Muslim Filipinos (NCMF). The appointment was endorsed by the Provincial Government of
Lanao del Sur, the NCMF National Capital Region (NCR) Office, and a broad network of civil society
organizations across sectoral lines.
The NCMF operates under Republic Act No. 9997, its founding charter, and serves as the primary national
government body responsible for the welfare, rights, and development of Muslim Filipino communities. Working
under NCMF Secretary Sabuddin N. Abdurahim, her official mandate as Commissioner encompasses:
Preserving and developing the culture, traditions, and rights of Muslim Filipinos at the level of national
executive policy
Scaling micro-enterprise frameworks, built from the cooperative model she developed in Lanao del Sur, into
national development strategies for underserved Muslim women
Strengthening local legal mechanisms, including providing cultural infrastructure and logistical support for
Special Shari'ah Bar candidates in Mindanao
RECOGNITION
"Iconic Woman Creating a Better World" Award, WEF Australia 2025
Cayongcat-Nuska was recognized at the Women Economic Forum (WEF) Australia 2025, held in Melbourne,
with the award title "Iconic Woman Creating a Better World." The award acknowledged her contributions to
transformative female leadership, grassroots entrepreneurship, and post-conflict community recovery, placing her
Marawi-based work within a global conversation on women's economic empowerment.
INACRAFT 2026 Panelist
She was invited as a principal panelist at the INACRAFT 2026 convention at the Jakarta International Convention
Center (JICC) in Indonesia, one of Asia's largest craft trade exhibitions. Her panel focused on empowering craft
small-to-medium enterprises (SMEs) and transforming regionally rooted culture into globally viable market
opportunities, drawing directly from the Raheemah cooperative's experience converting Meranaw heritage textiles
into sustainable enterprise.

PAGE 5
The Peace Walking Movement
National rehabilitation agencies recognized her role in organizing the Peace Walk, a cultural advocacy campaign
that uses indigenous pride and arts heritage as active counters to violent extremism in the region. The movement
reflects a philosophy central to her work: that cultural identity, when affirmed and celebrated, is one of the most
durable protections against radicalization and communal breakdown.
LEGACY
What makes Cayongcat-Nuska's story worth telling, beyond the titles and the awards, is the underlying argument
she has been making through her life's work: that post-conflict recovery doesn't have to choose between
humanitarian relief and cultural dignity. She built an organization that did both at the same time, and then proved
the model worked well enough to take it national.
Her trajectory from volunteer relief worker in 2019 to NCMF Commissioner in 2024 is really a story about what
happens when someone refuses to separate the practical from the cultural. The Raheemah Economic Hub didn't just
help displaced women earn income. It gave them something to weave toward, quite literally, in the tradition of their
ancestors. And in doing that, it demonstrated that Meranaw cultural heritage is not a relic to be protected behind
glass, but a living, breathing economic resource with real market value.
At the national level, her challenge now is to scale what worked in Lanao del Sur across the diversity of Muslim
Filipino communities, each with their own traditions, needs, and histories. The frameworks she developed through
years of direct grassroots work give her a credibility in that effort that is rare in national public administration.

Amai Pakpak Medical Center
Amai Pakpak Medical Center (APMC), known in Filipino as
Sentrong Medikal ng Amai Pakpak, is a government-owned tertiary
teaching and training hospital in Marawi City, Lanao del Sur, in the
Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM).
It is retained and directly funded by the national Department of
Health (DOH), and it holds the distinction of being Mindanao's
designated regional apex multi-specialty referral center, the hospital
where the region's toughest cases, from complicated heart conditions
to advanced cancers, eventually land when smaller facilities run out
of options.
What makes APMC's story worth telling isn't just its size or its
services. It's the sheer number of times this hospital has had to start
over. It has burned down, been fought over during one of the
deadliest urban battles in recent Philippine history, and still managed
to open a full cardiac surgery program less than a decade later. Few
hospitals anywhere carry that kind of history in their walls.
Contents

1.2 Lanao General Hospital Era (1910 to 1995)

PAGE 2

Website
apmc.doh.gov.ph
Phone
(063) 876-0001
Email
info@apmc.doh.gov.ph
Category
Institution: Hospital / Medical Center
Notability
Mindanao's designated regional apex
multi-specialty referral hospital, and the
only Level III tertiary center serving the
whole of Lanao del Sur and much of the
surrounding Bangsamoro region.
Known For
Surviving two fires and the five-month
Marawi siege of 2017, then rebuilding into
a facility now offering open-heart surgery
through its own Heart Institute.
Pull Quote
From a 25-bed cholera ward under a U.S.
Army tent in 1910 to an 800-bed regional
apex hospital a little over a century later,
Amai Pakpak Medical Center has never
really stopped rebuilding itself.
11 References
History
Early Origins (1903 to 1910)
The hospital's roots go back to 1903, when the United States Army's
27th Infantry Cavalry Division, under Captain John J. "Black Jack"
Pershing, set up a military medical facility on a 20-hectare stretch of
land then called Camp Marahui (later renamed Camp Keithley). It
wasn't yet a hospital for the public, just a facility built to keep
American soldiers alive during the occupation.
That changed in 1910. A cholera outbreak swept through the area,
killing both U.S. military personnel and local residents, and Captain
James Ames responded by organizing the facility into a proper 25-
bed hospital, becoming its first chief in the process. That moment,
arguably, is when Amai Pakpak's real story as a community hospital
begins.
Lanao General Hospital Era (1910 to 1995)
For most of the twentieth century, the facility operated as Lanao
General Hospital, a name locals eventually shortened to simply the
"Public Hospital." Its bed capacity grew slowly but steadily over the
decades: from 75 beds it was raised to 100 beds in 1992 through Republic Act No. 7217, then later doubled again
as demand from the province kept climbing.
In 1984, the hospital was folded into the Integrated Provincial Health Office of Lanao del Sur as part of a broader
integration program for the province's health system, a shift that placed it more firmly under local and provincial
coordination even as it remained a national facility.
Conversion to Medical Center (1995)
The hospital's biggest institutional leap came on March 3, 1995, when President Fidel V. Ramos signed Republic
Act No. 7943 into law. The measure, authored by the late Congressman Mamintal "Mike" Adiong Sr.,
renationalized the facility and elevated it from a general hospital into a full medical center, complete with the
personnel, equipment, and infrastructure the new classification demanded.
It was this same law that gave the hospital its present name, honoring Amai Pakpak, a 19th-century Maranao
military leader still remembered by the Maranao people as a symbol of resistance against Spanish colonial forces.
Naming a modern medical institution after him wasn't a small gesture. It tied the hospital's identity directly to
Maranao heritage and resilience, themes that would prove almost prophetic given everything the hospital would
later go through.
The hospital's bed capacity kept pace with its growing status. Republic Act No. 11103, signed by President Rodrigo
Duterte on October 30, 2018, raised the authorized bed count from 200 to 400, a threshold the DOH's own
implementing rules (Administrative Order No. 2014-0028) had already anticipated in laying out standards for a

PAGE 3
tertiary teaching and training hospital.
Fires and Reconstruction (2006, 2013)
Fire has twice threatened to undo decades of institutional growth. In 2006, a blaze triggered by a power overload
destroyed the hospital's main building entirely. Recovery came with international help: the U.S. Joint Special
Operations Task Force-Philippines funded and helped build a new facility, employing local workers and putting
roughly $660,058 into the reconstruction.
Barely seven years later, on October 16, 2013, another fire tore through the century-old hospital. Operations
resumed anyway, a pattern of quick recovery that would define APMC's next major test just four years later.
Marawi Siege (2017)
Nothing in the hospital's history compares to what happened during the Marawi siege, the five-month armed
conflict that engulfed the city from May 23 to October 23, 2017. Militants affiliated with the Islamic State stormed
the area around the hospital, and an ambulance driver was killed nearby. The battle zone around APMC saw such
intense bombardment that roughly 95 percent of the structures within it were heavily damaged or destroyed
outright. The hospital itself sustained losses estimated at ₱5,034,675 and was forced to close for the entire five
months of fighting.
Recovery began almost as soon as the guns quieted. An eight-man assessment team inspected the hospital on June
7, 2017, to gauge whether it could reopen. Days later, on June 13, 2017, APMC's doctors, nurses, and
administrative staff were redeployed to nearby district hospitals, evacuation centers, and the Philippine Red Cross,
so patient care in the wider area wouldn't collapse while the main facility rebuilt. When APMC finally reopened, it
didn't just resume normal operations. It went on to serve as one of the region's major facilities responding to the
COVID-19 pandemic a few years later, treating patients from well beyond Lanao del Sur.
Description and Overview
Today, Amai Pakpak Medical Center is classified as a Level III tertiary teaching and training hospital under the
Department of Health, and it functions as Mindanao's regional apex multi-specialty center. That means advanced
services once only available in Manila or Cebu, cardiovascular surgery, cancer treatment, advanced endoscopy, are
now offered right in Marawi.
As of 2026, the hospital runs on a 400-bed capacity, though Republic Act No. 12207, signed into law by President
Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr. on May 8, 2025, authorizes doubling that to 800 beds. The measure, sponsored by Lanao
del Sur's 1st District Representative Ziaur-Rahman "Zia" Alonto Adiong, followed years of advocacy from hospital
leadership, and it mandates that the hospital's services and facilities be upgraded in step with the added beds.
APMC is also PhilHealth-accredited and offers Zero Balance Billing (ZBB) for ward care, which in practice means
indigent patients can receive treatment without out-of-pocket costs.
Location and Geographic Context
APMC sits in Marawi City, Lanao del Sur, within BARMM, at coordinates 8°00′17″N 124°17′01″E. It's part of the
urban core of what's often called the "Islamic City of Marawi," specifically in Barangay Datu Saber, accessible via
Amai Pakpak Avenue. The hospital doesn't publish a precise street address on its official website, so anyone driving
in for the first time is generally advised to just call ahead at (063) 876-0001 for directions.

PAGE 4
Organization, Administration, and Governance
Ownership and Governance
APMC is owned and operated by the Department of Health, which makes it a DOH-retained hospital. In practical
terms, this means the hospital answers directly to the national health department for funding and oversight, rather
than to a local government unit, a structure that has helped it access national-level support during crises like the
2017 siege.
Legal Basis
The hospital's legal foundation runs through several pieces of legislation. Republic Act No. 7943 (1995) converted
it from a general hospital into a medical center. Republic Act No. 11103 (2018) expanded its bed capacity to 400.
And Republic Act No. 12207 (2025) authorizes the current push toward 800 beds. DOH Administrative Order No.
2014-0028 fills in the implementing details, setting standards for staffing, infrastructure, and administrative control
appropriate to a tertiary teaching and training hospital.
Leadership
The hospital has been led since August 15, 2018, by Dr. Shalimar Sani-Rakiin, who took over as Medical Center
Chief following the retirement of Dr. Amer A. Saber. Under her leadership, APMC has pushed through some of its
most significant modern milestones, including the opening of the Heart Institute and the successful lobbying for the
800-bed expansion. The hospital's organizational structure includes departments for surgery, internal medicine,
pediatrics, obstetrics-gynecology, radiology, and laboratory services, alongside specialized units like the Heart
Institute and the Women & Children Protection Unit.
Functions, Services, and Programs
Medical Services
APMC's service list has grown considerably in recent years:
Cardiovascular Services: The APMC Heart Institute opened its doors on August 11, 2023, under the
leadership of Dr. Ali T. Macatanong, offering advanced cardiac care including coronary artery bypass graft
(CABG) surgery. It was designed from the start as a regional referral center for complex cardiac cases, built
with support and guidance from the Philippine Heart Center and Northern Mindanao Medical Center. In
March 2025, PhilHealth-BARMM formally accredited the Heart Institute for the CABG Z Benefit Package,
which covers up to ₱550,000 per patient and effectively removes the financial barrier to open-heart surgery
for eligible members.
Oncology Services: Cancer treatment is offered as part of the hospital's broader multi-specialty programs.
Advanced Endoscopy: Endoscopic procedures are available for gastrointestinal and related conditions.
Surgical Services: General surgery, orthopedic surgery, and other specialized procedures.
Internal Medicine: Comprehensive adult medical care.
Pediatrics: Child health services.
Obstetrics and Gynecology: Maternal and reproductive health care.
Radiology and Imaging: X-ray, ultrasound, CT scan, and other diagnostic services.
Laboratory Services: Clinical testing and pathology.
HIV Treatment: APMC operates as an HIV Treatment Center under the DOH network.

PAGE 5
Women & Children Protection Unit (WCPU): Dedicated services for victims of violence and abuse.
Residency Training Programs
As a teaching and training hospital, APMC hosts residency programs in partnership with medical schools and
professional organizations, including established training tracks within its anesthesia department and other clinical
services, producing new physicians who often go on to serve elsewhere in the Bangsamoro region.
Public Health Programs
The hospital also participates in national health initiatives, among them Zero Balance Billing for indigent ward
patients, the Malasakit Center program that consolidates financial and medical assistance under one roof, and full
PhilHealth accreditation across multiple benefit packages, CABG surgery being the most recent addition.
Role and Significance
Regional Healthcare Hub
APMC functions as the primary referral hospital for Lanao del Sur and the surrounding provinces, taking on
complex cases referred up from district hospitals and rural health units across Mindanao. That referral role is really
what "regional apex center" means in practice: when smaller facilities can't handle a case, it usually ends up here.
Bangsamoro Context
Within BARMM, APMC carries weight beyond its medical charts. It provides advanced healthcare to a
predominantly Muslim population that has, historically, faced real disparities in access to specialized care. Its
reconstruction after the 2017 siege has come to symbolize the wider region's recovery and its determination to
rebuild essential services rather than simply move on. And as a government hospital operating in an Islamic city,
APMC has had to build cultural and religious sensitivity into how it serves patients, recognizing needs and
traditions that a generic facility elsewhere in the country might not think to accommodate.
Pandemic Response
During the COVID-19 pandemic, APMC operated well beyond its normal capacity, treating patients from across
Mindanao at a time when the health system was under enormous strain. Its reopening after the Marawi siege, just a
few years earlier, positioned it as one of the region's most critical facilities when the pandemic hit.

Legacy and Continuing Impact
Amai Pakpak Medical Center has become something of a case study in institutional persistence. From a 25-bed tent
hospital during a cholera outbreak in 1910 to a DOH-retained Level III tertiary teaching and training hospital more
than a century later, APMC has weathered fires, armed conflict, and a global pandemic without ever permanently
closing its doors to the people who depend on it.
Its rebuilding after the 2017 siege, and its frontline role during the COVID-19 pandemic that followed not long
after, say as much about the region's resilience as they do about the hospital itself. The opening of the Heart
Institute in 2023 and the PhilHealth accreditation for CABG surgery in 2025 mark the hospital's clearest steps yet
toward becoming a genuine regional apex center, one capable of keeping patients in Mindanao for procedures that
once meant a flight to Manila.
As BARMM continues to develop, APMC remains one of its most important pieces of public infrastructure, a place
that trains the region's next generation of doctors and nurses while still serving as the last stop for the most difficult
cases in Lanao del Sur and beyond.

Nasrollah Bacarat Conding
Sultan Atty. Nasrollah Bacarat Conding, MPA, JD, Al-Hajj, is a
Mranaw traditional leader, lawyer, government official, and Islamic
humanitarian from the Philippines, widely recognized for carrying
the Sultanate tradition of the Cando Clan into the modern era.
Born into a lineage tracing back to the revered titles of Sarip Batua sa
Madaya and Datu a Pitiilan sa Madaya, Sultan Nasrollah Conding did
not grow up chasing the Sultanate. He wasn't a fixture at family
councils or traditional political gatherings. Yet when the call of
lineage came, he answered it, and what followed was a series of
enthronements that placed him among the most widely titled
traditional leaders of Mranaw descent in the Philippines.
His legacy rests on three pillars: the preservation of adat and taritib
through his Sultanate responsibilities, the expansion of Islamic
charitable service through the One Peso Sadka Ogop sa Giginawa
Foundation, and a distinguished career in law and public service that
he built from the ground up, following in the footsteps of his father.
He's the first descendant of the Cando Clan to hold the title of Sultan
sa Visayas and later Panoroganan sa Sbangan a Unayan, Sultana
Dumalondong sa Butig, one of the highest Sultanate ranks in Lanao.
That's not just family history; that's a Mranaw milestone.
Contents
1 Background
2 Education
3 Career
3.1 Legal and Government Service
3.2 Traditional Sultanate Leadership
4 Humanitarian Service and Islamic Philanthropy
4.1 One Peso Sadka Ogop sa Giginawa Foundation
5 Contribution to the Preservation of Mranaw Culture
6 Recognition
7 Legacy
8 See Also
9 References
Background
The Mranaw people carry one of the richest traditions of Islamic sultanate governance in Southeast Asia, anchored
in the principles of honor, lineage, and community stewardship.

PAGE 2
Sultan Nasrollah Bacarat Conding is a proud descendant of the Cando Clan, a lineage connected to two respected
traditional figures: the Sarip Batua sa Madaya and the Datu a Pitiilan sa Madaya.
By his own admission, he was never deeply embedded in family gatherings or the informal political networks that
often lead to Sultanate succession. He never sought any traditional title, nor did he campaign for one.
What changed that was the collective voice of his elders, relatives, and friends, who saw in him the qualities and
the lineage that made him the right person to carry the responsibility forward.
His elders described the opportunity not as something that comes every decade, but perhaps once in a hundred
years, a generational moment where their branch of the Cando Clan was destined to occupy the traditional seat of
leadership.
Sultan Conding's forefathers were known as builders and protectors of the BATO Ali Masjid, a heritage of faith and
community service that he would continue and expand in his own generation.
Education
Sultan Nasrollah Conding holds a Juris Doctor (JD) degree and a Master of Public Administration (MPA),
credentials that reflect both his legal profession and his commitment to principled governance.
He completed his legal education at the University of the East College of Law, where he made his mark early. In
1996, he became the first elected Muslim Vice President of the UE College of Law student body, a distinction
that spoke to his ability to earn the trust and confidence of a diverse student community.
His academic leadership at UE followed an earlier recognition from Mindanao State University, where he was
named the First Muslim Leadership Awardee of MSU-JPIA in 1990.
He is also a Al-Hajj, having completed the Islamic pilgrimage to Mecca, which holds deep spiritual significance
for him personally and adds to his standing as a community leader grounded in faith.
Career
Legal and Government Service
Sultan Nasrollah Conding built his professional career in law and government, following the footsteps of his father,
Atty. Pilimpinas M. Conding, who was likewise a practicing lawyer.
Among his documented firsts in public service:
First Muslim Leadership Awardee of the MSU-JPIA (1990)
First elected Muslim Vice President of the University of the East College of Law (1996)
First Muslim Chief of the Legal Division of the Bureau of Internal Revenue (specific year on record)
These distinctions weren't just personal achievements. Each "first" represented a door opened for Muslim
professionals in spaces where they had previously been underrepresented.

PAGE 3
Traditional Sultanate Leadership
Sultan Conding's formal investiture into traditional leadership began in 2016 and continued through a series of
enthronements that expanded his reach across the Philippines.
On November 11, 2016, he was enthroned as Sultan sa Bacolod, Lima Datu ko Phamagsopa sa Marawi,
marking the beginning of his formal role in the traditional Mranaw leadership structure.
On December 10, 2024, he made history when Sultan Bob M. Datimbang, recognized as Sultan a Phangampong sa
Pilipinas, enthroned him as Sultan sa Visayas. This made him the first descendant of the Cando Clan to hold
this title, and it represented the extension of Mranaw traditional leadership into the Visayas region for the first time
through his lineage.
On February 23, 2025, he was enthroned as Panoroganan sa Sbangan a Unayan, Sultana Dumalondong sa
Butig, one of the highest-ranking Sultanate titles in Lanao. This enthronement came with not only honor, but also a
weighty responsibility to uphold adat, taritib, and the integrity of the Sultanate institution.
On November 2, 2025, Sultan Bob Datimbang once again conferred upon him the title of Sultan of Region 2,
further broadening his traditional mandate and making him one of the few traditional leaders entrusted with
Sultanate responsibilities spanning multiple regions of the country.
Humanitarian Service and Islamic Philanthropy
One Peso Sadka Ogop sa Giginawa Foundation
In December 2016, Sultan Nasrollah Conding founded the One Peso Sadka Ogop sa Giginawa Foundation, a
charitable organization rooted in Islamic principles of zakat and Baitul Mal.
The foundation was conceived as a modern expression of the timeless Islamic obligation to care for those in need.
It was not limited to family members or clan affiliates; from its inception, it was structured to serve all eight
categories of zakat beneficiaries recognized under Islamic teaching.
Through the trust and dedication of contributors and volunteers, the foundation grew far beyond its origins,
establishing chapters across all three major island groups: Mindanao, Visayas, and Luzon.
Under Sultan Conding's leadership, the foundation acquired three ambulances deployed to communities in:
Iligan City in Mindanao
Cebu City in the Visayas
Urdaneta City and Isabela in Luzon
The foundation also provides direct zakat financial assistance to individuals and families in need, with grants
ranging from ₱20,000 to ₱1,000,000, depending on circumstance and need.
In addition, the foundation supports the construction of masjid (mosques), with building assistance ranging from
₱500,000 to ₱2,500,000 per project.
Sultan Conding consistently reminded contributors that the foundation's success was not a product of human
ingenuity alone. He often said that true trust must not be placed merely in human capability, but in Allah (سبحانه
وتعالى). He humbly acknowledged that he did not consider himself a scholar or a saint, yet he believed that by
working sincerely for the sake of Allah, the Baitul Mal of Allah would continue to grow and benefit humanity.

PAGE 4
Contribution to the Preservation of Mranaw Culture
Sultan Conding's entrustment with multiple Sultanate titles across several regions is itself a testament to how
seriously the Mranaw traditional leadership community regards the preservation of adat (custom) and taritib
(protocol).
His investiture as Panoroganan sa Sbangan a Unayan, Sultana Dumalondong sa Butig placed on him a
responsibility that goes beyond ceremony. It means being a living custodian of Mranaw tradition, responsible for
upholding the dignity and continuity of the Sultanate institution in Lanao.
His enthronement as Sultan sa Visayas carried an additional cultural dimension: it signaled the expansion of
Mranaw traditional identity beyond Mindanao, reinforcing cultural ties among Muslim Filipino communities in the
Visayas.
Through the One Peso Sadka Foundation, he also continues the charitable heritage of his forefathers, who were
known as builders and protectors of the BATO Ali Masjid, a tangible expression of Islamic heritage and community
service.
Recognition
Sultan Nasrollah Conding has been recognized through both traditional and institutional channels:
First Muslim Leadership Awardee, MSU-JPIA (1990)
First elected Muslim Vice President, University of the East College of Law (1996)
First Muslim Chief, Legal Division, Bureau of Internal Revenue
Sultan sa Bacolod, Lima Datu ko Phamagsopa sa Marawi (enthroned November 11, 2016)
Sultan sa Visayas (enthroned December 10, 2024, by Sultan Bob M. Datimbang, Sultan a Phangampong sa
Pilipinas)
Panoroganan sa Sbangan a Unayan, Sultana Dumalondong sa Butig (enthroned February 23, 2025)
Sultan of Region 2 (enthroned November 2, 2025, by Sultan Bob M. Datimbang)
Legacy
Sultan Nasrollah Bacarat Conding's story is one of reluctant but purposeful leadership. He didn't pursue the
Sultanate; the Sultanate found him, through lineage, through community trust, and through a generational calling
that his elders described as a once-in-a-century opportunity.
What he built from that calling is substantial: four Sultanate titles, a nationally operating Islamic charity, a career
that opened doors for Muslim professionals, and a living example that traditional Mranaw leadership and modern
professional life aren't in conflict; they can, and should, coexist.
For the Cando Clan, his life marks a turning point. He surpassed many of his forefathers in the number and rank of
Sultanate titles, not through political maneuvering, but through the recognition of those who saw in him the
lineage, the character, and the capacity to serve.
His foundation, the One Peso Sadka Ogop sa Giginawa, has taken the charitable heritage of his ancestors and made
it national in scope, a quiet but steady expression of baitul mal in the modern Philippines.
His message to his community remains consistent: trust Allah, work sincerely, and the rest will follow.

Pilimpinas M. Conding
Atty. Pilimpinas M. Conding was a pioneering Maranao public servant, legal professional, and political figure
who blazed trails for Muslim Mindanao representation in Philippine governance during the late 20th century.
Known for his quiet strength and groundbreaking appointments, he became the first Maranao to hold several
critical positions in national and regional government, including Commissioner of the National Anti-Poverty
Commission under President Joseph Estrada, Secretary of the Department of Education, Culture, and Sports in the
Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (DECS-ARMM), and Speaker Pro-Tempore of the Regional Legislative
Assembly. His career spanned anti-poverty advocacy, education reform, tax administration, and regional
governance—opening doors for future generations of Bangsamoro leaders while championing the cause of
marginalized communities.
Contents
1 Early Life and Background
2 Education
3 Career
3.1 Tax Administration Pioneer
3.2 Anti-Poverty Advocacy
3.3 Education Leadership in ARMM
3.4 Regional Governance
3.5 Electoral Politics
4 Family and Personal Life
5 Legacy and Impact
6 External Links
Early Life and Background
Atty. Pilimpinas M. Conding was born into the Arindig royal
lineage of Lanao del Sur, the son of Sultan Conding Arindig and
Bae Mindarabao Cando H. Edres. Growing up in a Maranao
community that valued both traditional leadership and modern
education, he witnessed firsthand the challenges faced by Muslim
Mindanao in accessing national opportunities and representation.
His family background connected him to influential clans across
the region—his sister, the late Al Haj Bae Rassamala Pangarungan,
would become the grandmother of National Commission on
Muslim Filipinos (NCMF) Secretary Saidamen Pangarungan,
while his cousins included Sultan Ibrahim Marmay (former
Provincial Agrarian Reform Program Officer of the Department of
Agrarian Reform, Region X), Atty. Bato Ali Jr. (former
Commission on Audit Provincial Director), and Sultan Camid
Gandamra Sr. (father of Marawi City Mayor Atty. Majul U.
Gandamra).

PAGE 2
This network of kinship and governance would shape his understanding of how traditional authority and modern
bureaucracy could work together to serve the Bangsamoro people.
Education
Details of Atty. Conding's formal education, including where he obtained his law degree, remain to be documented
in publicly available sources. However, his successful legal career and appointment to high-level government
positions demonstrate that he met the rigorous academic and professional standards required for admission to the
Philippine Bar and for executive appointments during both the Marcos and post-Marcos eras.
Career
Tax Administration Pioneer
In 1974, during the Martial Law years under President Ferdinand Marcos, Atty. Conding made history as the first
Maranao designated as Bureau of Internal Revenue (BIR) Revenue District Officer in Ozamiz City. This
appointment was groundbreaking—at a time when Muslim Filipinos were largely underrepresented in the national
tax bureaucracy, his presence in this technical and politically sensitive role challenged prevailing biases and
demonstrated Maranao capability in public finance administration. His work in Ozamiz City laid the groundwork
for future generations of Maranao professionals in the BIR, including his own sons who would follow in his
footsteps decades later.
The role required not just legal expertise but also the ability to navigate the complex political landscape of Martial
Law while maintaining integrity and professionalism in revenue collection and taxpayer relations.
Anti-Poverty Advocacy
Atty. Conding's most nationally visible role came when President Joseph "Erap" Estrada appointed him as the first
Commissioner of the National Anti-Poverty Commission (NAPC). In this capacity, he became a key
implementer of the administration's signature "Erap Para sa Mahirap" (Erap for the Poor) program, which aimed to
address systemic poverty through direct intervention and community empowerment. As a Maranao leader in this
position, he brought attention to the specific poverty challenges faced by Muslim Mindanao, where armed conflict,
displacement, and historical marginalization had created especially acute development gaps.
His work at NAPC emphasized grassroots consultation, bringing the voices of the poorest Filipinos—including
those from conflict-affected areas—directly into national policy conversations. He understood that poverty in the
Bangsamoro context was not just about economics but about historical justice, cultural recognition, and political
inclusion.
Education Leadership in ARMM
Regional Governor Zacariah Candao appointed Atty. Conding as the first Secretary of the Department of
Education, Culture, and Sports of the Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (DECS-ARMM). This role
placed him at the helm of one of the most critical agencies in the young autonomous government, responsible for
shaping educational policy and cultural preservation across the Muslim-majority provinces. His tenure came during
a formative period when ARMM was still defining its identity and building institutions that could deliver basic
services while respecting the distinct cultural and religious character of Bangsamoro communities.

PAGE 3
As DECS-ARMM Secretary, he worked to address the chronic underfunding and neglect of education in the region,
advocated for culturally relevant curriculum that included Islamic studies and Maranao history, and fought to
improve teacher quality and school infrastructure in areas that had long been treated as peripheral by the national
government.
Regional Governance
Atty. Conding broke another barrier when he was elected as the first Maranao Speaker Pro-Tempore of the
Regional Legislative Assembly (RLA), the legislative body of ARMM that would later evolve into the
Bangsamoro Parliament. This position made him the second-highest-ranking official in the regional legislature and
gave him significant influence over the lawmaking process in Muslim Mindanao. His leadership in this role
demonstrated the growing political maturity of Maranao politicians and their ability to build coalitions across the
diverse ethnic groups within ARMM, which included not just Maranaos but also Maguindanaos, Tausūgs, and other
Bangsamoro communities.
As Speaker Pro-Tempore, he presided over legislative sessions, managed parliamentary procedure, and worked to
pass laws that addressed land rights, Islamic personal law, economic development, and peace-building—all while
navigating the complex power dynamics between the regional government, national government, and various
armed groups operating in the area.
Electoral Politics
In 1991, Atty. Conding ran as the official candidate for Mayor of Marawi City under a coalition between the
Partido Demokratiko Pilipino-Lakas ng Bayan (PDP-Laban) and the Liberal Party. The campaign was supported by
two of the most prominent opposition leaders of the time: Senator Jovito "Juvy" Salonga and Senator Aquilino
"Nene" Pimentel Jr. His candidacy represented an attempt to bring reformist politics to Marawi City, challenging
the entrenched political dynasties that had long dominated local governance.
While the outcome of the election is not documented in available sources, the mere fact that national opposition
leaders endorsed his candidacy speaks to his reputation as a principled public servant with a reform-oriented vision
for Marawi's future.
Family and Personal Life
Atty. Conding was married to Hadja Moumina Namraida Bacarat-Conding, with whom he raised five children,
each of whom would go on to make significant contributions to public service, business, and community
development:
1. Nasraili B. Conding, CPA, LLB – Founding President of the Bangsa Moro Federal Business Council Inc.
and Bureau of Internal Revenue Revenue District Officer. Married to Atty. Sittie Phamy C. Gandamra-
Conding, who serves as Commissioner of the National Labor Relations Commission (NLRC).
2. Atty. Nasrollah B. Conding, CPA, MPA – Supreme Chairman of the One Peso Sadka Foundation and
Bureau of Internal Revenue Assistant Regional Director. Married to Johaira "Rairai" Dida-agun Dimaporo-
Conding.
3. Norjaini B. Conding-Malamama – Wife of Engr. Abdulzaman R. Malamama, JD.
4. Ayubkhan B. Conding – Married to Rowena Abdullah Rakim-Conding.
5. Princess B. Conding-Dia – Married to Jamel Dia.

PAGE 4
His nephews and extended family also occupy prominent positions in government and professional life, including
Revenue District Officer Benjamin Gonsi Conding and Prof. Hassan Conding Cana. The Conding family's
continued presence in public service, tax administration, business development, and social welfare work reflects
the values he instilled—service to community, professional excellence, and commitment to the Bangsamoro cause.
His siblings included H. Aisha Conding-Ismael and H. Malik Conding, while his half-siblings from his father's side
were H. Sharifa/Boli Conding-Cana, H. Fatima/Delabi Conding-Gonsi, H. Amina/Timbang Conding-Aba, and H.
Abubacar Mustapha. From his mother's side, his sister Bae Rassamala Pangarungan-Asum would become the
matriarch of another influential political family.
Legacy and Impact
Atty. Pilimpinas M. Conding's life was defined not by personal ambition but by a quiet determination to open doors
for his people. In an era when Maranao representation in national governance was minimal and often tokenistic, he
proved through competence and integrity that Muslim Mindanao leaders could excel in the most demanding roles
in Philippine public service. His career spanned the authoritarian Marcos years, the democratic restoration under
Corazon Aquino, the populist presidency of Joseph Estrada, and the early years of regional autonomy—each phase
presenting unique challenges that he met with professionalism and principle.
His legacy is visible in multiple dimensions. Institutionally, he helped establish the precedent for Maranao
participation in national anti-poverty policy, regional education governance, and legislative leadership.
Professionally, his success in tax administration paved the way for his sons and other Maranao CPAs and lawyers
to enter the BIR and other technical agencies. Politically, his coalition-building and reformist credentials
demonstrated that Bangsamoro leaders could transcend clan-based politics and build alliances based on shared
values rather than just kinship.
Perhaps most importantly, his approach to public service—humble, bridge-building, focused on systemic change
rather than personal glory—set a standard that continues to inspire younger generations of Bangsamoro leaders. In
a region where political dynasties often prioritize family consolidation of power, he showed an alternative model:
raising children who would serve the public in their own right, based on merit and commitment, rather than simply
inheriting positions.
The institutions he helped build—NAPC's focus on community voices, ARMM's education system, the Regional
Legislative Assembly's parliamentary traditions—continue to shape governance in what is now the Bangsamoro
Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM). His work laid foundations that others are still building
upon.
May Allah grant him the highest station in Jannatul Firdausi. Ameen.
