Pull Quote
"A great leader leaves behind more than
achievements — he leaves wisdom, honor,
and a legacy that inspires generations."
Macmod Lolong Dalidig
Sultan Macmod Lolong Dalidig was a Sultan of Lanao, a former
Provincial Treasurer, and the President of the Federation of Royal
Sultanate of Lanao.
He spent his life in service to the Bangsamoro people, carrying both
the weight of traditional leadership and the responsibilities of
government with the same quiet dignity.
What set him apart wasn't just the titles he held. It was the way he
held them: with humility, sincerity, and a genuine concern for the
welfare of everyone around him, from fellow sultans to ordinary
community members.
He's remembered today as a leader, a mentor, an adviser, and a
father figure whose wisdom left a deep and lasting mark on the
people of Lanao.
Contents
1 Background
2 Government Service
3 Traditional Leadership
4 Character and Approach
5 Legacy
6 References
7 Categories
Background
Sultan Macmod Lolong Dalidig was a proud son of the Lanao
tradition, rooted in the heritage and customs of the Bangsamoro
people.
His identity as a Sultan was never just ceremonial. He carried the
responsibility that came with that title seriously, seeing it as an
obligation to protect, preserve, and serve the community he
represented.
Throughout his life, he remained deeply committed to the values of
his people: justice, unity, and peace, not as abstract ideals, but as
guiding principles in everything he did.

PAGE 2
Government Service
Sultan Macmod Lolong Dalidig served as the Provincial Treasurer of Lanao, bringing his trademark calm wisdom
and strong moral character into the realm of public administration.
He understood that government service and traditional leadership weren't separate worlds. For him, they were two
expressions of the same commitment: serving the people well.
In office, he was consistent. He listened with patience, acted with fairness, and treated every individual with equal
respect, regardless of their wealth, title, or position in life.
Traditional Leadership
As President of the Federation of Royal Sultanate of Lanao, Sultan Macmod Lolong Dalidig took on a role that
required both diplomacy and deep cultural knowledge.
He dedicated himself to strengthening unity among the Royal Sultanates, a task that called for constant dialogue,
trust, and the kind of genuine respect that he naturally extended to everyone he worked with.
He was a steady advocate for preserving the customs, values, and traditions of the Bangsamoro people, believing
that a community's identity is one of its most important assets.
He also worked consistently toward peace within the community, seeing peaceful coexistence not just as a goal but
as a responsibility that leaders must actively pursue and model.
Character and Approach
People who knew Sultan Macmod Lolong Dalidig often remarked on one thing above all else: he never let power
change him.
Despite the positions he held, he stayed humble and approachable. He didn't allow rank to create distance between
himself and ordinary people. Whether he was speaking with a fellow sultan, a government colleague, a community
member, or a stranger, he offered the same warmth, compassion, and dignity.
That consistency made him deeply loved. It also made him effective. People trusted him because they knew he saw
them, really saw them, as equals deserving of respect.
Many looked up to him not just as a leader but as a mentor and adviser, someone whose wisdom offered
encouragement and direction to those still finding their way.
Legacy
Sultan Macmod Lolong Dalidig has passed on, but what he left behind goes well beyond any formal record of
service.
He leaves a legacy of honorable leadership, humility, and compassion that continues to resonate in Lanao and
across the broader Bangsamoro community.

PAGE 3
His life is a reminder that the greatest leaders aren't remembered for the authority they wielded, but for the
kindness they practiced, the unity they built, and the lives they touched along the way.
His wisdom continues to inspire. His example of treating every person with equal dignity, regardless of where they
stand in life, remains one of the most enduring parts of his story.

Maisara Dandamun-Latiph
Atty. Maisara C. Dandamun-Latiph is a distinguished Maranao
jurist, legislator, and human rights advocate who has shaped post-
conflict recovery and institutional reform across the Bangsamoro
region.
Her career spans high-level state legal work, legislative innovation
in the Bangsamoro Transition Authority, and executive leadership
in one of the Philippines' most consequential reparations
programs: the Marawi Compensation Board.
As a Maranao woman in prominent executive and legislative
roles, she embodies a modern fusion of traditional Islamic values
and progressive legal reform, grounded in an unwavering
commitment to peacebuilding and the protection of the
marginalized.
Contents
1 Early Life and Heritage
2 Education
3 Professional Career
3.1 State Legal Practice
3.2 Bangsamoro Transition Commission (BTC)
3.3 Bangsamoro Transition Authority (2019-2022)
4 Signature Legislative Achievements

Early Life and Heritage
Atty. Latiph is a member of the Maranao ethnic group and was
raised in a Muslim community enclave in Metro Manila during
her formative years.
This upbringing in a minority setting, far from the Bangsamoro
heartland, sparked her lifelong commitment to educational access
and advocacy for the rights and dignity of the Bangsamoro people.

PAGE 2
She credits her family environment with instilling in her a deep sense of responsibility toward community service
and nation-building.
Education
Atty. Latiph's academic trajectory reflects a multidisciplinary approach that bridges law, education, organizational
leadership, and national security.
She earned her Masters in Educational Leadership and School Improvement with Honors from the University
of Manchester in the United Kingdom as a prestigious Chevering Scholar.
This achievement positioned her as an educational innovator and policy-level thinker before she fully committed to
legal and legislative careers.
She is a pioneering graduate of the Executive Master in National Security Administration (E-MNSA) from the
National Defense College of the Philippines (NDCP), one of the first women to complete this rigorous program.
Currently, she is pursuing a Doctor of Philosophy in Educational Administration and Development at the
University of the Philippines Diliman, demonstrating her sustained commitment to advancing knowledge in
institutional development and governance.
Professional Career
State Legal Practice
Before transitioning into regional leadership, Atty. Latiph served as a Senior State Solicitor at the Office of the
Solicitor General (OSG), where she handled complex constitutional and administrative law matters on behalf of the
Philippine government.
This role established her reputation as a skilled legal advocate capable of navigating high-stakes policy disputes
and defending state interests while maintaining principled positions on human rights.
Bangsamoro Transition Commission (BTC)
Atty. Latiph served as a Commissioner of the Bangsamoro Transition Commission, the body tasked with drafting
foundational legal frameworks for the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM).
In this capacity, she contributed substantially to the Bangsamoro Organic Law (BOL) or Republic Act No. 11054,
co-drafting key provisions and leading grassroots information campaigns to educate communities about the law
and the peace process.
Her work in the BTC positioned her as a bridge between government, civil society, and the communities most
affected by decades of conflict.
Bangsamoro Transition Authority (2019-2022)
As a Member of Parliament of the Bangsamoro Transition Authority from 2019 to 2022, Atty. Latiph authored and
championed some of the most consequential legislation in BARMM's interim period.

PAGE 3
She served as the women sector representative, bringing gendered perspectives and marginalized voices into
legislative deliberations.
Her legislative work demonstrates a clear pattern: protecting vulnerable populations and institutionalizing
programs that would outlive the transitional government.
Signature Legislative Achievements
Madaris Education Act: Atty. Latiph created the Office of the Director-General for Madaris Education to establish
a formal funding and institutional framework for Islamic educational institutions across the Bangsamoro region.
This act affirms the importance of Islamic pedagogy while ensuring quality standards and financial accountability.
Bangsamoro Communities outside BARMM (BTA Bill No. 15): She authored legislation creating an office
dedicated to protecting the rights and interests of Bangsamoro communities residing outside the autonomous
region. This forward-thinking measure addresses the reality that thousands of Bangsamoro citizens live in urban
centers and other regions, often isolated from institutional support networks.
RISE Act (BTA Bill No. 157): Promoted social enterprises as vehicles for sustainable development and
peacebuilding, recognizing that economic opportunity is inseparable from conflict prevention.
Child Protection and Gender Equality Measures: Atty. Latiph authored numerous bills and resolutions
addressing child abuse protection, establishing day care centers, and advancing gender equality in Bangsamoro
institutions. These measures reflect her conviction that protecting children and women is foundational to a just
society.
Healing Marawi: The Marawi Compensation Board
In January 2023, President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. appointed Atty. Latiph as Chairperson of the Marawi
Compensation Board (MCB), the quasi-judicial body mandated to implement Republic Act 11696 or the Marawi
Siege Victims Compensation Act of 2022.
The 2017 Marawi siege devastated 32 barangays across the city, displacing over 100,000 residents and destroying
an estimated 70 billion pesos in private property and commercial establishments.
For nearly two years, Atty. Latiph led the MCB's effort to receive, adjudicate, and award compensation to qualified
claimants.
Operational Milestones
Under her stewardship, the MCB achieved measurable progress in delivering justice and reparations to siege
victims:
Total Claims Received: 14,495 individual claims filed with the board
Compensation Processed: Over 1.5 billion pesos disbursed to qualified claimants
Approved Claims: Approximately 2,288 individuals received final awards
Payment Efficiency: The board achieved nearly 100 percent payment fulfillment for approved claims, with
payments reaching beneficiaries within six months of approval
The MCB's compensation structure reflected careful deliberation and legal precision:

PAGE 4
Concrete structures: 18,000 pesos per square meter
Mixed materials: 13,500 pesos per square meter
Light materials: 9,000 pesos per square meter
Death claims: Fixed amount of 350,000 pesos per individual
Leadership Philosophy
Atty. Latiph approached MCB leadership with a quasi-judicial mindset, emphasizing rigorous document review,
fraud prevention, and equitable treatment of all claimants.
She acknowledged the immense challenge of processing over 14,000 complex claims while maintaining
transparent and defensible adjudication standards.
She worked closely with civil society organizations, task forces, and community leaders to ensure the MCB's work
reflected the voices and needs of displaced residents themselves.
In March 2025, she transitioned leadership of the MCB to a successor, having established functional systems,
trained staff, and secured expanded funding for the board's continued operations.
Educational and Community Initiatives
Beyond legislative and executive roles, Atty. Latiph has founded and directed several educational and advocacy
centers that demonstrate her commitment to grassroots empowerment.
She co-founded the IQRA Kiddie Learning Center (2003), providing quality early childhood and primary
education to Muslim children in Metro Manila.
She established the Safia Learning Center (2014), extending educational access to urban Muslim communities
often overlooked by mainstream schooling systems.
She founded the Khadija Center for Muslim Women Studies, a non-stock, non-profit think tank dedicated to
evidence-based research on the lives, challenges, and aspirations of Muslim women in the Philippines.
This center has become a recognized voice in policy advocacy, informing legislation and institutional reform in
both national and Bangsamoro governance spaces.
Personal Life and Values
Atty. Latiph is married to Atty. Algamar Latiph, a fellow lawyer and human rights advocate with whom she
shares a deep commitment to social justice.
Together, they have two children.
The couple represents a prominent legal partnership within the Philippine human rights community, often
collaborating on advocacy initiatives and public interest cases.
Atty. Latiph's leadership style is frequently described as independent, principled, and advocacy-driven.
She has stated that her philosophy centers on "giving space" to those at the margins of society: women, youth,
children, internally displaced persons, and religious minorities.

PAGE 5
She practices Islam thoughtfully and sees no contradiction between Islamic values and progressive legal reform or
gender equality.
Legacy and Impact
Atty. Latiph's contributions to Bangsamoro governance extend across three distinct domains: institutional reform
through legislation, reparative justice through the MCB, and community empowerment through educational and
research initiatives.
Her legislative record demonstrates that peacebuilding requires not just political agreements but concrete
institutional investments in education, social safety nets, and economic opportunity.
Her leadership of the MCB showed that complex reparations programs can operate with efficiency, transparency,
and respect for claimants' dignity.
Her educational centers and research institute model how Bangsamoro intellectuals can build autonomous
knowledge systems that serve community-defined priorities rather than external agendas.
As a Maranao woman navigating male-dominated legal and political institutions, she exemplifies the possibility of
change and the power of principled advocacy.
"Isang malaking karangalan na maglingkod sa Bangsamoro para tugunan ang mandato ng MCB bilang
Chairperson" (It is a great honor to serve the Bangsamoro to fulfill the mandate of the MCB as
Chairperson). -- Atty. Maisara Dandamun-Latiph, upon stepping down from the MCB chairperson
role, March 2025
Her work continues to shape how the Bangsamoro region approaches education, justice, women's empowerment,
and the inclusion of marginalized voices in governance.

Mandangan P. Darimbang
A distinguished Maranao Muslim leader and public servant,
Sultan Mandangan Panomblayan Darimbang (commonly
known as "Manny") spent over four decades building trust
between Christian and Muslim communities in the Christian-
dominated city of Cagayan de Oro, demonstrating that traditional
Bangsamoro leadership could thrive alongside democratic
governance and civil service. Carrying the hereditary title of
Sultan from the Royal Sultanate of Kandanga Malungun,
Darimbang became a symbol of interfaith harmony and integrity
in Northern Mindanao, serving 30 years as Regional Director of
the Land Transportation Franchising and Regulatory Board
(LTFRB) with an untarnished record that was verified by the
Ombudsman, Civil Service Commission, and National Bureau of
Investigation.
Contents
1 Early Life and Background
2 Education and Early Career
3 Career in Public Service
3.1 LTFRB Regional Director (1987–2016)
3.2 Laguindingan Airport Integration (2013–2016)
3.3 Mindanao Railway Project Coordination
3.4 Other Concurrent Positions
4 Personal Values and Leadership Philosophy
5 Family and Political Legacy
6 Cultural Significance as a Sultan
7 Challenges and Context
8 Achievements and Recognition
9 Legacy
10 References
11 Further Reading
12 See Also
Early Life and Background
Darimbang was born into the Maranao ethnic community and
carries the noble lineage of the Royal Sultanate of Kandanga
Malungun. Unlike many of his peers who remained within the
predominantly Muslim Bangsamoro region, he made the
unconventional decision early in his career to pursue government
service in Cagayan de Oro City, a location where Muslims
represented a distinct minority.

PAGE 2
This choice reflected a deliberate commitment to challenge societal perceptions and prove that a Muslim leader of
royal heritage could excel, earn respect, and find genuine acceptance within a predominantly Christian community.
Rather than viewing his Maranao identity and Sultan title as obstacles, he saw them as assets that could help bridge
historical divides and foster mutual understanding.
Education and Early Career
Details regarding Darimbang's formal education remain limited in available sources, though his career trajectory
suggests professional training in administrative management and transportation governance. He entered the
Philippine Civil Service at the young age of 31, when he was appointed as the Regional Director of the LTFRB for
Region 10 (Northern Mindanao).
This appointment came during the administration of President Corazon Aquino in 1987. From his first day in
office, Darimbang brought a philosophy of fairness, professionalism, and public-centered service that would define
his three decades of leadership in the transportation sector.
Career in Public Service
LTFRB Regional Director (1987–2016)
Darimbang's most prominent and enduring role was his 30-year tenure as Regional Director of the LTFRB for
Northern Mindanao (Region 10).<ref name="ltfrb_longserving">From 1987 until his retirement in August 2016,
Darimbang held the record as the longest-serving regional director of an LTFRB office in Cagayan de Oro.</ref>
Starting at age 31, he navigated the complex and often contentious world of public transportation regulation with a
consistent commitment to balancing the interests of operators, drivers, and the riding public.
During his tenure, Darimbang earned widespread recognition for his fair-handed approach to franchise regulation,
fare adjustment petitions, and transport infrastructure coordination. He was known for hosting public consultations
before making major policy decisions, ensuring that stakeholders—from taxi associations to commuter groups—
had a voice in regulatory matters. His office processed countless franchise applications, meter calibrations, fare
reviews, and dispute resolutions.
Key initiatives under his leadership included the implementation of meter-calibration programs to prevent
overcharging of passengers, the regulation of transport services at the newly opened Laguindingan International
Airport, and the coordination of shuttle services connecting the airport to Cagayan de Oro's downtown area.
Laguindingan Airport Integration (2013–2016)
When Laguindingan International Airport opened in June 2013, Darimbang played a crucial coordinating role in
establishing the ground transportation network.<ref name="laguindingan_airport">The airport, located
approximately 40 kilometers from Cagayan de Oro's city proper, required careful planning to ensure passengers
had affordable, regulated, and reliable shuttle services.</ref> He worked with multiple transport cooperatives, taxi
associations, and the Civil Aviation Authority of the Philippines to establish fare matrices, approve franchises, and
regulate the flow of vehicles.
He secured exemptions from DOTC circular regulations to allow airport taxis to operate under specific conditions,
approved initial taxi booths within the airport premises, and ensured that passengers would not fall victim to the
"pakyaw" (flat-rate overcharging) system that had plagued other regional airports. The result was a transparent fare

PAGE 3
structure with regulated meter-based rates, preventing the exploitation of passengers unfamiliar with the route.
Mindanao Railway Project Coordination
Beyond his day-to-day LTFRB responsibilities, Darimbang served as Project Director of the Mindanao Railway
Project Office. This 1,544-kilometer infrastructure initiative aimed to connect Mindanao's key population centers
and economic hubs. His office coordinated the early planning and integration stages of the project, with particular
focus on Phase 1, the Tagum-Davao-Digos segment (100.2 kilometers).
Darimbang's role involved ensuring that the railway system would integrate smoothly with other critical transport
nodes, including the newly opened Laguindingan Airport, the Port of Cagayan de Oro, and the Mindanao Container
Port. This coordination work bridged civilian transportation regulation (his LTFRB mandate) with major
infrastructure development, showcasing his versatility as a government administrator.
Other Concurrent Positions
Throughout his career, Darimbang held several concurrent roles that reflected his standing in the regional
government hierarchy:
Chairman of the DOTC Regional Management Council Vice Chairman of the Infrastructure Committee for the
Regional Development Council Career Executive Service Officer (CESO V) President of the Organization of
Regional Officers Vice President of the National Council of Career Executive Service Officers
These positions placed him at the center of Northern Mindanao's governance and infrastructure planning networks,
allowing him to influence policy across multiple transportation and development domains.
Personal Values and Leadership Philosophy
At the heart of Darimbang's career lay a commitment to what he termed "borderless public service"—the idea that
government exists to serve all citizens equally, regardless of religious or cultural background. He embodied this
principle by choosing to work in a Christian-majority city and earning the trust of both Muslim and Christian
communities through consistent professionalism and integrity.
Darimbang's approach to transportation regulation prioritized the welfare of the riding public while acknowledging
the legitimate concerns of operators and drivers. He famously remarked that Northern Mindanao transport
operators were "not greedy" but "fair people" who deserved equitable treatment alongside commuters. This
balanced philosophy informed his handling of contentious fare increase petitions and his response to transport
strikes.
His commitment to transparency was evident in his practice of holding public consultations before major
regulatory decisions. Rather than imposing top-down rules, he created space for dialogue, believing that sustainable
policy emerged from genuine stakeholder engagement.
Family and Political Legacy
Darimbang's influence extended beyond his own career into his family's civic participation. His wife, Candy
Darimbang, made history in 2013 when she was elected as the Number 1 City Councilor of Cagayan de Oro—the
first person with a Muslim Maranao surname to achieve this distinction in the city.<ref

PAGE 4
name="candy_councilor">This achievement marked a symbolic milestone for Muslim political representation in a
Christian-dominated city government, building on the foundation of trust that Sultan Mandangan had cultivated
through decades of public service.</ref> Their children and grandchildren have continued this legacy, pursuing
careers in medicine, law, academics, and other professional fields within and beyond Mindanao, all guided by
principles of integrity and service.
Cultural Significance as a Sultan
Beyond his government career, Darimbang held the hereditary title of Sultan from the Royal Sultanate of Kandanga
Malungun. In Maranao tradition, a Sultan carries multiple responsibilities: mediating community disputes,
preserving cultural heritage, and serving as a spiritual and custodial figure for his clan and territory.
Darimbang's dual role—as a government civil servant and as a traditional Sultan—was itself revolutionary.
Historically, Sultanate authority and Philippine government administration operated in separate spheres, often in
tension. By successfully navigating both worlds, Darimbang demonstrated that Bangsamoro traditional leadership
and democratic governance were not incompatible but could reinforce one another.
As a Sultan, he applied traditional Maranao conflict resolution methods (Taritib and Igma) to community disputes,
serving as an informal mediator. As a government director, he brought the wisdom of collective deliberation and
consensus-building that characterizes Sultanate governance into his regulatory work. This synthesis made him a
unique figure in Northern Mindanao's public sphere.
Challenges and Context
Darimbang's career unfolded during a period of significant social and political change in Mindanao. The peace
process between the Philippine government and the Moro Islamic Liberation Front (MILF) intensified during his
tenure, creating an atmosphere of cautious dialogue but also lingering suspicions between Muslim and Christian
communities.
His presence as a visibly Muslim leader in a government office serving a Christian-majority city carried symbolic
weight. Every decision, every interaction with Christian counterparts, every family achievement became a small
affirmation that peaceful coexistence was possible and that Muslim Filipinos belonged fully in the nation's civic
institutions.
Late in his tenure, Darimbang faced scrutiny during a 2016 performance audit following complaints about alleged
corruption in the LTFRB office. Rather than contest the audit, he chose to retire on August 31, 2016, after 29 years
at the helm of the regional office. He cited personal reasons—that he had simply served long enough—rather than
accepting any implication of wrongdoing. His departure was marked by recognition of his unprecedented tenure
and clean personal record, which had been verified by the Ombudsman, Civil Service Commission, and National
Bureau of Investigation.
Achievements and Recognition
Darimbang's career was marked by numerous accolades and recognitions that reflected his standing among peers
and in the broader civil service:
Outstanding Regional Director Award for demonstrated excellence in transportation regulation and agency
management Outstanding Mindanaoan Award recognizing his contributions to the development and harmony of the
region Presidency of the Organization of Regional Officers, reflecting trust from his peer group Invitation to serve

PAGE 5
as Vice President of the National Council of Career Executive Service Officers Most significantly, an untarnished
government record verified by three major oversight bodies: the Ombudsman, Civil Service Commission, and
National Bureau of Investigation
These recognitions underscore that Darimbang's integrity was not merely a personal virtue but an institutional
legacy, one that would be difficult for future leaders to diminish.
Legacy
Sultan Mandangan Darimbang's legacy rests on a simple but profound contribution: he proved, through four
decades of quiet professionalism, that a Muslim Bangsamoro could excel in secular government service without
compromising his faith, culture, or heritage. He showed that traditional authority and modern governance could
coexist. He demonstrated that interfaith harmony arose not from grand gestures but from consistent, everyday
fairness and respect.
His career occurred at a critical juncture in Mindanao's history. During periods when Muslim-Christian relations
remained tense and when political violence occasionally erupted, Darimbang's presence in the public sphere served
as a steady counternarrative: that Muslims and Christians could work together, build trust, and serve a common
good.
The influence of his example extends to his family, whose achievements have continued to normalize Muslim
participation across Cagayan de Oro's civic and professional sectors. And in the broader context of Bangsamoro
aspirations for recognition and inclusion within the Philippines, his career—though centered on transportation
rather than explicitly political issues—has enduring significance as a model of dignity, competence, and belonging.

title: Datu Tampugaw -
text:
PAGE 1
Datu Tampugaw
Datu Amay-Tampugaw[4] (25 September 1886 –
c. 1934), also spelled Amai Tampugao,[5] known
as Sultan Tampugao of Tubaran,[6] was a Filipino
politician who became member of the House of
Representatives representing Mindanao and Sulu
from 1919 to 1925. Before becoming a member,
he was sultan of the Royal House of Pagayawan,
Confederate States of Lanao.
Biography
Tampugaw was born on September 25, 1886, in
Tubaran, Lanao province. As a devout Muslim, he
studied the Quran and attended a Maranao
school.[1] He then became the sultan of the Royal
House of Pagayawan, Confederate States of
Lanao.[6][1][b]
Moro Rebellion
In 1902, General Adna R. Chaffee wrote to Datu

to kill Moro rebel leaders and to make restitutions

also gave a stern warning for the three if they
don't comply.[7] As sultan, Tampugaw complied
with the demands of American authorities during
the Moro Rebellion due to the persuasion from an
Afghan high priest from Rio Grande.[5]
At first, the Americans were doubtful of trusting
Tampugaw of providing useful information to counter the rebellion. Tampugaw shared details about
the dangers posed by the cottas of Maciu and Bacolod, explaining their beliefs about killing Moros
would "displease the Almighty" while killing the Americans would guarantee a place in heaven.

On September 6, 1919, Tampugaw was appointed by Governor General Francis Burton Harrison as a

reappointed as member of the assembly in 1922 until 1925 representing Mindanao and Sulu.[9]
During the Fifth Legislature, he was member of the Navigation Committee. During the Sixth

title: Datu, Dimapuno Ramos
text:
PAGE 1
Dimapuno Ramos Datu
Sultan Atty. Dimapuno Ramos Datu, popularly known by his Maranaw name Pangnal (literally, "The Inquirer"),
is a Maranaw lawyer, educator, journalist, and elected public official from Raya, Balindong, Lanao del Sur, in the
Bangsamoro region of the Philippines.
Born on June 12, 1945, Pangnal is a Sultan of the Royal House of Raya Present and one of the top 50 model
Sultans of Iranaon. His career cuts across academia, law, broadcast media, civic leadership, and provincial
governance, making him one of the more genuinely multi-dimensional public figures in the history of Muslim
Mindanao.
He's best remembered for his years as Vice-Governor of Lanao del Sur, where his advocacy for clean and
transparent government earned him national recognition, and for his work in radio journalism, where his no-holds-
barred commentaries made him a trusted voice in the Maranaw community.
His life, as those who know him often put it, has been one of continuous involvement and relevance.
Contents
1 EARLY LIFE AND EDUCATION
2 ACADEMIC CAREER
3 JOURNALISM AND MEDIA
4 LEGAL AND PUBLIC SERVICE CAREER
5 CIVIC INVOLVEMENT
6 FAMILY
7 RECOGNITION AND AWARDS
8 LEGACY
9 REFERENCES
10 EXTERNAL LINKS
EARLY LIFE AND EDUCATION
Pangnal was born on June 12, 1945, in Raya, Balindong, Lanao del Sur, into a family with ties to the Royal House
of Raya.
He showed early on that he was built for excellence: he graduated as Valedictorian in both elementary and high
school.
He went to Manila for higher studies, enrolling at the University of the East (UE), where he earned his Bachelor of
Arts in Political Science graduating Cum Laude. He was also awarded the Dalupan Law Scholarship, through
which he completed his Bachelor of Laws (LLB) at the same institution.

PAGE 2

Not stopping there, he went on to take doctoral units in Political
Science at the University of the Philippines Diliman in Quezon
City, deepening a scholarly foundation that would inform
everything he did in public life afterward.
It's the kind of academic record that reflects genuine drive, not just
native ability.
ACADEMIC CAREER
Pangnal's most sustained academic role was at Mindanao State
University (MSU) in Marawi City, where he served as Dean of the
College of Business Administration from 1980 to 1985.
Those five years left a clear mark. Under his leadership, the
college produced two CPA board topnotchers and won the
University Leadership Award two successive times. The college
also bagged the Miss University Contest twice consecutively, a
testament to how Pangnal ran his unit: with energy, pride, and an
eye for developing the whole student.
He also had oversight of the MSU student publication
"PAGSIBOL" (meaning "DAWN"), the university's student organ,
reflecting his belief that student voices deserved a platform and a
home.
Beyond the deanship, he served as a Professional Lecturer and
Professor at MSU's College of Law and College of Business
Administration, and as the university's Chief Legal Counsel, a role
that put his legal training directly in service of the institution he
helped build.
He was also a former President of the Dansalan Junior College
Alumni Association in Marawi City. The association's membership
of roughly 2,000 professionals spread across the country formed a
significant backbone of the regional, provincial, city, and
municipal government bureaucracy in Muslim Mindanao and
especially in Lanao del Sur.
JOURNALISM AND MEDIA
Pangnal's media career is where many Maranaw people know him
best.

PAGE 3
State University (1980–
1985)
Spouse
Bai Hadja Zubaida "Aida"
Alonto Tagoranao
Children
11
Grandchildren
21
NOTABILITY
One of the top 50 model Sultans of Iranaon;
elected Vice-Governor of Lanao del Sur;
pioneer of the Maranaw press and civic
broadcast journalism; and founding president
of Muslim workers' and professional
organizations in Muslim Mindanao.
KNOWN FOR
Fearless radio commentary and expose
journalism; championing clean, transparent
governance; founding the Marawi City Press
and Radio Ranao Patrol "45"; leading MSU's
College of Business Administration through a
landmark decade; and lifelong service to the
Maranaw people across law, education, media,
and public life.
PULL QUOTE
"His life is one of continuous involvement and
relevance."
He was the publisher and editor of the Philippine Crescent, a local
newspaper tabloid that served Lanao del Sur and Marawi City.
Through it, he gave the province a local press voice that wasn't
afraid to name names or ask hard questions.
He was elected the first President of the Marawi City Press, and
also the first President of Radio Ranao Patrol "45," a broadcast
media outfit whose identity was built on exactly what the name
suggests: fearless, relentless reporting.
His radio commentaries and expose journalism became part of the
daily rhythm of life in Marawi City. He tackled the issues of the
day with the kind of directness people in the community needed,
and that earned him something real: the respect and reverence of
the Maranaw community and the common masses.
During the 1996 and 1998 elections, he volunteered as
NAMFREL representative and served as ANCHORMAN for the
radio program "Knowing the Issues and Candidates," a public
service broadcast over DXAD Radio Ranao, the only station
covering Marawi City and Lanao del Sur at the time.
That's civic work that doesn't stop when the microphone goes off.
It shapes how communities understand their choices, their
government, and themselves.
LEGAL AND PUBLIC SERVICE
CAREER
Pangnal's legal career reflected the same principles that drove his journalism: a commitment to truth,
accountability, and the rights of ordinary people.
He served as a human rights FLAG (Free Legal Assistance Group) lawyer for Marawi City and the Lanao del Sur
chapter, taking on cases that others might have passed on.
He held the post of Provincial Attorney of Lanao del Sur, serving as the province's chief legal officer.
He also served as Port Collector of Customs at two separate ports: the Port of General Santos City and the Port of
Parang, Cotabato City, roles that required both legal precision and an understanding of the country's broader
economic systems.
As elected Vice-Governor of Lanao del Sur, he brought all of this experience into the provincial government,
consistently pushing for clean, transparent, and responsible governance and maintaining a public media presence
that kept officials accountable.

PAGE 4
CIVIC INVOLVEMENT
Pangnal's civic contributions went well beyond any single office or institution.
He was the founding president of the Philippine Muslim Workers Association, Inc., the first mass-based
organization in the country dedicated to Muslim domestic and overseas Filipino workers.
The association was built to protect the rights of Filipino Muslim workers and to uplift their quality of life, at home
and abroad. It was a pioneering effort, and it came from someone who understood that advocacy doesn't wait for
the right political moment.
He's also an active member of the Mother of Rotary Club of Cotabato City, a reflection of his consistent pattern of
showing up for communities wherever he happened to be stationed.
FAMILY
Pangnal is married to Bai Hadja Zubaida "Aida" Alonto Tagoranao, who comes from the distinguished Alonto-
Tagoranao Clan, one of the prominent families in Maranaw society.
Together, they've been blessed with eleven children and twenty-one grandchildren.
It's a family grounded in the same values Pangnal built his public life on: deep roots in the Maranaw community, a
sense of responsibility to others, and the understanding that belonging to a family, a people, and a place is never
just background; it's the whole point.
RECOGNITION AND AWARDS
During his term as Vice-Governor of Lanao del Sur, Sultan Atty. Dimapuno Ramos Datu received the following
national-level recognitions from independent organizations:
Golden Service Award as Most Outstanding Provincial Vice-Governor of the Philippines, conferred by Fil-
Asia Research Society, Inc.
Golden Leadership-National Award as Most Outstanding Provincial Vice-Governor, conferred by United
Group of Charities and Human Development, Inc.
Golden Professional Award / Excellence Award as Most Outstanding Provincial Vice-Governor, conferred
by Exponent of People's Achievers Magazine
Humanitarian International Record Excellence Public Service Award as Most Outstanding Vice-
Governor and Exemplary Public Servant, conferred by Humanitarian International Record
Most Outstanding Vice-Governor, conferred by PHILMEDIA and Mindanao Congress
He was also cited as one of the Top 50 Model Sultans of Iranaon, an honor that recognizes not just royal standing
but lived commitment to the Maranaw people and their heritage.

PAGE 5
LEGACY
What makes Pangnal's story stand out isn't any single title or citation. It's the scope.
He was Valedictorian and Cum Laude. Dean and FLAG lawyer. Newspaper editor and radio anchor. Port Collector
and Provincial Attorney. Vice-Governor and founding president of organizations that put Muslim workers on the
national map.
Through it all, he never drifted far from the core of what genuine public service looks like: showing up, speaking
plainly, and staying accountable to the people who need you most.
For the Maranaw people of Lanao del Sur and for the broader Bangsamoro community, his career is a model of
what it looks like when someone uses every platform they're given, not for personal gain, but for the community
they came from.
His life, as it has been said, is one of continuous involvement and relevance. For Muslim Mindanao, that's not just
a description. It's a standard worth keeping.
REFERENCES

Dimapuno Alonto Datu-Ramos Jr
Dimapuno "Jun" Alonto Datu-Ramos Jr., MD, CESE, is a
Maranao physician and public servant from a prominent political
family in Lanao del Sur. He's best known these days as a Regional
Director of the National Commission on Muslim Filipinos (NCMF),
a role that capped off almost three decades of steady, patient climb
through the ranks of Philippine public service. Along the way he
wore a lot of hats: medical officer, spokesperson, quick response
team leader, and eventually the man steering NCMF's National
Capital Region office to one of the best-performing branches in the
whole Commission.
Contents
1 Early Life and Background
2 Education
3 Career
3.1 Early Government Service
3.2 Rise Within the NCMF
3.3 Building Institutional Systems
3.4 Regional Director, NCMF-NCR
4 Advocacies

Early Life and Background
Doc Jun, as most people call him, comes from the Alonto family, one
of the well-known political families of Lanao del Sur. Growing up
Maranao and rooted in that heritage shaped much of how he later
approached his work: always with an eye toward serving the
Bangsamoro people and making sure their voices reached the right
rooms.
Education
Before he became a familiar name in Muslim Filipino affairs, Doc
Jun built a solid academic and professional foundation. He trained
and became a licensed physician, and he's also a registered nurse,
giving him a rare dual footing in both medicine and healthcare
administration. He went on to earn a Master's degree in Hospital
Administration, and later received an honorary doctorate, a PhD
"Honoris Causa" in Public Administration with a focus on Good
Governance. To round things out, he also picked up a certification as

PAGE 2
Notability
Long-serving NCMF official who rose
from Medical Officer to Regional
Director, credited with building the
Commission's public transparency systems
and leading the NCMF-NCR office to a
top 2 Best Regional Office ranking.
Known For
Serving as NCMF Spokesperson,
championing the Bangsamoro people's
causes on social media, and advocating for
the recognition of NCR Muslim
Consultative Councils by local
government units.
Pull Quote
"A doctor by training, a public servant by
calling."
a halal industry practitioner from the Asian Institute of Management's
School of Executive Education and Lifelong Learning, a credential
that speaks to his ongoing interest in areas that matter deeply to
Muslim communities.
Career
Early Government Service
Doc Jun's public service career started at the ground level, working
as a Medical Officer in Lanao del Sur and later with the Office of
Muslim Affairs (OMA), the agency that eventually became the
NCMF. That early hands-on medical work in his home province gave
him a front-row seat to the health and welfare needs of Maranao
communities, something that stayed with him as he moved up the
ladder.
Rise Within the NCMF
As the OMA transitioned into the NCMF, Doc Jun's career transitioned right along with it. He eventually became
Director for the Bureau of External Relations, a position that put him at the center of how the Commission
communicated with the public and with other government bodies. He was appointed to his post by then President
Benigno Aquino Jr., and was later re-appointed by President Rodrigo Roa Duterte, a mark of continuity and trust
across two very different administrations.
From 2018 to the first quarter of 2022, he served as the official Spokesperson of the NCMF. During this stretch, he
became known for building up the Commission's public presence, largely through a strategic and very active social
media campaign. It wasn't just about visibility for its own sake either: he pushed for real transparency, helping
institutionalize the NCMF's official social media accounts, its official website, a digital magazine, regular media
interviews, and printed publications. He also helped put in place a formal Strategic External Communications Plan
so that all of this wouldn't just depend on one person's initiative but would carry on as an actual system.
Building Institutional Systems
Beyond communications, Doc Jun had a hand in shaping how the NCMF ran internally. He organized and
institutionalized the Commission's Customer Satisfaction Monitoring (CSAT) process, which involved regularly
collecting, recording, and analyzing feedback data before submitting monthly reports to the Planning Service and
quarterly reports to top management. He also led the creation of the NCMF's Occupational Safety and Health
Committee, an initiative that looked after the welfare of NCMF's own workforce.
When the COVID-19 pandemic hit, Doc Jun stepped into an even bigger role as Vice Chairperson for Operations
of the NCMF COVID-19 Quick Response Team. Under the pressure of nationwide lockdowns, the team
coordinated relief operations, burial assistance, and support for stranded Muslim Filipinos who had nowhere else to
turn.
His work on institutional integrity extended to finances too. He endorsed almost a million pesos in collected fees
from Certificate of Tribal Membership (CTM) applications to the National Treasury, doing this before the
Commission eventually announced that CTM processing would become a free service.

PAGE 3
Regional Director, NCMF-NCR
Doc Jun currently serves as Regional Director of the NCMF-NCR Regional Office, where he's widely recognized
for his contributions to Muslim Filipino communities across Metro Manila. Under his leadership, the NCMF-NCR
office achieved recognition as the top 2 Best Regional Office among the Commission's 11 regions nationwide, a
distinction that reflects both his management style and the team culture he built around him.
He also played a vital role, as ISO Core Team leader, in helping the NCMF secure its ISO 9001:2015 certification
in 2021, a milestone that speaks to the Commission's push toward more standardized, quality-driven public service.
In recognition of his years of experience and leadership, he was included in the Portfolio Assessment for the Career
Executive Service (PACES) Program through Career Executive Service Board Resolution No. 1652, and he was
recognized among the career executive service graduates during the CESB's 2024 annual convention, hence the
CESE distinction attached to his name.
Advocacies
Throughout his career, Doc Jun has been a consistent and vocal supporter of the Bangsamoro people and of tribal
leaders across different communities. He's also been an active champion for the NCR Muslim Consultative
Councils, continuously lobbying local government units to formally recognize these bodies. That advocacy bore
fruit in June 2026, when Parañaque City Mayor Edwin Olivarez signed a city ordinance recognizing the councils, a
concrete win for Muslim Filipino representation in the National Capital Region.
Legacy
Doc Jun's career traces an arc that's rare in Philippine bureaucracy: a licensed physician who found his true calling
not just in medicine, but in the quieter, harder work of building institutions. From frontline medical officer to
spokesperson to regional director, his fingerprints are on the systems, the transparency measures, and the
community relationships that continue to shape how the NCMF serves Muslim Filipinos, especially in the National
Capital Region.

Simeon Datumanong
Simeon Ampatuan Datumanong (June 17, 1935 – February 28, 2017) was a Maguindanaon lawyer, provincial
executive, regional administrator, legislator, and cabinet secretary whose public career spanned more than five
decades of Philippine history.
Born in Maganoy — now called Shariff Aguak — in the undivided province of Cotabato, he rose from provincial
board member to Secretary of Justice, serving at every tier of Philippine governance along the way: local, regional,
legislative, and executive.
He is best remembered as the first administrator to organize the provincial government of Maguindanao after its
creation under Presidential Decree 341 in 1973, a member of the Philippine government's negotiating panel for the
landmark 1976 Tripoli Agreement, a five-term congressman representing Maguindanao's Second District, and
twice Deputy Speaker of the House of Representatives.
His people knew him simply as Bapa Sim — an affectionate term of elder-familial respect that captured both his
stature and his style of leadership.

lineage: "datu" is the traditional Maguindanaon title for chieftain or
nobility. His father was Datu Dundoy Bapa-i Datumanong Giamad;
his mother, Bai Salama Ampatuan, was a daughter of Datu Alon
Ampatuan, the older brother of Sharif Aguak — a lineage that
explains the middle name "Ampatuan" that Simeon carried
throughout his life.
His early schooling was marked by consistent academic distinction.
He completed elementary school at Cotabato Central School in
1951 as class valedictorian, and then went on to Cotabato High
School, where he graduated in 1955 as first honorable mention.
These were no small achievements in mid-century Cotabato, where
formal education was still a scarce commodity in Muslim
communities that had long been pushed to the margins of the
Philippine state's modernizing ambitions.
What set him on a different path from many of his peers was his
decision to pursue law at the University of the Philippines College
of Law — then, as now, the country's most prestigious law school.
He completed his Bachelor of Laws and passed the Philippine Bar
Examinations in 1959.
The significance of this bears emphasis: a young Muslim man from
Cotabato entering UP's law program, completing it, and joining the
Philippine bar, all during a period when Muslim Mindanao was still
widely treated as a peripheral and suspect frontier of the republic.
After admission to the bar, he returned to Cotabato and practiced
law briefly before his trajectory was, almost inevitably, redirected
toward public life. Those who worked with him in those early years
described him as meticulous, measured, and constitutionally
inclined — qualities that would define every role he took on
afterward.
He later married Hadja Sittie Mariam Sigrid de Guzman
Datumanong, with whom he had four children: Borgiva Tasmi,
Merinisa Anisalam, Soraya Julie, and Rahma Anna Liza, and
eventually thirteen grandchildren.
ENTRY INTO PROVINCIAL POLITICS
Datumanong's formal entry into politics came in 1962 when he was
elected as a provincial board member of Cotabato — the bottom
rung of provincial governance, but a platform from which he
quickly demonstrated capacity.
In 1966, he was elected Vice-Governor of Cotabato. He became
Governor the following year under circumstances worth noting
precisely: in the November 1966 local elections, Congressman
Salipada K. Pendatun won the governorship of Cotabato, but chose

to return to Congress without taking his oath of office as Governor.
With the governorship vacant, Datumanong, as Vice-Governor,
ascended to the position in 1967 — a distinction the family has been
careful to preserve: he did not win the governorship by direct
election, but assumed it through constitutional succession. He held
the position until 1971.
Cotabato in the late 1960s was, in every sense, a pressure cooker.
The province was ethnically, religiously, and politically volatile.
Land disputes between Christian settlers and the indigenous Muslim
and lumad populations had been simmering for years — the result
of settlement policies enacted through national law long before
Datumanong's time, among them the Osmena Colony Act of 1912,
the Quirino-Recto Colonization Act of 1936, and the vigorous
resettlement programs of the Magsaysay administration. These were
decisions made by presidents and acts of Congress, not by local
executives. But their consequences fell squarely on the communities
Datumanong governed. The armed Moro resistance that would
eventually crystallize into the Moro National Liberation Front
(MNLF) was still taking shape underground, but its precursors —
grievances over land dispossession, political marginalization, and
cultural degradation — were visible to any governor willing to look
clearly at his constituents.
Datumanong governed Cotabato during this period as a pragmatic
administrator rather than an ideological warrior. His approach was
to work within the system, leverage his legal training, and push for
administrative solutions to structural problems. His reputation at
this stage was less that of a firebrand and more that of a capable
executive who understood that governance required patient
coalition-building.
In 1974, he was recognized nationally as one of the Ten Outstanding Young Men (TOYM) of the Philippines for
Public Administration — a distinction that marked his emergence not just as a regional politician but as a nationally
noticed figure.
ORGANIZING MAGUINDANAO: THE FIRST PROVINCIAL
ADMINISTRATOR
The political geography of Mindanao was dramatically redrawn in the early 1970s under the Marcos
administration. In November 1973, President Ferdinand E. Marcos Sr. issued Presidential Decree 341, creating
three new provinces out of the old undivided Cotabato: Maguindanao, Sultan Kudarat, and North Cotabato. The
power to create provinces belonged — and still belongs — exclusively to the President or to Congress, and by
1973, Marcos had padlocked Congress. PD 341 was the act that brought Maguindanao Province into legal
existence.
What Datumanong did was take that newly created entity and give it actual functioning shape. As the first governor
of Maguindanao from 1973 to 1975, he was the one who organized its administrative structures from the ground
up: recruiting staff, establishing offices, defining procedures, and putting operational government services in place
for a province that had never existed before. The family has been clear and precise on this point — he did not

PAGE 4
create Maguindanao Province, which was Marcos's act under PD 341. What he did was organize it, and that
distinction matters. Only a President or Congress can create a province; what a governor can do is build it into
something real.
That work was consequential in its own right. No inherited bureaucracy, no established precedents, no tested lines
of authority. Datumanong had to construct a provincial government from scratch while managing a constituency
simultaneously experiencing the ruptures of the Moro insurgency and the pressures of Martial Law.
He served in that role for two years before moving upward to a regional appointment. But those two years left a
structural imprint: the administrative skeleton he assembled became the frame within which all subsequent
Maguindanao governance operated. His successor governors inherited the offices, the procedures, and the
institutional groundwork that Datumanong had laid.
REGIONAL ADMINISTRATION AND THE 1976 TRIPOLI
AGREEMENT
In 1975, Datumanong transitioned from the provincial executive to the regional tier, serving as Regional
Commissioner of Region XII — a post he held until 1979. This role oversaw Central Mindanao's multi-province
administration and placed him squarely within the orbit of the Marcos government's regional development and
pacification strategies.
It was during this period, in 1976, that he participated in one of the most consequential diplomatic events in
contemporary Philippine history: the negotiations that produced the Tripoli Agreement.
Signed on December 23, 1976, in Tripoli, Libya, the agreement was the first formal compact between the
Philippine government and the Moro National Liberation Front (MNLF), pledging autonomy for thirteen provinces
in Mindanao and Sulu. Datumanong served as a member of the Philippine government's negotiating panel in
Tripoli, one of the few Muslim Filipino officials involved in crafting what would become the foundational
reference document for all subsequent Mindanao peace negotiations.
The following year, in 1977, he served as co-chairperson of the Provisional Government in the Southern
Philippines, the short-lived transitional structure envisioned under the Tripoli Agreement's framework. Though the
provisional government never fully materialized — Marcos ultimately chose to implement the agreement through
two separate autonomous regions rather than the single autonomous structure the MNLF demanded —
Datumanong's participation positioned him as one of the key Muslim Filipino architects of the early peace process.
From 1979 to 1984, he served as a regional assemblyman in the Autonomous Regional Government of Western
Mindanao and concurrently held the chairmanship of the Lupong Tagapagpaganap ng Pook (LTP), the executive
council of Autonomous Region XII, from 1980 to 1984. The LTP itself was a Marcos-created structure — another
institution brought into existence by presidential action rather than by the men who ran it. What Datumanong
brought to it was the same thing he had brought to Maguindanao Province: the administrative capacity to organize,
operationalize, and direct a regional governance structure that was new to the ground. His leadership of the LTP
gave him broad executive authority over Region XII's coordination and development functions during a critical
period of transition.

PAGE 5
THE BATASANG PAMBANSA AND THE OMACC
In 1984, Datumanong reached the apex of his Marcos-era career when he was elected to the Regular Batasang
Pambansa representing Maguindanao, while simultaneously being appointed the first Director General of the newly
created Office on Muslim Affairs and Cultural Communities (OMACC).
The OMACC was formed on June 30, 1984, through the merger of the Office of Muslim Affairs with the Office of
the Presidential Assistant on National Minorities (PANAMIN). It represented the Marcos administration's effort to
consolidate management of Muslim and indigenous peoples' affairs under a single government structure.
As OMACC's founding head, Datumanong bore responsibility for directing the agency's programs at a moment
when the question of how the Philippine state should relate to its Muslim citizens had never been more contested.
The Moro insurgency had not ended; the autonomous regions created under the Tripoli Agreement's flawed
implementation remained objects of resentment rather than satisfaction; and the broader Muslim community was
navigating profound tensions between traditional religious authority, modernist reform movements, and the
political economy of a Martial Law state.
His role at the OMACC — running concurrently with his Batasang Pambansa seat until 1986 — required him to
function simultaneously as a lawmaker and a cabinet-level administrator, balancing legislative and executive
functions that would become a characteristic feature of his career. He also served on the boards of the Philippine
Amanah Bank (1985–1986) and the United Coconut Planters Bank (1986–1992), extending his institutional
footprint into the financial sector.
When Corazon Aquino came to power following the EDSA People Power Revolution of February 1986, the
OMACC was dissolved and reorganized. On January 30, 1987, President Aquino divided the OMACC into three
separate offices: the Office for Muslim Affairs (OMA), the Office for Northern Cultural Communities (ONCC),
and the Office for Southern Cultural Communities (OSCC). The dissolution ended Datumanong's ministerial
appointment, but it did not remove him from public life. He returned to private practice and board service, waiting
for the democratic electoral system to be fully restored.
THREE TERMS IN THE HOUSE OF REPRESENTATIVES (1992–
2001)
When the restored Philippine democracy held its first post-Marcos congressional elections in 1987, Datumanong
did not immediately enter the fray. His return to elective office came in 1992, when he won the congressional seat
for Maguindanao's Second District. He would hold that seat for three consecutive terms, serving from 1992 to 2001
— a stretch of nine years that covered the presidencies of Fidel V. Ramos and Joseph Estrada, and briefly extended
into the early Arroyo administration.
As a congressman, his legislative agenda was consistently oriented toward Muslim Mindanao. He pushed for
infrastructure investments in the region, championed legislation supporting Muslim education and religious rights,
and engaged actively in the debates around the Organic Act that established and later amended the Autonomous
Region in Muslim Mindanao (ARMM). He sat on key House committees and used his seniority to advance
regional priorities that might otherwise have been overlooked in a House dominated by Luzon-based political
networks.
Between 1995 and 1998, during his second term, he served as Deputy Speaker of the House of Representatives —
one of the chamber's most senior positions, which gave him agenda-setting authority and placed him among the
handful of legislators who shaped what bills reached the floor.

PAGE 6
For a Muslim congressman from Maguindanao to hold that position in the mid-1990s was not merely a personal
achievement. It was a marker of how far the political representation of Muslim Filipinos had advanced in the
national legislature since the dark years of the early insurgency.
He was known within the House as a careful legislator: one who preferred to work through established procedures,
build alliances across political lines, and achieve incremental gains rather than dramatic confrontations. Former
President Gloria Macapagal-Arroyo, who would later bring him into her cabinet, described him as a man of
"uprightness" whose value in any institution came from his reliability and his deep knowledge of Mindanao's
political terrain.
CABINET SECRETARY UNDER PRESIDENT ARROYO
In January 2001, following President Arroyo's assumption of the presidency in the wake of EDSA II, Datumanong
left the House of Representatives to accept appointment as Secretary of the Department of Public Works and
Highways (DPWH). He served in this capacity from January 20, 2001 to January 15, 2003.
The DPWH portfolio was significant for Mindanao: infrastructure development — roads, bridges, flood control
systems, public buildings — was among the region's most pressing needs, and having a Maguindanaon Muslim at
the helm of the agency responsible for delivering it carried both substantive and symbolic weight.
After his stint at Public Works, Datumanong was moved to an even more visible portfolio. On January 16, 2003, he
was appointed Secretary of Justice, a position he held until December 23, 2003. The DOJ secretaryship placed him
at the apex of the Philippine legal system's administrative structure, responsible for directing the prosecution
service, overseeing the National Bureau of Investigation, managing the Bureau of Corrections, and handling a
broad range of politically sensitive legal matters.
His eleven-month tenure as Justice Secretary was brief but consequential. He entered the post during a period of
considerable political turbulence: 2003 was the year of the Oakwood Mutiny, when a group of junior military
officers seized a Makati hotel and briefly threatened civilian authority. Datumanong's DOJ was tasked with
processing the legal aftermath of that crisis, among other pressing matters.
Also during the Arroyo administration, he was appointed to serve on the government's panel for peace negotiations
with the Moro Islamic Liberation Front (MILF), an appointment that drew directly on his experience from the 1976
Tripoli negotiations. Government negotiators at the time described him as "very experienced in negotiations" who
"knows the problems on the ground and understands the issues very deeply."
RETURN TO CONGRESS: THREE MORE TERMS (2007–2013)
After completing his cabinet service, Datumanong returned to elective politics. In the 2007 congressional elections,
he recaptured his seat in the House of Representatives for Maguindanao's Second District, and went on to serve
three additional terms until 2013.
This second legislative stint included another term as Deputy Speaker of the House, a position he held from July
23, 2007 to June 30, 2010.
His return to Congress at an age when most politicians would have retired reflected both his personal stamina and
the degree to which his constituency continued to regard him as their most effective voice at the national level. In
Maguindanao's Second District, Datumanong was not just a political figure — he was an institution, a living
embodiment of the district's long engagement with Philippine national governance.

PAGE 7
He retired from electoral politics in 2013 at the age of seventy-nine, having completed five terms in the House of
Representatives and a career in public service spanning more than five decades. The last years of his life were spent
in the dignified elder statesman withdrawal that befits someone who has, by any measure, done everything an
ambitious public career can offer.
PASSING AND TRIBUTES
On the evening of February 28, 2017, a telephone call confirmed what many in Mindanao had feared. Simeon
Ampatuan Datumanong drew his final breath at the Philippine Heart Center in Quezon City. He was 81 years old.
Within hours, condolences poured in from governors, senators, and former presidents. The Department of Justice
flew its flag at half-mast. In Shariff Aguak, the town in Maguindanao where he was born and to which he would be
returned for burial, people wept.
That an announcement of a Muslim politician's death could draw such an outpouring of grief from all directions of
Philippine society — from Christian senators to Moro governors, from Catholic former presidents to rank-and-file
bureaucrats — says something about the kind of life Datumanong led.
Former President Arroyo released a statement describing him as "a strong voice for the equality of our Filipino
Muslims" who "exemplified the true Muslim spirit: committed, courageous, sincere, and loyal."
He was buried in Shariff Aguak according to Islamic rites, returned at last to the soil of Maguindanao from which
his extraordinary journey had begun.
LEGACY AND HISTORICAL SIGNIFICANCE
Simeon Datumanong's legacy is best understood by placing it within the contested history of Muslim Filipino
political integration. For much of the twentieth century, the relationship between the Philippine state and its
Muslim citizens was defined by exclusion, dispossession, and armed conflict. The Muslim south was treated as a
problem to be managed rather than a community to be genuinely included. Datumanong's career stands as evidence
that some Muslim Filipinos found a way to work within that hostile framework to carve out genuine representation
and institutional presence at the national level.
His involvement in the 1976 Tripoli Agreement alone would have been sufficient to secure him a place in the
historical record. The agreement, despite its ultimately flawed implementation, established the principle that
Muslim Mindanao's political status was a matter for formal negotiation between the Philippine government and
Moro representatives — a principle that would undergird every subsequent peace effort, from the 1996 Final Peace
Agreement with the MNLF to the Comprehensive Agreement on the Bangsamoro signed in 2014.
At the regional level, his work as the first governor to organize Maguindanao Province and his subsequent
leadership of the Marcos-created LTP Regional Executive Council helped give operational form to Central
Mindanao's administrative governance during one of its most chaotic periods. These were acts of institution-
building, and their effects outlasted any particular political agenda. The distinction the family rightly insists upon
— between creating a structure (which only a president or congress can do) and organizing it into something that
actually functions — does not diminish his contribution. If anything, it makes it more precise: Datumanong was not
a lawmaker conjuring provinces into existence. He was the administrator who showed up when the decree was
signed and made those provinces real.

PAGE 8
At the national level, his long House career — five terms, two Deputy Speakerships, and two cabinet appointments
— demonstrated that Muslim Filipino politicians could compete effectively in the structures of Philippine national
governance without abandoning their identities or their constituencies.
It would be incomplete, however, to present Datumanong's career as entirely without complexity. His political life
was inextricably entangled with the Marcos administration, during which he held ministerial and regional executive
posts under conditions of Martial Law. His collaboration with the Marcos state was not unique among Mindanao
politicians, but it was real, and the historical record requires honest acknowledgment of it.
In his later career, Datumanong was also a respondent in graft cases related to alleged irregularities in the use of his
Priority Development Assistance Fund (PDAF), with reports indicating that approximately 3.8 million pesos of his
PDAF may have been coursed through a fraudulent non-governmental organization. These charges were never
adjudicated during his lifetime, as Philippine law provides that criminal liability is extinguished by death. They
remain, however, part of the public record.
What emerges from all of this is the portrait of a politician who was simultaneously a genuine advocate for his
community and a pragmatic survivor in a system that demanded accommodation and compromise. These two
things are not mutually exclusive — they describe the condition of virtually every successful politician in
Philippine history. What distinguished Datumanong was the extraordinary duration of his relevance and the breadth
of his institutional footprint.
He carried Muslim Mindanao's voice into rooms it had rarely entered before, and he carried it with the authority of
someone who had done the hard, unglamorous work of building institutions from the ground up.

Datumanong dies at 81," March 1, 2017.

EDITORIAL NOTE
On June 2026, a family member of the late Simeon Ampatuan Datumanong submitted factual clarifications to
BangsamoroPedia. These corrections have been applied in full to this article. Specific corrections include: (1) the
names of his parents, Datu Dundoy Bapa-i Datumanong Giamad and Bai Salama Ampatuan, and the maternal
lineage through Datu Alon Ampatuan; (2) revision of his Board Member and Vice-Governor start dates from
1963/1967 to 1962/1966 respectively; (3) clarification that he became Governor of Cotabato through

PAGE 9
constitutional succession following Salipada Pendatun's decision not to take his oath, not by direct election to that
post; (4) correction of the characterization of his role in Maguindanao Province from "elected first governor" to
"first administrator to organize the provincial government," with the province itself created by PD 341 under
President Marcos; (5) clarification that the LTP was a Marcos-created structure; and (6) accurate attribution of
Mindanao settler migration policy to national legislation and presidential action, not to the actions of local
executives. BangsamoroPedia thanks the Datumanong family for their careful attention to the historical record.

Cosanie Mortaba Derogongan
Cosanie Mortaba Derogongan (DSc, MPA) is a Filipino peace
architect and the current Director of the Bureau of Peace and
Conflict Resolution (BPCR) at the National Commission on
Muslim Filipinos (NCMF). A member of the Meranao people
from Lanao, he is recognized for his unique ability to bridge hard-
edged security expertise with culturally grounded peacebuilding.
After spending over two decades as a disciplining authority in the
Philippine National Police system, Derogongan pivoted to become
one of the country's leading mediators in the Bangsamoro region,
pioneering frameworks that address rido (clan feuds) and prevent
violent extremism. He's known for translating complex peace
concepts into practical tools that speak the language of
communities on the ground, earning him the title of "Institutional
State-Builder" and making him the architect behind peace
initiatives that actually stick.
Contents

2 Education
3 Career

Conflict Resolution
