Background and Identity
Cosanie Mortaba Derogongan belongs to the Meranao people,
traditionally known as the "People of the Lake" from the Lanao
region of Mindanao. This cultural identity isn't just background
detail—it's the foundation of his entire approach to peacebuilding.
Growing up in a society where honor codes, lineage systems, and
Islamic faith form the backbone of social organization, he
developed an intimate understanding of how traditional structures
intersect with modern governance.

PAGE 2
He maintains strong ties to the Sultanate of Phangampong a Pilipinas, a connection that gives him what insiders
call "cultural currency"—the kind of legitimacy that can't be earned through government credentials alone. In
communities where traditional authority still carries more weight than official titles, this affiliation has proven
invaluable in his mediation work. It allows him to navigate the complex social webs of Mindanao's traditional
power structures while representing state interests.
His Meranao identity also shapes his understanding of rido—the traditional system of clan-based blood feuds that
can spiral from personal disputes into regional conflicts. Having grown up within these social dynamics,
Derogongan doesn't approach rido as an outsider trying to impose solutions, but as someone who understands the
underlying logic of honor, shame, and kinship that drives these conflicts.
Education
Derogongan's academic credentials reflect his commitment to backing cultural intuition with rigorous study. He
holds a Master of Public Administration (MPA), which gave him the technical foundation in governance,
administrative law, and policy implementation. This degree was critical during his years working within the
Philippine bureaucracy, where understanding the machinery of government was essential.
He later earned a Director Staff Course, a degree offered by the Philippine Public Safety College that bridges
social work, community intervention, and ethical frameworks for social change. This combination of "hard"
administrative training and "soft" social science created a unique skill set—he could operate fluently in both the
world of government regulations and the world of community-based conflict resolution.
His academic work also influenced his writing style. Unlike many bureaucrats who speak in impenetrable jargon,
Derogongan developed a talent for translating technical concepts into accessible frameworks. This ability would
later define his most influential contributions, from policy documents to grassroots training materials.
Career
The Disciplinarian Phase: DILG and NAPOLCOM
Before becoming known as a peacebuilder, Cosanie Mortaba Derogongan spent over 20 years in what he would
later describe as the "lion's den" of Philippine internal security. Working within the Department of the Interior
and Local Government (DILG) and the National Police Commission (NAPOLCOM), he served as a
disciplining authority—essentially the person responsible for making sure police officers followed the rules.
This wasn't a desk job. It involved investigating misconduct, adjudicating cases, and enforcing ethical standards in
one of the country's most challenging institutions. The work required a deep understanding of law enforcement
culture, administrative procedures, and the delicate balance between discipline and institutional loyalty. It was a
career defined by strict adherence to the law and what Derogongan calls the "hard side" of state power.
The experience gave him something invaluable for his later work: credibility with security forces. When he
eventually transitioned to peacebuilding, he could speak the language of generals and police chiefs because he had
been one of them. He understood the security mindset, the institutional pressures, and the practical constraints that
military and police leaders face when dealing with conflict zones.
This phase also taught him about the limits of pure enforcement. No matter how many disciplinary cases he
resolved, no matter how many rules were tightened, the problems kept recurring. It planted the seed for what would
become his life's work: the realization that lasting stability couldn't be imposed from above—it had to be built from

PAGE 3
within communities.
The Pivot to Peace: NCMF and Bureau of Peace and Conflict Resolution
When Derogongan moved to the National Commission on Muslim Filipinos (NCMF), he essentially "re-coded"
everything he had learned about security and law enforcement for a completely different mission: peacebuilding.
As the Director of the Bureau of Peace and Conflict Resolution (BPCR), he became the commission's point
person for some of the most intractable conflicts in Mindanao.
His role in the Bangsamoro peace process positioned him as a technical bridge between national government
agencies and local communities. While high-level peace talks grabbed headlines, Derogongan was doing the
unglamorous but critical work of translating agreements into community-level implementation. He helped design
the mechanisms that would allow transitional governance to function, working with traditional leaders to ensure
that peace frameworks respected local customs while meeting constitutional requirements.
One of his signature achievements has been his work on rido resolution. Unlike purely academic experts who
study clan feuds from a distance, Derogongan developed practical intervention models that could be deployed in
real-time conflicts. He trained mediators, created resolution protocols that incorporated Islamic law and customary
practices, and built networks of local peacemakers who could respond before disputes escalated into violence.
In the realm of counter-violent extremism, he took on leadership of the Religious Leaders Cluster under the
National Action Plan on Preventing and Countering Violent Extremism (NAP-PCVE). Rather than treating
radicalization as purely a security problem, Derogongan approached it as a crisis of faith and community. His
strategy focused on strengthening religious leadership, building community resilience, and addressing the
grievances that make extremist narratives attractive. It was a long game, focused on prevention rather than reaction.
Institutional Contributions and Frameworks
What distinguishes Derogongan from other peace practitioners is his ability to distill complex peacebuilding
concepts into frameworks that ordinary people can grasp and use. He doesn't just mediate conflicts—he builds
systems that allow others to become mediators.
The 7 F's of Peacebuilding
Inspired by the Quranic story of Ashab al-Kahf (The People of the Cave), Derogongan developed what he calls
the 7 F's of Peacebuilding—a framework that has been adopted across NCMF programs and beyond:
Faith: The spiritual foundation that serves as a shield against extremist ideologies. Derogongan argues that
genuine faith creates ethical boundaries that violence can't cross.
Fajr (Discipline): Named after the dawn prayer, this represents the discipline of early rising and God-
consciousness. It's about building daily habits that reinforce commitment to peace.
Forgiveness: The only mechanism that can break the cycle of vengeance. In rido contexts, this is the hardest
principle to apply but the most transformative when achieved.
Fasting: Beyond the religious practice, this represents building patience, self-control, and the ability to
endure hardship without resorting to violence.

PAGE 4
Family: The primary unit that must be protected from division. Derogongan sees family cohesion as the first
line of defense against both extremism and feuding.
Fulfillment: Finding contentment and purpose to avoid the lure of criminal enterprise or armed conflict. This
addresses the economic and psychological drivers of violence.
Fellowship: Building community ties that transcend clan boundaries. Strong inter-clan relationships make
rido less likely and easier to resolve when it occurs.
The 5 M's for a Peaceful Life
Alongside the 7 F's, Derogongan teaches a personal discipline framework called the 5 M's for a Peaceful Life,
focused on individual self-control:
Mouth: Guarding speech, avoiding gossip, slander, and inflammatory language that can trigger conflicts.
Mind: Cultivating pure intentions and examining the motivations behind actions.
Mood: Managing emotions, especially anger, through patience and reflection.
Manner: Reflecting ethical character in all interactions, treating others with dignity regardless of status.
Money: Using wealth responsibly, avoiding corruption, and practicing moderation.
These frameworks aren't just theoretical. They're embedded in NCMF training programs, peace education
curricula, and community workshops throughout Mindanao. The genius is in their simplicity—they're easy to
remember, culturally resonant, and actionable.
Publications and Thought Leadership
Derogongan has established himself as one of the leading voices on conflict resolution in Muslim Mindanao
through both policy documents and public scholarship. His most significant work is The Rido Conflict: Origins,
Challenges, and Paths to Peace, a comprehensive analysis that combines historical research, case studies, and
practical resolution strategies. The book has become required reading for mediators, local officials, and anyone
serious about understanding clan feuds in the region.
Beyond individual publications, he has been the driving force behind the NCMF Peacebook, a regularly updated
manual that serves as the commission's institutional knowledge base for conflict resolution. It compiles best
practices, case studies, mediation protocols, and training materials—essentially everything a new mediator needs to
know. The Peacebook represents Derogongan's commitment to institutionalizing peace work so that it doesn't
depend on individual personalities but becomes embedded in systems.
His writing style is distinctive. Unlike the dense academic prose that dominates peace studies, Derogongan writes
in a way that's accessible without being simplistic. He uses stories, metaphors drawn from Islamic tradition, and
concrete examples rather than abstract theory. This makes his work useful not just to scholars but to the grassroots
mediators who do the actual work of peace.

PAGE 5
Legacy and Recognition
In 2025, Cosanie Mortaba Derogongan received the Sultanate Golden Crescent Award in recognition of his
contributions as an "Institutional State-Builder." The award acknowledged not just his individual mediation
successes but his larger impact on creating the systems and frameworks that allow peace work to scale and endure.
His legacy extends beyond the specific conflicts he has resolved. He has trained a generation of mediators who
carry forward his methods. He has created frameworks that have been adopted by multiple government agencies
and civil society organizations. He has built bridges between traditional and modern governance structures,
between security forces and peace advocates, between Islamic scholarship and government policy.
What makes Derogongan's contribution particularly significant is the model he represents for Filipino Muslim
leadership. In a political landscape where Muslim Filipinos are often marginalized or stereotyped, he demonstrates
a different kind of power—one based on cultural authenticity, intellectual rigor, and practical impact rather than
electoral politics or armed struggle. He proves that you can be deeply rooted in traditional Islamic and Meranao
identity while also being a sophisticated, effective state institution builder.
Personal Philosophy
At the core of Derogongan's work is a simple but profound belief: you can't have security without peace, and you
can't have peace without a deep, respectful understanding of culture and faith. This philosophy emerged from
watching security-first approaches fail repeatedly. He saw that military operations might suppress violence
temporarily, but they couldn't address the underlying grievances, honor codes, and social dynamics that generated
conflict in the first place.
His move from discipline to reconciliation wasn't a rejection of his security background but an evolution. He still
believes in accountability, in rules, in the importance of strong institutions. But he learned that the most effective
discipline isn't punishment—it's teaching people how to reconcile, how to forgive, how to find contentment without
resorting to violence.
This is why his frameworks always integrate faith. For Derogongan, Islam isn't just a cultural identifier or a source
of metaphors—it's the ethical foundation that makes peace sustainable. He believes that when communities are
rooted in genuine spiritual practice, they develop the internal resources to resist both extremism and feuding. The 7
F's and 5 M's aren't secular peace techniques dressed up in religious language; they're arguments that the path to
peace runs through the heart of faith itself.

Macaurog B. Derogongan
Dr. Macaurog B. Derogongan is a prominent Filipino academic,
agricultural scientist, and university administrator. He is widely
recognized for his foundational role in expanding the Mindanao
State University (MSU) system, particularly serving as the first
head of what would become MSU-Maguindanao, and later
leading the academic arm of the entire MSU system during a
transformative era in the late 1980s.
Contents
1 Early Life and Cultural Roots
2 Academic Career and Institutional Contributions
2.1 Founding Leadership at MSU-Maguindanao (1973–
1974)
2.2 Dean of the College of Agriculture (1976–1977)
2.3 System Vice Presidency and Jurisprudential Footprint
(1989)
3 Cultural Significance and Legacy
4 See Also
5 References
Early Life and Cultural Roots
Macaurog B. Derogongan was born and raised in the province of
Lanao del Sur, Philippines, growing up immersed in the
traditional, deeply faithful culture of the Meranao (*people of the
lake*). Coming of age in a society that places immense value on
both customary ancestral lineage and Islamic scholarship,
Derogongan recognized early on that access to higher education
would be the most powerful tool to uplift his community.
Choosing to specialize in the agricultural sciences, he dedicated
his early academic career to studying sustainable farming
methods. His goal was to address a vital, practical need in the region: harnessing the fertile, rolling terrains of
Mindanao to ensure food security and economic self-reliance for local communities.
Academic Career and Institutional Contributions
Founding Leadership at MSU-Maguindanao (1973–1974)
By the early 1970s, the Mindanao State University system was actively seeking ways to foster regional integration
and peace through educational expansion. On October 10, 1973, the MSU Board of Regents passed BOR
Resolution No. 821, series of 1973, establishing a specialized branch in Dinaig (now Datu Odin Sinsuat),
Maguindanao.

PAGE 2
Then known as the MSU-Dinaig Agricultural and Technical College (MSU-DATC), the fledgling institution
required an organized leader to build its foundations from the ground up. Dr. Derogongan was appointed as its
**founding Director**, serving from 1973 to 1974. Operating on a shoestring budget during the second semester
of that academic year, he managed a tiny staff consisting of:
Seven (7) faculty members
Fifteen (15) administrative employees
One hundred and twenty-six (126) pioneering students
Despite these humble beginnings, the structural and academic framework laid down by Derogongan served as the
baseline blueprint for what has now evolved into the fully-fledged MSU-Maguindanao campus.
Dean of the College of Agriculture (1976–1977)
Following his foundational work in Maguindanao, Dr. Derogongan returned to the MSU Main Campus in Marawi
City. By the 1976–1977 academic year, he was appointed **Dean of the College of Agriculture**.
Serving alongside historic MSU figures—such as Acting Officer-in-Charge Mohamad-Ali Dimaporo and Vice
President for Academic Affairs Emily M. Marohombsar—Dean Derogongan shifted the college's focus toward
community-driven instruction. He realigned academic research with the real-world economic realities of local
farmers, transforming the college into an active engine for regional agricultural development rather than an isolated
ivory tower.
System Vice Presidency and Jurisprudential Footprint (1989)
By the late 1980s, Dr. Derogongan’s extensive administrative track record elevated him to the university system's
executive branch. In 1989, under Special Order No. 04-P, S. 1989, he was designated as the **Acting Vice
President for Academic Affairs** for the entire MSU System.
This particular chapter of leadership unexpectedly placed Dr. Derogongan at the center of a landmark legal battle
regarding university autonomy and state civil service regulations. A dispute over executive authority and shifting
university appointments culminated in the historic Philippine Supreme Court case Marohombsar vs. Alonto, Jr.
(G.R. No. 93711), decided on February 25, 1991. While the case fundamentally centered on the legality of
administrative designations, the official inclusion of Dr. Derogongan's appointment in the High Court's records
permanently etched his name into the legal history of public education management in the Philippines.
Cultural Significance and Legacy
Dr. Derogongan belongs to a pioneering generation of Bangsamoro intellectuals who successfully bridged
traditional Meranao society with modern, secular academic governance. During a highly volatile sociopolitical era
in modern Mindanao history, he weaponized education as a stabilizing force for peace.
His efforts helped transition MSU from a solitary provincial campus into a vast, decentralized university system
that continues to educate and empower thousands of youth across the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim
Mindanao (BARMM). Decades later, his lineage of public service remains deeply felt in the region, with members
of the Derogongan family continuing to lead in higher education administration and local civic development across
Lanao.

title: Diamaoden, Ansary Abdulrahman
text:
PAGE 1
Ansary Abdulrahman Diamaoden
Ansary Abdulrahman Diamaoden is a prominent Filipino development leader, peace advocate, and community
organizer from Lanao del Sur.
Born December 29, 1984, Diamaoden is recognized across the Bangsamoro region for his work in peacebuilding,
conflict transformation, and sustainable development.
As a Maranao leader and field-oriented practitioner, he bridges the historical struggles of the Bangsamoro
independence movement with contemporary efforts to build inclusive governance and development in the
Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM).
Diamaoden currently serves as Executive Director of UNYPAD-Relief Assistance Network and Organization, Inc.
(UNYPAD-RANAO), based in Marawi City, and holds leadership positions in civic and political organizations
across Lanao del Sur.
Contents
1 Early Life and Family Heritage
2 Education
2.1 Formal Academic Training
2.2 Peace Education and Professional Development
2.3 International Exposure
3 Professional Career and Leadership
3.1 UNYPAD and Youth-Led Development

4 Core Areas of Work
5 Legacy and Vision
6 Further Reading
7 See Also
Early Life and Family Heritage
Ansary Diamaoden was born into a family deeply rooted in the Bangsamoro struggle and Maranao nobility.
He traces his ancestry to the municipalities of Butig, Sultan Domalondong, and Lumbatan in Lanao del Sur, and
belongs to the royal lineage of Dianaton Naim of Butig.
His father was the late Mohammad Nassir Alhadj, widely known by his revolutionary nom de guerre, Commander
June Pha.
Commander June Pha was a highly respected figure in the Moro Islamic Liberation Front (MILF), serving as
Operational Commander of the Bangsamoro Islamic Armed Forces (BIAF-MILF), founding Chief of Task Force
Itehad, and co-founding Chair of the MILF Normalization Committee.
Diamaoden's upbringing within this revolutionary and peace-negotiation atmosphere significantly shaped his
commitment to public service and his focus on non-violent conflict transformation as a pathway to Bangsamoro
self-determination.

Diamaoden's educational foundation combines secular

He holds a Bachelor of Science in Secondary Education and a
Diploma in Agri-Business Management Entrepreneurship.
He furthered his expertise by earning a Master's Degree in Public
Administration (MPA), with focus on governance and institutional
management.
He pursued Arabic studies at Sanie Sanawie, deepening his
understanding of Islamic scholarship and Maranao cultural heritage.
Peace Education and Professional Development
His perspective on conflict resolution and peacebuilding was shaped
by specialized training at the Mindanao Peacebuilding Institute
(MPI) in Davao City and the ICF Asia School of Peace in India.
International Exposure
Diamaoden has participated in diverse international training and
study programs across multiple continents.
In Thailand, he underwent journalism advocacy training to
strengthen his communication skills.
Nepal provided him community organizing training grounded in
grassroots mobilization approaches.
He received human rights training in Hong Kong, broadening his
understanding of international standards and advocacy frameworks.
In Turkey, he engaged in administration and policy advocacy
training in Istanbul, gaining exposure to governance practices
beyond Southeast Asia.
An Indonesia study tour to Banda Aceh allowed him to analyze post-
conflict recovery mechanisms and regional autonomy arrangements
relevant to the Bangsamoro context.
These international exposures have informed his approach to development work, integrating global best practices
with local Maranao and Bangsamoro contexts.

PAGE 3
Professional Career and Leadership
UNYPAD and Youth-Led Development
Diamaoden is a central figure in the United Youth for Peace and Development (UNYPAD), a leading youth-led
non-governmental organization serving Muslim Mindanao.
As Executive Director of UNYPAD-RANAO, based in Marawi City, Diamaoden oversees regional development
programs addressing the complex needs of Lanao's post-conflict communities.
Simultaneously, he serves as the National Vice President for External Affairs of UNYPAD Inc., managing the
organization's partnerships and linkages with national and international stakeholders.
His work focuses on capacity building for community-based organizations and youth groups, conflict
transformation through dialogue facilitation and peace education, and sustainable development initiatives that
address social and economic challenges in the Bangsamoro region.
In August 2025, Diamaoden convened youth leaders from 20 barangays in Lanao del Sur for the Youth Peace
Summit 2025, themed "Empowered Youth, Inspiring Change."
Their voices, their leadership, and their courage are the strongest foundations upon which we can build
a more united Bangsamoro.
Diamaoden's leadership recognizes young people not merely as future stakeholders in peacebuilding but as present-
day leaders, innovators, and changemakers capable of transforming their communities.
Civic and Political Engagement
In addition to his NGO work, Diamaoden plays an active role in the political and governance landscape of Lanao
del Sur.
He serves as Provincial President for the ABOT Party, engaging in local governance and political reform initiatives.
He also holds the position of General Secretary within Sapolo Ago Isakalukes a Moriato Barakat, an organization
emphasizing community solidarity and collective leadership.
Core Areas of Work
Diamaoden's professional approach is characterized by direct field engagement and a commitment to grassroots
development.
His work prioritizes the voices and needs of marginalized sectors, fostering participatory development that centers
community agency rather than top-down interventions.
He integrates local customs and Islamic values into modern peacebuilding frameworks, recognizing that
sustainable peace requires cultural and religious grounding in Bangsamoro contexts.
As a lecturer, Diamaoden frequently discusses the historical roots of the Bangsamoro struggle for self-
determination, providing context for current peace and autonomy efforts.

PAGE 4
He serves as a bridge between the historical struggles of the older generation of Bangsamoro leaders and the
contemporary needs of a generation seeking inclusive development and reformed governance.
Legacy and Vision
Diamaoden embodies a generation of Bangsamoro leaders who inherited both the aspirations and unfinished work
of the independence struggle while seeking to channel these energies toward inclusive development and
institutional transformation.
His insistence on youth leadership, cultural integration, and field-oriented practice reflects a belief that lasting
peace emerges from communities taking ownership of their own futures rather than waiting for top-down solutions.
Through UNYPAD-RANAO and his civic roles, Diamaoden continues to expand the space for young Maranao and
Bangsamoro voices in both development and governance, modeling an approach that honors heritage while
building new institutions.

title: Diamaoden, Arsalan
text:
PAGE 1
Arsalan Diamaoden
Dr. Arsalan A. Diamaoden is a Meranaw public servant, academician, researcher, and traditional leader from
Butig in Lanao del Sur, Philippines. He currently serves as the Chairperson of the Bangsamoro Sports
Commission (BSC), the principal sports development body of the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim
Mindanao (BARMM). A man shaped as much by the lakes and highlands of Lanao as by the lecture halls of
Mindanao State University, Diamaoden has built a career that weaves together scholarship, faith-grounded
governance, and a genuine conviction that sports can be a doorway to lasting peace in the Bangsamoro.
He holds traditional titles that carry deep weight in the Meranaw world, including Sultan A. Cabugatan of the
Royal House of Poctan and Pat Ka Wata sa Mama of Dianaton Naim sa Butig, a combination of hereditary
standing and personal achievement that sets him apart in any room he enters. His trajectory from classroom dean to
regional commissioner reflects a generation of young Bangsamoro leaders who choose service over comfort, and
who understand that development means nothing if it does not reach the community.
Contents

2 Education
3 Career

3.2 Entry into Public Service: Bangsamoro Sports Commission
4 Chairmanship of the Bangsamoro Sports Commission

Early Life and Background
Arsalan A. Diamaoden grew up in Butig, a municipality nestled in the interior of Lanao del Sur that scholars and
local historians sometimes call the "cradle of Meranaw civilization."<ref name="butig2022">Diamaoden, A. A.
(2022). Butig, Lanao Del Sur, The Cradle of Meranaw Civilization: A Critical Analysis. Psychology and
Education: A Multidisciplinary Journal, 5(10), 863–871. https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.7364236</ref>
Butig is no ordinary hometown. It was among the earliest settlements where sharifs arriving from the Arabian
Peninsula planted the seeds of Islam in the Lanao highlands, establishing the sultanate system that would define
Meranaw political and social life for centuries. Growing up here meant inheriting a living tradition: a culture of

taritib (protocol) and igma (custom), a reverence for learning rooted in
the Quranic tradition, and a community that measures a man not just by
his title, but by his service to others.
This environment shaped Diamaoden early. He comes from the
Diamaoden family of Butig, a family with documented roots in the
Royal House of Poctan and a long history of community leadership in
Lanao del Sur.<ref name="butig2022"/> His upbringing exposed him to
the language of both traditional governance and grassroots need, and it
gave him a framework he has carried into every role he has held since.
Education
Diamaoden pursued his higher education at Mindanao State University
(MSU) in Marawi City, one of the country's premier public universities
and a historic center of Muslim Filipino learning. He completed his
undergraduate degree with a Bachelor of Arts in Islamic Studies,
Major in Shari'ah, followed by a Master of Arts in Islamic Studies,
both from MSU. These degrees grounded him in Islamic jurisprudence,
Meranaw cultural history, and the intellectual traditions of Muslim
Mindanao.
He then went on to earn a Doctor of Philosophy (Ph.D.) in Mindanao
Culture and Society from the College of Social Sciences and
Humanities at MSU. His doctoral dissertation tackled one of the most
consequential policy questions of his generation:
The Status, Challenges, and Prospects of the Implementation of
Political and Socio-Economic Tracks of the Comprehensive
Agreement on the Bangsamoro: A Basis for Implementation
Mechanism Intervention
The dissertation was not an armchair exercise. It dug into the real, lived
realities of the Comprehensive Agreement on the Bangsamoro (CAB)
and the structural gaps between what the peace agreement promised
and what communities were actually experiencing on the ground. It
positioned Diamaoden early on as both a scholar of Bangsamoro affairs
and a policy thinker with practical instincts.
He later enrolled in the executive course in Leadership, Innovation,
Communication, and Knowledge Management (DAP-GSPDM) at
the Development Academy of the Philippines (DAP), in a program
offered in collaboration with Aboitiz Equity Ventures (AEV) and the
National Union of Career Executive Service Officers (NUCESO). His
foresight paper for this program, titled Sports in Bangsamoro 2050:
Advancement or Downfall, would prove to be almost prophetic in
laying out the strategic case for sports development in the region.
On November 29, 2024, he completed a Post-Doctoral Degree in
Strategic Leadership and Management at Philippine Christian University, adding a second postgraduate research
credential to an already exceptional academic record.<ref name="docx-source">Source document:

PAGE 3
ARSALAN_A__DIAMAODEN.docx, uploaded biographical brief.</ref>
Career
Academic Career
Before stepping into public administration, Diamaoden built a name for himself as an educator. He served as the
Dean of Al-Bangsamoro Shari'ah and Professional Education College in Marawi City from 2017 to 2019, a
period that coincided with the aftermath of the Marawi siege and one of the most difficult chapters of
reconstruction in the city's modern history.<ref name="iesa2020">Bangsamoro Information Office. (March 2,
2020). Bangsamoro Young Educator receives International Education Awards. Luwaran.com.
https://www.luwaran.com/news/article/2011/bangsamoro-young-educator-receives-international-education-awards-
</ref>
His approach to academic leadership was anything but conventional. He pushed for innovative teaching methods
that engaged students beyond rote learning, established student clubs designed to tap into different types of
intelligence, and maintained a personal commitment to the communities around his institution. He volunteered in
feeding programs organized by both government and non-government organizations, and he personally initiated a
fundraising project to provide school supplies for orphaned students at a madrasa (Islamic school) in his hometown
of Butig.<ref name="iesa2020"/>
As an academic, he has also contributed meaningfully to scholarship on Bangsamoro history and culture. Among
his published works are a study on the decommissioning of Moro Islamic Liberation Front (MILF) combatants in
Butig and its implications for peace,<ref name="ijmaber2021">Diamaoden, A. A., et al. (2021). The
Decommissioning of the Moro Islamic Liberation Front Combatants in Camp Darul Arham, Butig Lanao Del Sur
and Its Implication to Peace. International Journal of Multidisciplinary: Applied Business and Education Research,
2(3). https://doi.org/10.11594/ijmaber.02.03.07</ref> and his 2022 critical analysis on Butig as the historical cradle
of Meranaw civilization.<ref name="butig2022"/> He has also produced research on Meranaw oral traditions,
including the Pananaroon (Meranaw proverbs), Islamic perspectives on land ownership, and peace-building
dynamics in Lanao del Sur.
Entry into Public Service: Bangsamoro Sports Commission
Diamaoden's transition from the college deanship to public service came through his appointment as
Commissioner for Lanao del Sur at the Bangsamoro Sports Commission (BSC). The BSC was established as a
key sports governance body of the BARMM, with a mandate to develop athletic programs, promote grassroots
sports participation, preserve traditional and indigenous games, and support Bangsamoro athletes in regional and
national competitions.<ref name="pna2022">Philippine News Agency. (March 29, 2022). PSC boosts ties with
Bangsamoro Sports Commission. https://www.pna.gov.ph/articles/1170938</ref>
In June 2023, he was elevated to Chairperson of the Bangsamoro Sports Commission, taking the helm of the
Commission and reorienting its strategic direction.<ref name="docx-source"/> He was subsequently re-appointed
as Chairperson in August 2025, a clear vote of institutional confidence from the Bangsamoro Government.<ref
name="docx-source"/>

PAGE 4
Chairmanship of the Bangsamoro Sports Commission
The 12-Point Agenda on Sports
Among Diamaoden's first significant acts as Chairperson was presenting a 12-Point Agenda to the Philippine
Sports Commission (PSC), outlining BSC's framework for sports development in the Bangsamoro.<ref
name="psc2023">Philippine Sports Commission. (November 29, 2023). Bangsamoro Sports Commission lays out
12-point agenda to PSC. https://psc.gov.ph/psc_site/bangsamoro-sports-commission-lays-out-12-point-agenda-to-
psc/</ref>
The agenda covered: sports facilities development, health and wellness programs, grassroots and youth sports,
sports education, human resource development, continuation of the Sports for All programs, elite sports
identification, traditional and indigenous sports preservation, gender equity in sports, regional linkages and
collaboration, sports tourism, and sports competition development. The scope of this agenda made it clear that his
vision for BSC was not simply about winning medals. It was about using sports as an instrument of Bangsamoro
identity, wellbeing, and peace.
Grassroots Programs and Athlete Incentivization
Under Diamaoden's leadership, the BSC expanded its reach into communities that had historically been
underserved by organized sports. The commission conducted sports clinics in Marawi City, Basilan, Sulu, and
Tawi-Tawi, with training sessions that covered not just athletic technique but also teamwork, sportsmanship, and
mental preparation for young participants.<ref name="barmm-sports-clinic">BARMM Official Website. (July 4,
2024). Young athletes in Marawi undergo intensive sports clinic. Bangsamoro Information Office.
https://bangsamoro.gov.ph/news/latest-news/young-athletes-in-marawi-undergo-intensive-sports-clinic/</ref>
The commission also institutionalized a cash assistance program for Bangsamoro athletes competing in national
and international competitions, ensuring that financial constraints would not prevent talented young athletes from
representing the region at the highest levels. In February 2025, for instance, the BSC provided cash grants to 24
Karatedo athletes from Mindanao State University-Marawi ahead of the 6th Karate Pilipinas National
Championships, with four of those athletes returning home with medals.<ref name="barmm-karate">BARMM
Official Website. (March 5, 2025). Mga atletang Bangsamoro tumanggap ng tulong pinansyal, nag-uwi ng medalya
sa nat'l competition. Bangsamoro Information Office. https://bangsamoro.gov.ph/news/barmm-ngayon/mga-
atletang-bangsamoro-tumanggap-ng-tulong-pinansyal/</ref>
The B-SMART ID and Talent Identification
One of the more innovative programs introduced during his tenure is the B-SMART ID, a talent identification
system designed to discover and develop young sports prospects across the Bangsamoro region. The program
reflects Diamaoden's belief that the region is full of athletic talent that simply hasn't had the right institutional
support to emerge. Mapping potential rather than waiting for it to surface on its own has become a defining feature
of how the BSC approaches youth development under his watch.<ref name="sobsa2025">Bangsamoro Sports
Commission. (October 8, 2025). 1st State of the Bangsamoro Sports Address highlights milestones in sports
promotion, development, and partnership building in BARMM. https://bsc.bangsamoro.gov.ph/2025/10/08/1st-
state-of-the-bangsamoro-sports-address-highlights-milestones-in-sports-promotion-development-and-partnership-
building-in-barmm/</ref>

PAGE 5
Preserving Indigenous Sports
Diamaoden has consistently championed the integration of traditional Bangsamoro games into the BSC's program
portfolio. Under his leadership, the Commission conducted Indigenous Peoples Games in South Upi, Maguindanao
del Sur, as part of the celebration of Indigenous Peoples Month 2025, gathering children from indigenous
communities to compete in traditional games that carry cultural memory as much as athletic value.<ref
name="ipgames2025">Bangsamoro Sports Commission. (November 3, 2025). BSC caps off 2-day Indigenous
Peoples Games in celebration of Indigenous Peoples Month 2025.
https://bsc.bangsamoro.gov.ph/2025/11/03/</ref>
This isn't just nostalgia. Diamaoden understands that when indigenous games disappear, a community loses
something it can't get back from a Wikipedia article. Bringing these games back into the public square, particularly
for children, is a quiet but powerful act of cultural continuity.
The 1st State of the Bangsamoro Sports Address
On October 6, 2025, Chairperson Diamaoden delivered the historic 1st State of the Bangsamoro Sports Address
(SOBSA) at the Shariff Kabunsuan Cultural Complex in Cotabato City. The event brought together athletes,
coaches, sports stakeholders, and Bangsamoro government officials in what became a milestone moment for sports
governance in the region. In his address, Diamaoden presented the accomplishments of the BSC from 2021 to 2025
and outlined the road ahead. He articulated a vision that was as much about social transformation as athletic
achievement:
"This occasion was more than just a meeting of minds. It is a celebration of unity, resilience, and
shared purpose among all who believe in the power of sports to transform lives and communities."
<ref name="pna-summit">Philippine News Agency. (November 9, 2025). Mindanao Sports Summit nurtures peace
through sports. https://www.pna.gov.ph/articles/1262908</ref>
The address highlighted key institutional achievements, including the formulation of the Bangsamoro Sports
Development Plan, the adoption of enabling policies for athlete and coach incentivization, the mapping of around
60 sports clubs and organizations across BARMM, and the development of key administrative frameworks
including the Commission's Operations Manual and Strategic Performance Management System (SPMS).<ref
name="sobsa2025"/>
Institutional Partnerships
Diamaoden has been active in building a network of partnerships for the BSC. He met with Philippine Sports
Commission (PSC) Chairman Patrick Gregorio to jointly plan the Mindanao Sports Summit held at Mindanao
State University in Marawi City on November 6–7, 2025, focused on grassroots sports development and talent
identification across Mindanao.<ref name="sunstar-psc">SunStar Davao. (October 22, 2025). PSC, BSC boost
BARMM sports. https://www.sunstar.com.ph/davao/sports/psc-bsc-boost-barmm-sports</ref>
He also led the BSC delegation in a partnership meeting with Otsuka-Solar Philippines (manufacturer of Pocari
Sweat) in January 2026, culminating in the signing of a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) covering athlete
hydration and wellness initiatives, as well as coordinated sports promotion across BARMM.<ref name="bsc-
otsuka">Bangsamoro Sports Commission. (January 28, 2026). BSC, Otsuka-Solar Philippines seal partnership for
sports promotion and development in BARMM. https://bsc.bangsamoro.gov.ph/2026/01/28/bsc-otsuka-solar-
philippines-seal-partnership-for-sports-promotion-and-development-in-barmm/</ref>

PAGE 6
In January 2026, he also received a courtesy visit from MILO Philippines at the BSC office in Cotabato City,
opening discussions on further collaboration to expand sports programs for Bangsamoro youth.<ref name="bsc-
milo">Bangsamoro Sports Commission. (January 28, 2026). MILO Philippines pays courtesy visit to Bangsamoro
Sports Commission. https://bsc.bangsamoro.gov.ph/2026/01/28/</ref>
Bangsamoro athletes, meanwhile, have been making their presence felt nationally and regionally. BARMM
representatives earned one gold, three silver, and four bronze medals at the 11th BIMP-EAGA (Brunei Darussalam,
Indonesia, Malaysia, Philippines-East ASEAN Growth Area) Friendship Games in Puerto Princesa City, a
performance that Diamaoden cited as proof that investment in Bangsamoro sports is paying off.<ref
name="sunstar-psc"/>
Traditional Leadership
Alongside his public service career, Diamaoden carries the hereditary distinction of Sultan A. Cabugatan of the
Royal House of Poctan and Pat Ka Wata sa Mama of Dianaton Naim sa Butig. These are not merely
ceremonial titles in the Meranaw world. The sultanate system remains a living institution in Lanao, with sultans
playing an active role in community mediation, social cohesion, and the preservation of taritib and igma, the twin
pillars of Meranaw customary law and protocol.<ref name="docx-source"/>
For Diamaoden, holding these titles means carrying a dual responsibility: to the people who elected him to public
office, and to the community that has entrusted him with ancestral authority. He has spoken about bridging the gap
between traditional sultanate leadership and the demands of modern democratic governance, and his career can be
read as a sustained effort to do exactly that.
Recognition and Awards
Outstanding Dean, International Education Summit and Awards (IESA) 2020, held at Divalux Resort,
Bangkok, Thailand (February 22, 2020). The IESA recognized Diamaoden among more than 250
distinguished educators from across Asia for his contributions to innovative academic leadership during his
tenure at Al-Bangsamoro Shari'ah and Professional Education College.<ref name="iesa2020"/>
Asia's Most Exceptional Leadership/Educator and Humanitarian Advocate of the Year (year of award
to be confirmed).<ref name="docx-source"/>
His 100 Days of Leadership at the BSC were noted as marking a new phase in the Commission's
institutional development.<ref name="docx-source"/>
Personal Values and Cultural Significance
Diamaoden has often spoken about the Meranaw concept of kambilangataw, meaning a role model in character
and good deeds, as the standard he holds himself to. This is not a management slogan for him. It's a code. It shows
up in his decision to volunteer at feeding programs when he was still a dean, in his commitment to bring sports
clinics to marginalized communities in Lanao del Sur, and in the way he speaks about athletes, not as statistics, but
as young people whose futures depend on whether the state shows up for them.<ref name="docx-source"/>
His Ramadan messages as BSC Chairperson have offered a window into how he integrates his Islamic faith with
his governance philosophy. He has written that Ramadan is a reminder that "true fulfillment comes not from
material wealth, but from humility, generosity, and a heart full of sincerity," framing the month not just as a

PAGE 7
religious observance but as a call to public service.<ref name="bsc-ramadan">Bangsamoro Sports Commission.
(March 3, 2025). Message of Bangsamoro Sports Commission Chairperson Dr. Arsalan Diamaoden on the
observance of the Holy Month of Ramadan 1446 AH. https://bsc.bangsamoro.gov.ph/2025/03/03/</ref>
He approaches governance through three overlapping lenses: moral accountability rooted in Islamic ethics,
traditional Meranaw values of communal responsibility, and a contemporary, evidence-based approach to policy
and institutional design. The combination is relatively rare in Philippine public life, and it's what makes him a
figure of genuine cultural significance in the Bangsamoro.
Legacy
It may be early in his career to speak of legacy in the past tense, but the shape of what Diamaoden is building is
already clear. He is constructing a sports governance system in the Bangsamoro that works not just for elite
athletes, but for the child in the barrio who has never seen a proper court. He is using sports as a language of peace
in a region that knows too well what the absence of peace looks like. And he is doing it while carrying the weight
of ancestral tradition in one hand and the framework of modern governance in the other.
His foresight paper at the Development Academy of the Philippines asked a blunt question: "Sports in Bangsamoro
2050: Advancement or Downfall?" The work he is doing now is his answer. He is betting, institution by institution
and program by program, that the answer is advancement, and that the Bangsamoro's best athletic years are still
ahead.

title: Diampuan-Sarip, Montia Jamilah
text:
PAGE 1
Montia Jamilah Diampuan-Sarip
Prof. Dr. Montia Jamilah Diampuan-Sarip, CESE, LPT, MAED, MAELT, Ph.D. is one of the most
distinguished academic leaders in the history of the Mindanao State University (MSU) System and a towering
figure in Philippine teacher education.
A Full Professor and former Dean of the College of Education at MSU-Main Campus in Marawi City, she has
spent more than four decades shaping how teachers are trained across the southern Philippines.
Her career is anchored in a simple but powerful belief: that education is the surest path to liberation, peace, and
dignity for the Bangsamoro people.
In 2019, the Professional Regulation Commission (https://prc.gov.ph) (PRC) of the Philippines named her the
Outstanding Professional of the Year in the field of Professional Teaching, making her widely recognized as the
first Filipino Muslim to receive this honor, the most prestigious national distinction the PRC confers on a practicing
professional.<ref name="prc2019">Professional Regulation Commission. (2019). 2019 Most Outstanding
Professionals of the Year Awardees. Retrieved from https://www.prc.gov.ph/2019-most-outstanding-
professionals</ref>
Beyond her academic work, Dr. Sarip carries a traditional royal title: Bae a Labi a Panoroganan ko Bayabao-
Masiu, a hereditary distinction that places her among the recognized leaders of Lanao's royal lineage.<ref
name="prc2019" />
Her life story moves from a community schoolhouse in Taraka, Lanao del Sur, to the national stage in Manila, and
eventually to international platforms in Thailand and the United States, all without losing the rootedness that
defines her: a Maranao Muslim woman who chose to build, not leave.

Early Life and Cultural Roots
Dr. Sarip was born and raised in the heartland of the Maranao
world, the lake province of Lanao del Sur in what was then the
Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (ARMM).
The exact date and municipality of her birth have not been publicly
disclosed, but what's well-established is the cultural environment
that shaped her: the world of the Maranao, one of the oldest and
most artistically rich communities in the Philippines, a people
whose identity is inseparable from the shores of Lake Lanao, the
traditions of the sultanate, and the deep commitment to learning
expressed through both Islamic scholarship and formal education.
She belongs to the broader world of Bangsamoro nobility.
Her royal title, Bae a Labi a Panoroganan ko Bayabao-Masiu,
formally recognized by traditional authorities, places her within the
aristocratic hierarchy of the Bayabao and Masiu domains, two of the
historical royal houses of Lanao del Sur.<ref name="prc2019" />
This isn't simply a ceremonial distinction.
In Maranao society, a bae (or bai) is a female member of the royal
class, and a labi is a title of further distinction within that class.
For Dr. Sarip, this identity has never been at odds with her scientific
or professional pursuits; if anything, it has deepened them.
She has actively used her position as a traditional leader to facilitate
conflict settlement and peace dialogues involving sultans, baes, and
community professionals across the region.<ref name="prc2019" />
Her faith in Islam has also been central to her worldview.
She approaches her work as an educator with a sense of calling
rooted in the Islamic concept of amanah (stewardship) and the duty
to pass on knowledge as an act of worship.
This blending of Maranao cultural pride, Islamic values, and
professional rigor forms the distinctive philosophical foundation of
everything Dr. Sarip has built.
Education
Dr. Sarip's academic credentials reflect a deliberate, layered
investment in the discipline she would spend her life teaching:
education itself.

PAGE 3

She holds a Licensure for Professional Teaching (LPT), a Master of
Arts in Education (MAED), and a Master of Arts in English
Language Teaching (MAELT), along with a Ph.D. in Education, the
terminal degree that qualified her for Full Professor rank at the
Mindanao State University.<ref name="son">Sarip, J. D. (2025).
Personal communication regarding Prof. Dr. Montia Jamilah
Diampuan-Sarip. [Family-provided biographical information from
her son, Prof. Jamilnur D. Sarip].</ref>
The MAELT in particular speaks to one of her core professional preoccupations: the quality of language instruction
in Bangsamoro classrooms, where students often navigate multiple languages and where English proficiency has a
direct bearing on board examination performance.
She is also a Career Executive Service Eligible (CESE), a distinction that recognizes her qualifications for the
highest career executive positions in the Philippine civil service.<ref name="son" />
While the specific institutions and years of her graduate studies have not been publicly disclosed, the arc of her
degrees tells its own story: a teacher who kept studying, kept deepening her expertise, and kept bringing that
deeper knowledge back to the students and institution she served.
Her doctoral research took her to international forums.
She earned a Best Oral Presentation award at the 1st International Conference on Education held in Songkhla,
Thailand in 2013, and has been nominated twice for inclusion in the Who's Who in the World directory published in
New Jersey, United States.<ref name="prc2019">Professional Regulation Commission. (2019). 2019 Most
Outstanding Professionals of the Year Awardees. Retrieved from https://www.prc.gov.ph/2019-most-outstanding-
professionals</ref>
Career
Beginnings in Basic Education: MSU-Taraka Community High School
Dr. Sarip's career didn't begin in the university halls of Marawi.
It began in the municipality of Taraka, where she served as Principal of the MSU-Taraka Community High School,
a basic education institution operated under the Mindanao State University System.<ref
name="source">Diampuan-Sarip, M. J. (n.d.). Dr. Montia Jamilah Diampuan-Sarip: The Trailblazer of
Bangsamoro Excellence [Biographical document]. Provided source material.</ref>
This posting gave her early, direct experience with the challenges of educating young people in a community that is
predominantly poor, predominantly rural, and often caught in the crossfire of the complex political landscape of
Lanao del Sur.
As principal, she demonstrated that quality school leadership isn't only possible in well-resourced urban settings,
but that it was urgently needed in places like Taraka, where many students come from farming families with limited
access to academic support.
Her time there laid the groundwork for a leadership philosophy she would carry into every role that followed:
every student, regardless of background, deserves the same standard of leadership and care.

PAGE 4
Director, Office of Admissions, MSU-Main Campus
Before and alongside her deanship, Dr. Sarip also served as Director of the Office of Admissions at MSU-Main
Campus in Marawi City.<ref name="source" />
In this role, she was responsible for upholding the university's admissions standards, a function that carries
enormous weight in an institution like MSU, which serves as the primary gateway to higher education for
thousands of young Bangsamoro people each year.
As admissions director, she maintained a commitment to meritocracy while navigating the realities of an institution
serving students from some of the most economically disadvantaged communities in the Philippines.
Dean, College of Education, MSU-Main Campus
Dr. Sarip's most consequential institutional role was as Dean of the College of Education at MSU-Main Campus.
In this position, she held full professor rank and oversaw the implementation of curricula prescribed by the
Commission on Higher Education (CHED), managing everything from faculty standards to research outputs to
student performance on the national Licensure Examination for Teachers (LET).<ref name="prc2019" />
Under her deanship, the college achieved sustained improvement in LET performance, consistently producing
topnotchers in the national board examinations.<ref name="source" />
This wasn't accidental.
She made curricular quality, faculty development, and student welfare simultaneous priorities, ensuring that the
promise MSU made to Bangsamoro youth, that world-class education is possible in Marawi, was actually
delivered.
Her administration also expanded scholarship access for students from government organizations (GOs) and non-
government organizations (NGOs), prioritizing poor but deserving students who might otherwise have been shut
out of higher education.<ref name="prc2019" />
She actively promoted paper presentations by both faculty and students at national and international conferences,
building a research culture within the college that had broad ripple effects on MSU's national academic standing.
<ref name="prc2019" />
She also pursued research collaboration with both GOs and NGOs, positioning the College of Education not just as
a teaching unit but as an active contributor to Philippine educational policy.<ref name="prc2019" />
Her tenure lasted long enough to be remembered not by administrators or colleagues alone, but by the hundreds of
licensed teachers she helped produce, many of whom are now educators across Mindanao and the broader
Bangsamoro region.

PAGE 5
National and International Influence
Philippine Association for Teacher Educators (PAFTE)
Dr. Sarip has been one of the most active Bangsamoro voices within the Philippine Association for Teacher
Educators (PAFTE), the national organization that sets professional standards and shapes curriculum development
for teacher education institutions across the Philippines.
She served as a National Board Member of PAFTE for two terms and led the PAFTE-ARMM Chapter as its
Chairperson, giving the Bangsamoro region a strong institutional voice in national teacher education policy.<ref
name="prc2019" />
In October 2018, PAFTE awarded her its highest distinction: the PAFTE Golden Award, in recognition of her
exceptional contributions to teacher education in the Philippines.<ref name="prc2019" />
Reading Association of the Philippines (RAP)
One of Dr. Sarip's most historically significant contributions to national educational policy came through her work
with the Reading Association of the Philippines (RAP), the country's foremost professional organization for
reading educators and literacy advocates.
RAP is affiliated with the International Literacy Association (ILA), formerly the International Reading Association
(IRA), which is based in the United States and serves as a global standard-setter for reading instruction and literacy
programming.
Dr. Sarip served as a National Board Director of RAP for two terms, making her the first Muslim to sit on the
national board of this organization, a landmark that brought inclusive representation for Mindanao and the
Bangsamoro into national literacy policy discussions.<ref name="source" /><ref name="prc2019" />
She was also the Founding President of the RAP-Lanao Chapter, establishing for the first time a formal
institutional home for reading advocacy within Lanao del Sur, a region where literacy challenges remain acute due
to conflict displacement, poverty, and limited access to reading materials.<ref name="prc2019" />
Other National Affiliations
Beyond PAFTE and RAP, Dr. Sarip has served on the Board of Directors of the Muslim Congress of the
Philippines and as a Member and Consultant to the RC-AKIC International College Foundation, Inc.<ref
name="prc2019" />
She also served as Secretary to the MSU Royalties, the formal body that represents the traditional leadership of the
MSU community, a role that bridges her academic and cultural identities.<ref name="prc2019" />
Following the 2017 Battle of Marawi, she was among the professionals consulted in designing the rehabilitation
plan for the Most Affected Area, specifically contributing to the education sector components of Marawi's post-
conflict reconstruction.<ref name="prc2019" />
International Recognition
Dr. Sarip's reach extends beyond Philippine shores.

PAGE 6
She was nominated twice for and included in the Who's Who in the World publication based in New Jersey, USA,
which profiles influential leaders across every significant field of endeavor worldwide.<ref name="prc2019" />
She has also been highlighted internationally for her work in promoting peace through education in conflict-
affected regions, an achievement cited in connection with her nomination for an Influential Educators of the World
citation from the United States.<ref name="source" />
Her Best Oral Presentation award at the 1st International Conference on Education in Songkhla, Thailand in 2013
further cemented her standing as a researcher and educator with international credibility.<ref name="prc2019" />
Peace and Community Advocacy
Dr. Sarip has never seen her role as purely academic.
She is a practicing peace advocate who draws on her royal title and community standing to bring warring parties to
the table, often working alongside sultans, baes, and other community leaders to resolve disputes through dialogue.
<ref name="prc2019" />
This work is especially significant given the decades-long armed conflict in Lanao del Sur and Marawi City.
In a region where trust in institutions has been tested repeatedly, traditional leaders like Dr. Sarip play a role that no
government program can fully replicate: the ability to speak to community members in their own language, cultural
framework, and emotional register.
She has also extended her community commitment to practical livelihood support, serving as a trainer for
livelihood programs aimed at the wives of farmers, helping women in rural communities gain economic skills that
improve household stability.<ref name="prc2019" />
This combination, academic scholarship plus grassroots community action, is what has made her legacy so durable.
The 2019 PRC Outstanding Professional Award
The single event that brought Dr. Sarip to national prominence outside Mindanao was her recognition at the 2019
Outstanding Professionals Awards Night, held on June 20, 2019, at the Fiesta Pavilion of the Manila Hotel, with
then-Chief Justice Lucas Bersamin as the guest of honor.<ref name="prcnight">Professional Regulation
Commission. (2019, June 28). PRC 2019 Outstanding Professionals Awards Night. Retrieved from
https://www.prc.gov.ph/article/prc-2019-outstanding-professionals-awards-night/4000</ref>
She was named the Outstanding Professional of the Year in the category of Professional Teaching, the highest
distinction the Professional Regulation Commission confers on a licensed teacher in the Philippines.
This recognition was historic on multiple levels.
She became widely recognized as the first professional from the MSU System to receive this national honor,
validating the quality of instruction within MSU's campuses at the highest official level.<ref name="source" />
She was also recognized as the first educator from what is now the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim
Mindanao (BARMM) to reach this distinction, demonstrating that educators from the Bangsamoro can lead the
entire Philippine professional landscape.<ref name="source" />

PAGE 7
For the broader Filipino Muslim community, it was a moment of rare national affirmation, a public and official
recognition that Muslim educators belong at the very top of the country's professional hierarchy.
The official PRC citation described her contribution to teaching as spanning 40 years, encompassing instruction,
research, and extension services, all oriented toward academic excellence and alleviating poverty in the
communities she serves.<ref name="prc2019" />
"Dr. Sarip is a researcher awarded internationally; serves as resource person to local, national and
international conferences; trainer for livelihood trainings to wives of farmers; involved in conflict
settlement being a traditional leader who holds royal title as 'Bae a Labi a Panoroganan ko Bayabao
Masiu'; and facilitate peace advocacy in the region with sultans, baes and professionals, shows her
commitment and professionalism in her field."
— Professional Regulation Commission, 2019 Citation<ref name="prc2019" />
Awards and Recognition
Dr. Sarip has received recognition at the barangay, municipal, regional, national, and international levels across a
career spanning four decades.
Her confirmed honors include the following:
The PRC Outstanding Professional of the Year in Professional Teaching (2019), the highest national
professional award in the Philippines, conferred by the Professional Regulation Commission at the 2019
Outstanding Professionals Awards Night in Manila.<ref name="prc2019" />
The PAFTE Golden Award (October 2018), given by the Philippine Association for Teacher Educators in
recognition of her exceptional contributions to teacher education.<ref name="prc2019" />
The Best Oral Presentation Award at the 1st International Conference on Education in Songkhla, Thailand
(2013), recognizing the quality of her research as presented before an international academic audience.<ref
name="prc2019" />
Twice nominated for and included in Who's Who in the World (New Jersey, USA), which spotlights leaders
making a global impact in their fields.<ref name="prc2019" />
Nominated for the Influential Educators of the World citation from the United States, recognizing her resilience
in promoting peace through education in conflict-affected regions.<ref name="source" />
Personal Life and Family
Behind every milestone in Dr. Sarip's public career is a partnership and a household that made it possible.
She is married to Mr. Mohammad Harby B. Sarip, Sr., a retired international banker who spent his career with Al-
Bank Al-Saudi Al-Fransi in the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, one of the prominent banking institutions of the Arab
world.<ref name="son" />
Their complementary worlds, his in international finance and hers in education, shaped a household where service,
excellence, and professional commitment were simply part of daily life.
Together, they raised seven children, all of whom have built distinguished careers in government, law, education,
medicine, and public service.<ref name="son" />

PAGE 8
Princess Sittie Habibah D. Sarip-Paudac (LPT, MAED) is recognized as the first Muslim news anchor in the
Philippines, having served under the Presidential Communications Operations Office (PCOO) at Malacañan.<ref
name="son" />
Mohammad Harby D. Sarip, Jr., serves with the Ministry of Health under the BARMM.
Mohammad Hajam D. Sarip (CSE, MPA) holds an Assistant Regional Director-equivalent position at the Land
Transportation Franchising and Regulatory Board (LTFRB) Region X.
Atty. Sittie Hadiya D. Sarip serves as a Prosecution Attorney at the Department of Justice (DOJ) under BARMM.
Precious Jawaher D. Sarip (LPT, MA, CAR) is a faculty member at MSU-Main Campus, continuing the family's
tradition of teaching at the institution their mother helped build.
Dr. Mohammad Jamjoom D. Sarip (RN) is a medical professional and former secretary of the Integrated Provincial
Health Office of Lanao del Sur.
The youngest, Prof. Jamilnur D. Sarip (LPT, DIS, MAIS, MPA, HC), currently serves as Director and former OIC
Dean of MSU-General Santos, and has held positions as Regional Consultant at the Bangsamoro Sports
Commission under BARMM and Project Manager for the Balay Mindanaw Foundation Inc. (BMFI) under projects
of the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) and Save the Children Philippines.<ref name="son" />
That seven children from one household hold professional positions spanning health, law, transportation regulation,
presidential communications, higher education, and international development isn't coincidence.
It is the long harvest of what Dr. Sarip and her husband planted together: a family culture where doing meaningful
work in service of the Bangsamoro was never optional, it was simply what you did.
Legacy
Forty years is a long time to do anything, but to sustain four decades of teaching with the same energy, idealism,
and rigor that Dr. Sarip has is genuinely extraordinary.
What distinguishes her legacy isn't just the list of positions she held or the awards she collected, though both lists
are impressive.
It's the texture of what she built: a College of Education that consistently sends out competent, licensed teachers
into Bangsamoro classrooms; a RAP-Lanao Chapter that brought literacy advocacy to a region that desperately
needs it; a PAFTE chapter that made sure the Bangsamoro's needs were heard in national teacher education policy;
a peace advocacy practice rooted not in politics but in cultural authority and personal conviction; and a family that
turned her values into a living, working inheritance spread across the institutions of this nation.
She made it clear, through the choices she made and the places she stayed, that a Maranao Muslim woman could be
both a traditional leader and a national standard-setter, both a community elder and a globally recognized educator.
For the next generation of Bangsamoro professionals, especially young women from Lanao del Sur and across the
region, that visibility matters enormously.
Dr. Sarip didn't just succeed.
She did it in a way that makes it easier for others to believe they can, too.

title: Dianalan, Jiamil Ismael Maruhom
text:
PAGE 1
Jiamil Ismael Maruhom

Jiamil Ismael Maruhom Dianalan
Jiamil Ismael Maruhom Dianalan (popularly known as Jimmy Dianalan) was a Filipino statesman, legislator,
agricultural administrator and Muslim welfare executive from Lanao del Sur, Mindanao.
Emerging from an influential Maranao royal lineage, he devoted his career to navigating the complex sociopolitical
landscape of the southern Philippines, moving between national legislative halls, executive offices in Manila, and
the grassroots realities of his home province.
He is best remembered as the founding Executive Director of the Office on Muslim Affairs (OMA), a pioneering
architect of Muslim institutional governance under the Philippine national government, and a dedicated voice for
agrarian development in Muslim Mindanao during one of the country's most turbulent political transitions.
Contents

EARLY LIFE AND ETHNIC
AFFILIATION
Jimmy Dianalan was born into the Maranao ethnic group, the
traditional "people of the lake," whose ancestral domain centers on
Lake Lanao in northwestern Mindanao.
Growing up in the shadow of the Pat a Pagampong sa Ranao, the
four traditional principalities of Lanao, he was immersed early in
the codes and responsibilities that define Maranao aristocratic life.
Central to that upbringing was maratabat, the layered Maranao
ethos of family honor, community obligation, and ancestral
prestige. For the Dianalans, maratabat was not an abstraction. It was
a lived standard, one that shaped how the family engaged with
neighbors, rivals, colonial administrations, and eventually the
Republic itself.

PAGE 2

national bureaucratic leadership
His family roots were planted firmly in the royal houses of Marawi
City and the surrounding municipalities, placing him squarely at the
center of Ranao's traditional hierarchy from birth.
FAMILY AND ALLIANCE NETWORKS
In Maranao political culture, no leader rises alone. Behind every
significant figure is a web of kinship, alliance, and reciprocal
obligation, and the Dianalan family understood this well.
Jimmy's brother, Sultan Omar Maruhom Dianalan, became a
historic figure in his own right. Sultan Omar served as the longest-
running mayor of Marawi City and was a regular assemblyman,
earning a reputation as one of the most durable political figures in
the history of the provincial capital.
That fraternal bond made the Dianalan household a stabilizing force
through decades of local and national upheaval, from martial law to
democratic restoration, from the AFP-MNLF conflicts to the slow,
complicated rise of autonomous governance in Muslim Mindanao.
On the personal front, Jimmy was married to Tamoki Isnihaya
Dangcal Indol, and together they raised a family committed to
continuing the tradition of public service.
His son, Jiamil "Troy" Dianalan Jr., distinguished himself as a
respected community leader and local representative before his
untimely passing in 2019, a loss that was mourned across the
province.
The family's multi-generational commitment to governance
continues today. Younger relatives, including Datu Madrigal
Dianalan II, have taken up technical and administrative roles in
agencies like the National Commission on Muslim Filipinos
(NCMF), carrying the family name into the modern era of
Bangsamoro institutional life.
EDUCATION
Dianalan's early schooling in Lanao followed a dual path common to young men of his generation and standing:
traditional Islamic studies alongside secular primary education.
As he grew older and surveyed the needs of his community, agriculture stood out as a field where professional
expertise could translate directly into real change for Mindanao's rural populations.
He pursued that conviction to Araneta University, where he graduated with a degree in agriculture.
That educational foundation set him apart. While many politicians from landed families governed through
patronage and ancestral authority alone, Dianalan brought a technical command of agrarian science to the table,
which later made him a credible and effective voice for rural workers and farming communities during some of the

PAGE 3
most consequential policy debates of the Marcos and Aquino eras.
PUBLIC CAREER
Legislative Service: Interim Batasang Pambansa (1978–1984)
Long before he held any executive appointment, Dianalan had already established himself on the national stage as
a legislator with a specific mission.
From 1978 to 1984, he served as a sectoral representative for agricultural labor in the Interim Batasang Pambansa,
the parliamentary body that operated during the latter years of the Marcos era.
His mandate was pointed: he went to bat for ancestral farmers and rural workers in Mindanao, people who were too
often invisible in the policy conversations happening in Manila.
In the Batasang, he was one of relatively few voices consistently arguing that agrarian development in Muslim-
majority provinces could not be separated from questions of land rights, indigenous authority, and community self-
determination.
Officer-in-Charge, Department of Agrarian Reform
The 1986 People Power Revolution reshuffled Philippine governance at nearly every level, and the Department of
Agrarian Reform was no exception.
When Secretary Heherson Alvarez stepped down from the DAR during the transition period, President Corazon
Aquino turned to Dianalan, appointing him as Officer-in-Charge of the entire department.
It was a significant trust. The DAR, even under ordinary circumstances, is one of the most politically loaded
agencies in the Philippines, sitting at the intersection of land ownership, poverty, rural politics, and national
ideology. For Dianalan, stepping into that role during a post-revolutionary transition meant navigating competing
pressures from landowners, peasant organizations, and a government still finding its footing.
Concurrently, he served as an Undersecretary working on agricultural policy and national planning committees,
where he focused on channeling infrastructure funds and development programs toward the agrarian economies of
Mindanao.
Founding Executive Director, Office on Muslim Affairs (1987)
January 30, 1987 marks what is arguably Jimmy Dianalan's most consequential day in public life.
On that date, President Aquino issued Executive Order No. 122-A, dissolving the older Ministry of Muslim Affairs
and Cultural Communities and replacing it with a streamlined new body: the Office on Muslim Affairs (OMA).
Dianalan was appointed as the OMA's founding Executive Director, which meant he was not stepping into an
existing institution. He was building one from the ground up.
The work was foundational in every sense. He established the OMA's initial personnel frameworks and created the
screening committees responsible for integrating Muslim professionals into the national bureaucracy, opening
pathways that had long been either closed or poorly mapped.

PAGE 4
He also structured state support for the Hajj pilgrimage, formalizing the Philippine government's role in facilitating
one of the most important religious obligations in a Muslim citizen's life.
That institutional architecture Dianalan put in place did not disappear when administrations changed. It evolved,
adapted, and eventually became the direct organizational blueprint for what is today the National Commission on
Muslim Filipinos (NCMF), the agency that continues to serve as the primary interface between the national
government and Filipino Muslim communities.
Lanao del Sur Gubernatorial Race (2010)
Dianalan's political journey came full circle in 2010, when he entered the gubernatorial race in Lanao del Sur under
the banner of Lapiang Manggagawa (LM).
The result did not go in his favor, as local power consolidated around other coalition blocs. But the campaign itself
was notable for what it was not: it was not a standard dynastic alliance play.
His platform centered on labor representation, agricultural equity, and regional economic self-reliance, themes
consistent with the entire arc of his career and decidedly out of step with the transactional politics that dominated
provincial contests of that era.
Even in defeat, the campaign underscored who Dianalan had always been: a man more interested in the substance
of governance than in the mechanics of political survival.
CULTURAL SIGNIFICANCE AND LEGACY
Jimmy Dianalan operated in a space that very few people of his generation managed to occupy comfortably: the
middle ground between traditional Maranao authority and the modern Philippine state.
Manila and Marawi have long spoken different languages, not just literally but politically and culturally. The
central government in the post-war decades struggled to understand the social architecture of Muslim Mindanao, its
sultanates, its codes of honor, its religious institutions, and its deep skepticism of outside authority.
Dianalan served as a bridge across that gap. He could sit in cabinet meetings in Malacañang Palace and argue
policy with national secretaries on their own terms, then return to Marawi and engage with the datus and sultans of
the Pat a Pagampong with the same fluency and respect.
That dual competence, bureaucratic and traditional, made him rare and valuable in ways that went beyond any
single appointment he held.
His family's legacy is also literally etched into the landscape of Marawi City. Sultan Omar Dianalan Boulevard,
named for his brother, runs as a central artery through the heart of the city. The boulevard survived heavy damage
during the 2017 Marawi Siege and has since been part of the long, difficult process of rebuilding the city. Its
continued presence in the restored urban landscape stands as a quiet marker of how deeply the Dianalan family is
woven into the identity of the place.
Dianalan passed away leaving behind a blueprint for what modern Moro leadership could look like: one that uses
the institutional mechanisms of the Philippine state not to assimilate or erase indigenous identity, but to safeguard
it, argue for it, and ensure it has a seat at the table.

Omar M. Dianalan
Sultan Atty. Omar Maruhom Dianalan (April 14, 1931 – 1990)
was a Filipino lawyer, traditional sultan, and public servant from
Marawi City, Lanao del Sur.
He served as Chief of Police of Marawi City, City Mayor of
Dansalan (later Marawi City) for nearly two decades, Assemblyman
in the Regular Batasang Pambansa under the Kilusang Bagong
Lipunan (KBL) banner, and Representative for the First District of
Lanao del Sur in the 8th Philippine Congress.
He is best remembered for leading the effort to officially designate
Marawi as the "Islamic City of Marawi" in 1980, and for his
steadfast advocacy on behalf of Bangsamoro communities during
some of the most turbulent decades in the history of Muslim
Mindanao.
Sultan Omar Dianalan Boulevard in Marawi City bears his name to
this day.

EARLY LIFE AND ROYAL HERITAGE
Omar Maruhom Dianalan was born on April 14, 1931, in what was
then the broader Lanao area of central Mindanao, the territory that
would later be formally constituted as Marawi City.

PAGE 2
Chief of Police, Marawi City
City Mayor of Dansalan / Marawi
City (c. 1968–1984)
Assemblyman, Regular Batasang
Pambansa (1984–1986)

Lanao del Sur, 8th Congress
(1987–1992)

Hadji Alawi Mandangan Dimakuta

(among others)

Notability
Maranao Sultan, Lawyer, and
Statesman from Lanao del Sur; one of
the longest-serving mayors in Marawi
City history; chief architect of Marawi's
