His middle name, "Maruhom," was not just a personal name: it
pointed directly to a lineage of respected noble leaders who had
long shaped the political and social landscape of the Maranao
world.
Dianalan belonged to the Royal House of Guimba-Marawi, one of
the traditional ruling structures within the sovereign confederation
of Lanao sultanates.
The Lanao sultanates are among the oldest continuously functioning
Islamic political institutions in the Philippines, and membership in a
royal house carried real, practical weight in Maranao society, not
just ceremonial prestige.
Over the course of his life, he earned the title of Sultan, a distinction
that carried with it both the weight of hereditary authority and the
expectations of a community that still looked to its traditional
leaders for moral and political guidance.
He came from two prominent clans: the Maruhom clan and the
Dianalan clan.
This dual heritage situated him at the intersection of multiple
respected lineages in the Mëranaw (Maranao) community, a Muslim
ethno-linguistic group centered around the shores of Lake Lanao in
central Mindanao, and one of the major Bangsamoro peoples of the
Philippines.
His upbringing, steeped in Islamic values, Maranao adat (customary
law), and the obligations of noble birth, shaped how he would later
approach public service: always with an eye toward community,
always anchored in the traditions that gave his people their identity.
EDUCATION AND LAW
Dianalan pursued formal legal education and earned a Bachelor of
Laws degree, later passing the Philippine Bar Examination to
become a licensed attorney.
His professional title, "Atty.," was not merely decorative in his
context.
In a country where the legal and political system had been
constructed largely around a Christian-majority, Manila-centric
framework, being a credentialed lawyer gave a Maranao leader from
Lanao del Sur something invaluable: the tools to operate within that
system on its own terms.
His legal training made him effective in halls of power where grassroots community connections alone were not
always enough to get things done.

PAGE 3
It was precisely this combination of traditional authority and modern professional credentials that made him such a
distinctive figure in Mindanao's political history.
PUBLIC SERVICE: POLICE, CITY HALL, AND BEYOND
Chief of Police
Dianalan began his public career in law enforcement, serving as Chief of Police of Marawi City.
In a city where tribal dynamics, clan relations, and community tensions were a daily reality for local governance,
the police chief's role was never simply about crime: it involved navigating complex social situations, mediating
disputes, and maintaining a working peace in an environment shaped by rido (clan conflict) and strong communal
loyalties.
City Mayor of Dansalan / Marawi City
From roughly 1968 to 1984, Dianalan served as City Mayor of Dansalan, which was later officially renamed
Marawi City.
That tenure of close to two decades made him one of the longest-serving elected mayors in the city's recorded
history.
His years in city hall coincided with a deeply turbulent period in Mindanao: the declaration of Martial Law in
1972, the armed conflict between the Moro National Liberation Front (MNLF) and the Philippine government, and
the broader struggle over Bangsamoro self-determination that would define Muslim Mindanao for generations.
Through all of that, Dianalan focused on what he could directly influence: infrastructure development, improving
the city's revenue base, encouraging investment, and maintaining enough stability to allow ordinary life to
continue.
The work was incremental, unglamorous, and necessary.
The Islamic City Declaration
The high point of his mayoral tenure, and arguably the achievement most associated with his name, came on April
15, 1980.
On that date, Dianalan signed City Council Resolution No. 19-A, which formally declared Marawi the "Islamic
City of Marawi."
The move was both culturally resonant and strategically calculated.
With roughly 92 percent of the population identifying as Muslim, Marawi already was, in every practical sense, an
Islamic city.
The official declaration formalized what the community already knew about itself, and it carried concrete strategic
value: it positioned Marawi to attract development assistance and investment from Muslim-majority countries and
organizations in the Middle East.

PAGE 4
It also sent a clear signal to Manila and to the broader Philippine public that Marawi's identity was not something
to be diluted or sidelined in the name of national uniformity.
The designation made Marawi the country's only predominantly Muslim chartered city, a distinction it holds to this
day.
NATIONAL LEGISLATURE
Batasang Pambansa (1984–1986)
Dianalan moved to the national stage in 1984, winning election as an Assemblyman in the Regular Batasang
Pambansa under the Kilusang Bagong Lipunan (KBL) banner, the ruling political party of the Marcos
administration.
His tenure in the Batasan covered the final years of Marcos rule, a period of intense political pressure that
culminated in the People Power Revolution of February 1986 and the restoration of democratic governance.
8th Philippine Congress (1987–1992)
After the restoration of the bicameral Congress under the 1987 Constitution, Dianalan won election as
Representative for the First District of Lanao del Sur in the 8th Philippine Congress, serving from 1987 to 1992.
His time in Congress was marked by consistent advocacy for his constituents and for the broader Bangsamoro
community.
Contemporaries described him as a fierce defender of Moro rights in the House, working to address historical
injustices and the structural marginalization that Muslim Mindanao had faced for decades.
Among his concrete legislative contributions was the sponsorship of House Bill No. 20077, which sought to
establish the Bubong District Hospital, a measure aimed at expanding access to healthcare in Lanao del Sur.
He also helped create the legislative framework for a Drug Addiction Rehabilitation Center in Barangay Amai-
Pakpak, Marawi City.
BOARD OF REGENTS, MINDANAO STATE UNIVERSITY
Beyond his roles in local and national government, Dianalan served on the Board of Regents of Mindanao State
University (MSU), the flagship state university of Muslim Mindanao and one of the most important educational
institutions in the Bangsamoro region.
His presence on the Board of Regents reflected both his community stature and his genuine interest in education as
a vehicle for Bangsamoro advancement.
FAMILY
Dianalan married into another prominent Lanao family: his wife was the daughter of the late Lanao Governor Datu
Hadji Alawi Mandangan Dimakuta.

PAGE 5
Their union linked two powerful political and traditional families, reinforcing the networks of clan and governance
that shaped political life in the Lanao region.
Among their children was Bae Omera Dimakuta Dianalan Lucman, who went on to build a distinguished public
career of her own, serving as Administrator of the Cooperative Development Authority, Vice Governor of Lanao
del Sur, and Secretary of the Office on Muslim Affairs.
LEGACY
Sultan Atty. Omar Maruhom Dianalan died in 1990.
Those who knew him remembered a man who kept his door open to anyone who came with a need, regardless of
faith or background.
In a political environment where personal enrichment was common, he stood apart: contemporaries noted that he
died without having accumulated great personal wealth, a quiet testament to the kind of public servant he had
chosen to be.
His integrity stayed intact through nearly three decades of public life, across the most difficult political terrain his
region had ever faced.
The city he served has not forgotten him.
Sultan Omar Dianalan Boulevard, the major commercial and arterial corridor of Marawi City, carries his name
today, a fitting monument for a man who spent his career building things that lasted.
His story is, in many ways, the story of Maranao leadership itself: how a person could hold two worlds at once, the
ancient obligations of a sultan and the modern responsibilities of an elected official, and serve both without
betraying either.

Bae Omerah Hafidah Dianalan-Lucman
Bae Omerah Hafidah D. Dianalan-Lucman (also rendered as Bai
Omera or Bai Omeira Dimakuta Dianalan-Lucman) is a Maranao
noblewoman, career public servant, and institutional pioneer who
served as the inaugural Secretary and Chief Executive Officer of the
National Commission on Muslim Filipinos (NCMF) from 2010 to
2012, making her the first woman to hold the cabinet-level position
overseeing the rights and welfare of Muslim Filipinos.<ref
name="ncmf_southluzon">National Commission on Muslim
Filipinos South Luzon Office. "About Us." NCMF-
Southluzon.weebly.com. Retrieved 2024.</ref>
Born into one of Lanao del Sur's most storied political dynasties, she
grew up watching her father, Sultan Atty. Omar Maruhom Dianalan,
govern Marawi City for nearly two decades, negotiate the tensions
between Islamic tradition and Philippine statehood, and sponsor
legislation that shaped the province for generations.
That upbringing became her template. Over a career spanning
provincial governance, social welfare, cooperative economics, and
executive administration, Dianalan-Lucman wove together the twin
threads of her identity: the daughter of a sultan who understood that
public service is an act of faith, and a Filipino technocrat who knew
that institutions matter just as much as intentions.
Her most enduring contribution was the transformation of the 23-
year-old Office on Muslim Affairs (OMA) into a fully empowered,
cabinet-level commission under Republic Act No. 9997.<ref
name="ra9997">Republic Act No. 9997, "National Commission on
Muslim Filipinos Act of 2009," signed into law by President Gloria
Macapagal-Arroyo on February 18, 2010.</ref>
The organizational bedrock she built during her two years at the
NCMF, including its functional bureaus, its operational manuals, and
its reconceived mandate as a policy body rather than a pilgrimage
office, remains the structural foundation of the Commission to this
day.

Early Life and Lineage
Bae Omerah grew up in Marawi City, the capital of Lanao del Sur and the only predominantly Muslim chartered
city in the Philippines. She was born into the Dianalan clan, one of the prominent royal clans of Ranao, whose
bloodlines run through the Sultanate of Guimba, one of the five united sultanates that historically governed
Marawi.<ref name="bangsa_sultan">Bangsa Ranao Blog. "Sultan Atty. Omar Maruhom Dianalan."
bangsaranao.blogspot.com. May 2013.</ref>
Her father, Sultan Atty. Omar Maruhom Dianalan (1931–1990), was a lawyer, a passionate advocate for the
Maranao people, and a man described by those who knew him as a servant-leader who died without much wealth
after nearly two decades as Mayor of Marawi City.<ref name="bangsa_sultan" /> He was also elected
Assemblyman and then Congressman of Lanao del Sur, representing the province's first district, and he served as a
member of the Board of Regents of Mindanao State University.<ref name="bangsa_sultan" />
Among his most visible legacies was the renaming of Marawi City as the "Islamic City of Marawi," formalized
through City Council Resolution No. 19-A on April 15, 1980, during his mayoral tenure.<ref
name="marawi_wiki">Wikipedia. "Marawi." en.wikipedia.org. Accessed 2024.</ref>
Her mother was the daughter of the late Lanao Governor Datu Hadji Alawi Mandangan Dimakuta of Watu, which
is why Bae Omerah carries the matronymic middle name "Dimakuta" in many official records, a sign of the dual
royal lineage she inherited from both sides of her family.<ref name="bangsa_sultan" />
The family home in Marawi was not simply a household. It was a meeting place for sultans, ulama, and politicians,
and growing up inside it gave Bae Omerah an unusually clear view of how traditional authority and modern
governance can either work together or tear each other apart.
In the Maranao culture, the title of Bae is given to women of noble rank, roughly equivalent to a princess or queen
in the context of the Ranao sultanates. For Bae Omerah, the title was never ceremonial. It carried an expectation of
service, and the community's understanding of her career was filtered through that expectation from the beginning.
She married Dr. Alibasher Lucman, a government official who served as Executive Director of the Office on
Muslim Affairs (OMA) from 1990 to 1992.<ref name="moroherald">Moro Herald. "New National Commission on
Muslim Filipinos (NCMF) Replaces Office on Muslim Affairs (OMA)." moroherald.com. April 22, 2010.</ref>
Their marriage brought together two of the most influential families in Lanao, the Dianalan clan of Marawi's
Guimba Sultanate and the Lucman clan, whose own political and intellectual contributions to the Bangsamoro
community span several generations.

PAGE 3
Education
Specific details of Dianalan-Lucman's formal educational credentials remain incompletely documented in publicly
available archives. Based on her career trajectory through legal and policy-intensive government positions,
including service at the Department of Social Welfare and Development (DSWD) at the undersecretary level,
researchers may consult the records of the National Library of the Philippines and the Civil Service Commission
for primary documentation of her academic background.
What is clear from her public record is that her professional formation was shaped as much by lived political
experience as by formal schooling. Growing up as the daughter of a lawyer-sultan who governed a city in one of
the Philippines' most politically complex provinces gave her a working knowledge of governance, Islamic
jurisprudence, and community negotiation that no classroom alone could have provided.
Career
Provincial Government and DSWD
Before her appointment to the cabinet, Bae Omerah served as Vice Governor of Lanao del Sur, giving her direct
experience in managing provincial governance under the pressures that define politics in Muslim Mindanao.<ref
name="bangsa_sultan" />
She later moved into national service, serving as an Undersecretary of the Department of Social Welfare and
Development (DSWD), where she worked on poverty alleviation and community welfare programs with particular
relevance to Muslim Filipino communities.<ref name="moroherald" />
Cooperative Development Authority
From her work at DSWD, Dianalan-Lucman transitioned to lead the Cooperative Development Authority (CDA),
where she served as Administrator and Chairperson for five years.<ref name="moroherald" />
At the CDA, she became a committed advocate for the cooperative movement as a tool for economic
empowerment in Muslim Mindanao. Her core argument was straightforward: you cannot build a lasting peace in a
community where people have no economic stake in the outcome. Financial literacy and access to capital, in her
view, were prerequisites for political stability, not luxuries to be addressed after the security situation improved.
Her years at the CDA also gave her a practical command of Islamic microfinance principles, particularly the
concept of Riba-free (interest-free) credit that aligns with Shari'ah law, a framework she would later formalize as
NCMF Secretary through the Bureau of Muslim Economic Affairs.
She also carried her advocacy into environmental and civil society spaces during this period. As president of the
Provincial Multi-sectoral Women's Council (PMWC), she championed the protection of Lake Lanao, calling for a
coalition of stakeholders from government, the private sector, and traditional community leaders to halt the
environmental degradation of the lake that is central to Maranao identity.<ref name="mgpnews">MAGKAISA
tungo sa GANAP na PAG-UNLAD News. "Lake Lanao Stakeholders' Conference." mgpnews2016.blogspot.com.
2006.</ref>

PAGE 4
The NCMF Appointment (2010)
On February 18, 2010, President Gloria Macapagal-Arroyo signed Republic Act No. 9997, the National
Commission on Muslim Filipinos Act of 2009, abolishing the 23-year-old Office on Muslim Affairs and replacing
it with a full-fledged commission with expanded powers.<ref name="ra9997" /> The law took effect on March 6,
2010.
Bae Omerah took her oath of office on March 10, 2010, one day before the constitutional ban on appointments took
effect ahead of the May 10 national elections.<ref name="ca_decision">Philstar.com. "CA Affirms Dismissal of 5
GMA Midnight Appointees." philstar.com. September 1, 2012.</ref>
President Arroyo officially designated her as the pioneer Secretary and Chief Executive Officer of the NCMF,
making her the first woman to lead the Philippines' primary government body for Muslim affairs.<ref
name="ncmf_southluzon" /><ref name="moroherald" />
The commission she inherited was brand new in name but burdened with the institutional inertia of the agency it
replaced. Her first task was not policy, but architecture: drafting the organizational structure, establishing the
functional bureaus, and defining what it actually meant for the NCMF to be a "policy body" rather than a logistical
office that mainly processed Hajj applications.
Tenure as NCMF Secretary (2010–2012)
Building the Institution
Dianalan-Lucman's two years at the NCMF were defined by a determined effort to expand what the agency thought
it was allowed to do. The OMA had largely defined itself around the annual Hajj pilgrimage and occasional cultural
events. She insisted that the NCMF's mandate under RA 9997 was far broader, and she moved quickly to build the
internal structures that could carry that mandate.
She established functional bureaus covering External Relations, Muslim Economic Affairs, and Legal Affairs,
ensuring that the NCMF could advise the President of the Philippines on matters ranging from international Islamic
diplomacy to the enforcement of Muslim Personal Laws in regions outside the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in
Muslim Mindanao (BARMM).<ref name="ncmf_wiki">Wikipedia. "National Commission on Muslim Filipinos."
en.wikipedia.org. Accessed 2024.</ref>
The Organizational Structure and Manual of Operations she developed during this period became the
administrative template that successive NCMF leaderships have built upon.<ref name="ncmf_southluzon" />
Hajj Reforms
One of her first major executive actions as Secretary was a total audit of the pilgrimage administration. The OMA's
Hajj operations had long been plagued by "ghost pilgrims," hidden fees, and unaccredited travel agencies
exploiting the process.
Dianalan-Lucman implemented stricter accreditation requirements for travel agencies and medical service
providers. She also worked to reduce the dependence on middlemen who extracted fees without providing
legitimate services to pilgrims.

PAGE 5
She actively engaged with Muslim communities across the country, launching a nationwide consultation and
dialogue with pilgrims and local communities to understand their concerns firsthand.<ref
name="phifocy">Philippine Foreign Policy (PHIFOCY) Blog. "Philippines/Islam: NCMF Consulting Moro
Communities Nationwide." phifocy-lavariaskarlao.blogspot.com. 2010.</ref>
She also recommended to Malacañang the official date of Eid'l Fitr as a national holiday, and formally requested an
Eid'l Fitr reception at Malacañang Palace from President Benigno Aquino III, reinforcing the symbolic visibility of
Muslim Filipinos within the national government.<ref name="abna">ABNA News Agency. "Eid'l Fitr in
Philippines on Sept. 10." en.abna24.com. August 30, 2010.</ref>
Madrasah Education and Shari'ah
Dianalan-Lucman directed the NCMF to collaborate with the Department of Education (DepEd) to standardize the
Arabic Language and Islamic Values Education (ALIVE) program, pushing for the formal integration of Madrasah
education into the national curriculum rather than its treatment as a peripheral or informal track.
She was also a vocal advocate for strengthening the Shari'ah court system in the Philippines, particularly in areas
outside the BARMM where Muslim Filipinos live in significant numbers but have limited access to Shari'ah
adjudication.
She initiated a formal review of the Code of Muslim Personal Laws (Presidential Decree No. 1083) to identify
implementation gaps in the Shari'ah court system, arguing that legal reform had to accompany institutional reform
if the NCMF was to genuinely protect the rights of Muslim Filipinos.
Islamic Microfinance
Drawing directly from her years at the CDA, she directed the NCMF's Bureau of Muslim Economic Affairs to
promote Islamic microfinance, specifically Riba-free credit facilities for small Muslim-owned businesses. The goal
was to give Muslim entrepreneurs access to capital without forcing them to choose between economic survival and
religious compliance with the prohibition on interest-bearing loans.
Interreligious Outreach
Her NCMF also extended its reach beyond internal Muslim affairs. She commended the cooperation of local
government units from predominantly Christian areas, such as Compostela Valley, that hosted the 38th Regional
Qur'an Reading Competition for Region XI, using the event as a model for interreligious goodwill and cultural
understanding.<ref name="oma_davao">National Commission on Muslim Filipinos (OMA Davao Blog).
"Regional Qur'an Reading Competition." omadavao.blogspot.com. Accessed 2024.</ref>
Challenges and Controversies
The Midnight Appointment Dispute
The transition from the Arroyo to the Aquino administration in 2010 placed Dianalan-Lucman at the center of a
politically charged constitutional dispute.

PAGE 6
Shortly after President Benigno Aquino III assumed office, his administration issued Executive Order No. 2, which
sought to revoke the appointments of nearly a thousand "midnight appointees" made by the Arroyo government in
the months before the May 2010 elections.
Dianalan-Lucman was among the appointees targeted. She fought back, filing a petition before the Supreme Court
of the Philippines, arguing that EO No. 2 unconstitutionally expanded the definition of a midnight appointment and
effectively amended a provision of law through executive action.<ref name="gma_news">GMA News Online.
"Aquino Hits SC Decision on 'Midnight Appointee.'" gmanetwork.com. October 14, 2010.</ref>
"[Executive Order No. 2] unduly expands the constitutional definition of appointments and must be
stricken down as void for over-breadth. In one fell swoop, through the mere issuance of EO 2,
Malacañang has cut down the term of the NCMF secretary, amending through executive action a
provision of the law which only Congress could lawfully amend."
The Supreme Court agreed with her preliminary arguments, issuing a status quo ante order that temporarily
prevented the Aquino administration from removing her from office.<ref name="gma_news" /> The case
eventually moved to the Court of Appeals, which remanded the factual issues from the Supreme Court.
In its ruling, the Court of Appeals held that Dianalan-Lucman was not a midnight appointee. The CA found that she
took her oath of office on March 10, 2010, one day before the constitutional ban on appointments took effect on
March 11, and that her right to enter the position was "plenary and complete" from the moment she was sworn in.
<ref name="ca_decision" />
The Aquino administration also argued, separately, that she was disqualified from leading the NCMF because, as a
woman, she could not serve as leader of the Hajj mission according to Islamic tradition. The Court of Appeals
rejected this argument, citing a sworn affidavit from Islamic law expert Aleem Said Ahmad Basher, who explained
that leading the Hajj mission is "more of a social, ceremonial or diplomatic function" and that a woman is fully
qualified to serve in that capacity.<ref name="ca_decision" />
Despite the favorable rulings, the political climate made her continued tenure untenable. She eventually accepted
the transition, turning over the agency in April 2012 to incoming Secretary Mehol K. Sadain.<ref
name="ncmf_southluzon" /><ref name="oma_davao" />
She remained as a Commissioner of the NCMF for the remainder of her four-year commission term, ending in
2014.
Personal Values and Leadership Style
Those who worked alongside Dianalan-Lucman consistently describe a leader who governed by consensus rather
than decree. Her approach to policy-making was grounded in the Islamic principle of Shura (consultation), and she
made a deliberate practice of engaging with religious leaders (Ulama) and traditional community elders before
finalizing policy directions.
This was not merely a political strategy. It reflected her genuine belief that government decisions affecting Muslim
communities should carry the endorsement of those communities' recognized spiritual and customary authorities,
not just the signature of a cabinet secretary.
She was also deeply comfortable operating in two worlds simultaneously. In Manila, she navigated the bureaucratic
machinery of the national government with the confidence of an experienced technocrat. In Lanao and in Muslim
communities across the country, she moved as a daughter of the sultanate, grounded in the Maranao concept of
Maratabat, the honor and sense of collective dignity that the Maranao people attach to their public representatives.

PAGE 7
Her decision to maintain her hijab and her traditional identity while serving in a cabinet-level role was itself a quiet
but powerful statement, one that demonstrated to Muslim women across the Philippines that the halls of
Malacañang and the institutions of the Philippine state were not spaces they were required to erase themselves to
enter.
Legacy and Cultural Significance
Bae Omerah Hafidah D. Dianalan-Lucman's place in Bangsamoro history rests on two pillars: what she built and
what she represented.
What she built is concrete and verifiable. The NCMF she inherited was an agency that barely existed on paper. The
NCMF she handed over in 2012 had an organizational structure, a set of functional bureaus, a reformed Hajj
administration, and a stated mandate to advise the Philippine presidency on the full spectrum of Muslim Filipino
concerns. She turned a 23-year-old government office into a commission with genuine policy ambitions.
What she represented is harder to quantify but no less significant. She was the first woman to serve as the head of
the Philippine government's primary agency for Muslim affairs, and she held that position while facing a politically
motivated challenge to her appointment, a legal argument questioning her religious authority, and the institutional
inertia of an agency transitioning from one identity to another.
The fact that she prevailed on each of those fronts, legally, institutionally, and symbolically, tells you something
about the caliber of the person behind the title.
For the Bangsamoro people, and particularly for Maranao women, her career stands as evidence of a proposition
that was not self-evident at the time: that a woman rooted in Islamic faith and Maranao tradition could lead the
most important Muslim affairs body in the country, and do so on her own terms.
Recognition
As the inaugural Secretary of the NCMF, Dianalan-Lucman occupies a permanent place in the institutional memory
of the Commission. Her name appears in the official history of the NCMF as the first in its line of Secretaries/Chief
Executive Officers.<ref name="ncmf_southluzon" />
Her work at the CDA before the NCMF also earned her recognition in the cooperative sector, where her advocacy
for Islamic microfinance and financial literacy programs in Mindanao was noted by stakeholders in both the
cooperative movement and the Muslim civil society.
Specific awards and formal recognitions have not been fully documented in publicly available sources, and
researchers are encouraged to consult the Official Gazette archives from the period of 2010 to 2012 and the records
of the National Library of the Philippines for primary documentation of her official recognitions.

title: Dilangalen, Didagen Piang
text:
PAGE 1
Didagen "Digs" Piang
Dilangalen
Personal Information
Born: January 8, 1954
Kabuntalan, Maguindanao
Died: November 6, 2021 (aged 67)
Heritage
Ethnicity: Maguindanaoan
Religion: Islam
Family
Father: Haji Datu Alamanza "Datu
Mongang" Dilangalen
Mother: Haja Bai Pangandongan
Piang
Spouse: Bai Zeny Dilangalen
Children: Bai Donna Dilangalen
(among others)
Political Career
Party: Various (KNP, pro-Estrada
coalition)
Positions held:
Representative, 1st District of
Maguindanao with Cotabato City
Didagen Piang Dilangalen
Atty. Didagen "Digs" Piang Dilangalen (January 8, 1954 – November 6, 2021) was a Filipino human rights
lawyer, constitutionalist, and congressman who represented the 1st District of Maguindanao with Cotabato City for
three consecutive terms, and later the lone district of Shariff Kabunsuan.
He was widely recognized for his thunderous oratory, unyielding
principles, and a fierce style of legislative debate that made him one
of the most recognizable faces on the floor of the House of
Representatives.
A descendant of Datu Piang (known historically as "Amai
Mingka"), one of the most consequential leaders in the history of
Muslim Mindanao, Dilangalen carried the weight of a remarkable
lineage into every courtroom and plenary session he entered. He
passed away on November 6, 2021, at the age of 67, following an
illness, mourned across party lines and across the breadth of
Bangsamoro society.

EARLY LIFE AND ROYAL HERITAGE
Didagen Piang Dilangalen was born on January 8, 1954, in
Kabuntalan, Maguindanao, into a family whose roots ran deep in
the political and spiritual history of the region.

PAGE 2
(1995–2004)
Representative, Shariff Kabunsuan
Lone District (2007–2010)
Legal Career
Human rights lawyer and trial attorney
Defense counsel, Estrada Impeachment
Trial (2000–2001)
Legal counsel, Marcos Jr. 2016 vice-
presidential canvassing
Notability
Maguindanaoan lawyer-legislator,
descendant of Datu Piang, firebrand
defender of Bangsamoro self-
determination, and one of the
Philippines' most recognizable
congressional voices of his era
Known For
"Shut Up, Mr. Speaker" outburst during
2004 presidential canvassing; defense
of Sarah Balabagan; three terms as 1st
District representative; EDSA III
leadership; Bangsamoro self-
determination advocacy
His father was Haji Datu Alamanza "Datu Mongang" Dilangalen, a
figure connected to the Raja Buayan Sultanate on the paternal side.
His mother, Haja Bai Pangandongan Piang, was the granddaughter
of the legendary Datu Piang, the dominant chieftain of the Pulangi
River valley who had navigated the Maguindanaoan world through
the tumultuous transitions of the Spanish colonial era, the American
period, and the early decades of Philippine state formation.
That maternal link to Datu Piang was not simply a matter of
genealogical prestige. It meant that Dilangalen grew up aware of a
particular tradition: the idea that political leadership and the defense
of Bangsamoro interests were inseparable from personal courage
and an uncompromising public voice. By all accounts, he lived that
tradition fully.
He pursued a legal education and emerged as an aggressive,
committed human rights defender and trial lawyer before he ever
entered electoral politics. The courtroom, for Dilangalen, was never
just a professional venue. It was, from the beginning, an arena for
the defense of the vulnerable.
LEGAL CAREER
The Sarah Balabagan Case
Of all the high-profile cases Atty. Dilangalen handled in his legal career, none drew more international attention
than the case of Sarah Balabagan.
Balabagan was a 14-year-old Filipina overseas worker who had been sentenced to death in the United Arab
Emirates after killing her employer, who had attempted to rape her. The case became a cause celebre in the
Philippines, igniting debates about the protection of overseas Filipino workers, the treatment of Muslim Filipinos
abroad, and the responsibilities of the Philippine government toward its most vulnerable citizens.
Dilangalen joined the defense effort and helped push for diplomatic and legal intervention. His work contributed to
securing Balabagan's release and her eventual return to the Philippines in 1997. The case remained one of the
defining moments of his legal career, and it illustrated something essential about Dilangalen as a lawyer: he was
most motivated when the stakes were highest and the client had the fewest resources.
The Estrada Impeachment Trial
When President Joseph Estrada faced impeachment proceedings in 2000 and 2001, Dilangalen was part of the core
defense counsel that represented the sitting president before the Senate acting as an impeachment court. The trial
was one of the most dramatic in Philippine constitutional history, stretching across months of televised hearings
that captivated the country.
Dilangalen's role in the proceedings reflected both his legal credentials and his personal loyalty to Estrada, a
loyalty that would prove defining in the years to come.

PAGE 3
The 2016 Marcos Vice-Presidential Canvassing
In 2016, Dilangalen served as the legal counsel for Ferdinand "Bongbong" Marcos Jr. during the congressional
canvassing of votes for the vice-presidential election. The canvassing was contested and politically charged, and
Dilangalen's involvement placed him again at the center of a nationally significant legal proceeding.
POLITICAL CAREER
First Congressional Stint: 1st District of Maguindanao with Cotabato City (1995–2004)
Dilangalen first won a seat in the House of Representatives in 1995, representing the 1st District of Maguindanao
with Cotabato City. He would go on to serve three consecutive terms in that position, covering the period from
1995 to 2004, which meant he had "graduated" from that seat in the Philippine term-limits sense, having served the
maximum consecutive terms allowed.
During his first term, he was recognized as one of the "10 Most Outstanding Congressmen of the Philippines," a
recognition that acknowledged both his legislative productivity and his early track record in bringing concrete
development to his constituents. He was notably described, in official Bangsamoro Parliament tributes, as the first
congressman in his district to distribute infrastructure and livelihood projects to every single barangay under his
jurisdiction during that initial term.
His legislative record was substantive. He authored House Bill 1933, which sought free preschool public education,
a measure ahead of its time in terms of its focus on early childhood education as a public good. He also sponsored
more than 3,000 scholars from Luzon, Visayas, and Mindanao, a program that extended the reach of his public
service well beyond the borders of his own district.
One of his most lasting physical contributions to the region was his donation of a significant portion of the five-
hectare land parcel on which the Sultan Haji Hassanal Bolkiah Mosque, the Grand Mosque of Cotabato, was
eventually built. The mosque stands today as the largest mosque in the Philippines, and Dilangalen's land
contribution was a direct expression of his commitment to the spiritual infrastructure of the Bangsamoro
community.
2004 Senatorial Bid
In 2004, Dilangalen ran for the Senate under the Koalisyon ng Nagkakaisang Pilipino (KNP), the coalition backing
presidential candidate Fernando Poe Jr. He did not win a Senate seat, but his loyalty to the Estrada-aligned political
network remained firm. Following the election, he served as Joseph Estrada's official spokesperson, a role that kept
him in the national political conversation even outside of formal office.
Second Congressional Stint: Shariff Kabunsuan Lone District (2007–2010)
Dilangalen returned to the House of Representatives in 2007, this time representing the newly created lone district
of Shariff Kabunsuan, a province carved out from Maguindanao. The arrangement was short-lived on a legal level:
the Supreme Court, in 2008, nullified the creation of Shariff Kabunsuan as a separate province in the case Sema v.
Commission on Elections, ruling that it had been created through a regional assembly ordinance rather than through
a national law. Despite the nullification, Dilangalen's representation of the district during the period remained part
of his formal legislative record.

PAGE 4
ICONIC CONTROVERSIES AND POLITICAL FIRE
No account of Didagen Dilangalen is complete without discussing what made him genuinely famous, not just in
political circles but across Philippine popular culture: his absolute fearlessness on the plenary floor and his
willingness to say, loudly and publicly, what others would only whisper.
"Shut Up, Mr. Speaker"
The moment that most Filipinos remember, if they remember Dilangalen at all, is a single outburst during the 2004
presidential canvassing at the Batasang Pambansa.
The canvassing was contentious. Dilangalen, representing the interests of the Estrada-aligned opposition and
arguing that election irregularities were being ignored, was in the thick of the protests on the floor. When his
arguments were cut off by Deputy Speaker Raul Gonzalez, Dilangalen did not pause to choose his words carefully.
He turned to the chair and said, directly and loudly: "Shut up, Mr. Speaker!"
The clip was replayed on national television for years afterward. It became a fixture of Philippine political blooper
compilations, a meme before the word existed in its current form, and a genuine marker of a particular era of
congressional drama. But those who knew Dilangalen's work emphasized that the moment, while memorable, was
not representative of a man given to theatrics for their own sake. It was representative of someone who genuinely
did not believe that decorum should trump accountability.
EDSA III Leadership
Following the ouster of Joseph Estrada in January 2001, Dilangalen was among those who refused to accept the
political transition quietly. He helped lead the "EDSA III" mobilization in April 2001, which brought a massive
crowd of working-class Estrada loyalists to the streets of Manila. The mobilization culminated in an attempt to
storm Malacañang Palace, and it represented one of the most intense episodes of post-Estrada political unrest.
Dilangalen's leadership in EDSA III was consistent with his broader political identity: a man who believed that
those in power owed a reckoning to those who had been pushed aside, and who was willing to put himself in the
middle of that confrontation.
PASSING AND LEGACY
Atty. Didagen Dilangalen passed away on the morning of November 6, 2021, following an illness. He was 67 years
old.
The mourning that followed crossed political lines in a way that spoke to the genuine respect he had accumulated
over decades in public life. The Bangsamoro Transition Authority Parliament passed Resolution No. 186 in his
honor, a formal tribute that documented his contributions to grassroots development, constitutional advocacy, and
Bangsamoro political representation.
Allies and former rivals offered tributes. Senator Imee Marcos, whose family Dilangalen had represented in a high-
stakes legal proceeding just five years before his death, was among those who praised him as a brilliant statesman
who combined fiery courage with profound humility. Regional Bangsamoro transition leaders added their voices to
the chorus.

PAGE 5
His political mantle passed to his family. His wife, Bai Zeny Dilangalen, and his daughter, Bai Donna Dilangalen,
carried the family's continuing presence in the political life of the region forward after his death.
What Dilangalen left behind was not just a legislative record or a list of courtroom victories. He left behind a
particular style of public advocacy: loud, loyal, principled, and deeply rooted in the conviction that the
Bangsamoro people deserved a full-throated voice at every table where their fate was being decided.
HONORS AND RECOGNITION
Named one of the "10 Most Outstanding Congressmen of the Philippines" during his early congressional
tenure
Subject of Bangsamoro Parliament Resolution No. 186, a formal tribute to his life and public service
Recognized by allies and political figures across the spectrum for his contributions to Bangsamoro
representation and human rights advocacy

title: Dilangalen, Mantil G.
text:
PAGE 1
Datu Mantil G. Dilangalen
Personal Information
Full Name: Datu Mantil G. Dilangalen
Ethnicity
Maguindanaon
Region
Cotabato, Mindanao, Philippines
Military Rank
Lieutenant Colonel (Lt. Col.)
Military Unit
People's Revolutionary Army; 10th
Military District (USAFFE)
Education
Los Baños College of Agriculture (now
part of the University of the Philippines
system)
Clan / Family
Dilangalen clan, Maguindanao region
Notable Descendants
Mantil G. Dilangalen
Datu Mantil G. Dilangalen (Lieutenant Colonel) was a prominent
Maguindanaon Moro leader and World War II guerrilla commander
from Mindanao, Philippines.
Operating in the Cotabato region during one of the most turbulent
periods in Philippine history, he is remembered for three things
above all: organizing early, structured anti-Japanese resistance when
most of the formal military had already collapsed, bringing together
diverse local forces under a single unified command, and protecting
both Muslim and Christian communities from foreign occupation at
a time when it would have been far easier to simply look the other
way.
His story is one of a traditional Moro datu who carried ancestral
responsibilities into a modern war, and who proved that those two
worlds were never as far apart as they seemed.
Contents
1 EARLY LIFE AND BACKGROUND
2 WORLD WAR II AND RESISTANCE LEADERSHIP
3 FORMATION OF THE PEOPLE'S REVOLUTIONARY
ARMY
4 THE LIBERATION OF MIDSAYAP
5 THE MARKETPLACE AMBUSH
6 INTEGRATION INTO THE 10TH MILITARY DISTRICT
7 POSTHUMOUS RECOGNITION AND LEGACY
8 FAMILY AND CONTINUED PUBLIC SERVICE
9 REFERENCES
EARLY LIFE AND BACKGROUND
Datu Mantil belonged to the Dilangalen clan, one of the influential
political and noble families rooted in the Maguindanao region.
Growing up in the traditional ruling class of the Moro people meant
that certain values came with the territory: community leadership,
ancestral land stewardship, and martial prowess were not just ideals
but expectations placed on every generation of the family.
Before the war upended everything, Datu Mantil pursued higher
education at the Los Baños College of Agriculture, which is now
part of the University of the Philippines system.

PAGE 2
Didagen "Digs" Dilangalen (former
Representative/human rights lawyer);
Datu Ramil Dilangalen (Municipal
Mayor, Northern Kabuntalan, BARMM)
Awards
Centennial Recognition Award, Ayala
Group of Companies (1998,
posthumous)
Notability
Maguindanaon Moro noble and WWII
guerrilla commander who organized
early anti-Japanese resistance in
Cotabato, co-founded the People's
Revolutionary Army, and led the
liberation of Midsayap in 1942.
Known For
Founding the People's Revolutionary
Army (1942); Liberation of Midsayap;
cross-community defense of Muslim and
Christian Mindanaoans during the
Japanese occupation.
That detail alone sets him apart. Archival records and family
photographs from this period document a young man navigating the
multicultural environment of a national university while never
losing sight of who he was. Photographs from that era show him in
traditional Maguindanaon Moro warrior attire even while studying
alongside students from across the Philippines, which speaks
volumes about both his confidence and his rootedness in his own
culture.
This early immersion in a world beyond Cotabato was far from
incidental. The relationships he built with non-Moro Filipinos
during those university years would later prove decisive when he
needed to forge alliances across ethnic and religious lines in the
middle of a war.
WORLD WAR II AND RESISTANCE
LEADERSHIP
When the United States Armed Forces in the Far East (USAFFE)
surrendered in May 1942, much of Mindanao found itself in a
dangerous limbo. Many areas either descended into chaos or fell
under direct Japanese military supervision, and for most of the
formal military structure, resistance was no longer an organized option.
Datu Mantil refused to accept that.
Rather than submit to the occupying forces, he began organizing a localized defense force from the ground up in
the Cotabato region, drawing on his clan's standing, his personal networks, and his own authority as a datu to bring
fighters together.
FORMATION OF THE PEOPLE'S REVOLUTIONARY ARMY
In September 1942, Datu Mantil made contact with Froilan Matas, who was leading another armed local group
operating in the same area.
Both men understood something that smaller resistance bands often failed to see: fragmented, isolated units were
easy targets. The Japanese could simply deal with them one by one. What the region needed was a unified front.
Recognizing this, Datu Mantil and Matas officially fused their followers into a single, cohesive unit named the
People's Revolutionary Army. The merger was both a practical military decision and a statement of intent: this
was not going to be a scattered, uncoordinated insurgency. It was going to be an organized force with a clear chain
of command.
Below is a simplified diagram of how the command structure came together:
[Datu Mantil Dilangalen]     [Froilan Matas]
 (Midsayap Guerrillas)    (Local Armed Forces)
          \                      /
           \                    /
            v                  v
      [People's Revolutionary Army]

PAGE 3
(Fused: September 1942)
                   |
                   v
         [Liberation of Midsayap]
       (Flag Raising: Oct 6, 1942)
THE LIBERATION OF MIDSAYAP
By early October 1942, the People's Revolutionary Army moved from organizing to action.
Town Occupation (October 2, 1942): Datu Mantil's joint command marched into the strategic town of Midsayap,
which Japanese troops had temporarily vacated, and took occupation of the area.
Flag Raising (October 6, 1942): Four days later, the forces formally took control of the municipal center. In a
moment that carried as much symbolic weight as military significance, they raised the American and Filipino flags
together, side by side, on the exact spot where the Japanese military emblem had been flying. It was a deliberate
and powerful act of defiance.
THE MARKETPLACE AMBUSH
The Japanese did not let the occupation of Midsayap go unanswered.
On October 8, 1942, Datu Mantil was in the middle of a public marketplace, in the process of inducting new
officers and volunteers into the People's Revolutionary Army, when two truckloads of Japanese reinforcement
troops arrived to launch a surprise counterattack near the Midsayap junction.
The setting could not have been more dangerous: a crowded civilian area, no advance warning, and an enemy force
arriving in force.
Despite the sudden chaos, Datu Mantil's forces quickly organized a defensive perimeter and engaged the enemy at
two distinct points simultaneously. When the battle ended, the guerrillas had successfully repelled the assault,
killing twenty-one Japanese soldiers and wounding several others. It was an early, significant tactical victory for
the Cotabato resistance, achieved under the most difficult possible conditions.
INTEGRATION INTO THE 10TH MILITARY DISTRICT
As the months wore on, the People's Revolutionary Army grew. More fighters joined, additional arms were
secured, and the unit's tactics became sharper through experience.
The Army continued to harass Japanese occupying forces across multiple fronts: at Bulanan, Lumopig, Salunayan,
and Libungan, keeping constant pressure on the enemy's grip over the region.
Eventually, Datu Mantil's forces were absorbed into the broader, unified network of the 10th Military District,
under the command of Colonel Wendell Fertig. This wider network received formal recognition from General
Douglas MacArthur's Southwest Pacific Area command, bringing the Cotabato resistance into the official Allied
military structure.
Throughout his active military service, Datu Mantil held the rank of Lieutenant Colonel (Lt. Col.).

PAGE 4
POSTHUMOUS RECOGNITION AND LEGACY
Datu Mantil's wartime leadership did something that outlasted the war itself: it established a working precedent for
cross-cultural cooperation between the Moro and Christian populations of Mindanao against a shared adversary.
At a time when communal divisions could easily have been exploited by an occupying force, he chose a different
path, one that placed the defense of all communities above ethnic or religious boundaries.
Centennial Award (March 16, 1998): As part of the nationwide Philippine Independence Centennial Celebrations,
Datu Mantil was honored posthumously in General Santos City. He received a prestigious Centennial Recognition
Award sponsored by the Ayala Group of Companies through the Ayala Business Club. The award formally
recognized his historical role as a defender of freedom who risked both his life and his status as a Moro noble to
maintain local autonomy during the occupation.
FAMILY AND CONTINUED PUBLIC SERVICE
The Dilangalen lineage remains deeply embedded in the civic and political landscape of the Bangsamoro region,
with the next generations carrying on a tradition of public service that their ancestor helped define.
Didagen "Digs" Dilangalen is a prominent human rights lawyer who served as a long-time member of the House
of Representatives, representing Cotabato City and the 1st District of Maguindanao.
Datu Ramil Dilangalen serves as a contemporary local chief executive, currently holding the position of
Municipal Mayor of Northern Kabuntalan within the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao
(BARMM).
Below is a simplified family lineage diagram:
         [Datu Mantil G. Dilangalen]
           (WWII Guerrilla Commander)
                      |
                      v
             [Prominent Descendants]
                      |
      +---------------+---------------+
      |                               |
      v                               v
[Didagen "Digs" Dilangalen] [Datu Ramil Dilangalen] (Former Representative/Lawyer) (Municipal Mayor,
BARMM)

title: Dimaampao, Japar B.
text:
PAGE 1
Japar B. Dimaampao
Japar Babay Dimaampao (born December 27, 1963) is the 191st Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the
Philippines, appointed on July 2, 2021, by President Rodrigo Duterte.<ref name="sc_profile">Justice Japar B.
Dimaampao, Supreme Court of the Philippines. https://sc.judiciary.gov.ph/justice-japar-b-dimaampao/</ref> He
made history as the first Maranao and only the second Muslim ever to sit on the Philippine High Court, breaking a
26-year absence of Muslim representation on the bench since Justice Abdulwahid Bidin of Tawi-Tawi retired in
1995.<ref name="wikipedia">Japar Dimaampao, Wikipedia.
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japar_Dimaampao</ref> Before that breakthrough came, he had to apply sixteen
times and survive thirteen JBC shortlists, turning what many would call a discouraging slog into something that the
Bangsamoro community now reads as a story of extraordinary faith and grit.<ref name="abs_cbn">Marawi native
is latest Supreme Court justice; only 2nd magistrate. ABS-CBN News, September 14, 2021. https://www.abs-
cbn.com/news/09/14/21/after-many-tries-marawi-native-finally-appointed-supreme-court-justice</ref>
Dimaampao is a rare combination in any court: a Certified Public Accountant turned lawyer turned jurist, with deep
specializations in Taxation law, Commercial law, and Shari'ah jurisprudence. He spent seventeen years at the Court
of Appeals before his elevation, producing technically precise decisions and building a reputation as the kind of
judge who reads a fiscal statute the way an auditor reads a balance sheet. His seat on the Supreme Court represents
more than personal achievement; for the BARMM and the broader Filipino Muslim community, it signals that the
promise of inclusive governance is slowly, finally, being kept.

Early Life and Family Background
Dimaampao was born in Marawi City, the cultural and spiritual
capital of the Maranao people, on December 27, 1963.<ref
name="sc_profile" /> Marawi sits at the heart of Lanao del Sur
and has long been the center of Islamic learning and Maranao
identity in the Philippines, where the faith and the traditional adat
(customary law) have shaped community life for centuries.<ref
name="bta_parliament">Justice Japar B. Dimaampao,
Bangsamoro Parliament.
https://parliament.bangsamoro.gov.ph/wp-
content/uploads/2022/03/AR-157-Justice-Japar-B.-
Dimaampao.pdf</ref> Growing up there meant growing up with
an acute awareness of what it meant to be Maranao in a national
system that, for much of its history, did not reflect that identity.
His father, the late Magdara Dimaampao, was no ordinary figure
either. The elder Dimaampao served as a Commissioner of the
Commission on Elections (COMELEC) and later as the Philippine
Ambassador to Iraq, a combination of democratic administration
and international diplomacy that shaped the household Justice
Dimaampao grew up in.<ref name="wikipedia" /> That
environment, defined by procedural rigor, public accountability,
and the weight of institutional responsibility, clearly left its mark.
The barangays of Poona Bayabao and Lumba-Bayabao in Lanao
del Sur are also connected to his lineage, anchoring him to the
traditional leadership structures of the Maranao.<ref
name="bta_parliament" /> These weren't just sentimental ties.
They provided the community networks and the cultural capital
that would later rally behind him during his long campaign for a
seat on the Supreme Court. When the appointment finally came in
2021, the Bangsamoro Parliament hailed him as "a proud son of
Marawi," framing his elevation as a collective victory.<ref
name="barmm_official">BTA Parliament, Chief Minister
Ebrahim commend Dimaampao's appointment as 2nd Muslim SC
Justice. BARMM Official Website.
https://bangsamoro.gov.ph/news/latest-news/bta-parliament-chief-
minister-ebrahim-commend-dimaampaos-appointment-as-2nd-
muslim-sc-justice/</ref>
That victory carried extra resonance because of the 2017 Marawi
Siege, which left the city's center in ruins and displaced tens of
thousands of residents.<ref
name="businessmirror">BusinessMirror, January 28, 2023. Issuu.

PAGE 3
https://issuu.com/businessmirror/docs/businessmirror_january_28_2023</ref> For a community still rebuilding,
having one of their own on the country's highest court became a symbol of resilience, a reminder that Marawi's
story is not just about destruction.
Education and Professional Credentials
Dimaampao took an unusual academic route that still shapes how he thinks about the law. He studied at the
University of the East in Manila for both his undergraduate and legal degrees, graduating with a Bachelor of
Science in Business Administration, majoring in Accounting, in 1982.<ref name="wikipedia" /> After passing the
board examinations, he became a Certified Public Accountant (CPA), a credential that gave him something most
law students never develop: the instinct to follow the numbers.<ref name="sc_profile" />
He then completed his Bachelor of Laws at the University of the East College of Law in 1987 and was admitted to
the Philippine Bar.<ref name="wikipedia" /> This CPA-plus-lawyer combination is not common in the Philippine
judiciary, and it's precisely what made him the go-to expert on tax law cases throughout his career. In 2024, the
University of the East recognized his lifetime of contribution to legal scholarship by conferring upon him the
degree of Juris Doctor.<ref name="ue_jd">Dimaampao and Tinga receive Juris Doctor degree from UE.
Inquirer.net. https://newsinfo.inquirer.net/1933675/dimaampao-and-tinga-receive-juris-doctor-degree</ref>
His alma mater has a strong legacy in Philippine law, counting former Chief Justice Lucas Bersamin among its
graduates.<ref name="ue_college_of_law">University of the East College of Law, Wikipedia.
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_the_East_College_of_Law</ref> For Dimaampao, UE wasn't just a
starting point; it was a place he later returned to as a faculty member, completing the loop between student and
teacher.
Academic and Professional Credentials of Japar B. Dimaampao

Executive Branch Career
Before ever sitting on any bench, Dimaampao spent years in the thick of the government's executive operations,
working across three different agencies and picking up practical legal experience that no classroom could fully
replicate.
He started as a legal officer at the National Bureau of Investigation (NBI), where the work was decidedly less
theoretical: criminal investigations, evidence gathering, and the unglamorous mechanics of the justice system at its
most basic level.<ref name="wikipedia" /> From there, he moved to the Metropolitan Waterworks and Sewerage
System (MWSS) as a senior corporate attorney, handling regulatory compliance and the legal complexities of
public utilities.<ref name="wikipedia" /> He also served at COMELEC, following in his father's institutional
footsteps and gaining a close look at how the country's electoral democracy actually runs from the inside.<ref
name="wikipedia" />

PAGE 4
His most significant role in the executive branch came as a Senior State Prosecutor at the Department of Justice
(DOJ), where he became the first Muslim to hold that position in the department's history.<ref name="wikipedia"
/> That distinction mattered not just symbolically; it placed him at the forefront of high-profile criminal
prosecutions and required him to operate in a bureaucracy that had rarely seen someone with his background in a
senior role. The prosecutorial experience gave him a "view from the trenches" of the criminal justice system that
would later inform his measured approach to criminal law cases as a judge, where he consistently demonstrated
sensitivity to both the state's duty to prosecute and the accused's right to due process.<ref name="philstar">CA
justice Japar Dimaampao, known Muslim jurist, appointed to Supreme Court. Philstar.com, September 14, 2021.
https://www.philstar.com/headlines/2021/09/14/2127103/ca-justice-japar-dimaampao-known-muslim-jurist-
appointed-supreme-court</ref>
Judicial Career
Regional Trial Court (2000–2004)
Dimaampao entered the judiciary in 2000 when he was appointed Presiding Judge of Branch 208 of the Regional
Trial Court of Mandaluyong City.<ref name="sc_profile" /> Trial court work is where law meets life, and his four
years there grounded him in the practical realities of docket management, courtroom proceedings, and the human
stakes of litigation. He rose to become the Executive Judge of the Mandaluyong RTC, a role that added significant
administrative responsibility to the judicial function, requiring oversight of other judges and coordination of the
court's operations.<ref name="sc_profile" />
Court of Appeals (2004–2021)
In March 2004, President Gloria Macapagal-Arroyo appointed Dimaampao as an Associate Justice of the Court of
Appeals, making him the youngest magistrate in the appellate court at that time, at just 40 years old.<ref
name="wikipedia" /> He succeeded Justice Alicia Austria-Martinez and began what would become a seventeen-
year career at the country's second-highest court.<ref name="wikipedia" />
During his time at the CA, he eventually became Chairperson of the court's 3rd Division and served on key internal
committees, including the Committee on Rules/Raffle and the Committee on Inventory and Audit of Caseload of
Retiring Justices.<ref name="sc_profile" /> His decisions during this period are noted for their technical precision,
particularly in tax cases, where his CPA background gave him an edge in reading complex financial structures that
most other justices might have found opaque.<ref name="sc_profile" />

Judicial Level

Supreme Court of the Philippines (2021–present)
His appointment as the 191st Associate Justice of the Supreme Court, filling the vacancy left by Justice Alexander
Gesmundo who had been elevated to Chief Justice, came on July 2, 2021.<ref name="wikipedia" /> He took his
oath of office on September 14, 2021, to widespread celebration across the Bangsamoro region.<ref

PAGE 5
name="wikipedia" />
The JBC Marathon: Sixteen Applications and Counting
The most well-known chapter of Dimaampao's story is the one that almost didn't have a happy ending. He applied
for a seat on the Supreme Court a total of sixteen times, and during the Duterte administration alone, he appeared
on the JBC shortlist thirteen separate times without being chosen.<ref name="wikipedia" /> Within the legal
community, this became known simply as the "JBC marathon," and it was a test of character as much as
credentials.<ref name="mb_barmm">BARMM endorses Dimaampao as next SC justice. Manila Bulletin, October
27, 2019. https://mb.com.ph/2019/10/27/barmm-endorses-dimaampao-as-next-sc-justice/</ref>
Throughout that process, his supporters in the Bangsamoro Parliament and among Moro representatives in the
House of Representatives campaigned actively for his appointment, calling it a fulfillment of long-overdue
commitments to historical justice.<ref name="wikipedia" /> His own response to being repeatedly passed over
was, by all accounts, remarkably composed.
When JBC members asked him why he kept coming back, he pointed to his faith:
"God is with those who patiently persevere," and "God is the final disposer of affairs."<ref
name="abs_cbn" />
He also told the JBC that he held onto the secular idea that "hope springs eternal," and that he trusted his time
would come when the "fullness of time" allowed.<ref name="abs_cbn" /> That combination of spiritual conviction
and professional steadiness made him a distinctive presence in JBC hearings, where candidates are often
scrutinized primarily for political connections or institutional backing. Dimaampao maintained a consistently
respectful stance toward the President's appointing power, stating that he honored the discretion of the executive
branch while continuing to offer his services.<ref name="abs_cbn" />
Legal Scholarship and Published Works
Parallel to his judicial work, Dimaampao has built a serious reputation as a legal author and educator. His
textbooks on tax law are used in some unexpected places: Harvard Law School and the Islamic Science University
of Malaysia are among the institutions that reference his work.<ref name="centralbooks">Justice Japar B.
Dimaampao, Centralbooks. https://central.com.ph/book-author/japar-b-dimaampao/</ref> That kind of reach isn't
typical for Philippine legal authors, and it says something about the quality and clarity of his writing.
His published works include:
Basic Approach to Income Taxation (Rex Book Store): A foundational text that bridges accounting principles
and tax law for students and practitioners.<ref name="wikipedia" />
Tax Principles and Remedies (Rex Book Store): A detailed guide to the administrative and judicial processes
in tax disputes.<ref name="wikipedia" />
Bar Essentials in Commercial Law (Central Books): A comprehensive Bar examination reference for
commercial law subjects.<ref name="wikipedia" />
Bar Q&A for the Past 10 Years: Taxation Law (Central Books): A study aid analyzing recurring Bar exam
patterns in taxation.<ref name="wikipedia" />
Statutory and Judicial Quick Guide to Local Government, Real Property, and Taxation: A specialized
reference for sub-national fiscal policy and real property law.<ref name="centralbooks" />

PAGE 6
As a classroom teacher, Dimaampao has taught at the University of the East, the University of Santo Tomas Faculty
of Civil Law, San Beda University (both Mendiola and Alabang campuses), and the De La Salle University Tañada-
Diokno School of Law.<ref name="sc_profile" /> His teaching style is known for making complex concepts
genuinely accessible, without dumbing them down, a quality that also runs through his judicial writing.<ref
name="philja_journal">Philippine Judicial Academy Journal, Vol. 16, Issue 41.
https://philja.judiciary.gov.ph/files/journal/vol16issue41.pdf</ref>
At the Philippine Judicial Academy (PHILJA), he serves as a Professorial Lecturer II at the Department of Shari'ah
and Islamic Jurisprudence, training judges and court personnel in Islamic law.<ref name="sc_profile" /> His
contributions to the field of taxation were recognized in 2018 when he was named the Metrobank Foundation
Professorial Chairholder in Taxation Law and the Pedro Concepcion Professorial Chairholder for
Commercial Law.<ref name="sc_profile" />
Shari'ah Advocacy and Islamic Law Integration
Dimaampao is probably the most visible advocate for the Shari'ah justice system within the mainstream Philippine
legal framework, and he's made it clear that his advocacy comes from principle, not just identity politics.
The Philippine Shari'ah courts were established by the 1977 Code of Muslim Personal Laws to govern the personal
and family matters of Muslims, but the system has long remained incomplete without a dedicated appellate
structure. When appeals from Shari'ah District Courts land in the secular Court of Appeals or the Supreme Court,
the reviewing justices may lack the theological and linguistic expertise needed to interpret Shari'ah doctrines
accurately.<ref name="sc_shariah">G.R. No. 211089, Maliga v. Tingao. SC E-Library.
https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/69172</ref> For Dimaampao, this is not a minor
administrative gap; it's a structural injustice.
He has been a consistent advocate for the creation of a Shari'ah Appellate Court and for the formal integration of
Shari'ah rules of procedure into the national judicial infrastructure.<ref name="bta_parliament" /> At the first
National Shari'ah Summit, he made the case that integrating Shari'ah is not about separating Muslim Filipinos from
the national system; it's about making the system genuinely whole:
Integrating Shari'ah into the Philippine legal framework is not about division but about binding the
nation's multicultural influences into a cohesive whole.<ref name="inquirer_shariah">SC embarks on
effort to strengthen PH's shari'ah justice system. Inquirer.net. https://newsinfo.inquirer.net/1738719/sc-
embarks-on-effort-to-strengthen-phs-shariah-justice-system</ref>
His practical contributions in this area include chairmanship of the 2020 Special Shari'ah Bar Examinations and
service as Co-Vice Chairperson of the Technical Working Group on Shari'ah.<ref name="wikipedia" /> He has also
pushed for the digitalization and modernization of Shari'ah court procedures, aligning them with the Supreme
Court's broader technology agenda under the Strategic Plan for Judicial Innovations 2022–2027.<ref
name="sc_shariah_indispensable">Justice Dimaampao: Shari'ah an Indispensable Component of the Philippine
Legal Framework. Supreme Court of the Philippines. https://sc.judiciary.gov.ph/justice-dimaampao-shariah-an-
indispensable-component-of-the-philippine-legal-framework/</ref>
Judicial Philosophy
Dimaampao's judicial philosophy centers on constitutional supremacy and a carefully defined version of judicial
activism. In his JBC interviews, he stated plainly that he would be guided by the definition of judicial power under
Article VIII, Section 1 of the 1987 Constitution, which he reads as authorizing the Court to check "grave abuse of

PAGE 7
discretion" by the other branches, even when the issue might otherwise be considered political.<ref
name="philstar" />
At the same time, he's not someone who believes courts should rewrite legislation from the bench. His opinions
reflect what might be called a pragmatic originalism: a preference for faithful interpretation of the law as written,
with reform properly left to the legislature.
He approaches institutional design through what he calls a "Black Swan" framework, borrowed from Nassim
Nicholas Taleb's concept of rare, high-impact events. He has argued that courts and rules of procedure must be built
to withstand crisis, not just routine business.<ref name="philja_journal" /> This view shapes his support for the
Strategic Plan for Judicial Innovations 2022–2027, which prioritizes technological advancement and proactive
access to justice.<ref name="sc_asean">Justice Dimaampao Discusses Access to Justice in the Philippines in
ASEAN Forum on Victim-Sensitive Adjudication of Trafficking Cases. Supreme Court of the Philippines.
https://sc.judiciary.gov.ph/justice-dimaampao-discusses-access-to-justice-in-the-philippines-in-asean-forum-on-
victim-sensitive-adjudication-of-trafficking-cases/</ref>
His philosophy also draws on the Islamic principle of Shura (consultation), which he connects to modern ideas of
open government and public participation. He has advocated for "Moral Governance" as a judicial framework,
arguing that transparency and accountability are the foundations of public trust in legal institutions.<ref
name="barmm_governance">BARMM Government signifies commitment to uphold open, good governance.
BARMM Official Website. https://bangsamoro.gov.ph/news/latest-news/barmm-govt-signifies-commitment-to-
uphold-open-good-governance/</ref>
Notable Supreme Court Opinions and Contributions
Taxation and Prescription: People v. Consebido (2025)
In People v. Consebido (G.R. No. 258563), Dimaampao filed a significant concurring and dissenting opinion
addressing the prescriptive period for violations of the National Internal Revenue Code (NIRC).<ref
name="lawphil_consebido">People v. Consebido, G.R. No. 258563. Lawphil.net.
https://lawphil.net/judjuris/juri2025/apr2025/pdf/gr_258563_dimaampao.pdf</ref> The majority opinion sought to
abandon long-standing doctrines and establish that the prescriptive period for tax fraud runs from the moment the
violation is discovered. Dimaampao, drawing on his detailed knowledge of the NIRC's legislative history,
cautioned against that approach. He argued for "obeisance to legislative intent," insisting that expanding or
contracting prescriptive periods is the legislature's job, not the Court's.<ref name="lawphil_consebido" /> The
opinion is a clear expression of his "pragmatic originalism" in action.
PhilHealth Funds Transfer Case (2025)
When the Supreme Court struck down the transfer of PHP 60 billion in excess PhilHealth funds to the National
Treasury as unconstitutional, Dimaampao agreed with the result but took a narrower view of the remedy.<ref
name="sc_philhealth">Press Briefer, December 5, 2025. Supreme Court of the Philippines.
https://sc.judiciary.gov.ph/press-briefer-december-05-2025/</ref> While the Court unanimously ordered the return
of the funds and voided the specific budget provision, Dimaampao argued against the wholesale invalidation of the
underlying Department of Finance circular (DOF Circular No. 003-2024). His position was that the circular could
be reconciled with the Universal Health Care Act and the Sin Tax Laws, and that the Court's corrective power
should be focused precisely on the illegal transfer, not on dismantling the broader regulatory framework.<ref
name="sc_philhealth" />

PAGE 8
Filipino Sign Language Rules
Dimaampao chaired the Technical Working Group that drafted the Rules on Filipino Sign Language (FSL)
Interpreting in the Judiciary, a set of rules designed to guarantee full participation by d/Deaf Filipinos in court
proceedings.<ref name="sc_pressbriefing">Press Briefer, October 29, 2025. Supreme Court of the Philippines.
https://sc.judiciary.gov.ph/press-briefer-october-29-2025/</ref> The process involved collaboration with the
Komisyon sa Wikang Filipino, Deaf organizations, and trial court representatives. The resulting FSL Rules align
the Philippine judiciary with the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities and mark a concrete
step toward an inclusive justice system.<ref name="sc_pressbriefing" />

Cultural and Symbolic Significance
For the Bangsamoro people, Dimaampao's place on the Supreme Court carries weight that goes far beyond his
individual career. He is widely regarded as a symbol of the community's long-standing aspiration to be represented
in the highest institutions of the republic, an aspiration that the 1996 Final Peace Agreement and the
Comprehensive Agreement on the Bangsamoro had, in principle, called for.<ref name="bta_parliament" />
Chief Minister Ahod "Al Haj Murad" Ebrahim of the BARMM specifically noted that Dimaampao's presence on
the bench helps the region's transition by ensuring that the Bangsamoro Organic Law is interpreted with a genuine
understanding of its historical and cultural context, not just its literal provisions.<ref name="barmm_official" />
The Bangsamoro Transition Authority (BTA) has repeatedly pointed to him as a model for the next generation of
Bangsamoro lawyers and as a sign that the national government is finally delivering on inclusive governance.<ref
name="barmm_official" />
For the Maranao people specifically, his appointment is a point of distinct pride. He is the first Maranao and only
the second Bangsamoro to ever sit on the High Court, and his presence there means that the legal traditions, the
lived realities, and the historical claims of the Maranao are now, for the first time, represented at the level of
national jurisprudence.<ref name="bangsamoro_parliament_pr">Republic of the Philippines, Bangsamoro
Parliament Press Release 516. https://parliament.bangsamoro.gov.ph/wp-content/uploads/2022/03/PR516.pdf</ref>
Personal Life and Values
Dimaampao is married to Maria Gina Perez Villapañe, and their partnership is often cited by those who know him
as the steady foundation that allowed him to endure the long years of repeated JBC applications without bitterness.
<ref name="sc_profile" />

PAGE 9
Those who have worked with him describe his character in terms that rarely appear in judicial profiles: humility,
rigorous intellectual discipline, and a genuine enjoyment of the classroom. His advice to Bar examinees captures
how he sees the relationship between faith and professional life:
"Trust God, simplify your answers, and pray for guidance."<ref name="youtube_bar">Justice Japar B.
Dimaampao, Message to 2022 Bar Examinees. YouTube. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Kh45-
bcFFGw</ref>
He has been described as a "devoted educator," and by all accounts that isn't just a polite formality. His classroom
work spans nearly four decades and multiple law schools, and the consistency of that commitment alongside an
active judicial career says something about what he considers important.
Recognition and Awards

region's foremost representative in the national judiciary<ref name="barmm_official" />
Participant, 2025 WIPO Intellectual Property Judges Forum, Geneva<ref name="wipo_forum">2025 WIPO
Intellectual Property Judges Forum Program.
https://www.wipo.int/edocs/mdocs/mdocs/en/wipo_ip_ju_ge_25/wipo_ip_ju_ge_25_program.pdf</ref>

Legacy
Dimaampao's service on the Supreme Court is expected to run until 2033, and the legacy taking shape around him
centers on three things: the entrenchment of Shari'ah justice as a proper and integrated part of the Philippine legal
system, the use of taxation expertise to clarify some of the country's most contested fiscal doctrines, and a quietly
persistent proof that merit and faith can carry someone all the way to the top of a national institution, even when
the door is closed thirteen times first.

PAGE 10
His work on the FSL Rules, his push for Shari'ah appellate structures, and his classroom commitment all point
toward the same belief: that a justice system is only as good as its capacity to actually reach the people it's
supposed to serve. That belief, expressed through decades of teaching, writing, and deciding, is probably his most
durable contribution.

title: Dimaampao, Magdara B.
text:
