SCHOLARLY WORKS
Doctoral Dissertation (2006)
Understanding Jihad is her foundational academic work. It argues for policy and educational programs for
Muslims in the Philippines grounded in a careful reading of jihad, and the 2021 moral governance chapter cites it.
[1][3]
Iran's Islamic Revolution and Filipino People Power (2017)
In "A Theoretical Study: Iran's Islamic Revolution and the Filipino People Power," she compares six theoretical
explanations of the Iranian Revolution with the Philippine People Power Revolution and maps where the two
converge and diverge.
The chapter appears on pages 50 to 62 of Philippine-Iran Relations: 50 Years and Beyond, edited by H. A. Sevilla
Jr. and published by the Asian Center, University of the Philippines Diliman.[13]
Moral Governance in the Bangsamoro (2021)
Co-authored with Dr. Nassef Manabilang Adiong, "Principles and Practice of Moral Governance in the
Bangsamoro" appears on pages 31 to 53 of Development for Peace, edited by U. S. Malik and published by MSU-
Marawi and Maven Media Asia.[3]
It's an exploratory, conceptual piece that asks how BARMM can move past secular "good governance" toward a
faith-informed moral governance built on five linked principles: Faith, Freedom, Moral Authority, Common Good,
and Social Ethics.
The framework draws on Islamic values while staying inclusive of Christians, Indigenous Peoples, and every other
group in the region.
It also takes on BARMM's practical problems: corruption legacies from the old ARMM era, the need for merit-
based systems, and accountable leadership.
Halal Policy Essay (2023)
On November 24, 2023, BusinessWorld published her essay "Gaps in the Halal Industry in the Philippines: Call for
Legislating Philippine Halal Authority."
She argues for a dedicated national halal agency with both regulatory and development functions. It's a policy
essay, not a peer-reviewed journal article, and it was also republished by HalalFocus.[14]
RECEPTION AND CITATIONS
Her work has traveled well beyond its original pages, and the moral governance chapter in particular has become a
reference point in Bangsamoro governance discussions.

PAGE 5
The Bangsamoro Parliament's Policy Research and Legal Services (PRLS) paper on merit-based recruitment
applies the five-principle framework to civil-service hiring and cites specific pages of the chapter for Faith,
Moral Authority, Common Good, and Social Ethics.[15]
A 2022 PRLS policy commentary, "How viable is moral governance?", treats the chapter as a foundational
formulation of the concept.[16]
The Berghof Foundation's study on implementing the Bangsamoro peace agreement identifies Adiong and
Diampuan (2021) as researchers who define moral governance in Islamic religious terms.[17]
The Institute for Autonomy and Governance's 2025 Review of the BARMM Transition cites the chapter in
discussing moral governance as the centerpiece of the transition and its anti-corruption agenda.[18]
A 2024 study titled Locus and Maxims of Moral Governance: A Framework for the Bangsamoro
Government cites the chapter in framing BARMM's moral governance commitment.
A 2025 study on moral governance and school heads' performance in the Bangsamoro Special Geographic
Area (SGA) uses the chapter in its conceptual discussion.[19]
A 2026 article in Muslim Politics Review on Aceh and Bangsamoro lists the chapter among its references.[20]
Her 2017 Iran chapter is also cited in a peer-reviewed article by H. A. Sevilla Jr. on Philippine-Iran relations in
Historia i Swiat (2023), which discusses her comparison of the Iranian Revolution and Philippine People Power.
[21]
Her dissertation also appears in the bibliography of the Sampung Piling Salitang Meranao and in the references of
other indexed works.
SCHOLARSHIP ABOUT HER
The 2024 article "Emanating Change: Fragments of Micro-Empowerment Among Women Leaders in Mindanao,
Philippines" studies twelve women leaders in the region, and Dr. Potre is one of them.
It treats her as a Meranaw educator and peacebuilder and discusses her peacebuilding in curricula and teacher
training, her grassroots work, the UK-Philippines Partners for Peace, her British Council fellowship, and her
interfaith leadership.[4]
LECTURES AND INTERFAITH CONTRIBUTIONS
"Revisiting the Narrative of Bangsamoro" (January 27, 2022): an invited virtual lecture for the Policy
Research and Legal Services of the Bangsamoro Parliament, covering Bangsamoro ethnolinguistic groups
and identity, narratives and historicity of Muslims in the Philippines, and a chronicle of Muslim affairs.[22]
Muslim contribution to the Interfaith Forum on Laudato Si (2016, Malate Parish, Manila): her
intervention connected religion, human development, climate change, sustainability, and the
interconnectedness of people and the planet.[23]
"Interfaith and the Future of Our Earth" (2013, Pasay City): she hosted this URI Southeast Asia and the
Pacific roundtable on how different faiths approach protecting the planet.[24]
"How I Came Into Interfaith" (2014): she interviewed Dr. Noemi Medina for the URI Southeast Asia-
Pacific archive, a documented oral-history contribution rather than a scholarly publication.[25]
LEGACY
Dr. Potre's career is a study in persistence and range.

PAGE 6
She moves between university halls, interfaith forums, government offices, halal trade dialogues, and Maranao
family gatherings, and she brings something substantive to each.
Her approach is rooted in faith and culture, practical about governance and development, and stubbornly hopeful
about dialogue.
She continues to consult, write, speak, and lead AHIP, with one conviction running through all of it: lasting peace
in Mindanao needs moral clarity, inclusive development, educational empowerment, and real respect across
differences.
RECOGNITION
British Council Fellow, University of Durham, United Kingdom (2005)
URI Regional Coordinator for Southeast Asia and the Pacific (c. 2012)
URI Senior Interfaith Advisor for the Philippines
URI Global Council Trustee for Southeast Asia and the Pacific (2018 to 2022)
Co-founder, United Kingdom-Philippines Partners for Peace (UKPPP)
CEO, Alliance for Halal Integrity in the Philippines Inc. (AHIP)
SELECTED WORKS
Diampuan, P. D. (2006). Understanding jihad: Basis for policy formulation and educational programs for
Muslims in the Philippines [Doctoral dissertation, Mindanao State University, Marawi City].
Diampuan, P. (2017). A theoretical study: Iran's Islamic Revolution and the Filipino People Power. In H. A.
Sevilla Jr. (Ed.), Philippine-Iran relations: 50 years and beyond (pp. 50-62). Asian Center, University of the
Philippines Diliman.
Adiong, N. M., & Diampuan, P. D. (2021). Principles and practice of moral governance in the Bangsamoro.
In U. S. Malik (Ed.), Development for peace: In pursuit of sustainable peace through inclusive development,
the case of the Bangsamoro (pp. 31-53). Mindanao State University-Marawi and Maven Media Asia.
Diampuan, P. D. (2023, November 24). Gaps in the halal industry in the Philippines: Call for legislating
Philippine Halal Authority. BusinessWorld.
NAME VARIANTS
Her name appears in several spellings across catalogs and publications, and they all refer to the same person: Potre
Dirampatan-Diampuan; Potre Dirampatan Diampuan; Potre D. Diampuan; Potre Diampuan; Potre Dirampaten-
Diampuan; and Potre Diramptan-Diampuan (the form URI uses).

RECEPTION AND CITATIONS
Her work has traveled well beyond its original pages, and the moral governance chapter in particular has become a
reference point in Bangsamoro governance discussions.

title: Dirampatan-Sharief, Minang Mujahida
text:
PAGE 1
Minang Mujahida Dirampatan-Sharief
Dr. Minang Mujahida Dirampatan-Sharief is a Meranaw academic, linguist, cultural heritage advocate, theater
artist, and peace weaver who spent close to five decades shaping the intellectual and cultural life of Mindanao from
her home base at Mindanao State University (MSU) in Marawi City.
She is one of the pioneering graduates of Mindanao State University (MSU) Main Campus, and later earned her
doctorate from the University of the Philippines, going on to spend close to five decades giving back to the very
institution that first formed her — alongside a generation of Meranaw women scholars who collectively redefined
what was possible for their community.
Her meticulous work documenting the Meranaw language for the national Filipino lexicon stands as one of the
most substantive Bangsamoro contributions to Philippine linguistic scholarship on record.
Beyond the classroom and the conference hall, she has consistently described herself in terms that say more about
her than any title could: guro, peace weaver, at culture bearer — teacher, peace weaver, and culture bearer —
words she offered not as biography but as a statement of life's purpose.
Contents
1 EARLY LIFE AND BACKGROUND
2 EDUCATION
3 ACADEMIC CAREER
4 LANGUAGE ADVOCACY: THE AMBAGANG WIKA PROJECT
5 IN DEFENSE OF WORDS: THE AMPATUAN CASE
6 CULTURAL HERITAGE AND PEACE ADVOCACY
7 LEGACY
8 EDITORIAL NOTES
9 REFERENCES
EARLY LIFE AND BACKGROUND
Minang Mujahida Dirampatan-Sharief was born around 1952 in Lanao, in the highland lake country of Mindanao
that the Meranaw people have called home for centuries.
She grew up in a community where Islamic faith, maratabat — that finely calibrated Meranaw sense of dignity,
honor, and communal pride — and the rhythms of Meranaw cultural life were not abstract principles but the actual
texture of daily existence.
Lanao in that era was not an easy place to grow up as an ambitious young woman with academic aspirations. Like
many Meranaw women of her generation, she came of age in a world that tended to prioritize men when it came to
schooling and professional formation. She and the women around her broke that tradition — not loudly or
dramatically, but steadily and with conviction — choosing the long road of learning at a time when that choice
carried real social friction.

PAGE 2
Dr. Minang Mujahida Dirampatan-
Sharief

Her deep immersion in Meranaw cultural identity — its oral
traditions, its language, its layered cosmology of faith and
community — would become the foundation for everything
she would later build in the academy and beyond. She did not
arrive at her life's work by accident. She was formed for it.
EDUCATION
Dr. Dirampatan-Sharief is one of the pioneering graduates of
Mindanao State University (MSU) Main Campus in Marawi
City — part of the foundational generation of students who
shaped the university's earliest academic culture and carried its
promise forward.
She later pursued advanced studies at the University of the
Philippines, where she earned her doctoral degree.
She and her contemporaries — among them fellow MSU
alumna and faculty luminary Dr. Medaylin B. Acraman —
were among the pioneering Meranaw women to hold doctoral
degrees from one of the country's most academically rigorous
institutions. This was no small thing for women from Lanao in
that era, and it spoke directly to the combination of intellectual
capacity and personal tenacity that defined their generation.
Returning to Mindanao after her graduate studies, Dr.
Dirampatan-Sharief came back to the institution that had first
formed her — this time as a faculty member, a researcher, and
a builder. She brought with her not only an advanced academic
credential but a clear sense of mission: to put what she had
learned in service of the community she had come from, at the
foot of Lake Lanao.
ACADEMIC CAREER
Dr. Dirampatan-Sharief's professional home for close to five
decades was Mindanao State University (MSU) in Marawi
City — the same institution where she had been a pioneering
student, and to which she returned as a faculty member
committed to deepening what the university could offer the
Meranaw people.
She and Dr. Acraman are recognized as two of the pioneering
MSU graduates who stayed on to become foundational voices
in the university's language education program, having shaped
its approach to English language instruction from the
institution's early years and continuing their contributions
through the 2010s — a tenure spanning close to five decades.

PAGE 3
Key Roles Held

(MSU)

(MSU)

Heritage Center (MCHC)

theater artist; one of the pioneering graduates of
MSU Marawi's Main Campus, who went on to
serve her alma mater for close to five decades as a
foundational voice in language education
Known For
Documenting Meranaw words for the
national Filipino lexicon through the UP
Ambagang Wika Project (2009)
Defending the indigenous linguistic dignity
of the word Ampatuan at a national language
conference
Close to five decades of leadership in MSU's
English and Pre-University programs
Cultural heritage and theater advocacy across
the Bangsamoro region
Pull Quote
"Ako po ay isang guro, peace weaver at culture
bearer."
("I am a teacher, a peace weaver, and a culture
bearer.")
— Dr. Minang Mujahida Dirampatan-Sharief
Her institutional responsibilities across that long career
covered significant ground.
As Chairperson of the English Department at MSU Marawi,
she led one of the university's most strategically important
academic units. The role was not merely administrative. It
demanded a sophisticated, culturally sensitive understanding of
the particular challenges that Meranaw students faced in
navigating English — a colonial-era language that functioned
simultaneously as a medium of instruction, a professional
credential, and a marker of social access. Getting that
navigation right, for students who often arrived at MSU as the
first in their families to reach higher education, required both
linguistic expertise and genuine empathy for the people in the
classroom.
As Director of the Pre-University Center at MSU, Dr.
Dirampatan-Sharief oversaw the foundational academic bridge
programs that prepared incoming students — many of them
from rural Lanao communities — for the demands of
university-level study. For a student population that often
arrived without the academic scaffolding that their counterparts
in Metro Manila or Cebu took for granted, the Pre-University
Center was frequently the difference between success and early
departure. Her leadership of that center was, in real and
practical terms, an act of community building.
In her later years at MSU, she served as a senior academic
consultant for the Meranaw Cultural Heritage Center (MCHC),
contributing her expertise to the center's work in preserving
Meranaw arts, oral literature, historical narrative, and
indigenous knowledge systems.
At the First MSU Applied Linguistics Conference in March
2014 — a milestone event for the university — she and Dr.
Acraman were the featured plenary speakers. Her address
covered current issues and trends in English Language
Teaching across the globe, a reminder that her intellectual
reach was never limited to Lanao, even as her sense of
obligation to Lanao never wavered.
LANGUAGE ADVOCACY: THE AMBAGANG WIKA PROJECT
One of Dr. Dirampatan-Sharief's most concrete and lasting contributions to Philippine cultural life is her work in
documenting the Meranaw language for the national Filipino lexicon.
Under the framework of the Ambagang Wika project — a national language initiative convened by the UP Sentro
ng Wikang Filipino in collaboration with the Filipinas Institute of Translation and the Office of the Chancellor of
UP Diliman — she presented a paper titled Sampung Piling Salitang Meranao (Ten Selected Meranaw Words) at a
national conference held at UP Diliman on March 5 to 6, 2009.

PAGE 4
The conference gathered language scholars and researchers from across the Philippine archipelago to contribute
words from regional languages into a planned national Filipino dictionary, the UP Diksiyonaryong Filipino. The
goal was ambitious: to build a monolingual Filipino dictionary that would finally reflect the country's actual
linguistic diversity, not just its Tagalog-dominant center.
Dr. Dirampatan-Sharief's contribution from Marawi went beyond a simple word list. She anchored each selected
Meranaw term in its cultural, historical, and societal context — treating the language as a living archive of
Meranaw civilization, not as a curiosity or an ethnographic footnote.
The methodology she brought to this work reflected years of deliberate, community-grounded research:
Linguistic Surveys — Broad surveys conducted among MSU students, faculty members, and Meranaw
community elders to identify candidate words and establish their range of usage
Informant Interviews — In-depth conversations with recognized culture-bearers who carried the living,
nuanced meanings of terms that dictionaries rarely capture
Lexical Mapping — Careful gathering and vetting of terms to identify proper linguistic equivalents and
contextual synonyms across registers
Historical and Etymological Research — Investigation of the deep roots, origins, and societal significance
of each selected word
Collaborative Translation — Coordinated work with MSU's Filipino-language faculty to render nuanced
Meranaw concepts as accurately as possible in the national language
The result was a rigorous scholarly contribution that insisted Meranaw deserved the same lexicographic
seriousness applied to Tagalog, Cebuano, or Ilocano — and demonstrated that the expertise to deliver that
seriousness existed right there in Marawi.
She framed the larger project in terms that were at once scholarly and deeply personal. In her own words at the
conference: Ang ating etnisidad ay di dapat maging sanhi ng di pagkakaunawaan — our ethnicity should not be
the cause of misunderstanding — and she offered a vision of a Filipino dictionary that would finally prove, as she
put it, that the more than a hundred languages of the Philippines belong to one people, and can serve as a road
toward mutual understanding, peace, and progress.
IN DEFENSE OF WORDS: THE AMPATUAN CASE
Perhaps no single episode captures Dr. Dirampatan-Sharief's intellectual courage and cultural commitment more
clearly than her intervention at a national language conference when the word Ampatuan was being evaluated as a
candidate for "Word of the Year."
The context was as charged as it gets. The November 2009 Maguindanao Massacre — one of the worst acts of
political violence in Philippine recorded history, in which 58 people including 32 journalists were killed in an
ambush attributed to members of the Ampatuan political clan — had exploded the name into national
consciousness under the darkest possible shadow. In its immediate aftermath, the name Ampatuan carried an almost
unbearable weight in Filipino public discourse. To many, it had become, in practice, a byword for political
warlordism and impunity.
When the word surfaced as a candidate for "Word of the Year" — a designation that would effectively fix its
massacre-era meaning into the national linguistic record — Dr. Dirampatan-Sharief stepped forward.
She reminded the assembled academics that the word Ampatuan had roots and a meaning that predated any
political dynasty or criminal event by centuries.

PAGE 5
In its original Bangsamoro linguistic context, the word carries two deeply significant components: tua, which
conveys the essence of power, inner strength, and dignity; and tuan, a term for a high Muslim religious authority or
spiritual leader. Far from a dark symbol, the word in its indigenous context was — and is — a dignified one. It
named a quality, a lineage, and a kind of authority rooted in spiritual and communal standing.
Her argument was not to deny the massacre or erase its victims from the historical record. She was not asking
anyone to forget or forgive. Her argument was more precise and more principled than that: if the word was going to
enter the national dictionary as a consequence of recent events, then its original, noble meaning had to stand in that
dictionary alongside the modern historical association. To allow the massacre to be the word's sole definition would
be to let violence accomplish a second act of destruction — this time not of lives, but of language, memory, and
identity.
The argument prevailed. The episode became, among those present, a marker of what linguistic advocacy actually
looks like when it takes seriously the stakes of cultural representation.
Dr. Dirampatan-Sharief's position grew directly from her core conviction: that language is not simply a
communication tool but a sacred vessel for a people's dignity, history, and self-understanding. Letting that vessel be
defined by the worst act ever committed in a family's name — without pushback, without the full linguistic record
— is, in her view, a cultural tragedy that compounds the original one.
CULTURAL HERITAGE AND PEACE ADVOCACY
Dr. Dirampatan-Sharief's reach has always extended well beyond the formal boundaries of university life.
She has served as a lecturer on Maranao cultural heritage for programs organized under the National Commission
for Culture and the Arts (NCCA), covering Meranaw historical perspective, Sultanate genealogy, traditional
cultural practices, and the performing arts traditions of the Meranaw people. Her work with the NCCA placed her
in national conversations about Indigenous cultural identity at a time when Mindanao's heritage was regularly
misrepresented or simply ignored in mainstream Philippine cultural programming.
She is also known, though not always acknowledged prominently in her academic profile, as a theater artist.
Theater, in the Meranaw cultural context, is far more than entertainment. It is memory work — a communal act of
passing history, identity, and values from one generation to the next through embodied performance. Her
engagement with theater has been, in this sense, a natural extension of the same cultural preservation instinct that
drives her linguistic work.
Her own articulation of her Muslim faith and Meranaw identity is worth sitting with directly. She has described her
jihad — her personal striving — as upang maging tunay na Muslim sa puso, sa isip at gawa: to be a true Muslim in
heart, mind, and deed. And her maratabat, her personal code of dignity, is ang ipagtanggol ang tama at mabuti at
iwasan ang mali at masama: to defend what is right and good, and to avoid what is wrong and bad.
These are not abstract religious formulas. They are the operating principles of a life lived under repeated pressure
— from the stigma that Muslim Mindanao has carried in the national imagination, from the physical and political
violence that has repeatedly descended on Marawi, from the long effort required simply to be taken seriously as a
Meranaw Muslim woman in Philippine academic and public life.
She has explicitly named and rejected the conflation of Meranaw Muslim identity with terrorism. In one public
address, she introduced herself in terms that were both a correction and a declaration: Isang Meranao, Muslim,
Bangsamoro Filipino, hindi terorista — a Meranaw, Muslim, Bangsamoro Filipino, not a terrorist. In the years that
followed the 2017 Marawi Siege, those words took on an even sharper urgency.

PAGE 6
LEGACY
Dr. Minang Mujahida Dirampatan-Sharief represents something that becomes rarer the more you look for it in
academic life: a scholar who never left her people.
She had the credentials, the training, and the connections to pursue a comfortable career at any major Philippine
university. She chose Marawi instead — and she stayed through decades of political instability, armed conflict, and
communal hardship that would have sent many people in the opposite direction.
Her legacy operates at several levels simultaneously.
As a linguist, she made the Meranaw language visible and legible within the national Filipino cultural framework
at a time when the languages of Mindanao were treated, at best, as regional curiosities. Her contributions to the
Ambagang Wika project gave Meranaw a place at the national lexicographic table that it had long deserved but
rarely been offered.
As an academic administrator, she built and led the institutional structures — the English Department, the Pre-
University Center — that gave successive generations of young Meranaw students a genuine path through higher
education. That is not a small thing. In communities where formal education was both a privilege and a daily act of
cultural navigation, steady, competent, culturally grounded academic leadership mattered enormously.
As a cultural advocate, she defended the integrity of Meranaw identity — in language, in the arts, in historical
narrative — with the precision and persistence that only genuine, long-term commitment produces. The Ampatuan
case alone would be enough to secure her place in the history of Bangsamoro intellectual life.
And as a peace weaver, she modeled, across decades, a way of being Meranaw, Muslim, and Filipino that refuses
both marginalization and caricature — insisting, by example, that these identities are not in contradiction and that
their bearer is not, and has never been, anyone's problem to define.
EDITORIAL NOTES
Her approximate birth year (c. 1952) is derived from a February 2010 Philippine Center for Investigative
Journalism profile that described her as 58 years old at that time.
The precise name, date, and venue of the national language conference at which she intervened in the
Ampatuan word debate have not been independently confirmed in the sources consulted for this article.

records are encouraged to supply this information.

title: Disamburun, Abdulrahman M.
text:
PAGE 1
Abdulrahman M. Disamburun
Hadji Alinog "Abdulrahman" M. Disamburun (born August 20, 1948) is a Filipino public servant, Islamic
scholar, and community leader from Tamparan, Lanao del Sur. Known for his multi-sector leadership spanning
local governance, religious education, and peacekeeping, he has dedicated over four decades to strengthening
grassroots institutions and advancing Islamic scholarship in the Bangsamoro region. His legacy rests on a rare
ability to bridge different fields—serving simultaneously as barangay official, provincial consultant, military
commander, and religious leader—embodying what his community describes as a versatile servant-leader whose
breadth of experience became his defining strength.
Contents
1 Early Life and Background
2 Education
3 Career
3.1 Local Governance and Community Development
3.2 Islamic Leadership and Religious Education
3.3 Military Service and Peacekeeping
4 Personal Life
5 Legacy and Recognition
6 External Links
Early Life and Background
Hadji Alinog "Abdulrahman" M. Disamburun was born on August 20, 1948, in Barangay Lumbaca-Ingud,
Municipality of Tamparan, Lanao del Sur. He was born into a family deeply committed to faith and community
service—his father, Imam Hadji Alim Disamburun, served as a respected religious leader, while his mother, Bae
Macalbe Tandong, upheld the values of Maranao tradition and family stewardship. Growing up in a community
where Islamic scholarship and public service were intertwined, young Abdulrahman absorbed these principles
early, shaping the trajectory of his later work.
The environment of Lumbaca-Ingud during his formative years was one where communal responsibility and
religious devotion formed the backbone of daily life. This upbringing instilled in him a natural inclination toward
leadership that would later express itself across multiple domains—from local government to religious education to
peacekeeping efforts.
Education
Disamburun's academic journey reflects both ambition and a commitment to continuous learning across several
decades. He began his formal education at Tamparan Central Pilot Elementary School, where he distinguished
himself academically, graduating as Salutatorian. This early recognition of his intellectual capabilities set the stage
for further educational pursuits.
For his secondary education, he attended two institutions that would deepen his Islamic knowledge: Kamilol Islam
College and Jamiatul Philippine Al-Islamia. These institutions provided him with a foundation in both secular and
religious studies, a dual education that would prove essential in his later roles bridging traditional Islamic

In 1968, he earned his Bachelor of Science in Commerce with a
major in Accounting from Iloilo University. This degree equipped
him with the technical and administrative skills necessary for
financial management and organizational leadership. Shortly after
completing his undergraduate studies, he underwent military
training at Camp Lapu-Lapu in Cebu City, earning the rank of 2nd
Lieutenant. This military education added another dimension to his
developing skillset—discipline, strategic thinking, and crisis
management.
Recognizing the importance of specialized training in public
administration, Disamburun returned to formal education later in
his career. In 1994, he completed his Master in Public
Administration at Bukidnon State College, strengthening his
theoretical understanding of governance systems and policy
implementation. This advanced degree came at a time when he
was already deeply involved in local government work, allowing
him to apply academic frameworks to real-world challenges he
was encountering in Tamparan and Lanao del Sur.
Career
Local Governance and Community Development
Disamburun's career in public service began in the education
sector, where he worked as an educator and commandant, helping
shape the next generation of community members. This early
teaching experience gave him insight into the challenges facing
young people in Tamparan and the broader region, particularly
around access to quality education and opportunities for
advancement.
His transition into local government came through a series of
increasingly responsible positions. He served as Municipal
Development Coordinator, where he worked to align community
needs with available resources and government programs. In this
role, he became known for his practical approach to development
—focusing on projects that had direct, measurable impacts on
people's daily lives rather than pursuing symbolic initiatives.
He later took on the role of Municipal Administrator, managing
the day-to-day operations of local government and ensuring that
services reached constituents effectively. This administrative
experience taught him the mechanics of governance—budgeting, personnel management, inter-agency
coordination, and regulatory compliance.

PAGE 3
His most direct connection to grassroots leadership came through his service as Barangay Chairman of Lumbaca-
Ingud, his home community. As chairman, he worked to strengthen local governance systems, support livelihood
programs, and promote coordination between the barangay and higher levels of government. His leadership style
emphasized participation and transparency, encouraging community members to take active roles in decision-
making processes.
Disamburun's influence extended beyond his own barangay when he was elected President of the Association of
Barangay Councils (ABC), a position that automatically made him a member of the Sangguniang Bayan
(Municipal Council). This role allowed him to represent the collective interests of all barangays in Tamparan,
advocating for policies and programs that addressed shared challenges across communities.
He later served as a member of the Sangguniang Panlalawigan (Provincial Board) of Lanao del Sur, giving him a
broader platform to influence provincial policy. In this capacity, he worked on issues affecting multiple
municipalities, helping to shape development strategies and resource allocation at the provincial level.
Later in his career, he was appointed Provincial Consultant on Barangay Affairs, a position that drew on his
decades of experience in grassroots leadership. In this consulting role, he advised provincial officials on barangay-
level concerns, helped develop training programs for local leaders, and served as a bridge between provincial
government and community-level realities.
Islamic Leadership and Religious Education
Parallel to his government service, Disamburun maintained a strong commitment to Islamic education and
leadership in Tamparan. He served as both President and Chairman of the Supreme Council on Islamic Affairs of
Tamparan, an organization dedicated to coordinating religious activities, supporting Islamic scholars, and
promoting Islamic values within the community.
In this capacity, he worked to strengthen the infrastructure of Islamic education, particularly the madaris system—
the network of Islamic schools that provides religious instruction alongside secular subjects. He advocated for
better integration of madaris education into the broader educational framework, recognizing that many young
Muslims in the region relied on these institutions for both spiritual formation and basic literacy.
He also served as Vice Chairman of Majlisul Qur'an Wal Hadith, an organization focused on the study and teaching
of the Qur'an and Hadith. This position placed him at the center of religious scholarship in the area, where he
helped guide curriculum development, supported teacher training, and facilitated gatherings of Islamic scholars to
discuss contemporary issues facing the Muslim community.
His involvement in these religious organizations spanned over two decades, making him a respected voice on
matters of Islamic practice and education. His dual role as both government official and religious leader gave him
unique credibility—he could speak the language of bureaucracy when dealing with government agencies and the
language of faith when engaging with religious communities, making him an effective advocate for Islamic
education within the public sphere.
Military Service and Peacekeeping
During a particularly challenging period in Mindanao's history, Disamburun took on the role of Battalion
Commander of the Civilian Home Defense Force (CHDF), a paramilitary organization that worked alongside the
Armed Forces of the Philippines to maintain peace and order in rural areas. This position reflected the trust placed
in him by both military authorities and local communities—he was seen as someone who understood the
complexities of the region and could work to prevent violence while maintaining community trust.

PAGE 4
As Battalion Commander, he balanced the difficult task of ensuring security while avoiding the heavy-handed
tactics that often alienated communities from government forces. His approach emphasized communication, local
intelligence networks, and de-escalation rather than purely military solutions. This peacekeeping role added yet
another dimension to his public service, demonstrating his willingness to take on difficult responsibilities during
times of crisis.
Personal Life
Hadji Alinog "Abdulrahman" M. Disamburun is married to Hja. Rahma Cayaranao Tominaman Disamburun, a
respected educator and school principal in her own right. Their partnership represents a union of shared values
around education, public service, and community leadership. Hja. Rahma's own career in education has
complemented her husband's work, as both have dedicated themselves to improving opportunities for young people
in Tamparan.
Together, they raised a family of nine children, many of whom have followed their parents' example by taking on
roles in leadership and public service. This intergenerational commitment to community involvement has extended
the Disamburun family's influence beyond the work of any single individual, creating a legacy of service that
continues through multiple family members.
Legacy and Recognition
Hadji Alinog "Abdulrahman" M. Disamburun's legacy is perhaps best understood not through any single
accomplishment but through the breadth of his service across multiple sectors. He represents a generation of
Filipino Muslim leaders who navigated the complex intersection of traditional religious authority, modern
democratic governance, and the practical demands of community development.
His ability to work effectively in different spheres—as elected official, religious scholar, military commander, and
educator—gave him a comprehensive understanding of his community's needs and the various levers available to
address them. While some leaders specialize deeply in one area, Disamburun's strength came from his versatility,
his capacity to move between different roles and bring insights from one domain to inform his work in another.
In his home community of Lumbaca-Ingud and the wider Tamparan area, he is remembered for practical
improvements to governance systems, for his support of Islamic education infrastructure, and for his commitment
to maintaining peace during difficult times. His work contributed to better coordination between communities and
government institutions, helping to strengthen the administrative structures that communities rely on for services
and support.
His life's work embodies what his community has described as a "jack of all trades" whose breadth became his
defining strength—a leader who refused to be confined to a single specialization but instead used his wide-ranging
experience to serve his community in whatever capacity was needed at any given moment.

title: Disimban-Ramos, Diamila
text:
PAGE 1
Diamila Disimban-Ramos
Diamila Disimban-Ramos (colloquially known as Jam) is a prominent Filipino legislator, women's rights
advocate, and Maranao cultural leader serving as a Member of Parliament in the Bangsamoro Transition Authority
(BTA). Appointed by President Rodrigo Duterte in 2019, she has become a central figure in the Bangsamoro
Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao's (BARMM) transitional governance, particularly noted for her
advocacy in women's empowerment, social justice, and the preservation of Bangsamoro cultural heritage. As both a
modern parliamentarian and traditional Maranao noble, Disimban-Ramos bridges institutional governance with the
cultural responsibilities of her inherited leadership role, embodying what she calls "untainted public service" rooted
in her deep commitment to her people's dignity and development.

Early Life and Heritage
Diamila Disimban-Ramos was born into a lineage deeply embedded in Bangsamoro regional leadership. Her father
hails from Taraka and Tamparan in Lanao del Sur, connecting her to the Maranao ethnic community, while her
mother traces roots to Kabuntalan in Maguindanao and Pikit in Cotabato, linking her to Maguindanaon heritage.
<ref name="heritage">Diamila Disimban-Ramos Official Profile, BTA Parliament.
https://parliament.bangsamoro.gov.ph/member-parliament/ramos-diamila-d/</ref> This dual lineage positions her
uniquely across the major ethnic groups of the Bangsamoro region, granting her a comprehensive understanding of
regional dynamics and shared values.
In November 2011, Disimban-Ramos underwent a formal rite of enshrinement as the Bae a Labi a Gaus (Great
Queen of Wealth and Power) in Bubong a Masiu, Taraka, Lanao del Sur. This traditional title reflects her significant
standing within Maranao socio-political structures and underscores her cultural responsibility to serve as a

Education and Early Government
Service
Disimban-Ramos earned her Bachelor of Science in Foreign
Service, majoring in Diplomacy, from the Lyceum of the
Philippines University, equipping her with formal training in
international relations and diplomatic engagement.
Before her appointment to the BTA Parliament, she accumulated a
decade of distinguished government service spanning multiple
sectors:
International Diplomacy: She served as a member of the
APEC Substantive Group under the Department of Foreign
Affairs during the 1995 APEC Summit, contributing to
Philippine positions on regional economic cooperation.<ref
name="apec">APEC Summit 1995 Delegation Records,
Department of Foreign Affairs Archives.</ref>
Youth and Social Development: From 1996 to 1999, she
worked with the National Youth Commission, focusing on
youth empowerment and civic engagement. Later, she
served in the Cooperative Development Authority (2011–
2016), where she promoted cooperative enterprise as an
engine for grassroots economic development.<ref
name="cda">Cooperative Development Authority Service
Records, 2011–2016.</ref>
Regional Agricultural Development: She served as the
ARMM Focal Person for Agribusiness and subsequently as
Chief of Staff at the Department of Agriculture and
Fisheries (DAF-ARMM), driving initiatives to strengthen
farming livelihoods and food security across the region.<ref
name="daf">DAF-ARMM Administrative Records, Chief
of Staff Unit.</ref>
Legislative Leadership in the BTA
Parliament
Diamila Disimban-Ramos assumed office in the Bangsamoro Transition Authority Parliament in 2019, where she
has shaped the institutional framework for the nascent autonomous region. Her parliamentary work centers on three
foundational pillars: Sustained Peace, Effective Governance, and Empowered Constituencies.

PAGE 3
Committee on Women, Youth, Children, and Persons with Disabilities
As chairperson of the Committee on Women, Youth, Children, and Persons with Disabilities (CWYCP), Disimban-
Ramos has positioned herself at the forefront of gender-responsive governance in BARMM. She led critical public
hearings on the Bangsamoro Gender and Development (GAD) Code, ensuring that regional policy reflects both
international human rights standards and the cultural values of Bangsamoro communities.<ref
name="gad">Bangsamoro Parliament Committee Minutes, CWYCP Hearings 2022–2023.</ref> Her leadership in
this committee directly contributed to the passage of the Bangsamoro Labor and Employment Code (approved in
early 2026), which aligns regional labor protections with moral governance principles grounded in Islamic values
and democratic accountability.<ref name="labor">Bangsamoro Labor and Employment Code, BTA Parliament
Third and Final Reading, 2026.</ref>
Key Legislative Measures
Disimban-Ramos has authored and co-authored several landmark bills addressing regional development, cultural
preservation, and social equity. Her legislative record reflects a consistent commitment to institutional capacity-
building and inclusive governance.
Ranaw Development Authority (Bill No. 111)
Perhaps her most significant initiative, Bill No. 111 proposes the creation of a Ranaw Development Authority to
govern and rehabilitate Lake Lanao and its surrounding natural resources. This measure balances economic
development with environmental preservation, addressing the ecological degradation of the lake while creating
sustainable livelihood opportunities for communities dependent on its waters and fisheries.<ref
name="ranaw">Bill No. 111, Ranaw Development Authority Act, BTA Parliament Archives.</ref>
Bangsamoro Cultural Heritage Act (Bill No. 204)
Co-authored with fellow parliamentarians, Bill No. 204 institutionalizes the protection and promotion of
Bangsamoro history, identity, and arts. The measure proposes a Regional Registry of Cultural Property to safeguard
intangible heritage including traditional weaving techniques (such as malong and ikat), oral epics (like the
Darangen), and ceremonial chants that form the backbone of Bangsamoro identity.<ref name="heritage_act">Bill
No. 204, Bangsamoro Cultural Heritage Act, BTA Parliament, 2021.</ref> This legislative approach treats culture
not as folklore but as living intellectual property worthy of institutional stewardship.
Other Bangsamoro Communities Peace and Culture Centers Act (Bill No. 203)
Bill No. 203 seeks to establish regional hubs (Peace and Culture Centers) dedicated to the "Other Bangsamoro
Communities" (OBCs), non-Moro groups and minorities living within and outside BARMM territory. The centers
would provide social, cultural, and economic services while fostering interfaith dialogue and peaceful coexistence.
<ref name="obc">Bill No. 203, OBC Peace and Culture Centers Act, BTA Parliament, 2021.</ref>
Bangsamoro Cooperative Act (Bill No. 210)
Continuing her long-standing interest in cooperative enterprise, Bill No. 210 empowers local communities and
social enterprises to foster economic prosperity through cooperative ownership models, building on her prior work
with the Cooperative Development Authority.<ref name="coop_act">Bill No. 210, Bangsamoro Cooperative Act,

PAGE 4
BTA Parliament Archives.</ref>
Women's Economic Empowerment Act (Bill No. 292)
This measure specifically targets the economic uplift of former Bangsamoro women combatants, recognizing their
sacrifice and contributions to the independence struggle while integrating them into civilian economic life through
targeted support, skills training, and access to microfinance.<ref name="women_econ">Bill No. 292, Economic
Empowerment of Former Bangsamoro Women Combatants Act, BTA Parliament, 2024.</ref>
Tamparan District Hospital Renaming (Bill No. 439)
In a gesture recognizing regional institutional growth, Disimban-Ramos filed Bill No. 439 to rename the Tamparan
District Hospital to the Lanao del Sur Provincial Hospital, reflecting its expanded regional importance and role in
provincial healthcare delivery.<ref name="hospital">Bill No. 439, Hospital Renaming Measure, BTA Parliament,
2025.</ref>
Role as Maranao Cultural Leader
Beyond her institutional parliamentary duties, Disimban-Ramos carries profound responsibilities within traditional
Maranao governance structures. Her title as Bae a Labi a Gaus positions her within the socio-political order
known as the Pat a Pangampong sa Ranao (Four Principalities of Lanao), a system of hereditary leadership that
predates colonial rule.
In this role, she functions as more than a symbolic figurehead. A Bae a Labi is traditionally expected to mediate
conflicts, uphold the maratabat (honor and rank) of her clan, represent her people in inter-ethnic dialogues, and
serve as guardian of communal welfare. Disimban-Ramos integrates these traditional duties seamlessly with her
modern parliamentary work, often viewing her legislative initiatives as extensions of her inherited cultural
responsibility to protect and advance Maranao interests.<ref name="cultural_leader">Maranao Leadership
Structures and Contemporary Governance, BTA Parliament Research Division, 2023.</ref>
Community Initiatives and Humanitarian Work
Disimban-Ramos is frequently recognized as a "fervid writer" and devoted Muslim mother who integrates personal
values into her public service. Her humanitarian commitments extend beyond legislation into direct community
engagement.
The Strings of Aspiration program stands as a defining example of her values in action. Through this initiative,
she organizes regular feeding and gift-giving programs for Bangsamoro children in partnership with organizations
like Save the Children Philippines, addressing immediate nutritional and material needs while building what she
describes as "pathways of hope" for vulnerable youth.<ref name="strings">Strings of Aspiration Program Records
and Social Media Documentation, 2022–2026.</ref>
Her commitment to what she calls "untainted public service" has earned her widespread respect among local
leaders, civil society organizations, and military commanders alike, transcending the usual political divisions that
characterize regional governance.<ref name="service">Disimban-Ramos Media Interviews and Public Statements,
2019–2026.</ref>

PAGE 5
Personal Philosophy and Public Advocacy
Disimban-Ramos frames her legislative and humanitarian work around the concept of Maratabat (Maranao
honor), understanding it not as historical nostalgia but as a living ethical framework for contemporary governance.
She advocates for policies that recognize Bangsamoro agency in nation-building, resist what she terms "colonial
residues" in national law, and center the voices of women, youth, and minorities in institutional decision-making.
In her public statements, she emphasizes that Bangsamoro empowerment is inseparable from women's
empowerment, arguing that the region's post-conflict rebuilding cannot succeed if half its population remains
economically marginalized or politically sidelined. This feminist orientation distinguishes her leadership from
some of her counterparts and has made her a vocal advocate for gender-responsive budgeting and accountability
within BTA institutions.<ref name="feminist">Diamila Disimban-Ramos Public Addresses, BTA Parliament
Proceedings, 2020–2026.</ref>
Challenges and Ongoing Work
As a parliamentarian in a transitional authority, Disimban-Ramos navigates the inherent tensions of building
democratic institutions in a region emerging from decades of conflict. Critics have occasionally questioned the
slow pace of certain legislative initiatives, particularly regarding land rights and justice mechanisms, though she
and her supporters argue that careful deliberation is necessary for sustainable, culturally grounded solutions.
Her work on Lake Lanao restoration, in particular, has faced resistance from entrenched economic interests, yet she
continues to push for this measure, viewing environmental restoration as central to regional health and long-term
prosperity.
Legacy and Future Directions
Diamila Disimban-Ramos represents a growing cohort of women leaders in the Bangsamoro region who navigate
traditional authority with modern democratic practice. Her career demonstrates how inherited cultural leadership
and formal institutional power can be integrated to serve broader peace-building and development goals.
As BARMM transitions from the Bangsamoro Transition Authority toward permanent democratic institutions,
Disimban-Ramos's work on cultural preservation, women's economic empowerment, and environmental restoration
will likely define her contribution to the region's foundational governance architecture. Her legislative record
suggests a vision of Bangsamoro autonomy that is economically vibrant, culturally proud, and radically inclusive.
Recognition
Disimban-Ramos has been featured in regional and national media for her parliamentary work and humanitarian
initiatives. She maintains active engagement with civil society organizations, academic institutions, and
international development agencies focused on peacebuilding and regional development in Mindanao.

title: Disomimba, Palawan D.
text:
PAGE 1
Palawan D. Disomimba
Panoroganan Palawan D. Disomimba was an influential traditional ruler and elected public official from Lanao
del Sur, widely recognized as one of the Maranao people's finest examples of a leader who could hold two worlds
together without losing either one.
A hereditary nobleman from the Royal House of Masiu and one of the 16 sovereign rulers of the historic Ranao
Confederation, he also served as the longest-sitting mayor in the history of Tamparan, holding office for over 32
consecutive years from 1959 to 1991.
His legacy rests on a simple but rare achievement: he showed that the old codes of the sultanate and the new rules
of the republic could work side by side, not against each other.
Contents
1 Background and Royal Heritage
2 Political Career
2.1 Mayor of Tamparan (1959–1991)
2.2 Vice Governor of Lanao del Sur (1980–1986)
3 Cultural Legacy
4 References
5 See Also
Background and Royal Heritage
Disomimba's roots trace directly to the Royal House of Masiu, one of the four founding principalities of the
Maranao political world.
These four houses form the Pat a Pangampong sa Ranao, the historic confederation of noble domains surrounding
Lake Lanao that defined Maranao political and cultural identity long before the Philippine republic existed.
Within this framework, Disomimba carried the hereditary title of Datu a Cabugatan sa Masiu, one of the most
senior crowns within the Masiu royal structure.
This wasn't a ceremonial role. The Datu a Cabugatan held actual authority under Maranao customary law (adat),
with the recognized right to sit in ancestral councils, mediate major community disputes, and weigh in on local
legal matters alongside Islamic religious scholars.
As one of the core 16 sovereign rulers of the Ranao Confederation, he also carried the broader duty of protecting
ancestral territorial boundaries, Islamic practices, and the cultural continuity of the Maranao people across the Lake
Lanao region.
His peers recognized him among the top 50 Model Sultans of the Iranaon lineage, a distinction earned through
consistent adherence to traditional codes of justice, ethical conduct, and peace-building diplomacy.<ref>Bilangatao
Guwani. (n.d.). Sultan Mayor Ambor Radianggaos, late Sultan sa Masiu, former Mayor of Taraka, Lanao del Sur.

Datu Masoi Blog. September 6, 2015. https://datumasoi.wordpress.com/2015/09/06/royal-blood-dalum-a-
masiu/</ref>
Political Career
Mayor of Tamparan (1959–1991)
Disomimba entered local politics in the late 1950s and never left, at least not willingly.
His run as Mayor of Tamparan lasted over 32 consecutive years, making him the longest-serving chief executive in
the municipality's entire history.
He took office during a period when many Mindanao municipalities were still consolidating after shifts in colonial-
era administrative organization, and Tamparan was no exception.
Under his watch, the town gained foundational public schools, expanded road infrastructure, and a degree of
communal stability that didn't come easy, given the political volatility that rippled through Mindanao during those
decades.
His governance wasn't just administrative. It carried the weight of the sultanate behind it, which meant residents
trusted him not only as a mayor but as a traditional authority figure whose word still mattered in the old sense.
The political legacy he built in Tamparan didn't end when he stepped down. His descendants eventually succeeded
him in local governance, extending the family's role in public service well beyond his own tenure.<ref>Philippine
Reports, Volume 661. Judiciary of the Philippines.
https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/assets/pdf/philrep_ebooks/Volume_661.pdf</ref>

PAGE 4
Vice Governor of Lanao del Sur (1980–1986)
While still serving as Tamparan's mayor, Disomimba expanded his reach to the provincial level, serving as Vice
Governor of Lanao del Sur from 1980 to 1986.
This was not a quiet period in Philippine history.
His vice-gubernatorial term overlapped with the final years of Ferdinand Marcos's Martial Law and the turbulent
transition that followed, leading eventually toward democratic restoration.
Navigating that atmosphere in a predominantly Muslim province, where central government policies were often
met with deep suspicion, required exactly the kind of dual credibility Disomimba had spent decades building.
He used the platform to advocate for public policies grounded in local Islamic values while actively defending
Maranao cultural integrity against pressures that came from heavy-handed central government integration efforts.
Cultural Legacy
Perhaps the most enduring thing about Palawan D. Disomimba isn't any single policy or infrastructure project. It's
the model he left behind.
He was one of the clearest demonstrations in Maranao political history that a traditional sultan and a constitutional
executive could exist in the same person, and that this combination didn't have to produce tension; it could produce
strength.
Historians and the Maranao community remember him today as a resilient diplomat, a stabilizing presence during
decades of conflict, and one of the foundational architects of modern governance in Lanao del Sur.
The Royal House of Masiu, to which he belonged, continues to be one of the cornerstones of Maranao cultural
identity, and Disomimba's life remains one of its most cited examples of leadership that genuinely served both
tradition and community.<ref>Bilangatao Guwani. (n.d.). Facebook post.
https://www.facebook.com/100046906275159/posts/2548776905140615/</ref>

Alizedney M. Ditucalan
Alizedney "Zed" M. Ditucalan (born in Bacolod-Kalawi, Lanao del Sur) is a Maranao
lawyer, competition law scholar, and the fourth Chancellor of Mindanao State University-
Iligan Institute of Technology (MSU-IIT). Elected on February 28, 2022, by the MSU Board
of Regents, he became the youngest person and the first alumnus ever to lead the institution.
More than a biographical milestone, that homecoming captures the through-line of his career:
a commitment to building institutions, not just inhabiting them. Whether he was designing the
Sarimanok Virtual Law Clinic to bring legal services to remote Lanao del Norte communities,
arguing in international handbooks that the Philippine Competition Act is a flawed but
salvageable regulatory transplant, or convening the first-ever MSU System-wide Academic
Summit, Ditucalan has consistently framed his work around one conviction: that a well-
designed institution serves its people far better than a poorly designed one, however
eloquently worded its founding documents may be.
