Background and Early Life
Ditucalan grew up in Bacolod-Kalawi in Lanao del Sur, in the cultural orbit of the Mindanao State University main campus in Marawi City.
That campus, established in 1961 as what its founding legislation called a "social laboratory" for peace and integration, has always been
more than a university; it is a statement about the place of the Bangsamoro in the Philippine national fabric.<ref name="iit-history">MSU-
IIT History, 54th Charter Day website, Mindanao State University-Iligan Institute of Technology, accessed March 10, 2026. Available at:
https://sites.google.com/g.msuiit.edu.ph/54thcharterday/iit-history</ref> Growing up in proximity to it gave Ditucalan an early exposure to
the layered world of Muslim Mindanao's legal life: a world where customary Maranao norms, specifically the Taritib and Igma that have
governed community relations for centuries, sit alongside a civil legal system whose authority over local disputes has never been entirely
uncontested.<ref name="bangsamoro-context">On Maranao customary law and the MSU social laboratory mandate, see MSU IIT History
(ibid., note 1). The concept of Taritib and Igma as traditional legal norms operating alongside civil law is widely acknowledged in
Bangsamoro legal literature, including the Bangsamoro Education Code of 2021.</ref>

PAGE 2
That environment was, in effect, his first classroom in legal theory. Long before he ever read a regulatory economics textbook in Japan, he
had already absorbed the practical lesson that law does not operate in a vacuum: it is always in conversation with history, with faith, and
with the particular grievances and aspirations of the community it purports to govern.
Education
Juris Doctor at MSU Marawi
Ditucalan completed his Juris Doctor at the MSU College of Law on the main campus in Marawi City. Legal education at Marawi has
always had a distinct character. Its students come of age understanding that law in Muslim Mindanao is never purely abstract: the tension
between Islamic jurisprudence and secular civil procedure is lived, not merely theorized. That formation would leave a permanent mark on
Ditucalan's scholarly sensibility, particularly in his later work on regulatory design, where his skepticism about transplanting foreign legal
frameworks onto unfamiliar soil has deep personal and historical roots.
Master of Laws, Kyushu University
After his initial years in practice, Ditucalan was selected for the Young Leaders' Program (YLP), a scholarship administered under Japan's
Ministry of Education, Culture, Sports, Science and Technology (MEXT), designed to cultivate future policy leaders from Asian nations
and foster durable intellectual connections with Japan.<ref name="mext-ylp">Young Leaders' Program, Ministry of Education, Culture,
Sports, Science and Technology (MEXT), Japan. Available at:
https://www.mext.go.jp/en/policy/education/highered/title02/detail02/sdetail02/sdetail02/1374094.htm</ref> He was the first recipient from
Mindanao to be selected for the program, a distinction that reflected both the strength of his candidacy and the degree to which Mindanao
had historically been passed over in elite international fellowship pipelines.<ref name="pmt">Ditucalan assumes as MSU-IIT new
chancellor, Philippine Muslim Today, March 14, 2022. Available at: https://philmuslimtoday.com/2022/03/14/ditucalan-assumes-as-msu-iit-
new-chancellor/</ref>
At the Kyushu University Graduate School of Law, he completed an LL.M. in International Economic and Business Law with a
specialization in Competition Law. The curriculum required twenty academic credits and a master's thesis of at least fifty pages, drawing on
comparative regulatory frameworks from the United States, the European Union, and Japan.<ref name="kyushu-ylp">Young Leaders'
Program (YLP) in Law (LL.M.), Kyushu University Graduate School of Law. Available at: https://www.law.kyushu-
u.ac.jp/programsinenglish/html/programs-admissions/academic-programs/ylp-ll-m/</ref> The experience also gave him something harder
to quantify: a deep familiarity with the Japanese administrative culture of long-term planning, accountability structured around clear
metrics, and what he would later describe as the institutional value of "predictability."<ref name="msu-newsletter">MSU Newsletter,
March 2023, MSU Main Campus. Available at: https://www.msumain.edu.ph/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/01-2023-March-MSU-
Newsletter.pdf</ref>
Graduate Studies at KU Leuven
Alongside his Japan-based training, Ditucalan completed additional graduate coursework at the Katholieke Universiteit Leuven (KU
Leuven) in Belgium, deepening his grounding in European competition law and comparative regulatory theory.<ref name="pmt"/>
Doctoral Research at Kyushu University
Ditucalan was subsequently selected under the JICA Knowledge Co-Creation Program (KCCP) as the first Filipino long-term scholar of the
Japan International Cooperation Agency (JICA) to undertake doctoral research at Kyushu University's Graduate School of Law. He was
also the first Filipino lawyer to pursue a doctorate specifically in competition law.<ref name="pmt"/> His research focused on the
institutional design of Philippine competition law, examining how the architecture of regulatory agencies, not merely the text of the
legislation, determines whether a competition regime actually works in practice.<ref name="nexus">Dean Zed Pursues LL.D. in Kyushu
University, Japan, The Nexus (MSU Law), February 4, 2018. Available at: https://msulawnexus.wordpress.com/2018/02/04/dean-zed-
pursues-ll-d-in-kyushu-univesity-japan/</ref>
A note on credentials: while multiple biographical sources describe Ditucalan as having pursued a Doctor of Laws (LL.D.) at Kyushu, the
official MSU-IIT directory lists his academic titles as J.D. and LL.M. only.<ref name="pmt"/> The 2018 announcement in The Nexus
confirmed that he began his three-year LL.D. program at Kyushu in February 2018.<ref name="nexus"/> The conferral of the LL.D. degree
had not been independently confirmed by official institutional records at the time this article was written.

PAGE 3
Career
Early Legal Practice
After completing his Juris Doctor, Ditucalan entered public service as a public attorney, essentially a public defender, gaining the front-line
litigation experience that would later distinguish his scholarship from more abstract legal theory. He was subsequently appointed University
Chief Legal Counsel of the MSU System and Director of the Legal Services Division, roles that required him to navigate the full
complexity of institutional law within a multi-campus state university.<ref name="pmt"/> He also served as President of the local chapter
of the Integrated Bar of the Philippines and as Managing Partner at Subejano and Ditucalan, handling appellate work.<ref name="pmt"/>
Dean of the MSU College of Law
Ditucalan served as Dean across three campuses of the MSU College of Law, a portfolio reflecting the confidence the MSU System placed
in his administrative capacity.<ref name="pmt"/> During this period, he also served as Vice Chancellor for Academic Affairs at MSU-IIT,
giving him a comprehensive view of how both legal education and university administration function from the inside.
His most consequential innovation as dean was the creation of the Sarimanok Virtual Law Clinic (SVLC), conceptualized in 2019. The
SVLC was built on the expanded permissions granted to law student practitioners under the Revised Rule 138-A of the Supreme Court of
the Philippines, which broadened the scope of activities law students could undertake under attorney supervision.<ref name="clep">The
First of a Thousand Voices: Stories of CLEP in the First Years of the Revised Rule 138-A. Available at:
https://fliphtml5.com/qzxkz/torf/The_First_of_a_Thousand_Voices%3A_Stories_of_CLEP_in_the_First_Years_of_the_Revised_Rule_138-
A/</ref>
Under Ditucalan's guidance, MSU became one of the first law schools in the country to leverage this expanded framework through a digital
delivery model. Students could conduct virtual client interviews and provide supervised legal advice through online platforms, effectively
removing the geographic barrier that had historically prevented residents of remote communities in Lanao del Norte from accessing legal
services.<ref name="clep"/> The SVLC was not an emergency pandemic response; it was operational before COVID-19 arrived in 2020,
making it one of the clearest examples in recent Philippine legal history of institutional leadership anticipating conditions rather than
merely reacting to them.
The clinic was developed in conversation with the highest levels of Philippine judicial leadership. Ditucalan participated in consultations
with then-Chief Justice Lucas Bersamin and Associate Justice Alexander Gesmundo, and was part of a Philippine delegation that visited
Harvard University, Georgetown University, and Suffolk University to study American clinical legal education models.<ref name="pmt"/>
The SVLC model has since been documented in The First of a Thousand Voices, a publication chronicling the early experience of clinical
legal education under the revised rule.<ref name="clep"/>
Election and Investiture as Chancellor of MSU-IIT
When the MSU Board of Regents convened in Manila on February 28, 2022, and elected Ditucalan as the fourth Chancellor of MSU-IIT,
the decision carried weight beyond the procedural.<ref name="iit-history"/> He was not only the youngest person to hold the
chancellorship in the institution's history; he was also the first of its alumni ever to return as its head, nearly 22 years after his own
graduation.<ref name="pmt"/>
His formal investiture took place on July 12, 2022, during MSU-IIT's 54th Charter Day, when MSU System President Atty. Basari D.
Mapupuno presented him with the Chancellor's Medallion and the University Mace, the first and only such mace approved by the MSU
Board of Regents.<ref name="investiture">Ditucalan lays out 10-year vision for IIT during investiture, MSU-IIT News, July 2022.
Available at: https://www.msuiit.edu.ph/news/news-detail.php?id=1473</ref> He succeeded Dr. Sukarno D. Tanggol.<ref name="iit-
history"/>
From his first days in office, Ditucalan set a tone that was deliberately different from the detached formality often associated with
university leadership. He toured every unit on campus, conducted listening sessions with faculty and staff in their own spaces rather than
summoning them to his, and engaged directly with local radio to share his vision with the broader Iligan community.<ref name="one-
year">ChanZed's ONE-credible Year at MSU-IIT, MSU-IIT News. Available at: https://www.msuiit.edu.ph/news/news-detail.php?
id=1568</ref> In one candid moment, speaking in the easy Visayan that characterizes daily life in Iligan, he admitted that had he known
fully what the role entailed, he might have thought twice before accepting it. It was a moment of genuine self-disclosure that his
constituents, by all accounts, appreciated.<ref name="one-year"/>

PAGE 4
Scholarship and Intellectual Contributions
Competition Law as Institutional Architecture
Ditucalan's standing as one of the Philippines' leading competition law scholars rests on a body of work that is coherent in a way that much
legal scholarship is not: every piece contributes to a single sustained argument rather than ranging across disconnected topics.
The backdrop is a specific legislative history. For roughly 25 years, the Philippine Congress struggled to pass a national competition law,
leaving the economy exposed to cartel arrangements and the abuse of dominant market positions.<ref name="msu-newsletter"/> When the
Philippine Competition Act (PCA) was finally enacted in 2015, it drew on two distinct regulatory traditions: the American model, grounded
in economic efficiency analysis, and the European Union model, which foregrounds market structure and restricts dominant firms from
excluding rivals.<ref name="elgar">Ditucalan, Alizedney M., The Philippine Competition Law Dilemma: US-EU Fusion and Tension, in
Van Uytsel, Hayashi, and Haley (eds.), Research Handbook on Asian Competition Law (Edward Elgar Publishing, 2020). Available at:
https://www.e-elgar.com/shop/usd/research-handbook-on-asian-competition-law-9781785361821.html</ref>
In his contribution to the Research Handbook on Asian Competition Law (Edward Elgar, 2020), Ditucalan argued that the PCA is better
understood as a "fusion" of these two models than as a transplant from either, and that this fusion creates an internal regulatory tension the
Philippine Competition Commission (PCC) must navigate on a case-by-case basis.<ref name="elgar"/>
His earlier work, "Institutional Design of Philippine Competition Law," published in the KLRI Journal of Law and Legislation in 2018,
took a more structural approach: the PCA's effectiveness depends less on its substantive text than on the organizational architecture of the
PCC itself. Independence from political interference, technical expertise in the agency's professional staff, and accountability mechanisms
that are transparent without being crippling: these, he argued, are the prerequisites for effective competition enforcement in any developing
economy, and the Philippines had not yet fully satisfied them at the time of writing.<ref name="klri-2018">Ditucalan, Alizedney M.,
Institutional Design of Philippine Competition Law, KLRI Journal of Law and Legislation, Volume 8, Number 1 (2018). Available at
SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3489788</ref>
A 2019 article in the same journal, "The Philippine Competition Act: A Mestiza?," extended the analysis through the lens of mixed legal
systems, arguing that the PCA's hybrid American-European-Filipino character creates both flexibility and uncertainty in its application.<ref
name="klri-2019">Ditucalan, Alizedney M., The Philippine Competition Act: A Mestiza?, KLRI Journal of Law and Legislation, Volume
9, Number 2 (2019). Available at SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3499045</ref> His chapter in Leniency in
Asian Competition Law (Cambridge University Press, 2022) added a further dimension, examining how cartel self-reporting mechanisms
(leniency programs) function in Asian jurisdictions where institutional trust may be lower than in Western contexts.<ref
name="cambridge">Ditucalan, Alizedney M., Chapter contribution to Leniency in Asian Competition Law (Cambridge University Press,
2022). Available at: https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/leniency-in-asian-competition-law/</ref>
The core proposition running through all of this work is direct: law reform without institutional reform is insufficient; transplanted legal
frameworks require active redesign to function in their recipient environments; and the measure of a competition law is not the elegance of
its text but the quality of the agency charged with enforcing it.
Administration as Chancellor
Vision 2032 and "Influencing the Future"
His 10-year strategic vision, Vision 2032, was approved by the MSU Board of Regents on December 22, 2022.<ref name="one-year"/> It
gave direction and specificity to a trajectory MSU-IIT had been moving toward for years, organized around six pillars: Education; Research
and Innovation; Student Support; Public Service; Governance; and Infrastructure.<ref name="investiture"/> The vision's five-year
operational plan carries the tagline "Influencing the Future," and the phrase is more than marketing: it captures Ditucalan's conviction that a
regional university's highest obligation is not to mirror what institutions elsewhere have already achieved, but to shape what comes next.
The "One MSU" Mandate
One of the most ambitious of Ditucalan's early initiatives was convening the 2022 MSU System-wide Academic Summit, the first in the
MSU System's history.<ref name="msu-newsletter"/> Bringing together academic heads from all thirteen MSU campuses, the summit
addressed faculty development pathways, learning outcomes alignment with international benchmarks, blended and digital-first teaching
methods, program alignment across campuses, student support services, and quality assurance mechanisms.

PAGE 5
The goal was not to make every campus identical, but to achieve what Ditucalan consistently calls "systemness": the coherence of shared
standards and shared ambitions operating through institutional diversity.<ref name="msu-newsletter"/> This "One MSU" philosophy
carries particular resonance given the historical complexity of the relationship between MSU-Marawi and MSU-IIT, two campuses roughly
90 kilometers apart, in different provinces, with different demographic compositions and primary disciplines. By positioning MSU-IIT as a
partner of the main campus rather than a rival, and by embodying that position through his own biography as a Marawi-formed scholar
leading the Iligan institution, Ditucalan has sought to make the integration he advocates personally credible.<ref name="investiture"/>
Research Intensity and Rankings
At the time of Ditucalan's appointment, the data offered both encouragement and urgency. In 2022, MSU-IIT broke into the Times Higher
Education Impact Rankings, placing in the 801-1000 band in recognition of its performance against the United Nations Sustainable
Development Goals.<ref name="iit-history"/> In the QS World University Rankings: Asia, it had held a position in the 551-600 range for
several consecutive years, with academic reputation as its strongest asset.<ref name="wiki-msuiit">Mindanao State University-Iligan
Institute of Technology, Wikipedia, accessed March 10, 2026. Available at:
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mindanao_State_University%E2%80%93Iligan_Institute_of_Technology</ref> In the Webometrics Ranking,
MSU-IIT had climbed to sixth among Philippine institutions in July 2021, and ranked fourth among Philippine universities in the UI
GreenMetric worldwide rankings.<ref name="iit-history"/> In the same year, it received ISO 9001:2015 certification.<ref name="iit-
history"/>
Physics Professor Jan Mickelle Maratas was ranked as the Philippines' top scientist by the AD Scientific Index in 2022, a recognition that
reflected the kind of sustained investment in individual researchers that Ditucalan's administration has worked to amplify and
institutionalize.<ref name="iit-history"/> The university's designation as the first Center for Sustainable Polymers in the Philippines
reinforced the seriousness of its research ambitions.
His administration has also pursued active partnerships with the Department of Science and Technology. A 2022 visit to the DOST
Advanced Science and Technology Institute (DOST-ASTI) explored collaborative work in satellite data science under the PEDRO
initiative, AI-assisted agricultural applications through the Gul.AI platform, and disaster risk mitigation.<ref name="dost">DOST-ASTI
Features Initiatives to MSU-IIT, DOST Advanced Science and Technology Institute, 2022. Available at:
https://asti.dost.gov.ph/communications/dost-asti-features-initiatives-to-msu-iit/</ref>
Industry Partnerships and Micro-credentials
At the Times Higher Education Asia Universities Summit in 2023, Ditucalan elaborated a practical argument about the future of university
credentials: that automation and artificial intelligence will simultaneously displace existing jobs and generate demand for competencies that
conventional degree programs do not yet supply.<ref name="the-summit">Agenda and Speaker Profile, Alizedney Ditucalan, THE Asia
Universities Summit 2023. Available at: https://www.timeshighered-events.com/asia-universities-summit-
2023/agenda/speakers/3070008</ref> His response has been to forge partnerships with Coursera and with global technology firms
including Google, Meta, and IBM, embedding professional certificates into the MSU-IIT curriculum as stackable credentials that
complement academic degrees and are legible to employers in markets far beyond Iligan.<ref name="the-summit"/>
On the international academic front, he has continued to cultivate his relationship with Kyushu University, facilitating faculty exchanges
and joint research, and has pursued collaborative programs with the University of the Philippines Diliman.<ref name="nexus"/> In 2025,
MSU-IIT formalized a strategic partnership with Thailand's Bansomdejchaopraya Rajabhat University through a memorandum of
understanding, extending the university's internationalization agenda into Southeast Asia.<ref name="msuiit-mou">MSU-IIT and
Thailand's Bansomdejchaopraya Rajabhat University forge strategic partnership through MOU, MSU-IIT News, 2025. Available at:
https://www.msuiit.edu.ph/news</ref>
Equity, Inclusion, and Peace Education
The values that appear in Ditucalan's policy decisions are consistent with those that appear in his scholarship: that institutions earn
legitimacy through transparency and accountability, and that an institution failing to serve all of its constituents is, by definition, poorly
designed.
One notable example is the implementation of an inclusive dress code policy at MSU-IIT, which permits students to wear attire
corresponding to their gender identity and preference.<ref name="pia">Education, PIA Northern Mindanao (WordPress), accessed March
10, 2026. Available at: https://pianormin.wordpress.com/tag/education/</ref> In a region where conservative social norms carry real
weight, and at a university drawing students from across Mindanao's diverse communities, this was an institutional statement with
implications far beyond dress codes. Ditucalan explained it in straightforward terms: a learning environment must be one where every
student feels safe and respected, and that principle extends to the most visible markers of identity.<ref name="pia"/>

PAGE 6
In 2024, under his oversight, MSU-IIT approved a formal Peace Education Policy and moved to strengthen the Institute for Peace and
Development in Mindanao (IPDM).<ref name="msu-2024">MSU Newsletter, September 2024, MSU Main Campus. Available at:
https://www.msumain.edu.ph/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/05-2024-September-MSU-Newsletter.pdf</ref> These steps align with the
Bangsamoro Education Code of 2021, which calls for the integration of peace education across all levels of the school system in the
Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao.<ref name="bec">Bangsamoro Education Code of 2021. Available at:
https://rasmitmug.com/ebooks/Bangsamoro-Education-Code-1.pdf</ref> For MSU-IIT, which sits in a city adjacent to the Bangsamoro
peace process without being formally within the BARMM, these policies are also a form of institutional positioning: a declaration that the
university intends to play a substantive role in regional reconciliation.
Legacy and Cultural Significance
There is a dimension of Ditucalan's career that resists easy categorization under scholarship or administration: its symbolic function for the
communities that shaped him. He represents a profile that remains rare in Philippine public life: a Maranao Muslim from Lanao del Sur
who has published in Edward Elgar handbooks, studied in Kyushu, Brussels, and Cambridge, and now leads one of the country's better-
ranked technological universities. That profile matters in ways that extend beyond the individual.
In his commencement addresses, including the 53rd Commencement Exercises of MSU-IIT and the 61st Commencement of MSU-Marawi,
he has returned consistently to a formulation that captures his sense of obligation:
A graduate's success is the country's hope.
The phrase sounds simple; in context, it is dense with meaning. For graduates of a university still rebuilding from the 2017 siege of Marawi
City, or from an Iligan campus that received thousands of Marawi evacuees during that crisis, the injunction carries a weight that it simply
would not carry at a Manila institution.<ref name="commencement-msuiit">Welcome Address by Chancellor Alizedney Ditucalan during
the 53rd Commencement Ceremonies of MSU-IIT. Available at: https://www.msuiit.edu.ph/announcements/detail.php?id=1773</ref><ref
name="msu-marawi-61">61st Commencement Exercises Souvenir Program, MSU Main Campus, 2024-2025. Available at:
https://www.msumain.edu.ph/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/61st-Commencement-Exercises-Souvenir-Program-(2nd-Sem-2024-
2025).pdf</ref>
His emergence as the first Filipino JICA long-term doctoral scholar at Kyushu, and as the first Mindanaoan recipient of the YLP fellowship,
has also altered perceptions, both within the region and within the JICA network, of what Mindanao-based scholars can achieve in
international competitive processes. One of the most persistent structural obstacles to Mindanao's development is the underrepresentation of
Mindanao professionals and academics in the national and international networks where research agendas and policy priorities are set.
Ditucalan's career has pushed, visibly and verifiably, against that pattern.
Recognition and Awards
First alumnus of MSU-IIT to serve as Chancellor of the institution (2022)
Youngest Chancellor in MSU-IIT's institutional history (2022)
First grantee from Mindanao for Japan's Young Leaders' Program (YLP)
First Filipino long-term JICA scholar at Kyushu University's Graduate School of Law
First Filipino lawyer to undertake doctoral research specifically in competition law
Speaker, Times Higher Education Asia Universities Summit (2023)
MSU-IIT recognized in the Times Higher Education Impact Rankings (801–1000 band, 2022) and QS World University Rankings:
Asia (551–600 band) during his chancellorship
MSU-IIT ranked 6th among Philippine institutions in Webometrics (July 2021) and 4th in the UI GreenMetric worldwide rankings
Challenges
No account of Ditucalan's chancellorship would be complete without acknowledging the structural conditions in which it operates. MSU-
IIT, for all its rankings achievements, remains a regional state university in a part of the Philippines that continues to carry the weight of
decades of armed conflict, economic underdevelopment, and institutional neglect. Transforming such a university into a research-intensive
institution requires not just vision and strategy but sustained external funding, stable political conditions, and a faculty pipeline that takes
years to build.
The credential discrepancy around his doctoral degree, noted in scholarly sources, has not been definitively resolved by official institutional
records, and remains an open question for future documentation.<ref name="pmt"/><ref name="nexus"/>

PAGE 7
The inclusive dress code policy, while principled, was implemented in a social environment where it was not without controversy, and its
long-term acceptance within the MSU-IIT community reflects an ongoing process of institutional culture change rather than a settled
outcome.<ref name="pia"/>
More broadly, Ditucalan's administration faces the challenge common to any reforming leader in a complex institution: that the coherence
of a vision in the chancellor's office does not automatically translate into coherence at the level of departments, programs, and individual
faculty members who have their own ideas about what the university is for.
Personal Reflections
Ditucalan has spoken publicly, with characteristic directness, about what the chancellorship has demanded of him. In one exchange with the
Iligan community, he admitted in the easy Visayan of everyday life in the city that, had he fully understood what the role entailed, he might
have hesitated before accepting it.<ref name="one-year"/> Coming from someone whose career has been defined by taking on firsts, the
remark reads less as regret than as honest testimony about the weight of institutional leadership, and about the gap between the theory of
institutional design and the daily reality of running an institution through that design.

Abdulgani Maulana Sarip Domado
Dr. Abdulgani Maulana Sarip Domado was a distinguished
academic leader, administrator, and educator whose four-decade
career at Mindanao State University (MSU) profoundly shaped the
institution and mentored generations of students and professionals.
A Bangsamoro intellectual whose expertise spanned statistics,
Islamic jurisprudence, and institutional management, Domado
earned historic distinction as the first and only individual to
receive a PhD from MSU in 1993. His life embodied the
principles of leadership, friendship, and service, bridging social
divides with rare humility and connecting sincerely with
colleagues across all organizational levels.
Contents
1 Early Life and Educational Foundation
2 Historic Achievement: Pioneer PhD Graduate
3 Professional Career and Administrative Leadership
4 International Experience and Global Perspective
5 Leadership Philosophy: The Alpha Phi Omega Legacy
6 Character and the Common Touch
7 Mentorship and Pedagogical Legacy
8 Family and Personal Values
9 Spiritual Foundation
10 Legacy and Recognition
11 See Also
12 References
13 Further Reading
Early Life and Educational Foundation
Dr. Domado's relationship with Mindanao State University began early and remained unbroken throughout his life.
A four-time MSU alumnus, he built his academic credentials across multiple disciplines and institutions. He earned
his Juris Doctor degree from the University of the East in Manila in 1983, demonstrating his commitment to legal
scholarship. Recognizing the intersection between Islamic law and modern governance, he completed specialized
Sharia training in 1991, deepening his expertise in Islamic jurisprudence. This multidisciplinary foundation
positioned him uniquely at the crossroads of law, Islamic studies, and statistical analysis.
Historic Achievement: Pioneer PhD Graduate
In 1993, Domado achieved a milestone that would forever mark his place in MSU's institutional history. He
became the first and only individual to earn a PhD from Mindanao State University, a watershed moment for the
university's academic credibility and research standing. This accomplishment was not merely personal

PAGE 2
achievement; it validated MSU's capacity to produce doctoral-level research and scholarship. As an accredited
statistician who chaired the Graduate School Panel in 1993, Domado helped establish rigorous standards for high-
level academic inquiry at the institution.
Professional Career and Administrative Leadership
Domado's professional journey began in 1975 at the Jamiatul Philippines Al-Islamia Foundation (JPI), where he
served as a full-time instructor before rising to pioneering professor status in the Graduate School. His career
spanned over four decades, the vast majority dedicated to MSU's advancement.
By the early 2000s, Domado had ascended to increasingly significant administrative roles. His crowning
institutional responsibility came as Director of the Board of Regents (BOR), Supply, Property, and Auxiliary
Services, where he oversaw critical operational, procurement, and resource management functions for the entire
university system. He carried this responsibility until his retirement in 2019, ensuring that MSU's physical
infrastructure, supply chains, and auxiliary services operated with integrity and efficiency.
International Experience and Global Perspective
Beyond the Philippines, Domado's professional footprint extended to the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, where he
served as an Administrative Officer at the Revenue Attaché Office. He also worked as a General Consultant for
Yellow Pages in Riyadh, managing a diverse team of 24 managers and bringing Filipino professional standards to
an international marketplace. This international experience enriched his understanding of organizational dynamics
and cross-cultural management.
Leadership Philosophy: The Alpha Phi Omega Legacy
Domado's approach to leadership was fundamentally shaped by his early involvement in collegiate civic
organizations. As a pioneering member of Alpha Phi Omega (Beta Upsilon Chapter, MSU), he internalized the
fraternity's cardinal principles of leadership, friendship, and service. These weren't mere organizational slogans;
they became the ethical framework guiding his four-decade career.
Leadership through stewardship manifested across multiple roles. Beyond his MSU directorship, he served as:
Grand Chancellor of the JPI Mother Chapter of Mindanao (1975–1977)
President of the MSU ILS Federated Organization
President of the JPI Faculty Association
Vice President of the RIR Forum
Each role prepared him for progressively greater institutional responsibility.
Character and the Common Touch
The principle of friendship took on distinctive meaning in Domado's life. Colleagues and students consistently
remarked on his humility and "common touch," a rare ability to treat security guards, drivers, and high-ranking
government officials with equal sincerity and respect. He demonstrated that authentic leadership isn't measured by
hierarchy but by genuine human connection. This egalitarian spirit made him beloved across the university
community, earning affection from those at every organizational level.

PAGE 3
Mentorship and Pedagogical Legacy
Service became Domado's lifelong vocation, expressed through both administrative stewardship and passionate
teaching. As a pioneering professor in the Graduate School, he inspired generations of students through mentorship
grounded in intellectual rigor and moral guidance. His students valued not just his expertise but his willingness to
invest in their professional and personal growth. This mentorship legacy extended beyond the classroom; former
students often credited Domado's encouragement as pivotal to their career trajectories.
Family and Personal Values
The cornerstone of Domado's life was family. Alongside his wife, Bae Alabi sa Ramain Ombae Sarip Domado,
he prioritized the education and success of their ten children. The couple instilled values of discipline, sacrifice,
and perseverance that yielded remarkable results. Their children pursued diverse professional paths, achieving
success across multiple fields:
Two earned doctoral degrees
Four became engineers
One became a nurse
Two entered management professions
One pursued advanced studies in biology
Domado viewed his role as a father and husband as his most profound service, understanding that family
excellence reflects larger institutional commitment.
Spiritual Foundation
Throughout his life, Domado attributed his many successes to the grace of Allah, reflecting a faith-centered
worldview. His identity as a Muslim intellectual contributed meaningfully to MSU's mission as the nation's premier
Muslim university and research institution. He modeled how Islamic values of discipline, integrity, and service-to-
community could animate academic and administrative work.
Legacy and Recognition
Dr. Domado's retirement in 2019 marked the conclusion of institutional service but not the end of his influence. His
legacy persists through:
The first and only MSU PhD graduate, establishing a precedent for institutional research excellence
Generations of mentored students and professionals scattered across Philippine and international institutions
A family of accomplished professionals whose success exemplifies his personal values
A standard of humble, servant-centered leadership that contrasts sharply with ego-driven administration
His life demonstrated that great institutional achievement needn't rely on self-promotion or hierarchical distance
from those being served. Instead, it emerges from sustained commitment, intellectual rigor, ethical consistency, and
genuine care for others' development.

title: Domado, Metalicop A.
text:
PAGE 1
Metalicop A. Domado
Born
Lanao del Sur, Philippines
Nationality
Filipino

Metalicop A. Domado
Atty. Metalicop A. Domado (rahimahullah) was a Filipino
Muslim lawyer and public administrator who played a central role
in building many of the institutional programs that supported
Muslim Filipino cultural affairs in the late twentieth century.
Serving as Director of the Bureau of Muslim Cultural Affairs
within the Office on Muslim Affairs, he quietly helped construct
systems that strengthened Qur'anic education, Shari'ah legal
training, madrasah development, and cultural recognition for
Muslim communities across the Philippines.<ref
name="tamano"/>
His work rarely attracted headlines, yet the structures he designed
continue to shape Muslim Filipino cultural and religious life.
Colleagues often described him as an “institution builder,”
someone who believed that lasting change happens when strong
systems are carefully created and patiently maintained.
Contents
1 Background
2 Education
3 Early Career at Mindanao State University
4 Service in the Office on Muslim Affairs
5 Qur'an Reading Competition Programs
6 Shari'ah Training and Legal Development
7 Cultural Programs and Community Engagement
8 Madrasah Education Initiatives
9 Character and Leadership Style
10 Transition to the National Commission on Muslim Filipinos
11 Legacy
12 Death
13 See Also
14 Further Reading
15 References
Background
Metalicop A. Domado came from Lanao del Sur, a province widely known as one of the cultural centers of the
Maranao people in Mindanao. Growing up in a region deeply connected to Islamic tradition, he developed a strong
awareness of the social realities facing Muslim Filipinos.
Friends and colleagues later recalled that Domado carried a strong sense of responsibility toward ordinary people
in his community. The stories of farmers, small traders, and families struggling to navigate government institutions
stayed with him, shaping his view that public service should focus on practical solutions rather than public

PAGE 2
recognition.
Education
Domado pursued legal studies and eventually passed the Philippine Bar, entering the legal profession during a
period when Muslim representation within national institutions remained limited. His training in law gave him the
tools to navigate the country's legal system while remaining rooted in Islamic legal traditions recognized under
Philippine law.
His legal background later proved essential when working on programs related to Shari'ah implementation and
Muslim personal law.
Early Career at Mindanao State University
In 1976, Domado joined Mindanao State University in Marawi City as Director of Personnel Management and
Training Services. At the time, the university served as an important educational center for Muslim Mindanao.
While his official responsibilities focused on personnel management, many who worked with him remember a
different side of his daily routine. Community members often approached the university seeking help or advice,
and Domado regularly took time to listen to their concerns.
The law for him was never about arguments in courtrooms. It was about justice for people who could
not afford lawyers. |source=Former MSU colleague
These interactions gradually shaped his understanding that meaningful service required engagement beyond the
walls of a single institution.
Service in the Office on Muslim Affairs
The creation of the Office on Muslim Affairs (OMA) in 1987 through Executive Order No. 122-A marked an
important moment for Muslim Filipino representation within the Philippine government.<ref name="eo122"/>
Domado joined the new institution through its Plans and Policy Services division. Much of his work took place
behind the scenes, drafting program structures, preparing policy proposals, and helping translate the broad mandate
of the OMA into workable initiatives.
Colleagues quickly noticed his long-term perspective. Instead of focusing only on launching programs, he
constantly asked how those programs would survive changes in administration or funding.
In five years, where will this office be? In ten years, what will we have accomplished?
|source=Ashary S. Tamano, former OMA official
Eventually, Domado became Director of the Bureau of Muslim Cultural Affairs (BMCA), the position where he
made his most lasting contributions.

PAGE 3
Qur'an Reading Competition Programs
One of Domado's most visible achievements involved strengthening the national structure for the Qur'an Reading
Competition (QRC).
Before his reforms, local competitions existed but lacked a consistent pathway that could bring talented reciters
from local communities to the international stage.
Domado introduced several institutional improvements:
standardized judging criteria
structured selection procedures
training and accreditation of judges
coordinated national competitions
These changes helped transform the Philippine QRC system into a reliable pipeline for international participation.
The results were remarkable. Filipino competitors began winning major titles in global competitions. Among the
most notable champions was Abdul Bashit Imam, who won multiple international championships including
victories in Dhaka and Tehran.<ref name="qrc"/>
Female competitors also achieved recognition. Isnairah Bantayao won a major international competition in Kuala
Lumpur, while Potre Salacayan and Norania Cabugatan secured victories in regional ASEAN contests.
In 2000, the Philippines hosted the ASEAN Qur'an Reading Competition at the Philippine International Convention
Center in Pasay City. The event demonstrated the country's growing role in the international community of
Qur'anic reciters.
Shari'ah Training and Legal Development
Another major focus of Domado's work involved the implementation of Presidential Decree No. 1083, also known
as the Code of Muslim Personal Laws of the Philippines.<ref name="pd1083"/>
Although the law recognized Shari'ah in matters such as marriage, divorce, and inheritance, the system required
trained personnel to function effectively.
To address this need, the OMA established Shari'ah Training Centers in several locations:
Marawi City
Cotabato City
Zamboanga City
National Capital Region
Jolo, Sulu
Between 1989 and 2009, nine training cycles were conducted, reaching more than two thousand participants
interested in Islamic jurisprudence and its relationship with Philippine law.<ref name="shariah"/>
More than one thousand candidates later took the Special Bar Examination for Shari'ah Counselors, with several
hundred successfully passing the rigorous process.
Through these initiatives, Domado helped build the human infrastructure necessary for the practical application of
Muslim personal law.

PAGE 4
Cultural Programs and Community Engagement
Domado believed that culture should not remain confined to government archives. Instead, it should be visible,
celebrated, and experienced in everyday life.
During the 1990s, the OMA partnered with community organizations to support public celebrations of major
Islamic holidays. Among the most prominent were the International Eid'l Fitr Festivals organized in Metro
Manila by the Kasañangan Foundation.<ref name="eid"/>
These events provided Muslim Filipinos living in the capital with an opportunity to gather, celebrate, and share
their cultural heritage with a wider audience.
The Bureau also supported public awareness campaigns informing Muslim Filipinos of their officially recognized
religious holidays under Philippine law.
Madrasah Education Initiatives
Domado also worked to strengthen the role of the madrasah system in the national education framework.
Islamic schools had long served as centers for religious learning in Muslim communities, yet their graduates often
faced difficulties when entering the formal educational system.
The OMA helped reactivate the National Federation of Arabic Madaris to create a coordinated national network
of Islamic schools. Regional chapters were organized across Mindanao and the Sulu archipelago.
Cooperation between the OMA and the Department of Education eventually produced a framework for integrating
madrasah education into the national curriculum.<ref name="madrasah"/>
Financial assistance was also provided to hundreds of madaris and ustadzes, offering modest but meaningful
support to Islamic educators.
Character and Leadership Style
Those who worked closely with Domado consistently described him as disciplined, humble, and deeply committed
to public service.
He was the first to arrive and the last to leave. He believed every minute of work was a chance to serve
someone who needed help.
|source=Former staff member
Rather than seeking attention, he preferred careful planning and quiet execution. His leadership style emphasized
consultation with community leaders, religious scholars, educators, and youth groups.
Despite limited budgets and shifting political priorities, he continued building programs that could survive
institutional change.

PAGE 5
Transition to the National Commission on Muslim Filipinos
In 2010, Republic Act No. 9997 abolished the Office on Muslim Affairs and created the National Commission on
Muslim Filipinos (NCMF).<ref name="ra9997"/>
Although the agency structure changed, many programs originally developed during Domado's tenure continued
under the new institution. These included Qur'an reading competitions, Shari'ah training programs, and madrasah
education initiatives.
The survival of these programs demonstrated the strength of the institutional foundations he helped create.
Legacy
Atty. Metalicop A. Domado is remembered as a public servant who believed that institutions matter. His work
focused on building systems that allowed Muslim Filipino communities to preserve their faith, culture, and legal
traditions within the national framework.
Many of the programs he helped design continue to operate decades later, supporting new generations of scholars,
educators, and Qur'anic reciters.
For those who worked alongside him, his legacy can be summed up in a simple idea: real progress happens quietly,
when institutions are built carefully and allowed to grow over time.
Death
Details surrounding the date of Domado's passing are not widely documented in public sources. Within Muslim
communities and among former colleagues, he is remembered with the prayer rahimahullah (may Allah have
mercy on him), a traditional expression honoring a departed believer.

Sha Elijah Biruar Dumama-Alba
Atty. Sha Elijah Biruar Dumama-Alba is a Maguindanaoan
lawyer, legislator, and public servant widely regarded as one of the
most consequential figures in the young history of the Bangsamoro
Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM).
A woman of firsts, she served as the inaugural Attorney General of
the BARMM and later became the first woman to head the Ministry
of the Interior and Local Government (MILG) in the region.
Her career is anchored on a principle she has championed publicly
and personally: Moral Governance, the idea that public service
must be grounded in integrity, transparency, and the lived values of
the Bangsamoro people.
She completed both the regular Philippine Bar and the special
Shari'ah Bar, placing third nationally in the 2018 Shari'ah Bar
Examinations, a distinction that positions her as a rare legal voice
capable of navigating both the secular and Islamic legal traditions of
the Philippines.
As a member of the Bangsamoro Transition Authority (BTA)
Parliament, she served as Floor Leader and Chairperson of the
Committee on Rules, helping lay down the foundational laws that
would define how the region governs itself for generations.
She belongs to the Maguindanaoan ethnic group, one of the
principal Moro peoples of Mindanao.
Contents
1 Early Life and Family Background
2 Education
3 Career
3.1 Bangsamoro Attorney General (2019–2023)
3.2 Legislative Leadership in the Bangsamoro Transition
Authority
3.3 Minister of the Interior and Local Government (2023–
present)
3.4 Deputy Speaker, Bangsamoro Parliament (2025–
present)
4 Institutional Contributions

6 Legacy and Cultural Significance
7 Recognition
8 See Also

PAGE 2
Early Life and Family Background
Sha Elijah Biruar Dumama-Alba was born in the early 1980s in Cotabato City, a city that sits at the political and
cultural heart of the Bangsamoro region.
She grew up in a household shaped by public service. Both of her parents were doctors and government workers,
and that dual commitment to professional excellence and community duty left a deep impression on her.
She was a remarkably fast learner from the start. She completed high school at just 14 years old, a fact that points
to the kind of intellectual drive that would later define her career.
In her early college years, she followed her father's preference and enrolled in a pre-medical course. By her third
year, however, she had made a decisive turn toward law, a shift that would eventually take her to the highest legal
office in the Bangsamoro.
That pivot, from medicine to law, turned out to be one of the most consequential decisions in Bangsamoro legal
history.
Education
Atty. Dumama-Alba's educational path reflects both academic rigor and a deliberate orientation toward public life.
She earned her Bachelor of Science in Public Administration from the University of the Philippines Diliman,
one of the country's most competitive and respected public universities.
She went on to complete her Juris Doctor at San Beda University, a law school with a strong national reputation
for producing bar topnotchers and public interest lawyers.
She later added a Master's Degree in Public Management, with a specialization in Regional and Local
Governance, from the Development Academy of the Philippines, deepening her understanding of how
government actually works at the ground level.
Her most distinctive academic achievement came in 2018, when she placed 3rd in the Special Shari'ah Bar
Examinations, making her one of a very small number of lawyers in the Philippines admitted to both the regular
Philippine Bar and the Shari'ah Bar.
That dual admission is not just a credential. It reflects a genuine commitment to serving a community whose legal
needs span two distinct systems of law.
Career
Bangsamoro Attorney General (2019–2023)
When the BARMM was formally established in 2019 under the Bangsamoro Organic Law, it needed legal
infrastructure as much as it needed political leadership.
Atty. Dumama-Alba stepped into that need as the first-ever Attorney General of the BARMM, serving as the
chief legal advisor to the Chief Minister and the entire Cabinet.

PAGE 3
The role placed her at the center of some of the most complex legal questions facing a newly autonomous region:
How do you translate a peace agreement into workable governance structures? How do you build institutions that
respect both national law and the unique legal traditions of the Bangsamoro?
She held the position from 2019 to 2023, a period that coincided with the critical early years of the region's
transition.
Legislative Leadership in the Bangsamoro Transition Authority
As a Member of Parliament in the BTA, Atty. Dumama-Alba took on a legislative leadership role that went well
beyond representing a constituency.
She served as Floor Leader of the BTA Parliament and as Chairperson of the Committee on Rules, two
positions that put her squarely in charge of how the parliament functioned as a body.
In that capacity, she helped shepherd the passage of two foundational laws: the Bangsamoro Electoral Code and
the Bangsamoro Local Governance Code.
These aren't routine pieces of legislation. They are the legal backbone of how the region elects its leaders and how
its local governments operate. Getting them right mattered enormously.
Minister of the Interior and Local Government (2023–present)
In December 2023, Atty. Dumama-Alba was appointed Minister of the Interior and Local Government (MILG)
of the BARMM, becoming the first woman to lead that ministry.
In this role, she oversees local government units across the Bangsamoro, leads disaster preparedness efforts
through the BARMM-READi framework, and manages public safety functions across the region.
The ministry sits at the intersection of governance, security, and community service. It's not a comfortable desk job.
It's a position that demands constant engagement with local leaders, first responders, and the communities they
serve.
Deputy Speaker, Bangsamoro Parliament (2025–present)
In November 2025, Atty. Dumama-Alba was sworn in as one of the Deputy Speakers of the Bangsamoro
Parliament, adding another layer of legislative leadership to an already substantial career.
Institutional Contributions
Beyond her formal positions, Atty. Dumama-Alba played a significant institutional role through her co-leadership
of the Joint Secretariat of the Intergovernmental Relations Body (IGRB), the key coordination mechanism
between the national government in Manila and the Bangsamoro government in Cotabato City.
That kind of intergovernmental work is often invisible but always essential. It's the plumbing of federalism: making
sure the different levels of government can actually talk to each other and resolve disputes without things breaking
down.

PAGE 4
Her consistent presence in that mechanism helped keep the Bangsamoro transition on track during some of its most
delicate moments.
Moral Governance Advocacy
Atty. Dumama-Alba has been one of the clearest and most consistent voices for Moral Governance in the
Bangsamoro.
The principle, as she has articulated it, is about more than just avoiding corruption. It's about integrating the ethical
and spiritual values of the Bangsamoro people, rooted in Islamic principles, into the everyday practice of public
administration.
For a region that has spent decades negotiating its place within the Philippine state, this kind of value-driven
governance is not abstract philosophy. It's a practical framework for building institutions that the Bangsamoro
people can genuinely trust and own.
Legacy and Cultural Significance
Atty. Dumama-Alba represents something genuinely new in Bangsamoro public life: a woman who has succeeded
at the highest levels of both legal and political leadership, in a context where those doors were not always open.
Her success in passing both the Philippine Bar and the Shari'ah Bar, and her career that spans the Attorney
General's office, the parliament, and a cabinet ministry, makes her one of the most versatile and accomplished
public servants the Bangsamoro has produced.
She has advanced the cause of women's empowerment not through speeches alone but through the accumulation
of firsts: first woman to hold this position, first woman to lead that ministry.
She has also helped legitimize and formalize the Shari'ah justice system within the Philippine legal framework,
demonstrating through her own career that Islamic law and constitutional law can coexist and reinforce each other.
As a Maguindanaoan woman who has navigated both the national institutions in Manila and the regional
institutions of the Bangsamoro, she functions as a living bridge between two worlds that sometimes struggle to
understand each other.
Recognition
2025 TOWNS Award
Recognized by the TOWNS Foundation, Inc. for exceptional contributions to Peacebuilding and Good
Governance.
2019 Obama Foundation Leader (Asia-Pacific)
Selected as one of the Obama Foundation Leaders from the Asia-Pacific region, a program that identifies and
supports emerging public leaders across the region.
Asia Foundation Development Fellow
Recognized as a Development Fellow by the Asia Foundation, an international development organization
focused on governance and civil society.

Faydah Maniri Dumarpa
Atty. Faydah Maniri Dumarpa (born May 7, 1983) is a Filipino
lawyer, public administrator, and human rights advocate serving as
a Commissioner of the Commission on Human Rights of the
Philippines (CHR). She was appointed by President Ferdinand
Marcos Jr. on December 28, 2022, joining the Sixth Commission En
Banc to serve a full seven year term running until 2029. A Maranao
attorney with roots in Lanao del Sur, Dumarpa is the first Muslim
woman ever appointed Commissioner in the history of the CHR, a
distinction she herself has affirmed in public remarks before the
United Nations.
Before stepping into this role, Dumarpa built a career of over two
decades that touched all three branches of Philippine government.
She worked in statutory research as a legislative officer in both the
House of Representatives and the Senate, moved into corporate law
with the National Power Corporation, and later took on senior
administrative and financial posts in the executive branch, including
at the National Nutrition Council and the Procurement Service of
the Department of Budget and Management.
At the Commission, she now serves as Focal Commissioner for
some of its most sensitive portfolios: gender equality and women's
rights through the Gender Equality and Women's Human Rights
Center (GEWHRC), the protection of persons deprived of liberty
(PDLs), and the emerging field of human rights in technology,
covering issues like data privacy, cybersecurity, and AI governance.
Contents
1 EARLY LIFE AND FAMILY
2 EDUCATION
3 CAREER
4 COMMISSION ON HUMAN RIGHTS
5 LEGACY AND SIGNIFICANCE
6 SEE ALSO
7 REFERENCES
EARLY LIFE AND FAMILY
Dumarpa hails from Lanao del Sur in the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM), and
she comes from a family with deep ties to Philippine law and regional politics. Her father, Atty. Sultan Salic Biston
Dumarpa, is a lawyer and former Commissioner of the National Labor Relations Commission (NLRC). Her
mother, Faysah Racman Pimping Maniri Dumarpa, served as Congresswoman for the 1st District of Lanao del Sur.

PAGE 2
EDUCATION
Dumarpa's academic path wove together business, management, and law. She earned her Bachelor of Science in
Business Administration, majoring in Marketing, from the Philippine School of Business Administration (PSBA).
She then pursued a Master's degree in Business Administration (MBA) at Far Eastern University (FEU).
She went on to study law at San Beda University, completing her Bachelor of Laws (LL.B.) in 2010. She passed
the Philippine Bar Examinations and was admitted to the Philippine Bar in 2012.
CAREER
Legislative and Corporate Law (2001-2020)
Dumarpa's public service career began in 2001, when she joined the House of Representatives as a Political Affairs
Officer, a post she held for nine years while building a foundation in statutory research and legislative policy work.
She later moved to the Senate of the Philippines as a Legislative Staff Officer, taking on a supervising role within
the office by 2013.
She then shifted into corporate practice, serving as a corporate lawyer for the National Power Corporation
(NAPOCOR) starting in 2013. She also held a legal role with the Land Bank of the Philippines during this period.
Executive Bureaucracy (2021-2022)
In 2021, Dumarpa was appointed Deputy Executive Director III for Administrative and Financial Service at the
National Nutrition Council (NNC) under the Department of Health. In this post, she coordinated with international,
local, and private stakeholders to help fund and implement nutrition programs on the ground.
In September 2022, she joined the Procurement Service of the Department of Budget and Management (PS-DBM)
as Director IV of the Administrative and Finance Group, overseeing budgeting, human resource operations, and
general services for the agency.
COMMISSION ON HUMAN RIGHTS
Gender Equality and Women's Rights
As the lead of the Gender Equality and Women's Human Rights Center (GEWHRC), Dumarpa carries out the
CHR's mandate as the state's Gender and Development Ombud under the Magna Carta of Women (RA 9710). Her
work touches on compliance with laws such as the Safe Spaces Act, the Anti-Violence Against Women and Their
Children Act, and the Responsible Parenthood and Reproductive Health Act.
Persons Deprived of Liberty
Dumarpa also serves as Focal Commissioner for Persons Deprived of Liberty (PDLs), leading jail visitation
programs across the country. Her work in this space centers on assessing overcrowding, sanitation, and the specific
health risks faced by women in detention, using international standards as a benchmark for reform.
Emerging Technologies and Cybercrime

PAGE 3
As Focal Commissioner for Emerging Technologies, Dumarpa leads CHR discussions on how digital tools intersect
with human rights, from data privacy to AI surveillance to government cybersecurity. She has issued public
statements on hacking incidents targeting government agencies, framing them as threats to Filipinos' right to
privacy under the Data Privacy Act of 2012.
LEGACY AND SIGNIFICANCE
As a high ranking Muslim Filipino woman in a constitutional office, Dumarpa represents a rare and important
voice for Mindanao and the Bangsamoro region within the country's national human rights machinery. Her own
words to the United Nations Human Rights Council in March 2023 underscored this milestone, noting that in the
38 years since the Commission's creation, she was the first Muslim woman ever appointed as Commissioner.
Some civil society groups initially viewed her appointment with caution, given that her background came from
executive bureaucracy rather than grassroots activism. Over time, her command of institutional finance,
administrative law, and public policy has been credited with helping turn advocacy work into funded, structurally
sound government programs.

Notability
Faysah Racman Pimping Maniri Dumarpa
Faysah Racman Pimping Maniri Dumarpa (born March 1952) is
a Filipina educator, social servant, and politician from Marawi City,
Lanao del Sur. She spent the better part of two decades in public
service, first as a regional legislator in the Autonomous Region in
Muslim Mindanao (ARMM), then as a three-term member of the
House of Representatives representing Lanao del Sur's 1st District
from 2001 to 2010.<ref name="geni">Template:Cite web</ref>
She's remembered as one of the more prominent Moro women to
hold national office, and her legislative record leans heavily toward
carving out space for Islamic identity within Philippine law,
strengthening social services, and staying involved in the peace
process between the government and the Moro Islamic Liberation
Front (MILF).
She's the mother of Atty. Faydah Maniri Racman-Pimping
Dumarpa, who currently serves as a Commissioner at the
Commission on Human Rights (CHR), appointed by President
Ferdinand Marcos Jr. in December 2022.<ref
name="chr">Template:Cite web</ref>
Contents
1 EARLY LIFE AND FAMILY BACKGROUND
2 EDUCATION
3 EARLY PUBLIC SERVICE AND REGIONAL CAREER
4 CONGRESSIONAL CAREER (2001 TO 2010)
5 INSTITUTIONAL AND LEGISLATIVE CONTRIBUTIONS
5.1 TECHNICAL LEGISLATIVE OVERVIEW
6 MARAWI SIEGE REHABILITATION ADVOCACY
7 AWARDS AND RECOGNITION
8 SEE ALSO
EARLY LIFE AND FAMILY
BACKGROUND
Faysah grew up in Marawi City, Lanao del Sur, immersed in
traditional Meranao culture from childhood. That grounding in
Meranao custom and community life later became the backbone of
her academic and political career, shaping how she approached
sociology, anthropology, and eventually, legislation touching on
Bangsamoro identity.

PAGE 2
Three-term Representative of Lanao del
Sur's 1st District who authored the law
making Eid'l Adha a national holiday
Known For
Championing Islamic identity in
national law, Moro women's political
representation, and post-Marawi Siege
advocacy
Her husband, Atty. Salic Biston Dumarpa, worked as a human rights
lawyer and later served as a Commissioner of the National Labor
Relations Commission (NLRC). Their daughter, Atty. Faydah
Maniri Racman-Pimping Dumarpa, has carried the family's tradition
of public service forward through her own work at the CHR.
EDUCATION
Faysah built her academic foundation around teaching first, then
broadened into cultural studies later in her career.
She earned her Bachelor of Science in Education at Pangarungan Islamic College in Marawi City, the degree that
set her on the path toward classroom teaching. She went on to complete a Master of Arts in Anthropology at Centro
Escolar University in Manila, a credential that gave her the analytical tools to connect national policymaking with
Moro cultural systems and representation.
EARLY PUBLIC SERVICE AND REGIONAL CAREER
Long before she reached national office, Faysah built her career around education and social welfare work across
Mindanao.
She started out as a classroom instructor at Pangarungan Islamic College, teaching in the same institution where
she'd earned her own degree. From there, she moved into government service as an Undersecretary at the
Department of Social Welfare and Development (DSWD) under the ARMM, where she oversaw relief operations
for communities caught in the crossfire of armed conflict.
In 1993, she stepped into elected office for the first time as a Regional Legislative Assemblywoman, representing
Lanao del Sur in the 3rd ARMM Regional Legislative Assembly, a position she held until 2001.<ref name="geni"
/> That stretch in regional government marked her real entry into policymaking.
Her profile grew from there. She served as a peace negotiator, reportedly the only woman on the government's
peace panel engaging the MILF, and was later tapped by President Gloria Macapagal Arroyo to sit on the 2005
Constitutional Commission as a charter consultant.
CONGRESSIONAL CAREER (2001 TO 2010)
Faysah won her seat in the House of Representatives in 2001 and went on to serve three consecutive terms
representing Lanao del Sur's 1st District, stepping down in 2010 after completing the maximum number of terms
allowed.<ref name="geni" /> During her time in Congress, she chaired the Committee on Social Services and
served as Vice-Chairperson of the Committee on Muslim Affairs.
INSTITUTIONAL AND LEGISLATIVE CONTRIBUTIONS
Her legislative work centered on three things: giving Islamic identity a rightful place in national law, protecting
minorities from discrimination, and building infrastructure for her district back home.

PAGE 3
She authored Republic Act No. 9849, the law that declared the tenth day of Zhul Hijja, the twelfth month of the
Islamic calendar, a nationwide holiday for the observance of Eid'l Adha.<ref name="ra9849">Template:Cite
web</ref><ref name="ra9849author">Template:Cite web</ref> Signed into law on December 11, 2009, the
measure embedded one of Islam's two major feast days into the national holiday calendar, applied nationwide and
not just in Muslim-majority areas.
She also pushed for the expansion of Shari'ah court funding and jurisdiction across Mindanao, and championed
anti-profiling measures aimed at protecting Muslim Filipinos and indigenous groups from religious and racial
profiling.
On the education front, she authored Republic Act No. 9921, which converted the RPMD National High School in
Barangay Papandayan Caniogan, City of Marawi, into the RPMD National Science High School, opening up
dedicated STEM education access for Moro youth in Lanao del Sur.<ref name="ra9921">Template:Cite web</ref>
<ref name="ra9921author">Template:Cite web</ref>

MARAWI SIEGE REHABILITATION ADVOCACY
Faysah stayed active in civic life well after leaving Congress. Following the 2017 Marawi Siege, she stood with
displaced Meranao families, pressing Task Force Bangon Marawi to return ancestral lands to their rightful owners
and pushing back against commercial development plans for what became known as the "Ground Zero" area of the
city.
AWARDS AND RECOGNITION
Her decades of work earned her recognition on multiple fronts:
ASEAN Gintong Ina Award
Sultan Kudarat Award for Most Outstanding Muslim Educator
Bangsamoro Woman of Distinction Award

Salic Biston Dumarpa
Sultan Atty. Salic Biston Dumarpa is a Filipino lawyer, jurist, and
respected Meranaw civic leader whose career carried him from the
prosecutorial trenches of Lanao del Sur all the way to the national
labor bench, and eventually into decades of grassroots advocacy for
the Bangsamoro people.
He is best remembered for three overlapping identities that rarely sit
in one man: a career prosecutor who rose to become a Regional
State Prosecutor for the Department of Justice, a Presiding
Commissioner of the National Labor Relations Commission who
spent over a decade ruling on labor disputes across Mindanao, and a
traditional Sultan whose word still carries weight among the
Meranaw of Lanao del Sur.
Contents
1 EARLY LIFE AND FAMILY
2 EDUCATION
3 CAREER AND INSTITUTIONAL CONTRIBUTIONS
3.1 Department of Justice (1980s–1999)
3.2 National Labor Relations Commission (1999–2010)
4 POLITICAL ACTIVITIES AND JURISPRUDENCE
5 INVOLVEMENT IN BANGSAMORO CIVIC MOVEMENTS
5.1 The Post-Siege Marawi Rehabilitation Campaign
(2019)
5.2 Electoral Integrity and Anti-Corruption Mobilization
5.3 Advocacy for Federalism in the Bangsamoro
6 AWARDS, RECOGNITION, AND LEGACY
7 SEE ALSO
8 REFERENCES
EARLY LIFE AND FAMILY
Dumarpa was born and raised in Lanao del Sur, the landlocked
heartland of the Meranaw people on the shores of Lake Lanao. He
grew up immersed in two systems of order at once: Islamic tradition
and the Meranaw concept of Maratabat, the clan honor and status
system that still shapes public life in the province. In time, he was
elevated to the traditional royal title of Sultan, a recognition that
placed him at the head of both a clan and a broader responsibility to
the Moro community around him.
Public service runs deep in the Dumarpa household. He is married
to Hon. Faysah Racman Pimping Maniri Dumarpa, who represented
the 1st District of Lanao del Sur in the House of Representatives

PAGE 2
Notability
Filipino lawyer, jurist, and Meranaw
Sultan known for a long public service
career spanning provincial prosecution,
regional prosecution, and labor
adjudication, followed by decades of civic
leadership in the Bangsamoro region.
Known For
Serving as Presiding Commissioner of
the NLRC Fifth Division; leading the
2019 Marawi IDP mandamus suit against
Task Force Bangon Marawi; advocacy for
federalism and electoral integrity in
Lanao del Sur.
before he himself sought the same seat after her term ended. Their
daughter, Atty. Faydah Maniri Dumarpa, carries the family's legal
tradition forward: she was appointed by President Ferdinand
Marcos Jr. as a Commissioner of the Commission on Human Rights
in December 2022, taking her seat on the Sixth Commission En
Banc for a term running to 2029.
EDUCATION
Dumarpa studied in Manila before returning home to practice law.
He is said to have earned a Bachelor of Science in Business
Administration, majoring in Accounting, from the National College
of Business and Arts, and later a Bachelor of Laws from the
University of the East College of Law, a school with a long track
record of producing lawyers and public officials. He subsequently passed the Philippine Bar Examination, which
opened the door to his decades in public service. (Note: these educational details come from a submitter-provided
source and are pending independent confirmation. See internal notes.)
CAREER AND INSTITUTIONAL CONTRIBUTIONS
Department of Justice (1980s–1999)
Dumarpa's career in public prosecution began at home, where he served as Provincial Fiscal of Lanao del Sur (the
position now called Provincial Prosecutor) through the late 1980s. It was in this role that he found himself at the
center of a Supreme Court case that still gets cited in law school today.
In 1988, a legal opinion issued by Dumarpa's office, regarding who rightfully held the mayoralty of Marogong,
Lanao del Sur, put him on a collision course with the Commission on Elections. COMELEC found Dumarpa and
two colleagues in contempt over the opinion, fining them 500 pesos each. Dumarpa fought back, and in Dumarpa
v. Dimaporo (G.R. Nos. 87014-16, September 13, 1989), the Supreme Court reversed the contempt finding, ruling
that there was no clear showing of intent to undermine COMELEC's authority and that the fiscals had simply been
doing their job when asked for a legal opinion. The case remains a reference point on good-faith legal advice given
by government lawyers in the course of their duties.
In January 1991, Dumarpa was promoted to Regional State Prosecutor for DOJ Region XII, covering Central
Mindanao. He held the post for roughly eight years, overseeing every Provincial and City Prosecution Office in the
region during a period when the area was, as it still can be, a difficult place to keep the machinery of justice
running smoothly. He is credited with pushing for faster, more efficient preliminary investigations across offices
that were often stretched thin.
National Labor Relations Commission (1999–2010)
In January 1999, Dumarpa moved from criminal prosecution into labor adjudication when he was appointed
Presiding Commissioner of the NLRC's Fifth Division, based in Cagayan de Oro. He held the post for more than a
decade, until March 2010, and his name appears on a long list of Supreme Court cases from that period as the
presiding officer whose division decisions were being reviewed on appeal, among them Retuya v. Dumarpa (G.R.
No. 148848, August 5, 2003) and disputes involving companies and workers across Northern and Central
Mindanao.

PAGE 3
As Presiding Commissioner, Dumarpa sat at the head of a division that heard appeals from labor arbiters across the
region, weighing workers' rights against employers' obligations under the Labor Code. Reporting from that period
shows him signing off on decisions that favored reinstated workers as often as those that sided with management,
the ordinary rhythm of a quasi-judicial body doing its job on a contested, case-by-case basis.
POLITICAL ACTIVITIES AND JURISPRUDENCE
After stepping down from the NLRC in 2010, Dumarpa made a run at elected office, contesting the congressional
seat for the 1st District of Lanao del Sur, the very seat his wife had just vacated, in the May 10, 2010 automated
national elections.
The race against his opponent, Hussin Pangandaman, turned into one of the messier contests of that election cycle.
COMELEC declared a total failure of elections in seven municipalities, three of them in Dumarpa's own district:
Masiu, Lumba Bayabao, and Kapai. Special elections were rescheduled more than once because of missing ballots
and election officials unwilling to serve. When COMELEC issued Resolution No. 8965 governing how those
special elections would be run, Dumarpa, who was narrowly leading in the areas where voting had gone through
cleanly, challenged two of its provisions before the Supreme Court, arguing they were adopted without proper
notice and would tilt the special elections against him.
The Court never got to rule on the merits in the way Dumarpa hoped. In Dumarpa v. Commission on Elections
(G.R. No. 192249, April 2, 2013), the justices found the petition moot: the special elections had already gone
forward, and Pangandaman had already been proclaimed the winner. Still, the Court used the case to affirm
COMELEC's broad constitutional and statutory authority to re-cluster precincts, reconstitute boards of election
inspectors, and adjust residency requirements for poll workers during emergencies, powers that election lawyers
still point to today. The case is a routine but real part of the country's election jurisprudence, even if it did not end
the way Dumarpa wanted.
INVOLVEMENT IN BANGSAMORO CIVIC MOVEMENTS
Retirement from government did not slow Dumarpa down. If anything, the years after 2010 are when his civic
profile in Lanao del Sur grew the most, built around post-conflict rehabilitation, clean elections, and constitutional
reform for the Bangsamoro.
The Post-Siege Marawi Rehabilitation Campaign (2019)
The 2017 Marawi Siege left tens of thousands of Meranaw residents displaced, many of them barred for years from
returning to the city's "Most Affected Area" while government clearance and unexploded ordnance disposal
dragged on. By December 2019, frustration had turned into legal action.
Acting as chairman of the Go Right Foundation Inc., Dumarpa helped lead close to 400 displaced Marawi residents
in filing a class suit before the Marawi Regional Trial Court. The petition, a writ of mandamus with a prayer for
preliminary mandatory injunction, was directed at HUDCC Secretary Eduardo del Rosario, who chaired Task Force
Bangon Marawi, and Marawi City Mayor Majul Gandamra. Dumarpa argued publicly that the bureaucratic delay
had wrecked residents' livelihoods, businesses, and their children's schooling. The pressure appears to have
worked, at least in part: government reporting from that period shows building permits finally being released to
Marawi residents in the months that followed.

PAGE 4
Electoral Integrity and Anti-Corruption Mobilization
Dumarpa has also been a persistent voice against the political warlordism, vote-buying, and electoral fraud that
have long plagued Lanao del Sur and the old ARMM. He is said to have worked with retired Moro officers from
the AFP and PNP to mobilize hundreds of voters into filing formal affidavits documenting local corruption and
fraudulent election practices, and to have carried those grievances directly to Malacañang. (Note: this specific
mobilization is sourced from submitter materials and is pending independent confirmation. See internal notes.)
Advocacy for Federalism in the Bangsamoro
As a man who understood both the Philippine legal code and Meranaw Adat (customary law), Dumarpa became an
advocate for federalism as a long-term fix for a region he felt had long been shortchanged by centralized rule from
Manila. He is said to have served as Provincial Chairman of the Marawi City and Lanao del Sur chapters of the
MRRD-NECC (Masa Masid / Movement for Reform and Regional Development - National Executive
Coordinating Committee), campaigning alongside other Moro leaders for a shift to a federal system that would
guarantee the Bangsamoro genuine self-determination and fiscal autonomy. (Note: this civic role is sourced from
submitter materials and is pending independent confirmation. See internal notes.)
AWARDS, RECOGNITION, AND LEGACY
Over the course of his career, Dumarpa is said to have received recognition from regional organizations, legal
fraternities, and Islamic civic groups for his work on justice and peaceful dispute resolution. (Note: specific awards
are not yet itemized or independently verified. See internal notes.)
What is well documented is the shape of his legacy: a Moro jurist who built a career inside the country's secular
legal institutions while never setting aside his role as a traditional Sultan. That dual footing, part magistrate, part
customary leader, let him move between two systems of law that do not always speak to each other, and to be taken
seriously in both. In Marawi City and across Lanao del Sur, he remains regarded as an elder statesman of sorts,
someone whose opinion on both legal and communal matters still carries weight.

title: Dumpa, Alexander Diamla
text:
PAGE 1
Alexander Diamla Dumpa
Alexander Diamla Dumpa (born June 3, 1996) is a Filipino jurist, educator, and public official from Tamparan,
Lanao del Sur.
A proud Maranao, he is best known for his extraordinary academic record at Mindanao State University, where he
made history as the first student ever to graduate with Magna Cum Laude distinction from the MSU College of
Law.
From selling watermelons at a public market in Tamparan to becoming a national policymaker at 25, Dumpa's life
story has become one of the most compelling narratives in Bangsamoro legal history, a testament to what discipline
and education can do for a young person from a marginalized community.
He served as a Commissioner of the Legal Education Board (LEB) from 2021 to 2026, where he championed law
student welfare and helped embed Shari'ah legal studies into the national legal education framework.
Contents
