Early Life and Background
Dumpa grew up in Tamparan, a municipality in Lanao del Sur in the heart of the Bangsamoro region.
His early years were not easy.
To support his schooling, he worked as a watermelon vendor at the local public market in Tamparan, a detail that
has since become central to how he's described and celebrated in Philippine legal circles.
That experience, he has noted, shaped the values that carried him through his academic and professional life:
perseverance, humility, and an abiding belief in the power of education to change lives.

in 2016.
Juris Doctor (2022)
Dumpa went on to earn his law degree at the MSU College of
Law, again graduating as University Class Valedictorian and
Magna Cum Laude, with a General Point Average of 1.39.
He became the first student in the entire history of the MSU
College of Law to earn the Magna Cum Laude distinction, a
milestone that marked a new standard for academic excellence
in that institution.
Master of Laws (2025)
He completed his graduate legal studies at the Polytechnic
University of the Philippines (PUP) under the Public
Governance Track, finishing with a General Weighted
Average of 1.10.
His thesis, Governing the Mind: A Doctrinal Analysis of
Philippine Supreme Court Jurisprudence on Academic
Freedom, was awarded the Best Thesis Award.

PAGE 3
Term
2021 to 2026 (Legal Education
Board)
Professional Career
Legal Education Board (2021 to 2026)
In September 2021, President Rodrigo Duterte appointed Dumpa as a Regular Board Member of the Legal
Education Board, representing the Law Students' Sector.
He was 25 years old at the time of his appointment.
During his five-year tenure, Dumpa served as one of the primary proponents of LEB Memorandum Order No.
32, s. 2024, which established the first-ever national policy framework for Law Student Welfare and Development
in the Philippines.
He also contributed to the integration of the Shari'ah academic track into the national legal education system, a
significant step toward recognizing the distinct legal traditions of Muslim Filipinos within the mainstream legal
curriculum.
Bar Admission
Dumpa successfully passed the 2023 Philippine Bar Examinations, formally completing his credentials as a
member of the Philippine bar.
University Service
In early 2026, he was appointed as legal consultant to the Mindanao Varsitarian, the official student publication of
MSU Marawi, bringing his legal expertise back to the university that shaped him.
Cultural Significance
As a Maranao lawyer and former national board official, Dumpa carries a particular kind of weight in the
Bangsamoro community.
His story, rising from a market vendor's stall to the boardroom of a national regulatory body, has resonated widely
among students and youth in Mindanao, especially those from underserved communities who see in him a model of
what meritocratic achievement can look like.
In Philippine legal circles, particularly on platforms like Abogado PH, he has been consistently portrayed as a
symbol of earned success within a demanding and often inaccessible profession.
His advocacy for law student welfare also gives his cultural profile a practical dimension: he did not just succeed
within the system, he worked to make that system more equitable for those who come after him.
Legacy and Recognition
Dumpa's legacy rests on several pillars.
He is the first Magna Cum Laude graduate in MSU College of Law history, a record that stands on its own
regardless of everything else he has accomplished.

PAGE 4
He helped author the first national policy on law student welfare, an achievement that has practical and lasting
consequences for thousands of law students across the country.
His Best Thesis Award at PUP for a work on academic freedom reflects not just scholarly ability, but a consistent
commitment to the intersection of education, governance, and rights.
And across all of it, he has been an unmistakably Maranao voice in national legal and educational policy,
representing his community at a level and in spaces where that community has historically been underrepresented.
Challenges
Dumpa's path was built on overcoming material poverty and geographic disadvantage.
Growing up in Lanao del Sur, far from the major urban centers where legal education and professional networks
are concentrated, he had to outperform his circumstances at every stage.
His background as a market vendor is not just a human interest detail; it reflects a structural reality about the
barriers that face students from conflict-affected regions like the Bangsamoro, and why representation in
institutions like the LEB matters.

Al Haj Murad Ebrahim
Al Haj Murad Ebrahim (born October 2, 1949) is a Filipino Moro revolutionary leader, politician, and the
founding chairman of the Moro Islamic Liberation Front (MILF) following the death of Salamat Hashim. He is the
first Chief Minister of the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM), playing a central
role in the transition from armed struggle to autonomous governance and development in the Bangsamoro region.
<ref name="milf2020">Moro Islamic Liberation Front. Leadership Profile: Al Haj Murad Ebrahim. MILF Official
Website, 2020.</ref><ref name="usip2020">United States Institute of Peace. The Bangsamoro Transition and
Governance under Murad Ebrahim. USIP, 2020.</ref>
---
Early Life and Education
Murad Ebrahim was born in Barangay Pandan, Cotabato City, to a Maranao family with deep Islamic roots.
He studied at local Madrasah schools and later pursued higher education in Islamic studies, political science,
and leadership development.
His early exposure to the Moro struggle and Islamic scholarship shaped his commitment to Moro self-
determination and governance.<ref name="milf2020" />
---
MILF Leadership
Following the death of MILF founder Salamat Hashim in 2003, Murad Ebrahim was appointed chairman of
the MILF.
Under his leadership, the MILF continued to pursue the goal of Moro autonomy while engaging in sustained
peace negotiations with the Philippine government.
Murad emphasized discipline, ideological coherence, and institution-building within the MILF, preparing the
organization for political participation and governance.<ref name="milf2020" />
---

PAGE 2
Role in the Bangsamoro Peace Process
Murad Ebrahim played a pivotal role in negotiating the Comprehensive Agreement on the Bangsamoro
(CAB) signed in 2014 between the MILF and the Philippine government.
He coordinated with the Bangsamoro Transition Commission to draft the Bangsamoro Organic Law, which
laid the legal framework for the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao.
Murad’s leadership ensured that the transition process balanced security, governance, and the preservation of
Moro culture and identity.<ref name="usip2020" />
---
Chief Minister of BARMM
On February 22, 2019, Murad Ebrahim was officially appointed as the first Chief Minister of BARMM
following the ratification of the Bangsamoro Organic Law.
As Chief Minister, he oversees the Bangsamoro Transition Authority, regional governance, economic
development programs, education initiatives, and the implementation of Sharia-compliant laws in the region.
His administration emphasizes reconciliation, post-conflict rehabilitation, and the integration of former
combatants into society.<ref name="milf2020" /><ref name="usip2020" />
---
Vision and Legacy
Murad Ebrahim is recognized for transforming the MILF from an armed separatist movement into a political
and governance-oriented organization.
He advocates for a peaceful, autonomous, and development-oriented Bangsamoro region while preserving
Islamic culture and Maranao traditions.
His leadership symbolizes the success of Moro self-determination through political negotiation, institution-
building, and regional autonomy.<ref name="milf2020" /><ref name="usip2020" />
---

Hamza Eshmael
Hamza Eshmael is a prominent Moro financial professional and
risk management expert who currently serves as Senior Vice
President and Head of Risk at Salmon Bank (Rural Bank of Sta.
Rosa), confirmed by the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas in February
2024. Originally from Marawi City in Mindanao, Eshmael has
built a distinguished career spanning nearly 15 years in enterprise
risk governance and compliance, rising to executive roles in
Bonifacio Global City while remaining grounded in his
commitment to proving that Moro professionals belong in
finance's highest decision-making spaces. His work advocates for
secure-by-design financial systems and financial inclusion, and his
story embodies the principle that systemic integrity and cultural
belonging are inseparable.
Contents
1 Early Life and Background
2 Education
3 Professional Career
3.1 Early Career and Foundational Years
3.2 2016 Australian Regulatory Assignment
3.3 Salmon Bank and Current Leadership
4 Industry Leadership and Advocacy
5 Legacy and Influence
6 Recognition and Public Profile
7 Vision and Future Direction
8 Religion and Personal Values
9 References
10 Further Reading
11 See Also
Early Life and Background
Hamza Eshmael was born and raised in Marawi City, a historic
center of Bangsamoro culture and commerce in Lanao del Sur
province on the island of Mindanao. His upbringing shaped his
understanding of resilience and responsibility, values reinforced by his maternal grandfather's enduring counsel: "If
you cannot bring honor, at least do not bring dishonor." This principle became the moral compass guiding his
professional journey, anchoring his belief that success measured only in titles or earnings rings hollow without
integrity and service.
Coming from a city often left out of national conversations, Eshmael carried with him an awareness that his
presence in elite professional spaces would be read as either a breakthrough or an intrusion, depending on who was
watching. This awareness, rather than paralyzing him, focused his work. He committed early to building systems

PAGE 2
that could protect trust and uphold the kind of governance that works for people who feel they don't belong.
Education
Eshmael earned his Bachelor of Science in Accountancy from the Philippine School of Business Administration,
establishing a strong technical foundation in financial systems and corporate governance. Recognizing the value of
international exposure and rigorous academic training, he pursued advanced studies at California State University
under a prestigious Fulbright scholarship, where he made the honor's list. The Fulbright experience exposed him to
global best practices in financial regulation and reinforced that risk management is not a compliance box to check,
but a discipline that shapes institutional culture and trustworthiness.
He holds certifications in ISO 31000 (Risk Management), positioning him among a select cadre of professionals
qualified to design enterprise-wide risk frameworks aligned with international standards. He is also a certified Six
Sigma Yellow Belt (CSSYB), reflecting his commitment to operational excellence and process efficiency.
Professional Career
Early Career and Foundational Years
Eshmael's career began in roles that built his expertise in governance and risk assessment. Over nearly 15 years in
the sector, he worked across diverse financial institutions, including international banks, one of the country's largest
insurers, licensed digital banks, and rural banking institutions backed by regional fintech groups. Each role added
layers to his understanding of how risk frameworks must be tailored to institutional context, regulatory
environment, and the communities they serve.
Early in his career, Eshmael confronted the weight of being a minority professional in majority spaces. He recalled
periods when he felt compelled to prove his belonging at every meeting, when self-doubt and impostor syndrome
threatened to undermine his confidence. A pivotal conversation with a former supervisor changed his trajectory.
Sensing Eshmael's sense of marginalization, his boss reminded him directly:
"You're not an outsider anymore. You help shape direction. And it's time you see yourself that way."
The words stuck with him, reframing his role from supplicant to stakeholder.
2016 Australian Regulatory Assignment
A transformative moment came in 2016 when Eshmael was deployed to Australia to support a regulatory
remediation effort. Fighting jet lag on his first overseas assignment, he was tasked with drafting key policy and
governance frameworks for a financial institution under review by Australia's Securities and Investments
Commission (ASIC).
Immersed in ASIC's Responsible Lending Guidelines (RG 209), Eshmael crafted a comprehensive framework
designed not simply to appease regulators, but to embed responsible lending culture into organizational DNA. The
framework was independently reviewed by KPMG Australia and found to be aligned with regulatory expectations.
The experience taught him a critical lesson:
"That experience taught me how to unlearn, relearn, and adapt. I wasn't just writing a policy. I was
learning how to lead with substance even in unfamiliar terrain."

PAGE 3
This principle, forged in the unfamiliar landscape of Australian securities law, became his signature approach:
frameworks must be tailored, not transplanted; governance must serve institutional purpose, not just compliance
aesthetics.
Salmon Bank and Current Leadership
In February 2024, Eshmael was confirmed by the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas as Senior Vice President and Head
of Risk at the Rural Bank of Sta. Rosa, a fintech-backed institution serving underserved markets in Southeast Asia.
His portfolio encompasses enterprise risk management, model governance, policy development, cybersecurity
oversight, and direct regulatory interface.
His leadership philosophy prioritizes building systems that balance internal controls with operational efficiency. He
advocates for "secure-by-design" approaches to fraud prevention, embedding anti-fraud culture into everyday
decision-making rather than treating it as a bolt-on compliance function. Under his oversight, Salmon Bank's risk
governance framework reflects both international best practices and the realities of serving communities for whom
financial services are gateways to economic dignity.
Industry Leadership and Advocacy
Eshmael is a frequent speaker and panelist at major financial summits and governance forums across the region.
At the TransUnion Financial Services Summit, he addressed the challenge of de-risking fraud threats while
building organizational cultures where fraud prevention is everyone's responsibility, not just the compliance
department's burden. His framing shifted the conversation from "How do we catch fraud?" to "How do we design
systems where fraud becomes structurally difficult?"
On the Diligent Panel addressing Asia Pacific regulations, Eshmael discussed the intersection of governance, risk,
and compliance technology, advocating for GRC solutions that empower decision-makers rather than drowning
them in data. His approach reflects a core conviction: technology serves governance when it clarifies choices, not
when it multiplies noise.
Legacy and Influence
Eshmael's significance extends beyond technical expertise. He represents a deliberate break from the narrative that
Bangsamoro representation in Philippine finance is incidental or tokenistic. His rise to C-suite rank in a major
financial institution, achieved through demonstrated competence and principled leadership, serves as both blueprint
and challenge to younger Moro professionals. He regularly speaks about the responsibility that comes with
occupying decision-making spaces, particularly when one comes from communities historically excluded from
those spaces.
His maternal grandfather's maxim, "If you cannot bring honor, at least do not bring dishonor," is not simply family
wisdom. It became his professional creed.
"This is my way of bringing honor to my family, my parents, and my grandparents. Every policy I
write, every risk framework I help build, is part of that promise not to forget where I come from, and
to prove that people like me belong in these conversations."
He views his career not as personal ascent, but as a contribution to institutional resilience and systemic inclusivity.

PAGE 4
"Coming from a city often left out of the national conversation, I carry that reminder every day that
risk management isn't just a technical function. It's a responsibility to make systems work for
everyone, especially those who feel they don't belong."
Recognition and Public Profile
Eshmael's trajectory caught national attention following the publication of an in-depth profile in Bilyonaryo News
Channel in July 2025, titled "From Marawi to the Boardroom: Moro Yuppie Champions Risk Management in
Philippine Finance." The article traced his journey from Marawi City, a city rebuilding after the 2017 siege by the
Maute Group, to the financial boardrooms of Metro Manila. The profile resonated across sectors because it
articulated a larger truth: that Moro talent, given opportunity and recognition, advances not just individual careers
but national financial resilience.
Vision and Future Direction
Eshmael advocates for a new generation of Filipino risk management professionals who understand that the
discipline serves not just institutions, but people. He has expressed hope that younger Filipino professionals will
venture into risk management careers, helping to "future-proof" the nation's financial system through sound
governance, regulatory compliance, and inclusive design.
His message to the industry is unambiguous: frameworks matter, but they matter only insofar as they serve the
people they protect. And the people they protect include Moro professionals proving their belonging, rural
depositors trusting financial institutions with their livelihoods, and communities building resilience through access
to reliable financial systems.
Religion and Personal Values
Eshmael is a Muslim professional grounded in Islamic values of integrity, justice, and stewardship. His family's
counsel and his own articulated principles reflect the Islamic concept of amana (trust and responsibility), viewing
professional work as a form of worship when executed with integrity and in service of the community's wellbeing.

Rosa. February 2024.</ref> </references>

title: Espaldon, Romulo M.
text:
PAGE 1
Romulo M. Espaldon
Romulo Mercader Espaldon (September 16, 1925 – August 27, 2005) was a Filipino military officer, statesman,
diplomat, and peacemaker who rose to become the first Rear Admiral in the history of the Philippine Navy. Born to
Bicolano Christian schoolteachers and raised in the predominantly Muslim province of Tawi-Tawi, he inhabited the
cultural borderland between two worlds from his earliest years — and spent the rest of his life building bridges
between them. He commanded the AFP in the south during the height of the Moro insurgency and pioneered the
"Policy of Attraction" — a strategy built on dialogue, amnesty, and development that brought more than 40,000
rebels back from armed opposition without a single battle being fought to compel them. He was a guerrilla fighter
at sixteen, a valedictorian at Kings Point at twenty-five, a governor, regional commissioner, commissioner of
Islamic affairs, congressman, and ambassador — and at some point along that extraordinary journey, he embraced
Islam, completing a lifelong journey home to the communities that had shaped him. When he retired from
command in 1980, the Muslim communities of the Autonomous Region IX gave him the title Sultan
Makasanyang — Sultan of Peace — and the words of their citation told the whole story: before Espaldon, the
military was the enemy; after him, it had become something else entirely.

Early Life and Formation
Roots in Sorsogon, Childhood in Tawi-Tawi
Romulo Mercader Espaldon was born on September 16, 1925, in
Donsol, Sorsogon, a coastal municipality on the southeastern tip of
Luzon. His parents, Cipriano Espaldon and Claudia Mercader, were
schoolteachers — the kind of dedicated civil servants who answered
the government's call to serve in the country's most remote corners,
far from the comforts of home province.<ref name="wiki">Romulo
Espaldon. (n.d.). Wikipedia. Retrieved 2025, from
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romulo_Espaldon</ref> The family
relocated to Tawi-Tawi, the southernmost island province of the
Philippines, where they served as pioneer educators in communities
that were predominantly Tausug and Sama-Bajau in heritage, Islamic
in faith, and centuries deep in maritime tradition.<ref name="wiki"/>
Young Romulo did not grow up watching this world from a distance.
He grew up inside it. He learned Tausug and Sinama with native
fluency, absorbed Islamic customs as part of everyday life, and
participated in community rituals alongside neighbors who had no
reason to see him as an outsider.<ref name="wiki"/> The fishing
villages, the stilt houses over the sea, the call to prayer at dawn —
these were simply the texture of childhood. That immersion would
later give him something almost no other officer in the Philippine
military possessed: the genuine ability to see the Moro question
through Muslim Filipino eyes.
His academic record from the start was exceptional. He graduated
valedictorian from Bongao Elementary School in Tawi-Tawi in 1938,
and with honors from Sulu High School in 1942.<ref name="wiki"/>
Both achievements came against the backdrop of the Japanese

PAGE 3
Awards
Légion d'honneur (France)
Bintang Yudha Dharma
Pratama (Indonesia)
Congressional Gold Medal
(USA, posthumous)
USMMA Hall of
Distinguished Graduates

First Governor of Tawi-
Tawi

Commissioner, Region IX
First Commissioner,
Commission on Islamic
Affairs

Sudan, Somalia
Ambassador to Saudi
Arabia and Yemen
Member of Congress (8th
Congress, Tawi-Tawi)
occupation of the Philippines, which had turned the southern islands
into a theater of guerrilla warfare and transformed the line between
schooling and survival into something barely visible.
World War II Service
The Teenage Guerrilla
Espaldon didn't wait to be old enough. In 1941, at sixteen, he
volunteered for the USAFFE Bolo Battalion in Sulu and Tawi-Tawi
to fight the invading Japanese forces.<ref name="wiki"/> He served
as intelligence officer of the 1st Battalion, 125th Infantry Regiment
under Lieutenant Colonel Alejandro Suarez, commander of the Sulu
Area Command, and acted as liaison officer between that command
and the American landing forces — the Sulu White Task Force —
during the liberation campaign in Tawi-Tawi.<ref name="wiki"/> He
also served as Garrison Commander of the Cagayan de Sulu Forces.
<ref name="wiki"/>
These were not peripheral roles for a teenager. They required linguistic skill, cultural trust, and personal courage —
and the boy who spoke Tausug like a native was far better equipped for that work than most. His guerrilla years
formed the character that would animate every subsequent chapter of his career: direct, trusted across cultural lines,
and comfortable in situations where institutional support was thin and individual judgment mattered most.
The Plane That Left Without Him
After liberation, Espaldon was commissioned as a Second Lieutenant in the Philippine Army and enrolled in the
Cook and Bakers School at Camp Olivas, graduating First Honor. What happened next has a quality that stays with
you. On March 23, 1946, as he and his classmates were about to board a Douglas C-47 aircraft back to Mindanao,
orders came that he was to be retained at Camp Olivas as an instructor — a consequence of having topped his
class. The plane took off without him. It crashed on Mount Banahaw, killing most of the military passengers on
board.<ref name="wiki"/>
After his instructorship at Camp Olivas, he pursued a degree in aeronautical engineering at FEATI University on a
scholarship<ref name="wiki"/> — a detail that speaks to the breadth of his intellectual curiosity long before his
naval career had taken shape.
Naval Education and Military Formation
Kings Point: Valedictorian Again
In 1947, Espaldon was selected through nationwide competitive examinations as one of fifty Filipino scholars for
midshipman training at the United States Merchant Marine Academy (USMMA) at Kings Point, New York,
pursuant to the Philippine Rehabilitation Act of 1946.<ref name="wiki"/> Among his classmates were future
notable figures including political activist Nemesio Prudente and Navy Captain Danilo Vizmanos. He graduated
valedictorian of the USMMA Deck Class of 1950 with a ninety-percent average, and was commissioned as an
Ensign in the new Philippine Navy.<ref name="wiki"/>

PAGE 4
The pattern continued. In 1952, he took the Anti-Submarine Warfare Deck Officers Course at the Naval Training
College and finished first with a remarkable rating of ninety-nine percent.<ref name="wiki"/> He later graduated
from the Naval Command Course at the US Naval War College in 1968<ref name="wiki"/>, and obtained a
Master's degree in National Security Administration from the National Defense College of the Philippines, where
his performance was rated "Superior."<ref name="wiki"/> Out of thirteen foreign and local courses he attended
across his career, he topped six and finished the rest with honors.<ref name="wiki"/>
In 1995, the USMMA inducted Espaldon as only the third Filipino in its Hall of Distinguished Graduates —
recognizing him as the first Academy graduate to attain the rank of Rear Admiral, and for his successful efforts in
bringing peace to Southern Philippines.<ref name="wiki"/> When he received that distinction, he described it in
words that said everything about the man: the most memorable day of his lifelong efforts at living in God's way
and in the service of his fellowmen.<ref name="arabnews">Arab News. (2005, September 5). Former Philippine
envoy to Riyadh dies at 79. Arab News. https://www.arabnews.com/node/272519</ref>
Naval Career and Intelligence Service
Early Commands and Diplomatic Posting
After commissioning in 1950, Espaldon took command of patrol ships RPS Capiz and later RPS Iloilo.<ref
name="wiki"/> He was later appointed naval attaché to Indonesia and Malaysia, where he became fluent in Bahasa
Indonesia and built regional relationships that would serve him in later negotiations.<ref name="wiki"/>
The Senior Ranks: Intelligence, Command, and Politics
His career advanced through increasingly senior positions: Chief of Naval Intelligence in 1966, Acting Chief of the
Intelligence Service of the AFP (ISAFP) in 1969, Vice Commander of the Philippine Navy in 1971, and Deputy
Chief of Staff of the Armed Forces of the Philippines in 1972.<ref name="wiki"/>
That last posting should have been the stepping stone to the top. It wasn't. The Marcos administration reportedly
preferred a loyalist — specifically Fabian Ver — in the top military position.<ref name="wiki"/> AP correspondent
Gil Santos later noted that Espaldon was one of the few "good guys" in the military who genuinely wanted to
restore professionalism, and paid for it by being sidelined.<ref name="wiki"/>
Cleaning Up Customs
Even pushed to the margins, Espaldon kept working. From October 25, 1972, to August 31, 1973, he served as
Military Supervisor of the Bureau of Customs — then one of the most corrupt agencies in the Philippine
government.<ref name="wiki"/> He computerized entry procedures, dismantled the racketeering "cabo" system at
the North Harbor, and prosecuted 37 cases of customs irregularities. The result: revenue collection rose twenty-four
percent over the previous year, and processing time collapsed from ten days to seventy-two hours.<ref
name="wiki"/> He received the Outstanding Achievement Medal for his work there — but more than the medal,
the episode revealed something important. Wherever Espaldon went, things worked better than they had before.

PAGE 5
Commanding the South: The Moro Insurgency
The Conflict He Inherited
By the early 1970s, the Moro National Liberation Front (MNLF), founded by Nur Misuari, had launched a full-
scale secessionist insurgency across Mindanao, the Sulu archipelago, and Palawan. At its peak in 1974, the MNLF
could field between 50,000 and 60,000 armed fighters<ref name="wiki"/>, with as many as 20,000 reportedly
trained in Sabah with Libyan financial backing.<ref name="wiki"/> Decades of land dispossession, political
marginalization, and cultural condescension had finally boiled over into open revolt. The AFP's initial response —
a search-and-destroy approach under Commodore Gil Fernandez as SOWESCOM Commander — was making
things worse, not better. Communities were more alienated by the day.
A New Commander, A Different Approach
In 1973, Commodore Espaldon replaced Fernandez as commanding officer of the AFP Southwest Command
(SOWESCOM). The replacement wasn't routine. The MNLF's "Magic Eight" rebel commanders had reportedly
sought Fernandez's relief as a precondition for peace discussions — citing his lack of sympathy for Muslims.<ref
name="wiki"/> Espaldon's appointment was itself a signal. His predecessor's Vietnam-style tactics of body counts
and search-and-destroy were abandoned in favor of what became known as the "Policy of Attraction" — dialogue,
amnesty, reintegration, and development.<ref name="wiki"/>
Central to this campaign of reconciliation was Rear Admiral Romulo M. Espaldon, a native of Tawi-
Tawi, tasked to dialogue with the MNLF in the thrust for finding a lasting peace in
Mindanao.|Amilpasa "Caloy" Bandaying, former MNLF Top 90 member and Espaldon's aide-de-
camp, in The Bangsamoro Story
The personal dimension of the change mattered as much as the strategic one. In October 1973, word came that the
Magic Eight rebel commanders wanted to surrender to Espaldon personally, along with their 2,000 fighters. The
agreed plan called for Espaldon to anchor offshore and wait. By noon, no one had come. When a single commander
finally arrived by pump boat and asked Espaldon to come ashore instead, Espaldon agreed — with nothing but trust
and eight unarmed men on a small pump boat. The rebels rushed to embrace him, weeping, saying the government
was sincere. It wasn't a military victory. It was something harder to achieve.
The Results
The results were real. By late 1978, Espaldon announced the collapse of the Northern Mindanao Revolutionary
Command led by Abul Khayr Alonto, with 1,215 rebels surrendering in that operation alone — bringing the total to
35,411.<ref name="wiki"/> By the early 1980s, over 40,000 rebels had laid down their arms under his amnesty
program.<ref name="wiki"/> Some independent observers have raised questions about whether the official figures
were overstated<ref name="wiki"/>, but the reduction in armed conflict across the Zamboanga provinces and the
Sulu archipelago was widely documented and acknowledged as genuine.
Many surrendering fighters were integrated into the AFP through officer training as part of the broader peace effort.
<ref name="wiki"/> Espaldon even designated a former MNLF Top 90 member, Amilpasa "Caloy" Bandaying, as
his aide-de-camp — over the objections of SOUTHCOM officers.<ref name="wiki"/> The message that sent was
clear: these men weren't just former enemies. They were future colleagues.

PAGE 6
Governor of Tawi-Tawi: Father of a Province
When Tawi-Tawi became a separate province on September 11, 1973, through Presidential Decree No. 302,
Espaldon became its first Military Governor.<ref name="wiki"/> He had actually proposed the separation himself.
He had gone to President Marcos directly and made the case: the Sama people of Tawi-Tawi were tired of being
administratively subordinated to Sulu; they wanted their own leaders, their own provincial government, their own
future. If the government wanted to address the insurgency in a meaningful way, creating a separate province was
the practical answer.<ref name="wiki"/> Marcos listened. That's how Romulo Espaldon earned the moniker Father
of Tawi-Tawi.<ref name="wiki"/>
What followed was a run of infrastructure development that has few parallels in the region's history. In the first 730
days of Tawi-Tawi's existence as a province, Espaldon and Vice Governor Nur Jaafar led the construction or
completion of over 100 civilian projects: the provincial capitol, a hospital, a public market, fifty mosques,
schoolhouses, a radio station, airstrips, piers, houses, bridges, roads, and a water system.<ref name="wiki"/> This
wasn't token development. It was a deliberate statement that the Philippine state could show up for a Muslim-
majority province — and that Espaldon was proof it could be done.
In 1974, he was also designated second Military Governor of Basilan, administering the province through Colonel
Florencio E. Magsino.<ref name="wiki"/> Basilan's own official government records would later describe him as
"a tactful and able administrator, respected by Muslim and Christian alike."<ref name="arabnews"/>
On December 29, 1973, Espaldon made history: he became the first naval officer ever promoted to the rank of Rear
Admiral in the Philippine Navy.<ref name="wiki"/> That same day, Commodore Hilario Ruiz, then Flag Officer-
in-Command of the Philippine Navy, was likewise promoted.<ref name="wiki"/>
Regional Commissioner of Region IX
On July 7, 1975, Espaldon was appointed the first Regional Commissioner of Region IX, covering Basilan, Sulu,
Tawi-Tawi, and the Zamboanga provinces.<ref name="wiki"/> In that same month, he led the signing of the
Philippines-Indonesia Agreements on Border Crossing and Border Patrol — a maritime security cooperation
framework that Indonesia later recognized with the Bintang Yudha Dharma Pratama, its second-highest military
order of merit, awarded in 1978.<ref name="wiki"/>
Espaldon served as Region IX's first and only Regional Commissioner until the office was reorganized into the
Lupong Tagapagpaganap ng Pook (LTP) in 1979, when he was succeeded by Ulbert Ulama "Bob" Tugung.<ref
name="wiki"/>
In 1976, when SOWESCOM was reorganized into the AFP Southern Command (SOUTHCOM), Espaldon became
its inaugural commander — with full authority to deploy troops in the south without seeking clearance from the
service chiefs, an explicit recognition that his methods were working where other approaches had not.<ref
name="wiki"/>
The Tripoli Agreement and the Ceasefire of 1977
The Tripoli Agreement of December 23, 1976, brokered with Libyan mediation, set up a ceasefire framework and
opened the path toward some form of autonomy for Muslim Mindanao. On January 20, 1977, in Zamboanga City,
Espaldon signed the ceasefire agreement with Dr. Tham Manjoorsa, the MNLF's authorized representative.<ref
name="wiki"/> A subsequent plebiscite led to the creation of two autonomous regions — Regions IX and XII — in
Mindanao.<ref name="wiki"/>

PAGE 7
Marcos's government never fully honored the Tripoli Agreement's autonomy provisions, and armed conflict
eventually resumed elsewhere. But the ceasefire Espaldon negotiated and enforced in his zone of command
represented a genuine pause in the killing. The partial autonomy structures he helped establish planted seeds that
would eventually grow into the Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (ARMM) in 1989, and into today's
Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM), formally inaugurated in 2019.
Crisis Negotiations: Hostages, Ships, and Trust
Alongside the broader strategic work, Espaldon was repeatedly called upon to resolve acute crises that demanded
something harder to find than military firepower: patience, nerve, and the ability to communicate across deep
cultural suspicion. He proved equal to every one of them.
The MV Don Carlos Hijacking (1978)
On April 30, 1978, the MV Don Carlos of Sulpicio Lines was seized and its 56 hostages held by terrorists
demanding 700,000 pesos for their release. After twenty-three days, with Espaldon's decisive assistance,
government forces obtained the release of all hostages — without a single centavo of ransom being paid.<ref
name="wiki"/> The Sulpicio Lines vice-president, retired BGen. Emilio Alcoseba, was direct about what made the
difference: without Espaldon and General Luga, the terrorists would never have released anyone.<ref
name="wiki"/>
The Suehiro Maru (1975)
On September 26, 1975, the Japanese freighter Suehiro Maru was seized in Zamboanga, its 29 crew members held
by 40 terrorists demanding $133,000. Espaldon assembled a blockade of eleven Navy ships and applied steady
pressure until the rebels progressively dropped their demands and eventually released the ship and crew — again,
with no ransom paid.<ref name="wiki"/>
The Pierre Huguet Kidnapping (1978)
On February 26, 1978, Pierre Huguet, a senior official of the French Ministry of Cultural Affairs, was abducted
while photographing stilt houses in Zamboanga Bay and held on Basilan for a ransom of $132,000. Espaldon
coordinated directly with French Ambassador Raphaël-Léonard Touze and eventually secured Huguet's peaceful
release — consistent with the government policy of paying no ransom.<ref name="wiki"/> France responded by
awarding Espaldon the Légion d'honneur — the highest French order of merit — in 1978.<ref name="wiki"/>
The Eunice Diment Case (1976)
On February 28, 1976, British missionary-translator Eunice Diment was kidnapped off Basilan Island. She was
released unharmed on March 17 with no ransom paid.<ref name="wiki"/> The Hong Kong-based Far Eastern
Economic Review described the episode as a good illustration of how Espaldon and his officers worked.<ref
name="wiki"/>

PAGE 8
The Battle of Jolo: A Commander's Hardest Moment
Not every episode was a clean success. On February 7, 1974, government forces launched a military offensive
against MNLF positions in the municipality of Jolo, resulting in heavy civilian and military casualties and
significant damage to the town. Documented accounts indicate that Espaldon opposed the military operation but
was overruled by the central government in Manila.<ref name="mindanews">Santos, S. M. Jr. (2025, March 28).
Commentary: Addendum to 'The Jolo Siege of 1974, half a century hence.' Mindanews.
https://mindanews.com/mindaviews/2025/04/commentary-addendum-to-the-jolo-siege-of-1974-half-a-century-
hence/</ref> He was later remembered as the "prime mover" who sent naval ships to the Jolo pier to evacuate
thousands of stranded civilians to safety.<ref name="wiki"/>
After the battle, Espaldon was made part of the Executive Committee of the Inter-Agency Task Force for the
Rehabilitation of Jolo. Six years later, the Municipality of Jolo presented him a formal citation — signed by Mayor
Habib Aminkadra Barlie Abubakar — that read in part:
Thanks to the work and love of Rear Admiral Romulo M. Espaldon for the people of Jolo, we Taosugs
now possess a new image of ourselves.|Municipality of Jolo Citation, December 28, 1980, signed by
Mayor Habib Aminkadra Barlie Abubakar
The citation credited him with rebuilding roads and houses, and erecting a new mosque in place of the one
destroyed during the fighting.<ref name="wiki"/>
Sultan of Peace: The Retirement Citation
Upon his retirement on December 31, 1980, the Muslim communities of Autonomous Region IX gave him a send-
off no government decoration could replicate. On December 28, 1980, in Zamboanga City, they conferred upon
him the honorary title Sultan Makasanyang — Sultan of Peace.<ref name="wiki"/> The formal citation was
unambiguous about what it meant:
Before Espaldon assumed command, the military was looked upon by us as an enemy. He transformed
a situation of potential fratricidal war into one of cooperative brotherliness and of fruitful co-existence,
and elevated the Muslims of Region IX into first class citizens attended to by the government on equal
footing with our Christian brothers.|Citation of Sultan Makasanyang, Autonomous Region IX,
December 28, 1980
Those words, from the communities he had served, are the truest measure of his career.<ref name="wiki"/>
Commission on Islamic Affairs and the Ministry of Muslim Affairs
Espaldon's commitment to Muslim Filipinos didn't stop when the uniform came off. In 1979, while still serving as
Regional Commissioner, he was appointed the first Commissioner of the newly created Commission on Islamic
Affairs.<ref name="wiki"/> That agency was elevated into the Ministry of Muslim Affairs in 1981, and Espaldon
continued to lead it as its inaugural minister.<ref name="wiki"/>
Under his leadership, the Philippine Shari'ah Institute was established, and the Code of Muslim Personal Laws was
translated from English into Arabic.<ref name="wiki"/> The first Madrasa policy conference was convened —
bringing together educators and officials to discuss integrating Madrasa education into the national Philippine
educational system, a forward-thinking initiative that anticipated policy debates that would continue for decades.
<ref name="wiki"/> He also served as Chairman of the Philippine Pilgrimage Authority and as Amirul Hajj in both
1981 and 1984, leading the Philippines' annual Hajj mission to Mecca.<ref name="wiki"/>

PAGE 9
Congress: First Elected Representative of Tawi-Tawi
A chapter of Espaldon's career that often gets overlooked is his time in the Philippine Congress. In 1990, after
winning an election protest against Alawadin T. Bandon Jr., he was seated as representative of the lone legislative
district of Tawi-Tawi during the 8th Congress of the Philippines, serving from December 12, 1990, to June 30,
1992.<ref name="wiki"/>
He was the first elected representative of Tawi-Tawi — a province he had personally lobbied President Marcos to
create. That singular loop — the man who made the province becoming its first voice in the national legislature —
captures something essential about his relationship with Tawi-Tawi. It was never just a posting. It was a
responsibility.
Among the bills he filed as legislator were House Bill No. 35166, creating the Sulu Archipelago Development
Authority, and House Bill No. 35187, requiring conspicuous identification markings on water vessels — the kind
of practical, security-conscious legislation that only a former naval commander would think to introduce.<ref
name="wiki"/> He also received an appointment as Honorary Ambassador-at-Large to Guam in 1990.<ref
name="wiki"/>
Diplomatic Career: From Cairo to Riyadh
After retiring from the AFP in 1980 and completing his work at the Ministry of Muslim Affairs, Espaldon entered
the Philippine Foreign Service. His appointment as Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary to Egypt,
Sudan, and Somalia from 1984 to 1986<ref name="wiki"/> placed him at the heart of the Arab world during a
period of considerable regional turbulence. His cultural familiarity with Islam, his personal networks in the Muslim
world, and his hard-won fluency in Bahasa Indonesia made him an unusually effective representative.
He later served as Ambassador to Saudi Arabia and Yemen from 1993 to 1998<ref name="wiki"/> — arguably the
most important diplomatic posting available to a Filipino, given the presence of millions of Overseas Filipino
Workers (OFWs) in the Kingdom. During his time in Riyadh, he consistently reminded embassy personnel that
their primary mission was to serve and protect OFWs.<ref name="wiki"/>
Even in retirement from diplomacy, his name carried weight where it counted. During the 2000 Sipadan hostage
crisis, the Abu Sayyaf Group declared it would release three female hostages if the government agreed to a
negotiating panel composed of Espaldon, Senator Ramon Magsaysay Jr., and Sultan Rodinood Kiram.<ref
name="wiki"/> The government declined the request<ref name="wiki"/>, but the fact that an armed extremist
organization named him as a trusted interlocutor — more than two decades after his retirement from military
command — speaks to the enduring depth of his credibility in the south.
In 2003, he served as adviser to a government panel that met with Prof. Shariff Julabbi, founder of the MILF
splinter group Bangsamoro Mujahideen Alliance.<ref name="wiki"/> To the end of his active public life, he
remained engaged with the effort to find a negotiated solution to the conflict he had spent a lifetime trying to
resolve.

PAGE 10
Faith and Personal Values
Embracing Islam
At some point during his career, Romulo Espaldon formally embraced Islam.<ref name="wiki"/> He never sought
public attention for the decision and never used it as political currency. For those who had known him across the
decades, it wasn't a surprise — it was the formalization of something that had been true of him for a long time. He
had grown up in a Muslim world, learned to see it from the inside, and his entire approach to the Moro question
had been built on recognizing the dignity and humanity of Muslim Filipinos. His family reportedly received the
news with joy.<ref name="arabnews"/>
He adopted devout practices thereafter, living modestly, praying daily, and conducting himself in ways that those
around him recognized as genuinely of their own — not a convert performing identity, but a believer living his
faith. He was known for the principle he articulated at his USMMA Hall of Fame induction: living in God's way
and in the service of his fellowmen.<ref name="arabnews"/> That phrase, spoken at a moment of international
recognition, captures the compass that oriented his entire life.
Character Under Pressure
Throughout the martial law era, when corruption and patronage were normalized across both the civilian and
military bureaucracy, Espaldon neither accumulated personal wealth through his offices nor permitted troops under
his command to abuse civilians. He received honors with visible humility. When asked what drove him, he spoke
of faith and duty — never of ambition or ideology. The Sultan of Peace title was not a political gesture from the
communities who gave it. It was their recognition of a man who had, against considerable institutional pressure,
chosen to be good.
Civic Involvement
Beyond his official roles, Espaldon maintained broad civic engagement. He served as Vice-President of the Boy
Scouts of the Philippines from 1981 to 1984, and as District Governor of Lions Clubs International from 1983 to
1984.<ref name="wiki"/> In 1977, Don Moser of National Geographic captured him in action at a community
dialogue — watching Espaldon thunder at a slow-moving local official: "You, commissioner, will go to Manila
yourself and get the funds!" — to an audience that applauded.<ref name="wiki"/> He appeared on the cover of
Asiaweek twice<ref name="wiki"/>, and in January 1984 was featured on the cover of Mr. & Ms. magazine and
named among the fifty most capable people to lead the Philippines.<ref name="wiki"/>
Honors and Recognition
Philippine Awards
Espaldon received a distinguished array of Philippine military and civilian decorations, including the Presidential
Merit Award, multiple Outstanding Achievement Medals, Distinguished Service Stars, Military Merit Medals,
Presidential Unit Citations, the Philippine Liberation Medal, the Jolo Campaign Medal, the Anti-Dissidence
Campaign Medal, and Long Service Medals.<ref name="tracesofwar">Espaldon, Romulo Mercader. (n.d.).
TracesOfWar.com. Retrieved from https://www.tracesofwar.com/persons/88438/Espaldon-Romulo-

PAGE 11
Mercader.htm</ref> He also received the Aurora Aragon Quezon Award in 1979, and in 1988 both the Gintong
Ama Award for Government and Public Service and the Distinguished Achievement Award from the National
Defense College of the Philippines.<ref name="wiki"/>
Foreign Honors
France: Légion d'honneur (1978) — for securing the release of French national Pierre Huguet without
ransom.<ref name="wiki"/>
Indonesia: Bintang Yudha Dharma Pratama (1978) — for leading the Philippines-Indonesia Border Crossing
and Border Patrol Agreements.<ref name="wiki"/>
United States: Congressional Gold Medal for Filipino Veterans of World War II — awarded posthumously
by the US Congress in 2022.<ref name="wiki"/>
United States Merchant Marine Academy: Inducted into the Hall of Distinguished Graduates in 1995 as
only the third Filipino ever so recognized.<ref name="wiki"/>
Community Citations
Beyond institutional awards, the most meaningful tributes were those from the communities he served. The Sultan
Makasanyang citation of December 28, 1980, from the Muslim communities of Autonomous Region IX —
acknowledging that the military had been the enemy before Espaldon arrived — stands as a tribute no medal can
replicate.<ref name="wiki"/> The Municipality of Jolo's citation credited him with giving the Tausug people "a
new image of ourselves."<ref name="wiki"/>
Legacy
Espaldon is widely regarded today as one of the most significant figures in the modern history of Muslim
Mindanao — a judgment made more meaningful, not less, by his Christian birth and his choice to cross every
boundary that had kept others on one side or the other. In the folklore of Mindanao he is remembered as the Father
of Tawi-Tawi. In the academic literature on the Moro conflict, he is cited as the model of a leader who chose
outreach over confrontation, integration over annihilation, and development over dependency.
Many analysts of the Mindanao peace process credit him with laying significant groundwork for what eventually
became the Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (ARMM) in 1989 and today's Bangsamoro Autonomous
Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM), formally inaugurated in 2019. The ceasefire he signed, the amnesty
programs he ran, the institutional frameworks for Muslim participation in government he helped build, the Shari'ah
Institute and Madrasa education reforms he championed — all contributed to the political and institutional
architecture that later administrations would formalize into autonomous governance.
His approach — integrating security with social upliftment, treating surrendered fighters as future citizens rather
than defeated enemies, building development programs as instruments of reconciliation — anticipated by decades
the frameworks now known in peace and conflict studies as whole-of-nation peacebuilding and comprehensive
peace strategies. That these approaches are now standard vocabulary in the field is, in part, his intellectual and
practical legacy.
His life story is taught in Philippine military and civilian institutions as a case study in cultural sensitivity,
principled leadership, and human-centered engagement with conflict. His methodology is studied. His name is
remembered. And the region he devoted his life to is still, imperfectly and with great effort, working toward the
peace he helped make thinkable.

PAGE 12
Death
Rear Admiral Romulo M. Espaldon passed away on August 27, 2005, in Makati, Philippines, from colon cancer.
He was seventy-nine years old. He was laid to rest at the Libingan ng mga Bayani — the Heroes' Cemetery — in
Metro Manila.<ref name="arabnews"/> He had served the Philippine state as guerrilla fighter, naval officer, Rear
Admiral, military governor, regional commissioner, minister of Muslim affairs, congressman, and ambassador,
across more than five decades of public life. Each chapter was full. Each was demanding in a different way. And
each was animated by the same essential conviction: that human conflict is never finally about irreconcilable
differences, but about unaddressed grievances and the failure of genuine respect.
The Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao, inaugurated in 2019 after decades of painful
negotiation, represents the most complete political expression to date of the vision that Espaldon helped make
thinkable. It is fragile, imperfect, and still contested. But it exists. And those who study its origins will find, at the
foundation, the work of a man who understood — decades before his government's policies caught up — that the
only bridge strong enough to hold the weight of Mindanao's history was one built from genuine human respect.
Further Reading

reconciliation in Southern Mindanao.]

hence.'" Mindanews. https://mindanews.com/mindaviews/2025/04/commentary-addendum-to-the-jolo-siege-
of-1974-half-a-century-hence/

title: Galo, Arafat Lamping
text:
PAGE 1
Arafat Lamping Galo
Arafat Lamping Galo is a prominent Maranao civil servant, first Maranaw and Bangsamoro Real Estate Consultant
who pass the licensure board examination, and as real estate enthusiast serving as Regional Supervisor of the
Bureau of Local Government Finance (BLGF) in the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao
(BARMM). Widely known as Sir Raffy, Galo has become a fiscal steward of Bangsamoro autonomy, bridging
Philippine national financial standards with the region's evolving self-governance framework. His dual expertise in
property valuation and treasury management has positioned him as a key architect of local government financial
independence across BARMM's 111 Municipalities, 5 Provinces and 3 Cities. Through capacity building,
modernized assessment systems, and strategic revenue generation initiatives, Galo embodies the professional
excellence and cultural pride that define contemporary Bangsamoro public service.

Early Life and Family
Arafat Lamping Galo was born and raised in Lanao del Sur, a province deeply rooted in Maranao culture and
heritage. His hometown is Lumba Bayabao, specifically Barangay Cabasaran, where his family has maintained
strong community ties and a reputation for public service. The Galo family is known for their commitment to civic
duty and educational advancement, values that have shaped Arafat's professional trajectory.
Growing up in Lanao del Sur during a period of significant political transitions, Galo witnessed the evolution of
local governance structures and the complexities of regional administration. His early exposure to community
leadership through family networks and cultural traditions like Kandorei (thanksgiving gatherings) instilled in him
a sense of responsibility toward collective welfare and organizational excellence.

Education and Professional Development
Galo's formal education reflects a deliberate progression toward
governance and fiscal expertise. He holds a Master of Public
Administration, a degree that prepared him for the administrative
complexities of government service. He also earned a Master of
Business Administration, equipping him with business acumen
essential for understanding financial systems and organizational
management.
Beyond academic credentials, Galo pursued specialized professional
certifications in real estate, a field critical to property valuation and
local government revenue generation. He obtained his License as a
Real Estate Appraiser in July 2013, demonstrating technical
competence in property assessment methodologies. This
accomplishment was followed by his certification as a Licensed Real
Estate Consultant in December 2021, a prestigious national credential
that ranks among the highest qualifications in the Philippine real
estate industry. The five-year gap between these two licenses reflects
his commitment to continuous professional development and
deepening expertise.
His academic background and professional licenses have earned him
the distinction of being frequently addressed as Professor,
recognizing his contributions to specialized training and knowledge
transfer within BARMM government circles.
Career in Fiscal Administration
Role as Regional Supervisor, BLGF
Arafat Lamping Galo currently serves as Regional Supervisor for the
Bureau of Local Government Finance (BLGF) within the BARMM.
In this capacity, he oversees the financial management systems,
treasury operations, and fiscal performance of local government units
(LGUs) across all 39 municipalities in Lanao del Sur and other
BARMM provinces.
The BLGF is a technical bureau under the Department of Finance
tasked with improving the fiscal capacity and financial autonomy of
local governments. Galo's role bridges the gap between national
fiscal standards and the unique administrative needs of the
autonomous region, ensuring that BARMM municipalities can
manage their finances effectively while maintaining compliance with
national auditing and budgeting requirements.

PAGE 3
Property Valuation and Tax Reform
One of Galo's most significant contributions has been his modernization of property assessment systems in Lanao
del Sur. Leveraging his expertise as a Licensed Real Estate Consultant, he has championed the systematic updating
of Schedules of Market Values (SMVs) across municipalities. SMVs form the basis for calculating real property
taxes, and outdated assessments directly limit local government revenue.
His valuation work addresses a critical challenge: many municipalities in BARMM rely heavily on the National
Tax Allotment (NTA) rather than locally sourced revenues. By ensuring that property assessments reflect current
market conditions, Galo helps municipalities increase their real property tax collections, thereby reducing fiscal
dependency and strengthening local government financial independence. This initiative directly supports the
Bangsamoro Organic Law's emphasis on fiscal autonomy.
Treasury Operations and Financial Oversight
Galo oversees the supervision of provincial, city, and municipal treasurers across his jurisdiction. He conducts
Local Treasury Operations Evaluations (LTOE) to assess how effectively local treasurers manage funds, collect
revenues, and comply with BLGF standards. These evaluations identify best practices and areas for improvement,
creating accountability mechanisms that strengthen financial governance at the municipal level.
His oversight extends to monitoring compliance with electronic payment systems and digital financial reporting
tools, helping LGUs transition from paper-based to technology-enabled treasury operations.
Key Initiatives and Achievements
Capacity Building for Local Finance Officers
Recognizing that technical expertise must be distributed across the region, Galo has become a prominent organizer
of training programs for municipal and city finance committees. These workshops cover contemporary financial
management topics including electronic payment systems, the Electronic Statement of Receipts and Expenditures
(eSRE), financial reporting standards, and debt sustainability practices for LGU credit financing.
By investing in the professional development of local finance officers, Galo multiplies his impact beyond his direct
supervisory role. Finance officers trained in modern practices can then lead their municipalities toward greater
fiscal sophistication and self-reliance.
BLGF Regional Office Inauguration
A landmark achievement in Galo's tenure was his supporting role in the inauguration of the BLGF Regional Office
in Marawi City on July 30, 2025. This facility represents a permanent institutional presence dedicated to providing
technical assistance and financial oversight to all LGUs in Lanao del Sur and surrounding BARMM provinces. The
office serves as a headquarters for BLGF personnel and a hub for municipal treasurers seeking guidance on
complex financial matters.
The establishment of this regional office strengthens BARMM's capacity to implement fiscal policies aligned with
both national standards and the specific provisions of the Bangsamoro Organic Law.

PAGE 4
Digitalization and Financial Systems Modernization
Galo oversees the rollout of the Enhanced LGU Integrated Financial Tools (LIFT) System across Lanao del Sur.
This initiative digitalizes local financial reporting and data submission, allowing municipalities to file their
Statements of Receipts and Expenditures electronically rather than through cumbersome paper processes. The LIFT
System increases transparency, reduces errors, and enables real-time fiscal monitoring at the regional level.
Seal of Good Local Governance Administration
Galo is instrumental in administering the Seal of Good Local Governance (SGLG) program in Lanao del Sur,
specifically in the Financial Administration category. The SGLG program recognizes municipalities that
demonstrate excellence in governance, and Galo's work ensures that performance criteria are fairly applied and that
top-performing municipalities serve as benchmarks for the region.
Cultural Significance and Community Identity
Maranao Representation in Government
Arafat Lamping Galo stands as a visible representative of Maranao professional excellence in regional governance.
His prominence in BARMM fiscal administration demonstrates that Muslim Filipinos, particularly Maranaos,
continue to lead in complex, technical government roles requiring both cultural credibility and modern expertise.
His career validates the educational and professional aspirations of younger Maranaos entering public service and
specialized fields. By holding prestigious national licenses and wielding significant influence over regional
financial policy, Galo challenges stereotypes and affirms the capacity of Bangsamoro communities to excel in
administrative and technical domains.
Integration of Faith and Civic Duty
Galo's public profile consistently emphasizes the integration of Islamic faith and professional responsibility. In his
public acknowledgments, he frequently expresses gratitude to Allah for his achievements and credits community
support for his successes. This integration reflects a broader Bangsamoro approach to governance in which spiritual
grounding and civic responsibility are viewed as complementary rather than contradictory.
Kandorei and Community Celebration
In his home municipality of Lumba-Bayabao, Galo is frequently honored during Kandorei events, traditional
Maranao thanksgiving gatherings where community members celebrate shared achievements and express collective
gratitude. These occasions recognize his professional accomplishments as a source of family and community pride,
positioning him as a role model for aspiring professionals within the Maranao community.
His work is thus embedded in a cultural context that views individual achievement as an expression of family
honor and collective identity.

PAGE 5
Legacy and Regional Impact
Arafat Lamping Galo's work has redefined what fiscal stewardship looks like within an autonomous region. Rather
than viewing national standards and regional autonomy as opposing forces, he has demonstrated that BARMM can
maintain compatibility with Philippine financial systems while exercising genuine fiscal independence. His
initiatives have strengthened local government financial capacity across 39 municipalities, reduced administrative
dependency, and created pathways for younger finance professionals to develop expertise in both traditional and
emerging governance contexts.
His emphasis on property valuation, revenue generation, and capacity building reflects a long-term vision of fiscal
sustainability in which municipalities are not perpetually reliant on national subsidies but instead generate locally
sourced revenues through efficient, fair, and transparent systems.
The BLGF Regional Office in Marawi City stands as a physical manifestation of this legacy, a permanent
institution designed to ensure that BARMM local governments continue to access world-class financial technical
assistance for generations to come.
Recognition and Professional Standing
Galo's credentials and track record have earned him recognition within BARMM government and among
professional associations serving local government finance. His appointments as Regional Supervisor and his
frequent designation as Professor reflect institutional confidence in his judgment and expertise. His involvement in
national and local government units GOCC agencies, he is recognized as Outstanding Educator by various research
organization.

Ombra C. Gandamra
Ombra C. Gandamra (born in Lanao del Sur) is a Filipino lawyer, career public servant, and cultural advocate
whose decades-long service to the Muslim Filipino community has left a quiet but enduring mark on government
institutions in the Philippines. Known for bridging the gap between traditional Maranao leadership and the modern
Philippine bureaucracy, he built his reputation through methodical work in legal governance, regional
administration, and Muslim affairs. After a long career that spanned the transition from the Office on Muslim
Affairs (OMA) to the National Commission on Muslim Filipinos (NCMF), he retired as Regional Director of
NCMF Region X in 2018. He currently serves as the City Administrator of Marawi City, where he brings that same
institutional knowledge to bear on one of the country's most challenging post-conflict recovery efforts.
His legacy is not built on dramatic moments or headline-grabbing
decisions. It's built on sustained, deliberate service, on being the person
in the room who understood the law, remembered the institutional
history, and knew how to get things done for a community that has long
had to fight for its place in national policy. In Marawi, a city still
recovering from the devastating 2017 siege, his work as City
Administrator is a continuation of that same mission.
