Background and Early Life
Ombra C. Gandamra was born in Marawi City, the Islamic City of the Philippines and the heart of the Meranao
homeland in Lanao del Sur, a predominantly Meranao province with a rich tradition of Islamic scholarship,
customary governance, and political leadership. The Gandamra family is among the prominent political and
professional clans in Marawi City and the surrounding province, maintaining a lineage of public service that spans
multiple generations and branches of government.
The details of his early childhood and secondary schooling remain largely private, which is not unusual for public
servants of his generation. What is known is that he pursued a degree in law and passed the Philippine Bar
Examination, the rigorous national licensing process that qualifies individuals to practice law in the Philippines.
His decision to enter public service rather than private legal practice would shape the entire arc of his career.
Education
Atty. Gandamra earned his law degree from San Beda College in Manila, completing his legal studies in 1980.
That same year, he sat for and passed the Philippine Bar Examination, administered by the Supreme Court of the
Philippines. Passing the Bar in the same year as graduation is no small achievement, and it signaled early on the
kind of focused, disciplined mind that would define his decades of public service. His legal formation at San Beda,

PAGE 3
one of the Philippines' most respected law schools with a strong tradition of producing public servants and jurists,
gave him both the doctrinal grounding and the professional rigor he would carry throughout his career in Muslim
affairs governance.
Career
Legal Officer at the Office on Muslim Affairs
Atty. Gandamra began his public service career at the Office on Muslim Affairs (OMA), the government agency
established to address the cultural, educational, and socioeconomic concerns of Muslim Filipinos across the
archipelago. He joined the institution as a Legal Officer, a role that placed him at the intersection of national
legislation and the day-to-day concerns of a minority community whose rights and identity were, in many ways,
still being negotiated within the Philippine legal system.
His early work involved reviewing policies, advising on matters touching on Islamic law and its accommodation
within the Philippine legal framework, and ensuring that the agency's programs were on sound legal footing. It was
painstaking, unglamorous work, the kind that rarely generates public attention but is absolutely essential to the
functioning of any government institution.
Director of Legal Services
Through years of dedicated service and demonstrated legal expertise, Atty. Gandamra rose to become the Director
of Legal Services at OMA. This was a significant elevation in responsibility. As Director, he was no longer just
reviewing documents but was actively shaping the legal direction of the agency. He oversaw the legal affairs of an
institution dealing with questions that were, and remain, deeply sensitive: the integration of Shari'ah principles in a
predominantly secular national legal system, the rights of Muslim communities under national and international
law, and the institutional protection of Muslim cultural identity.
His tenure in this role gave him a breadth of institutional knowledge that few colleagues could match. He
understood not just the statutes and regulations but the reasoning behind them, the political negotiations that
produced them, and the practical realities of implementing them in communities spread across the country.
Regional Director, OMA/NCMF Region X
One of the defining chapters of Atty. Gandamra's career was his appointment and long service as Regional
Director of the OMA, and later the NCMF, Regional Office X, based in Cagayan de Oro City. Region X, or
Northern Mindanao, covers a geographically and culturally diverse area where Muslim Filipinos live alongside
Lumad and Christian communities, making effective regional governance both complex and consequential.
As Regional Director, he was the face of the national agency at the regional level. The position required diplomatic
skill, legal knowledge, and a genuine understanding of the communities he served, and Atty. Gandamra brought all
three to the role.
Implementing National Laws, Policies, and Programs
A core part of the Regional Director's mandate was ensuring that the laws, rules, regulations, policies, programs,
and projects of the Commission were actually put into practice on the ground in Region X, not just on paper in
Manila. That gap between policy and practice is where a lot of well-meaning government programs quietly die, and

PAGE 4
Atty. Gandamra made it his business to close it.
Among the flagship programs his office implemented was the annual Qur'an Reading Competition, a regional
event that brought together Muslim youth from across Northern Mindanao to demonstrate their mastery of Qur'anic
recitation and tajweed. More than a contest, the competition served as a visible affirmation of Islamic identity and
scholarship in a region where Muslim Filipinos are a minority, and it gave young people a concrete occasion to take
pride in their faith and culture.
His office also organized the annual regional Shari'ah trainings and seminars, which were aimed at deepening
awareness and understanding of Islamic law among community members, local officials, and government workers
who regularly interact with Muslim Filipinos. These sessions were practical and applied, addressing real questions
about how Shari'ah principles intersect with everyday life, civil transactions, family law, and the Philippine legal
system. For a community whose legal identity has often been misunderstood or overlooked by mainstream
institutions, these trainings were more than educational exercises. They were a form of institutional respect.
The office also managed the processing of applications for the annual Hajj operation, coordinating the
documentation, eligibility assessments, and logistical arrangements for Muslim Filipinos in the region who seek to
fulfill one of the five pillars of Islam by making the pilgrimage to Mecca. The Hajj operation is one of the most
visible and personally significant services the NCMF provides, and managing it properly at the regional level
requires both administrative precision and genuine sensitivity to what the pilgrimage means to the people
undertaking it.
Establishing Hajj Coordinating and Monitoring Units
Atty. Gandamra's office was also tasked with establishing and maintaining regional and provincial Hajj
coordinating and monitoring units across the coverage area of Region X. These units served as local touch points
for pilgrims at various stages of the Hajj process, from initial inquiry and application all the way through post-
pilgrimage monitoring and documentation. By decentralizing the coordination function down to the provincial
level, his office made the Hajj application process more accessible to Muslim communities in areas that couldn't
easily reach the regional center in Cagayan de Oro City. It was an acknowledgment that effective service delivery
isn't just about having the right programs. It's about making sure people can actually reach them.
Delivering Services to Muslim Filipinos
Underpinning all of these specific programs was a broader mandate that Atty. Gandamra took seriously throughout
his tenure: providing efficient and effective service to Muslim Filipinos in the region. That phrase is easy to write
into a law or a mission statement. Actually delivering on it, in a country where Muslim communities have
historically faced marginalization, underfunding, and institutional neglect, is a different matter entirely.
Under his leadership, the Regional Office worked to ensure that services were not only available but responsive
and dignified. This meant reducing bureaucratic friction for community members navigating government
processes, ensuring that staff understood and respected the cultural and religious context of the people they were
serving, and maintaining the kind of consistent presence in the region that communities could rely on.
Coordinating with Local Government Units and Regional Agencies
No government agency operates in isolation, and the NCMF Regional Office under Atty. Gandamra functioned as
an active partner within the broader ecosystem of Northern Mindanao's governance landscape. His office
maintained regular coordination with local government units (LGUs) across the region, working alongside
mayors, governors, and their respective departments to align programs and avoid duplication.

PAGE 5
He also coordinated with the regional offices and agencies of the Executive Department operating in Region X,
including agencies responsible for education, social welfare, health, and infrastructure. This whole-of-government
approach was essential to serving Muslim communities effectively, since the needs of those communities often cut
across multiple government mandates. A Muslim family displaced by conflict might need housing assistance,
educational support for their children, livelihood programs, and documentation services all at once, and no single
agency can provide all of that on its own. Atty. Gandamra understood this, and his office consistently positioned
itself as a connector and bridge within that larger system.
His tenure spanned the significant institutional transition from OMA to NCMF, triggered by the enactment of
Republic Act No. 9997 in 2010, which abolished OMA and created the NCMF as its successor agency with a
broader mandate and strengthened legal basis. Managing an agency through such a transition is no small feat.
Personnel, programs, legal authorities, and institutional relationships all had to be reconfigured while essential
services continued. His ability to manage that transition in Region X without disrupting service delivery was a
mark of his administrative skill.
He continued serving as Regional Director under NCMF until his retirement on March 3, 2018, completing a run at
the regional helm that spanned multiple national and local administrations.
Board Member and Vice Chairman, LASURECO
Alongside his government service, Atty. Gandamra also took on a leadership role in the energy sector, serving as
Board Member and Vice Chairman of the Lanao del Sur Electric Cooperative (LASURECO). LASURECO is
the electric cooperative responsible for providing power distribution services across Lanao del Sur, including
Marawi City — a province where reliable electricity has long been critical to both economic development and the
delivery of basic public services. His position on the Board placed him at the intersection of public utility
governance and community welfare, consistent with his broader career of service to the people of Lanao del Sur.
Current Role: City Administrator of Marawi City
Following his retirement from national government service, Atty. Gandamra took on what may well be the most
consequential role of his career: City Administrator of Marawi City. He serves under Mayor Majul Gandamra,
part of the same prominent Gandamra political family that has long been active in Marawi's governance.
The significance of this appointment cannot be overstated. Marawi City is not an ordinary local government unit. It
is a city still working through the aftermath of the 2017 Marawi Siege, a five-month urban battle between
government forces and militants affiliated with the Islamic State that left the city's central district in ruins,
displaced hundreds of thousands of residents, and inflicted trauma on an entire generation of Meranao families. The
rehabilitation of Marawi has been one of the most complex post-conflict reconstruction efforts in Philippine
history, involving multiple national agencies, billions of pesos in funding, and the extraordinarily difficult task of
balancing physical rebuilding with cultural and psychological healing.
As City Administrator, Atty. Gandamra functions as the chief administrative officer of the city government,
managing the daily operations of the local bureaucracy, coordinating with department heads, and ensuring that the
mayor's directives are translated into concrete programs and timely execution. In the context of Marawi's recovery,
this means keeping rehabilitation projects on track, navigating bureaucratic processes with national agencies, and
managing the enormous logistical complexity of a city in transition.

PAGE 6
Inter-Agency Coordination
One of his most critical functions as City Administrator is serving as the city's primary inter-agency liaison.
Marawi's recovery involves a long list of national government bodies: the Task Force Bangon Marawi, the National
Housing Authority, the Department of Public Works and Highways, the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in
Muslim Mindanao (BARMM) government, and cultural agencies like the National Commission for Culture and the
Arts (https://ncca.gov.ph) (NCCA), among others.
Atty. Gandamra's decades of experience navigating national government institutions, understanding how agencies
work, who to call, and how to get things moving, makes him particularly effective in this coordination role. He
understands both sides of the table, having spent his career inside the national bureaucracy before stepping into
local government service.
Cultural Advocacy and the Meranao Identity
Beyond his administrative functions, Atty. Gandamra has been a vocal advocate for the preservation and
promotion of Meranao culture and heritage. This advocacy is particularly significant in the context of Marawi's
recovery, where the risk of cultural erasure is real. When communities are displaced, when traditional structures are
destroyed, and when rebuilding is driven primarily by efficiency and cost, cultural memory is often what gets left
behind.
The Marawi Museum and School of Living Traditions
He has been a consistent supporter of the establishment of a Marawi Museum and a School of Living Traditions
in the city. These are not merely symbolic proposals. They represent a strategic approach to rebuilding that
recognizes culture as infrastructure. A museum would serve as a repository of Meranao history, art, and material
culture, providing future generations with a tangible connection to their heritage even as the physical landscape of
the city changes around them. A School of Living Traditions would ensure that living cultural practices, the crafts,
the music, the oral traditions, the performing arts, continue to be transmitted from one generation to the next.
The Torogan and Architectural Heritage
He has also been a strong advocate for the preservation of the Torogan, the traditional grand house of Meranao
royalty, recognized as a National Cultural Treasure under Philippine law. The Torogan is one of the most distinctive
examples of indigenous Philippine architecture, characterized by its elevated design, intricate okir wood carvings,
and the symbolic panolong projections that mark the home of a royal family. Many Torogans in Marawi were
damaged or destroyed during the 2017 siege, making efforts to document, protect, and restore surviving structures
both urgent and culturally vital.
His advocacy in this space reflects a broader understanding that rebuilding Marawi isn't just about putting up new
buildings. It's about recovering a civilization. The Meranao people have a rich, sophisticated cultural heritage, and
that heritage is as much a part of the city's future as its roads and drainage systems.
Arts as Healing
Atty. Gandamra has also championed the promotion of local arts as a means of psychological and social healing
for Marawi's displaced and traumatized population. This is consistent with a growing body of research and practice
in post-conflict societies that recognizes cultural expression as a critical component of community recovery, not a

PAGE 7
luxury but a necessity. His engagement with the NCCA and other cultural agencies has been part of this effort to
bring arts programming and cultural recognition into the recovery process.
Family and Political Connections
The Gandamra name carries significant weight in Marawi City and Lanao del Sur. The family has maintained a
presence in local politics and public life over many decades, with members holding positions at various levels of
government.
Mayor Majul Gandamra currently leads the city government of Marawi, and Atty. Ombra Gandamra serves in his
administration as City Administrator. Shaquille Gandamra, who formerly served as Sangguniang Kabataan (SK)
President, is currently a member of the Sangguniang Panlungsod (City Council) of Marawi City. The family
represents a continuity of civic engagement that is characteristic of the Meranao political tradition, where
leadership roles are often carried across generations as expressions of community responsibility.
Recognition and Legacy
Atty. Gandamra's career has been built less on formal awards and more on something harder to quantify:
institutional memory and trust. In a government agency where turnover is constant and institutional knowledge is
often lost when people leave, he was one of those rare officials who stayed long enough to become the living
memory of the institution. Colleagues and community members who worked with him during his years at OMA
and NCMF have cited his reliability, his depth of legal knowledge, and his genuine commitment to the welfare of
Muslim Filipinos as defining qualities.
His transition from national agency work to local government in Marawi also speaks to a particular kind of legacy:
the career public servant who doesn't retire into inactivity but redirects decades of accumulated skill toward a new
and urgent challenge. In taking on the City Administrator role, he chose to pour that institutional capital back into
the community that most needs it.
His legacy is, in many ways, the story of an institution that got better because the right person was willing to do the
unglamorous work for long enough to make it matter.
Challenges
No account of Atty. Gandamra's career would be complete without acknowledging the enormity of the challenges
he has worked within. Serving Muslim Filipinos within the Philippine government has always meant navigating
institutions that were not designed with that community's interests as a primary consideration. OMA and later
NCMF were created precisely to fill that gap, but gaps in funding, political will, and institutional capacity have
always been present.
The challenge in Marawi is of a different scale entirely. The city's rehabilitation has faced chronic delays,
bureaucratic bottlenecks, funding gaps, and the immense difficulty of rebuilding a community whose trauma is still
raw. As City Administrator, Atty. Gandamra operates in the middle of all of these pressures, with the weight of
community expectations on one side and the limitations of government process on the other.
His work is a reminder that institutional service in complex, underserved, and conflict-affected communities is not
for the faint of heart. It requires patience, persistence, and a willingness to keep showing up even when the
problems seem bigger than the tools available.

title: Gubat, Janoden Masbud
text:
PAGE 1
Janoden Masbud Gubat
Janoden Masbud Gubat (born March 30, 1974) is a Maranao electrical engineer, government official, civic
leader, and Sultan a Cabugatan sa Maul of the Royal Sultanate of Maul in Marantao, Lanao del Sur.
He carries a rare combination of credentials: a licensed electrical engineer who has worked on billion-peso
infrastructure projects in both the Philippines and the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, a government executive who
helped shape national land reform and data privacy policy, and a hereditary sultan who continues to serve his
community through organized civic work.
Over more than two decades of professional life spanning Mindanao, Metro Manila, and the Arabian Peninsula,
Gubat has built a track record rooted in technical excellence, public service, and Maranao cultural leadership. He is
perhaps best understood as a builder in every sense of the word: of power plants, of government systems, of civic
institutions, and of the communities he belongs to.

Background
Janoden Masbud Gubat is Maranao, a member of one of the indigenous Muslim peoples of Lanao del Sur in the
Bangsamoro region of Mindanao.
His connection to the Royal Sultanate of Maul in Marantao is not just historical or ceremonial. As Sultan a
Cabugatan sa Maul, he holds a living position within the traditional Maranao royal system, a responsibility that
runs alongside his professional and civic roles rather than separate from them.
He currently resides in Bacoor City, Cavite, in the Camella Homes community, which reflects the broader reality of
many Maranao professionals who have settled in Luzon while maintaining deep ties to their Bangsamoro roots.
He is also Executive Vice President of the Royal Sultanate of Lanao, further anchoring his role within the broader
network of Maranao traditional governance.

He later studied law at Mindanao State University, one of the premier
institutions serving the Muslim Filipino community, though his

He holds a Doctor of Humanities from Piedmont College of

Kingdom of Saudi Arabia.
Career
Early Practice in Mindanao
Gubat began his professional engineering career with BRIMA
Construction in Iligan City, where he served as Project Electrical
Engineer from April 2000 to February 2008.
During this period, he worked on government facilities across the
Mindanao region, gaining foundational experience in project
supervision, electrical systems installation, and coordination across
engineering disciplines.
This Mindanao chapter gave Gubat his professional footing: planning
electrical works, evaluating materials, preparing progress reports, and
working within multi-disciplinary construction teams. It was the kind
of on-the-ground experience that would serve him well in far larger
theatres.

In 2008, Gubat moved to the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, where he
would spend the next eight years working on some of the most
consequential military and infrastructure projects in the region.
He joined Al-Arab Contracting Company in Al-Taif from May 2008
to May 2010 as Project Electrical Engineer, assigned to two major
projects.
The first was the Typhoon Project, covering Royal Saudi Air Force aircraft facilities at King Fahad Airbase in Al-
Hawiya, Al-Taif, with a project cost of 1 billion Saudi Riyals. This involved Typhoon jet fighter facilities, bomb
shelters, and comprehensive military infrastructure.
The second was the Taif Handicap Hospital, a 300-bed facility within Taif Military Camp, under the General
Directorate of Military Works, valued at 100 million SAR.
In 2010, Gubat moved into a consultancy role as Senior Regional Electrical Engineer Consultant with the Ministry
of Defense (MOD) and General Directorate of Military Works (GDMW), based at King Khalid Military City in
Hafar Al-Batin, Northern Region, Kingdom of Saudi Arabia.
He held this role from September 2010 to September 2016, sponsored successively by Abdullah Al-Saif and
Partners for Engineering Consulting (2010 to 2013) and Al-Rajhi Engineering Consulting (2013 to 2016).
During this six-year tenure, he oversaw a remarkable portfolio of projects, including the following:
The 25 MW, 13.8 KV Gas Turbine and Generator Power Plant (Project No. 2/7/186), valued at 90 million SAR,
was completed between November 2010 and May 2013.
The 800 Military Housing Units (Project No. 1/7/9), valued at 650 million SAR, ran from September 2010 to July
2012.
The Hawk Missiles Storage Facility (Project No. 5/7/2), valued at 7 million SAR, was completed between
September 2010 and August 2012.
Primary Substation upgrading and Telephone Communication Facilities projects were completed between October
2011 and April 2013, at a combined cost of 17 million SAR.
The Sewer Treatment Plant (Project No. 2/7/277D), valued at 15 million SAR, was completed between March 2011
and October 2013.
Multiple school projects were completed between 2011 and 2015, including boys and girls elementary,
intermediate, and high school facilities valued at a combined 81.5 million SAR.
The Missiles Launcher Patriot project for the Royal Saudi Air Defense (Project No. 13/12/4), covering three sites,
was valued at 245 million SAR and ran from March 2013 to November 2015.
The Royal Saudi Air Defense General Headquarters (Project No. 3/7/4), valued at 260 million SAR, and the Royal
Saudi Air Force Housing project (Project No. 3/7/5), valued at 250 million SAR, were both completed through
2015 and 2016.

PAGE 4
His responsibilities across these projects included reviewing shop drawings, evaluating contractor claims,
conducting manufacturer inspections, representing the Regional Director in executive meetings, overseeing
electrical commissioning and testing, and preparing weekly and monthly progress reports.
Return to the Philippines: Private Sector
Returning to the Philippines after his Saudi contract ended, Gubat joined Solid South Engineering Services in Pasig
City as Senior Electrical Engineer Consultant from November 2016 to December 2018.
He oversaw electrical designs, coordinated multi-discipline construction activities, and supported project
management functions across multiple concurrent construction projects.
In September 2020, he joined Design Science, Inc. as Senior Electrical Engineer Consultant on the Metro Manila
Skyway Stage 3 project (the NLEX-SLEX Link) under San Miguel Corporation, a role he held until February
2021.
His duties included evaluating contractor and subcontractor performance, reviewing technical submittals, attending
executive-level meetings between San Miguel Corporation and project contractors, and serving as the
representative of the Project Manager in key transactions.
Government Service: Department of Agrarian Reform
Gubat entered government service with the Department of Agrarian Reform (DAR), initially as Technical Staff-1 in
the Office of the Undersecretary for Special Concerns from January to June 2019.
In this capacity, he provided legal and technical inputs for the nationwide Validation of Certificate of Land
Ownership Awardees (CLOAs) and Emancipation Patents (EPs), participated in Technical Working Group
discussions on the Rice Tariffication and Liberalization Law (RA 11203), and represented the Undersecretary in
public occasions and agrarian reform beneficiary engagements.
He returned to DAR from July 2021 to June 2022 as Executive Assistant III and concurrent Chief of Staff of the
Undersecretary for Special Concerns Office.
In this senior role, he led the planning of all activities of the Undersecretary's office, represented the DAR in inter-
agency meetings, reviewed project proposals, special orders, and policy memoranda, and directed the office's staff
functions.
Critically, he was appointed Team Leader of the DAR-Data Privacy Act Task Force under Special Order No. 343,
Series of 2021, mandated to bring the Department into full compliance with the Data Privacy Act of 2012 (RA
10173).
This task force work included leading Privacy Impact Assessment clustering exercises across Mindanao, Visayas,
Luzon, and the DAR Central Office, crafting the Department's control framework for personal data processing, and
representing DAR in data-sharing agreement negotiations with other government agencies.
He also served as Team Leader for the Validation of Certificate of Land Ownership Awarded/Emancipation Patent
(CLOA/CCLOA/EP), covering both privately acquired and government-owned distributed agricultural lands under
Special Order No. 610, Series of 2021.

PAGE 5
Organizational Affiliations and Civic Leadership
Gubat has been deeply embedded in civic life across multiple organizations, reflecting a consistent personal
commitment to community building alongside his professional and royal responsibilities.
Within the Fraternal Order of Eagles-Philippine Eagles, he served as Charter and Regional Governor of NCR 68,
with his region earning the "2023 Remarkable Region" award. He was also Commissioner of the National
Commission on Education for 2023 and 2024, Charter President of the Luminous Eagles Club (NCR 3, which
received "Best Club" and "Best Club President" recognitions), and Club Secretary of the Premier Eagles Club
(NCR 3, earning "Most Active Regional Member" recognition).
In Rotary International, he served as Charter President and "Hope Creating President" of the Rotary Club of
Diliman International (District 3780), which received the Club Excellence Award. He also served as "Life
Changing President" of the Rotary Club of Manila Quiapo Central (District 3810), which he led to receive "Most
Outstanding Club" and "Most Outstanding Club President" designations, alongside eight major and 34 minor
awards during his term.
He is a Board of Trustee and Founder of the Greenhills Muslim Business Club Foundation Inc., a Founding
Chairman and President of Samahan ng Maharlikang Pilipino, and serves as National Chairman on Muslim Affairs
of Community Force Multipliers for Peace Inc. (CFMPI).
He has served as Secretary General and National Executive Director for Operation of United Christian Muslim
Against Crime and Corruption Inc., as Vice President for Anti-Corruption and Criminal Investigation of the
Association of Chief of Police of the Philippines, and as Director for Muslim Affairs of Apila ng Bayan Inc.
He is a member of Xi Kappa Sigma, Mu Kappa Phi Exclusive Law Fraternity, the Saudi Council of Engineers, and
the Institute of Integrated Electrical Engineers of the Philippines (IIEE).
Legacy
Janoden Masbud Gubat's legacy sits at the intersection of technical mastery, public service, and Maranao cultural
continuity.
He belongs to a generation of Muslim Filipinos who carried their professional skills far beyond the boundaries of
Bangsamoro, building military cities in the Arabian Peninsula and infrastructure corridors in Metro Manila, while
never stepping away from the responsibilities of community and identity back home.
His work in the Department of Agrarian Reform connected his engineering precision to the cause of land justice for
Filipino farmers, and his role in the DAR-Data Privacy Act Task Force reflects an understanding that governance in
the 21st century requires technical fluency, not just administrative rank.
As Sultan a Cabugatan sa Maul and Executive Vice President of the Royal Sultanate of Lanao, he continues the
Maranao tradition of leadership as a form of accountability: to one's lineage, one's community, and one's faith.
Across his civic affiliations, from Rotary to the Fraternal Order of Eagles to interfaith organizations working
against crime and corruption, his consistent theme has been bridge-building: between communities, between
institutions, and between generations.

PAGE 6
Recognition
Gubat has received recognition in multiple civic arenas:
His region (NCR 68) received the "2023 Remarkable Region" award under the Fraternal Order of Eagles-
Philippine Eagles during his term as Regional Governor.
The Luminous Eagles Club (NCR 3), which he founded and led as Charter President, earned "Best Club" and "Best
Club President" designations.
During his presidency of the Rotary Club of Manila Quiapo Central (District 3810), the club was recognized as
"Most Outstanding Club," and Gubat was named "Most Outstanding Club President," with the club earning a total
of eight major and 34 minor awards in that period.
The Rotary Club of Diliman International (District 3780) received the Club Excellence Award during his tenure as
Charter President.
He holds honorary doctoral degrees from Piedmont College of Theology (Doctor of Humanities) and Brethren
Evangelical School of Theology International (Doctor in Philosophy in Executive Leadership, Honoris Causa),
recognizing his service, leadership, and public contributions.
Challenges
Gubat's career illustrates the resilience required of Muslim Filipino professionals navigating spaces where their
identity and credentials are not always recognized together.
Building a licensed engineering career that spans Philippine government service, international military
infrastructure, and civic leadership simultaneously is not a straightforward path. Each domain carries its own
demands, expectations, and gatekeeping, and Gubat has had to demonstrate competence and credibility across all
of them.
His work on data privacy compliance at DAR reflects the additional complexity that comes with technical roles
inside bureaucratic environments, where institutional resistance and legacy practices often slow the implementation
of needed reforms.
His simultaneous responsibilities as sultan, engineer, civic leader, and government executive also speak to the
weight carried by individuals who belong to communities that are underrepresented in national institutions, and
who feel obligated to represent those communities with distinction in every room they enter.

title: Guiling, Janalodin Talon
text:
PAGE 1
Janalodin Talon Guiling
Datu Janalodin "Johnny" Talon Guiling, PhD, CSP is a respected public servant and community leader in the
Philippines. He has built a career dedicated to Muslim rights advocacy, civic engagement, and local governance.
Contents
1 Early Career
2 Government Service
3 Organizational Leadership
4 Civic Engagement
5 Awards and Recognition
6 Academic Honors
7 Legacy
Early Career
Datu Johnny Guiling first gained recognition as Chairman of the Metropolis Muslim Traders Association Inc. from
2010 to 2014 and as President of the Muntinlupa Muslim Association Islamic Propagation Center Inc. from 2009 to
2015. His early leadership roles reflected his commitment to empowering Muslim communities through trade,
education, and religious propagation.
Government Service
In 2014, he became the Director and Department Head of the Muntinlupa City Muslim Affairs Office, the first
Muslim Affairs Office established by a local government unit in Metro Manila. He continues to serve in this role,
ensuring representation and welfare for Muslim residents in the city.
Organizational Leadership
Beyond government service, Guiling has held multiple leadership positions:
Chairman, Committee on Muslim Affairs, The Fraternal Order of Eagles – Philippine Eagles Inc. (2021–
present)
Regional Governor, EMPIRE Eagles NCR XII (2021–present)
Overall Chief Marshall and Chief Protocol Officer for National Elections, TFOE-PE Inc. (2022–present)
National Coordinator and NCR Vice President, Salam Police Advocacy Group (2025–present)
He also serves as Goodwill Ambassador of the SPMUDA International Organization for Peace and Development
Philippines.

Datu Johnny Guiling is widely recognized as a passionate
advocate for Muslim rights and welfare. His leadership has
strengthened community representation, promoted peace and
order, and advanced the role of Muslims in civic and national
development.

title: Guiling, Ramy Lawi
text:
PAGE 1

Guiling Al-Haj
Occupation
Regional State Prosecutor, Department of
Justice (ARMM/BARMM); lawyer,
educator, businessman
Education
Manuel L. Quezon University (AB
Political Science, 1973; Bachelor of Laws,
1977)
Bar Admission
Philippine Bar Examinations, 1978 (Top
20 Bar Passer; perfect score in Civil Law)
Spouse
Bae Norania Laut Al-Hadja
Parents
Sultan of Masiu Guiling O. Buntalis Al-
Haj and Sitte Nafsia Dehaliya Lawi
Guiling Al-Hadja
Heritage
Royal Sultanates of Lanao: Masiu,
Borocot, and Bansayan
Notability
One of the highest-ranking Meranaw legal
officials to serve as Regional State
Prosecutor, capping a government career
that spanned the Department of Islamic
Affairs, the Bureau of Lands, the Office of
the Ombudsman, and the Provincial
Prosecutor's Office of Maguindanao.
Known For
Ramy Lawi Guiling
Atty. Ramy "Mohammad Sedic" Lawi Guiling Al-Haj is a
Filipino jurist, educator, businessman, and member of the Royal
Sultanates of Lanao, best known for his long career as a Regional
State Prosecutor of the Department of Justice for the Autonomous
Region in Muslim Mindanao (ARMM), now the Bangsamoro
Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM). Over the
decades, he built a reputation not just as a careful and principled
prosecutor, but as a teacher, orator, and quiet pillar of the Meranaw
community.
Contents
1 Early Life and Education
2 Career in Public Service
3 Legal Practice and Advocacy
4 Academic Career
5 Personal Life
6 Royal Heritage and Recognition
7 Public Image
8 Legacy
9 See Also
10 References
Early Life and Education
Atty. Guiling comes from a lineage deeply rooted in the traditional
leadership of Lanao. He is the son of Sultan of Masiu Guiling O.
Buntalis Al-Haj and Sitte Nafsia Dehaliya Lawi Guiling Al-Hadja,
herself the daughter of Sultan of Masiu Lawi Belok Osangan. He is
also a grandson of Sultan Mamatod of Gapa, Balindong, placing him
firmly within a family whose name carries weight across several
Meranaw sultanates.
He pursued his college education at Manuel L. Quezon University
(MLQU), where he completed his Bachelor of Arts in Political
Science in 1973, finishing the program in just seven semesters
instead of the usual eight, a small detail that already hinted at the
discipline he would carry into the rest of his career. He stayed on at
the same university for law school, earning his Bachelor of Laws in
1977.
The following year, in 1978, he took and passed the Philippine Bar
Examinations, landing among the Top 20 Bar Passers nationwide. He
also posted a perfect score of 100% in Civil Law, a rare feat that said

PAGE 2
Fondly called "The Singing Prosecutor"
for his artistic gifts, and widely admired as
an orator, declaimer, and debater whose
eloquence left a lasting mark on
Bangsamoro legal and civic circles.
Pull Quote
"True greatness is measured not merely by
titles, honors, or professional
accomplishments, but by a steadfast
commitment to serving humanity with
honesty, compassion, courage, and
righteousness."
as much about his grasp of legal principle as it did about the hours he
must have poured into mastering it.
Career in Public Service
Atty. Guiling's government service began in 1978 with the
Department of Islamic Affairs under the Department of Foreign
Affairs (DFA), a fitting starting point given his background and faith.
From there, his career moved steadily through a series of demanding
posts: District Land Officer of the Bureau of Lands in Iligan City,
City Prosecutor of Marawi, Deputy Ombudsman for Mindanao, and
Provincial Prosecutor of Maguindanao.
He eventually rose to become Regional State Prosecutor of the Department of Justice for the ARMM (now
BARMM), a position he held until his compulsory retirement, closing out a government career that spanned several
decades and touched nearly every layer of the justice system in the region.
Legal Practice and Advocacy
Outside of government, Atty. Guiling also built a respected private legal practice. Among the cases that stand out in
his career was his work representing victims and their families in litigation connected to the SuperFerry tragedy,
many of whom were Maranao passengers. It was work that called for more than legal skill: it demanded patience
and compassion for families still grappling with loss, and Atty. Guiling took on that responsibility with evident
seriousness.
Academic Career
Convinced that legal knowledge should never stay locked away in the courtroom, Atty. Guiling also spent years
teaching. He served as a professor at St. Michael's College, at Jamiatu Philippine Al-Islamia (JPI) in Marawi City,
and at the Mindanao State University College of Law. Generations of law students passed through his classes,
many of them carrying forward the same values he emphasized: competence, integrity, ethical leadership, and
respect for the rule of law.
Personal Life
Atty. Guiling is married to Bae Norania Laut Al-Hadja, daughter of Sheik Ismael Laut, the Sultan of Rogan and a
former Senior Board Member of Lanao del Sur from Poon A Bayabao. Together they raised a family grounded in
faith, honor, and service to their community.
Away from the courtroom and the classroom, Atty. Guiling is also a successful businessman with a taste for golf,
tennis, and precision shooting, pursuits that reflect the same discipline and focus he brought to his legal career.

PAGE 3
Royal Heritage and Recognition
As a member of the Royal Sultanates of Lanao, Atty. Guiling carries a heritage tied to Masiu and, through his
family line, to Gapa, Balindong. In recognition of his leadership, integrity, and years of distinguished service, he
has been honored by three Royal Sultanates of Lanao: Masiu, Borocot, and Bansayan, a distinction that reflects the
esteem in which he is held by both traditional and modern institutions in the region.
Public Image
Beyond his legal and academic credentials, Atty. Guiling is known across Lanao for his charisma and artistic talent,
earning him the affectionate nickname "The Singing Prosecutor." He has also long been admired as a skilled orator,
declaimer, and debater, qualities that made him a memorable and commanding presence at gatherings throughout
his career.
Legacy
Atty. Ramy "Mohammad Sedic" Lawi Guiling Al-Haj's career reflects a rare combination: a jurist's precision, a
teacher's patience, and a performer's warmth. From his early academic distinctions to his decades in public service
and legal practice, his story continues to serve as an example for lawyers, prosecutors, judges, and educators across
the Bangsamoro region, a reminder that a life of service can be measured in integrity as much as in title.

title: Guinomla, Bahnarim A.
text:
PAGE 1
Ambassador Bahnarim A.
Guinomla
Personal Information
Born: Dulawan (now Datu Piang),
Maguindanao del Sur, Philippines
Ethnicity
Maguindanaon (Bangsamoro)
Profession
Career Diplomat, Philippine Foreign
Service
Appointing Authority
President Gloria Macapagal-Arroyo
(Saudi Arabia posting, 2002)
Diplomatic Posts
Consul General, Jeddah, Saudi Arabia
(1994–1998)
Bahnarim A. Guinomla
Bahnarim A. Guinomla (born in Dulawan, Datu Piang, Maguindanao del Sur) was a career diplomat of the
Republic of the Philippines and one of the most accomplished Moro foreign service officers in the history of the
Philippine Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA). He is widely recognized as the first Maguindanaon career
diplomat to attain the rank of Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary, a milestone that opened new
ground for Bangsamoro representation on the world stage. Over a career that spanned decades and crossed
continents, Guinomla served in high-profile postings across the Middle East, the Caucasus, and South Asia, earning
a reputation as a dedicated public servant with a genuine commitment to the welfare of overseas Filipino workers
(OFWs) and the dignity of the Bangsamoro people.
Contents
1 BACKGROUND AND HERITAGE
2 EARLY CAREER AND RISE IN THE FOREIGN SERVICE
3 CONSULAR SERVICE IN JEDDAH
4 AMBASSADORIAL POSTING: KINGDOM OF SAUDI
ARABIA
5 AMBASSADORIAL POSTING: REPUBLIC OF TURKEY
6 AMBASSADORIAL POSTING: PEOPLE'S REPUBLIC OF
BANGLADESH
7 ACHIEVEMENTS AND INSTITUTIONAL
CONTRIBUTIONS
8 PERSONAL VALUES AND CHARACTER
9 LEGACY AND SIGNIFICANCE
10 NOTES
11 SEE ALSO
BACKGROUND AND HERITAGE
Guinomla was born in Dulawan, a historic settlement that is now
part of the municipality of Datu Piang in Maguindanao del Sur. The
town carries deep historical weight: it sits in the heartland of the old
Sultanate of Buayan, one of the major Maguindanaon political
centers that shaped the identity of Muslim Mindanao for centuries.
Growing up in that environment gave Guinomla an early and
grounded sense of who he was and where he came from.
His lineage was connected to the traditional leadership and noble
heritage of the historic realms of Buayan, lending him a cultural
authority and a bridge-building instinct that would later define his
diplomatic style. He was not someone who needed to manufacture
gravitas; it came naturally from his roots.
That background also gave him something rarer: a quiet confidence
that he belonged in rooms where decisions were made, even when
Bangsamoro representation at those levels was far from common.

PAGE 2
Ambassador to Saudi Arabia (2002–
2006)
Ambassador to Turkey, with concurrent
accreditation to Georgia and Azerbaijan
Ambassador to Bangladesh, with
concurrent accreditation to Maldives
and Sri Lanka
Award
Gawad Mabini (DFA Distinguished
Service Award)
Notability
First Maguindanaon career diplomat to
reach the rank of Ambassador
Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary;
pioneering figure in Bangsamoro
representation in the Philippine Foreign
Service
Known For
OFW welfare advocacy; strengthening
Philippines-Saudi Arabia, Philippines-
Turkey, and Philippines-Bangladesh
relations; bridging the Bangsamoro
region with national and international
diplomacy
His rise through the DFA would eventually prove that point in the
most concrete way possible.
EARLY CAREER AND RISE IN THE
FOREIGN SERVICE
Guinomla entered the Department of Foreign Affairs as a career
diplomat, meaning he earned his positions through the professional
ranks rather than through political appointment. This distinction
matters. Career diplomats build their expertise over years of
ground-level consular and administrative work, and Guinomla's
trajectory reflected exactly that kind of steady, unglamorous
dedication.
One of his notable early roles was as Head of the DFA Office for
Mindanao. This was a position that put him at the intersection of
regional concerns and national foreign policy, a space where he
could actively work to make foreign affairs services more accessible
to Mindanaoans and help integrate the region's particular needs into
broader diplomatic considerations. It was, in many ways, a fitting
entry point for someone with his background.
He was also involved with the Philippine Political Science
Association in Mindanao during this period, which points to an
intellectual engagement with questions of political integration and governance that went beyond his administrative
brief. He was not just processing documents; he was thinking seriously about the country and the region's place
within it.
CONSULAR SERVICE IN JEDDAH
From 1994 to 1998 (with some accounts placing the tenure's later years closer to 1997), Guinomla served as
Philippine Consul General in Jeddah, Saudi Arabia. This was a posting that put him face-to-face with some of the
most pressing realities of Filipino migration: workers in distress, legal cases requiring intervention, documentation
backlogs, and the everyday challenges facing hundreds of thousands of Filipinos living and working far from
home.
Consular work in a labor-intensive post like Jeddah is rarely glamorous. It involves long hours, difficult cases, and
the kind of patient negotiation that never makes headlines. Guinomla's years there gave him firsthand knowledge of
the Saudi system, its institutions, and the dynamics of the Filipino community, knowledge that would prove
directly useful when he later returned to the Kingdom in a much higher capacity.
His Jeddah experience was more than just a resume line. It was the foundation for much of what he became as a
diplomat.

PAGE 3
AMBASSADORIAL POSTING: KINGDOM OF SAUDI ARABIA
In 2002, President Gloria Macapagal-Arroyo appointed Guinomla as Ambassador Extraordinary and
Plenipotentiary to the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia. This was, by any measure, one of the most consequential bilateral
postings in Philippine diplomacy. At the time, hundreds of thousands of Filipinos were living and working in the
Kingdom, making Saudi Arabia one of the top destinations for OFW deployment and one of the largest sources of
remittances to the Philippines.
Guinomla hit the ground running. His prior Jeddah experience meant he did not need an orientation period; he
already understood the terrain. He focused his tenure on three interconnected priorities: protecting the welfare of
Filipino workers, deepening bilateral relations between Manila and Riyadh, and supporting the broader Filipino
community in the Kingdom.
Worker protection, in particular, was a constant concern. He played an active role in the repatriation of distressed
workers, working through the bureaucratic and sometimes diplomatic complexities that such cases inevitably
involved. His accessible personal style helped; he was known as someone workers and community members could
actually approach, not a remote figure behind thick embassy walls.
The posting was not without its difficulties. Security concerns sometimes constrained embassy activities and
required careful management. Guinomla navigated these challenges with the kind of measured professionalism that
his career had prepared him for. He served in Riyadh until 2006, leaving behind a record of steady, people-centered
service.
AMBASSADORIAL POSTING: REPUBLIC OF TURKEY
After Riyadh, Guinomla moved on to Turkey, where he served as Philippine Ambassador with concurrent
accreditation to Georgia and Azerbaijan. This was a geographically and strategically different assignment: Turkey
sits at the crossroads of Europe and Asia, and the South Caucasus region, including Georgia and Azerbaijan, was
undergoing significant political and economic transformation in the mid-2000s.
He presented his credentials in Azerbaijan in 2007, formally establishing the diplomatic relationship at the
ambassadorial level for that concurrent posting. His work in Turkey and the Caucasus involved promoting
diplomatic, economic, and cultural ties in a region where the Philippines had real interests but relatively limited
institutional presence. It was the kind of assignment that rewarded intellectual curiosity and adaptability, qualities
Guinomla had demonstrated throughout his career.
AMBASSADORIAL POSTING: PEOPLE'S REPUBLIC OF
BANGLADESH
Guinomla's final major ambassadorial assignment took him to Dhaka, where he served as Philippine Ambassador
to Bangladesh from approximately 2010 to 2013. His concurrent accreditations extended to the Maldives and Sri
Lanka, giving him responsibility for Philippine interests across a significant stretch of South Asia.
In Bangladesh, he engaged actively with local institutions. A visit to the American International University-
Bangladesh was among his documented activities, reflecting his interest in educational and professional
connections between the two countries. He also explored opportunities such as the potential hiring of Filipino
nurses by Bangladeshi hospitals, a practical form of people-to-people diplomacy that reflected his consistent focus
on creating tangible benefits from his postings.

PAGE 4
He made farewell calls on leaders in the Maldives in 2013 before completing his assignment, a customary
diplomatic courtesy that also marked the close of a long and distinguished career in active service.
ACHIEVEMENTS AND INSTITUTIONAL CONTRIBUTIONS
Guinomla received the Gawad Mabini, the Department of Foreign Affairs' high distinction for exemplary service
by a Filipino diplomat. The award recognized the cumulative weight of his contributions across multiple postings
and decades of professional life.
Beyond the formal recognition, his career built something harder to quantify: a demonstration that Bangsamoro
professionals could and did serve at the highest levels of Philippine diplomacy. Every posting he held, every
credential he presented, every negotiation he conducted added to a body of evidence that the Moro peoples of
Mindanao were not peripheral to the Philippine national story but central to it.
His work advancing OFW welfare, strengthening bilateral trade and cultural relations, and representing Philippine
interests in Muslim-majority countries also carried a particular resonance for the Bangsamoro community. He
understood the cultural and religious contexts of postings like Saudi Arabia and Turkey in ways that a diplomat
without his background might not, and that understanding made him more effective.
PERSONAL VALUES AND CHARACTER
Those who worked with and knew Guinomla consistently described him in terms that pointed to the same core
qualities: dedication, professionalism, compassion, and a genuine commitment to public service. These are words
that appear on many eulogies and tributes, but in his case, they are grounded in a traceable record of actual conduct
over decades.
He was known as approachable, someone who took the time to meet with community members and workers, not
just officials and counterparts. That quality is not universal among senior diplomats, and its presence in Guinomla's
career says something real about his priorities.
His pride in his Maguindanaon roots never wavered across decades of international postings. He remained, by all
accounts, deeply connected to his identity and his homeland even as he represented the Philippine state in some of
the world's most consequential capitals.
LEGACY AND SIGNIFICANCE
The tribute messages and condolences that followed Guinomla's passing came from embassies, community
organizations, and colleagues across the world he had spent a career building relationships in. That response was
not simply protocol; it reflected the genuine respect he had earned through decades of quiet, competent service.
His legacy operates on multiple levels. For the Bangsamoro community, he is a proof of concept: that one of their
own could rise through the most competitive and demanding professional ranks in Philippine public service and
succeed with distinction. For younger Filipinos from Mindanao who dream of careers in foreign service, his story
is a direct and unambiguous precedent.
For Philippine diplomacy more broadly, his career illustrated something worth remembering: that cultural
groundedness is not a liability in the foreign service. Guinomla's deep roots in Maguindanaon identity and his
understanding of Muslim societies made him a more effective diplomat in the regions he served, not a less
professional one.

PAGE 5
He leaves behind a legacy that bridges regions, cultures, and communities, and that, in the end, is what the best
diplomats do.
NOTES
Specific details of Guinomla's early formal education have not been fully documented in publicly available
sources. Editorial note: BangsamoroPedia welcomes contributions from family members and researchers
with verified information on this aspect of his biography.
Some sources record his Jeddah consul general tenure as 1994–1998; others indicate the later years of
service extended to approximately 1997. Both are noted here for accuracy.
Details of his work with the Philippine Political Science Association in Mindanao require further
documentation. This item is retained as a credible reference pending fuller sourcing.

Mary Joyce Guinto-Sali
Mary Joyce Z. Guinto-Sali is a Filipino academic administrator,
scholar, and peace advocate who serves as the Chancellor of the
Mindanao State University-Tawi-Tawi College of Technology and
Oceanography (MSU-TCTO), the institution widely known as TCTO.
Appointed in late 2020, she made history as the first woman to lead the
university, shattering a long-standing gender barrier in one of the most
remote and culturally distinct corners of the Philippines. A proud
product of the very community she now leads, Chancellor Guinto-Sali
embodies what scholars of island Mindanao have come to call
"homegrown success," the idea that transformational leadership doesn't
have to come from outside but can grow naturally from the land, the sea,
and the people of the Sulu Archipelago.<ref
name="narrative">Chancellor Mary Joyce Z. Guinto-Sali: Narrative
Research. Prepared for BangsamoroPedia. Retrieved 2025.</ref>
Her leadership philosophy is anchored in a Culture of Peace, a
framework she didn't simply inherit from a textbook but shaped through
lived experience in a region that has known both conflict and resilience.
Under her watch, MSU-TCTO has moved toward what she calls
"SMART" governance, modernizing infrastructure, strengthening
academic programs, and repositioning the institution as a serious player
in marine research and the Blue Economy of the southern seas.

Early Life
Mary Joyce Z. Guinto-Sali was born and raised in Tawi-Tawi, the southernmost province of the Philippine
archipelago, a stretch of islands and straits shaped as much by ocean currents as by centuries of Malay, Islamic, and
indigenous cultural exchange.<ref name="narrative" />
Growing up in Tawi-Tawi wasn't just a geographic fact for her; it was a formative education in itself. The region's
"peripheral" reality, where distance from Manila often translated into distance from national attention and
resources, sharpened her understanding of what it means to be left behind by systems designed for someone else.
<ref name="narrative" /> That awareness never left her. It would later define every institutional decision she made
as chancellor.
Her early years were spent in a community where the sea was not a backdrop but a livelihood, and where education
was seen not as a luxury but as a lifeline. The people of Tawi-Tawi, drawn from the Sama, Tausug, and other
indigenous groups of the Sulu Sea, taught her something no graduate program could: that development means
nothing if it doesn't begin with dignity.<ref name="narrative" />
Family
Chancellor Guinto-Sali has maintained a quiet privacy around her immediate family life, a choice that reflects both
personal preference and a deliberate commitment to letting her work speak for itself.<ref name="narrative" />
What the record does show is that she grew up within a community that treated the Mindanao State University not
merely as an institution but as part of the social fabric of the region. Her background is rooted in a local
professional culture where academic achievement and public service were understood as inseparable, and that
orientation became the quiet but steady current running through her entire career.<ref name="narrative" />
She has spoken about her sense of identity as a "daughter of the MSU system," a phrase that signals not just
institutional loyalty but a genuine feeling of belonging to something larger than herself.<ref name="narrative" />
That relationship with MSU, stretching back long before she ever held any title, remains one of the most consistent
threads in her story.
Education
If there is one decision in Chancellor Guinto-Sali's life that explains everything that followed, it's the academic
path she chose. At a time when many scholars from the region pursued degrees in engineering, business, or the
hard sciences, she turned toward something far less conventional and far more urgent: she earned a Ph.D. in Peace
and Development.<ref name="narrative" />
The choice was neither accidental nor idealistic. It was strategic. A doctoral focus in peace and development gave
her the theoretical tools to read Tawi-Tawi's history not as a story of backwardness or perpetual conflict, but as a
complex human situation shaped by colonial legacies, resource inequality, and the unfinished business of
reconciliation.<ref name="narrative" />

PAGE 3
She completed her higher education entirely within the MSU system, which meant she never had to leave the
region to become the kind of scholar it needed.<ref name="narrative" /> That decision, staying close to home
rather than seeking prestige elsewhere, became something of a signature move for her: investing in place, not just
in personal advancement.
Career
Faculty and Early Academic Life
Chancellor Guinto-Sali began her professional life as a faculty member at MSU-TCTO, doing the quiet, essential
work of classroom teaching in a university that sits at the edge of the country's administrative map.<ref
name="narrative" />
Her trajectory from that starting point to the chancellor's office wasn't fast or flashy. It was built on consistency:
showing up, delivering, and earning the trust of colleagues and students through the long, ordinary work of
academic life.<ref name="narrative" /> That kind of institutional credibility is harder to manufacture than a title,
and it became one of her most durable assets.
Dean of the College of Arts and Sciences
Her most significant pre-chancellorship role was as the Dean of the College of Arts and Sciences (CAS) at MSU-
TCTO.<ref name="narrative" />
In that position, she took on a task that might look simple on paper but was genuinely complicated in practice:
integrating a strong liberal arts curriculum into a university whose identity was built around technical programs in
fisheries, oceanography, and maritime studies.<ref name="narrative" /> The humanities and the hard sciences don't
always make comfortable neighbors, but she understood that the kind of graduates Tawi-Tawi needed, graduates
who could navigate both a fishing boat and a bureaucracy, required both.
Her deanship was, in this sense, a dress rehearsal for the balancing act she'd later perform as chancellor: holding
technical excellence and cultural rootedness in the same hand.
Appointment as Chancellor
In late 2020, Chancellor Guinto-Sali was appointed the Chancellor of MSU-TCTO, becoming the first woman in
the university's history to hold that office.<ref name="narrative" />
The appointment came at a difficult moment. The country was in the grip of the global pandemic, higher education
was navigating an abrupt shift to remote and hybrid learning, and MSU-TCTO, like most regional universities, was
doing so with less resources and less attention than its urban counterparts. That she took the helm precisely then,
and moved forward with a vision rather than retreating into maintenance mode, says something important about her
character.<ref name="narrative" />
Her appointment wasn't just a personal milestone. For the women of Tawi-Tawi and the broader BARMM region, it
was a signal: that leadership in a traditionally male-dominated institution was no longer a closed door.<ref
name="narrative" />

PAGE 4
Contributions and Achievements
SMART Governance
One of Chancellor Guinto-Sali's most deliberate moves as administrator has been the push toward what she frames
as "SMART" governance at MSU-TCTO.<ref name="narrative" /> This approach isn't just a catchy label; it
reflects a genuine commitment to systematic, measurable, and accountable institutional management in a setting
where informal and personality-driven leadership had long been the default.
SMART governance, in her practice, means making decisions based on data and strategic planning, holding the
university to external quality standards, and building systems that will outlast any individual leader's tenure. That
last point matters. She's not building MSU-TCTO around herself; she's building it to continue without her.<ref
name="narrative" />
Blue Economy and Marine Research
Under her leadership, MSU-TCTO has leaned into one of its most natural and underutilized strengths: the ocean.
<ref name="narrative" />
The university sits in one of the most biologically diverse marine environments on the planet, the Coral Triangle,
and Chancellor Guinto-Sali has made it a priority to position TCTO as a serious institutional player in marine
research and sustainable aquaculture. She has championed what development economists call the Blue Economy,
the idea that coastal and island communities can build lasting prosperity by managing marine resources wisely
rather than extracting them recklessly.<ref name="narrative" />
For Tawi-Tawi, whose communities have depended on the sea for centuries, this isn't an abstract development
theory. It's a recognition that the region's future and its past are pointing in the same direction.
Infrastructure and Campus Modernization
She oversaw significant improvements to the physical infrastructure of the Sanga-Sanga campus, including the
renovation of academic laboratories and the upgrading of facilities that had long been underfunded.<ref
name="narrative" />
In a region where university infrastructure is often an afterthought in national budget discussions, these
improvements carried a clear message: that MSU-TCTO's students deserved the same learning environment as
students anywhere else in the country. Chancellor Guinto-Sali has been consistent in treating physical infrastructure
not as a perk but as a prerequisite for quality education.<ref name="narrative" />
Academic Accreditation
One of her most consequential institutional pushes has been the drive for AACCUP (Accrediting Agency of
Chartered Colleges and Universities in the Philippines) accreditation across multiple programs at MSU-TCTO.<ref
name="narrative" />
Accreditation is the unglamorous, paperwork-heavy work of proving to external evaluators that your programs
meet national quality benchmarks. It matters enormously for students: accredited programs carry more weight in
the job market and in graduate school applications. It also matters for the institution's credibility and its ability to

PAGE 5
attract funding and partnerships. Chancellor Guinto-Sali has pushed this process forward not because it's easy, but
because she understands that quality is the only argument a regional university can make against the gravitational
pull of larger, better-resourced institutions.<ref name="narrative" />
Values and Philosophy
At the center of Chancellor Guinto-Sali's leadership is a concept she returns to again and again: the Culture of
Peace.<ref name="narrative" />
For someone who earned a doctorate in peace and development, this could easily have remained a theoretical
commitment. Instead, she has woven it into the day-to-day reality of running a university. That means designing
programs that foreground the history and traditions of the Sama, Tausug, and other indigenous communities of the
Sulu Archipelago, not as cultural add-ons but as core to the institution's identity.<ref name="narrative" />
Her leadership style has been described as "Empathetic Governance," a phrase that might sound soft but is, in
practice, politically demanding.<ref name="narrative" /> It means actively listening to constituencies that are often
overlooked, students from remote barangays, faculty from non-dominant cultural backgrounds, communities at the
margins of the margins. It means treating equity not as an aspiration but as an operational principle.
She views education as a tool for social justice, which is to say she doesn't see teaching and research as ends in
themselves but as instruments for changing the material conditions of people's lives.<ref name="narrative" /> In
Tawi-Tawi, that's not a rhetorical position. It's a daily practice.
Cultural Significance
In the Bangsamoro, where the relationship between women and public leadership has often been complicated by
both cultural tradition and institutional history, Chancellor Guinto-Sali's position carries a weight that goes beyond
administration.<ref name="narrative" />
She is, as scholars of the region have noted, a symbol of "homegrown success," the proof that the Sulu Archipelago
doesn't need to import its leaders or export its talent to Manila in order to govern itself well.<ref name="narrative"
/> Her career was built here, her education was earned here, and her commitment has remained here. That
continuity of place is, in itself, a form of advocacy.
For young women in Tawi-Tawi and across the BARMM, her chancellorship is a data point against every
institutional message that told them their ambitions should be smaller or their voices quieter.<ref name="narrative"
/> She hasn't had to say that explicitly. Her presence in the office says it for her.
She also serves as a cultural bridge, holding together the university's aspiration for international academic
standards with a genuine respect for local heritage.<ref name="narrative" /> That balance, between the global and
the rooted, is one of the most difficult things any regional institution has to manage, and it's one she's navigated
with unusual skill.
Recognition
Chancellor Guinto-Sali's most historically significant recognition is her appointment itself: becoming the first
female Chancellor of MSU-TCTO in the university's history stands as a landmark milestone in Bangsamoro
academic leadership.<ref name="narrative" />

PAGE 6
Within the MSU system, her work has been recognized as a model for how a geographically peripheral campus can
achieve institutional transformation without losing its cultural grounding. Her leadership during the pandemic-era
disruptions, maintaining forward momentum on accreditation, infrastructure, and research positioning while
managing the immediate operational pressures of the health crisis, has drawn attention from education
administrators across the region.<ref name="narrative" />
Manuel T. Corpus Outstanding Quality Champion Award (2026)
In 2026, Chancellor Guinto-Sali received one of the most prestigious honors in Philippine higher education quality
assurance: the Manuel T. Corpus Outstanding Quality Champion Award, conferred during the 39th Annual
National Conference and General Assembly of the AACCUP.<ref name="corpus2026">MSU-TCTO Facebook
Page. Official statement of Chancellor Mary Joyce Z. Guinto-Sali on the Manuel T. Corpus Outstanding Quality
Champion Award. Posted 2026.</ref>
The Manuel T. Corpus Award is named in honor of one of the founding figures of the Philippine higher education
accreditation movement, and it recognizes institutional leaders who have demonstrated exceptional commitment to
academic quality, institutional integrity, and the relentless pursuit of excellence in their campuses. Receiving it is a
recognition not just of individual merit but of what an entire institution has achieved under a leader's direction.
Chancellor Guinto-Sali dedicated the award to her faculty and staff, whom she has called "Team Dolphins," in a
public statement that captured both her characteristic warmth and the collective spirit she has worked to build at
MSU-TCTO.<ref name="corpus2026" />
I am honored and deeply grateful to receive the Manuel T. Corpus Outstanding Quality Champion
Award during the 39th Annual National Conference and General Assembly 2026. I dedicate this
recognition to Team Dolphins. Your unwavering support, teamwork, and shared passion made this
achievement possible. This is as much yours as it is mine.
She also extended congratulations to fellow awardee Chancellor Alizedney M. Ditucalan of MSU-Iligan Institute of
Technology (MSU-IIT), describing the shared recognition as an honor.<ref name="corpus2026" />
The award affirms what the accreditation record at MSU-TCTO has been building toward under her tenure: that a
university at the geographic edge of the country, with all the structural disadvantages that entails, can meet and
exceed the standards by which Philippine higher education measures itself.
Challenges
No honest account of leading MSU-TCTO omits the structural difficulties that Chancellor Guinto-Sali has had to
navigate.<ref name="narrative" />
Tawi-Tawi's geographic isolation is not merely a scenic fact. It translates directly into logistical costs, delayed
deliveries, infrastructure gaps, and the constant challenge of recruiting and retaining faculty in a location far from
most professional networks. National budget processes are rarely designed with the archipelagic university in
mind, and arguing for the needs of MSU-TCTO within a centralized allocation system requires persistent political
and bureaucratic labor.<ref name="narrative" />
The region's history of armed conflict and political instability has also shaped the environment in which the
university operates. Building a Culture of Peace is not an abstract exercise in Tawi-Tawi; it's a response to lived
social realities that affect students, faculty, and the communities the university serves.<ref name="narrative" />

PAGE 7
Against these headwinds, Chancellor Guinto-Sali's record of institutional progress is not just administratively
notable. It reflects a quality of leadership that holds its course under conditions that would cause many
administrators to retreat into caution.<ref name="narrative" />

City: BARMM-MBHTE.

title: Gundarangin, Ibra
text:
PAGE 1
Ibra Gundarangin
Sultan Ibra Gundarangin was one of Lanao's most distinguished traditional and political leaders during the
American colonial era.
He served as Congressman of Mindanao and Jolo from 1931 to 1934, making him one of the earliest Maranao
figures to hold formal legislative office under the American-administered Philippine government.
Beyond his political role, Sultan Ibra Gundarangin carried an even weightier title: he was traditionally recognized
as the first Sultan sa Ranao — or Sultan of Undivided Lanao — a designation that placed him at the symbolic
center of Maranao political and cultural unity.
Contents
1 BACKGROUND
2 TRADITIONAL TITLE: SULTAN SA RANAO
3 CONGRESSIONAL SERVICE (1931–1934)
4 BRIDGING TWO WORLDS
5 LEGACY
6 SEE ALSO

BACKGROUND
Sultan Ibra Gundarangin hailed from Lanao, the ancestral homeland of the Maranao people in what is now the
Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM).
The Maranaos had long been governed through a sophisticated system of royal houses and principalities rooted in
Islamic law and adat (customary law).
This system was organized under the historic Confederation of the Sultanates of Lanao, a decentralized alliance
of royal courts and principalities collectively known as the Pat a Phangampong a Ranao — the Four
Principalities of Lanao.
Each principality held its own royal lineage and governance structure, and leadership among them was never
simply inherited: it was recognized, negotiated, and affirmed through complex traditions that had been practiced
for centuries before colonial rule arrived.
TRADITIONAL TITLE: SULTAN SA RANAO
The title Sultan sa Ranao — Sultan of Undivided Lanao — was not merely ceremonial.
It represented a rare form of cross-principality recognition: an acknowledgment by the royal houses and
communities of Lanao that one leader could stand as a unifying symbol across all four principalities.
Sultan Ibra Gundarangin's recognition as the first to hold this title signals the enormous respect he commanded
among the Maranao datus and sultans of his time.

PAGE 2
Sultan Ibra Gundarangin

Notability
The title itself reflects the deep political philosophy of the
Maranao: that unity across the Pat a Phangampong was not a
given — it was something earned and conferred through
demonstrated leadership, lineage, and character.
CONGRESSIONAL SERVICE (1931–
1934)
Sultan Ibra Gundarangin's entry into the Philippine legislature
placed him in a politically complex position.
The Philippine Legislature under the American administration was
both a colonial institution and, increasingly, a platform through
which Filipino leaders — including those from Mindanao —
could advocate for their communities.
His role as Congressman for Mindanao and Jolo (the legislative
district covering the Muslim-majority south) meant he spoke not
just for Lanao, but for a broad constituency of Muslim Filipinos at
a time when the political future of Mindanao was still very much
an open question.
He represented Lanao during a period when American colonial
policy toward the Moro peoples was shifting — transitioning from
the earlier era of military administration toward civilian
governance and, eventually, greater integration with the broader
Philippine Commonwealth framework.
BRIDGING TWO WORLDS
What makes Sultan Ibra Gundarangin's story particularly
significant is what it represents: the meeting point of the old and
the new.
He was, at once, a product of the Maranao royal tradition — with
a title that connected him to centuries of Islamic sultanate
governance — and a participant in the emerging modern political
system that the Americans were building across the archipelago.
That dual identity wasn't a contradiction. For many Maranao
leaders of his generation, engaging with colonial institutions was a
strategic choice — a way to ensure that the voice of Lanao wasn't
left out of conversations shaping the Philippines' political future.
Sultan Ibra Gundarangin embodied that pragmatic, forward-
looking leadership: grounded in tradition, but willing to engage
the wider world on behalf of his people.

PAGE 3

LEGACY
Sultan Ibra Gundarangin's legacy rests on two pillars.
The first is his pioneering role in Maranao political representation
— his congressional service opened a path that later generations
of Maranao and Bangsamoro leaders would continue to walk.
The second is his enduring place in Maranao traditional history as
the first Sultan sa Ranao, a title that continues to carry cultural
and symbolic weight in Lanao's royal discourse.
Together, these roles place him among the foundational figures in
the political and cultural history of the Maranao people and the
broader Bangsamoro nation.

title: Gutoc, Alexis Ali A.
text:
PAGE 1
Alexis Ali A. Gutoc
Dr. Alexis Ali A. Gutoc (also referred to as Alexis A. Gutoc or Alexis Gutoc), MD, FPOA, FPCS, FAPOA, is a
Muslim Filipino board-certified orthopedic and trauma surgeon based primarily in Marawi City (Lanao del Sur)
and Iligan City (Lanao del Norte), with practice extending to Cagayan de Oro in Northern Mindanao. He
specializes in orthopedic surgery and traumatology, arthroscopic surgery, reconstructive shoulder and elbow
surgery, musculoskeletal diagnostic and interventional ultrasound, musculoskeletal regenerative medicine, and
perineural injection therapy.
He serves as Chairperson (or Head) of the Orthopedic Department at Amai Pakpak Medical Center (APMC)
in Marawi City, a Department of Health facility, and holds affiliations with several other hospitals in the region. He
is a Diplomate of the Philippine Board of Orthopaedics and a Fellow of the Philippine Orthopaedic
Association, Philippine College of Surgeons, Philippine Shoulder Society, and Philippine Orthopaedic Wound Care
and Diabetic Limb Society.
