title: Laidan, Zenaida P. Hadji Raof
text:
PAGE 1
Zenaida P. Hadji Raof Laidan
Dr. Hadja Sittie Shayma Zenaida P. Hadji Raof Laidan is a pioneering Maranao academician, science and
technology advocate, and the first woman Regional Director of the Department of Science and Technology
Regional Office XII (DOST XII) in the Philippines. Best known for championing Halal science development and
establishing critical technology infrastructure across Mindanao, she's a bridge-builder who's connected
government, academe, and private sector stakeholders to drive inclusive regional development. Her career has been
defined by rigorous science, cultural rootedness, and a genuine passion for lifting up underserved communities,
particularly in the Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (ARMM) and Soccsksargen region.
Contents
1 Early Life and Family Background
2 Education and Academic Preparation
3 Academic Career at Mindanao State University
4 Government Service: DOST XII Regional Director
4.1 Core Programs and Initiatives
4.2 Institutional Leadership Roles
5 Halal Science: A Global Leadership Agenda
6 International Engagement and Speaking
7 Recognition and Royal Honors
8 Publications and Research
9 Dimensions of Her Impact
10 Further Reading
11 See Also
Early Life and Family Background
Dr. Laidan hails from a distinguished Bangsamoro royal family. She's the daughter of Rajah Pangadapun
Sumandar, Rajah Pangadapun sa Ganasi, heir to the thrones of Sultan sa Tugaya and Sultan sa Ramain, and a
former mayor of Tugaya in Lanao del Sur. Her mother was Hadja Sittie Aishah Hadji Raof Sumandar, Baiya-
Diamla (Muslim female regent) sa Tugaya. This noble lineage gave her both heritage and responsibility, though it
was her own intellectual drive that ultimately shaped her remarkable journey.
The combination of royal lineage and her Maranao identity became central to her worldview. Growing up, she
witnessed firsthand the challenges facing her community and the critical need for modern science and technology
to address them. She carries the weight of that responsibility with dignity.
Education and Academic Preparation
Dr. Laidan's educational path was marked by excellence and determination. She earned her Bachelor of Science in
Inland Fisheries from Mindanao State University (MSU) in Marawi City, her hometown. Her academic talent
earned her a prestigious National Science Development Board (NSDB, now DOST) scholarship, which supported
her graduate studies.

PAGE 2
In 1982, she completed her Master of Arts degree in Teaching General Science at her alma mater, MSU. Twelve
years later, in 1994, she earned her Doctor of Philosophy degree in Science Education with a major in Biology
from De la Salle University in Manila. Dr. Laidan was also conferred an Honorary Doctor of Philosophy degree in
Institutional Development and Management from Sultan Kudarat State University and Akamai University in
Hawaii in 2008, recognizing her professional contributions and leadership.
Academic Career at Mindanao State University
Before her government appointment, Dr. Laidan spent twenty-two years as an Associate Professor (Level V) at the
Mindanao State University-University Training Center (MSU-UTC), where she taught Chemistry, Biology, and
General Science courses. Her colleagues knew her affectionately as "Zeny," and she earned a reputation as both a
rigorous educator and someone genuinely invested in student development.
Beyond classroom instruction, Dr. Laidan took on leadership roles in professional organizations. She served as
President of the Muslim Development Exponents Foundation of the Philippines, Inc., and as Board Director of the
Muslim Educators League of the Philippines, Inc., both based in Marawi City. Through these roles, she pursued her
passion for expanding educational access to Maranao women and underserved communities. In 1996, she founded
the Science Learning Center in Marawi City to help preschoolers develop their full learning potential, reflecting her
belief that education must start early and reach everyone.
Government Service: DOST XII Regional Director
In 1991, Dr. Laidan was appointed Action Officer on Science and Technology in the Autonomous Region in
Muslim Mindanao (ARMM), giving her her first opportunity to influence policy at scale.
Her appointment as Regional Director of DOST XII in 1999 marked a watershed moment not only for her career
but for the region. She became the first woman to hold this position in the department's history. Since assuming
office, she's distinguished herself through unwavering personal integrity and exemplary public service. As Regional
Director, Dr. Laidan oversees the implementation of national science and technology agendas across Region XII
and ARMM, with direct responsibility for fostering a competent, competitive, and socially conscious S&T
community.
Core Programs and Initiatives
Dr. Laidan's tenure has been defined by aggressive, results-oriented implementation of transformative programs:
Small Enterprise Technology Upgrading Program (SETUP): Her office has helped thousands of small
and medium enterprises (SMEs) across food processing, marine and aquaculture, horticulture, metals and
engineering, woodcraft, and furniture sectors. Interventions include technology infusion, equipment
provision, manpower training, technical assistance, product standardization, food safety protocols, and
energy auditing.
Technology Institutional Support Program (TISP): Rolling out emerging technologies to rural and remote
areas, with special focus on ARMM and Region 12 communities.
Virtual Center in Technology Innovation in Information Technology (VCTI-IT): Established to bridge
academe and private sector, promoting globally competitive ICT-driven industries.
Tissue Culture and Clonal Nursery Development: Advancing high-value fruit crops and ornamental plant
production through modern biotechnology.

PAGE 3
Regional Food Processing Centers: She initiated establishment of a major food processing facility in
Isulan, Sultan Kudarat, creating local employment and value-added opportunities.
Metrology Program: Ensuring product standardization and competitiveness through rigorous testing and
measurement protocols.
Philippines Science High School Campus, SOCCSKSARGEN Region: Through her initiative and strong
local networks, this prestigious science education facility was established in 2012 and immediately opened to
scholars.
S&T Program for the Poor, Vulnerable and Disabled: Reflecting her commitment to inclusive
development.
All of these programs reflect a consistent philosophy: technology and science must serve the people, especially
those without easy access to innovation.
Institutional Leadership Roles
Dr. Laidan holds significant governance positions across Region XII's higher education landscape. She serves as
Regent/Trustee of the Governing Board of University of Southern Mindanao (USM), Sultan Kudarat State
University (SKSU), Cotabato City State Polytechnic College (CCSPC), Cotabato Foundation College of Science
and Technology (CFCST), and Adiong Memorial Polytechnic State College (AMPSC). She's also a Trustee of the
Environmental Protection and Conservation Center (ECPC) in Sarangani Province.
Additionally, Dr. Laidan chairs six major consortia coordinating science, technology, and development initiatives
across South Central Mindanao: the Regional Information Technology and Electronic Commerce Committee
(RITECC XII), Cotabato Region Industry and Energy Research and Development Consortium (CRIERDC),
Region XII Analytical Laboratories Consortium (LABCON XII), Region XII Health Research and Development
Consortium (HRDC XII), Region XII Nutrition and Communications Network (NUTRICOMNET XII), and the
Halal S&T Consortium.
Halal Science: A Global Leadership Agenda
If one achievement defines Dr. Laidan's career trajectory, it's her pioneering advocacy for Halal science and
technology development. As a devout Muslim holding a senior position in the Philippines' premier S&T agency,
she recognized a critical gap: the country lacked coherent scientific frameworks for Halal product development and
certification, even as global Halal markets surged.
Dr. Laidan authored and now implements the Philippine Science and Technology Program for the Development
of the Halal Industry, which became DOST's flagship Halal initiative. She chairs the National Halal Forum-
Philippines, the country's leading Halal event, which evolved into the Philippine Halal Assembly and ultimately the
World Halal Assembly Philippines, establishing the country as a credible voice in global Halal standardization.
More tangibly, she's the Founder and Administrator of the Halal Laboratory in Cotabato City, operational since
2010. In 2019, after a decade of her persistent advocacy and fundraising, the Philippine Halal Science Center and
National Halal Laboratory opened in Koronadal City, commissioned as a clearing house for all Halal products
entering and exiting the country. The facility provides comprehensive laboratory services for Halal standardization,
testing, forensics analysis, and research and development, serving both MSMEs and multinational corporations.

PAGE 4
This work earned her international recognition. The Standards and Metrology Institute for Islamic Countries
(SMIIC) of the Organization of Islamic Cooperation (OIC) granted DOST XII permission to adopt and implement
its Unified Global Halal Standards, noting specifically SMIIC's confidence in Dr. Laidan's expertise and leadership.
International Engagement and Speaking
Dr. Laidan's Halal Science expertise has made her a sought-after international speaker. She has presented at major
global forums, including:
World of Halal Science, Industry and Business (WHASIB) International Conference, Phuket, Thailand (June
2010)
World Halal Forum 2008, Malaysia (May 2008)
2nd International Conference and Expo on Halal Industry, Lahore, Pakistan (January 2012)
Saudi Food Forum, Jeddah, Kingdom of Saudi Arabia (December 2013)
Japan Halal Summit 2014, Tokyo (August 2014)
Halal Korea Expo 2015, Seoul (August 2015)
World Halal Summit Istanbul 2016, Turkey
World Halal Convention East Europe 2017, Poznan, Poland (September 2017)
World Halal Summit 2017, Istanbul, Turkey (November 2017)
Halal International Conference 2017, Bangkok, Thailand (November 2017)
Iran Halal Conference 2017, Mashhad, Iran (December 2017)
World Halal Assembly Oman 2018 (May 2018)
Thailand Halal Assembly 2018 (December 2018)
She has also led benchmarking missions, including a significant study mission to Malaysia in 2014 to explore best
practices in Halal industry strengthening. In 2015, she organized the Philippine Halal Assembly International
Conference and Expo at the Marriott Manila, where SMIIC formally granted DOST XII its global standards
authorization.
Recognition and Royal Honors
Dr. Laidan's contributions have been recognized through numerous awards. During Kamindanawan 2011, she was
honored as one of the Outstanding Top Women Mindanao Achievers for "breaking new ground" through science,
technology, and innovation, particularly for championing Halal science in the Philippines.
On May 15, 2014, Dr. Laidan was conferred a distinguished royal honor, being crowned and enthroned as Bai-a-
Zeybaaleem sa Masiu, a noble Bangsamoro women's title with the equivalent rank of Sultan in the Royal
Sultanate of Lanao. This recognition honored both her professional accomplishments and her embodiment of
Maranao cultural values and leadership.
Publications and Research
Dr. Laidan is a licensed fishery biologist and prolific researcher. Her academic work has been published in peer-
reviewed international journals and presented at science and technology conferences. Notable publications include:
"Status of Bachelor of Science for Secondary Programs Major in Biology Offered by Selected Institutions in
the National Capital Region," published in Asia Life Sciences (International Journal of Life Sciences),
Volume 4, No. 2 (July-December 1995)
"Some Effects of Water Hyacinths (Eichhornia crassipes, Linn.) on Some Physico-Chemical Parameters of
Lake Lanao," published in BIOTA Journal (February 1996)

PAGE 5
Dimensions of Her Impact
What makes Dr. Laidan's leadership distinctive is her holistic approach to development. Early in her career, she
focused on particular sectoral needs; as DOST XII Regional Director, her vision expanded to address
interconnected challenges across food security, economic competitiveness, environmental sustainability, education,
and cultural preservation. She's simultaneously a scientist, educator, administrator, cultural ambassador, and bridge-
builder among disparate stakeholders.
Her work has generated measurable outcomes: thousands of SMEs upgraded with new technologies; numerous
food and fruit processing centers established; the loom-weaving industry in ARMM and Cotabato City revitalized;
a premier science high school opened to talented but under-resourced scholars; and a world-class Halal science
infrastructure built to serve both the Philippines and the global Muslim business community.
Perhaps most importantly, Dr. Laidan has demonstrated that Bangsamoro leadership in science, technology, and
development is not aspirational, it's achievable, and it can be done with both rigor and cultural integrity.
Further Reading

Directories.

title: Lanto, Macabangkit B.
text:
PAGE 1
Macabangkit B. Lanto
Atty. Macabangkit B. Lanto (1942 – October 15, 2024) was a Filipino lawyer, diplomat, university administrator,
and writer.
As one of the most prominent intellectual figures from the Bangsamoro region, he spent over five decades working
across public service, international affairs, and higher education.
He was widely respected for his leadership in building up the Mindanao State University system, for representing
the Philippines on the world stage, and for his sharp socio-political commentary in national media.
A proud Maranao from Lanao del Sur, Lanto served as a living bridge between the Muslim communities of
Mindanao and the institutions of the Philippine national government.
Contents
1 EARLY LIFE AND EDUCATION
2 LAYING THE GROUNDWORK AT MSU
3 INTERNATIONAL DIPLOMACY AND NATIONAL ROLES
4 MEDIA AND JOURNALISM
5 RETURN TO MARAWI AS CITY ADMINISTRATOR
6 FAMILY, VALUES, AND LEGACY
EARLY LIFE AND EDUCATION
Lanto was born in 1942 in Lanao del Sur, Philippines.
Growing up immersed in the rich cultural and spiritual traditions of the Maranao, his childhood in Mindanao laid
the foundation for his lifelong commitment to fighting for minority rights and regional progress.
He moved to Manila for university and earned his law degree from the University of the Philippines — one of the
country's most prestigious institutions.
Demonstrating exceptional academic ability, he later won a Fulbright fellowship, which brought him to New York
University (NYU) for his postgraduate legal studies.
LAYING THE GROUNDWORK AT MSU
Before making his mark on the national stage, Lanto directed his energy toward building up local institutions in
Mindanao.
In the late 1970s, his deep understanding of law and public administration brought him to the attention of regional
leaders, leading to his appointment as Secretary of the Board of Regents (BOR) of the Mindanao State University
(MSU) System.
At the time, MSU was navigating significant growing pains as it worked to expand from a single campus in
Marawi City into a multi-campus network serving communities across conflict-affected Mindanao.

Lanto stepped in and helped reshape the institution on several
fronts.
He legally unified campus operations, placing scattered
community colleges under one central management system and
giving the expanding network a firmer institutional footing.
He drafted and signed the documentation to establish new
extension campuses, bringing higher education within reach of
remote Muslim and indigenous communities across the region.
Known for his compassionate approach to administration, he
frequently used his authority to resolve bureaucratic obstacles and
credit blockages that kept underprivileged students from
completing their degrees.
INTERNATIONAL DIPLOMACY AND
NATIONAL ROLES
Lanto's expertise eventually carried him far beyond academia into
high-level government service.
As a diplomat, he served as the Philippine Ambassador to Egypt
and Sudan, where he worked to strengthen bilateral ties and
protect the welfare of Filipino workers overseas.
Back home, he served as Undersecretary for two major national
agencies: the Department of Justice (DOJ) and the Department of
Tourism (DOT).
These roles placed him among a very small circle of Bangsamoro
professionals to have held senior executive positions across
multiple branches of the Philippine national government.
MEDIA AND JOURNALISM
In his later years, Lanto transitioned into journalism and became a
widely-read voice in national media.
Writing a regular column for the Daily Tribune, he used the
platform to bridge the gap between complex government policies
and general public understanding.
His columns regularly analyzed contemporary legal issues, public
administration challenges, and national peace initiatives.
He was particularly passionate about the Bangsamoro peace
process, applying his deep legal background to advocate for
constitutional solutions to the historical conflicts in Mindanao.

through the written word."
Through his writing, he remained an active and influential voice
in national conversations long after leaving formal government
posts.
RETURN TO MARAWI AS CITY
ADMINISTRATOR
In his final years, Lanto chose to bring his decades of experience
back to local government in his home region.
He was appointed City Administrator of the Islamic City of
Marawi — a critical role he held until his death in October 2024.
Taking up the post during a sensitive period in the city's history,
Lanto focused heavily on supporting Marawi's recovery and
rebuilding in the aftermath of the devastating 2017 Marawi Siege.
He reorganized operations at city hall, improving the delivery of
municipal services to local residents and streamlining day-to-day
administrative functions.
He was committed to bringing people and institutions together —
just days before his passing, he hosted key meetings for local
lawyers that helped Marawi successfully stage the Western
Mindanao Integrated Bar of the Philippines (IBP) Convention.
He remained a fierce advocate for internally displaced families
from the siege, working alongside cultural organizations to ensure
that Marawi's rebuilding process respected the city's unique
historical and Islamic identity.
FAMILY, VALUES, AND LEGACY
To the friends, colleagues, and young lawyers he mentored
throughout his career, Lanto was a man of deep wisdom,
approachable humility, and unwavering personal integrity.
Outside of his professional life, he was an avid golf enthusiast
who found rest and enjoyment on the course.
As a Maranao intellectual in the truest sense, Lanto served as an
essential cultural bridge between the central government in
Manila and the Muslim communities of Mindanao.
By breaking through barriers in international diplomacy and
executive governance, he demonstrated what was possible for
religious and cultural minorities in the Philippines.

PAGE 4
Through his foundational work at MSU, his insightful national journalism, and his commitment to local
government in his home city, he championed education and public service as the most enduring tools for peace and
lasting social progress.
Atty. Macabangkit B. Lanto passed away on October 15, 2024. He is remembered as one of the most consequential
Bangsamoro figures of the twentieth and early twenty-first century.

title: Lao, Mamarinta B.
text:
PAGE 1
Brigadier General Mamarinta B. Lao
Born
February 29, 1916 at Macadar, Lumbatan,
Lanao del Sur, Philippines
Died
2005 (aged 89), Macadar, Lumbatan, Lanao del
Sur, Philippines
Ethnicity
Meranao
Religion
Islam
Allegiance
Republic of the Philippines
Branch of Service
Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP);
Philippine Constabulary (PC)
Rank
Mamarinta B. Lao
Brigadier General Mamarinta B. Lao (February 29, 1916 -
2005) was a decorated Filipino military officer, a Meranao royal
noble, and one of the most consequential figures in the history of
Muslim Filipinos in national service.
Born into a centuries-old royal lineage from the shores of Lake
Lanao, he went on to break one of the most enduring barriers in
the Armed Forces of the Philippines: he became the first career
Filipino-Muslim and the first Meranao officer to ever attain
the rank of General in the AFP's regular standing forces.
His story spans World War II guerrilla heroics, decades of
peacetime military command, provincial governance during
Mindanao's most turbulent years, and a cultural legacy that
continues to resonate with the Meranao people and the
Bangsamoro region to this day.
Contents
1 Background and Royal Lineage
2 Education
3 World War II: The Lanao Bolo Battalion
4 Career: Rising Through the Ranks
4.1 The First Muslim General: Context and Distinction
5 Governance: Governor of Lanao del Sur
6 Legacy: Camp General Mamarinta B. Lao
7 Cultural Significance
8 Death and Final Rest
9 Recognition and Honors
10 See Also
11 References
12 External Links
Background and Royal Lineage
Mamarinta Lao came into the world on a date that comes around
only once every four years: February 29, 1916, in the ancestral
settlement of Macadar, in the municipality of Lumbatan, Lanao
del Sur.
He wasn't just a child of that lakeside community; he was born
into one of its most distinguished noble families.

PAGE 2
Brigadier General
Commands Held
Lanao Bolo Battalion (1942), Provincial
Commander, PC Sulu
Wars and Conflicts
World War II, Philippine Resistance, 1942-
1945)
Political Office
Governor of Lanao del Sur (1975-1976)
Royal Title
Noble of the Pat ka Lokes sa Macadar (Four
Royal Ancestors of Macadar); descendant of the
Unayan principality
Resting Place
Macadar, Lumbatan, Lanao del Sur
NOTABILITY
First career Filipino-Muslim and first Maranao
officer to attain the rank of General in the
Armed Forces of the Philippines
KNOWN FOR
Commanding the Lanao Bolo Battalion during
the Japanese Occupation; bridging Meranao
royal authority with Philippine national military
service; namesake of Camp General Mamarinta
B. Lao in Marawi City
PULL QUOTE
"He proved that you could be a fiercely loyal
soldier of the Republic without surrendering a
single thread of your Islamic faith or Meranao
identity."
Both of his parents traced their ancestry directly to the Pat ka
Lokes sa Macadar, which translates roughly as the Four Royal
Ancestors of Macadar, the foundational ruling houses of that
settlement.
According to local salsila (genealogical records), his bloodline ran
deep into the Unayan principality, descending from the royal
ancestor Akonga and the princess Paramata Andong.
His father, Datu Abdullah, was a direct descendant of a lineage of
regional leaders that included Sultan Mardan, Datu Kalipa, and
Tomindug.
Growing up surrounded by this heritage, the young Mamarinta
was raised with a clear understanding that leadership wasn't
optional for him; it was a responsibility that came with his
bloodline.
Education
Long before he ever wore a uniform, Lao earned a reputation as a
sharp and driven student, which was no small feat in a time when
formal education was still finding its footing in rural Mindanao.
He completed his primary schooling in Macadar and Managan,
finishing consistently at the top of his classes.
For his secondary education, he attended the Lumbatan
Agricultural High School (LAHS), where he graduated as
Valedictorian.
He then continued his studies at the Lanao Provincial Normal
School, completing a two-year collegiate program with high
honors.
By the time he was ready to take on greater responsibilities, Lao
was that rare combination: a deeply rooted Meranao noble who
was also fully conversant in the legal and administrative realities of the American Commonwealth government.
World War II: The Lanao Bolo Battalion
When Japanese Imperial Forces swept through the Philippines in early 1942, the regular USAFFE units were
quickly overwhelmed.
U.S. Brigadier General Guy Fort recognized that the fiercely independent warrior spirit of the Moro people could
be organized into a formidable resistance force.
In January 1942, Fort formally authorized the creation of the Lanao Bolo Battalion, a specialized guerrilla unit
built around the fighting traditions and territorial knowledge of the Meranao people.

PAGE 3
The young Lieutenant Mamarinta Lao was appointed as the battalion's overall commander.
It was a role that demanded far more than battlefield courage.
The challenge was administrative and diplomatic as much as military: Lao had to unify localized combat sectors
commanded by proud, fiercely independent Datus who traditionally answered to no outside authority.
Armed with kampilans, bolos, and whatever firearms they could secure, the Lanao Bolo Battalion harassed
Japanese supply lines, executed intelligence operations, and held the rugged mountain terrain of Ranao against a
determined occupying force.
The Japanese never fully subdued the interior of Lanao del Sur, and Lao's coordination of these resistance networks
was a major reason why.
Career: Rising Through the Ranks
After the war, Lao returned to a peacetime military that was still largely unfamiliar with the idea of a Muslim
officer climbing the institutional ladder of the regular AFP.
He climbed anyway.
Over a multi-decade career marked by tactical competence, peacekeeping operations across Mindanao, and steady
institutional service, Lao worked his way from wartime lieutenant to full general officer.
One of his most significant mid-career postings was as the Provincial Commander of the Philippine
Constabulary (PC) in Sulu, where he was deployed during the height of the mid-century anti-insurgency
campaigns of the 1950s.
National Artist for Literature F. Sionil Jose, who covered the Kamlon Campaign in Sulu as a journalist during that
period, explicitly noted serving alongside then-Colonel Mamarinta Lao during those tense years.
When he was finally elevated to Brigadier General, it wasn't just a personal milestone; it was a watershed moment
for Muslim Filipinos everywhere.
The First Muslim General: Context and Distinction
It's worth pausing to be precise about this claim, because the history can get a bit tangled.
Other legendary Muslim Filipinos, including Salipada K. Pendatun of Cotabato, also held the title of Brigadier
General.
But Pendatun's rank was primarily rooted in his wartime guerrilla command and subsequent political-military
appointments.
What made Lao's achievement historically distinct was that he earned his generalship by climbing the regular,
peacetime promotion ladder of the AFP's standing forces, proving that a Filipino-Muslim officer could advance
through the standard institutional hierarchy on the strength of merit and service alone.
Historical records, including documentation from UP Diliman ROTC Vanguard logs, confirm that General Lao is
recognized as the first career Filipino-Muslim and first Meranao officer to attain a generalship in the regular
AFP officer corps.

PAGE 4
Governance: Governor of Lanao del Sur
After retiring from active military duty, Lao's service to his people wasn't finished.
During the volatile mid-1970s in Mindanao, when political stability in the region was fragile at best, he stepped
into civilian governance.
He served as Governor of Lanao del Sur from 1975 to 1976, succeeding Princess Tarhata Alonto-Lucman and
preceding Mohammad Ali Dimaporo in that office.
His term was a critical stabilizing interlude, drawing on both his military authority and his deep personal credibility
among the Meranao people to hold the province steady through a difficult transition.
Legacy: Camp General Mamarinta B. Lao
The most visible tribute to his enduring legacy stands in Marawi City.
Through Regional Legislative Assembly (RLA) Bill No. 26, the historic military reservation formerly known as
Campo Ranao, the strategic nerve center of military operations in Lanao del Sur, was officially renamed Camp
General Mamarinta B. Lao.
This wasn't a ceremonial gesture.
Campo Ranao had been the tactical heart of military activity in the province since the American colonial era, and
giving it General Lao's name tied the identity of that institution permanently to the legacy of indigenous Muslim
military leadership.
Every soldier who passes through its gates today does so under a name that stands for something: that being
Meranao and being Filipino aren't in conflict.
Cultural Significance
To the Meranao people, General Lao was something the formal record can't fully capture: a bridge.
He lived during a period when the relationship between Manila and the Muslim communities of Mindanao was
frequently strained by distrust, distance, and competing interests.
Lao occupied a unique middle ground that few people could claim.
Because of his royal lineage, the Datus and Sultans of Ranao trusted him as one of their own.
Because of his military record, the top brass in Manila took his counsel seriously.
He used that position not just for personal advancement but to defuse local conflicts, push for infrastructure and
educational investment in Lanao, and open doors for a younger generation of Muslim Filipinos who wanted to
serve their country in uniform.
He lived his entire career as proof that Islamic faith, Meranao identity, and loyal Philippine military service could
coexist without contradiction.

PAGE 5
Death and Final Rest
General Mamarinta B. Lao passed away in 2005, at the age of 89.
In a fitting final chapter, he was returned to his roots.
He was laid to rest with full military honors in his ancestral hometown of Macadar, Lumbatan, the same
community where he was born nearly nine decades earlier.
He left behind not just a decorated military record but a template: a living demonstration that the sons and
daughters of the Lake could serve, lead, and excel at the highest levels of national life without losing themselves in
the process.
Recognition and Honors
Brigadier General, Armed Forces of the Philippines (highest military rank, career track)
Valedictorian, Lumbatan Agricultural High School
Commander, Lanao Bolo Battalion (World War II resistance)
Provincial Commander, Philippine Constabulary, Sulu
Governor of Lanao del Sur (1975-1976)
Camp Namesake: Campo Ranao in Marawi City officially renamed Camp General Mamarinta B. Lao (RLA
Bill No. 26)

title: Lao, Sadick A.
text:
PAGE 1
Sadick A. Lao
Engr. Sadick A. Lao is a Meranaw engineer, cooperative leader, and infrastructure entrepreneur from Marawi City,
Lanao del Sur, in the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM). He is best known as the
Board Chairperson of the Lanao del Sur Electric Cooperative (LASURECO), where he has dedicated himself to
restoring reliable electricity service to one of the most underserved regions in the Philippines.
Alongside his work in the energy sector, he is the proprietor of Andong Builders and General Merchandise, a
construction firm that by early 2026 was managing infrastructure projects worth over one billion pesos across
Lanao del Sur. His dual role as both a power sector leader and a physical infrastructure builder has positioned him
as one of the key figures in the post-siege reconstruction and development of the province.
More than just a technical professional, Engr. Lao is seen by many in the Meranaw community as a guardian of
socio-economic stability: the kind of leader who understands that lights, roads, and water systems aren't just
engineering problems; they're the foundation on which culture and community survive.
Contents
1 Early Life and Background
2 Family
3 Education
4 Career
4.1 Board Chairperson, LASURECO
4.2 Proprietor, Andong Builders and General Merchandise
5 Contributions
6 Values and Leadership Philosophy
7 Cultural Significance
8 Recognition
9 Challenges and Obstacles
10 See Also
11 Further Reading
Early Life and Background
Engr. Sadick A. Lao grew up in Marawi City, the storied "City of Flowers" at the heart of Lanao del Sur. He came
of age during a particularly meaningful transition for the Meranaw, a period when deeply rooted Islamic traditions
were beginning to intersect with modern secular education and governance.
That intersection shaped him in a lasting way. He didn't have to choose between honoring his heritage and
engaging with the demands of a changing world; he learned early on that the two could coexist and, in fact,
strengthen each other. Growing up in the heart of the province also meant he had a front-row seat to the everyday
struggles his community faced: unstable power supply, underdeveloped roads, and the persistent fragility of the
local economy. Those early observations would eventually define his life's work.

PAGE 2
Family
For Engr. Lao, family is the lens through which he views leadership. He was raised within a traditional Meranaw
social structure where collective welfare consistently takes precedence over individual gain. That upbringing didn't
stay at home; it followed him into the boardroom and the construction site.
People who work with him often note that he checks in not just on project progress, but on the personal lives and
family situations of his staff, whether at LASURECO or at Andong Builders. He's been known to treat his
professional teams as extensions of his own household. In his view, a worker who is stable and supported at home
is a more committed and effective contributor to the mission. It's a leadership philosophy rooted in Meranaw values
of bayanihan and communal responsibility, and it colors everything he does.
Education
Engr. Lao pursued a degree in Engineering, building the technical foundation he would need to navigate the
complex realities of power infrastructure and large-scale construction. His academic formation was, like that of
many Bangsamoro professionals, deeply shaped by the Mindanao State University (MSU) Main Campus in
Marawi City, one of the most significant institutions in the entire Bangsamoro region.<ref name="msu">Mindanao
State University is the primary state university in the Bangsamoro region and has produced a significant proportion
of Lanao del Sur's professional class.</ref>
His bond with MSU didn't end at graduation. He has continued to collaborate with the university on regional
development initiatives, reflecting his belief that education is not a phase of life but an ongoing commitment. That
conviction has also led him to support local institutions such as the Senator Ninoy Aquino College Foundation,
where he has engaged students on the importance of energy sustainability and technical literacy as tools for
community development.
Career
Board Chairperson, LASURECO
The Lanao del Sur Electric Cooperative (LASURECO) is the primary electricity distribution utility serving Lanao
del Sur, and Engr. Lao's role as its Board Chairperson has placed him at the center of one of the region's most
pressing crises: chronic power instability and service inequity.
In this position, he serves as the critical link between the local communities who depend on electricity for their
daily lives and the national regulatory bodies, particularly the National Electrification Administration (https://nea.g
ov.ph) (NEA), that govern the cooperative sector. Navigating that relationship requires a combination of technical
expertise, political acumen, and, perhaps most importantly, a deep understanding of what power outages actually
mean for families and small businesses on the ground.
One of his landmark contributions has been the push to dismantle the so-called "pakyaw system," a bulk billing
practice that had been in place for years and was widely criticized for its lack of transparency and fairness.<ref
name="pakyaw">The "pakyaw system" in the context of electric cooperatives refers to a bulk metering
arrangement where an entire community or cluster of households is billed collectively, a practice that has
historically led to inequitable cost distribution among consumers.</ref> Advocating for individual metering, Engr.
Lao helped bring accountability to the billing process, giving consumers a clearer picture of their actual usage and
a fairer share of costs.

PAGE 3
In 2025, he organized a major Stakeholders Forum that brought together a notably broad coalition: government
officials, cooperative members, civil society groups, and even local content creators and vloggers who document
community life in the province. The forum was designed to open up a transparent, inclusive conversation about the
cooperative's challenges and the path forward, a gesture that signaled his commitment to accountability over optics.
Proprietor, Andong Builders and General Merchandise
Parallel to his LASURECO work, Engr. Lao has built Andong Builders and General Merchandise into a significant
player in BARMM's infrastructure development landscape. The firm has been a primary contractor for projects
under the Bangsamoro government's infrastructure agenda.
By early 2026, Andong Builders was managing a portfolio of projects valued at over one billion pesos.<ref
name="infra">Figure cited from available documentation as of early 2026; actual contract values are subject to
official government procurement records.</ref> These projects range from road networks and lake protection
structures to water systems in rural communities. The firm has worked on lake walls designed to protect coastal
settlements along Lake Lanao, fish landing facilities that support the province's fishing economy, and Level II
water systems that bring potable water to communities with no prior access.
Engr. Lao has also been a participant in the broader Marawi Rehabilitation Program, contributing to the physical
reconstruction of infrastructure in areas affected by the 2017 siege of Marawi. For families displaced by that
conflict, the completion of roads, drainage systems, and community facilities represents far more than a
construction milestone: it's the material condition for coming home.
Contributions
Engr. Lao's contributions cut across two sectors that, taken together, define the basic infrastructure of modern life
in Lanao del Sur: energy and physical construction.
In the energy sector, his reform of billing practices at LASURECO and his advocacy for systemic improvements in
power delivery have made a tangible difference for ordinary consumers. The 2025 Stakeholders Forum, in
particular, demonstrated a model of cooperative governance that prioritizes communication and community input
over top-down administration.
In construction, the scale and variety of Andong Builders' portfolio reflects a comprehensive approach to
development. Rather than focusing on a single type of project, the firm has taken on work that addresses multiple
layers of need simultaneously, from agricultural support (fish landings) to disaster resilience (lake walls) to basic
sanitation (water systems). The connection between these projects is a coherent vision of what Lanao del Sur needs
to become a fully functioning, self-sustaining province.
His integration of both roles, energy leader and infrastructure builder, is arguably his most distinctive contribution.
He didn't choose one lane and stay in it. He recognized that rebuilding a province requires working on several
fronts at once, and he structured his career accordingly.
Values and Leadership Philosophy
Those who work alongside Engr. Lao consistently point to three qualities that define how he operates: simplicity,
patience, and compassion.

PAGE 4
His reputation for simplicity comes from his insistence on clarity. He doesn't rely on technical jargon to create
distance between himself and the communities he serves. When explaining complex infrastructure problems,
whether to a boardroom of officials or a room full of cooperative members, he finds ways to make the issues
accessible and actionable. It's a quality that has made him effective as a public communicator and as a leader.
His patience is especially significant given the context in which he works. Lanao del Sur has experienced decades
of conflict, underdevelopment, and political instability. Quick fixes are tempting but usually ineffective in this
environment. Engr. Lao has consistently advocated for long-term, phased approaches to infrastructure repair and
development, prioritizing solutions that will hold up over time rather than ones that look good in the short term.
His compassion shows up in specific, practical ways. He is known for his sensitivity to the concerns of low-income
consumers, particularly those who struggle with the cost of electricity, and he has used his platform at LASURECO
to advocate for equitable billing and consumer protection. In a region where poverty remains widespread, that
advocacy carries real weight.
Cultural Significance
In the Meranaw community, Engr. Lao occupies a role that goes beyond his job titles. He is often described as a
modern "Engineer-Leader," a figure who carries the responsibilities of both technical expertise and communal
stewardship.
This matters because, for the Meranaw people, the stability of infrastructure is inseparable from the survival of
culture. Reliable electricity powers the workshops, markets, and schools where Meranaw artisans, traders, and
students carry their heritage forward. Functional roads connect the communities where the traditions of torogan
(royal house) culture, okir art, and kulintang music are kept alive. When Engr. Lao works to keep the lights on and
the roads passable, he is, in a very real sense, working to keep the culture viable.
His work in the Marawi Rehabilitation Program adds another layer to this cultural role. The 2017 siege left the
most historically rich area of the city in ruins. Rebuilding it isn't just an infrastructure project; it's a cultural
reclamation effort. By participating in that reconstruction, Engr. Lao has tied his legacy to the return and revival of
Meranaw civilization in its ancestral home.
Recognition
While formal awards and official recognition specific to Engr. Lao are not comprehensively documented in public
records, his standing in the Bangsamoro engineering and cooperative sectors speaks for itself. His firm's selection
as a major contractor for BARMM government infrastructure projects reflects the confidence that the regional
government has placed in his work. His continued leadership at LASURECO, amid the formidable challenges
facing the cooperative, reflects the trust of the members and the oversight bodies that he serves.
His organization of the 2025 Stakeholders Forum was itself a form of recognition by the sector that transparent,
community-centered governance in the cooperative space is both necessary and possible.
Challenges and Obstacles
Engr. Lao has operated in one of the most challenging environments for infrastructure development in the
Philippines. Lanao del Sur's geography, with its mountainous terrain, lake basin, and dispersed rural communities,
presents formidable logistical obstacles for any construction or electrification effort.

PAGE 5
Beyond geography, the region has had to contend with decades of armed conflict and political instability, both of
which have disrupted infrastructure projects, frightened away investment, and drained public resources. The 2017
siege of Marawi was only the most dramatic of these disruptions; the underlying fragility of governance structures
in the province has been a persistent challenge for anyone trying to build or repair public systems.
At LASURECO specifically, the cooperative has faced systemic issues including power supply shortfalls, aging
infrastructure, and the cultural inertia of longstanding practices like the pakyaw system that took years of advocacy
to reform. Managing a public utility under those conditions, while maintaining the trust of consumers who have
every reason to be skeptical, requires a level of resilience and steady commitment that defines Engr. Lao's
approach.

Acram A. Latiph
Dr. Acram A. Latiph is a Professor of Economics at Mindanao State
University (MSU) in Marawi City and the Executive Director of the
Institute for Peace and Development in Mindanao (IPDM). He is
known for treating economics and peacebuilding as one job: figure
out why some places stay stuck in conflict, then use policy, research,
and training to help them get unstuck.
Contents
1 Education
2 Academic Career
3 Institute for Peace and Development in Mindanao
4 Policy Work and Consultancy
5 Commentary on the Bangsamoro Elections
6 References
Education
Dr. Latiph took his Bachelor of Science in Economics at San Beda
College and his Master of Science in Finance at the University of the
Philippines Diliman. At the Maxwell School of Citizenship and
Public Affairs at Syracuse University in New York, he completed an
Executive Master of Public Policy and an Advanced Certificate in
Conflict Resolution. His PhD in Development Economics came from
the Australian National University (ANU).
His dissertation, "What's Wrong with Mindanao? The Unequal
Development in the Philippines," examined the structural economic
gaps behind the region's uneven progress. It was nominated for the
ANU Award for Academic Excellence. He is a recipient of the
Fulbright Scholarship, the Australian Leadership Award, and the
NISGP Scholarship.
Academic Career
Dr. Latiph teaches in the Department of Economics at MSU Marawi.
His research covers rural development, fiscal autonomy, poverty
alleviation, Islamic economics and finance, political economy,
regional planning, and the prevention of violent extremism, all with a
focus on the Bangsamoro and Muslim Mindanao.

Institute for Peace and Development in
Mindanao
The MSU Board of Regents created IPDM in December 2001. Today
it serves as the central coordinating unit for the university's peace and
development programs. Under Dr. Latiph, it runs three programs: peace education, peace research and conflict
studies, and peace action. The institute's larger aim is to help the MSU System grow into a National Peace
University.
Much of the work happens on the ground. IPDM has partnered with UNDP Philippines on peace education training
for MSU campuses. It works with the Office of the Presidential Adviser on Peace, Reconciliation and Unity
(OPAPRU) to implement and monitor educational assistance for the children and next-of-kin of decommissioned
MILF combatants. At one of those turnovers, Dr. Latiph said that education is a powerful catalyst for
transformation.
With World Vision, IPDM trained barangay Lupon representatives in conflict transformation and moved to place
the partnership under a formal Memorandum of Agreement. In July 2024, the institute welcomed the Indonesian
Leimena Group to Marawi, where the discussions covered preventing and countering violent extremism and a
proposed Youth Peace Security certificate course.
Policy Work and Consultancy
Dr. Latiph serves as a consultant and resource person for government institutions, international organizations, and
civil society groups, including the Lanao del Sur provincial government and BARMM authorities. His
contributions include development plans, poverty alleviation measures, socioeconomic impact assessments, and
studies on peace, conflict, and violent extremism.
On March 23, 2026, he presented an economic risk analysis to the Lanao del Sur Provincial Economic Crisis
Management Committee, which Governor Mamintal A. Adiong Jr. created after fuel costs climbed. He explained
that the province relies on supply routes through Iligan and Cagayan de Oro and has limited local production, so
price swings reach households quickly.
His recommendations were practical: expand access to affordable rice, strengthen links with local producers, and
provide targeted fuel assistance for transport workers, farmers, and fisherfolk. For government operations, he
proposed trimming fuel allocations for nonessential activities and adopting a four-day workweek, which the
provincial government has begun implementing.
Commentary on the Bangsamoro Elections
When the Bangsamoro held its first parliamentary elections on September 14, 2026, Dr. Latiph shared his
reflections in an interview with CounterCheck. He traced the road from the 1976 Tripoli Agreement, signed under
President Ferdinand Marcos Sr., to this milestone under President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. He also recalled that he
never imagined former MILF commanders would one day take part in elections through institutions the peace
process created.
He welcomed the voter turnout, which the Commission on Elections placed at 84.34 percent, and noted that Lanao
del Sur voted peacefully and in an orderly manner. To him, the inaugural election is a milestone and not the
destination, and the real work is building a mature, resilient, and accountable democracy.

Atty. Jehan-Jehan A. Lepail
Atty. Jehan-Jehan A. Lepail is a Filipino lawyer and public official who serves as the Deputy Executive Director
of the National Commission on Muslim Filipinos (NCMF), the Philippine government body mandated to protect
and promote the rights and welfare of Muslim Filipinos.<ref name="profile">Profile summary from uploaded file
on Atty. Jehan-Jehan A. Lepail.</ref> Her public career has moved from private legal practice to local government
service and then to national leadership in Muslim affairs. Across those roles, one theme keeps showing up: bringing
the law closer to communities that have long felt distant from it.<ref name="profile" />
She is associated with efforts to widen access to justice, improve community-level dispute resolution, and
strengthen government service delivery for Muslim communities in the Philippines.<ref name="profile" /> In that
sense, her legacy isn't just about holding office. It's about using public institutions in a way that makes them feel
reachable, practical, and culturally aware.
Background
Atty. Lepail emerged as part of a generation of Muslim Filipino professionals whose careers crossed formal legal
institutions, local politics, and national public service.<ref name="profile" /> Her professional path reflects a mix
of technical legal training and hands-on administrative work, especially in areas where questions of law, identity,
and governance overlap.

PAGE 2
Her later work would place her in settings where legal problems were rarely abstract. They involved ordinary
people dealing with access, representation, mediation, and state services. That community-facing dimension
became central to her public profile.<ref name="profile" />
Education
Atty. Lepail studied at Ateneo de Manila University, where she earned a bachelor's degree in Legal Management
with honors and later completed her law degree.<ref name="profile" /> Her Ateneo training gave her a classical
grounding in Philippine legal education, one shaped by rigorous legal method and public service formation.
She also pursued masteral units at the University of the Philippines Institute of Islamic Studies, an academic step
that deepened her understanding of Islamic thought, Muslim social realities, and the place of Shari'ah-related
concerns within the Philippine setting.<ref name="profile" /> That combination, mainstream legal training on one
hand and Islamic studies on the other, helps explain her later role as a bridge between state institutions and Muslim
community concerns.
Career
Early legal practice
Atty. Lepail began her professional career in 2008 at the Quasha, Ancheta, and Peña Law Office in Makati.
Working in an established law firm gave her early exposure to the discipline, precision, and demands of legal
practice in the Philippines.
Though this stage of her career was relatively brief, it laid the technical foundation for the public roles that
followed. It also gave her firsthand experience with the formal legal system before she entered governance and
community-oriented service.
Local government service
In 2009, she moved into public administration as a Municipal Administrator in a local government unit in
Mindanao.<ref name="profile" /> That shift mattered. It took her from formal legal work into the everyday
mechanics of governance, where policy, administration, and public need meet in very direct ways.
During the 2010 to 2013 term, she also served as Vice Mayor of Datu Saudi Ampatuan, Maguindanao.<ref
name="profile" /> Her time in local government placed her inside the realities of grassroots administration in a
politically sensitive region. It also strengthened her understanding of how law and governance actually function
outside major urban institutions.
National Commission on Muslim Filipinos
Atty. Lepail joined the National Commission on Muslim Filipinos in 2017 as head of the Bureau of Legal Affairs.
<ref name="profile" /> In that position, she oversaw part of the NCMF's mandate to provide legal assistance to
indigent Muslim Filipinos, especially those who lacked ready access to legal representation and state support.

PAGE 3
In 2019, she was appointed Deputy Executive Director of the NCMF.<ref name="profile" /> In that role, she
became part of the commission's senior leadership, helping oversee operations that included legal concerns,
community relations, policy implementation, and matters connected to the annual Hajj pilgrimage.<ref
name="profile" />
Her rise within the NCMF showed continuity rather than abrupt promotion. She moved upward through legal
service, administrative responsibility, and institutional familiarity, which gave her both technical and operational
credibility.
Contributions
Community-based legal access
One of the most significant themes in Atty. Lepail's work has been the push for community-based legal guidance.
<ref name="profile" /> Rather than treating justice as something available only through expensive litigation or
distant courts, she supported approaches that help communities identify legal problems early and address them
through practical guidance, mediation, and local support structures.
Working in partnership with the Hanns Seidel Foundation, she helped advance initiatives that trained community-
level personnel to assist marginalized residents in recognizing and responding to legal issues.<ref name="profile"
/> This approach reflected a grounded reading of reality: many people do not begin with lawyers or courts, they
begin with confusion, uncertainty, and the need for trusted local help.
Community-based legal guidance allows people to understand and address legal issues in ways that are
closer to their daily realities.|source=Based on the uploaded profile summary of Atty. Jehan-Jehan A.
Lepail.
Hajj administration
As part of the NCMF leadership, Atty. Lepail has also been involved in the complicated work of Hajj
administration.<ref name="profile" /> This includes logistical, financial, and policy dimensions tied to the annual
pilgrimage of Filipino Muslims to Saudi Arabia. Hajj administration is one of the most sensitive and visible
functions of the NCMF, since it affects both religious obligation and public trust.
Her participation in this area placed her within a field that requires coordination with foreign authorities, oversight
of processes affecting pilgrims, and attention to equity in the handling of fees and services.<ref name="profile" />
In practical terms, this meant dealing with one of the commission's most demanding mandates, where
administration, religion, and public accountability all meet.
Institutional reform and dispute resolution
Atty. Lepail has also been linked to efforts to adjust NCMF strategies toward more community-level dispute
resolution, including greater emphasis on mediation and arbitration.<ref name="profile" /> This matters in
communities where formal courts may be geographically distant, financially burdensome, or socially intimidating.
By supporting approaches that recognize the value of accessible settlement mechanisms, she has helped frame
justice not only as courtroom process but also as social repair, negotiated fairness, and culturally informed
resolution.<ref name="profile" /> That thread runs through much of her public work.

PAGE 4
Legacy
Atty. Lepail's public legacy centers on legal access with cultural understanding. She has worked in spaces where
technical legality alone is not enough, and where public trust often depends on whether institutions can speak to
people's lived realities.<ref name="profile" />
That legacy also carries symbolic weight. As a Muslim woman in a senior government position, she stands as part
of a broader shift in Muslim Filipino leadership, one in which women increasingly occupy visible roles in law,
governance, and institutional reform.<ref name="profile" /> Her career suggests that leadership in Muslim affairs is
not limited to inherited authority or symbolic representation. It can also be administrative, legal, practical, and
reform-minded.
The phrase that best captures her public imprint is this: bringing justice closer to the community. It fits the arc of
her work, from legal aid to dispute resolution to service delivery.
Recognition
Atty. Lepail has been recognized within government and partner institutions for her work in legal affairs, Muslim
community service, and administrative leadership.<ref name="profile" /> Part of that recognition comes from her
role in strengthening programs aimed at indigent and marginalized Muslim Filipinos.
She has also come to represent a form of leadership that resonates beyond formal office. For many observers, her
career reflects the growing presence of professionally trained Muslim women in national governance, especially in
sectors tied to rights, law, and public administration.<ref name="profile" />
Challenges
Like many public officials working in Muslim affairs, Atty. Lepail has operated within difficult institutional terrain.
The challenges attached to her work include bureaucratic limitations, uneven access to legal services, the
complexity of service delivery across marginalized communities, and the continuing task of aligning national
systems with local realities.<ref name="profile" />
In the NCMF setting, those challenges become even sharper because the commission deals with issues that are both
administrative and deeply personal, including religious practice, legal vulnerability, and community representation.
Her work has therefore required not only legal skill but also patience, negotiation, and institutional discipline.
Death
As of the latest available information in the uploaded file, there is no indication that Atty. Jehan-Jehan A. Lepail is
deceased. She is described as actively serving in government as Deputy Executive Director of the National
Commission on Muslim Filipinos.<ref name="profile" />

title: Lidasan, Tahir S. Jr.
text:
PAGE 1
Tahir S. Lidasan Jr.
Tahir S. Lidasan Jr., CESO II, is a Filipino civil servant, and public administrator who currently serves as the
Executive Director of the National Commission on Muslim Filipinos (NCMF). Drawing on a family legacy deeply
rooted in Muslim Mindanao and shaped by more than two decades of work inside the country's Muslim affairs
bureaucracy, he has become one of the most recognizable technocrats in the Bangsamoro civil service landscape.
His career is defined by a steady, determined push to bring the Halal industry, Shari'ah law, and Muslim Filipino
cultural identity into the mainstream of Philippine governance and the national economy.
Lidasan's story isn't one of overnight rise or dramatic breaks. It's the story of someone who did the work quietly
and consistently, building expertise in legal affairs, international relations, and institutional reform one role at a
time, until he was in a position to shape the agency that shapes the lives of millions of Filipino Muslims.
Contents
1 Early Life and Family Background
2 Education
3 Career
3.1 Entry into Public Service
3.2 Positions within the OMA and NCMF
3.3 Officer-in-Charge and Appointment as Executive Director
4 Major Contributions
4.1 Halal Industry Development
4.2 Administrative and Institutional Reform
4.3 Shari'ah System Strengthening
5 Legacy and Cultural Significance
6 Recognition
7 See Also
8 Further Reading
Early Life and Family Background
Tahir S. Lidasan Jr. comes from a family where public service and advocacy weren't abstractions but daily realities.
He belongs to the Iranun and Maguindanaon communities, two of the major ethnolinguistic groups in Muslim
Mindanao, and both sides of his family carry histories of leadership and education.
His father, Tahir Lidasan Sr., was a pioneering Iranun widely known for his pro-bono legal work on behalf of the
marginalized. In a region where access to legal representation has long been uneven, the elder Lidasan carved out a
practice grounded in empathy and justice, qualities that would visibly shape his son's approach to governance
decades later.
His mother, Bai Ulanbai Ayunan Sinsuat, comes from the prominent Sinsuat clan of Maguindanao and holds a rare
distinction in her own right: she was among the first Muslim women from Mindanao to pursue higher education in
Manila in the 1950s. Her decision to study in the capital at a time when such a path was far from conventional
speaks to a family culture that valued education as a serious and necessary investment, not just a personal
achievement.

PAGE 2
Growing up shaped by these two figures, Lidasan developed early the values of legal rigor, cultural grounding, and
service that would come to define his professional life.
Education
Lidasan built his academic foundation at the University of the Philippines College of Law, one of the most
respected law schools in the country. During his time there, he served as a legal intern for the Child Justice League
and worked alongside human rights advocates, an early signal of where his interests and commitments lay: at the
intersection of law, human rights, and the welfare of the vulnerable.
Recognizing that effective public administration required more than legal training alone, he went on to take
graduate units in Business Administration at the Ateneo de Manila Graduate School of Business. That combination
of law and management has served him well across the various roles he has held in government, particularly in
efforts to modernize and formalize the Halal economy.
Career
Entry into Public Service
Lidasan began his government career in the legislative branch, serving as a legal staff member for Representative
Ranjit Ramos Shahani. In that capacity, he was part of the team that helped draft the law creating the National
Youth Commission (NYC), an early experience in translating advocacy into legislation.<ref name="nyc">Lidasan
was among the legal staff involved in drafting the law establishing the National Youth Commission of the
Philippines.</ref>
He also chaired the UNICEF Committee on Children in Armed Conflict during his early career, a role that placed
him at the center of conversations about protecting children in conflict-affected areas, including those in Mindanao.
These formative experiences with youth rights and humanitarian concerns would remain a thread running through
his public service even as his roles evolved.
Positions within the OMA and NCMF
The bulk of Lidasan's career unfolded inside the Office on Muslim Affairs (OMA) and its successor agency, the
National Commission on Muslim Filipinos (NCMF). He held a series of director-level positions that collectively
gave him a comprehensive view of how the agency worked, and where it needed to go.
As Director of the Bureau of Legal Affairs, he handled the legal framework surrounding Muslim Filipino rights,
including matters touching on Shari'ah law and its interface with the national legal system.
As Director of the Bureau of External Relations, he pivoted to the international dimension of his work, focusing
on diplomatic engagement and the development of the Philippine Halal industry in the context of global Halal
markets and standards.
These two directorships gave him the dual lens that would come to define his leadership as Executive Director: a
firm grounding in the legal architecture of Muslim affairs, paired with a forward-looking engagement with the
global Halal economy.

PAGE 3
Officer-in-Charge and Appointment as Executive Director
In July 2017, Lidasan was designated Officer-in-Charge (OIC) Executive Director of the NCMF, serving in that
interim capacity until July 2018. His subsequent confirmation as full Executive Director formalized what had
already become evident during his OIC tenure: that he had the institutional knowledge, the relationships, and the
vision to lead the agency.
He is a member of the Career Executive Service (CES), the third tier of the Philippine Civil Service, and was
conferred his CES Eligibility in January 2009. He currently holds the rank of CESO II.<ref name="ces">Lidasan
was conferred Career Executive Service Eligibility in January 2009 and rose to the rank of CESO II.</ref>
Major Contributions
Halal Industry Development
If there is one area where Lidasan has left the clearest institutional fingerprints, it's in the Halal sector. He is
credited with managing and actively developing the Philippine Halal industry, which involves not just domestic
regulation but meaningful engagement with international standards bodies and trading partners.
He represented the Philippines in global conferences on Halal, working to align local certification and standards
with international requirements, a prerequisite for the country's products to gain access to the growing global Halal
market. One concrete result of this engagement was the signing of a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) with
the Philippine Chamber of Commerce and Industry (PCCI)-Makati, aimed at establishing a dedicated "Halal Hub"
in Makati City.<ref name="halalhub">Lidasan signed an MOU with PCCI-Makati to establish a Halal Hub in
Makati City as part of NCMF's efforts to grow the Philippine Halal industry.</ref>
For Lidasan, this work isn't purely economic. It's cultural. Embedding Halal standards and Islamic Finance into the
mainstream national economy is also a way of affirming the legitimacy and presence of Muslim Filipino identity in
the broader Philippine story.
Administrative and Institutional Reform
Under his leadership, the NCMF undertook important internal modernization efforts. The agency automated its
payroll system, a practical reform that improved efficiency and reduced administrative friction for NCMF
personnel across the country.
He also initiated a national census of Muslim Filipinos, a foundational exercise in ensuring that government
resources, programs, and policies are calibrated to the actual size, distribution, and needs of the Muslim Filipino
population. Accurate data, as Lidasan has demonstrated through his administrative priorities, is not a bureaucratic
nicety but a precondition for effective governance.
Shari'ah System Strengthening
Lidasan has been a consistent voice in efforts to expand and strengthen the Shari'ah legal system in the Philippines.
He has participated in dialogues with the Supreme Court of the Philippines aimed at extending the reach of Shari'ah
courts beyond the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM), to serve Muslim populations

PAGE 4
in other parts of the country where no formal Shari'ah court currently exists.<ref name="shariah">Lidasan engaged
with the Supreme Court of the Philippines in discussions on expanding the Shari'ah legal system to serve Muslim
Filipinos outside the BARMM.</ref>
This advocacy reflects a broader vision: that the rights and legal traditions of Filipino Muslims should be accessible
regardless of where they live in the archipelago, not just in the recognized Muslim homeland of the south.
Legacy and Cultural Significance
Those who have worked with or observed Lidasan often describe his style as "quietly effective." He doesn't lead
through spectacle or loudness but through consistency, preparation, and a willingness to engage with complex
problems across legal, economic, and cultural dimensions.
His career represents something significant in the landscape of Bangsamoro governance: the emergence of a
Muslim Filipino technocrat who is simultaneously rooted in cultural identity and fluent in the language of modern
bureaucracy. He carries the Iranun values of empathy and justice modeled by his father, while navigating the
institutional realities of a national government commission.
His focus on Islamic Finance and the Halal economy is a good lens for understanding his larger vision. These aren't
simply policy priorities. They're expressions of a conviction that Muslim Filipino traditions don't have to be held
apart from national development but can be, with the right frameworks, fully integrated into it.
In the broader arc of the Bangsamoro digital and institutional ecosystem, Lidasan represents the kind of civil
servant that the community's development has long needed: someone with deep roots, broad training, and the
patience to work through systems rather than around them.
Recognition
Lidasan's elevation to CESO II is one of the formal markers of recognition within the Philippine civil service
system, representing a high level of competence and professional standing within the Career Executive Service.
<ref name="ces"/> His appointment as full Executive Director of the NCMF, following his OIC tenure, reflects
institutional confidence in his capacity to lead one of the most sensitive and consequential agencies in the
Philippine government structure.
His work on Halal standards and international alignment has also brought him visibility in regional and global
Halal industry circles, representing the Philippines in forums where policy direction and trade standards intersect.

Ismael Sheikh-adatu Londo
Si Sultan Police Major (PMaj) Ismael Sheikh-adatu Londo ay
isang senior officer ng Philippine National Police (PNP) at ang
kinikilalang Sultan ng Marantao, Lanao del Sur, mula sa
marangal na angkan ng AMITO royal bloodline. Sa loob ng
mahigit dalawang dekada ng serbisyo publiko, pinagsama niya
ang dalawang daigdig na bihirang magkasama: ang disiplina ng
batas at ang dignidad ng tradisyon. Bilang pulis, lider-
komunidad, lider-tradisyunal, at lider-relihiyoso, siya ay isang
patunay na ang tunay na paglilingkod sa bayan ay hindi
nagtatapos sa opisina — lumalagpas ito sa hangganan ng kultura,
pananampalataya, at pamana.

Pagpapalaki at Pinagmulan
Si Sultan PMaj Ismael Sheikh-adatu Londo ay nagmula sa isang
pamilyang may malalim na ugat sa kultura at tradisyon ng
Maranao. Siya ang anak ng yumaong Shiek Ahmad Baraocor
Londo at Hadja Fatima Shiek-Adatu Marohombsar Amerol.
Pinalaki siya sa isang tahimik na pagpapahalaga sa pamilya,
pananampalataya, at pananagutang panlipunan. Ang kanyang
pagpapalaki sa ilalim ng tradisyunal na pagpapahalaga ng
Maranao ay naging pundasyon ng kanyang disiplinado at
serbisyo-oriented na pamumuhay.

PAGE 2
Siya ay ama ng sampung anak, at kilala siya sa kanyang malalim na dedikasyon sa pamilya kahit na abala ang
kanyang buhay-propesyonal. Para sa kanya, ang pamilya at ang komunidad ay hindi magkahiwalay na
responsibilidad kundi iisa.
Edukasyon at Mga Propesyonal na Kwalipikasyon
Si Sultan PMaj Londo ay may tatlong degree sa akademya:
Bachelor of Science in Accountancy
Bachelor of Elementary Education
Master of Public Administration
Bukod sa akademikong paghahanda, siya ay isang Registered Criminologist at hawak niya ang apat na
propesyonal na eligibilidad:
1. RA 6506 Criminologist Eligibility
2. Civil Service Commission (CSC) Professional Career Service Eligibility
3. CSC Police Officer Examination Eligibility
4. NAPOLCOM Police Officer Eligibility
Ang kanyang pinagsanib na edukasyon sa criminology, accountancy, edukasyon, at pampublikong administrasyon
ay nagbibigay sa kanya ng natatanging kakayahan na tingnan ang mga hamon ng paglilingkod sa publiko mula sa
maraming anggulo.
Karera sa Serbisyong Sibil at Kepolisyahan
Simula ng Karera (1999 pababa)
Nagsimula si Sultan PMaj Londo sa PNP bilang Police Officer 1 (patrolman) noong 1999. Mula sa
pinakamababang antas, dahan-dahan niyang inakyat ang hagdan ng serbisyo publiko. Sa kanyang panahon bilang
non-commissioned officer, nakatanggap siya ng anim na promosyon, hanggang sa maabot niya ang ranggong
Senior Police Officer 3 (SPO3).
Ang bawat promosyon ay hindi basta ibinibigay. Para kay Sultan PMaj Londo, ang bawat hakbang pataas ay resulta
ng patuloy na dedikasyon, integridad sa trabaho, at malasakit sa komunidad na kanyang pinaglilingkuran.
Pagiging Commissioned Officer (2018 hanggang kasalukuyan)
Noong 2018, isang makasaysayang pagbabago ang dumating sa kanyang karera nang siya ay maging
commissioned officer. Mula noon, dalawang beses pa siyang na-promote, hanggang sa maabot niya ang kanyang
kasalukuyang ranggo bilang Police Major (PMaj). Sa ngayon, inaasahan ang kanyang promosyon sa ranggong
Police Lieutenant Colonel (PLTCOL), In shaa Allah.
Mga Posisyon sa Lanao del Sur
Sa loob ng kanyang serbisyo sa lalawigan ng Lanao del Sur, nagsilbi si Sultan PMaj Londo sa iba't ibang kritikal na
posisyon:

PAGE 3
Chief Investigator
Deputy Chief of Police
Officer-in-Charge (OIC) Chief of Police ng Marantao Municipal Police Station (dalawang beses)
Ang kanyang matagal at paulit-ulit na pagiging OIC Chief of Police sa Marantao ay patunay ng tiwala ng
institusyon sa kanyang kakayahan at integridad.
Kasalukuyang Posisyon
Sa kasalukuyan, siya ay nagsisilbing Provincial Chief ng PNP Community, Human Development and Welfare
Service (CHS) ng Lanao del Sur Provincial Police Office (LSPPO) sa ilalim ng Police Regional Office
Bangsamoro Autonomous Region (PRO BAR).
Ang kanyang opisina ay kinikilala bilang Best Provincial Office of the Year 2023, isang pagkilala na
sumasalamin sa kahusayan ng pamumuno at ang kahusayan ng buong koponan sa ilalim ng kanyang patnubay.
Tradisyunal at Pamayanan na Pamumuno
Pagtatatag Bilang Sultan ng Marantao
Noong Hunyo 22, 2024, si PMaj Ismael Sheikh-adatu Londo ay pormal na iniluklok bilang Sultan ng Marantao,
mula sa kilala at marangal na angkan ng AMITO royal bloodline. Ang pagluluklok na ito ay hindi lamang isang
seremonya; ito ay isang pagkilala ng komunidad na ang kanilang pinuno ay taong subok na sa serbisyo,
pananampalataya, at katapatan sa tradisyon ng Ranao.
Para sa mga Maranao, ang pagiging Sultan ay higit pa sa titulo. Ito ay responsibilidad na may bigat ng kasaysayan,
kultura, at kolektibong kinabukasan ng isang bayan.
Pamumuno sa FEROSULA at Imam Council
Bilang isang kinikilalang lider sa loob ng mas malawak na komunidad ng Ranao, si Sultan PMaj Londo ay
nagsisilbing Chairman ng 28 Legislative Council (kilala rin bilang 28 Mbabaya ko Taritib sa Ranao) ng
Federation of Royal Sultanate of Lanao (FEROSULA). Sa posisyong ito, siya ay aktibong bahagi ng
pamamahala ng mga tradisyunal na batas at kaugalian ng Ranao.
Siya rin ay miyembro ng Imam Council of the Philippines Inc., na nagpapakita ng kanyang papel bilang isang
lider-relihiyoso na kumikikilala sa kahalagahan ng malalim na pag-unawa sa Islam sa loob ng lipunan.
Mga Organisasyonal na Kaugnayan
Si Sultan PMaj Londo ay aktibong miyembro at lider sa iba't ibang organisasyon:
Ranao Finest Inc. (dalawang terminong Presidente)
Philippine Eagles Club
Upsilon Phi Sigma 1935
Almanar Philippines
Imam Council of the Philippines Inc.
Federation of Royal Sultanate of Lanao (FEROSULA) — Chairman, 28 Legislative Council

PAGE 4
Ang kanyang aktibong pakikilahok sa iba't ibang grupo, mula sa mga propesyonal na organisasyon hanggang sa
mga grupong pangkultura at panrelihiyon, ay nagpapakita ng isang lider na hindi nagtatago sa kanyang opisina.
Mga Parangal at Pagkilala
Ang kanyang opisina bilang Provincial Chief ng PNP CHS LSPPO PRO BAR ay kinilala bilang Best
Provincial Office of the Year 2023.
Iniluklok bilang Sultan ng Marantao noong Hunyo 22, 2024, isang pagkilala mula sa komunidad ng
Marantao sa kanyang pamumuno, integridad, at serbisyo.
Dalawang beses na naging Presidente ng Ranao Finest Inc., na nagpapakita ng patuloy na tiwala ng
organisasyon sa kanyang kakayahang pamuno.
Pamana at Kabuluhan
Ang kwento ni Sultan PMaj Ismael Sheikh-adatu Londo ay hindi simpleng karera; ito ay isang halimbawa ng isang
Maranao na naglingkod sa bayan sa lahat ng antas, mula sa pagiging patrolman hanggang sa pagiging Sultan. Sa
loob ng mahigit dalawang dekada sa PNP, pinagtibay niya na ang batas at tradisyon ay hindi magkalaban, kundi
magkasamang pag-iingat ng kapayapaan at kaayusan sa Ranao.
Bilang Sultan, lider-relihiyoso, at opisyal ng PNP, pinapatunayan niya na ang tunay na lider ay hindi naglilingkod
sa iisang titulo lamang kundi sa buong komunidad, sa kanyang buong pagkatao.
