Bantuas M. Lucman
Bantuas "Banjo" M. Lucman is a Filipino lawyer, academic,
and public servant who serves as the Bangsamoro Attorney
General. He was officially appointed to the position on April 14,
2025, by BARMM Chief Minister Abdulraof Macacua.
As the head of the Bangsamoro Attorney General's Office
(BAGO), Lucman acts as the chief legal counsel of the
Bangsamoro Government and the principal legal advisor to the
Chief Minister. With over two decades of experience in litigation
and corporate law, his tenure is defined by efforts to harmonize
Philippine civil law, indigenous customary traditions, and Shari'ah
jurisprudence into a cohesive regional framework.
Contents
1 Early Life and Cultural Background
2 Education and Legal Career
2.1 Private Practice
2.2 Academia
3 Institutional Contributions
3.1 The Tri-Justice Framework
3.2 National-Regional Inter-Agency Alignment
3.3 Shari'ah and Civil Law Integration
3.4 Unification of Regional Legal Officers
4 Cultural and Social Significance
5 See Also
6 References
Early Life and Cultural Background
Lucman was born and raised in the province of Lanao del Sur, a region deeply rooted in Meranau culture and
complex socio-political history. He is recognized by his local community as a prominent Moriatao Diwan
(descendant of noble ancestry), with close ancestral ties to the municipality of Bayang.
Growing up in the Meranau heartland, Lucman was exposed early to the intersections of traditional customary
laws, Islamic principles, and the formal Philippine legal system. This unique cultural environment profoundly
shaped his approach to public administration, instilling a lifelong focus on defending marginalized and underserved
communities.

PAGE 2
Education and Legal Career
Lucman pursued his legal education at the University of the East (UE) College of Law. After admission to the
Philippine Bar, he embarked on a private legal practice spanning more than twenty years, establishing himself as a
formidable litigator.
Private Practice
Throughout his career in the private sector, Lucman managed a diverse legal portfolio encompassing civil,
criminal, commercial, maritime, and labor law. He served as a leading partner in notable firms, including Balbin |
Lucman | Del Rosario & Partners, which later evolved into Lucman Calde Law Partners. In the courtroom, he
earned a reputation for combining sharp corporate strategy with a dedicated pro-bono practice focused on
individuals who lacked access to the justice system.
Academia
In addition to active courtroom litigation, Lucman entered academia as a law professor at the University of the
East. For several years, he taught future attorneys the complexities of the Law on Partnership and Corporation,
emphasizing the role of corporate ethics and social responsibility in modern legal practice.
Institutional Contributions
Upon taking the helm of BAGO in April 2025, Lucman initiated several structural and policy reforms aimed at
modernizing the BARMM legal apparatus while respecting its unique autonomy.
The Tri-Justice Framework
Lucman is a leading proponent of an inclusive "Tri-Justice Framework" for the region. He has consistently
advocated that a truly functional regional legal system must seamlessly balance state law, customary law, and
Islamic jurisprudence by actively engaging both local justice dispensers and grassroots communities.
National-Regional Inter-Agency Alignment
In mid-2025, Lucman spearheaded crucial bilateral dialogues with the national government's chief lawyer, Solicitor
General Darlene Marie B. Berberabe. This historic coordination aligned the mandates of BAGO and the Office of
the Solicitor General (OSG), ensuring that BARMM's unique autonomous legal interests are accurately represented
in national court proceedings without jurisdictional friction.
Shari'ah and Civil Law Integration
To better understand dual-legal governance, Lucman personally led a high-level BAGO delegation to Malaysia to
study its parallel civil and Shari'ah court mechanisms. Under his leadership, BAGO began adapting these
international strategies—focusing on digital case-tracking systems, institutionalized mediation, and legally
enforceable fatwas—to build a culturally responsive legal framework in the Bangsamoro.

PAGE 3
Unification of Regional Legal Officers
Lucman serves as the chairperson of the Legal Officers Network (LLN) Board. In this capacity, he has worked to
unify and standardize the legal strategies across all ministries, agencies, and offices within the Bangsamoro
government, ensuring a cohesive institutional defense of the public good.
Cultural and Social Significance
Beyond administrative duties, Lucman's leadership is characterized by a strong humanitarian focus. He expanded
BAGO's reach by launching **Community Legal Service** programs in remote municipalities like Madamba,
Lanao del Sur. These programs translate and demystify complex state legislation (such as anti-violence laws) for
rural populations while explicitly validating women's rights under Islamic traditions.
Furthermore, his office established the BAGO Gender and Development Focal Point System (GFPS). This
initiative drives localized social welfare actions, such as distributing essential healthcare and maternity starter kits
to expectant mothers in impoverished communities, reflecting his core philosophy that a strong regional state must
be built on a foundation of community care.

Diamael "James" M. Lucman
Prof. Diamael "James" M. Lucman (rahimahullah) was a Filipino
academic, public administrator, and civic leader whose name carries
real weight across Mindanao's socio-political landscape.
He is best remembered for his lifelong bond with Mindanao State
University (MSU), a relationship that took him from wide-eyed
student to campus leader to, eventually, the university's Acting
President in 1999.
Along the way, he also found time to serve his country in national
government, keep the lights on for entire rural communities, and lead
one of the country's most storied fraternities. It's the kind of resume
that reads less like a single career and more like four.
Contents
1 Early Life and Academic Foundation
2 Institutional and Academic Contributions
3 Public Service and Utility Management
4 Civic Leadership and Fraternity Status
5 Personal Life and Family Legacy
6 See Also
7 References
Early Life and Academic Foundation
Lucman grew up in Marawi City and Bayang, Lanao del Sur, right in
the heart of Maranao culture and history.
His connection to Mindanao State University started early: he
attended MSU Preparatory High School, graduating in 1968.
He never really left. Lucman stayed on at MSU for his college years,
earning his bachelor's degree in Community Development and Public
Administration in 1975.
Even as a student, he was already a leader in the making. He was
elected Student Council President, a post that came with a seat on the
university's highest governing body, the MSU Board of Regents.
Hungry to sharpen his understanding of governance, Lucman
eventually made his way to Manila, where he completed a Master in
Public Administration at the University of the Philippines Manila in
1977.

PAGE 2
Guided Mindanao State University
through a critical transition period as its
Acting President in 1999, stepping in right
after the university's first female president
and steadying the institution before
handing it over to his successor.
Known For
A rare career that moved seamlessly
between the classroom, the halls of
national agrarian reform, and the wiring
and utility lines of rural Lanao del Sur, all
while rising to the top leadership post of
the Beta Sigma Fraternity.
Pull Quote
"A blueprint for Maranao leadership:
academic excellence, utility management,
and a deep-seated love for public service."
Institutional and Academic Contributions
Degree in hand, Lucman went home to Marawi City to teach,
choosing to pour his knowledge back into the next generation of
Mindanao's leaders.
He rose through the academic ranks at MSU, eventually earning the
title of Professor VI, with a specialization in public administration
and regional development.
The high point of his institutional career came in 1999, when he was
designated Acting President of the entire Mindanao State University
System.
He stepped into the role right after the historic term of Hadja Sittie
Nurlaylah Emily M. Marohombsar, MSU's first female president, and
carried the university through a delicate stretch: keeping academic
operations stable, looking after student welfare, and holding the line
on day-to-day campus management before passing the baton to his successor.
Public Service and Utility Management
Lucman's talents were never confined to the university gates.
He was called into national service as Undersecretary for the Department of Agrarian Reform, where he helped
steer land reform initiatives and rural development, bringing a genuinely southern, Mindanaoan perspective to
national agrarian policy.
Closer to home, he took on the very grounded, very practical job of Manager of the Lanao del Sur Electric
Cooperative (LASURECO). Running a utility cooperative isn't glamorous work, but it mattered enormously: it
meant grappling with the everyday energy challenges of the province and working to bring dependable power to
rural Maranao communities.
Civic Leadership and Fraternity Status
Within Philippine student culture and civic circles, Lucman holds something close to legendary status.
He was among the very first pioneer members of the MSU chapter of the Beta Sigma Fraternity, and his
commitment to its ideals of brotherhood and community service eventually carried him all the way to the top of the
organization, as President of Beta Sigma Philippines.
Personal Life and Family Legacy
Lucman came from a prominent regional lineage and built a family just as devoted to public welfare as he was.
He was married to Bae Tondogun Disomimba, a respected civic figure in her own right who served as a manager
for human settlements and was the sister of former mayor Topaan Disomimba.

PAGE 3
Prof. James Lucman passed away leaving behind a blueprint for Maranao leadership that blended academic
excellence, utility management, and a deep, unwavering commitment to public service.

title: Lucman, Esnairah Macabato
text:
PAGE 1
Esnairah Macabato Lucman
Police Captain Esnairah Macabato Lucman is a senior law enforcement officer serving under the Philippine
National Police (PNP) in the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM).
She's built her career in one of the most historically complex provinces in the southern Philippines, Lanao del Sur,
a region shaped by deep Islamic tradition, Meranao clan culture, and decades of social tension.
What makes her story stand out isn't just her rank. It's the fact that she got there by consistently bridging two
worlds: the formal demands of the Philippine state's police framework and the deeply personal, relationship-driven
culture of Meranao communities.
She's recognized as a trailblazer in gender-sensitive policing, juvenile justice advocacy, and community-centered
public safety reform in post-conflict Mindanao.
Contents

2 Education and Training
3 Career

Early Life and Family Background
Esnairah Macabato Lucman comes from a well-established Meranao lineage with roots in Lanao del Sur.
She belongs to two families that carry real civic weight in the region: the Lucman and Macabato clans, both
historically active in local leadership, traditional governance, and public service.
Growing up in that environment means growing up with Maratabat, the Meranao code of honor that governs
dignity, family responsibility, and how communities resolve their differences. That background gave her an
unusually sharp understanding of how Lanao del Sur actually works, not just on paper, but in practice.
Choosing law enforcement as a career meant pushing against significant cultural expectations. Command positions
in the region's police establishment had long been dominated by men, and for a Meranao woman, joining that track
was itself a statement.

PAGE 2
Police Captain Esnairah Macabato Lucman

Her reason was straightforward: she wanted women and children
in her community to have a trusted, credible voice within the
system. Someone who understood where they were coming from,
who could navigate both the law and the culture on their behalf.
Education and Training
Captain Lucman completed her criminal justice and tactical
training through the PNP's standardized professional
development pathway.
But she didn't stop at the basics. She pursued a substantial
portfolio of specialized training focused on gender-sensitive law
enforcement, juvenile justice systems, and human rights
advocacy.
She also trained extensively in alternative dispute resolution
(ADR), psycho-social emergency intervention, and specialized
dialogue techniques suited for communities where Islamic
principles and Meranao customs significantly shape how people
respond to authority and conflict.
That combination of state policing standards and culture-
informed tools is what allowed her to operate effectively in a
region where a by-the-book approach, without cultural fluency,
often fails.
Career
Command at Bayang Municipal Police Station
Captain Lucman's field career began in earnest when, as a Police
Lieutenant (PLT), she was assigned as Chief of Police for the
Bayang Municipal Police Station under the Lanao del Sur Police
Provincial Office (LDS PPO).
It was a frontline posting, and it tested her early.
During the peak of the COVID-19 pandemic, she personally led
maritime and land-based patrols across Lake Lanao, reaching
remote barangays like Barangay Sapa to ensure both public
safety and the delivery of basic resources. Getting to those
communities required navigating the lake's terrain and the trust
deficits that came with sending uniformed personnel into areas
with complicated histories with the state.
She did it anyway, and consistently.

PAGE 3
Promotion and Transition to Marawi City
Upon her promotion to Police Captain (P/Capt), she transitioned from the Bayang command to collaborative roles
with the Marawi City Police Office and the provincial government of Lanao del Sur.
Her portfolio shifted from territorial security operations toward something arguably more complex: inter-agency
social protection work in a city still navigating the aftermath of the 2017 Marawi siege and its long tail of
displacement, trauma, and institutional distrust.
Institutional Contributions
Juvenile Justice and Child Protection
As the Marawi City Police Office's representative to the Local Council for the Protection of Children (LCPC),
Captain Lucman played a central role in getting the Comprehensive Local Juvenile Intervention Program of
Marawi City off the ground.
The program is designed to redirect at-risk youth away from exploitation and localized radicalization, a real and
persistent concern in communities still dealing with post-conflict fragility.
Her contribution went beyond representation. She helped operationalize the program's structures, making sure that
police involvement in child protection felt supportive rather than punitive.
Anti-Trafficking and Violence Against Women
Through the Local Council Against Trafficking and Violence Against Women (LCAT-VAW), Captain Lucman
worked to standardize how police units in the area respond to domestic violence and trafficking cases.
One of her most significant contributions here was establishing confidential, trusted reporting pathways for female
victims. In a cultural environment where speaking out about domestic abuse or trafficking carries serious social
risk, those pathways weren't just procedural improvements. They were lifelines.
Women who might never walk into a police station could reach out through channels that felt safer, more discreet,
and handled by someone who genuinely understood the cultural stakes of doing so.
Inter-Agency Coordination
Captain Lucman has also served as a key connector between the Marawi City Police Office, the provincial
government of Lanao del Sur, and BARMM's regional social welfare offices.
That kind of inter-agency coordination is harder than it sounds. Each body has its own priorities, mandates, and
internal cultures. Getting them to operate as a coherent network for peace and order, rather than parallel but
disconnected systems, requires sustained relationship-building and credibility on all sides.
She's built that credibility through consistent, accountable work.

PAGE 4
Cultural Significance
Captain Lucman's significance in the broader BARMM context goes beyond her specific programs and
assignments.
She's a hijab-wearing Muslim police officer in a region that has, historically, had complicated and sometimes
adversarial relationships with uniformed government forces. In that environment, her presence as a senior officer
humanizes the institution in ways that policy memos simply can't.
For young Meranao women watching her career, the message is tangible: it's possible to hold executive command
without abandoning your faith, your identity, or your community.
More broadly, she's demonstrated that progressive gender protection policies and deep respect for indigenous
cultural frameworks aren't contradictory goals. They can reinforce each other, especially when the person leading
the work understands both from the inside.
Her career is a working proof of concept for community policing in post-conflict Muslim Mindanao.
Legacy
Captain Esnairah Macabato Lucman's legacy is still being written, but its outlines are already clear.
She's changed how women and children in Lanao del Sur and Marawi City experience the PNP. She's built
structures for youth protection and victim reporting that will outlast any single posting. And she's shown that
policing in the BARMM doesn't have to choose between effectiveness and cultural sensitivity.
In a region that has seen more than its share of institutional failure, she represents something more durable:
institutional trust, earned one community at a time.

title: Lucman, Halil Al Rashid
text:
PAGE 1
Atty. Halil Al Rashid Lucman
Personal Information
Born: Lanao del Sur, Philippines
Nationality: Filipino
Religion: Islam
Ethnicity: Maranao
Education
Bachelor of Laws (LL.B.)
Philippine Bar Examination Passer
Profession
Lawyer
Civil Servant
Agricultural Technocrat
Government Service
Halil Al Rashid Lucman
Atty. Halil Al Rashid Lucman is a Filipino lawyer, civil
servant, and agricultural technocrat who has spent more than
three decades as a senior director at the National Food
Authority (NFA), the Philippine government agency
responsible for food supply stabilization and grain regulation.
He is a son of Haroun Al-Rashid Lucman, the Sultan of
Bayang and Sultan Paramount of MINSUPALA who also
served as Congressman of Lanao del Sur, and Princess
Tarhata Alonto-Lucman, the first female Governor of Lanao
del Sur.
Atty. Lucman represents a distinct archetype within the
Bangsamoro narrative: a scion of Maranao royalty who chose
institutional civil service over partisan politics, planting his
career in the mechanics of national food policy rather than the
volatility of regional electoral contests.
EARLY LIFE AND ARISTOCRATIC
ROOTS
Atty. Halil Al Rashid Lucman was born into one of the most
storied political and royal dynasties in the Muslim south.
His father, Haroun Al-Rashid Lucman (June 23, 1924 – July
21, 1984), was a man of remarkable range: a World War II
guerrilla commander, a journalist, a Congressman of Lanao
del Sur (1965–1969), the Sultan of Bayang, and eventually
the Sultan Paramount of MINSUPALA — a royal title
encompassing Mindanao, Sulu, and Palawan — which was
conferred upon him in 1974.<ref>Bantayog ng mga Bayani.
"Haroun Al Rashid Lucman." bantayogngmgabayani.org.
</ref>
His mother, Princess Tarhata Alonto-Lucman (June 26, 1926
– February 26, 2021), was a pioneering political figure in her
own right — the first woman ever to govern the province of
Lanao del Sur, serving as its Governor beginning in 1971.
<ref>GMA News Online. "Princess Tarhata Alonto Lucman,
1st woman governor of Lanao del Sur, dies." February 26,
2021.</ref>
Through his mother, Atty. Lucman is a direct grandson of
Sultan Alauya Alonto of Ramain, a towering figure of the
early Philippine Commonwealth who served as the first

PAGE 2
Director, Business Regulation Department
— National Food Authority (NFA)
Director, Industry Services Department —
National Food Authority (NFA)
Family
Father: Haroun Al-Rashid Lucman (Sultan
of Bayang; Sultan Paramount of
MINSUPALA; Congressman, Lanao del Sur)
Mother: Princess Tarhata Alonto-Lucman
(first female Governor of Lanao del Sur)
Maternal Grandfather: Sultan Alauya
Alonto of Ramain (first Muslim senator,
Philippine Commonwealth)
Maternal Uncles: Senator Ahmad Domocao
Alonto; Gov. and Ambassador Abdul Gaffur
Madki Alonto
Sibling: Haroun Al-Rashid Alonto Lucman
Jr. (former ARMM Vice Governor)
Notability
Maranao royal turned national technocrat; long-
serving NFA Director and food security policy
advocate
Known For
Over three decades of service at the National
Food Authority
Regulatory and licensing enforcement in
grain trading
Post-harvest grain management and surplus
preservation
Advocacy for systemic reforms in Philippine
agricultural policy
Representing Bangsamoro professionals in
national governance
Pull Quote
Muslim senator of the Commonwealth Government and as a
delegate to the 1934 Constitutional Convention.
<ref>Wikipedia. "Alauya Alonto." en.wikipedia.org.</ref>
His maternal uncles carried the family's tradition of public
service forward in equally impressive ways.
Senator Ahmad Domocao Alonto — Tarhata's eldest brother
— served as a Senator of the Philippines (1955–1961), and
later as a delegate to the 1971 Constitutional Convention and
as a commissioner of the 1986 Philippine Constitutional
Commission; he is widely credited as the legislative architect
of the Mindanao State University system.<ref>Wikipedia.
"Domocao Alonto." en.wikipedia.org.</ref>
His other uncle, Abdul Gaffur Madki Alonto, served both as
Governor of Lanao del Sur and as an Ambassador, adding
diplomatic achievement to the family's already formidable
public record.<ref>Wikipedia. "Tarhata Alonto-Lucman."
en.wikipedia.org.</ref>
Growing up inside this layered world of sultanic authority and
democratic politics, Atty. Lucman absorbed an early
education in what governance actually costs — and what it's
for.
FAMILY CONTEXT AND MARTIAL
LAW EXILE
The decade of the 1970s hit the Lucman-Alonto family hard.
When Ferdinand Marcos declared Martial Law in September
1972, Princess Tarhata — by then a sitting Governor —
became a vocal critic of the dictatorship, openly encouraging
Moro youth activism and supporting the push for autonomy.
<ref>Wikipedia. "Tarhata Alonto-Lucman." en.wikipedia.org.
</ref>
Marcos removed her from office in 1975.
Her husband, Congressman Rashid Lucman, had already
distinguished himself as a thorn in Marcos's side — it was
Lucman who, from the floor of Congress in 1968, called for
the impeachment of Marcos over the state-sponsored Jabidah
massacre, in which 68 Tausug military recruits were
massacred.<ref>Wikipedia. "Rashid Lucman."
en.wikipedia.org.</ref>
The family ultimately went into exile in Saudi Arabia, where
Rashid Lucman continued his opposition work until his death
in Riyadh in 1984.

PAGE 3
"State interventions must directly benefit local
farmers — not intermediaries."
This formative experience — living through political
dispossession, royal displacement, and exile — shaped how
Atty. Halil understood the relationship between law, power,
and the protection of vulnerable communities.
Among the children of Rashid and Tarhata, his sibling Haroun Al-Rashid Alonto Lucman Jr. later entered electoral
politics, winning election as Vice Governor of the Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (ARMM) in both
2013 and 2016, serving until the region was reconstituted as the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim
Mindanao (BARMM) following the 2019 plebiscite.<ref>Fandom Military History Wiki. "Rashid Lucman."
military-history.fandom.com.</ref>
Atty. Halil, by contrast, chose a different road entirely.
LEGAL EDUCATION AND BAR PASSAGE
Atty. Lucman is among the pioneering graduates of the Mindanao State University (MSU) in Marawi City — the
very institution his maternal uncle, Senator Ahmad Domocao Alonto, helped legislate into existence.
That connection is worth pausing on.
Senator Domocao Alonto authored the charter that established MSU in 1957. The university was formally
organized on September 1, 1961, opened its first classes on June 13, 1962, and held its inaugural commencement
exercises on April 26, 1966.<ref>MSU-IIT Official Facebook Page. "56th Commencement Ceremonies — First
Semester Graduation Issue of the IITians." facebook.com/MSUIITPH.</ref><ref>Mindanao State University Main
Campus. "About MSU." msumain.edu.ph.</ref>
Atty. Lucman's place among its pioneering batch of graduates means the family didn't just build the institution —
they sent their own through it.
He pursued a degree in law at MSU and went on to pass the Philippine Bar Examination, earning the right to
practice as a licensed attorney in the Philippines.
The specific year of his bar passage is not available in the source record, but his credentials are well-established
through his long-standing professional designation as Atty. and his recognized standing as a lawyer-official within
the NFA — confirmed in published news accounts identifying him as "Lawyer Halil Al Rashid Lucman, director of
NFA's Industry Services Department."<ref>GMA News Online. "NFA audit team to probe reported rice
anomalies." July 2010. gmanetwork.com.</ref>
CAREER AT THE NATIONAL FOOD AUTHORITY
The career of Atty. Lucman is, in many ways, the story of a man who decided to master one of the most
unglamorous but consequential corners of Philippine governance: making sure the country has enough rice, that the
rice is safe, and that the people profiting from grain don't game the system.
That's no small thing in a country where food security has historically been both a political flashpoint and an
economic lever.

PAGE 4
Regulatory Leadership: Business Regulation Department
In the late 2000s, Atty. Lucman served as Director of the NFA's Business Regulation Department.
The work was as technical as it sounds — and as critical.
In this role, he led the legal and operational framework governing grain trading across the country: private sector
licensing, anti-smuggling task forces, and the enforcement mechanisms that kept the grain supply chain from being
captured by unscrupulous intermediaries.
The timing was particularly consequential. The global food crisis of 2008 sent rice prices soaring worldwide. Atty.
Lucman was a key institutional voice during the multi-sectoral negotiations that followed, as the government
scrambled to calibrate rice import tariff policies to shield Filipino consumers from price shocks.
Post-Harvest Management: Industry Services Department
He later served as Director of the NFA's Industry Services Department, a role that shifted his focus from
enforcement to operations.
This meant warehouse management, post-harvest surplus preservation, and grain recovery logistics — the less
visible but foundational work of actually keeping national rice stocks intact.
GMA News reported him in this capacity during a 2010 controversy over rice anomalies at the NFA, when he
publicly addressed questions about the condition of the agency's stored grain reserves, describing himself as "hurt"
by the allegations being raised against the NFA.<ref>GMA News Online. "NFA audit team to probe reported rice
anomalies." July 2010. gmanetwork.com.</ref>
It was a moment that captured something consistent about his career: he's been, throughout, the kind of official
who shows up to defend the institution when it's under fire — not by deflecting responsibility, but by engaging the
substance head-on.
During major calamities, he was also tasked with managing post-typhoon grain recovery strategies, ensuring that
weather-damaged harvests were processed and preserved to the maximum extent possible.
PHILOSOPHY AND POLICY STANCE
Atty. Lucman isn't one to keep his views on agricultural policy abstract.
He has consistently argued that state interventions in food supply — import tariffs, price floors, licensing regimes
— must be designed to directly benefit local farmers, not the traders and middlemen who stand between the farmer
and the consumer.
He has been openly critical of policy reforms that stripped the NFA of its enforcement powers or disrupted local
farm-gate pricing mechanisms, arguing that such changes effectively abandoned the rural poor in favor of market
convenience.
Underneath the technocratic language, there's a philosophy at work here that draws from deep Maranao roots:
Maratabat — the concept of dignity, honor, and collective responsibility — filtered through the lens of
administrative accountability.

PAGE 5
In that sense, Atty. Lucman doesn't separate his cultural formation from his professional practice. The two, for him,
seem to be the same project: protecting people who deserve protection, through whatever institutional tools are
available.
CULTURAL SIGNIFICANCE
Within Bangsamoro history, the figure of the royal politician has long been the dominant archetype: the sultan who
becomes a congressman, the datu who runs for governor.
Atty. Halil Al Rashid Lucman represents something different — and arguably more durable.
He is a member of the Lucman-Alonto dynasty who chose the merit-based terrain of the national civil service over
the patronage networks of regional politics. He didn't just participate in the bureaucracy; he rose to lead major
departments within it, shaping food policy that touched the lives of Filipinos far beyond Lanao.
That choice — sustained over three decades — is its own kind of statement about what Bangsamoro professionals
can do when they bring both legal training and cultural groundedness into national institutions.
His long career at the NFA also illustrates something the broader public rarely recognizes: Moro men and women
have been quietly shaping the national state from within, not just advocating for it from without.
EDITORIAL NOTES
The following factual clarifications are flagged for transparency:
The source document describes Rashid Lucman as "Paramount Sultan of Bayang." More precisely, he was
the Sultan of Bayang and was separately proclaimed Sultan Paramount of MINSUPALA in 1974 — two
distinct honors, not a single compounded title.
The source describes Sultan Alauya Alonto as "the first Muslim nationally elected to the Philippine Senate."
Historical records confirm he was the first Muslim senator of the Philippine Commonwealth Government;
the first Muslim senator in Philippine history overall was Hadji Butu Abdul Bagui (pre-Commonwealth
period). The distinction matters and has been reflected accurately in this article.
The source describes Domocao Alonto as "Constitutional Commissioner Senator" — he did hold both roles
(Senator 1955–1961; 1986 Constitutional Commission member), though not simultaneously. This article
presents his career in its correct sequential context.
Specific dates for Atty. Lucman's birth, educational completion, and bar passage year are not available in the
source record and have not been assumed.

text:

Lucman

Saudi Arabia

Haroun al-Rashid Lucman
Sultan Haroun al-Rashid Lucman (June 23, 1924 – July 21, 1984)
was a Filipino statesman, World War II guerrilla commander,
journalist, and one of the most consequential figures in the history
of the modern Bangsamoro self-determination movement.
Born into Maranao royal lineage in the municipality of Bayang,
Lanao del Sur, Lucman carried the weight of ancestry and the
ambitions of a people who had never been fully absorbed into the
Philippine state's idea of nationhood. His life traced a remarkable
arc: from a teenage guerrilla fighter in the mountains of Lanao, to a
congressman on the floor of the House of Representatives, to a
revolutionary organizer building networks across Southeast Asia
and the Middle East, to an exile in Riyadh spending his final months
in quiet but determined resistance.
The defining moment of his political career came in March 1968,
when he filed the first formal resolution to impeach President
Ferdinand Marcos following the Jabidah Massacre, the alleged
extrajudicial killing of young Tausug military trainees by Philippine
government operatives. When Congress blocked the move, Lucman
concluded that the existing democratic system was structurally
broken, at least for the Moro people. That conclusion changed the
direction of his life, and arguably changed the direction of
Bangsamoro history.
He is posthumously honored at the Bantayog ng mga Bayani Wall
of Remembrance in Quezon City, recognized as a national
champion of democracy who stood against the Marcos dictatorship
at a time when very few dared to.

13 FURTHER READING
EARLY LIFE AND ETHNIC
AFFILIATION
Haroun al-Rashid Lucman was born on June 23, 1924, in Bayang, a
municipality tucked into the southern shores of Lake Lanao in what
is now Lanao del Sur. He belonged to the Maranao people, one of
the major Muslim ethnolinguistic communities indigenous to the
Lake Lanao region of Mindanao, a group known historically for
their warrior tradition, their intricate artistic heritage, and their
fierce resistance to outside domination.
His family background was not ordinary. Through the salsila (the
traditional genealogical record maintained by Maranao royal
houses), Lucman's ancestry traced back to two foundational figures:
Sharif Kabungsuan, the 16th-century Islamic missionary credited
with bringing Islam to mainland Mindanao, and Angintabu, a
daughter of the chieftain of Malabang. This lineage connected him
directly to his father, Sharif Maka-alang, who had inherited the role
of traditional chieftain of their region.
To understand what this ancestry meant in practice: in Maranao society, genealogical legitimacy is not ceremonial.
It confers real authority, shapes political alliances, and determines who gets listened to and who does not. Lucman
grew up knowing exactly who he was in that world, and he would spend the rest of his life deciding how to use it.
FAMILY AND PERSONAL LIFE
Lucman's marriage placed him at the intersection of two of Lanao's most influential families. His wife, Tarhata
Alonto-Lucman, was the daughter of Sultan Alauya Alonto of Ramain, one of the most respected Maranao leaders
of his generation. The union was both personal and political, cementing ties between powerful royal houses at a
time when those alliances still carried tremendous weight in local and national governance.
Tarhata herself was no passive figure. She broke significant ground in 1971 when she was elected Governor of
Lanao del Sur, becoming one of the few women to hold a provincial executive position in Muslim Mindanao at that
time. She stood alongside her husband through his anti-dictatorship campaigns and paid a price for it: Ferdinand
Marcos, after declaring Martial Law, had her unseated from the governorship in 1975.
Their children carried the family's tradition of public service forward. Their son, Haroun Alrashid Alonto Lucman
Jr., later served as Vice Governor of the Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (ARMM).
WORLD WAR II GUERRILLA SERVICE
When the Pacific War reached the Philippines and American and Filipino forces formally surrendered to the
Japanese Imperial Army in 1942, Haroun al-Rashid Lucman was still a young man. He had enlisted in the United
States Armed Forces in the Far East (USAFFE) before the fall, but surrender was not something he was prepared to
accept.

PAGE 3
Rather than lay down his arms, Lucman retreated into the mountains of Lanao and began organizing what would
become the first homegrown guerrilla resistance force in Mindanao. He was in his late teens when he did this. The
operations he led against Japanese occupying troops were described as fierce, and his tactical command earned him
a reputation that spread well beyond his home province.
The restored Commonwealth government took notice. In 1944, the 20-year-old Lucman was appointed Deputy
Governor of Lanao, a post that recognized both his wartime contributions and his traditional standing in the region.
He held the position until 1949. It was an extraordinary level of trust placed in an extraordinarily young man, and it
set the tone for a career that would move between formal governance and unconventional resistance for the next
four decades.
MEDIA AND CIVIL CAREER
When his term as Deputy Governor ended in 1949, Lucman made a notable pivot. He moved into journalism,
taking up work as a Mindanao correspondent for the Manila Chronicle. In a pre-television era when the print media
was the primary channel for shaping public opinion in Manila, the role gave him a platform to document what was
actually happening in the Muslim south: the post-war dislocation, the land disputes, the persistent economic
marginalization that Manila's reconstruction priorities tended to overlook.
He held that post until returning to civil service in 1959, when he was appointed as Regional Development Officer
of the Commission on National Integration (CNI) in Marawi City. The CNI was a government agency established
to address the socioeconomic conditions of the country's cultural minorities, including the Bangsamoro
communities of Mindanao. Lucman served in this capacity until 1961, working within the system to advocate for
the welfare of his people, even as his confidence in that system was gradually eroding.
LEGISLATIVE CAREER AND THE IMPEACHMENT OF MARCOS
In 1961, Lucman re-entered electoral politics and won a seat in the House of Representatives, representing the lone
district of Lanao del Sur under the Liberal Party. He served two consecutive terms as congressman, from 1961 to
1969.
His years in Congress were, by most accounts, those of a principled and engaged legislator. But the defining
moment of his legislative career, the one that would shape the rest of his life, came in March 1968 following the
Jabidah Massacre.
The massacre involved the alleged execution of young Tausug men, recruited as military trainees by Philippine
government operatives and covertly trained to infiltrate Sabah as part of a project to press Manila's territorial
claims. When the trainees balked at the mission and attempted to escape, government forces allegedly killed most
of them. Exact figures remained disputed, but the shock among Muslim Filipinos was immediate and profound.
Here was state violence directed at Muslim men serving the state's own covert agenda.
Congressman Lucman responded with a resolution to impeach President Ferdinand Marcos. It was the first formal
impeachment attempt against Marcos in Philippine history.
The Marcos-aligned majority in Congress killed the resolution. But the experience of filing it, of watching the
democratic machinery absorb the blow and continue running without consequence, was clarifying for Lucman. He
concluded that the Philippine state's democratic institutions were structurally incapable of delivering justice for the
Moro people. That conclusion did not arrive as despair. It arrived as a decision.

PAGE 4
INSTITUTIONAL CONTRIBUTIONS AND REVOLUTIONARY
LEADERSHIP
Having exhausted his faith in constitutional remedies, Lucman founded the Bangsamoro Liberation Organization
(BMLO), an organization openly committed to campaigning for an independent Moro republic. The BMLO was
distinctive from the start: it was rooted in traditional Maranao aristocratic authority and Islamic conservatism, and
it operated as much through diplomacy and coalition-building as through armed preparation.
Lucman leveraged his stature aggressively in the international arena. He traveled extensively to Muslim-majority
nations to secure funding and military training for the Moro cause, finding particularly receptive partners in
Malaysia, where the government's own standoff with Manila over the Sabah dispute made support for Moro
independence both principled and geopolitically convenient.
He facilitated the transit of young Muslim recruits to undergo guerrilla warfare training in Malaysia. Among the
men he personally recruited for this initial group was a young University of the Philippines lecturer named Nur
Misuari, who would later break away to found the Moro National Liberation Front (MNLF) and become the
dominant figure of the armed Moro revolution during the Martial Law years.
From 1968 to 1972, Lucman also chaired the Union of Islamic Forces and Organizations and presided over the
Supreme Revolutionary Council, bodies that sought to coordinate the fragmented landscape of Moro resistance into
a unified front. The BMLO eventually merged its tactical operations with Misuari's MNLF, though the alliance was
always an uneasy one and would not hold.
ROYAL SUCCESSION AND TRADITIONAL LEADERSHIP
In 1974, with Mindanao convulsed by military operations and thousands of Moro civilians displaced, the traditional
royal houses convened to consolidate Bangsamoro leadership under a single recognized authority. Lucman was
formally enthroned as the Second Paramount Sultan of Mindanao and Sulu.
He used this platform immediately and pointedly. Wielding the full symbolic weight of the sultanate title, he issued
a formal proclamation rejecting Philippine sovereignty over the Bangsamoro homeland and demanding absolute
self-rule for the Bangsamoro people. The move was as much a statement of legitimacy as it was of defiance:
Lucman was saying, in effect, that the authority of the sultanates predated the Philippine republic and was not
extinguished by it.
TACTICAL AND IDEOLOGICAL DIFFERENCES: BMLO VS.
MNLF
Sultan Haroun al-Rashid Lucman's BMLO and Nur Misuari's MNLF both emerged from the same post-Jabidah
Massacre resistance impulse. Lucman even personally financed and facilitated the Malaysia training that produced
Misuari's foundational "Top 90" fighters. But the two organizations splintered rapidly, driven by fundamentally
different ideas about who should lead the Bangsamoro struggle and what it was ultimately for.
The core tension was ideological. The BMLO sought to anchor the Moro cause within the historical legitimacy of
the traditional sultanates. For Lucman, the royal houses and traditional datus were the rightful custodians of
Bangsamoro governance. Their authority was not a relic but a living institution, grounded in genealogy, Islamic
tradition, and centuries of recognized rule.

PAGE 5
Misuari saw it very differently. Influenced by Marxist frameworks, he viewed the traditional datu system as feudal
and as itself complicit in the historical marginalization of ordinary Muslims. The MNLF promoted an egalitarian
social order where royal titles carried no political weight. Rather than emphasizing Islamic identity as a primary
frame, Misuari focused on forging a unified "Moro" identity built around the shared historical experience of
resisting Spanish, American, and Filipino colonization across all Muslim communities, regardless of class or
lineage.
The tactical approaches also diverged sharply. Lucman's BMLO prioritized geopolitical diplomacy, international
coalition-building, and selective armed defense, seeking to force the Philippine state to the negotiating table for
genuine autonomy. Misuari's MNLF pursued total guerrilla war aimed at full secession, rejecting collaboration with
Christian politicians or mainstream opposition figures.
The following table summarizes the key distinctions between the two organizations:

The MNLF's capacity for sustained mass armed mobilization ultimately gave it dominance on the ground during
the Martial Law years, eclipsing the BMLO as the primary armed face of the Moro revolution. But the two
organizations represented genuinely different visions for Bangsamoro society, not merely competing factions
within the same movement.
EXILE AND THE ANTI-MARTIAL LAW MOVEMENT
When Marcos declared Martial Law in September 1972, Lucman became an immediate target. In 1976, after years
of operating under increased danger, he evaded state forces and fled into self-exile in Saudi Arabia. He settled in
Riyadh.
From there, he did not stop. He directed international resistance networks, maintained communication with
underground operations inside Mindanao, and provided welfare support for thousands of displaced Moro refugees
who had fled the war at home. Exile, for Lucman, was a base of operations, not a retreat.
He also expanded his coalition. In the United States, he linked up with Christian and secular anti-Marcos
opposition groups, forging the kind of broad-front alliances that his BMLO philosophy had always favored. In
1984, he was elected Vice-President of the Ninoy Aquino Movement (NAM) in San Francisco, California. His final
months were spent working to bring together the Bangsamoro independence movement, the mainstream
democratic opposition represented by the Aquino network, and the underground left-wing resistance inside the
Philippines.

PAGE 6
COLLABORATION WITH NINOY AQUINO IN EXILE
Sultan Haroun al-Rashid Lucman and Senator Benigno "Ninoy" Aquino Jr. built one of the more consequential
political alliances of the Marcos opposition era. Both men were in exile, both recognized Marcos's Martial Law
regime as the immediate common enemy, and both understood that defeating it would require a coalition broader
than any single movement could provide. They found in each other what the other lacked: Lucman brought the
weight of Islamic tradition, royal legitimacy, and deep Middle Eastern connections; Aquino brought the prestige of
mainstream Philippine democratic opposition and international media attention.
The Taif Summit and Saudi Diplomacy
In July 1981, Lucman and his nephew Atty. Macapanton "Jun" Abbas Jr., who served as Secretary-General of the
BMLO, pulled off what can only be described as a diplomatic coup for the anti-Marcos cause. Drawing on
Lucman's status as Paramount Sultan and his extensive contacts in the Arab world, they arranged for Ninoy Aquino
to travel from Boston to Saudi Arabia and secured him an audience with King Khaled of Saudi Arabia in the city of
Taif.
Getting that meeting required bypassing active protests from the Philippine Embassy, which did everything it could
to prevent Aquino from gaining a reception in a country where the Marcos government had significant diplomatic
standing. Lucman's connections were strong enough to make it happen anyway.
The significance of the Taif meeting was substantial on multiple levels. For Aquino personally, being received by a
sitting head of state elevated his profile from domestic dissident to internationally recognized political figure,
giving him leverage over other U.S.-based opposition leaders. For the broader movement, the meeting opened
conversations about using Saudi Arabia's geopolitical influence and oil leverage as pressure on the Marcos
administration to restore democratic institutions and respect Muslim rights.
The two men also used their time together in exile to negotiate a recalibrated vision for the Bangsamoro struggle.
Lucman had previously demanded full secession. Aquino persuaded him that a post-Marcos democratic
government would be prepared to offer genuine, constitutional regional autonomy within a sovereign Philippine
republic. This blueprint would later form the ideological foundation that Aquino's widow, President Corazon
Aquino, used to establish the Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (ARMM) under the 1987 Constitution.
The "Marcial Bonifacio" Passport
By 1983, Aquino had resolved to return to the Philippines despite Marcos having revoked his passport and
pressured international airlines to refuse him passage. The problem was practical: he needed travel documents.
Lucman solved it. Using his intelligence and diplomatic network, he obtained a blank Philippine passport through
an operative inside the Philippine Consulate in Jeddah. His team completed the passport under the alias "Marcial
Bonifacio," a name that was not chosen casually.
"Marcial" was a direct reference to Martial Law. "Bonifacio" pointed to Fort Bonifacio, the military detention
facility where Aquino had been imprisoned for nearly eight years. The name was a small act of defiance folded into
a travel document.
That passport, prepared by Lucman's network, was the document Benigno Aquino Jr. carried in his pocket when he
boarded his flight back to Manila on August 21, 1983. He was assassinated on the tarmac of Manila International
Airport shortly after landing. The assassination, and the public outrage that followed, ultimately set in motion the
events that would bring down the Marcos dictatorship three years later.

PAGE 7
DEATH AND POSTHUMOUS RECOGNITION
The assassination of Ninoy Aquino in August 1983 hit Lucman hard. The two men had been close, and the loss
compounded the toll that years of exile, resistance work, and deteriorating health had already taken. Less than a
year after Aquino's death, on July 21, 1984, Sultan Haroun al-Rashid Lucman died in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia. He
was 60 years old.
He did not live to see the People Power Revolution of February 1986, which ended the Marcos dictatorship and
opened the way for the democratic restoration he had worked toward from exile. But the transition that followed
formally acknowledged his contributions.
Lucman was posthumously inducted into the Bantayog ng mga Bayani (Monument of Heroes) in Quezon City, the
national monument dedicated to Filipinos who resisted the Marcos dictatorship. The inscription on the Wall of
Remembrance recognized him as a national champion of democracy who had fought Martial Law at cost to himself
and his family.
The Grand Lodge of the Philippines also honored his legacy by chartering the Sultan Haroun Al-Rashid M.
Lucman Masonic Lodge No. 406 in Lanao del Sur.
CULTURAL SIGNIFICANCE AND IMPACT
Sultan Haroun al-Rashid Lucman occupies a distinctive place in Philippine history precisely because he refused to
stay in any single lane. He was simultaneously a product of the traditional Maranao aristocracy and a revolutionary
who built transnational resistance networks. He deployed royal legitimacy not to protect privilege but to press
demands the Philippine state had consistently refused to hear.
His legislative battle over the Jabidah Massacre provided the catalytic moment that shifted Muslim political
consciousness, at least in part, away from seeking accommodation within mainstream Manila politics and toward
insisting on substantive autonomy. The trajectory from that 1968 impeachment resolution, through the founding of
the BMLO, through the Aquino alliance, and through the post-Marcos constitutional settlement, is not a straight
line, but it is a line. The ARMM and today's Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM)
carry the imprint of the arguments Lucman was making decades before either existed.
He spent the last years of his life in exile, working to hold a coalition together across enormous ideological
distances, with his health failing and his closest ally freshly murdered. That he kept working is, perhaps, the most
revealing thing about him.

title: Lucman, Jamil Pangadapun
text:
PAGE 1
Jamil Pangadapun Lucman
Jamil Pangadapun Lucman, better known by his legendary nom de guerre Commander Jungle Fox, was one of
the founding commanders of the Moro National Liberation Front (MNLF) and a key figure in the Bangsamoro
struggle for self-determination in the Southern Philippines.
A member of the historic Top 90, the elite cohort of young Moro fighters trained in guerrilla warfare abroad in the
late 1960s, Lucman built his name in the jungles of Lanao, where his tactical genius earned him a reputation that
outlasted the war itself.
He's one of those rare figures who carried a rifle and a gavel in the same lifetime. After years commanding MNLF
forces across Lanao del Sur and del Norte, he transitioned into civilian life as a regional legislator and community
builder, helping thousands of former fighters find their footing as farmers and citizens in the newly autonomous
Bangsamoro.
His story is fundamentally Maranao: shaped by nobility, defined by maratabat, and driven by an unwavering belief
that his people deserved better.
Contents
1 Early Life and Family Roots
2 The Top 90 and Foreign Military Training
3 Commanding the MNLF in Lanao
4 Transition to Peace and Agrarian Reintegration
5 Political Career and Regional Legislation
6 Legacy and Cultural Significance
7 See Also
8 References
9 External Links
Early Life and Family Roots
Jamil Lucman came from the very top of Maranao society. Born into the royal and political aristocracy of Lanao
del Sur, his lineage connected him to traditional clan structures that held real cultural and political weight across
the Lake Lanao region.
His uncle was Sultan Haroun Rashid Lucman, a decorated World War II guerrilla veteran, former Philippine
Congressman, and a paramount traditional leader in Mindanao and Sulu. That's a heavy family legacy to grow up
under, and it clearly left its mark.
Coming of age in an era defined by land dispossession, political marginalization, and simmering resentment toward
Manila, Jamil absorbed his uncle's early radicalization and political worldview. By the late 1960s, he was ready to
act on it.

PAGE 2

He was married to Bae Diamond Tanog Lucman, a prominent
Maranao noblewoman who made the extraordinary decision to
leave comfort and security behind to join her husband in the
underground movement. She's remembered in her own right as a
symbol of resilience and sacrifice in the Bangsamoro struggle.
The Top 90 and Foreign Military
Training
The origin story of the MNLF's military wing begins with a
single shock: the Jabidah Massacre of 1968. When news broke
that Moro recruits had been killed by their own government,
traditional leaders across Muslim Mindanao began quietly
organizing something bigger than protests.
In 1968, Jamil Lucman was selected as part of a historic group of
92 young Moro men, known collectively as the Top 90 or the
Blackshirts. The group included future movement icons like Nur
Misuari and Abul Khayr Alonto.
The cohort was smuggled out of the Philippines and transported
to Malaysia, where they underwent intensive guerrilla warfare
and commando training, primarily on the island of Pangkor and
in the jungles of Sabah. The training was clandestine, backed by
the Malaysian government as strategic leverage during its
ongoing diplomatic dispute with the Philippines over the Sabah
claim.
It was here, and in the early armed skirmishes that followed, that
Jamil earned the name Jungle Fox. The moniker stuck because
he was uncanny in dense terrain, navigating Mindanao's
rainforests to execute ambushes and disappear before
reinforcements arrived.
Commanding the MNLF in Lanao
When the Top 90 returned to the Philippines, they became the
military backbone of the newly formed Moro National Liberation
Front. Lucman was designated a founding member of the MNLF
Central Committee, sitting alongside Misuari, Alonto, and other
pioneer commanders.
The declaration of Martial Law in September 1972 changed
everything. What had been low-intensity guerrilla skirmishes
exploded into full-scale conventional warfare. Commander
Jungle Fox took operational command of MNLF forces across
Lanao del Sur, Lanao del Norte, and adjacent provinces.

PAGE 3
Spouse
Bae Diamond Tanog
Lucman
Relatives
Sultan Haroun Rashid
Lucman (uncle)
His strategy leaned on the geography he knew best. Using the
complex terrain around Lake Lanao to maximum advantage, he
kept large AFP contingents bogged down, denying them the clean
battlefield victories they needed. His forces were fast, elusive,
and deeply familiar with every ridge and valley in the region.
Through the bloodiest years of the 1970s insurgency, he kept the
revolutionary momentum alive in the Lanao sector.
Transition to Peace and Agrarian Reintegration
By the late 1970s and into the early 1980s, Commander Jungle Fox had seen enough. The war's humanitarian cost
on ordinary Maranao civilians was immense, and Lucman knew that continuing to fight was no longer the most
responsible choice.
He entered localized peace dialogues with the national government under President Ferdinand Marcos Sr.,
negotiating through the AFP's Southern Command (SouthCom) under Admiral Romulo Espaldon. Lucman and his
battle-hardened fighters formally returned to civilian life under an amnesty framework, but he didn't just hand over
his arms and walk away.
He used his considerable leverage to secure something structural for his men. The result was Proclamation No.
2046, signed into law in 1981, which legally carved out a substantial tract of public agricultural land on the Kalaga
Plateau, covering the municipalities of Wao and Bumbaran in Lanao del Sur.
Under the administration of the Southern Philippines Development Authority (SPDA), Lucman established the
Kalaga Plateau Agro-Industrial Cooperative Settlement. The initiative successfully transitioned thousands of
former MNLF fighters into self-sustaining agrarian farmers, giving them land, livelihoods, and a reason to stay at
peace. It was, by any measure, one of the most thoughtful rebel reintegration programs the Philippines had seen up
to that point.
Political Career and Regional Legislation
With the creation of the Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (ARMM) following the Tripoli Agreement,
Lucman made his full transition to civilian statecraft.
He ran for office under the Lakas–Ompia party and was elected as an Assemblyman representing the 2nd
District of Lanao del Sur in the 2nd ARMM Regional Legislative Assembly, serving from 1993 to 1996. As a
regional lawmaker, his priorities were clear: veterans' welfare, cultural preservation, and agricultural development.
He consistently pushed the position that any autonomous governance framework must genuinely empower Moro
communities, not just create new layers of administration.
He remained a formidable political kingmaker in the province well into the 2000s, including notable electoral
contests against established post-war political dynasties in gubernatorial races.
Legacy and Cultural Significance
In contemporary Bangsamoro history, Commander Jungle Fox holds a place that's hard to replicate. He represents
what the Top 90 generation stood for at its best: elite privilege set aside, personal safety abandoned, and decades of
one's life given to a cause larger than the self.

PAGE 4
A few specific threads run through his legacy:
Founding Generation Idealism
He's revered as part of the original cohort that built the modern Moro national identity from the ground up, before
the MNLF was a household name, when joining the movement meant real sacrifice.
The Warrior-Statesman Model
Unlike commanders who remained in exile or stayed in perpetual conflict, Lucman demonstrated that a
revolutionary's final duty is the welfare of the people he fought for. His pivot to peace, and the creative
reintegration program he built, is frequently cited as a model for post-conflict transitions.
Maranao Resilience and Maratabat
Alongside his wife Bae Diamond, Lucman's life story appears regularly in regional oral histories and local political
discourse as an example of maratabat, the Maranao concept of honor and dignity, expressed not just through
resistance but through the responsibility to rebuild.

title: Lucman, Macacna Deragun
text:
PAGE 1
Colonel Macacna "Abdulwahid"
Deragun Lucman
Full Name
Macacna "Abdulwahid" Deragun
Lucman
Also Known As
Colonel Lucman; Abdulwahid Lucman
Ethnicity / Community
Bangsamoro (Lanao region)
Education
Bachelor of Arts in Political Science,
University of Manila (1969)
Military Branch
Philippine Constabulary (PC) /
Philippine National Police (PNP),
Armed Forces of the Philippines
Macacna Deragun Lucman
Colonel Macacna "Abdulwahid" Deragun Lucman was a Filipino Muslim military and police officer who
served in the Philippine Constabulary (PC) and the Philippine National Police (PNP) across a career spanning 27
years. Born into a Mindanao shaped by cultural pride, political tension, and armed conflict, he rose through the
ranks on the strength of competitive achievement, battlefield grit, and a deep sense of duty to both his institution
and his community.
He is remembered not only for his decorated combat record but for something rarer: the kind of quiet, persistent
leadership that showed up after the firefights, in the barangay halls, the college campuses, and the crowded alleys
of the city, long after most soldiers had hung up their boots.
Contents
1 BACKGROUND
2 EDUCATION
3 MILITARY AND POLICE CAREER
3.1 Entry and Commission
3.2 Combat Years in Mindanao
3.3 Capital Command (CAPCOM)
3.4 Provincial Directorships
4 DECORATIONS AND AWARDS

5.1 The 1976 Hostage Recovery
5.2 MSU Marawi Campus Stabilization (1997)
5.3 Islamic Center, Manila
6 FAMILY
7 CIVIC AND FRATERNAL LIFE
8 LEGACY
9 EDITORIAL NOTES
10 SEE ALSO
11 REFERENCES
BACKGROUND
Colonel Lucman came of age at a time when Mindanao was
anything but quiet. The region was in the thick of decades of
conflict, with Moro communities caught between armed
movements, state military operations, and the everyday pressures of
living under policies that did not always reflect their realities.
Growing up Bangsamoro in that environment meant carrying a
particular kind of weight, one that demanded both cultural
rootedness and a willingness to engage with larger national
institutions.

PAGE 2

Constabulary (1970)

(date unverified)
Notability

to serve as Director for Logistics at the
Capital Command (CAPCOM) since its
activation in 1967; decorated combat
veteran with 13 years of active duty in
Mindanao and the Sulu Archipelago;
community peacekeeper at Manila's
Islamic Center post-retirement
Known For
Bridging Bangsamoro military service
and civilian community work; leading
the bloodless recovery of a kidnapped
MSU director in 1976; maintaining
order at MSU Marawi (1997) and at
He chose engagement. Rather than turn away from the Philippine
state, he moved toward it, not in spite of who he was, but very much
as who he was: a Muslim man from Mindanao who believed that
service and community were not in conflict with each other.
That posture, principled participation in a system that was imperfect
and sometimes hostile, would define everything he did over the next
several decades.
EDUCATION
Lucman earned his Bachelor of Arts in Political Science from the
University of Manila in 1969. The choice of discipline was fitting:
political science is, at its core, the study of power, governance, and
the relationship between citizens and the state. For a young
Bangsamoro man navigating a country with deep questions about
who belongs and who gets to lead, it was the right lens.
His years at the University of Manila also planted the roots of
fraternal connections that would last a lifetime. He became a life
member of the Alpha Phi Omega fraternity (Tau Chapter), a service-
oriented organization with deep ties to the scouting movement, as
well as Kappa Beta Phi.
MILITARY AND POLICE CAREER
Entry and Commission
In 1970, just a year after finishing his degree, Lucman took on one
of the most competitive entry points into the Philippine military
establishment: the qualifying examination for Regular Officers in
the Philippine Constabulary (PC), then an arm of the Armed Forces
of the Philippines (AFP). It was a punishing field. Over 800
applicants sat for the exam nationwide. Only 114 passed. Lucman
ranked No. 20 among them.
That ranking earned him a commission as a 2nd Lieutenant in the
PC, and with it, the start of a career that would take him from the
jungles of Mindanao to the halls of the Capital Command in Taguig.

PAGE 3
Manila's Islamic Center during his
retirement years
Combat Years in Mindanao
For 13 years, Lucman served in active combat roles across some of
the most volatile provinces in the country: Central Mindanao, Tawi-Tawi, Basilan, Sulu, and Zamboanga City.
These were not desk postings. The Moro insurgency was at its peak in the 1970s and early 1980s, and officers like
Lucman were deployed into situations where the margin between life and death was thin.
His record from this period includes direct combat engagements against armed groups, hostage recovery
operations, and extended deployments in areas where ambushes were a routine hazard.
What made his position unusual, and in many ways remarkable, was that he was a Muslim officer serving in
operations that were often directed against Moro armed factions. That was not a simple thing to navigate. It
required a clear sense of institutional duty alongside a personal compass that kept him grounded in who he was.
Capital Command (CAPCOM)
Later in his career, Lucman was assigned to the Capital Command (CAPCOM) at Camp Bicutan, Taguig, one of
the more prestigious postings within the AFP structure. There he served on the general staff as Director for
Logistics, a senior administrative and operational role.
The significance of that appointment goes beyond the title. He became the first Muslim officer in recent memory to
hold that position since CAPCOM's activation in 1967. In an institution that has historically been dominated by
officers from other parts of the country and other faith communities, that milestone mattered: not as a token, but as
evidence that Bangsamoro professionals could and did reach the upper tiers of the national security apparatus.
Provincial Directorships
His regional assignments included serving as Provincial Director for the Lanao del Sur PNPO, based at Camp
Bagong Amai Pakpak in Marawi City, and later as Provincial Director in Maguindanao. These were leadership
postings in provinces where the PNP's role was layered and complicated: keeping peace in communities still raw
from decades of armed conflict, navigating relationships between state forces, local government, and Moro
constituencies.
He also served as Regional Adjutant for Regional Command 9 (RECOM 9) in Zamboanga City from 1981 to 1982,
an administrative and coordination role that recognized his organizational competence as much as his field
experience.
Earlier, in 1981, he served as Chief of Police in Malabang, Lanao del Sur, maintaining civil order during the final
years of martial law. That posting coincided with active operations by the 25th Infantry Battalion, and his role was
to keep the community from fracturing further under that pressure.
DECORATIONS AND AWARDS
Colonel Lucman's award record reflects both his courage in the field and his effectiveness in administrative
command. Key decorations include:
Bronze Cross Medal

PAGE 4
Awarded for heroism during a 1980 encounter with armed terrorists in Barangay Lower Kidama, Parang,
Maguindanao.
Military Merit Medal with Spear Device (twice)
Awarded twice for bravery in combat: first for actions against armed groups in Basilan in 1983, and earlier
for actions against the Tonda Force in Lanao del Sur in 1972.
Military Merit Medal with Anahaw Leaf (twice)
Awarded twice for administrative excellence during his service as Regional Adjutant in RECOM 9,
Zamboanga City (1981-1982).
Wounded Military Personnel Medal
Received following his 1972 engagement against the Tonda Force in Lanao del Sur, where he sustained
combat injuries.
Kagitingan Badge as Commander
Recognized his leadership under fire.
Campaign Ribbons
He carried ribbons for the Sulu Campaign, Mindanao Campaign, and anti-dissident operations, along with
various commendations and plaques from different commands.
KEY ACCOMPLISHMENTS
The 1976 Hostage Recovery
One of the most dramatic episodes in Lucman's career came in 1976, when Mindanao State University director
Eduardo Ulindang was kidnapped. Lucman led the recovery operation and secured Ulindang's safe release without
the payment of any ransom. In a period when such situations routinely ended badly or dragged on indefinitely, that
outcome stood out. It reflected not just tactical skill but the kind of trust and community intelligence that only
comes from an officer who is genuinely known and respected in the region.
MSU Marawi Campus Stabilization (1997)
Decades later, in 1997, Lucman was called on again when unrest broke out on the main campus of Mindanao State
University in Marawi City. He helped restore peace and order on campus, a role that drew on both his authority and
his standing as someone the Marawi community recognized as one of their own.
Islamic Center, Manila
From the late 1990s onward, one of Lucman's most sustained contributions was in Quiapo's Islamic Center in
Manila, a dense, historically significant migrant community that had been established in the 1960s by prominent
Moro leaders as a base for students and families from Mindanao and Sulu coming to the capital.
By the time Lucman became a fixture there, the area had grown complex and difficult: overcrowded, under-
resourced, and increasingly touched by drug trafficking and other forms of disorder. He moved in not as a passive
presence but as an active force for stability, pushing back against drug lords and criminal networks, enforcing
community discipline, and working to make the enclave cleaner and more orderly.

PAGE 5
Accounts from the community describe him as someone who clashed directly with criminal elements, willing to
put himself in the middle of dangerous situations even in retirement. He kept at it until his health began to fail.
FAMILY
He married Bae Norhaina Macabato Alonto, who served as Barangay Chairwoman of Barangay 648 (Zone 67,
District VI, Manila), the barangay that encompasses the Islamic Center. Her community leadership complemented
his; together, they represented a kind of dual presence in a migrant enclave that needed both security and civic
stewardship.
The Alonto name carries significant weight in Bangsamoro political and social history, and Bae Norhaina's
community work in Manila kept those connections alive in an urban setting far from Mindanao.
CIVIC AND FRATERNAL LIFE
Beyond his military affiliations, Lucman maintained a wide network of fraternal and civic memberships throughout
his life. In addition to Alpha Phi Omega and Kappa Beta Phi from his university years, he held life membership in:
LAMUSPROF (Lanao Muslim Professionals), connecting him to the network of Maranao and Lanao-origin
professionals across the country
Bayang United Youth Fraternity, a fraternal organization with roots in the Bangsamoro community
Crossed Swords Fraternity, an exclusive organization for AFP officer candidates and officers
In 1988, he joined the Free and Accepted Masons of the Philippines, specifically Lodge No. 148 Noli Me
Tangere in Ermita, Manila. His membership in Masonry, alongside his identity as a practicing Muslim, reflects the
kind of pluralist engagement that characterized his whole life: building bridges across different traditions without
abandoning his own.
LEGACY
Colonel Lucman's life resists easy categorization. He was a Muslim military man who served loyally in institutions
that were sometimes in tension with Moro communities. He was a decorated combat officer who spent as much of
his energy on civic peacekeeping as on battlefield operations. He was a Mindanaoan who became a fixture in
Manila's most prominent Muslim community.
What ties it all together is a consistent commitment to order, dignity, and community: not order imposed from
outside, but the kind built from inside, by someone who understood the people he served and who they were.
His path, from a top-ranking PC examiner to provincial director to neighborhood guardian, illustrates something
the broader story of the Philippines too often overlooks: the role that Bangsamoro professionals have played in
building and maintaining the country's institutions, often at great personal cost, and often without the recognition
those contributions deserve.

PAGE 6
His medals capture the risks. His legacy lives in the communities that are safer, more stable, and more dignified
because he was there.

Muhammad Amin Jammal Khan Lucman
Datu Muhammad Amin Jammal Khan Lucman, widely known
as "Magic," is a Filipino Muslim corporate leader and public
servant who has made significant contributions to
telecommunications infrastructure development and humanitarian
service in Mindanao. As Area Sales Manager of DITO
Telecommunity Corporation, he oversees strategic operations
across multiple provinces in Northern Mindanao and manages
service delivery for millions of subscribers while championing
digital inclusion in underserved communities. His legacy is
defined by a rare combination of corporate excellence and
frontline courage—particularly during the 2017 Siege of Marawi,
where he left his corporate role to serve as a rescuer, and through
his pioneering work bringing telecommunications infrastructure to
conflict-affected areas.
Contents
1 Early Life and Background
2 Telecommunications Career
2.1 Early Years with DITO
2.2 Pioneering Work in Marawi City
2.3 Current Role and Responsibilities
3 Public Service and Humanitarian Work
3.1 The Siege of Marawi
