(KAS)
Ali Macabalang
Ali G. Macabalang is a veteran Filipino journalist, columnist, and
peace advocate whose name has become almost synonymous with
serious, sustained reporting on the Bangsamoro people and their long
struggle for self-determination. Over a career spanning almost five
decades (he is currently on his 48th year in the media profession), he has
served as the primary chronicler of the Bangsamoro peace process, the
transformation of regional governance in Muslim Mindanao, and the
living culture and identity of Muslim Filipinos in the southern
Philippines. His peers and readers have long called him the "Mindanao
Voice," a title earned not through self-promotion but through an
unyielding presence in stories that most national media either
overlooked or parachuted into briefly. Macabalang stayed. He reported
from the inside, and that commitment to staying, to being rooted in the
communities he covered, has defined every chapter of his life's work.
Contents
1 Early Life and Cultural Roots
2 Professional Career
2.1 The Manila Bulletin and Major Bylines
2.2 Covering the Peace Process
2.3 Regional Commission to BARMM: Tracking the Transition
2.4 The Marawi Siege
3 Notable Achievements and Recognition
4 Personal Values and Cultural Significance
5 Academic and Policy Contributions
6 Legacy
7 Further Reading
8 See Also
Early Life and Cultural Roots
Macabalang's exact birthdate isn't widely documented in public records, which is fitting for a journalist who has
always found the story more interesting than the storyteller. What the record makes clear is that he is deeply rooted
in the Lanao and Maguindanao regions of Mindanao, and that rootedness has never been incidental to his
journalism. It has been the foundation of it.
He identifies as a Muslim Filipino, and his reporting reflects a lived familiarity with Maranao and Maguindanaon
traditions that goes well beyond surface-level cultural literacy.<ref name="source1">Source material on Ali G.
Macabalang, archived profile document.</ref> He didn't cover these communities from the outside looking in. He
reported from within, where the prayers, the genealogies, the political structures, and the grievances of the
Bangsamoro people were things he understood personally, not just professionally.

PAGE 2
He is a product of the Mindanao educational system, and over the years he has written frequently about the need to
strengthen regional education as what he calls the "foundation of BARMM."<ref name="source1" /> That
perspective, at once that of a reporter and an advocate, has made him a sought-after voice in academic and policy
discussions about the Mindanao State University system and educational development in autonomous regions.
Professional Career
Macabalang built his reputation across some of the most dangerous and historically significant decades in the
modern history of the southern Philippines. His career is not a story of ambition climbing a media ladder. It's a
story of commitment to a place and its people, sustained through instability, conflict, and the particular pressures
that come with reporting the truth in volatile regions.
The Manila Bulletin and Major Bylines
He is best known for his long association with the Manila Bulletin (https://mb.com.ph), one of the Philippines'
oldest and most respected newspapers, where he served for decades as a senior correspondent for the Mindanao
bureau.<ref name="source1" /> That posting wasn't a desk assignment. It meant being on the ground during some
of the most consequential moments in southern Philippine history, often as one of the only national-level journalists
present.
His bylines have also appeared in The Manila Times (https://manilatimes.net), the Philippine Daily Inquirer (http
s://inquirer.net), Philippine Muslim Today, and Philippine News Today.<ref name="source1" /> Across these
platforms, his reporting carried Mindanao stories to audiences far beyond the region, ensuring that what happened
in Cotabato, Marawi City, and Maguindanao didn't stay invisible to the rest of the country.
Covering the Peace Process
If there is one subject that defines Macabalang's professional life above all others, it is the Bangsamoro peace
process. He covered the negotiations between the Philippine government and both the Moro Islamic Liberation
Front (MILF) and the Moro National Liberation Front (MNLF) with a depth and consistency that few journalists
matched.<ref name="source1" /> His reporting didn't simply describe what happened at the negotiating table. It
explained what was at stake for the communities living in the shadow of those negotiations, the farmers, the ulama,
the displaced families who had been waiting for peace their entire lives.
Regional Commission to BARMM: Tracking the Transition
Macabalang has followed the long and complicated transition from the Regional Commission (characterized by the
so-called Batasan Pampook and Lupong Tagapagpaganap ng Pook established in 1978 under former President
Ferdinand Marcos Sr.), to the Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (ARMM), and to the Bangsamoro
Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM) with the patience of someone who knows that this story did
not begin with any single law or referendum.<ref name="source1" /> His coverage has helped readers understand
the layered history, competing interests, and questions of identity that make the BARMM project both necessary
and genuinely difficult to get right.

PAGE 3
The Marawi Siege
Perhaps the most dramatic chapter of his career came with the Marawi Siege of 2017, when armed conflict
engulfed Marawi City for five months and displaced hundreds of thousands of residents. Macabalang reported from
the ground during the fighting and continued to cover the slow, painful rehabilitation that followed.<ref
name="source1" /> His on-the-ground presence during the siege, and his sustained attention to what came after the
cameras left, became a model of crisis journalism in the region, one that kept the humanity of the displaced front
and center long after the international news cycle had moved on.
Notable Achievements and Recognition
Macabalang's career has drawn attention not just from readers but from scholars, media institutions, and
humanitarian organizations that study journalism under pressure.
He is a primary subject in the book Invisible Ink: Stories of Muslim Filipino Journalists in Mindanao, which
documents the professional ethics and survival strategies of journalists working in one of the world's most
dangerous environments for media practitioners.<ref name="source1" /> His inclusion in that volume marks him as
a figure whose individual experience captures something larger about the conditions facing Muslim Filipino
reporters in conflict zones.
He has also been recognized for his practice of Peace journalism, an approach that prioritizes de-escalation,
nuance, and giving voice to displaced communities. In the Mindanao context, this has meant centering the accounts
of bakwits (internally displaced persons) and refusing to frame complex political conflicts in ways that serve only
one side of the story.<ref name="source1" />
His reports from the 1980s have been cited in academic journals and in legal and humanitarian documents
produced by organizations including the International Committee of the Red Cross (https://icrc.org) (ICRC), where
they serve as primary sources for regional history and human rights documentation.<ref name="source1" /> That
kind of archival weight is unusual for a working journalist. It speaks to how seriously researchers and institutions
have regarded his firsthand accounts of events that shaped the modern Bangsamoro.
Personal Values and Cultural Significance
What makes Macabalang more than a skilled reporter is the set of values that have guided his work and, in turn,
shaped a generation of younger Mindanao journalists who came after him.
He is a vocal advocate for what he calls "Moral Governance" in the BARMM, the conviction that Islamic piety and
political transparency are not competing values but deeply intertwined ones.<ref name="source1" /> His columns
on this theme have contributed to an ongoing public conversation about what accountable governance should look
like in a Muslim-majority autonomous region, one that doesn't have to choose between its faith and its
responsibilities to its citizens.
Through his writing, Macabalang has worked to preserve the history of the Moro quest for self-rule, ensuring that
this narrative stays in the public record rather than being absorbed and flattened by national historical narratives
that have often marginalized Bangsamoro perspectives.<ref name="source1" /> In his columns and reports, the
names, decisions, and sacrifices of Bangsamoro leaders are treated as history worth remembering.
He is also, in a detail that has taken on near-symbolic significance in Philippine media studies, a reporter who has
carried a firearm for self-defense.<ref name="source1" /> That fact is not a dramatic flourish. (He is a survivor of
an ambush on March 20, 1995 in Cotabato City where he sustained an almost fatal wound in the nape). It is a

PAGE 4
precise description of the conditions under which journalism in Mindanao has had to be practiced, and of the
personal courage that has always been inseparable from Macabalang's professional commitment.
Macabalang's career represents the literal and metaphorical "fighting" for truth in volatile regions, a
phrase used in media scholarship to describe both the physical dangers he has faced and the ethical
weight of the journalism he has consistently produced.
Academic and Policy Contributions
Beyond his daily reporting, Macabalang has functioned as what might be called a "Bridge Researcher," someone
who moves between journalism and scholarship without fully belonging to either, and who makes both disciplines
richer for his presence.<ref name="source1" />
He has regularly synthesized complex regional policies into accessible documents for academic and public
audiences, making the machinery of Bangsamoro governance legible to readers who would otherwise have no way
into the subject. This work of translation, turning policy language into human-scale meaning, has been as important
as his front-line reporting in shaping how the Bangsamoro story has been understood.
His bylines are preserved in the archives of the Institute for Autonomy and Governance (IAG) and the Konrad-
Adenauer-Stiftung (KAS), where they serve as foundational records for researchers studying security,
development, and autonomy in the southern Philippines.<ref name="source1" /> The fact that a journalist's
newspaper articles end up in serious institutional archives is a measure of how thoroughly his work has entered the
historical record, not as context for someone else's analysis, but as primary evidence in its own right.
Legacy
Ali G. Macabalang represents a kind of journalism that has become increasingly rare: the long-term beat reporter
who stays, who accumulates knowledge and trust over decades, and who becomes part of the landscape of the story
he is covering. The Bangsamoro peace process didn't happen only in conference rooms and signed agreements. It
happened in the stories told about it, and Macabalang told more of those stories, with more context, more cultural
grounding, and more sustained courage, than almost anyone else.
His legacy rests on three pillars. He has been a primary documenter of one of the most significant political and
humanitarian transformations in Philippine history. He has modeled a form of Muslim Filipino journalism rooted in
cultural understanding rather than external observation. And he has, through sheer persistence across more than
three decades, helped ensure that the voices of Bangsamoro communities reached audiences that would not
otherwise have heard them.
The "Mindanao Voice" is not a nickname. It is a description of a lifelong commitment to the idea that the
Bangsamoro story deserves to be told with accuracy, dignity, and care.
Further Reading

available sources)

peace process

development

PAGE 5

documentation

title: Macabato, Khaliquzzaman M.
text:
PAGE 1
Khaliquzzaman M. Macabato
Atty. Khaliquzzaman M. Macabato, CPA, CSEE, is a Filipino public health administrator, legal educator, and
certified public accountant who served for over two decades as the PhilHealth Regional Vice President for the
Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM), previously the Autonomous Region in Muslim
Mindanao (ARMM).
He is one of the few Bangsamoro professionals in the country to hold triple qualifications as a lawyer, a Certified
Public Accountant (CPA), and a Career Service Executive Eligible (CSEE), a combination that gave him a rare
institutional edge in navigating the complex intersection of public health governance, fiscal management, and legal
administration.
His career tells a story about what sustained public service can look like in a region that has long been defined by
conflict, underrepresentation, and unmet need. For more than two decades, he worked to extend the reach of social
health insurance to some of the most remote, conflict-affected communities in the Philippines, while
simultaneously mentoring a generation of Bangsamoro lawyers and accountants at the Mindanao State University
(MSU) College of Law in Iligan City.

Early Life and Background
Khaliquzzaman Macabato traces his roots to Mindanao, with strong communal ties to Marawi City and the
surrounding provinces that now form the BARMM.
His name itself carries meaning: "Khaliquzzaman" combines Al-Khaliq (the Creator, one of the 99 Names of Allah
in Islamic tradition) with zaman (Arabic for era or time), a name that speaks to the faith-rooted culture of the
Bangsamoro people.

PAGE 2

Like many Muslim Mindanao professionals of his generation, Macabato
came of age in a region where access to quality education and government
service was not a given. The region's history of armed conflict, political
neglect, and economic marginalization made it all the more significant
when young Bangsamoro men and women chose the path of professional
public service.
Specific biographical details of his birth and early childhood are not on
public record.
Education and Professional Qualifications
Atty. Macabato built his academic and professional credentials across
multiple disciplines, which would define the unusual range of his public
service career.
He earned qualifications as a Certified Public Accountant (CPA) and as
an Attorney-at-Law, two demanding and distinct professional
examinations in the Philippines that together position him in a small,
specialized category of legal-accounting practitioners.
He also holds the distinction of being a Career Service Executive
Eligible (CSEE), the highest civil service eligibility in the Philippines for
senior government executives, qualifying him for Career Executive
Service positions in the bureaucracy.
For advanced professional development in his area of public health
practice, Macabato completed the prestigious Flagship Course on
Sustainable Social Health Insurance at the Asian Institute of
Management (AIM) in Makati City.
This combination of legal training, accounting expertise, and executive
civil service eligibility is what made him particularly effective in a role
that demanded both technical compliance management and high-stakes
policy leadership.
Career
Early Career: Accounting at MSU-General Santos City
(1988–1994)
Macabato began his professional life in the public sector as an Accountant at Mindanao State University (MSU) in
General Santos City, where he served from 1988 to 1994.
This early post grounded him in the fundamentals of government financial management and gave him hands-on
experience with the fiscal demands of a public university serving a diverse, largely underserved student population.

PAGE 3
Legal Education: MSU College of Law (2001–Present)
In May 2001, Macabato took on a parallel role that would run alongside his executive career for decades: he joined
the faculty of the Mindanao State University - Iligan Institute of Technology (MSU-IIT) College of Law in
Iligan City as a Professorial Lecturer, specializing in Taxation Law.
His lectures have covered core areas of Philippine fiscal law, including the National Internal Revenue Code,
income tax, Value Added Tax (VAT), estate taxes, and the provisions of the TRAIN Law (Tax Reform for
Acceleration and Inclusion).
What makes his approach distinctive is what his students describe as the "CPA-lawyer perspective," the ability to
bridge the mathematical and computational rigor of accounting with the doctrinal and interpretive demands of legal
practice.
He's known for clarifying foundational concepts like the Lifeblood Doctrine of taxation (the principle that taxes are
the lifeblood of the government and their prompt collection a paramount duty) in ways that connect legal theory to
real government operations.
Beyond taxation, his portfolio at MSU College of Law has included Commercial Law and Corporate
Governance, drawing from his executive experience at PhilHealth to contextualize how large government-owned
and controlled corporations (GOCCs) operate under the law.
Several of his lectures have been made available online through video platforms, extending his reach beyond the
classroom to aspiring bar reviewees and practicing lawyers across the country.<ref name="msu-youtube">Atty.
Khaliquzzaman Macabato. Taxation Law lectures. Available at: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9QnrduN1yVg
and https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RMxHXJGWNeQ</ref>
PhilHealth ARMM/BARMM: Regional Vice President (2002–2025)
In December 2002, Macabato joined the Philippine Health Insurance Corporation (PhilHealth) and was assigned to
the PhilHealth Regional Office – ARMM (which later became the PhilHealth Regional Office – BARMM
following the ratification of the Bangsamoro Organic Law in 2019).
He would remain in this position for over two decades, becoming the longest-serving regional executive in the
history of PhilHealth's operations in the Bangsamoro region.
As Regional Vice President (RVP), he held authority over the implementation of the National Health Insurance
Program (NHIP) across the provinces and component cities under the region, a mandate that required him to
navigate conditions no other PhilHealth regional executive faced in quite the same way: areas affected by active
armed conflict, fragmented local governance structures, and communities with among the lowest health literacy
and PhilHealth membership rates in the entire country.
"It is truly a privilege for us at PhilHealth Regional Office ARMM to have presented the concrete
testimony of how the government has helped change lives through the PAMANA project. Bringing
social health protection to the most far-flung areas in the country, including conflict-affected and
conflict-vulnerable communities, is another milestone towards realizing PhilHealth's vision of making
bawat Pilipino miyembro, bawat miyembro protektado, kalusugan natin, segurado."
This quote, delivered by Macabato at the 2nd PhilHealth Forward in 2015, reflects the mission that anchored his
tenure: making universal health care a reality even in communities that most of the country had overlooked.<ref
name="philhealth-2015">PhilHealth. "2nd PhilHealth Forward for 2015 Held." Philippine Health Insurance

PAGE 4
Corporation. December 23, 2015. https://www.philhealth.gov.ph/news/2015/2nd_forward.html</ref>
Governance and Procurement Leadership
During his tenure, Macabato led significant modernization efforts within the regional office.
He approved procurement contracts for the upgrading of information technology infrastructure, including desktop
computers, laptops, and flatbed scanners, to digitize member records and improve claims processing in remote
Bangsamoro areas.<ref name="philhealth-procurement">PhilHealth Regional Office ARMM. Notices to Proceed,
IT Resources and Flatbed Scanners. 2015.
https://www.philhealth.gov.ph/about_us/bidsNprojects/2015/Regional/PROARMM/</ref>
His legal background made him particularly adept at ensuring regional operations complied with the Republic Act
9184 (Government Procurement Reform Act) and its Revised Implementing Rules and Regulations. He oversaw
multiple Annual Procurement Plan (APP) amendments, balancing the corporate operating budget with the unique
demands of health service delivery in conflict-affected provinces.
He also oversaw the expansion of Group Enrollment Programs and the implementation of the Konsulta
Package, which prioritized primary health consultations and preventive care for indigents and organized groups
throughout the Bangsamoro region.
Board of Trustee: Philippine Integrated School, Marawi City (2001–Present)
Alongside his PhilHealth and MSU roles, Macabato has served since 2001 as a Board of Trustee member of the
Philippine Integrated School in Marawi City, one of the key private educational institutions serving Bangsamoro
youth in Lanao del Sur.
This role has kept him directly connected to the community-level realities of Bangsamoro education, long before
his executive commitments required him to operate from regional capitals.
Contributions and Legacy
Advancing Social Health Insurance in the Bangsamoro Region
Macabato's most enduring contribution is the sustained institutional presence of PhilHealth in a region where
government services have historically been erratic, incomplete, or absent altogether.
For over two decades, he built and maintained the operational infrastructure that allowed PhilHealth to function in
the ARMM and then the BARMM, including during periods of intense armed conflict, the Battle of Marawi in
2017, and through the political transition from ARMM to BARMM in 2019.
He was a consistent advocate for the PAMANA Program (Payapa at Masaganang Pamayanan), a government
initiative aimed at extending social services to conflict-affected and conflict-vulnerable communities, which
PhilHealth participated in through health insurance coverage for residents in far-flung Bangsamoro areas.

PAGE 5
Legal and Fiscal Literacy Advocacy
Beyond his executive role, Macabato has been a sustained voice for fiscal transparency and legal literacy in the
Bangsamoro region.
He has consistently educated local government units (LGUs), private employers, and civil society organizations on
the legal obligations and social importance of PhilHealth remittances, framing mandatory contributions not merely
as regulatory compliance but as a social contract with Bangsamoro workers and families.
His outreach through MSU College of Law has contextualized national tax and commercial laws within the
governance structure of the Bangsamoro Organic Law, helping future lawyers understand how RA 11054 reshapes
the application of national statutes within autonomous Bangsamoro institutions.
The Rawaten Awards
During his years of leadership at PhilHealth BARMM, the regional office institutionalized the Rawaten Awards
("Rawaten" being the Maranao word for "model" or "to be emulated"), a recognition program honoring healthcare
facilities and employers that demonstrate exceptional compliance with PhilHealth mandates and commitment to
employee health security.
The awards program stands as part of Macabato's legacy of building a culture of accountability and recognition
within the regional health insurance ecosystem.
Recognition and Departure
In July 2025, PhilHealth held a formal leadership turnover ceremony marking Macabato's transition after more
than two decades at the helm of the regional office.
During the ceremony, PhilHealth leadership acknowledged that his tenure had been defined by a consistent push
for inclusive healthcare access across the Bangsamoro provinces.
His colleagues credited him with being a stabilizing force in regional health operations, particularly during the
turbulent political transition from ARMM to BARMM and during the post-conflict rehabilitation period following
the Battle of Marawi in 2017.
Atty. Macarambon was named as Acting Regional Vice President, taking over the leadership of PhilHealth
BARMM from Macabato.
Personal Values and Professional Philosophy
What stands out across Macabato's decades of service is a consistent philosophy: that professional expertise carries
a social obligation, especially in a region as historically underserved as the Bangsamoro.
His simultaneous maintenance of three distinct professional roles, as a regional health executive, a law professor,
and a school trustee, reflects a belief that leadership in the Bangsamoro context means showing up in multiple
arenas at once.
His integration of legal rigour and accounting precision within public health administration helped him translate
complex national policy into operational realities on the ground in Maguindanao, Lanao del Sur, Basilan, Sulu, and
Tawi-Tawi.

PAGE 6
His students at MSU College of Law have noted his ability to make taxation law human and relevant, connecting
abstract fiscal doctrine to the lived realities of government service and business practice in Muslim Mindanao.

Abdulraof Macacua
Abdulraof Abdul Macacua (also known as Sammy Al Mansour) is a Filipino Moro revolutionary leader and
politician currently serving as the Chief Minister of the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao
(BARMM). He is a senior leader of the Moro Islamic Liberation Front (MILF) and previously served as Governor
of Maguindanao del Norte and as a Member of the Bangsamoro Transition Authority.<ref
name="barmm2024">Bangsamoro Government. Profile of Chief Minister Abdulraof Macacua. Official BARMM
Website, 2024.</ref><ref name="pia2024">Philippine Information Agency. Macacua assumes leadership in
BARMM transition. 2024.</ref>
---
Early Life and Background
Abdulraof Macacua was born in Maguindanao and is part of the Maguindanaon Moro community.
He became involved in the Moro struggle at a young age, joining the Moro Islamic Liberation Front (MILF)
during the height of the armed resistance movement.
He later emerged as one of the trusted leaders within the MILF’s central committee and military structure.
<ref name="pia2024" />
---
Role in the Moro Islamic Liberation Front
Macacua is a senior MILF commander and political leader, known by his nom de guerre Sammy Al
Mansour.
He served as Chief of Staff of the Bangsamoro Islamic Armed Forces (BIAF), the MILF’s armed wing.
He played a role in maintaining organizational cohesion during the transition from armed struggle to peace
negotiations with the Philippine government.<ref name="barmm2024" />
---

PAGE 2
Political Career
Governor of Maguindanao del Norte
Macacua served as the first Governor of Maguindanao del Norte following the division of the province of
Maguindanao.
His administration focused on local governance, public service delivery, and development initiatives in the
province.
Bangsamoro Transition Authority
He was appointed as a Member of the Bangsamoro Transition Authority (BTA), the interim governing body
of BARMM.
In Parliament, he contributed to legislative work, governance reforms, and institutional development during
the transition period.
---
Chief Minister of BARMM
Abdulraof Macacua became Chief Minister of BARMM following leadership transition within the
Bangsamoro government.
As Chief Minister, he oversees the regional government, including policy implementation, development
programs, and peace-building initiatives.
His leadership continues the MILF-led transition toward a fully functioning parliamentary government in
BARMM.<ref name="pia2024" />
---
Leadership and Contributions
Advocates for peace, stability, and socio-economic development in the Bangsamoro region.
Supports the institutionalization of Bangsamoro governance under the Bangsamoro Organic Law.
Promotes unity among Moro groups and cooperation with the Philippine national government.
---
Legacy and Significance
Macacua represents the new generation of Moro leaders who transitioned from revolutionary struggle to
formal governance.
His leadership symbolizes continuity within the MILF while advancing the goals of autonomy, peace, and
development in BARMM.
He plays a crucial role in guiding the Bangsamoro region toward full political normalization and democratic
elections.
---

Sacar D. Macadindang
Sacar D. Macadindang is a Filipino civil engineer, entrepreneur,
and community leader who made history in 1976 as the first
Muslim Meranao to rank in the top four of the Civil
Engineering Board Examination in the Philippines. A trailblazer
who opened doors for succeeding generations of Mindanao Muslim
engineers, Macadindang built a distinguished career spanning four
decades across the Philippines and Saudi Arabia, becoming a
respected figure in both structural engineering and Islamic
community development. His journey from Mindanao State
University to international construction projects represents the
aspirations and capabilities of Bangsamoro professionals in nation-
building and global infrastructure development.
Contents
1 Background
2 Education
3 Career
3.1 Early Professional Work in the Philippines
3.2 Overseas Career in Saudi Arabia
3.3 Return to the Philippines
4 Entrepreneurship
5 Institutional Contributions
6 Legacy and Impact
7 Recognition and Significance
8 Challenges and Context
9 See Also
10 External Links
Background
Sacar D. Macadindang hails from the Meranao people, one of the
largest Muslim ethnolinguistic groups in the Philippines,
predominantly residing in the provinces surrounding Lake Lanao in
Mindanao. Growing up in a region where educational and
professional opportunities for Muslims were historically limited,
Macadindang pursued engineering at a time when Filipino
Muslims were vastly underrepresented in technical and
professional fields. His decision to study civil engineering during
the 1970s, a period marked by social and political challenges in Mindanao, demonstrated both personal
determination and family support for higher education.
The Meranao community has a rich tradition of craftsmanship and architectural heritage, evident in their intricate
woodcarving and the iconic torogan traditional houses. Macadindang's choice of civil engineering can be seen as a
modern extension of this cultural legacy, translating indigenous design sensibilities into contemporary structural

PAGE 2
practice. His achievement in 1976 would become a landmark moment for Meranao representation in the Philippine
engineering profession.
Education
Macadindang earned his Bachelor of Science in Civil Engineering from Mindanao State University (MSU), the
premier institution of higher learning in Muslim Mindanao. Founded in 1961, MSU was established specifically to
provide educational opportunities for Filipino Muslims and other cultural communities in Mindanao, making it the
natural choice for aspiring Meranao professionals.
His academic journey culminated in a historic achievement during the May 1976 Civil Engineering Board
Examination. Ranking fourth overall in the nationwide licensure exam, Macadindang became the first Muslim
Meranao to place in the top tier of the highly competitive test. This breakthrough was particularly significant given
the systemic barriers faced by Muslim students from Mindanao, including limited access to review centers,
financial constraints, and the linguistic challenge of taking exams primarily designed for Tagalog and English
speakers.
The 1976 board exam result shattered prevailing stereotypes about the capabilities of Muslim engineers and served
as a powerful statement about MSU's educational quality. Macadindang's achievement inspired a generation of
Meranao and Maguindanao students to pursue engineering and other technical fields, contributing to the gradual
diversification of the Philippine engineering profession.
Career
Early Professional Work in the Philippines
After passing the board exam, Macadindang began his career as a Research Aide at Mindanao State University, his
alma mater. This position allowed him to contribute to the academic institution that had shaped his professional
foundation while gaining practical experience in engineering research and applications.
He subsequently joined the National Irrigation Administration (NIA), where he applied his civil engineering
expertise to agricultural infrastructure projects critical to Mindanao's farming communities. His work at NIA
involved the design and construction of irrigation systems that directly impacted food security and rural
development in the region.
Macadindang then moved to the private sector, working as a Civil Engineer at Erectors Inc., Philippines, a
construction company where he gained experience in commercial and industrial projects. This phase of his career
provided exposure to diverse construction methodologies and project management practices that would prove
invaluable in his later international work.
Overseas Career in Saudi Arabia
In 1982, Macadindang joined the wave of Filipino Overseas Filipino Workers (OFWs) seeking opportunities in the
Middle East. His decision to work abroad came during a period of massive infrastructure development in Saudi
Arabia, driven by oil wealth and rapid urbanization. As a licensed civil engineer with proven credentials, he was
well-positioned to contribute to the Kingdom's construction boom.
His Saudi Arabian career spanned multiple phases and companies, demonstrating progressive professional growth:

PAGE 3
He began as a Junior Civil Engineer at a construction company in Jeddah, steadily advancing to senior positions as
he proved his technical competence and project management capabilities. His work involved the construction of
commercial buildings, residential complexes, and infrastructure projects in one of Saudi Arabia's fastest-growing
cities.
Macadindang then served as Senior Cost Engineer at Kara Establishment, a role that required sophisticated
understanding of construction economics, budgeting, and resource allocation. This position expanded his skill set
beyond pure structural engineering into the financial and managerial aspects of large-scale construction.
His career reached a significant milestone when he became Technical Services Department Manager and Project
Engineer at SAMACO (Saudi Arabian Marketing Company), where he worked for seven years. In this role,
Macadindang oversaw the construction of multiple multi-story buildings serving as showrooms, offices, and hotels.
The scale and complexity of these projects required coordination of diverse engineering disciplines and
management of substantial construction teams.
Perhaps the most prominent phase of his overseas career was his six-year tenure as Technical Manager and Project
Engineer at Abdul Latif Jameel Co., Ltd., one of Saudi Arabia's largest and most prestigious conglomerates.
Macadindang's primary responsibility was the design and construction of automotive showrooms and service
centers for Toyota and Lexus, two of the world's leading car brands. These projects demanded exceptional attention
to detail, as automotive showrooms require specific spatial configurations, lighting systems, and structural supports
for vehicle displays. His work contributed to the expansion of Japanese automotive presence in the Saudi market.
His final position before retirement was as Project Management Consultant at Dr. Fuoad Ghazali & Arch. Adel
Moemen Engineering Consultant, where he worked for seven years on continued automotive showroom projects
for Abdul Latif Jameel. This consultancy role represented the pinnacle of his professional career, drawing on
decades of accumulated expertise in project management, cost engineering, and technical oversight.
Throughout his two decades in Saudi Arabia, Macadindang not only built buildings but also built bridges between
Filipino engineering professionals and Middle Eastern employers, establishing a reputation for competence and
reliability that benefited other OFWs who followed.
Return to the Philippines
After retiring from his consultancy work in Saudi Arabia, Macadindang returned to the Philippines, bringing with
him decades of international experience and technical knowledge. Rather than settling into full retirement, he
remained professionally active in multiple capacities.
Currently, he works as a supervising engineer for several private commercial building projects in the Philippines.
This role allows him to mentor younger engineers while applying the sophisticated project management techniques
he mastered during his Saudi Arabian career to Philippine construction contexts.
Entrepreneurship
Demonstrating the entrepreneurial spirit common among successful OFWs, Macadindang established Happy
Family Hardware, a business that serves the construction industry by providing building materials and supplies.
The enterprise represents a strategic application of his engineering knowledge to the commercial sector, as his
technical expertise allows him to advise customers on appropriate materials and construction solutions.

PAGE 4
Happy Family Hardware also serves as a tangible legacy for his family, creating employment opportunities and
contributing to the local economy. The business name reflects Meranao cultural values that prioritize family
cohesion and collective prosperity.
Institutional Contributions
Beyond his engineering career, Macadindang has been deeply involved in Islamic community development. He is
one of the four founding members of the Insan Islamic Assembly, Inc., an organization dedicated to religious
education, community service, and the strengthening of Islamic identity among Filipino Muslims.
The Insan Islamic Assembly represents Macadindang's commitment to giving back to the Meranao community and
ensuring that future generations maintain strong connections to their faith and cultural heritage. As a founder, he
helped establish the organization's vision, governance structure, and programmatic priorities. His involvement
reflects a holistic understanding of Muslim community needs that extends beyond economic development to
include spiritual and cultural dimensions.
The organization's work is particularly important in contexts where Muslim communities face marginalization or
stereotyping, providing spaces for religious practice, Islamic education, and community solidarity. Macadindang's
dual identity as a successful engineer and religious community leader demonstrates that professional achievement
and Islamic faith are mutually reinforcing rather than contradictory.
Legacy and Impact
Macadindang's most enduring legacy is his role as a pathbreaker for Muslim Meranao engineers. His 1976 board
exam achievement demonstrated that students from Muslim Mindanao could compete at the highest levels of the
Philippine engineering profession when given access to quality education. The psychological impact of this
achievement cannot be overstated, as it challenged deficit narratives about Muslim intellectual capacity and
inspired countless young Meranao to pursue technical education.
His career trajectory from MSU to international construction projects provides a template for professional success
that other Mindanao Muslims have followed. Many engineers from Lanao del Sur and Lanao del Norte cite
Macadindang's example as proof that geographic and cultural background need not limit professional ambitions.
On a practical level, his overseas work contributed to the positive reputation of Filipino engineers in the Middle
East, helping to secure opportunities for subsequent generations of OFWs. His technical competence and
professionalism in managing multi-million dollar construction projects reinforced the perception of Filipinos as
skilled and reliable workers.
His establishment of Happy Family Hardware and continued work as a supervising engineer demonstrate a
commitment to knowledge transfer, ensuring that the expertise gained abroad benefits the Philippine construction
industry. By remaining professionally active after retirement, he continues to mentor younger engineers and
contribute to infrastructure development in his home country.
Recognition and Significance
While formal awards and honors are not extensively documented, Macadindang's recognition comes primarily
from the respect accorded to him within the Meranao engineering community and among Filipino engineers who
worked in Saudi Arabia. His name is frequently mentioned in discussions about pioneering Muslim professionals
who broke barriers in technical fields during the 1970s and 1980s.

PAGE 5
The establishment of Insan Islamic Assembly, Inc. stands as institutional recognition of his leadership within the
Muslim community. Being selected as one of four founders indicates the trust and esteem in which he is held by
fellow community members.
His continued employment as a supervising engineer for multiple commercial projects in his senior years reflects
the confidence that private sector clients place in his judgment and expertise, a form of professional recognition
that speaks to decades of proven competence.
Challenges and Context
Macadindang's achievements must be understood against the backdrop of significant challenges faced by Muslim
Filipinos in the 1970s. The period of his board exam was marked by the escalation of the Moro conflict in
Mindanao, the declaration of Martial Law in 1972, and widespread displacement of Muslim communities. Pursuing
higher education and professional certification during this turbulent period required extraordinary focus and
resilience.
As a Muslim engineer working in the Philippines during the late 1970s and early 1980s, Macadindang likely
encountered both subtle and overt forms of discrimination. The decision to work overseas in 1982 may have been
driven partly by limited opportunities for Muslim professionals in the Philippine private sector and government,
where Christian Filipinos dominated executive and technical positions.
His work in Saudi Arabia, while professionally rewarding, came with the typical challenges faced by OFWs,
including family separation, adaptation to different cultural norms, and the vulnerability of being a foreign worker
in a kafala system that often favored employers over employees. Despite these challenges, Macadindang
persevered and achieved success, demonstrating the adaptability and work ethic for which Filipino OFWs are
renowned.

Omar Macarimbang Alawi Macalandong
Datu Shiekh Omar Macarimbang Alawi Macalandong (March 21, 1915 – December 5, 1985) was a Maranao
Islamic scholar, educator, Hajj guide, and public servant from the historic region of Lanao in Mindanao,
Philippines.
Over the course of four decades, he wove together the dual roles of religious leader and government official,
serving his communities not as separate callings but as complementary expressions of a single commitment: to
uplift the Maranao people through faith, education, and principled governance.

EARLY LIFE AND FAMILY
BACKGROUND
Datu Shiekh Omar Macarimbang Alawi Macalandong was born on
March 21, 1915, in the historic region of Lanao, into a family that
carried both aristocratic standing and deep religious conviction.
His father, Datu Macalandong Abuat Angnie, and his mother, Bae
Rene Macarimbang, were members of respected Maranao families
from Madalum, Lanao del Sur, whose lineages were bound up with
generations of traditional leadership, Islamic scholarship, and
community stewardship.
Growing up in this environment, young Omar was surrounded by
the kind of formation that shaped leaders: the discipline of Islamic
learning, the responsibility of the datu class, and the expectation of
service that came with belonging to distinguished families.
The Datu Macalandong Angni Abuat and Macarimbang lineages
were not merely names of prestige. They represented an ongoing
tradition of governance and religious guidance among the Maranao,
a people whose identity has long been inseparable from their faith
and their sense of place along the shores of Lake Lanao.

RELIGIOUS LEADERSHIP AND
ISLAMIC EDUCATION
From the 1940s through the 1980s, Datu Shiekh Omar devoted the
larger part of his life to Islamic education and religious leadership,
earning the title Sheikh through years of dedicated study and
community guidance.
He is recognized as one of the pioneering figures involved in the
establishment and early development of the Jamiatu Muslim
Mindanao (JMM) in Matampay, Marawi City, an institution that
has served as a vital center of Islamic learning for communities
across Mindanao.
His contributions to JMM went beyond symbolic participation. He
helped nurture the institution's early growth, worked to attract
students and teachers, and lent his religious authority to give the
school legitimacy in the eyes of Maranao families who looked to
recognized scholars before entrusting their children's Islamic
education to any institution.
Through this work, he contributed to the formation of future
scholars, educators, and Muslim leaders, a quiet but generational
investment in the intellectual and spiritual life of the region.
His approach to religious leadership was rooted in accessibility. He
was known not as a remote authority but as a guide who met people
where they were, whether in matters of faith, family, or civic life.
This combination of learning and approachability made him widely
respected across communities in Lanao.
PUBLIC SERVICE AND REGIONAL
LEADERSHIP
Datu Shiekh Omar's public career reflected the reality of his time: in
the Lanao of the mid-twentieth century, the division between
religious and civic leadership was not sharp. Respected scholars
were also expected to serve their communities in governance, and
he answered that expectation directly.
From 1953 to 1959, he served as Deputy Governor-at-Large (Vice
Governor) during a period when the undivided Province of Lanao
maintained leadership structures representing different territorial jurisdictions.
In this capacity, he represented the Lanao del Norte area, working to strengthen cooperation between local
communities and the provincial government at a time when the administrative landscape of Mindanao was still
taking shape.

PAGE 3
Following the division of the Province of Lanao into Lanao del Norte and Lanao del Sur, he remained engaged in
public affairs and later sought election as Board Member of Lanao del Norte, running under the political banner of
Mamintal Tamano, a figure of considerable influence in the political life of Muslim Mindanao during that era.
His willingness to remain in public life even after his tenure as vice governor reflected a sense of civic duty that
was consistent with his religious convictions: service was not a phase of life but a permanent orientation.
HAJJ GUIDANCE AND SPIRITUAL SERVICE
Among the roles that defined Datu Shiekh Omar in the eyes of ordinary Maranao families, perhaps none was more
personal than his work as a Murshid, a Hajj guide who assisted pilgrims from Mindanao in performing the sacred
pilgrimage to Makkah.
The Hajj is among the most significant obligations in Islamic life, and for many Maranao families of that
generation, undertaking the pilgrimage meant navigating unfamiliar logistics, languages, and rituals in a distant
land. A trusted Murshid was not simply a travel facilitator; he was a spiritual anchor.
Datu Shiekh Omar served hundreds of pilgrims in this capacity, drawing on his deep knowledge of Islamic
teachings, his patience, and his genuine care for the people who placed their trust in him. Those who made the
journey with him remembered him for ensuring that the Hajj was performed not merely as ritual but with proper
understanding, discipline, and devotion.
This aspect of his life speaks to a kind of service that left no government record but lived on in the memories and
gratitude of the families he accompanied.
INFLUENCE IN LANAO DEL NORTE
A significant chapter of Datu Shiekh Omar's life unfolded in Lanao del Norte, where he extended his influence well
beyond his native Madalum.
He became especially respected in the municipalities of Munai, Kauswagan, Karomatan (now Sultan Naga
Dimaporo), Bacolod, and Magsaysay, areas where Maranao communities looked to him as both a religious
authority and a community elder.
Through sustained engagement across these communities, he worked to foster cooperation among Maranao groups
and to encourage a way of living together grounded in Islamic values and mutual respect.
He also maintained a close and lasting relationship with the Datu Cablangan, a bond founded on shared
commitments to leadership, religious scholarship, and community service. These relationships were the kind built
not through formal alliance but through years of shared work and consistent presence.
FAMILY AND EDUCATIONAL LEGACY
The values that shaped Datu Shiekh Omar's life did not stay with him alone. They passed to his children, whose
careers extended his legacy into education and local governance.
His eldest daughter, Faridah Ali Macabato Macarimbang, served as School District Supervisor of Ganassi,
Lanao del Sur, where she contributed meaningfully to educational leadership and the development of the
provincial school system. Her career reflects the emphasis on education that her father championed through his

PAGE 4
work at JMM and in his broader role as a community teacher.
His daughter Hadji Norjannah Omar Malawi Macarimbang served as Municipal Councilor of Madalum,
carrying the family's tradition of civic engagement into local governance at the barangay and municipal level.
Together, their careers illustrate what it means for a family legacy to take root in a community: not through
monuments, but through the continued presence of people who carry the same values forward into new generations
of work.
LEGACY
Datu Shiekh Omar Macarimbang Alawi Macalandong passed away on December 5, 1985, leaving behind a record
of service that cut across the religious, educational, civic, and spiritual dimensions of Maranao life.
He served as a government official when governance in Lanao was still finding its footing in the postwar era. He
helped build an institution of Islamic learning that would outlast him by generations. He guided hundreds of
pilgrims through one of the most sacred experiences of their lives. And he did all of this while raising children who
would carry the same commitments into their own careers.
His legacy is not the kind that fills history books with dramatic episodes. It is the quieter, more durable kind: a man
who showed up, served faithfully, and left behind communities a little better than he found them.
For the Datu Macalandong Angni Abuat and Macarimbang families, and for the communities of Lanao del Sur and
Lanao del Norte that knew him, his memory remains a living part of the heritage of Bangsamoro leadership.

Hejira Nefertiti S. Macalandong-Limbona
Dr. Bai Hejira Nefertiti Sinsuat Macalandong-Limbona is the 4th
elected Chancellor of Mindanao State University-Maguindanao
(MSU-Maguindanao), one of the eight constituent universities of the
Mindanao State University System in the southern Philippines.<ref
name="biosketch">Template:Cite web</ref>
A daughter of the university's legacy, a practitioner of public
administration, and a champion of women's rights in conflict-affected
communities, Chancellor Limbona has spent her entire professional
life building up a single institution, and in doing so, she has become
one of the most consequential academic leaders the Bangsamoro
region has produced in recent decades.
Her chancellorship has been defined by a clear conviction: that the
university is not merely a place for degrees, but a vehicle for genuine
peace and development in Mindanao.
She was among the first to push MSU-Maguindanao toward what
would become its most globally recognized milestone, a pioneering
academic program on Women, Peace and Security that earned
recognition across Southeast Asia and drew partnerships with the
United Nations Development Programme (UNDP), the British
Government, and universities in Indonesia.<ref
name="gov.uk">Template:Cite web</ref>

Background and Family
Dr. Limbona was born and raised in Cotabato City, the bustling urban center at the heart of the Bangsamoro region
in central Mindanao.
Her family background is deeply intertwined with the history of MSU-Maguindanao itself.
She is the eldest daughter of Prof. Bai Yasmin Q. Sinsuat, a former Chancellor of MSU-Maguindanao, and Prof.
Nazarollah R. Macalandong, who served as Vice President for Administration and Finance of the MSU System.
<ref name="biosketch"/>
Growing up in a household where academic governance, public service, and Bangsamoro heritage were not just
dinner-table topics but lived realities gave her a distinct vantage point that few of her peers could match.
The Sinsuat name itself carries weight in Maguindanao history, associated with civic leadership and institutional
memory in a region that has long struggled to balance political turbulence with the aspiration for progress.
She is married to the Honorable Asnawi S. Limbona, and they are blessed with four children.
Education
Dr. Limbona's educational path reflects an unusually wide intellectual curiosity, moving from computing to
business management to public leadership, and ultimately to the academic study of governance.
She began with a Bachelor of Science in Information and Computer Science from St. Paul College of Manila,
completing the degree in 1999.<ref name="biosketch"/>
Three years later, in 2002, she earned a second bachelor's degree, a Bachelor of Science in Business Administration
with a major in Computer Applications, from De La Salle-College of Saint Benilde in Manila.<ref
name="biosketch"/>
That dual foundation in technology and business would prove prescient: decades later, she would be the one
advocating for digital connectivity as a tool for integrating Muslim communities into the national mainstream.
In 2003, she completed the Building Leadership program at the Asian Institute of Management in Manila, a
formative experience that sharpened her orientation toward institutional reform and organizational leadership.<ref
name="biosketch"/>
She then turned her formal studies toward public governance.
In 2010, she finished her Master in Public Administration degree from MSU-Maguindanao, the very institution she
would later lead.<ref name="biosketch"/>
In 2012, she completed the Administrative Excellence Service Executive Development Program for State
Universities and Colleges (SUCs) through the Development Academy of the Philippines.<ref name="biosketch"/>

PAGE 3
The following year, 2013, she earned her Doctor of Philosophy in Public Administration from Cotabato City State
Polytechnic College, which also awarded her the Certificate of Academic Excellence in recognition of her
scholarly performance.<ref name="biosketch"/>
Career at MSU-Maguindanao
Early Service and Administrative Roles
Chancellor Limbona's career at MSU-Maguindanao did not begin at the top. It began at the entry level, and she
worked her way up methodically over more than a decade.
She was appointed as an instructor at the age of 23, barely out of her own undergraduate studies, stepping into a
teaching role at the same university where her mother had served as chancellor.<ref name="biosketch"/>
It's worth pausing on that detail: walking into an institution your parent once led as a junior instructor takes a
certain confidence, and it set the tone for her entire professional trajectory.
In 2003, she joined the Internal Audit System of MSU-Maguindanao, a role that placed her at the intersection of
administrative accountability and institutional governance.<ref name="biosketch"/>
That same year, she became Managing Editor of the university's Newsletter Editorial Board, a post she held until
2007, helping shape institutional communication during a period of growth for the campus.<ref
name="biosketch"/>
From 2004 to 2007, she served concurrently as Director of the Division of Student Affairs, a role that brought her
directly into the lives of the student population, many of them coming from underserved communities across
Maguindanao and neighboring provinces.<ref name="biosketch"/>
Vice Chancellor for Administration and Finance
From 2008 to 2014, Dr. Limbona served as Vice Chancellor for Administration and Finance, one of the most
demanding executive positions in any university's organizational structure.<ref name="biosketch"/>
That six-year tenure gave her a thorough understanding of institutional finance, human resources, and operational
management, the kind of ground-level fluency in how a university actually functions that chancellors who come in
as pure academics often lack.
By the time she was elected chancellor, she had accumulated nine years of leadership and managerial experience
across student affairs, editorial work, internal audit, and university-wide finance.
Election as Chancellor
Dr. Limbona was elected as the 4th Chancellor of MSU-Maguindanao, succeeding the line of chancellors who had
built the institution from its agricultural college origins in 1973 into a full-service university serving the
Bangsamoro region.<ref name="biosketch"/>
She was subsequently reappointed as chancellor, continuing in the role with the formal designation as the Fourth
Regular Chancellor of the institution.<ref name="reappointed">Template:Cite web</ref>

PAGE 4
Vision and Institutional Leadership
Chancellor Limbona has articulated a clear, consistent vision for MSU-Maguindanao: to make it globally
recognized as a premiere innovative institution that provides excellent quality education, exceptional research
advancement, and a diverse study environment.<ref name="biosketch"/>
What makes that vision more than just aspiration is the specificity with which she has pursued it through
partnerships, programs, and policy advocacy.
She has consistently framed the university's mission in terms of its Bangsamoro context, insisting that an excellent
university in Maguindanao is not just an academic project but a contribution to the peace process.
Her approach to governance blends a service ethic drawn from Islamic values with a practical administrator's
attention to institutional mechanics.
In 2022, speaking after a meeting with Bangsamoro Chief Minister Ahod Ebrahim, she said:
"Our plan will be a milestone for MSU and will be a trademark for BARMM in developing the
academe and to produce more excellent Bangsamoro professionals in the different courses offered by
MSU in the future."
During a 2025 stakeholders' meeting in Paglat, she was equally direct about what she expected students to gain
from their time at the university:
"What we want is for our students to be provided with what they need so that when they finish college,
they will pass the board exam or bar and, hopefully, the skills and competence they acquire at MSU-
Maguindanao will be enough for them to secure a decent job in their chosen field."
Contributions and Initiatives
Diploma in Women, Peace and Security
Perhaps the most historically significant achievement of Chancellor Limbona's tenure is her role in establishing the
Diploma in Women, Peace and Security (DWPS), widely recognized as the first academic diploma of its kind in
Southeast Asia.
Developed in partnership with the Philippine Center for Islam and Democracy (PCID), and supported by the
European Union, the UNDP, and the British Embassy Manila, the diploma program is offered fully online across
three semesters, making it accessible to students and practitioners who would otherwise be unable to attend
traditional on-campus programs.<ref name="icwps"/>
Chancellor Limbona captured the program's ambition in precise terms when she said:
"DPWPS is not merely a diploma, it is a platform of praxis of WPS champions, practitioners and
leaders, enabling the vision of WPS pillars and frameworks in institutions across all sectors,
procedural systems and geopolitical borders."
The program has drawn international attention.

PAGE 5
In October 2024, a delegation led by Chancellor Limbona attended the International Conference on Women, Peace
and Security (ICWPS) at the Philippine International Convention Center (PICC) in Manila, a landmark global
event that convened 691 delegates from 84 countries, including 27 ministerial-level officials and parliamentarians.
<ref name="icwps"/>
MSU-Maguindanao maintained a prominent presence at the event, showcasing the DWPS program as a model for
academic institutions seeking to embed gender, peace, and security into their core offerings.
International Academic Partnerships
Under Chancellor Limbona's leadership, MSU-Maguindanao has built a series of meaningful international
partnerships, particularly in the area of women, peace, and security.
In 2025, with support from the UK Government's Indo-Pacific Governance Fund and the UNDP, the university led
an international learning exchange in Yogyakarta, Indonesia, which resulted in the signing of Memoranda of
Understanding with three major Indonesian universities: Universitas Gadjah Mada, Universitas Muhammadiyah
Yogyakarta, and Universitas Ahmad Dahlan.
These agreements aim to advance cooperation in gender education, research, and community engagement across
Southeast Asia.
Chancellor Limbona described what the exchanges meant in practice:
"These learning exchanges spark the curiosity that drives meaningful research and action, exactly
what we need to not only mainstream the WPS agenda, but to truly transform the challenging
situations facing our women, communities and families."
She also led MSU-Maguindanao's signing of scholarship Memoranda of Agreement with the European Union and
the Magbassa Kita Foundation, Inc., expanding access to higher education for Bangsamoro students.
The university has also signed a MOA with Nueva Ecija University of Science and Technology (NEUST) for the
joint offering of a Diploma in WPS with a specialization in Indigenous Peoples' Perspectives, further extending the
reach of MSU-Maguindanao's flagship peace education program to other regions of the Philippines.
Peace Education and the UNDP Partnership
In a separate but related initiative, MSU-Maguindanao under Chancellor Limbona partnered with the United
Nations Development Programme (UNDP) Philippines and the MSU Institute for Peace and Development in
Mindanao (IPDM) to conduct a training workshop on the effective integration of peace into the university
curriculum.
The initiative was part of MSU's transition toward becoming a National Peace University, a mandate rooted in the
university's foundational legislation, Republic Act 1387, which charged it with advancing national unity through
education.
The workshop involved college deans, directors of the Graduate School, heads of academic offices, program
advisers, and faculty, working collectively to develop peace-integrated course modules, syllabi, and assessment
mechanisms.

PAGE 6
BARMM Development Partnerships
In June 2022, Chancellor Limbona led a delegation to the office of BARMM Chief Minister Ahod Ebrahim to
present three strategic development proposals for the university: an Academic Center focused on Islamic Studies
and Peace Education, an Eco-tourism Development project, and a Housing Project for faculty, staff, and students.
<ref name="barmm"/>
The meeting signaled a growing alignment between the university's institutional ambitions and the BARMM
government's priority of building Bangsamoro professionals.
In May 2024, she presided over the signing of a Memorandum of Agreement with the Ministry of Trade,
Investments, and Tourism of BARMM (MTIT-BARMM) under the Rural Agro-Industrial Partnership for Inclusive
Development (RAPID) Growth Project.
The MOA committed MSU-Maguindanao's ABM Department to providing business and advisory services to
smallholder farmers in Maguindanao, particularly in the coconut, cacao, and coffee industries, connecting them
with supplies, marketing channels, and training programs.
After the signing, Chancellor Limbona offered a remark that reflected both her faith and her sense of public duty:
"Alhamdulillah for today, serbisyo para sa bayan."<ref name="rapid"/>
Climate Resilience and DOST Partnership
In 2024, MSU-Maguindanao signed a Memorandum of Agreement with the Technology Transfer and Promotion
Division of the Department of Science and Technology's Philippine Council for Agriculture, Aquatic and Natural
Resources Research and Development (DOST-PCAARRD) for a climate resilience project in Datu Blah Sinsuat,
Maguindanao.
The project focuses on rehabilitating 10 hectares of land using agroforestry techniques, establishing community
nurseries, and training farmers on climate adaptation practices, directly responding to the devastation caused by
Typhoon Paeng in October 2022.<ref name="dost"/>
Chancellor Limbona expressed the project's significance in terms of the university's contribution to the UN
Sustainable Development Goals, particularly SDG 13 on Climate Action.
Digital Connectivity
In May 2023, MSU-Maguindanao and MSU-Tawi-Tawi College of Technology and Oceanography (MSU-TCTO)
jointly received a digital connectivity project through the Development Academy of the Philippines (DAP),
selected from 114 State Universities and Colleges across the country.
Chancellor Limbona framed the project's importance in terms that went beyond infrastructure: "The need and
importance of digital connectivity is critical, and it will help in achieving the mandate of MSU-System to integrate
the Muslims and the other cultural minorities into the mainstream of national life."
Women's Empowerment and Gender Equality
Chancellor Limbona signed a Memorandum of Understanding on the Diploma on Women, Peace and Security with
Bangsamoro Women Commission (BWC) Chairperson Hadja Bainon G. Karon during the Culmination Program of
the National Women's Month 2024, reaffirming her personal and institutional commitment to advancing women's

PAGE 7
rights in the Bangsamoro region.
She has also participated in high-level international discussions on gender and security, including speaking at the
7th International Forum on Law and Religion on the subject of Institutional WPS Structures and Regional
Networks.
Personal Values and Cultural Identity
Chancellor Limbona's leadership style is informed by a set of values that are deeply Bangsamoro in character: a
sense of familial duty, a commitment to public service grounded in Islamic ethics, and an abiding awareness that
the work of building institutions in conflict-affected communities is never finished.
Her frequent use of phrases like "Alhamdulillah" and "serbisyo para sa bayan" in public addresses reflects a
personal approach to her role that integrates faith with civic obligation.
She comes from a family that has spent generations in public service and academic governance, and she carries that
lineage not as a burden but as a framework for accountability.
Her support for the Women, Peace and Security agenda is not simply a programmatic choice. It reflects her
understanding of what it means to grow up as a Bangsamoro woman, navigating expectations of tradition and the
demands of modern institutional leadership simultaneously.
She has spoken in formal and international settings about the need to transform, not just mainstream, the WPS
agenda in communities where women have historically been undervalued despite their central role in
peacebuilding.
Recognition
Among the formal recognitions of her academic work, Chancellor Limbona received the Certificate of Academic
Excellence from Cotabato City State Polytechnic College upon the completion of her doctoral degree in Public
Administration.
MSU-Maguindanao's DWPS program, which she championed, has been internationally recognized as the first of its
kind in Southeast Asia, and the university's role in hosting learning exchanges and building regional WPS networks
has drawn formal acknowledgment from the United Nations, the British Government, and partner academic
institutions in Indonesia and beyond.
She has been invited to deliver speeches and messages at national and international forums including the
International Conference on Women, Peace and Security, the 7th International Forum on Law and Religion, and
events organized by the UNDP Philippines.
Institutional Legacy
When historians of the Bangsamoro peace process look back at MSU-Maguindanao's arc from a modest
agricultural college in Dinaig in 1973 to a globally engaged peace university in the 2020s, Chancellor Limbona's
tenure will occupy a significant chapter.

PAGE 8
She did not inherit an institution waiting to be globalized. She led a deliberate transformation, anchoring the
university's research, extension, and academic programs to the realities of peacebuilding, gender justice, climate
vulnerability, and rural development in Muslim Mindanao.
More than that, she demonstrated that a Bangsamoro woman, born and raised in Cotabato City, educated across
Manila's major universities, rooted in a family of public servants, could lead an autonomous university into
international prominence without losing sight of its most basic obligation: to give Bangsamoro students what they
need to build decent lives.
Her phrase, "serbisyo para sa bayan," distilled in ordinary Tagalog, remains the most honest summary of what she
has pursued across more than two decades in the same institution.

title: Macalawi, Modrica Ebrahim
text:
PAGE 1
Modrica Ebrahim Macalawi
Personal Information
Born: 1956, Masiu, Lanao del Sur,
Philippines
Died: 1993 (aged 37), Butuan City,
Philippines
Cause of Death: Motor vehicle
accident
Ethnicity and Faith
Maranaw (Muslim Mindanao)
Education
Bachelor of Laws, University of the East
(UE), Manila, 1979
Bar Admission
Philippine Bar, 1980 (Rating: 82.5%)
Professions
Modrica Ebrahim Macalawi
Atty. Modrica Ebrahim Macalawi (1956–1993), more widely known by his nickname Roger, was a Maranaw
lawyer, public prosecutor, reserve military officer, and community advocate from Lanao del Sur, Mindanao. In the
span of just thirty-seven years, he built a reputation that crossed courtrooms, corporate boardrooms, military
barracks, and the informal gathering spaces of Muslim migrant communities in northern Mindanao. He is
remembered as one of the pioneering Maranaw professionals who brought both legal expertise and genuine cultural
advocacy to regions far from his hometown.
Contents
1 ROOTS AND EARLY LIFE
2 EDUCATION AND LEGAL CREDENTIALS
3 A DYNAMIC PROFESSIONAL CAREER
3.1 From Private Practice to Corporate Rooms
3.2 Stepping into the Prosecutor's Office
4 INSTITUTIONAL IMPACT AND MILITARY SERVICE
4.1 Breaking New Ground in Alpha Phi Omega
4.2 Serving in Uniform
5 CULTURAL SIGNIFICANCE AND LEGACY
6 A SUDDEN END
7 SEE ALSO
8 REFERENCES
9 EXTERNAL LINKS
ROOTS AND EARLY LIFE
Roger Macalawi was born in 1956 in Masiu, a lakeside municipality
in Lanao del Sur nestled along the shores of Lake Lanao. Masiu is
known for its deep cultural roots within the Maranaw world, and it
was in that environment of tradition, pride, and community identity
that Roger grew up. From an early age, people around him noticed
something different about the boy: he had a way with words that
went beyond ordinary conversation.
By the time he reached high school, that gift had sharpened into
something formidable. He became a fixture on the debate circuit,
collecting best debater awards and earning a reputation as the
teammate everyone wanted in their corner. His logic was quick, his
delivery confident, and his arguments hard to rattle.
But Roger was not just a debater with books under his arm. He had
a voice, literally, that could stop a room. He loved to sing and was a
regular on local stages, competing in singing contests with genuine
enthusiasm. His all-time favorite artist was the British balladeer
Matt Monro, whose smooth, measured style apparently matched

PAGE 2
Trial Lawyer, Corporate Counsel, Public
Prosecutor, Reserve Military Officer
Government Position
1st Assistant Prosecutor, Butuan City
(appointed 1988)
Military Rank
Major, Armed Forces of the Philippines
(Reserve)
Fraternity
Alpha Phi Omega (APO) International;
one of the first Maranaw members
Notability
Pioneer Maranaw Lawyer and Public
Prosecutor; Pro Bono Advocate for
Muslim Communities in Northern
Mindanao
Known For
Cultural bridge-building between
Muslim and non-Muslim communities
in Butuan City and Agusan province;
Member of Alpha Phi Omega fraternity;
legal advocacy for indigent Muslim
migrants
something in Roger's own sensibility. Friends who knew him across
decades would later remember how he could pivot from a heated
political conversation straight into a Matt Monro number, and do
both with equal conviction.
EDUCATION AND LEGAL
CREDENTIALS
When Roger decided to pursue law, he made the move that many
ambitious young men from the provinces made at the time: he
headed to Manila. He enrolled at the University of the East (UE), an
institution with a track record of producing sharp, street-smart legal
practitioners. He took to the environment naturally, channeling the
same intensity he had brought to high school debates into his legal
studies.
In 1979, he completed his Bachelor of Laws degree, graduating
with flying colors. The following year came the real proving
ground: the 1980 Philippine Bar Examination. It is one of the most
demanding professional licensure exams in the country, and many
well-prepared candidates fall short. Roger did not. He passed with a
rating of 82.5 percent, earning his license and the standing to
practice law in the Philippines.
A DYNAMIC PROFESSIONAL
CAREER
From Private Practice to Corporate Rooms
Roger began his legal career in private practice, and the courtroom suited him well. His debating background
translated directly into the work of a trial lawyer: reading the room, anticipating arguments, and making a case hold
together under pressure. He was a tough opponent, and word of that got around.
By the late 1980s, his growing profile caught the attention of the business world. He was brought on as legal
counsel for the Villar family, serving their expanding business empire. The move into corporate law stretched his
skills in new directions and gave him exposure to high-stakes commercial dealings, but it was never really where
his heart was. His instinct kept pulling him toward public service.
Stepping into the Prosecutor's Office
In 1988, Roger made the turn that would define the last chapter of his career. He was appointed as the 1st Assistant
Prosecutor of Butuan City, the commercial and administrative hub of the Caraga region in northern Mindanao. The
role was a serious one. As a prosecutor, he carried responsibility for evaluating criminal complaints, directing state
investigations, and deciding which cases would move forward to trial.

PAGE 3
His appointment was also significant in ways that went beyond the job description. A Maranaw professional
stepping into that kind of institutional role in Butuan City brought a perspective the local justice system had not
often seen. It was a milestone for representation, and for the idea that the Muslim south could produce
professionals who belonged in every room of Philippine civic life.
INSTITUTIONAL IMPACT AND MILITARY SERVICE
Breaking New Ground in Alpha Phi Omega
Roger's record of opening doors began well before his legal career. Back in his college years in the early 1970s, he
joined Alpha Phi Omega (APO) International, a fraternity organized around the values of leadership, friendship,
and service. He holds the distinction of being among the very first Maranaw members of the fraternity, a fact that
carries more weight when you consider how unusual his presence must have been in those spaces at the time.
His involvement helped shift the culture of the fraternity in subtle but meaningful ways, making room for other
Muslim students and signaling that the organization's values were genuinely universal. His pioneering membership
is also credited with helping lay the groundwork for APO's growth across Mindanao, particularly around the
Mindanao State University (MSU) system.
Serving in Uniform
On top of his legal work and civic engagements, Roger carried one more identity: that of a uniformed officer. He
joined the citizen soldiery as a reserve officer in the Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP) and did not stop there.
Through sustained commitment and demonstrated competence, he rose through the ranks to attain the grade of
Major. Balancing a demanding courtroom career with the discipline of military service earned him a kind of respect
that cut across different circles, from regional officials and legal peers to ordinary citizens who saw in him
someone who showed up fully in every role he took on.
CULTURAL SIGNIFICANCE AND LEGACY
Perhaps the most human part of Roger's story is what he did without fanfare, in the spaces between his official
roles. During the late 1980s and into the early 1990s, Butuan City and the surrounding Agusan province were
receiving a growing number of Muslim families from Mindanao, people who had migrated northward in search of
better opportunities. Many of them arrived with very little, unfamiliar with the legal system, facing language
barriers, and vulnerable to exploitation.
Roger became a fixture in that community. He drew on his legal knowledge and his position to provide pro bono
assistance to families who could not afford counsel. When someone was being taken advantage of, or when a
family did not know where to turn, Roger was the name that came up. Over time, he earned the informal title that
meant more than any official designation: the "voice of the Muslims" within the Butuan city government. He made
sure a community that often felt invisible had someone advocating for them in the halls of justice.
This work was not part of any official mandate. It was simply who he was.

PAGE 4
A SUDDEN END
Roger Macalawi lived with an open throttle. He could argue a complex case before a judge in the morning, attend a
military briefing in the afternoon, and spend the evening singing Matt Monro with his friends, laughing and trading
stories. That rhythm, full, warm, and genuinely engaged with life in all its dimensions, was the essence of the man.
In 1993, that life was cut short without warning. At only thirty-seven years old, Roger was killed in a sudden
vehicular accident. The news struck hard across Lanao del Sur, Butuan City, and the broader legal community. He
had been doing so much, for so many people, and the abruptness of it made the loss feel even more unfair.
But the work he did lives on in the community he fought for. The migrant families he helped navigate the legal
system. The Muslim students who found a path into places like APO because he had walked it first. The colleagues
who watched a Maranaw lawyer carry himself with excellence and earn the respect of a city that had never seen
one quite like him.
His story is a short one by the measure of years, but by any other measure, it runs deep.
