title: Macalawi, Sayradz Ebrahim
text:
PAGE 1
Sayradz Ebrahim Macalawi
Sayradz Ebrahim Macalawi is a distinguished Filipino diplomat and public servant who dedicated over 30 years
to the Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA) of the Philippines. Throughout a career spanning three decades, he
held various high-level consular and administrative positions, particularly across the Middle East and North Africa,
where he became a prominent advocate for the welfare of Overseas Filipino Workers (OFWs). His signature legacy
lies in his unwavering commitment to the "Third Pillar" of Philippine Foreign Policy—the protection and
promotion of Filipino citizens abroad—earning him recognition as a bridge-builder between the Republic of the
Philippines and the Islamic world. As a member of the Maranao ethnic community from Lanao, Macalawi
represents a generation of Bangsamoro public servants who brought cultural depth and diplomatic finesse to
Philippine foreign relations.
Contents

2 Education and Professional Training
3 Diplomatic Career

3.4 International Expansion: China and Bahrain

Background and Early Life
While comprehensive public records about Sayradz Ebrahim Macalawi's earliest years remain select, his name
carries deep roots in the Maranao ethnic tradition of the Lanao region in Mindanao. The name "Sayradz" reflects
the rich Islamic heritage of the Bangsamoro people, a community that has historically maintained strong cultural
and religious ties with the broader Muslim world. Within the context of Philippine diplomacy, Macalawi emerged
as part of a pioneering generation of Bangsamoro public servants who would serve as vital cultural ambassadors
between the predominantly Catholic Philippines and the Islamic nations of the Middle East and North Africa.

PAGE 2

His upbringing in Mindanao, a region characterized by its vibrant
Islamic traditions and complex socio-political landscape, likely
shaped his diplomatic sensibilities and equipped him with the
cultural competence necessary to navigate diverse international
environments. This background proved invaluable throughout his
career, particularly in assignments that required deep
understanding of Islamic customs, protocols, and social dynamics.
Education and Professional Training
Although specific details of Macalawi's formal education are not
extensively documented in public records, his career trajectory
suggests a high level of specialized training in consular
administration, international relations, and diplomatic protocol.
His ability to assume increasingly complex roles across multiple
countries indicates comprehensive preparation in areas such as:
Consular law and migrant protection frameworks
International diplomatic conventions and protocols
Cross-cultural communication and cultural diplomacy
Crisis management and emergency response
Administrative leadership and institutional management
The Department of Foreign Affairs typically requires its foreign
service officers to undergo rigorous training programs, and
Macalawi's progression through various diplomatic ranks suggests
he successfully completed these professional development
requirements.
Diplomatic Career
Early Career and Consular Foundations (1980s)
Macalawi began his diplomatic journey in the 1980s, a
transformative period for Philippine foreign relations marked by
increasing labor migration to the Middle East. His first
international assignment was at the Philippine Embassy in the
Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, a critical posting due to the massive
concentration of Filipino workers in the Gulf region. During this
formative period, he developed foundational expertise in consular
and administrative work, learning to navigate the complex legal
and cultural environment that would define much of his subsequent career.
The Saudi Arabia assignment exposed Macalawi to the daily realities faced by OFWs—from labor disputes and
contract violations to medical emergencies and legal challenges. This early exposure would shape his lifelong
commitment to migrant welfare and inform his approach to consular service delivery.

PAGE 3
Crisis Management in North Africa (1991–1996)
From 1991 to 1996, Macalawi served as Administrative Officer at the Philippine Embassy in Tripoli, Libya. This
tenure coincided with a complex and often volatile political era in Libya's history, requiring diplomatic personnel to
maintain operations amid regional instability and shifting political dynamics. As Administrative Officer, Macalawi
was responsible for:
Managing embassy operations and logistical coordination
Ensuring the safety and welfare of Filipino nationals in Libya
Coordinating with Libyan authorities on consular matters
Overseeing administrative procedures and documentation
Conducting field operations to assist distressed Filipino workers
His work in Libya demonstrated his capacity for crisis management and his ability to maintain effective diplomatic
operations even in challenging environments. The experience reinforced his reputation as a reliable and resourceful
foreign service officer capable of handling high-pressure situations with professionalism and calm.
Cultural Diplomacy in Egypt (1999–2005)
Macalawi's career took a strategic turn when he was appointed Cultural Attaché at the Philippine Embassy in
Cairo, Egypt, serving from 1999 to 2005. This assignment represented a shift from purely administrative and
consular work toward soft-power diplomacy and cultural exchange. In this capacity, he was responsible for:
Promoting Philippine heritage, arts, and culture within the Arab Republic of Egypt
Strengthening bilateral ties through academic and cultural exchange programs
Fostering mutual understanding between Philippine and Egyptian diplomatic communities
Organizing cultural events, exhibitions, and educational initiatives
Building networks with Egyptian cultural institutions and academic organizations
The Cairo posting allowed Macalawi to leverage his cultural background and Islamic heritage to create meaningful
connections between the Philippines and one of the Arab world's most influential nations. His work contributed to
enhancing the Philippines' cultural presence in the region and demonstrated the strategic value of deploying
diplomats with deep cultural competence.
International Expansion: China and Bahrain
Further broadening his diplomatic portfolio, Macalawi served as an Attaché and member of the diplomatic staff in
the People's Republic of China. This assignment represented a significant geographic and cultural shift, requiring
him to adapt his diplomatic skills to East Asian contexts while maintaining his core focus on consular services and
migrant protection.
Additionally, Macalawi rendered four years of service in the Kingdom of Bahrain, returning to the Gulf region
where he once again focused on migrant welfare and the protection of the Filipino community. His Bahrain
assignment reinforced his expertise in Gulf consular operations and allowed him to apply lessons learned from his
earlier Saudi Arabia posting to a different Gulf state context.

PAGE 4
Institutional Leadership
Director, DFA NCR West (2016–2018)
Prior to his retirement, Macalawi returned to the Philippines to assume a leadership role at the Department of
Foreign Affairs' home office. From 2016 to 2018, he was designated as Director at the West Office of the
Department of Foreign Affairs in Manila, specifically at DFA NCR West located at SM City Manila. This
appointment represented the culmination of his three-decade career and placed him in charge of one of the busiest
consular satellite offices in the country.
As Director, Macalawi's responsibilities included:
Supervising the operations of a high-volume consular office serving thousands of Filipino citizens
Implementing streamlined processes to improve service delivery and reduce wait times
Advocating for more efficient and responsive foreign service support for the general public
Mentoring junior foreign service officers in the nuances of consular law and migrant protection
Coordinating with other DFA offices to ensure consistent policy implementation
Managing staff performance and professional development
His leadership at DFA NCR West was characterized by a focus on customer service excellence and a commitment
to making consular services more accessible to ordinary Filipinos. He brought his extensive field experience to
bear on institutional operations, ensuring that the home office maintained the same level of dedication to citizen
welfare that he had demonstrated abroad.
Core Contributions and Advocacy
Champion of Migrant Welfare
Macalawi's career was fundamentally defined by his commitment to the "Third Pillar" of Philippine Foreign
Policy: the protection of the rights and promotion of the welfare of Filipinos overseas. This pillar, alongside the
promotion of national security and economic diplomacy, represents the Philippines' recognition that millions of its
citizens work abroad and require robust consular protection.
Throughout his postings in the Middle East and North Africa, Macalawi was particularly noted for his skill in
resolving complicated and sensitive cases involving OFWs. These cases often involved:
Labor disputes and wage claims
Contract violations and illegal recruitment
Medical emergencies and repatriation
Legal assistance and detention cases
Domestic worker abuse and exploitation
Cultural misunderstandings requiring mediation
Macalawi frequently worked behind the scenes, leveraging his cultural understanding and diplomatic relationships
to secure the safety and legal rights of citizens in distress. His approach combined legal expertise with cultural
sensitivity, recognizing that effective consular protection in Islamic countries required both procedural competence
and cultural intelligence.

PAGE 5
Professional Integrity and Ethical Leadership
Throughout his three decades of service, Macalawi maintained a reputation for professionalism and integrity. In a
field where diplomatic personnel sometimes face ethical challenges and temptations, he remained steadfast in his
commitment to serving the Filipino people without compromise. His colleagues and subordinates remember him as
a leader who led by example, demonstrating that effective diplomacy requires both technical competence and moral
clarity.
Legacy and Cultural Significance
As a prominent Muslim Filipino diplomat, Macalawi's service in key Islamic centers—Saudi Arabia, Libya, Egypt,
and Bahrain—highlights the strategic role of Bangsamoro professionals in Philippine foreign relations. His career
demonstrates that effective diplomacy in the Islamic world benefits greatly from deploying officials who share
cultural and religious affinities with host nations.
Macalawi's legacy in the DFA is characterized by:
A lifelong commitment to the Filipino people, both at home and abroad
The establishment of best practices in consular protection and migrant welfare
The mentoring of a new generation of foreign service officers
The demonstration that cultural diversity within the Foreign Service strengthens Philippine diplomacy
The bridging of understanding between Christian-majority Philippines and the Islamic world
He remains a respected figure among the "archival" generation of Filipino diplomats who laid the groundwork for
modern consular services, and his contributions continue to influence DFA policies and practices related to OFW
protection.
Recognition and Honors
While specific awards and formal recognitions are not extensively documented in public records, Macalawi's three-
decade career and progression through increasingly senior positions represent a form of institutional recognition.
The trust placed in him to lead DFA NCR West during the final years of his career reflects the high regard in which
he was held by DFA leadership.
Within the Filipino community in various countries where he served, Macalawi earned informal recognition as a
trusted advocate and reliable source of assistance during times of crisis. This grassroots recognition, while not
reflected in formal awards, represents perhaps the most meaningful acknowledgment of his service.
Challenges and Complexities
Macalawi's diplomatic career unfolded against a backdrop of significant challenges that tested his skills and
resilience:
Political Instability
Serving in countries like Libya and navigating the complex political landscapes of the Middle East required
constant adaptation to changing circumstances. Macalawi had to maintain effective consular operations even as
host countries experienced political transitions, regional conflicts, and shifting diplomatic relationships.

PAGE 6
OFW Vulnerability
The systemic vulnerabilities faced by OFWs—particularly domestic workers in the Gulf region—presented
ongoing challenges. Despite the best efforts of consular personnel, structural issues such as the kafala sponsorship
system, cultural barriers, and inadequate legal protections for migrant workers meant that many cases could not be
fully resolved. Macalawi had to balance advocacy with diplomatic realities, knowing that aggressive intervention
could sometimes jeopardize broader bilateral relationships.
Resource Constraints
Like many DFA personnel, Macalawi often worked with limited resources—insufficient staff, tight budgets, and
inadequate facilities. Managing high caseloads while maintaining service quality required creative problem-solving
and personal dedication beyond normal duty hours.
Cultural Navigation
As a Muslim Filipino diplomat, Macalawi occupied a unique position—able to navigate Islamic cultural contexts
more effectively than many colleagues, yet still representing a predominantly Christian nation. This required
careful balance and the ability to bridge different cultural perspectives while maintaining professional neutrality.
Retirement and Later Years
Following his retirement from the Department of Foreign Affairs in 2018, specific details about Macalawi's
activities are not extensively documented in public records. Like many career diplomats, he likely maintained
connections with the foreign service community and may have provided informal mentorship to younger
diplomats. His three decades of experience represent an invaluable institutional memory that continues to inform
DFA practices and policies.

title: Macalimbon, Maungangun Dimakuta
text:
PAGE 1
Col. Maungangun "Misangkad"
Dimakuta Macalimbon
Sulutan sa Sundigan a Piagapo
Reign: Singular, posthumously
unrepeated
Military Rank
Colonel, Philippine Army
Military Mayor of Piagapo
Term: 1977 to 1981 (appointed by Pres.
Ferdinand E. Marcos)
Born
Malaig, Wato-Balindong, Lanao del Sur
Ethnicity
Maranao
Notability
Only crowned Sultan of Western
Piagapo (Sulutan sa Sundigan a
Piagapo) in local tradition; pioneer
Muslim Army officer; Top Ten
Outstanding Municipal Mayor, 1979
Known For
Maungangun Dimakuta Macalimbon
Col. Maungangun "Misangkad" Dimakuta Macalimbon was a
Maranao military officer, military mayor, and traditional royal
figure whose name is tied permanently to the municipality of
Piagapo, Lanao del Sur. He carried several distinct identities across
his lifetime: a Colonel in the Philippine Army, an appointed Military
Mayor of Piagapo during the Marcos era, an advocate for peace and
clan reconciliation across both Lanao provinces, and, in a
distinction nobody else has matched before or since, the only person
ever formally crowned Sulutan sa Sundigan a Piagapo, the Sultan
of Western Piagapo.
That last title is the one people in Piagapo still bring up first when
his name comes up. Plenty of men in Lanao have worn military rank
or held a mayor's seat. Far fewer get enthroned into a sultanate seat
that, by community account, has never been filled again since, and
fewer still spent decades after their term in office working to settle
clan wars instead of stepping away from public life altogether.
Contents
1 EARLY LIFE AND LINEAGE
2 MILITARY CAREER
3 MILITARY MAYOR OF PIAGAPO
4 THE SULTANATE OF SUNDIGAN A PIAGAPO
5 PEACE ADVOCACY AND RIDO SETTLEMENT
6 LEGACY
7 SEE ALSO
8 REFERENCES
EARLY LIFE AND LINEAGE
Macalimbon's roots trace back to Malaig in Wato-Balindong, Lanao
del Sur, a town whose name carries weight in Maranao royal
genealogy. On his mother's side, he descended from a line
connected directly to one of the more storied figures in that history.
His maternal grandfather was Mama sa Paigoay, sibling of the
historical Datu Dimakuta, a name that surfaces again and again in
tarsila records tracing royal descent across the Pat A Pangampong a
Ranao, the Four Principalities of Lanao.
Mama sa Paigoay's daughter, Bae Maulad, became Macalimbon's
mother. That maternal line is part of why his eventual enthronement
as sultan carried real legitimacy in the eyes of the community rather
than being a ceremonial gesture. In Maranao tradition, a sultanate

PAGE 2
Soldier, military mayor, crowned sultan,
and Rido settlement advocate across
Lanao del Sur and Lanao del Norte
seat isn't handed out casually. It has to connect to bloodline, and
Macalimbon's connection ran straight through the house of
Dimakuta.
MILITARY CAREER
Macalimbon's path into public life started in uniform, and he became known as a pioneer Muslim officer within the
Armed Forces of the Philippines at a time when that distinction genuinely meant something. He served as Battalion
Commander of the 25th Infantry Battalion in Balabagan, Lanao del Sur, from 1984 to 1985, leading troops through
a stretch of Lanao's history that demanded both military discipline and cultural sensitivity in equal measure.
His career carried him well beyond Mindanao too. He became the first Muslim Assistant Commandant of Far
Eastern University in Manila, a post that placed him at the intersection of military training and civilian academic
life in the national capital. He went on to serve as ROTC Commandant at Mindanao State University and later at
Gregorio Araneta University, shaping the next generation of officer candidates in both regions. Along the way he
also held the post of Brigade S5 (civil-military operations officer) of the 23rd Brigade in Ditucalan, Iligan City, and
served as S5 officer of the 1st Tabak Division based in Polakan, Zamboanga del Sur. Eventually, he rose to the rank
of Colonel in the Philippine Army, the rank by which he is most remembered.
MILITARY MAYOR OF PIAGAPO
In 1977, President Ferdinand E. Marcos appointed Macalimbon Military Mayor of Piagapo, Lanao del Sur, a post
he held until 1981. He served as one of the town's chief executives alongside other notable figures of the period,
including Bashier Amairomag and Guimba Mandangan, in a stretch of years when military officers regularly
stepped into Piagapo's top civilian post, a reflection of the security situation across Lanao at the time and the
practical need for leadership that could navigate both worlds at once.
His time in office coincided with one of the most difficult periods for the region. He was responsible for processing
hundreds of MNLF rebel returnees back into civilian life, and he took part in the rescue of foreign nationals during
and after Martial Law. For his record in office, he received various awards and commendations from government
and private-sector bodies recognizing his gallantry, bravery, and loyalty to both country and constituents. In 1979,
he was adjudged one of the Top Ten Outstanding Municipal Mayors in the Philippines by President Marcos
himself, a national distinction that placed Piagapo, a small Maranao town, on a list usually dominated by far larger
municipalities.
Piagapo itself carries deep royal significance bigger than any one administration. Local history holds that the area
was once ruled by a queen, Dayang Labi, a descendant of Sharief Kabungsuan, the missionary credited with
introducing Islam to Maguindanao. She was enthroned as the Bai sa Radapan, and a barangay in Piagapo was
named after her title to preserve her legacy. Claimants to sultanate leadership across the different areas of Piagapo
trace their genealogical legitimacy back to her, which is the same cultural framework that gave weight to
Macalimbon's own enthronement generations later.
THE SULTANATE OF SUNDIGAN A PIAGAPO
Within the traditional governance structure of the Pat A Pangampong a Ranao, Piagapo sits inside the larger
Pangampong a Bayabao, one of the four historic principalities making up the Lanao confederation. Piagapo itself is
internally divided into three districts, one of which is Sundigan a Piagapo (also rendered Sendigan a Piagapo), the

PAGE 3
western portion of the municipality that gave Macalimbon's title its name.
He was enthroned as the Sulutan sa Sundigan a Piagapo, Sultan of Western Piagapo. What makes this distinction
stand out in local memory is that, by community account, he remains the only person ever formally crowned with
this exact title. Other Piagapo sultanates carry on through succeeding generations, but this particular seat has stayed
tied to his name alone, posthumously and without a successor claiming the same crown.
This kind of singular, unrepeated title isn't unusual in the decentralized Lanao sultanate system, where royal houses
can rise, go dormant, or remain attached permanently to the figure who held them, depending on lineage,
community consensus, and circumstance. For Macalimbon, it means his legacy in Piagapo isn't measured only by
years served in uniform or in the mayor's office. It's measured by a crown that, as far as local tradition goes,
nobody else has worn.
PEACE ADVOCACY AND RIDO SETTLEMENT
After his time as mayor, Macalimbon's public life didn't end, it shifted direction. He became widely recognized
across both Lanao del Sur and Lanao del Norte as an advocate for settling Rido, the clan-based conflicts that have
historically strained Maranao communities and, left unresolved, can stretch across generations. His work in this
area is remembered as a genuine milestone, helping translate his standing as a soldier, statesman, and sultan into
tangible peace and reconciliation between feuding clans on both sides of the Lanao provincial line.
That body of peacebuilding work is, for many who knew him, just as central to his legacy as either his military
record or his crown.
LEGACY
Colonel Macalimbon's life traces a path that's genuinely rare even within a region accustomed to leaders wearing
multiple hats. Soldier, military mayor, sultan, and peace advocate are four very different kinds of authority and
responsibility, and he held all of them across one lifetime.
In Piagapo today, his name remains attached to a title nobody else has carried, and to a body of Rido settlement
work that left both Lanao del Sur and Lanao del Norte more peaceful than he found them, a distinction that keeps
his memory alive well past his years in active service.

Macapanton Abbas, Sr.
Macapanton H. Abbas, Sr. (February 1910 to August 3, 1964) was a
Maranao lawyer, jurist, and public servant from Dayawan, Dansalan
(now Marawi City), Lanao.
He's remembered today as the first Muslim Filipino to pass the
Philippine Bar Examinations and, more remarkably, the first Muslim
Filipino to place in the Top 10, finishing 2nd in his cohort. That double
distinction didn't just make him a personal trailblazer; it cracked open a
door that had never been opened before for the Bangsamoro people in
the country's legal and judicial system.<ref
name="mb2020">Template:Cite news</ref>
From the courts of Lanao del Sur to the benches of Sulu and Davao,
Abbas spent his career building firsts: first Muslim fiscal, first Muslim
district judge, first Muslim judge of the Court of First Instance. He
served under five presidents, survived a war, lost a child to its brutality,
and still came out the other side with his integrity intact. His story isn't
just about a man who passed a bar exam. It's about what one person's
determination can unlock for an entire people.

Early Life and Family
Macapanton Abbas was born in February 1910 in Dayawan, a village in
Dansalan, the town that would eventually grow into Marawi City.<ref
name="everybodywiki">Template:Cite web</ref>

PAGE 2
His biological father was Hadji Darapa Abbas, the Datu of Marawi, and his mother was Dalumabi, who held the
royal title of Bai-a-labi sa Dayawan, meaning she was of the royal women of that settlement.
His paternal lineage traced directly to Hadji Okur, the Rajah Muda (crown prince) of Marawi, and from him to
Rampatan, the Datu of Marawi. The Abbas name carried enormous weight in Lanao; it was associated with the
traditional chief ruler and defender of Marawi going back multiple generations.
Upon Macapanton's birth, he was adopted by his maternal uncle in accordance with an accepted practice in
Maranao culture, where children are sometimes raised by relatives as a mark of honor and family solidarity. His
adoptive father was Sultan Cotawato of Dayawan and Wato, the brother of his mother Dalumabi. Sultan
Cotawato became popularly known as Amai Macapanton, meaning "Father of Macapanton," and it was through
this adoption that the young Abbas grew up connected to both the Dayawan and Wato royal houses.<ref
name="everybodywiki" />
Royal Lineage
Few lawyers in Philippine history came from a background as deeply rooted in traditional governance as
Macapanton Abbas.
Through his biological and adoptive family lines, he held rights of succession in several of the most prominent
royal houses of Lanao: Dayawan, Marantao, Marawi, Wato, Madaya, and Taraka. He was also connected to the
more recently established Sultanate of Lanao, whose first Sultan was his uncle, Ibra Gundarangin, who also
served as the first Congressman (Representative) of Lanao.<ref name="everybodywiki" />
This multi-layered royal heritage meant that Abbas moved through both indigenous political structures and the
modern Philippine legal system with a foot in each world. His very name, Macapanton, was a traditional one; and
the world he eventually entered as a lawyer and judge was, for most of his people, a foreign institution. He bridged
both with deliberate ease.
Education
Abbas finished his elementary schooling in Dansalan, completing the basic level of formal education that was still
relatively uncommon for Maranao children in the early twentieth century.
For secondary school, he traveled far from home, enrolling at the American-run Torres High School in Tondo,
Manila. He was among the first Maranaos to complete a high school education, a distinction that in itself spoke to
both his family's foresight and his own willingness to navigate an unfamiliar world far from Lake Lanao.<ref
name="everybodywiki" />
He then enrolled at the Philippine Law School, one of the leading private law schools of the era. He completed his
Bachelor of Laws (LL.B.) degree in 1935, and in the same year, he sat for and passed the Philippine Bar
Examinations. He was admitted to the Philippine Bar in 1935, making him the very first Muslim Filipino lawyer in
the country's history.<ref name="everybodywiki" />
The Philippine Bar Examinations: A Historic Achievement
Passing the bar was already an exceptional feat. Placing 2nd in the entire country was something else entirely.

PAGE 3
According to records from the National Commission on Muslim Filipinos (NCMF), Macapanton Abbas, Sr. was
the first Maranao, and the first Muslim Filipino, to place in the Top 10 of the Philippine Bar Examinations,
finishing in 2nd place.<ref name="mb2020" /> No Muslim Filipino had ever come close to that kind of national
ranking in the bar exams before him.
The significance of this is hard to overstate. The Philippine Bar was, and still is, one of the most competitive
professional examinations in the country. For a young man from Dansalan who grew up far from Manila's law
schools and libraries to place 2nd nationally was a statement. It said, clearly and without ambiguity, that the
Bangsamoro mind was just as sharp, just as capable, and just as ready to lead as anyone else in the Philippine legal
profession.
Abbas carried that credential with him into every courthouse and every courtroom he ever entered. It was never just
a personal achievement. It was, in the words of those who followed him, the key that unlocked the door.
"The first Maranao second placer was the late Macapanton Abbas Sr., who pulled off the feat in the
1940s on his way to becoming the country's first Muslim lawyer." — Manila Bulletin, citing National
Commission on Muslim Filipinos records, May 1, 2020<ref name="mb2020" />
Student Activism and Leadership
Abbas wasn't just studying law at Philippine Law School; he was building networks and shaping ideas about what
the Philippines could be.
At the law school, he joined the Mystical Order of the Swastika, a fraternal student organization (using the
ancient symbol of good fortune, well before its later associations). He rose through its ranks to become its
Mahatma Grand Lama, the organization's top student leader.<ref name="everybodywiki" />
More consequentially for Philippine political history, Abbas co-founded the Young Philippines Party alongside
Wenceslao Vinzons, a charismatic young lawyer who would later become one of the most celebrated guerrilla
commanders of World War II. The founding members of the Young Philippines Party were a remarkable group,
including names that would go on to define Philippine public life: Arturo Tolentino, Lorenzo Sumulong,
Diosdado Macapagal, Domocao Alonto, and Jose Laurel Jr., among others.<ref name="everybodywiki" /><ref
name="vinzons">Template:Cite news</ref>
Abbas was also a member of the Nucleus Group of the Pan Malayan People's Union, a student-led organization
that sought solidarity among the peoples of the Malay Archipelago. Even as a student, he was thinking in broad,
regional terms about identity, politics, and community.
Entry into the Legal Profession
After his admission to the bar in 1935, Abbas began what would become a series of historic firsts in the Philippine
legal profession. He wasn't just practicing law; he was, by his very presence in each role he entered, opening that
role to an entire community for the first time.
He became the first Moro First Assistant City Attorney, the first Moro Provincial Fiscal, the first Moro District
Judge, and the first Moro judge of the Court of First Instance (now the Regional Trial Court). Each of these titles
came with its own significance, and together they traced the arc of a career spent not just serving the law but
expanding who that law could speak for and who could speak for it.<ref name="everybodywiki" />

PAGE 4
The 1938 National Assembly Elections
Politics called Abbas early, though his first encounter with electoral politics was a painful one.
In the run-up to the 1938 Second National Assembly elections, Abbas entered the race at the last minute. His
opponent was Tomas Cabili, a prominent figure who had served as Lanao's delegate to the 1935 Constitutional
Convention. Cabili had earned tremendous goodwill among the Maranaos by refusing to sign the Constitution, the
only delegate to do so, on the grounds that it failed to protect the rights of the Moro people, especially the
Maranaos.<ref name="everybodywiki" />
The timing of Abbas's late entry created an awkward situation: many of his own relatives had already committed to
campaign for Cabili, including his own father, Hadji Abbas, who was one of Cabili's campaign leaders. They had
pledged in good faith because Abbas had earlier said he wasn't going to run.
A new block voting law heavily favored the governing Nacionalista Party, and all 98 seats of the National
Assembly went to Nacionalista candidates that year. The contest between Abbas and Cabili was close, but it ended
bitterly. Relatives who had pledged to the Quran to support Cabili burned the voting precinct in Dansalan, which
was Abbas's own hometown. It was a wound that went deeper than any election loss.
After that experience, Abbas stepped back from electoral politics entirely. He turned, instead, to the law.
World War II: Resistance and Sacrifice
When the Japanese forces occupied the Philippines in the early 1940s, Macapanton Abbas faced the same
impossible choices that every Filipino did, but with an added layer of pressure directed specifically at the Moro
community.
The Japanese made deliberate efforts to recruit young Moros, framing their occupation as an opportunity to take
leadership away from Christian Filipinos. Many were tempted. Abbas wasn't. He refused to collaborate, and the
consequences were immediate: the Japanese placed him on a wanted list.<ref name="everybodywiki" />
What followed was a grinding, dangerous months-long flight. Abbas, his wife, his mother-in-law, four young
daughters (the youngest just a few months old at the time), and their household servants moved from village to
village across Lanao. They survived thanks to the Maranao tradition of hospitality rooted in the torogan (the royal
house), where travelers, especially those of royal lineage, could find shelter. Relatives and friends opened their
homes. Communities protected them.
But the war took its toll. Abbas was wounded, and the wound became infected. He needed massive doses of
antibiotics to recover. And then, in the most devastating moment of those years, his youngest daughter Salma died.
She was still an infant.<ref name="everybodywiki" />
That loss broke something. Abbas made the decision to surrender.
When he finally turned himself in, the Japanese commander did not arrest him. Instead, he offered Abbas the post
of Justice of the Peace. It was, in its own way, an acknowledgment of his standing. Abbas accepted, and from that
position he began rebuilding what the war had tried to destroy.

PAGE 5
Post-War Career and Presidential Appointments
On July 22, 1943, Abbas was formally appointed Justice of the Peace of the Momungan groups of municipal
districts, Lanao, by President Jose P. Laurel. He was 33 years old. It was his first judicial appointment, and it
wouldn't be his last.<ref name="og1943">Template:Cite book</ref>
The appointments that followed tracked the rise of a lawyer who was consistently recognized by the country's
highest executive office, across administrations and across regions.

Abbas served under five presidents spanning more than fifteen years of the post-war Philippine Republic, and at
every step he was breaking new ground for Muslim Filipinos in the judiciary.
Campaigning for President Magsaysay
By 1953, Abbas had been serving as Provincial Fiscal of Sulu for several years. When Ramon Magsaysay entered
the 1953 presidential race, Abbas made a decision that would shape both his career and the political outcome in
Lanao: he resigned his post as Fiscal to campaign for Magsaysay full-time.
He returned to Lanao and united his clan behind the candidate. The result was a resounding margin: Magsaysay
carried Lanao by a wide vote, in no small part because of the network Abbas had mobilized.<ref
name="everybodywiki" />
Magsaysay kept faith with his supporters. In 1954, he appointed Abbas as District Judge of the Sixteenth Judicial
District of Sulu and Basilan City. Two years later, in 1956, he elevated Abbas to the Court of First Instance of Sulu,
the highest trial court at the time. It was the culmination of everything Abbas had worked toward: a Muslim
Filipino, born in Dayawan, sitting as a judge in the country's highest trial court.

PAGE 6
Personal Life
Macapanton Abbas married Hadja Sitti Rahma Yahya, a woman who was herself remarkable in her own right.
She was the first Moro woman to receive her education in Cebu, where she studied from elementary through
college level in the 1920s up to 1936, an extraordinary achievement for a Moro woman of that generation.<ref
name="everybodywiki" />
Hadja Sitti Rahma was the daughter of Sheikh Ismail Yahya, from Bayang and Yemen, and Bai Rosa Peralta,
whose family roots spanned Malita, Davao, Buayan (Cotabato), Ilocos Norte, and Yemen. She was an heiress to a
hacienda in Malita, Davao that belonged to her family.
Together, Macapanton and Hadja Sitti Rahma raised thirteen children.
Their eldest daughter, Hadja Potri Zorayda Abbas, married Senator Mamintal Tamano, one of the most
prominent Muslim Filipino statesmen of the twentieth century.
Their eldest son, Macapanton Rashid Abbas, Jr., became a lawyer and businessman, and served as former Sultan
of Dayawan.
Their second son, Dr. Firdausi Ismail Abbas, also became a lawyer, and holds the title of Sultan of Lanao.
The Abbas children and their descendants have continued to be significant figures in Bangsamoro civic, legal, and
cultural life, a legacy directly traceable to the values their father embodied.
Legacy
Macapanton Abbas didn't set out to be a symbol. He set out to be a lawyer. But the two things turned out to be
inseparable.
Before Abbas, there was no Muslim Filipino in the Philippine legal profession. There was no Muslim fiscal, no
Muslim district judge, no Muslim CFI judge. The doors to those offices existed, but no one from the Bangsamoro
had walked through them. Abbas walked through all of them, and in doing so, he made it possible for others to
follow.
His 2nd place ranking in the Philippine Bar Examinations was particularly meaningful, not because bar rankings
define a lawyer's worth, but because it demolished any lingering assumption that Muslim Filipinos couldn't
compete at the highest levels of national professional life. In a country where the legal system was built largely
around Christian Filipino political and social norms, Abbas's ranking was an argument, made in numbers, that the
Bangsamoro people belonged in that system and could excel within it.<ref name="mb2020" />
The National Commission on Muslim Filipinos (NCMF) counts Abbas among the most consequential figures in the
history of Muslim Filipino participation in Philippine public life. His daughter's marriage into the Tamano family,
and his sons' continuation of the legal profession, suggest that the values he modeled were transmitted not just
through stories but through lived example.
Death
Macapanton H. Abbas, Sr. died on August 3, 1964. He was in his mid-fifties, leaving behind a family of thirteen
children, a distinguished judicial career, and a legacy that the Bangsamoro legal community still looks to as a
foundational chapter in its history.<ref name="everybodywiki" />

PAGE 7
He had spent nearly three decades in public service, surviving a world war, political defeat, personal tragedy, and
the isolation that came with being always the first of his kind in every room he entered. He did it with the bearing
of a man who knew exactly who he was, where he came from, and what he owed to the people he represented.

Imelda Macapundag
Imelda Macapundag Panolong (born January 9, 1968) is a
Meranaw career diplomat from the Bangsamoro region who carved a
singular path through the Philippine Department of Foreign Affairs
(DFA).
She's the first Maranao woman in Philippine diplomatic history to
rise to the rank of Career Minister and, later, Chief of Mission —
making her the highest-ranking Bangsamoro woman ever to serve in
the Philippine foreign service.
Her appointment in 2020 as the seventh Philippine Ambassador to
Oman capped a career built on decades of quiet, consistent service
across the Middle East, South Asia, Southeast Asia, and North
America.
Panolong didn't just break barriers. She carried the weight of
representing her people, her faith, and her country simultaneously,
and she did it in some of the world's most consequential postings for
Overseas Filipino Workers and Muslim Filipinos abroad.

Early Life and Background
Panolong was born on January 9, 1968, in Malaysia, though her roots are firmly planted in the Bangsamoro
homeland.
She traces her heritage to the Meranaw people, the indigenous Muslim community of the Lake Lanao region —
one of the major ethnolinguistic groups within the Bangsamoro collective.
The circumstances of her birth in Malaysia are consistent with the historical reality of many Bangsamoro families
who maintained cross-border ties with the Malay world long before the modern Philippine state drew its southern
boundaries.
Growing up, Panolong would carry both worlds with her: the identity of a Meranaw Muslim and the formal
credentials of a Filipino citizen navigating national institutions built far from the shores of Lanao.
That dual awareness would become one of her defining strengths as a diplomat, particularly in Muslim-majority
countries where her cultural fluency opened doors that career credentials alone could not.
Education
Panolong pursued higher education at the University of the Philippines Diliman, the country's premier state
university, where she earned a Bachelor of Arts degree in Political Science in 1989.<ref name="wiki-
panolong">Template:Cite web</ref>
She followed that up with graduate academic units in International Studies between 1990 and 1991, a period that
coincided with her transition into the foreign service.<ref name="wiki-panolong"/>
Her academic background in political science and international studies gave her an analytical foundation that
would prove useful throughout a career spent navigating the geopolitics of the Middle East, the welfare of migrant
workers, and the intricacies of bilateral diplomacy.
Diplomatic Career
Entry into the Foreign Service
Panolong began her connection to the DFA in the early 1990s, starting as a contractual clerk at the Office of
Cultural Affairs and Public Information Services.<ref name="wiki-panolong"/>
She formally entered the Philippine Foreign Service in 1991, and her initial years in the Home Office were spent in
administrative and consular affairs roles, including stints as a Principal Assistant at the Passport Division, Office of
Consular Affairs, and as a Special Assistant at the Office of the Undersecretary for Migrant Workers Affairs.<ref
name="jeddah-cv">Template:Cite web</ref>
These early assignments weren't glamorous, but they gave her hands-on experience with two of the DFA's most
operationally demanding portfolios: passport services and migrant worker welfare, both of which would later
become central to her work overseas.

PAGE 3
First Overseas Assignment: Islamabad, Pakistan (1995–1996)
Her first posting abroad took her to the Philippine Embassy in Islamabad, Pakistan, where she served as Third
Secretary and Vice Consul from 1995 to 1996.<ref name="wiki-panolong"/>
It was a baptism by fire in the complexities of South Asian diplomacy, and it set the tone for a career that would
keep returning to the arc connecting Southeast Asia to the Muslim world.
Jeddah: First Consular Tour (1996–2001)
From Islamabad, Panolong moved to the Philippine Consulate General in Jeddah, Saudi Arabia, where she served
as Consul from 1996 to 2001, focusing on Assistance-to-Nationals (ATN) matters.<ref name="wiki-panolong"/>
The Jeddah consulate is one of the busiest Filipino diplomatic posts in the world, given the massive concentration
of Overseas Filipino Workers (OFWs) in the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia.
Her five years there gave her an unmatched familiarity with the legal, logistical, and human dimensions of
protecting Filipino workers in the Gulf.
Home Office: North Africa Division (2001–2003)
Returning to Manila, Panolong served as Director of the North Africa Division under the Office of Middle East and
African Affairs from 2001 to 2003.<ref name="wiki-panolong"/>
It was a policy-level role that broadened her strategic view of the Philippines' engagement with the Arab and
African world, a perspective she'd continue to develop in subsequent postings.
Manama, Bahrain (2003–2006)
From 2003 to 2006, Panolong was posted to the Philippine Embassy in Manama, where she served as First
Secretary and Consul.<ref name="wiki-panolong"/>
Bahrain's Filipino community is significant, and her work there deepened her expertise in OFW welfare across
Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) states.
Toronto, Canada (2006–2009)
Panolong took her career west when she was assigned as Deputy Consul General at the Philippine Consulate
General in Toronto from 2006 to 2009.<ref name="wiki-panolong"/>
Toronto is home to one of the largest Filipino diaspora communities in North America, and her posting there gave
her a different dimension of the Filipino overseas experience, far from the labor-heavy Gulf postings that had
defined much of her earlier career.
Home Office: Middle East Division (2009–2011)
Back in Manila from 2009 to 2011, Panolong served as Director of the Middle East Division under the Office of
Middle East and African Affairs.<ref name="wiki-panolong"/>

PAGE 4
It was her second directorship in the same office, this time focused on the region where she had spent the most
formative years of her career.
Jakarta, Indonesia (2011–2014)
Panolong's assignment to the Philippine Embassy in Jakarta as Minister and Consul General from 2011 to 2014
marked a significant step up.<ref name="jeddah-cv"/>
Indonesia is the world's largest Muslim-majority country, and her posting in Jakarta reflected the DFA's recognition
of her stature as a diplomat with both senior rank and cultural credibility in the Islamic world.
Los Angeles, California (2014–2015)
She returned to North America for her posting as Deputy Consul General at the Philippine Consulate General in
Los Angeles, California, from 2014 to August 2015.<ref name="wiki-panolong"/>
Jeddah: Historic Return as Consul General (2015–2017)
In September 2015, Panolong was appointed Consul General of the Philippine Consulate General in Jeddah,
completing a full circle back to the post where she had begun her Gulf career two decades earlier, this time as its
head.<ref name="wiki-panolong"/>
It was a historic appointment on multiple fronts.
She was the first Filipina ever to hold the position of Consul General in Jeddah, and the first Asian woman to
become Consul General in Saudi Arabia.<ref name="wiki-panolong"/>
Her exequatur was received from the Saudi Ministry of Foreign Affairs on September 7, 2015.<ref name="wiki-
panolong"/>
The timing couldn't have been more demanding.
Between 2016 and 2017, two of Saudi Arabia's largest construction firms, Saudi Oger and Saudi Binladin Group,
underwent catastrophic closures, leaving thousands of OFWs stranded without pay or documentation.
Under Panolong's leadership, the Jeddah consulate coordinated the repatriation of at least 683 displaced Filipino
workers from those two firms.<ref name="wiki-panolong"/>
As the consulate's jurisdiction also covered Mecca, she was additionally responsible for the welfare of Muslim
Filipinos performing the annual Hajj, a responsibility that carried both logistical and spiritual weight for the
Bangsamoro communities she represented.<ref name="wiki-panolong"/>
On March 25, 2017, she was designated as Chargé d'Affaires at the Philippine Embassy in Riyadh during a historic
state visit by President Rodrigo Duterte, making her the de facto head of the Philippine diplomatic mission in the
Saudi capital during one of the highest-profile bilateral engagements of the period.<ref name="wiki-panolong"/>
Promotion to Chief of Mission
Panolong's ascent through the ranks of the foreign service produced two watershed moments for the Bangsamoro
community.

PAGE 5
She became the first Maranao woman in the Philippine diplomatic corps to be promoted to the rank of Career
Minister and later to Chief of Mission, Class II.<ref name="wiki-panolong"/>
She was subsequently confirmed by the Commission on Appointments to the rank of Chief of Mission, Class I, the
highest career rank in the Philippine Foreign Service.<ref name="ca-confirmation">Template:Cite web</ref>
No Bangsamoro woman had ever reached that level before her.
Ambassador to Oman (2020–2024)
In February 2020, President Rodrigo Duterte nominated Panolong to serve as Philippine Ambassador to the
Sultanate of Oman, succeeding outgoing Ambassador Narciso Castañeda.<ref name="wiki-panolong"/>
The Commission on Appointments confirmed her appointment on March 4, 2020.<ref name="dfa-
confirmation">Template:Cite web</ref>
Panolong arrived in Muscat on August 16, 2020, and formally presented her credentials to Sultan Haitham bin
Tarik on November 8, 2020.<ref name="wiki-panolong"/>
She became the seventh Philippine Ambassador to Oman and the first woman to hold the post.<ref name="wiki-
panolong"/>
At the time of her appointment, Oman accommodated approximately 45,000 Filipinos, making them the fourth
largest expatriate population in the country, with numbers that had been growing steadily before the COVID-19
pandemic disrupted global migration patterns.<ref name="wiki-panolong"/>
She served in Muscat until 2024.
Cultural Significance and Bangsamoro Legacy
What makes Panolong's story remarkable isn't just the list of firsts she accumulated across a three-decade career.
It's what those firsts meant for a community that had long been underrepresented in the national institutions of the
Philippine government.
The Bangsamoro people, including the Meranaw, have historically navigated a complicated relationship with
Manila's bureaucratic structures, shaped by decades of armed conflict, peace negotiations, and an ongoing struggle
for political recognition and self-governance.
For Panolong to rise to the top of the Philippine diplomatic corps as a Muslim woman from Lanao was, in a very
real sense, a demonstration of what's possible when the barriers are crossed, not by abandoning one's identity, but
by carrying it into the halls of power.
Her postings across the Muslim world weren't incidental. They were consequential. Wherever she served, she
brought a cultural literacy and a lived understanding of Islam that career diplomats from other backgrounds simply
couldn't replicate.
In Jeddah, in Manama, in Jakarta, and in Muscat, she wasn't just a Filipino diplomat. She was a Meranaw Muslim
speaking to governments and communities whose worldview she genuinely shared.
That's the kind of cultural diplomacy that no briefing book can fully prepare a person for.

PAGE 6
Personal Values and Family Life
Panolong is married to Jamel "Jim" Panolong, and the couple has three sons named Mohammad, Mohsen, and
Mohaisen.<ref name="wiki-panolong"/>
Her family accompanied her through many of her foreign assignments, a choice that reflects both the personal
sacrifices of a diplomatic career and the value she placed on keeping family at the center of her service.
Her sons' names, all rooted in Islamic tradition, signal the deliberate continuity of faith and identity that she
maintained throughout a career that took her far from Lanao and into the most formal rooms of global diplomacy.
Friends and colleagues have described her approach to public service as grounded, principled, and deeply attentive
to the welfare of Filipinos on the ground, particularly the migrant workers whose precarious lives in the Gulf she
witnessed up close for years.
Recognition and Honors
Panolong's career has been recognized through her formal advancement within the DFA career ladder, from
contractual clerk to Chief of Mission Class I, one of the highest career distinctions in the Philippine Foreign
Service.
Her confirmation by the Commission on Appointments as both an Ambassador and as Chief of Mission Class I is
itself a form of institutional recognition of her record and qualifications.<ref name="ca-confirmation"/>
She is widely cited as a trailblazer for Muslim Filipinas in public service, and her career is frequently referenced in
discussions of gender and religious minority representation in Philippine diplomacy.
Legacy
Imelda Macapundag Panolong's legacy rests on a simple but profound truth: she went where no Bangsamoro
woman had gone before, and she went there well.
From her early years processing OFW cases in Jeddah to her final years as the Philippines' top envoy in Muscat,
she built a body of work defined by service to ordinary Filipinos far from home, by skilled navigation of one of the
world's most diplomatically complex regions, and by the quiet, persistent assertion that a Meranaw Muslim woman
belongs at the table wherever the Philippines' interests are represented.
Her career is a landmark in Bangsamoro history not because it was celebrated loudly, but because it was built
steadily, assignment by assignment, for more than three decades.
For the next generation of Bangsamoro women in public life, she is proof that the ceiling, while real, can be
broken.

title: Macarambon, Benasing Jr.

Benasing Macarambon Jr.
Benasing Onayan Macarambon Jr. is a Bangsamoro politician
and public servant who served as Representative of the 2nd
District of Lanao del Sur in the House of Representatives of the
Philippines for three consecutive terms from 1998 to 2007.
He is a leader of the Moro National Liberation Front (MNLF)
and a longtime advocate for the ecological protection of Lake
Lanao.
His career spans regional assembly service, three terms in the
national legislature, a gubernatorial bid, and a post-congressional
appointment to the Subic Bay Metropolitan Authority (SBMA)
board.
Contents
1 BACKGROUND
2 EARLY GOVERNMENT SERVICE
3 ARMM REGIONAL LEGISLATIVE ASSEMBLY
4 MEMBER OF THE HOUSE OF REPRESENTATIVES
5 LEGISLATIVE WORK
6 POST-CONGRESSIONAL CAREER
7 ADVOCACY
8 MNLF AFFILIATION
9 PLACE IN THE BANGSAMORO NARRATIVE
10 SEE ALSO
11 CATEGORIES
BACKGROUND
Macarambon was born in Lanao del Sur, Philippines.
He comes from a prominent family in the province.
The Macarambon family is associated with Fiat Construction
Services, one of the largest construction firms in Mindanao.
His public service began well before his congressional career,
rooted in regional governance structures that predated the formal
ARMM.

PAGE 2
Kabalikat ng Malayang Pilipino (KAMPI)
Moro National Liberation Front (MNLF)
Legislative Office
Representative, 2nd District of Lanao del
Sur House of Representatives of the
Philippines 1998 to 2007 (Three
consecutive terms)
Prior Legislative Service
Assemblyman, 2nd District of Lanao del
Sur 3rd ARMM Regional Legislative
Assembly (1996 to 2001)
Earlier Government Service

December 29, 1987

Notability
Three-term Representative of the 2nd
District of Lanao del Sur (1998 to 2007),
MNLF leader, and advocate for the
ecological protection of Lake Lanao.
Known For
Authoring legislation on education and
cooperative broadcasting; infrastructure
development across Lanao del Sur; post-
EARLY GOVERNMENT SERVICE
On December 29, 1987, Macarambon was designated by then-
Secretary of Local Government Luis T. Santos as a member of
the Sangguniang Pampook (Regional Assembly) in Region XII.
The Sangguniang Pampook was an interim regional body that
operated under the framework of regional autonomy in Muslim
Mindanao prior to the formal establishment of the ARMM.
His tenure in that body ended when it was abolished by the
enactment of Republic Act No. 6734 in 1989, which set the stage
for the 1990 ARMM elections.
ARMM REGIONAL LEGISLATIVE
ASSEMBLY
Macarambon later served as Assemblyman for the 2nd District of
Lanao del Sur in the 3rd ARMM Regional Legislative Assembly,
which sat from 1996 to 2001.
This regional legislative experience gave him direct exposure to
the governance challenges of Muslim Mindanao, including
questions of autonomy, development funding, and the
administration of communities with distinct cultural and
religious identities.
MEMBER OF THE HOUSE OF
REPRESENTATIVES
Macarambon was elected Representative of the 2nd District of
Lanao del Sur in 1998, succeeding Pangalian Balindong, who
had held the seat from 1995 to 1998.
He served three consecutive terms, covering the 11th, 12th, and
13th Congress of the Philippines, until 2007.
As a member of the House of Representatives, his work included
drafting and filing legislation, representing the interests of his
district's constituents, participating in congressional committees,
and contributing to national policy discussions affecting Muslim
Mindanao.
His tenure coincided with significant national debates on
Bangsamoro autonomy and the ongoing peace process with the
MNLF and the Moro Islamic Liberation Front (MILF).

PAGE 3
congressional service on the SBMA board.
Pull Quote
"His role in Congress connects local
realities in Lanao del Sur with national
decision-making."
LEGISLATIVE WORK
Macarambon authored numerous House bills during his
congressional service.
Among the legislation he authored that became law:
Republic Act No. 8912 created a secondary school in the
municipality of Sultan Gumander, Lanao del Sur.
Republic Act No. 9171 granted the Muslim Development
Multipurpose Cooperative a broadcast franchise.
The Senate Legislative Reference Bureau also records his authorship of measures providing for the construction of
infrastructure across Lanao del Sur, including municipal halls, bridges, roads, and sports development centers in
municipalities such as Tugaya, Marogong, Balabagan, Ganassi, and Madalum.
He likewise authored bills establishing and expanding schools, including measures creating national high schools
in Malabang and Balabagan, and converting the Balabagan Trade School into a state polytechnic college.
POST-CONGRESSIONAL CAREER
After completing his three terms in the House, Macarambon ran for Governor of Lanao del Sur in the 2007
elections under Kabalikat ng Malayang Pilipino (KAMPI) but was unsuccessful.
In 2018, President Rodrigo Duterte appointed him as a member of the Board of Directors of the Subic Bay
Metropolitan Authority (SBMA), where he represented the business and investment sectors.
He replaced outgoing board member Stefani C. Sano in that post.
His appointment papers were signed on May 8, 2018, and his term ran until September 22, 2022.
ADVOCACY
Beyond his legislative record, Macarambon has been a consistent advocate for the ecological protection of Lake
Lanao, one of the most significant bodies of water in Mindanao and a lake of deep cultural and ecological
importance to the Maranao people and the broader Lanao del Sur community.
MNLF AFFILIATION
Macarambon is identified as a leader of the Moro National Liberation Front, the historic Bangsamoro organization
founded by Nur Misuari that played a central role in negotiating the first formal peace agreement between the
Bangsamoro and the Philippine government under the 1996 Final Peace Agreement.
His affiliation with the MNLF situates him within the tradition of Bangsamoro leaders who pursued autonomy and
recognition through both armed struggle and political engagement.

PAGE 4
PLACE IN THE BANGSAMORO NARRATIVE
Benasing Onayan Macarambon Jr. represents the generation of Bangsamoro politicians who moved between
regional governance structures and the national legislature during the critical decades of the peace process.
His career arc, from the Sangguniang Pampook to the ARMM Regional Assembly to the House of Representatives
to the SBMA board, reflects the layered nature of Bangsamoro political participation in Philippine institutions.
His legislative record in the House, particularly in education and infrastructure, left a concrete mark on
communities in the 2nd District of Lanao del Sur.

Sinaolan T. Macarambon
Sinaolan T. Macarambon is widely recognized as the first Muslim
Filipino woman civil engineer — a distinction that carries weight
not just as a biographical footnote but as a defining chapter in the
story of the Bangsamoro people's integration into the Philippine
national mainstream. She built her career entirely within the
Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH), where she
spent more than three decades shaping the roads, bridges, and flood
control systems that keep Mindanao functioning. From a pioneering
student at Mindanao State University (MSU) in the 1960s to a
Presidential appointee under President Benigno Aquino III, her
journey is the story of what happens when institutional purpose meets
individual determination — and what it looks like when someone
refuses to let barriers define their ceiling.
Contents
1 Background and Early Life
2 Education at Mindanao State University
3 Career at the Department of Public Works and Highways
3.1 Early Career and Administrative Foundations
3.2 District Engineer, Cotabato 2nd Engineering District
3.3 Regional Director, DPWH Region XII
(SOCCSKSARGEN)
3.4 The Mindanao River Basin Crisis and Flood
Rehabilitation
3.5 Regional Director, DPWH Region XI (Davao)
3.6 National Appointment: Acting Director III
4 Legacy and Cultural Significance
4.1 The First, Not the Last
4.2 Integration Through Participation
4.3 The MSU Ripple Effect
4.4 Contribution to DPWH Institutional Memory

Background and Early Life
Macarambon grew up in a Mindanao that was, in many ways, still finding its footing. The southern Philippines had
long felt the weight of historical neglect — underdeveloped infrastructure, limited access to higher education, and a
Muslim-majority population that remained largely outside the circles of national professional life. It was into this

PAGE 2
landscape that she was born and raised, and it was this landscape that she would spend her career rebuilding, one
project at a time.
Understanding where she came from means understanding the world the Mindanao State University was built to
change. When MSU was established in the early 1960s in Marawi City, its mandate was both educational and
geopolitical: to bring Muslims and other cultural minorities into the national fold by training a homegrown
generation of professionals.<ref name="msu-coe-history">College of Engineering – History (unofficial), MSU
Main Campus – Marawi City. Retrieved March 15, 2026, from https://www.msumain.edu.ph/coe-history/</ref>
That mission wasn't just aspirational — it was urgent. The southern provinces needed engineers, doctors, teachers,
and administrators who understood their communities from the inside.
For Macarambon, choosing engineering wasn't just a career decision. It was, in the context of her time and place, a
quiet act of defiance — against regional stereotypes, against gender expectations, and against the assumption that
Muslim women from Lanao del Sur didn't belong in technical fields.
Education at Mindanao State University
Macarambon enrolled in the Mindanao State University College of Engineering (COE) shortly after its founding in
1964. The curriculum was deliberately modeled after that of the University of the Philippines, with the explicit goal
of producing graduates who could hold their own against the best engineers from any institution in the country.<ref
name="msu-coe-history" />
What that looked like in practice was tough. The early COE years were lean — major courses were offered with
minimal laboratory equipment, and the "end-to-end" system was in full effect.<ref name="msu-coe-history" />
Under this approach, students tackled two courses at a time in intensive six-week blocks, a format designed to
compress the curriculum without cutting corners on rigor.<ref name="msu-coe-history" /> It was the kind of
academic environment that either broke people or built them into something extraordinary. For Macarambon and
her classmates in the pioneering batch, it built them.
The Civil Engineering Department, also established in 1964, had a clear sense of regional purpose from day one.
Students weren't just learning to pass board exams — they were being trained to solve the specific hydrological,
geological, and infrastructural problems of the MINSUPALA region (Mindanao, Sulu, and Palawan).<ref
name="msu-cedept">Civil Engineering Department – MSU Main Campus – Marawi City. Retrieved March 15,
2026, from https://www.msumain.edu.ph/college-of-engineering/cedept/</ref> That grounding in regional reality
would prove invaluable throughout Macarambon's entire career.
She graduated as part of what the department would later honor as its pioneering batch — a cohort whose members
went on to establish a tradition of excellence that has since produced over a thousand registered civil engineers
with impact not just locally, but globally.<ref name="msu-cedept" />
Career at the Department of Public Works and Highways
Early Career and Administrative Foundations
After completing her degree, Macarambon joined the Department of Public Works and Highways, where she would
remain for the bulk of her professional life. Her early career placed her at the intersection of engineering and
administration — a combination that would become her hallmark.

PAGE 3
By 1983, she had taken on roles tied to the delineation of functions, authority, and responsibility in connection with
the construction and supervision of government buildings.<ref name="dpwh-do">Department Order | Page 368 |
Department of Public Works and Highways. Retrieved March 15, 2026, from
https://dpwh.gov.ph/DPWH/references/issuances/DO?page=367</ref> Through Department Order No. 58 and
related issuances, she helped define the accountability structures that govern how public infrastructure gets built —
and who answers when something goes wrong.<ref name="dpwh-do" /> That kind of foundational work doesn't
make headlines, but it shapes everything that follows.
Mastering the bureaucratic side of engineering — budget management, regulatory compliance, inter-agency
coordination — was as important to her as the technical craft itself. She understood that in the Philippine civil
service, the best engineer in the room isn't always the one who gets things done. The one who gets things done is
the one who can navigate systems as well as survey land.
District Engineer, Cotabato 2nd Engineering District
In September 1994, Macarambon was assigned as District Engineer of the Cotabato 2nd Engineering District in
Region XII.<ref name="dpwh-so-region12">Reassignment of Engr. SINAOLAN T. MACARAMBON as Regional
Director of DPWH Region XII. Department of Public Works and Highways. Retrieved March 15, 2026, from
https://dpwh.gov.ph/dpwh/issuances/special-order/8042</ref> It was a significant step up — the District Engineer
is the key link between the national department and the local government units, the person responsible for keeping
roads passable, bridges safe, and drainage systems functional in communities that often don't have much margin for
failure.
The Cotabato basin is not an easy place to build. Seasonal flooding, varying accessibility, and the security
complexities of Central Mindanao all made the job demanding. Managing infrastructure in that environment
required more than engineering knowledge — it required trust-building, community awareness, and the kind of
steady hand that doesn't rattle when conditions change without warning. She handled it.
Her tenure as District Engineer laid the groundwork for the regional leadership roles that followed. It gave her field
credibility that no administrative posting could manufacture — the kind of credibility that comes from knowing
what a flooded road looks like at 5 a.m. and what it takes to get it functional by noon.
Regional Director, DPWH Region XII (SOCCSKSARGEN)
In January 2009, Macarambon was designated as Regional Director of DPWH Region XII, the SOCCSKSARGEN
region — South Cotabato, Cotabato, Sultan Kudarat, Sarangani, and General Santos City.<ref name="dpwh-so-
region12" /> It was one of the most senior field positions in the department, overseeing a region whose economy
depends heavily on agriculture, and whose infrastructure is constantly tested by the Mindanao River system and its
tributaries.
Her appointment came at a critical time. The region had been grappling with recurring catastrophic floods, and the
2008–2009 flooding events had displaced thousands of residents and devastated agricultural land across the
Cotabato basin.<ref name="ptf-mrbrd">Mindanao River Basin Flood Report. Presidential Task Force on Mindanao
River Basin Rehabilitation and Development. Retrieved March 15, 2026, from
https://www.scribd.com/presentation/34165470/PTF-MRBRD-BRIEF-25August2009</ref> The scale of the
disaster prompted the creation of the Presidential Task Force on Mindanao River Basin Rehabilitation and
Development (PTF-MRBRD), and Macarambon was squarely at the center of the response effort.

PAGE 4
The Mindanao River Basin Crisis and Flood Rehabilitation
The Mindanao River Basin is one of the country's most complex hydrological systems — a web of major rivers
including the Ala, Pulangi, and Mindanao rivers, all draining through the Ligawasan Marsh before exiting into
Illana Bay.<ref name="ptf-mrbrd" /> When that system overflows, the consequences are enormous. The PTF-
MRBRD was established through executive orders specifically to deal with the aftermath: displaced communities,
destroyed dikes, ruined farms, and broken roads.<ref name="ptf-mrbrd" />
As Regional Director, Macarambon's role went well beyond issuing repair orders. She was involved in aerial
surveys to assess the extent of flooding, coordinated relief and reconstruction timelines, and oversaw the repair of
flood control structures along the Ala River and other major waterways.<ref name="ptf-mrbrd" /> The work
demanded constant coordination across multiple government agencies — a logistical challenge as demanding as
the engineering itself.
The management of the Mindanao River Basin required not just infrastructure repair, but a
comprehensive approach to how water moves through the region's marshlands and into the bay — a
challenge that defined much of Macarambon's tenure in Region XII.|Presidential Task Force on
Mindanao River Basin Rehabilitation and Development (PTF-MRBRD), 2009
In 2010, she also reported on the commencement of a ₱412.4-million road project in Region XII, designed to be
operational by January 2012.<ref name="pia-caraga">2010-05-23 – PIA – Caraga Regional Office. Retrieved
March 15, 2026, from http://www.piacaraga.com/2010_05_23_archive.html</ref> Projects of that scale are rarely
just about pavement — they're about connecting farmers to markets, cutting travel time for medical access, and
signaling to communities that the national government hasn't forgotten them. The fact that she was managing
budgets of that magnitude speaks to the level of institutional trust she had earned.
Regional Director, DPWH Region XI (Davao)
By September 2010, Macarambon had been reassigned as Regional Director of DPWH Region XI, based in Davao
City.<ref name="dpwh-region11">Designation SINAOLAN T. MACARAMBON Regional Director XI.
Department of Public Works and Highways. Retrieved March 15, 2026, from
https://dpwh.gov.ph/dpwh/tags/designation-sinaolan-t-macarambon-regional-director-xi-178</ref> The move was a
notable shift — from Region XII's vast river basins and agricultural flatlands to Region XI's rapidly urbanizing,
economically dynamic Davao landscape.
Region XI presents a different set of infrastructure challenges: urban road congestion, port development,
metropolitan drainage, and the demands of a fast-growing city that was quickly emerging as one of the most
significant urban centers in Mindanao. That the DPWH moved Macarambon from one type of challenge to an
entirely different one says something about how the department viewed her: not as a specialist in one kind of
problem, but as someone who could read any landscape and deliver results.
Her rotation across two of Mindanao's most consequential regions in a relatively short span was a clear institutional
statement — she was being used as a problem-solver, not just a placeholder.
National Appointment: Acting Director III
In December 2012, President Benigno S. Aquino III appointed Macarambon as Acting Director III within the
Department of Public Works and Highways, with the appointment taking effect in early 2013.<ref name="aquino-
mop">Full text of "Messages of the President Book 15: Benigno S. Aquino III (Volume 2)." Internet Archive.

PAGE 5
Retrieved March 15, 2026, from https://archive.org/stream/MOP-Vol2-Benigno-S-Aquino-III/13AD%20-
%20BSA_djvu.txt</ref>
This appointment moved her from regional execution to national policy — a shift that required compliance with
stringent Career Executive Service (CES) qualifications and aligned with the Aquino administration's Daang
Matuwid platform of transparency and accountable governance.<ref name="aquino-mop" /> It was the capstone of
a career built on merit: not through political connections, but through three decades of showing up, delivering, and
building things that still stand.
Legacy and Cultural Significance
The First, Not the Last
Macarambon's designation as the first Muslim Filipino woman civil engineer isn't a ceremonial title — it's a
historical marker. In the 1960s, engineering in the Philippines was essentially a male profession. For a Muslim
woman from Lanao del Sur to enter that space, graduate at a high standard, and then spend decades climbing
through one of the country's most hierarchical government agencies was genuinely unprecedented.
Her career provides the clearest possible proof of what the MSU founding mandate was designed to produce: a
professional class of Muslim Filipinos who could compete — and lead — at the national level.<ref name="msu-
coe-history" /> She didn't just benefit from that mission. She became its most visible evidence.
Her career demonstrates that technical excellence can be a powerful tool for social integration. By
excelling in a field that is inherently objective and evidence-based, she was able to command respect
across cultural and political divides.|Research on Macarambon's career trajectory, 2026
Integration Through Participation
What makes Macarambon's legacy particularly valuable for the Bangsamoro community is the model it represents.
She didn't occupy a tokenistic or symbolic role — she ran engineering districts and regional offices that served the
entire population of Central and Southern Mindanao, regardless of faith or ethnicity. The flood control systems she
oversaw, the roads she built, the administrative frameworks she helped design — these served Christian, Muslim,
and Lumad communities alike.
That's what genuine integration looks like. Not absorption, not assimilation, but full participation in the national
project while remaining rooted in one's own identity and community.
The MSU Ripple Effect
As a member of the pioneering batch of the MSU Civil Engineering Department, Macarambon stands as a
founding figure of an institution that has since produced over a thousand registered engineers with global impact.
<ref name="msu-cedept" /> Every student who came after her did so in a department that her cohort helped build
— and with the knowledge that the ceiling they might be looking at had already been broken by someone who
looked like them.
The department's ongoing commitment to research relevant to the MINSUPALA region — hydrological systems,
geotechnical challenges, ASEAN-context engineering — continues to trace back to the intellectual framework that
was established during Macarambon's time as a student.<ref name="msu-cedept" />

PAGE 6
Contribution to DPWH Institutional Memory
Her 1983 work on the delineation of functions within the DPWH — helping to clarify which offices are responsible
for what during the construction and supervision of government buildings — is an often-overlooked part of her
legacy.<ref name="dpwh-do" /> Administrative frameworks don't get the same attention as ribbon-cutting
ceremonies, but they're what make ribbon-cutting ceremonies possible. The accountability structures she helped
define ensured that public infrastructure was built to standard, within budget, and with clear lines of responsibility.
That kind of contribution shapes institutions long after the people who made it are gone.
Recognition
Recognized as the first Muslim Filipino woman civil engineer in the Philippines
Served as one of the most senior Muslim professionals in the Department of Public Works and Highways
Appointed by President Benigno S. Aquino III as Acting Director III, DPWH (2012–2013)<ref
name="aquino-mop" />
Member of the pioneering batch of the Mindanao State University College of Engineering, Class of
approximately 1968<ref name="msu-newsletter">Official Newsletter of Mindanao State University – MSU
Main Campus. Retrieved March 15, 2026, from https://www.msumain.edu.ph/wp-
content/uploads/2025/03/03-2023-December-MSU-Newsletter.pdf</ref>
Managed one of the largest government-led flood rehabilitation operations in Mindanao's history through the
PTF-MRBRD<ref name="ptf-mrbrd" />
Death
Details regarding the date and circumstances of Sinaolan T. Macarambon's passing have not been formally
published in accessible public records at the time of this article's writing. BangsamoroPedia welcomes
contributions from family members, colleagues, and researchers who can provide verified information about her
later years and passing.

title: Macaraya, Tocod D. Sr
text:
PAGE 1
Tocod D. Macaraya Sr
Atty. Tocod D. Macaraya Sr. was a prominent Maranao lawyer, legal scholar, academic administrator, and
statesman who left a lasting and definitive mark on the legal, political, and educational landscape of Mindanao. He
was a Delegate to the 1971 Constitutional Convention representing Lanao del Sur.
He's recognized today as one of the premier legal minds from the region, a foundational pillar of the Mindanao
State University (MSU) System, and the principal architect behind the early structures of regional autonomy for
Muslim Mindanao.
Contents
1 Legal Career and Bar Distinction
2 University Administration and Reform
2.1 Officer-in-Charge (1974–1975)
2.2 First Executive Vice President (1989–1990)
3 Regional Autonomy and Statecraft
3.1 The RCC's Consultations
3.2 Drafting the Organic Act for ARMM
4 Literary and Scholarly Contributions
5 Legacy
6 References
7 See Also
Legal Career and Bar Distinction
In 1954, Macaraya sat for the Philippine Bar Examination, a year that turned out to be one of the most storied in
the history of the Philippine legal profession.
That batch produced Florenz Regalado, who achieved what remains the highest bar exam score ever recorded in
the country: 96.7%.
Against that extraordinary field, Macaraya finished with a general average of 92.65%, placing him among the Top
15 topnotchers nationwide.
For a young Maranao lawyer in post-war Philippines, that ranking wasn't just a personal achievement. It was a
statement, clear proof that Muslim Mindanao had legal talent that belonged on the national stage, at a time when
few from the region had found their way there.
University Administration and Reform
Macaraya gave a major portion of his career to the growth and stability of the Mindanao State University (MSU)
System, a landmark institution founded in Marawi City to advance peace and socio-economic development in the
south of the Philippines.

PAGE 2
Atty. Tocod D. Macaraya Sr.
Ethnicity
Maranao
Nationality
Filipino
Professions
Lawyer · Legal Scholar · Academic
Administrator · Statesman
Institution
Mindanao State University System
