Key Positions Held
Delegate to the 1971 Constitutional Convention;
Officer-in-Charge, MSU (1974–1975) · First
Executive Vice President, MSU System (1989–
1990) · Chairman, Regional Consultative
Commission for Muslim Mindanao
He served in two pivotal administrative capacities across different
periods of the university's history.
Officer-in-Charge (1974–1975)
During a period of intense socio-political turbulence in the region,
Macaraya stepped in as the interim head of the university.
His main task was keeping MSU functional and its academic
mission on track while the broader Mindanao landscape was in
upheaval.
It wasn't a glamorous role, but it was a necessary one, and
Macaraya handled it with the steady hand the institution needed.
First Executive Vice President (1989–1990)
A decade and a half later, Macaraya came back to MSU in a much
more formal and historic capacity.
Under Special Order No. 03-P issued in 1989, he was designated
as the university system's very first Executive Vice President,
making him the inaugural holder of that office in MSU System
history.
In that capacity, he formalized structural expansions across the
growing system and introduced administrative reforms that laid
operational groundwork still felt in the MSU of today.
Regional Autonomy and Statecraft
If there's one chapter of Macaraya's career that eclipses the others
in terms of national impact, it's his chairmanship of the Regional
Consultative Commission (RCC) for Muslim Mindanao.
Following the ratification of the 1987 Philippine Constitution, he
was appointed to lead this body, which carried a mandate of real
historical weight: conduct genuine grassroots consultations across
Muslim Mindanao and produce a legal framework for regional
self-governance.
The RCC's Consultations
Operating out of Zamboanga City through 1988, the commission
went on the ground. They conducted extensive multi-sectoral
consultations across communities throughout Mindanao, making
sure ordinary Moros had a voice in shaping the structure of their
own political future.

PAGE 3
Major Legislation
Republic Act No. 6734 (Organic Act for the
ARMM)
Notability
One of the first Maranao lawyers to rank among
the national Top 15 bar topnotchers, and the
principal architect of the legislative framework
that officially created the Autonomous Region in
Muslim Mindanao (ARMM).
Known For
1954 Bar Top 15 Topnotcher · Pioneering MSU
Executive Vice President · Chairman of the
Regional Consultative Commission · Co-drafter
of Republic Act No. 6734
Pull Quote
"Knowledge conquers all evils, and individual
professions must ultimately serve the
community."
This wasn't a top-down exercise in paper drafting. It was
deliberate, community-by-community listening, structured to give
the eventual legislation real democratic roots.
Drafting the Organic Act for ARMM
Under Macaraya's chairmanship, the RCC consolidated those
consultations into a legislative draft that would serve as the
foundation for one of the most consequential pieces of legislation
in post-Marcos Philippine history.
That draft became the primary basis for what Congress enacted as
Republic Act No. 6734, the Organic Act that officially created the
Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (ARMM).
Without the foundational work of the RCC under his leadership,
the path toward Moro political self-determination would've looked
considerably different.
Literary and Scholarly Contributions
Outside the halls of government and the boardrooms of the university, Macaraya was also a writer and a thoughtful
documentarian of Maranao and Islamic intellectual tradition in the Philippines.
His most noted scholarly work is a 1988 publication titled Nomination Letter for the 1988 King Faisal
International Award for Service of Islām and other Related Papers.
The text centers on statesman Ahmad Domocao Alonto and draws out the intersections between Islamic identity,
governance, and the long peace struggle in Mindanao, illuminating how faith and politics were never entirely
separate in the Bangsamoro experience.
It remains a key secondary source for historians studying the socio-political dimensions of Muslim Filipino
leadership.
Legacy
Atty. Tocod D. Macaraya Sr. is remembered as a bridge-builder, a Maranao son who worked the difficult ground
between minority aspirations and national legal structures, and who did it with intellectual rigor, institutional
patience, and a genuine sense of purpose.
His philosophy, recorded in the annals of the MSU, puts it plainly: knowledge conquers all evils, and one's
profession must ultimately serve the community, not just the individual.<ref name="msuPresidents"/>
That guiding belief shows up clearly in everything he built. He used law to assert worth, academia to prepare a
generation, and statecraft to open constitutional doors for a region that had long been waiting for them.
His central role in drafting the Organic Act for the ARMM places him among a very small number of Maranao
statesmen who directly shaped the constitutional future of their people, not through words alone, but through the
legal architecture they left standing.<ref name="senate6734"/><ref name="stanford"/>

Marjanie M. Macasalong
Marjanie Macasalong is a Filipino Moro politician and public servant from Lanao del Sur. He currently serves as
a Member of the Bangsamoro Parliament under the Bangsamoro Transition Authority (BTA) and is the former
Governor of Lanao del Sur. He is recognized for his leadership in regional governance, disaster response, and
institutional development in the Bangsamoro region.<ref name="pia2020">Philippine Information Agency.
Macasalong leads Lanao del Sur recovery efforts. 2020.</ref><ref name="barmm2023">Bangsamoro
Government. Profiles of Bangsamoro Parliament Members. Official BARMM Website, 2023.</ref>
---
Early Life and Education
Marjanie Macasalong hails from Lanao del Sur and is part of a respected Maranao family.
He pursued higher education in the Philippines, preparing for a career in governance and public service.
His early exposure to community leadership and public administration shaped his commitment to regional
development.<ref name="pia2020" />
---
Political Career
Governor of Lanao del Sur
Macasalong served as Governor of Lanao del Sur, where he led the province during a critical period
following the Siege of Marawi (2017).
His administration focused on rehabilitation, infrastructure rebuilding, and restoration of government
services in affected communities.

PAGE 2
Bangsamoro Parliament
He was appointed as a Member of the Bangsamoro Transition Authority Parliament, contributing to the
legislative work of BARMM.
As a parliament member, he participates in policy-making, governance reforms, and institutional
strengthening during the transition period.<ref name="barmm2023" />
---
Contributions to Bangsamoro Governance
Played a key role in post-conflict recovery and rehabilitation efforts in Lanao del Sur.
Advocates for infrastructure development, education, and public service delivery in the Bangsamoro region.
Supports peace-building initiatives and the institutionalization of BARMM governance under the
Bangsamoro Organic Law.
---
Legacy and Significance
Marjanie Macasalong is recognized as a leader who guided Lanao del Sur during a critical period of recovery
and transition.
His work bridges provincial governance and regional legislative development in BARMM.
He continues to contribute to the strengthening of Bangsamoro institutions and long-term regional stability.
---

Lead
Fahad Cali Macasimbar is a Filipino development practitioner,
youth leader, and peacebuilding advocate from Marawi City,
Lanao del Sur, in the Bangsamoro region of Mindanao. With over
seven years of grassroots engagement, Macasimbar has emerged
as a committed voice for inclusive, participatory development in
conflict-affected communities. His work bridges local realities
with broader institutional frameworks, focusing on water
sanitation and hygiene (WASH), food security, livelihood
development, and democratic governance. Currently serving as Project Coordinator at UNYPAD-Relief Assistance
Network and Organization, Inc. (UNYPAD-RANAO), he continues to champion community resilience and lasting
peace in the Bangsamoro region.
Macasimbar's significance lies not in titles alone, but in his deliberate commitment to empowering marginalized
communities. His career reflects a philosophy of public service rooted in trust-building, stakeholder collaboration,
and the principle that sustainable development emerges when local voices lead the conversation. As both a
practitioner and organizational leader, he exemplifies how technical expertise and grassroots connection can
advance peace and governance simultaneously.

PAGE 2
Early Life and Background
Fahad Cali Macasimbar was born and raised in Marawi City, the capital of Lanao del Sur province in the
Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM). Growing up in this historic city, Macasimbar
witnessed firsthand the complexities of conflict-recovery and community resilience. Marawi City's strategic
location and cultural significance in the Muslim-Mindanao region exposed him to diverse development challenges,
from post-conflict reconstruction to livelihood gaps and governance gaps affecting vulnerable populations.
His upbringing in a historically significant Muslim community shaped his understanding of peacebuilding not as an
abstract concept, but as a lived necessity. This formative context became the foundation for his later commitment to
inclusive, participatory development that respects local culture and agency.
Education
Macasimbar earned his Bachelor of Public Administration from Mindanao State University (MSU) Main
Campus, located in Marawi City.<ref name="educ1">Fahad Cali Macasimbar. Professional Biography. UNYPAD-
RANAO Documentation, 2024.</ref> His academic training in public administration provided him with formal
grounding in governance structures, institutional management, and policy frameworks, critical competencies for
navigating development work in complex regional contexts.
Beyond his undergraduate degree, Macasimbar obtained his Licensed Professional Teacher (LPT) credential in
2025, signaling his deliberate investment in education and capacity-building as a development strategy.<ref
name="lpt1">Fahad Cali Macasimbar. Professional Records. UNYPAD-RANAO, 2025.</ref> This additional
qualification reflects his conviction that knowledge transfer and human development form the backbone of
sustainable community change.
Throughout his career, he has participated in numerous specialized trainings covering conflict transformation,
disability inclusion, legal literacy, culture of peace, social protection, project management, and leadership
communication. These continuous learning engagements have deepened his ability to respond to multifaceted
development challenges in diverse, politically sensitive contexts.
Professional Career
Early Work as Community Organizer
Macasimbar began his development career as a Community Organizer with UNYPAD-Relief Assistance Network
and Organization, Inc. (UNYPAD-RANAO), a civil society organization focused on relief, recovery, and
sustainable development in the Bangsamoro region.<ref name="career1">Fahad Cali Macasimbar. Professional
History. UNYPAD-RANAO Organizational Records, 2017.</ref> In this foundational role, he developed extensive
experience in grassroots mobilization, stakeholder engagement, and field-level program facilitation. His work
involved direct engagement with barangay officials, community leaders, and vulnerable populations to understand
local needs, build trust, and mobilize collective action around shared development goals.
This phase of his career was marked by a strong field-based orientation. Rather than relying solely on institutional
frameworks, Macasimbar prioritized face-to-face engagement, listening processes, and participatory
methodologies. His coordination skills and authentic community connection became hallmarks of his approach,
contributing to improved development outcomes and deepened community ownership of programs.

PAGE 3
Current Role as Project Coordinator
Since advancing to the position of Project Coordinator at UNYPAD-RANAO, Macasimbar has assumed broader
responsibility for program design, implementation, monitoring, and reporting across multiple thematic areas.<ref
name="career2">Fahad Cali Macasimbar. Position Description and Organizational Role. UNYPAD-RANAO,
2024.</ref> His current portfolio encompasses:
Peacebuilding and conflict transformation: Designing and facilitating programs that promote dialogue,
address underlying causes of conflict, and strengthen social cohesion in post-conflict communities.
Water sanitation and hygiene (WASH): Overseeing water access, sanitation infrastructure, and hygiene
promotion initiatives that address fundamental health and dignity needs.
Food security and livelihood development: Managing interventions that strengthen agricultural
productivity, household income diversification, and economic resilience among vulnerable populations.
Governance and civic participation: Supporting institutional strengthening, legal literacy, and citizen
engagement in democratic processes and local governance.
As Project Coordinator, Macasimbar bridges multiple stakeholders: government agencies, donor organizations,
civil society partners, and community members. He ensures alignment between project activities and donor
requirements, institutional policies, and community priorities, a balancing act that demands both technical rigor and
political sensitivity.
Institutional Contributions and Organizational Leadership
Beyond his project management responsibilities, Macasimbar serves as Provincial Secretary of the UNYPAD
Lanao del Sur Chapter. In this leadership role, he supports administrative coordination, member communication,
documentation, and partner relations at the provincial level.<ref name="institutional1">Fahad Cali Macasimbar.
Organizational Leadership Record. UNYPAD Lanao del Sur Chapter, 2024.</ref> This position reflects his
demonstrated organizational capability and his broader commitment to institutional effectiveness and democratic
participation within civil society structures.
His work at the provincial level involves:
Supporting coordination among UNYPAD members across Lanao del Sur
Facilitating communication between local chapters and national leadership
Documentation of organizational activities and institutional learning
Strengthening partnerships with local government units (LGUs) and barangay officials
Advocating for member interests and supporting collective action on development priorities
Areas of Thematic Focus
Peacebuilding and Conflict Transformation
Macasimbar's peacebuilding work is grounded in the recognition that Bangsamoro communities have experienced
prolonged conflict and require deliberate, culturally sensitive approaches to peace consolidation. Rather than
viewing peace as the mere absence of violence, his programs emphasize positive peace: the building of trust,
strengthening of institutions, and creation of dialogue spaces where former adversaries can envision shared futures.
His training in conflict transformation has equipped him to facilitate dialogues that move beyond blame toward
problem-solving. He understands that sustainable peace in the Bangsamoro region requires addressing both formal
institutional dimensions (governance reforms, security sector reform) and relational dimensions (inter-community

PAGE 4
reconciliation, narrative change).
Water, Sanitation, and Hygiene (WASH)
WASH interventions in the Bangsamoro region are inseparable from governance and dignity. Macasimbar's WASH
work ensures that water and sanitation become not just technical infrastructure projects, but expressions of
government responsiveness and community agency. His approach integrates health education, institutional
coordination with LGUs, and community participation in planning and maintenance.
Food Security and Livelihood
In a region marked by poverty, conflict-induced displacement, and agricultural vulnerability, Macasimbar's
livelihood work focuses on building household and community resilience. His programs promote diversified
income sources, strengthen agricultural knowledge, and create linkages between small producers and market
opportunities. This work reflects an understanding that food security emerges when communities control the means
of their own productive life.
Governance and Institutional Strengthening
As someone trained in public administration, Macasimbar views governance strengthening as integral to
development. His work supports local government units in improving service delivery, transparency, and citizen
participation. He recognizes that weak governance perpetuates poverty and conflict, while responsive, inclusive
institutions create foundations for sustainable development.
Continuous Learning and Professional Development
A defining characteristic of Macasimbar's career is his commitment to ongoing professional development. Beyond
his formal degrees, he has completed specialized trainings in:
Conflict transformation and peace education
Disability inclusion and social protection
Legal literacy and citizen rights
Culture of peace and community dialogue facilitation
Project management and monitoring and evaluation (M&E)
Leadership communication and organizational development
This investment in learning reflects his belief that development professionals must continuously deepen their
understanding of complex realities and emerging best practices. It also signals his humility, his recognition that
technical credentials alone are insufficient for navigating the real-world messiness of development work in
conflict-affected regions.
Legacy and Professional Impact
Over seven years of dedicated service, Fahad Cali Macasimbar has contributed to multiple dimensions of
development and peacebuilding in the Bangsamoro region. His work has touched vulnerable communities,
strengthened civil society institutions, and helped bridge local communities with broader development initiatives.
His impact manifests not in dramatic headlines, but in sustained community trust, improved service delivery,
reduced conflict tensions, and strengthened local capacity.

PAGE 5
His legacy is that of a bridge-builder: someone who understands how to translate development principles into
culturally appropriate, locally owned programs. He demonstrates that peacebuilding and development are not
separate domains, but interconnected efforts that succeed only when rooted in genuine community participation
and local leadership.
As the Bangsamoro region continues navigating post-conflict recovery and institutional consolidation, practitioners
like Macasimbar remain essential. His work embodies the principle that sustainable peace and development emerge
from inside communities, from individuals who choose to stay, build relationships, and invest their lives in
collective transformation.
Challenges and Context
Macasimbar's work occurs within significant structural constraints. The Bangsamoro region carries legacies of
prolonged conflict, limited state capacity, development gaps, and ongoing political transition. Development
practitioners in this context operate with limited resources, complex stakeholder dynamics, and competing
priorities between relief, recovery, and transformation.
Despite these constraints, Macasimbar's career represents a commitment to working within local realities rather
than imposing external solutions. His approach reflects awareness that sustainable development requires patience,
cultural humility, and genuine partnership with communities affected by conflict and poverty.

Abdulgani M. Macatoman
Abdulgani M. Macatoman is a prominent Filipino public
servant, business leader, and economic development advocate. As
a Mindanao-rooted professional, he has championed the growth of
micro, small, and medium enterprises across the Philippines,
advocated for the protection of overseas Filipino workers, and
emerged as a leading voice in the global halal economy. His career
spans high-level government service, corporate leadership, and
civic engagement, positioning him as a key figure in regional
economic cooperation and private sector development in the
Bangsamoro region and beyond.
Contents
1 Early Life and Education
2 Government Career
2.1 Department of Trade and Industry
2.2 Commission on Filipinos Overseas
3 Corporate and Civic Leadership
4 Global Halal Economy and Media Presence
5 Awards and Recognition
6 Legacy and Impact
7 Further Reading
8 See Also
Early Life and Education
Macatoman was born and raised in Mindanao, a heritage that has
shaped his lifelong commitment to the region's economic and
social development. His educational journey established a
rigorous foundation in commerce, law, and business management.
He earned a Bachelor of Science in Commerce with a major in
accounting from the University of the East (UE) in 1991. Continuing at UE, he completed his Bachelor of Laws in
1995, followed by a Master of Business Administration in 1999. Beyond formal education, he also became a
Certified Public-Private Partnership Consultant and completed the Phronetic Leadership Class through the
Development Academy of the Philippines in partnership with JICA, strengthening his expertise in development
economics and strategic governance.

PAGE 2
Government Career
Department of Trade and Industry
Appointed by President Rodrigo Duterte, Macatoman served as Undersecretary of the Department of Trade and
Industry (DTI), overseeing the Trade Promotions Group (TPG) and the Office of Special Concerns. In this capacity,
he led transformational initiatives across multiple sectors:
His work in investment promotion focused on attracting global investors and enhancing the competitiveness of
Philippine industries on the world stage. Recognizing that small businesses form the backbone of the Philippine
economy, Macatoman emerged as a fierce advocate for MSME development, spearheading programs to empower
micro and small entrepreneurs across the nation.
He chaired the Export Development Council, positioning Philippine exports for greater international
competitiveness. Additionally, Macatoman served as Senior Official for the BIMP-EAGA, facilitating regional
economic cooperation and trade facilitation among member nations.
Commission on Filipinos Overseas
Macatoman's tenure at the Commission on Filipinos Overseas (CFO) as Acting Secretary and Officer-in-Charge
reflected his deep commitment to the welfare of the global Filipino diaspora. During this period, he championed
initiatives to strengthen the protection of overseas Filipino workers (OFWs) and expanded engagement programs
connecting millions of Filipinos abroad with opportunities and support services in the home country.
Corporate and Civic Leadership
Beyond government service, Macatoman built an influential presence in both the private sector and civil society.
As Founder, President, and CEO of the Global Empire International Group of Companies, he directed a diverse
portfolio of business ventures focused on trade, investment facilitation, and economic development.
He served as Chairman of the Foreign Chamber Council of the Philippines (FCCP), fostering collaboration
between foreign investors and local Philippine industries. His leadership helped position the Philippines as an
attractive investment destination while supporting local business growth.
Recognizing the untapped economic potential of the Bangsamoro region, Macatoman assumed the role of
Chairman of the Bangsamoro Business Council, advocating for inclusive investment, inclusive growth, and
sustainable economic development in the Mindanao region.
His commitment to public service extended to the Armed Forces of the Philippines, where he holds the rank of
Reserve Lieutenant Colonel.
Global Halal Economy and Media Presence
Macatoman has positioned himself as a thought leader in the emerging global halal economy. He authored the book
Global Halal Economy, which explores the vast economic opportunities within the halal industry and its potential
for catalyzing international trade, fostering interfaith dialogue, and creating prosperity across Muslim-majority
regions.

PAGE 3
His expertise reaches the public through media platforms. He hosts Kabuhayan at Negosyo (Livelihood and
Business), a weekly program broadcast on Channel 23 and DWIZ 882 (AM radio), where he discusses business
opportunities, entrepreneurship, and livelihood development for Filipino workers and entrepreneurs.
Awards and Recognition
Macatoman's contributions to economic development, public service, and corporate leadership have earned him
numerous distinctions:
Management Man of the Year (2017), Philippine Council of Management
Asian Humanitarian Businessman of the Year, 5th Global Officials of Dignity (G.O.D.) Awards at the
United Nations
Most Outstanding Alumnus, University of the East
Ten Outstanding Young Filipinos (2012)
Paul Harris Fellow, Rotary International
Legacy and Impact
Macatoman's career represents a bridge between government, private enterprise, and civic engagement. His
advocacy for MSMEs has contributed to policy frameworks that support small business growth and resilience. His
leadership in the halal economy has elevated the Philippines' position within the global Islamic economy, opening
new markets and partnerships. Through his work on behalf of overseas Filipino workers and the Bangsamoro
business community, he has demonstrated commitment to inclusive development and regional prosperity.
Further Reading

title: Madale, Abdullah Timan
text:
PAGE 1
Dr. Abdullah T. Madale
Personal Information
Born: October 25, 1937
Ramain-Ditsaan, Lanao del Sur,
Philippines
Died: 2014
Ethnicity
Maranao ("People of the Lake")
Spouse
Abdullah Timan Madale
Abdullah Timan Madale (October 25, 1937 – 2014) was a
Maranao educator, anthropologist, author, and cultural
administrator from Lanao del Sur, Philippines.
Over a career spanning more than four decades, he became one of
the most consequential Maranao voices in Philippine scholarship:
expanding access to secondary education across Muslim Mindanao
through Mindanao State University, and producing a body of
ethnographic work that gave the Maranao people an authoritative,
insider-authored place in the national historiography.
His books remain core references for anyone studying the culture,
governance, and heritage of the Lake Lanao communities.
Contents
1 EARLY LIFE
2 EDUCATION
3 CAREER
3.1 Public School Service
3.2 National Museum of the Philippines
3.3 Mindanao State University
3.4 Post-Retirement Service
4 SCHOLARSHIP AND MAJOR WORKS
5 PERSONAL LIFE
6 LEGACY
7 SEE ALSO
EARLY LIFE
Abdullah Timan Madale was born on October 25, 1937, in a
teacher's cottage at the Ramain-Ditsaan Central Elementary School
in Lanao del Sur.
He was the fourth child of Macasolong Madale, a school
superintendent, and Hadja Faida Timan Madale, and grew up
steeped in both Islamic faith and the intellectual culture his parents
embodied.
His early childhood was shaped by the disruptions of World War II
and the Japanese occupation, during which his first classroom
lessons included singing and counting in Japanese.

PAGE 2
Hadja Nurjanna C. Madale
Education
Elementary Teacher's Certificate,
Philippine Normal College
B.S. Elementary Education, Philippine
Normal College
M.A. Supervision and Administration,
Philippine Normal College
Ph.D. Psychology, University Planning
and Administration, Al-Azhar
University, Cairo
Occupation
Educator, Anthropologist, Author,
Cultural Administrator
Institutions
Mindanao State University
National Museum of the Philippines
Philippine Normal College
ARMM
Notability
Pioneer educator and anthropologist
who expanded university access across
Muslim Mindanao and produced
foundational scholarship on Maranao
culture and heritage.
Known For
Establishing MSU's external high school
network; authoring The Maranao, The
Remarkable Maranaws, The Maranaw
Torogan, and Muslims: The
After liberation, he returned to a more formal schooling path and
distinguished himself from the start: he graduated as valedictorian
of Tamparan Central School, then went on to Lanao High School,
where he finished with second honors.
EDUCATION
Madale pursued his higher education at the Philippine Normal
College in Manila, where he earned three consecutive credentials:
Elementary Teacher's Certificate
Bachelor of Science in Elementary Education
Master's Degree in Supervision and Administration
While studying in Manila, he was far more than just a high-
achieving student. He served simultaneously as Student Council
President and Editor-in-Chief of The Torch, the college's official
student publication — a combination that speaks to both his
intellectual drive and his instinct for community leadership.
For his doctorate, Madale crossed continents. He earned his Doctor
of Philosophy from Al-Azhar University in Cairo, Egypt, one of the
oldest continuously operating universities in the world.
He specialized in Psychology, University Planning, and
Administration, and graduated with a rare distinction of Excellent,
Second Degree — a mark of exceptional academic performance.
CAREER
Public School Service
Madale began his professional life in the public school system,
working first as a Head Teacher before advancing to Assistant
Principal under the Bureau of Public Schools.
National Museum of the Philippines
In 1961, his deep familiarity with Maranao culture brought him to
the National Museum of the Philippines, where he served as an
anthropologist specializing in Muslim culture.
This role positioned him as a bridge between community
knowledge and formal institutional research.

PAGE 3
Misunderstood Filipinos; Ph.D. graduate
of Al-Azhar University with a distinction
of Excellent, Second Degree.
Mindanao State University
When Mindanao State University opened in Marawi City in July
1962, Madale was there from day one as its inaugural Public
Relations Officer.
What followed was a 20-year tenure at the institution, during which he held some of its most important
administrative positions:
Principal of the MSU Laboratory Elementary School (now the Integrated Laboratory School)
College Dean
Executive Assistant to the President
Assistant Vice President
Vice President for External Studies
It was in that final role where his impact on access to education was most felt. As Vice President for External
Studies, he pioneered the creation of MSU's external high school branches across the region, bringing secondary
education to communities in remote Mindanao that had previously been cut off from it.
His peers widely acknowledged that his qualifications and record would have made him a strong candidate for the
university presidency itself, but political dynamics within the institution ultimately meant that path was not taken.
He retired from formal MSU administration in 1982.
Post-Retirement Service
Retirement did not slow Madale down. He went on to serve as an educational consultant during the formative years
of the Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (ARMM), contributing institutional knowledge at a critical
moment in Bangsamoro governance.
In 1991, he briefly entered national politics, running for a seat in the Philippine Senate under the People's Reform
Party, led by Miriam Defensor Santiago.
He later returned to MSU as a full-time professor under the leadership of Dr. Emily M. Marohomsar, the
university's first Muslim woman president.
SCHOLARSHIP AND MAJOR WORKS
Madale was a prolific writer throughout his life, publishing hundreds of articles and several books that have
become standard references in the study of Maranao culture and Muslim Filipino identity.
His core published works include:
Title
Year
Focus
The Maranao (co-edited with
Mamitua Saber)
1975
Sociological and cultural frameworks of the Lake Lanao
communities.
The Remarkable Maranaws
1976
Customary laws, folklore, and social hierarchies of the region.
The Maranaw Torogan
1996
The architectural, social, and political significance of the
Maranao royal house.

PAGE 4
Muslims: The Misunderstood
Filipinos
2012
Essays challenging institutional biases and stereotypes directed
at Muslim Filipinos.
The significance of these works goes beyond documentation. At a time when Maranao culture was often filtered
through Eurocentric or Manila-centric lenses, Madale wrote from the inside. He mapped the structures of the Lanao
Sultanate, explained the cultural and political role of the torogan (the Maranao royal house), detailed traditional
land allocation systems, and systematically pushed back against the misrepresentations that had long shaped how
Muslim Filipinos were understood in mainstream Philippine society.
PERSONAL LIFE
Madale was married to Hadja Nurjanna C. Madale, and together they raised twelve children: Hyasminth, Rizaminh,
Sultan Alykhan, Sittie Aleyah, Sittie Nirveenh, Abdullah Junior, Abdul Lateef, Nurhirahma, Mirashna, Nazrallah
"Pinky," Muhamed Abdel Nasser, and Abdel Hamid Shams.
He remained an active presence in the Lanao community as an elder and scholar until his passing in 2014.
LEGACY
Dr. Abdullah T. Madale left two enduring marks on Mindanao and on Philippine history more broadly.
The first is structural: through his work establishing MSU's external high school network, he created real academic
pathways for thousands of young Muslim Filipinos in areas that had no secondary schools to speak of. The ripple
effects of that expansion are still felt in the region today.
The second is scholarly: at a moment when the dominant narratives about Muslim Filipinos were shaped by
outsiders, he provided an authoritative internal voice. His ethnographic texts on the Maranao gave the community's
history, laws, traditions, and rights a permanent, credible presence in Philippine academia.
Together, those two contributions make him a foundational figure in modern Bangsamoro intellectual and
institutional history.

title: Madale, Nagasura Timan
text:
PAGE 1
DR. NAGASURA T. MADALE
Personal Information
Born: February 1942
Marawi City, Lanao del Sur, Philippines
Ethnicity
Meranaw (Maranao)
Education
B.S. in Elementary Education, Mindanao
State University, 1968
M.A. in Asian Studies, University of the
Nagasura Timan Madale
Nagasura Timan Madale (born February 1942, Marawi
City) is a Meranaw cultural anthropologist, peace educator,
and one of the most respected voices in Bangsamoro
intellectual life.
A professor of cultural anthropology at Mindanao State
University for several decades, he devoted his career to two
intertwined missions: recovering the deep literary and ritual
traditions of the Maranao people from the margins of
Philippine scholarship, and then turning that recovered
heritage into practical tools for conflict resolution and
interfaith dialogue in Mindanao.
He is perhaps best known outside academic circles for
founding the School for the Living Tradition under the
National Commission for Culture and the Arts (NCCA), and
for leading the Access Philippines Youth Leadership Training
Program, a U.S. Department of State-funded initiative that
brought Muslim, Christian, and Lumad youth from Mindanao
to Northern Illinois University for intensive peace and
mediation training.
Contents

2 EDUCATION
3 ACADEMIC CAREER AT MINDANAO STATE
UNIVERSITY

5 NATIONAL CULTURAL GOVERNANCE

PEACEBUILDING
7 LITERARY AND ANTHROPOLOGICAL WORKS
8 ADVOCACY AFTER THE MARAWI SIEGE
9 RECOGNITION AND LEGACY
10 SEE ALSO
11 REFERENCES
EARLY LIFE AND ROOTS
Nagasura Timan Madale was born in Marawi City, Lanao del
Sur, the cultural and political heartland of the Meranaw
people, in February 1942.

PAGE 2
Philippines Diliman, 1973
Ph.D. in Philippine Studies, University of the
Philippines Diliman, 1987
Academic Positions
Professor of Cultural Anthropology, Mindanao
State University
Chair, Department of History, MSU (1975–
1976)
Vice Chancellor for Research and Extension,
MSU (since 1992)
Director, Southern Philippines Center for
Peace Studies (1981–1984)
Public Service
Commissioner, Organic Autonomy Law for
Muslim Mindanao (1980s)
Founding Chair, NCCA Sub-Commission on
Muslim Communities

and Letters (1991)

University Center for Postdoctoral Studies,
Dubrovnik (1983)

He is the son of Serapion A. Madale and Faidah T. Madale,
and grew up in a community where Islamic faith, customary
law, and oral tradition were not separate categories but woven
into the fabric of everyday life.
Lake Lanao, the body of water that defines Meranaw identity
(the name literally means "people of the lake"), shaped his
earliest intellectual instincts: a sense that the rhythms of oral
poetry, the rules of *adat* and *taritib* (customary law and
protocol), and the imperatives of *maratabat* (honor and
dignity) were not quaint survivals but living, functioning
frameworks with real explanatory power.
That sensibility, that the indigenous was not inferior to the
imported but was in fact irreplaceable, would run through
everything he wrote and built for the next six decades.
EDUCATION
Madale completed his Bachelor of Science in Elementary
Education at Mindanao State University in Marawi City in
1968.
He then moved to Quezon City to pursue graduate studies at
the University of the Philippines Diliman, earning his Master
of Arts in Asian Studies in 1973.
His doctoral work at the same institution, completed in 1987,
earned him a Ph.D. in Philippine Studies, with a research
focus on the oral literature and cultural anthropology of
Mindanao's Muslim communities.
In between those milestones, he pursued further scholarly
formation internationally: a postdoctoral fellowship in
nonviolence studies at the Inter-University Center for
Postdoctoral Studies in Dubrovnik, Yugoslavia in 1983, and a
Folklore Fellowship at the Finnish Academy of Sciences and
Letters in 1991.
These fellowships signaled that his work was being
recognized well beyond the Philippines, and they gave him
comparative frameworks for thinking about indigenous oral
traditions and conflict resolution that he would bring back to
Mindanao.

PAGE 3
Tales from Lake Lanao and Other Essays
(2001)
Maranao (2002)
Notability
Pioneering Maranao cultural anthropologist,
peace educator, and author; first chair of the
NCCA Sub-Commission on Muslim
Communities; founder of the School for the
Living Tradition; recognized by Marquis
Who's Who as a noteworthy university
administrator and anthropologist.
Known For
Documenting Maranao oral literature and
indigenous cultural traditions; bridging
Islamic heritage and modern peacebuilding;
co-founding the Access Philippines Youth
Leadership Training Program; shaping the
organic autonomy law for Muslim Mindanao.
ACADEMIC CAREER AT
MINDANAO STATE UNIVERSITY
Madale spent the core of his professional life at Mindanao
State University in Marawi City, one of the few institutions
whose geographic and cultural positioning made it possible to
produce scholarship about the Meranaw people from the
inside.
He served as Chair of the Department of History from 1975 to
1976, and as Director of the Southern Philippines Center for
Peace Studies from 1981 to 1984, at a time when the Moro
insurgency and the consequences of the Marcos dictatorship
made peace studies anything but an abstract academic
enterprise.
He later rose to the position of Vice Chancellor for Research
and Extension, a role he held from 1992 onward, giving him
institutional authority to shape how MSU engaged with the
communities surrounding it.
In the classroom, he introduced generations of students to
what was then a relatively unusual combination: ethnography,
indigenous epistemology, and conflict resolution theory,
taught together as an integrated body of knowledge rather
than separate disciplines.
His core argument, repeated across his lectures, publications,
and public addresses, was that a durable peace in Mindanao could not be engineered from outside but had to be
built on the foundation of local knowledge systems: the *salsila* (genealogical traditions), the oral epics, the
customary protocols of *taritib*, and the Islamic values of the Meranaw and other Bangsamoro peoples.
CONSTITUTIONAL AND POLICY WORK
In the 1980s, Madale served as one of 53 commissioners tasked with drafting the organic autonomy law for
Muslim Mindanao, the legal architecture that would eventually give rise to the Autonomous Region in Muslim
Mindanao (ARMM).
His contribution was not primarily technical but substantive: he argued, and helped ensure, that cultural identity,
indigenous governance traditions, and the distinct historical experience of Muslim Filipinos were properly reflected
in the language and structure of that law, rather than being subordinated to the homogenizing logic of the central
state.
He was also appointed Regional Consultant Commissioner, further extending his policy influence into the
mechanisms of regional governance.

PAGE 4
NATIONAL CULTURAL GOVERNANCE
Madale served as the founding chair of the Sub-Commission on Muslim Communities under the National
Commission for Culture and the Arts (NCCA).
In that role, he established the School for the Living Tradition, a national program designed to address the
accelerating loss of endangered indigenous crafts, music, performing arts, and oral traditions by pairing master
practitioners with younger students in structured apprenticeships.
The program operated on a simple but powerful premise: that the most effective way to preserve a living tradition
is not to archive it but to transmit it, person to person, across generations, within the communities where it
originally lived.
He also authored the Maranao monograph (2002), published as part of the NCCA's Katutubo: Profiles of
Philippine Cultural Communities series, providing one of the most authoritative brief introductions to Meranaw
society and culture available to a general Philippine readership.
ACCESS PHILIPPINES AND INTERFAITH PEACEBUILDING
One of Madale's most consequential contributions to Mindanao peacebuilding grew out of a relatively modest
starting point: a small peace research grant from the International Peace Research Association (IPRA) Foundation
for a project he called "Buddy Buddy for Peace."
That initial grant, focused on documenting a model for interfaith dialogue, eventually became the springboard for a
much larger initiative, the Access Philippines Youth Leadership Training Program, which he coordinated in
partnership with the Center for Southeast Asian Studies at Northern Illinois University and the U.S. Department of
State's Bureau of Educational and Cultural Affairs.
The program ran for at least six consecutive years, recruiting young adults and adult leaders from Mindanao's three
communities: Muslims, Christians, and Lumad (indigenous peoples).
Qualified participants were brought to Northern Illinois University in DeKalb, Illinois for a one-month intensive
training in peace, mediation, and conflict resolution.
After returning to Mindanao, participants implemented small community peace projects, then assembled three
months later for a follow-on gathering to share results and discuss challenges.
In Madale's own words, the program "was responsible for the establishment of a network of youths and adults in
Mindanao for peace and development."
He also noted that the original IPRA research grant gave his office the opportunity to document a model for
interfaith dialogue that, in the post-September 11 environment, became a widely used case study in peace studies
programs across the region.
LITERARY AND ANTHROPOLOGICAL WORKS
Madale's bibliography spans several decades and ranges from academic monographs to cultural essays accessible
to general readers.

PAGE 5
His foundational anthology, The Muslim Filipinos: A Book of Readings (1981), offered an insider's account of the
history, identity, and social institutions of Muslim communities across the Philippine archipelago, at a time when
such perspectives were largely absent from mainstream Philippine publishing.
Possibilities for Peace in Southern Philippines (1990) gathered his political essays on how traditional Islamic
concepts and indigenous frameworks for reconciliation could be applied to the Mindanao conflict, a contribution
that anticipated many of the arguments that would later shape formal peace negotiations.
The Sarimanok in Myths and Living Tradition (published by Cagayan Capital College, 2000) is arguably his most
distinctive work: a deep scholarly investigation into the iconic mythical bird of the Maranao people, tracing its
origins across multiple epic traditions and clarifying its ritual, symbolic, and artistic functions within Meranaw
society.
In his *Sarimanok* research, Madale cross-examined competing origin stories, including the connection to Prince
Radia Indarapatra in the Maranao epic Darangen, and meticulously parsed where authentic Meranaw tradition
diverged from later accretions or popular retelling.
His monograph Mindanao (1999) and his NCCA-published Tales from Lake Lanao and Other Essays (2001)
brought Meranaw mythology, folklore, and oral literature to a wider public, translating the richness of traditions
like the Darangen epic cycle and the *Kashawing* rice ritual into prose accessible beyond the academic
community.
His chapter-length essays on "The Future of the Moro National Liberation Front as a Separatist Movement in
Southern Philippines" (1984, published by the Institute of Southeast Asian Studies, Singapore) and "The
Resurgence of Islam and Nationalism in the Philippines" (1986, same publisher) remain standard references in
Southeast Asian studies and in the academic literature on the Bangsamoro question.
ADVOCACY AFTER THE MARAWI SIEGE
Following the 2017 Marawi Siege, which devastated the city where Madale was born and spent his career, he
became a vocal advocate for integrating peace education into the core school curriculum for the Bangsamoro
region and across Mindanao.
His argument was consistent with the logic of his entire scholarly career: that rebuilding Marawi required more
than physical reconstruction, that the real work was healing young minds, countering the narratives of violent
extremism with deep cultural literacy, and restoring the sense of Meranaw identity and dignity that the siege had
disrupted.
He contended that the most durable counter-narrative to radicalization was not political messaging but the living
cultural heritage of the Meranaw people itself, including its oral epics, its customary law, its art forms, and its
Islamic ethical tradition.
RECOGNITION AND LEGACY
Madale was listed in Marquis Who's Who as a noteworthy university administrator and anthropologist.
He received the Governor's Award from Rotary International District 387 in 1989, followed by a Meritorious
Award in 1990.

PAGE 6
His family includes his wife, Milagros A. Pabular (married April 6, 1968), and seven children: Namil, Faridah,
Zuraydah, Fatima, Nagasura Junior, Rajah, and Amir.
His legacy is difficult to reduce to a single category because his life's work deliberately refused those categories.
He was an academic who wrote policy, a cultural preservationist who built peace programs, a Meranaw insider who
engaged with Finnish folklorists and Yugoslav nonviolence scholars, and a storyteller who believed that the epics
of Lake Lanao were not museum pieces but living instruments for navigating conflict, building identity, and
imagining a better future for Mindanao.
The School for the Living Tradition, the Access Philippines network, the *Sarimanok* scholarship, the organic
autonomy law framework, and the dozens of students he trained at MSU are all, in their different ways,
continuations of that single coherent project.

title: Magarang, Leng Rohaniah Guro
text:
PAGE 1
Leng Rohaniah Guro Magarang
Leng Rohaniah Guro Magarang (also known as Leng Rohann and affectionately called Lengleng) is a Maranao
chef-entrepreneur, community leader, culinary peace advocate, and government employee based in Iligan City,
Lanao del Norte. She is the founder and owner of Kitchenommy Delights, and has served as the elected president
of the Iligan Hotels and Resorts Restaurants Association (IHARRA) for six consecutive years. A working solo
parent who built her culinary career from a childhood spent in her grandmother's kitchen, she is best known for
championing the philosophy of "food for peace," using halal cuisine as a bridge between Muslims, Christians, and
indigenous peoples across Northern Mindanao.
Recognized by USAID as an Empowered Woman and honored by Nestlé Halal Philippines and One Halal Global
as a Chef Ambassador, she has brought Bangsamoro and Iligan cuisines to international stages, including the
International Battle of the Chefs in Penang, Malaysia. Her decade-long Free Iftar Program, her disaster relief
operations, and her youth culinary training initiatives have made her one of the most consequential figures in
Mindanao's food and community empowerment landscape.

Early Life and Heritage
Leng Rohaniah Guro Magarang was born in Butlig, Lanao del Sur, into a family where cooking wasn't just a skill,
it was a way of keeping the peace.<ref name="tribune2024">Template:Cite web</ref>

PAGE 2

Her family's torogan, the traditional ancestral home of Maranao nobility,
was renowned throughout the community for the quality of its food. And
this reputation did real work: warring parties who entered the dining hall
laid down their arms. Differences were settled not at the negotiating table
but over her grandmother's cooking.<ref name="tribune2024" />
Growing up in that environment, Leng didn't play with ordinary toys.
While her grandmother measured and stirred, young Leng was right there
beside her, playing with miniature kitchen sets, already learning by
instinct that cooking was her calling.<ref name="tribune2024" />
Her nickname, "Lengleng," is a warm derivative of malingkat, a Tausug
word that means beautiful, and it captures the affection with which her
community has always regarded her.<ref name="tribune2024" />
Education and Early Training
Leng's formal culinary education was not the conventional restaurant-
school path. She started her hands-on training as an apprentice to chef
Dennis Barazon, assisting in cooking demonstrations focused on
Malaysian cuisine and everyday Filipino staples. That early exposure to
cross-cultural cooking would later define her signature style.<ref
name="tribune2024" />
In 2014, she took a short culinary course at the Alternative Learning
School in Iligan City, formalizing skills she had been refining since
childhood.<ref name="tribune2024" />
Career
Burp Diner and the Road to Kitchenommy
In 2015, Leng co-founded Burp Diner in Iligan alongside a classmate and
two professional chefs. The restaurant carved a niche serving students in
the city, with its standout item being Albaik chicken, a version of breaded
fried chicken inspired by the famous Saudi fast-food chain Albaik.
Muslim pilgrims returning from Mecca raved about the original, brought
her samples, and Leng developed her own version that closely matched
the original's taste.<ref name="tribune2024" />
The Marawi Siege of 2017 disrupted the business severely, as it did for
countless entrepreneurs in Northern Mindanao. But Leng and her business partner Angelica Dagondon kept going
by pivoting to catering work for fundraising events, including events hosted by prominent names such as Senator
Tito Sotto and actor Kier Legaspi. Many friends and relatives displaced by the siege found comfort in Leng's
kitchen during this difficult period.<ref name="tribune2024" />
When the COVID-19 pandemic hit, she set up Kitchenommy Cocina Studio at her husband's office as an
improvised commissary. During Ramadan, orders for iftar meals poured in, proving the demand was there. But
family concerns about viral exposure pushed her to look for a more permanent space. She returned to the old Burp

PAGE 3
Diner building, reopened the kitchen, and gave jobs to former workers who had lost their livelihoods during the
pandemic, initially paying them in free meals until the delivery business stabilized. Eventually, the team received
professional wages.<ref name="tribune2024" />
Kitchenommy Delights grew steadily. It is now a concessionaire at Mindanao State University Iligan Institute of
Technology (MSU-IIT), serving students through its signature chicken wing variants.<ref name="tribune2024" />
Restaurant Consultancy
Beyond running her own kitchen, Leng has built a respected restaurant consultancy practice. She works with
establishments on menu design, staff training, hospitality standards upgrading, and the organization of culinary
events and competitions. As IHARRA president, she also makes rounds of Iligan City's restaurants to check on
food safety and industry standards.<ref name="tribune2024" />
Government Service
Leng is also a government employee, though specific details about her government position have not been publicly
disclosed in available sources. This dual life as a public servant and private entrepreneur reflects her broader
orientation: using every platform available to serve her community.
IHARRA Leadership
Leng was elected president of the Iligan Hotels and Resorts Restaurants Association (IHARRA), a post she has
held for six consecutive years.<ref name="sourceprofile">Leng Rohaniah Guro Magarang professional profile
document, provided by subject.</ref> Under her leadership, IHARRA has become more than a trade association. It
has served as a platform for culinary competitions to elevate local cuisines, a hub for industry training, and a
headquarters kitchen during disaster relief operations.
One of her most significant achievements as IHARRA head was organizing a culinary training program for out-of-
school youth under the USAID Opportunity 2.0 Program, working alongside Iligan Mayor Frederick Siao.
IHARRA members committed to helping program graduates find employment after completing their training.<ref
name="tribune2024" />
She also served as Former President of Rotary East Iligan, extending her community leadership beyond the
culinary sector into broader civic service.<ref name="sourceprofile" />
Culinary Philosophy and Signature Dishes
Leng's cooking philosophy is rooted in a simple but powerful idea: halal food is food for everyone. She believes
that when people sit together and share a meal, differences dissolve. This isn't just ideology for her; it comes from
lived experience in her grandmother's torogan, where the same principle played out across generations.<ref
name="tribune2024" />
Her signature dish is Chicken Pindiyalokan, a Maranao preparation of chicken cooked with palapa, the iconic
condiment made from ginger, shallots, turmeric, chilies, and shredded coconut. She also prepares a Roasted
Pindiyalokan variant that has drawn attention at public culinary events.<ref name="tribune2024" />
"I always dedicate my food to everyone to promote peace." — Chef Leng Rohaniah Guro Magarang,
as quoted in the Daily Tribune, January 2024

PAGE 4
"Strength isn't about standing alone, it's about building a table where everyone has a place." —
Kitchenommy Delights
Her dishes have been featured in the Daily Tribune and showcased at the International Battle of the Chefs in
Penang, Malaysia, where she represented both Bangsamoro and Iligan cuisines on an international stage.<ref
name="sourceprofile" /><ref name="tribune2024" />
Community Initiatives
Free Iftar Program
For ten consecutive years, Leng has personally prepared and distributed free iftar meals, the evening meal that
breaks the daily fast during Ramadan, to communities in need, including the Torel Orphanage and local mosques.
<ref name="sourceprofile" /> This program has become one of the most sustained individual charitable feeding
initiatives in Iligan City.
Disaster Relief Operations
When Typhoon Basyang struck, Leng mobilized Kitchenommy Delights and IHARRA's resources to serve as the
association's headquarters kitchen for relief operations, producing and distributing thousands of hot meals to
typhoon victims. This relief work is ongoing, reflecting her view that a professional kitchen is a community
resource in times of crisis.<ref name="sourceprofile" />
Interfaith Culinary Advocacy
In December 2023, following a bombing at Mindanao State University in Lanao del Sur that claimed four lives,
Leng joined the Tri-People Cuisine for Interfaith Solidarity event at The Alemania Hotel in Iligan City. The event,
organized during the island's annual Week of Peace, brought together Muslim, Christian, and Higaunon Lumad
chefs to cook and share food as a collective act of mourning and hope. Leng prepared her signature Chicken
Pindiyalokan and Roasted Pindiyalokan for the occasion.<ref name="uri2024">Template:Cite web</ref>
The event was a collaboration between Pakigdait, Inc., IHARRA, the Iligan City Tourism Office, and other civic
groups, and it drew attendance from security sector members of the PNP and the AFP, indigenous elders, city
officials, media, and youth.<ref name="uri2024" />
Youth Empowerment Through Food
Through the USAID Opportunity 2.0 Program, Leng channeled IHARRA's resources into vocational culinary
training for out-of-school youth. The commitment extended beyond skills training: IHARRA members pledged to
help graduates find actual employment.<ref name="tribune2024" />
"I couldn't give them dole-outs, but I could teach them how to cook. Many have since gotten jobs as a
result." — Chef Leng Rohaniah Guro Magarang, as quoted in the Daily Tribune, January 2024

PAGE 5
Nestlé Halal Cooking Demonstrations
As a Chef Ambassador for Nestlé Halal Philippines, Leng has led halal cooking demonstrations that bring
professional culinary education to wider audiences, helping normalize halal standards in mainstream food culture.
<ref name="sourceprofile" />
Ambassadorial Roles
Leng has served as Chef Ambassador for two major halal food organizations:
Nestlé Halal Philippines — Her role involves promoting halal cooking standards and demonstrating how
mainstream food brands can integrate halal practices seamlessly.<ref name="sourceprofile" />
One Halal Global — This international platform gave her a broader reach to advocate for Bangsamoro and
Filipino halal cuisine on a global stage.<ref name="sourceprofile" />
She also serves as Chef Consultant for IHARRA, advising on culinary programming and hospitality standards for
the association's member establishments.<ref name="sourceprofile" />
Recognition and Awards
Leng's work has earned her recognition from both domestic and international organizations:
USAID Empowered Woman Award for strengthening community resilience and empowering people
through food and culinary heritage.<ref name="sourceprofile" />
Philippine Halal Excellence Award for Community Service for her sustained advocacy in halal cuisine
and community feeding programs.<ref name="sourceprofile" />
Higala Communities Initiative Inc. Empowered Women 2026 award, recognizing her as a standout
empowered woman in her community.<ref name="sourceprofile" />
Featured in the Daily Tribune for her signature regional dishes and her community service model.<ref
name="tribune2024" />
Personal Life
Leng married Abdul Salam Magarang in 2009, a contractor and a second cousin of her mother. She is a working
solo parent, managing her restaurant enterprise, consultancy work, and government duties alongside raising her
child.<ref name="tribune2024" />
Her Muslim faith is integral to her identity as a chef. Halal cooking isn't simply a market category for her; it's an
expression of her values, her heritage, and her belief that food prepared with care and conscience nourishes more
than the body. Ramadan, with its rhythms of fasting and feasting, is one of the most active periods in her kitchen,
both commercially and in terms of charitable work.<ref name="sourceprofile" />
Cultural Significance
Leng Rohaniah Guro Magarang stands at the intersection of several important conversations in contemporary
Philippine society. She is a Maranao woman who navigated a male-dominated industry, rebuilt a business through a
siege and a pandemic, and emerged as one of the most recognized voices in Northern Mindanao's food scene.

PAGE 6
Her work speaks directly to the challenge of inter-communal peace in a region that has experienced decades of
conflict. By positioning the dining table as a place of reconciliation, she draws on a tradition that goes back to her
grandmother's torogan, where warring parties once set down their weapons to eat together. This is not symbolic
performance for Leng; it's a working methodology that she deploys through events, programs, and her daily
cooking practice.
She also represents a model of leadership that doesn't separate professional excellence from social responsibility.
Kitchenommy Delights is simultaneously a restaurant, a relief kitchen, a training ground, and an expression of
Bangsamoro culinary heritage.

Mangigin D. Magomnang
Brig. Gen. Mangigin D. Magomnang was a Bangsamoro military
officer who later stepped into a very different kind of leadership role,
guiding Mindanao State University (MSU) through one of the most
sensitive chapters in Philippine political history. He is best
remembered as the university's Regent In-Charge in 1986, right when
the country and the institution were both figuring out what came next
after a national upheaval.
His story is a bit unusual. Not many officers move from the
discipline of the barracks straight into the halls of a university
administration building, but for Magomnang, it was less a career
pivot and more a call to duty in a different uniform.
Contents
1 Military Career
2 Transition to Academic Leadership
3 Role at Mindanao State University
4 Leadership in a Time of Transition
5 Legacy
6 See Also
7 References
8 Categories
Military Career
Magomnang built his career the traditional way, working his way up through the ranks of the Philippine military.
He served for a time as a Lieutenant Colonel, where he picked up the kind of experience that shapes a career:
command decisions, coordination across units, and the discipline that comes with responsibility over people's lives.
He eventually reached the rank of Brigadier General, a rank that placed him firmly within Mindanao's security
landscape at a time when military presence and regional stability were deeply intertwined. Years spent navigating
that terrain gave him an instinct for order and structure, an instinct that would matter more than he probably
expected once he crossed over into academic life.
Transition to Academic Leadership
1986 was not a quiet year for the Philippines. The EDSA People Power Revolution had just reshaped the national
leadership, and that shockwave rippled through institutions across the country, including universities. MSU was
one of them.
It was in this climate that Magomnang was appointed Regent In-Charge of MSU, and it is worth pausing on just
how unusual that appointment was. This was not a routine handover. Consider what was happening all at once:
National leadership had just changed

PAGE 2
Universities everywhere were adjusting to new political directions from Manila
MSU itself needed to hold its footing within a complex and sometimes volatile regional environment
Stepping into that role meant Magomnang had to carry both authority and restraint at the same time, enough
authority to keep the institution functioning, and enough restraint to avoid making a fragile moment worse.
Role at Mindanao State University
As Regent In-Charge, his job was less about building something new and more about making sure nothing fell
apart. That meant:
Maintaining order within the campus
Ensuring academic operations kept running without interruption
Managing the practical details of institutional transition
Coordinating with government authorities during a period when lines of communication mattered more than
usual
His military background turned out to be exactly the right toolkit for this moment. Stability was the priority, and
stability was something he knew how to hold onto even when the ground around him was still shifting.
Leadership in a Time of Transition
If there is one word that defines Magomnang's time at MSU, it is timing. He was not there to overhaul the
university or chart a bold new direction. He was there to hold it steady, to make sure students kept learning and the
institution kept functioning while the rest of the country sorted itself out.
It is the kind of leadership that rarely gets celebrated in the moment. Nobody writes headlines about an institution
that simply did not collapse, but that quiet continuity is exactly what a fragile period like 1986 needed, and it is
exactly what he delivered.
Legacy
Mangigin D. Magomnang's story sits at an interesting crossroads between two very different worlds, the military
and the academe. His time at MSU stands out precisely because it shows how leadership can cross over into
unfamiliar territory when the moment demands it.
Within the broader Bangsamoro context, he represents a generation of leaders who moved fluidly between service,
discipline, and institution-building, the kind of people who held structures together when stability could not be
taken for granted.

Sahawi S. Malik
Sahawi S. Malik is a Filipino academic, engineer, and
interdisciplinary scholar recognized for bridging educational
leadership with technological innovation and environmental
stewardship. He holds multiple doctoral degrees spanning
education, technology management, sustainable development, and
computer engineering—a rare combination that positions him as a
visionary in integrated solutions for contemporary challenges.
Currently serving as Teacher VI and Assistant Professor II, Dr.
Malik is distinguished by his commitment to transformative
education and sustainable innovation, earning recognition as a
Scientific and Technological Specialist under Presidential Decree

Early Life and Background
Details regarding Dr. Malik's early life, family background, and formative years remain largely private. What is
documented is his consistent pursuit of academic excellence across multiple disciplines, suggesting a deep
intellectual curiosity and commitment to lifelong learning from an early age.
Education
Dr. Malik's educational journey reflects an extraordinary commitment to interdisciplinary mastery, accumulating
credentials that span engineering, business, education, and environmental sciences.
Undergraduate Studies
Dr. Malik began his academic pursuit with a Bachelor of Science in Computer Engineering, establishing the
technical foundation for his later work in systems, computing, and engineering solutions. This undergraduate
training provided the backbone of his expertise in technological applications and digital systems.
Graduate and Doctoral Studies
His graduate education demonstrates a strategic expansion into multiple domains:
Master of Engineering with specialization in Computer Engineering, deepening his technical expertise
Master in Business Administration (MBA), equipping him with strategic and operational business insights
necessary for institutional leadership
Doctor of Philosophy in Computer Engineering, anchoring his technical acumen in advanced research and
innovation
PhD in Educational Administration and Supervision, grounding his expertise in institutional leadership,
academic governance, and policy implementation
PhD in Technology Management, sharpening his vision for managing technological innovation and digital
transformation in educational and organizational contexts
Doctor in Sustainable Development Studies (Major in Sustainable Environmental Engineering), reflecting
his commitment to environmental resilience, green technologies, and sustainable practices
This multi-doctoral trajectory is unusual in academia and represents a deliberate effort to integrate knowledge
systems that are typically siloed in conventional academic structures.
Professional Credentials and Recognition
Dr. Malik holds several significant professional certifications that validate his expertise:
Licensed Professional Teacher (LPT)
Accredited by the Professional Regulation Commission of the Philippines, this credential certifies his qualifications
to practice teaching at professional levels in the Philippine educational system.

PAGE 3
Professional Computer Engineer (PCpE)
Also accredited by the Professional Regulation Commission, this certification recognizes his technical competence
and professional standing in the field of computer engineering.
Scientific and Technological Specialist (STS)
Under Presidential Decree 997 (PD 997), Dr. Malik has been recognized as a Scientific and Technological
Specialist—an honor bestowed upon individuals demonstrating exceptional contributions to science and
technology in the Philippines. This designation acknowledges his significant impact in advancing scientific and
technological development in the country.
Career and Institutional Contributions
Dr. Malik currently serves in dual academic roles as Teacher VI and Assistant Professor II, positions that reflect
both his pedagogical expertise and research capabilities. Throughout his career, he has engaged in:
Multidisciplinary research spanning education, technology, and sustainability
Capacity-building initiatives aimed at developing human resources and institutional capabilities
Academic consultancy providing expert guidance to educational institutions and organizations
Championing sustainable innovation in technological and educational contexts
Transformative education initiatives that integrate modern pedagogical approaches with technological
advancement
His work is characterized by a commitment to bridging theoretical knowledge with practical applications,
particularly in contexts where educational leadership intersects with technological advancement and environmental
stewardship.
Areas of Expertise
Dr. Malik's interdisciplinary background enables him to contribute across multiple domains:
Educational Leadership and Governance
Drawing from his PhD in Educational Administration and Supervision, he brings expertise in institutional
leadership, academic policy implementation, and educational governance structures.
Technology Management and Innovation
His PhD in Technology Management, combined with his computer engineering background, positions him to lead
digital transformation initiatives and manage technological innovation in educational and organizational settings.
Sustainable Development and Environmental Engineering
Through his doctoral work in Sustainable Development Studies with a focus on Sustainable Environmental
Engineering, Dr. Malik contributes to environmental resilience strategies, green technology implementation, and
sustainable practice development.

PAGE 4
Systems and Computing
His foundational training and advanced degrees in Computer Engineering provide deep technical expertise in
computing systems, engineering solutions, and technological infrastructure.
Strategic Business Operations
His MBA credentials equip him with capabilities in strategic planning, operational management, and business-
oriented decision-making within academic and organizational contexts.
Research and Scholarly Contributions
Dr. Malik's research interests lie at the intersection of education, technology, and sustainability. His scholarly
approach emphasizes:
Integration of educational methodologies with technological tools
Application of engineering principles to sustainable development challenges
Development of frameworks for managing technological innovation in educational institutions
Exploration of environmental engineering solutions within educational contexts
His dynamic portfolio reflects a passion for creating integrated solutions that address contemporary challenges
through interdisciplinary approaches.
Legacy and Vision
Dr. Malik's professional trajectory embodies a vision of integrated solutions that transcend traditional disciplinary
boundaries. His work demonstrates that contemporary challenges—whether in education, technology, or
environmental sustainability—require leaders who can synthesize knowledge across multiple domains.
His legacy is being built on several foundations:
Interdisciplinary Excellence: Demonstrating that mastery across multiple fields creates unique value in
solving complex problems
Sustainable Innovation: Consistently advocating for technological and educational advancement that
considers environmental and social sustainability
Transformative Education: Championing educational approaches that prepare learners for rapidly changing
technological and environmental contexts
Professional Integrity: Maintaining multiple professional certifications and recognitions that validate
expertise and commitment to ethical practice
Challenges and Future Directions
Like many interdisciplinary scholars, Dr. Malik operates in spaces where traditional academic structures may not
fully accommodate cross-cutting expertise. The challenge of maintaining depth across multiple doctoral-level
disciplines while creating meaningful integration remains ongoing work.
Future directions likely include:

PAGE 5
Expanding research that demonstrates practical applications of integrated educational-technological-
environmental approaches
Contributing to policy development that recognizes the value of interdisciplinary expertise
Mentoring emerging scholars and professionals in navigating interdisciplinary careers
Developing institutional models that effectively leverage integrated expertise
Recognition and Impact
Dr. Malik's recognition as a Scientific and Technological Specialist under PD 997 represents formal
acknowledgment of his contributions to Philippine science and technology. This designation places him among a
select group of professionals whose work has demonstrable impact on national scientific and technological
advancement.
His academic positions as Teacher VI and Assistant Professor II indicate progression through academic ranks and
recognition by institutional peers of his teaching effectiveness and scholarly contributions.
Philosophy and Approach
Dr. Malik's work is characterized by both scholarly rigor and practical orientation. His approach emphasizes:
Scholarly Excellence: Maintaining high academic standards across multiple disciplines
Practical Application: Ensuring that theoretical knowledge translates into actionable solutions
Integration: Building bridges between traditionally separate fields of knowledge
Innovation: Seeking new approaches to persistent challenges
Sustainability: Considering long-term environmental and social implications of technological and
educational decisions

Atty. Abdullah "Dabs" Derupong Mama-o is a Filipino lawyer,
diplomat, and government official who served as the inaugural
Secretary of the Department of Migrant Workers (DMW) under
President Rodrigo Roa Duterte.
A Maranao leader with deep engagement in Middle Eastern
diplomacy, he became known for applying what has been described

draws on shared religious and cultural identity to resolve labor crises
and secure the welfare of Overseas Filipino Workers (OFWs).

Early Life and Background
Abdullah Derupong Mama-o is of Maranao descent, one of the
major Muslim ethnolinguistic groups in the Philippines.
His background within a Muslim Filipino community shaped his familiarity with Islamic culture and social
structures, which later informed his diplomatic engagements in the Middle East.
Education
Mama-o pursued his legal education at San Beda College of Law in Manila, where he graduated as part of the
Class of 1972. :contentReference[oaicite:1]{index=1}

PAGE 2
He was a classmate of Rodrigo Duterte, a connection that would later intersect with his role in government service
during Duterte’s presidency.
Government Career
Presidential Adviser on OFW and Muslim Concerns (2016–2022)
Following the assumption of President Duterte in 2016, Mama-o was appointed as Presidential Adviser on
Overseas Filipino Workers and Muslim Concerns. :contentReference[oaicite:2]{index=2}
In this role, he functioned as a senior adviser and field negotiator, frequently deployed to the Middle East to
address urgent labor and diplomatic concerns involving Filipino workers.
His work included direct engagement with foreign officials, employers, and diplomatic counterparts to resolve
disputes, facilitate repatriation, and improve labor conditions.
Special Envoy to Kuwait (2018)
In 2018, Mama-o was designated as Special Envoy to Kuwait during a diplomatic crisis between the Philippines
and Kuwait. :contentReference[oaicite:3]{index=3}
The crisis emerged following the death of an Overseas Filipino Worker and subsequent tensions involving embassy
rescue operations.
Mama-o played a key role in de-escalating the situation through diplomatic negotiations, contributing to the
eventual easing of tensions and the lifting of the deployment ban after securing improved protections for Filipino
workers.
Secretary of the Department of Migrant Workers (2022)
On March 9, 2022, Mama-o was appointed as the first Secretary of the Department of Migrant Workers in an ad
interim capacity. :contentReference[oaicite:4]{index=4}
He oversaw the initial organization and transition of the department, which consolidated multiple government
agencies into a unified institution dedicated to protecting the rights and welfare of OFWs.
This role placed him at the center of institutional reform aimed at streamlining services for millions of Filipinos
working abroad.
Major Achievements and Institutional Contributions
Mama-o’s government service involved several high-impact interventions, including:
Leading negotiations in Saudi Arabia for the repatriation of approximately 11,000 stranded Filipino workers
affected by a construction sector crisis
Participating in diplomatic efforts in Libya that secured the release of abducted Filipino workers
Overseeing the foundational establishment of the Department of Migrant Workers as a centralized
government agency

PAGE 3
These efforts highlight his role in crisis response, labor diplomacy, and institutional development.
Diplomatic Approach and Cultural Significance
A defining aspect of Mama-o’s work is his use of the "Islamic Factor of Diplomacy", a method grounded in
shared religious and cultural understanding. :contentReference[oaicite:5]{index=5}
This approach enabled him to establish rapport with leaders and officials in Muslim-majority countries, creating
communication channels that complemented formal diplomatic protocols.
His work has been recognized by the National Commission on Muslim Filipinos for addressing both the specific
concerns of Muslim Filipino workers and the broader needs of the OFW community.

Legacy
Atty. Abdullah D. Mama-o’s career reflects a model of diplomacy that integrates cultural identity with practical
negotiation.
His contributions lie in both crisis resolution and institutional development, particularly in advancing government
mechanisms for the protection of Filipino workers abroad.
His role in establishing the Department of Migrant Workers marks a significant development in Philippine labor
governance, with long-term implications for OFW welfare and state accountability.
Challenges
Much of Mama-o’s work took place in complex and high-pressure environments involving international labor
disputes, diplomatic tensions, and humanitarian concerns.
Navigating these situations required balancing national policy, foreign relations, and the immediate needs of
distressed workers, often under urgent and sensitive conditions.
