Alexander Pumbaya Mama-o
Datu Alexander P. Mama-o (Hadji AbdulRauf Pumbaya Mama-o),
Cabugatan sa Bayang, is a Bangsamoro public servant and
transportation reformer from Rinabor, Bayang, Lanao del Sur. He
spent most of his career in one demanding corner of government:
regulating the transportation sector. Along the way he kept pushing
for better governance and for programs that make daily life easier for
ordinary people.
His working life covers a lot of ground. There were years in
government offices, years as a worker overseas, and years leading
communities. It took him from small towns in Mindanao to national
government institutions, and it makes him a fine example of what a
Bangsamoro professional can offer the country.
Contents
1 Early Years and Life Abroad
2 Reshaping Transportation in Caraga
3 Results and Recognition
4 Studies
5 Royal Title and Bangsamoro Roots
6 Civic Leadership
7 Two Careers, One Thread
Early Years and Life Abroad
Datu Alexander earned his Bachelor of Science in Social Work at
Philippine Christian University in 1974. He started working a year
later, with stints in banking, education, and social welfare.
By 1976 he was wearing two hats: college instructor at Pacasum
College in Marawi City, and Senior Social Welfare Officer of the
Department of Social Welfare and Development (DSWD) in
Malabang, Lanao del Sur. He helped set up social welfare services
for the province, and he led the split of DSWD Lanao del Sur into
two district offices so that more people could reach essential
services. He then headed the 2nd District.
In 1978 he went to the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia as an Overseas
Filipino Worker. His job at Jeddah International Airport was in
aviation and production control. Off the clock, he pioneered a
Jeddah-based Filipino group that helped repatriate hundreds of
Muslim and Christian Filipino workers who had left their employers
and sought refuge at the Philippine Embassy.

PAGE 2
Bayang royal heritage into civic
leadership.
Pull Quote
"From Rinabor to Jeddah to Caraga, the
work stayed the same: keep people and
services moving, and make life a little
easier for ordinary folks."
Reshaping Transportation in Caraga
He came home in 1986 and went back into government, this time on
the road of transportation administration and reform. He held
leadership posts in the Land Transportation Franchising and
Regulatory Board (LTFRB), the Land Transportation Office (LTO),
and the former Telecommunications Office (TELOF), all under the
Department of Transportation and Communications (DOTC), now
the Department of Transportation (DOTr).
When the Caraga region was created, he became the pioneer and founding Regional Director of the DOTC there,
separating its operations from DOTC Region X in Cagayan de Oro City.
Over his years of service he was assigned to Marawi City, Cagayan de Oro City, Butuan City, Cebu City,
Zamboanga City, and Baguio City. Caraga is where he left some of his biggest marks:
One roof for transport offices. He pioneered an integrated DOTC Caraga Regional Office that brought the
LTO, the LTFRB, and the National Telecommunications Commission (NTC) together.
Easier trips within cities. He helped establish intra-city routes in Caraga, giving students, professionals,
workers, and other commuters a way to get around.
Wider links between provinces. In 1997, working with local government officials, he helped expand
interprovincial routes to keep people, goods, and services moving and to support the region's economic
growth.
Government offices closer to the people. In 1997 he pioneered the LTO Patin-ay District Office and the
LTO Trento Extension Office, and in 1998 he oversaw the reopening of the LTO Dapa Office.
Telecommunications projects delivered. He completed seven NTC projects serving communities in
Butuan, Nasipit, Magallanes, Surigao City, Prosperidad, Mangagoy, and other parts of Caraga.
Results and Recognition
The numbers from his later years in Caraga speak for themselves. From January to June 2017, while he served as
Regional Director of the DOTr Caraga Regional Office, the office's revenue collections rose by ₱24,832,365.88, a
16.23% increase over baseline collections.
He is also a recipient of a Presidential Trophy from former President Gloria Macapagal Arroyo, given for the strong
performance of the regional transportation agencies in Caraga and their contribution to national revenue
collections. It came with the administration's recognition of the LTO's achievements in 2001.
In 2016 he was re-appointed DOTr Regional Director for Caraga Region XIII, and he took his oath of office before
then Court of Appeals Associate Justice Japar B. Dimaampao. His appointments as a DOTC executive carry the
signatures of four presidents in turn: Fidel V. Ramos, Joseph Estrada, Gloria Macapagal Arroyo, and Rodrigo Roa
Duterte.
Studies
After his social work degree in 1974, he completed a Master in Business Administration at the Agusan Institute of
Technology in 1997, under a consortium with Southwestern University.

PAGE 3
Royal Title and Bangsamoro Roots
In 2015, Datu Alexander was proclaimed a crowned Prince (Cabugatan) of the Royal House of Bayang, Lanao del
Sur, one of the 16 Royal Houses of Lanao.
He was crowned Cabugatan sa Bayang as a descendant of Cabugatan, who was the son of Amerodin, son of
Amdag, son of Diwan. Under the traditional system of succession based on the ancient local law known as Ijma
ago Taritib, Cabugatan is next in line to the throne of the Sultanate of Bayang during the turn of Amerodin, the
eldest son of Amdag, in the order of succession. On his mother's side, he also traces his royal lineage to the
Sultanate of Pagayawan, as a grandson of Cali sa Unayan.
Civic Leadership
Since 2008 he has chaired the Moriatao Diwan (Descendants of Diwan) National Directorate Council, and since
2012 he has chaired the Filipino Muslim Alliance for Integrity and Reform Movement. His civic involvement also
reaches Muslim community organizations and initiatives tied to peace, democracy, and federalism.
His years in Saudi Arabia in the late 1970s and early 1980s had a Bangsamoro side too. He took an active part in
the efforts of the Bangsa Moro Liberation Organization, founded by the late Haroun Al-Rashid Lucman, which
worked to unite Moro leaders in the Middle East behind a call for a peaceful resolution of the armed conflict in
Mindanao.
These roles are a big part of how he is known publicly. They tie his professional career back to his roots and to the
continuing importance of traditional institutions in Lanao del Sur.
Two Careers, One Thread
Datu Alexander P. Mama-o's working life shows the many ways Muslim Filipinos and Bangsamoro leaders have
contributed to Philippine public administration, regional development, and community life.
He started with social welfare work in Lanao del Sur, led transportation offices in Caraga, helped fellow Filipino
workers in Saudi Arabia, and took part in traditional leadership institutions at home. The thread through all of it is
steady engagement with public service and with the communities around him.

Amer Hussein Naga Mambuay
Atty. Amer Hussein Naga Mambuay is a Filipino attorney and a
Senior Partner at SyCip Salazar Hernandez & Gatmaitan
(SyCipLaw), widely recognized as the largest and most prestigious
full-service law firm in the Philippines.
He serves as the Partner-in-Charge and Head of SyCipLaw's
Davao City branch office, where he oversees the firm's regional
commercial, litigation, and corporate operations across the southern
Philippines.
A proud member of the Meranaw ethnic group, Mambuay occupies
a historically significant place within the Philippine legal
profession. He is one of the very few Muslim-Filipino lawyers to
reach the apex of elite corporate practice, earning consistent
recognition from global legal intelligence directories for his work in
complex commercial litigation, international alternative dispute
resolution, and industrial relations.
His career is not just a professional story, it's a breakthrough: proof
that a Moro lawyer from Lanao can stand toe-to-toe with the biggest
names in Philippine corporate law, and win.
EARLY LIFE AND FAMILY
Amer Hussein Naga Mambuay was born and raised in the Lanao
region of Mindanao, rooted in a family belonging to the Meranaw
(People of the Lake) cultural minority of the Lanao del Sur
province.
Growing up in Lanao del Sur gave him an early, lived understanding
of civic responsibility and the rule of law in one of the Philippines'
most structurally complex and culturally rich regions. The
intersection of Indigenous governance traditions, Islamic
jurisprudence, and the Philippine national legal system wasn't just
academic context for him, it was the environment he came of age in.
That grounding in place and identity has never left him. Throughout
his career, he has maintained strong professional, civic, and
institutional ties with his home province and the broader Meranaw
community, even as his practice expanded to the national and
international stage.

a Senior Partner and Branch Head at

PULL QUOTE
"Cultural roots can successfully coexist
with elite, globalized corporate legal
practice."
EDUCATION
Mambuay pursued his higher education at the University of the
Philippines (UP), the country's premier national university.
He completed his undergraduate studies at UP before earning his
Juris Doctor (Bachelor of Laws) from the UP College of Law,
widely considered the most competitive law school in the
Philippines and a training ground for Chief Justices, legislators, and
leading public figures.
During his time at UP Law, he was initiated into the Alpha Phi
Beta Fraternity, an organization within the UP College of Law
known for producing some of the most influential figures in
Philippine law and governance. The fraternity's culture of rigorous
academic engagement and institutional legal service shaped the
professional philosophy he carried into his career.
CAREER
After earning his law degree, Mambuay joined SyCipLaw, the
country's largest full-service law firm, and steadily built his
reputation within its ranks until he advanced to the position of
Senior Partner.
Recognizing the economic expansion and geopolitical significance
of Mindanao, he took on the additional responsibility of managing
SyCipLaw's strategic presence in the south as Head of the Davao
City branch office. From that post, he directs the firm's regional
operations covering corporate advisory, litigation, and dispute
resolution across the southern Philippines.
His practice spans three core operational areas:
Litigation and Dispute Resolution
Mambuay brings extensive trial and appellate experience to the
table. He represents foreign and local conglomerates, maritime
operators, and financial institutions before regular trial courts,
appellate courts, and specialized regulatory bodies across the
country.
His track record in this space covers high-stakes commercial
disputes where the clients involved often have significant
operational exposure across multiple jurisdictions.

PAGE 3
Employment, Labor, and Immigration
He serves as a principal advisory lead for large corporate boards navigating the Philippines' worker-centric legal
framework. His work here covers employment litigation, management-side defense strategies, and the structuring
of cross-border corporate immigration policies for multinational companies operating in the Philippines.
Corporate Services
Mambuay routinely advises clients on the operational risks, asset acquisitions, and regulatory compliance
requirements tied to doing business within regional economic corridors, particularly in Mindanao and the broader
southern Philippines.
MAJOR WORKS AND CONTRIBUTIONS
Over the course of his career, Mambuay's contributions to Philippine legal practice have taken shape across several
significant areas:
Corporate Restructuring and Rehabilitation. He has guided major corporations through financial distress,
debt recovery, asset liquidation, and strategic reorganizations, helping clients navigate some of the most
complex phases of corporate life.
Industrial Relations and Labor Advisory. Mambuay regularly serves as lead management counsel in high-
stakes collective bargaining negotiations, industrial strikes, and multi-tier labor disputes. He also consults on
the labor implications of mergers and acquisitions (M&A), an area requiring simultaneous command of
employment law, corporate law, and negotiation strategy.
International Alternative Dispute Resolution. He has successfully argued commercial arbitration matters
under international jurisdiction, including before tribunals constituted under the International Chamber of
Commerce (ICC) International Court of Arbitration, one of the world's most prominent arbitral bodies.
MCLE Lectureship. He is formally accredited by the Supreme Court of the Philippines as a lecturer for
labor law under the Mandatory Continuing Legal Education (MCLE) program, training practicing
attorneys nationwide on evolving labor standards and statutory developments.
Multicultural Corporate Advocacy. He leads SyCipLaw's interactive Kapihan sessions, which orient
multinational corporate groups, including Korean and Japanese expatriate business communities, on the
unique cultural and practical dimensions of Filipino labor law and workplace mandates. It's the kind of cross-
cultural legal guidance that goes well beyond the four corners of a contract.
AWARDS AND RECOGNITION
Mambuay's professional standing has been independently vetted and consistently validated by global legal
intelligence platforms:
The Legal 500 Asia Pacific. A consistent presence in individual rankings, Mambuay was historically cited as
a "Leading Individual" in the Philippines. In the latest 2025 and 2026 editions, he has maintained his peak
tiering, formally ranked as a Leading Partner specifically for Labour and Employment.
asialaw Rankings. Peer and client review data formally classify him as a Notable Practitioner in the
Philippines for Labour and Employment, with SyCipLaw's team earning outstanding marks across all
evaluated categories.

PAGE 4
IBP Lanao del Sur Chapter Recognition. The Integrated Bar of the Philippines (IBP) Lanao del Sur
Chapter formally acknowledged him as the only Muslim recognized as a Leading Lawyer in the
Philippines by global ranking platforms, underscoring both his professional achievement and its historic
cultural significance.
Client Feedback. Global research entities quote corporate clients describing Mambuay's regional team as
exceptionally "responsible, proactive," and known for producing legal briefs that are "thorough, well-studied,
and accurate."
PERSONAL LIFE
Mambuay keeps his personal life firmly private.
He divides his time between corporate obligations in Metropolitan Manila and Davao City, and civic networks in
Lanao del Sur. Beyond his formal legal work, he operates as a low-profile mentor to young minority law students
and professionals seeking to enter institutional corporate law firms, a sector historically dominated by practitioners
from metropolitan Luzon.
He doesn't make much noise about it. But for Meranaw and broader Bangsamoro students eyeing careers in
corporate law, he's the kind of figure whose example speaks loudly enough.
LEGACY, IMPACT, AND CULTURAL SIGNIFICANCE
Mambuay's most enduring contribution may not be found in any court filing or arbitration award, but in what his
career represents for the broader Bangsamoro community.
Historically, Muslim-Filipino lawyers concentrated their practice within Shari'ah courts, public service, local
politics, or human rights advocacy in Mindanao. Corporate law at the national and international level remained
largely out of reach, not because of lacking talent, but because of the structural barriers and networks that gatekeep
elite institutional practice.
Mambuay took a non-traditional route and broke through.
His career demonstrated that a Moro lawyer can ascend to the absolute apex of elite corporate law, multinational
dispute resolution, and international commercial arbitration, and be ranked there by the same global platforms that
evaluate the best in the world.
His recognition by the IBP Lanao del Sur Chapter as the only Muslim to be classified as a Leading Lawyer in the
Philippines by international platforms is more than an individual honor. It's a benchmark, a visible proof point for
minority law students that cultural identity and global professional excellence are not in conflict. They can, and do,
coexist.

title: Mambuay, Amina T.
text:
PAGE 1
Amina T. Mambuay
Amina T. Mambuay (née Tominaman) is a pioneering Filipino Muslim peacebuilder, educator, and the first
Maranao woman to become an internationally certified trainer with the Center for Nonviolent Communication
(CNVC). Born and raised in Marawi City, Mambuay has spent over two decades championing interfaith dialogue,
compassionate communication, and social healing across the Philippines and internationally. She holds the
distinction of being the only CNVC-certified trainer in the Philippines, a credential she earned in 2016 after nearly
a decade of dedicated practice and training. Her work bridges the deeply personal practice of nonviolent
communication with broader peacebuilding efforts in Mindanao, a region historically marked by Muslim-Christian
conflict and the devastating 2017 Marawi siege. Through her leadership of Kalilintad Pilipinas Inc. and her role as
Muslim Coordinator for the Silsilah Forum in Cagayan de Oro, Mambuay has touched thousands of lives, offering
tools for empathy, conflict transformation, and reconciliation. Her family's collective advocacy earned them the
prestigious Jollibee Family Values Award, recognizing their commitment to fostering unity across religious divides.
Contents

2 Education
3 Professional Career
3.1 Academic and Research Work
3.2 Discovery of Nonviolent Communication
3.3 Certification and Expertise Development

Early Life and Background
Amina Tominaman was born and raised in Marawi City, the capital of Lanao del Sur province in Mindanao and
known as the "Islamic City of Marawi." She comes from a Muslim-Maranao family, belonging to the Maranao
people—the largest Muslim ethnolinguistic group in the Philippines, whose name literally means "people of the
lake" in reference to Lake Lanao. The Maranao community, numbering over 1.4 million, is renowned for its rich
cultural heritage, including the UNESCO-recognized Darangen epic, intricate okir woodcarvings, and the
distinctive torogan royal houses.
Growing up in Marawi during a period of ongoing Muslim-Christian tensions in Mindanao, Mambuay witnessed
firsthand the cycles of conflict, discrimination, and misunderstanding that plagued her homeland. The Maranao
people had long resisted colonial powers—from Spanish conquistadors to American forces—and maintained a

strong sense of cultural identity and Islamic faith despite centuries
of external pressure. This historical context of resistance and
marginalization would later inform Mambuay's deep commitment
to peacebuilding and dialogue.
Her upbringing in a predominantly Muslim city that nonetheless
housed Christians and other faiths gave her early exposure to the
possibilities of interfaith coexistence, even as broader societal
forces worked against it. Marawi, situated on the shores of Lake
Lanao at an elevation that provides a cooler climate than
surrounding areas, served as both a center of Islamic learning and
a flashpoint for broader conflicts over land rights, political
representation, and religious identity in Mindanao.
Education
Mambuay pursued higher education at Ateneo de Cagayan
University, now known as Xavier University, one of Mindanao's
premier Catholic institutions located in Cagayan de Oro City.
There she earned a Bachelor of Arts degree in Philippine Studies,
followed by a Master of Arts in Sociology-Anthropology. Her
choice to study at a Catholic university as a Muslim woman
demonstrated an early openness to crossing religious boundaries—
a theme that would define her life's work.
Her academic training in sociology and anthropology equipped her
with analytical frameworks for understanding the complex social
dynamics, cultural traditions, and structural inequalities that
characterized Muslim-Christian relations in Mindanao. The
interdisciplinary nature of her studies allowed her to examine
Philippine society from multiple angles, considering historical
legacies, cultural practices, power structures, and identity
formation.
This educational foundation proved invaluable when she later
began working in research and education, as it gave her the tools
to both analyze conflict systematically and communicate insights
across different audiences. Her time at Xavier University also
exposed her to progressive Catholic thought on interfaith dialogue,
particularly ideas emerging from the Second Vatican Council's
declaration Nostra Aetate, which encouraged respectful
engagement with other religions.

PAGE 3
Professional Career
Academic and Research Work
After completing her education, Mambuay worked as a researcher at Xavier University, where she explored issues
confronting Muslims and Lumad (indigenous) communities in Mindanao. Her research delved into the historical
grievances, economic disparities, and social marginalization faced by these communities, providing empirical
documentation of patterns of discrimination and structural inequality.
From June 1990 to May 1995, she served as a college instructor at Mindanao State University (MSU) in Marawi
City, one of the country's premier institutions for higher education serving Muslim Filipinos. MSU's main campus
in Marawi was established in 1961 to address the educational needs of Muslim communities in Mindanao and
promote understanding between Muslims and Christians. Teaching at MSU allowed Mambuay to directly influence
the next generation of Maranao leaders and professionals, sharing both academic knowledge and her growing
insights about peaceful coexistence.
However, the late 1990s brought significant challenges. Mambuay and her husband Nathaniel Mambuay, also a
Muslim-Maranao, faced severe employment discrimination in the private sector. As Nathaniel recounted, finding
jobs as Muslims proved extremely difficult: "Sa private sector, napakahirap ng employment para sa isang Muslim.
Sa Iligan maswerte na kung may isang Muslim na naka-employ sa isang kumpanya" (In the private sector,
employment for a Muslim is very difficult. In Iligan you're lucky if even one Muslim is employed in a company).
These personal experiences of marginalization deepened their resolve to work toward greater understanding and
equality.
Discovery of Nonviolent Communication
Mambuay's transformative encounter with Nonviolent Communication came through an unexpected source—a
Catholic nun friend who gave her a copy of Marshall Rosenberg's seminal book, "Nonviolent Communication: A
Language of Life." Rosenberg, an American psychologist who developed NVC in the 1960s and 1970s, created a
communication approach based on empathy, honesty, and compassionate connection. His work emerged from his
own experiences with violence and antisemitism growing up in Detroit, and he spent decades teaching NVC as a
tool for reconciliation in conflict zones worldwide.
The book resonated deeply with Mambuay, offering a practical methodology for the kind of understanding and
peace she sought. In 2007, another friend—this time a priest—recommended her for NVC training in Ruhpolding,
Germany. This international training proved to be a turning point in her life. The intensive workshop exposed her to
practitioners from diverse backgrounds and conflict zones, showing her that the principles of empathic listening
and compassionate communication could transcend cultural and religious boundaries.
Mambuay immediately recognized NVC's potential for addressing the deep-seated conflicts in Mindanao. As she
later explained, "NVC promotes better relations and understanding between Muslims, Christians, and people of
other living faiths. It is a calling and a mission, because we work as volunteers. And I am happy with our choice. It
meets our desire to contribute to the well-being of others and to contribute to peace and understanding."
Her husband Nathaniel joined her in this advocacy the same year, and together they began introducing NVC to
various sectors in Philippine society, from educational institutions to faith communities to conflict-affected areas.
Even before earning official certification, Mambuay was already conducting workshops and training sessions,
determined to share these transformative tools with her community.

PAGE 4
Certification and Expertise Development
Mambuay's journey toward CNVC certification was long and rigorous. The certification process through the Center
for Nonviolent Communication has been compared to an independent study master's degree program in its depth
and requirements. Candidates must demonstrate extensive practice, undergo multiple levels of training, receive
assessments from certified trainers, and show competency in teaching NVC to diverse audiences.
In 2016, after nearly a decade of dedicated study and practice, Mambuay became a certified trainer—the first
Maranao and the first Muslim-Filipino to achieve this distinction, and the only certified NVC trainer in the entire
Philippines. This milestone reflected not just her personal mastery of the methodology but also her pioneering role
in bringing systematic communication training to Filipino communities.
The certification was supported by visits from German NVC trainers to the Philippines. In the summer of 2015,
four German certified trainers—Gitta Zimmermann, Klaus Karstadt, Esther Gerdts, and Friederike Kahlau-Karstadt
—conducted multiple workshops across the Philippines, working alongside Mambuay and her husband. These
workshops reached diverse audiences: prisoners and military chaplains in Tagaytay, children in conflict with the
law at the Cebu City Minor Dorm, BJMP personnel and social workers, University of San Carlos staff, and
religious groups at the Cebu Seminary. The German trainers' visit provided crucial endorsement for the continued
promotion of NVC in the Philippines and supported Mambuay's path to certification.
As a certified trainer, Mambuay's expertise spans multiple areas: Education, Mind-Body-Spirit integration,
Parenting and Family dynamics, Conflict Resolution, and Social Change. She leads transformative workshops and
trainings both locally and internationally, offering empathy sessions grounded in NVC principles. Her work focuses
particularly on reducing prejudice and bias among people of different faiths and empowering youth as agents of
change.
Institutional Contributions and Leadership
Kalilintad Pilipinas Inc.
In 2010, witnessing the profound suffering caused by calamities and the ongoing animosities between Muslims and
Christians in Mindanao, Mambuay and her family established Kalilintad Pilipinas Inc., a non-governmental
organization dedicated to education and peacebuilding. The organization's founding reflected the family's belief
that proper education for children offered the greatest hope for peace—if not in the present generation, then for
future ones.
Kalilintad Pilipinas runs a shelter for students from grades 4 through 8, providing housing, education, and care for
children who would otherwise lack access to schooling. At its peak, the shelter housed 17 students—six Muslims
and nine Christians—many of them orphans or from impoverished families whose parents could not afford to send
them to school. This intentional mixing of Muslim and Christian children under one roof embodied the
organization's commitment to building bridges across religious divides from an early age.
Beyond the educational shelter, the organization conducts community outreach including distribution of slippers
and school supplies to children in remote areas, medical missions, and relief goods for indigent families. As
Mambuay explained to her own children when starting these initiatives: "Kasi nakita namin yung mga bata
especially yung nakatira sa liblib, pumapasok sa school walang tsinelas, tapos yung lagayan ng school materials
nila plastic bag... Sabi ko sa mga anak ko baka pwede tayo makabigay kahit konting tulong" (We saw children,
especially those living in remote areas, going to school without slippers, and their school materials were kept in
plastic bags... I told my children maybe we could give even a little help).

PAGE 5
The family eventually relocated from Marawi to Misamis Oriental to continue this work, establishing their
permanent residence there while maintaining connections to their Maranao homeland.
Silsilah Forum Cagayan de Oro
Mambuay serves as the Muslim Coordinator for Silsilah Forum Cagayan de Oro, a local chapter of the broader
Silsilah Dialogue Movement. Silsilah, which means "chain," "bond," or "family tree" in Arabic, was founded in
1984 by Italian PIME missionary Fr. Sebastiano D'Ambra in Zamboanga City as an autonomous movement for
dialogue formed by Christians and Muslims. The movement envisions "a life-in-dialogue for all Muslims,
Christians and peoples of other living faiths in respect, trust and love for one another."
The Silsilah Movement emerged in response to the violent conflicts in Mindanao, including clashes between the
Moro National Liberation Front and Philippine military forces. Fr. D'Ambra, who studied Islam and Arabic in
Rome before returning to the Philippines, created Silsilah as a "common house" where people of all faiths could
meet as equals. The movement emphasizes dialogue not just as conversation but as a spirituality—dialogue with
God, with oneself, with others, and with creation.
As Muslim Coordinator in Cagayan de Oro, Mambuay helps lead the local Silsilah Forum, organizing activities
that promote friendship and mutual trust between Christians and Muslims. These include workshops, seminars,
community gatherings, and participation in the annual World Interfaith Harmony Week celebrated each February.
Silsilah Forum groups focus on building grassroots relationships that can withstand political tensions and violent
provocations.
The movement's work proved particularly crucial during the 2013 Zamboanga siege when MNLF forces attacked
the city. The Interfaith Council of Leaders of Silsilah appeared on television to announce that the siege was not a
religious war, helping to prevent broader Muslim-Christian violence. A former MNLF commander later told Fr.
D'Ambra that seeing this appeal on television convinced him to cancel a planned rebel offensive in the city.
Mambuay's role integrates her NVC expertise with Silsilah's dialogue methodology, offering communication tools
that help participants move beyond talking about peace to actually practicing it in their daily interactions.
Interfaith Forum for Peace and Harmony
Mambuay is also an active member of the Interfaith Forum for Peace and Harmony in Cagayan de Oro, where she
regularly facilitates trainings, talks, and community engagements that promote understanding across cultures and
religions, both locally and internationally. This forum brings together leaders from different faith traditions to
address shared concerns and build collaborative responses to social challenges.
Her involvement in multiple interfaith organizations reflects a strategic approach to peacebuilding—working
through different networks and platforms to reach diverse audiences and create multiple points of connection
between communities. Where Silsilah focuses specifically on Muslim-Christian dialogue rooted in spiritual
practice, the Interfaith Forum for Peace and Harmony encompasses a broader range of religious traditions and
emphasizes concrete collaborative action on social issues.
In 2022, Mambuay served as a resource person for the Interfaith Cooperation Forum's five-day in-person Training
of Trainers on Nonviolent Communication, held in Dumaguete City. She co-facilitated alongside her daughter Lara
Mambuay, demonstrating how the family's commitment to NVC has extended across generations. Nine participants
from four Asian countries—Bangladesh, Philippines, Timor-Leste, and Nepal—attended the training, representing
Muslim, Christian, and Hindu traditions. The training covered NVC components and principles, empathy exercises,
receiving difficult messages, and the "13 NVC Dance Steps" for navigating challenging conversations.

PAGE 6
Navigating the Marawi Siege
The 2017 Marawi siege represented one of the darkest chapters in recent Philippine history and had profound
implications for Mambuay's work and identity as a Maranao peacebuilder. On May 23, 2017, militants affiliated
with the Islamic State—primarily from the Maute Group and Abu Sayyaf—attacked Marawi City in an attempt to
establish a caliphate in Southeast Asia. The Philippine military's response involved five months of intense urban
warfare, aerial bombardment, and ground combat that left the city in ruins.
The siege displaced over 360,000 people from Marawi and surrounding areas, killed more than 1,200 people
(including civilians, soldiers, and militants), and destroyed approximately 20% of the city's infrastructure. Entire
neighborhoods were reduced to rubble. The city where Mambuay was born and raised—the center of Maranao
culture and Islamic learning—became a symbol of the violent extremism that she had spent years working to
prevent.
For Mambuay and the broader Maranao community, the siege was a profound trauma. The Maute brothers who led
the attack were themselves Maranaos from a wealthy, politically connected family in Butig, Lanao del Sur. Their
radicalization and the participation of other young Maranaos in the siege raised painful questions about what had
failed in Maranao society and how extremist ideologies had taken root among the youth.
In the aftermath of the siege, all mayors of Lanao del Sur issued a manifesto labeling the Maute Group and its
sympathizers as "enemies of the Maranao people," attempting to distance the broader community from the
extremists. Yet the damage to Marawi's infrastructure and social fabric—not to mention the stigmatization of
Muslims and Maranaos in national discourse—created enormous challenges for reconstruction and reconciliation.
During the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020, Mambuay gave an interview reflecting on how the Ramadan holy month
was being observed amid both the pandemic and the lingering effects of the 2017 siege. She emphasized the
resilience of the Muslim community: "I am one with all those observing the Holy month of Ramadan. I am hopeful
that with our prayers, we will be able to face the challenges brought about by the COVID-19 pandemic, and other
challenges knowing that Allah (s.w.t) is there to guide us."
The siege reinforced for Mambuay the urgent necessity of her work. The violent extremism that destroyed her
hometown represented the antithesis of everything she advocated—connection instead of division, empathy instead
of hatred, dialogue instead of violence. In the years following the siege, her efforts to promote understanding,
reduce prejudice, and equip young people with communication skills took on even greater significance.
Recognition and Awards
In recognition of their collective family advocacy for interfaith peace and unity, Mambuay and her family received
the prestigious Jollibee Family Values Award. The Jollibee Family Values Awards, initiated by the Philippines'
leading fast-food chain, honor Filipino families who exemplify positive values and make significant contributions
to their communities through various advocacies.
The award recognized the Mambuay family's noble work in seeking peaceful ways to build unity between Christian
and Muslim faiths. Jollibee honored them alongside other Filipino families from Luzon, Visayas, Mindanao, and
the United States for their noteworthy advocacies that made significant impacts in the lives of their fellowmen.
Winners received cash prizes, trophies designed by renowned brass sculptor Michael Cacnio, and public
recognition at the Gabi ng Parangal para sa Pamilyang Pilipino (Night of Honor for Filipino Families).
The award highlighted how the family's work embodied core Filipino values—bayanihan (communal unity),
malasakit (compassion), and pagkakaisa (solidarity)—while specifically addressing one of the most challenging
divides in Philippine society: the Muslim-Christian relationship. The recognition brought greater visibility to their

PAGE 7
work and validated their approach of starting with the family unit as the foundation for broader social
transformation.
Beyond the Jollibee award, Mambuay's pioneering status as the Philippines' only CNVC-certified trainer has
brought her international recognition within the global NVC community. She is listed on the Center for Nonviolent
Communication's official website and has been featured in various NVC networks and publications. Her profile
notes her mission: "to share NVC to people, both in groups and individuals to inspire and support them in giving
and receiving from the heart & speaking and listening from the heart."
Personal Philosophy and Approach
Mambuay's work is grounded in several interconnected philosophical commitments. At the core is her belief that
"connection is why we're here; it is what gives purpose and meaning to our lives"—a quote from researcher Brené
Brown that Mambuay frequently cites. This emphasis on connection directly counters the forces of division,
othering, and dehumanization that fuel conflict.
Her integration of NVC with Islamic spirituality offers a unique contribution to peacebuilding discourse. While
NVC was developed by a secular Jewish psychologist primarily for Western contexts, Mambuay demonstrates how
its principles align with Islamic teachings about compassion, justice, and the unity of humanity. She views NVC
not merely as a communication technique but as "a way of life" that reflects spiritual values.
In interviews, Mambuay emphasizes that NVC is particularly liberating for interfaith work: "We can sit down
together and share experiences, not looking at each other as Muslims or Christians but all as creations of one God.
This is liberating, thanks to Nonviolent Communication." This framing allows participants to transcend identity-
based divisions and connect at the level of shared humanity and shared needs.
Her approach to training emphasizes experiential learning over intellectual understanding. NVC workshops
typically involve extensive role-playing, where participants practice empathic listening and honest expression in
simulated difficult conversations. Exercises like "Four Chairs" (giving empathy to others) and "Four Ears"
(receiving hard-to-hear messages) provide concrete skills for navigating real conflicts.
Mambuay also brings attention to the intersection of communication and power. She continually develops her skills
in "integrating NVC to reduce prejudice and bias—particularly among people of different faiths and youth." This
recognizes that communication patterns both reflect and reinforce social hierarchies, and that transforming these
patterns requires addressing underlying prejudices and structural inequalities.
Family and Generational Transmission
Mambuay is married to Nathaniel Mambuay, also a Muslim-Maranao who shares her commitment to peacebuilding
and nonviolent communication. Their partnership models the egalitarian, collaborative approach that NVC
promotes, with both spouses actively engaged in advocacy work as equals.
The couple's children, including Lara Mambuay and Sarah Adrianne Mambuay, have also become NVC
practitioners and facilitators. Lara co-facilitated the 2022 Interfaith Cooperation Forum Training of Trainers
alongside her mother, while Sarah Adrianne led sessions on empathy exercises during the same training. This
generational transmission ensures that the family's work will continue and demonstrates how NVC principles can
be lived within family systems.

PAGE 8
The children's involvement in community outreach from a young age—helping distribute slippers and school
supplies, participating in feeding programs, engaging in interfaith activities—reflects the family's commitment to
raising socially conscious, empathetic young people. As Mambuay noted, the Jollibee Family Values Award
recognition made each family member "more enthusiastic and dedicated in involving themselves with the outreach
programs we participate in."
The family's decision to run a shelter for both Muslim and Christian students further exemplifies their commitment
to creating spaces of coexistence and mutual respect. Living alongside children from different faith backgrounds,
the Mambuay children learned practically what their parents taught theoretically—that religious differences need
not be barriers to friendship and solidarity.
Legacy and Continuing Impact
Amina T. Mambuay's legacy is multifaceted. As the Philippines' first and only internationally certified NVC trainer,
she has pioneered the systematic teaching of empathic communication in a country where indirect communication
styles and hierarchical social structures often make honest expression difficult. Her workshops have reached
thousands of Filipinos across sectors—educators, religious leaders, youth, families, government officials, and
community organizers.
Her particular contribution lies in demonstrating NVC's applicability to interfaith peacebuilding in contexts of
entrenched conflict. While NVC is often taught as a tool for interpersonal relationships or workplace
communication, Mambuay shows how it can address collective trauma, historical grievances, and identity-based
conflicts. Her work proves that even in situations as complex and painful as Muslim-Christian relations in post-
siege Mindanao, tools for empathy and understanding remain relevant and powerful.
As a Maranao woman, Mambuay also challenges stereotypes about Muslim women's roles and agency. In a context
where Muslim women are often portrayed as passive or oppressed, she exemplifies active leadership, international
engagement, and cross-cultural bridge-building. Her authority as a certified trainer and her partnerships with
Catholic religious orders demonstrate her ability to command respect across gender and religious boundaries.
The institutional structures she has helped build—Kalilintad Pilipinas Inc., the network of NVC practitioners in the
Philippines, the active Silsilah Forum chapters—provide infrastructure for ongoing peacebuilding work that will
outlast any individual leader. By training other facilitators and creating systems of support, Mambuay ensures that
the impact of her work multiplies beyond her direct reach.
Her life also offers testimony to the power of unlikely friendships and cross-boundary partnerships. That a nun
gave her the book that changed her life, that a priest recommended her for international training, that German
trainers traveled to the Philippines to support her certification—all these moments illustrate how peacebuilding
requires people willing to transcend their own tribal loyalties and invest in others' flourishing.
Looking forward, Mambuay's work becomes ever more critical as the Philippines grapples with ongoing challenges
around religious pluralism, violent extremism, historical injustice, and social cohesion. The tools and approaches
she offers—empathic listening, honest expression, needs-based dialogue, conflict transformation—provide
practical pathways toward the peaceful, just society that policy declarations and military operations alone cannot
achieve.
In her own words, reflecting on NVC's significance: "It is not only a tool for peace building, it is a way of life."
This simple statement captures the essence of Mambuay's contribution—she has spent decades not just talking
about peace but embodying it, not just teaching communication skills but living them, not just hoping for
understanding but systematically creating the conditions for it to emerge.

title: Mambuay, Raslany
text:
PAGE 1
Raslany Mambuay
Engr. Raslany Mambuay, REE, CEM, CEA, SO2, PCO, LFA, is a distinguished Filipino electrical engineer,
civic leader, and emerging legal professional whose career exemplifies the convergence of technical excellence,
transformative leadership, and public service commitment. As the first Muslim president of the Rotaract Club of
Manila Metro and recipient of the Overall Most Outstanding President award in District 3810, he has demonstrated
exceptional capacity to lead diverse organizations toward measurable impact while breaking barriers for Maranao
representation in professional and civic spaces. With credentials spanning electrical engineering, energy
management, environmental compliance, safety, and financial advisory—combined with ongoing legal education—
Mambuay represents a new generation of Filipino professionals integrating technical expertise with governance
and public policy.

Background
Engr. Raslany Mambuay belongs to the Maranao people, one of the Philippines' largest Muslim ethnolinguistic
groups predominantly based in the Lanao provinces of Mindanao. His professional journey reflects a conscious
effort to pursue excellence across multiple disciplines while maintaining strong connections to his cultural and
religious identity. As a member of the Maranao community, he has actively worked to increase representation and
visibility of Muslim professionals in mainstream Filipino civic organizations, particularly in Metro Manila's
leadership circles. His career trajectory demonstrates how technical competence, cultural authenticity, and inclusive
leadership can coexist and mutually reinforce one another in contemporary Philippine professional life.

Education
Mambuay's educational background reflects a progressive
expansion from engineering fundamentals to public administration
and legal studies, positioning him at the intersection of technical
practice, governance, and law.
Undergraduate Studies
He earned his Bachelor of Science in Electrical Engineering
from Rizal Technological University (RTU), where he
distinguished himself not only academically but also through
pioneering student leadership. At RTU, he became the university's
first Maranao board member of the RTU Supreme Student
Council, marking an important milestone for Mindanao Muslim
representation in the institution's student governance structure.
This early leadership experience would prove foundational to his
subsequent civic and professional trajectory.
Graduate and Professional Studies
Building on his engineering foundation, Mambuay pursued a
Master of Public Administration at the University of Perpetual
Help System DALTA, with one semester remaining toward
completion. This graduate program reflects his strategic interest in
understanding governance frameworks, public policy
development, and institutional management—competencies
increasingly relevant to senior engineering leadership and public
sector engagement.
Currently, he is a second-year Juris Doctor student at the
University of Nueva Caceres, undertaking legal education while
maintaining active professional practice and civic leadership
responsibilities. This pursuit of legal training signals a long-term
professional vision that integrates engineering expertise with legal
literacy, potentially positioning him for specialized practice in
infrastructure law, environmental compliance, energy regulation,
or public-private partnerships.
Professional Career
Mambuay's professional trajectory spans diverse sectors including
fast-moving consumer goods, construction, and industrial
solutions, with progressive advancement through technical and
managerial roles.

PAGE 3
Early Career
His professional journey began at Unilever, one of the world's leading consumer goods companies, where he
served as a Project Engineer. In this capacity, he gained exposure to large-scale manufacturing operations, process
optimization, and the integration of electrical systems within complex production environments. This experience in
a multinational corporate setting provided him with foundational project management skills and an understanding
of global engineering standards.
He subsequently joined Xing Solutions Corporation as a Direct Manager Assistant, expanding his competencies
beyond pure engineering toward organizational management and strategic coordination.
Infrastructure and Construction Leadership
Mambuay's career took a significant step forward when he assumed the role of Area Project Manager at Unimax
Steel Structure and Construction Corporation. In this position, he managed multiple construction sites
simultaneously, overseeing electrical installations, safety protocols, and project delivery within tight timelines and
budget constraints. This role demanded integration of technical engineering knowledge with contractor
coordination, regulatory compliance, and stakeholder management.
Current Position
Currently, he serves as Project Manager at Lead Tech Industrial Solutions Corporation, where he oversees
comprehensive project lifecycles from design and procurement through installation, commissioning, and client
handover. His role involves coordinating multidisciplinary teams, ensuring adherence to electrical codes and safety
standards, managing energy efficiency initiatives, and maintaining environmental compliance across industrial
installations.
Professional Credentials
Mambuay holds an exceptional array of professional certifications that distinguish him within the Philippine
engineering community:
Registered Electrical Engineer (REE) – licensed by the Professional Regulation Commission to practice
electrical engineering in the Philippines
Certified Energy Manager (CEM) – recognized expertise in energy management systems and efficiency
optimization
Certified Energy Auditor (CEA) – qualified to conduct comprehensive energy audits and recommend
conservation measures
Safety Officer 2 (SO2) – certified under Department of Labor and Employment regulations to implement
occupational safety and health programs
Pollution Control Officer (PCO) – authorized to manage environmental compliance and pollution
prevention systems
Licensed Financial Advisor (LFA) – qualified to provide financial planning and advisory services
This combination of credentials reflects a holistic approach to professional development, integrating technical
engineering with safety, environmental stewardship, energy sustainability, and financial planning.

PAGE 4
Leadership and Civic Engagement
Beyond his professional engineering practice, Mambuay has demonstrated transformative leadership in civic
organizations, particularly within the Rotary movement.
Rotaract Club of Manila Metro
In 2022-2023, Mambuay served as President of the Rotaract Club of Manila Metro, making history as the
organization's first Muslim president. His presidency was characterized by exceptional performance across multiple
service dimensions, culminating in unprecedented recognition at the district level.
At the District Conference and Grand Appreciation Night 2023, the club under his leadership received the
following awards:
Overall Most Outstanding President (awarded to Engr. Raslany Mambuay) – District 3810, out of more
than 60 club presidents
Public Image Award – Platinum Distinction
Professional Development Award – Platinum Distinction
International Service Award – Platinum Distinction
Club Service Award – Platinum Distinction
Community Service Award – Platinum Distinction
District Affairs Award – Platinum Distinction
Disaster Risk Reduction Citation – Platinum Distinction
Outstanding Flagship Project – Metro Cares
Excellence in Fundraising Award – Bronze Distinction
Leadership Excellence Award – PLP Raslany Mambuay
This extraordinary recognition across nearly all award categories reflects comprehensive organizational excellence
and Mambuay's capacity to mobilize volunteers, implement high-impact projects, and build institutional culture
during his presidential year. The "Imagine Rotary" year under his leadership set new standards for the club's service
delivery and organizational effectiveness.
Rotary Club of Tondo Metro
Mambuay's leadership within the Rotary movement continues with his upcoming service as Vice President of the
Rotary Club of Tondo Metro for the 2026-2027 term. This appointment represents progression from youth
Rotaract leadership to senior Rotary responsibilities, positioning him for potential district-level roles in the coming
years.
Youth Leadership Training
He has completed the Youth Leadership Program, earning a Light Blue Cord designation with merit certificate
recognition, reflecting his investment in continuous leadership development and mentorship capacity.
Institutional Contributions
Mambuay's contributions extend beyond individual achievement to institutional impact across several dimensions.

PAGE 5
Representation and Inclusion
As the first Maranao student leader at RTU and the first Muslim president of Rotaract Club of Manila Metro,
Mambuay has opened pathways for greater Mindanao Muslim participation in mainstream Filipino civic and
professional organizations. His success challenges stereotypes and demonstrates that leadership excellence can
emerge from any cultural or religious background when talent is recognized and nurtured.
Service Innovation
During his Rotaract presidency, the "Metro Cares" flagship project addressed critical community needs while
mobilizing youth volunteers toward sustainable service models. His emphasis on disaster risk reduction earned
platinum distinction, reflecting attention to resilience-building in a disaster-prone nation.
Professional Standards
Through his accumulation of multiple professional credentials and commitment to continuing education, Mambuay
models the importance of lifelong learning and multidisciplinary competence for engineering professionals
navigating increasingly complex technical and regulatory environments.
Legacy and Recognition
Mambuay's legacy is being built on several foundations: technical excellence in electrical engineering and energy
management; transformative civic leadership within the Rotary movement; and pioneering representation as a
Maranao Muslim professional in Metro Manila's organizational landscape.
His recognition as Overall Most Outstanding President among more than 60 peers in District 3810 stands as a
defining achievement, demonstrating that cultural and religious identity can coexist with—and even enhance—
leadership effectiveness in pluralistic settings.
The platinum-level distinctions across nearly all service categories during his presidential year establish
benchmarks for future club leaders and demonstrate how focused leadership can elevate organizational
performance across multiple dimensions simultaneously.
His ongoing legal studies suggest a future legacy that may extend beyond engineering practice toward policy
advocacy, regulatory development, or public sector leadership where technical expertise and legal literacy
converge.
Current Pursuits and Future Trajectory
Mambuay currently balances multiple professional and educational commitments: full-time project management
responsibilities at Lead Tech Industrial Solutions Corporation, second-year law studies at the University of Nueva
Caceres, near-completion of his Master of Public Administration degree, and upcoming vice-presidential duties
with the Rotary Club of Tondo Metro.
This demanding portfolio reflects an individual comfortable with complexity and committed to continuous growth
across technical, legal, and civic domains.

PAGE 6
His trajectory suggests potential future roles in infrastructure development, public-private partnerships, energy
policy, or public sector leadership positions where engineering expertise, legal knowledge, and proven civic
leadership can be leveraged for broader institutional impact.

title: Manansala, Brian Magat
text:
PAGE 1
Brian Magat Manansala
G. Brian Magat Manansala (also known as Brian M. Manansala, and Zul Kifli Manansala, in literary circles)
is a Filipino educator, author, motivational speaker, cultural advocate, youth leader, and Balik-Islam revert based in
Calumpit, Bulacan.
He is recognized across Bulacan and Filipino Muslim communities for weaving together a life of creative
expression, grassroots leadership, and sincere spiritual transformation.
Before his reversion to Islam, he had already carved out a reputation as a multi-awarded educator, published poet,
Baybayin (ancient Filipino script) advocate, and one of the country's Outstanding Scoutmasters.
After embracing Islam, he channeled that same energy into founding Calumpit Muslims Inc. and building a Muslim
community in a predominantly non-Muslim province, making him a bridge-builder in the truest sense of the word.
His signature legacy is best captured this way: he didn't abandon his past when he found his faith; he redirected it
toward something larger.

Background
Brian grew up in Calumpit, Bulacan, where his roots run deep in the local educational and cultural landscape.

Details about his early childhood remain largely private, but what
is known paints a picture of someone shaped early by creativity,
restlessness, and a drive to connect with people.
His mother, Teresita Magat, remains a visible presence in his
personal life and appears prominently in accounts of his journey,
reflecting the kind of close family bond that often anchors people
through significant life transitions.
As a young man, Brian explored performance arts and even went
through a phase as a rapper before channeling his energy toward
education, scouting, and community service.
That early creative restlessness never left him; it simply found
more structured and purposeful expressions over time.
Education
Brian earned a Bachelor of Secondary Education, major in
Filipino, from Bulacan State University.
That academic foundation in language, literature, and pedagogy
became the bedrock of practically everything he has done since:
teaching, writing, speaking, cultural advocacy, and community
organizing.
His training in Filipino language and literature put him in a natural
position to champion indigenous Philippine writing systems like
Baybayin, a passion that would later become one of his most
recognized contributions.
Career
Teaching and Mentoring
Brian has taught at Frances National High School in Calumpit,
Bulacan, where his role extends well beyond the classroom.
He serves as a scouting adviser and functions as a general mentor
to the young people under his care.
His approach to teaching reflects a philosophy of education as
empowerment: not just delivering lessons, but shaping character,
building resilience, and inspiring students to see their own
potential.

PAGE 3
Institutions
Frances National High
School, Calumpit; Calumpit
Muslims Inc.; New Muslim
Academy
Performance Arts and Early Creative Work
Before settling into his identity as an educator and cultural
advocate, Brian explored performance arts, including a stint as a
rapper.
That background in performance gave him a comfort with audiences and a natural flair for public engagement that
has served him well throughout his career as a speaker and community leader.
Literary Contributions
Brian is a published author whose works reflect his deep commitment to Filipino language, literature, and
indigenous heritage.
His published titles include Walang Pamagat: Kalipunan ng mga Tula (a poetry collection), D' Adventures of Eagle
Man, Ang Sasakyang Aparador, and Anatomya ng Baybayin, a work dedicated to the study and promotion of
Baybayin, the precolonial Philippine script.
He has served as a literary contest judge for BulPriSA (Bulacan Provincial Schools Press Association) and
MaCiPriSA (Malolos City Press), contributing his expertise to competitions that nurture young Filipino writers.
Baybayin Advocacy
One of Brian's most consistent passions is the promotion and preservation of Baybayin, the ancient Filipino
writing system that predates Spanish colonization.
He has spoken about Baybayin at public platforms including TEDx MHPNHS Youth and has been featured in I-
Witness documentary segments, bringing indigenous script awareness to broader audiences.
His book Anatomya ng Baybayin stands as one of his more academically oriented contributions, offering both
educators and enthusiasts a structured resource on the script.
Scouting and Youth Development
Brian's involvement in scouting is longstanding and nationally recognized.
He represented the Philippines at the 22nd World Scout Jamboree in Sweden (held in 2011), a major
international gathering of scout leaders and youth from around the world.
His dedication to the scouting movement earned him recognition as one of the Outstanding Scoutmasters of the
Philippines.
At the local level, his scouting work complements his classroom teaching, giving young people in Calumpit
structured opportunities for leadership development, community service, and character formation.
Motivational Speaking
Alongside his work as an educator and author, Brian has built a reputation as a motivational speaker, particularly
among youth audiences.

PAGE 4
His speaking engagements cover themes of culture, identity, indigenous heritage, personal transformation, and
service.
His recognition as Philippines' Most Inspiring Motivational Speaker (2023) reflects the reach and impact of this
dimension of his career.
Conversion to Islam and New Chapter
Brian's reversion to Islam marks a significant turning point in his life, and it's the kind of story that tends to
resonate precisely because it's so personal and so public at the same time.
After years of building a career in education, arts, and public service, he embraced Islam and took on the name Zul
Kifli Manansala in Muslim community contexts.
He is open about the fact that his reversion wasn't a rejection of who he was before; rather, it was a deepening, a
redirection of his talents and platform toward faith-centered service.
In his own telling, years of chasing recognition, influence, and identity through the arts and public life eventually
led him to seek something more grounding, and he found it in Islam.
Institutional Contributions
Founding of Calumpit Muslim Community and Calumpit Muslims Inc.
Following his reversion, Brian founded the Calumpit Muslim Community, which grew and was formalized into
Calumpit Muslims Inc.
Operating in a predominantly non-Muslim province, this organization focuses on Islamic awareness, community
service, humanitarian outreach, brotherhood (ukhuwwah), and peaceful coexistence.
It serves both the local Muslim population and the broader community by promoting dialogue and mutual
understanding between people of different faiths.
The organization also actively supports fellow Balik-Islam reverts, providing guidance, community, and resources
for those navigating a similar journey.
New Muslim Academy
Brian has contributed content to the New Muslim Academy, a platform dedicated to guiding individuals who have
embraced Islam.
His involvement reflects his commitment to accompanying others along the path he himself has walked, offering
practical and spiritual support rooted in lived experience.
Personal Values and Cultural Significance
Brian's life and work embody a blend of Filipino resilience, artistic depth, and service-oriented leadership.

PAGE 5
He holds education as a form of empowerment, indigenous culture (especially Baybayin and local literature) as a
form of identity, and Islamic principles of unity, compassion, and truth-seeking as a moral compass.
What makes his story particularly compelling in Philippine Muslim discourse is that he brings credibility from a
deeply Filipino, non-Muslim background into the Balik-Islam narrative.
He doesn't just preach coexistence; he lives it, operating simultaneously as a scouting adviser, Baybayin scholar,
literary judge, and Muslim community leader in a Catholic-majority province.
Culturally, he helps keep alive Filipino literary and indigenous script traditions while adapting them for
contemporary youth, ensuring they stay relevant rather than merely historical.
In Bulacan and Filipino Muslim circles alike, he is seen as a genuine bridge-builder: someone whose journey
challenges both Muslims and non-Muslims to reconsider their assumptions about identity, transformation, and
community.
Recognition
Brian has received a wide range of awards at local, national, and regional levels, recognizing his contributions to
education, culture, and humanitarian service.
Award

2026

(year not specified)

(year not specified)
Asia's Humanitarian Hero
(year not specified)
Outstanding Scoutmaster of the Philippines
(year not specified)
Provincial and local government units in Bulacan have also recognized him multiple times for his cultural and
educational contributions.
Challenges
Brian's path has not been without its complexities.
Building a Muslim community in a predominantly Catholic province like Bulacan requires sustained patience,
diplomacy, and the kind of credibility that can only come from being genuinely known and respected by the
surrounding community.
His work with Calumpit Muslims Inc. involves not just serving existing Muslims but engaging neighbors, local
governments, and institutions that may have limited familiarity with Islam.

PAGE 6
His personal transformation from a celebrated educator and performance artist into a faith-driven community
organizer also required navigating questions of identity, social perception, and continuity of purpose.
The source file notes that details about his early childhood and full family background remain relatively private,
which reflects his careful management of the boundary between his public advocacy and his personal life.
Legacy
Brian Zul Kifli Manansala's legacy is still being written, and that's part of what makes his story worth telling now.
He represents a generation of Filipino educators who understand that their classroom is not four walls but a whole
community, and that their responsibilities don't end at the school bell.
As a Balik-Islam revert, he gives voice to a growing but often misunderstood segment of Filipino society, people
who come to Islam not by birth but by conviction, and who carry with them the full texture of a Filipino
upbringing.
His advocacy for Baybayin places him in a tradition of Filipino intellectuals who believe that knowing where you
came from is inseparable from knowing who you are.
And his founding of Calumpit Muslims Inc. is a quiet but significant act of institution-building in a place where no
such institution existed before.
He continues to show up: for his students, for his faith community, for his country's literary heritage, and for
anyone who needs to know that transformation is possible at any stage of life.

Dr. Yusoph J. Mando
Yusoph J. Mando is a Filipino public servant, entrepreneur, and
cultural advocate best known for serving as Commissioner of the
National Commission on Muslim Filipinos (NCMF). Over time, he
built a reputation not just as a government official, but as a
connector of worlds, someone who consistently worked to bring
Muslim Filipino identity into the center of national life. His public
message stayed simple and steady across roles: peace, dignity, and
shared nationhood.

Background
Yusoph J. Mando was born in 1972 in Tipo-Tipo, Basilan, a
province shaped by deep Yakan cultural traditions and a long history
of resilience. Growing up in Basilan meant living in a place where
identity, faith, and community were tightly woven into daily life. It
was also a place marked by tension and conflict, which exposed him
early to the realities of marginalization and misunderstanding faced
by Muslim communities.

PAGE 2
Leadership at the NCMF under
President Rodrigo Duterte; championing
Vision 2040 for Muslim Filipino
development; Hajj program reforms;
Yakan-English-Tagalog dictionary
project; peacebuilding and interfaith
dialogue
His upbringing was not isolated from hardship. Like many from
Basilan, he grew up navigating both opportunity and limitation.
These early conditions shaped how he later understood leadership,
not as authority from above, but as responsibility rooted in lived
experience.
At a young age, he moved to Manila in search of better
opportunities. The transition from Basilan to the capital exposed
him to a completely different social environment. He had to adapt, learn quickly, and survive in a competitive
urban setting. This period of adjustment played a critical role in shaping his outlook, especially his ability to move
between cultural spaces with ease.<ref name="blog1" />
Education

Mando’s educational journey reflects both formal study and lived experience. His early academic formation was
shaped by exposure to fields such as public administration, criminology, and Islamic perspectives on governance,
areas that later informed his work in public service.
His learning, however, did not stop within the classroom. Much of his development came from direct engagement,
running businesses, working with communities, and navigating different social environments from Basilan to
Manila. These experiences gave him a working understanding of both institutional systems and grassroots realities.
Over time, this combination of formal education and practical exposure shaped a leadership style that is grounded,
adaptive, and closely connected to the communities he serves.

Entrepreneurial Formation
Before entering government service, Mando spent years building himself through entrepreneurship. His early work
involved a range of small-scale ventures, reflecting both necessity and ambition. He took on different roles, from
informal trade to service-based work, gradually learning how systems function at the ground level.
This phase of his life is important because it grounded his later policies in real-world experience. He understood
how ordinary people earn, struggle, and survive.
Pamanganan Halal House
One of his most visible entrepreneurial ventures was Pamanganan Halal House in Quiapo, Manila. The restaurant
was not simply a business. It was an expression of identity and discipline.
Every aspect of the operation followed halal standards, from sourcing ingredients to food preparation. This strict
adherence was not just about compliance, but about demonstrating that halal could be practiced fully even in a
dense urban environment.<ref name="blog1" />
What made the restaurant stand out was its openness. It attracted both Muslims and non-Muslims, quietly breaking
down barriers. Customers did not just come for food, they encountered a way of life. In that sense, the restaurant
became an informal space for cultural exchange.
Entry into Public Service
In August 2020, Mando was appointed Commissioner of the National Commission on Muslim Filipinos by
President Rodrigo Duterte.<ref name="pia1" />
The appointment marked a shift from private enterprise to national responsibility. It placed him within a
government institution tasked with addressing the needs of Muslim Filipinos across the country.

PAGE 4
He also served as a spokesperson, which made him one of the more visible faces of the NCMF. This role required
him to translate policy into language that communities could understand, something he handled with a
conversational and grounded approach.
Public Service at the National Commission on Muslim Filipinos
Mr. Yusoph Mando previously served as a Commissioner of the National Commission on Muslim Filipinos
(NCMF), where he held several key leadership roles, including Commission Spokesperson, Crime-Free Czar, and
later Officer-in-Charge Secretary of the Commission.
As NCMF Spokesperson, Mando was responsible for communicating the Commission’s programs, policies, and
initiatives to the public and to Muslim communities across the Philippines. In this role, he helped strengthen
engagement between the Commission, community leaders, and various government agencies.
During his tenure as Crime-Free Czar, he worked with local officials, law-enforcement agencies, and community
leaders to support peace-building initiatives and promote community-based approaches to conflict prevention and
public safety within Muslim communities.
Mando later served as Officer-in-Charge Secretary of the NCMF, overseeing the Commission’s programs and
administrative operations. During this period, he introduced several operational reforms aimed at improving
institutional coordination and program delivery.
One of the most notable initiatives during his leadership was the development of improved operational systems for
the Philippine Hajj program, particularly in the preparation and implementation of Hajj 2024. These reforms
included strengthened coordination mechanisms, improved service-provider arrangements, and upgraded
accommodation and service systems for Filipino pilgrims. The reforms contributed to a more organized and hassle-
free Hajj experience, and the operational framework established during that period continues to guide the
management of Hajj services for Filipino pilgrims.
In addition, Mando supported initiatives related to Halal industry development, Shari’ah-related programs, the
welfare of Muslim Overseas Filipino Workers (OFWs), and community-based mediation efforts aimed at resolving
tribal and local conflicts.
Vision 2040
One of the major frameworks associated with his tenure was the NCMF "Vision 2040" initiative. The program laid
out long-term goals for Muslim Filipino communities.
The framework focused on:
Strengthening halal economic systems
Improving pilgrimage services
Expanding access to Sharia education
Integrating Muslim Filipinos into national development
Rather than treating Muslim communities as separate, the framework emphasized participation in the broader
national economy and governance.<ref name="pna1" />

PAGE 5
Contributions
Halal Advocacy
Mando’s work in halal advocacy predates his government role. Through business and later through policy, he
promoted halal as a system of life, not just a dietary rule.
He framed halal in terms of discipline, cleanliness, and ethical conduct. This approach made it easier for non-
Muslims to understand its broader value.
He also supported the development of local halal products and industries, recognizing their potential to create jobs
and strengthen economic independence.
"Halal is not only about what we eat. It is about discipline, cleanliness, and accountability in how
we live our daily lives." Yusoph J. Mando
Cultural Preservation
One of his notable contributions is his work on a Yakan–English–Tagalog dictionary. This project aimed to
preserve the Yakan language and make it accessible beyond Basilan.<ref name="blog1" />
The effort reflects a deeper concern. Many indigenous languages in the Philippines face gradual decline, especially
among younger generations who migrate to cities. By documenting the language, he contributed to safeguarding
cultural memory.
"If we lose our language, we lose a part of who we are. Preserving Yakan is preserving our identity
as a people." Yusoph J. Mando
Peacebuilding and Interfaith Engagement
Mando has long been involved in peacebuilding efforts. His approach is grounded in interaction rather than
abstraction.
He participated in interfaith dialogues, community initiatives, and collaborative programs that brought together
Muslims and Christians. These were not limited to formal settings. Much of the work happened through everyday
encounters, shared spaces, and open conversations.
This approach helped build trust over time, especially in areas where suspicion and misunderstanding had long
existed.<ref name="pia1" />
"Peace and love. That is how we move forward as one people." Yusoph J. Mando
Public Communication
As a public figure, Mando developed a communication style that emphasized clarity and relatability. He avoided
technical language when addressing communities, choosing instead to speak in terms that people could connect
with.

PAGE 6
This approach made government programs feel more accessible, especially to sectors that often feel excluded from
formal institutions.
Recognition
In 2021, Mando received recognition as one of the Most Outstanding Public Servants, highlighting his
contributions to public service, peacebuilding, and community engagement.
His work has also been acknowledged in leadership circles for advancing Muslim Filipino representation within
national discourse.
Challenges
Mando’s career has unfolded within a complex national context. Muslim Filipinos continue to face structural
challenges, including economic inequality, limited access to services, and persistent stereotypes.
Working within government, he had to navigate these realities while maintaining credibility among both state
institutions and local communities.
Balancing these expectations required constant negotiation, especially in an environment where trust is not easily
given.
Legacy
Yusoph J. Mando’s legacy is defined by connection. Across entrepreneurship, governance, and cultural work, he
consistently worked to bridge divides.
He presented Muslim identity not as separate from the Filipino story, but as part of its foundation. His work reflects
a vision of a country where diversity is not simply tolerated, but actively integrated.
For many observers, his impact is not only in programs or policies, but in the tone he set. A tone that insists
dialogue is possible, that shared values exist, and that national identity can expand without losing its core.
