Major General / Police Director Akod Kodaong Mangondato,
PC, PNP, Al-Hadj is remembered as one of the first and most
distinguished Maranao-Muslim officers to rise through the ranks of
Philippine public service.
He came from Barangay Calilangan-Mangondato in Masiu, Lanao
del Sur, a place that also recognized him with a title beyond his
military and police career. He held the position of Sultan sa Lumbac
a Masiu, Lanao del Sur, carrying both a traditional and a public
service role for his community.
Contents
1 Education and Training
2 Career and Public Service
3 Legacy and Character
4 See Also
5 References
Education and Training
General Mangondato completed the General Staff Course (GSC) in
Indonesia, a program reserved for officers being groomed for high
level command and strategic leadership. It was training that placed
him among a select group prepared to take on senior responsibilities
within the armed services.
He also served for a long stretch as Commandant of Mindanao State
University (MSU) Main Campus in Marawi City, where he oversaw
order and security for the university during his tenure.
Career and Public Service
General Mangondato rose to the rank of Police Director, equivalent
to a 2-Star General, within the Philippine National Police. Along the
way, he held several key posts that shaped his legacy in public
service.
He served as General Staff R1 and R5 stationed at Camp Alagar in
Cagayan de Oro City, where he took charge of peace and order
efforts across the whole of Northern Mindanao.
He was also appointed Chief Intelligence/Security officer for the
entire Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (ARMM) during
the term of Regional Governor Atty. Lininding Pangandaman.

PAGE 2
Mangondato, and serving as a trusted ally
of President Fidel V. Ramos.
Pull Quote
"True leadership is measured by service to
others, especially in times when they need
it most."
Beyond his official duties, he was known as a close friend and
trusted confidant of former President Fidel V. Ramos.
Interestingly, his influence reached beyond security and governance.
He was also recognized as an official and administrator in the field of
Track and Field in the Philippines, playing a part in shaping the sport
in the country.
Legacy and Character
General Akod K. Mangondato was not just known as a successful police official and community leader. He also
stood as a protector of his people during times of danger.
During the years of Martial Law, when fear and unrest spread across many parts of the country, he did not hesitate
to act. Together with his brother, Brigadier General Diamongen Kodaong Mangondato, PC, who was also a senior
officer of the Philippine Constabulary, they used their positions and influence to rescue, assist, and protect their
fellow Maranao across Mindanao.
Many families and individuals were kept safe from harm because of what they did, a reminder that true leadership
is measured by service to others, especially in times when they need it most.
He completed the Al-Hadj, the sacred pilgrimage to Mecca, and throughout his life he served as a bridge of
understanding between the government and the Moro community. His career also helped open the door for other
Muslim officers who would go on to rise through the ranks of public service.

Khalil Oga Mangurun Mapupuno
Atty. Khalil Oga Mangurun Mapupuno (widely known as Atty.
Oga Mapupuno) was a Filipino lawyer, statesman, and educator
who left a quiet but enduring mark on two very different stages: the
national halls of constitutional lawmaking and the classrooms of
Mindanao State University in Marawi City.
He is best remembered as one of the elected delegates to the historic
1971 Philippine Constitutional Convention, where he sat alongside
other prominent Muslim figures to represent the legal interests and
political aspirations of the Bangsamoro people at a moment when
the republic was rethinking its foundational charter.
Outside of politics, his deeper and more lasting work was in the
academy. For much of his later career, he shaped the legal minds of
Bangsamoro lawyers as a senior professor at the MSU College of
Law, where students recalled him not just for his command of the
law, but for the sheer force of his presence and oratorical skill.

FAMILY BACKGROUND AND ETHNIC
AFFILIATION
Atty. Oga Mapupuno was Maranao, born and raised in Wato-
Balindong, Lanao del Sur, a municipality that carries a long history
of traditional royalty and political leadership among the People of
the Lake.
His family connections ran deep into the political and civic fabric of
Lanao.

PAGE 2
Political Career

Convention (elected November 10,
1970)
Academic Appointment

President for Administration, Mindanao
State University

Administrative Law at Mindanao State
University

Representing Muslim Mindanao at the

case on electoral due process; decades
of legal mentorship at MSU College of
Law
He was married to Maimona S. Dimakuta-Mapupuno, through
whom he became linked to the prominent Dimakuta political
lineage.
His mother-in-law and the wife of the celebrated Lanao leader Datu
Ali Dimaporo were sisters, which drew him into close familial orbit
with veteran Mindanao statesman former Congressman Abdullah
Dimakuta-Dimaporo.
These ties were not just genealogical. They formed part of a broader
network of civic duty, public service, and community leadership
that defined elite Maranao families of his generation.
That sense of duty clearly passed to the next generation. His son,
Atty. Basari Dimakuta Mapupuno, went on to serve as Provincial
Prosecutor of Lanao del Sur, earned the title Sultan of Malaig, and
became the 8th Regular President of the Mindanao State University
System, one of the most significant academic leadership roles in
Muslim Mindanao.
EDUCATION AND EARLY LIFE
Atty. Oga Mapupuno grew up in the post-World War II years of
Lanao del Sur, a period when rebuilding, both physical and
institutional, was the urgent project of every community across the
Philippines.
He showed an early aptitude for rhetoric, reasoning, and leadership, qualities that would define every role he later
held.
He pursued legal education and passed the Philippine Bar Examination, earning the right to practice law as a full-
fledged attorney.
His formal training gave him more than legal technique. It instilled in him a deep respect for statutory construction,
institutional design, and the mechanics of governance, a reverence that would later shape both his teaching
philosophy and his approach to national service.
Specific details regarding the institutions he attended and the year he passed the Bar are pending verification.
Template:Fact
CAREER AND NATIONAL SERVICE
The 1971 Constitutional Convention
The pinnacle of Atty. Oga Mapupuno's national political career came on November 10, 1970, when he was elected
as one of six delegates representing the lone district of Lanao del Sur to the 1971 Philippine Constitutional
Convention.

PAGE 3
This was no ordinary assignment. The Convention had been convened to draft an entirely new constitution for the
republic, replacing the 1935 Constitution that had governed the Philippines through independence, the Second
World War, and the postwar decades.
Mapupuno worked alongside other prominent Muslim delegates, including Domocao Alonto and Pangalian
Balindong, as part of a small but consequential bloc that fought to embed the interests, legal frameworks, and
autonomy of the Muslim minority into the new constitutional order.
It was meaningful, principled work, and it was cut short.
The Convention was overtaken by events when President Ferdinand Marcos declared Martial Law in 1972,
effectively suspending the normal processes of democratic governance and altering the trajectory of the
constitutional project.
For the Muslim delegates who had come to Manila hoping to secure formal protections for their communities, the
declaration was a bitter interruption. But the groundwork they laid, the arguments they made, and the positions they
staked out in the Convention hall did not disappear. They became part of the long historical record of Bangsamoro
advocacy within the Philippine republic.
Legal Practice and Philippine Jurisprudence
Beyond his role at the Convention, Atty. Oga Mapupuno was an active legal practitioner whose name found a
permanent place in Philippine case law.
He is named in the landmark consolidated petitions of Bashier v. Commission on Elections and Oga Mapupuno,
docketed as G.R. No. L-33692 before the Supreme Court of the Philippines.
The case touched on electoral law and due process safeguards during a turbulent transitional period in Philippine
governance, contributing to the body of jurisprudence governing how local elections are administered and how
procedural rights are protected.
Being cited in a Supreme Court decision is not a minor footnote. It places Atty. Oga Mapupuno in the official legal
record of the country, where his name will remain as long as Philippine jurisprudence is studied.
INSTITUTIONAL CONTRIBUTIONS TO MINDANAO STATE
UNIVERSITY
After his years in national service, Atty. Oga Mapupuno turned his focus almost entirely to the Mindanao State
University (MSU) Main Campus in Marawi City, where he would spend the better part of his later career building
something arguably more durable than any single case or political campaign: a generation of Bangsamoro lawyers.
Vice President for Administration
He served as the University's Vice President for Administration, taking on critical structural oversight during the
institution's formative years.
MSU was still finding its institutional footing during this period, and executives like Mapupuno helped shape its
administrative culture, its operational systems, and its identity as a university of and for the Bangsamoro people.

PAGE 4
The specifics of his term as Vice President, including exact dates of service, are pending documentary verification.
Template:Fact
Professor of Administrative Law
His role as a senior faculty member at the MSU College of Law was perhaps the chapter of his life that touched
the most people.
He specialized in Administrative Law, the branch of public law governing the authority, procedures, and
accountability of government agencies, a field of immediate practical relevance in a region where the relationship
between community and state has often been contested.
His students remembered him with unmistakable warmth.
He was described as eloquent, meticulous, and strict, a professor who held high standards and made no apologies
for it, but who also possessed an exceptional command of language and a gift for oratory that made his lectures not
just instructive but genuinely memorable.
For many of the lawyers who passed through his classroom, he was not simply a professor. He was a model of what
it meant to be a Bangsamoro professional: rigorous, principled, and fully at home in the world of national
institutions without surrendering an inch of cultural identity.
PERSONAL VALUES AND CULTURAL SIGNIFICANCE
Atty. Oga Mapupuno's life was, in many ways, a living argument for a particular idea: that engagement, not
withdrawal, is the Bangsamoro path to justice.
At a time when the Moro people were fighting for institutional recognition within the broader Philippine republic,
and when many of that struggle's loudest voices were those of armed resistance, Mapupuno chose a different
instrument. He used education and constitutional reform, working within systems while pushing those systems to
expand.
His personal philosophy centered on the conviction that education is the most powerful equalizer available to a
marginalized community.
He carried that conviction into every role he held, from the convention hall in Manila to the law classrooms of
Marawi, and he carried it with the kind of personal integrity that makes a life not just accomplished but exemplary.
His legacy is legible in his son's career, in the Supreme Court record, and in the countless Bangsamoro lawyers
who studied Administrative Law under his instruction and went on to serve their communities in courts,
government offices, and civic institutions across the region.
The synthesis he embodied, of traditional Maranao culture, Islamic values, and modern constitutional practice, was
not incidental to his professional life. It was the source of it.

Abdul A. Marohombsar
Atty. Abdul A. Marohombsar was an eminent Maranao trial lawyer,
jurist, and statesman from Lanao del Sur, Philippines. He is widely
recognized for his trailblazing contributions to regional governance
and national electoral administration, having served as the Vice
Governor of Lanao del Sur, an Assemblyman for the regional
legislative body (Batasan Pampook) of Region XII, and a national
Commissioner of the Commission on Elections (COMELEC).
He was married to Dr. Hadja Sittie Nurlayla "Emily"
Marohombsar (https://wiki.maranaw.com/index.php/Hadja_Sitti
e_Nurlaylah_%22Emily%22_Marohombsar), the first Muslim
female president of the Mindanao State University (MSU)
System. Standing as a foundational pillar of modern Maranao
leadership, Marohombsar’s career was defined by a strict adherence
to judicial integrity, local administrative reform, and ethical modesty.
Contents
1 Early life and familial ties
2 Education and legal career
3 Political and public service career
3.1 Local and regional governance
3.2 COMELEC Commissionership
4 Personal life and incorruptibility
5 Legacy and cultural significance
6 Reference
7 See also
Early life and familial ties
Abdul A. Marohombsar was born into an influential and noble
Maranao clan in the undivided province of Lanao. His family
possessed a strong tradition of military and civil leadership. The
legendary patriarch Col. Louis Marohombsar—a Bataan Death
March survivor and the first post-WWII military governor of
undivided Lanao, was his father-in-law. Abdul grew up heavily
immersed in the complexities of tribal dynamics, civic
responsibilities, and regional public leadership, which later defined
his approach to law. He was married to his paternal cousin, Dr. Hadja
Sittie Nurlayla "Emily" Marohombsar, making Col. Luis
Marohombsar both his biological uncle and his father-in-law.

PAGE 2
the Maranao people, and for founding a
multi-generational family tradition of
public service across ARMM and
COMELEC
Pull Quote
"True leadership is measured not by the
offices one holds, but by the modesty one
keeps."
Education and legal career
Marohombsar pursued higher education with a focus on law and
governance. He obtained his Bachelor of Laws degree and
successfully passed the Philippine Bar Examination, qualifying him
as a trial lawyer. His formal legal education equipped him with a
profound understanding of constitutional and statutory frameworks,
enabling him to bridge the gap between national statutory laws and
the traditional socio-cultural structures (adat) inherent to the Muslim
populations of Mindanao.
Before transitioning into regional and national politics, Marohombsar built an exceptional reputation as a
formidable trial lawyer in the Lanao region. He was highly regarded for his litigation skills, legal intellect, and
ethical courtroom demeanor. He frequently handled volatile and sensitive disputes, earning the trust of both the
local Maranao royalty and national judicial institutions.
Political and public service career
Local and regional governance
Marohombsar eventually entered provincial politics, where he achieved the unique status of being an undefeated
Vice Governor of Lanao del Sur. Serving alongside key regional executives, his tenure focused on maintaining
institutional peace, introducing bureaucratic reforms, and fostering civic development during eras marked by
political shifts and local conflicts.
As the Philippine government attempted to institute regional autonomy structures in the late 1970s and 1980s,
Marohombsar was elected as an Assemblyman for the Batasan Pampook (Regional Legislative Assembly) of
Autonomous Region XII. In this legislative capacity, he helped draft and sponsor regional resolutions that aimed to
address the economic, educational, and legal needs of Muslim Mindanao.
COMELEC Commissionership
Recognizing his stellar legal background and unassailable integrity, Marohombsar was appointed by the President
of the Philippines as a national Commissioner of the Commission on Elections (COMELEC). As a COMELEC
commissioner, he was tasked with overseeing the enforcement and administration of all election laws throughout
the archipelago. His presence on the commission was vital in ensuring equitable democratic representation and
managing complex electoral exercises in historically conflict-prone areas of Western and Central Mindanao.
Personal life and incorruptibility
Marohombsar was married to Dr. Hadja Sittie Nurlayla "Emily" Marohombsar, a fellow Maranao intellectual
who went on to become an iconic figure in Philippine academia. Dr. Emily Marohombsar was a pioneering faculty
member of the Mindanao State University (MSU) Main Campus in Marawi when it opened in 1961. She steadily
rose through the academic ranks to become a Dean, Vice President, and ultimately the 4th President of the MSU
System, securing her place in history as the university's first female and first Muslim head.

PAGE 3
Despite holding some of the highest, most influential offices in regional and national governance, Atty.
Marohombsar and his wife were celebrated for their extraordinary honesty and financial incorruptibility. Observers
and relatives frequently noted that the couple never utilized their offices for personal enrichment. They lived out
their retirement decades modestly, choosing to reside in a standard government-provided cottage on the MSU Main
Campus in Marawi City rather than amassing luxury vehicles or personal estates.
The marriage was blessed with five children:
Abdul Marohombsar Jr.
Shainulla Marohombsar
Samerah Marohombsar
Alamina Marohombsar
Ahmad Marohombsar
Atty. Abdul A. Marohombsar passed away prior to the demise of his wife, who died in May 2013.
Legacy and cultural significance
Atty. Marohombsar’s legacy continues to heavily reverberate across Lanao del Sur and the broader Bangsamoro
region:
The Anti-Graft Standard: In a political landscape often scrutinized for corruption, Marohombsar and his
wife are held up by modern historians and public administration scholars as paragons of absolute integrity.
Their choice to live an unblemished, modest life within university housing while commanding national
agencies remains an inspirational benchmark for young Moro public servants.
Multi-Generational Public Service: The family tradition of public service established by Atty. Abdul and
Dr. Emily Marohombsar was successfully transferred to their children. Their immediate offspring and
descendants went on to fill critical roles in state governance, with various family members serving as
municipal judges, provincial vice governors, regional assemblymen in the Autonomous Region in Muslim
Mindanao (ARMM), and subsequent COMELEC executives.
Socio-Cultural Upliftment: Through his legal defenses and structural execution of election mechanisms,
Marohombsar directly contributed to the normalization of civil democratic participation among the Maranao
people, proving that traditional Islamic societies could seamlessly engage with and excel within the wider
Philippine constitutional republic.

title: Marohombsar, Abdulmajid P.
text:
PAGE 1
Abdulmajid P. Marohombsar
Atty. Abdulmajid P. Marohombsar — more warmly known as Atty. Majid in the circles he moves through — is
a Maranao Muslim lawyer, educator, and policy advocate from Lanao del Sur who has built his career at the
intersection of two legal worlds that don't always speak to each other: the Philippine national justice system and the
Shari'ah tradition that governs the lives of millions of Muslim Filipinos.
He's the kind of figure who's harder to spot on a headline but impossible to miss in the rooms where policy gets
shaped. In September 2024, the Integrated Bar of the Philippines (IBP) appointed him as the first-ever Deputy
Director for Muslim Concerns at the National Center for Legal Aid (NCLA) — a historic appointment that put a
dedicated Muslim legal aid office inside the IBP's national structure for the first time.
His work spans courtrooms, classrooms, and policy tables — from litigating in both regular and Shari'ah courts, to
teaching at the Philippine Judicial Academy, to writing on Islamic finance instruments like Sukuk, to sitting in on
summits that quietly shape how justice reaches the Bangsamoro region.
Contents
1 Background
2 Education
3 Career
4 Institutional Contributions
5 Legacy
6 Recognition
7 Categories
Background
Marohombsar comes from a Maranao family with roots planted deep in Lanao del Sur — the heartland of Maranao
culture, framed by Lake Lanao and the skyline of Marawi City.
He grew up shaped by the particular texture of Muslim Mindanao: a region of extraordinary cultural richness, long-
running conflict, slow peace, and a community that has had to fight hard just to be seen and served by its own
national institutions.
His parents — Mr. Saidamen Tamano Marohombsar and Mrs. Almirah Pandapatan Marohombsar — are central
figures in how he talks about his life and work. He credits them with the quiet, foundational kind of support that
rarely makes it into official biographies: "infinite love" and real sacrifices that made his path possible. He's invoked
the Islamic legal principle that hardship begets facility — a phrase that reads like a window into the values they
passed on to him.
The Marohombsar name carries weight in Mindanao's professional and academic networks, connecting to
generations of figures in education and public service. But what stands out in how he talks about himself isn't
lineage — it's gratitude, and a sense that everything he's been given creates an obligation to give back.

PAGE 2

Education
If there's one thing that defines Marohombsar's formation as a
lawyer and thinker, it's the sheer range of where he chose to study
— and what that range says about the kind of work he was
preparing himself for.
He earned his Juris Doctor in the Philippines and cleared both the
Philippine Bar and the Shari'ah Bar — a dual qualification that
very few Filipino lawyers hold, and that sits at the core of what
makes his IBP role possible.
For graduate-level Islamic scholarship, he went to the University
of the Philippines Diliman, where he earned a Master of Arts in
Islamic Studies (MAIS) — and did it as a university scholar,
which says something about how seriously he brought himself to
the work.
He also trained at the Hague Academy of International Law in the
Netherlands, one of the most prestigious institutions in
international legal education. He took his Islamic finance studies
to INCEIF University in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia — a specialized
institution that trains professionals in the technical frameworks of
Islamic banking and capital markets.
And he's not done. He's currently a candidate for a Master of
Public Policy at the London School of Economics — signaling
that he sees law not just as a courtroom craft but as a tool for
shaping systems and governance.
On top of all that, he serves as a professorial lecturer at the
Philippine Judicial Academy in the Department of Shari'ah and
Islamic Laws and Jurisprudence — which means he's not just
absorbing the law, he's teaching the judges and court practitioners
who apply it.
Career
Marohombsar's career doesn't fit neatly into one category — and
that's probably intentional.
He's worked in both government and the private sector, including
roles with the National Commission on Muslim Filipinos
(NCMF), which gives him firsthand familiarity with the
institutional landscape that shapes Muslim Filipino life from the
policy side.
He's also an author. His written work on Sukuk — the Islamic
bond instrument — and on Islamic capital markets puts him in a
relatively small group of Filipino legal scholars who understand

Pull Quote

greatest benefit to many others." — Hadith cited
by Atty. Marohombsar as a guiding principle of
service
Islamic finance not just in theory but in its technical and
regulatory dimensions. That expertise matters increasingly as the
Philippines looks at integrating Islamic finance into its broader
financial architecture.
But the appointment that marks the clearest milestone in his career
came in September 2024, when the IBP named him Deputy
Director for Muslim Concerns at the National Center for Legal
Aid. The NCLA is the IBP's primary legal aid arm, and this new
office within it represents something that hadn't existed before: a
structured, institutionalized pathway for Muslim Filipinos —
especially those in remote or conflict-affected areas of the
Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao
(BARMM) — to access legal help in both regular courts and
Shari'ah courts.
The position aligns directly with ongoing reforms from the
Supreme Court to improve access to justice, and Marohombsar has
been active in making it more than a title — participating in
Shari'ah summits, legal aid caravans, and collaborative work
between the IBP, NCMF, and the judiciary.
Institutional Contributions
The deeper significance of Marohombsar's IBP role is what it
represents structurally: for the first time, there's a formal Muslim
legal aid office inside the country's national lawyers' organization.
Muslim Filipinos have long navigated a dual legal reality — the
national civil and criminal law system on one side, and the Code
of Muslim Personal Laws on the other, which governs family
matters, inheritance, and personal status under Shari'ah principles.
For communities in Mindanao, especially in the BARMM, the gap
between legal rights on paper and legal access in practice has
historically been wide.
Marohombsar's work is aimed at closing that gap. His office
supports cases in both legal systems, helps communities
understand their rights, and builds the connective tissue between
institutions that too often operated in silos.
He's also contributed to the broader peace-building conversation in
Mindanao, approaching it through the lens of legal inclusion: the idea that genuine peace requires not just absence
of conflict but presence of justice, and that justice has to be accessible to be real.
His connections to institutions like Mindanao State University (MSU) and networks across the Muslim Filipino
professional community strengthen his ability to translate policy work into on-the-ground impact.

PAGE 4
Legacy
Atty. Marohombsar represents something that's still uncommon in the Philippine legal establishment: a lawyer
who's equally at home in a Manila courtroom, a Shari'ah court in Mindanao, a lecture hall at the Judicial Academy,
and an international law seminar in The Hague.
That range isn't accidental. It reflects a deliberate choice to build the kind of credibility and competence that makes
it harder for institutions to ignore the communities he serves.
He's become a model for younger Maranao and Muslim Filipino professionals — proof that a person can be deeply
rooted in Islamic identity and tradition while also moving fluently through the highest levels of national and
international legal education. He doesn't treat those two things as contradictions. He treats them as the whole point.
His reference to the hadith — "the best among us are those who bring the greatest benefit to many others" — isn't
just a quote. It functions as a mission statement. And in a country where Muslim Filipinos have spent decades
pushing for recognition, representation, and a justice system that actually serves them, Marohombsar's quiet,
rigorous, institution-building work is exactly the kind of contribution that outlasts headlines.

Arsad A. Marohombsar
Arsad "RPK" Alawi Marohombsar is a prominent Filipino public
servant, military veteran, administrator, and former politician from
the province of Lanao del Sur. He established himself as an
influential fixture in local governance within the Mindanao region,
initially managing administrative regional portfolios before moving
into elective office.
Marohombsar is best remembered for his historic tenure as the vice
governor of Lanao del Sur, serving three consecutive terms from
2007 to 2016. Running alongside Governor Mamintal "Bombit"
Adiong Jr., Marohombsar built an undefeated electoral record in
provincial politics. Before capturing elective office, he served as a
First Lieutenant (1st Lt.) in the Philippine Army, the Provincial
Director of the Department of the Interior and Local Government
(DILG) for Lanao del Sur, and the regional secretary of the DILG for
the Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (ARMM).

Early Life, Family, and Education
Marohombsar belongs to the prominent Alawi-Marohombsar
political family, a traditional clan rooted in the municipal politics of
Madalum and the broader lake region of Lanao del Sur. His family
tree is deeply intertwined with regional diplomacy and local
governance: his relative, Kasan Alawi Marohombsar, served as the
vice governor of Lanao del Sur from 1968 to 1972 and later became
the Philippine Ambassador to Egypt from 1986 to 1993.
Details regarding his exact birth date, childhood years, and early
schooling remain limited in standard public registries. His higher
education background and specialized degree focus are similarly

office in 2016.

unverified in official biographical archives, though his subsequent
technocratic appointment to director-level positions suggests a
foundational tracking in public administration or legal studies.
Career and Public Service
Administrative Bureaucracy (DILG ARMM)
Before his political breakthrough, Marohombsar spent years climbing the civil service ranks. His primary
administrative milestone was his appointment as the Regional Secretary of the DILG for the ARMM. This director-
level position tasks its executive with bridging the gap between national government directives and local execution
in one of the country's most socio-politically complex regions.
In this role, Marohombsar was responsible for overseeing capacity-building initiatives for local government units
(LGUs). He prioritized programs that aimed to professionalize local bureaucracies, enhance structural
accountability, and establish peace-and-order parameters in volatile provincial areas.
Vice Gubernatorial Career (2007–2016)
Marohombsar transitioned to elective politics during the 2007 Philippine general elections. He secured a spot as the
vice gubernatorial running mate of Mamintal Adiong Jr., campaigning under the Lakas–CMD banner. The tandem
secured victory against competitive local factions, including configurations led by former Marawi City Mayor
Omar Ali and Assemblyman Jamil Lucman.
       ARSAD MAROHOMBSAR'S VICE GUBERNATORIAL TIMELINE

 [ June 2016 Turn Over     ] ---> Official Retirement / End of 3rd Term
Marohombsar was successfully re-elected in 2010. The 2010 provincial elections in Lanao del Sur encountered
severe logistical and security disruptions, leading the Provincial Board of Canvassers (PBOC) to delay official
proclamations for the vice gubernatorial and congressional slots due to pending special elections. Despite the hold,
initial election tabulations demonstrated Marohombsar's wide margin, where he led early counts with 97,115 votes.
He was eventually confirmed and sworn into office.
In July 2012, ahead of the next electoral cycle, Marohombsar joined Governor Adiong and 163 other high-profile
ARMM officials in a mass oath-taking to shift allegiances to the ruling Liberal Party (LP). Under the LP ticket in
2013, he ran for his final consecutive term. He handily defeated opponents Elias Abdusalam of the Ompia Party
and independent candidates Mosa Alapa and Abdul Latiph Usman. On July 4, 2013, he took his final oath of office
before Regional Trial Court Executive Judge Wenida Papandayan.

PAGE 3
Having served three consecutive three-year terms (the maximum term limit allowed by the Philippine
Constitution), Marohombsar officially completed his vice gubernatorial run on June 30, 2016. He stepped down
and ceremonially turned over the official leadership documents to his former running mate, Mamintal Adiong Jr.,
who succeeded him as vice governor.
Leadership Roles and Contributions
As the presiding officer of the Sangguniang Panlalawigan (the Provincial Board) of Lanao del Sur for nearly a
decade, Marohombsar steered provincial legislative dynamics. His leadership style was defined by stabilizing local
legislative friction and balancing the complex, often conflicting demands of traditional Maranao clan structures
with modern governmental laws.
His core contributions centered around:
LGU Capacity Standardization: Utilizing his background from DILG ARMM to raise fiscal and
developmental reporting metrics among municipal governments.
Cultural and Civic Festivals: Co-leading historical community milestones, such as the grand Karimbaran
sa Ranao celebrations during the annual Araw ng Lanao del Sur, which institutionalized traditional Maranao
brass-making, culinary arts, and malong weaving into regional tourism frameworks.
Peace and Order Mediation: Actively participating in multi-sectoral security councils tasked with
mediating local blood feuds (rido) that historically disrupted agricultural and infrastructure development
around Lake Lanao.
No records exist detailing any major solo-authored books, academic papers, or standalone literary works published
by Marohombsar. His written contributions are limited to provincial ordinances, legislative resolutions, and
administrative manuals produced during his time with the DILG. Furthermore, while he received regional
commendations from the ARMM government and local civic organizations for maintaining an undefeated, peaceful
political record, documentation of formal national or international civilian awards remains unavailable.
Personal Life
Marohombsar maintains a relatively low personal profile outside his public service identity. His immediate family
ties continue to influence the regional landscape. His relative, Mohammad Joharden "RPK Jojo" Mangotara
Marohombsar, carries on the political moniker and serves the public sphere, running for seats such as Provincial
Board Member for the first district of Lanao del Sur under the Lakas-CMD banner. Marohombsar’s personal
interests, everyday life details, and activities following his 2016 political retirement are kept strictly private.
Legacy and Significance
Marohombsar occupies a unique niche in the political history of Lanao del Sur. In a region historically
characterized by volatile shifts in political power, intense inter-clan rivalries, and highly contested democratic
races, his ability to secure three consecutive legislative terms without a single electoral defeat is a rare feat.
His legacy is tied to the concept of collaborative, technocratic governance. Rather than seeking the highest
executive office after his statutory limit expired, his smooth institutional handover in 2016 demonstrated a respect
for constitutional term limits that is sometimes lacking in provincial politics. He left behind a modernized
Sangguniang Panlalawigan framework that bridged traditional Islamic leadership customs with modern Philippine
administrative policies.

title: Marohombsar, Hadja Sittie Nurlaylah Emily
text:
PAGE 1
Hadja Sittie Nurlaylah "Emily" Marohombsar
Hadja Sittie Nurlaylah "Emily" Marohombsar (September 7, 1935 – May 24, 2013) was a Filipino educator,
university administrator, and peace negotiator from Lanao del Sur who made history as the first, and to date only,
woman to serve as president of the Mindanao State University (MSU) System, and as the first Moro woman
appointed to the Government of the Republic of the Philippines (GRP) peace panel in negotiations with the Moro
Islamic Liberation Front (MILF). A graduate of the Philippine Women's University with the highest academic
distinction, she pursued advanced studies at Ateneo de Manila University, the East-West Center at the University of
Hawaii, and Harvard University before joining MSU's founding faculty in 1961. Over a career spanning more than
four decades, she served successively as professor, Dean of the College of Liberal Arts, Vice President for
Academic Affairs, Vice President for External Studies, and ultimately as the 4th MSU System President from 1993
to 1998, where she championed the vision of a "world-class MSU by 2020," forged international academic
linkages, and institutionalized a generation of Bangsamoro women leaders through systematic mentorship and
scholarship expansion. Her subsequent service as a civilian member of the GRP peace panel from 1998 to 2003
established a precedent for inclusive, gender-representative peace diplomacy in the Philippines. She died on May
24, 2013, in Marawi City, and was laid to rest in her hometown of Ganassi, Lanao del Sur.

Early Life and Family Background
Marohombsar was born on September 7, 1935, in Ganassi, a
municipality in the interior of Lanao del Sur, in what was then the
undivided Lanao Province.<ref>Macabalang, Ali G. "Death of
Muslim lady educator mourned." Mindanao Pagadian Frontline,
May 27, 2013. http://pagadianfrontline.blogspot.com/2013/05/death-
of-muslim-lady-educator-mourned.html</ref> Her birth came five
years before the Philippines gained Commonwealth status and a
decade before independence — a period when Maranao identity,
rooted in the ancient lake region of Mindanao and woven through
with Islamic faith and clan honor, was being tested by the expanding
apparatus of colonial and post-colonial governance.
Her father, Luis Marohombsar, was a figure of exceptional
distinction: the first Muslim graduate of the Philippine Military
Academy (PMA) and the former military governor of the then-
unified Lanao Province.<ref>Macabalang, Ali G. "Death of Muslim
lady educator mourned." Mindanao Pagadian Frontline, May 27,
2013. http://pagadianfrontline.blogspot.com/2013/05/death-of-
muslim-lady-educator-mourned.html</ref> His career represented a
deliberate and consequential act of engagement with the Philippine
national project at a time when many Maranao leaders viewed the
Manila government with deep suspicion. By entering the state's most
prestigious military institution and serving in civil authority, Luis
Marohombsar demonstrated to his daughter that service to the nation
and fidelity to Maranao identity are not contradictions but can be
lived as a single, integrated vocation.
The Maranao Cultural Context
The Maranao people — whose name derives from ranao, the
Maranao word for lake, referring to Lake Lanao — are among the
most culturally distinctive of the Philippines' Muslim communities.
Their society is organized around the torogan (royal households), the
taritib (customary law), and an Islamic faith filtered through
centuries of local tradition. In Maranao culture, ilmu — knowledge in
the Islamic theological sense — is regarded not merely as an
intellectual virtue but as a religious obligation, grounded in the
Prophet Muhammad's reported instruction to "seek knowledge, even
unto China."<ref>Macabalang, Ali G. "Death of Muslim lady
educator mourned." Mindanao Pagadian Frontline, May 27, 2013.
http://pagadianfrontline.blogspot.com/2013/05/death-of-muslim-
lady-educator-mourned.html</ref> Young people from prominent
families were historically expected to master the Quran, the Arabic
language, and the practical arts of governance and community
leadership.

PAGE 3

Yet the formal public sphere — the university presidency, the
government negotiating table — had been almost exclusively male.
The traditional Maranao noblewoman, the bae, commanded genuine
moral authority within her community, but formal institutional power
remained largely inaccessible to women. This was the structural
limitation Emily Marohombsar was born into — and which her
career would systematically dismantle.
Name and Honorifics
Her formal name carries layered significance. "Hadja" denotes one
who has completed the Hajj pilgrimage to Mecca, marking deep
religious commitment and social standing in the Muslim world.
"Sittie" is a Maranao honorific for a woman of noble birth.
"Nurlaylah" is an Arabic compound meaning "Light of the Night" —
nur (light) and laylah (night) — a name that would prove prophetic
across the most turbulent decades of the Bangsamoro struggle.
<ref>Macabalang, Ali G. "Death of Muslim lady educator mourned."
Mindanao Pagadian Frontline, May 27, 2013.
http://pagadianfrontline.blogspot.com/2013/05/death-of-muslim-
lady-educator-mourned.html</ref> The nickname "Emily," accessible
and two-syllabled, navigated the boundary between Filipino and
international contexts and was the name by which she was known to
students, colleagues, and peace-negotiation counterparts throughout
her career.
Education
Undergraduate Studies
In the 1950s, Marohombsar traveled to Manila to study at the
Philippine Women's University (PWU) — a significant act during a
period when the cultural and political distance between Manila and
Muslim Mindanao was profound. She graduated Summa Cum Laude with a Bachelor of Science in Education, the
highest academic distinction the university conferred, in open competition with students from across the
Philippines.<ref>Macabalang, Ali G. "Death of Muslim lady educator mourned." Mindanao Pagadian Frontline,
May 27, 2013. http://pagadianfrontline.blogspot.com/2013/05/death-of-muslim-lady-educator-mourned.html</ref>
She was among the very few Muslim Moro women of her generation to study at PWU.<ref>Luwaran/Key
Philippine Military and Insurgency-Related Events. "Thousands mourn death of Moro educator Dr. Emily
Marohombsar." Luwaran, May 28, 2013. https://retiredanalyst.blogspot.com/2013_05_28_archive.html</ref>
Impressed by her combination of academic excellence and physical grace, PWU officials reportedly encouraged
her to enter a national beauty pageant — an invitation her devout Muslim family declined.<ref>Macabalang, Ali G.
"Death of Muslim lady educator mourned." Mindanao Pagadian Frontline, May 27, 2013.
http://pagadianfrontline.blogspot.com/2013/05/death-of-muslim-lady-educator-mourned.html</ref> The family's
response was an early articulation of the principle that would guide her entire career: she was being educated to
serve, not to be displayed.

PAGE 4
Post-Graduate and International Studies
Marohombsar pursued post-graduate studies at Ateneo de Manila University, one of the Philippines' premier
research institutions, deepening her grounding in education theory, linguistics, and social development.
<ref>Macabalang, Ali G. "Death of Muslim lady educator mourned." Mindanao Pagadian Frontline, May 27,
2013. http://pagadianfrontline.blogspot.com/2013/05/death-of-muslim-lady-educator-mourned.html</ref>
<ref>Arguillas, Carolyn O. "Moro women, second to none." MindaNews, March 29, 2008.
https://mindanews.com/top-stories/2008/03/moro-women-second-to-none/</ref> She subsequently earned a
scholarship to the East-West Center at the University of Hawaii, established by the United States Congress in 1960,
where she engaged in the comparative study of educational systems, development economics, and the challenges of
nation-building and cultural identity in the post-colonial Asian context.<ref>Macabalang, Ali G. "Death of Muslim
lady educator mourned." Mindanao Pagadian Frontline, May 27, 2013.
http://pagadianfrontline.blogspot.com/2013/05/death-of-muslim-lady-educator-mourned.html</ref><ref>Arguillas,
Carolyn O. "Moro women, second to none." MindaNews, March 29, 2008. https://mindanews.com/top-
stories/2008/03/moro-women-second-to-none/</ref>
She then undertook studies at Harvard University, which at the time was developing influential models of
institutional governance and international development policy.<ref>Macabalang, Ali G. "Death of Muslim lady
educator mourned." Mindanao Pagadian Frontline, May 27, 2013.
http://pagadianfrontline.blogspot.com/2013/05/death-of-muslim-lady-educator-mourned.html</ref><ref>Arguillas,
Carolyn O. "Moro women, second to none." MindaNews, March 29, 2008. https://mindanews.com/top-
stories/2008/03/moro-women-second-to-none/</ref> From these experiences she drew a philosophy that would
define her career: a university in a developing Muslim region was not simply a knowledge factory but a social
institution — a proof-of-concept for the proposition that academic excellence and cultural identity need not
conflict.
Honorary Doctorate
In 1978, the Philippine Women's University conferred upon her an honorary doctorate, honoris causa, in
recognition of her leadership in Philippine higher education.<ref>Macabalang, Ali G. "Death of Muslim lady
educator mourned." Mindanao Pagadian Frontline, May 27, 2013.
http://pagadianfrontline.blogspot.com/2013/05/death-of-muslim-lady-educator-mourned.html</ref> The honor was
symbolically complete: the student who had arrived in Manila in the 1950s from Lanao del Sur had returned,
decades later, as one of the country's recognized educational leaders.
Career
Early Teaching: Jamiatul Philippine Al-Islamia
Before joining a state university, Marohombsar taught English at the Jamiatul Philippine Al-Islamia in Marawi
City, an Islamic institution that predated MSU and served as one of the principal centers of Muslim education in the
Lanao region.<ref>Macabalang, Ali G. "Death of Muslim lady educator mourned." Mindanao Pagadian Frontline,
May 27, 2013. http://pagadianfrontline.blogspot.com/2013/05/death-of-muslim-lady-educator-mourned.html</ref>
This posting was formative: it established the synthesis she would maintain throughout her career — that mastery
of the modern world's languages and knowledge systems fulfilled rather than contradicted the Quranic command to
seek knowledge. Teaching English to Bangsamoro youth was, in the post-colonial Philippines, both a practical
instrument of upward mobility and a form of advocacy.

PAGE 5
Founding Faculty of Mindanao State University (1961)
Mindanao State University was established through Republic Act No. 1387, as amended by R.A. 1893, authored by
the late Senator Domocao Alonto, and formally opened in Marawi City on September 1, 1961 — a state institution
expressly designed to bring quality higher education to the Muslim South.<ref>Mindanao State University.
Wikipedia. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mindanao_State_University</ref> Marohombsar joined MSU's founding
faculty in 1961, becoming part of what colleagues called the "pioneering faculty workforce" — the small cohort
who built the institution's academic culture from the ground up, when the library was still sparse and the question
of what it meant to be a Muslim university within a nominally secular state was still being worked out in practice.
<ref>Macabalang, Ali G. "Death of Muslim lady educator mourned." Mindanao Pagadian Frontline, May 27,
2013. http://pagadianfrontline.blogspot.com/2013/05/death-of-muslim-lady-educator-mourned.html</ref> Her
teaching subjects were English and Liberal Arts.
Administrative Rise: Dean and Vice President
Over the following decades, Marohombsar rose steadily through every level of MSU's academic and administrative
structure. She served as Dean of the College of Liberal Arts, overseeing the foundational disciplinary programs on
which MSU's professional schools depended. She subsequently served as Vice President for External Studies — a
position documented in Philippine Supreme Court records from a case in which she was the petitioner — in which
capacity she cultivated the East-West Center alumni network and began building the international linkages that
would define her presidential tenure.<ref>Dr. Emily M. Marohombsar v. Ahmad E. Alonto, Jr., et al., G.R. No.
93711. Supreme Court of the Philippines, February 25, 1991. https://lawlibrary.chanrobles.com/index.php?
option=com_content&view=article&id=31259</ref> She also served as Vice President for Academic Affairs,
responsible for the quality and direction of MSU's teaching and research programs across all campuses.
<ref>Macabalang, Ali G. "Death of Muslim lady educator mourned." Mindanao Pagadian Frontline, May 27,
2013. http://pagadianfrontline.blogspot.com/2013/05/death-of-muslim-lady-educator-mourned.html</ref>
Her tenure at MSU was not without institutional conflict. In 1989, then-MSU President Ahmad E. Alonto, Jr.
attempted to reclassify her permanent position, leading Marohombsar to bring the matter before the Philippine
Supreme Court. In a landmark decision dated February 25, 1991, the Supreme Court ruled in her favor, holding that
her removal was unlawful and ordering her reinstatement as Vice Chancellor for the remainder of her term.<ref>Dr.
Emily M. Marohombsar v. Ahmad E. Alonto, Jr., et al., G.R. No. 93711. Supreme Court of the Philippines,
February 25, 1991. https://lawlibrary.chanrobles.com/index.php?
option=com_content&view=article&id=31259</ref> The ruling affirmed the security of tenure of permanent civil
service officials and is cited in Philippine administrative law.
4th MSU System President (1993–1998)
In February 1993, President Fidel V. Ramos appointed Emily Marohombsar as the 4th President of the Mindanao
State University System.<ref>Mindanao State University Main Campus. "The MSU System Presidents." MSU
Main Campus official website (n.d.). https://www.msumain.edu.ph/the-msu-system-presidents/</ref>
<ref>Arguillas, Carolyn O. "[Special Report] The women in the Bangsamoro peace process: History, herstory."
MindaNews, January 28, 2014. https://cmfr-phil.org/womensvoices/resources/special-report-the-women-in-the-
bangsamoro-peace-process-history-herstory/</ref> The appointment was historic on multiple counts: she was the
first woman ever to serve as MSU System President, the first woman to lead any major state university system in
Mindanao, and one of a small number of women heading large, multi-campus public university systems anywhere
in the Philippines at the time. She remains, to date, the only woman ever to have served in this role.<ref>Arguillas,
Carolyn O. "[Special Report] The women in the Bangsamoro peace process: History, herstory." MindaNews,
January 28, 2014. https://cmfr-phil.org/womensvoices/resources/special-report-the-women-in-the-bangsamoro-

PAGE 6
peace-process-history-herstory/</ref><ref>Mindanao State University Main Campus. "The MSU System
Presidents." MSU Main Campus official website (n.d.). https://www.msumain.edu.ph/the-msu-system-
presidents/</ref>
Her administration was guided by the vision of a "world-class MSU by the year 2020" — a phrase embedded in
subsequent MSU strategic plans and student handbooks and one that continued to shape the university's
institutional aspirations long after her presidency.<ref>Mindanao State University Main Campus. MSU Student
Handbook 2019–2020. https://www.msumain.edu.ph/wp-content/uploads/2023/10/Student_Handbook_2019-
2020.pdf</ref> She moved on three fronts: raising the quality of instruction and research to internationally
competitive standards; building physical and technological infrastructure; and forging international educational
partnerships.
Her emphasis on producing topnotchers — graduates ranked at or near the top of national professional licensure
examinations in medicine, nursing, engineering, and law — was a deliberate strategy for building MSU's national
reputation and demonstrating that Muslim students from Mindanao, trained at a Mindanao university, could
compete with and outperform graduates from the country's most elite institutions.<ref>Arguillas, Carolyn O.
"Moro women, second to none." MindaNews, March 29, 2008. https://mindanews.com/top-stories/2008/03/moro-
women-second-to-none/</ref>
She forged formal academic linkages with universities in the United States and with institutions in the Brunei-
Indonesia-Malaysia-Philippines East ASEAN Growth Area (BIMP-EAGA), opening pathways for MSU faculty to
pursue advanced degrees abroad and creating student exchange opportunities previously unavailable to Mindanao
scholars.<ref>Arguillas, Carolyn O. "Moro women, second to none." MindaNews, March 29, 2008.
https://mindanews.com/top-stories/2008/03/moro-women-second-to-none/</ref> These partnerships embedded
MSU within a regional Malay-Islamic academic geography that the internal boundaries of the Philippine state had
historically obscured.
Colleagues consistently described her administration as energetic, demanding, meticulous, and above all, honest —
she was characterized as a "human dynamo" in the academic community.<ref>Macabalang, Ali G. "Death of
Muslim lady educator mourned." Mindanao Pagadian Frontline, May 27, 2013.
http://pagadianfrontline.blogspot.com/2013/05/death-of-muslim-lady-educator-mourned.html</ref> Her personal
lifestyle was notable for its modesty: her family was known for not building lavish homes despite many years of
government service — a quality that stood in marked contrast to patterns of personal enrichment frequently
observed among officials with access to government resources in the same era and region.<ref>Macabalang, Ali G.
"Death of Muslim lady educator mourned." Mindanao Pagadian Frontline, May 27, 2013.
http://pagadianfrontline.blogspot.com/2013/05/death-of-muslim-lady-educator-mourned.html</ref> Her tenure as
MSU System President ended in December 1998, following the transition from the Ramos to the Estrada
administration.<ref>Arguillas, Carolyn O. "[Special Report] The women in the Bangsamoro peace process:
History, herstory." MindaNews, January 28, 2014. https://cmfr-phil.org/womensvoices/resources/special-report-the-
women-in-the-bangsamoro-peace-process-history-herstory/</ref>
Member, GRP–MILF Peace Panel (1998–2003)
Following her MSU presidency, Marohombsar joined the Government of the Republic of the Philippines (GRP)
peace panel in negotiations with the Moro Islamic Liberation Front, becoming the first Moro woman ever to sit at
the official government negotiating table with the MILF.<ref>Arguillas, Carolyn O. "[Special Report] The women
in the Bangsamoro peace process: History, herstory." MindaNews, January 28, 2014. https://cmfr-
phil.org/womensvoices/resources/special-report-the-women-in-the-bangsamoro-peace-process-history-
herstory/</ref><ref>Luwaran/Key Philippine Military and Insurgency-Related Events. "Thousands mourn death of
Moro educator Dr. Emily Marohombsar." Luwaran, May 28, 2013.
https://retiredanalyst.blogspot.com/2013_05_28_archive.html</ref> Her appointment broke the gender barrier in

PAGE 7
Philippine peace negotiations at the highest level, bringing to the table a figure whose credentials were impeccable
on both sides of the cultural divide: Harvard-trained, honored by the Philippine Women's University, deeply rooted
in the Maranao community, and fluent in the Maranao language as well as English and Filipino.
UN Women researcher Irene Santiago, in a foundational study of women's participation in the Mindanao peace
process, documented Marohombsar as a full member of the government panel — not an observer or adviser —
meaning she participated in substantive negotiations, held a vote, and bore responsibility for the government's
formal positions.<ref>Santiago, Irene M. "The participation of women in the Mindanao peace process." UN
Women. https://wps.unwomen.org/pdf/research/Santiago.pdf</ref> She participated in technical working groups on
ancestral domain and social development — the substantive committees where the practical terms of any eventual
peace agreement on land rights, resource sharing, and community development were being defined.
When President Gloria Macapagal-Arroyo reconstituted the GRP peace panel as an all-civilian body in February
2001 under Presidential Adviser Jesus Dureza, she retained Marohombsar and added Irene Santiago of the
Mindanao Commission on Women, making it the first time a majority of the civilian panel members were women
with Bangsamoro ties or women's rights backgrounds.<ref>Arguillas, Carolyn O. "[Special Report] The women in
the Bangsamoro peace process: History, herstory." MindaNews, January 28, 2014. https://cmfr-
phil.org/womensvoices/resources/special-report-the-women-in-the-bangsamoro-peace-process-history-
herstory/</ref>
In 2003, before the 2004 presidential elections, Marohombsar and another female panel member resigned,
reportedly disillusioned with what they viewed as the insincerity of the Arroyo administration's handling of the
negotiations with the MILF.<ref>Luwaran/Key Philippine Military and Insurgency-Related Events. "Thousands
mourn death of Moro educator Dr. Emily Marohombsar." Luwaran, May 28, 2013.
https://retiredanalyst.blogspot.com/2013_05_28_archive.html</ref><ref>Arguillas, Carolyn O. "[Special Report]
The women in the Bangsamoro peace process: History, herstory." MindaNews, January 28, 2014. https://cmfr-
phil.org/womensvoices/resources/special-report-the-women-in-the-bangsamoro-peace-process-history-
herstory/</ref> The substantive proposals developed during her tenure in the technical working groups — on
ancestral domain, social development, and the mechanics of genuine autonomy — laid groundwork that informed
the 2014 Comprehensive Agreement on the Bangsamoro and the Bangsamoro Organic Law of 2018.
Historic Significance
Marohombsar's career occupies a foundational position in the history of Bangsamoro women's public leadership.
Her MSU presidency broke a structural barrier specific to Muslim Mindanao: the formal institutional leadership of
a major state university in a region where patriarchal clan structures, religious conservatism applied to gender
roles, and the dislocations of prolonged conflict had combined to restrict Bangsamoro women's access to formal
authority. Her appointment was, in the specific context of Marawi City and Lanao del Sur, more radical than
national precedents — such as the 1986 presidency of Corazon Aquino — would suggest, given the distinct social
pressures operating in the Muslim South.<ref>Arguillas, Carolyn O. "[Special Report] The women in the
Bangsamoro peace process: History, herstory." MindaNews, January 28, 2014. https://cmfr-
phil.org/womensvoices/resources/special-report-the-women-in-the-bangsamoro-peace-process-history-
herstory/</ref>
Her presence on the GRP peace panel established a precedent for gendered representation in Philippine peace
diplomacy. Women's organizations, including the Mindanao-based Women's Peace Table and national NGOs
engaged with the Bangsamoro peace process, have cited her participation as having "legitimized the Bangsamoro
peace negotiations" in the eyes of Muslim constituencies — not merely through formal appointment but through
the deeper legitimacy of community recognition.<ref>Santiago, Irene M. "The participation of women in the
Mindanao peace process." UN Women. https://wps.unwomen.org/pdf/research/Santiago.pdf</ref> The Philippine

PAGE 8
Commission on Women's 2025 statement on the twenty-ninth anniversary of the 1996 Final Peace Agreement
names Marohombsar among "the first Moro women appointed to government peace panels" — a milestone in
ensuring that women's perspectives would shape the future of Mindanao.<ref>Philippine Commission on Women.
"Statement on the 29th anniversary of the signing of the 1996 Final Peace Agreement." September 2, 2025.
https://pcw.gov.ph/philippine-commission-on-women-statement-on-the-29th-anniversary-of-the-signing-of-the-
1996-final-peace-agreement/</ref>
By living simultaneously as a devout Muslim woman — completing the Hajj, observing her faith, maintaining
Islamic dress — and as a Harvard-trained educator, university president, and peace negotiator, she demonstrated
through practice what could not be established through argument alone: that Islamic identity and modern
institutional leadership are complementary, not contradictory.<ref>Macabalang, Ali G. "Death of Muslim lady
educator mourned." Mindanao Pagadian Frontline, May 27, 2013.
http://pagadianfrontline.blogspot.com/2013/05/death-of-muslim-lady-educator-mourned.html</ref>
Educational Philosophy and Contributions
Marohombsar's approach to education was guided by the conviction that "knowledge conquers all evils" — a
principle she rooted both in Islamic teaching and in the founding ideals of MSU.<ref>Macabalang, Ali G. "Death
of Muslim lady educator mourned." Mindanao Pagadian Frontline, May 27, 2013.
http://pagadianfrontline.blogspot.com/2013/05/death-of-muslim-lady-educator-mourned.html</ref> The Islamic
concept of ilmu — knowledge as a religious obligation and a path toward the divine — informed her view that a
degree granted to a Maranao student was not merely a credential but a contribution to the collective capacity of a
people to govern themselves, represent their interests in national forums, and withstand the political and economic
marginalization that had historically defined Bangsamoro relations with the Philippine state.
Under her administration, Arabic language instruction, Islamic jurisprudence (fiqh), and Maranao cultural studies
were offered alongside standard professional programs in education, nursing, engineering, agriculture, and law —
not as cosmetic additions but as an integrated expression of the conviction that a Bangsamoro professional whose
religious and cultural knowledge was shallow was not fully educated regardless of board examination performance.
<ref>Arguillas, Carolyn O. "Moro women, second to none." MindaNews, March 29, 2008.
https://mindanews.com/top-stories/2008/03/moro-women-second-to-none/</ref> She wanted MSU to produce
graduates who were excellent by the standards of both the national mainstream and their own tradition, so that they
would never be required to choose between being Muslim and being modern.
She placed particular and sustained emphasis on expanding access to higher education for Muslim women,
expanding scholarship programs, recruiting women faculty, and personally mentoring numerous young Maranao
women who went on to academic and professional careers. The effect compounded over time, generating
successive cohorts of Bangsamoro women leaders in and beyond the university system.
Public Reception and Tributes
When Marohombsar died on May 24, 2013, thousands gathered in Marawi City before her burial rites, arriving
from university campuses, mosques, and surrounding barangays of Lanao del Sur.<ref>Macabalang, Ali G. "Death
of Muslim lady educator mourned." Mindanao Pagadian Frontline, May 27, 2013.
http://pagadianfrontline.blogspot.com/2013/05/death-of-muslim-lady-educator-mourned.html</ref> The breadth of
tributes was notable: they came from university presidents and village elders, from women's rights advocates and
Islamic scholars, from the Philippine Commission on Women in Manila and from the MILF's communications
portal in Cotabato.

PAGE 9
MILF Peace Panel chairman Mohagher Iqbal, who had sat across the negotiating table from Marohombsar in the
late 1990s and early 2000s, sent formal condolences and described her as "a very amiable personality" who was "so
easy to deal with," adding: "We missed another good person and may Allah bless her soul."<ref>Luwaran/Key
Philippine Military and Insurgency-Related Events. "Thousands mourn death of Moro educator Dr. Emily
Marohombsar." Luwaran, May 28, 2013. https://retiredanalyst.blogspot.com/2013_05_28_archive.html</ref> That
the MILF's own leadership mourned her passing as a personal loss spoke to the quality of human relationships she
had built across a politically charged divide.
A tribute published in connection with her death described her as "an icon of integrity, beauty, and brain."
<ref>Macabalang, Ali G. "Death of Muslim lady educator mourned." Mindanao Pagadian Frontline, May 27,
2013. http://pagadianfrontline.blogspot.com/2013/05/death-of-muslim-lady-educator-mourned.html</ref> The
placement of "integrity" first in this formulation was characteristic of how her community valued her: among
everything she had accomplished, the manner in which she conducted herself was regarded as the most important
thing.
She was laid to rest according to Islamic burial rites in her hometown of Ganassi, Lanao del Sur, on May 25, 2013.
<ref>Luwaran/Key Philippine Military and Insurgency-Related Events. "Thousands mourn death of Moro educator
Dr. Emily Marohombsar." Luwaran, May 28, 2013.
https://retiredanalyst.blogspot.com/2013_05_28_archive.html</ref>
Awards and Recognition
Ten Outstanding Women of the New Society (TOWNS) Award (1977) — a national award recognizing
Filipino women achievers.<ref>Macabalang, Ali G. "Death of Muslim lady educator mourned." Mindanao
Pagadian Frontline, May 27, 2013. http://pagadianfrontline.blogspot.com/2013/05/death-of-muslim-lady-
educator-mourned.html</ref><ref>Arguillas, Carolyn O. "Moro women, second to none." MindaNews,
March 29, 2008. https://mindanews.com/top-stories/2008/03/moro-women-second-to-none/</ref>
Honorary Doctorate, honoris causa, Philippine Women's University (1978) — conferred in recognition of
her leadership in Philippine higher education.<ref>Macabalang, Ali G. "Death of Muslim lady
educator mourned." Mindanao Pagadian Frontline, May 27, 2013.
http://pagadianfrontline.blogspot.com/2013/05/death-of-muslim-lady-educator-mourned.html</ref>
Sultan Kudarat Award for Most Outstanding Muslim Educator (1988) — the Muslim community's own
recognition of distinguished service to the Bangsamoro educational mission.<ref>Macabalang, Ali G. "Death
of Muslim lady educator mourned." Mindanao Pagadian Frontline, May 27, 2013.
http://pagadianfrontline.blogspot.com/2013/05/death-of-muslim-lady-educator-mourned.html</ref>
<ref>Arguillas, Carolyn O. "Moro women, second to none." MindaNews, March 29, 2008.
https://mindanews.com/top-stories/2008/03/moro-women-second-to-none/</ref>
Gintong Ina (Golden Mother) Award — recognizing the integration of distinguished public service with
exemplary family life.
Bangsamoro Woman of Distinction citation.
East-West Center Outstanding Alumni Award — from the institution that was the principal international
turning point in her intellectual formation.<ref>Macabalang, Ali G. "Death of Muslim lady educator
mourned." Mindanao Pagadian Frontline, May 27, 2013.
http://pagadianfrontline.blogspot.com/2013/05/death-of-muslim-lady-educator-mourned.html</ref>
In institutional form, the most enduring honor is the scholarship established in her name at MSU's Institute for
Peace and Development in Mindanao (IPDM), which continues to support graduate education for scholars who
might not otherwise have access to it.

PAGE 10
Legacy
Marohombsar's legacy operates on several levels simultaneously. At MSU, the foundational mission she helped
define — an academically excellent, culturally grounded Bangsamoro university embedded in both the national
mainstream and the broader Malay-Islamic world — was institutionalized in strategic plans, student handbooks,
and institutional culture. The international linkages she built during her presidency continued to generate
opportunities for MSU faculty and students after her departure. The pipeline of Bangsamoro women educators and
administrators that she cultivated through mentorship produced successive generations of women leaders in
Mindanao higher education.
In the Bangsamoro peace process, the substantive proposals developed during her tenure on the GRP peace panel
laid groundwork that influenced the 2014 Comprehensive Agreement on the Bangsamoro and ultimately the
Bangsamoro Organic Law of 2018 (Republic Act 11054), which created the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in
Muslim Mindanao (BARMM) and included explicit provisions for women's representation in its governance
structures.<ref>Philippine Commission on Women. "Statement on the 29th anniversary of the signing of the 1996
Final Peace Agreement." September 2, 2025. https://pcw.gov.ph/philippine-commission-on-women-statement-on-
the-29th-anniversary-of-the-signing-of-the-1996-final-peace-agreement/</ref>
The principles she embodied throughout her career — women's full participation in public life, the inseparability of
cultural identity and modern professional competence, the state's obligation to invest in the education of its Muslim
citizens — have been progressively codified in Philippine law, including the Magna Carta of Women (Republic Act
9710, 2009) and the BARMM's governance framework.
Her name is cited in the Philippine Commission on Women's 2025 statement as part of a lineage of women
peacebuilders that runs from her 1998 appointment through Irene Santiago and Miriam Coronel-Ferrer — who
served as chief government negotiator when the 2014 Framework Agreement on the Bangsamoro was signed —
and continues into the current generation of Bangsamoro women in governance and civil society.<ref>Philippine
Commission on Women. "Statement on the 29th anniversary of the signing of the 1996 Final Peace Agreement."
September 2, 2025. https://pcw.gov.ph/philippine-commission-on-women-statement-on-the-29th-anniversary-of-
the-signing-of-the-1996-final-peace-agreement/</ref><ref>Arguillas, Carolyn O. "[Special Report] The women in
the Bangsamoro peace process: History, herstory." MindaNews, January 28, 2014. https://cmfr-
phil.org/womensvoices/resources/special-report-the-women-in-the-bangsamoro-peace-process-history-
herstory/</ref>
The MSU Institute for Peace and Development in Mindanao (IPDM) maintains the scholarship and lecture series in
her name as active expressions of her conviction that education is the most durable instrument of social
transformation in Mindanao.
Personal Life
Marohombsar married Abdul Marohombsar, a lawyer who served as Vice Governor of Lanao del Sur and
subsequently as a Commissioner of the Commission on Elections (COMELEC) — a parallel public service career
that made their household a living argument for the Bangsamoro community's future in trained, ethical, and
civically engaged citizens.<ref>Macabalang, Ali G. "Death of Muslim lady educator mourned." Mindanao
Pagadian Frontline, May 27, 2013. http://pagadianfrontline.blogspot.com/2013/05/death-of-muslim-lady-educator-
mourned.html</ref> Their children were raised in a home where intellectual discipline, Islamic values, and civic
commitment were integral to domestic life.

PAGE 11
She was the maternal aunt of Robert Maulana M. Alonto, who served as a senior member of the MILF Peace
Negotiating Panel and concurrently as a member of the Bangsamoro Transition Commission (BTC).
<ref>Luwaran/Key Philippine Military and Insurgency-Related Events. "Thousands mourn death of Moro educator
Dr. Emily Marohombsar." Luwaran, May 28, 2013.
https://retiredanalyst.blogspot.com/2013_05_28_archive.html</ref> Through this family connection, she was
personally linked to both sides of the peace process she participated in — a position she navigated with the same
integrity that characterized all of her public conduct.
She completed the Hajj pilgrimage, earning the honorific "Hadja," and maintained her Islamic practice throughout
her academic and public career. She is universally remembered by those who knew her as having been
constitutionally incapable of separating her professional conduct from her religious values — the two were, in her
life, the same thing.

title: Marohombsar, Johnny III Lucman Derogongan
text:
PAGE 1
Johnny III Lucman Derogongan Marohombsar
Johnny III Lucman Derogongan Marohombsar, widely known as "JB" to family and close friends, is a Filipino
naval officer and one of the most decorated graduates of the Philippine Military Academy (PMA) in recent history.
He's a Maranao from Lanao del Sur and comes from a distinguished lineage of statesmen, lawyers, and military
leaders who helped shape Bangsamoro history. His appointment in 2017 as the first Maranao and second Muslim
cadet to serve as PMA Class Baron marked a watershed moment for Muslim Filipino representation in the country's
premier military institution.
Contents
1 Background and Family
2 Education
3 A Historic Milestone at PMA
4 Chief of Staff Saber
5 Service in the Philippine Navy
6 Legacy
7 Recognition
8 References
Background and Family
JB was born into a respected Maranao family rooted in Lanao del Sur. On his mother's side, he is the son of Hannia
Kuzbari Lucman Derogongan, daughter of Dr. Macaurog B. Derogongan of Poona Bayabao, Lanao del Sur, and
Bai Rohanifa Monaoray Kuzbari Lucman Derogongan of Bayang, Lanao del Sur. Through this line, he is the great-
grandson of the late Congressman Sultan Haroun Al-Rashid M. Lucman, a prominent statesman and respected
Bangsamoro leader whose legacy looms large in Mindanao's political history.
On his paternal side, his grandfather is Atty. Johnny Marohombsar, regarded by many as one of Mindanao's
respected legal minds, remembered particularly for contributions associated with the development of autonomy in
the Philippines. JB is also connected through his paternal heritage to Gen. Luis R. Marohombsar, among the early
graduates of the Philippine Military Academy and a former governor of the then undivided Lanao.
This family background, spanning law, governance, and military service, formed a strong foundation for JB's own
path in public life.
Education
JB pursued his military education at the Philippine Military Academy in Baguio City. Throughout his cadet years,
he distinguished himself not only in military discipline and command, but also in academic performance, earning
recognition as a Valedictorian candidate by the time of his graduation in 2017. His record at PMA reflected a rare
combination of intellectual rigor and leadership ability that set him apart from his peers.

PAGE 2

A Historic Milestone at PMA
The single most defining chapter of JB's cadet career came in
2017, when he was appointed Class Baron of the PMA
"Salaknib" Class of 2017, making him the first Maranaw and the
first Muslim cadet in PMA history to hold this position.
The Class Baron is the highest-ranking cadet in the Corps of
Cadets, carrying responsibility for military discipline, command
leadership, and representing the entire cadet corps. It's the most
prestigious role a cadet can hold, and JB earned it on the strength
of his performance, character, and the confidence of both his
peers and the institution.
His appointment was celebrated across Mindanao and resonated
deeply within the Muslim Filipino community, many of whom
saw it as a long-overdue recognition of Bangsamoro excellence
in the national military.
One of the most memorable moments of his cadet life came at
PMA's 2017 graduation ceremonies, where he led the graduating
class and personally escorted then President and Commander-in-
Chief Rodrigo Duterte during the Presidential Inspection of the
Line. This ceremonial duty is traditionally reserved for the
academy's top cadet leader and stands as one of the most visible
honors a graduating cadet can receive.
Chief of Staff Saber
Upon graduating from PMA, JB received the Chief of Staff
Saber, one of the most prestigious awards the academy confers.
The saber recognizes outstanding institutional leadership,
command ability, and exemplary service throughout a cadet's
time at the academy. Receiving this award, alongside his
recognition as a Valedictorian candidate, cemented his standing
as one of the most accomplished graduates of PMA Salaknib
Batch 2017.
Service in the Philippine Navy
After his commissioning, JB joined the Philippine Navy and
continued building his record in military service. In August 2021,
he and three fellow Filipino naval officers took part in the
International Combat Information Center Watch Officer Course,
held at the International Surface Warfare Officers School in
Newport, Rhode Island, USA. The four Filipino officers swept
the top four places in the course, a remarkable collective

PAGE 3
achievement that drew attention to the high caliber of Filipino military officers in international settings. JB's
performance in this course was consistent with the standard of excellence he had established at PMA.
Legacy
JB's story is significant on multiple levels. As a Maranao officer in the Philippine Navy with historic distinctions at
PMA, he represents the kind of leadership that the Bangsamoro region can offer the nation. His journey challenges
the narrow narratives often applied to Muslim Filipinos and offers a compelling counter-narrative: that faith,
discipline, and dedication can carry a young man from Lanao del Sur to the top of the country's most demanding
military institution.
He continues to be a source of inspiration for young people in Mindanao and across the Bangsamoro region, many
of whom see in him a living proof that the path to national service and excellence is open to them, too.

title: Marohombsar, Kasan A.
text:
PAGE 1
Ambassador Atty. Kasan A.
Marohombsar
Ethnic Affiliation
Maranao (Meranao), Bangsamoro
Region of Origin
Lanao del Sur, Bangsamoro Autonomous
Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM)
Clan / Family
Alawi-Marohombsar political family of Lanao
del Sur
Education
Kasan A. Marohombsar
Ambassador Atty. Kasan A. Marohombsar was a Maranao
lawyer, judge, local government official, and diplomat from
Lanao del Sur who served as Vice-Governor of Lanao del Sur
from 1968 to 1972 and as Philippine Ambassador to Egypt
from 1986 to 1993 under President Corazon C. Aquino. A
member of the Alawi-Marohombsar political family, one of
Lanao del Sur's most enduring clans in public service, he was
also among the rare Muslim Filipinos from Mindanao to gain
entry into the University of the Philippines and the prestigious
Upsilon Sigma Phi fraternity in the early 1950s. His career
spanned local governance, the judiciary, and international
diplomacy at a time when Moro Filipino representation in
Philippine institutions was neither common nor guaranteed.
He is remembered as part of a generation of Bangsamoro
professionals who worked steadily within the system to keep
the bridges intact.
Contents
1 BACKGROUND
2 EDUCATION
3 CAREER
3.1 Local Governance
3.2 Judiciary
3.3 Diplomacy
4 FAMILY AND CLAN
5 INSTITUTIONAL CONTRIBUTIONS
6 LEGACY
7 RECOGNITION
8 SEE ALSO
9 REFERENCES
BACKGROUND
Ambassador Atty. Kasan A. Marohombsar came from a
family that knew what public life demanded long before he
entered it himself.
Born into the Alawi-Marohombsar clan of Lanao del Sur,
with roots tied to the municipality of Ganassi, Kasan grew up
in a household where service to community wasn't optional; it
was expected.
The Marohombsar name already carried weight.

PAGE 2
University of the Philippines (undergraduate,

(institution unspecified in available records)
Profession
Lawyer, Judge, Politician, Diplomat

1950s–1990s
