Deceased (exact date not widely recorded in
public sources)
Notability
One of the few Maranao Muslims from
Mindanao to serve as a Philippine
Ambassador; appointed by President Corazon
Aquino to lead the Philippine mission in
Luis R. Marohombsar, widely recognized as the first Muslim
graduate of the Philippine Military Academy and a governor
of undivided Lanao, was a connection that the family bore
proudly.
In Maranao society, that kind of lineage matters: it shapes
how a person is received, what doors open, and what
responsibilities they inherit.
His exact birth date isn't clearly documented in accessible
public records, which is true of many public figures from
Mindanao whose stories were seldom covered by Manila-
centered media of that era.
What is clear is that he grew up at a time when Muslim
Filipinos navigating national institutions had to be
exceptionally prepared, exceptionally resilient, and willing to
move between worlds.
EDUCATION
Kasan's path to UP was unusual for a young Muslim man
from Mindanao in the late 1940s.
He earned his place at the University of the Philippines and
became a member of Upsilon Sigma Phi, one of the country's
oldest and most prestigious fraternities, listed under the Class
of '50.
That affiliation placed him in company with some of postwar
Philippines' most influential professionals and statesmen.
He went on to earn a law degree, taking on the title that
would follow him through governance and diplomacy: "Atty.
Kasan."
He also served as a judge, which points to a man who didn't
just study the law but chose to administer it, quietly anchoring
legal accountability in a province that often felt the edges of
Philippine institutional reach.
CAREER
Local Governance
Kasan served as Vice-Governor of Lanao del Sur from 1968
to 1972, years that coincided with rising tensions across
Mindanao, the early stirrings of armed resistance, and the
eventual declaration of Martial Law in 1972.

PAGE 3
Egypt from 1986 to 1993, a posting with
significant implications for Muslim Filipino
representation in the Arab world.
Known For
Bridging Mindanao's realities with national
institutions; serving as Vice-Governor of
Lanao del Sur during a turbulent decade of
Mindanao unrest; advancing Moro Filipino
presence in Philippine foreign service;
membership in the elite Upsilon Sigma Phi
fraternity at UP as one of the rare Muslim
Filipinos in that circle during the early 1950s.
Pull Quote
"His life reminds us that history in
Mindanao isn't just about conflict; it's also
about steady builders who kept the bridges
intact."
Governing during that period was no small thing.
It meant managing a constituency increasingly caught
between state power and community grievance, between
loyalty to the Philippine republic and the demands of Moro
identity.
He appears in historical photographs alongside prominent
figures like Senator Ahmad Domocao Alonto, a marker of his
standing in the political circles that shaped Mindanao's
relationship with Manila during those pivotal years.
Judiciary
Alongside his political career, he served in the judiciary as a
judge in Lanao del Sur.
This dual role, as both an elected local official and an officer
of the court, reflected the pattern of his generation: Maranao
leaders who pursued professional credentials as a way of
asserting legitimacy within Philippine institutions while
remaining grounded in their communities.
Diplomacy
The capstone of Kasan's public life was his appointment as
Philippine Ambassador to Egypt, a position he held from 1986 to 1993 under President Corazon C. Aquino.
Egypt was no ordinary posting for a Filipino ambassador from Mindanao.
Cairo sits at the center of the Arab world, hosts the Arab League, and holds deep symbolic significance for Muslim
communities globally.
For the Philippine government to send a Maranao Muslim to that post during a period when the Bangsamoro
struggle for self-determination was drawing international attention was, in its way, a deliberate signal.
Kasan's presence in Cairo helped strengthen Philippine ties with an important partner nation while quietly asserting
that Moro Filipinos could represent their country with competence and dignity on the global stage.
FAMILY AND CLAN
The Alawi-Marohombsar family of Lanao del Sur is one of those political clans that spans generations without
losing its foothold.
Kasan's vice-governorship was followed years later by Arsad "RPK" Alawi Marohombsar, who held the same
position from 2007 to 2016, an indication of how deeply the family's public service commitments run.
Abdul Marohombsar, likely a close relative, carved out his own distinguished record as a trial lawyer, an
undefeated vice-governor, and eventually a COMELEC commissioner.

PAGE 4
Abdul's wife, Dr. Hadja Sittie Nurlayla Emily M. Marohombsar, herself from the Luis Marohombsar line, was a
respected educator, which speaks to the family's multi-generational investment in both public service and learning.
Kasan's own personal life was kept largely private, consistent with many Moro leaders of his era who preferred that
public records reflect their service, not their households.
INSTITUTIONAL CONTRIBUTIONS
What Kasan contributed most wasn't captured in a single legislation or a named landmark.
It was the steady accumulation of presence: a Maranao lawyer sitting on a provincial bench, a Maranao politician
navigating the turbulent 1970s, a Maranao ambassador representing the Philippines in Cairo.
Each of those roles pushed back, quietly and persistently, against the assumption that leadership and national
service were things that happened somewhere north of Mindanao.
His tenure as ambassador came at a time when the Bangsamoro cause was visible in international discourse.
Having a Muslim Filipino in that diplomatic seat mattered, even if the record of specific negotiations or agreements
from that period remains sparse in public documentation.
LEGACY
Kasan Marohombsar belongs to a generation of Maranao intellectuals and professionals who worked within the
system at considerable personal cost to prove that Moro Filipinos could and should hold space in every layer of
Philippine public life.
He embodied the Maranao concept of maratabat, which carries the weight of honor, dignity, and reputation, not
just for oneself but for one's family and community.
He's remembered within Upsilon Sigma Phi's historical records, within Lanao del Sur's political genealogy, and in
the memories of families who knew what the Marohombsar name represented in those years.
In the era of the BARMM, when the question of Bangsamoro representation and self-governance has taken on new
institutional dimensions, figures like Kasan serve as reminders that this path was walked long before it had formal
recognition.
He passed away some years ago, though his death, like much of his quieter personal life, was not widely covered in
major media.
His story lives in family remembrance, in fraternity archives, and in the patient, persistent record of Mindanao
history that BangsamoroPedia exists to preserve.
RECOGNITION
No major national awards are prominently documented in available public sources, which is not uncommon for
civil servants from the regions whose contributions were significant but seldom spotlighted by Manila-centric
media.

PAGE 5
His sustained service across decades of local governance, judiciary, and international diplomacy stands as its own
testament.

title: Marohombsar, Luis R.
text:
PAGE 1
Luis R. Marohombsar
General Luis R. Marohombsar was a Maranao soldier, military intelligence officer, and provincial governor who
holds a singular place in Philippine history as the first Muslim cadet to complete the full four-year program at the
Philippine Military Academy and receive a commission as an officer of the Philippine Constabulary.<ref
name="pma">Wikipedia. "Philippine Military Academy." Accessed March 7, 2026.
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philippine_Military_Academy. See also: Philippine Military Academy Alumni
Records (Office of the PMA Registrar, Fort del Pilar, Baguio City).</ref> Born into the royal genealogical tradition
of the Pangampong a Masiu, one of the four great confederations of Lake Lanao, he was a custodian of the
Maranao concept of Maratabat, the inherited duty of honor, collective dignity, and ancestral responsibility that
defines conduct for those of royal lineage.<ref name="maranao">Echoes of Kinship: The Untold Meranaw and
Higaonon Connections in Lanao and Mindanao. International Journal of Social Sciences: Current and Future
Research Trends. ISRRA. Accessed March 7, 2026.
https://ijsscfrtjournal.isrra.org/Social_Science_Journal/article/download/1868/260/2446</ref>
He fought through the Battle of Bataan as the S-2 Intelligence Officer of the 1st Philippine Constabulary Regiment,
survived the Bataan Death March, and returned after the war to serve as Governor of Lanao, becoming one of the
very few figures in Philippine history to hold simultaneous authority within both the traditional Islamic political
order and the modern apparatus of the national republic. His life was, in the most direct sense, a proof that the
Bangsamoro could participate fully in national institutions without setting aside the cultural identity that defined
them.

Background and Origins
The Lake Lanao World
The Maranao people take their name from the land they have
inhabited for centuries: Maranao means people of the lake, a
reference to Lake Lanao, which sits on a plateau deep in the
interior of Mindanao.<ref name="maranao" /> Long before the
Spanish arrived in the archipelago, the communities around the
lake had organized themselves into a sophisticated political
system anchored by two governing principles: the Taritib (the
established customary order) and the Igma (a system of
consensus-based traditional law).<ref name="royalhouses">Royal
Houses of Lanao. Borneo History. February 2017. Accessed
March 7, 2026.
https://borneohistory57.blogspot.com/2017/02/royal-houses-of-
lanao.html</ref> Within this framework, authority is not simply
elected or appointed; it is genealogically inherited, validated by
royal lineage records called Salsila, and recognized by
neighboring houses.
The political geography of Lanao is organized around the Pat a
Pangampong sa Ranao, the four traditional confederations:
Masiu, Unayan, Bayabao, and Baloi.<ref
name="sultanate">Jamel, R. "Short Historical Background of
Maranao Royalty (Sultanate)." Scribd. Accessed March 7, 2026.
https://www.scribd.com/doc/283071887/Short-Historical-
Background-of-Maranao-Royalty-Sultanate</ref> Each
confederation encompasses a network of sultanates ranked
according to prestige, with sixteen pagawian (higher-prestige
sultanates) and twenty-eight pagawid (lower-prestige royal
houses) making up the full hierarchical structure.<ref
name="royalhouses" />
Royal Lineage and the Marohombsar Family
The Marohombsar family's standing in this world traces to the
Pangampong a Masiu, whose constituent municipalities include
Taraka, Tamparan, and Masiu proper.<ref name="sultanate" />
Their genealogy runs back to Sharif Muhammad Kabungsuan, the
Arab-Malay missionary from Johore whose arrival in Malabang in
1515 is accepted as the formal introduction of Islam and the
sultanate system to Mindanao.<ref name="kabungsuan">Jamel,
R. "Short Historical Background of Maranao Royalty
(Sultanate)." Scribd. Accessed March 7, 2026.

PAGE 3
Lineage
Descended from Sharif
Muhammad Kabungsuan
Religion
Islam
Notable role
First Muslim graduate of the
Philippine Military Academy
https://www.scribd.com/doc/283071887/Short-Historical-
Background-of-Maranao-Royalty-Sultanate</ref> By marrying
into the family of Macaapun Rajah Simbaan of Malabang,
Kabungsuan established the bloodline from which the primary
Muslim royal houses of Mindanao would descend.<ref
name="kabungsuan" />
The crucial figure connecting that founding generation to Lanao
was Sharif Dimasangcay Adel, the fourth-generation descendant of Kabungsuan, whose descendants established
the ruling sultanates of the lake region.<ref name="kabungsuan" /> The Marohombsar family traces its royal status
through this line, a claim codified in the Salsila and validated by centuries of recognition from neighboring houses.
Luis Marohombsar entered the world not as an ordinary subject of Lanao but as a custodian of Maratabat, the
moral weight of ancestral reputation that defines conduct for those born into the royal genealogical tradition.<ref
name="maranao" /> That awareness shaped everything he did. When he walked into the Philippine Military
Academy, when he held his position on the killing fields of Bataan, and when he governed the most politically
complex province in the newly independent republic, he was not acting for himself alone. He was acting for every
Maranao who would follow.
Education
The Policy of Attraction
The early decades of American colonial rule in the Lake Lanao region were characterized by what administrators
called pacification, a series of military campaigns that culminated in pitched battles at Bayang and other sites
where Maranao warriors demonstrated that their resistance was organized and deeply principled.<ref
name="lanaodelsur">Provincial Government of Lanao del Sur. "History of Lanao del Sur." Accessed March 7,
2026. https://lanaodelsur.gov.ph/history/</ref> After those conflicts, colonial policy shifted toward what became
known as the Policy of Attraction, a deliberate effort to recruit the children of Moro nobility into government
schools and military academies, with the goal of creating a new generation of Muslim leaders whose institutional
loyalties would include the government in Manila.
Whatever its political intentions, this policy produced a small cohort of highly capable Muslim officers who would
go on to serve the Philippines with genuine distinction. General Marohombsar was the most consequential product
of this educational moment in Lanao history.
First Muslim Graduate of the Philippine Military Academy
The Philippine Military Academy, established in its modern form under the National Defense Act of 1935 and
modeled on the United States Military Academy at West Point, was during the pre-war Commonwealth period an
institution shaped almost entirely by the culture of Christian lowland Luzon.<ref name="pma" /> Its honor code, its
discipline system, its rituals and traditions all reflected a world that a young Maranao nobleman had not been raised
within. For Luis R. Marohombsar to enter that institution and graduate as a commissioned officer required more
than academic and physical competence. It required a form of cultural endurance that is easy to underestimate from
a distance.
As the first Muslim cadet to complete the PMA's full four-year program and receive a commission, Marohombsar's
graduation was a landmark in Philippine military history.<ref name="pma" /> He proved that the Maranao could
participate fully in the machinery of the modern state without abandoning the Maratabat that defined their identity.

PAGE 4
His commissioning into the Philippine Constabulary was not simply a career appointment. It was a proof of
concept for the entire enterprise of Muslim integration into national institutions, and it changed what was
imaginable for every Maranao who came after him.
Military Career
Philippine Constabulary and Intelligence Work
In the years between his commissioning and the outbreak of the Pacific War, Captain Marohombsar built his
professional reputation within the Philippine Constabulary, the security force that served simultaneously as the
national police and the reserve combat backbone of the Commonwealth government. Deployment to Mindanao
gave him an advantage that few officers could match: his fluency in Maranao, his knowledge of customary law, and
his recognized standing within the royal houses of Lanao transformed him from an ordinary officer into an
invaluable institutional asset.
By mid-1941, the strategic situation in the Pacific had deteriorated to the point that war was no longer a distant
contingency. The Philippine Constabulary began organizing its units into a wartime structure under the United
States Armed Forces in the Far East. The 1st Philippine Constabulary Regiment was among the first units inducted
into this structure, formally activated on October 15, 1941, by Brigadier General George M. Parker at Camp
Crame, Quezon City.<ref name="pcrecords">GUARDIAN LAW: Philippine Constabulary Wartime Records.
University of the Philippines Diliman Main Library Repository. Accessed March 7, 2026.
https://repository.mainlib.upd.edu.ph/omekas/files/original/cfa53a4c3e857dc4df7e33f8d77995662a312a76.pdf. See
also: Wikipedia. "Philippine Constabulary." Accessed March 7, 2026.
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philippine_Constabulary</ref>
Captain Marohombsar was assigned to this regiment as S-2 Intelligence Officer, responsible for threat assessment,
counter-espionage operations, and the collection of battlefield information.<ref name="pcrecords" /> Intelligence
work in the pre-war Constabulary demanded more than the ability to read maps and interrogate suspects. It
required an officer who could interpret the complex social dynamics of communities under threat, someone who
understood what certain kinds of loyalty and certain kinds of silence meant. For those tasks, Marohombsar's
grounding in the tradition-bound political culture of Lanao made him exceptionally well-suited.<ref
name="pcrecords" />
The Battle of Bataan
When Japanese forces launched their assault on the Philippines on December 8, 1941, the 1st Philippine
Constabulary Regiment found itself at the center of a strategic crisis that unfolded with terrifying speed.<ref
name="bataan">Wikipedia. "Battle of Bataan." Accessed March 7, 2026.
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Bataan. For a comprehensive study, see: Young, D. J. (2009). The Battle of
Bataan: A Complete History. McFarland & Company.</ref> The initial Japanese landings on northern Luzon
overwhelmed the Philippine-American defensive positions within days. General Douglas MacArthur's
implementation of War Plan Orange-3 set in motion a fighting withdrawal into the Bataan Peninsula, where
Filipino and American forces were meant to hold out long enough for a relief force that would, in the event, never
come.
The 2nd Battalion of the 1st PC Regiment was ordered directly to Bataan at the outbreak of hostilities, while other
regimental elements were initially assigned to metropolitan Manila for counter-espionage duties before eventually
following their comrades into the peninsula.<ref name="pcrecords" /> Once consolidated on Bataan, the regiment

PAGE 5
became part of the dense defensive structure that Filipino and American commanders assembled along the Abucay-
Mauban and later the Orion-Bagac lines.
For Captain Marohombsar in his S-2 role, the intelligence environment on Bataan had no real peacetime
equivalent. The Japanese 14th Army under General Masaharu Homma employed infiltration tactics at a high level
of sophistication, using small units and snipers to probe and exploit gaps in the defensive perimeter. Identifying
these infiltrations, mapping them, and providing the regimental commander with the intelligence necessary to
respond was Marohombsar's daily work throughout those months.<ref name="bataan" /> And he carried out that
work under conditions of genuine privation: malaria and dysentery were ravaging the defenders, rations had been
cut to subsistence levels, and ammunition reserves were depleting without resupply.
The Bataan Death March
When Major General Edward P. King Jr. negotiated the surrender of the Bataan-based Filipino-American forces on
April 9, 1942, approximately 76,000 soldiers became prisoners of war overnight.<ref name="bataan" /> What
followed, the forced march from Mariveles to Camp O'Donnell in Capas, Tarlac, across approximately 105
kilometers of tropical terrain in sweltering heat and without adequate food or water, became known to history as
the Bataan Death March. Thousands of Filipino and American prisoners perished during the march or in the
internment that followed.
Captain Marohombsar survived both the march and the period of imprisonment. His survival was not incidental. It
was essential to everything that would follow in his career and in his service to his people.
The defense of Bataan remains one of the most remarkable episodes in Philippine military history, a
demonstration that Filipino soldiers fighting for a republic not yet three decades old were capable of
extraordinary sacrifice.
Governor of Lanao
Appointment and the Logic of Dual Authority
The liberation of the Philippines in 1944 and 1945 found the country in a state of profound institutional disruption.
Infrastructure had been devastated, communities had been displaced, and the traditional bonds of provincial
governance had been strained by the years of Japanese occupation and resistance warfare. In Mindanao, these
challenges carried an extra layer of complexity because of the underlying tensions between the Muslim
communities of Lanao and a national government that was still, in many respects, unfamiliar with the Islamic
south.
Into this environment, the central government appointed Luis Marohombsar as Governor of Lanao, recognizing
that the province needed a leader who could command respect from both the traditional elite and the administrative
apparatus of the new republic. The logic of the appointment was clear: here was a man who held a general officer's
rank, had bled for the Philippines on Bataan, and simultaneously held unimpeachable credentials within the royal
genealogical hierarchy of Lanao. No one else in the country occupied that precise intersection.

PAGE 6
Governance Through Taritib and Igma
As Governor, Marohombsar did not govern through the imposition of central government authority. He governed
through the patient work of mediation. His deep familiarity with the Taritib and Igma of the Lake Lanao tradition
allowed him to intervene in land disputes and interclan conflicts before they could escalate into the blood feuds that
had historically destabilized the region.<ref name="royalhouses" /> The customary law of the Maranao is not
simply a set of rules; it is a living social compact, constantly being renegotiated through the authority of recognized
leaders. A governor without standing in that system had almost no leverage in resolving disputes. A governor with
the Marohombsar name had enormous leverage.
Under his administration, the province made meaningful progress in rebuilding infrastructure and establishing the
basic institutions of democratic local governance. Roads were repaired, schools reopened, and the mechanisms of
provincial administration began to function again. His approach was consistent throughout: wherever possible, he
worked with the traditional authority structures rather than around them, offering the central government's
resources and legal frameworks as complements to the customary order rather than replacements for it.
The Division of Lanao Province
One of the most consequential administrative outcomes of the post-war period was the passage of Republic Act No.
2228 on May 22, 1959, which formally divided the unified Province of Lanao into Lanao del Norte and Lanao del
Sur.<ref name="ra2228">Republic Act No. 2228. "An Act to Create the Provinces of Lanao del Norte and Lanao
del Sur." Approved May 22, 1959. Supreme Court E-Library. Accessed March 7, 2026.
https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/2/13574. See also: Provincial Government of Lanao del
Norte. "History." Accessed March 7, 2026. https://lanaodelnorte.gov.ph/history/</ref> The new provinces were
inaugurated on July 4, 1959, with Iligan City designated as the capital of Lanao del Norte and Marawi City as the
capital of Lanao del Sur.<ref name="ra2228" /> While this division occurred after Marohombsar's gubernatorial
tenure, the administrative foundation he had helped build during his years as governor made it possible to divide
the province without precipitating a governance crisis.
Legacy
A Family That Continued the Work
The fullest measure of a leader is often found not in his official record but in the lives of those he raised and
mentored. By that measure, General Marohombsar was one of the most successful leaders in Maranao history. His
children extended his work into domains he himself could not enter, carrying the family's tradition of service into
education, law, engineering, and peace diplomacy.
The most celebrated of his children is Dr. Sittie Nurlayla Emily M. Marohombsar, who served as President of
Mindanao State University from 1992 to 1998, becoming the first woman ever appointed to lead that institution.
<ref name="msu">MSU System Has New President. Philippine Muslim Today. March 12, 2022. Accessed March 7,
2026. https://philmuslimtoday.com/2022/03/12/msu-system-has-new-president/</ref> Her achievement was
recognized formally at a public ceremony in Lanao del Sur, where she was honored alongside other pioneering
women of the province as the first female educator elevated to the MSU presidency.<ref name="pia">March 2012
(Lanao del Sur In Focus). Philippine Information Agency. March 27, 2012. Accessed March 7, 2026.
https://lanaodelsurinfocus.blogspot.com/2012/03/. See also: BlogWatch. "Money and Mosque-Making, Marks of
the Meranao People." July 17, 2012. https://blogwatch.tv/2012/07/money-and-mosque-making-marks-of-the-
meranao-people/</ref> Beyond education, Dr. Emily Marohombsar made history again in 1997 when President
Fidel Ramos appointed her as the first woman to serve on the government peace panel in negotiations with the

PAGE 7
Moro Islamic Liberation Front, marking the first time a woman had ever sat at the table in the Bangsamoro peace
process.<ref name="wps">Santiago, Miriam. "The Participation of Women in the Mindanao Peace Process."
October 2015. UN Women. Accessed March 7, 2026. https://wps.unwomen.org/pdf/research/Santiago.pdf</ref>
The General's other children built careers across multiple fields. Atty. Johnny Marohombsar served as a
respected member of the Philippine bar, embodying the family's commitment to the rule of law that their father had
served in uniform. Dr. Rebekah Marohombsar Alawi pursued an academic career at Mindanao State University,
rising to the position of Dean of the Graduate School, where she sustained the family's investment in Maranao
scholarship and education.<ref name="msuprofiles">Mindanao State University Faculty and Administrative
Profiles (MSU-Main Campus, Marawi City). See also: Supreme Court of the Philippines. G.R. No. 126481,
Marohombsar v. Court of Appeals. February 2000.
https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/59594</ref> Engr. Usaffe Marohombsar and Engr.
Samson Marohombsar contributed to national development through their professional engineering work. Engr.
Usaffe's given name was drawn directly from the wartime acronym for the United States Armed Forces in the Far
East, a quiet memorial to their father's years on Bataan.
The Meaning of Being First
The significance of being the first Muslim graduate of the Philippine Military Academy cannot be measured only in
terms of what it meant to General Marohombsar personally. It was a structural opening, a precedent that made
every subsequent Maranao officer possible. Before him, the proposition that a Maranao nobleman could thrive at
the PMA was untested. After him, it was proven. That kind of first carries a particular gravity because it changes
the horizon of possibility for an entire community.
The same quality of firstness runs through his entire biography. He was the first to demonstrate that a Constabulary
intelligence officer of Maranao extraction could perform effectively under the extreme pressure of Bataan. He was
the first Governor of Lanao to hold simultaneous authority in the traditional and modern political systems of the
province. And through his daughter, he was the father of both the first female president of Mindanao State
University and the first woman peace negotiator in the Bangsamoro talks.
None of this was accidental. Marohombsar navigated each of these firsts through personal excellence, cultural
intelligence, and the deeply internalized sense of obligation that Maratabat demands. He understood that in a
society structured around genealogical prestige, the honor of being first is simultaneously a burden. To fail would
have reflected on every Maranao who came after him. To succeed, as he consistently did, was to open doors that
could not easily be closed again.
Relevance to the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region
General Marohombsar's legacy has taken on renewed relevance in the era of the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region
in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM). The institutional framework of the BARMM, the aspiration to create governance
structures that are genuinely responsive to the cultural and political identity of the Bangsamoro people, reflects in
large part the argument that Marohombsar made with his life. He proved, decades before the peace agreements, that
the Muslim people of Mindanao did not have to choose between their ancient identity and full participation in the
Philippine republic. The architects of Bangsamoro self-governance are, in a real sense, working in the space he
opened.

PAGE 8
Recognition
General Luis R. Marohombsar is recognized in Maranao historical memory as a foundational figure in the
integration of Muslim Mindanao into the national life of the Philippines. His pioneering graduation from the
Philippine Military Academy is documented in official alumni records at Fort del Pilar, Baguio City.<ref
name="pma" /> His daughter, Dr. Sittie Nurlayla Emily M. Marohombsar, has been honored by the Philippine
Information Agency and the Mindanao State University system as part of her own recognition for pioneering
achievements in education and peacebuilding.<ref name="pia" /><ref name="wps" /> Within the Pangampong a
Masiu, his name remains part of the living genealogical record that defines royal standing in the lake region.
Death
The specific date and circumstances of General Luis R. Marohombsar's death have not been formally documented
in public records. He passed away in Lanao, Philippines, leaving behind a family that has carried his legacy
forward across multiple generations and professional fields.

Willie Dangane Marohombsar
General Willie Dangane Marohombsar is a retired senior law
enforcement executive and military veteran from the Philippines.
Following a career in public safety spanning several decades across
Mindanao, he transitioned to academic and civic leadership. As an
elder of the prominent Marohombsar clan of Lanao del Sur, he holds
the traditional, honorary title of "General Dean" within his
community. This title recognizes his role as a senior adviser,
custodian of cultural values, and academic administrator.

4 Civic Contributions and Policy Views

6 Research Assessment
6.1 Verified Facts
6.2 Information Not Yet Verified
6.3 Research Gaps
Early Life and Family
General Marohombsar belongs to the Marohombsar clan, a
historically influential and well-respected family lineage based in the
province of Lanao del Sur within the Bangsamoro region. Raised in
an environment heavily shaped by Meranao culture and civic
expectations, he was taught early on the core values of honor,
integrity, and responsibility to the community. Within his extended
family network, he remains a unifying figure who regularly
spearheads initiatives aimed at preserving the clan's historical legacy.
This includes active participation in major clan milestones, such as
the United Marohombsar Grand Reunion hosted at the Dimaporo
Gymnasium on the Mindanao State University (MSU) Main Campus
in Marawi City.
Education and Military Foundation
His foundational discipline and leadership training began in the mid-
1970s within the armed forces.

PAGE 2
MILF ceasefire committees to maintain
peace in conflict-prone areas, and later
guiding curriculum development for
public safety education as an academic
dean
Pull Quote
"From frontline command to the dean's
office, the title 'General Dean' carries both
a soldier's discipline and an elder's duty to
his people."
Military Enlistment: On September 1, 1974, Marohombsar
entered military service as a civilian recruit and military
trainee at Camp General Servillano Aquino in San Miguel,
Tarlac.
Initial Unit: He was part of a cohort of 600 recruits who took
their formal oaths under Brigadier General Miguel M.
Villamor, then the Brigade Commander of the 5th Infantry
Brigade, Philippine Army.
Training Battalion: He completed his rigorous instruction
under the 1st Probational Battalion, an early operational
experience that established the technical and strategic
framework for his later career in national security and law enforcement.
Career and Public Service
Law Enforcement Leadership
Marohombsar transitioned his security career into the Philippine National Police (PNP), where he rose through the
officer ranks to hold critical field commands in conflict-prone areas of Mindanao. He primarily operated within
police intelligence and strategic field operations, securing a reputation for mitigating urban crime, kidnapping
syndicates, and local insurgencies.
Cotabato City Police Director: During the late 2000s, Marohombsar served as a Police Senior
Superintendent (equivalent to Police Colonel) and the City Police Director for Cotabato City. His tenure was
marked by navigating highly complex security issues, including investigating high-profile ambushes,
tracking down fugitive political figures, and handling urban disasters.
Anti-Kidnapping Campaigns: He managed local security during a period of frequent kidnapping incidents
orchestrated by organized syndicates. Marohombsar notably challenged broader institutional frameworks by
publicly noting that several apprehended suspects admitted to receiving protection from corrupted
government figures. He also coordinated closely with regional stakeholders, Muslim clerics, and the joint
ceasefire committees of the government and the Moro Islamic Liberation Front (MILF) to maintain territorial
stability.
Sarangani Provincial Director: He later extended his institutional leadership across south-central
Mindanao, serving as the Provincial Director of the Sarangani Police Provincial Office.
Post-Retirement and Academic Transition
After retiring from active duty in the PNP, Marohombsar entered the education sector. Utilizing his administrative
background and legal knowledge in criminology and public safety, he took on institutional management roles. He
serves as an academic administrator and Dean at Goldenstate College, a higher education institution located in
General Santos City. In this capacity, he guides curriculum development and professional training for future public
safety practitioners.
Civic Contributions and Policy Views
Marohombsar continues to be an active voice in community governance, public safety policy, and regional legal
issues. He regularly engages with regional media outlets to champion structural changes in law enforcement.

PAGE 3
Police Visibility: He advocates for heightened police visibility and the institutional deployment of proactive
patrols to deter street-level criminality.
Student Safety Infrastructure: Leveraging his platform as an academic dean, he has publicly urged local
government units in Mindanao to implement stringent safety perimeters and specialized protection protocols
around schools and university zones to shield students from urban criminal threats.
Community Partnerships: He maintains that effective law enforcement relies entirely on strong
community-police partnerships, encouraging civilian cooperation and local government integration to sustain
peace and order.
Cultural and Historical Significance
Within the cultural framework of Lanao del Sur and the wider Bangsamoro community, Marohombsar carries
distinct significance as a clan elder. The traditional title of "General Dean" represents a unique fusion of modern
institutional achievements (his rank as a police general/senior commander and his role as a college dean) with
traditional Meranao governance structures, where senior professionals are formal asset-holders of family values,
dispute resolution, and historical lineage.
Research Assessment
Verified Facts
Formal enlistment and oath-taking as a military trainee on September 1, 1974, at Camp General Servillano
Aquino, Tarlac, under the 1st Probational Battalion, 5th Infantry Brigade.
Service as a Police Senior Superintendent and City Director of the Cotabato City Police Office during the
late 2000s.
Service as the Provincial Director for the Sarangani Police Provincial Office.
Post-retirement transition to academe, currently serving as a Dean at Goldenstate College in General Santos
City.
Traditional recognition as an elder and "General Dean" within the Marohombsar clan of Lanao del Sur.
Information Not Yet Verified
Specific dates of his promotions through the police ranks (e.g., the exact year he achieved the rank of
Superintendent/Senior Superintendent).
The specific years marking the beginning and end of his tenure as Sarangani Provincial Director.
Exact date of his official retirement from the Philippine National Police.
Research Gaps
Detailed Educational Background: Official records detailing his undergraduate degree, the higher education
institution he attended, or any specialized post-graduate degrees in criminology, public administration, or
military science are currently missing from the public record.
Official Awards Registry: A comprehensive list of specific military or PNP commendations, medals, and
institutional merit awards received during his decades of active service remains undocumented in open
source materials.
Complete Chronological Timeline: Precise transitional dates mapping his movement from the Philippine
Army training environment into the active ranks of the Philippine National Police.

PAGE 4

purposes based on public institutional records, historical news archives, and verified family documents. It does not
contain professional, legal, or security advice.

Nashmyleen A. Marohomsalic
Nashmyleen A. Marohomsalic is a distinguished Filipino jurist and human rights advocate who made history in
August 2024 as the first Filipina and first Bangsamoro lawyer to be admitted as counsel to the International
Criminal Court (ICC). yes A Meranao from Lanao del Sur, Atty. Marohomsalic represents a generational
milestone for the Bangsamoro community, proving that indigenous and minority legal professionals can reach the
highest echelons of international justice. Her work bridges international humanitarian law with the Philippine
judicial system, particularly through her role in developing landmark refugee protections and capacity-building
initiatives alongside the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR).
Early Life and Family
Atty. Marohomsalic was born into a prominent family of public servants in Lanao del Sur, the heart of Meranao
territory. She is one of six children of the late Atty. Nasser A. Marohomsalic and Hadja Omensalam Benito
Adap Cotigal.
Her father's legacy profoundly shaped her commitment to human rights and social justice. Atty. Nasser A.
Marohomsalic was a renowned human rights champion, historian, and former Commissioner of the Commission on
Human Rights (CHR) (https://chr.gov.ph), as well as a member of the National Amnesty Commission. He authored
the seminal work Aristocrats of the Malay Race: A History of the Bangsa Moro in the Philippines, which
established the intellectual foundation for modern Bangsamoro legal scholarship. A fierce advocate for "moral

As a Meranao, Atty. Marohomsalic belongs to one of the major
ethnic groups within the Bangsamoro community, often called the
"People of the Lake" in reference to Ranao, the geographic and
cultural heart of Meranao civilization.
Education
Her academic foundation is rooted in two of the Philippines' premier
universities.
She obtained a Bachelor's degree in Philosophy from the
University of the Philippines (UP), one of Asia's oldest and most
respected institutions. This philosophical grounding in ethics and
critical thinking would later inform her approach to humanitarian
law.
She earned her Juris Doctor (J.D.) degree from the Ateneo de
Manila University, a Jesuit institution known for producing socially
conscious lawyers. During her legal training, she became an alumna
of the Ateneo Human Rights Center, where she began her
specialization in human rights advocacy and peace-building—a
trajectory that would define her entire career.<ref
name="source2">Extracted from uploaded DOCX on Atty.
Nashmyleen A. Marohomsalic.</ref>
Career and Institutional Contributions
Supreme Court Role
Atty. Marohomsalic currently serves as a lawyer in the Office of the
Chief Justice (OCJ) of the Supreme Court of the Philippines. In this
pivotal institutional role, she has been instrumental in shaping landmark judicial initiatives that protect vulnerable
populations, particularly refugees and stateless persons.
The Rule on Facilitated Naturalization of Refugees and Stateless Persons
Her most significant institutional contribution is her work on the Rule on Facilitated Naturalization of Refugees
and Stateless Persons (A.M. No. 21-07-22-SC), which the Supreme Court approved as the first judiciary-led
initiative globally designed specifically to simplify citizenship pathways for displaced persons.

PAGE 3
As a member of the Supreme Court's Special Committee Secretariat under the Office of the Chief Justice, Atty.
Marohomsalic helped draft and refine legal procedures that allow recognized refugees and stateless individuals to
acquire Philippine citizenship through an expedited and more affordable judicial process. The rule addressed
systemic barriers that had historically prevented displaced populations from attaining citizenship:
Financial Barriers: Previous laws required expensive physical publication of petitions in newspapers for
three consecutive weeks. The new rule permits electronic publication on official websites such as the
Supreme Court or Official Gazette, drastically reducing application costs.
Procedural Inflexibility: The rule mandates an expedited and continuous hearing process to prevent cases
from languishing in court for years.
Documentation Vulnerabilities: Recognizing that displaced persons flee without complete records, the rule
adopts the principle of absolute liberality. Courts must consider the unique circumstances and lack of
traditional documentary requirements inherent to forced displacement.
Protection for Minors: It introduced a groundbreaking provision allowing unaccompanied children to file
for naturalization with assistance from government or child-caring agencies, fulfilling international
obligations under the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child.
Social Integration: The rule allows petitioners to request a local name as part of their naturalization,
facilitating smoother assimilation into Philippine society.
This rule is the first judiciary-led initiative globally aimed specifically at simplifying naturalization for
displaced persons, marking the Philippines as a regional leader in protecting vulnerable populations.
Capacity Building and Judicial Training
Working alongside the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) Philippines, Atty.
Marohomsalic has been a key organizer and resource person for training programs that translate complex
international humanitarian laws into local judicial practice.
She has participated in organizing and facilitating capacity-building seminars for Regional Trial Court (RTC)
judges across the Philippines. These sessions ensure judges handle naturalization cases with "absolute liberality"
and a deep understanding of the vulnerabilities of forcibly displaced persons. Her training contributions extend to
the 1st National Refugee Day Forum in 2024, where she delivered messages of solidarity and discussed the
"whole-of-society" approach to forced displacement.<ref name="source3">UNHCR Philippines, National Refugee
Day Forum 2024.</ref>
Public Advocacy and Awareness
Atty. Marohomsalic has supported institutional advocacy within the Supreme Court to foster a culture of inclusion:
She was instrumental in the Hope Away from Home photo exhibit at the Supreme Court, a collaboration
with UNHCR to raise awareness about the plight of refugees among court personnel and the public.
She has represented the Philippine judiciary's progress on refugee rights in international settings, such as
meetings with the International Association of Refugee and Migration Judges (IARMJ), showcasing the
Philippines as a regional leader in protecting displaced populations.<ref name="source4">Supreme Court of
the Philippines, Rule on Facilitated Naturalization international engagement, 2024.</ref>

PAGE 4
Historic ICC Admission
In August 2024, Atty. Marohomsalic achieved a historic milestone: she was admitted to the International
Criminal Court (ICC) Bar Association. This admission marked her as the 5th Filipino lawyer and the very first
Filipina and first Bangsamoro to be accredited to represent parties before the court.
Her admission was based on rigorous evaluation of her litigation skills and professional experience, qualifying her
to appear in cases involving international crimes such as genocide and crimes against humanity. The Bangsamoro
Parliament formally commended her achievement, recognizing its significance not only for the Bangsamoro people
but for the entire Philippine legal profession and women in international law.<ref name="source5">Bangsamoro
Parliament Resolution, August 2024.</ref>
This milestone represents a turning point: for the first time, a Bangsamoro lawyer—and a Muslim woman at that—
can represent clients, states, or international organizations in the world's premier tribunal for justice on the gravest
crimes.
Legacy of Her Father: Atty. Nasser A. Marohomsalic
Atty. Nashmyleen's commitment to marginalized communities and humanitarian law is a direct continuation of the
work pioneered by her late father. His intellectual, institutional, and moral contributions created the foundation
upon which his daughter's career stands.
Human Rights Advocacy
As a former Commissioner of the Commission on Human Rights (CHR) and the National Amnesty Commission,
Atty. Nasser A. Marohomsalic was a "fierce advocate" for ensuring the voices of the oppressed were heard at the
national level. His work centered on accountability, reconciliation, and protecting the rights of marginalized
communities, particularly the Bangsamoro.
Historical Scholarship
He authored Aristocrats of the Malay Race: A History of the Bangsa Moro in the Philippines, a seminal work
that wove Bangsamoro identity and dignity into the national historical discourse. His intellectual defense of the
compatibility between Islam and democracy served as a foundation for modern Bangsamoro legal scholarship and
remains required reading in law schools and policy circles.
Institutional Pioneering
He made history as the first Meranao elected National Secretary of the Integrated Bar of the Philippines (IBP),
breaking institutional barriers and proving that Bangsamoro voices belonged at the highest levels of the legal
profession. His daughter mirrored this pioneering spirit by becoming the first Bangsamoro counsel admitted to the
ICC.

PAGE 5
Peace-Building Architecture
He played an active role in drafting the Bangsamoro Basic Law and championed "moral governance" as a guiding
principle for Bangsamoro political and legal institutions. His focus on inclusive justice and reconciliation directly
informed Nashmyleen's work on humanitarian law and refugee protection.
Cultural Significance and Bangsamoro Pride
Atty. Marohomsalic's rise represents a landmark for the Bangsamoro community, particularly for young Meranao
women aspiring to careers in law, governance, and international diplomacy. As a "Bangsamoro Pride," she
embodies the principle that indigenous and minority professionals can reach the highest echelons of international
justice while remaining rooted in their cultural and spiritual identity.
Her visibility in traditional Meranao dress during formal settings sends a powerful message: professional
excellence and cultural pride are not mutually exclusive. She serves as a living testament to the Bangsamoro
people's intellectual capacity, moral leadership, and rightful place in global governance and justice systems.
Her work—bridging international humanitarian standards with local judicial practice—demonstrates that
marginalized communities are not merely subjects of international law; they are architects and practitioners of
justice.
Contributions to the Bangsamoro Struggle
Atty. Marohomsalic has been a consistent voice in forums discussing the Mindanaoan Struggle and the road to
sustainable peace. She emphasizes the intersection of cultural identity and legal rights, arguing that genuine peace
requires both institutional justice and cultural recognition.
Her work with the UNHCR on refugee and stateless persons protection addresses one of the most pressing
humanitarian consequences of conflict in the region. By streamlining citizenship pathways for displaced
populations, she directly serves communities affected by decades of armed conflict and displacement.
Recognition and Awards
In August 2024, the Bangsamoro Parliament adopted a formal resolution commending and congratulating Atty.
Marohomsalic for her historic ICC admission. The resolution recognized her achievement not only as a personal
milestone but as a breakthrough for the Bangsamoro people in international legal institutions.<ref
name="source6">Bangsamoro Parliament Resolution Commending Atty. Nashmyleen A. Marohomsalic, August
2024.</ref>
Further Reading
Marohomsalic, Nasser A. Aristocrats of the Malay Race: A History of the Bangsa Moro in the Philippines.

on refugee protection and naturalization.

Atty. Nasser A. Marohomsalic
Atty. Nasser A. Marohomsalic (July 21, 1955 to July 6, 2024) was a Maranao lawyer, historian, novelist, and
human rights advocate who spent his career championing justice for the Bangsamoro people and advocating for the
intersection of Islamic tradition and democratic governance.<ref name="NDBC">Peace Sec. Galvez on passing of
NAC Commissioner Nasser Marohomsalic. Notre Dame Broadcasting Corporation (NDBC) News, 2024.</ref> He
served as the first Bangsamoro commissioner of the Commission on Human Rights (CHR) during the 2nd
Commission term, spanning from May 5, 1994, to May 5, 2001,<ref name="CHR">Commission on Human Rights
Commission En Banc. CHR Official Records, 1994-2001.</ref> and was sitting as a commissioner of the National
Amnesty Commission at the time of his death. Marohomsalic left an indelible mark on Philippine human rights,
peace advocacy, and Bangsamoro intellectual life through his institutional work, his prolific historical and literary
writings, and his unwavering belief that amnesty and dialogue were the pathways to national healing.
Early Life and Education
Marohomsalic was born on July 21, 1955, in Lumba-Bayabao, Lanao del Sur, the heart of Meranaw territory. He
began his tertiary education at Mindanao State University-Main Campus as an honors student before relocating to
Manila to complete his undergraduate studies. He earned his Bachelor of Arts in Political Science from Far Eastern
University in 1977, then pursued legal studies at the University of the Philippines, where he completed his
Bachelor of Laws in 1981.<ref name="NDBC" />

He was married to Hadja Omensalam Benito Adap Cotigal and
fathered six children, among them Atty. Nashmyleen A.
Marohomsalic, who would go on to become the first Filipina and

Colleagues and friends knew him affectionately as "Tito Nas," a
mentor figure described by those close to him as more like family
than a professional peer, known for his lighthearted humor and
ready willingness to help anyone in need.<ref
name="Memoir">Personal memoir, author acquaintance. 2025.
</ref>
Legal Career and Institutional Roles
Commission on Human Rights (1994-2001)
In 1994, President Fidel Ramos appointed Marohomsalic as a
Commissioner of the Commission on Human Rights, marking a
historic moment: he became the first Bangsamoro to sit on the
CHR.
<ref name="NDBC" /> During his seven-year tenure, he earned a
reputation as a vocal champion for the marginalized, particularly
indigenous Muslim communities. He was known for visiting
displaced communities and wounded security personnel alike,
emphasizing that their human rights were equally protected under
law. When Mayor Alfredo Lim's administration in Manila
launched the notorious "spray-painting" campaign against
suspected drug pushers in 1997, Marohomsalic was among the
CHR voices that publicly tangled with this extrajudicial practice,
refusing to see human rights as selective.<ref
name="OnMaranao">On Maranao. Blogspot, 2025.</ref>
His work at the CHR transcended bureaucratic procedure. He
published Towards Peace, Autonomy, and Human Rights (1999), a
collection of his speeches and positions from those years, arguing
that true peace requires both institutional accountability and community healing.
Integrated Bar of the Philippines (National Secretary)
Marohomsalic made history as the first Maranao elected as National Secretary of the Integrated Bar of the
Philippines,<ref name="NDBC" /> a position that gave him a platform to ensure Muslim Filipino representation in
the Philippine legal community. His tenure underscored his belief that the bar itself should reflect the diversity of
the nation it served, not exclude it.

PAGE 3
National Amnesty Commission (1990s-2024)
At the time of his death in July 2024, Marohomsalic was serving as a Commissioner of the National Amnesty
Commission (NAC), where he had become instrumental in implementing the government's reconciliation
programs.
<ref name="NAC">National Amnesty Commission Official Records.</ref> His role overseeing amnesty
processing touched thousands of applications from the Moro Islamic Liberation Front (MILF), Moro National
Liberation Front (MNLF), and former communist rebels.
Marohomsalic held a philosophical view of amnesty that transcended legalism. He famously stated that "everything
follows after peace,"<ref name="SourceDoc">Nasser A. Marohomsalic. NAC Position Papers and Speeches,
1990s-2024.</ref> viewing amnesty not as a mere legal procedure but as a "motherhood of all virtues" essential for
national stability and the reintegration of former combatants. He clarified a crucial legal principle: that amnesty
covers crimes committed in pursuit of political beliefs but does not erase civil liabilities, a distinction he
championed to encourage former rebels to return to the fold of law.
He was instrumental in establishing Local Amnesty Boards (LABs) across the country, ensuring that eligible
individuals in remote or conflict-affected areas could access the amnesty process without traveling to distant
offices. This was not mere procedural convenience; it was an expression of his belief that peace infrastructure
should reach the people, not require the people to reach it.
Philippine Center for Islam and Democracy (PCID)
Marohomsalic was a founding member of the Philippine Center for Islam and Democracy, where he worked
alongside other Muslim and non-Muslim intellectuals to counter the false narrative that Islam and democratic
governance were inherently incompatible.
<ref name="PCID">Philippine Center for Islam and Democracy Official Records. https://www.pcid.com.ph</ref>
His intellectual contribution to this organization centered on bridging two traditions that many in the West (and
regrettably, some in the Philippines) falsely opposed. He demonstrated through institutional work and scholarly
writing that Islamic principles of justice and consultation (shura) not only coexist with democratic ideals but enrich
them.
Scholarship and Literary Work
Marohomsalic's intellectual legacy rests on his dual identity as historian and novelist, roles that allowed him to
serve Bangsamoro consciousness on multiple registers.
Aristocrats of the Malay Race (1995/2001)
His seminal work, Aristocrats of the Malay Race: A History of the Bangsa Moro in the Philippines, was self-
published in 2001 after a decade of research and writing. The book provides a comprehensive historical account of
Bangsamoro resistance to Spanish, American, and Philippine central authority, framed explicitly as a registry of
both aspirations and grievances.<ref name="OnMaranao" /> It is widely used as a primary text in understanding
the Bangsamoro struggle from a local, humanizing perspective, shifting the narrative from "rebellion" to a defense
of noble identity.

PAGE 4
The book sold out immediately upon release, a testament to its resonance with readers seeking a Bangsamoro-
authored account of Bangsamoro history.
<ref name="Amazon">Aristocrats of the Malay Race: A History of the Bangsa Moro in the Philippines.
Amazon.com Book Review Database, accessed 2024.</ref>
Maratabat: A Novel on Rido and Revenge Justice (2024)
In his final work, launched in June 2024 at Mindanao State University-Marawi just weeks before his passing,
Marohomsalic shifted to fiction to explore the Meranaw concept of maratabat (personal and lineal honor) and how
it fuels rido (clan feuding). The novel is structured around two central, deeply embedded concepts that dictate
social behavior and conflict resolution in Lanao:
Maratabat is a deep sense of personal honor, dignity, and self-esteem, but unlike Western concepts of
individual pride, it is collective. It is tied to one's lineage (bangsa) and rank. Upholding one's honor is
synonymous with protecting the reputation of the entire clan.
The novel portrays maratabat as a double-edged sword: a source of immense pride and resilience, but also a force
that can lead to what Marohomsalic called "an irrational choice of death over loss of face." Rido, by contrast, is a
cyclical system of retaliatory violence between families, often triggered by offenses to maratabat ranging from
petty insults to serious crimes, and capable of persisting across generations.
The thematic heart of Maratabat is a warning to younger generations: while maratabat was historically a code of
nobility and chivalry, it has been modernly "warped" into a justification for destructive revenge violence. Through
his characters, Marohomsalic advocated for a "Maratabat Reimagined," shifting the focus from retaliation to
finding honor in peacebuilding, community service, and education. This was not Marohomsalic abandoning
tradition; it was him honoring it by asking Meranaw society to remember what maratabat truly means in the service
of life.
The Mujahidin (Unfinished)
At the time of his passing, Marohomsalic had been working on The Mujahidin, a novel set in the conflict zones of
Mindanao. The manuscript remains with close friends and family, incomplete but bearing the promise of his final
artistic vision.
<ref name="OnMaranao" />
Cultural Significance and Peace Advocacy
Marohomsalic's intellectual work, whether historical or literary, served a singular purpose: to document, defend,
and elevate Bangsamoro identity and agency in Philippine consciousness. He was a custodian of Bangsamoro
memory in an era when that memory was often marginalized or distorted.
Beyond the written word, he served as a publicity ambassador for Heavenly Culture, World Peace, Restoration
of Light (HWPL) Philippines,<ref name="SourceDoc" /> cementing his status as a voice for harmony at regional
and global levels.
His belief in dialogue over demonization, in amnesty over vengeance, and in the dignity of his people permeated
every role he held. Whether sitting on the CHR, chairing amnesty boards, or writing novels late into the evening,
Marohomsalic treated peacebuilding not as a policy goal but as a moral imperative rooted in Islamic tradition and

PAGE 5
democratic principle.
Family Legacy and Continuing Impact
Atty. Nashmyleen A. Marohomsalic and the International Criminal Court
Marohomsalic's commitment to justice and education continues through the achievements of his daughter, Atty.
Nashmyleen A. Marohomsalic. In 2024, she became the first Filipina and first Bangsamoro lawyer to be
admitted as counsel before the International Criminal Court.<ref name="BARMM" /> She is one of only five
Filipino lawyers accredited by the International Criminal Court Bar Association, allowing her to represent victims,
defendants, or witnesses in cases involving genocide, war crimes, and crimes against humanity.
Her achievement was formally recognized by the Bangsamoro Parliament through Resolution No. 492, which
commended her for breaking ground in international legal representation. She holds a degree in Philosophy from
the University of the Philippines and a Juris Doctor from Ateneo de Manila University.<ref name="BARMM" />
Nasser Marohomsalic Lecture Series on Justice, Peace, and Liberty
In late 2025, nearly a year after Marohomsalic's passing, the Philippine Center for Islam and Democracy launched
the Nasser Marohomsalic Lecture Series on Justice, Peace, and Liberty in his honor, serving as a platform for
intellectual discourse on the values he championed throughout his life.<ref name="PCID" />
The inaugural session was opened by Atty. Christian Monsod, a framer of the 1987 Constitution of the Philippines.
Lectures focus on the intersection of social justice, the rule of law, and the empowerment of marginalized
communities. The series explicitly bridges Islamic principles and democratic ideals, reflecting Marohomsalic's
lifelong commitment to showing that these traditions are not enemies but allies in the pursuit of justice.
Death and Commemoration
Atty. Nasser A. Marohomsalic passed away on July 6, 2024, at the age of 68. The Bangsamoro Parliament passed a
resolution recognizing his immense contributions to peacebuilding, human rights, and civil service. At the moment
of his death, he remained a sitting commissioner of the National Amnesty Commission, a role he held with the
same dedication and moral clarity that defined his entire career.
His final novel, Maratabat, was launched posthumously, a final gift to Bangsamoro and Philippine letters from a
man who believed that literature and law were both instruments of human dignity.

Otengue Masnar
Dr. Otengue Masnar is a distinguished Filipino academic
administrator and researcher who shaped the research landscape at
Mindanao State University (MSU) in Marawi City. Belonging to the
Maranao ethnic group—the "People of the Lake" centered around
Lake Lanao—Dr. Masnar stands out for his unique achievement of
being designated twice as the university's Vice Chancellor (later Vice
President) for Research and Extension, a position that put him at the
helm of MSU's knowledge production engine. His signature legacy
revolves around strengthening the OneMSU philosophy, which uses
education as the primary tool for peace-building in the conflict-
scarred MINSUPALA region (Mindanao, Sulu, and Palawan). Dr.
Masnar's work bridges traditional Maranao cultural values with
modern scientific administration, ensuring that university research
stays globally competitive while remaining deeply rooted in local
needs.

Early Life and Background
Dr. Masnar hails from a family with deep institutional ties to Mindanao State University. The Masnar lineage
represents a multi-generational commitment to academic service, with relatives like Sohra B. Masnar and
Mohammad Ayyub C. Masnar continuing the tradition in administrative and research roles at MSU's Main Campus
in Marawi City. Growing up within the Maranao community, which has historically faced marginalization and
conflict in the southern Philippines, Dr. Masnar developed an early understanding of the critical role education
plays in social transformation and peace-building.
The Maranao people, known for their rich Islamic heritage and intricate cultural traditions around Lake Lanao,
have long contributed scholars and leaders to the region's academic institutions. Dr. Masnar's background in this
community deeply influenced his later emphasis on indigenous knowledge systems and cultural integration in
university research programs.
Education
Dr. Masnar's academic journey reflects a deliberate progression from technical agricultural expertise to high-level
administrative leadership. His educational credentials include:
Bachelor of Science in Agriculture — Mindanao State University, Marawi City. This foundational degree
grounded him in the practical challenges of agricultural development in Mindanao, particularly issues
affecting rural and indigenous communities.
Master in Public Administration (1995) — Mindanao State University, Marawi City. This degree marked
his transition from technical work to institutional leadership, equipping him with the skills needed for
university governance.
Doctoral Studies in Philippine Studies — Mindanao State University, Marawi City. These studies
deepened his understanding of the socio-political dynamics of the Philippines, particularly the historical
context of Muslim Mindanao.
Doctor of Management, major in Leadership and Organization — Liceo de Cagayan University. This
terminal degree formalized his expertise in organizational behavior and strategic leadership, preparing him
for executive-level academic administration.
This educational path—combining agriculture, public administration, cultural studies, and management—uniquely
positioned Dr. Masnar to understand the multifaceted challenges facing Mindanao State University as both an
academic institution and a social catalyst.

PAGE 3
Career
Dr. Masnar's professional trajectory is inseparable from the institutional development of Mindanao State
University. His career followed a steady ascent through the university's research infrastructure, culminating in his
unprecedented double designation as Vice Chancellor (later renamed Vice President) for Research and Extension.
Early Academic Positions
After completing his agricultural studies, Dr. Masnar initially worked in roles that combined teaching with
agricultural extension work. These early positions exposed him to the realities of knowledge transfer between
university researchers and rural communities, particularly indigenous groups and farming families around Lake
Lanao.
Vice Chancellor/Vice President for Research and Extension
Dr. Masnar's most significant contribution came through his leadership of the Office of the Vice Chancellor for
Research, Extension, and Development (OVCRED). Being designated to this position twice represents an
extraordinary vote of confidence in his administrative capabilities—a rare achievement in Philippine higher
education. In this role, he succeeded notable Maranao scholars such as Dr. Mamitua Saber, inheriting and
expanding upon a legacy of using research as a tool for regional development.
His responsibilities encompassed:
Knowledge Production: Dr. Masnar oversaw research initiatives that directly addressed the socio-cultural and
economic challenges facing the Bangsamoro region. He prioritized studies that documented indigenous knowledge
systems, assessed institutional effectiveness, and explored pathways to peace in conflict-affected areas.
Community Extension: He transformed how MSU's research reached surrounding communities. Rather than
treating research as a purely academic exercise, he ensured that innovations and technologies developed at the
university were actively disseminated to indigenous peoples, farming communities, and local government units.
Sustainable Development: Dr. Masnar championed research and extension programs focused on environmental
conservation, particularly the protection of the Lake Lanao watershed—a critical ecological and cultural resource
for the Maranao people.
Consultant and Advisor
Beyond his university roles, Dr. Masnar served as a consultant and resource person for regional government
projects in Marawi City and the Lanao provinces. His expertise was particularly sought after for initiatives
involving public policy, indigenous integration, and peace-building strategies.
Institutional Contributions
Dr. Masnar's impact on MSU extends far beyond administrative efficiency. He fundamentally reshaped how the
university approached research, community engagement, and its role in regional peace-building.

PAGE 4
OneMSU Philosophy
Dr. Masnar is credited with strengthening and operationalizing the OneMSU philosophy, which positions
education—particularly research and extension work—as the primary mechanism for achieving lasting peace in
Mindanao. This philosophy emerged from the recognition that MSU, as a state university serving a predominantly
Muslim region, has a unique responsibility to bridge cultural divides and counter narratives of conflict.
Under Dr. Masnar's leadership, the OneMSU philosophy translated into concrete programs:
Integration of peace-building concepts into research methodologies and extension curricula
Support for studies examining student and community perceptions of the Mindanao conflict
Development of conflict resolution training programs for students and community members
Promotion of interfaith dialogue and cultural exchange within the university
Professionalization of Research Culture
Dr. Masnar is widely recognized for professionalizing MSU's research environment. When he assumed leadership,
the university's research output was fragmented and lacked systematic coordination. He introduced:
Standardized research protocols and ethics review processes
Mentorship programs for early-career researchers and faculty members
Incentive structures that rewarded publication in peer-reviewed journals
Partnerships with national and international research institutions
These reforms elevated MSU's research profile and increased its competitiveness for research grants and academic
recognition.
Cultural-Scientific Integration
One of Dr. Masnar's signature contributions was his insistence that modern scientific methods could—and should
—coexist with respect for traditional knowledge systems. He supported interdisciplinary research projects
documenting ethnoscience among indigenous groups in Mindanao, which preserved traditional ecological
knowledge while subjecting it to rigorous academic inquiry. This approach resonated deeply with Maranao cultural
values while advancing the university's scientific mission.
Research and Publications
Dr. Masnar's scholarly work focuses on the intersection of organizational management, institutional trust, and the
social dynamics of higher education in conflict-affected regions.
Organizational Health Studies
One of his most cited works examines Organizational Health at Mindanao State University, a quantitative and
qualitative study assessing how administrative structures impact faculty effectiveness and the overall academic
environment. This research provided empirical evidence for administrative reforms and highlighted the challenges
of maintaining institutional integrity in a post-conflict setting.

PAGE 5
Institutional Trust Research
Dr. Masnar conducted groundbreaking research on the factors affecting institutional trust among students at
MSU. This study examined how social trust, perceived corruption, and institutional performance influence
students' confidence in their university—a critical factor in retention and academic success. His findings have
implications for university governance across the Philippines, particularly in regions with histories of political
instability.
Peace Education Scholarship
Through his administrative role, Dr. Masnar supported and contributed to research on student perceptions of the
Mindanao conflict. These studies aimed to understand how young people in the region process narratives of
conflict and how education can foster national unity and solidarity. This research directly informed curriculum
development and extension programming.
Publications and Dissemination
Dr. Masnar's work has been published in regional and international journals, and he has presented at academic
conferences focused on higher education in Southeast Asia. His research is frequently cited in studies on
institutional governance, peace education, and indigenous knowledge systems.
Recognition and Awards
Dr. Masnar's career is distinguished by numerous institutional honors that reflect his impact on MSU and the
broader academic community.
Institutional Leadership Honors
Dual Vice Chancellor Designation: The rare distinction of being designated twice as Vice Chancellor/Vice
President for Research and Extension represents the highest level of institutional confidence in his leadership
abilities.
Loyalty and Service Awards: Dr. Masnar has been honored multiple times during MSU's annual Loyalty
Awards ceremonies, which recognize personnel who have dedicated decades to the university's growth and
stability.
Senior Academic Leadership: His status as a veteran administrator earned him positions on elite university
bodies, including advisory roles with the MSU Board of Regents and participation in system-wide strategic
planning committees.
Professional Distinctions
Expert in Public Administration: Regional government agencies have recognized Dr. Masnar as a leading
expert on public policy and indigenous integration, frequently calling on him as a consultant.
Research Mentorship Excellence: He has been commended for his role in developing the next generation
of scholars at MSU, with many of his mentees now leading research initiatives across the university system.
Peace and Cultural Advocacy Awards: Local and regional peace-building organizations have recognized
Dr. Masnar's efforts in promoting intercultural understanding and dialogue within academic settings.

PAGE 6
Challenges and Controversies
While Dr. Masnar's career has been marked by notable achievements, his tenure also coincided with significant
challenges facing MSU and the broader Marawi community.
Institutional Resource Constraints
Like many state universities in the Philippines, MSU has long struggled with inadequate funding and infrastructure.
Dr. Masnar frequently faced the challenge of maintaining research quality and supporting faculty development with
limited resources. His ability to secure external grants and partnerships became crucial to sustaining OVCRED's
operations.
Navigating Political Dynamics
MSU operates within a complex political environment, where regional, ethnic, and religious affiliations can
influence university governance. Dr. Masnar had to navigate these dynamics carefully, balancing the interests of
different stakeholder groups while maintaining academic integrity and institutional neutrality.
Post-Marawi Siege Impact
The 2017 Siege of Marawi—a five-month armed conflict that devastated the city—profoundly impacted MSU. The
university was forced to relocate temporarily, and many facilities were damaged or destroyed. While the timeline of
Dr. Masnar's tenure in relation to this event is not definitively documented, the institutional trauma affected all
MSU administrators and faculty. Rebuilding research capacity in the aftermath required extraordinary resilience
and strategic planning.
Legacy
Dr. Otengue Masnar's legacy at MSU is multifaceted, extending beyond his administrative accomplishments to
encompass a vision of education as a transformative force in conflict-affected regions.
Institutionalization of Peace Education
Dr. Masnar's most enduring contribution may be his role in making peace education a core institutional value at
MSU. By integrating peace-building concepts into research and extension work, he ensured that future generations
of students and faculty would approach their academic work through a lens of social responsibility and conflict
resolution.
Model for Cultural-Scientific Integration
His success in harmonizing traditional Maranao values with modern scientific standards provides a replicable
model for other universities serving indigenous and minority communities. Dr. Masnar demonstrated that
respecting cultural heritage and pursuing academic excellence are not mutually exclusive—they can reinforce each
other when approached thoughtfully.

PAGE 7
Development of Research Infrastructure
The professionalization of MSU's research culture under Dr. Masnar's leadership created lasting institutional
capacity. The systems, mentorship networks, and quality standards he established continue to shape research
practices at the university.
Inspiration for Future Leaders
As a Maranao scholar who rose to the highest levels of academic administration, Dr. Masnar serves as an
inspiration for students from marginalized communities. His career trajectory demonstrates that excellence,
integrity, and cultural pride can coexist and propel individuals to positions of institutional leadership.
Personal Values and Philosophy
Throughout his career, Dr. Masnar emphasized several core values that shaped his leadership style and institutional
priorities:
Academic Integrity: He maintained strict standards for research ethics and transparency, even when political or
financial pressures might have suggested shortcuts.
Evidence-Based Practice: Dr. Masnar insisted that administrative decisions be grounded in data and research,
modeling the scientific approach he expected from faculty.
Social Impact: He consistently evaluated research and extension programs based on their potential to improve
lives in surrounding communities, particularly among vulnerable populations.
Inclusiveness: Dr. Masnar advocated for research that gave voice to marginalized groups, including indigenous
peoples, women, and conflict-affected populations.
Preservation of Indigenous Identity: While embracing modern academic standards, he remained committed to
documenting and preserving the cultural knowledge systems of Mindanao's diverse ethnic groups.
