Bai Dimple I. Mastura
Bai Dimple I. Mastura is a Filipino politician serving as the
representative of the lone district of Maguindanao del Norte in the
House of Representatives of the Philippines. She is part of a new
generation of leaders in the Bangsamoro region and is recognized
for her role as a Muslim woman in national governance.
Her public life reflects a continuing shift in Bangsamoro politics,
where women are increasingly taking on visible leadership roles at
both local and national levels.
Background
Bai Dimple Mastura comes from a political family in Maguindanao
del Norte, a province within the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in
Muslim Mindanao (BARMM). Her background is rooted in local
governance and public service, shaped by the political and social
environment of central Mindanao.
Her identity as a bai (a traditional title for a noble or respected woman in Moro society) also carries cultural
weight, signaling both heritage and leadership within the community.

PAGE 2
Education
Publicly available information on her formal education is limited in widely accessible sources. However, her
professional trajectory indicates training and experience aligned with governance, administration, and public
leadership.
Political career
Entry into public service
Bai Dimple Mastura entered public life through local governance in Maguindanao, where she became involved in
administrative and political roles prior to her election to Congress.
Her rise reflects a broader pattern in Bangsamoro politics, where local leadership often serves as a pathway to
national office.
Member of the House of Representatives
She was elected as the representative of the lone district of Maguindanao del Norte following the division of the
former Maguindanao province into two separate provinces, Maguindanao del Norte and Maguindanao del Sur.
As a member of the House of Representatives of the Philippines, she participates in national legislation while
representing the interests of her constituency in the Bangsamoro region.
Her role includes:
crafting and supporting legislation
addressing local development concerns
linking national policy with regional realities
Contributions
Bai Dimple Mastura’s contributions are often seen in the context of representation and inclusion.
Regional representation – giving voice to Maguindanao del Norte in national policymaking
Women in leadership – serving as an example of Muslim women participating in high-level governance
Community engagement – maintaining links between local communities and national institutions
Her presence in Congress reflects ongoing efforts to ensure that Bangsamoro concerns are part of national
conversations.
Legacy
Bai Dimple Mastura’s public image is tied to the idea of emerging leadership in the Bangsamoro.
She represents a shift from traditionally male-dominated political structures toward more inclusive participation,
particularly for women in Muslim Mindanao.

PAGE 3
Her career continues to evolve, but her role already signals a broader transformation in how leadership is defined in
the region.
Recognition
She is recognized within her constituency and the wider Bangsamoro region as a key political figure representing
Maguindanao del Norte.
Her position in Congress places her among the visible Muslim women leaders in the Philippines today.
Challenges
Her role comes with challenges that include:
navigating complex local political dynamics
addressing development issues in underserved communities
balancing national legislative work with constituency needs
These challenges are part of the broader realities of governance in the Bangsamoro region.
Death
As of available information, Bai Dimple I. Mastura is alive and actively serving as representative of Maguindanao
del Norte.

Michael O. Mastura
Atty. Michael Ong Mastura (born March 14, 1941) is a Filipino
lawyer, legislator, historian, and peace negotiator who has spent
more than six decades at the intersection of Philippine constitutional
law, Islamic jurisprudence, and Bangsamoro political history. Born
into the royal lineage of the Sultanate of Maguindanao in Sultan
Kudarat, he grew up with a foot in two very different worlds: one
shaped by the centuries-old rituals and authority structures of a pre-
colonial Sultanate, the other by the demands of a modern
democratic republic. The remarkable thing about his career is that
he didn't choose between those worlds. He spent his life making
them talk to each other.
He is the lead researcher behind Presidential Decree No. 1083, the
Code of Muslim Personal Laws of the Philippines (1977), and the
man most responsible for designing the country's Shari'ah court
system. He served three terms as a congressman for the First
District of Maguindanao and Cotabato City, where he shepherded
landmark legislation on Islamic banking and regional education.
After leaving Congress, he joined the Moro Islamic Liberation
Front (MILF) Peace Negotiating Panel as its constitutional expert,
earning a label that stuck when the Manila Standard used it in 2025:
the "Moro Constitutionalist."<ref name="bta2025">Template:Cite
news</ref>
That label captures something essential. Mastura has never argued
that the Bangsamoro should walk away from the Philippine
republic. His position, held consistently across six decades of legal
and political work, is that the republic is spacious enough to
accommodate the full diversity of its peoples, including those who
trace their lineage to pre-colonial Sultanates, observe Islamic law in
family matters, and carry a collective memory of sovereign
governance that predates Spanish colonization by more than a
century. Making that case, through legislation, litigation,
scholarship, and negotiation, is the thread that runs through
everything he has done.

Early Life and Royal Lineage
Birth and Origins in Sultan Kudarat
Michael Ong Mastura was born on March 14, 1941, in Sultan
Kudarat, a municipality in the province of Maguindanao.<ref
name="wikipedia">Wikipedia. "Michael Mastura." Last modified
November 17, 2025. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Mastura</ref> The town itself is named after the most
celebrated ancestor of the Mastura clan, Sultan Muhammad Dipatuan Kudarat, the 7th Sultan of Maguindanao,
who reigned from approximately 1619 to 1671 and earned a place in Philippine history for his sustained resistance
against Spanish colonial invasions.<ref name="kudarat_wiki">Wikipedia. "Muhammad Kudarat." Last modified
December 2025. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad_Kudarat</ref>
Growing up in a place named after your forefather is not a small thing. It means history isn't something you
encounter in a textbook. It is the road under your feet, the title people use when they address your family, and the
weight carried by your surname at every gathering of elders.

PAGE 3
Mastura's father, Datu Usngan Mastura, was a prince and the custodian of the family's Tarsila, the genealogical
manuscript that traces the lineage of Maguindanaon royal houses across generations. In Maguindanaon culture, the
Tarsila is far more than a family tree. It functions as a legal document, a proof of sovereignty, and a political
instrument: recording not just birth and descent, but the succession of titles, the allocation of territorial authority,
and the covenants made between ruling families and their subjects.<ref name="rulers_book">Mastura, Michael O.
The Rulers of Magindanao in Modern History, 1515-1903: Continuity and Change in a Traditional Realm of
Southern Philippines. Quezon City: Ateneo de Manila University Press, 2023.</ref> Mastura would eventually
draw on this tradition in his scholarly work to build a case for the historical sovereignty of the Maguindanao
Sultanates under international law, a legal argument with direct implications for the Bangsamoro peace process.
One detail in his family background adds another dimension to his identity: Mastura is of Chinese ancestry on one
side of his family, with grandparents who migrated to the Philippines in the early 20th century.<ref
name="wikipedia" /> He is, in other words, simultaneously a Datu heir to a Sultanate, a Filipino citizen shaped by
colonial and post-colonial institutions, and the descendant of immigrants who wove themselves into the fabric of
Mindanao society. It is a quietly fitting biography for someone who spent his career weaving together strands that
others assumed could not be combined.
The Sultanate of Maguindanao and Its Historical Weight
The Sultanate of Maguindanao was one of the most powerful Islamic polities in Southeast Asia during the 17th and
18th centuries. Under Sultan Muhammad Dipatuan Kudarat, it reached its territorial apex, encompassing vast areas
of what is now Central and Southern Mindanao, including regions corresponding to modern-day Cotabato, Sultan
Kudarat province, Maguindanao, and parts of Zamboanga. The Sultan maintained diplomatic and trade
relationships with the Dutch East India Company, the Brunei Sultanate, and other regional powers, generating a
body of written treaties that Mastura would later study and document as evidence of the Sultanate's standing under
international law.<ref name="rulers_book" />
To grow up inside this tradition is to carry a keen, lived awareness that the Philippine state, as currently organized,
represents a particular, and contestable, set of choices about governance, sovereignty, and identity. For Mastura,
that awareness became not a source of separatism but of something more precise: a demand that the Philippine
legal order take seriously the pre-colonial and colonial-era political realities of Muslim Mindanao, and find ways to
integrate them within a shared constitutional framework.
Education and the Formation of a Legal Mind
For all the grandeur of his lineage, Mastura was a serious student in the formal Western legal tradition. He earned
both his Bachelor of Arts and his Bachelor of Laws from Notre Dame University in Cotabato City.<ref
name="nd_alumni">Notre Dame University, Cotabato City. College of Law. Alumni records listing Mastura's BA
and LLB degrees.</ref> Notre Dame Cotabato, operated by the Oblates of Mary Immaculate, was a notably
ecumenical institution in the heart of Muslim Mindanao. Learning the tools of Philippine law inside a Catholic
university in a Muslim-majority region was, in itself, an early preparation for the career Mastura would build: one
that required genuine comfort with difference and a steady ability to think across cultural and religious boundaries.
He went on to complete his Master of Laws (LL.M.) at the University of the Philippines.<ref
name="up_profile">University of the Philippines. UP Tuklas Research Portal. "Author Profile: Michael O.
Mastura." Confirms LL.M. from UP and documents graduate research focus on legal pluralism.</ref> UP's College
of Law, the intellectual engine of the Philippine legal establishment, sharpened him on the hardest constitutional
questions the country was capable of generating. His graduate work centered on the concept of legal pluralism: the
idea that a single national jurisdiction can, and in some cases must, accommodate more than one system of law for
different communities within it.

PAGE 4
Legal pluralism was not a radical notion in comparative jurisprudence. Nations from India to Indonesia to Morocco
had found ways to maintain civil codes alongside customary or religious law for personal and family matters. What
was genuinely bold, in the Philippine context, was arguing that the country's secular republican framework could
and should make room for Shari'ah, not as a foreign concession, but as the legitimate legal heritage of an
indigenous people who had been part of the archipelago long before Spanish colonization arrived. That became
Mastura's core legal argument, and he spent the rest of his career building it, clause by careful clause.
The 1971 Constitutional Convention
Mastura's first major appearance on the national stage came when he was elected as a delegate from Maguindanao
to the 1971 Philippine Constitutional Convention, the body convened to draft a new Philippine constitution.<ref
name="concon">Philippine Archives. Records of the 1971 Constitutional Convention: Delegate Interventions,
Maguindanao. Manila: National Historical Commission of the Philippines.</ref> He was already, by then, a young
man with a sharp legal mind and a clearly articulated political vision, and the Convention was his first opportunity
to translate those qualities into formal constitutional advocacy.
His interventions focused on a single overarching critique: that the Philippine Constitution operated on
assumptions of a homogeneous Filipino national identity that effectively erased the distinct cultural, legal, and
historical identities of Muslim Filipinos. This was not a polite suggestion. It was a challenge to the foundational
assumptions of the republic itself.
Mastura argued that genuine national unity, the kind that holds over time, cannot be built by ignoring the distinct
character of constituent peoples. It requires affirmative recognition of difference and the construction of
institutional arrangements that allow different communities to participate in governance on terms they can actually
accept.
The Convention's work was ultimately derailed by Marcos's declaration of martial law in 1972 and replaced by the
1973 Constitution. But Mastura's arguments did not vanish with the Convention. They entered the policy record,
shaped the thinking of younger Bangsamoro scholars and advocates, and eventually found partial expression in the
legislation he would help draft just a few years later.
Presidential Decree No. 1083: The Code of Muslim Personal Laws
Background and the Brief
In 1977, the Marcos administration promulgated Presidential Decree No. 1083, formally known as the Code of
Muslim Personal Laws of the Philippines. The law recognized Shari'ah in the Philippines for the first time as a
formal legal system, governing matters of marriage, divorce, inheritance, and family relations among Muslim
Filipinos.<ref name="pd1083">Republic of the Philippines. Presidential Decree No. 1083, Code of Muslim
Personal Laws of the Philippines. Promulgated February 4, 1977.
https://lawphil.net/statutes/presdec/pd1977/pd_1083_1977.html</ref> It was a landmark not only in Philippine
legal history but in the broader history of pluralist governance in Southeast Asia.
Mastura was the lead researcher on the committee that drafted the Code. His academic work on legal pluralism
provided the theoretical scaffolding; his political relationships and cultural credibility gave him access to
community leaders and religious scholars whose input shaped the substantive provisions. The result was a law that
drew on classical Islamic jurisprudence while being carefully calibrated to operate within the framework of the
Philippine civil law system. Getting that balance right required exceptional legal dexterity.

PAGE 5
Designing the Shari'ah Court System
Perhaps even more significant than the Code itself was the institutional infrastructure Mastura designed to carry it
out. He was the key figure in establishing the Shari'ah District Courts and Shari'ah Circuit Courts, specialized
judicial bodies with jurisdiction over personal law matters involving Muslim Filipinos.<ref name="pd1083" />
Crucially, he insisted that these courts be integrated into the national judiciary under the supervisory authority of
the Supreme Court of the Philippines, rather than being set up as a parallel or external system.
This was a deliberate choice, and a politically important one. It meant that Shari'ah justice in the Philippines was
not a carve-out for separatism but an expression of inclusive constitutional governance. The courts Mastura
designed were not foreign bodies grafted onto Philippine law. They were Filipino courts, staffed by Filipino judges,
operating under Philippine procedural rules, but applying substantive Islamic law to matters where Muslim
Filipinos were entitled to be governed by the legal traditions of their own faith.
The Luwaran and the Recovery of Indigenous Legal Tradition
Alongside his work on PD 1083, Mastura conducted foundational scholarship on the Luwaran, the traditional
Maguindanao code of laws that had governed customary matters in the region before the introduction of Philippine
civil law.<ref name="luwaran">Mastura, Michael O. "The Luwaran: Maguindanao Customary Law and Its
Relationship to the Code of Muslim Personal Laws." Scholarly monograph.</ref>
Critics of Shari'ah in the Philippines had sometimes argued that Islamic law was a foreign imposition that didn't
reflect the authentic indigenous legal tradition of Mindanao. Mastura's research on the Luwaran dismantled that
argument point by point. He demonstrated that the Maguindanao people had a sophisticated, written legal tradition
in continuous use for centuries; that this tradition drew on Islamic jurisprudence as one of its sources but was
thoroughly adapted to local conditions and social structures; and that its principles were broadly compatible with
the Muslim Personal Law code being developed under PD 1083.
Legally, this scholarship provided a basis for arguing that PD 1083 was not imposing foreign law on unwilling
communities but rather recognizing and codifying a tradition that was already alive and operative. Politically, it
gave the Bangsamoro case for legal autonomy a historical depth and indigenous legitimacy that no outside critic
could easily dismiss.
Legislative Legacy: Three Terms in Congress
Mastura served as Representative for the First District of Maguindanao and Cotabato City in the House of
Representatives from 1987 to 1995, three successive terms under the restored democratic order of the post-Marcos
era.<ref name="senate_issuances">Senate of the Philippines. Legislative Record of Representative Michael O.
Mastura (1987-1995). Issuances Library. https://issuances-library.senate.gov.ph/congress-author/mastura-michael-
o</ref> His legislative record in this period stands out not for sheer volume but for its strategic coherence: virtually
everything he worked on was oriented toward building the institutional foundations of a self-governing,
economically capable Muslim Mindanao.
Republic Act No. 6848: The Al-Amanah Islamic Investment Bank
The most economically significant legislation of his congressional years was Republic Act No. 6848 (1990), which
restructured and rechristened the existing Philippine Amanah Bank into the Al-Amanah Islamic Investment Bank
of the Philippines.<ref name="ra6848">Republic of the Philippines. Presidential Decree No. 264, Establishment of

PAGE 6
the Philippine Amanah Bank (1973), subsequently restructured under Republic Act No. 6848, Al-Amanah Islamic
Investment Bank of the Philippines Charter, enacted January 26, 1990. The founding concept is attributed to the
late Senator Mamintal A.J. Tamano.</ref>
The original institution was not Mastura's creation. The Philippine Amanah Bank was established through
Presidential Decree No. 264, signed by President Marcos in 1973, and the founding concept was developed by the
late Senator Mamintal A.J. Tamano, who recognized early that Muslim Mindanao needed a financial institution
aligned with Islamic principles. What Mastura contributed through RA 6848 was the institutional strengthening and
rechartering of that original vision, transforming it into a formally constituted Islamic investment bank operating
explicitly on the principle of profit-sharing rather than interest, in accordance with the Islamic prohibition on riba
(usury).
This was more than a technical financial reform. For Muslim Filipinos who observed the Islamic prohibition on
interest, conventional banking was a system they could not fully participate in on their own terms. The Al-Amanah
bank gave them access to formal financial services, savings accounts, business financing, trade credit, structured in
a way consistent with their religious obligations.
Mastura had, in fact, served as the bank's first President and Chief Executive Officer from 1984 to 1986, giving
him firsthand operational knowledge of what the institution needed to function effectively. The RA 6848 charter
reflected that practical experience directly.
Higher Education and Regional Development
Mastura was also instrumental in strengthening the educational infrastructure of his region. He played a key role in
legislation formalizing the Mindanao State University System as a regional academic anchor, and he authored the
bill that converted agricultural schools in Maguindanao into what became the Maguindanao State College, an
institution designed to provide practically oriented post-secondary education to a historically underserved
population.<ref name="ra7474">Republic of the Philippines. Republic Act No. 7474, Establishment of
Maguindanao State College. Enacted April 10, 1992. https://www.officialgazette.gov.ph/1992/04/10/republic-act-
no-7474/</ref> He also worked on measures to increase national government financial support to municipalities in
the region, giving local governments greater fiscal capacity to deliver basic services.
Taken together, his legislative record shows a coherent governing philosophy: that Bangsamoro autonomy is not
simply about political recognition but about the practical capacity to govern. That capacity requires courts, banks,
universities, and locally controlled financial resources. Mastura was building the scaffolding of a functioning sub-
national government, piece by piece, through the tools available to him in Congress.
First Deputy Minister for Muslim Affairs
Before his congressional terms, Mastura was appointed in 1981 as the first Deputy Minister of the Ministry of
Muslim Affairs under Minister Romulo Espaldon. This placed him at the center of the government's effort to
institutionalize its relationship with the Muslim minority, a relationship defined until then largely by conflict and
neglect. As Deputy Minister, he worked to build the bureaucratic architecture for state engagement with Muslim
communities, drawing on his legal training, his cultural authority as a Datu, and his relationships with both
government officials and religious leaders.
He also served as a member of the Board of Regents of Mindanao State University, the Southern Philippines
Development Authority, and the Mindanao Economic Council, positions that gave him direct influence over
regional education, economic planning, and development policy at a critical juncture in Mindanao's history.

PAGE 7
The MILF Peace Process: Constitutional Imagination at the Negotiating
Table
Transition to Peace Work
When Mastura's congressional terms ended in 1995, he moved into a different but equally influential role: senior
member and legal adviser on the Moro Islamic Liberation Front (MILF) Peace Negotiating Panel. The transition,
from a representative of the state to a representative of an armed opposition seeking a negotiated political
settlement with that same state, was significant. But in Mastura's framing, it was not a contradiction. He had always
argued that the Bangsamoro question was ultimately a constitutional question, not a military one, and that its
resolution required legal imagination rather than armed force.
On the MILF panel, he served as the movement's constitutional expert, the person responsible for ensuring that
peace agreements were drafted with what he called "constitutional elasticity": language and frameworks that could
be interpreted broadly enough to accommodate meaningful Bangsamoro autonomy without requiring the kind of
explicit constitutional amendment that Manila's political class would be unable to accept. This was technically
demanding, politically delicate work. Peace agreements are not just political documents. They are quasi-legal
instruments that will be interpreted, litigated, and argued over in courts for years after the signing ceremony.
The Substate Framework and the Concept of "Sui Generis"
At the heart of Mastura's contribution to the negotiations was his development of the concept of an asymmetric
political relationship between the Bangsamoro and the Philippine state. In interviews during the negotiations, he
described the proposed Bangsamoro entity as "sui generis," a class by itself, within the Philippine constitutional
order. This was not rhetorical flourish. It was a legally precise claim: that the Bangsamoro's situation is distinct
enough, historically, culturally, and legally, that it requires a constitutional arrangement with no exact parallel
elsewhere in the Philippine system.
Mastura was also careful about what this claim did not include. He consistently emphasized that the MILF was not
seeking secession or independence.
"We are not leaving the Republic. We are not leaving the nation state."<ref
name="gma2012">Arguillas, Carolyn O. "Amid peace negotiations, MILF to stage show of force in
Maguindanao." GMA News Online. July 5, 2012.
https://www.gmanetwork.com/news/topstories/specialreports/264357/</ref>
What the MILF sought, as Mastura articulated it, was devolution: a structural adjustment of the Philippine state to
allow for meaningful self-governance by the Bangsamoro within the republic, rather than mere administrative
decentralization. By keeping the MILF's position within a recognizable constitutional vocabulary, autonomy,
devolution, asymmetric federalism, substate arrangements, Mastura made it possible for government negotiators to
engage with it without having to confront questions of national unity that Manila could not politically process.
The MOA-AD Crisis and Its Lessons
The most painful episode of the peace process during Mastura's tenure on the panel was the collapse of the
Memorandum of Agreement on Ancestral Domain (MOA-AD) in 2008. The agreement, years in the making, was
struck down by the Supreme Court of the Philippines before it could be signed, following a campaign of political
opposition from local officials and national politicians who argued it was unconstitutional. The decision triggered
armed hostilities and a major humanitarian crisis in Central Mindanao.

PAGE 8
Mastura's public analysis of the MOA-AD crisis was direct. In remarks at a forum organized by the Human
Development Network and the UP School of Economics in September 2009, he argued that the collapse
demonstrated not a problem with the agreement's content but with the Philippine state's institutional capacity for
constitutional imagination.
"...a mindset that cannot accept another form [of political arrangement]."<ref name="hdnph">Mastura,
Michael O. "Prepared Remarks." Public Forum: GRP-Moro Conflict: Is There an End in Sight?
Human Security and Human Development Revisited. Human Development Network and UP School of
Economics, September 19, 2009. https://www.hdnph.org/prepared-remarks-of-dr-michael-o-
mastura/</ref>
The MOA-AD crisis did not end the peace process. It reset it, painfully and at great cost. The negotiations
eventually produced the Comprehensive Agreement on the Bangsamoro in 2014, and the Bangsamoro Organic Law
that followed, creating the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM), represented a
partial but significant vindication of the constitutional framework Mastura and the MILF panel had spent years
developing.
The Bangsamoro Transition Authority and Continuing Relevance
Even in his eighties, Mastura has remained an active and influential voice on Bangsamoro governance. In March
2025, he was quoted in the Manila Standard defending the legality of presidential appointments to the Bangsamoro
Transition Authority (BTA), the interim governing body overseeing the transition to full BARMM operations. His
argument was characteristic: the appointments were legally sound, the Transition Authority needed performance-
based and competent leadership to function effectively, and critics were confusing process with substance.<ref
name="bta2025" />
The Manila Standard identified him in that report as the "Moro Constitutionalist," a phrase that has since become a
standard descriptor for his career. He is not simply an advocate for Bangsamoro interests in the way a community
organizer or political campaigner might be. He is, specifically and distinctively, a constitutionalist: someone who
believes that the path to Bangsamoro dignity and self-determination runs through the Philippine constitutional
order, not around it.
He has also continued to appear as amicus curiae before the Supreme Court of the Philippines in cases involving
Shari'ah and indigenous rights.<ref name="sc_amicus">Supreme Court of the Philippines. Mastura has appeared as
amicus curiae in multiple cases involving Shari'ah and indigenous rights. Specific case citations available through
the SC e-Library at https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph</ref> It is a role that places him in the peculiar position of
being simultaneously an advocate for the Bangsamoro and an authoritative expert operating within the very
institutional framework he has spent his career trying to reform.
Scholarly Works: History as Political Intervention
Mastura's published books are not purely academic exercises. They are political interventions, careful, evidence-
based arguments for propositions with direct bearing on the legal and governance status of Muslim Mindanao, and
they have to be understood in that context.

PAGE 9
The Rulers of Magindanao in Modern History, 1515-1903 (2023 Edition)
This book, published in an updated edition in 2023 by the Ateneo de Manila University Press, is Mastura's most
comprehensive historical work, covering nearly four centuries of dynastic rule in the Maguindanao Sultanate.<ref
name="rulers_2023">Mastura, Michael O. The Rulers of Magindanao in Modern History, 1515-1903: Continuity
and Change in a Traditional Realm of Southern Philippines. Quezon City: Ateneo de Manila University Press,
2023. https://unipress.ateneo.edu/product/rulers-magindanao-modern-history-1515-1903-continuity-and-change-
traditional-realm-southern</ref>
At its core is what Mastura calls the "Mastura List," a documented inventory of international treaties signed by the
Maguindanao Sultanates with foreign powers, including Spain, the Netherlands, and Great Britain. The legal
significance is substantial. International law recognizes that sovereign entities have the capacity to make treaties;
conversely, a treaty record is evidence of sovereignty. By documenting 35 such international agreements, Mastura
is making a concrete argument, in the language of international law, that the Maguindanao Sultanate was a
sovereign state, treated as such by the major powers of its day, and that the historical basis for Bangsamoro claims
to political recognition is considerably stronger than critics have acknowledged.
A review in MindaNews described the book as the work of "an intellectual giant" and praised its combination of
documentary rigor with accessibility for general readers.<ref name="mindanews_review">MindaNews. "Review:
Great Book by an Intellectual Giant." April 2023. https://mindanews.com/booksmindanews/2023/04/review-great-
book-by-an-intellectual-giant/</ref> The 2023 edition incorporates newly available archival material and updated
scholarly commentary.
Bangsamoro Quest: The Birth of the Moro Islamic Liberation Front (2012)
This book provides the definitive insider account of the MILF's origins, ideology, and evolution as a political and
military organization.<ref name="bangsamoro_quest">Mastura, Michael O. Bangsamoro Quest: The Birth of the
Moro Islamic Liberation Front. Cotabato City: MILF Peace Negotiating Panel, 2012.</ref> Written with the
authority of someone who sat on the MILF's peace panel, it traces the ideological distance between the MILF and
its predecessor, the Moro National Liberation Front (MNLF), a distinction that matters enormously for
understanding the different political visions competing within the Bangsamoro peace process.
Where the MNLF began with a primarily nationalist orientation rooted in the idea of a Moro homeland, the MILF,
as Mastura traces it, developed a more specifically Islamic identity grounded in the religious obligations of Muslim
Filipinos and a vision of governance rooted in Islamic political philosophy. The book argues that this distinction
has concrete implications for the kind of political settlement that can satisfy MILF's core constituency.
Muslim Filipino Experience (1984)
Mastura's earliest major work, a collection of essays on the sociopolitical identity of Muslims in a majority-
Christian state, remains relevant precisely because the questions it raises are still not fully resolved.<ref
name="muslim_exp">Mastura, Michael O. Muslim Filipino Experience: Essays on a Minority Experience in a
Pluralist Society. Manila: 1984.</ref> Written in 1984, in the shadow of martial law and an ongoing insurgency, it
grapples with questions of citizenship, belonging, and the relationship between religious identity and national
identity that continue to shape debates about the Bangsamoro today.
What distinguishes these essays from polemical writing on the same themes is Mastura's insistence on engaging
seriously with the Philippine state's perspective, on understanding why it has responded to the Bangsamoro
question the way it has, and on identifying the legal and institutional levers that could move that response in a more

PAGE 10
constructive direction. The voice throughout is that of a pluralist: someone who wants the republic to be better, not
dismantled.
Awards, Recognition, and Institutional Roles
In 1981, Mastura was named one of the Ten Outstanding Young Men (TOYM) of the Philippines in the category of
Law and Muslim Affairs.<ref name="toym">Junior Chamber International Philippines. "TOYM Awardees, 1981:
Law and Muslim Affairs, Michael O. Mastura." Award records on file with JCI Philippines.</ref> The TOYM
Award, administered by Junior Chamber International Philippines, is one of the country's most prestigious citations
for young professionals, and Mastura's recognition in it reflected both his early legal accomplishments and his
broader civic contributions.
He has also received the Datu Order of Kalantiao, the highest recognition for legal service in the Philippines, and
has been repeatedly invited to appear as amicus curiae before the Supreme Court of the Philippines in cases
touching on Shari'ah, indigenous rights, and the legal status of the Bangsamoro. The latter role is particularly
telling: the highest court in the country has turned to Mastura, repeatedly, as its authoritative expert on matters at
the intersection of Islamic jurisprudence and Philippine constitutional law.
Beyond his legal and legislative work, Mastura has been an institution-builder. He co-founded the Southeast Asian
Shari'ah Law Association and the Sultan Kudarat Islamic Academy, and established the Islamic Welfare Society of
the Philippines. These efforts, undertaken alongside everything else, reflect his understanding that changing the
situation of Muslim Filipinos requires not just legal reform but the development of civil society infrastructure
capable of sustaining advocacy, education, and community development over the long term.
Legacy
Assessing the legacy of someone still actively engaged in the work his life has been about is not a simple task.
With Mastura, the challenge is compounded by the fact that the project he has devoted himself to, the
constitutionalization of Bangsamoro identity, the integration of Islamic legal traditions into the Philippine legal
order, the creation of durable political institutions for Muslim Mindanao, is genuinely unfinished. The BARMM
exists, but its transition is incomplete. The Shari'ah courts function, but they face resource constraints and
unresolved jurisdictional questions. The peace process has produced agreements, but their implementation remains
contested and fragile.
In this context, Mastura's most important legacy may not be any single law, treaty, or book. It may be a way of
thinking about the problem, a constitutional imagination, to borrow his own vocabulary, that has made it possible
to approach the Bangsamoro question as one capable of legal solution rather than as a permanent conflict requiring
permanent military management.
He demonstrated, through his career, that it is possible to be simultaneously committed to the integrity of the
Philippine constitutional order and to the full recognition of Bangsamoro identity within it. These are not
contradictory positions. The apparent tension between them can be worked through with sufficient legal creativity
and political will. That is not a trivial demonstration. In a political environment where both extreme nationalism
and separatism have powerful constituencies, the case for constitutional pluralism is difficult to make and easy to
ignore. Mastura has spent more than sixty years making it, patiently and with remarkable consistency.
The young Bangsamoro scholars, lawyers, and civil servants now working within the BARMM apparatus, drafting
codes, litigating cases, running institutions, are in a meaningful sense working within a framework that Mastura
helped design. That may be the most lasting form of legacy a legal scholar can have: not a monument with his
name on it, but a way of working that outlasts him because it was absorbed by the people who came after.

PAGE 11
Further Reading

Traditional Realm of Southern Philippines. Quezon City: Ateneo de Manila University Press, 2023.

MILF Peace Negotiating Panel, 2012.

Philippines. 1977.

Online. July 5, 2012.

Udtog Matalam
Datu Udtog Matalam (born c. late 1890s, Pagalungan, Cotabato;
died 1983) was a Maguindanaoan statesman, military leader, and
hereditary aristocrat whose life spanned the American colonial
period, the Japanese occupation, the birth of the Philippine republic,
and the opening of the modern Bangsamoro self-determination
struggle.
He governed the undivided "Empire Province" of Cotabato for five
terms, making him one of the most powerful local executives in
20th-century Mindanao.
He is best remembered for founding the Muslim Independence
Movement (MIM) on May 1, 1968, a watershed act that redirected
Moro political energy away from accommodation with Manila and
toward a formal demand for sovereignty.
His actions did not produce an independent state, but they set in
motion a chain of events that led directly to the armed struggle of
the Moro National Liberation Front (MNLF) and, later, the Moro
Islamic Liberation Front (MILF), movements whose legacy
continues to shape the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim
Mindanao today.

EARLY LIFE AND LINEAGE
Datu Udtog Matalam was born in Pagalungan, in the heart of the
Cotabato valley, sometime in the final decade of the 19th century.

PAGE 2
Multiple (polygamous household, per
Maguindanaoan custom)
Children (notable)
Datu Guimid "Jimmy" Matalam
Datu Udtog "Jun" Matalam Jr.
Datu Norodin Matalam
Notability
The Maguindanaoan statesman who
formalized the Bangsamoro
independence struggle, founding the
Muslim Independence Movement in
1968 and catalyzing the rise of the
MNLF and MILF.
Known For
Five-term Governor of the Empire
Province of Cotabato; founding of the
Muslim Independence Movement
(MIM); co-founding of Central
Mindanao Colleges; anti-Japanese
guerrilla leadership during World War
II
He was Maguindanaoan, a member of the ethnic group traditionally
described as the "people of the flood plains," who for centuries
dominated the broad river basin that runs through central Mindanao.
His birth placed him squarely inside the region's hereditary ruling
class.
His father held the title of Sultan of Pagalungan, a royal house
historically aligned with the Buayan Sultanate, one of the most
powerful Islamic polities in pre-colonial and early colonial
Mindanao.
Tragedy struck the family when Udtog was only four years old.
His father was defeated in battle and beheaded by Datu Mantawil,
the Sultan of Kabuntalan, at a site still known today as Pagagawan,
a Maguindanaoan word that translates roughly as "the Battlefield."
The killing was part of the endemic clan warfare that characterized
datu politics during the early colonial era, when American
administrators had not yet fully consolidated control over the
interior.
Despite losing his father so young, Matalam inherited the full weight of his family's socio-political prestige.
In Maguindanaoan aristocratic culture, lineage and blood rank carried enormous authority, and the son of a sultan
was still a son of a sultan regardless of the circumstances of the father's death.
That inherited standing would become the platform from which Matalam built his entire public life.
EDUCATION AND COLONIAL-ERA CAREER
Matalam's formal schooling was shaped by the practical demands of the American colonial administration rather
than by any aspiration to a professional degree.
Unlike his brother-in-law Congressman Salipada Pendatun, who traveled to Manila and earned a law degree,
Matalam received a basic education that combined traditional Islamic instruction with the civic and administrative
training the American colonial system provided for local leaders in Muslim Mindanao.
His early career showed that he understood exactly what role the colonizers expected Muslim elites to play, and he
played it well.
In 1914, when Matalam was still a young man, American authorities appointed him as Assistant Colony
Superintendent of a mixed agricultural colony in Pagalungan.
The colony was deliberately designed to settle both Muslim and Christian settlers in the same area, and Matalam's
job was to manage the Muslim half of that experiment, acting as a trusted intermediary between the colonial
bureaucracy and the local population.
He also served as a District School Inspector, traveling across the region to encourage Muslim families to enroll
their children in the Western-style colonial school system.

PAGE 3
This was no small task. Conservative Muslim communities were understandably cautious about sending their
children into schools run by Christian American administrators, and it took someone with both standing and tact to
make any headway.
Matalam's willingness to serve in these roles spoke to a pragmatic intelligence: he recognized that working within
the colonial system, rather than against it, was the most effective way to protect and advance the interests of his
people during that particular moment in history.
WORLD WAR II AND GUERRILLA LEADERSHIP
When Japan invaded the Philippines in December 1941, Datu Udtog Matalam made a clear and unambiguous
choice: he refused to collaborate with the occupiers and organized an armed resistance instead.
This was not an automatic or cost-free decision.
Collaboration offered material rewards, personal security, and continued political influence under Japanese
patronage.
Matalam chose the harder path.
He organized an effective guerrilla network across central Mindanao, operating alongside his brother-in-law
Salipada Pendatun and American officers who had evaded capture after the fall of organized Philippine resistance.
His forces protected civilian populations from Japanese reprisals and disrupted Japanese communication lines,
limiting the occupiers' ability to move freely across the interior.
The wartime experience transformed Matalam's public image in ways that proved lasting.
He had already been a figure of hereditary authority, a man people followed because of who his family was.
The guerrilla campaign added something different to that: the reputation of a man people followed because of what
he himself had done.
His wartime bravery converted traditional royal prestige into broad, modern political capital, and when the war
ended and the Philippine republic was reestablished, Matalam was positioned perfectly to enter electoral politics.
POLITICAL CAREER AND EXECUTIVE GOVERNANCE
The restoration of Philippine independence in 1946 opened a new chapter in Matalam's life.
He entered civilian politics and almost immediately established himself as the dominant executive figure across the
entire undivided "Empire Province" of Cotabato, a territorial unit so vast that it has since been divided into five
separate provinces: Cotabato, South Cotabato, Sarangani, Maguindanao del Norte, and Maguindanao del Sur.
Matalam served five terms as Provincial Governor, holding office from 1946 to 1949 and again from 1955 to 1968.
Together with Salipada Pendatun, he co-led what was effectively the dominant political machine of central
Mindanao for more than two decades.
His governance style combined the instincts of a traditional datu lord with the administrative responsibilities of a
modern elected official.

PAGE 4
He was known for maintaining relative peace across a province that had its share of inter-clan tensions, working to
resolve bloody feuds (known in Maguindanaoan as mrando or rido) through mediation and the allocation of public
land rather than through force alone.
This approach kept large portions of the province functional and relatively stable during a period when much of the
Philippine countryside was caught up in political violence.
Matalam voluntarily stepped away from the governorship in 1968.
By that point, he felt increasingly marginalized by the national political shifts taking place under President
Ferdinand Marcos Sr., whose administration favored younger, nationalistic politicians over the old guard of
traditional local lords who had dominated provincial politics since independence.
It was, in many ways, a signal that the era of the hereditary datu-as-governor was drawing to a close.
What Matalam did next, however, ensured that his name would not simply fade from history.
INSTITUTIONAL CONTRIBUTIONS AND MAJOR WORKS
Beyond his executive role, Matalam left concrete institutional legacies that outlasted his time in office.
Central Mindanao Colleges
On July 3, 1947, Governor Matalam co-founded the Central Mindanao Colleges (CMC) in Kidapawan City, an
institution designed to provide accessible higher education to young people across central Mindanao, both Muslim
and Christian.
The founding of CMC reflected a genuine conviction on Matalam's part that education was one of the few tools
that could improve the material circumstances of his constituents across generational timescales.
Creation of Municipalities
Using his influence as governor, Matalam worked to convert booming agricultural settlements into properly
recognized municipal units with their own local governments.
The most personally significant of these efforts came on December 29, 1961, when President Carlos P. Garcia
signed Executive Order No. 461, formally separating a strategic section of Kabacan to create the Municipality of
Matalam in what is now North Cotabato.
The new municipality was named entirely in the Governor's honor, a recognition of his decades of service and his
role in the development of the region.
The Municipality of Matalam continues to exist as a functioning local government unit to this day, and its name
keeps the governor's memory embedded in the daily life of central Mindanao in the most literal way possible.
THE MUSLIM INDEPENDENCE MOVEMENT (MIM)
The defining act of Datu Udtog Matalam's later life came on May 1, 1968, and it was triggered by an event that
shocked and outraged Muslim Filipinos across the country.

PAGE 5
The Jabidah Massacre, which occurred in March of that year, involved the killing of young Moro military recruits
by Philippine Army officers on Corregidor Island.
The recruits had been trained as part of a covert operation aimed at destabilizing the Malaysian state of Sabah, but
when the operation was exposed and the recruits threatened to reveal what they knew, Christian officers executed a
number of them, with the full death toll remaining disputed and contested.
For many Muslims in Mindanao, the massacre crystallized longstanding grievances about their treatment within the
Philippine state: second-class citizenship, land dispossession, institutional neglect, and now state violence directed
at their young men.
Matalam responded from Pagalungan by issuing a bold manifesto.
The document established the Muslim Independence Movement (MIM), which openly and formally advocated for
the complete secession of Mindanao, Sulu, and Palawan from the Republic of the Philippines, calling for the
creation of an independent, sovereign Islamic state in the southern Philippines.
This was not a quiet or ambiguous statement.
It was a public declaration by one of the most senior Muslim political figures in the country, and it carried
enormous symbolic weight precisely because of who Matalam was: a five-term governor, a decorated guerrilla
veteran, a descendant of sultans, a man who had spent decades working within the Philippine system and was now
publicly declaring that the system had failed his people.
Matalam's original intention for the MIM appears to have been primarily political rather than military.
He likely hoped that the threat of secession would serve as a serious enough lever to force the Marcos
administration and the national government to address Muslim grievances through negotiation and reform.
The MIM did catch the attention of international actors, however, particularly Libya under Muammar Gaddafi and
Malaysia, who saw the movement as aligned with their own regional interests.
What happened next was something Matalam may not have fully anticipated.
Radicalized younger members within the MIM, most notably the student leader Nur Misuari, used the
organization's platform and international connections to access foreign military training abroad.
That training pipeline became the foundation for the Moro National Liberation Front (MNLF), formally established
by Misuari in 1972.
The MNLF's armed campaign against the Philippine government brought Mindanao to full-scale war by the early
1970s.
A subsequent split within the MNLF eventually produced the Moro Islamic Liberation Front (MILF) in 1984, a
movement that pursued its own armed struggle and eventually negotiated the peace agreement that gave birth to the
current Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao.
The direct line of causation runs from Jabidah to Matalam's manifesto to Misuari's MNLF to the MILF to the
Bangsamoro Organic Law.
Datu Udtog Matalam is, in a very real sense, the founding grandfather of the modern Bangsamoro political project.

PAGE 6
PERSONAL LIFE AND POLITICAL DYNASTY
Matalam lived according to the customs and values of traditional Maguindanaoan aristocracy throughout his life.
He maintained a polygamous household with multiple Muslim wives, consistent with both Islamic practice and the
structural logic of datu politics, where marriage alliances between ruling families served as one of the primary tools
for building and maintaining political coalitions.
This stood in contrast to many Westernized Muslim politicians of his era who married Christian women and
adopted more outwardly monogamous, modern domestic arrangements.
Matalam's commitment to traditional Maguindanaoan custom was not mere personal preference. It was also a
statement about identity, about whose side he stood on, and about what kind of leader he intended to be.
His family produced a political dynasty that has remained active in Maguindanao governance for decades after his
death.
His son Datu Guimid "Jimmy" Matalam became a Congressman and Speaker of the ARMM Regional
Legislative Assembly, and was the principal author of Republic Act No. 6734, the Organic Act that formally
established the Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao. The father sowed the seeds of Bangsamoro self-
governance; the son helped write its first legal framework.
His son Datu Udtog "Jun" Matalam Jr. served for multiple terms as the Mayor of Pagalungan, Maguindanao,
keeping the family rooted in the municipality where the patriarch was born and from which he had issued his
famous 1968 manifesto.
His son Datu Norodin Matalam served as both Vice-Governor and Provincial Governor of Maguindanao,
sustaining the family's role in provincial executive governance well into the post-ARMM period.
LEGACY, IMPACT, AND CULTURAL SIGNIFICANCE
Datu Udtog Matalam died in 1983, fifteen years after the act that defined his place in Bangsamoro history.
He did not live to see the full consequences of what the MIM set in motion, including the ARMM, the peace
agreements, or the eventual passage of the Bangsamoro Organic Law in 2018.
But his legacy is embedded in each of those developments in ways that are difficult to overstate.
He is widely regarded as the father of modern Moro secessionism, the first major political figure in the Philippines
to formally and publicly articulate the concept of an independent Moro nation as a concrete political demand rather
than a distant aspiration.
Earlier generations of Muslim political leaders, including Matalam himself in his earlier career, had sought
integration into the Philippine state on favorable terms, negotiating for autonomy, land rights, and representation
within the republic.
Matalam's 1968 manifesto broke with that tradition and established a new political vocabulary, one centered on
sovereignty, self-determination, and the right of the Bangsamoro people to govern themselves on their own terms.
He also represents one of the more remarkable personal transitions in 20th-century Philippine political history.

PAGE 7
He came to adulthood as the son of a beheaded sultan in a society still organized largely around hereditary
aristocratic authority.
He navigated the American colonial bureaucracy, the Japanese occupation, independence-era electoral politics, and
the Marcos era, adapting at each stage without losing the essential elements of who he was or where he came from.
By the time he issued the MIM manifesto, he had converted the legitimacy of a royal bloodline into the moral
authority of a democratic elder statesman, and then used that authority to challenge the very state he had spent
decades serving.
The Municipality of Matalam in North Cotabato stands as a permanent geographic reminder of his decades of local
leadership, a town that carries his name on every government document and road sign in that part of central
Mindanao.
His family continues to govern in Maguindanao.
And the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao, however imperfect, exists in part because a datu
from Pagalungan decided in 1968 that enough was enough.

title: Matuan, Inoyag Mamaroba
text:

Inoyag Mamaroba Matuan
Inoyag Mamaroba Matuan, PhD (born June 19, 1958) is a
retired Filipino hydroelectric engineer and plant manager who
dedicated over four decades to the National Power Corporation's
Agus 2 Hydroelectric Plant in Lanao del Sur. A Maranao
professional from the Bangsamoro region, Dr. Matuan rose
through the ranks from Control Operator to Plant Operations and
Maintenance Manager, becoming one of the most accomplished
technical leaders in Mindanao's energy sector. His career is
distinguished by pioneering work in computerizing operations
reporting, spearheading multiple ISO certifications, and achieving
consecutive Outstanding Ratings in plant performance audits—
cementing his legacy as a transformative figure in Philippine
hydroelectric power generation.

PAGE 2
Early Life and Background
Inoyag Mamaroba Matuan was born on June 19, 1958, in Buntong, Lanao del Sur, in the heart of the Bangsamoro
region. He comes from a Maranao family—his father, Panda Matuan Mamko, and his mother, Mamaroba Kakasi
Macalimpao, raised him with values that would later define his professional integrity and community commitment.
Growing up in a predominantly Muslim province, Matuan witnessed firsthand the challenges and opportunities
facing Mindanao's development, particularly in infrastructure and energy access.
He completed his elementary education at Marinaut Elementary School from 1966 to 1968, then moved to
Dansalan College High School for his secondary education, graduating in 1972. These formative years in Lanao del
Sur's educational institutions shaped his understanding of the region's needs and potential, particularly in technical
fields that could drive economic progress.
Matuan married Saripha Hadji Ali Matuan, and together they raised twelve children: Nasibah, Mohammad Sadiq,
Asiya, Mohammad Jamshyd, Mohammad Jamal, Jamilah, Norjannah, Norhidayah, Mohammad Jarir, Mohammad
Jamil Yahya, Mohammad Jalal, Mohammad Jabir, and Jora'nah. His ability to balance a demanding career in
hydroelectric plant operations with family responsibilities reflects the strong support system that sustained him
throughout his professional journey.
Education
Dr. Matuan's educational trajectory demonstrates a rare commitment to continuous learning across multiple
engineering disciplines and management fields. He pursued dual undergraduate degrees at Mindanao State
University (MSU), earning a Bachelor of Science in Mechanical Engineering in 1980 and a Bachelor of Science in
Electrical Engineering in 1986. This dual expertise in both mechanical and electrical systems would prove
invaluable in understanding the complex interplay of turbines, generators, and control systems at hydroelectric
plants.
Beyond his engineering foundation, Matuan recognized the importance of management competencies for
leadership roles. He enrolled at Liceo de Cagayan University in Cagayan de Oro City, completing a Master in
Management with a major in Business Management in 2001. Not content with a master's degree, he continued his
studies and earned a Doctor in Management from the same institution in 2004, becoming one of the few engineers
in the Philippine power sector to hold both technical engineering credentials and advanced management
qualifications.
In 1984, Matuan also completed a vocational course in Basic Computer Programming at Computrade in Iligan City
—a forward-thinking decision that would later enable him to computerize critical plant operations and reporting
systems.
Professional Credentials
Dr. Matuan holds an impressive array of professional licenses and eligibilities that underscore his technical
mastery:
Registered Mechanical Engineer – He passed the board examination on April 1, 1981, with a rating of 77.35%,
receiving Professional Regulation Commission (PRC) License No. 21339.
Registered Electrical Engineer – He obtained his electrical engineering license on October 1, 1987, with a rating
of 75.20% and PRC License No. 0017514.

PAGE 3
Professional Mechanical Engineer – On April 1, 1989, he earned the Professional Mechanical Engineer
designation with a rating of 76.37% and License No. 0002888, demonstrating advanced competency in his field.
Career Executive Service Eligibility – On June 25, 2006, he received Career Executive Service Eligibility (CESB
Resolution No. 6074, Series of 2008) in Cagayan de Oro City with a score of 109, qualifying him for top-level
executive positions in the Philippine government.
This combination of dual engineering licenses, professional certifications, and executive eligibility positioned
Matuan as one of the most credentialed technical leaders in the National Power Corporation system.
Career at National Power Corporation
Dr. Matuan spent his entire professional career at the Agus 1 & 2 Hydroelectric Plant Complex of the National
Power Corporation (NPC) in Pawak, Saguiaran, Lanao del Sur. His 42-year tenure from 1981 to 2023 represents
one of the longest and most distinguished careers in Philippine hydroelectric operations.
Control Operator (1981–1984)
Matuan began his career on December 21, 1981, as a Control Operator B at Agus 2 Hydroelectric Plant, reporting
to Ramon F. Ko. In this foundational role, he was responsible for the hourly recording of meter and gauge readings
from the plant's three generating units and their auxiliaries. Even at this entry level, Matuan demonstrated
innovation by converting the elevation chart into a working table for computing water stored in the forebay
elevation and calculating spilled water—an achievement that improved operational efficiency and data accuracy.
Acting Hydro Control Engineer (1984–1985)
On October 16, 1984, Matuan was promoted to Acting Hydro Control Engineer A, a role he held until August 29,
1985. Under the supervision of Pedro C. Ambos, Jr., he took on greater analytical responsibilities, including the
analysis of hourly recorded readings and making recommendations to the Plant Hydroelectric Operations Engineer.
He contributed to the preparation and submission of the Plant Statistical Report to NPC Head Office in Manila,
demonstrating his growing competence in technical reporting and plant performance documentation.
Control Engineer (1985–1988)
From August 30, 1985, to March 31, 1988, Matuan served as Control Engineer A. During this period, he
contributed to the preparation of procedures for the Managed Maintenance Program for implementation, helping to
systematize the plant's preventive maintenance protocols. His work ensured that the plant's equipment received
timely and effective maintenance, reducing downtime and extending asset life.
Principal Engineer (1988–1991)
Matuan was promoted to Principal Engineer C on April 1, 1988, continuing in this position through June 30, 1989,
and then again from July 1, 1989, to December 31, 1991. In this role, he was responsible for analyzing the hourly
recorded readings of meters and gauges and making technical recommendations to the Plant Superintendent. He
contributed significantly to the preparation of Preventive Maintenance Work Orders for implementation by
operating and maintenance personnel across both Agus 1 and Agus 2 Hydroelectric Plants.

PAGE 4
Operations/Maintenance Superintendent (1992–1993)
On January 1, 1992, Matuan advanced to the role of Operations/Maintenance Superintendent A, a position he held
through December 31, 1993. This marked his transition into supervisory and managerial responsibilities,
overseeing the overall operation of the plant's three generating units and their auxiliaries while reporting to the
Manager of the Operations Division.
Superintendent (1994–2003)
Matuan served as Superintendent A from January 1, 1994, to July 15, 2001, and then as Superintendent from July
16, 2001, to February 28, 2003. During these years, he was responsible for the overall operation of the three
generating units at Agus 2 Hydroelectric Plant, continuing to report to the Operations Division Manager, Dr.
Mangurun T. Bautil.
During this period, Matuan achieved one of his most significant contributions to plant operations: the
computerization of the Monthly Operations Report. This innovation minimized delays and reduced errors in
submitted reports to NPC headquarters, improving data reliability and operational transparency. He also developed
the Superintendent's Patrol Checklist, which served as a systematic guide during routine inspection tours,
enhancing the consistency and thoroughness of plant monitoring.
A brief termination occurred from February 28 to March 2, 2003, after which he was reinstated and continued his
service.
Plant Superintendent (2003–2013)
From March 3, 2003, to May 19, 2013, Matuan served as Plant Superintendent, reporting to Dr. Mangurun T.
Bautil. In this role, he bore full responsibility for the overall operation of the plant's three generating units and their
auxiliaries. His continued refinement of computerized operations reporting and the Superintendent's Patrol
Checklist became standard operating procedures that improved plant efficiency and safety.
Division Manager, Plant Technical Services (2013–2018)
On May 20, 2013, Matuan was promoted to Division Manager for Plant Technical Services, a position he held until
July 31, 2018. Reporting directly to Dr. Palawan A. Lomondaya, he managed Safety, Health, Environment,
Information Systems, and Technical Services for the plant complex.
During this period, Dr. Matuan achieved remarkable institutional milestones:
He spearheaded the acquisition of Integrated Management System (IMS) Certification covering ISO 9001:2008
(Quality Management), ISO 14001:2004 (Environmental Management), and OHSAS 18001:2007 (Occupational
Health and Safety). This certification demonstrated the plant's commitment to international standards in operations,
safety, and environmental stewardship.
Under his leadership, the plant received the Corporate Safety and Health Excellence Award from the
Department of Energy for four consecutive years, a testament to the robust safety culture he cultivated.
He also spearheaded the acquisition of the Certificate of Completion from the Energy Regulatory Commission for
four consecutive years, ensuring regulatory compliance and operational excellence.

PAGE 5
Acting Plant Operations and Maintenance Manager (2018–2019)
On August 1, 2018, Matuan was appointed Acting Plant Operations and Maintenance Manager for the Operations
Division at Agus 2 Hydroelectric Plant, serving in this capacity until May 15, 2019. Reporting directly to the Plant
Manager, Dr. Mangurun T. Bautil, he was responsible for the management of the overall operation and maintenance
of the entire facility.
During this period, he spearheaded the transition to the latest versions of the Integrated Management System
standards: ISO 9001:2015, ISO 14001:2015, and OHSAS 18001:2007, ensuring the plant remained current with
evolving international best practices.
He also led the plant to achieve an Outstanding Rating in the Plant Performance Measurement Audit conducted
by the Power Sector Assets and Liabilities Management Corporation (PSALM), Manila—one of the highest
recognitions for operational excellence in the Philippine power sector.
Plant Operations and Maintenance Manager (2019–2023)
On May 16, 2019, Matuan was officially appointed as Plant Operations and Maintenance Manager, the culminating
position of his distinguished career. He served in this role until his retirement on June 20, 2023, reporting to Dr.
Mangurun T. Bautil and bearing ultimate responsibility for all operations and maintenance at Agus 2 Hydroelectric
Plant.
In this final chapter of his career, Dr. Matuan continued to lead the plant to excellence. He maintained the
certifications for ISO 9001:2015, ISO 14001:2015, and OHSAS 18001:2007, and sustained the plant's Outstanding
Rating in PSALM audits. His tenure as Plant Manager represented the apex of a career built on technical mastery,
management excellence, and unwavering commitment to service.
Institutional Contributions
Dr. Matuan's contributions to the National Power Corporation and the broader Philippine energy sector extend far
beyond his operational responsibilities:
Computerization Pioneer – At a time when most plant operations relied on manual record-keeping, Matuan
introduced computerized systems for the Monthly Operations Report, significantly reducing errors and delays. This
innovation became a model for other NPC facilities and demonstrated how technology could enhance operational
efficiency and data integrity.
ISO and Quality Management Leadership – His role in securing and maintaining multiple ISO certifications
(9001, 14001, OHSAS 18001) across successive standard versions positioned Agus 2 as a benchmark for quality,
environmental stewardship, and occupational health and safety in the Philippine power sector. These certifications
required systemic changes in documentation, training, and continuous improvement processes, all of which Matuan
championed and institutionalized.
Safety Culture Champion – The four consecutive Corporate Safety and Health Excellence Awards from the
Department of Energy reflect not just compliance, but a deep-rooted safety culture that Matuan cultivated
throughout the plant. His Superintendent's Patrol Checklist became an enduring tool for consistent safety
monitoring and risk mitigation.

PAGE 6
Regulatory Excellence – Achieving four consecutive Certificates of Completion from the Energy Regulatory
Commission demonstrated Matuan's commitment to regulatory compliance and transparent governance—critical
factors in maintaining public trust and operational legitimacy.
Operational Excellence – His consistent achievement of Outstanding Ratings in PSALM audits speaks to the high
standards of plant performance, maintenance quality, and operational reliability that he maintained throughout his
leadership.
Legacy and Recognition
Dr. Inoyag Mamaroba Matuan's legacy is multifaceted. As a Maranao professional, he exemplified how indigenous
and Muslim Filipinos can achieve the highest levels of technical and managerial excellence in the Philippine civil
service. His 42-year career at a single facility—rising from Control Operator to Plant Manager—demonstrates the
rewards of sustained dedication, continuous learning, and institutional loyalty.
His work had tangible impacts on Mindanao's energy security. The Agus 2 Hydroelectric Plant, under his
stewardship, consistently delivered reliable power to the Mindanao grid, supporting economic development,
industrial growth, and the daily lives of millions of Filipinos. His commitment to safety meant that workers
returned home safely, and his environmental stewardship ensured that operations were conducted responsibly.
For young engineers and professionals in Lanao del Sur and the broader Bangsamoro region, Dr. Matuan's career
serves as proof that technical excellence and ethical leadership can thrive regardless of one's ethnic or regional
background. He navigated a complex bureaucratic environment, led diverse teams, and achieved international
standards of quality—all while remaining rooted in his Maranao identity and community.
His dual engineering degrees, advanced management qualifications, and Career Executive Service Eligibility make
him one of the most credentialed professionals ever to serve at the Agus Hydroelectric Complex. His innovations in
computerization, quality management, and safety protocols have become part of the institutional fabric of the
National Power Corporation.
Challenges and Resilience
Dr. Matuan's career was not without challenges. The brief termination in early 2003—though quickly resolved—
reflects the institutional and political complexities that government employees sometimes face. His resilience and
reinstatement demonstrate both his value to the organization and his personal fortitude in navigating difficult
circumstances.
Working in a hydroelectric facility in a region that has experienced social and political challenges required not only
technical competence but also cultural sensitivity, community engagement, and an understanding of the broader
socio-political context. Matuan's long tenure and the respect he commanded suggest that he successfully balanced
these demands.
The transition through multiple ISO standard versions (from 2004/2007 standards to 2015 standards) also presented
significant challenges, requiring retraining, documentation overhauls, and cultural shifts within the organization.
Matuan's successful leadership through these transitions speaks to his adaptability and his ability to manage
institutional change effectively.

PAGE 7
Personal Life
Beyond his professional achievements, Dr. Matuan is a family man who raised twelve children with his wife,
Saripha Hadji Ali Matuan. The children—Nasibah, Mohammad Sadiq, Asiya, Mohammad Jamshyd, Mohammad
Jamal, Jamilah, Norjannah, Norhidayah, Mohammad Jarir, Mohammad Jamil Yahya, Mohammad Jalal,
Mohammad Jabir, and Jora'nah—represent a legacy that extends beyond the professional realm.
He has maintained his residence at the Agus 2 HE Plant Compound in Pawak, Saguiaran, Lanao del Sur, living at
the site he dedicated his life to managing. This proximity to his workplace reflects a deep commitment to his
responsibilities and a life fully integrated with his professional mission.
Retirement
Dr. Matuan retired on June 20, 2023, after 42 years of exemplary service to the National Power Corporation and
the Filipino people. His retirement marked the end of an era at Agus 2 Hydroelectric Plant, where his institutional
knowledge, technical expertise, and leadership had shaped operations for over four decades.
In retirement, he leaves behind systems, protocols, and a culture of excellence that will continue to benefit the plant
and its employees for years to come. His career stands as a testament to what can be achieved through dedication,
continuous learning, ethical leadership, and a commitment to public service.

Nash B. Maulana
Nash B. Maulana (born in Datu Piang, Cotabato, now Maguindanao del Sur) is a Filipino journalist, author,
inventor, and public information director from the Bangsamoro region of Mindanao.
He is widely recognized for his decades of frontline reporting on the Moro conflict and the southern Philippine
peace process, work that often placed him in direct physical danger.
Outside the newsroom, Maulana pursued a second life in engineering, eventually patenting the Tri-Mode Power
Generator System (T-MPG), a renewable energy utility model designed to bring electricity to off-grid, conflict-
affected schools in the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM).

EARLY LIFE AND EDUCATION
Nash B. Maulana was born in Datu Piang, a municipality in the
province of Cotabato, now administratively part of Maguindanao
del Sur in the BARMM.
He completed his elementary education at the Datu Gumbay Piang
Central Elementary School in his hometown, then pursued high
school at Notre Dame of Dulawan, also located in Datu Piang.
For college, Maulana moved to Manila, where he enrolled in BS
Electrical Engineering at National University.
Though he did not finish the engineering degree, his exposure to
electronics and technical problem-solving would prove formative
years later, when he returned to engineering not as a student but as a
self-taught inventor.

PAGE 2
Journalist, Columnist, Public
Information Director, Inventor
Region
Bangsamoro, Mindanao, Philippines
Patent
Tri-Mode Power Generator System (T-
MPG), IPOPHL Utility Model
Notability

veteran Moro conflict reporter who
patented a renewable energy system to
