He eventually completed a Bachelor of Arts in Journalism and
Communications at the Polytechnic University of the
Philippines in Manila, the credential that would anchor his long
career in media.
While studying, he worked as a student employee at the BSP Kiosk
in Luneta Park, Manila (1983), balancing the demands of work
and academics in the country's capital.
CAREER IN JOURNALISM AND
PUBLIC SERVICE
Early Employment and Public Information Work
After finishing his studies, Maulana began his career in public
service before formally entering national media.
He served as an Office Clerk and later as an Information Officer
at the Office of Muslim Affairs and Cultural Communities
(OMACC) from 1984 to 1985 and again from 1987 to 1989.
These positions gave him early exposure to the intersection of government communication and Muslim community
affairs, experience that would inform his later journalism and his years as a public information director.
National Media Career
Maulana entered mainstream journalism in the late 1980s, joining the Philippine Daily Globe as a news
correspondent from 1988 to 1992.
From 1989 onward, he took on a column at The Mindanao Cross, a byline he has maintained to the present day,
making it one of the longest continuous writing engagements in his career.
In 1992, he joined the Philippine Daily Inquirer as a news correspondent, covering the Bangsamoro beat out of
Cotabato City.
He held that post until 2017, a run of twenty-five years that positioned him as one of the most experienced
reporters on southern Philippine affairs in the country.
He also contributed to the Philippine Free Press in 2007, lending his perspective on Mindanao to one of the
Philippines' oldest English-language publications.
Reporting the Bangsamoro Peace Process
For over three decades, Maulana's primary beat was the Moro conflict and its many iterations: ceasefire
negotiations, ancestral domain disputes, civilian displacement, and the slow, uneven construction of autonomous
governance in Muslim Mindanao.

PAGE 3
He chronicled the evolution of the peace tracks from the early autonomous experiments under the Autonomous
Region in Muslim Mindanao (ARMM) through to the formal establishment of the BARMM under the Bangsamoro
Organic Law.
In 2014, his reporting on the Comprehensive Agreement on the Bangsamoro (CAB) drew particular attention,
especially his coverage of the weapons decommissioning process involving the Moro Islamic Liberation Front
(MILF).
Maulana's reporting highlighted what many observers considered the most difficult element of the peace deal: the
disarmament of MILF fighters, who held deep cultural and security attachments to their firearms.
He documented the creation of the Independent Decommissioning Body (IDB), the multilateral mechanism
tasked with overseeing the phased disarmament and normalization of former combatants, and his accounts helped
audiences outside Mindanao understand why this phase of peace-building required particular patience and trust-
building.
The 1996 Ambush
The risks of covering Mindanao's conflict zones were not abstract for Maulana.
On March 20, 1996, he and fellow journalist Ali Macabalang were ambushed by a gunman in Cotabato City.
Macabalang sustained a wound to the neck.
Maulana was shot twice in the leg.
He survived the attack and, after recovering, returned directly to his beat, an act that drew wide respect from
colleagues and deepened his standing as one of the region's most committed press figures.
Government Service: ARMM Bureau of Public Information
In addition to his journalism, Maulana served as Director III of the ARMM Bureau of Public Information from
2010 to 2013.
In that role, he helped shape the communication strategy of the autonomous regional government during a critical
period in the Bangsamoro peace track, translating policy decisions and peace initiatives into language accessible to
the region's diverse communities.
THE TRI-MODE POWER GENERATOR SYSTEM (T-MPG)
From Reporter to Inventor
Alongside decades of reporting, Maulana pursued a parallel interest in electronics and engineering, one that traced
back to his unfinished engineering degree in Manila.
The problem he set out to solve was not abstract: rural schools across the BARMM remained cut off from the
national power grid, limiting children's access to computers, lights, and basic learning tools.

PAGE 4
In communities that had already lost years of education to armed conflict, the absence of reliable electricity
compounded an already severe disadvantage.
Maulana's response was practical.
He spent years designing and refining a generator system that could operate independently of grid infrastructure,
using a self-charging battery mechanism that could sustain output in remote, conflict-affected areas.
The Patent
The result was the Tri-Mode Power Generator System (T-MPG), officially recognized by the Intellectual
Property Office of the Philippines (IPOPHL) as a patented Utility Model.
The T-MPG is a self-charging, battery-driven generator prototype that draws its distinctiveness from its operational
design: rather than relying on a single energy source, the system routes power conversion through three separate
operational paths.
This multi-channel architecture allows the generator to maintain stable electrical output even in areas entirely off-
grid, making it particularly suited to the geography and infrastructure gaps of rural Bangsamoro communities.
The patent made Maulana something of a regional celebrity in technology circles, celebrated as a veteran political
reporter who had successfully crossed into green energy engineering.
PROJECT ENERGIZING SCHOOLS
Maulana did not develop the T-MPG as a commercial product.
His goal, from the beginning, was deployment: getting working units into underfunded classrooms across the
BARMM.
To that end, he launched Project Energizing Schools, an initiative structured around two interlocking goals.
The first is direct electrification: providing rural schools with immediate, reliable power so that students and
teachers can use computers, lighting, and modern educational materials.
The second is skills transfer: introducing the mechanics of the T-MPG to local youth and former combatants
classified as peace beneficiaries.
By teaching community members how to build and maintain the generators themselves, Maulana embeds a
practical science and technology curriculum into communities that have had limited access to vocational training,
and that have often known only conflict as the backdrop to their daily lives.
LEGACY AND SIGNIFICANCE
Nash B. Maulana represents an unusual figure in Philippine journalism: a frontline correspondent who did not stop
at documenting a region's problems, but who used his own hands, and his own patent, to address one of them.
His career spans the full arc of the Bangsamoro peace process, from the early ceasefire negotiations of the 1990s
through the ratification of the Bangsamoro Organic Law and the formal creation of the BARMM.

PAGE 5
He survived an assassination attempt that might have ended another journalist's career, and returned to reporting.
He earned a national patent in a technical field entirely outside his primary profession.
And he built a community program that ties renewable energy infrastructure directly to the education of a
generation growing up in post-conflict Mindanao.
In that sense, Maulana's legacy is not simply that of a chronicler of Bangsamoro history.
He became, in the most literal sense, part of it.
SELECTED WORKS AND CONTRIBUTIONS
Coverage of the Bangsamoro peace process, Philippine Daily Inquirer (1992 to 2017)
Column, The Mindanao Cross (1989 to present)
Contributor, Philippine Free Press (2007)
2014 report on MILF weapons decommissioning and the Comprehensive Agreement on the Bangsamoro
(CAB), published in the Inquirer
Patented Utility Model: Tri-Mode Power Generator System (T-MPG), IPOPHL
Project Energizing Schools, BARMM

Amilbahar S. Mawallil
Amilbahar S. Mawallil is a Filipino Moro politician and public servant from Tawi-Tawi. He currently serves as a
Member of the Bangsamoro Parliament under the Bangsamoro Transition Authority (BTA) and previously served
as Governor of Tawi-Tawi. He is known for his leadership in regional governance, maritime development, and
representation of island provinces within the Bangsamoro region.<ref name="pia2021">Philippine Information
Agency. Mawallil leads development initiatives in Tawi-Tawi. 2021.</ref><ref name="barmm2023">Bangsamoro
Government. Profiles of Bangsamoro Parliament Members. Official BARMM Website, 2023.</ref>
---
Early Life and Education
Amilbahar Mawallil hails from Tawi-Tawi, one of the southernmost provinces of the Philippines, composed
of island communities with strong Sama-Bajau and Tausug cultural influences.
He pursued his education in the Philippines, focusing on governance and public service.
His early exposure to the socio-economic challenges of island provinces shaped his commitment to regional
development and representation.<ref name="pia2021" />
---
Political Career
Governor of Tawi-Tawi
Mawallil served as Governor of Tawi-Tawi, where he focused on improving local governance, public
services, and infrastructure in island communities.
His administration emphasized maritime development, connectivity, and economic opportunities for coastal
populations.

PAGE 2
Bangsamoro Parliament
He was appointed as a Member of the Bangsamoro Transition Authority Parliament, contributing to
legislative processes and governance reforms in BARMM.
As a parliament member, he represents the interests of island provinces, ensuring their inclusion in regional
policy-making.<ref name="barmm2023" />
---
Contributions to Bangsamoro Governance
Advocates for inclusive development for island and coastal communities in the Bangsamoro region.
Supports infrastructure development, maritime economy, and transportation connectivity in Tawi-Tawi.
Promotes peace, stability, and integration of diverse ethnolinguistic groups within BARMM.
---
Legacy and Significance
Amilbahar Mawallil is recognized as a key representative of island-based Moro communities in Bangsamoro
governance.
His leadership highlights the importance of including geographically remote areas in regional development
planning.
He continues to contribute to strengthening governance and representation within BARMM.
---

title: Mimbalawag, Mansawi Dariday
text:
PAGE 1
Mansawi Dariday Mimbalawag
Mansawi Dariday Mimbalawag, widely known by his alias KNA-MDM and often addressed as Aleem
Mansawi, is a prominent Maranao Islamic scholar, academic, and political figure in the Bangsamoro region. As a
researcher affiliated with the University of the Philippines Diliman Institute of Islamic Studies, Mimbalawag has
become a recognized voice for Islamic leadership in governance and social justice advocacy, particularly around
Marawi Siege reconstruction and internally displaced persons (IDPs) rights. His work bridges traditional Islamic
scholarship with contemporary public policy, earning him prominence as both a spiritual guide (Ajem) and
institutional thought leader in the Bangsamoro.
Contents
1 Early Life and Background
2 Education
3 Academic and Research Career
4 Religious Leadership and Civic Advocacy
5 Marawi Rehabilitation and IDP Advocacy
6 2025 Electoral Campaign
7 Personal Values and Cultural Significance
8 Further Reading
9 See Also
Early Life and Background
Mimbalawag was born on November 30, 1970, to a Maranao family deeply rooted in the Lanao region's socio-
religious traditions. His background reflects the distinctive Maranao heritage, where leadership typically combines
royal lineage, religious scholarship, and community service. He is married to Asnia M. Guro-Mimbalawag.
Education
Mimbalawag's academic training emphasizes public administration and Islamic studies. He holds a Bachelor's
degree in Public Administration and a Master's degree in Public Policy. His formal education laid the groundwork
for his later institutional work at the University of the Philippines, where he has developed expertise in the
intersection of Islamic governance, community development, and policy implementation.
Academic and Research Career
Since his affiliation with the UP Diliman Institute of Islamic Studies, Mimbalawag has established himself as an
active researcher and scholar. His academic work focuses on Islamic leadership constructs and their integration
with modern bureaucratic systems in the Bangsamoro region. Key research areas include:
Indigenous Muslim Leadership: Exploring how traditional Maranao and Bangsamoro leadership models
adapt to contemporary governance frameworks.
Madrasah Education and Institutionalization: Investigating the development and integration of Islamic
education within the Philippine national education system.

Mimbalawag regularly contributes to scholarly dialogues through
paper presentations at international conferences focused on Islam
in Southeast Asia, and participates actively in UP IIS research
collaborations on Muslim orature and intercommunal cooperation
in Mindanao.
Religious Leadership and Civic Advocacy
Beyond academia, Mimbalawag serves as a recognized Ajem
(Islamic Movement Speaker), providing moral and spiritual
guidance within the Bangsamoro community. His religious
teachings emphasize faith-based resilience and ethical leadership,
with recurring themes such as "Fear Allah, Not People," which
underscore the spiritual duty of leaders to serve their communities.
Mimbalawag is also a key figure in the League of Bangsamoro
Organizations, where he has been instrumental in coordinating
national solidarity movements and advocating for international
human rights. He has been notably vocal in supporting Palestinian
rights and has led civil society initiatives centered on humanitarian
and justice concerns affecting Muslim communities.
Marawi Rehabilitation and IDP Advocacy
One of Mimbalawag's most prominent contributions has been his
sustained advocacy for Marawi Siege survivors and internally
displaced persons. His advocacy encompasses:
Demanding the release of stagnant rehabilitation funds to
accelerate physical reconstruction of the city.
Advocating for IDP property rights and pushing for "win-
win solutions" that prioritize vacant lots over existing
private properties in reconstruction planning.
Monitoring the implementation of Republic Act No. 11696
(the Marawi Siege Victims Compensation Act), emphasizing
that compensation should be calculated using replacement
costs rather than depreciated fair market values to ensure
justice for survivors.
Participating in civil society dialogues to ensure
rehabilitation efforts remain culturally sensitive and
inclusive of traditional Maranao leadership structures.
His efforts reflect his commitment to ensuring that post-conflict
recovery prioritizes both material reconstruction and the preservation of Maranao cultural and historical heritage.

PAGE 3
2025 Electoral Campaign
In 2025, Mimbalawag sought election as Vice Governor of Lanao del Sur under the Reform PH Party, running on a
platform of "Moral Governance" and regional self-determination. His campaign emphasized the integration of
Islamic leadership principles into local public policy and advocated for the advancement of Bangsamoro autonomy.
Though his candidacy did not succeed at the ballot, his campaign reinforced his public profile as a vocal advocate
for faith-based governance and IDP rights.
Personal Values and Cultural Significance
Mimbalawag is widely viewed as a bridge between traditional Islamic values and contemporary public
administration. His public life is characterized by emphasis on integrity, excellence, and the role of faith in
fostering peace and prosperity. He represents a generation of Bangsamoro leaders who leverage academic research
and institutional credentials to strengthen Bangsamoro identity and autonomy while maintaining deep roots in
Islamic tradition.

Abdul-Aziz Mimbantas
Aleem Abdulaziz S. Mimbantas (d. 2012) was a Filipino Moro revolutionary leader, Islamic scholar, and senior
official of the Moro Islamic Liberation Front (MILF). He served as Vice Chairman for Military Affairs and was a
key figure in the Bangsamoro armed struggle and subsequent peace negotiations with the Philippine government.
<ref name="pia2024">Philippine Information Agency. Healthcare workers in Lanao del Sur push for a new
hospital in Masiu. August 15, 2024.</ref><ref name="gulfnews2018">Felongco, G. Senior MILF official dies of
heart attack. Gulf News, 2018.</ref>
---
Early Life and Background
Abdulaziz Mimbantas was a native of Masiu, Lanao del Sur, a stronghold of the Maranao people and an
important area in the Moro resistance movement.<ref name="pia2024" />
He was trained in Islamic scholarship, earning the title “Aleem,” reflecting his deep grounding in Islamic
teachings and leadership within the Moro community.
His early life was shaped by the political and social struggles of the Bangsamoro people during the post-
colonial Philippine period.
---
Role in the Moro Islamic Liberation Front
Mimbantas became one of the senior leaders of the MILF under Chairman Salamat Hashim.
He served as Vice Chairman for Military Affairs, overseeing aspects of the Bangsamoro Islamic Armed
Forces (BIAF).<ref name="pia2024" /><ref name="gulfnews2018" />
He also played a role in the MILF peace negotiations with the Philippine government, contributing to
dialogue efforts that would later lead to the Bangsamoro peace process.<ref name="gulfnews2018" />
As a close associate of Salamat Hashim, he was instrumental in sustaining the organization’s structure and
strategy during critical periods of armed struggle and negotiation.

PAGE 2
---
Death
Abdulaziz Mimbantas died in 2012 from cardiac arrest following engagements related to peace and
development efforts.<ref name="gulfnews2018" />
In accordance with Islamic tradition, he was buried shortly after his death in Camp Bushra Somiorang in
Butig, Lanao del Sur, near the grave of Salamat Hashim.<ref name="gulfnews2018" />
---
Legacy
Mimbantas is remembered as one of the central military and ideological leaders of the MILF.
His contributions to both armed resistance and peace negotiations helped shape the trajectory of the
Bangsamoro struggle for self-determination.
His legacy continues to be honored in the Bangsamoro region:
 * His burial site, together with that of Salamat Hashim, has been declared a protected heritage and memorial site under 
Bangsamoro law.<ref name="baa60">Bangsamoro Autonomy Act No. 60, 2024.</ref>  
 * A hospital in Masiu, Lanao del Sur has been established in his honor, recognizing his service to the Bangsamoro people.
<ref name="pia2024" />  
---
Significance in Bangsamoro History
Abdulaziz Mimbantas represents the generation of Moro leaders who transitioned from armed struggle to
political negotiation.
His role helped lay the groundwork for later agreements such as the Comprehensive Agreement on the
Bangsamoro and the establishment of the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao.
---

dies of heart attack. Gulf News, 2018.</ref> <ref name="baa60">Bangsamoro Autonomy Act No. 60. Official

Panambulan M. Mimbisa
Panambulan M. Mimbisa (born February 8, 1950) is a retired
Filipino jurist, lawyer, and public administrator from the Meranaw
(Maranao) ethnic group of Lanao, Mindanao.
He is best known for his long and distinguished tenure as
Presiding Judge and Executive Judge of the Regional Trial
Court (RTC), Branch 37, in General Santos City, where he served
until his compulsory retirement on February 8, 2020, exactly on
his 70th birthday.
Before ascending to the bench, Mimbisa built a solid foundation
across both the executive branch of government and the private
practice of law, making him one of the more well-rounded legal
figures to emerge from the Bangsamoro community in the latter
half of the twentieth century.

ETHNIC AFFILIATION AND
CULTURAL BACKGROUND
Mimbisa belongs to the Meranaw (also spelled Maranao), the
"People of the Lake," an Islamized indigenous group native to the
Lanao region of Mindanao and recognized as one of the major
ethnolinguistic communities of the Bangsamoro.
His Meranaw identity wasn't just a biographical footnote; it
shaped the texture of how he practiced and administered law.

PAGE 2

Manila

Notability

instrumental in advancing Alternative
Dispute Resolution (ADR) in Mindanao.
Known For
Founding Secretary General of the United
Muslim Democrats of the Philippines
(UMDP); Landmark rulings on
fraudulent land titles; championing
court-annexed mediation; bridging Moro
customary law and Philippine statutory
jurisprudence.
Growing up within a cultural tradition anchored in the Taritib (the
traditional order governing Meranaw social conduct), ancestral
lineage, and Islamic values, he carried a dual awareness
throughout his career: the formal demands of Philippine statutory
law on one hand, and the moral logic of customary Moro law
(Adat) and Islamic cultural frameworks on the other.
This dual grounding became one of the defining characteristics of
his approach to justice, particularly in a region as complex and
contested as Mindanao.
EARLY LIFE AND EDUCATION
Mimbisa was born on February 8, 1950, and his parents named
him Panambulan at birth.
He completed his elementary education at the Dansalan Central
Elementary School in Lanao, a school tied to the civic and
educational heartbeat of the old Dansalan (now Marawi City)
community.
For high school, he attended the Mindanao State University Preparatory High School, where he distinguished
himself enough to earn a full scholarship, completing his secondary education in 1965.
The scholarship opened the door to further studies at MSU, but his uncle had other plans.
At his uncle's urging, Mimbisa set aside the MSU scholarship and made the leap to Manila, enrolling at the
University of Manila for a Bachelor of Science in Business Administration, with a major in Economics.
The move proved to be a good one: he landed on the honor list, earning induction into Beta Sigma Phi, the
Association of Honor Students of the College of Business Administration.
He eventually rose to become the Most Exalted Betan, the organization's highest student honor.
Beyond academics, Mimbisa had a talent for argumentation that went far beyond the classroom.
He won the title of Best Debater in the Yearly Inter-collegiate Debate Tournament during his undergraduate years,
a distinction that hinted at the courtroom presence he would later develop.
After completing his business degree, he stayed at the University of Manila to pursue a Bachelor of Laws (LL.B.).
As a law freshman, he entered the Annual Inter-Collegiate Oratorical Contest and won the championship, taking
home the Presidential Trophy, a clean sweep of the university's most competitive student platforms.
He took the Philippine Bar Examination in 1975.
That particular bar was widely considered one of the most difficult in recent memory: the passing mark had to be
reduced to 70% to ensure that at least a workable number of examinees would qualify, with fewer than 20% of
takers ultimately making the cut.
Mimbisa passed with an average of 76.96%, comfortably clearing the adjusted bar and officially entering the legal
profession.

PAGE 3
EARLY GOVERNMENT SERVICE
Mimbisa launched his professional career in government in 1976, a year after passing the bar, taking on the role of
Executive Officer of the Government Peace Panel for Mindanao.
The posting placed him at the heart of one of the most politically sensitive assignments of the era: managing the
formal government machinery tasked with engaging the peace process in Mindanao.
This early experience in conflict management and institutional negotiation would leave a lasting mark on his
professional temperament.
In subsequent years, he served as a key official within the Office of Muslim Affairs (OMA), where he sat as a
representative to the National Economic and Development Authority (NEDA) Board.
In that capacity, he contributed to policy directions aimed at the socioeconomic development and cultural
integration of Muslim Filipino communities into the national framework, work that coincided with the "Philippines
2000" economic push during the Ramos administration.
JUDICIAL CAREER
Presiding Judge, RTC Branch 37
Mimbisa eventually transitioned into the judiciary, taking on the post of Presiding Judge of the Regional Trial
Court, Branch 37, in General Santos City.
The RTC in General Santos handles a wide and demanding docket: civil, criminal, and special proceedings
covering one of Mindanao's major urban centers and its surrounding provinces.
Mimbisa presided over Branch 37 for years, building a reputation for steady, deliberate jurisprudence.
Executive Judge
Recognizing his leadership capabilities and his record on the bench, the Supreme Court of the Philippines
elevated Mimbisa to the position of Executive Judge for the region.
As Executive Judge, he carried additional administrative responsibilities overseeing court operations, managing
personnel and docket flow, and acting as the regional judicial authority for executive matters such as writs, urgent
applications, and inter-court coordination.
Advocacy for Alternative Dispute Resolution
One of Mimbisa's most lasting institutional contributions was his championing of Alternative Dispute Resolution
(ADR) as a practical tool for decongesting Philippine courts.
He partnered with the Philippine Dispute Resolution Center, Inc. (PDRCI) to conduct ADR road shows and
training seminars in General Santos City, helping introduce court-annexed mediation and judicial dispute resolution
protocols to litigants, lawyers, and court personnel across the region.

PAGE 4
The effort was part of a broader national push to reduce litigation costs and resolve disputes more efficiently, and
Mimbisa's participation as a sitting Executive Judge gave the program institutional credibility in Mindanao.
MAJOR RULINGS AND JUDICIAL ACTIONS
TRO Against Fraudulent Land Titles (2016)
In 2016, Judge Mimbisa issued a significant Temporary Restraining Order (TRO) halting the processing and
sale of a 707-hectare government-owned land tract in Davao that had been flagged by the Land Registration
Authority (LRA) for carrying spurious mother titles.
The ruling froze all transactions involving the disputed land, protecting legitimate corporate leaseholders and
shielding public forest areas from fraudulent conversion and privatization.
The case drew attention to the persistent problem of manufactured land titles in Mindanao and signaled the
judiciary's willingness to act decisively against such schemes.
Change of Venue for Trial of Suspects in Broadcaster Killings
Mimbisa's court was also involved in the administrative coordination surrounding the transfer of venue for the trial
of suspects in the killings of prominent local broadcasters in General Santos City.
Pursuant to directives from the Supreme Court, his bench coordinated the swift transmittal of court records and
case files from General Santos City to the Makati City RTC, ensuring that the proceedings would be conducted in a
neutral venue free from local influence.
The move was consistent with concerns about the safety of court proceedings and the integrity of the judicial
process in high-profile media cases.
RETIREMENT
Judge Mimbisa reached the mandatory retirement age for Philippine judges and took his compulsory retirement
on February 8, 2020, the same day he turned 70.
The timing, a birthday that doubled as a farewell from the bench, was a fitting capstone to a career that had
spanned more than four decades of public service across executive and judicial roles.
LEGACY AND SIGNIFICANCE
For the Meranaw people and the broader Bangsamoro community, Panambulan Mimbisa's career carries a
significance that goes beyond his individual rulings or administrative record.
He is the founding Secretary General of the United Muslim Democrats of the Philippines (UMDP)
His rise to Executive Judge of a Regional Trial Court represents a meaningful instance of indigenous Moro
representation within a national legal system that has historically been shaped by and for the majority population.

PAGE 5
He demonstrated, through sustained professional work rather than tokenism, that a Muslim Filipino from the Lanao
highlands could master the full apparatus of Philippine law, from the bar exam to the Supreme Court-level
administrative machinery, while remaining rooted in the cultural and communal values of his people.
His dual career in executive government and the judiciary gave him a breadth of perspective rare among jurists: he
had sat on both sides of the policy-implementation divide, and that experience informed how he ran his courtroom
and how he approached conflict.
His support for ADR, in particular, reflects a sensibility shaped as much by Moro traditions of dialogue and
communal resolution as by formal legal training.
In retirement, he remains an esteemed elder within Moro society, frequently sought out as a witness and moral
authority at significant cultural events, clan assemblies, and traditional peace pacts across Mindanao.
His story belongs in the Bangsamoro record not because it is exceptional in the way of myth, but because it is real:
a man from Dansalan who earned a presidential trophy in Manila, passed one of the hardest bar exams in
Philippine history, served his community through decades of often unglamorous institutional work, and left the
bench with his integrity intact.

Amer Manalao Mindalano
Amer Manalao Mindalano (also known as Amir Manalao Mindalano)
was a Maranao Muslim guerrilla commander, decorated war hero, and
legislator from Lanao Province in Mindanao, Philippines.
During World War II, he was the first Maranao leader to launch organized
offensive strikes against Japanese occupation forces in Lanao, earning
him a reputation for fearlessness that spread across both sides of the
conflict.
He served as a Major and regimental commander of the 127th Infantry
Regiment under the United States Forces in the Philippines (USFIP), and
was awarded the Silver Star for gallantry in action on September 14, 1943
— one of the highest military decorations granted to Filipino soldiers by
the American government during the war.
After liberation, Mindalano carried his leadership from the battlefield into
the halls of government, representing Lanao in the 1st Congress of the
Philippines from 1946 to 1949.
His story is inseparable from the larger history of Maranao resistance: a
people who, with kris blades and guerrilla cunning, effectively contained
Japanese forces around Lake Lanao before American-led forces had even
begun to consolidate their own guerrilla movement in Mindanao.
Contents
1 Background and Early Life
2 World War II and the Lanao Resistance
2.1 The Japanese Occupation of Mindanao
2.2 The First Strike: Mindalano Moves Before Anyone Else
2.3 Organizing the Resistance
2.4 Silver Star: The Battles That Defined His Legacy

5 Legacy and Recognition

PAGE 2
5.1 The Silver Star as Formal Vindication
5.2 A Forgotten Chapter, Slowly Remembered
6 Death
7 Further Reading
8 See Also
Background and Early Life
Amer Manalao Mindalano was born into the Maranao Muslim community of Lanao, the indigenous people living
around the shores of Lake Lanao in the heart of Mindanao.
The Maranaos — whose name literally translates to "People of the Lake" — were part of the broader confederation
of Muslim sultanates known as the Pat a Pangampong a Ranao (Confederation of Sultanates in Lanao), a deeply
rooted political and cultural structure that shaped the identity and governance of the region long before colonial
rule.<ref name="wikipedia_moros">Wikipedia. "Moros during World War II." Retrieved from
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moros_during_World_War_II</ref>
Mindalano's honorific title, Amir, reflects his standing within this community: a title of leadership, dignity, and
trust, not merely ceremonial, but functional within the social hierarchy of Maranao political life.
Precise records of his birth year, parentage, and early schooling are not fully documented in available public
archives, a gap that reflects the broader historical marginalization of Muslim Mindanao in Philippine national
records.
What is documented, however, is that by the time the Japanese arrived in Mindanao in 1941 and 1942, Mindalano
was already a recognized community leader, a man who commanded enough personal authority to organize fighters
and inspire loyalty in the most dangerous of circumstances.
His personal motivation for resistance was, by multiple accounts, deeply rooted: he had vowed to avenge the death
of his father, a vow that transformed private grief into a very public act of defiance against occupation.<ref
name="docx_source">Source document: Amer Manalao Mindalano (uploaded reference file, BangsamoroPedia
research collection).</ref>
World War II and the Lanao Resistance
The Japanese Occupation of Mindanao
The Japanese invasion of Mindanao began in earnest in early 1942.
By May 27, 1942, Brigadier General Guy O. Fort, commanding officer of the 81st Division, had surrendered the
last formal Filipino-American forces in the region to Japanese commanders at Dansalan, the town now known as
Marawi City.<ref name="metrocdo">Metro Cagayan de Oro. "The USAFFE Visayas-Mindanao Force Surrender in
1942." Retrieved from https://www.metrocagayandemisamis.com/2025/08/30/the-usaffe-visayas-mindanao-force-
surrender-in-1942/</ref>
For most commands, surrender meant the end of organized resistance. For the Maranaos, it meant something very
different.

PAGE 3
General Fort, familiar with the culture of the Moro people, allowed the Moro Bolo Battalion fighters to keep their
rifles and go home, knowing that men who had sworn an oath before the Holy Quran to fight to the death could not
simply be ordered to lay down arms.<ref name="metrocdo"/>
The Japanese occupiers quickly moved to disarm the broader Maranao civilian population, demanding households
surrender firearms while limiting access to chopping tools — a move that the Maranaos largely treated with
contempt, handing over only a few defective rifles and rusty blades.<ref name="positively_filipino">Positively
Filipino. "The Battle of Tamparan and the Forgotten Moro Heroes of World War II." May 4, 2022. Retrieved from
https://www.positivelyfilipino.com/magazine/the-battle-of-tamparan-and-the-forgotten-moro-heroes-of-world-war-
ii</ref>
When the Japanese began publicly executing violators, the result was not submission. It was ignition.
The First Strike: Mindalano Moves Before Anyone Else
Amer Manalao Mindalano was, by every available account, the first Maranao leader to launch organized armed
attacks against the Japanese forces in Lanao.
This wasn't a spontaneous uprising; it was deliberate, purposeful resistance rooted in his personal vow and his
conviction that no foreign power had the right to occupy Maranao land.
The Japanese garrison in Dansalan took notice quickly.
In June 1942, the Japanese commander of the garrison dispatched a punitive expedition to Watu, a small village on
the western shore of Lake Lanao, specifically to find Manalao Mindalano.
The surprised villagers of Watu, who had no connection to Mindalano, were trapped against the
lakeshore as they tried to escape the soldiers, who methodically bayoneted men and women alike,
killing 24 in all.
This account, reported by American educator Edward Kuder, captured in the article "The Battle of Tamparan and
the Forgotten Moro Heroes of World War II," illustrates how seriously the Japanese took the Mindalano threat from
the very beginning of the resistance.<ref name="positively_filipino"/>
The fact that the Japanese mounted a dedicated punitive operation in June 1942, just weeks after the formal
surrender, tells you everything: Mindalano was already hurting them.
Organizing the Resistance
Mindalano didn't fight alone.
He was part of a broader network of Maranao resistance that also included figures like Datu Busran Kalaw of
Momungan, Naguib Juanday, Datu Laguindas of Ganassi, Joseph Sanguilla, and Datu Buntalis of Masiu, among
others.<ref name="wikipedia_moros"/>
He traveled across Lanao to recruit fighters and persuade local leaders to join the guerrilla movement, reportedly
vowing not to shave his beard until the Japanese had been driven from Philippine soil — a visible, daily declaration
of his unbroken commitment to resistance.<ref name="docx_source"/>
By the latter half of 1942, Maranao resistance forces had made Japanese inland operations increasingly suicidal.

PAGE 4
On September 12, 1942, an estimated 130 Japanese troops were slaughtered in towns around Lake Lanao, forcing
Japanese commanders to avoid the interior altogether and freeing Mindalano and his colleagues to push their
operations toward the coastal northern region.<ref name="militaryfandom">Military Wiki, Fandom. "Moros during
World War II." Retrieved from https://military-history.fandom.com/wiki/Moros_during_World_War_II</ref>
Within months, the three Japanese garrisons around Lake Lanao were cut off from one another, with one under
active siege.
Edward Kuder, who made contact with the American guerrilla force under Colonel Wendell Fertig in late 1942,
witnessed what the Maranaos had already accomplished and wasted no time connecting Fertig with these local
resistance leaders — men like Mindalano who had subdued the Japanese occupiers before the American-led
guerrilla movement had fully taken shape.<ref name="positively_filipino"/>
Silver Star: The Battles That Defined His Legacy
Mindalano's war record was formalized under the United States Forces in the Philippines (USFIP), where he served
as a Major and regimental commander of the 127th Infantry Regiment, 108th Infantry Division, 10th Military
District.<ref name="docx_source"/>
Two specific actions stand at the center of his military record, both cited explicitly in the official Silver Star citation
issued under Department of the Army, General Orders No. 73 (August 9, 1951):
The Interception at Ganassi (September 14, 1943)
On September 14, 1943, Mindalano led his men in an operation to intercept a Japanese patrol returning to Ganassi.
He personally led the attack, displaying what the citation calls "dauntless courage," and destroyed ten enemy
soldiers in the engagement.<ref name="silverstar">Department of the Army, General Orders No. 73 (August 9,
1951). Silver Star Citation for Major Manalao Mindalano. Valor Military Times, retrieved from
https://valor.militarytimes.com/recipient/recipient-109194/</ref>
This single action earned him the Silver Star, but the citation is careful to note that it doesn't stand alone.
The Battle of Malabang (April 1, 1945)
The second action cited is arguably the more strategically significant of the two.
On April 1, 1945, a portion of Mindalano's regiment, then operating at Malabang, Lanao, was completely
surrounded by a Japanese force that outnumbered them and outgunned them.
In a situation where many commanders would have surrendered or attempted to withdraw, Mindalano did the
opposite.
He launched a surprise attack from the rear and left flanks of the encircling Japanese force.
The Silver Star citation describes what followed:
He led a surprise attack from the rear and left flanks and succeeded in penetrating the enemy line,
creating havoc among the foe and inflicting heavy casualties on the invaders. During this daring action
against a force superior in number, arms, and equipment, Major Mindalano, despite a severe loss of

PAGE 5
men, rallied his soldiers, dispersed the enemy, and saved the entire regiment from annihilation. Major
Mindalano's inspiring leadership and sustained devotion to duty reflect great credit on himself and the
Philippine Army.
The full text of the citation, issued by the President of the United States under the authority of the Act of Congress
of July 9, 1918, records these two engagements as the basis for the award.<ref name="silverstar"/>
The Silver Star Award (Formal Record)
The following details constitute his formal Silver Star record as registered with the U.S. military:

The Broader Maranao War Record
Mindalano's campaigns need to be understood alongside the larger Maranao resistance, which represents one of the
most effective grassroots anti-Japanese movements in Philippine history.
The Maranao Moros fought the Japanese 108th Division almost every week from 1943 to October 1944, operating
in Lanao in southern Mindanao.<ref name="wikipedia_moros"/>
Historians have noted that the Moro guerrilla campaign was so effective that it confined Japanese forces to a few
coastal detachments, with any inland move into Moro-held territory typically resulting in the annihilation of the
intruding force.
Contemporary accounts describe Maranao fighters using both firearms and traditional bladed weapons, including
the kris, the barong, and the campilan, to compensate for ammunition shortages and to exploit close-quarters terrain
advantages.<ref name="filipiknow">FilipiKnow. "Meet the Terrifying Moro Warriors and Heroes of WWII."
January 21, 2022. Retrieved from https://filipiknow.net/moros-during-world-war-2/</ref>
Some historians have argued that six months before the American return in late 1944, the Moros had already
effectively driven the Japanese from their territories in Mindanao, with Japanese soldiers reportedly preferring to
surrender to American forces rather than face the Moros.<ref name="filipiknow"/>

PAGE 6
Post-War Political Career
Congressman for Lanao (1946–1949)
When the war ended, Mindalano's transition from battlefield commander to elected legislator was both natural and
necessary.
His people needed representation, and few in Lanao had the credibility, the name recognition, and the moral
authority he had earned through three years of resistance.
He was elected to represent Lanao in the 1st Congress of the Philippines, which convened from May 25, 1946 to
December 13, 1949 — the first legislature of the newly independent Republic of the Philippines, operating under
the presidencies of Manuel Roxas and, later, Elpidio Quirino.<ref name="1stcongress">Wikipedia. "1st Congress
of the Philippines." Retrieved from https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1st_Congress_of_the_Philippines</ref>
It was historically significant: the 1st Congress passed a total of 421 laws (Republic Acts No. 1 to 421) focused on
national reconstruction and the establishment of republican government after the devastation of occupation.<ref
name="1stcongress"/>
Mindalano was part of that legislative body, one of the very few Muslim Mindanao voices in a national legislature
still finding its post-war footing.
His presence mattered beyond symbolism.
He also served as a member of the 2nd Congress of the Commonwealth of the Philippines in 1946, immediately
preceding the Republic's inauguration, giving him continuity across the Commonwealth-to-Republic transition.<ref
name="bangsa">Bangsamoro Political Profiles. "Bangsa Ranao." Retrieved from
https://bangsaranao.blogspot.com/</ref>
Legislative Contributions
Among the documented acts of his legislative work, Mindalano used his position as Congressman to manage the
transfer of the Lanao Agricultural High School to Malabang, Lanao Province in 1946, an act of educational
foresight that shaped the region's post-war institutional landscape.<ref name="msulnac">MSU-Lanao del Norte
Agricultural College. "VMGC and History." Retrieved from https://msusnd.edu.ph/about/vmgc</ref>
As a veteran who had led men through the hardest campaigns of the war, he was also a natural advocate for the
recognition and benefits of Filipino guerrillas who had served under the USFIP, a community whose wartime
sacrifices were sometimes overlooked in the rush of post-war reconstruction.<ref name="docx_source"/>
His title of Amir — carried into his legislative service — signaled that he remained not just a congressman, but a
bridge figure: a man whose authority within the Muslim community of Lanao gave him a unique capacity to
translate the concerns of that community to a national government that was still, in many ways, learning to include
Muslim Mindanao in its vision of the republic.<ref name="docx_source"/>

PAGE 7
Values, Character, and Cultural Significance
A Vow as a Political Statement
Mindalano's decision to vow not to shave his beard until the Japanese were expelled was not merely personal. In
Maranao culture, such public vows carry the weight of community witness: they bind the person who makes them
to a public standard of conduct and create a form of social accountability.
By making his vow visible and known across Lanao, Mindalano turned his private grief — the death of his father
— into a communal statement of defiance.
He was also reportedly among the most active recruiters of the resistance, traveling from community to community
to persuade Maranao leaders and ordinary folk to join the fight, an effort that required not just bravery but political
skill, patience, and the kind of personal trust that can't be manufactured.<ref name="docx_source"/>
The Kris and the Koran
Mindalano's story sits at the intersection of two powerful Maranao traditions: the warrior ethos of the maratabat
(Maranao honor-dignity) and the faith commitments of Islam.
The Moro fighters' willingness to resist even after formal surrender, their oath-taking before the Quran, their use of
bladed weapons alongside firearms — these weren't just tactics. They reflected a deeply held belief that certain
things were worth dying for, and that dishonor was a worse outcome than death.
Mindalano embodied both dimensions: a man who fought with military discipline under an American-recognized
command structure, while also operating within the cultural logic of his own people.
A Maranao Among Moro Heroes
Mindalano is consistently grouped with the most celebrated Moro anti-Japanese resistance leaders: Salipada
Pendatun, Datu Busran Kalaw, Sultan Mohamad Ali Dimaporo, Domocao Alonto, and others.<ref
name="filipiknow"/><ref name="wikipedia_moros"/>
What distinguishes him in this company is the specific honor of being described as the first Maranao to strike —
not just a participant in the resistance, but the one who, in the dark days of mid-1942, chose to move before there
was any guarantee of American support, before there was a functioning guerrilla network, and before it was clear
the resistance could survive at all.
That willingness to act first, at greatest risk, is the core of his historical significance.
Legacy and Recognition
The Silver Star as Formal Vindication
The Silver Star, awarded by the U.S. government in 1951, was more than a medal. It was formal acknowledgment
by the most powerful military in the world that Manalao Mindalano had performed with extraordinary gallantry in
defense of shared values.

PAGE 8
That the citation was issued in 1951 — six years after the war's end — reflects both the bureaucratic lag in
processing wartime awards for Filipino soldiers under the USFIP and the larger, often frustrating story of delayed
recognition that many Filipino veterans experienced in the post-war decades.
A Forgotten Chapter, Slowly Remembered
Mindalano's name appears in Philippine military and legislative records, but he remains underrepresented in
mainstream national historiography.
This is not unique to him: Muslim Mindanao heroes of World War II have long occupied a marginal place in the
dominant narrative of Philippine wartime resistance, which has historically centered on Luzon-based figures and
events.
Efforts by historians, cultural advocates, and digital platforms like BangsamoroPedia are working to change that,
surfacing the stories of men like Mindalano and restoring their rightful place in the national memory.
His legacy is best understood not just as a military story, but as a statement about the Bangsamoro people's deep,
historically rooted commitment to their homeland — a commitment that they have demonstrated, repeatedly, in the
face of every occupying force that has underestimated them.
Death
The exact date and circumstances of Amer Manalao Mindalano's death are not fully documented in available public
sources.
He is confirmed to have served in the 1st Congress of the Philippines through 1949; further biographical details
from this period onward remain to be verified through archival research.
Further Reading
Tan, Samuel K. The Muslim South and Beyond. University of the Philippines Press.
Abinales, Patricio N. Making Mindanao: Cotabato and Davao in the Formation of the Philippine Nation-
State. Ateneo de Manila University Press, 2000.
Kuder, Edward. Personal reports and correspondence cited in Positively Filipino, "The Battle of Tamparan
and the Forgotten Moro Heroes of World War II," 2022.

https://valor.militarytimes.com/recipient/recipient-109194/

Mindanao State University – Main Campus
Sindangan Extension
Mindanao State University – Main Campus Sindangan Extension
(commonly called MSU-MCSE) is a public university extension
campus of the Mindanao State University System, located in
Barangay Balok, Sindangan, Zamboanga del Norte, Philippines. It
stands as one of the youngest yet fastest-growing extension campuses
in the MSU System, built through a partnership between the Local
Government Unit (LGU) of Sindangan and MSU Main Campus in
Marawi City. Since its establishment in 2021, MSU-MCSE has
grown from a pioneering batch of 301 students into a campus of
nearly 800 enrollees, offering programs in engineering,
environmental science, fisheries, psychology, mathematics, statistics,
and secondary education.

Pull Quote
"What began as a visionary aspiration has
become a thriving university campus, a
beacon of hope for Sindangan and the
entire Zamboanga Peninsula."
Overview
MSU-MCSE was created to answer a long-standing need in
Sindangan and its neighboring municipalities: access to free, quality
tertiary education without having to travel far from home. As an
extension of the MSU System, which was chartered to serve Muslim
and Indigenous communities across the MINSUPALA (Mindanao-
Sulu-Palawan) region, the campus carries forward that same mission
while also opening its doors widely to the broader population of
Zamboanga del Norte, including the Subanen communities native to
the area. Today it offers eleven degree programs, supports a growing
roster of licensed professionals among its graduates, and continues to
expand its facilities and academic offerings year after year.
History and Founding
The story of MSU-MCSE traces back to the early days of Hon. Rosendo "Dodoy" S. Labadlabad's term as
Municipal Mayor of Sindangan, which began in July 2019. Education was one of his top priorities from day one,
with local leaders already dreaming of a homegrown institution of higher learning even before the idea had a name.
That dream took clearer shape in November 2019, when Mayor Labadlabad learned about the MSU Charter during
a gathering he attended. Realizing that MSU's mandate to serve Muslim and Indigenous communities, including the
Subanens of Zamboanga del Norte, aligned perfectly with what Sindangan needed, he began exploring the idea in
earnest.
The real spark, though, came from a casual conversation. Former Sangguniang Bayan (SB) Member Hon. Floro
"Dodong" S. Ricaborda of Titay, Zamboanga Sibugay, ran into Dr. Florencio "Anjun" D. Recoleto Jr., then Vice
Chancellor for Academic Affairs of MSU Main Campus, and Prof. Elpidio "Pids" S. Ricaborda, JD, while
discussing an entirely different MSU extension project. Somewhere in that conversation came the question that
changed everything: why not put up an MSU extension in Sindangan too?
From there, momentum built quickly. Mayor Labadlabad and Hon. Dodong Ricaborda rallied local officials such as
SB Secretary Dr. El B. Jimenez, SB Member Hon. Jerome E. Ochavo, Municipal Administrator Mr. Jie Archie D.
Reluya, CPA, Mr. Michael A. Masalta, and Municipal Health Officer Dr. Rex V. Samson, with strong backing from
Vice Mayor Hon. Nilo Florentino "Boy" Z. Sy and the Sangguniang Bayan, which passed supportive resolutions to
move things along.
On July 23, 2020, Mayor Labadlabad formally wrote to MSU System President Dr. Habib W. Macaayong to open
discussions about establishing the extension campus. By August 12, 2020, the group, now joined by Hon.
Congresswoman Glona G. Labadlabad (who later became Mayor of Sindangan herself), LGU Legal Officer Atty.
Lunrey B. Bagor, and MSU officials including Vice President for Planning and Development Dr. Rasid M. Paca
and Vice President for Academic Affairs Dr. Alma E. Berowa, met in Iligan City for the first exploratory talks with
MSU's Deans and Department Chairs.
That December, the University issued Special Order No. 747-OP, Series of 2020, creating a Technical Working
Committee (TWC) chaired by Dr. Paca, with Dr. Recoleto as Vice Chairperson. OVCAA Special Assistants Dr.
Joel V. Araya, Dr. Alyanah G. Pantao, and Prof. Ian Randy F. Gallego handled the heavy lifting of preparing the
feasibility study and supporting documents, work that paid off when the Academic Planning Committee approved
the proposal on March 9, 2021.

PAGE 3
The breakthrough moment arrived on March 22, 2021, when the MSU Board of Regents officially approved the
creation of MSU-MCSE. A Memorandum of Agreement (MOA) between the LGU of Sindangan and MSU Main
Campus followed on April 8, 2021, cementing the partnership. Soon after, Dr. Recoleto was designated as the
campus's First Campus Director through a special order, with a six-year term as laid out in the MOA.
Institutional Development
Entrance exams came fast on the heels of the Board's approval. The MSU System Admission and Scholarship
Examination (MSU-SASE) was held on March 28, 2021, followed by the MSU College Entrance Test (MSU-CET)
on May 22 and July 10, 2021. Enrollment for the pioneering batch ran from July 21 to 30, 2021, at the Old
Municipal Building of Sindangan, and 301 students made the cut across ten founding degree programs.
The campus held its first Flag Raising Ceremony on September 8, 2021, at the Misok Campus, followed the next
day by its official inauguration at the Balok campus site and its first University Convocation, marking the true start
of academic life at MSU-MCSE.
From there, growth has been steady and, at times, dramatic. By the Second Semester of AY 2024–2025, enrollment
had climbed to 757 students. The campus celebrated its 4th Founding Anniversary on March 22, 2025, in
partnership with the LGU of Sindangan, and just months later, on July 4, 2025, it held its historic First Pre-
Commencement Exercises, presenting 113 pioneering graduates, five of them Magna Cum Laude and forty Cum
Laude. These degrees were formally conferred at the 61st Commencement Exercises of MSU Main Campus in
Marawi City on July 24, 2025.
By the Second Semester of AY 2025–2026, enrollment had grown further still, to 792 students across ten
pioneering programs, with a new eleventh program (BSEd Mathematics) approved to start in AY 2026–2027.
Etymology
The name "Mindanao State University – Main Campus Sindangan Extension" reflects its administrative status as a
satellite or extension campus of MSU Main Campus in Marawi City, rather than an independent chartered
university. "MCSE" is simply shorthand built from "Main Campus Sindangan Extension," and it is this acronym,
MSU-MCSE, that the campus and its community use in everyday reference.
Vision, Mission, and Core Values
While MSU-MCSE operates under the broader mandate of the Mindanao State University System, its guiding
purpose has consistently centered on bringing accessible, quality, and free higher education closer to the people of
Sindangan and the neighboring municipalities of Zamboanga del Norte, particularly underserved communities who
would otherwise have to travel far for a college education. Its 5th Founding Anniversary theme, "MSU-MCSE at 5:
Strengthening Connections, Sustaining Academic Excellence, and Advocating for Peace, Innovation, and Inclusive
Education," captures much of what the campus continues to stand for: connection, excellence, peace, innovation,
and inclusion.
Founders and Early Leadership
The founding of MSU-MCSE was very much a community effort. Key figures include:

PAGE 4
Hon. Rosendo "Dodoy" S. Labadlabad, Municipal Mayor of Sindangan, whose administration championed
the establishment of the campus from the very beginning
Hon. Floro "Dodong" S. Ricaborda, whose conversation with MSU officials sparked the idea
Dr. Florencio "Anjun" D. Recoleto Jr., then Vice Chancellor for Academic Affairs of MSU Main Campus,
who became the campus's First Campus Director
Prof. Elpidio "Pids" S. Ricaborda, JD, OVCAA Special Assistant, later Special Assistant to the Campus
Director
Dr. Rasid M. Paca, RME, JD, then Vice President for Planning and Development, who chaired the Technical
Working Committee
Dr. Alma E. Berowa, then Vice President for Academic Affairs
Dr. Habib W. Macaayong, MSU System President at the time of the initial talks
Hon. Congresswoman Glona G. Labadlabad, later Mayor of Sindangan, who supported the campus from its
earliest exploratory discussions
Vice Mayor Hon. Nilo Florentino "Boy" Z. Sy and the members of the Sangguniang Bayan, who provided
legislative backing through supportive resolutions
Historical Development
The campus's growth since 2021 has moved along several fronts at once: enrollment, academic programs, faculty
and staff, research culture, and institutional partnerships. What started as a ten-program offering with 301
pioneering students has, within five years, become an eleven-program campus with nearly 800 students, a growing
base of licensed professional graduates, and a deepening relationship with both the MSU System Administration
and the LGU of Sindangan.
Campus and Location
MSU-MCSE is situated in Barangay Balok, Sindangan, Zamboanga del Norte, with academic operations also held
at the Misok Campus. Enrollment activities in recent years have made use of venues such as the Sindangan
Cultural and Sports Complex, while the Office of the Campus Director has operated out of the 2nd Floor of the Old
Municipal Building in Poblacion, Sindangan. In April 2026, the campus adopted a blended learning modality as
part of austerity measures aimed at conserving fuel resources, with face-to-face classes held Mondays, Tuesdays,
and Saturdays at the Misok Campus, and online classes conducted Wednesdays through Fridays via Google Meet
and Google Classroom. All examinations remained face-to-face to protect academic integrity.
Academic Structure
The campus is led by the Office of the Campus Director, supported by a Special Assistant to the Campus Director
and administrative staff. As of the Second Semester of AY 2025–2026, MSU-MCSE maintained 52 personnel
across its academic departments, categorized as follows:
Organic Faculty (28): hired directly at MSU-MCSE, with salaries funded by the LGU of Sindangan under
the MOA
Organic Faculty with Item (5): originally LGU-funded, now covered under MSU-Main Campus plantilla
items
Mobile Faculty (9): MSU-Main Campus faculty who rotate teaching duties, typically every other week,
between Marawi and Sindangan
Full-Time Faculty (4): MSU-Main Campus faculty whose entire teaching load is dedicated to MSU-MCSE
Campus Administration and Staff (6): including the Campus Director, Special Assistant, and LGU-assigned
administrative personnel

PAGE 5
Ten of the faculty members additionally serve as Program Coordinators for their respective degree programs.
Academic Programs and Curriculum Offerings
MSU-MCSE currently offers eleven degree programs:
1. Bachelor of Science in Agricultural and Biosystems Engineering (ABE)
2. Bachelor of Science in Chemical Engineering (CHE)
3. Bachelor of Science in Civil Engineering (CE)
4. Bachelor of Science in Electrical Engineering (EE)
5. Bachelor of Science in Mechanical Engineering (ME)
6. Bachelor of Science in Psychology (PSY)
7. Bachelor of Science in Environmental Science (ES)
8. Bachelor of Science in Fisheries (FIS)
9. Bachelor of Science in Mathematics (MAT)
10. Bachelor of Science in Statistics (STT)
11. Bachelor of Secondary Education Major in Mathematics (BSEd Math), approved May 21, 2026, to begin
First Semester, AY 2026–2027
For the Second Semester of AY 2025–2026, Civil Engineering had the highest enrollment among the ten
established programs with 126 students, followed by Environmental Science with 109 and Psychology with 103.
Research, Extension, and Community Engagement
Building a culture of research has been a growing priority for the campus. From March 19 to 21, 2026, MSU-
MCSE held a 3-Day Reecho Seminar on Research Capacity Building, IDP Integration, and Faculty Research
Orientation, helping align faculty research work with the University's Institutional Development Plan. This was
followed on May 9, 2026, by a Faculty and Student Research Seminar titled "Foundations of Research in the Age
of AI: Building Ethical, Data-Driven, and AI-Assisted Researchers," which tackled research conceptualization, data
analysis, ethical AI use, academic writing, and scholarly integrity.
On the community front, the Environmental Envoys and Conservationists Society (EnvironECS), working with the
Supreme Student Government (SSG), led a Mangrove Planting Activity in Barangay R.G. Macias, Sindangan,
during Earth Month 2026, joined by LGU Sindangan Mayor Hon. Glona G. Labadlabad and various government
agencies. The campus also took part in Gabay Zanorte: Division Career Guidance Expo 2026 on March 4, 2026, at
the Sindangan Cultural and Sports Complex, where faculty and student leaders guided junior and senior high
school learners on higher education pathways.
Student Life and Organizations
Student life at MSU-MCSE runs through bodies like the Supreme Student Government (SSG), which has organized
events such as the Month of Love celebration on February 13, 2026, featuring interactive booths, departmental
games, and cultural performances. The Environmental Envoys and Conservationists Society (EnvironECS) leads
sustainability initiatives such as mangrove planting. Weekly Monday Flag Ceremonies serve as a regular gathering
point for announcements, recognitions, and introducing new faculty to the community, as seen on February 9,
2026, when eight newly hired faculty members were formally welcomed.

PAGE 6
Traditions and Culture
Founding anniversaries are a big deal at MSU-MCSE. The 5th Founding Anniversary, held March 19 to 23, 2026,
featured a torch lighting ceremony, salute performances, cultural presentations, and the introduction of Mr. and Ms.
MSU-MCSE 2026 candidates representing four cluster teams: Dauntless, Erudite, Amity, and Candor. The five-day
celebration wove together academic, cultural, sports, and student development activities into one big campus-wide
affair.
The campus also observes broader civic milestones. In February 2026, it marked the 40th Anniversary of the EDSA
People Power Revolution with a screening of the film "Batas Militar," encouraging reflection on democracy,
human rights, and responsible citizenship. Meanwhile, the Hard Hatting and Pinning Ceremony has become an
annual rite of passage for students from Engineering, Environmental Science, Fisheries, Psychology, Mathematics,
and Statistics as they step into apprenticeship, internship, and on-the-job training.
Administration and Governance
MSU-MCSE operates under a Campus Director appointed through a special order from the MSU System, with a
six-year term as stipulated in the MOA between the LGU of Sindangan and MSU Main Campus. The Office of the
Campus Director (OCD) is supported by a Special Assistant and administrative staff. Governance decisions,
particularly on funding, faculty plantilla, and infrastructure, are coordinated through regular dialogue between the
MSU System Administration and the LGU of Sindangan, most recently formalized in a Bilateral Meeting held May
14, 2026, which addressed proposed amendments to the MSU-LGU MOA, funding arrangements, faculty plantilla
requirements, student assistance programs, and the long-term goal of institutional autonomy for the campus.
Presidents, Chancellors, or Heads
Dr. Florencio D. Recoleto Jr., PhD: First and current Campus Director of MSU-MCSE, designated in April
2021 with a six-year term
Prof. Elpidio S. Ricaborda, JD: Special Assistant to the Campus Director
Atty. Paisalin P.D. Tago, CPA: MSU System President, who made his first official visit to Sindangan and
MSU-MCSE from May 13 to 15, 2026
Dr. Minerva-Saminah M. Naga: Vice President and Vice Chancellor for Academic Affairs, who approved the
lowering of the SASE cut-off score in May 2026 to expand access to admission
Facilities and Landmarks
The main academic site sits at the Balok campus, with additional operations at the Misok Campus, where the
pioneering Flag Raising Ceremony was held in 2021 and where face-to-face classes continue under the current
blended learning arrangement. The GAD Building has also been used for face-to-face sessions when needed.
Large-scale institutional events, from enrollment to founding anniversary celebrations, are typically held at the
Sindangan Cultural and Sports Complex, while the Office of the Campus Director is based at the 2nd Floor of the
Old Municipal Building, Poblacion, Sindangan.

PAGE 7
Accreditation and Recognition
MSU-MCSE's academic quality has been reflected in a series of licensure examination results. In January 2026, the
Department of Psychology and Related Services achieved a 100% passing rate in the Certified Human Resource
Associate (CHRA) Assessment Examination, with all nine examinees passing, placing the campus among the top-
performing schools in the country for that exam. The campus's first batch of BS Fisheries graduates achieved an
85.71% passing rate in the Fisheries Professional Licensure Examination (FPLE), well above the national passing
rate of 69.61%. In the April 2026 Registered Electrical Engineers Licensure Examination, MSU-MCSE posted a
100% passing rate among its four examinees. Engr. Aaron O. Mateo became the campus's first Civil Engineering
Licensure Examination passer in March–April 2026, while Engr. Joscel Ijurpe became its first Registered Chemical
Engineer after passing the 2026 Chemical Engineer Licensure Examination.
Significant Milestones

March 22, 2021: MSU Board of Regents approves the creation of MSU-MCSE
April 8, 2021: MOA signed between LGU Sindangan and MSU Main Campus
September 8-9, 2021: First Flag Raising Ceremony and official inauguration
March 22, 2025: 4th Founding Anniversary
July 4, 2025: First Pre-Commencement Exercises, 113 pioneering graduates
January 2026: 100% passing rate in the CHRA Assessment Examination
March 4, 2026: Participation in Gabay Zanorte Division Career Guidance Expo
March 19-21, 2026: Research Capacity Building and IDP Integration Seminar
March 19-23, 2026: 5th Founding Anniversary
April 6, 2026: Implementation of austerity measures and blended learning modality
April 26, 2026: MSU College Entrance Test (CET) 2026 administered, 212 examinees
May 4, 2026: MSU SASE results released; October 2025 exam produced 210 initial passers
May 9, 2026: Faculty and Student Research Seminar on AI-assisted research
May 13-15, 2026: First official visit of MSU System President Atty. Paisalin P.D. Tago, CPA
May 14, 2026: 3rd Crème de la Crème Recognition Program and Bilateral Meeting between MSU System
and LGU Sindangan
May 20, 2026: SASE cut-off score lowered from 80 to 69, raising qualified enrollees to 408
May 21, 2026: Approval of the Bachelor of Secondary Education Major in Mathematics, the campus's 11th
degree program
May 28, 2026: 3rd Hard Hatting and Pinning Ceremony

Sharifah A. Galvez, RFP: Faculty member and Registered Fisheries Professional
Contributions to Education, Society, and the Bangsamoro Community
As an extension of the Mindanao State University System, MSU-MCSE carries forward MSU's founding mandate
to serve Muslim and Indigenous communities across the MINSUPALA region, while also opening opportunities to
the wider Subanen and general population of Zamboanga del Norte. By keeping tuition and testing fees free and
lowering admission barriers where possible (as seen in the 2026 SASE cut-off score adjustment), the campus has
made higher education genuinely reachable for families in Sindangan and neighboring towns who might otherwise
have had to send their children far from home to study. Its growing list of licensed professionals, engineers,
fisheries specialists, and psychology-related practitioners, is already feeding back into the local workforce and
economy of the Zamboanga Peninsula.
Legacy and Impact
In just five years, MSU-MCSE has gone from an idea floated in a casual conversation between local leaders and
MSU officials to a campus of nearly 800 students, eleven degree programs, and a growing track record of board
exam passers. Its story reflects what can happen when local government units, university administrators, and
community leaders align around a shared goal: accessible, quality education for a region that needed it. As the
campus continues pursuing its long-term goal of institutional autonomy, it remains anchored to the same vision that
started it all, bringing MSU's mission of inclusive, transformative higher education closer to the people of
Sindangan and the entire Zamboanga Peninsula.

Abdulkarim Misuari
Abdulkarim Misuari is a Filipino Moro political figure and public servant from Sulu. He currently serves as a
Member of the Bangsamoro Parliament under the Bangsamoro Transition Authority (BTA). He is associated with
the Moro National Liberation Front (MNLF) and is part of a prominent political family in the Bangsamoro
struggle.<ref name="barmm2023">Bangsamoro Government. Profiles of Bangsamoro Parliament Members.
Official BARMM Website, 2023.</ref><ref name="pia2022">Philippine Information Agency. MNLF leaders join
Bangsamoro governance. 2022.</ref>
---
Early Life and Background
Abdulkarim Misuari hails from Sulu, a historic center of the Sultanate of Sulu and the Moro resistance
movement.
He is part of the Misuari family, which has played a major role in the Moro struggle for self-determination.
His background is closely tied to the political and revolutionary developments in the Bangsamoro region.<ref
name="pia2022" />
---
Political Career
Moro National Liberation Front
Abdulkarim Misuari is associated with the Moro National Liberation Front (MNLF), one of the earliest Moro
revolutionary organizations advocating for autonomy and self-determination.
He has been involved in political and organizational activities related to the MNLF’s participation in
governance and peace processes.

PAGE 2
Bangsamoro Parliament
He was appointed as a Member of the Bangsamoro Transition Authority Parliament, representing MNLF
interests within the Bangsamoro government.
As a parliament member, he participates in legislative deliberations, policy-making, and governance reforms
during the BARMM transition period.<ref name="barmm2023" />
---
Contributions to Bangsamoro Governance
Represents MNLF constituencies within BARMM, contributing to inclusive governance that incorporates
different Moro revolutionary groups.
Supports peace-building initiatives and the political integration of former revolutionary movements into
formal governance structures.
Advocates for development programs in Sulu and other Bangsamoro areas.
---
Legacy and Significance
Abdulkarim Misuari symbolizes the integration of MNLF leadership into the Bangsamoro political
framework.
His participation in BARMM governance reflects the broader peace process that brought together different
Moro groups under a unified regional government.
He contributes to strengthening political inclusivity and representation in the Bangsamoro Parliament.
---

text:

Nur Misuari
Nur Misuari (born March 3, 1939) is a Filipino Moro revolutionary leader, politician, and academic, widely
recognized as the founder and former chairman of the Moro National Liberation Front (MNLF). He played a
central role in the struggle for Moro self-determination and autonomy in Mindanao and the Sulu archipelago,
advocating for the rights, welfare, and political recognition of the Bangsamoro people.<ref
name="mcginty2011">McGinty, C. Muslims in the Philippines: Nur Misuari and the Moro Struggle. Asian Affairs
Journal, 2011.</ref><ref name="jolo2005">Jolo, A. The MNLF Movement: Origins and Leadership. Mindanao
Studies, 2005.</ref>
---
Early Life and Education
Nur Misuari was born in Tapul, Sulu, to a Tausug family with strong Islamic values.
He studied at various local schools before earning a degree in political science at the University of the
Philippines Diliman.
He pursued graduate studies in the United States, earning a master’s degree in political science from the
University of the Philippines and engaging in research on autonomy, governance, and minority rights.<ref
name="mcginty2011" />
---
Academic Career
Misuari worked as a professor and researcher, focusing on Philippine politics, Muslim history, and minority
governance.
His academic work laid the foundation for understanding Moro identity, history, and grievances, shaping his
vision for autonomy and self-determination.<ref name="jolo2005" />
---

PAGE 2
Formation of the Moro National Liberation Front
In 1972, following the declaration of Martial Law by President Ferdinand Marcos, Misuari established the
Moro National Liberation Front (MNLF) to advocate for Moro self-determination and political autonomy.
The MNLF initially aimed to create an independent Bangsamoro homeland in Mindanao, Sulu, and Palawan,
citing historical marginalization and the failure of the Philippine government to protect Moro rights.
Under Misuari’s leadership, the MNLF conducted organized armed resistance against government forces
while also pursuing diplomatic engagement with international actors, including the Organization of Islamic
Cooperation (OIC).<ref name="mcginty2011" /><ref name="jolo2005" />
---
Political Leadership and Governance
Following peace negotiations mediated by the OIC and the signing of the Tripoli Agreement in 1976, Misuari
became the first governor of the autonomous region of the former Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao
(ARMM) in 1996.
As governor, he focused on institution-building, socio-economic development, and establishing autonomous
governance structures.
His tenure was marked by political challenges, including factionalism within the MNLF, disputes with the
Philippine national government, and tensions with emerging groups like the Moro Islamic Liberation Front
(MILF).<ref name="mcginty2011" />
---
Later Years and Controversies
Misuari faced multiple arrests and accusations of rebellion and inciting violence, including during the 2001
Mindanao rebellion.
Despite controversies, he remained a symbolic figure for Moro identity, autonomy, and political struggle.
He continues to advocate for peace and dialogue between the Philippine government and Moro communities,
emphasizing education, culture, and self-determination.<ref name="jolo2005" />
---
Legacy
Nur Misuari is widely regarded as the father of the Moro nationalist movement and a pivotal figure in the
history of the Bangsamoro struggle.
His leadership of the MNLF contributed to the establishment of autonomous governance structures,
including the ARMM and later the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao.
Misuari’s life reflects the complex interplay of armed struggle, political negotiation, and cultural advocacy in
the Moro quest for self-determination.<ref name="mcginty2011" /><ref name="jolo2005" />
---

title: Morados, Macrina Hannah A.
text:
PAGE 1
Macrina Hannah A. Morados
Macrina Hannah A. Morados is a Filipino Muslim legal scholar, educator, and public intellectual who has spent
her career making Islamic law legible, just, and relevant, not just inside the classroom but in courtrooms, policy
tables, and communities where it actually shapes people's lives. She holds the rank of Associate Professor 7 at the
UP Institute of Islamic Studies (UP IIS), University of the Philippines Diliman, and served as the institute's 8th
Dean from 2016 to 2018, becoming only the second woman in UP IIS history to hold that position. Her signature
contribution is the bridge she has built between Islamic jurisprudence and Philippine law, particularly the Code of
Muslim Personal Laws (Presidential Decree 1083), which governs the lives of millions of Filipino Muslims on
matters of family, marriage, inheritance, and children's rights. Contextual evidence, including her foundational
education at the Mindanao State University in Marawi City and her deep familiarity with Maranao communities
and concerns, strongly suggests she is of Maranao heritage, though this has not been explicitly confirmed in
publicly available sources.
Contents

2 Education
3 Career

Background
Macrina A. Morados came of age academically in Marawi City, the heart of Maranao Muslim civilization in
Mindanao. She completed her undergraduate education at Mindanao State University (MSU), one of the most
significant centers of Islamic learning in the Philippines, earning her Bachelor of Arts in Islamic Studies in 1991
in MSU-General Santos. MSU's main campus sits within a predominantly Maranao environment, and the
institution has historically been the alma mater of many prominent Muslim Filipino scholars, lawyers, and public
servants. Her decision to pursue Islamic Studies there reflects both a personal rootedness in Muslim Filipino
identity and an early intellectual commitment to understanding the intersection of faith, law, and community. She
went on to earn her Bachelor of Laws at the MSU College of Law, Marawi Campus, completing her legal
education in 2001. In March 2019, the Mindanao State University formally confirmed the retroactive elevation of
her Bachelor of Laws to a Juris Doctor degree, aligning her credential with contemporary Philippine legal
education standards. This confirmation, retroactive to 2001, recognized not just the formality of a title change but

Career
Academic Career at UP Diliman
Morados has built her academic home at the UP Institute of Islamic
Studies, where she now holds the rank of Associate Professor 7.
Her teaching and research spans a wide range of subjects: Muslim
Personal and Family Relations Law, the Shari'ah Court system in
the Philippines, Muslim women and children's rights, Islamic
education, interfaith relations, theo-centrism and pluralism, and the
history of Muslims in the Philippines. She served as Dean of the
UP IIS with a three-year term beginning January 1, 2016, affirmed
by UP Diliman Chancellor Michael L. Tan on March 30, 2016. As
the second woman ever to lead the institute (following Dr. Carmen
Abubakar), her deanship was marked by an ambitious agenda:
curriculum reform to respond to global trends in Islamic banking,
Halal, and Shari'ah studies; revival of the IIS academic journal; and
the strengthening of the institute's role as a voice against extremism
and radicalization. She was also a Faculty Affiliate of the UP
Center for International Studies from 2015 to 2019, and served as
Convener of the UP Center for Integrative and Development
Studies, Islamic Studies Program (UP CIDS-ISP) from 2017 to
2021.
Role in the Shari'ah Justice System
Morados has been a trusted figure in the Philippine judiciary's
engagement with Islamic law. She served as Shari'ah Bar
Examiner in 2008, covering Islamic Inheritance Law, and again in
2014, covering Persons and Family Relations. In November 2021,
