by virtue of an En Banc Resolution of the Supreme Court of the
Philippines, she was designated Chairperson of the 2022 Shari'ah
Bar Examinations, the first time the examinations were held at UP
Diliman since 1983. Apart from her examining role, she has served
as a lecturer for the PHILJA-NCMF Shari'ah Training Seminar
during the 18th and 19th Shari'ah Bar Examinations. She was also
invited by the Philippine Judicial Academy (PHILJA) to participate
in and lecture at the Judges Career Enhancement Program, where
she delivered a comparative lecture on PD 1083 and the Civil Code
on Persons and Family Relations for an audience of Shari'ah Court
and Regional Trial Court judges in Tagaytay City (August 1 to 3,
2024). She currently serves as Team Leader of the Supreme Court
project on the Institutional Review and Assessment of the Shariah
Justice System, with outputs submitted in 2025.
Government and Policy Engagements
In 2015, she was appointed as a member of the Transitional Justice
and Reconciliation Commission (TJRC) for the Historical
Injustice Study Group, a body formed to address the roots of
conflict in Muslim Mindanao as part of the peace process between
the Philippine government and the Moro Islamic Liberation Front
(MILF). Her role in that commission was a recognition of her
standing as a credible voice in Muslim Filipino affairs and her
ability to situate historical grievances within the framework of law,
justice, and reconciliation. In 2008, she received a Cultural
Exchange Program grant under the Interfaith Program of the US
Department of State and Purdue University, which broadened her
engagement with international interfaith dialogue.
Research and Publications
Morados is a prolific researcher whose published work consistently engages the real-world stakes of Islamic law in
the Philippine context.
Muslim Personal Laws in the Philippines (PD 1083): A Policy Review using the Gender Perspective
(Lead Author, commissioned by the International Development Law Organization [IDLO], 2021) -- her most
directly policy-oriented publication, applying gender analysis to the Code of Muslim Personal Laws.
Islamic Law and International Humanitarian Law: A Philippine Ulama Perspective on their
Convergences and Divergences (Co-author, UP IIS and ICRC, 2021) -- a scholarly contribution to the
conversation between Islamic jurisprudence and international human rights frameworks.
Balik-Islam in Luzon and Metro Manila (Co-author, in Research on Balik-Islam in the Philippines, IAG-
UPIIS, 2020) -- examining the return to Islam among Filipino converts in urban and northern Philippine
communities.
Philippine Muslim History: Challenges and Prospects (Co-author, UP CIDS and UPIIS, 2019) -- a
collaborative historiographical work addressing the contested and complex history of Filipino Muslims.
CRC and Islamic Law Divergences and Convergences: The Philippine Case (Co-author, commissioned
by UNICEF and the National Commission on Muslim Filipinos [NCMF], 2007) -- an early and influential
contribution examining the compatibility of the Convention on the Rights of the Child with Islamic legal
principles in the Philippine context.

PAGE 4
She has also written opinion pieces in Philippine national media, including the Philippine Daily Inquirer,
addressing issues such as the conceptual framework for rebuilding Marawi City as an Islamic community grounded
in the principle of Tawheed.
Institutional Contributions
During her deanship of UP IIS, Morados articulated a clear vision for the institute as more than an academic unit;
she saw it as a corrective voice in a national conversation too often distorted by misconception and fear. She
advocated for the IIS to offer a major in Shari'ah and to develop Halal-related programs in response to growing
global demand, framing both as opportunities for Filipino Muslims to participate meaningfully in national
economic and legal life. She called for the revival of the IIS academic journal as a platform for balanced and
liberating knowledge, particularly as a counterweight to the rise of radicalism and extremism. Through her work
with UP CIDS-ISP, she helped institutionalize a space for interdisciplinary Islamic studies research within one of
the Philippines' premier policy research centers. She has built a reputation as a go-to expert for media, international
organizations, and government bodies seeking nuanced, informed perspectives on Muslim Filipino law, gender, and
social issues.
Legacy
Macrina A. Morados represents a generation of Muslim Filipino women scholars who refused to be peripheral to
the intellectual and policy conversations that shape their communities' lives. She has worn many hats: professor,
dean, bar examiner, bar chair, policy reviewer, reconciliation commissioner, and public intellectual. In each of
those roles, she has brought the same core conviction: that Islamic law, properly understood and justly applied, is
compatible with human dignity, women's rights, and the aspirations of Filipino Muslims for peace and self-
determination. Her research on Muslim personal law from a gender perspective, her advocacy for raising the
minimum age of Muslim marriage, and her work on children's rights within Islamic jurisprudence mark her as a
reformist scholar in the best tradition of Islamic legal thought. As she completes her doctorate and leads the
Supreme Court's review of the Shariah justice system, her scholarly and institutional work continues to shape the
legal landscape for Filipino Muslims.
Recognition
Appointed as the 8th Dean of the UP Institute of Islamic Studies (2016-2018), only the second woman to
hold the position
Designated Chairman of the 2022 Shari'ah Bar Examinations by the Supreme Court of the Philippines
(2021)

(2015)

University, 2008)

Convener, UP CIDS Islamic Studies Program (2017-2021)
Team Leader, Supreme Court Institutional Review and Assessment of the Shariah Justice System
(output submitted 2025)

PAGE 5
Current Research
Morados is presently finishing a research study on Preventing and Countering Violent Extremism (P/CVE)
among High-Profile Muslim Inmates in the Philippines. This research sits at the intersection of her expertise in
Islamic law, her long engagement with Muslim communities under stress, and the urgent national conversation on
deradicalization and justice reform. It reflects her sustained commitment to research that is not merely academic
but directly useful to the state, communities, and the people most affected by the policies she studies.

title: Moxsir, Ebra M.
text:
PAGE 1
Ebra M. Moxsir
(PCOL) Ebra M. Moxsir (Ret.) is a prominent Filipino Muslim religious leader, retired high-ranking police
official, and the current National President of the Imam Council of the Philippines (ICPI). A proud Maranao from
Mindanao, Moxsir has carved out a unique career path that bridges law enforcement and Islamic leadership,
making him one of the most influential voices for the Filipino Muslim community in contemporary Philippine
society. He is best known for his dual role as a police officer and Imam, particularly his service as acting "top cop"
of Marawi City during the devastating 2017 Marawi Siege, where his spiritual guidance and law enforcement
expertise proved crucial in navigating one of the most challenging chapters in Mindanao's recent history. With a
Doctorate in Public Administration and decades of service in the Philippine National Police (PNP) Chaplain
Service, Moxsir embodies a philosophy that unites moral authority with civic duty, positioning him as both a
cultural navigator and bridge-builder between Muslim Filipinos and the broader national community.
Contents
1 Early Life and Education
2 Police Career and Service
3 Role During the 2017 Marawi Siege
4 Religious Leadership and the Imam Council of the Philippines
5 Awards and Recognition
6 Institutional Contributions and Cultural Significance
7 Legacy and Public Presence
8 See Also
9 External Links
Early Life and Education
Ebra Moxsir was born and raised in the Lanao region of Mindanao, the ancestral homeland of the Maranao people.
His heritage connects him deeply to the rich cultural and religious traditions of one of the Philippines' most
prominent Muslim ethnolinguistic groups. Growing up in a region where Islamic faith and Maranao identity are
inseparable, Moxsir developed a strong sense of spiritual calling from an early age. While specific details about his
childhood remain largely private, his trajectory suggests a household that valued both religious devotion and
educational achievement.
Moxsir pursued his undergraduate education at Mindanao State University (MSU), the premier state university
serving Mindanao's Muslim communities and a key institution in preserving Maranao cultural heritage. MSU
provided him with not only academic credentials but also a broader exposure to the diverse social and political
landscape of Mindanao. His commitment to lifelong learning would later drive him to earn a Doctorate in Public
Administration (DPA), an advanced degree that equipped him with the theoretical frameworks and practical skills
to navigate complex bureaucratic systems. This combination of religious scholarship and public administration
expertise became the foundation for his dual career, allowing him to speak fluently in both the language of Islamic
jurisprudence and the operational vocabulary of government service.

Police Career and Service
Moxsir's professional journey took him into the ranks of the
Philippine National Police (PNP), where he would eventually rise
to the rank of Police Colonel (PCOL). Unlike many of his peers
who pursued traditional law enforcement tracks, Moxsir found his
niche in the PNP Chaplain Service, a specialized unit tasked with
providing spiritual guidance and moral support to police personnel
across the country. He served as Deputy Director of the Chaplain
Service, a position that placed him at the intersection of
operational policing and pastoral care.
In this role, Moxsir was responsible for overseeing the spiritual
welfare of Muslim officers within the PNP, ensuring that their
religious obligations were respected while maintaining the
discipline and professionalism expected of law enforcement
personnel. He became known within the force as a principled
leader who could balance the demands of police protocol with the
spiritual needs of Muslim Filipinos in uniform. His presence in the
Chaplain Service also helped to institutionalize Islamic practices
within the PNP, making the force more inclusive and culturally
sensitive to the country's Muslim minority.
Moxsir's approach to policing was deeply informed by his
religious training. He often spoke about the alignment between a
police officer's duty to protect and serve the public and an Imam's
mission to guide believers toward moral righteousness. For him,
law enforcement was not merely a profession but a form of
spiritual service—a way to manifest Islamic values of justice,
compassion, and communal responsibility in the secular realm of
public safety.
Role During the 2017 Marawi Siege
The defining moment of Moxsir's career came during the 2017
Marawi Siege, a five-month urban conflict between government
forces and ISIS-affiliated militants that devastated the Islamic City
of Marawi. As the siege unfolded, Moxsir was thrust into a critical
leadership position as the acting "top cop" of Marawi City, a
role that demanded both tactical acumen and profound cultural
sensitivity.
During this period, Moxsir's dual identity as a police officer and
Imam proved invaluable. He served as a trusted intermediary
between the military-led government response and the traumatized
local population, many of whom were displaced from their homes
and caught between warring factions. His religious authority
allowed him to communicate with community leaders, religious

PAGE 3
scholars, and ordinary Maranao residents in ways that military commanders could not. At the same time, his police
credentials gave him operational credibility within the security apparatus coordinating the government's response.
Moxsir worked tirelessly to maintain public trust during a time of extraordinary chaos and fear. He provided
spiritual counseling to displaced families, facilitated dialogue between civilian leaders and military officials, and
helped ensure that humanitarian relief efforts respected Islamic customs and practices. His efforts to de-escalate
tensions and promote calm were widely recognized, and he became a symbol of resilience and moral leadership in
the midst of one of the darkest chapters in Marawi's history.
The siege left deep scars on the city and its people, but Moxsir's presence during that time reinforced his reputation
as a leader who could navigate crises without compromising his principles. His work during the conflict
highlighted the importance of cultural competence in law enforcement and underscored the need for leaders who
understand the communities they serve—not just in theory, but through lived experience and genuine solidarity.
Religious Leadership and the Imam Council of the Philippines
Following his retirement from active police duty, Moxsir dedicated himself fully to religious leadership, assuming
the role of National President of the Imam Council of the Philippines (ICPI). The ICPI is one of the most
significant Islamic organizations in the country, representing Imams and Muslim religious leaders from across the
Philippine archipelago. Under Moxsir's stewardship, the council has grown into a well-structured and increasingly
influential institution that advocates for the welfare of Imams, promotes Islamic education, and works to strengthen
the voice of Muslim Filipinos in national affairs.
As National President, Moxsir has focused on several key initiatives. He has worked to professionalize the role of
the Imam in the Philippines, pushing for better training, clearer standards of religious scholarship, and improved
compensation and support for those who dedicate their lives to Islamic ministry. He has also emphasized the
importance of interfaith dialogue, regularly engaging with Christian, Buddhist, and indigenous religious leaders to
promote mutual understanding and combat religious prejudice.
Moxsir has been instrumental in positioning the ICPI as a partner to government agencies on issues affecting
Muslim communities. He has met with officials from the Bureau of Jail Management and Penology (BJMP) to
ensure that Muslim detainees have access to halal food, prayer facilities, and religious guidance. He has also
worked with local government units to address the unique needs of Muslim Filipinos during public health
emergencies, natural disasters, and social welfare programs.
One of his most visible contributions has been the establishment of practical community services under ICPI's
umbrella. This includes an emergency response vehicle donated by Senator Robin Padilla, which provides
transportation for medical emergencies and cadaver services for Muslim families. These initiatives reflect Moxsir's
belief that religious leadership must go beyond preaching and ritual—it must translate into tangible support for the
community's everyday needs.
Awards and Recognition
Moxsir's contributions to public service and religious leadership have earned him significant recognition both
within the Muslim community and in broader Philippine society. In 2018, he was awarded the Medalya ng
Pambihirang Paglilingkod (Special Service Medal) by the Philippine National Police, the organization's highest
honor for outstanding and meritorious service. The award specifically recognized his leadership during the 2017
Marawi Siege, acknowledging his role in maintaining stability and trust during an unprecedented crisis.

PAGE 4
Beyond formal honors, Moxsir is frequently celebrated as a bridge-builder between Muslim Filipinos and the wider
national community. He is regularly invited to high-profile events such as the annual Saudi National Day
celebrations, where he represents the Filipino Muslim community on an international stage. These appearances
underscore his status not only as a religious leader but also as a cultural ambassador who helps to strengthen ties
between the Philippines and the broader Islamic world.
Moxsir's media presence has also contributed to his public recognition. He is a sought-after commentator during
major Islamic observances such as Ramadan and Eid al-Adha, where he helps to educate non-Muslim Filipinos
about the significance and spiritual depth of these celebrations. His clear and accessible explanations have made
him a trusted voice for journalists and broadcasters seeking to present Islam in a balanced and respectful manner.
Institutional Contributions and Cultural Significance
Beyond his individual achievements, Moxsir's legacy lies in the institutional footprint he has built over decades of
service. His work has helped to strengthen the infrastructure of Muslim religious leadership in the Philippines,
making the ICPI a more effective advocate for the rights and welfare of Filipino Muslims.
Moxsir has been a vocal proponent of interfaith unity, regularly participating in dialogues with leaders from other
religious traditions. He believes that mutual respect and understanding are essential to building a cohesive and
peaceful society, particularly in a country as religiously diverse as the Philippines. His efforts have contributed to a
growing recognition within government circles that Muslim communities must be active partners in policymaking,
not passive subjects of top-down programs.
He has also worked to ensure that Islamic institutions are better integrated into the broader social fabric of the
Philippines. This includes advocating for the inclusion of Islamic perspectives in public health campaigns, disaster
response protocols, and social welfare initiatives. His approach reflects a pragmatic understanding that effective
governance requires not just technical expertise but also cultural sensitivity and genuine engagement with the
communities being served.
Moxsir's cultural significance extends to his role as a mentor and model for younger Muslim Filipinos. His career
demonstrates that it is possible to honor one's religious identity while excelling in mainstream institutions like the
police force or public administration. He has shown that Muslim Filipinos can be leaders in both sacred and secular
spheres, and that these roles are not mutually exclusive but mutually reinforcing.
Legacy and Public Presence
At the core of Ebra Moxsir's legacy are the values of unity, leadership, and collaboration. He has spent his career
demonstrating that a police officer's duty and a religious leader's mission are fundamentally aligned: both seek to
protect the vulnerable, uphold justice, and foster moral and spiritual transformation within the community. This
philosophy has guided his work in both the PNP and the ICPI, shaping him into a leader who is respected across
sectarian and institutional boundaries.
Moxsir's public presence remains strong even in retirement. He continues to be a go-to voice for the media during
significant religious holidays, public controversies involving Muslim communities, and national discussions about
interfaith relations. His ability to communicate complex religious concepts in accessible language has made him an
invaluable resource for journalists, educators, and policymakers seeking to understand the Filipino Muslim
experience.

PAGE 5
His leadership of the ICPI has also ensured that the next generation of Imams will have a stronger institutional
foundation to build upon. Through training programs, advocacy campaigns, and community outreach initiatives,
Moxsir has helped to elevate the status of Islamic religious leaders in the Philippines, ensuring that they are
recognized not just as spiritual guides but as vital contributors to the nation's social and moral fabric.
As the Philippines continues to grapple with questions of identity, pluralism, and national unity, figures like Ebra
Moxsir will remain essential. His life and work remind us that true leadership transcends institutional titles and
formal positions—it is measured by the trust one earns, the bridges one builds, and the communities one uplifts.
For the Maranao people of Mindanao, for Muslim Filipinos across the archipelago, and for the broader Philippine
society, Moxsir stands as a testament to the power of faith, service, and unwavering commitment to the common
good.

title: MSU Main Extension - Bataraza
text:
PAGE 1
MSU Main - Bataraza Extension
Mindanao State University Main Campus – Bataraza Extension (MSU-MCBE) is an extension campus of
Mindanao State University (MSU) Main Campus in Marawi City. It is located in Bataraza, southern Palawan, and
stands as the first MSU campus established outside the island of Mindanao. As part of the MSU System, it operates
under the university’s broader mandate to deliver quality higher education, promote national integration, and
support development across the Mindanao, Sulu, and Palawan (MinSuPala) regions. It functions as a non-
autonomous extension of MSU-Main rather than a full constituent university or college. Students are admitted
primarily through the MSU System Admission and Scholarship Examination (MSU-SASE), and academic records
are managed in coordination with the main campus registrar.
Contents
1 History and Founding
2 Campus and Location
3 Academic Programs
4 Significant Milestones
5 Administration and Governance
6 Contributions and Impact
7 Research Assessment
7.1 Verified Facts
7.2 Information Not Yet Verified or Limited
7.3 Research Gaps
History and Founding
The proposal for an MSU presence in Bataraza gained formal traction in early 2021. The MSU Board of Regents
(BOR) approved the establishment of the extension campus on March 22, 2021, following an ocular inspection and
evaluation conducted in late February of that year. Local government support, particularly from then-Mayor
Abraham Ibba of Bataraza, played a key role in the initiative. A parallel proposal for a campus in nearby Brooke’s
Point was deferred at the time.
Classes began on October 13, 2021, with an initial enrollment of 147 students. Instruction started in temporary
facilities on the second floor of the Bataraza Town Center in Barangay Marangas while permanent infrastructure
was prepared. Many early classes were delivered virtually, with faculty support drawn largely from MSU-Marawi.
Groundbreaking for the permanent six-hectare campus in Barangay Inogbong took place on December 6, 2021.
The event was attended by MSU System President Dr. Habib W. Macaayong, Palawan Governor Jose C. Alvarez,
and Mayor Ibba. An initial three-storey building with 18 classrooms was planned as part of the PGP-MSU-Bataraza
School Complex.
Dr. Hernando P. Bacosa, a professor of environmental science at MSU-Iligan Institute of Technology and a native
of nearby Brooke’s Point, served as the founding Campus Director. He later returned to faculty roles at MSU-IIT.
As of recent official listings, Prof. Donnabelle L. Abdullah serves as Director/Campus Head.
↑

PAGE 2
Campus and Location
The permanent campus occupies a six-hectare site in Barangay Inogbong, Bataraza, Palawan. Pre-admission and
other activities have been held at the Center for Learning and Innovation Building on this site. Earlier operations
used the Bataraza Town Center (second floor) in Barangay Marangas as temporary classrooms. Contact details
include the email msubataraza@msumain.edu.ph, phone (+63) 968-773-7545, and the Facebook page Mindanao
State University Main Campus-Bataraza Extension. A campus website is listed as msubataraza.msumain.edu.ph.
Academic Programs
MSU-MCBE offers undergraduate programs aligned with those of the main campus:
Bachelor of Science in Nursing
Bachelor of Science in Civil Engineering
Bachelor of Secondary Education major in English
Bachelor of Secondary Education major in Sciences
Bachelor of Elementary Education major in General Education
Bachelor of Arts in Islamic Studies major in Shari’ah
Admission is based on MSU-SASE scores, with cut-offs varying by year and program (commonly around 80 or
higher for most bachelor’s programs in recent cycles, with higher thresholds for scholarships). Some earlier
references also mentioned technology-related pathways or Arabic teaching, but the core listed programs above
appear consistently in official announcements.
Significant Milestones
In June 2025 the campus held its first pre-commencement exercises at the Mini Coliseum in Bataraza, graduating
59 students from the colleges of Education, Engineering, Health Sciences, and the King Faisal Center for Islamic,
Arabic and Asian Studies. Thirty of these graduates earned Latin honors (25 cum laude, 4 magna cum laude, and 1
summa cum laude). Deans and officials from MSU-Main attended to mark the occasion. The first batch of BS
Nursing graduates achieved a 100% passing rate (16 out of 16) in the November 2025 Nursing Licensure
Examination.
Administration and Governance
MSU-MCBE falls under the administrative oversight of MSU-Main Campus and the MSU System Board of
Regents. The System President (currently Atty. Paisalin P. Tago as of mid-2025 listings) holds ultimate authority,
with the campus headed by a Director. Faculty and staff recruitment follows system processes, with applications
often routed through the campus director and addressed to the System President.
Contributions and Impact
As the first MSU campus outside Mindanao, MSU-MCBE extends the university’s long-standing mandate of
providing accessible, quality higher education to underserved areas of the MinSuPala region. Local leaders have
highlighted its potential to raise educational standards and support economic development in southern Palawan. Its

PAGE 3
programs in education, nursing, engineering, and Islamic studies respond to regional needs in teacher training,
healthcare, infrastructure, and cultural-religious education. The strong performance of its first nursing cohort has
been noted as an early marker of quality.
Research Assessment
Verified Facts
BOR approval: March 22, 2021.
Classes started: October 13, 2021 (147 students, temporary site).
Groundbreaking of permanent 6-hectare campus in Brgy. Inogbong: December 6, 2021.
First MSU campus outside Mindanao.
Current programs as listed above.
First pre-commencement: June 28, 2025 (59 graduates).
100% first-time nursing licensure pass rate (November 2025 batch).
Campus Head: Prof. Donnabelle L. Abdullah (official MSU System listing).
Founding Campus Director: Dr. Hernando P. Bacosa.
Information Not Yet Verified or Limited
Detailed independent vision, mission, or core values statements specific to the extension (it inherits the
System’s).
Full list of current faculty, exact student enrollment figures beyond the opening year, or complete facilities
inventory.
Formal CHED Certificates of Program Compliance or external accreditation status specific to Bataraza
programs (as a young extension, these may still be in process or covered under Main Campus recognition).
Comprehensive list of student organizations, traditions, or notable alumni (understandable given the
campus’s short history).
Precise construction timeline and current status of all permanent buildings beyond the Center for Learning
and Innovation Building references.
Research Gaps
Publicly available official documentation remains limited. Most detailed operational information comes from the
campus Facebook page, local news reports (especially Palawan News), and MSU System pages. No extensive
institutional archive, yearbooks, or peer-reviewed historical studies specifically on MSU-MCBE were located.
Future updates from the official campus website, CHED records, or MSU System annual reports would help fill
remaining gaps on governance details, research/extension activities, and long-term outcomes.
The campus is still in its early developmental phase. Its rapid progress from approval in 2021 to first graduates and
strong licensure results by 2025 demonstrates institutional commitment and local support. Continued monitoring of
official MSU and CHED sources will provide the most reliable updates.

contribute information, please message the administrator through the official Facebook page: Notable Muslim

title: MSU-General Santos City
text:
PAGE 1
MSU-General Santos City
Mindanao State University – General Santos (MSU-GenSan or MSU Gensan) is a public state higher education
institution and a constituent university of the Mindanao State University System. Located primarily in Barangay
Fatima, General Santos City, Philippines, it serves as a key provider of accessible tertiary education in the
SOCCSKSARGEN region and neighboring areas of Southern Mindanao.
It operates under the broader MSU mandate, established by Republic Act 1387 (as amended), to educate the youth
of Mindanao, Sulu, and Palawan (MINSUPALA), support regional economic development through trained
manpower, and promote the integration of Muslims, Indigenous Peoples, and other cultural communities into
national life. As part of the only state university system with this explicit integration and peace-oriented charter,
MSU-GenSan emphasizes inclusive education, research, extension, and community engagement.
The university reports more than 9,500 students (over 8,600 undergraduates in recent figures), with colors of
maroon and gold, the motto “Learn, Achieve, Excel,” and the alma mater song Himno ng Pamantasang Mindanao
(music by Lucio San Pedro, lyrics by Prof. Angelito G. Flores). Its official website is msugensan.edu.ph.
Contents
1 History and Founding
2 Vision, Mission, and Core Values
3 Campus and Location
4 Academic Structure and Programs
5 Research, Extension, and Community Engagement
6 Administration and Governance
7 Accreditation, Recognition, and Milestones
8 Student Life, Traditions, and Culture
9 Notable Alumni and Faculty
10 Contributions and Legacy
11 Research Assessment
History and Founding
MSU-GenSan began in September 1967 as a community high school, six years after the founding of the MSU main
campus in Marawi in 1961. It was initially hosted inside Dadiangas West Elementary School in central General
Santos City. Local support, including involvement from figures such as Jacobino Java Sr. (principal of Dadiangas
West), helped establish it.
To address growing enrollment, the city government donated a 3.3-hectare lot in the city center for the high school.
It expanded into a junior college around 1971, limited at first to two-year general education programs. On October
10, 1973, by Board of Regents (BOR) Resolution No. 822, it became a full-fledged collegiate campus of the MSU
System, initially offering two-year degree courses and focusing on areas such as agribusiness.
Engr. Abedin Limpao Osop served as the first director of the then MSU Community College and later as the first
chancellor. The campus underwent physical transfers as it grew. In 1980 (or 1983 according to some university
summaries), Presidential Proclamation No. 2029 reserved land in what is now Barangay Fatima (formerly part of
Tambler) as a civil reservation for the MSU General Santos unit (and human settlements). Official university pages

PAGE 2
and Wikipedia commonly cite 1983 and a 156-hectare main campus; the proclamation text itself is dated November
11, 1980, and describes a larger aggregate area of which the university portion became the core campus. This
acquisition enabled significant expansion of degree programs and facilities.
The university gained greater autonomy around 1981. It has continued to expand academic offerings,
infrastructure, and roles in research and community service. In June 2026, a major Mindanao earthquake caused
substantial damage estimated near ₱870 million to buildings and facilities; recovery and rehabilitation efforts
followed, with some activities shifting online temporarily.
Vision, Mission, and Core Values
According to the official university site (updated via BOR Resolution No. 386, Series of 2025):
Vision: A leading transformative University driving excellence, research, innovation, and sustainable peace
and development.
Mission: To produce competent human resources committed to the development of the Philippines and to
help uplift the living conditions of Muslims, Indigenous Peoples, and other underserved communities.
Core Values (I-RISE): Integrity, Respect, Inclusivity, Service, Excellence. Earlier statements described a
vision of becoming a globally competitive university in Southern Philippines and a mission focused on
competent human resources for Southern Mindanao while improving conditions for Muslims and Indigenous
Peoples. The 2025 revision aligns more explicitly with system-wide goals of transformation, peace, and
inclusive development.
Campus and Location
The main campus covers approximately 156 hectares in Barangay Fatima, General Santos City (coordinates
roughly 6°03′59″N 125°07′34″E). It houses most academic colleges, administrative offices, and facilities, and
includes a Philippine Institute of Volcanology and Seismology (PHIVOLCS) seismic station. Additional sites
include:
A 3.3-hectare campus in the city center (Dadiangas/CETD area) used for the College of Medicine, School of
Graduate Studies, College of Law (extension), laboratory high school, and related programs, often with
evening or weekend classes.
A field laboratory/research station of about 3.1 hectares in Barangay Siguel (or Bawing in some references)
for the College of Fisheries and Aquatic Sciences. The university also operates a laboratory junior high
school (MSU-CETD) and Senior High School Department under the College of Education.
Academic Structure and Programs
MSU-GenSan comprises multiple colleges and institutes, including Agriculture; Business Administration and
Accountancy; Education; Engineering; Fisheries and Aquatic Sciences; Health Sciences (Nursing); Natural
Sciences and Mathematics; Social Sciences and Humanities; the Institute of Islamic, Arabic, and International
Studies; College of Medicine (established 2021, first graduates in 2025); and a College of Law extension of the
main campus.
Undergraduate offerings span BS programs in Agricultural Business Management, Agricultural & Biosystems
Engineering, Agriculture, Accountancy, Economics, Business Administration, Elementary and Secondary
Education, Physical Education, Civil/Electrical/Electronics/Mechanical Engineering, Engineering Technology,
Fisheries, Marine Biology, Nursing, Biology, Information Technology, Mathematics, Chemistry, Physics, various

PAGE 3
BA degrees (English Language Studies, Literary and Cultural Studies, Filipino, History, Political Science,
Sociology, Psychology), Islamic Studies (including Shariah major), and International Relations, among others.
Diploma and certificate programs exist in technical fields.
Graduate programs include master’s degrees in Agribusiness Management, Business Management (various
majors), Education, Teaching, Public Administration, Sustainable Development (multiple majors), Biology,
Mathematics, Information Technology, Philippine Studies, Filipino, and a PhD in Educational Management, plus a
Doctor in Sustainable Development Studies. The Doctor of Medicine is a post-baccalaureate program. Admission is
primarily through the MSU System Admission and Scholarship Examination (MSU-SASE). Tuition is generally
free under RA 10931 for eligible students.
Research, Extension, and Community Engagement
The university maintains research and extension functions aligned with regional needs in agriculture, fisheries,
education, sustainable development, peace, and health. Units include research and extension divisions, a Halal
Research and Training Center, and the Institute for Peace and Development in Mindanao. It engages communities
through outreach, supports peacebuilding consistent with the MSU charter, and has produced publications in
indexed journals. CHED has recognized it in areas such as Center of Excellence in Fisheries, Provincial Institute
for Agriculture, and Center of Training in Education.
Administration and Governance
As a constituent university, MSU-GenSan is headed by a chancellor (elected for a five-year term) who sits on the
MSU Board of Regents. The current chancellor is Atty. Shidik T. Abantas, MDM, LLM (seventh regular
chancellor, inaugurated around April 2025). The MSU System president is Atty. Paisalin P. Tago. Vice chancellors
oversee Academic Affairs, Administration and Finance, Research/Extension/Innovation, Planning and
Development, and Student Affairs and Services.
Early leadership included Engr. Abedin Limpao Osop (first director/chancellor), followed by figures such as Dr.
Datumanong A. Sarangani (second chancellor), and later leaders including Dr. Anshari P. Ali (who advanced the
College of Medicine). Full historical lists of all chancellors are not comprehensively detailed in publicly accessible
official summaries.
Accreditation, Recognition, and Milestones
MSU-GenSan joined the Accrediting Agency of Chartered Colleges and Universities in the Philippines (AACCUP)
on December 31, 2014, and has pursued program accreditations (including Level III for some programs such as BA
Islamic Studies). It has received CHED’s Excellence in Quality Assurance in Teacher Education (EQUATE) Award,
performed strongly in licensure examinations (including multiple topnotchers in the LET), and earned placements
in rankings such as Webometrics (around 63rd in the Philippines in one recent edition) and Times Higher Education
Sustainability Impact Ratings. The College of Medicine marked a regional milestone as the first of its kind in
Region XII, with its inaugural graduates in 2025. ISO 21001:2018 processes have also been pursued.
Significant milestones include the 1967 founding as a high school, 1973 elevation to collegiate status, land
acquisition enabling campus growth, expansion of graduate and professional programs (including Medicine), and
ongoing quality assurance efforts amid challenges such as the 2026 earthquake.

PAGE 4
Student Life, Traditions, and Culture
Student life includes organizations, cultural activities, sports, and the laboratory schools. The university reflects
Mindanao’s diversity (Bangsamoro, Lumad/Indigenous, Christian, and other communities) and emphasizes peace,
inclusivity, and service. Specific longstanding traditions beyond the system alma mater song and commencement
exercises (recent batches named such as Maragsâ and Magdarani) are not extensively detailed in official public
materials reviewed. The official seal features a lamp of knowledge, Okir (Maranao) motifs, three rays representing
MINSUPALA, and a SOCCSKSARGEN map reference.
Notable Alumni and Faculty
Publicly highlighted alumni include actress and comedian Melisa Cantiveros (noted on Wikipedia, though primary
verification is limited). Faculty and leadership include deans and researchers contributing to regional scholarship in
education, engineering, fisheries, social sciences, Islamic studies, and medicine (e.g., College of Medicine Dean
Dr. Edwin C. Alconcel). Comprehensive lists of notable alumni or faculty are not centrally published in the sources
consulted; many graduates serve in education, government, agriculture, health, engineering, and community
leadership roles across Southern Mindanao and beyond.
Contributions and Legacy
MSU-GenSan contributes to regional human capital development, particularly in agriculture, fisheries, teacher
education, engineering, health, and Islamic/Arabic studies relevant to Bangsamoro and broader Mindanao
communities. It supports peace education, cultural integration, and economic needs in SOCCSKSARGEN while
advancing the MSU System’s national integration mandate. Its growth from a community high school to a multi-
campus institution with professional programs (including the region’s first College of Medicine) illustrates
sustained local and system support. The 2026 earthquake underscored both vulnerability and resilience as
rehabilitation continues.
Research Assessment
This article draws primarily from the official MSU-GenSan website (msugensan.edu.ph), the MSU Main Campus
site (msumain.edu.ph), Wikipedia entries cross-checked against official pages, government proclamations (e.g.,
Proclamation No. 2029 via Lawphil), CHED-related announcements, news reports on recent events (e.g., Rappler
on earthquake damage), and secondary academic or public references. Priority was given to institutional and
government sources.
Verified Facts: Founding as community high school in 1967; elevation via BOR Resolution 822 on October 10,
1973; main campus land via Presidential Proclamation 2029 (1980 text, commonly referenced as 1983 acquisition);
current chancellor Atty. Shidik T. Abantas; vision/mission/core values per 2025 BOR resolution; approximate
campus sizes and locations; major colleges and sample programs; AACCUP membership from 2014; College of
Medicine establishment and first graduates; student population figures around 9,500; earthquake damage in 2026.
Information Not Yet Verified or Incomplete: Exact complete chronological list of all chancellors/directors with
precise terms; detailed founding individuals beyond Osop and early local supporters; comprehensive inventories of
accredited programs with current levels; exhaustive lists of notable alumni/faculty; precise breakdown of research
outputs or extension impact metrics; full historical enrollment trends; detailed traditions or student organization
histories; exact current land area reconciliation (156 ha commonly stated vs. proclamation aggregate).

PAGE 5
Research Gaps: Limited publicly digitized institutional archives or annual reports for early decades; sparse
independent academic histories; incomplete cross-verification of some Wikipedia details against primary
documents; evolving post-2026 recovery data; and the need for official confirmation of any program-specific
CHED Centers of Excellence status beyond summarized claims. Future research would benefit from direct access
to BOR minutes, university yearbooks, and local government records. The article maintains a neutral, factual tone
based on available authoritative sources. Discrepancies (such as the 1980 vs. 1983 dating of the land proclamation
or minor variations in campus size reports) are noted where they appear; the official university narrative and
primary legal text are preferred where conflicts arise.

administrator to help ensure historical accuracy. If you would like to suggest corrections, share sources, or
contribute information, please message the administrator through the official Facebook page: Notable Muslim
Filipinos.

title: MSU-LNCAT
text:
PAGE 1
MSU-Lanao National College of Arts
and Trades
Also Known As
LNCAT, MSU-LNCAT
Type
Constituent college (technical-vocational,
arts and trades, and basic education)
Founded
Early 1920s as Lanao High School;
integrated into the MSU System on
January 10, 2001
Location
Saduc, Marawi City, Lanao del Sur,
Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in
Muslim Mindanao (BARMM)
Parent System
Mindanao State University (MSU) System
MSU System President
Paisalin P. Tago
Campus Head
Supt. Cairany D. Dia-Gandamra, JD, RN,
MPA
Notability
One of the few CHED-supervised schools
folded into the MSU System through
CHED Order No. 27 S. 2000 and RA
8760, making it a key provider of
technical-vocational education in the
Bangsamoro region.
Known For
MSU-Lanao National College of Arts and Trades
Mindanao State University-Lanao National College of Arts and
Trades (MSU-LNCAT) is a constituent college of the Mindanao
State University (MSU) system. It is located in Marawi City, Lanao
del Sur, in the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim
Mindanao (BARMM). The institution specializes in technical-
vocational education, arts, trades, and basic education, serving as a
key provider of skills-oriented programs in the region.
Contents
1 Overview
2 History and Founding
3 Institutional Development and Historical Development
4 Campus and Location
5 Academic Structure, Programs, and Curriculum Offerings
6 Research, Extension, and Community Engagement
7 Student Life, Organizations, Traditions, and Culture
8 Administration and Governance
9 Presidents, Chancellors, or Heads
10 Facilities and Landmarks
11 Accreditation and Recognition
12 Significant Milestones
13 Notable Alumni and Faculty
14 Contributions to Education, Society, and the Bangsamoro
Community
15 Legacy and Impact
16 Research Assessment
Overview
MSU-LNCAT operates as an integrated campus within the broader
MSU system, focusing on practical education in arts and trades
alongside junior high school, senior high school (with academic and
TVL tracks), and select collegiate programs. It sits at a high elevation
(around 3,700 feet above sea level) in the Marawi area, emphasizing
technical skills, cultural heritage, civic responsibility, and community
development in a region rich with Meranao and diverse Mindanao
traditions. As part of the MSU mandate, it contributes to national
integration, manpower development, and educational access for local
communities, particularly in the Bangsamoro area.

PAGE 2
TVL specializations in ICT, Home
Economics, and Industrial Arts, alongside
complete junior and senior high school
programs rooted in Meranao culture and
civic values.
Pull Quote
"From a provincial high school on a
mountaintop to a pillar of technical
education in the Bangsamoro: that's the
LNCATizen story."
History and Founding
The roots of MSU-LNCAT trace back to the early 20th century as
Lanao High School, which later became Lanao Provincial High
School. It evolved into a focus on arts and trades, eventually
becoming the Lanao National College of Arts and Trades (LNCAT),
a CHED-supervised institution. On January 10, 2001, LNCAT was
integrated into the MSU system along with two other institutions
(Lanao del Norte Agricultural College and Maigo School of Arts and
Trades). This occurred through CHED Order No. 27 S. 2000 and
Republic Act No. 8760, which facilitated the integration of CHED-
supervised schools into chartered state universities. A memorandum of agreement was signed between MSU and
the relevant regional director.
This integration aligned with MSU's broader mission to expand access to quality education across Mindanao.
Institutional Development and Historical Development
Post-integration, MSU-LNCAT transitioned from a standalone vocational school into a component of the MSU
system. It maintained its emphasis on technical and vocational training while expanding basic education offerings.
The campus has faced regional challenges, including impacts from conflicts in Marawi, but has continued
operations and community engagement. Recent activities include graduations, visits from MSU system leadership,
and participation in system-wide events like athletic competitions.
Campus and Location
The campus is in Saduc, Marawi City, Lanao del Sur. Its elevated position offers scenic views and reflects the
highland setting of the area. Facilities support vocational training, basic education, and administrative functions. As
part of the MSU system, it benefits from system-level resources while maintaining a local focus.
Academic Structure, Programs, and Curriculum Offerings
MSU-LNCAT offers a range of programs:
Basic Education: Complete junior high school and senior high school with academic tracks (e.g.,
Humanities and Social Sciences) and Technical-Vocational-Livelihood (TVL) tracks.
TVL Specializations: Information and Communications Technology (major in Computer Servicing), Home
Economics (Food Trades, Dressmaking), Industrial Arts (e.g., Automotive Servicing, Electrical Installation
and Maintenance).
Collegiate Programs: Four-year courses in arts, trades, and related fields (specific current listings may vary;
refer to official channels for details). The curriculum blends technical skills with general education, cultural
pride, and civic values.
Research, Extension, and Community Engagement
As part of MSU, the campus engages in extension activities supporting local communities, skills training, and
regional development. Details on dedicated research centers are limited in public sources, but it aligns with the
system's mandates for instruction, research, and extension.

PAGE 3
Student Life, Organizations, Traditions, and Culture
Students participate in system-wide activities, such as the MSU Sports and Athletic Association (MSUSAA). The
institution fosters a sense of identity as "LNCATizens" or MSUans, emphasizing cultural heritage (particularly
Meranao), faith, and community. Traditions likely include local celebrations and graduations highlighting regional
pride.
Administration and Governance
MSU-LNCAT operates under the MSU System, headed by President Paisalin P. Tago. The campus head (often
titled Superintendent or similar) is currently Cairany D. Dia-Gandamra, JD, RN, MPA (also referred to with
honorifics like Hadja). Governance follows MSU policies and BARMM contexts.
Presidents, Chancellors, or Heads
Current campus leadership: Supt. Cairany D. Dia-Gandamra (as of recent records). • Broader MSU leadership
applies system-wide.
Facilities and Landmarks
Specific landmarks are not extensively documented publicly, but the campus includes facilities for vocational
training, classrooms, and basic education. It is part of the larger MSU network in Marawi.
Accreditation and Recognition
As an MSU constituent, it falls under the system's accreditation processes (e.g., AACCUP for programs). Specific
program-level accreditation details for LNCAT are not prominently detailed in top-level sources but are pursued as
part of system efforts.
Significant Milestones
Early 1920s: Origins as Lanao High School / Provincial High School.
2001: Integration into MSU system.
Ongoing: Hosting system events, graduations, and resilience through regional challenges.
Notable Alumni and Faculty
Publicly available information on widely recognized notable alumni or faculty is limited. Many graduates
contribute locally in trades, education, and community roles in the Bangsamoro region. Further archival research
would be needed for specifics.

PAGE 4
Contributions to Education, Society, and the Bangsamoro Community
MSU-LNCAT provides accessible technical and vocational education, helping develop skilled manpower in arts,
trades, and technology. It supports national integration goals, cultural preservation, and economic development in
Lanao del Sur and the Bangsamoro area by offering practical pathways for youth.
Legacy and Impact
The institution embodies the evolution from a provincial high school to a modern vocational component of a major
state university system. It plays a role in equipping locals with skills while fostering pride in regional identity.
Research Assessment
Verified Facts: Founding roots in early 20th-century high school, 2001 integration into MSU via CHED
Order and RA 8760, location in Marawi, focus on TVL and basic education, current leadership under Supt.
Cairany D. Dia-Gandamra, and alignment with MSU's mission. These are corroborated across official MSU
sites, Wikipedia (sourced), and institutional social media.
Information Not Yet Verified: Exact founding date of the original high school (described as "early part of
nineteen twenty"), comprehensive lists of current collegiate degree programs, detailed accreditation statuses
for specific programs, and exhaustive notable alumni/faculty lists. Some promotional videos provide useful
context but contain transcription variations.
Research Gaps: Deeper primary sources like official institutional histories, annual reports, or archives from
pre-2001 era would strengthen details on founders, early leadership, specific milestones, and quantitative
impacts (e.g., enrollment, graduate outcomes). Official campus website or dedicated publications could fill
many gaps; public online presence is primarily through MSU main pages and Facebook. No major conflicts
in facts were found, though details vary slightly in informal sources.
This article draws from cross-checked official MSU publications, government-related integrations, and reputable
references. It is ready for BangsamoroPedia-style publication following any final copyediting.

administrator to help ensure historical accuracy. If you would like to suggest corrections, share sources, or
contribute information, please message the administrator through the official Facebook page: Notable Muslim
Filipinos.

title: MSU-TCTO

Mindanao State University–Tawi-Tawi
College of Technology and
Oceanography
Also Known As
MSU-TCTO (https://msutcto.edu.ph/)
Website: https://msutcto.edu.ph/
Type
Public autonomous university campus
Established
1964 (as MSU Preparatory High School,
Bongao); formalized as MSU-Sulu
College of Technology and Oceanography
through Republic Act No. 6060 on August
4, 1969; renamed Tawi-Tawi College of

Colleges and Institutes
Mindanao State University–Tawi-Tawi College of
Technology and Oceanography
Mindanao State University–Tawi-Tawi College of Technology
and Oceanography (MSU-TCTO) stands as a vital autonomous
campus of the Mindanao State University System. Located in the
heart of the Sulu Archipelago in Bongao, Tawi-Tawi, it blends
academic excellence with a deep commitment to marine sciences,
cultural preservation, and community upliftment in one of the
Philippines' most remote and biodiverse regions.
The university serves as a beacon for inclusive education,
particularly for Muslims and other cultural minorities, while
advancing research and sustainable practices tied to the area's rich
marine environment. Its tagline, "Creating Opportunities •
Transforming Lives," captures its ongoing role in regional
development.

PAGE 2
College of Arts and Social Sciences
(CASS), College of Islamic Arts and
Sciences (CIAS), College of Education
(COED), College of Business,
Accountancy, and Management (CBAM),
College of Mathematical Sciences (CMS),
College of Fisheries, Oceanography,
Environmental Science, and Technology
(COFEST), College of Computer Studies
(CCS), College of Law (COL)
Accreditation

(including College of Law), CHED
Certificates of Program Compliance
Notability
The only oceanography and fisheries-
focused university campus in the Sulu
Archipelago, ranking among the top
Philippine higher education institutions in
the Times Higher Education Sustainability
Impact Ratings for SDG 14 (Life Below
Water)
Known For
Producing graduates in marine biology,
fisheries, education, and Islamic studies
while advancing inclusive education for
Muslim and indigenous communities in
one of the country's most remote and
biodiverse regions
Pull Quote
"From a small high school in Bongao to a
beacon of marine science and inclusive
education, MSU-TCTO has spent six
decades transforming the Sulu
Archipelago, one graduate at a time."
History and Founding
MSU-TCTO's story begins modestly in 1964 as the Mindanao State
University Preparatory High School in Bongao, an extension of the
MSU Marawi Preparatory High School. This early initiative aimed to
bring secondary education to the islands.
A major milestone came with Republic Act No. 6060, signed by
President Ferdinand Marcos on August 4, 1969. This law created the
MSU-Sulu College of Technology and Oceanography (MSU-
SCTO), focused on fisheries technology degrees and diplomas to
support resource exploitation, conservation, fish processing research,
and oceanographic studies in the Sulu Seas.
When Tawi-Tawi separated from Sulu as a province in 1973, the
institution adapted. Batas Pambansa Blg. 197, signed on March 16,
1982, renamed it the Tawi-Tawi College of Technology and
Oceanography and formalized its place as an autonomous campus
in the MSU System. Full autonomy as a university campus
solidified around 1990.
Expansion included more secondary schools across island
municipalities from 1967 to 1977, reaching about 20 by 1990. In
1984, the MSU-TCTO Science High School and Child Development
Center – Laboratory Elementary School opened, broadening its basic
education footprint.
Etymology
The name reflects its geographic and academic focus. "Tawi-Tawi"
honors the province, while "College of Technology and
Oceanography" underscores its original mandate in technical and
marine fields. Earlier iterations tied it to "Sulu" before provincial
division necessitated the change.
Vision, Mission, and Core Values
The university envisions itself as a center of excellence in fisheries, oceanography, marine sciences, and related
disciplines, responsive to southern Philippines' socio-economic, peace, and development needs. It positions itself as
a renowned institution in the Sulu Archipelago for marine and environmental science, driving sustainable
development.
Its mission centers on delivering globally competitive instruction, research, extension, and production in these
areas, with emphasis on quality education for Muslims and indigenous groups, environmental stewardship,
knowledge transfer, and stakeholder engagement for peace and progress. These align with the broader MSU
System's emphasis on integration, excellence, and service. Annual reports highlight alignment with UN SDGs,
especially SDG 4 (Quality Education) and SDG 14 (Life Below Water).

PAGE 3
Founders and Early Leadership
Founding ties to national legislation under President Marcos and the MSU System's broader vision for Mindanao
education. Early leadership included Dr. Filemon G. Romero, the first regular Chancellor, a noted oceanographer
and environmental scientist who advanced marine research and conservation. He later contributed significantly to
organizations like WWF-Philippines.
Institutional and Historical Development
From a high school adjunct, MSU-TCTO grew through program expansion, research centers (e.g., the Institute of
Oceanography and Environmental Science operations starting around 1996), and infrastructure. It navigated
challenges like the COVID-19 pandemic by shifting to distance learning while maintaining operations. Recent
decades emphasize quality assurance, internationalization, Scopus-indexed publications, and facility upgrades.
Annual reports document steady progress in governance, student support, and community reach, even during
crises.
Campus and Location
The main campus occupies Boheh Sallang, Sanga-Sanga, Bongao, Tawi-Tawi 7500, in a prime marine
biodiversity hotspot. A Manila Liaison Office aids coordination. Recent additions include student residence halls
turned over by BARMM in 2026, a new College of Law building, Halal Research Center plans, and a Medical and
Wellness Services Building.
Academic Structure
Colleges and institutes include the:
College of Arts and Social Sciences (CASS)
College of Islamic Arts and Sciences (CIAS)
College of Education (COED)
College of Business, Accountancy, and Management (CBAM)
College of Mathematical Sciences (CMS)
College of Fisheries, Oceanography, Environmental Science, and Technology (COFEST)
College of Computer Studies (CCS)
College of Law (COL). It also maintains basic education units.
Academic Programs and Curriculum Offerings
Programs span undergraduate to graduate levels, including BS Marine Biology, BS Fisheries, education degrees,
Islamic studies (e.g., BS Teaching Arabic, BA Islamic Studies), business, IT, mathematics, public administration,
and Juris Doctor. Many hold AACCUP accreditation and CHED Certificates of Program Compliance.

PAGE 4
Research, Extension, and Community Engagement
Research thrives in marine biodiversity, small-scale fisheries, coral reefs, and social sciences, with numerous
ongoing projects and Scopus publications. Extension delivers literacy programs, capability-building, and
partnerships (e.g., with barangays, AHA Learning Center, PCID for women, peace, and security). It ranks strongly
in THE Sustainability Impact Ratings, topping Philippine HEIs in SDG 14.
Student Life and Organizations
Student-centered approaches include scholarships, co-curricular activities, residence halls, and support services.
Organizations foster leadership, with emphasis on inclusivity and diversity.
Traditions and Culture
Campus life integrates local Tawi-Tawi and Bangsamoro cultural elements, Islamic observances, and marine-
themed activities. Events like foundation anniversaries, graduations, and PRAISE Awards celebrate achievements
and community.
Administration and Governance
Governed under the MSU Board of Regents per RA 8292, it features a Chancellor supported by vice chancellors
for academic affairs, administration, research/extension, and planning. Chancellor Mary Joyce Z. Guinto-Sali, PhD,
has led with focus on quality assurance (earning national recognition), research, and partnerships.
Chancellors, or Heads
Chancellor Guinto-Sali serves as the current (4th regular) leader, noted for multi-year advancements.
Dr. Filemon G. Romero was an early key figure. Details on all interim leaders remain less documented
publicly.
Facilities and Landmarks
Key sites include the Henry V. Kong Gymnasium, academic halls, research facilities, and new dormitories. The
campus map highlights its island setting.
Accreditation and Recognition
Strong AACCUP Level II performance (ranking high nationally), ISO 9001:2015 certification (including
College of Law), CHED COPCs, and global sustainability rankings affirm quality.
Significant Milestones
Legal foundations (1969, 1982)
Autonomy and program growth

PAGE 5
Pandemic resilience
Recent: SDG rankings, new infrastructure, AACCUP awards, international partnerships (e.g., UP), and
digital initiatives.
Notable Alumni
Graduates include Roben Abdella (first Badjao magna cum laude), summa cum laude honorees like Amin
Kadra A. Sarapuddin, and professionals in education, fisheries, and leadership. Alumni associations remain
active.
Notable Faculty
Figures like Dr. Filemon G. Romero (marine scientist), current leaders in research (e.g., Dr. Richard N. Muallil),
and dedicated educators in various colleges contribute prominently.
Contributions to Education, Society, and the Bangsamoro Community
MSU-TCTO expands educational access, trains teachers and professionals, advances marine conservation critical
to local economies, and supports peace-building and cultural continuity. It empowers communities through
extension and produces graduates who serve regionally.
Legacy and Impact
Over six decades, MSU-TCTO evolved from a small high school into a dynamic institution fostering resilience,
innovation, and opportunity in Tawi-Tawi. It continues to bridge traditional knowledge with modern science,
contributing to a stronger Bangsamoro and Philippine south.
Research Assessment
This article incorporates official website content, annual reports (2020–2024), legal documents, and cross-verified
sources. Chronology and mandates are consistent.
Verified Facts: Founding laws and dates, current leadership and vision/mission, recent achievements in
research and facilities, accreditation status.
Information Not Yet Verified: Exhaustive past chancellor lists or complete alumni databases beyond
examples.
Research Gaps: Older internal archives for granular historical data, long-term impact studies, and full
faculty/alumni profiles. Annual reports provide strong recent coverage but vary in depth for earlier periods.

title: Muallam, Mukhtar Muhana
text:
PAGE 1
Mukhtar Muhana Muallam
Mukhtar Muhana Muallam (born September 16, 1940, in Talipao, Sulu) was a career diplomat and Foreign
Service Officer who spent more than 25 years representing the Philippines across Asia, Africa, and the Middle East.
He rose from a Tausug family in the Sulu Archipelago to become a senior figure in the Department of Foreign
Affairs (DFA), serving his highest posting as Ambassador Plenipotentiary and Extraordinary to Tripoli, Libya
from 1997 to 2003.
A valedictorian, a Commission on National Integration (CNI) scholar, and a multilingual professional fluent in
Arabic, Spanish, and Bahasa, Muallam carried the cultural heritage of Sulu into the corridors of Philippine
statecraft.
His career is often cited as a quiet but compelling example of Bangsamoro excellence in the country's mainstream
institutions—proof that the children of Sulu could succeed not through conflict or compromise of identity, but
through education, competence, and service.
Contents
1 Early Life and Background
2 Education
3 Diplomatic Career
3.1 Entry into the Foreign Service
3.2 Jakarta, Indonesia (1975-1980)
3.3 Tarsakan Posting (1980-1984)
3.4 Islamabad, Pakistan (1986-1990)
3.5 Lagos, Nigeria and Riyadh, Saudi Arabia
3.6 Ambassador to Libya (1997-2003)
4 Home Office Roles and Multilateral Work
5 Family and Personal Life
6 Cultural Significance and Legacy
7 Recognition and Honors
8 Sources and Notes
9 References
Early Life and Background
Mukhtar Muhana Muallam was born on September 16, 1940, in Talipao, a municipality in the island province of
Sulu, in what is now part of the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM).
He was the son of Muallam Halifa and Muhana Sayadi, both of whom have since passed.
Like many young Tausugs of his generation, he grew up immersed in the deeply communal, culturally rich life of
the Sulu Archipelago—an environment shaped by centuries of Islamic tradition, seafaring history, and a strong
sense of community identity.

PAGE 2
Ambassador Mukhtar Muhana Muallam
Born
September 16, 1940
Talipao, Sulu, Philippines
Nationality
Filipino
Ethnicity
Tausug
Education
B.S. Political Science (1966),
University of the Philippines
Diliman
M.A. (1969), University of the
Philippines Diliman
Occupation
Diplomat, Foreign Service Officer
Known for
Ambassador Plenipotentiary and
Extraordinary to Libya (1997-2003);
ASEAN Executive Director;
advocate for Bangsamoro
representation in diplomacy
Spouse
Hadja Nurulyn Nujum Jikiri (m.
1979)
Children
Fatima Rhaisieta, Fatima Rhaihana,
Fatima Rhailina
The Tausug people, whose name translates roughly to "people of
the current," have long been recognized for their fierce sense of
independence and their tradition of producing leaders in
governance, scholarship, and the arts.
Muallam would go on to embody those qualities in a career that
carried his hometown's spirit across several continents.
Education
Muallam attended Sulu High School, graduating as valedictorian
of the Class of 1958.
That class is now remembered as one of the most consequential
in the province's history.
Among his batchmates were Nur Misuari, who later founded and
led the Moro National Liberation Front (MNLF) and served as
governor of the Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao
(ARMM); Parouk Hussein, a physician who also eventually
served as ARMM governor; Alan Timbayan, who likewise went
on to become an ambassador; and several others who became
scholars, lawyers, and educators.
The concentration of leadership talent in that single graduating
class reflects the intense intellectual energy and aspiration that
ran through Sulu's communities in the late 1950s, even as the
country was navigating the challenges of a young republic.
After high school, Muallam pursued higher education as a scholar
of the Commission on National Integration (CNI), which was
the government's program for supporting students from Muslim
and indigenous communities.
He earned a Bachelor of Science in Political Science in 1966
from the University of the Philippines in Diliman, Quezon City,
and followed it with a Master of Arts degree in 1969 from the
same institution.
His multilingual ability set him apart early: he was fluent in
Arabic, Spanish, and Bahasa Indonesia in addition to Filipino and
English, a combination that made him a natural fit for diplomatic
postings across Muslim-majority and Spanish-speaking regions.

PAGE 3
Parents
Muallam Halifa (father), Muhana
Sayadi (mother)
Languages
Filipino, English, Arabic, Spanish,
Bahasa Indonesia
Diplomatic Career
Entry into the Foreign Service
Muallam joined the Department of Foreign Affairs and rose
steadily through the ranks of the Foreign Service over the course of more than two and a half decades.
His career traced a wide arc across Southeast Asia, South Asia, Africa, and the Arab world, giving him a breadth of
exposure that few diplomats of his era matched.
His approach throughout was consistent: careful, competent, and dedicated rather than flashy.
Colleagues and institutional records portray a professional who advanced because of the quality of his work and the
reliability of his service.
Jakarta, Indonesia (1975-1980)
Muallam's first overseas posting placed him at the Philippine Embassy in Jakarta, Indonesia, where he served as
Third Secretary and Vice Consul from 1975 to 1980.
Indonesia was a significant early posting, given the two countries' shared Southeast Asian geography, their ASEAN
membership, and the cultural and historical ties between the Sulu Archipelago and the Indonesian archipelago.
His fluency in Bahasa would have been a genuine asset here.
Tarsakan Posting (1980-1984)
From 1980 to 1984, he served as Officer-in-Charge (OIC) Principal Officer at the Philippine consular office in
Tarsakan, extending his experience in managing diplomatic operations at a field level.
Islamabad, Pakistan (1986-1990)
One of his most significant early postings followed: First Secretary and Consul General at the Philippine
Embassy in Islamabad, Pakistan, from 1986 to 1990.
Pakistan was a key diplomatic partner during this period, particularly in the context of the Philippines' relations
with the Islamic world and multilateral forums involving Muslim-majority states.
Muallam's command of Arabic and his Tausug Muslim background likely strengthened his rapport in this
environment.
Lagos, Nigeria and Riyadh, Saudi Arabia
Records also place him in Lagos, Nigeria, and list him as Chargé d'Affaires in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia at various
points during his career, expanding his exposure to Sub-Saharan Africa and the Gulf region.
These assignments further demonstrated the DFA's confidence in his ability to handle a range of diplomatic
environments.

PAGE 4
Ambassador to Libya (1997-2003)
The capstone of his overseas career was his appointment as Ambassador Plenipotentiary and Extraordinary to
Tripoli, Libya, a posting he held from 1997 to 2003.
This was a diplomatically sensitive assignment.
Philippine-Libyan relations during this period were intertwined with the broader landscape of the Mindanao peace
process: Libya had long positioned itself as a supporter and interlocutor in talks involving Moro groups,
particularly the MNLF, under the framework of the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation (OIC).
Ambassador Muallam's Tausug identity and his deep understanding of the Bangsamoro context made him a fitting
envoy to navigate these relationships.
He served in Tripoli until retirement, closing out a career that had taken him from the Indonesian archipelago to the
heart of North Africa.
Home Office Roles and Multilateral Work
Muallam's career wasn't confined to overseas postings alone.
Between field assignments, he held a series of important positions at the DFA's central offices in Manila.
These included:
Director of ASEAN Affairs (1984)
OEA Director (1985-1986)
Executive Director of ASEAN (1995-1997), a role he occupied just before his Libya appointment
Work with the Presidential Management Staff
Involvement with the GRP Peace Process, connecting his professional role to the ongoing effort to find a
lasting settlement in Mindanao
His repeated engagement with ASEAN affairs underscored his regional expertise and his value as an institutional
resource in multilateral diplomacy.
His work on the peace process also meant that his Bangsamoro heritage wasn't just a biographical footnote—it was
a professional asset that the Philippine government recognized and drew upon.
Family and Personal Life
In 1979, Mukhtar Muhana Muallam married Hadja Nurulyn Nujum Jikiri (also affectionately referenced in
community notes as Nur Ain).
Together they raised three daughters: Fatima Rhaisieta, Fatima Rhaihana, and Fatima Rhailina.
Family and community accounts suggest a life that balanced the demands of a peripatetic diplomatic career with
strong private roots, including ties to Sulu and later connections in Maharlika Village, one of Metro Manila's
established Muslim communities.
His family life reflected the values common to many Tausug households: faith, family cohesion, and a quiet sense
of continuity with ancestral roots even amid life in foreign postings.

PAGE 5
Cultural Significance and Legacy
Ambassador Mukhtar Muhana Muallam belongs to a generation of Bangsamoro professionals who pursued
excellence within the Philippine state at a time when that choice carried real weight.
The 1960s through the 1980s were decades of tremendous upheaval for Muslim Mindanao, marked by armed
conflict, displacement, and deep questions about identity and belonging.
Against that backdrop, Muallam's path—from a CNI scholarship to the University of the Philippines to a quarter-
century in the foreign service—offered a different kind of narrative: one defined not by confrontation but by
competence.
He was, in the words of one community tribute, "one of those quietly impressive figures who rose from the heart of
Sulu to represent the Philippines on the world stage with dignity and skill."
His career demonstrated the value of linguistic and cultural fluency as diplomatic tools—qualities that Tausug and
other Bangsamoro professionals were uniquely positioned to bring to international service.
For younger generations from Muslim Mindanao, Muallam's story carries a straightforward message: a kid from
Talipao who topped his high school class could master languages, earn degrees from the country's premier
university, and spend decades representing the republic from Jakarta to Tripoli.
That's not a minor legacy. That's the kind of biography that reshapes how a community sees itself.
Recognition and Honors
Ambassador Muallam's contributions are documented and recognized through a 2023 tribute published by the Sulu
Tawi-Tawi Cultural and Historical Society, which drew directly from his DFA Personal Information Sheet (PIS)
and photographs provided by DFA officials.
His inclusion in institutional records of the Department of Foreign Affairs, embassy histories, and cross-referenced
peace process documentation reflects the scope and significance of his career.
He was part of the historic Sulu High School Class of 1958, a cohort that has been formally recognized for
producing an unusually high concentration of national leaders, diplomats, physicians, and public servants.
Sources and Notes
The primary source for this biography is the 2023 tribute by the Sulu Tawi-Tawi Cultural and Historical Society,
based on Ambassador Muallam's DFA Personal Information Sheet and photographs provided by DFA officials.
Cross-checks with Philippine embassy historical records, OIC-related peace process documentation, and University
of the Philippines alumni notes are consistent with the information provided, with no significant discrepancies
identified.
Ambassador Muallam did not publish memoirs or seek extensive media coverage, which is characteristic of many
career diplomats of his generation.

PAGE 6
References
Sulu Tawi-Tawi Cultural and Historical Society. (2023). Tribute to Ambassador Mukhtar Muhana Muallam.
Based on DFA Personal Information Sheet (PIS) and official photographs.
Department of Foreign Affairs of the Philippines. Embassy records and personnel histories.
University of the Philippines Diliman. Alumni records, College of Social Sciences and Philosophy.
Commission on National Integration. Scholar records (historical).

title: Musa, Abdulkhabir Isa
text:
PAGE 1
Abdulkhabir Isa Musa
Ustadz Abdulkhabir Isa Musa is a Filipino Islamic scholar, educator, and public servant who currently serves as a
Commissioner of the National Commission on Muslim Filipinos (NCMF), holding the seat dedicated to the
Ulama Sector.
He's one of the more respected voices in Muslim Mindanao today, the kind of scholar whose work doesn't stay
inside the mosque walls. Whether he's delivering a khutbah at the Sadik Grand Mosque in Zamboanga City, sitting
with regional ulama on matters of community guidance, or now advising national policy from his seat at the
NCMF, Ustadz Musa has always carried the same steady message: Islam in the Philippines is a faith of peace,
moderation, and service.
His appointment by President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr. in May 2026 brings a theological voice directly into national
governance, ensuring that the perspectives of the country's religious scholars aren't just heard in prayer halls but in
the halls of government as well.
Contents
1 Background
2 Education
3 Religious and Community Leadership
3.1 Khateeb and Public Preacher
3.2 Ulama Supreme Council of Zamboanga Peninsula
3.3 Interfaith Advocacy and Dialogue
4 Appointment as NCMF Commissioner
5 Philosophical and Scholarly Contributions
5.1 Unity (Wahdah)
5.2 Moderation (Wasatiyyah)
5.3 Madrasah Education Reform
6 Legacy
7 Recognition
8 See Also
Background
The specifics of Ustadz Musa's early life are kept private, as is common for many ulama who prefer their public
legacy to speak through their work rather than personal biography.
What is well established is that his roots are in the Zamboanga Peninsula, a region that sits at the crossroads of
multiple Muslim Filipino communities, from the Tausug and Yakan to Sama and Chavacano-speaking Muslims.
Growing up in that kind of diversity likely shaped the deeply pluralistic and unifying outlook that has come to
define his scholarship and community work.
