Education
Ustadz Musa received his formation in one of the most respected
centers of traditional Islamic learning in the world: Damascus,
Syria.
His studies there covered the three pillars that serious students of
Islam pursue at that level: Islamic Jurisprudence (Fiqh),
Theology (Aqidah), and Arabic Linguistics.
That combination isn't incidental. Fiqh gives a scholar the tools to
apply Islamic law to real-life situations. Aqidah grounds the faith
in sound theological principles. And fluency in classical Arabic
makes it possible to work directly from the original sources, not
just translations or commentaries.
Together, those disciplines produced a scholar who can engage
both the tradition and the present moment with equal confidence.
Religious and Community Leadership
Khateeb and Public Preacher
Ustadz Musa has long been a regular presence on the pulpit, most
prominently at the Sadik Grand Mosque in Zamboanga City.
His sermons aren't the fire-and-brimstone variety. He's known for
drawing connections between classical Islamic texts and the real
social challenges his community faces, touching on themes like
family values, civic responsibility, and the importance of peace.
That ability to make the tradition feel alive and relevant, rather
than distant and legalistic, is a big part of why he's become a
trusted voice across different generations of Filipino Muslims.
Ulama Supreme Council of Zamboanga Peninsula
Beyond the pulpit, Ustadz Musa plays an active role in the Ulama
Supreme Council of the Zamboanga Peninsula, one of the
regional bodies that handles religious rulings and community
guidance for the area's Muslim population.
That kind of institutional involvement means his influence
extends well past individual congregations. Regional ulama
councils shape how Islamic teaching gets applied across a wide
range of social and legal questions, and being a contributing
member of that body reflects a significant level of trust within the
scholarly community.

PAGE 3
Interfaith Advocacy and Dialogue
Ustadz Musa has also been a consistent participant in interfaith symposia and dialogue initiatives, working across
the religiously plural communities of Mindanao and Tawi-Tawi.
He's a proponent of "Pagkasilasa", a concept that translates roughly as mutual love and affection among people of
different backgrounds. That framing, drawn from local cultural vocabulary rather than imported terminology,
reflects an approach that feels genuinely rooted in the communities he serves.
His interfaith work isn't performative. It's part of a coherent vision of what Muslim Filipino citizenship looks like:
engaged, confident in its faith, and open to building bridges across difference.
Appointment as NCMF Commissioner
In May 2026, President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr. appointed Ustadz Musa as Commissioner of the National
Commission on Muslim Filipinos, assigning him to the Ulama Sector seat.
He was formally sworn into office by NCMF Secretary Sabuddin N. Abdurahim.
The NCMF is the primary government body tasked with promoting the welfare of Muslim Filipinos, coordinating
Islamic cultural and religious affairs, and ensuring that state programs are responsive to the needs of the country's
Muslim communities.
As Commissioner for the Ulama Sector, Ustadz Musa's specific mandate covers several areas:
Advising the Commission on how Islamic principles can be integrated meaningfully into government
programs.
Representing the interests of religious educators, Islamic scholars, and Madrasah communities at the national
level.
Coordinating religious and cultural affairs, including the management and logistics of the annual Hajj
pilgrimage for Filipino Muslims.
His appointment signals a recognition that theological expertise has a legitimate and necessary role in shaping how
the Philippine government engages with its Muslim citizens.
Philosophical and Scholarly Contributions
Unity (Wahdah)
One of the central themes running through Ustadz Musa's work is the idea of unity, which he frames in the Islamic
concept of Wahdah.
For him, the diversity of Muslim Filipino ethnolinguistic communities, Maranao, Tausug, Yakan, Sama,
Maguindanao and others, isn't a source of fragmentation but a feature of the community's richness that needs to be
managed with care and intentionality.
His advocacy consistently calls Muslim Filipinos to look past tribal and regional loyalties toward a shared identity
grounded in faith and collective purpose.

PAGE 4
Moderation (Wasatiyyah)
Ustadz Musa is firmly in the tradition of Islamic scholarship that champions Wasatiyyah, often translated as the
middle path or moderation.
He rejects extremism in both its theological and political forms, and consistently advocates for an understanding of
Islam that is compatible with peaceful coexistence within the Philippine state.
That isn't always an easy position to hold, especially in a region that has seen prolonged armed conflict. But his
credibility as a trained scholar gives his moderation position genuine weight within the community.
Madrasah Education Reform
Ustadz Musa is a vocal champion of modernizing the Madrasah education system in the Philippines.
His argument is practical: Filipino Muslim students shouldn't have to choose between deep religious formation and
the secular competencies they need to participate fully in society. A well-designed Madrasah curriculum can deliver
both.
That advocacy connects directly to his role at the NCMF, where education policy and community development are
central concerns.
Legacy
Ustadz Abdulkhabir Isa Musa represents a generation of Muslim Filipino scholars who've chosen engagement over
withdrawal.
Rather than confining his learning to religious circles alone, he's taken his training from Damascus into mosques,
council chambers, interfaith forums, and now a national government commission.
His legacy, still being written, is one of a scholar who understood that serving the community means meeting it
where it is: in its complexity, its diversity, and its ongoing search for dignity and justice.
The appointment to the NCMF is, in many ways, a natural culmination of that long arc of service. He brings to
public office what he's always brought to the pulpit: grounded knowledge, a genuine care for people, and a vision
of Islam as a foundation for civic life, not a retreat from it.
Recognition

Frequent resource speaker at major mosques and interfaith platforms across Mindanao and the Zamboanga

Editorial Note on Representation
BangsamoroPedia and the Notable Muslim Filipinos initiative aim to document notable individuals across the
entire Bangsamoro, not limited to any single ethnolinguistic group. The distribution shown above reflects the
available and verifiable profiles included in this article, and does not represent a fixed or exclusive selection. As
more qualified individuals from different communities are documented, representation is expected to broaden
further.
Education and Academic Leadership
Emily R. Marohombsar (1977)
Field: Education
Ethnicity: Maranao
Emily Marohombsar, born in Ganassi, Lanao del Sur, was the first Muslim woman to receive the TOWNS award.
She later became the first female President of the Mindanao State University system.
Her leadership helped sustain MSU as a space for social integration in Mindanao. She also served as part of the
government peace panel negotiating with the Moro Islamic Liberation Front.
Her career marked an early breakthrough for Maranao women in academic and national leadership.
Marlene Hofer Tamano (1986)
Field: Education
Ethnicity: Maranao
Marlene H. Tamano focused her career on strengthening education in the Bangsamoro. Coming from the Hofer
family of Cebu/Zamboanga Sibugay and the Tamano family of Tugaya, Lanao Sur, she worked on curriculum
development that integrates Islamic values with national standards.
Her work helped create a more grounded and identity-based learning experience for Moro students.
Bai Rohaniza Sumndad-Usman (2019)
Field: Education and Peacebuilding
Ethnicity: Maranao
Bai Rohaniza Sumndad-Usman founded the Teach Peace Build Peace Movement, an initiative that promotes peace
education among children in conflict-affected communities.
Through her programs, tens of thousands of learners have been introduced to peace-centered values at an early
stage.

PAGE 3
Peacebuilding, Law, and Governance
Atty. Sha Elijah Biruar Dumama-Alba (2025)
Field: Peacebuilding and Governance
Ethnicity: Maguindanaoan
Atty. Sha Elijah Dumama-Alba serves as Attorney General of the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim
Mindanao.
She played a key role in drafting foundational laws of BARMM, including the Administrative Code, Civil Service
Code, and Electoral Code. Her work supports institutional stability in the region.
Mayor Sitti Djalia Turabin-Hataman (2025)
Field: Governance
Ethnicity: Yakan
Mayor Sitti Djalia Turabin-Hataman has served in both national and local leadership roles, including as Executive
Director of the National Commission on Muslim Filipinos and as a party-list representative.
As Mayor of Isabela City, she focused on socio-economic development while supporting Yakan cultural
preservation, particularly traditional weaving.
Samira Ali Gutoc (2019)
Field: Peace Advocacy
Ethnicity: Maranao
Samira Gutoc is a former legislator in the ARMM Regional Legislative Assembly. She gained national attention
after resigning from the Bangsamoro Transition Commission during the declaration of Martial Law in 2017.
She founded the Ranao Rescue Team, which provided assistance to civilians affected by the Marawi Siege.
Public Service and Social Work
Deputy Minister Nur-Ainee Tan-Lim (2025)
Field: Public Service
Ethnicity: Tausug
Nur-Ainee Tan-Lim serves as Deputy Minister of the Ministry of Social Services and Development in BARMM.
Her work focuses on improving service delivery in remote areas, especially in Sulu, and promoting transparency in
aid distribution.

PAGE 4
Noraida Adang Abdullah Karim (2013)
Field: Social Work
Ethnicity: Maguindanaoan
Noraida Karim has led humanitarian efforts in conflict-affected areas, particularly in Maguindanao.
Her approach emphasizes conflict-sensitive resource management, ensuring that aid delivery does not aggravate
local tensions such as clan conflicts.
Journalism
Jamela Aisha Martinez Alindogan (2025)
Field: Journalism
Ethnicity: Mindanao-based, mixed heritage
Jamela Alindogan is a journalist known for her field reporting in conflict zones, including the Marawi Siege and
other major events in Mindanao.
She is also the founder of Sinagtala, which supports women and children affected by conflict through livelihood
and safe-space initiatives.
Representation and Impact
These awardees reflect the diversity of the Bangsamoro, representing multiple ethnolinguistic groups across the
region.
Their work highlights the growing role of Muslim Filipina leaders in shaping education, governance, and
peacebuilding, both within Mindanao and at the national level.

title: Muslim, Macapado A.
text:
PAGE 1
Macapado A. Muslim
Macapado Abaton Muslim (born July 4, 1956) is a Filipino political scientist, public administrator, and
peacebuilding scholar from Marawi City, Lanao del Sur—the heartland of the Meranaw people. Over more than
four decades, he built one of the most distinctive careers in Mindanao's academic and governance landscape: a
scholar who refused to stay in the ivory tower, and an administrator who never stopped thinking like a researcher.
As the 6th Regular President of the Mindanao State University (MSU) System, he modernized an eleven-campus
institution while simultaneously producing a body of work that helped reshape how the Philippine government and
the broader academic world understand the Bangsamoro struggle. His most enduring intellectual contribution—the
theory of Autonomy Plus Compensatory Justice—gave peacebuilders a framework that went beyond simply
drawing lines on a map, insisting instead that political self-governance must be paired with a serious reckoning for
decades of historical injustice. That idea didn't just stay in his books; it found its way into the structural logic of the
Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM).

Early Life and Cultural Background
Macapado Muslim was born and raised in Marawi City, a city that
sits at the edge of Lake Lanao and carries the weight of centuries of
Meranaw identity, Islamic tradition, and colonial resistance. Growing
up in the post-independence Philippines of the late 1950s and 1960s,
he came of age during a time when Moro consciousness was
beginning to find political shape—when the grievances of
Bangsamoro communities, long simmering under colonial and post-
colonial governance, were edging toward open conflict.
That environment shaped his thinking from the start. Unlike analysts
who studied the so-called "Moro Problem" from a comfortable
distance in Manila, Muslim was an insider. He wasn't reading about
displacement and marginalization in academic journals—he was
living in a community that embodied both the richness of Meranaw
culture and the real consequences of institutional neglect. Rather than
pushing him toward radicalism, this proximity to conflict convinced
him early on that education and political engineering were the most
powerful tools available for lasting change.
His faith as a Muslim in the Philippine south also anchored his later
thinking on governance. He would eventually articulate a philosophy
of "moral governance"—a vision of public administration grounded
in Islamic ethical principles—that grew directly from his upbringing
in a city where religion, culture, and politics were never separate
conversations.
Education
Undergraduate Studies at MSU
Muslim completed his Bachelor of Science at Mindanao State
University in Marawi City—the same institution he would one day
lead. Founded explicitly as a "laboratory for peace" and social
integration in Mindanao, MSU shaped his conviction that universities
aren't just places for producing graduates; they're institutions with a
civic mission in divided societies.
Master of Public Administration, UP Diliman
After finishing at MSU, he moved to Quezon City to pursue a Master
of Public Administration (MPA) at the University of the Philippines
Diliman's National College of Public Administration and Governance

PAGE 3
Association;

Society for Public
Administration;

Philippines

Political Science, Public

Peacebuilding
(NCPAG), completing the degree in 1980. The UP Diliman years
gave him a precise understanding of how the Philippine state works
—and, critically, where and why it fails. Those failures, he would
argue throughout his career, were not accidental; they were structural,
and they had everything to do with the marginalization of minority
communities in the country's south.
Doctoral Studies at the University of Hawaii
The most formative chapter of his intellectual life unfolded in
Honolulu, Hawaii. As an East-West Center scholar—a prestigious program that brings together researchers from
across the Asia-Pacific—he enrolled at the University of Hawaii at Manoa, where he earned both a Master of Arts
and a Doctor of Philosophy in Political Science, completing his doctorate in 1990.
At the University of Hawaii, he worked under the mentorship of the late Dr. Glenn Paige, a pioneering figure in
political science who founded the Center for Global Nonviolence and developed the field of "nonkilling" political
theory. Paige's influence was lasting. Muslim would go on to become a long-standing associate of the Center for
Global Nonviolence, and Paige's insistence on the moral and strategic superiority of nonviolent political solutions
runs through virtually everything Muslim has written and done.
His doctoral dissertation, The Moro Armed Struggle in the Philippines: The Nonviolent Autonomy Alternative,
became the foundational text of his career—a rigorous, deeply personal argument that the Moro conflict was not a
security problem to be managed militarily, but a political problem demanding a political and constitutional
solution.

Career
Early Academic Career at MSU
Muslim started as an Instructor at Mindanao State University in June 1980, right after finishing his MPA. He
moved steadily through the ranks: Associate Professor V by January 1986, then Professor VI in January 1991
following his doctoral graduation. In March 2016, he was conferred the title of University Professor—the highest
academic distinction in the Philippine university system, and one that's not handed out lightly. It's reserved for
scholars whose records of research, publication, and service set them apart across decades of work.

PAGE 4
Dean, College of Public Affairs (1991–1994)
From January 1991 to November 1994, Muslim served as Dean of the College of Public Affairs at MSU-Marawi. It
was during this period that his major research outputs on the Moro struggle began appearing in print, laying the
groundwork for the policy influence he'd later exercise at the national level. He ran the college not just as an
administrative function, but as a platform for producing research with real-world consequence.
Campus Chancellor, MSU–General Santos (1995–2007)
His most telling test as a manager came during two full five-year terms as Chancellor of MSU–General Santos
City, from December 1995 to March 2007. General Santos City sits in a multicultural urban landscape where ethnic
and political tensions have historically made institution-building complicated. His success in nurturing an effective
and peaceful campus environment in that setting established his reputation as someone who could manage
complexity without sacrificing principle—a quality that would later define his MSU System presidency.
The MSU System Presidency (2008–2016)
Acting President (2008–2010)
In 2008, Muslim was designated Acting President of the MSU System after topping the selection process. His
regular appointment, however, was held up for more than two years by what observers described as political
maneuvering both within and outside the university. When President Gloria Macapagal-Arroyo finally signed his
appointment on March 5, 2010, critics attached the "midnight appointment" label to it—but his peers pushed back
firmly on that framing.
Template:Quote
The delay was, for many who watched it unfold, a case study in the political vulnerabilities of academic leaders in
regions where governance and patronage are tangled together.
Regular President (2010–2016)
Muslim was formally installed as the 6th Regular President of the Mindanao State University System on July 1,
2010. He led an institution spread across eleven campuses, with a mandate as old as the university itself: to serve as
an instrument of peace and development in the southern Philippines.
His administration organized its work around several connected pillars:
Academic Meritocracy
He pushed hard to insulate MSU's promotions and admissions from political patronage—a persistent
problem in institutions embedded in regional power structures. Raising standards wasn't popular everywhere,
but it was, in his view, non-negotiable.
Infrastructure and Equipment Build-up
Particularly in his final years as president, Muslim prioritized large-scale infrastructure development across
the campuses—new laboratories, upgraded academic buildings, modernized facilities. The goal was
straightforward: an institution that aspires to be globally competitive has to look and function like one.
Income Generation

PAGE 5
Aware that relying entirely on national government appropriations was a structural weakness, he launched
income-generating initiatives through land use development and other entrepreneurial programs, giving
MSU a measure of financial resilience.
Strategic Rationalization
He oversaw a review and realignment of academic programs to ensure they served the actual development
needs of Mindanao and met international academic standards—not just on paper, but in practice.
Internationalization
Muslim consistently pushed for MSU to engage with the broader ASEAN region. On August 6, 2015, he
hosted a major forum on Malaysian Foreign Policy and ASEAN, making the case that higher education
institutions in the south have a specific role to play in regional peacebuilding and socio-economic
development.
His leadership style was described by colleagues as "decisive and strategic," always oriented toward what he called
the "equipoise of technology and moral-spiritual values."
Scholarly Contributions
Dissertation and First Book
Muslim's 1994 book, The Moro Armed Struggle in the Philippines: The Nonviolent Autonomy Alternative,
published from his doctoral dissertation, is the work that established his standing as the foremost academic voice
on the Moro conflict from within the Bangsamoro community itself. It drew on human needs theory and political
engineering to argue that armed struggle was not an irrational impulse but a rational—if ultimately destructive—
response to systemic exclusion. The solution, he argued, was also political: not suppression, but genuine structural
reform.
The Theory of Autonomy Plus Compensatory Justice
The concept that defines his academic legacy is Autonomy Plus Compensatory Justice. It's a deceptively simple
formulation that addresses one of the most common failure modes of peace agreements: granting autonomy without
actually fixing the damage that made autonomy necessary in the first place.
Political autonomy alone is insufficient to end conflict if it is not paired with compensatory justice—a
massive, focused effort to undo the historical and systematic marginalization and economic destitution
caused by decades of conflict and neglect.|author=Macapado A. Muslim|source=The Moro Armed
Struggle in the Philippines: The Nonviolent Autonomy Alternative (1994)
In Muslim's framework, compensatory justice isn't charity—it's an obligation. It requires the Philippine state to
channel significant resources into the autonomous region specifically because that region was impoverished
through state action (or inaction) over generations. This theory offered the intellectual scaffolding for moving
beyond the limited autonomy of the 1990s Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (ARMM) toward the more
ambitious and better-resourced design of the BARMM.

PAGE 6
Research Output and Current Thrusts
Over his career, Muslim published more than 60 research papers and books spanning governance reforms, political
leadership, peacebuilding, and federalism. His current research focus centers on constitutional design and
institutional innovation in divided and unequal societies—work that remains directly relevant as the BARMM
moves toward regular parliamentary governance.
His work is among the most frequently cited in studies on the Moro conflict and post-conflict reconstruction in the
Philippine south.
Policy Contributions to the National Government
Beyond publishing, Muslim has consistently offered his expertise to national governance through voluntary policy
papers submitted directly to the President of the Philippines. These submissions have addressed:
Managing the COVID-19 pandemic at the regional level, with specific frameworks for high-risk and
conflict-affected areas
Strengthening BARMM governance during its transition from an interim to a regular parliamentary
government
The role of morally upright and competent political leadership in fragile, divided societies
This willingness to translate academic work into actionable policy advice—without waiting for a formal
appointment or compensation—reflects his view that scholarship carries a social responsibility, especially in
communities that have historically been underserved by the state.
Legacy and Impact
The Scholar-Manager Model
Muslim's career offers what is perhaps the most fully realized example in the contemporary Philippines of the
"scholar-manager" model—someone who demonstrates, through sustained practice, that rigorous academic work
and effective institutional leadership aren't in tension. They reinforce each other.
Sixty-plus publications alongside the successful management of an eleven-campus university system isn't common
anywhere. In a conflict-affected region with chronic resource constraints and political volatility, it's remarkable. He
showed a generation of administrators at MSU and beyond that you don't have to choose between thinking
carefully and acting decisively.
Moral Governance in the BARMM
His most far-reaching contribution to governance may be the influence of his thought on what the BARMM has
adopted as "Moral Governance"—a philosophy that grounds public administration in Islamic ethical values:
justice (adl), transparency (amanah), and compassion (rahmah). Muslim didn't invent this concept from scratch,
but his decades of writing and teaching about the indispensability of morally upright leadership in divided societies
gave it an academic and policy anchor.
Studies on the BARMM's education and governance reforms have found that where moral governance frameworks
have been institutionalized, stakeholder trust and institutional performance have improved measurably. Muslim's
fingerprints are on those frameworks, not through coercion or appointment, but through the gradual absorption of

PAGE 7
ideas into policy culture.
Advancing the Bangsamoro Cause Internationally
Through his work at the East-West Center, his affiliations with international organizations, and his role in bringing
diplomatic forums to Mindanao, Muslim helped present the Bangsamoro struggle as a legitimate question of self-
determination and constitutional design—not a regional insurgency to be managed through security operations.
That reframing mattered, both for international audiences and for Bangsamoro leaders themselves.
Controversies and Critical Perspectives
The Presidential Appointment Controversy
The two-year gap between his designation as Acting President and his formal appointment as Regular President
remains the most discussed episode of his institutional career. His peers saw it as a political squeeze play—using
bureaucratic delay to stall reforms that would reduce the influence of patronage networks. His critics, a smaller
number, used the "midnight appointment" framing to question the legitimacy of the appointment itself. The weight
of evidence, and the professional consensus, favored his colleagues' view: this was a qualified candidate who had
been made to wait.
Critique of the Marawi Rehabilitation
After the devastating 2017 Marawi Siege left much of the city's core destroyed and tens of thousands of families
displaced, Muslim became one of the loudest and most credible voices criticizing the government's reconstruction
approach.
He called the proposed "New Marawi" a pie in the sky fantasy, a phrase that landed hard in policy circles because
it came from someone with decades of credibility on Bangsamoro affairs—not from an opposition politician
looking for a sound bite.
His critique had several specific threads:
The government's reconstruction priorities favored prestige projects—cultural centers, sports complexes—
over the urgent work of rebuilding homes in the Ground Zero areas
Thousands of internally displaced persons (IDPs) had effectively become permanent displacees because
residential reconstruction was crawling while infrastructure projects moved faster
He argued that restorative rebuilding had to come first; modernization could follow once original residents
were back in their homes
These were not abstract academic arguments. They were the application of his "compensatory justice" framework
to a real, ongoing catastrophe—and they kept him in the public conversation long after his formal MSU tenure
ended.
Awards and Professional Affiliations
Muslim's contributions have been recognized by several national and international organizations:
Vice President, Philippine Political Science Association

PAGE 8
Vice President, Philippine Society for Public Administration
Vice President, East-West Center Alumni Association – Philippines
Associate, Center for Global Nonviolence (founded by Dr. Glenn Paige, University of Hawaii)
These affiliations span both the academic and policy dimensions of his career—political science on one side, public
administration on the other, and nonviolence studies threading through both.
Personal Philosophy
Running through everything Muslim has done—his scholarship, his administration, his public criticism—is a
consistent philosophical commitment: that governance is a moral act, not just a technical one. In a region where
public administration has too often meant the distribution of patronage along ethnic and political lines, his
insistence on merit, accountability, and ethical leadership reads as both an academic position and a personal one.
His concept of "the transformative magic of education" isn't mere rhetoric. It's the animating conviction of a man
who grew up in a community at the center of a protracted conflict and chose to spend his life building institutions
rather than fighting battles.

title: Mutia, Solaiman C.
text:
PAGE 1
Solaiman C. Mutia
Atty. Solaiman "Soler" C. Mutia is a Filipino lawyer, diplomat, and public servant who pioneered the Philippine
government's approach to Hajj pilgrimage coordination and has spent decades protecting the rights of overseas
Filipino workers in the Middle East. He's best known as the country's first-ever Hajj Attaché under the former
Office on Muslim Affairs (OMA), a founding Commissioner of the National Commission on Muslim Filipinos
(NCMF), and currently serves as Labor Attaché for the Migrant Workers Office in Al Khobar, Saudi Arabia. A
Muslim Filipino from Lanao del Norte with deep roots in both grassroots and international public service, Mutia
established the protocols that continue to govern how the Philippines manages its annual Hajj operations and has
been at the forefront of labor diplomacy during some of the region's most challenging crises, including the 2023
Sudan evacuations and ongoing Middle Eastern tensions in 2026.
Contents

2 Education

Background
Long before Solaiman Mutia became a name in Philippine diplomacy, he was a local leader in Lanao del Norte. He
was elected three times as a Provincial Board Member in his home province, building a reputation as someone who
understood the needs of Muslim communities in Mindanao. His early career also included management work with
the Lanao del Norte Electric Cooperative (LASURECO), where he got hands-on experience with infrastructure and
public utilities. These grassroots experiences gave him the foundation he'd later need when coordinating large-scale
operations like the Hajj pilgrimage and managing the welfare of thousands of overseas workers. Unlike many
diplomats who start in Manila and work their way outward, Mutia's path went the other direction. He came from
the communities he would eventually represent on the international stage.

PAGE 2

Education
Mutia earned his law degree from Mindanao State University's
College of Law, one of the premier institutions for Islamic studies
and legal education in the southern Philippines. MSU has long
been a training ground for Muslim Filipino professionals who go
on to serve in government, the judiciary, and international
organizations. After establishing himself as a lawyer, Mutia
pursued further studies at the Asian Institute of Management,
focusing on development studies. This combination of legal
expertise and development training made him uniquely qualified
for the kind of work he'd take on later: navigating both the legal
frameworks of international agreements and the practical realities
of managing large-scale social programs.
Career
The First Philippine Hajj Attaché
Before the National Commission on Muslim Filipinos even
existed, there was the Office on Muslim Affairs (OMA), and that's
where Mutia made his first major mark. He was appointed as the
first-ever Philippine Hajj Attaché, stationed at the Philippine
Consulate General in Jeddah. This wasn't just a ceremonial role.
He was tasked with coordinating the annual pilgrimage for
thousands of Filipino Muslims, which meant handling logistics,
negotiating with Saudi Arabian Hajj authorities, and making sure
pilgrims had the support they needed in a foreign country. The
position didn't have a precedent, so Mutia essentially had to build
the playbook from scratch. His work set the standard for how the
Philippine government would manage Hajj operations for years to
come, long before the role became a permanent presidential
appointment in 2019.
Building the NCMF (Commissioner Era, 2010-2014)
When Republic Act No. 9997 abolished the OMA and created the
National Commission on Muslim Filipinos in 2010, Mutia didn't
just stick around. He was elevated. He served as one of the
founding Commissioners from 2010 to 2014, helping steer the
brand-new agency through its early years. As Commissioner, he
was a primary advocate for the cultural and socio-economic rights
of Muslim Filipinos nationwide. He also held the post of Deputy
Executive Director within the commission, which gave him a deep
view of both policy formulation and ground-level operations.
During this time, the NCMF was figuring out how to move
beyond just Hajj coordination and become a comprehensive

PAGE 3

policy-making body for Muslim rights. Mutia's legal background
and his previous experience as Hajj Attaché made him one of the
key architects of that transition.
Protector of OFWs (Labor Attaché Era)
In the latest chapter of his career, Mutia shifted his focus to the
millions of Filipinos working in Saudi Arabia. As Assistant Labor
Attaché in Jeddah, he was part of the critical team that welcomed
and processed Filipino evacuees fleeing the conflict in Sudan in
2023. It was high-stakes work: coordinating with multiple
agencies, managing logistics for distressed workers, and ensuring
everyone got home safely. In September 2024, he was officially
promoted to Labor Attaché II. By early 2026, he was serving as
Labor Attaché for the Migrant Workers Office in the Eastern
Region, based in Al Khobar, under the Philippine Embassy in
Riyadh. His office covers a massive jurisdiction of Filipino workers in Saudi Arabia's industrial heartland.
Institutional Contributions
Policy Architect for RA 9997
As one of the pioneering Commissioners of the National Commission on Muslim Filipinos, Mutia's legal
background from Mindanao State University was critical during the agency's transition from the old Office on
Muslim Affairs. He was instrumental in drafting the implementing rules and regulations for Republic Act No. 9997,
which formally established the NCMF. His goal was to move the agency beyond just Hajj coordination and into a
comprehensive policy-making body for Muslim rights. He wanted the NCMF to have teeth, not just advisory
power.
Expansion of Shari'ah Legal Aid
Mutia was a vocal advocate for strengthening the Shari'ah legal system in the Philippines. During his term as
Commissioner, he pushed for more government-funded legal assistance for Muslim Filipinos, ensuring that their
specific religious and cultural laws were respected in the national legal framework. He understood that for many
Muslim communities, access to justice meant access to Shari'ah courts, and he worked to make sure those courts
had the resources they needed.
Institutionalizing the Hajj Attaché Role
Drawing from his experience as the first-ever Hajj Attaché, Mutia helped institutionalize the role within the NCMF
structure. This ensured that future Hajj operations had a permanent legal standing and a dedicated budget within the
Philippine diplomatic corps. Before his work, the Hajj Attaché position was informal and underfunded. After his
tenure, it became a recognized and essential part of how the Philippines serves its Muslim citizens abroad.

PAGE 4
Current Operations: MWO Al Khobar (2026)
Since his promotion to Labor Attaché II, Mutia has been leading the Migrant Workers Office in the Eastern
Province of Saudi Arabia. His office is located at the Al Khobar Mall and covers a massive jurisdiction of Filipino
workers in the kingdom's industrial heartland. The work is relentless. Just in April 2026 alone, Mutia joined
Ambassador Raymond Balatbat at King Fahad International Airport to send off a batch of OFWs requesting
repatriation due to ongoing regional tensions. He's also been strengthening corporate ties, recently meeting with top
officials from Saeed R. Al Zahrani Company (SRACO), one of the largest employers of Filipinos in Saudi Arabia,
to ensure that labor contracts and worker protections remain a priority during the current crisis. His office works
closely with the Philippine Embassy in Riyadh to provide "Serbisyo Caravans," bringing services like SSS, Pag-
IBIG, and PhilHealth directly to OFWs in Al Khobar so they don't have to travel long distances. It's what Mutia
calls the "One Country Team" approach.
Core Services in Al Khobar
Under Mutia's leadership, the MWO Al Khobar currently prioritizes three main areas: contract verification (making
sure every OFW's job contract meets Department of Migrant Workers standards for fair pay and safety), dispute
resolution (acting as a mediator between Filipino workers and their Saudi employers to settle grievances without
needing long court cases), and crisis assistance (managing the evacuation and welfare of distressed Filipinos,
especially those affected by the airspace restrictions and regional conflicts currently impacting the Middle East).
The office doesn't just react to problems. It tries to prevent them by staying in constant contact with employers and
making sure workers know their rights before disputes escalate.
Legacy
Mutia's legacy is written in two major areas: Hajj administration and labor diplomacy. On the Hajj side, he set the
blueprint. Before him, there was no clear protocol for how the Philippine government should coordinate with Saudi
authorities. After him, there was an institutionalized system that's been running for over a decade. On the labor
diplomacy side, his work during the Sudan crisis and the ongoing Middle Eastern tensions has shown that the
Philippine government can respond quickly and effectively when its citizens are in danger abroad. He's also proven
that you don't need to be flashy to be effective. His approach has always been methodical, building systems that
outlast individual administrations. Whether it's drafting regulations for the NCMF or mediating disputes between
OFWs and employers, Mutia's work has been about creating structures that protect people long after he's moved on
to the next role.
Recognition
While Mutia hasn't sought public accolades, his contributions have been recognized by those who've worked with
him. Colleagues from the NCMF era describe him as someone who could balance the legal technicalities of policy-
making with the human realities of community service. OFWs in Al Khobar know him as the attaché who shows
up at the airport during repatriations and takes the time to meet with workers individually. His three successful
terms as Provincial Board Member in Lanao del Norte speak to his ability to maintain trust with his home
constituency even while taking on national and international roles. For Muslim Filipinos, especially those from
Mindanao, he represents the kind of leader who never forgets where he came from, even when working on global
stages.

PAGE 5
Challenges
Mutia's career hasn't been without challenges. Managing Hajj operations meant navigating complex relationships
with Saudi authorities, where diplomatic protocols and religious sensitivities intersect. The NCMF's early years
were marked by limited budgets and competing priorities, and Mutia had to fight for resources to expand programs
like Shari'ah legal aid. His current work as Labor Attaché in Al Khobar comes during one of the most volatile
periods in Middle Eastern geopolitics in recent decades. The 2023 Sudan evacuations tested the limits of what a
small diplomatic team could accomplish under pressure. The ongoing regional tensions in 2026 have meant
constant crisis management, with Mutia and his team working around the clock to ensure OFW safety. Despite
these challenges, he's maintained his focus on the fundamental mission: protecting Filipino lives and dignity,
whether they're pilgrims on Hajj or workers building Saudi Arabia's infrastructure.

title: Mutilan, Mahid M.
text:
PAGE 1
Mahid M. Mutilan
Dr. Mahid M. Mutilan (1943 – December 6, 2007) was a Maranao scholar, politician, peace advocate, and
religious leader from Tamparan in Lanao del Sur, Philippines. He served three consecutive terms as Governor of
Lanao del Sur from 1992 to 2001, and later as Vice-Governor of the Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao
(ARMM). Before entering politics, he spent more than a decade as a Muslim missionary in Japan, building bridges
between cultures and faiths long before "interfaith dialogue" became a catchphrase in Philippine governance.
What made Mutilan unusual, even in a region full of remarkable figures, was how completely he defied the mold.
In Lanao del Sur, political power had long been the exclusive territory of entrenched dynasties. Mutilan came in
with something different: a doctorate from Al-Azhar University in Cairo, a platform built on Islamic principles, and
a genuine belief that governance could be guided by moral accountability rather than lineage. He called his
movement Ompia, the Maranao word for reform, and the name said everything about his vision.
He is perhaps remembered most widely as a co-founder of the Bishops-Ulama Conference (BUC), the landmark
body that brought together Catholic bishops, Protestant leaders, and Muslim scholars to work toward peace in
Mindanao. His death on December 6, 2007, in a vehicular accident just one day after what would be his final public
address, cut short a life that had been fully dedicated to reconciliation, education, and the upliftment of the
Bangsamoro people.

Early Life and Background
Mahid Mutilan was born in 1943 in the municipality of Tamparan, a predominantly Maranao community sitting
along the shores of Lake Lanao in Lanao del Sur. He grew up in a region where Islamic tradition ran deep, where
the Ulama (religious scholars) carried enormous moral authority, and where political power was heavily tied to
one's family name.

PAGE 2

From early on, it was clear that Mutilan wasn't going to follow a
conventional path. He had an appetite for learning that went well
beyond what was available locally, and he pursued his education with
the kind of seriousness that would eventually take him thousands of
miles from home, all the way to one of the most prestigious Islamic
institutions in the world.
Education
Mutilan earned his Doctorate in Islamic Theology from Al-Azhar
University in Cairo, Egypt. At the time of his graduation, he was
among a very small number of Filipinos to have attained that level of
religious academic distinction from Al-Azhar, an institution founded
in 970 CE and widely regarded as the foremost authority in Sunni
Islam.
His education at Al-Azhar didn't just give him credentials. It gave
him a worldview. He came back not only as a deeply trained faqih
(Islamic jurist) but also as someone who had seen how Muslim
communities could engage with the wider world without losing their
identity. That perspective shaped everything he would do afterward,
from his missionary work to his political career.
Missionary Work in Japan
Before politics ever entered the picture, Mutilan served as a Muslim
missionary in Japan for somewhere between eleven and nineteen
years, a stretch of time that tells you a great deal about his patience
and his commitment. Japan is not an easy place to do religious
outreach. It's a society with deep cultural cohesion, and Islamic
communities there have historically been small and scattered.
Mutilan's work in Japan centered on intercultural dialogue and the
construction of Islamic centers, physical spaces where Muslims in
Japan could gather, pray, and feel a sense of community. This wasn't
just charity work. It was the beginning of a lifelong practice: finding
common ground across difference, and building institutions that
could outlast any single person's efforts.
When he eventually returned to the Philippines, he brought that same
instinct with him. And Lanao del Sur, a region caught between
entrenched tradition and urgent need for change, gave him a much
larger stage.

PAGE 3
Term of
office
Governor: 1992–2001
Vice-Governor, ARMM:
2001
Political Career
The Ompia Movement
By the late 1980s, the political landscape of Lanao del Sur was, bluntly, a closed system. Traditional Maranao
leadership, the datus and their extended clans, held political power as something close to a birthright. Elections
happened, but they largely shuffled influence within the same social circles. The idea that an Ulama-backed
movement could break through was, to most observers, far-fetched.
Mutilan proved them wrong.
He founded the Ompia Party, taking its name directly from the Maranao word for reform. The party's platform
was built around Islamic populism, which in practical terms meant: moral governance, public accountability, and a
shift away from clan loyalty as the basis of political support. He didn't campaign against any specific family. He
campaigned against the entire system of governance that put lineage above competence and loyalty above integrity.
The voters of Lanao del Sur responded.
Mayor of Marawi City (1988–1992)
Mutilan's first major electoral win came in 1988, when he was elected Mayor of Marawi City, the regional center of
Lanao del Sur and the only predominantly Islamic city in the Philippines. His term as mayor gave him a platform to
demonstrate what the Ompia platform actually looked like in practice: attention to basic services, an emphasis on
education, and a governing style informed by Islamic ethical principles rather than transactional politics.
His mayoralty also gave him the credibility and name recognition to aim higher.
Governor of Lanao del Sur (1992–2001)
In 1992, Mutilan won the governorship of Lanao del Sur, a victory that signaled a genuine shift in the province's
political culture. He would go on to win re-election twice, serving three consecutive terms through 2001.
During his tenure as governor, his administration was guided by the same convictions that powered the Ompia
movement. He pushed the Ulama into a more active role in public affairs, not as figures who blessed whoever
happened to be in power, but as genuine stakeholders in the direction of the province. By doing so, he created a
new kind of political accountability, one rooted in Islamic moral authority rather than clan hierarchy.
His governorship coincided with some of the most turbulent years in the Mindanao peace process, and he used his
position to engage consistently with national-level discussions about the future of Muslim Mindanao.
ARMM Vice-Governorship and Educational Reform
In 2001, Mutilan stepped into regional leadership as the Vice-Governor of the Autonomous Region in Muslim
Mindanao (ARMM), serving alongside Governor Parouk Hussin. Alongside that role, he served concurrently as
the ARMM Secretary of Education, a portfolio that he approached with characteristic seriousness.
His most significant push during this period was the effort to integrate the Madaris curriculum (the curriculum of
traditional Islamic schools) into the standard Philippine educational framework. For decades, Muslim students in
the region had faced a stark and unnecessary choice: religious education or secular education. Mutilan pushed back

PAGE 4
against that false choice. He wanted Muslim students to receive a solid grounding in both Islamic studies and the
broader academic subjects that would prepare them for university and professional life.
This wasn't purely an educational vision. It was a political one too. A generation of Bangsamoro youth that was
both religiously grounded and academically equipped would be far less vulnerable to radicalization and far more
capable of participating in governance, law, medicine, and other fields where the region desperately needed local
expertise.
His tenure wasn't free of difficulty. One persistent challenge was the non-remittance of GSIS (Government Service
Insurance System) premiums for regional teachers, a systemic problem embedded in the ARMM's bureaucratic
structure that proved difficult to untangle despite his efforts. It's worth acknowledging that reform at scale is rarely
clean, and Mutilan was working inside one of the most complex administrative environments in the Philippine
government.
Architect of Peace and Interfaith Dialogue
If there is one aspect of Mutilan's career that transcended the local and spoke to something national, even universal,
it was his role as a peacemaker.
Bishops-Ulama Conference
In 1996, Mutilan co-founded the Bishops-Ulama Conference (BUC), a historic initiative that brought together
Catholic bishops, Protestant leaders, and Muslim scholars in a shared commitment to reducing religious tensions in
Mindanao and building a culture of mutual respect between communities that had, in many cases, been living in
fear of each other for decades.
The BUC was not a ceremonial body. It did real work: facilitating dialogue in conflict-affected areas, issuing joint
statements at critical moments, and providing a platform where religious leaders from different traditions could
speak to their own communities with credibility about the importance of coexistence.
Mutilan's involvement in the BUC was entirely consistent with everything else he stood for. He never saw Islam as
something to be defended by pushing others away. He saw it as a tradition rich enough to engage with the world
generously and honestly.
Peace Negotiations with the MILF
Mutilan also served as a member of the government's peace panel during the administration of President Joseph
Estrada, working as a moderate bridge between the Moro Islamic Liberation Front (MILF) and the Republic of the
Philippines. His role was not simply representational. He brought to the table the kind of credibility that comes
from being genuinely trusted by the Muslim community, someone the MILF leadership could recognize as a
serious interlocutor rather than a government mouthpiece.
His participation in these negotiations reflected his core conviction: that the Bangsamoro struggle was not a
conflict between religions, but between neglect and justice, between indifference and recognition. He held that
position consistently throughout his public life.

PAGE 5
Recognition and Legacy
Mutilan is often referred to posthumously as a Grand Mufti, though this was an honorific recognition of his
scholarly stature rather than a formally appointed title. The designation reflects how his peers and the broader
Muslim community in the Philippines regarded him: as someone whose religious knowledge and moral authority
were of a genuinely senior order.
The continued existence of the Bishops-Ulama Conference is the most visible institutional legacy of his work. The
BUC has outlasted many of the political arrangements that surrounded its founding, and it continues to function as
a venue for interfaith engagement in Mindanao.
The integration of the Madrasah curriculum into the Bangsamoro educational system, while still a work in progress
long after his death, traces a direct line back to the advocacy he led during his time as ARMM Education Secretary.
In Lanao del Sur, his legacy is more personal. He changed the terms of political competition in the province,
demonstrating that a candidate could win, govern, and win again, if the platform was honest and the commitment
was real.
Death
On December 6, 2007, Dr. Mahid M. Mutilan died in a vehicular accident in Gitagum, Misamis Oriental, while he
was traveling to catch a flight to Manila. He was 63 or 64 years old.
The accident came just one day after what would be his final public address, delivered in Marawi City on
December 5, 2007. In that speech, he spoke about peace, about the obligations of faith, and about justice. Those
who were present described it as a summation of everything he had spent his life saying.
His death was mourned across the Philippines. Leaders from the Muslim and Christian communities alike offered
condolences. The loss was felt not just as the passing of a politician or a scholar, but as the removal of a voice that
had, for decades, argued consistently and credibly for a better way of doing things in a region that desperately
needed exactly that.
"Islam is a religion of peace. Our struggle is not against people of other faiths, but against injustice and
the neglect of our moral responsibilities."
— Dr. Mahid M. Mutilan, Final Public Address, Marawi City, December 5, 2007

Yousef T. Naeem
Dr. Yousef Tahamid Naeem (born May 3, 1999) is a Filipino Tausug
physician, registered nurse, and public health practitioner who placed
9th in the October 2025 Physician Licensure Examination with a rating
of 88.92 percent. His academic background, which combines nursing,
medicine, and public health, reflects a multidisciplinary approach to
healthcare rooted in both clinical practice and community-based
systems.
He is recognized for his work on culturally informed healthcare,
particularly his research on traditional and alternative medicine, as well
as his commitment to serving communities in Western Mindanao.
Contents
1 Early Life and Background
2 Education
3 Physician Licensure Examination
4 Research and Academic Work
5 Clinical Practice and Work
6 Skills and Competencies
7 Professional Outlook
8 Notes
Early Life and Background
Dr. Naeem was born in Tetuan, Zamboanga City, to Mohammad Naeem
and Rokarna T. Naeem. He traces his roots to the Tausug people of the
Sulu archipelago, a community historically associated with Islamic
scholarship, trade, and leadership in southern Philippines.
Growing up within this cultural context, his formation reflects both
local identity and exposure to diverse environments, having completed
part of his early education in Saudi Arabia.
Education
Dr. Naeem completed his Doctor of Medicine – Master of Public
Health (MD–MPH) at the Ateneo de Zamboanga University School of
Medicine (2019–2025), where he was recognized as an Academic
Achievement Awardee in 2025.
The institution is known for its socially accountable medical education
model, which emphasizes community immersion and service in
underserved areas. This training framework shaped his orientation
toward patient-centered care and public health practice.

PAGE 2
Prior to medicine, he earned his Bachelor of Science in Nursing (BSN), graduating magna cum laude from Western
Mindanao State University in 2019. He passed the Philippine Nursing Licensure Examination the same year.
His earlier education includes secondary and primary schooling in Jeddah and Makkah, Saudi Arabia, where he
graduated in the top percentile of his class.
Physician Licensure Examination
In October 2025, Dr. Naeem ranked 9th nationwide in the Physician Licensure Examination administered by the
Professional Regulation Commission, achieving a score of 88.92 percent.
His performance placed him among the top examinees in a national cohort of thousands of medical graduates and
contributed to the strong showing of Ateneo de Zamboanga University School of Medicine during that examination
cycle.
Research and Academic Work
Dr. Naeem has contributed to research focused on community health and culturally responsive medicine. His works
include:
Naeem, Y. T., Ynawat, R. A. (2025). The acceptance of traditional and alternative medicine among medical
doctors in Zamboanga City. Philippine Journal of Health Research and Development.
Naeem, Y. T. (2023). The acceptance of chlorination, boiling, SODIS, and Sawyer Water Filter as means of
water purification in Barangay Sta. Cruz, Mahayag, Zamboanga del Sur. Western Mindanao Health
Research Journal.
His research explores how medical practitioners engage with non-conventional healing practices, particularly in
communities where traditional medicine remains part of everyday health behavior.
He also received several recognitions in research competitions, including:
Poster Competition Winner, 6th Regional Health Research Summit (2024)
Policy Pitch Finalist, Philippine Academy of Family Physicians (2025)
5th Placer, ZCHRD Region IX Oral Research Presentation (2025)
3rd Placer, ZCHRD 3-Minute Pitch to Policymakers Competition (2025)
Clinical Practice and Work
Dr. Naeem practices general medicine with a focus on patient-centered care, health education, and preventive
medicine. His clinical background includes experience in vaccination programs, where he served as a volunteer
nurse during the COVID-19 vaccination rollout.
He is also engaged in digital health through telemedicine platforms, allowing him to extend care to patients in
geographically isolated areas.
In addition to clinical work, he has been involved in academic and review settings, contributing as a lecturer for
Physician Licensure Examination review programs.

PAGE 3
Skills and Competencies
His professional competencies include:
Clinical care, triage, and emergency response
Public health and community-based healthcare
Research and academic writing
Health education and patient communication
He is fluent in English and Arabic, with conversational proficiency in Tagalog.
Professional Outlook
Dr. Naeem has expressed a commitment to developing as a physician grounded in compassion, efficiency, and
continuous learning. His career direction reflects an integration of clinical medicine, public health, and research,
with the goal of contributing to improved healthcare delivery in underserved communities.
Notes
This profile was reviewed and updated with input from Dr. Naeem to ensure accuracy and proper representation of
his professional background.

Hadji Urang Menor Naga
Hadji Urang Menor Naga (January 2, 1901 – February 15, 1987)
was a Maranao leader, public servant, and civic innovator whose
influence shaped governance, infrastructure, and community life in
Lanao. He is remembered as the “Most Honest Provincial Treasurer
of Lanao del Sur” and as a quiet builder of modern institutions in
Marawi City.
Contents
1 Early Life
2 Government Service
3 Civic Contributions
4 Education and Faith
5 Agricultural Innovation
6 War and Resistance
7 Legacy
Early Life
Born in 1901, Naga grew up during a time of administrative and
social transformation in Mindanao. His fluency in English allowed
him to bridge local governance with national and international
networks.
Government Service
He served as Provincial Treasurer of the undivided Lanao, later
continuing in Lanao del Sur after the province was divided in 1959.
His reputation for integrity became legendary, earning him
recognition upon retirement in the mid-1960s as the “Most Honest
Provincial Treasurer of Lanao del Sur.”
Civic Contributions
Naga’s vision extended beyond government. In Marawi City, he
helped establish:
The first printing press
The first electric company
The first radio station
The first taxi company
MATELCO, the first telephone company
These initiatives modernized civic life, giving Marawi access to communication, mobility, and information.

PAGE 2
Education and Faith
He was a member of the first Board of Incorporators of the Kamilol Islamic Society School, supporting education
for future generations. As a Hadji, he embodied moral leadership, and as the 3rd Sultan sa Bayabao, he carried
traditional authority within Maranao society.
Agricultural Innovation
Together with his son-in-law and grandson, Sacar M. Basman of the International Rice Research Institute, Naga
helped introduce “Miracle Rice” in Bubong, Lanao del Sur. This shortened harvest cycles to three months,
transforming livelihoods in the Basak area.
War and Resistance
Naga was a war veteran during the Japanese and American occupations and fought in the Tamparan War in Lanao
del Sur, carrying forward the resilience of his people.
Legacy
His name itself reflects contrasts: “Urang” (scorpion) for vigilance and defense, “Naga” (water dragon) for depth
and adaptability. He passed away on February 15, 1987, leaving behind no stone monument, but a legacy etched in
institutions, honesty, and community progress.
Profile provided by Hayree Alug Basman (https://www.facebook.com/eyepatch11)

title: Naga, Minerva-Saminah Mambuay
text:
PAGE 1
Minerva-Saminah Mambuay Naga
Minerva-Saminah Mambuay Naga, commonly known as Dr. Naga, is a Filipino educator, academic
administrator, and researcher who currently serves as the Vice President for Academic Affairs (in Concurrent
Capacity) of the Mindanao State University (MSU) System, one of the largest and most culturally significant state
university systems in Mindanao.<ref name="msugensan2025">Mindanao State University Marawi City. (2025,
December 12). Dr. Minerva-Saminah M. Naga, Vice President for Academic Affairs. MSU Marawi City. Retrieved
from https://msugensan.edu.ph/dr-minerva-saminah-m-naga-new-vice-president-for-academic-affairs/</ref>
She built her career entirely within the MSU system, rising from classroom teacher to the highest academic policy
post in a university network that serves over 69,000 students across Mindanao, Sulu, and Palawan. Before her
elevation to the system-wide VPAA role, she served as Dean of the College of Education at MSU-Marawi and as
Vice Chancellor for Academic Affairs at MSU-Marawi.<ref name="msumain">Mindanao State University Main
Campus. (n.d.). Personnel Profile: Minerva-Saminah M. Naga. Office of the Dean, College of Education, MSU
Main Campus. Retrieved from https://www.msumain.edu.ph/personnel/minerva-saminah-m-naga/</ref>
Her career is best understood through one thread that runs from her earliest classroom work all the way to the top
of the MSU system: a determination to make quality education meaningful for Meranaw and Bangsamoro learners,
not just adequate. She navigated an AusAID scholarship to the University of Melbourne, survived the
administrative crisis that followed the 2017 Battle of Marawi, and helped steer MSU through the pandemic-era
shift to flexible learning, all while staying rooted in the cultural and spiritual soil of Lake Lanao.
Contents
