Background
Growing Up in Meranaw Country
Minerva-Saminah Mambuay Naga grew up in the cultural
heartland of the Meranaw people, the communities surrounding
Lake Lanao in the province of Lanao del Sur in central Mindanao.
Biographical and Professional Study: Dr. Minerva-Saminah
Mambuay Naga. (n.d.). Unpublished institutional document. The
Meranaw are one of the largest Islamic ethno-linguistic groups in
the Philippines, known for a rich tradition of scholarship,
craftsmanship, and a deeply held cultural code called maratabat,
which ties personal and family honor to excellence in conduct and
achievement.
Growing up within that culture meant that pursuing higher
education wasn't simply a career choice. It carried the weight of
family and community expectations. For a woman aspiring to
academic leadership in a traditionally structured society, the path
required not just intelligence but persistence. What makes Naga's
trajectory particularly striking is that she chose to channel that
drive into education itself, making the improvement of teaching
and learning her life's work rather than simply climbing out of her
community.
Her full name reflects both her Meranaw heritage and her
interfaith identity. The name "Saminah" is of Arabic origin and is
commonly used among Muslim Filipinos, while "Minerva,"
drawn from Roman tradition, signals a family that was
comfortable bridging worlds, an instinct she'd carry into her
professional life as a bridge-builder between global educational
standards and local Bangsamoro realities.

PAGE 3
Education
Undergraduate Studies
Naga completed her Bachelor of Science in Home Economics at Mindanao State University in Marawi City in
April 1997. Her undergraduate thesis, titled "A Survey in Iodized Salt Awareness and Utilization: MSU-ILS
Preschoolers' Parents," gave her an early grounding in community-based research and household dynamics. Home
Economics at MSU-Marawi was, and remains, a discipline with strong community extension dimensions, so Naga's
undergraduate years weren't spent entirely in lecture halls. They gave her a practical sense of how families and
communities actually function, knowledge that would later shape how she thought about education policy.
Early International Exposure
Before she ever finished her doctorate, Naga had already begun building an international perspective on education.
In April and May 2005, she joined the Philippines-Australia BEAM (Basic Education Assistance for Mindanao)
Teacher Educators Training and Study Tour as a Visiting Scholar at the University of South Australia (UniSA) in
Adelaide. That short but consequential tour introduced her to Australian frameworks for teacher education at a time
when the Philippine Department of Education was actively reshaping the madrasah and public school curriculum in
Muslim Mindanao. Coming back from Adelaide with fresh eyes on how teacher preparation programs are designed
would matter enormously later, when she eventually sat in the Dean's office overseeing the preparation of future
teachers herself.
Master of Assessment and Evaluation, University of Melbourne
The bigger international turning point came in January 2007, when Naga was selected as an AusAID-PAHRDF
(Philippines-Australia Human Resource Development Facility) long-term training scholar through the MSU
Academic Professional Development Program (APDP).<ref name="msumain" /> She spent a year and a half, from
January 2007 to August 2008, at the University of Melbourne in Victoria, Australia, completing a Master of
Assessment and Evaluation.<ref name="msumain" />
The Melbourne years were formative in ways that went beyond coursework. She was immersed in one of the
world's leading educational research environments at a time when outcomes-based approaches to assessment were
gaining momentum globally. She returned to MSU-Marawi in 2008 not just with a degree but with a
methodological toolkit and a vocabulary for reforming how student learning gets measured. That Melbourne
experience became the intellectual engine behind much of her later research and her advocacy for outcomes-based
education in Philippine higher education institutions.
She had earlier completed her Master of Arts in Education with a major in Reading at Mindanao State University
in Marawi in April 2004, before the Melbourne scholarship.<ref name="msumain" /> The Reading specialization
gave her a concrete understanding of foundational literacy, a background that proved directly useful years later
when she was designing post-conflict literacy recovery programs for communities displaced by the Marawi Siege.
Doctoral Research
Naga completed her Doctor of Philosophy in Educational Administration at Central Mindanao University
(CMU) in Musuan, Bukidnon, in March 2015, supported by a grant from the MSU Academic Professional
Development Program.<ref name="msumain" /> Her doctoral dissertation focused on outcomes-based evaluation
of classroom assessment competencies in higher education institutions, directly tying together the threads of her

PAGE 4
Melbourne training and her practical experience as a faculty member at MSU-Marawi.<ref name="docbio" /> The
research asked a straightforward but urgent question: are college teachers actually competent to assess student
learning in ways that align with the outcomes their programs promise? The findings had direct policy implications
for how MSU and similar institutions train and evaluate their teaching faculty.
Career
Early Faculty Life and Peace Education Work
Naga joined the faculty of the College of Education at MSU-Marawi in the years following her undergraduate
completion in 1997. Her teaching areas spanned educational administration, assessment and evaluation, reading
education, home economics, pre-service practicum supervision, and pedagogical strategies with a focus on
educational technology, as well as peace education integration.<ref name="msumain" /> That last specialization,
peace education, took on particular significance given the recurring cycles of armed conflict that have marked life
in Lanao del Sur and greater Mindanao.
She began documenting peace-related forums and dialogue sessions in the early 2000s. In 2009, she participated in
the National Conference on Secondary Arabic Language and Islamic Values Education (ALIVE) and the Standard
Madrasah Curriculum (SMC), organized by the DepEd Bureau of Madrasah Education.<ref name="msumain" /> In
2010, she documented the Consultative Meeting on the MSU Peace Education Module Exemplars and Strategic
Planning Workshop, a project of MSU-IPDM under the UN ACT for Peace Programme Partnership.<ref
name="msumain" /> These weren't just resume entries. They reflected a genuine investment in the peace
architecture of Mindanao at a time when formal peace negotiations between the Philippine government and the
Moro Islamic Liberation Front (MILF) were slowly gaining ground.
Documenting the Framework Agreement on the Bangsamoro
In December 2012, Naga served as documenter for the two-day Forum on the Basic Understanding and
Popularization of the Framework Agreement on the Bangsamoro (FAB), organized by the Consortium of
Bangsamoro Civil Society (CBCS-Ranaw) in Marawi City.<ref name="msumain" /> The FAB, signed in October
2012, was a landmark peace accord that would eventually lead to the creation of the Bangsamoro Autonomous
Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM). Being in the room for those community-level discussions, and being the
one responsible for accurately recording what was said, gave Naga a ground-floor perspective on how peace
agreements are received, debated, and processed by ordinary educators and community members. In 2012, she also
documented a Teachers' Forum on Interfaith Dialogue, again under CBCS-Ranaw.<ref name="msumain" />
In 2016, she was involved in the My Lake Lanao Project, a participant teachers' training organized by the Embassy
of the United States in Manila in partnership with MSU-IIT and the MSU College of Education Extension Services.
<ref name="msumain" /> The project centered on environmental advocacy and community engagement around
Lake Lanao, connecting teachers to both ecological and cultural stewardship.
Director of Admissions, MSU-Marawi
From 2016 to 2021, Naga served as Director of the Office of Admissions at MSU Main Campus in Marawi City,
concurrently serving as a Special Assistant in the Office of the Vice President for Academic Affairs at the system
level.<ref name="msumainadmissions">Office of Admissions, MSU Main Campus. (n.d.). Admissions Directors.

PAGE 5
Retrieved from https://www.msumain.edu.ph/admissionsoffice/</ref> The Admissions Directorship put her at the
front door of the entire university, overseeing the processes by which thousands of students from across the
Bangsamoro and wider Mindanao entered MSU's academic community every year.
Her five years in Admissions (2016 to 2021) overlapped directly with the catastrophic Battle of Marawi in 2017,
one of the most devastating urban conflicts in recent Philippine history. Managing student enrollment and records
continuity while the city was under siege and the campus evacuated its population was not a theoretical
administrative challenge. It was a crisis that required improvisation, coordination with displaced faculty and
students, and a steady hand during institutional chaos.
Post-Siege Recovery and the "3Rs" Initiative
The Battle of Marawi, which began in May 2017, forced the temporary closure of the MSU campus and displaced
tens of thousands of Marawi residents.<ref name="wikipedia_msu">Wikipedia contributors. (2025). Mindanao
State University. Wikipedia, The Free Encyclopedia. Retrieved from
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mindanao_State_University</ref> For the College of Education, the siege created an
acute educational emergency: an entire generation of students in Lanao del Sur had their schooling disrupted, and
the learning losses were deep.
In August 2017, even as the conflict was still ongoing, Naga was among the contributors to the Marawi City
Education Master Plan, which formed part of the Recovery, Rehabilitation, and Reconstruction Plan for 2017
onwards, commissioned by the City Government of Marawi.<ref name="msumain" /> The same month saw the
Multi-Stakeholders Forum for Lanao del Sur, co-organized with Task Force Bangon Marawi and the National
Economic and Development Authority, where she served as documenter.<ref name="msumain" />
In the years that followed, Naga became instrumental in the "3Rs" (Reading, Writing, and Arithmetic) recovery
initiatives, designed specifically to diagnose and address the learning gaps that accumulated in Lanao del Sur I
during and after the siege.<ref name="docbio" /> This wasn't just a matter of going back to basics. It involved
systematically mapping which competencies had been lost, identifying which student populations were most
affected, and designing a Curricular Development Plan that could realistically bridge those gaps given the
emotional and logistical weight students and teachers were carrying. The recovery work blended her expertise in
reading, her Melbourne-honed assessment methodology, and her longstanding peace education sensibility.
Dean, College of Education, MSU-Marawi
Naga eventually rose to the position of Dean of the College of Education at MSU-Marawi, the largest and most
historically rooted college in the MSU system's flagship campus.<ref name="mbhte2024">Ministry of Basic,
Higher, and Technical Education, MEISO. (2024, July 31). Director General Tahir Nalg graced the Tribute to
Parents, Recognition Rites, and Hooding Ceremony for the College of Education graduates at MSU Marawi.
Retrieved from https://mbhte-meiso.bangsamoro.gov.ph/2024/07/31/</ref> As Dean, she oversaw the academic
programs responsible for training the teachers who would serve the schools of the Bangsamoro and wider
Mindanao. Her office was in the New Building of the College of Education on the MSU Main Campus in Marawi
City.<ref name="msumain" />
Her tenure as Dean was defined by a push toward international-standard quality assurance and outcomes-based
program delivery, including active engagement with the ASEAN University Network Quality Assurance (AUN-
QA) framework.<ref name="docbio" /> AUN-QA is one of the most rigorous benchmarking systems in Southeast
Asian higher education, and working toward it required the College of Education to demonstrate, with evidence,
that its graduates were actually achieving the learning outcomes its programs promised. This was precisely the
terrain that Naga had been preparing for since her Melbourne years.

PAGE 6
She also led international academic missions to forge institutional partnerships. Among the notable linkages were
visits to Kastamonu University in Turkey and Universitas Diponegoro in Indonesia, seeking to align early
childhood and higher education frameworks at MSU with international best practices, and to place Meranaw
academic leadership on a global map.<ref name="docbio" />
During her deanship, she also oversaw the navigation of the COVID-19 pandemic and the shift to flexible and
online learning modalities, a transition that required not just technology adoption but a compassionate rethinking of
how assessment and instruction work when students are learning from homes in communities with limited internet
access.
Vice Chancellor for Academic Affairs, MSU-Marawi
After her service as Dean at MSU-Marawi, Naga was appointed Vice Chancellor for Academic Affairs at MSU-
Marawi City, the largest constituent universities of the MSU System located in Lanao del Sur.<ref
name="msugensan2025" /> As VCAA, she was the chief academic officer of Marawi campus. The posting
demonstrated the confidence the MSU system's leadership placed in her cross-campus versatility.
It was during her tenure as VCAA that the Turkish Cooperation and Coordination Agency (TİKA) engaged with
MSU officials to discuss joint initiatives on medical education, with Naga representing the university in those
discussions.<ref name="tika">TİKA Philippines. (n.d.). [Post on joint initiatives with MSU officials]. X (formerly
Twitter). Retrieved from https://x.com/tikaphilippines/status/1986300694547341522</ref> This was part of a
broader pattern of her career: leveraging international partnerships not as prestige exercises but as mechanisms for
genuinely improving what MSU campuses can offer their students.
Vice President for Academic Affairs, MSU System
In December 2025, Naga was designated as the Vice President for Academic Affairs of the Mindanao State
University System in a concurrent capacity, while retaining her VCAA position at MSU-General Santos.<ref
name="msugensan2025" /> The VPAA is the highest academic policy position in the MSU System, responsible for
setting the direction of curriculum, quality assurance, and academic standards across all eight constituent
universities and three constituent colleges of the network.
"May you continue to lead with wisdom and dedication in advancing quality education and
transformative service for Mindanao."<ref name="msugensan2025" />
This congratulatory message from the MSU-General Santos community at the time of her designation captures the
esteem in which she is held across the system. Her elevation to the VPAA role marks the culmination of a career
built entirely within MSU, from undergraduate student to the person now responsible for shaping the academic life
of over 69,000 students across Mindanao, Sulu, and Palawan.
Contributions and Advocacy
Outcomes-Based Education and Assessment Reform
If there is one intellectual legacy that defines Naga's academic career, it's her sustained push to make assessment
meaningful rather than just procedural. Her doctoral research at Central Mindanao University examined whether
college faculty in higher education institutions were genuinely competent to assess student learning in alignment

PAGE 7
with outcomes-based frameworks.<ref name="docbio" /> This was a pointed question, because the shift to
outcomes-based education (OBE) in the Philippines had been mandated by the Commission on Higher Education
but wasn't always implemented with rigor.
Her Melbourne training gave her the theoretical and methodological grounding to distinguish between assessment
that merely documents student performance and assessment that actually informs teaching and improves learning.
She brought that distinction back to MSU and tried to build it into faculty development, curriculum review, and
program evaluation processes. This contribution is less visible than a policy announcement but more durable: it
shapes how individual faculty members think about what they're measuring and why.
Post-Conflict Academic Recovery
Naga's involvement in the post-Marawi Siege recovery efforts represents one of the most concrete public services
of her career. Contributing to the Marawi City Education Master Plan in 2017, designing the "3Rs" learning
recovery initiatives for Lanao del Sur I, and working through the Multi-Stakeholders Forum with national and local
government bodies, she helped ensure that the educational consequences of the siege were taken seriously as policy
problems and not just humanitarian footnotes.<ref name="msumain" /><ref name="docbio" />
The population displacement caused by the battle didn't just interrupt schooling for a few months. It scattered
families, traumatized students and teachers, and disrupted academic records. The interventions Naga helped
architect addressed not just what students had missed but how the system could rebuild enough trust and stability to
make learning possible again in a post-conflict context.
Peace Education Integration
Naga has been a consistent voice for integrating peace education into the formal curriculum at all levels, from pre-
service teacher preparation to in-service faculty development.<ref name="msumain" /><ref name="docbio" /> This
isn't a peripheral interest. In a region where armed conflict has periodically reshaped the educational landscape,
training teachers to facilitate peace-oriented dialogue in their classrooms is as practical as teaching them literacy
instruction methodology.
Her documented involvement in peace education forums spans from 2009 to 2018, covering the National
Conference on Secondary Arabic Language and Islamic Values Education (ALIVE), the UN ACT for Peace
Programme's MSU Peace Education Module workshops, the community-level popularization of the Framework
Agreement on the Bangsamoro, and interfaith dialogue sessions for teachers.<ref name="msumain" /> This body of
work positions her not as a detached academic observer of peace processes but as an active participant in building
the civic and pedagogical infrastructure that makes sustainable peace more likely.
Research on the Bangsamoro Education Landscape
Naga's research portfolio covers three overlapping themes: educational administration and school leadership,
assessment and outcomes-based evaluation, and the socio-economic and professional context of educators and
communities in the Bangsamoro.
Her collaborative publications include a 2024 study on school principals' experiences implementing School
Improvement Plans in Lanao del Sur, published in Education Quarterly Reviews;<ref
name="balindong2024">Balindong, N. A., Naga, M. M., et al. (2024). The experiences of the school principals on
the implementation of the School Improvement Plan (SIP) in Lanao del Sur. Education Quarterly Reviews, 7(1).
</ref> a 2024 qualitative study on how MBHTE-BARMM supervisors balance work-life responsibilities;<ref

PAGE 8
name="datumaas2024">Datumaas, N. M., Naga, M. M., et al. (2024). A qualitative study on MBHTE-BARMM
supervisors' approaches to achieving work-life responsibilities. Education Quarterly Reviews, 7(1).</ref> and a
2025 study on the perceived effectiveness of In-Service Training (INSET) programs as a basis for an INSET
manual, published in the International Journal of Research and Innovation in Social Science (IJRISS).<ref
name="mangoda2025">Mangoda, N. S., Naga, M. M., et al. (2025). Perceived effectiveness of In-Service Training
(INSET) programs: Basis for an INSET manual. IJRISS, 9(10).</ref>
Her doctoral dissertation itself, completed in 2015, remains a reference point for researchers examining outcomes-
based evaluation in Philippine higher education:<ref name="naga2015">Naga, M. M. (2015). Outcomes-based
evaluation on classroom assessment competencies in higher education institutions (Doctoral dissertation). Central
Mindanao University, Musuan, Bukidnon.</ref>
Faith-Integration as a Protective Factor
One of the less widely cited but meaningful dimensions of Naga's research involves the intersection of professional
identity and religious practice among educators in the Bangsamoro. Her work has explored how faith-integration,
specifically the sense of vocation and ethical grounding that comes from Islamic practice, functions as a protective
and stabilizing factor for the well-being of Muslim educators working in high-stress environments like post-
conflict schools.<ref name="docbio" /> This is a distinctive contribution to a literature that often treats religiosity
and professional performance as separate domains.
International Academic Linkages
Naga has personally led or participated in high-level academic delegation visits to partner institutions abroad,
including Kastamonu University in Turkey and Universitas Diponegoro in Semarang, Indonesia.<ref
name="docbio" /> These visits were aimed at benchmarking MSU's early childhood and higher education
programs against international frameworks and building institutional agreements that could support faculty
exchange, collaborative research, and curriculum development. The Turkey connection also reflects MSU's
historical and religious ties with the broader Turkic and OIC world, given Marawi's significance as a center of
Islamic scholarship in Southeast Asia.
Institutional Quality Assurance
Naga has been actively involved in the ASEAN University Network Quality Assurance (AUN-QA) processes
within MSU, which involve rigorous peer review of academic programs, learning outcomes, curriculum design,
faculty qualifications, and student support systems.<ref name="docbio" /> AUN-QA membership and compliance
is a significant institutional marker in Southeast Asian higher education, and her sustained work in this area has
contributed to pushing MSU's programs toward regional benchmarks. The pursuit of AUN-QA accreditation is not
just about prestige; it's about giving MSU graduates credentials that are recognized and respected across the
ASEAN region.
Legacy
Dr. Naga's career is, at its core, a story about what it means to serve an institution and a people simultaneously.
Every administrative role she took on, from Admissions Director to Dean to VCAA and VPAA, was filled during a
period of significant institutional stress. The Marawi Siege, the post-conflict recovery, the pandemic, the shift to
flexible learning: she navigated all of these not as external disruptions to her career but as the actual substance of
her work.

PAGE 9
What she leaves behind at each level is a more rigorous, more outward-looking, and more culturally grounded
approach to academic management. She showed that it's possible to hold global standards (Melbourne-trained,
AUN-QA oriented, outcomes-based) and local rootedness (Meranaw identity, peace education, community
research) in the same professional life without compromising either.
For future Bangsamoro educators, particularly women aspiring to academic leadership, her ascent from a Home
Economics undergraduate at MSU-Marawi to the Vice President for Academic Affairs of the entire MSU System is
a concrete proof of what that path can look like.
Recognition
Naga's contributions have been recognized at various institutional levels. The MSU community formally
congratulated her on her designation as system-wide Vice President for Academic Affairs in December 2025, with
the university describing her leadership as distinguished by wisdom and dedication to quality education and
transformative service for Mindanao.<ref name="msugensan2025" /> Her selection as an AusAID-PAHRDF
scholar in 2006 was itself a competitive award, reflecting recognition of her academic potential at the national and
binational level.<ref name="msumain" />
She has been acknowledged by external government bodies, including the Bangsamoro Ministry of Basic, Higher,
and Technical Education (MBHTE), at official recognition ceremonies for College of Education graduates under
her deanship.<ref name="mbhte2024" /> Her research work has been published in peer-reviewed journals
including Education Quarterly Reviews and the International Journal of Research and Innovation in Social Science
(IJRISS).<ref name="mangoda2025" /><ref name="balindong2024" />
Challenges
Naga's career unfolded in one of the most persistently difficult educational environments in the Philippines. The
Bangsamoro region has historically suffered from underinvestment in public education, recurring armed conflict,
high poverty rates, and geographic isolation. Serving as an academic administrator in Marawi during and after the
2017 siege meant managing institutional survival alongside strategic development, with very little margin for error.
As a woman in a leadership role in a society that maintains traditional gender hierarchies, her rise to the deanship
and then to system-level leadership was itself a navigation of cultural terrain that not all institutional contexts in the
Bangsamoro would have supported easily. The documentation available does not detail the specific internal
resistance or challenges she may have faced along the way, but the cultural context makes clear that her ascent was
not simply the product of credentials alone.
The broader challenge she continues to face, now as VPAA of the entire MSU System, is the tension between the
system's mandate to serve the Bangsamoro and Muslim Mindanao on their own cultural terms, and the pressures of
national and international accreditation, standardization, and resource competition. Navigating that tension is the
central task of her current role.
Further Reading

of the School Improvement Plan (SIP) in Lanao del Sur. Education Quarterly Reviews, 7(1).

PAGE 10

title: Naga, Pipalawan O.
text:
PAGE 1
Pipalawan O. Naga
Pipalawan O. Naga is a distinguished Filipino civil engineer, environmental administrator, and public policy
expert who gained national recognition as one of the 1989 Bagong Bayani Awardees. He's best known for his
decades-long advocacy to protect Lake Lanao, pioneering the "Heartware" philosophy that bridges indigenous
cultural preservation with modern environmental governance. Of Meranaw descent, Naga's work stands as a
landmark example of how technical expertise and ancestral stewardship can unite to safeguard threatened
ecosystems in the Bangsamoro region.
Contents
1 Early Life and Ethnic Identity
2 Education and Academic Distinction
3 Professional Career
3.1 The 1989 Bagong Bayani Award
3.2 Transition to Environmental Governance
4 Institutional Contributions
4.1 Save Lake Lanao Movement (SALAM)
4.2 Policy Milestones
5 Environmental Philosophy: "Heartware"
6 Legacy and Recognition
7 Fact Sheet
8 References
9 External Links
Early Life and Ethnic Identity
Pipalawan Naga belongs to the Meranaw (Maranao) people, an indigenous ethnic group indigenous to the Lanao
region of Mindanao who call themselves the "People of the Lake." Born and raised in the communities surrounding
Lake Lanao, Naga's cultural upbringing was deeply intertwined with the Ranao—the ancient lake that serves as the
spiritual, cultural, and economic heartbeat of Meranaw civilization.
Growing up in this environment shaped his later professional trajectory. The lake wasn't just a body of water to him
—it was a living testament to Meranaw identity, embedded in oral histories, ceremonial practices, and the daily
rhythms of lakeside communities. This connection would later become the foundation of his environmental
advocacy, grounding his technical work in something more profound than engineering alone.
Education and Academic Distinction
Naga's educational journey reflects a deliberate expansion from technical engineering into broader systems of
governance and environmental policy.

PAGE 2
His foundational training was in Civil Engineering and Management Engineering, equipping him with the
technical skills that would later define his early career as an Overseas Filipino Worker. But recognizing that
infrastructure projects carried social and political dimensions, he pursued a Master of Public Administration
(MPA) with a major in Organization and Management.
The turning point came in 2011 when he completed his Master in Public Management (MPM) at the prestigious
Ateneo School of Government (ASoG). His cohort recognized him as one of the Outstanding Graduates that
year, largely due to his pioneering research on integrated lake basin management. This research wasn't just
academic—it became a technical blueprint for advocating policy reforms that would later influence national
environmental legislation.
Professional Career
The 1989 Bagong Bayani Award
In 1989, while working in the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, Pipalawan Naga was honored as one of the Ten Bagong
Bayani Awardees, receiving the Award for Outstanding Employee. This remains the highest national recognition
conferred upon Overseas Filipino Workers, awarded by the Bagong Bayani Foundation, Inc., in coordination with
the Philippine government.
The award wasn't just ceremonial. It recognized Naga's professional excellence, technical integrity, and the way he
represented Filipino competence on the global stage. At a time when many OFWs faced exploitation and
discrimination, Naga's achievements stood as proof of Filipino engineering expertise. His work abroad built the
credibility he would later leverage when returning to advocate for his homeland's most threatened natural resource.
Transition to Environmental Governance
After his overseas career, Naga returned to the Philippines and shifted his focus entirely. He accepted a role as
Consultant for Environment and Natural Resources for the Provincial Government of Lanao del Sur,
applying his engineering background to environmental challenges facing the lake basin.
In 2013, he represented the Philippines at the International Symposium on Integrated Lake Basin Management
in Shiga, Japan. There, he presented his research to an international audience of environmental scientists, drawing
global attention to the ecological crisis unfolding at Lake Lanao—a crisis largely invisible to the world beyond
Mindanao.
Institutional Contributions
Save Lake Lanao Movement (SALAM)
Naga emerged as a pivotal founding leader of the Save Lake Lanao Movement (SALAM), a grassroots coalition
formed in response to the direct damming of Lake Lanao for the Agus-1 Hydroelectric Plant. The dam's
construction threatened to disrupt the lake's natural water cycles, endangering its endemic species and undermining
the socio-religious practices of Meranaw communities who depend on the lake's seasonal rhythms.

PAGE 3
What set Naga apart was his ability to translate indigenous concerns into technical language that policymakers
couldn't ignore. He provided the engineering substantiation used to challenge the project, demonstrating with data
and models that artificial water level fluctuations would trigger cascading ecological failures—biodiversity
collapse, shoreline erosion, and the disruption of traditional fishing practices central to Meranaw subsistence.
Policy Milestones
Naga's advocacy directly contributed to two landmark policy achievements:
Presidential Proclamation No. 871 (1992) declared the Lake Lanao Watershed a protected reservation, legally
recognizing the lake's ecological and cultural significance. This wasn't just symbolic—it established a legal
framework for limiting extractive activities and prioritizing conservation.
Memorandum Order No. 421 created the Lake Lanao Watershed Protection and Development Council
(LLWPDC), an inter-agency body tasked with coordinating conservation efforts. Naga's research and advocacy
provided much of the technical foundation for the Council's early work, shaping its priorities and strategic
approach.
Environmental Philosophy: "Heartware"
Naga is the architect of the "Heartware" approach to conservation—a philosophy that challenges purely
technocratic models of environmental management.
He argues that while "hardware" (infrastructure) and "software" (legislation) are necessary, they're insufficient for
sustainable management. What's missing, he insists, is Heartware—the integration of local culture, collective
memory, and the spiritual connection that indigenous communities maintain with their environment.
For Naga, conservation isn't just about enforcing regulations or building better water treatment facilities. It's about
honoring the worldview of the Meranaw people, for whom the lake is not a resource to be managed but a sacred
entity deserving of respect. This philosophy has influenced how conservation projects in Bangsamoro are designed,
encouraging participatory approaches that center indigenous knowledge rather than sidelining it.
Legacy and Recognition
Pipalawan Naga's legacy is multifaceted. As an OFW, he demonstrated Filipino engineering excellence on the
international stage. As an environmental advocate, he pioneered methods for integrating indigenous knowledge into
environmental policy. And as a public intellectual, he challenged the assumption that modernization requires
abandoning traditional ecological wisdom.
His "Heartware" framework has been cited in regional environmental planning documents and continues to
influence how conservation projects are conceptualized in Muslim Mindanao. The protections established for Lake
Lanao, while incomplete and often undermined by development pressures, remain legal testaments to the
effectiveness of his advocacy.
Perhaps most importantly, Naga proved that local communities—especially indigenous groups often excluded from
decision-making—can drive policy change when their concerns are backed by rigorous technical analysis and
strategic coalition-building.

PAGE 4
Fact Sheet
Full Name: Pipalawan Ombawa Naga
Ethnic Group: Meranaw (Maranao)
Key Award: 1989 Bagong Bayani Award (Outstanding Employee)
Major Legacy: Protection of the Lake Lanao Watershed
Signature Philosophy: "Heartware" (Culture-based Environmentalism)
Educational Distinction: Outstanding Graduate, Ateneo School of Government (2011)
International Representation: 2013 International Symposium on Integrated Lake Basin Management,
Shiga, Japan
References
Bagong Bayani Foundation, Inc. (1989). Roll of Honor: 1989 Awardees. Manila.
Ateneo School of Government. (2011). Commencement Records: Outstanding Graduates. Quezon City.
Naga, P. O. (2011). Lake Lanao: An ancient lake in distress. Shiga University, Japan.
Office of the President. (1992). Presidential Proclamation No. 871. Official Gazette of the Philippines.

title: Naga-Marohombsar, Salma L.
text:
PAGE 1

Known for

member, MSU Main
Mathematics Department;
leader of the Balik MSU
campaign during the 2017
Marawi Siege

Filipino

Salma L. Naga-Marohombsar
Dr. Salma L. Naga-Marohombsar is a Filipino mathematician,
educator, and institutional leader from the Bangsamoro region of
Mindanao, recognized as one of the most consequential figures in
the academic life of the Mindanao State University (MSU)
system.
She holds a PhD in Mathematics and has been a faculty member
of the Mathematics Department at MSU Marawi since 1999, when
she became the first Muslim woman to join that department, a
milestone that opened doors for generations of Bangsamoro
women in STEM. She is currently the Chairperson of the
Mathematics Department (2023 to present).
Her career brings together three threads that rarely converge in a
single person: rigorous mathematical research, deeply rooted
community service, and fearless academic leadership.
When the 2017 Marawi Siege displaced thousands and shuttered
the university, Dr. Naga-Marohombsar didn't step back. She
stepped forward, leading the campaign that brought students home
to campus before the conflict had even fully ended.
Her legacy is built on firsts and on the willingness to keep
showing up, whether in the classroom, the boardroom, the
badminton court, or a peace consultation table.
Contents
1 Background
2 Education
3 Career
4 Leadership During Crisis and Peace Advocacy
5 Institutional Contributions
6 Research Excellence
7 University Life and Sports
8 Legacy
9 Recognition
10 See Also
11 External Links
Background
Dr. Naga-Marohombsar belongs to the Bangsamoro community and has built her life's work within and alongside
the people of Marawi City and the broader Bangsamoro region of Mindanao.

PAGE 2
Her identity as a Bangsamoro woman in mathematics is not incidental to her career. It's central to it.
From the very beginning, she entered spaces where women like her were not yet represented, and she stayed, grew,
and eventually led those same spaces.
Her commitment to education as a vehicle for community uplift has been the consistent thread running through her
academic, administrative, and advocacy work across more than two decades.
Education
Dr. Naga-Marohombsar holds a Doctor of Philosophy (PhD) in Mathematics, a credential that anchors her
scholarly contributions in one of the most demanding disciplines in higher education.
The source document does not specify the institution where she completed her doctoral studies, but her academic
career has been centered within the MSU system, where she has taught, researched, and led since 1999.
Her doctoral formation shaped both her research output and her approach to institutional development, allowing
her to contribute meaningfully to curriculum, policy, and graduate studies frameworks at the university level.
Career
Dr. Naga-Marohombsar joined the Mathematics Department of Mindanao State University Marawi in 1999 as its
first Muslim woman faculty member, a distinction that was historic at the time and remains part of her enduring
identity within the institution.
Over the course of more than two decades, she has grown from faculty member to one of the most broadly
experienced academic administrators in the College of Natural Sciences and Mathematics (CNSM).
She is the only CNSM faculty member to have served as Chairperson of two distinct departments within the
college: the Mathematics Department and the Graduate Studies Department.
As Chairperson of the Mathematics Department, she served her first term from 2012 to 2013 and is currently in her
second term, which began in 2023.
She also served as Chairperson of the Graduate Studies Department from 2019 to 2022, a role that ended when the
department was dissolved.
Beyond department leadership, she has held advisory roles at the highest levels of the MSU system, serving as
Special Assistant to the Vice President for Academic Affairs and as Special Assistant to the Vice Chancellor for
Research and Extension.
These appointments reflect the breadth of trust the institution has placed in her across academic, research, and
policy domains.
Leadership During Crisis and Peace Advocacy
Perhaps the most defining chapter of Dr. Naga-Marohombsar's career came in the aftermath of the 2017 Marawi
Siege, when the city was devastated by months of armed conflict and MSU Marawi was left empty and uncertain.

PAGE 3
As the Over-all Team Leader of the Balik MSU: Somombak Tano sa Pantaw a Mareg campaign, she led the
critical effort to bring students back to campus even before the siege had fully concluded.
The campaign's name, which translates roughly to "Return to MSU: Let Us Go Back to the Shore of the Lake,"
carries with it the spirit of belonging, resilience, and homecoming that defined the initiative.
In a time when many institutions would have waited for clearer skies, Dr. Naga-Marohombsar and her team made a
deliberate choice to treat education itself as an act of peace and recovery.
Her advocacy for peace doesn't stop at the campus gates. She has served as a consultant for the Principles for
Peace Key Sectoral Consultations, contributing her perspective and expertise to broader conversations about
peacebuilding in Mindanao.
She also served as the Marawi Area Focal Person for the Mindanao Young Women Leaders Forum, a platform
dedicated to amplifying the voices of young Bangsamoro women in peace and development work.
On the international stage, she has presented on the topic Science + Peace: What's Math Got to Do with It?, a
talk that bridges her academic discipline with her deep commitment to building a more just and peaceful society.
This question, what mathematics has to do with peace, is one that speaks to who she is: a scientist who sees her
field not in isolation, but in conversation with the world around it.
Institutional Contributions
Dr. Naga-Marohombsar has left lasting marks on the policy and governance infrastructure of the MSU system.
She contributed to the crafting of the MSU Graduate Studies Handbook, a document that shapes how graduate
education is structured and delivered across the MSU system.
She also contributed to the Evaluation Guidelines for MSU Chancellors, a framework that governs one of the
most consequential leadership positions in the university system.
These contributions place her among the small circle of faculty members who have helped define not just the
culture of the university, but its formal rules and standards.
Her dual role as both a practitioner (teaching, researching, leading departments) and a policy architect gives her
contributions a durability that extends well beyond any single term or position.
Research Excellence
As a mathematician, Dr. Naga-Marohombsar has produced scholarly work that has earned international recognition
and placement in high-quality academic venues.
Her research has been published in ISI and Scopus-indexed journals, including Ars Combinatoria and Advances
and Applications in Discrete Mathematics, two respected venues in the field of discrete mathematics and
combinatorics.
This publication record places her among a relatively small group of MSU faculty whose research meets the
standards of international peer review and indexing.

PAGE 4
In 2020, her contributions to scholarship were formally recognized when she was named Distinguished Faculty
Member in the Field of Research by the university.
Her research profile also made her a qualifier for the prestigious CHED Republica Award, a national recognition
that reflects the quality and impact of her scholarly output.
University Life and Sports
Academic excellence and institutional leadership aside, Dr. Naga-Marohombsar is also a celebrated figure in
university sports.
She is actively engaged as a coordinator, coach, and champion in women's badminton for the university, a
dimension of her campus life that speaks to her all-around presence and energy within the MSU community.
Her involvement in sports reflects the same spirit that defines her broader career: full commitment, genuine
participation, and a will to win.
Legacy
Dr. Naga-Marohombsar's legacy in the MSU system is built on a rare combination of academic depth, institutional
courage, and community rootedness.
She is remembered as the woman who broke the gender barrier in the MSU Marawi Mathematics Department in
1999, and as the leader who chose to bring students home during one of the most difficult moments in Marawi's
history.
Her work proves that a mathematician can also be a peacebuilder, that a department chair can also be a badminton
champion, and that a Bangsamoro woman can lead in every room she enters.
For young women in the Bangsamoro region considering careers in STEM and public service, Dr. Naga-
Marohombsar is not just a role model. She is proof of what is possible.
Her story continues to be written, with her second term as Mathematics Department Chairperson (2023 to present)
adding yet another chapter to a career that has never stopped moving forward.
Recognition

Qualifier, CHED Republica Award (Commission on Higher Education), for research excellence

title: Naga-Pangadapun, Salam Pacasum
text:
PAGE 1
Salam Pacasum Naga-Pangadapun
Bae Salam Pacasum Naga-Pangadapun (also known as Salam Naga Pangadapun, or by her Hajj name Norhayah;
affectionately called "Ate Salam") was a Maranao political figure and traditional leader who served as mayor of
Marawi City, Lanao del Sur, from 1985 to 1986. She holds the distinction of being the first woman to occupy that
office. Her short tenure came at a turbulent moment in Philippine history, bridging the final period of the Marcos
administration and the early months after the 1986 People Power Revolution.
Contents
1 Early Life and Family
2 Education
3 Career and Public Service
4 Leadership Roles and Cultural Contributions
5 Personal Life and Children
6 Legacy and Historical Significance
Early Life and Family
She was born on December 12, 1945, into a prominent Maranao political and traditional family. She was the only
child of Sultan Cosain Naga (also referred to as Sheik Cosain Naga), who served as appointed mayor of Marawi
City from 1954 to 1957, and Bae Saripa Ali Pacasum (also known as Hadja Saripa Ali Pacasum-Naga).
Her maternal grandparents are identified in available family accounts as Sheik Abdul Rahman Pacasum and
Baialabi a Gaos Pala Ali. She later married the late Judge Yusoph Pangadapun of the Regional Trial Court in
Marawi City (Branch 10). He is now deceased. The marriage linked a traditional political lineage with the local
judiciary.
Education
According to the primary reference document, she studied at the Philippine Women’s University in Manila. She
earned a Bachelor of Arts in Psychology and later a master’s degree in public administration from the same
institution. Independent public records confirming the exact degrees and years of attendance were not located in
available official or institutional sources during this research.
Career and Public Service
Bae Salam entered local government service in Marawi City during a period of significant political change in the
Philippines. She assumed the position of mayor in 1985 and held office through 1986, becoming the first woman
to serve as the city’s chief executive.
Her time in office coincided with the final months of the Marcos administration and the early days of the new
national leadership that followed the February 1986 People Power Revolution. As part of the broader
reorganization of local governments under the incoming administration, Officers-in-Charge were appointed across
the country, and she stepped down from the mayoralty during that transition.
Paragraph
Insert
Save changes…

PAGE 2
Despite the relatively short duration of her term, her service marked a notable moment in the city’s political history
as the first instance of a woman holding the top municipal post in a setting long shaped by traditional male
leadership.
Leadership Roles and Cultural Contributions
Beyond formal office, family and local accounts describe her as active in traditional Maranao conflict resolution,
particularly kapamasad sa rido (the mediation and settlement of blood feuds). Rido refers to inter-family conflicts
that can persist across generations and involve land, honor, or political disputes. Mediation of this kind draws on
traditional authority, Islamic principles, and interpersonal skill. Independent contemporary documentation of
specific cases she mediated was not located in publicly available primary sources, though the practice itself is well-
attested in Maranao culture.
Personal Life and Children
She and Judge Yusoph Pangadapun had several children who have continued in public service in Marawi City and
the broader Bangsamoro region:
Rawia N. Pangadapun has served as City Civil Registrar of Marawi City.
Yasmira Pangadapun-Muti (also referred to as Bai Yasmira Pangadapun) has held the position of
Provincial Social Welfare Officer under the Ministry of Social Services and Development / DSWD-
BARMM.
Yusoph “Popoy” Pangadapun served as vice mayor of Marawi City (listed in some records for the period
around 1998–2004).
Yanisah Pangadapun-Lanto has been active at the barangay level; Norhaya Village in Marawi is named in
connection with her mother’s Hajj name and appears in official barangay listings.
Legacy and Historical Significance
Her principal historical marker is her status as Marawi’s first female mayor. In a region where traditional and
formal politics have long been male dominated, her assumption of the office, even for a limited period resulting
from an election protest and succession, represented a break with precedent. The family’s continued presence in
local civil registration, social welfare administration, the city legislature, and barangay leadership illustrate
intergenerational continuity common in Philippine local politics, particularly in Lanao del Sur.

Hassan Sharief Noor
Ustadz Hassan Sharief Noor (born January 15, 1942) is a Filipino
Muslim Qur’an reader (qari), educator, and Islamic scholar from
Punud-Taporog, Poona Bayabao, Lanao del Sur. He is widely
recognized as a pioneer of Qur’anic recitation in the Philippines and
the first Filipino Muslim to win an international Qur’an reading
competition, bringing global recognition to Filipino Muslim
scholarship.
---
Early Life and Education
Hassan Sharief Noor was born on January 15, 1942, in Punud-Taporog, Poona Bayabao, Lanao del Sur.
He was raised in a religious household, where his father, an Arabic teacher, trained him in Qur’anic reading
at an early age.
He completed his elementary education at Talagian Elementary School, where he studied alongside future
Lanao del Sur governor Dr. Mahid Mutilan.
He later pursued higher education at Jamiatul Philippine Al-Islamiah in Marawi City, where he earned a
Bachelor of Science in Education.
---
Teaching Career
Noor began his professional career as a public school teacher at Talagian Elementary School in Poona
Bayabao, serving from 1962 to 1980.
He subsequently joined Jamiatul Philippine Al-Islamiah as an instructor from 1981 to 1987.
From 1987 to 2008, he served at the Mindanao State University – King Faisal Center for Islamic, Arabic and
Asian Studies in Marawi City, where he:

PAGE 2
- Taught basic Arabic subjects  
 - Served as Director for Extension Services  
Beyond formal institutions, he taught Qur’anic recitation continuously from 1971 to 2015, mentoring
generations of students in proper pronunciation (tajwid) and recitation techniques.
---
Qur’an Recitation and International Recognition
Ustadz Noor gained national and international recognition for his excellence in Qur’anic recitation, known
for:
 - A melodious and disciplined voice  
 - Mastery of correct Arabic pronunciation (tajwid)  
In September 1979, he became the **first Filipino Muslim champion** in an International Qur’an Reading
Competition held in Tripoli, Libya.
This achievement marked a historic milestone, demonstrating that Filipino Muslims could compete at the
highest level in Islamic scholarship and recitation.
His victory drew attention from Muslim countries, many of which were previously unaware of the depth of
Islamic learning in the Philippines.
---
Role as International Judge
Due to his expertise and reputation, Noor was invited to serve as a hakam (judge) in international Qur’an
reading competitions held in Bangkok, Thailand in:
 - 1991  
 - 1993  
 - 2000  
His participation as a judge reflects his standing in the global Qur’anic recitation community.
---
Legacy and Influence
Ustadz Hassan Sharief Noor is regarded as one of the key figures in the development of Qur’anic recitation
in the Philippines.
He trained numerous students who later excelled in national and international competitions, including:
 - Abdul Basit Tomara  
 - Isnairah Bantayao  
His lifelong dedication to teaching helped sustain and strengthen the tradition of Qur’an reading among
Muslim Filipinos.

PAGE 3
He is widely considered one of the reasons why Qur’anic recitation remains vibrant and active in the
Bangsamoro community.
---
Significance
Noor’s achievements elevated the profile of Filipino Muslims in the global Islamic community.
He bridged traditional Islamic learning and modern educational institutions in the Philippines.
His contributions continue to influence Islamic education, particularly in Qur’anic studies, in the
Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao.

Acmad D. Omar Sr
Acmad D. Omar Sr. is a distinguished Filipino retired police general and former diplomat who served as the
Philippine Ambassador to the Sultanate of Oman from 2005 to 2010. Known as a decorated "Top Cop" for his
heroic rescue operations and criminal apprehension efforts in the Philippine National Police, Omar successfully
transitioned to international diplomacy where he championed the welfare of overseas Filipino workers and
strengthened Philippine-Omani relations. A Filipino Muslim from Mindanao, his career exemplifies the bridge
between security expertise and cultural diplomacy in Southeast Asian-Middle Eastern relations.

Early Life and Background
Acmad D. Omar Sr. was born around 1948, making him
approximately 56 years old when he received his diplomatic
appointment in early 2004. As a Filipino Muslim, his ethnic and
religious background positioned him uniquely for leadership roles
in Muslim Mindanao and later diplomatic assignments in the
Middle East. His upbringing in a Muslim Filipino community
gave him deep cultural insights that would prove invaluable in

PAGE 2
both his law enforcement career in the Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (ARMM) and his subsequent
diplomatic posting to an Islamic nation.
Family
Omar's legacy of public service extends to the next generation through his son, Acmad Omar Jr., who rose to the
rank of Brigadier General in the Philippine Air Force. This father-son dedication to national service reflects a
family tradition of commitment to the Philippines. The younger Omar has been noted for his own distinguished
military career, continuing the family's reputation for excellence in uniformed service.
Law Enforcement Career
Philippine National Police Service
Before entering diplomatic service, Acmad D. Omar Sr. built a remarkable career in the Philippine National Police
(PNP), ultimately retiring in 2003 with the rank of Regional Director. His tenure was marked by exceptional
courage and tactical brilliance in some of the most challenging security environments in the Philippines.
Command in ARMM
As the Regional Director and commander of police forces in the Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao
(ARMM), Omar led operations in one of the country's most volatile regions. His leadership was characterized by a
combination of cultural sensitivity and operational decisiveness that earned him widespread respect. The ARMM
posting required navigating complex tribal politics, religious dynamics, and active insurgent threats—challenges
that Omar met with distinction.
Notable Operations and Commendations
Omar earned his reputation as a "Top Cop" through several high-profile successful operations that captured
national and international attention.
Rescue of Jeffrey Schilling
One of the defining moments of Omar's police career was his instrumental role in the 2001 rescue of American
national Jeffrey Schilling, who had been held hostage for over seven months by the Abu Sayyaf Group in Jolo,
Sulu. The successful recovery operation required sophisticated intelligence work, tactical coordination, and cultural
negotiation skills. This operation brought Omar international recognition and demonstrated his capability to handle
complex hostage situations involving foreign nationals.
Criminal Apprehension Success
Throughout his tenure in ARMM, Omar led numerous missions that resulted in the capture of notorious criminals
and the dismantling of kidnap-for-ransom cells that had terrorized communities across the southern Philippines.
His operational successes contributed significantly to improved security conditions in the region and earned him
multiple departmental honors prior to his retirement.

PAGE 3
Diplomatic Service
Appointment to Oman
In February 2004, President Gloria Macapagal-Arroyo appointed Omar as Ambassador Extraordinary and
Plenipotentiary to the Sultanate of Oman. He officially assumed his post in May 2005, bringing his unique
combination of security expertise and cultural understanding to Philippine diplomatic efforts in the Gulf region.
The appointment reflected recognition of Omar's ability to navigate Muslim-majority societies and his
demonstrated leadership capabilities.
Labor Welfare Advocacy
Omar made the welfare of thousands of Overseas Filipino Workers (OFWs) in Oman his top priority throughout his
ambassadorship. He stated that "the welfare of the Filipino workers in Oman is on top of our agenda," a
commitment he pursued vigorously. One of his major diplomatic victories was successfully advocating for the
lifting of Oman's ban on certain Filipino workers, ensuring continued employment opportunities for thousands of
Filipino families dependent on remittances from the Gulf.
Economic and Infrastructure Development
Air Services Agreement
In December 2009, Ambassador Omar facilitated the signing of a Memorandum of Understanding on air services
between the Philippines and Oman. This agreement was a crucial step in establishing direct air links between
Manila and Muscat, making travel more accessible and affordable for Filipino workers and their families. The air
services MoU represented a significant milestone in bilateral economic relations and practical connectivity between
the two nations.
Philippine School Sultanate of Oman
In June 2007, Omar inaugurated the new building of the Philippine School Sultanate of Oman, providing critical
educational infrastructure for the children of the Filipino expatriate community. The school serves as an anchor
institution for maintaining Filipino cultural identity and educational standards abroad. This infrastructure
development demonstrated Omar's holistic approach to supporting the Filipino diaspora beyond just employment
issues.
Political and Cultural Diplomacy
Peace Process Support
Omar effectively leveraged Omani support for the peace process in the Southern Philippines, drawing on both his
law enforcement experience in Mindanao and his diplomatic position. The Sultanate's backing provided valuable
Muslim-world endorsement for Philippine peace initiatives.

PAGE 4
Organization of Islamic Cooperation
He advanced the Philippines' bid for observer status in the Organization of Islamic Cooperation (OIC),
strengthening the country's engagement with the Islamic world and opening new diplomatic channels for
addressing Mindanao peace issues.
Achievements and Recognition
Omar's career trajectory from decorated police general to successful diplomat represents a unique path in
Philippine public service. His ability to translate field operations experience into diplomatic effectiveness set him
apart from traditional career diplomats. He is recognized for bridging cultural gaps between the Philippines and the
Arab world, using his Muslim Filipino identity and his professional accomplishments to enhance bilateral
understanding.
Legacy and Impact
Acmad D. Omar Sr.'s career demonstrates how specialized regional expertise and cultural competency can be
leveraged in international diplomacy. His success in both law enforcement and diplomatic arenas offers a model for
career transitions in public service. His work in Oman created lasting improvements in the conditions and
protections for Filipino workers in the Gulf, affecting the lives of thousands of families. The bilateral agreements
and institutional infrastructure he developed continue to benefit Philippine-Omani relations.
Personal Values and Philosophy
Throughout both phases of his career, Omar's work was defined by a commitment to public safety and
humanitarian welfare. Whether rescuing hostages in Mindanao or advocating for worker rights in Oman, his focus
remained on protecting Filipino lives and interests. His emphasis on practical results over diplomatic protocol
earned him respect both in law enforcement circles and among the OFW community he served.

title: Omar, Acmad Umpa Jr
text:
PAGE 1
Acmad Umpa Omar Jr
Acmad Umpa Omar Jr. (born 24 May 1970, Iligan City) is a Brigadier General of the Philippine Air Force (PAF)
and one of the most consequential figures in the intersection of military affairs and national legislation in the
Philippines today. Since 05 March 2021, he has served as the Chief of the Office for Legislative Affairs (OLA) of
the Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP), the officer primarily responsible for representing the AFP's interests
before both houses of the Philippine Congress and the Commission on Appointments. A seasoned combat
helicopter pilot with 3,000 flying hours to his name, a holder of three graduate degrees, and a proud member of the
Maranao community from the Lanao region of Mindanao, BGen. Omar is a rare figure in Philippine military
history. His career is the story of a man who learned to fight in the skies above Mindanao, lead across some of the
AFP's most demanding commands, and then take that same energy into the deliberative halls of the legislature,
where some of the country's most significant defense and security laws of the past several years bear his
fingerprints.
Early Life and Heritage
Acmad Umpa Omar Jr. was born on 24 May 1970 in Iligan City, a city that has long sat at the crossroads between
the Christian and Muslim worlds of Northern Mindanao. He is of Maranao descent, belonging to the "People of
the Lake," the ethnolinguistic community historically rooted at the shores of Lake Lanao in the Lanao region. The
Maranao are known for their warrior tradition, their intricate arts (particularly the okir), and a deep cultural code of
honor that prizes dignity, excellence, and the defense of one's name and community. Those values were not abstract
for the young Acmad. They were lived.
He took his early schooling in the city that shaped him. He completed his elementary education at Diliman
Preparatory School and his secondary education at La Salle Academy, Iligan City, a school known for forming
young men of discipline and character. After finishing high school, he entered the University of Santo Tomas
(UST) in Manila, where he was pursuing a degree in Civil Engineering and was already in his second year of
college when he made a decision that would change the course of his life. In 1990, he left his engineering studies
behind and walked into the Philippine Military Academy as a plebe. He never looked back.
Education and Academic Formation
Philippine Military Academy
He entered the Philippine Military Academy (PMA) in 1990 as a plebe and graduated in 1994 as a commissioned
officer of the Philippine Air Force with the "Bantay Laya" Class of 1994, a batch whose name, meaning
"Guardian of Freedom," set the tone for everything that followed.
Military Training and Specialization
Fresh out of the Academy, he immediately threw himself into the specialized training pipeline that turns
commissioned officers into Air Force professionals. He completed the Basic Air Force Officers Course
(BAFOC), the prerequisite that every Air Force officer must go through, and then moved on to pilot training at the
Philippine Air Force Flying School (PAFFS).

PAGE 2

At PAFFS, he didn't just complete the course. He topped it. In
1996, he graduated and was conferred the prestigious Vicente
Rivera Award for Number One in Instrument Flying, a
recognition given to the cadet who demonstrates the highest level
of proficiency in flying on instruments. That kind of distinction
early in a pilot's career says a lot about the officer you're dealing
with.
His training didn't stop there. In 2003, he traveled to Lackland
Air Force Base in Texas, USA, where he completed the United
States Air Force (USAF) Advanced Logistics Readiness
Operation Course, deepening his expertise in the logistical
backbone of air operations. Back home, he completed the AFP
Intelligence Officers Collection Course, the PAF Squadron
Officers Course, and the Command and General Staff College
at Camp Aguinaldo, Quezon City, all of which are key rungs on
the ladder toward senior leadership.
He also brought international exposure into areas beyond pure
military operations. He attended Civil-Military Operations
training in Stockholm, Sweden, and the Civil-Military
International Cooperation Course in Fort Dickson, Malaysia,
building the cross-cultural, inter-agency sensibility that would
later define his work as a legislative affairs officer. Additional
professional courses included Defense Resource Management
Training and Finance Accountable Officer programs, rounding out
a training record that covers the full spectrum of modern military
leadership.
Graduate Academic Degrees
BGen. Omar's commitment to education didn't end with his
commission. Over the course of his career, he pursued and
completed three graduate degrees, making him one of the more
academically credentialed flag officers in the AFP today.
He earned a Master in National Security Administration
(MNSA) from the National Defense College of the Philippines
(NDCP), the AFP's premier institution for strategic and security
studies. He also holds a Master in Public Administration, Major
in Development and Security (MPA-DevSec), from the
Development Academy of the Philippines (DAP). Most recently,
he completed a Doctorate in Development Administration,
Major in Public Governance, from Philippine Christian
University (PCU).
Together, these degrees reflect a career-long effort to understand
not just how to command, but how institutions work, how
governance functions, and how security and development
intersect. That grounding shows clearly in the work he has done as
Chief, OLA.

PAGE 3
Children
4 (1LT Jaafar, Atty. Gabriel
Acmad, Raphael Hamzah,
Zaina Arriana)
Notable Award
Vicente Rivera Award, No.
1 in Instrument Flying,
PAFFS (1996); Officer of
the Year (2012)
Military Career and Command Positions
Over the course of 35 years in uniform, BGen. Omar has
accumulated a command record that spans air operations,
intelligence, search and rescue, combat deployments, and
institutional management. Some of his major assignments include:
Commander, Tactical Operations Group of Sulu and
Tawi-Tawi (TOG SULTAW) — one of the AFP's most
operationally demanding commands, covering a region historically central to internal security challenges in
the Southern Philippines.
Commander, Trilateral Air Patrol (TAP), Indonesia-Malaysia-Philippines (INDOMALPHI) — a
multinational air patrol arrangement among the three neighboring countries, reflecting BGen. Omar's
capacity for regional security cooperation.
Deputy Assistant Chief of Staff for Reservist and Retirees Affairs, OA9
Director for Operations, Tactical Operations Wing Western Mindanao (TOWWESMIN)
Commander, PAF Search and Rescue Squadron
Director, PAF Inspection Division
Air Force Inspector General (AFIG) — a role that requires both moral authority and institutional
knowledge, as the AFIG is responsible for ensuring the Air Force maintains its standards and values.
Director, Plans and Program, PAF
Assistant Chief of Air Staff for Personnel, OA1
Commanding Officer, Executive Officer/Plans, Program, and Budget Unit, AFP Pension Gratuity
Management Center
Chief, Management Fiscal Office, AFP Pension Gratuity Management Center
Each of these positions added a layer to his understanding of how the AFP works, both at the tactical and
institutional levels. By the time he assumed the OLA post in 2021, he brought to it a career's worth of operational
credibility, administrative experience, and the kind of personal rapport that only 35 years of service can build.
Flying Career
One of the defining dimensions of BGen. Omar's identity as an Air Force officer is his life in the cockpit. He is a
seasoned combat helicopter pilot who has accumulated 3,000 flying hours over the course of his career, a figure
that puts him among the AFP's most experienced aerial operators.
That record includes the 2,500 Flying Hours Accident-Free Award, a recognition of not just the volume of flight
time he has logged but the discipline and professionalism with which he has done so. He holds the PAF Command
Rating Pilots Badge, one of the Air Force's highest distinctions for pilots.
His flying career began with the Vicente Rivera Award at PAFFS in 1996 and continued through decades of
operational deployments, including his time commanding TOG SULTAW, where helicopter operations are often
central to the mission. That cockpit experience grounds everything else about him. It gives him a kind of credibility
that no desk assignment can manufacture.
Service as Chief, Office for Legislative Affairs, AFP
BGen. Omar assumed designation as Chief of the Office for Legislative Affairs (OLA) of the AFP on 05 March
2021, and his tenure in that role has been one of the most productive in the office's history.

PAGE 4
The OLA's job is both simple to describe and difficult to execute. It serves as the primary interface between the
AFP, one of the country's largest and most complex institutions, and the Philippine Congress, the body that
ultimately controls the AFP's budget, legal framework, and policy environment. The Chief of OLA is, in practice,
the AFP's voice to the legislature. That voice has to be credible, consistent, and well-informed.
BGen. Omar has brought all three to the role. He has built what his colleagues describe as a genuinely strong
rapport with members of both the Senate and the House of Representatives, as well as with the Commission on
Appointments (CA), the body that confirms presidential appointments to senior military and civilian positions.
That relationship didn't happen by accident. It was built through sustained, respectful engagement, and through
delivering on commitments.
A concrete expression of that relationship has been the construction of a new facility that will serve as the
headquarters for the OLA team and satellite offices for the Senate and House of Representatives. The building,
which includes a VIP lounge, conference room, library, and roof deck, is designed to function as a hub of
operational coordination between the AFP and its congressional stakeholders. It is, in a very practical sense, a
monument to the kind of trust BGen. Omar has built between the two institutions during his tenure.
Legislative Achievements
Perhaps the most tangible measure of BGen. Omar's impact as Chief, OLA, is the list of laws that were enacted
under his leadership. These are not minor administrative measures. They include some of the most consequential
legislation affecting the AFP, national security, and Philippine sovereignty in recent years:
Anti-Terrorism Act of 2020 (Republic Act 11479) — the law that defines and penalizes terrorism and
establishes the legal framework for counter-terrorism operations.
Republic Act 11709 — prescribing fixed terms for key AFP officers, increasing the mandatory retirement
age of Generals and Flag Officers, and providing for a more effective attrition system.
Republic Act 11939 — the amendment to RA 11709, refining its provisions.
Defense Acquisition Act (Republic Act 12009) — governing how the AFP procures defense equipment and
systems, a critical piece of legislation for the AFP Modernization Program.
Self-Reliant Defense Posture Act (Republic Act 12024) — promoting the development of a domestic
defense industry to reduce the AFP's dependence on foreign military equipment.
Philippine Maritime Zone Act (Republic Act 12064) — defining and asserting the country's maritime
zones, a measure of significant strategic importance given the Philippines' ongoing territorial challenges.
Archipelagic Sea Lanes Act (Republic Act 12065) — establishing the legal basis for the designation and
management of sea lanes through Philippine archipelagic waters.
Free Legal Assistance Act (Republic Act 12177) — providing free legal assistance to AFP personnel, a
welfare measure that directly benefits the men and women in uniform.
Each of these laws required sustained legislative advocacy, careful relationship management, and the ability to
communicate complex security and defense concerns in terms that legislators and their staff could understand and
act on. That's what BGen. Omar has done, consistently, across his years in the role.
Family
BGen. Omar is married to Dr. Melanie Sarmiento-Omar, FPSOUG, a fellow professional whose academic and
medical credentials reflect a household that takes excellence seriously. They are blessed with four children.
Their eldest, 1LT Jaafar Omar, is a graduate of the Philippine Military Academy Class of 2018, carrying on the
family's tradition of military service into the next generation. Their second child, Atty. Gabriel Acmad Omar, has
pursued a career in law. Their younger children are Raphael Hamzah and Zaina Arriana.

PAGE 5
The family is, in its own way, a reflection of BGen. Omar's values: service, education, and the kind of
groundedness that only comes from knowing where you come from.
Awards and Recognition
BGen. Omar's 35 years of service have been recognized through a long and varied list of military honors,
commendations, and special recognitions:
Three (3) Outstanding Achievement Medals
Distinguished Service Star
Distinguished Service Medal
Bronze Cross Medal
Silver Wing Medal
Combat Kagitingan Badge
Military Merit Medals
Long Service Medal Achievement
Military Commendation Medals
Military Civic Action Medal
Visayas and Mindanao Campaign Medal
People Power II Award
Disaster Relief Badges
Marksmanship Badge
Inspector General's Badge
Intelligence Badge
Wing Commander's Well Done Award
Presidential Streamer Award
Officer of the Year Award for 2012
PAF Command Rating Pilots Badge
2,500 Flying Hours Accident-Free Award
Forty-two (42) commendations
Thirty (30) certificates of appreciation and recognition
That is not a short list. It's the accumulated recognition of a career lived fully and in service to others.
Legacy
BGen. Acmad Umpa Omar Jr. carries two legacies, and both of them matter.
The first is institutional. Within the AFP, he has demonstrated that the Office for Legislative Affairs is not just a
liaison function. It is a strategic asset. Under his leadership, the office has been the fulcrum on which some of the
most important defense legislation of the decade has turned. He has built lasting relationships, created permanent
infrastructure, and expanded the OLA's capacity to serve the AFP's legislative needs long after his own tenure ends.
The second legacy is personal and communal. As a senior Maranao officer in the Philippine Air Force, BGen.
Omar represents something that goes beyond rank and position. In a country where Muslim Filipinos have
historically been underrepresented in the national military establishment, a Brigadier General from Iligan City with
a Maranao heart, a combat pilot's record, and a doctorate is not a small thing. For the young people of the
Bangsamoro who are watching, he is proof that you don't have to set aside who you are to serve the nation at the
highest level. You carry it with you. And it makes you stronger.

PAGE 6
He leads by what he calls Integrity, Professionalism, and Excellence, the three values he has consistently put at
the center of his leadership philosophy. Those aren't catchphrases for BGen. Omar. They're the operating system.
