Dr. Rasid M. Paca (also referred to as Rashid M. Paca), RME, JD,
DPA, is a longtime Filipino academic administrator, educator, and
institutional leader who has spent over three decades building his
career within the Mindanao State University (MSU) System, based
primarily in Marawi City. He is known for wearing many hats
throughout his professional life, moving fluidly between engineering,
agriculture, law, and public administration, and using that broad
foundation to serve MSU through some of its most difficult chapters,
including the aftermath of the 2017 Marawi Siege and the disruptions
of the COVID-19 pandemic. Much of what is publicly known about
him comes from official MSU sources, institutional announcements,
and public records, since he has generally kept his personal life out
of the spotlight even as his professional profile grew within the
university system.
Contents
1 Early Life and Education
2 Career at Mindanao State University
3 OIC Presidency (2025)
4 Public Engagement and Contributions
5 Legacy
6 See Also
7 References
Early Life and Education
Details about Dr. Paca's early life, including his exact birth date and
family background, are not extensively documented in publicly
available materials, a reflection of how private he has remained even
as his career in academic administration flourished. What is well
recorded is his academic journey, which reads like a study in lifelong
learning. He earned his Bachelor of Science in Mechanical
Engineering from Mindanao State University in Marawi City back in
1989, laying the technical foundation that would later distinguish
him among his peers in university leadership. He returned to the
classroom repeatedly over the following decades. In 1996, he
completed a Certificate in Governmental Management at MSU. By
2001, he had earned a Master of Science in Agricultural Engineering
from the University of the Philippines Los Baños, where he studied
as an APDP Scholar. He did not stop there. In 2007, he obtained his
Bachelor of Laws (LLB) from MSU Marawi, adding legal expertise
to his growing set of credentials. He later pursued a Doctor in Public
Administration (DPA) at MSU, completing it in 2021, and around
2004 he also earned units toward a Ph.D. in Sustainable

PAGE 2
Development at MSU Iligan City. Alongside all this, Dr. Paca holds the distinction of being a Registered
Mechanical Engineer (RME). Early in his career, before his long tenure at MSU took full shape, he worked as a
technical instructor at a Qatar Independent Technical School and later served as founding president of the
Philippine Engineering and Agro-Industrial College, Inc. (PEACI), an engineering focused institution in Marawi
City. This combination of engineering, agriculture, law, and public administration would go on to shape how he
approached university leadership: practical, grounded, and always attentive to sustainable development and good
governance.
Career at Mindanao State University
Dr. Paca's relationship with MSU spans more than thirty years, and it shows in the steady progression of roles he
has held. He started out as a faculty member and moved through the ranks as department chairperson, then college
dean, then Vice President for Planning and Development, and eventually Executive Vice President, one of the
highest administrative posts in the university system. Along the way, he frequently stepped in as Officer-in-Charge
whenever the university president was away on official travel, a role that quietly built the institutional trust that
would later matter a great deal. During his time in these positions, he became closely associated with MSU's
recovery efforts following the Marawi Siege, working on partnerships such as the one with the International
Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) for humanitarian and educational initiatives in the aftermath of the conflict.
He was also active in community engagement work and in promoting integrity and national loyalty within the
university, themes that came up often in his public statements.
OIC Presidency (2025)
The most defining chapter of Dr. Paca's career so far came in 2025. Following the passing of the MSU System's 8th
President, Atty. Basari D. Mapupuno, in May of that year, the MSU Board of Regents designated Dr. Paca as
Officer-in-Charge (OIC) President. He held this interim post from May 27, 2025 to June 27, 2025, guiding the
university system through a sensitive leadership transition before formally turning over the presidency to the 9th
president, Atty. Paisalin P.D. Tago, CPA, in early July 2025. It was a short stretch as caretaker leader, but a
significant one. During this period, he met with President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. in Marawi City in June 2025,
where discussions touched on rehabilitation efforts, agro-fishery projects, and MSU's broader role in regional
development across Mindanao. MSU communications from this period describe his leadership style as one built on
presence and resilience, qualities that had already been tested through crises like the Marawi Siege and the
pandemic, and that carried over into his brief but consequential time at the helm.
Public Engagement and Contributions
Beyond his formal administrative roles, Dr. Paca has been a visible presence in efforts tied to MSU's broader
mission as an institution for education, peace-building, and development in Mindanao. He has taken part in events
centered on cultural unity, sustainable practices, and community resilience, consistently framing his public
statements around integrity, the rejection of corruption, and service to both the Bangsamoro people and the wider
Filipino nation. His official MSU profile notes that detailed lists of publications, research projects, or specific
courses taught are still being compiled, marked as "updating soon" in available institutional records. No significant
controversies or conflicting accounts have surfaced in official or reputable sources reviewed for this article.

PAGE 3
Legacy
In the broader story of Philippine higher education, especially within Mindanao, figures like Dr. Paca represent
something important: continuity. His multidisciplinary background, spanning engineering, law, agriculture, and
public administration, has equipped him to navigate a region where academic excellence has to coexist with socio-
economic challenges and peace-related priorities. As of mid-2025, he continues to serve MSU in a senior capacity,
carrying forward decades of institutional knowledge at a university system that has weathered no shortage of
storms. Further primary materials, such as a full curriculum vitae, archival university records, or in-depth
interviews, could add more depth to his scholarly output and personal motivations, though these remain limited in
the materials currently available.

Potri Ali Pacasum
Princess Potri Ali Pacasum is a Maranao political figure, educator,
and entrepreneur from Balo-i, Lanao del Norte, in the
predominantly Muslim region of the Lanao provinces in Mindanao,
Southern Philippines.
She holds the distinction of being the first Bangsamoro woman to
represent the industrial and labor sectors of Mindanao in the
Philippine Parliament, serving as an assemblywoman in the Interim
Batasang Pambansa from 1978 to 1984.
Princess Potri is also a traditional leader, having been crowned
Muslim Princess of Lanao del Norte and recognized with the
lifetime title of Bai a Labi a Gaos of Balo-i, Lanao del Norte.
Contents
1 BACKGROUND AND FAMILY
2 EDUCATION
3 LEGISLATIVE SERVICE
3.1 Assemblywoman, Interim Batasang Pambansa (1978–
1984)

5 ADVOCACY AND FOUNDATIONS
6 TRADITIONAL TITLES AND HONORS
7 AWARDS AND RECOGNITION

BACKGROUND AND FAMILY
The Pacasum clan is one of the well-known and respected families
in the Lanao provinces, with deep roots in the predominantly
Maranao communities of both Lanao del Sur and Lanao del Norte.
Princess Potri comes from a family of recognized Muslim
community leaders.
Her father, Sheikh Abdul Racman Pacasum, and her mother, Bai
Alabi Pala Ali Pacasum, are described in biographical records as
principal figures in the predominantly Muslim communities of both
Lanao provinces.
The family's influence spans both Lanao del Sur and Lanao del
Norte, reflecting the cross-provincial reach that distinguishes many
of Mindanao's leading Muslim families.

The Pacasum family has maintained institutions and properties in
the Lanao region, including Pacasum Colleges, which has served as
an educational pillar in the area.
In the wider public record, the Pacasum clan is noted for
connections to civic and community life in the Lanao provinces,
including ties that extend to well-known figures in Mindanao
society.
EDUCATION
Princess Potri holds a degree in Political Science, a background that
shaped her approach to governance and public service as she later
transitioned into the Philippine legislature.
Specific details about the institution where she completed her
degree have not been independently verified in available sources
and are reserved for editorial confirmation.
LEGISLATIVE SERVICE
Assemblywoman, Interim Batasang Pambansa (1978–
1984)
Princess Potri Ali Pacasum served as a member of the Interim
Batasang Pambansa (IBP), the unicameral legislature of the
Philippines under the 1973 Constitution promulgated during the
administration of President Ferdinand Marcos.
The Interim Batasang Pambansa was inaugurated on June 12, 1978,
and operated until June 5, 1984, when it gave way to the Regular
Batasang Pambansa.
Alongside regionally elected representatives, the Interim Batasang
Pambansa seated sectoral representatives chosen through their
respective Electoral Councils, covering groups such as youth,
agriculture, and labor.
Princess Potri held a sectoral seat representing the industrial and
labor constituencies of Mindanao, making her the first
Bangsamoro woman to hold such a representative position in the
Philippine Parliament.
This was no small distinction: the Batasang Pambansa era was a
period of concentrated political power, and Maranao women
entering national legislative halls were still a rarity.

PAGE 3
presidency of Pacasum Colleges; and
her lifetime title as Bai a Labi a Gaos of
Balo-i.
Her committee engagements during her tenure covered a wide and
practical range of concerns, including:
Ecology and human settlements
Labor, employment, and manpower development
National cultural communities
Industry, trade, and investments
Public works, transportation, and communications
The committee portfolio tells its own story: Princess Potri was not simply a symbolic figure.
Her legislative focus placed the realities of Muslim workers, minority community rights, and Mindanao's economic
infrastructure at the center of her work in the national parliament.
In 1981, she was recognized as one of the outstanding members of the Batasang Pambansa for her meritorious
services to the cause of Islam and her sustained efforts to improve the economic and labor conditions of the
Muslim population of Southern Philippines.
PROFESSIONAL AND ENTREPRENEURIAL CAREER
Outside the legislature, Princess Potri built a substantial presence across education, banking, business, and
transport.
As President of Pacasum Colleges, she oversaw one of the Pacasum family's key contributions to education in the
Lanao region, an institution that has served Maranao students through generations.
She also served as Principal Organizer of the Rural Bank of Greater Balo-i, a role that placed her at the heart of
grassroots financial access for communities in Lanao del Norte.
Her corporate directorships spanned several enterprises:
Director, Islam International Travel and Tours Corp.
Director, Islam Development Co., Inc.
Director, Greater Balo-i Mining and Warehouse Co., Inc.
Chairperson, Transpotri Corp.
Chairperson, Mohammad Anggandug Construction and Services Co., Inc.
Taken together, this portfolio of roles reflects a woman who understood that lawmaking alone does not uplift a
community: economic infrastructure, credit access, education, and mobility all have to move alongside political
representation.
ADVOCACY AND FOUNDATIONS
Princess Potri Ali Pacasum is the Founding Chairperson of the Princess Potri Ali Pacasum Foundation, an
institution that channels her commitments to social development, youth welfare, and community uplift.
She is also described as the moving spirit behind Manarath Philippines, an organization whose name and
mission reflects the Maranao and broader Bangsamoro tradition of communal care and forward-looking
development.

PAGE 4
Specific programmatic details about Manarath Philippines and the Foundation have not been fully verified in
independently accessible public sources, and additional documentation would strengthen the treatment of these in
any future revision.
TRADITIONAL TITLES AND HONORS
Beyond her legislative and professional achievements, Princess Potri holds recognized traditional standing within
Maranao society.
She was crowned Muslim Princess of Lanao del Norte, and she carries the lifetime title of Bai a Labi a Gaos of
Balo-i, Lanao del Norte.
The title Bai a Labi in Maranao society designates a woman of noble rank, typically from a recognized royal or
chiefly lineage within the traditional structure of the Lanao sultanate system.
Conferment of such a title as a lifetime designation speaks to her standing not merely as a politician or
businesswoman, but as someone whose identity is rooted in the taritib and adat that govern the social order of the
Maranao people.
AWARDS AND RECOGNITION
Her public service earned her national recognition through two formal awards:
In 1979, she received the Filipino Youth Achievement Award for Outstanding Service and Dedication to Youth
Welfare and Development.
In 1980, she was honored with the Achievement Award for Integrity, Leadership Excellence and Exemplary
Dedication to National Development.
In 1981, the Batasang Pambansa itself recognized her as one of its outstanding members, citing her service to the
cause of Islam and her determined efforts to improve the economic and labor conditions of the Muslim
communities of Southern Philippines.

title: Pacasum, Sabdulah Ali
text:
PAGE 1
Sabdulah Ali Pacasum
Sulutan sa Baloi Sabdulah Ali Pacasum, more widely known as Bobby, was a Meranaw philanthropist, civil
servant, and the longest-reigning Sultan of Balo-i in Lanao del Norte, Philippines.
He was the second son of Sheik Abdulrahman Pacasum of Marawi City, Lanao del Sur, and Bai a labi a Gaos Pala
Ali of the Royal House of Balo-i.
In a career that moved between the courts, the halls of government, the deserts of Mecca, and eventually the throne
of his royal house, Bobby Pacasum became one of the more quietly extraordinary figures the Bangsamoro region
has produced.
He died in December 2005 due to health complications, having reigned as Sultan for over two decades.
Contents
1 Background and Family
2 Education
3 Career in Government
4 Detention at Camp Crame
5 Service to Filipino Pilgrims in Mecca
6 The Sultanate of Balo-i
7 OMPONGAN and the Organization of the 15 Royal Houses
8 Legacy and Character
9 Recognition and Honors
10 References
11 See Also
Background and Family
Bobby Pacasum came from two distinguished bloodlines.
His father, Sheik Abdulrahman Pacasum, was a respected figure in Marawi City, Lanao del Sur.
His mother, Bai a labi a Gaos Pala Ali, belonged to the Royal House of Balo-i in Lanao del Norte, the very house
Bobby would one day lead as Sultan.
He was the second son of the family, and while he would grow up to hold titles and offices that commanded
respect, people who knew him described a man who never really let any of that go to his head.
He was, by most accounts, an introvert who genuinely preferred a quiet private life, though life rarely gave him the
chance to live one.

PAGE 2
Sabdulah Ali Pacasum

Education
Bobby Pacasum pursued his Bachelor of Arts degree at the
University of the Philippines, already a prestigious path for any
student from Mindanao.
He then went on to pursue his Bachelor of Laws (LL.B) at the
Ateneo de Manila University School of Law, where he became
the lone Maranaw student enrolled during his time there.
Being the only student from his community in that environment
could have been isolating. Instead, it became the backdrop for
what is arguably one of the most remarkable runs of student
leadership in Philippine legal education.
While at Ateneo Law, Bobby simultaneously held three elected
positions: President of the Junior Class (a race he won over his
friend and classmate, former First Gentleman Mike Arroyo),
President of the Fraternal Order of Utopia Honor Society (where
he was the 5th in the Wall of Presidents, immediately followed
by former Chief Justice Renato Corona as the 6th), and President
of the Ateneo Law Student Council.
All three, at the same time.
He also attended the prestigious Senior Executive Development
Course at Mindanao State University, along with several other
seminars and trainings in management and leadership.
In January 1975, the business school of Ateneo de Manila
recognized his academic distinction with its Highest Award in
Management Studies.
Career in Government
Bobby Pacasum went on to serve as Regional District Collector
of the Bureau of Customs, a significant post that put him at the
center of the country's trade and customs administration in the
region.
His performance in that role was recognized at the highest level:
he received the Most Outstanding District Collector of Customs
award from then President Ferdinand E. Marcos.
The same President Marcos who, in a sharp twist of fate, would
later order his arrest.

PAGE 3

Malacanang
PULL QUOTE
"He was a lot of things to a lot of people, an
uncle, a kuya, a friend, a brother... but to his
children, he was simply the most loving and
sweetest father any one could possibly have."
Detention at Camp Crame
At some point during the Marcos years, Bobby Pacasum was
accused on grounds of "rebellion" and ordered detained.
He was taken to Camp Crame in Quezon City and held in
solitary confinement for eight months.
It was a jarring turn for a man who had just been honored by the
very administration that now held him behind bars.
He was eventually acquitted of all charges against him, with the
sustained effort of a loyal and prominent group of lawyer friends,
and the unwavering support of his family, securing his release.
The experience left a mark, but it didn't define him. He returned
to his community and continued serving.
Service to Filipino Pilgrims in Mecca
One of the defining moments in Bobby Pacasum's life as a public
servant came when over 3,000 Filipino Hajj pilgrims found
themselves stranded in Mecca, Kingdom of Saudi Arabia.
He stepped in to assist them personally.
The scale and significance of what he did earned him a
recommendation for a Presidential Citation, a recognition that
speaks to the seriousness with which his intervention was
regarded.
The details of how he facilitated that assistance are not
elaborated in the available source, but the outcome, rescuing
thousands of stranded Filipino Muslims from a precarious
situation far from home, is on record.
The Sultanate of Balo-i
On January 31, 1981, Bobby Pacasum was formally enthroned as
the Sultan of Balo-i.
He would hold that position until his death in December 2005, making him the longest-reigning Sultan of Baloi on
record.
Despite the weight of the title and the regular stream of people who would flock to his home the moment word got
out that he was in town, Bobby remained, at heart, a private man.
He wasn't a politician, and he made no pretense of wanting to be one.

PAGE 4
OMPONGAN founder Sultan Sabdulah Ali Pacasum
audience with President Marcos, Sr.
But the help he gave to those who came seeking his guidance and influence, quietly and without fanfare,
encompassed what many public officials in far more prominent positions never managed to do for their Meranaw
constituents.
OMPONGAN and the Organization of the 15 Royal Houses
Beyond his own sultanate, Bobby Pacasum took on a
broader role that placed him at the center of Meranaw
traditional governance as a whole.
He founded OMPONGAN, the Organization of the 15
Royal Houses of Lanao, and served as its chairman.
To understand the weight of that, a bit of context helps.
<ref>The 15 Royal Houses of Lanao, known as the
Panoroganan, form the executive body of the Confederate
States of Lanao. They are complemented by the 28
M'babaya ko Taritib, the legislative houses, together
forming the traditional governance structure of the Pat a
Pangampong a Ranao (the four states of Ranao). See:
Macabando (2008), cited in academic literature on Lanao
Sultanate political structure.</ref>
<ref>The 28 Council of Ministers referenced here
correspond to the M'babaya ko Taritib, the 28 legislative
houses of the Lanao Sultanate, whose role is to legislate
local customs, traditions, and laws in concurrence with the
15 royal sultans. Source: Bang Ali Pacasum (personal
account); corroborated by academic literature on the Lanao
Sultanate political structure.</ref>
The Confederate States of Lanao, or Pat a Pangampong a
Ranao, is made up of four states: Bayabao, Masiu, Unayan,
and Baloi. The 15 Royal Houses, known as the
Panoroganan, are the executive core of that confederation,
each led by a sultan. They work alongside 28 legislative
houses, the M'babaya ko Taritib, whose role is to enact
customs, traditions, and laws within the confederation.
Getting those sultans to agree on anything collectively is no
small feat. Getting them, along with the 28 Council of
Ministers and other traditional leaders, to travel together to
Manila and sit down with the President of the Philippines is
something else entirely.
Bobby Pacasum did exactly that, not once but twice.
He convened the 15 sultans, the 28 Council of Ministers, and other traditional leaders for a formal dialogue at
Malacanang Palace with then President Ferdinand E. Marcos.

PAGE 5
He later repeated the same feat with former President Corazon Aquino, bringing the same coalition of Lanao royal
leadership to the Palace for another high-level engagement.
These weren't ceremonial visits. They were deliberate acts of political bridge-building, using the weight of
traditional Meranaw authority to open lines of communication between the royal houses of Lanao and the national
government.
As founder and chairman of OMPONGAN, Bobby Pacasum was the one who made that table possible.
Legacy and Character
Those who knew Bobby Pacasum describe a man of contrasts.
He could be feared for a mercurial temper, but he was deeply loved by the many people whose lives he touched
through discreet, personal acts of kindness and intervention.
He was, depending on who you asked, an uncle, a kuya, a friend, a brother. Not just to his own family, but to
anyone who treated him with sincerity and respect.
His children remember him as the most loving and sweetest father they could have asked for, and they credit Allah
SWT for the gift of having such a man in their lives.
One reflection, offered by his family, reached for the image of Don Vito Corleone from the Godfather as a way to
capture the kind of quiet, powerful, community-anchored presence Bobby had in Marawi and Balo-i. Not in any
sinister sense, but in the way he became a figure people turned to, a man who got things done for his people
through loyalty, relationships, and personal integrity.
He died in December 2005, leaving behind a family, a royal seat, and a community of people who remembered him
not for any single headline, but for the thousand small things he did that nobody else thought to do.

Lawyer; Government Official; Islamic Da'wah
Advocate
Years of Government Service
Paisal Amerol Padate
Atty. Paisal Amerol Padate is a Maranao lawyer, long-
serving government official, and Islamic da'wah advocate
from Lanao del Sur, widely recognized as the patriarch of one
of the most accomplished legal families in the Bangsamoro
region. Over a career spanning nearly four decades, he served
the Philippine government in roles that cut across agrarian
reform, criminal prosecution, election administration, and
infrastructure law — retiring in 2016 as the Chief Legal
Officer of the Department of Public Works and Highways
(DPWH) Regional Office XII. Beyond public service, he is
known for his deep commitment to the faith, having
embraced the Tabligh Jama'ah movement in 1990 and devoted
much of his personal life to da'wah work, community-
building, and the propagation of Islamic values throughout
Mindanao.
Contents
1 BACKGROUND
2 EDUCATION
3 CAREER
3.1 Early Legal Practice: Agrarian Reform (1979)
3.2 The Prosecution Years: Lanao del Sur (1986)
3.3 Election Administration: Basilan Province (2007)
3.4 Chief Legal Officer, DPWH Region XII (2009–
2016)
4 FAITH AND DA'WAH WORK
5 FAMILY AND THE PADATE LEGAL DYNASTY

BACKGROUND
Paisal Amerol Padate was born into a family for whom public
service was not a profession but a calling.
His father, the late Judge Macapandi M. Padate, carried two
weighty distinctions: he was a Municipal Trial Court Judge
and, simultaneously, the Sultan of the Royal House of Tubok

PAGE 2
1979 – 2016 (approx. 37 years)
Spouse
Bai Zenaida Jamil Padate (retired public
school teacher)
Children
9 children; 5 of whom became lawyers and
public servants
Father
Judge Macapandi M. Padate (Sultan of the
Royal House of Tubok; Municipal Trial Court
Judge)
Sibling
Atty. Abdul-Aziz Amerol Padate (Bureau of
Customs; deceased)
Religious Affiliation
Islam; Tabligh Jama'ah (since 1990)
Key Government Posts
Legal Officer, Department of Agrarian Reform
(1979)
Associate Provincial Prosecutor, Lanao del
Sur (1986)
Provincial Election Supervisor, Basilan
Province (2007)
Chief Legal Officer, DPWH Region XII
(retired 2016)
NOTABILITY
One of the founding patriarchs of the Padate
legal dynasty of Lanao del Sur, a family
lineage credited with producing at least 14
lawyers from a single bloodline — among the
highest concentrations of legal professionals
from one family in the Bangsamoro region.
KNOWN FOR
Nearly four decades of government legal
service across agrarian reform, criminal
prosecution, election administration, and
public works; active leadership in Islamic
da'wah through the Tabligh Jama'ah
movement; and raising five children who
became lawyers and distinguished public
servants.
PULL QUOTE
— a man who understood, perhaps better than most, that law
and leadership are inseparable in the Maranao tradition.
That dual inheritance, of jurisprudence and sultanic
responsibility, defined the household Paisal grew up in.
His elder brother, the late Atty. Abdul-Aziz Amerol Padate,
followed their father into the legal field as a lawyer of the
Bureau of Customs, cementing an early pattern in the family:
service through law, generation after generation.
Paisal would carry that pattern further than anyone might
have anticipated.
EDUCATION
For his undergraduate studies, Padate pursued the sciences,
earning a Bachelor of Science in Biology from Far Eastern
University in 1973.
The turn toward law came shortly after.
He enrolled at Manuel Luis Quezon University and
completed his Bachelor of Laws degree in 1977 — a course
that would anchor the next four decades of his professional
life.
In April 1979, he cleared the Philippine Bar Examinations
and was formally admitted to the Philippine Bar, joining the
ranks of Filipino lawyers at a time when Mindanao was
navigating profound political and social transformation.
CAREER
Early Legal Practice: Agrarian Reform (1979)
Padate began his government career almost immediately after
passing the bar.
In 1979, he joined the Department of Agrarian Reform as a
Legal Officer — entering public service during the height of
the Marcos-era land reform program, when agrarian cases
were among the most contested and consequential legal
proceedings in rural Philippines.
It was entry-level work by title, but formative by nature: it
placed a young lawyer squarely at the intersection of land
rights, rural justice, and community welfare.

PAGE 3
"True success is not measured by titles,
positions, or worldly recognition, but by
sincere service to God and humanity."
— Atty. Paisal Amerol Padate
The Prosecution Years: Lanao del Sur (1986)
Seven years into his career, Padate's responsibilities expanded
significantly.
In 1986, he was appointed Associate Provincial Prosecutor
of Lanao del Sur — a posting that brought him into the heart
of criminal justice administration in one of Mindanao's most complex provinces.
As provincial prosecutor, he represented the state in criminal proceedings, carried the responsibility of building
cases, and worked within a justice system that, in Lanao del Sur, had to operate amid persistent security concerns
and the particular sensitivities of a predominantly Muslim society.
He would serve in this capacity for over two decades, building a reputation as a steady, principled presence in the
provincial legal community.
Election Administration: Basilan Province (2007)
In 2007, Padate took on a different kind of legal responsibility when he was appointed Provincial Election
Supervisor of Basilan Province under the Commission on Elections (COMELEC).
Election supervision in Basilan — a province with its own history of armed conflict and political volatility —
demanded more than technical knowledge of electoral law. It required diplomacy, steadiness under pressure, and
the kind of credibility that only a long career in government service can build.
His appointment to this post spoke to the confidence that national institutions had placed in him.
Chief Legal Officer, DPWH Region XII (2009–2016)
In 2009, Padate transitioned to the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) Regional Office XII,
joining as Attorney III.
Over the following years, he climbed steadily through the office, eventually assuming the role of Chief Legal
Officer — the top legal position in a regional infrastructure agency responsible for roads, bridges, and public
facilities across central Mindanao.
He held that position until his honorable retirement in 2016, completing what would prove to be a nearly forty-
year arc of uninterrupted government service.
FAITH AND DA'WAH WORK
If Atty. Padate's professional career is the part of his life most easily recorded, his life in faith may be the part he
considers most defining.
In 1990, he joined the Tabligh Jama'ah movement — a global Islamic renewal movement focused on grassroots
da'wah, the strengthening of personal faith, and the revival of Islamic practice in everyday life.
For Padate, this was not a casual affiliation. He became an active participant in Tabligh activities, traveling to
communities across Mindanao and beyond to engage in da'wah — the invitation to faith — and to foster
brotherhood and reconciliation among Muslim communities.

PAGE 4
He often describes himself simply as a "Lawyer and Tabligh," a self-identification that reveals his own sense of
priority: the bar card is a credential, but the faith is the compass.
His engagement with the Tabligh Jama'ah also shaped the values he passed on to his children — values that show
up not just in their personal lives but in how they've approached public service.
FAMILY AND THE PADATE LEGAL DYNASTY
The most striking chapter of Atty. Padate's legacy is one he wrote not alone, but with his wife, Bai Zenaida Jamil
Padate, a retired public school teacher, and their nine children.
Five of those children became lawyers and entered public service:
Atty. Nasif Numeiry Padate — President of the Integrated Bar of the Philippines (IBP), Lanao del Sur
Chapter, where he has led the chapter's recognition of lifetime achievers in the legal profession.
Atty. Abol Alam Padate — Former Assistant City Prosecutor of Cagayan de Oro City, and former
Assemblyman of the Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (ARMM).
Atty. Faizal Padate, Jr. — Former Senior Assistant City Prosecutor of Davao City, and former Regional
Director of the Department of Social Welfare and Development (DSWD).
Atty. Wallad Abdani Padate — Incumbent Assistant Regional Prosecutor, National Prosecution Service
Region XII.
Atty. Danieza Julaida Padate — Incumbent Officer-in-Charge City Prosecutor of Koronadal City.
Together with lawyer-grandchildren and relatives descended from Judge Sultan Macapandi Padate, the extended
Padate family has produced at least 14 lawyers from a single lineage — a concentration of legal professionals
from one bloodline that is virtually unmatched in the history of Lanao del Sur and the broader Bangsamoro region.
The breadth of jurisdictions they cover — from Marawi to Cagayan de Oro to Davao to Koronadal — reflects not
just family achievement, but a family-wide commitment to the rule of law across the length and breadth of
Mindanao.
INSTITUTIONAL CONTRIBUTIONS
Over the course of his career, Atty. Padate contributed to legal practice and governance in at least four distinct
agencies: the Department of Agrarian Reform, the National Prosecution Service, the Commission on Elections, and
the Department of Public Works and Highways.
Each posting represented a different domain of public law, and his willingness to move across these domains —
rather than building a career in a single bureaucratic niche — gave him an unusually broad understanding of how
Philippine government legal work actually functions on the ground.
His tenure as Chief Legal Officer of DPWH Region XII placed him at the center of infrastructure governance in
central Mindanao during a period of significant development investment, including road and bridge projects vital to
connecting Bangsamoro communities with the rest of the country.

PAGE 5
LEGACY
What sets Atty. Paisal Amerol Padate apart is not any single appointment or achievement, but the coherence of a
life lived across law, faith, and family — and the way those three threads have reinforced rather than competed
with each other.
He chose public service over private practice, not because it was more lucrative (it wasn't), but because he
understood government legal work as a form of service to the community.
He embraced the Tabligh Jama'ah not as a departure from his professional identity, but as its spiritual grounding —
a reminder that lawyers, like everyone else, are accountable to something beyond the docket.
And he raised a family whose collective legal footprint across Mindanao now reads, in many ways, as the most
durable expression of everything he believed in.
The Padate legal dynasty — rooted in Judge Sultan Macapandi Padate, extended by Atty. Paisal and his siblings,
and now flourishing across a third generation of lawyers — stands as one of the most remarkable family stories in
Bangsamoro legal history.
RECOGNITION
Honorable retirement from government service, DPWH Region XII (2016)
Recognized as the patriarch of the Padate legal family, which has produced at least 14 lawyers from a single
lineage in Lanao del Sur and the Bangsamoro region
CHALLENGES
Atty. Padate's career unfolded in provinces — Lanao del Sur, Basilan — that were among the most conflict-
affected in the Philippines.
Serving as a prosecutor and election supervisor in environments where political violence was a recurring reality
required not just legal competence but personal courage and a willingness to uphold institutions that were
themselves under pressure.
His ability to carry out his mandates across these postings, and to do so with integrity over the course of nearly four
decades, is itself a form of public service that goes beyond what any formal commendation can fully capture.

Samsia M. Paitao-Dumrang
Dr. Samsia M. Paitao-Dumrang (affectionately called AVCAA by her colleagues and subordinates) is a Filipino
academic administrator and education advocate who has served as the Assistant Vice Chancellor for Academic
Affairs (External Units) of the Mindanao State University System. She is widely regarded as the "mother of the
13 MSU External Units" scattered across Lanao del Sur, Lanao del Norte, and Misamis Occidental, overseeing the
academic and institutional affairs of these campuses with remarkable steadiness and care. Her career is a story of
quiet, sustained dedication: starting as a Special Assistant in the same office where she would eventually rise to a
senior leadership post, she's built her authority not through shortcuts but through decades of firsthand experience
with the communities she serves.
Contents
1 Background
2 Career
3 Leadership Style
4 Research and Professional Development
5 Contributions to Academic Scholarship
6 Legacy
Background
Dr. Samsia M. Paitao-Dumrang's roots in the Mindanao State
University system run deep. Long before she held the title of
Assistant Vice Chancellor, she worked as a Special Assistant within
the same administrative office, familiarizing herself with the
complex machinery of multi-campus governance. That experience,
sustained over several decades, gave her an unusually grounded
understanding of how the 13 MSU External Units function, what
challenges they face, and what kind of leadership they need. Her rise
through the ranks wasn't a dramatic leap; it was the kind of steady,
earned ascent that comes from showing up consistently, doing the
work, and earning the trust of the people around her.
Career
Dr. Paitao-Dumrang's formal senior leadership career spans at least
two administrations of the MSU System. She served under the late MSU System President Atty. Basari D.
Mapupuno and has continued in her role under the current MSU System President, Atty. Paisalin PD. Tago, CPA.
As AVCAA for External Units, she provides oversight and administrative direction for 13 MSU satellite campuses
spread across Lanao del Sur, Lanao del Norte, and Misamis Occidental. These units are often located in
geographically dispersed and underserved communities, which means her work carries a development dimension
beyond just academic administration. She coordinates with campus administrators, monitors academic programs,
and serves as the institutional bridge between the external units and the MSU System's central leadership.

PAGE 2
Her long tenure in the office, beginning from her years as Special Assistant, has given her an institutional memory
that few in her position can match.
Leadership Style
People who work with Dr. Paitao-Dumrang consistently describe her approach to leadership as one centered on
empowerment and upliftment. Rather than managing from a distance or relying strictly on hierarchy, she's known
for fostering a collaborative environment among her subordinates and the wider community of the 13 External
Units. She leads by example, and those who've worked under her recognize her as someone who genuinely invests
in the growth of the people around her. Colleagues and students alike have called her a pillar of strength and an
advocate for positive change in the academic community.
Research and Professional Development
Dr. Paitao-Dumrang doesn't limit herself to administrative duties. She actively participates in research and
professional development activities, including international academic conferences. She has attended events abroad,
including a conference in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia, reflecting her interest in engaging with the broader global
academic conversation and bringing those insights back to her institution.
Contributions to Academic Scholarship
Beyond her administrative work, Dr. Paitao-Dumrang has contributed to the intellectual life of the university as a
panelist for master's theses and doctoral dissertations at the College of Education at Mindanao State University.
This role puts her at the center of graduate-level academic review, where she helps shape the quality and direction
of research emerging from one of the university's key academic colleges.
Legacy
Dr. Paitao-Dumrang's legacy in the Mindanao State University system is grounded in longevity, consistency, and
genuine care for the communities she serves. She represents a model of academic leadership built not on quick
wins or high-profile appointments, but on years of patient service and institutional memory. Her work across the 13
MSU External Units has made her a familiar and trusted figure in communities throughout Lanao del Sur, Lanao
del Norte, and Misamis Occidental. The affectionate nickname AVCAA has become inseparable from her identity, a
sign that her colleagues and subordinates see her not just as a title, but as a person who's made that role her own.

Other Names
Datu Akadir Akobar
Title
Datu (Chieftain) of Marawi, Lanao
Notability

two major Spanish expeditions, one of the

Known For

Datu Amai Pakpak
Datu Amai Pakpak (died March 10, 1895), also known as Datu
Akadir Akobar, was a Maranao military leader and chieftain from
Lanao who led the resistance against Spanish colonization in the
1890s. He is best remembered for defending Kota Marawi (Fort
Marawi) during the two Battles of Marawi in 1891 and 1895, a stand
that made him one of the most celebrated heroes of the Maranao
people.
He was a native of Marawi who rose to become the principal
defender of the Lanao region against Spanish military expeditions in
the closing years of the 19th century. His leadership in the two major
Battles of Marawi, first against Governor-General Valeriano Weyler's
forces in 1891 and again against Governor-General Ramón Blanco's
much larger expedition in 1895, cemented his place in Philippine
history as a symbol of Moro resistance and Maranao sovereignty. He
died in combat on March 10, 1895, during the second Battle of
Marawi.
Contents
1 Early Life and Background
2 Military Leadership
3 First Battle of Marawi (1891)
4 Second Battle of Marawi (1895)
5 Resistance Against Colonization
6 Bangsamoro Context
7 Honors and Recognition
8 Historical Markers
9 See Also
10 References
Early Life and Background
Datu Amai Pakpak was born in Buadi sa Kayo, Marawi, in what is
now Lanao del Sur. His given name was Akadir Akobar, though he
became known among the Maranao as Amai Pakpak, which
translates to "father of Pakpak," a name taken from his daughter. As a
datu, he held authority over his community and carried the
responsibility of its defense and welfare, a role that would define the
rest of his life.

PAGE 2
Military Leadership
Amai Pakpak maintained and commanded a fortification known as Fort Marawi or Kota Marawi, built near the
northern shore of Lake Lanao, close to what is now the site of the Agus 2 hydroelectric dam and Camp Amai
Pakpak. This earth-and-stone kota stood as the primary line of defense against Spanish incursions into the Lanao
region, and it was here that Amai Pakpak would make his stand, twice, against forces that far outnumbered his
own.
First Battle of Marawi (1891)
The first major confrontation came on August 21, 1891, when Spanish forces under Governor-General Valeriano
Weyler launched an expedition against the Maranao. The Spanish force, numbering around 1,242 soldiers, arrived
in Iligan aboard the warships Manila, Cebu, San Quintin, and Marquez de Duero before pushing on toward Kota
Marawi.
Under Amai Pakpak's leadership, the Maranao defenders put up a fierce resistance. The Spaniards eventually
managed to burn the kota after a two-hour siege, but they withdrew back to Iligan, wary of Maranao
reinforcements arriving by vinta, the traditional boats used across Lake Lanao. Amai Pakpak and his warriors
wasted no time rebuilding the fortification, bracing for the attack they knew would come again.
Second Battle of Marawi (1895)
Four years later, on March 10, 1895, Governor-General Ramón Blanco returned, this time with a force of over
5,000 soldiers and four gunboats hauled all the way to Lake Lanao. It was a far better equipped expedition, and
Spain was determined to finally secure its conquest of Lanao.
The Maranao warriors, once again under Amai Pakpak, mounted a determined defense of Kota Marawi. Despite
fierce resistance that slowed the Spanish advance, the fort was eventually overrun. Amai Pakpak, his son Anggay,
and 23 other datus perished inside the kota that day. According to some accounts, Amai Pakpak and his son had
escaped into a secret chamber (digo-digo) within the fort before launching one final, suicidal attack against the
Spanish, in which the datu was killed. His body was never identified, as fellow Maranao concealed his identity out
of pity and respect.
The Spanish would eventually withdraw from Lanao following the outbreak of the Spanish–American War in 1898,
never having fully conquered the region.
Resistance Against Colonization
Datu Amai Pakpak's resistance against Spanish forces stands as one of the most significant episodes of Moro
defiance during the 317-year Moro-Spanish War. His leadership helped preserve Maranao sovereignty and Islamic
traditions at a time of intense colonial pressure. The Battles of Marawi in 1891 and 1895 are counted among the
largest battles for independence fought before the Philippine Revolution broke out in 1896.

PAGE 3
Bangsamoro Context
Amai Pakpak's struggle is woven into the fabric of Bangsamoro history and identity. The National Historical
Commission of the Philippines (NHCP) and the Bangsamoro Commission for the Preservation of Cultural Heritage
(BCPCH) have both recognized his contributions as part of the wider story of Bangsamoro resistance and nation-
building. In August 2024, historical markers honoring Amai Pakpak and the defense of Marawi were unveiled in
Marawi City, affirming the Meranaw people's place in Philippine history.
Honors and Recognition
Datu Amai Pakpak is widely regarded as a Maranao hero and a symbol of Moro resistance against foreign
colonization. In 1970, the Lanao General Hospital was renamed the Amai Pakpak Medical Center in his honor.
Several institutions and places in Marawi still carry his name today, including:
Amai Pakpak Medical Center
Amai Pakpak Central Elementary School
Amai Pakpak Avenue
Camp Amai Pakpak (formerly Camp Keithley), the military reservation that now occupies the ground where
his kota once stood
Historical Markers
In August 2024, the NHCP and BCPCH unveiled four historical markers in Marawi City: one for "Amai Pakpak,"
one for "Pagtatanggol sa Marawi" (Defense of Marawi), one for "Labanan sa Marawi" (Battle of Marawi), and one
for "Kota Marawi." These were installed at the Lanao People's Park and Public Library, Amai Pakpak Central
Elementary School, and Marawi City Hall.
NHCP Chairperson Regalado Trota Jose, Jr. noted that the markers stand as proof of the significant role the
Meranaw people played in Philippine social history and nation-building. BCPCH Chairperson Salem Y. Lingasa
added that recognizing the contributions of the Meranaw and Bangsamoro is part of correcting long-standing
historical injustices.

title: Pala-Mohamad, Aniza

Aniza Pala-Mohamad
Dr. Aniza Barandia Pala-Mohamad is a distinguished Maranao physician, educator, and healthcare leader whose
career has centered on bridging specialized medical care gaps across the BARMM. As the first Maranao
endocrinologist to establish practice in the cities of Marawi and Iligan, Dr. Pala-Mohamad has spent over a decade
advancing clinical excellence, training the next generation of internal medicine specialists, and championing health
equity through both private and charitable care. Her institutional contributions at Amai Pakpak Medical Center in
Marawi City and her pioneering research on genetic markers of diabetes in Filipino populations have cemented her
legacy as both a clinician-researcher and an advocate for accessible, specialized healthcare in underserved
communities.

Early Life and Background
Dr. Aniza Barandia Pala-Mohamad was born and raised in Brgy.
Poblacion, Kauswagan,Lanao del Norte, the land of beauty and
bounty, where Muslims and Christians coexist in peace and unity. She
is the daughter of Alice Mohamad Barandia and Marcone Pala. Her
identity as a Maranao woman from a region historically marginalized
in healthcare infrastructure shaped her understanding of the deep
inequities in access to specialized medical care. The Maranao, often
called the "People of the Lake" for their residence around Lake
Lanao, have faced systemic barriers to quality healthcare, particularly
in subspecialties like endocrinology, where expertise concentrates
overwhelmingly in urban centers like Metro Manila and Cebu City.
Her decision to return to her roots as a trained endocrinologist would,
years later, prove transformative for her community.
Academic Journey
Dr. Pala-Mohamad's educational trajectory reflects consistent
academic excellence and deliberate pursuit of specialized training.
Undergraduate and Medical School
She earned her M.D. from the MSU College of Medicine in 2005,
graduating in the Top 10 of her class. This achievement at one of the
Philippines' leading medical schools signaled her intellectual caliber
and clinical aptitude early in her career. Her MSU degree rooted her
in the academic traditions of Mindanao and connected her to an
alumni network deeply invested in the region's health workforce.
Residency in Internal Medicine
Following her medical degree, Dr. Pala-Mohamad completed her
internal medicine residency at the Vicente Sotto Memorial Medical
Center in Cebu City in 2010. This three-year training exposed her to
the breadth of systemic diseases and prepared her for the specialized
study of metabolic disorders.
Fellowship in Endocrinology
In 2014, she completed her fellowship in Endocrinology, Diabetes,
and Metabolism at the prestigious Philippine General Hospital (PGH)
in Manila, one of the country's premier teaching institutions. This
subspecialty training equipped her with advanced diagnostic and
therapeutic expertise in disorders of the endocrine system, including diabetes, thyroid disease, and metabolic
syndrome. Her completion of PGH's rigorous fellowship marked the culmination of nearly a decade of
postgraduate training and positioned her among the select cohort of endocrinologists in the Philippines.

PAGE 3
Advanced Management Training
Beyond clinical medicine, Dr. Pala-Mohamad pursued formal training in institutional leadership, earning a Master
of Hospital Administration (MHA) and a Master of Business Administration (MBA). These credentials
demonstrate her strategic vision for healthcare systems and her commitment to leading not just at the bedside, but
at the institutional level.
Professional Career and Practice
Since 2014, Dr. Pala-Mohamad has maintained a dual-city clinical practice, serving patients in both Marawi and
Iligan. She operates in private fee-for-service settings and, critically, continues to offer charity clinic hours to
ensure that specialized endocrine care reaches those unable to afford private consultation. This dual commitment to
clinical excellence and health equity is the ethical cornerstone of her practice.
Primary Institutional Role: Amai Pakpak Medical Center
Dr. Pala-Mohamad's most significant institutional contribution has been her leadership at the Amai Pakpak Medical
Center (APMC) in Marawi City, a key tertiary referral hospital serving the BARMM and the surrounding Lanao
provinces. Her roles at APMC span both clinical leadership and workforce development.
Internal Medicine Residency Program
One of Dr. Pala-Mohamad's most enduring legacies is her instrumental role in establishing the first Internal
Medicine Residency Training Program in Lanao del Sur. Prior to her involvement, the province had no
accredited program to train internal medicine specialists locally, forcing aspiring physicians to migrate to other
regions or cities. By pioneering this program at APMC, she created a pathway for medical graduates from Lanao
del Sur and neighboring provinces to specialize without geographic dislocation.
The program's impact has been measurable and sustained. Under her leadership and mentorship, it has produced 49
accredited Internal Medicine specialists. Many of these trainees have pursued further subspecializations,
returning to serve their communities as cardiologists, nephrologists, gastroenterologists, and endocrinologists. In
this way, Dr. Pala-Mohamad's program has seeded the development of subspecialty care across the BARMM
region itself.
Departmental Leadership
Dr. Pala-Mohamad currently serves as the Chairperson of the Internal Medicine Department at APMC. In this
role, she oversees clinical standards, resident training, and the strategic direction of the department. She previously
served as the Training Officer, a position in which she ensured that resident education met Philippine Medical
Association and specialty board standards.
Private Practice and Community Outreach
In Iligan City, Dr. Pala-Mohamad operates at the FK Specialists Clinic, where she sees patients with endocrine and
metabolic disorders on a fee-for-service basis. Her clinical focus spans:
Type 1 and Type 2 diabetes management and complication prevention
Thyroid disorders (hypothyroidism, hyperthyroidism, thyroiditis)

PAGE 4
Adrenal and pituitary disorders
Obesity and metabolic syndrome management
Hormonal therapy and hormone replacement
Beyond individual consultations, she leads lay health education forums throughout Marawi and Iligan, teaching
patients and community members about chronic disease prevention, medication adherence, and lifestyle
modification. These public education sessions reflect her conviction that healthcare literacy is as essential to health
equity as clinical expertise.
Research and Academic Contributions
Dr. Pala-Mohamad is not only a clinician but a researcher engaged in translational work that directly addresses the
health needs of Filipino populations.
Pharmacogenomics Research
In 2023, she co-authored a peer-reviewed study published in the Journal of the ASEAN Federation of Endocrine
Societies (JAFES) examining genetic variants associated with poor sulfonylurea response in Filipino diabetic
patients. This research is particularly significant because it identifies molecular explanations for why certain
Filipino patients fail to respond adequately to a commonly prescribed class of diabetes medications. The
implications are direct: understanding population-specific genetic markers can guide more personalized drug
selection and prevent futile or ineffective treatment courses. This type of pharmacogenomic research is still nascent
in the Philippines, making Dr. Pala-Mohamad's contributions especially valuable for tailoring global diabetes
guidelines to local genetic realities.
Clinical Outcomes and Nutrition Research
She has also investigated the relationship between malnutrition and mortality in hospitalized Type 2 Diabetes
patients, a study addressing an often-overlooked intersection of metabolic disease and nutritional status in acute
care settings. This research speaks to real-world clinical challenges: how do clinicians manage patients whose
diabetes coexists with undernutrition or malnutrition, a surprisingly common scenario in resource-limited
healthcare settings? Her work in this area informs both clinical protocols and institutional policies around
nutritional support in diabetic inpatients.
Teaching and Mentorship
For over a decade, Dr. Pala-Mohamad has mentored medical students at MSU College of Medicine, where she
conducts clinical rotations and lectures on endocrinology and metabolic disease. She has trained hundreds of
interns and residents at APMC, many of whom now serve as physicians across Mindanao. Her didactic teaching
includes both foundational lectures for trainees and continuing medical education seminars for practicing
physicians in Marawi City, ensuring that local doctors remain current with advances in endocrinology, diabetes
management, and metabolic disease.

PAGE 5
Legacy and Impact
Dr. Aniza Pala-Mohamad's significance lies not in a single discovery or award, but in her embodiment of a
principle that remains rare among specialist physicians in the Philippines: the commitment to build capacity and
care in one's own community rather than consolidate expertise in privilege. Her career achievements cluster around
three interconnected themes: pioneering representation, institutional capacity building, and equitable access.
Pioneering Representation
As the first Maranao endocrinologist to establish fulltime practice in Marawi and Iligan, Dr. Pala-Mohamad
serves as a visible symbol of what is possible. Her presence in these cities challenges the historical assumption that
specialized medicine is an urban or Manila-centric privilege. For Maranao women, in particular, she models both
medical excellence and cultural rootedness, demonstrating that professional ambition and community commitment
are not mutually exclusive. Her photo, her name, and her practice are themselves educational, signaling to the next
generation of Maranao students that medicine at the highest levels is accessible to them.
Institutional Capacity Building
The Internal Medicine Residency Program she established at APMC is a permanent infrastructure, likely to outlast
her tenure and continue training specialists decades into the future. By investing in systems rather than individual
heroics, she has created scalable solutions to the workforce shortage in internal medicine across the BARMM. The
49 specialists trained under her watch are already embedded across the region, multiplying her impact
exponentially.
Health Equity Through Dual Practice
Her maintenance of both a private practice and a charity clinic embodies a stance on healthcare justice: that
specialized care should not be rationed by ability to pay. This is not merely idealistic; it is practical commitment,
every week, to treating the uninsured alongside private patients. It reflects the values she articulates publicly:
compassion, integrity, and empowerment.
Recognition and Professional Memberships
Dr. Pala-Mohamad holds full fellowship status with the Philippine College of Physicians (PCP), the professional
organization for Philippine physicians and the issuing body for medical licensure standards. She is also an active
Fellow of the Philippine Society of Endocrinology, Diabetes and Metabolism (PSEDM), the national
subspecialty college for endocrinologists and metabolic disease specialists.
Challenges and Limitations
Despite her achievements, Dr. Pala-Mohamad's work occurs within constrained circumstances. The BARMM
region, while developing, faces infrastructure limitations, irregular PhilHealth reimbursement rates that
disadvantage rural providers, and ongoing security challenges that periodically disrupt healthcare delivery in
Marawi proper. Her efforts to establish specialist care and training programs have frequently required her to
improvise solutions and advocate for institutional support in an environment of scarcity. Her ability to persist and
innovate within these constraints is itself remarkable.

PAGE 6
Personal Values and Approach
In interviews and public statements, Dr. Pala-Mohamad emphasizes three core values that drive her professional
life:
Compassion: Recognition that illness brings both physical and emotional suffering, and that healing requires
attentiveness to the whole person.
Integrity: Commitment to evidence-based practice, honest communication with patients, and ethical
decision-making even when convenience might suggest otherwise.
Empowerment: Belief that patients and trainees thrive when equipped with knowledge, agency, and hope.
Her educational forums and mentorship reflect this commitment to building capability in others.
Future Directions
Looking forward, Dr. Pala-Mohamad continues to expand endocrine care access within the BARMM and to mentor
the next cohort of internal medicine residents at APMC. She remains engaged in clinical research, particularly in
pharmacogenomics and outcomes research relevant to Filipino populations. Her vision, as articulated in various
institutional forums, centers on sustainable, locally-rooted healthcare systems that neither depend indefinitely on
external resources nor accept the inevitability of specialist care shortages.

Nihara Macabando Panandigan
Nihara Macabando Panandigan is a Maranao political leader, community builder, and royal titleholder from
Mulondo, Lanao del Sur, in the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM). She served
two terms as Municipal Mayor of Mulondo and previously as its Vice Mayor, earning recognition for her inclusive
governance style and her genuine care for the community's most vulnerable members. Beyond her political career,
she carries the prestigious royal title of Bae A Labi sa Ulo a Masiu, a distinction that places her among the
respected women leaders of the Maranao people.
Her legacy is defined by a hands-on approach to public service, from pioneering orphan care and social welfare
programs to actively supporting the region's religious educators and institutions. She built her political foundation
from the ground up, starting as a barangay chairwoman, and worked her way to becoming one of Mulondo's
longest-serving chief executives. Today, she remains a central figure in the municipality's civic and family life.
Contents

2 Career
3 Social Welfare Programs
4 Support for Religious Institutions
5 Cultural Heritage and Royal Title
6 Legacy and Family
7 See Also
Background
Nihara Macabando Panandigan comes from Mulondo, a municipality
in Lanao del Sur within the BARMM. Her roots in the Maranao
community run deep, evidenced both by her decades of public
service and by her recognition as a royal titleholder under the
traditional Maranao leadership structure.
Her public service story didn't start at the top. She first served as
Barangay Chairwoman in Marinaut, Marawi City, where she
developed a reputation for being responsive and community-
centered. That grassroots foundation shaped the kind of leader she
would become, someone who understood the day-to-day realities of
her constituents before she ever took on a municipal office.
Career
Panandigan's career in elective politics spans multiple decades and
positions. She served as Vice Mayor of Mulondo from 2013 to 2019,
a six-year stint that prepared her well for the chief executive role. In
2019, she was elected Municipal Mayor of Mulondo, a position her
constituents gave her with a clear mandate. She went on to serve two
terms as mayor.

PAGE 2
During her time as mayor, she led infrastructure improvements, telecommunications access initiatives, and public
health and welfare programs across the municipality. Her administration consistently prioritized lifting living
conditions for ordinary residents while strengthening the mechanisms of local governance.
Social Welfare Programs
One of the defining features of Panandigan's tenure was her focus on the most vulnerable members of her
community. She is credited with pioneering two notable social welfare programs in the BARMM region.
The first is the SIYAP KO MGA WATA ILO Program, a care initiative for orphaned children. The second is the
SIYAP KO MGA TIBAYO Program, which extends support to other disadvantaged groups. These programs
reflect a clear philosophy in her governance: inclusive development means no one gets left behind, especially
children and families with the least resources.
Support for Religious Institutions
Panandigan also made the support of the religious sector a priority during her administration. Under her watch,
Imams and Bilal serving each Masjeed in the municipality received regular assistance from the Office of the
Mayor. Madrasah institutions were similarly supported, and the Asatidz (faculty members) of these Madrasah
received consistent aid as well.
This commitment to the religious and educational sector reflects her understanding of the central role that Islamic
institutions and their leaders play in Maranao community life, not just in spiritual guidance but in moral formation
and community cohesion.
Cultural Heritage and Royal Title
Beyond her political roles, Panandigan holds a significant position in the traditional leadership structure of the
Maranao people. She carries the title of Bae A Labi sa Ulo a Masiu, a prestigious royal distinction bestowed upon
women leaders who are recognized for their standing, character, and service within the community.
This title is not merely ceremonial. It connects her to a long tradition of Maranao women who have held respected
positions within the datu system, and it adds a layer of cultural legitimacy to her public service that resonates
deeply with her constituents.
Legacy and Family
Panandigan's public service legacy is now woven into her family's continued involvement in Mulondo's
governance. Her husband, Abdulhakim O. Panandigan, currently serves as the municipality's mayor, while their
son, Khalid Macabando Panandigan, serves as Vice Mayor. This continuity reflects the trust the community has
extended to her family and the durable impact of her years in office.
As the First Lady of Mulondo, she remains an active and influential presence in the municipality's civic life,
carrying forward the same advocacy for community welfare that defined her own years in leadership.

Ali Bangcola Panda
Prof. Dr. Ali Bangcola Panda (born January 2, 1963) is a
distinguished Filipino Muslim scholar, educator, researcher, and
policy advocate who has dedicated over three decades to
advancing Islamic scholarship, governance reform, and
peacebuilding in the Bangsamoro region and across the
Philippines. A member of the Meranao ethnic group from Lanao
del Sur, Panda is widely recognized for bridging the worlds of
academia, policy advocacy, and grassroots community
engagement through his signature commitment to nonviolent
political participation and institutional reform.
As Professor VI at Mindanao State University (MSU) and former
Dean of the King Faisal Center for Islamic, Arabic and Asian
Studies, Panda has shaped generations of Muslim scholars while
authoring groundbreaking research on ulama leadership, Islamic
education, and Bangsamoro governance. His most notable work,
Meranao Ulama in Philippine Politics: A Nonviolent Approach
(2009), established him as a leading voice in understanding how
Islamic scholars navigate political engagement without resorting
to armed conflict—a critical contribution to Philippine peace
studies. Beyond academia, he actively engages with legislative
bodies, submits policy recommendations to the Bangsamoro
Parliament and Philippine Congress, and uses radio broadcasting
to reach communities across Mindanao.
