Early Life and Background
Ali Bangcola Panda was born on January 2, 1963, in Poblacion, Lumbatan, a municipality in Lanao del Sur
province on the island of Mindanao. Growing up in a predominantly Meranao community during a period of
significant political and social transformation in Muslim Mindanao, Panda was exposed early to the intersections of
Islamic tradition, Filipino nationalism, and the struggles for Muslim autonomy. His formative years coincided with
the height of the Moro conflict in the 1970s, which would later inform his scholarly focus on nonviolent political
engagement and governance reform.
As a young Meranao Muslim in Lanao del Sur, Panda witnessed firsthand the challenges faced by his community
—limited educational opportunities, political marginalization, and the tension between traditional Islamic
governance structures and the Philippine secular state. These experiences shaped his lifelong commitment to
finding peaceful solutions to Muslim Filipino grievances through education, scholarship, and policy advocacy
rather than armed struggle.
Education
Panda's academic journey reflects a deep commitment to both Islamic scholarship and social science research,
making him one of the few Filipino Muslim scholars with extensive training in both traditional Islamic studies and
Western academic frameworks.
Undergraduate Studies
Panda began his higher education at Mindanao State University (MSU) in Marawi City, where he earned a
Bachelor of Arts in Islamic Studies (Shariah) from 1980 to 1985 as a full scholar. Recognizing the importance of
understanding international relations for Muslim communities in a globalized world, he pursued a second
undergraduate degree, completing a Bachelor of Science in International Relations at MSU from 1985 to 1986,
also as a full scholar.

PAGE 3
During his undergraduate years, Panda distinguished himself academically, earning full scholarship support that
allowed him to focus entirely on his studies. His dual degrees in Islamic studies and international relations
positioned him uniquely to analyze Muslim Filipino issues through both religious and political science lenses.
Graduate Studies
Building on his undergraduate foundation, Panda pursued graduate education at the University of the Philippines
Diliman, one of the country's most prestigious academic institutions. From 1986 to 1989, he completed his Master
of Arts in Islamic Studies at the Institute of Islamic Studies, supported by a Graduate Scholarship. His MA thesis,
titled "Ulama Political Participation in Lanao del Sur," examined the role of Islamic scholars in local politics and
laid the groundwork for his later doctoral research.
From 1989 to 1993, Panda earned his Doctor of Philosophy in Philippine Studies with a specialization in
bureaucracy from UP Diliman. His doctoral studies were supported by two prestigious scholarships: the UP
Presidential Scholar program and a grant from the Muslim World League, reflecting both national and international
recognition of his scholarly potential. His PhD dissertation, "Meranao Ulama Political Leadership," became the
foundation for his most influential book and established him as an expert on Islamic leadership in Philippine
politics.
Professional Qualification
In addition to his academic credentials, Panda completed the Shariah Training Program required under Presidential
Decree 1083, which governs Muslim personal law in the Philippines. This qualification demonstrates his expertise
in Islamic jurisprudence and his commitment to understanding the legal frameworks that affect Muslim Filipino
communities.
Academic Career
Panda's academic career at Mindanao State University spans more than three decades, during which he has risen
from instructor to the highest professorial rank while making significant contributions to Islamic scholarship and
education.
Teaching Trajectory
Panda began his teaching career in the early years of his academic life as an instructor, lecturer, and literacy
teacher. After completing his PhD in 1993, he was appointed Assistant Professor III at MSU, a position he held
from 1992 to 1998. He was promoted to Associate Professor I in 1999 and steadily advanced through the
Associate Professor ranks (I–V) from 1999 to 2013. In 2014, he achieved the highest academic rank of Professor
VI (Salary Grade 29, Step 4), a position he continues to hold, reflecting both his scholarly excellence and sustained
contributions to the university.
Throughout his teaching career, Panda has trained hundreds of students in Islamic studies, political science, and
research methodology, many of whom have gone on to become scholars, government officials, and community
leaders themselves.

PAGE 4
Administrative Leadership at MSU
Beyond teaching, Panda has held numerous administrative positions at MSU, demonstrating his capacity for
institutional leadership and governance.
Dean of King Faisal Center
From 2012 to 2015, Panda served as Dean of the King Faisal Center for Islamic, Arabic and Asian Studies
(KFCIAAS), one of MSU's most important academic units for Islamic scholarship in Southeast Asia. During his
tenure, he worked to strengthen the center's research capacity, internationalize its academic programs, and maintain
its reputation as a leading institution for Islamic studies in the Philippines.
Prior to becoming dean, he served as Assistant Dean of KFCIAAS from 1997 to 1999, giving him extensive
experience in managing the center's operations.
Graduate School Leadership
Panda played a crucial role in MSU's graduate education, serving as Acting Dean of the Graduate School from
2000 to 2001 and Assistant Dean of the Graduate School from 1999 to 2000. In these positions, he oversaw
graduate programs, supervised thesis and dissertation committees, and worked to maintain academic standards for
advanced degrees.
He also served as Department Chair for Graduate Studies from 1994 to 1996, directly managing graduate-level
curriculum and faculty.
Other Administrative Roles
Panda's administrative experience includes:
Assistant Vice Chancellor for Academic Affairs (External Units) – 2016
Project Director, Research and Extension Services – 1996–1997
Community and Extension Director – 1996–1997
College Secretary – 1992–1994
These diverse roles gave him comprehensive understanding of university operations, from academic affairs to
research management to community engagement.
Research and Scholarship
Panda is a prolific scholar whose research focuses on Islamic education, Muslim governance, peacebuilding, and
the socio-political development of Bangsamoro society.
Published Books
His most significant published works include:

PAGE 5
1. Meranao Ulama in Philippine Politics: A Nonviolent Approach (2009) – This groundbreaking book examines
how Meranao Islamic scholars engage in political leadership without resorting to armed conflict, offering a
counternarrative to militant approaches in Muslim Mindanao. The work draws on his doctoral research and
extensive fieldwork in Lanao del Sur.
2. Islamic Economy and Globalization in Muslim Filipino Areas (2005) – This work analyzes the economic
challenges and opportunities facing Muslim communities in the context of global economic integration.
Unpublished Manuscripts
Panda has authored numerous unpublished manuscripts on critical topics:
Islamic Education and Peaceful Coexistence
Islamic Education: Challenges and Progress in Philippine Secular State
Ulama in Philippine Politics: Challenges and Development
Islamic Finance and Economic Development: Contemporary Challenges and Progress in the Philippines
Islam and Political Influence in the Philippines
Research Methodology: Questions and Answers
Al Fiqh: Questions and Answers
Al Salah: Questions and Answers
Al Sawm: Questions and Answers
A Glossary of 200 Key Terms in Al Fiqh
These unpublished works demonstrate the breadth of Panda's scholarly interests, ranging from political science to
Islamic jurisprudence to pedagogical materials for Islamic education.
Research Themes
Panda's scholarly contributions consistently address:
Islamic education reform in secular contexts
Muslim governance and political leadership
Peacebuilding and conflict resolution in Muslim Mindanao
Socio-political development of Bangsamoro society
Islamic resurgence and modernization in the Philippines
Policy Engagement and Legislative Advocacy
Unlike many academics who remain confined to university settings, Panda actively engages with policymakers and
government institutions to translate his research into practical reforms.
Bangsamoro Parliament Engagement
Panda is a regular contributor to the Bangsamoro Transition Authority (BTA) and the Bangsamoro Parliament,
submitting position papers on proposed legislation affecting Muslim Mindanao. His expertise in Islamic
governance and Bangsamoro politics makes him a valued voice in regional legislative processes.

PAGE 6
Philippine Congress Advocacy
Beyond regional engagement, Panda submits policy recommendations to the Philippine Congress on matters of
governance, education, peace, and Muslim affairs. His work helps bridge the gap between Muslim Mindanao's
concerns and national policymaking in Manila.
Public Advocacy Letters
Panda has authored numerous formal complaint and advocacy letters to government agencies, demonstrating his
commitment to accountability and institutional reform. These letters have been addressed to:
National Commission on Muslim Filipinos (NCMF)
Lanao del Sur Electric Cooperative (LASURECO)
Bangsamoro Parliament (BTA/BPA)
National Power Corporation (NPC), including concerns about proposed privatization
Various other government agencies
These advocacy efforts address governance accountability, public utilities, community welfare, and institutional
reform, showing Panda's willingness to confront bureaucratic failures and demand better service for Muslim
communities.
International Academic Engagement
Panda has established himself as a scholar of international standing through participation in conferences and
academic exchanges across Asia and the Middle East.
Countries of Engagement
He has presented research and delivered keynote addresses in Indonesia, Malaysia, Brunei Darussalam, Thailand,
Turkey, Kuwait, and the Philippines.
Notable International Roles
Keynote Speaker – International Conference on Islamic Studies (Indonesia, 2023)
Keynote Speaker – Islamic Leadership and Governance Conference (Indonesia, 2022)
Presenter – Prince of Songkla University (Thailand, 2017)
Speaker – Universiti Islam Sultan Sharif Ali (Brunei, 2016)
Speaker – International Islamic Thought Conference (Malaysia, 2011)
Contributor – Kuwait Islamic World Encyclopedia Project (2012–2013)
Speaker – International Conference on Palestine and Islamic Resurgence (Indonesia, 2011–2012)
These international engagements have enhanced Panda's scholarly network and brought Philippine Islamic
scholarship to global audiences.
Media and Broadcasting
Recognizing that scholarship must reach beyond academic journals, Panda has maintained an active presence in
Islamic media and public communication.

PAGE 7
Radio Broadcasting
News Caster – Saksi Islamic Radio Forum, Inc. (Present)
Former President – Tarompong sa Ranao Radio Forum
Regular Resource Speaker on Islamic education, governance, and peacebuilding
Through radio, Panda reaches audiences across Lanao del Sur and surrounding areas, making complex political and
religious issues accessible to ordinary citizens. His broadcasting work complements his academic research by
creating direct channels for public education.
Media Organizations
Panda founded the Lanao Association of Media Practitioners, serving as its founding president. This
organization brings together journalists and media professionals committed to responsible reporting on Muslim
Mindanao issues.
Civic and Organizational Leadership
Panda's commitment to community service extends to leadership roles in multiple civic and Islamic organizations.
Current Leadership Positions
President – Bangsamoro Multisectoral Development Council, Inc.
Vice President – Ranao Federal State Movement, Inc.
President – Almorshid Research and Da'wah Center
Member – Ulama Supreme Council of the Philippines
These positions reflect Panda's standing within Meranao and broader Muslim Filipino communities as both a
scholar and community organizer.
Legacy and Impact
Prof. Dr. Ali Bangcola Panda's significance lies in his ability to operate effectively across multiple domains—
academia, policy advocacy, media, and community organizing—while maintaining a consistent commitment to
nonviolent reform and institutional change.
His scholarship on ulama political leadership provides crucial insights into how Islamic scholars can engage
constructively with democratic politics without abandoning their religious principles or resorting to armed struggle.
In the context of decades of violent conflict in Muslim Mindanao, this research offers an alternative model
grounded in education, dialogue, and institutional reform.
Panda represents a generation of Muslim Filipino intellectuals who pursued advanced education in mainstream
Philippine universities while maintaining deep roots in Islamic scholarship and Meranao culture. This dual
positioning allows him to serve as a bridge between Muslim communities and the Philippine state, translating
Islamic concepts for secular audiences and explaining constitutional governance to traditional communities.

PAGE 8
Core Expertise
Panda's areas of expertise include:
Islamic Studies and Shariah Governance
Bangsamoro Governance and Autonomy
Peacebuilding and Conflict Resolution
Public Policy and Legislative Advocacy
Islamic Education Reform
Socio-political Development of Muslim Communities
Media and Public Communication
Recognition and Continuing Service
Currently serving as Professor VI at Mindanao State University and maintaining active roles in civic organizations,
broadcasting, and policy advocacy, Panda continues to contribute to Philippine Islamic scholarship and Muslim
Filipino development. His work addresses contemporary challenges facing the Bangsamoro region, including the
implementation of the Bangsamoro Organic Law, Islamic education reform, and economic development.
His residence on the MSU campus in Marawi City, with his office at the King Faisal Center, symbolizes his
lifelong connection to the institution that shaped his career and to the Meranao community he has spent decades
serving.

title: Panda, Asma Masacal Alauya
text:
PAGE 1
Asma Masacal Alauya Panda
Template:Italic title
Atty. Asma Masacal Alauya Panda is a Maranao legal scholar, financial regulator, and pioneering woman in
Philippine central banking. She serves as the Senior Director and Deputy General Counsel of the Bangko Sentral
ng Pilipinas (BSP), making her the first woman, first Muslim, and first Maranao to hold this position in the
institution's history. Over a 22-year career with the BSP, Panda has authored the legal frameworks for landmark
financial modernization legislation, including the Islamic Banking Law (Republic Act No. 11439), which
established Shari'ah-compliant banking regulation across the Philippines and significantly advanced financial
inclusion for Bangsamoro and Muslim Filipino communities.
Contents
1 Early Life and Lineage
2 Education
3 Professional Career

4.4 The FIST Act (Republic Act No. 11523)
4.5 The Agri-Fisheries Financing Enhancement Act (Republic Act No. 11901)
5 Cultural Significance and Role in Bangsamoro Governance
6 Personal Life
7 Legacy and Recognition
8 See Also

10 External Links
Early Life and Lineage
Asma Masacal Alauya was born into one of Lanao del Sur's most distinguished families of legal scholarship and
public service. Her father, Atty. Saaduddin A. Alauya, Sr., was a seminal figure in Philippine Islamic
jurisprudence, serving as a Jurisconsult in Islamic Law and as the Vice-Governor of Lanao del Sur. Her mother,
Hadja Maimuna Masacal Alauya, held the traditional Maranao title of Bai sa Bayabao, signifying her status as a
respected community leader and keeper of cultural heritage.
The Alauya household was one where law, faith, and public service were interwoven into daily life. This
foundation would profoundly shape Asma's professional identity and her later commitment to bridging Islamic
principles with financial governance.

PAGE 2

Her siblings have similarly pursued institutional leadership across finance,
education, medicine, and Islamic law. Arifa Alauya-Ala serves as Senior
Assistant Governor at the BSP, where she has become a leading figure in
Islamic finance regulation and central bank operations. Saaduddin M.
Alauya, Jr. holds the position of Vice Chancellor at Mindanao State
University. Dr. Aslama Alauya-Lamping is a medical professional.
Aninding M. Alauya practices as a Shari'ah Lawyer. This constellation of
achievement across sectors reflects not privilege alone, but a family ethos
of meritocratic excellence and service.
Education
Panda's academic record at Mindanao State University established her as
an exceptional scholar in two distinct fields. She earned her Bachelor of
Science in Business Administration with a specialization in
Management, graduating Magna Cum Laude. Recognizing her analytical
strengths, she subsequently pursued legal studies at the same institution.
In the College of Law, she distinguished herself further, graduating Cum
Laude and earning the honor of Class Valedictorian. Her dual expertise
in business administration and law would later prove invaluable in
navigating the complexities of central bank governance, where technical
regulatory acumen must align with institutional finance.
Her postgraduate trajectory took her to the United States. As a BSP BEST
Scholar (a competitive fellowship for promising civil servants), she was
selected to pursue advanced legal studies at New York University. There,
she earned her Master of Laws (LL.M.) in Corporate Law, a
specialization that positioned her to grapple with the intricate legal
structures underlying modern financial regulation and central bank
operations.
Professional Career
Early Years at the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas
Panda joined the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas in 2002 as a junior lawyer in
the Office of the General Counsel and Legal Services (OGCLS). At that
time, the BSP's legal function was primarily reactive, focused on contract
review and institutional defense. Over the subsequent two decades, the
role of the General Counsel's office would transform dramatically as the Philippine financial system itself
underwent modernization.
She rose through the ranks of the OGCLS with steady recognition for her technical precision, cultural insight, and
capacity to translate complex financial and regulatory concepts into coherent legal frameworks. Her peers recalled
her as intellectually rigorous, culturally grounded, and unafraid to ask difficult questions when ambiguity arose.

PAGE 3
Deputy General Counsel and Senior Director
In 2019, Panda was promoted to Deputy General Counsel, and her title was later elevated to Senior Director in
recognition of her strategic scope. As the second-most senior lawyer in the institution, she oversaw major legal
policy initiatives, advised the Governor's office on regulatory matters, and coordinated the bank's litigation and
compliance functions.
Her technical purview expanded to include monetary policy law, banking regulation, financial crime prevention,
payment systems law, and—most significantly—Islamic finance regulation. She became the institutional authority
on the legal frameworks governing Bangsamoro-Muslim financial participation in the Philippine banking system.
In a temporary designation, Panda also served as Chief of Staff to the Governor of the Bangko Sentral ng
Pilipinas, placing her at the strategic center of the institution's administrative decision-making. However, in
interviews and institutional communications, she has consistently expressed her preference for the disciplined,
detail-oriented work of legal drafting and regulatory analysis over administrative management. This choice
reflected her core conviction that law, when precisely crafted, is the most powerful instrument for institutional
integrity.
Legislative Architecture
Panda's most consequential contributions to Philippine governance lie in her role as a primary legal architect of five
landmark pieces of financial legislation that have fundamentally reshaped the banking and payment systems
landscape.
The Islamic Banking Law (Republic Act No. 11439)
The passage of the Islamic Banking Law in 2019 represented a historic milestone in financial inclusion. For
decades, the Philippine financial system was structured around conventional interest-based banking, which is
prohibited under Shari'ah law. This created a structural barrier to Bangsamoro and Muslim Filipino participation in
the formal financial system, effectively excluding millions of citizens from credit, savings products, and investment
opportunities.
Panda served as the principal legal author of the statutory framework governing Shari'ah-compliant banking
institutions. The law established a specialized regulatory regime allowing banks to offer Islamic banking services
(murabaha, musharaka, ijarah, and other Shari'ah instruments) alongside conventional banking. It also created the
Islamic Banking Supervisory Board and outlined prudential standards specific to Islamic financial products.
More than a technical achievement, this law represented cultural recognition. As Panda herself has noted in
institutional settings, Islamic banking regulation was not merely a financial inclusion tool, it was a statement that
the Philippine banking system could accommodate the ethical and religious obligations of its Muslim citizens
without compromise. The law has since enabled the establishment of multiple Islamic banking windows and, in
2023, the establishment of the first fully-fledged Islamic bank in the Philippines.
Amendments to the New Central Bank Act (Republic Act No. 11211)
In 2018, the New Central Bank Act underwent substantial amendment to modernize the BSP's institutional
architecture and expand its powers. Panda contributed to the legal framework for several key amendments,
including provisions that increased the BSP's statutory capital to 200 billion pesos (from 50 billion) and expanded
its corporate governance and supervisory authorities over non-bank financial institutions.

PAGE 4
These amendments reflected a global consensus (post-2008 financial crisis) that central banks required broader
prudential authority to manage systemic financial risk. Panda's contribution ensured that the Philippine
amendments aligned with international best practices while respecting the nation's constitutional constraints on
central bank authority.
The National Payment Systems Act (Republic Act No. 11127)
The National Payment Systems Act of 2018 established the first comprehensive statutory framework governing
payment system operators, clearing houses, and settlement systems in the Philippines. Panda's contributions to its
legal drafting ensured that the act addressed emerging risks in digital payments and fintech while preserving the
stability and interoperability of the nation's payment infrastructure.
The law was enacted at a moment of rapid fintech innovation, where unregulated digital payment platforms
threatened both consumer protection and systemic stability. The statute created clearer boundaries around what
constitutes a payment system operator, defined settlement obligations, and empowered the BSP to establish
prudential standards and technical requirements.
The FIST Act (Republic Act No. 11523)
During the COVID-19 pandemic, the Philippine financial system faced unprecedented stress as borrowers
struggled to service debts. The Financial Institutions Strategic Transfer (FIST) Act of 2020 provided a legal
framework allowing banks to transfer non-performing assets (NPAs) to Asset Management Corporations (AMCs)
at a faster pace, without triggering immediate loss recognition that would impair bank capital.
This technical legal mechanism was critical to the financial system's ability to absorb pandemic-related distress
without triggering a credit crunch. Panda's role in drafting the statutory mechanics of NPA transfer, pricing
methodologies, and the legal status of transferred assets was essential to the law's effectiveness.
The Agri-Fisheries Financing Enhancement Act (Republic Act No. 11901)
The Agri-Fisheries Financing Enhancement Act of 2022 aimed to expand credit access for agricultural, fisheries,
and rural development sectors, which have historically faced credit constraints. Panda contributed to its legal
framework, which simplified collateral requirements for farm and fishery loans and incentivized lending to
underserved rural communities.
This legislation reflected a broader policy aim: ensuring that financial modernization benefited not only urban and
formal sector participants but also the agricultural and fishing communities that form the backbone of Philippine
food security.
Cultural Significance and Role in Bangsamoro Governance
Panda's presence in the senior executive leadership of the BSP carries significance that extends beyond technical
legal achievement. She represents a cultural breakthrough in Philippine institutional governance, one that did not
occur through tokenism or symbolic gesture, but through 22 years of meritocratic advancement and demonstrated
technical mastery.

PAGE 5
In the context of Bangsamoro governance, her prominence signals something profound: that the highest levels of
Philippine financial administration are not closed to Muslims or Maranao professionals. When she championed the
Islamic Banking Law, she was not merely advancing an economic policy; she was translating the financial ethical
requirements of her faith into a statutory framework that enables her community's economic participation. This is
bridge-building at the most fundamental level, because it operates not through rhetoric but through the mechanics
of law and regulation.
Her father's legacy as a Jurisconsult in Islamic Law had provided the intellectual foundation; Asma's career has
extended that legacy into the sphere of modern financial governance. In doing so, she has demonstrated that
Islamic jurisprudence and contemporary central banking are not incompatible domains, but can be harmonized
through careful legal craft.
Personal Life
Panda is married to Cairoden C. Panda. The couple has two daughters who have continued the family's tradition
of academic and professional distinction.
Amal Jayieda A. Panda is a dual-qualified professional, holding credentials as both a Certified Public
Accountant (CPA) and a practicing Lawyer. Her dual expertise positions her for careers spanning financial
auditing, corporate advisory, or financial law.
Anon Jarya Panda continues the family's commitment to higher education and professional achievement.
Legacy and Recognition
Atty. Asma Masacal Alauya Panda's career embodies a rare combination of attributes: intellectual rigor, technical
mastery, institutional loyalty, and cultural consciousness. She has been a bridge between traditional Maranao values
and modern Philippine governance, demonstrating that these are not opposing forces but complementary
dimensions of a complete professional identity.
Her legislative contributions have reshaped the Philippine financial landscape in ways that will outlast her tenure at
the BSP. The Islamic Banking Law, in particular, is likely to be remembered as a turning point in financial
inclusion and the recognition of minority religious communities within the formal economy.
Her ascent to one of the most senior legal positions in the nation's central bank stands as a quiet but unmistakable
statement about the capacity of Philippine institutions to recognize excellence regardless of gender, religious
identity, or regional origin. She has not merely broken a glass ceiling; she has built institutions that will be more
inclusive because she has held them.

Ahdel Sambulayang T. Pangandaman
Ahdel Sambulayang T. Pangandaman was a Filipino legislator, military officer, and public official from Lanao
del Sur who served as an assemblyman (Mambabatas Pambansa) in the Interim Batasang Pambansa from 1978 to
1984.
He represented Region XII, which at the time covered the provinces of Lanao del Sur, Lanao del Norte,
Maguindanao, North Cotabato, and Sultan Kudarat, along with Marawi City.
Pangandaman was a Maranao leader who navigated one of the most turbulent chapters in the history of Muslim
Mindanao: the Martial Law era and its aftermath, when the question of Moro autonomy was at the center of
national and regional politics.
His career straddled two worlds, the legislative hall in Manila and the ground realities of a region in the middle of a
secessionist conflict, and he brought both a soldier's instincts and a politician's pragmatism to the role.
He is counted among the foundational figures of the Pangandaman political dynasty of Lanao del Sur, a family that
has produced governors, cabinet secretaries, diplomats, and congressional representatives well into the 21st
century.
Contents
1 BACKGROUND
2 POLITICAL CAREER
2.1 The Road to the Batasang Pambansa (1978)
2.2 Legislative Tenure (1978–1984)
3 MILITARY SERVICE
4 INSTITUTIONAL CONTRIBUTIONS

7 SEE ALSO

BACKGROUND
Ahdel Sambulayang T. Pangandaman came from the Maranao
people, the Muslim ethnolinguistic group native to the Lake Lanao
region of Lanao del Sur.
The Maranao are one of the largest Muslim communities in the
Philippines, with a cultural identity deeply rooted in the traditions of
the sultanate system, the weaving arts, the torogan (royal house),
and the okir design tradition.
Pangandaman was a member of the Pangandaman political clan,
one of the most enduring family networks in Lanao del Sur's
modern political history.

PAGE 2
June 12, 1978 – June 5, 1984
Region Represented

including Marawi City
Votes Received (1978)
271,393
Military Classification

classification)
Political Clan

del Sur
Notability
One of the Maranao legislators elected
to the Interim Batasang Pambansa
under the Marcos administration;
served the full six-year legislative term
from 1978 to 1984 representing Region
XII and Marawi City.
Known For
Legislative advocacy for Moro
autonomy and regional stabilization
during the post-Tripoli Agreement
period; dual career as legislator and
military officer; founding generation of
the Pangandaman political dynasty.
This was not simply a family with political connections. It was a
dynasty with staying power, producing leaders across multiple
generations and across multiple branches of government: executive,
legislative, diplomatic, and administrative.
His entry into public life combined two tracks that were common
for prominent Maranao men of his generation: civic leadership
rooted in community standing, and a military or paramilitary role
that gave regional leaders real authority on the ground during an era
of armed conflict.
POLITICAL CAREER
The Road to the Batasang Pambansa (1978)
The political context that shaped Pangandaman's legislative career
was the Marcos Martial Law regime, declared in 1972.
When Marcos suspended the regular Congress and governed by
decree, conventional electoral politics were put on hold for several
years.
By 1978, Marcos moved to reconstruct a legislative body that would
give his administration a parliamentary face while keeping real
power concentrated in the executive.
The result was the Interim Batasang Pambansa, a transitional
parliament elected through the 1978 Philippine parliamentary
elections.
Pangandaman ran under the banner of the Kilusang Bagong Lipunan (KBL), the ruling party that Marcos had built
as the political vehicle of his administration.
Running in the multi-seat regional constituency of Region XII, which encompassed the provinces of Lanao del Sur,
Lanao del Norte, Maguindanao, North Cotabato, and Sultan Kudarat, Pangandaman secured one of the contested
seats with 271,393 votes.
This was a meaningful electoral result in a region where political competition was intense and where the presence
of armed conflict made political activity complicated and, at times, dangerous.
Legislative Tenure (1978–1984)
Pangandaman assumed office on June 12, 1978, and served the full duration of the Interim Batasang Pambansa
until it dissolved on June 5, 1984.
His six-year tenure placed him squarely in the middle of one of the most critical periods in the history of Muslim
Mindanao.
The Moro secessionist movement, led primarily by the Moro National Liberation Front (MNLF), had been fighting
the Philippine government since the early 1970s.

PAGE 3
The 1976 Tripoli Agreement, brokered with the help of Libya and the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation, had
established a framework for regional autonomy, but its implementation was contested and incomplete.
Within this environment, Pangandaman's legislative work focused on regional stabilization, the advancement of
Moro autonomy within the existing constitutional framework, and the coordination between local government
structures and the national administration.
He served on parliamentary committees focused on regional development, local government coordination, and the
integration of cultural minorities into the national socio-political fabric.
His position was that of an interlocutor: a Maranao politician who worked within the system while advocating for
the interests of the Bangsamoro people through institutional channels.
MILITARY SERVICE
Historical archives, including the institutional repository Tuklas at the University of the Philippines, classify
Pangandaman under the dual categories of "Legislators" and "Soldiers."
This dual classification was not unusual for prominent Maranao leaders of his era.
During the mid-20th century, regional leaders across Mindanao often held military or paramilitary commissions
alongside their civilian roles.
For men like Pangandaman, a military background was not separate from political leadership; it was part of the
same integrated role of community authority in a region where security and governance were deeply intertwined.
His military service gave him credibility in local peacekeeping, provided him with a role in counter-insurgency
mediation, and positioned him as someone who understood the realities of armed conflict from the inside.
The specifics of his military rank, branch of service, and the dates of his commissions are not fully documented in
available sources and would benefit from further archival research.
INSTITUTIONAL CONTRIBUTIONS
Pangandaman's most significant institutional contribution was his role in the KBL Moro coalition, the group of pro-
administration Moro leaders who chose to work within the Marcos political framework rather than join or support
the armed insurgency.
This was a deliberate political choice that had real consequences for the trajectory of Moro autonomy negotiations.
Alongside contemporaries like Datu Blah Sinsuat, Pangandaman was part of a faction that bet on institutional
engagement as the path toward addressing Moro grievances, even as others pursued armed struggle.
Within the Batasang Pambansa, his advocacy for regional concerns helped keep the question of Muslim
Mindanao's political status on the legislative agenda during a period when the central government might otherwise
have treated it purely as a security problem.
His work on committees dealing with regional development and cultural minorities was aimed at building the
administrative and legislative groundwork for eventual autonomy, even if the political conditions of the Marcos era
limited how far that work could actually go.

PAGE 4
LEGACY
The Pangandaman name in Lanao del Sur politics carries a continuity that traces back directly to Ahdel
Sambulayang T. Pangandaman's generation.
His participation in the Interim Batasang Pambansa helped establish the family's standing as a political force
capable of operating at the national level, not just within the local politics of the Lake Lanao region.
The generations that followed built on that foundation.
Lininding Pangandaman went on to serve as Governor of the Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (ARMM)
and as a veteran diplomat.
Amenah "Mina" Pangandaman became one of the most visible figures in the Marcos Jr. administration as Secretary
of the Department of Budget and Management (DBM).
Nasser, Solaiman, and Mohammed Hussein Pangandaman served as Congressional and Party-List Representatives
in the House of Representatives of the Philippines.
This pattern of multi-generational leadership, spanning executive administration, legislative service, and
diplomacy, reflects the durable political capital that the founding generation of the dynasty, including Ahdel
Sambulayang, helped build.
At a broader level, his legacy is that of a Maranao leader who chose to engage the Philippine state during one of its
most authoritarian chapters, working within a constrained political system to advance the interests of his
community in the ways that were available to him.
Whether that choice is viewed as pragmatic collaboration, principled engagement, or accommodation of a difficult
power structure is a question that historians of the Bangsamoro continue to explore.
RECOGNITION
Pangandaman's service in the Interim Batasang Pambansa is documented in institutional archives, including the
University of the Philippines Tuklas repository, which classifies him among both legislators and soldiers of his era.
His political career is recognized within the broader narrative of Maranao and Bangsamoro participation in national
governance during the Martial Law period.

Amenah F. Pangandaman
Amenah "Mina" F. Pangandaman is a Filipino Moro public
servant, economist, and government official currently serving as Secretary of the Department of Budget and
Management (https://dbm.gov.ph) (DBM) of the Philippines. She is the first Muslim woman to hold the position
and has been a key figure in advancing inclusive governance, public financial management, and Bangsamoro
development.<ref name="dbm2022">Department of Budget and Management. Profile of Secretary Amenah
Pangandaman. Official DBM Website, 2022.</ref><ref name="pia2022">Philippine Information Agency.
Pangandaman named DBM Secretary. 2022.</ref>
---
Early Life and Education
Amenah Pangandaman hails from Marawi City, Lanao del Sur, and belongs to a prominent Maranao family
with a legacy in public service.
She earned her degree in Business Administration and pursued further studies in development economics and
public administration.
Her educational background laid the foundation for her career in fiscal policy, governance, and development
planning.<ref name="dbm2022" />
---
Career in Government
Pangandaman has held several key positions in government prior to her appointment as DBM Secretary,
including:
 * Assistant Governor of the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (https://bsp.gov.ph) (BSP)  
 * Executive Director at the Board of the World Bank Group for Southeast Asia  
 * Secretary of the Department of Budget and Management in BARMM

PAGE 2
She played a critical role in managing fiscal policy, budgeting systems, and development financing for both
national and Bangsamoro institutions.<ref name="pia2022" />
---
Role in Bangsamoro Governance
As DBM Secretary of BARMM, Pangandaman was instrumental in establishing the region’s budgeting
systems during the transition period.
She helped institutionalize transparency, accountability, and efficient public financial management in the
Bangsamoro government.
Her work supported the early operationalization of the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim
Mindanao under the Bangsamoro Organic Law.
---
Secretary of Budget and Management
In 2022, Pangandaman was appointed as Secretary of the Department of Budget and Management, becoming
the first Muslim woman to hold the position in Philippine history.
As DBM Secretary, she oversees the national budget, public expenditure management, and fiscal policy
implementation.
She has promoted digitalization, open governance, and inclusive budgeting to ensure equitable development
across regions, including Mindanao.<ref name="dbm2022" />
---
Advocacy and Contributions
Advocates for women’s leadership and representation in government.
Promotes inclusive economic development, particularly for underserved communities in Mindanao.
Supports transparency, accountability, and modernization of public financial systems.
---
Legacy and Significance
Amenah Pangandaman represents the growing role of Moro women in national leadership and governance.
Her career bridges Bangsamoro regional governance and Philippine national institutions.
She is regarded as a trailblazer in public finance and a symbol of inclusive leadership in the Philippines.
---

Juhary B. Pangandaman
Dr. Juhary B. Pangandaman is a Meranaw public administrator,
educator, and university executive who has spent more than nineteen
years building a career inside the halls of Mindanao State University
(MSU) in Marawi City. He currently serves as Director II at the MSU
Main Campus and holds the position of Special Disbursing Officer of
the University, a role that puts him squarely in charge of some of the
institution's most sensitive fiscal responsibilities. Before that, he
headed the Property Division, where he led the university through a
milestone that had never happened before in its long history.

Early Life
Dr. Pangandaman was born in Marinaut, Marawi City, Lanao del Sur.
His roots run deep into two communities that Meranaw people know
well for their cultural weight: Tugaya, his mother's hometown and
the center of centuries-old Meranaw artistry and craftsmanship, and
Bubong, Barangay Panalawan, where his father's family comes from.
Growing up between these two lineages gave him an early
appreciation for heritage and craftsmanship, themes that would later
echo in his work protecting and preserving institutional resources.
He finished elementary school at Marinaut Elementary School, then
went on to secondary school at the Mindanao State University
University Training Center (MSU-UTC) in Marawi City, staying
close to the institution that would eventually define his entire
professional life.
Education
Dr. Pangandaman's academic path stayed almost entirely within
Mindanao State University, a rare kind of loyalty that speaks to how
much the institution shaped him. He earned his undergraduate degree

at MSU-Marawi, then went on to complete both his Master's and
Doctoral degrees at the same university.
His academic credentials reflect a wide range of interests: a Bachelor
of Science in Public Administration with a major in Fiscal
Administration, a Master of Public Administration, and a Doctor of
Philosophy in Philippine Studies. He also completed the academic
requirements for a second doctorate, this time in Educational
Management, and picked up certifications in Governmental
Management and Professional Teaching along the way. As a
Licensed Professional Teacher, education isn't just something he
administers, it's something he's personally trained and licensed to do.
Career
Dr. Pangandaman's MSU career began at the rank-and-file level,
where he spent nine years earning a reputation for dependability and
hard work before moving into leadership. For the past decade, he has
held a string of directorial posts, each one adding to his experience in
university governance.
Over the years he served as Director of the MSU Cultural Affairs
Office, Director of the Division of Student Affairs, and Director of
the Property Division. In each of these posts, he pushed programs
forward in student development, cultural preservation, resource
management, and community engagement, building a track record
that touches nearly every corner of university life.
His time at the Property Division stands out as a defining chapter. Under his leadership, all sixteen academic and
administrative buildings of Mindanao State University, along with their contents, were insured under the
Government Service Insurance System (GSIS) for the first time in the university's history. It was a milestone years
in the making, one that finally gave the institution real protection against unforeseen risks and secured public
property for future generations of students.
He currently holds the itemized position of Director II at the MSU Main Campus and continues to serve as Special
Disbursing Officer, a role entrusted with key fiscal and administrative duties for the University.
Awards and Recognition
Dr. Pangandaman's contributions to MSU have not gone unnoticed. He is a two-time consecutive recipient of the
MSU Model Employee Award, winning it in both 2007 and 2008, an honor recognizing his proactive attitude, sense
of duty, and humanitarian service to the university community.
In 2008, the Office of the President of Mindanao State University conferred on him the Distinguished University
Service Award, recognizing his exceptional performance and contributions to the institution. He was also
recognized for producing one of the Best Doctoral Dissertations at MSU, a nod to his commitment to research and
scholarly work.

PAGE 3
Most recently, his tenure at the Property Division earned the university a Special Recognition Award from GSIS,
honoring the historic insurance of all sixteen university buildings. In accepting the award, Dr. Pangandaman
credited the achievement to the collective effort of the Property Division staff, university officials, and the
guidance of MSU System President Atty. Paisalin P. D. Tago, CPA.
Personal Life
Dr. Pangandaman traces his heritage to Tugaya and Bubong, two towns in Lanao del Sur known for their distinct
contributions to Meranaw culture, one for artistry and craftsmanship, the other as his ancestral home. This dual
heritage remains part of who he is, grounding his public service work in a strong sense of cultural identity.
Legacy
Dr. Pangandaman's career reflects a steady, decades-long commitment to public service inside one institution. From
rank-and-file employee to university director, his path shows what patience, integrity, and consistent performance
can build over time. His work protecting MSU's physical assets, developing its students, and preserving its culture
continues to shape how the university manages both its resources and its people. As he continues in his current role,
he remains focused on strengthening the systems of accountability, transparency, and good governance that have
defined his career so far.

title: Pangandaman, Lininding P.
text:
PAGE 1 Lininding P. Pangandaman 2nd Governor of the Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao In office 1993 – 1996 President Fidel V. Ramos Vice Governor Nabil Tan Preceded by Zacaria Candao Succeeded by Nur Misuari Philippine Ambassador to Saudi Arabia In office December 1973 – 1981 President Ferdinand Marcos Preceded by Position established Succeeded by Benjamin T. Romualdez Commissioner, Commission on Elections (Philippines) In office c. 1973 President Ferdinand Marcos Delegate, 1971 Constitutional Convention District represented Lanao del Sur Personal Information Born c. 1925
Masiu, Lanao del Sur, Philippines Lininding P. Pangandaman Atty. Lininding P. Pangandaman (c. 1925 – October 15, 2013), popularly referred to as "Lindy," was a Filipino lawyer, diplomat, and politician who served as the second elected Governor of the Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (ARMM) from 1993 to 1996. An ethnic Maranao from Masiu, Lanao del Sur, Pangandaman is widely regarded by historians and political analysts as a "Diplomatic-Institutional Architect" of the Bangsamoro political order — a leader uniquely capable of bridging the cultural imperatives of traditional Moro society with the constitutional and bureaucratic demands of the Philippine state. His career spanned three transformative decades of Philippine history, encompassing his election as a delegate to the 1971 Philippine Constitutional Convention, his landmark appointment as the first Philippine Ambassador to the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia in December 1973, his role as the chief government negotiator that produced the 1976 Tripoli Agreement, and finally his tenure as the second ARMM Governor during the crucial period of regional institutionalization under President Fidel V. Ramos. Philippines Nationality Filipino Ethnicity Maranao Religion Islam Spouse Ester Pangandaman Political party Lakas-NUCD-UMDP Profession Lawyer, Diplomat, Politician Notability Second elected Governor of the ARMM (1993–1996); first Philippine Ambassador to Saudi Arabia (1973–1981); chief government negotiator of the 1976 Tripoli Agreement; first Muslim COMELEC Commissioner; delegate to the 1971 Philippine Constitutional Convention representing Lanao del Sur. Known For Negotiating the 1976 Tripoli Agreement — the foundational peace instrument between the Philippine state and the Moro National Liberation Front — and serving as the first Philippine Ambassador to the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, establishing the bilateral diplomatic mission in Jeddah at the height of the Moro secessionist conflict. 10 External Links 11 Categories Early Life Lininding P. Pangandaman was born circa 1925 in the municipality of Masiu in the province of Lanao del Sur in the Lanao region of Mindanao, in the southern Philippines. He was the son of Pangandaman Gandawali and Paramata Pangandaman, a family deeply embedded in the cultural and traditional leadership hierarchies of the Maranao people. Masiu, historically recognized as one of the four traditional principalities of the Ranao confederacy — the Pat a Pangampong sa Ranao — conferred upon him both the social capital of dynastic lineage and the cultural grounding of the Maranao nobility. His upbringing was shaped by the twin pillars of Maranao social organization: the concept of maratabat (collective honor and dignity) and the taritib (the codified body of customary law and social hierarchy). These principles governed the obligations of the aristocratic class and instilled in the young Pangandaman an acute sense of communal responsibility that would define his public life. He came of age during the Japanese occupation of the Philippines and the subsequent period of national reconstruction, formative experiences that deepened his awareness of the structural vulnerabilities of the Bangsamoro within the Philippine nation-state. Education Pangandaman pursued a formal legal education, earning his degree as an Attorney-at-Law. His training in Philippine law was instrumental in equipping him with the technical expertise required to navigate the national legal system during a period when the Muslim south was experiencing increasing marginalization through land dispossession and the centralization of governmental authority in Manila. The precise institution where he obtained his law degree has not been established by available public records; however, his legal practice and his subsequent appointment to constitutional bodies confirm his professional standing within the Philippine bar. His intellectual formation was also shaped by his engagement with the broader Bangsamoro intelligentsia. He was a co-founder of the Basak Muslim Professionals Fraternity and Sorority, an organization dedicated to cultivating a professional class from among the first generation of post-war Muslim graduates in the Philippines. PAGE 3 Career Professional Foundations and the Basak Muslim Professionals Movement Pangandaman's earliest and most enduring institutional contribution was his co-founding of the Basak Muslim Professionals Fraternity and Sorority, an organization that functioned as a crucible for the first generation of modern Muslim professionals in post-war Philippines. The Basak region of Lanao del Sur — notable for its agricultural fertility and intellectual output — lent its name to a movement that was simultaneously social, political, and aspirational in character. The professionalizing mission of the organization was a deliberate response to the so-called "Moro Problem" as then framed by the central government in Manila, which viewed the Muslim south primarily through the lens of pacification and integration. Pangandaman and his contemporaries inverted this framing: they viewed education not as a tool of assimilation but as a mechanism of assertion. By encouraging the Maranao community to pursue professional degrees in law, medicine, and government, they sought to create a cadre of leaders competent to advocate for Moro rights within the very constitutional and legal structures that had historically marginalized them. 1971 Philippine Constitutional Convention In 1971, Pangandaman was elected as a delegate to the 1971 Philippine Constitutional Convention (ConCon), representing the province of Lanao del Sur. This placement positioned him at the center of the most consequential constitutional debates concerning the status of the Muslim south within the Philippine republic. Within the convention, Pangandaman was a key figure in the Bangsamoro Unity Bloc, a coalition of Muslim delegates that formally coalesced on July 15, 1971, and sought to secure constitutional recognition of Moro identity and a framework for meaningful regional autonomy. Working alongside fellow delegates including Michael Mastura and others, the Bloc advocated for several landmark reforms: the structural reform of the Philippine political system to accommodate Muslim traditions and customary governance, the constitutional security of ancestral land rights, and the formal institutionalization of Islamic practices — including the nascent framework for Sharia law — within the national legal order. The Bloc's monograph, The Moro Problem: An Approach Through Constitutional Reforms, remains a foundational document in the intellectual history of the Bangsamoro struggle for self-determination. Though the convention was overtaken by the declaration of Martial Law by President Ferdinand Marcos in September 1972, the constitutional frameworks it proposed — autonomy for the Muslim south, recognition of Sharia courts, ancestral domain protection — became the blueprints for every subsequent peace process, from the Tripoli Agreement to the Bangsamoro Organic Law of 2018. Following the proclamation of Martial Law, Pangandaman was appointed to the Ad Hoc Custodial Committee of the 1971 Constitutional Convention, established pursuant to Presidential Proclamation No. 1102. This body was tasked with the liquidation of convention affairs and the custodial preservation of its records — a role that demonstrated the institutional trust placed in Pangandaman even as the political landscape was transformed by authoritarian rule. Commissioner, Commission on Elections Under the 1973 Constitution promulgated by President Marcos, Pangandaman was appointed as a Commissioner of the Commission on Elections (https://comelec.gov.ph) (COMELEC), becoming the first Muslim to serve in this capacity in Philippine history. His appointment coincided with the expansion of the commission from three to nine PAGE 4 members under the new constitutional framework, which also reduced the term of office from nine to seven years and mandated staggered appointments to protect institutional independence. Pangandaman's presence on the COMELEC served as a visible signal of Muslim inclusion within the central constitutional machinery of the republic. His tenure was cut short when he was subsequently appointed to the diplomatic corps. His unexpired term was assumed by Commissioner Hashim R. Abubakar, preserving a degree of Muslim representation on the body responsible for administering the nation's elections. Philippine Ambassador to Saudi Arabia (1973–1981) In December 1973, at the height of the Moro secessionist conflict, President Marcos appointed Pangandaman as the first Philippine Ambassador to the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia — a posting that coincided with the inauguration of the first Philippine diplomatic mission in Jeddah. This appointment was strategically motivated: the government of Marcos recognized that international pressure from the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation (OIC), much of it channeled through Saudi Arabia and Libya, was strengthening the diplomatic position of the Moro National Liberation Front (MNLF). Pangandaman's tenure in Jeddah (1973–1981) was distinguished by his role as a cultural and religious interlocutor between the Philippine state and the Islamic world. As an ethnic Maranao and a practicing Muslim, he was uniquely equipped to engage with his Saudi counterparts on a basis of shared faith and heritage. Among his notable intellectual contributions during this period was his report, The Muslim Referendum Vote: A Mandate with the New Society, which analyzed the 1973 plebiscite results in the Muslim provinces of Mindanao and sought to demonstrate, for international audiences, that the Muslim populace broadly supported the national government's development agenda. The Jeddah mission also became a vital node in Philippine migration diplomacy, as the 1970s oil boom accelerated the movement of Filipino workers to the Middle East. Pangandaman's administration of the mission laid the institutional groundwork for the modern Philippine diplomatic presence in the Arabian Peninsula, including consular services for the growing community of overseas Filipino workers and the facilitation of the annual Hajj pilgrimage. His successor, Benjamin T. Romualdez, inherited a post that Pangandaman had institutionalized as a strategic platform for Philippine national security and economic interests. Chief Negotiator: The 1976 Tripoli Agreement The mid-1970s represented the most violent phase of the Moro secessionist conflict, with casualties in the tens of thousands and significant swaths of western Mindanao in open rebellion. In 1975, Pangandaman was recalled from his ambassadorial post to lead the Government of the Republic of the Philippines (GRP) negotiating panel in peace talks with the MNLF. The panel, which Pangandaman chaired, included the following members: Member Capacity Ambassador Lininding P. Pangandaman Panel Head / Chief Negotiator Hashim Abubakar COMELEC Commissioner Simeon Datumanong Governor, Maguindanao Brig. Gen. Mamarinta Lao Acting Governor, Lanao del Sur Sheikh Abdul Hamid Camlian Representative, Zamboanga PAGE 5 Between April and June 1975, Pangandaman's panel undertook field consultations across "Moroland," organizing dialogue sessions with insurgents at designated assembly points — an approach operating in parallel with the military's "Policy of Attraction" program led by Admiral Romulo Espaldon, which combined amnesty offers with targeted development projects. This "two-track" strategy — simultaneous top-down diplomacy and ground-level engagement — was a hallmark of Pangandaman's negotiating methodology. The culminating achievement of these negotiations was the signing of the 1976 Tripoli Agreement on December 23, 1976, in Tripoli, Libya, under the auspices of the OIC's Quadripartite Ministerial Commission. The agreement established the framework for "autonomy for the Muslims in the Southern Philippines within the realm of the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Republic of the Philippines." Pangandaman's central contribution was his capacity to bridge the MNLF's maximalist demand for formal independence with the Philippine government's absolute insistence on territorial integrity — a diplomatic tension that no preceding negotiator had managed to reconcile into a signed instrument. Although the Tripoli Agreement ultimately faced significant implementation challenges — owing partly to Libyan influence over the MNLF and to the ambiguities of the autonomy provisions — it is widely recognized by scholars of the Bangsamoro question as the foundational document of the entire peace architecture. Every subsequent agreement, including the 1996 Final Peace Agreement and the Bangsamoro Organic Law, traces its normative lineage to the framework first articulated in Tripoli. Governor, Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (1993–1996) Nearly two decades after the Tripoli Agreement, Pangandaman returned to the political arena. At the personal urging of President Fidel V. Ramos, he contested the second ARMM gubernatorial election. On March 25, 1993, he was elected as the second Regional Governor of the ARMM, with Nabil Tan as his Vice Governor, succeeding the inaugural governor Zacaria Candao. His administration's primary mandate was the institutionalization of the fledgling regional government, which was still largely a paper entity when Pangandaman assumed office. Key governance achievements and challenges during his term included: The establishment of a functioning regional executive structure through a series of regional executive orders, notably Executive Order No. 9 (signed December 12, 1994), which defined the integrated administrative framework of the ARMM. Major infrastructure development linking the two principal cities of the region — Cotabato City (seat of the ARMM government) and Marawi City (the cultural capital of the Maranao) — through the strengthening of the Cotabato-Marawi road corridor, a project carrying both logistical and symbolic significance in uniting the Maguindanaon and Maranao peoples. The translation of the Organic Act (Republic Act No. 6734) into functional government offices, regional ordinances, and service-delivery mechanisms, providing the institutional substrate upon which subsequent administrations would build. The administration was not without criticism. Reports from the period noted a bloated bureaucracy of over 19,000 regional personnel and allegations that patronage networks influenced appointments, including the reported placement of relatives — among them Pangandaman's wife Ester and several cousins and nephews — in key executive positions. Critics characterized portions of the administration as functioning more as a large-scale employment mechanism than a self-governing polity. These structural deficiencies, however, reflected systemic problems endemic to the early ARMM rather than being unique to Pangandaman's tenure. PAGE 6 The 1996 Transition: A Political Sacrifice for Peace As the government of President Ramos neared the finalization of the 1996 Final Peace Agreement with the MNLF, a political consensus emerged that MNLF Chairman Nur Misuari should assume the ARMM governorship as a concrete manifestation of the peace settlement. Pangandaman, who had intended to seek re-election, withdrew his candidacy entirely to give way to Misuari's uncontested election. This act — the voluntary relinquishment of an elective office to an erstwhile adversary for the sake of a broader peace — is widely cited among historians of the Bangsamoro as one of the most consequential acts of political magnanimity in the history of Muslim Mindanao. The institutional stability that Pangandaman had constructed during his three-year term provided Misuari with a functional regional government — however imperfect — as the foundation from which to implement the Final Peace Agreement's Phase II provisions. Historic Significance Pangandaman's career constitutes a rare instance of a single leader traversing all three dimensions of statecraft simultaneously: constitutional lawmaking, foreign diplomacy, and executive governance. Scholars of the Bangsamoro have periodized his contributions into three interlocking historical roles: 1. The Diplomatic Bridge Builder (1970s–1980s): As the first Philippine Ambassador to Saudi Arabia, Pangandaman managed the difficult balance between representing a state that was waging war against a Muslim insurgency while simultaneously cultivating goodwill within the broader Islamic community. His reports on the Muslim referendum and his management of the Jeddah mission helped contain international hostility toward the Philippines within the OIC framework. 1. The Peace Negotiator (1975–1976): As chief of the GRP panel, he authored the first formal framework for autonomy in Muslim Mindanao — the 1976 Tripoli Agreement — under extraordinarily complex international conditions involving Libyan patronage of the MNLF and Saudi mediation. 1. The Regional Executive (1993–1996): As ARMM Governor, he oversaw the foundational institutionalization of autonomous governance and, in his final act of service, stepped aside to enable the peaceful transfer of power to a former revolutionary, cementing the structural link between the 1976 diplomatic framework and the 1996 political settlement. Jurisprudential and Intellectual Contributions Beyond executive and diplomatic roles, Pangandaman made substantive intellectual contributions to the legal and jurisprudential architecture of Muslim Mindanao: As a member of the Bangsamoro Unity Bloc at the 1971 ConCon, he co-authored The Moro Problem: An Approach Through Constitutional Reforms, which remains a primary source document in Philippine constitutional law as it relates to Muslim autonomy. His advocacy for the formal recognition and integration of Islamic personal law — including Muslim inheritance law — within the regional legal framework of the ARMM contributed to the eventual codification of Sharia-based jurisprudence in the region. At the General Santos City consultations in 1995, Pangandaman advanced a "Two-Track Proposal" for the parallel implementation of the peace agreement and the regional governance framework, a pragmatic mechanism to manage the political transition from military integration to civilian governance. In his later years, he served in an advisory capacity to the Department of Social Welfare and Development (DSWD) for the ARMM, advocating during a 2007 JICA-sponsored workshop for funding for core shelters PAGE 7 and income-generating projects for internally displaced persons (IDPs) in conflict-affected Bangsamoro communities. Public Reception Public assessments of Pangandaman's legacy have been generally favorable within the Bangsamoro community, though not without acknowledgment of the structural imperfections of his administration. Community leaders and historians cited in regional accounts tend to emphasize his long-term contribution to institutional state-building over the shorter-term patronage issues that characterized his ARMM governorship. His death on October 15, 2013, prompted a formal statement of condolence from the ARMM's Bureau of Public Information, describing the region as being "in deep sorrow" over the loss of a founding leader. The simultaneous death of fellow ARMM figure Ali Bashir Lucman in the same week underscored the sense that a founding generation of Bangsamoro institutional leaders was passing from the scene. The Philippine Senate passed Senate Resolution No. 585 honoring the memory and contributions of Pangandaman, a recognition of the national significance of his career across multiple presidential administrations. Legacy The enduring legacy of Atty. Lininding P. Pangandaman may be assessed at three levels: Institutional: The administrative structures, executive orders, and regional ordinances produced during his ARMM governorship provided the functional scaffolding within which the 1996 Final Peace Agreement was implemented. While the ARMM was subsequently replaced by the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM) pursuant to the Bangsamoro Organic Law (Republic Act No. 11054, 2018), the precedents and institutional frameworks that Pangandaman helped establish remain embedded in the governance architecture of the successor body. Diplomatic: His successful negotiation of the 1976 Tripoli Agreement — the first formal instrument of peace between the Philippine state and the Bangsamoro revolutionary movement — established the normative and diplomatic parameters within which all subsequent peace negotiations were conducted. The Tripoli Agreement is described by scholars as the "Ur-text" of the Bangsamoro peace process. Cultural and Generational: Through the Basak Muslim Professionals movement, Pangandaman helped inaugurate a tradition of professional and intellectual leadership among the Maranao that influenced subsequent generations of politicians, lawyers, academics, and civil servants. Members of the Pangandaman family have continued to serve in prominent public roles in the Philippine government, including at the national level. His career embodies a governing philosophy that may be summarized as follows: that the legitimate grievances of the Bangsamoro are most durably addressed not through armed resistance alone, but through mastery of law, skilled diplomacy, and the construction of functioning institutions — a philosophy that retains its relevance in the ongoing project of Bangsamoro self-governance under the BARMM. Personal Life Pangandaman was married to Ester Pangandaman, who served as a senior official in the ARMM regional executive during his governorship. He was the father of several children; members of the Pangandaman family subsequently entered Philippine public life in various capacities at the regional and national PAGE 8 levels. He was a practicing Muslim whose faith informed both his diplomatic orientation — particularly in his role as ambassador to an Islamic state — and his advocacy for the formal recognition of Sharia law within the Philippine legal system. Pangandaman died in the early hours of Tuesday, October 15, 2013, at approximately 88 years of age. He was survived by members of his family and by a generation of Bangsamoro leaders whose political formation was shaped in significant part by the institutional framework he helped construct. Mohammed Hussein Pacasum Pangandaman (born January 17,
1978), more commonly known simply as Hussein Pangandaman
or by his initials HPP, is a Filipino politician and government
administrator from Lanao del Sur. He represented the 1st District of
Lanao del Sur in the House of Representatives during the 15th
Congress (2010 to 2013), and since 2023 he has served as
Administrator and Chief Executive Officer of the Authority of the
Freeport Area of Bataan (AFAB).
He comes from one of the most recognized political families in the
Bangsamoro region, and over the years his career has touched both
ends of the country: legislative work rooted in Mindanao and
executive leadership steering a major economic zone up north in
Luzon. Whether in Congress or at the helm of a freeport authority,
his work has consistently circled back to one theme, getting
investment and development moving in places that need it.

Early Life and Family
Pangandaman was born on January 17, 1978, into a Maranao
Muslim family with deep political roots in Lanao del Sur. His father
is Nasser C. Pangandaman Sr., a veteran public official who has
held several national-level posts over the years, including a stint as
Secretary of Agrarian Reform and, more recently, as Presidential
Adviser for Marawi Rehabilitation and Development under the
Marcos administration. His mother is Yasmin Pacasum-
Pangandaman, and the "Pacasum" in his own full name traces
directly back to her side of the family.

PAGE 2

Known For
Leading freeport investment growth in
Bataan; legislative advocacy for Lanao
del Sur cooperatives; member of the
Pangandaman political family of
Mindanao.
The Pangandaman name carries weight across Lanao del Sur, with
relatives who have served as mayors and provincial officials over
the decades. Hussein grew up inside that network of public service,
and it's not much of a stretch to say politics was less a career choice
for him than a family inheritance.
He is married, and photos from his 2023 oath-taking ceremony
show him and his wife alongside President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.
Beyond that, he keeps his immediate family life fairly private, and
details about children have not been made public.
Education
Information about Pangandaman's formal schooling is thin on the
public record. Like many figures from established political families
in the region, he most likely started out in schools in or around
Lanao del Sur before moving on to higher studies elsewhere, though
no specific university or degree has turned up in available records or
major profiles. This is one area where the public record simply
hasn't caught up with the man.
Career
Congressional Service (2010 to 2013)
Pangandaman entered electoral politics in 2010, running for the 1st District seat of Lanao del Sur under the Lakas-
Kampi-CMD banner. He won the seat in the May 2010 elections, though because of voting delays in parts of the
district, he didn't actually take his oath of office until November 15, 2010. He went on to serve out the remainder of
the term, until June 30, 2013, later sitting in the chamber as an independent.
During his time in the House, he filed legislation addressing local concerns, including House Bill No. 4706, and
pushed for measures supporting cooperatives and community development programs in his home district.
His tenure wasn't without controversy. Between 2008 and 2011, he was linked to a pair of physical altercation
incidents, one involving a golf course confrontation and another involving a security guard at Technohub, both of
which drew media coverage and prompted inquiries within the House. The matters were eventually resolved
through apologies issued by family members, and the complainants in at least one case later withdrew their
charges.
Authority of the Freeport Area of Bataan (2023 to present)
After leaving Congress, Pangandaman stayed active in public life, and in 2023 his career took an unexpected turn
northward. On April 28, 2023, President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. appointed him Administrator and CEO of the
Authority of the Freeport Area of Bataan, with the appointment formally announced by the Presidential
Communications Office on May 7, 2023, as part of a batch of fifteen appointees. He took his oath shortly after, in a
ceremony attended by President Marcos himself.

PAGE 3
Stepping into the role, Pangandaman has leaned into stakeholder engagement and operational efficiency as his twin
priorities, framing his job as building on what was already a functioning agency rather than reinventing it. Under
his leadership, AFAB has pursued international partnerships, including outreach trips to companies in Spain, South
Korea, and the United Arab Emirates, aimed at drawing fresh investment into the freeport. He has also pushed the
agency to widen its scope beyond traditional manufacturing into tech-based and knowledge-based industries, a shift
he has described as necessary for keeping the freeport relevant in a changing global economy.
Closer to home, his administration has worked on freeport infrastructure and community concerns alike, from
water supply improvements done in coordination with private partners, to the revival of the freeport's golf course
for leisure and tourism purposes, to regular dialogue with groups like the Bataan Economic Zone Neighborhood
Association on housing and security issues affecting freeport residents.
Major Works and Institutional Contributions
As a legislator, Pangandaman's contributions centered on cooperative-based poverty alleviation and economic
interventions tailored to Lanao del Sur's needs.
At AFAB, his leadership has focused on:
Positioning the freeport as a hub for business, industry, and community development.
Expanding international outreach to attract fresh investment.
Strengthening coordination with oversight bodies such as the Commission on Audit and the Bureau of
Customs.
Supporting diversification into sectors like manufacturing, defense-related production, and emerging
technology and aeronautics industries.
Reporting strong investment growth, with AFAB citing over seventeen billion pesos in committed
investments between May 2023 and May 2024 alone.
In recognition of his appointment, the Bangsamoro Parliament adopted Resolution No. 353 in June 2023,
congratulating him and citing his record of legislative leadership.
Awards and Recognition
Pangandaman has received a Leadership Award from the Bureau of Customs, Port of Limay, in recognition of his
contributions to trade facilitation and inter-agency cooperation. He continues to be recognized in AFAB
institutional events and Bangsamoro Parliament resolutions for his work in governance and public service.
Personal Life
Pangandaman keeps a fairly private personal life outside of his official duties. He is a Muslim of Maranao descent,
consistent with his family's heritage, and his wife has appeared alongside him at official functions, including his
2023 oath-taking. He divides his public life between two distinct communities nowadays, his roots in Lanao del
Sur and his current post in Bataan.

PAGE 4
Legacy and Impact
Pangandaman's career traces an unusual arc for a Philippine public official, moving from representing a conflict-
affected district in Mindanao to running a major economic freeport zone in Luzon. That shift says something about
adaptability in Philippine public administration, and at AFAB he has continued building on themes that go back to
his congressional years: investment, development, and service delivery, just at a different scale and in a different
setting. His earlier legislative work on cooperatives and local advocacy aimed at improving conditions in Lanao del
Sur, while his current role places him at the center of national economic strategy. The controversies from his
congressional years remain part of the public record, a reminder of the scrutiny that comes with public office, but
they have not prevented his continued appointment to leadership positions since.
Cultural Significance
As a Maranao politician turned national administrator, Pangandaman represents one thread of how Bangsamoro
voices have found their way into mainstream Philippine governance. His family's long-standing prominence
reflects the broader role that established clans continue to play in Bangsamoro political life and in regional peace-
building efforts. His current post at AFAB also stands as an example of a Mindanao-rooted leader stepping into a
national economic institution, bridging regional identity with broader national development goals.
References
Basic biography and photo provided by Bang Pacasum. (https://www.facebook.com/pacasum)

Diamond Ali Pacasum Pangarungan
Princess Diamond Ali Pacasum Pangarungan is a Maranao civic
leader, former legislator, and cultural heritage advocate from Lanao
del Sur. She spent the better part of three decades moving between
public office and community work, first as an Assemblywoman in
the Regional Legislative Assembly of the Autonomous Region in
Muslim Mindanao, and later as a fixture in nearly every major civic
organization Marawi City had to offer. Her name carries weight not
just because of the offices she held, but because of the institutions
she helped build from scratch, among them the Lanao People's Park
and Public Library and the Lanao Cultural Heritage Foundation,
both of which still serve her home province today. She is married to
Atty. Saidamen Balt Pangarungan, who would go on to serve as
Secretary of the National Commission on Muslim Filipinos and
later as Chairman of the Commission on Elections.
