BACKGROUND
Princess Diamond Ali Pacasum Pangarungan was born to Sheik
Abdul Rahman Pacasum and Bai a Labi Pala Ali of Baloi, Lanao del
Norte. Her family ties run deep into Maranao tradition, and that
grounding would later shape much of the cultural preservation work
she became known for. She is the spouse of Atty. Saidamen Balt
Pangarungan, former Secretary of the National Commission on
Muslim Filipinos and former Chairman of the Commission on
Elections, and together they have three children: Nikkolai,
Saidamer, and Ramayana Saidamen.

PAGE 2
cultural heritage leader from Lanao del
Sur
Known For
Founding the Lanao Cultural Heritage
Foundation and the Lanao People's Park
and Public Library
EDUCATION
She began her schooling at Raya Madaya Elementary School in
Marawi City before moving on to Jamiatul Philippines Al-Islamia
for her secondary education, also in Marawi City. She pursued her
college degree at the Philippine Women's University along Taft
Avenue in Manila, and later took her post graduate studies at the
University of Asia and the Pacific in Ortigas Center, Pasig City,
where she completed a one year study grant in Strategic Business and Economic Planning from 1996 to 1997.
CAREER
Pangarungan's career began in the halls of national government before it shifted toward regional politics and civic
work back home. From 1973 to 1975, she served as Executive Assistant at the Batasan Pambansa, which later
became the House of Representatives, in Batasan Hills, Quezon City. From there she moved to the Philippine
Amanah Bank in Manila, where she worked as Budget Officer from 1974 to 1976.
Her entry into elected office came in 1990, when she was elected Assemblywoman for the 1st District of Lanao del
Sur in the Regional Legislative Assembly of the Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao, based in Cotabato City.
She served that term until 1994, and was re-elected for a second term that ran from 1992 to 1997. During her years
in the assembly, she also took on national-level roles, serving as Commissioner of the National Commission on the
Role of Filipino Women from 1998 to 2000, where she represented Indigenous Cultural Communities for the
Autonomous Region in Mindanao, and as a Board of Governor for the Philippine National Red Cross National
Headquarters during that same period.
LEGISLATIVE WORK
As a legislator, Pangarungan authored the bill creating the Bureau of Cultural Heritage for the ARMM, a measure
that reflected her long standing interest in preserving Maranao and broader Bangsamoro culture through formal
institutions. She also filed several resolutions pushing for pilot projects in her home province, including the
establishment of a food terminal for Lanao del Sur, a drug rehabilitation center in Marawi City, intensified
irrigation canals for the province's low lying farming areas, and an integrated farming program spanning both
Lanao del Sur and Lanao del Norte.
INSTITUTIONAL CONTRIBUTIONS
Beyond her legislative work, Pangarungan built a long record of hands on civic projects in Lanao del Sur. She
established the first Provincial Skills and Livelihood Training Center at People's Park in Marawi City in 1993, and
between 1991 and 1996 oversaw the establishment of all 18 municipal plazas across the 1st District of Lanao del
Sur. From 1992 to 1994, she promoted a comprehensive livelihood training program aimed at barangay women and
out of school youth, and she also donated books to municipal libraries and public schools throughout the province.
In 1992, she played a catalyst role in establishing the Lanao People's Park and Public Library in Marawi City, an
institution she would go on to chair from 1990 to the present. That same civic instinct carried into her cultural
heritage work: in 2000, she founded the Lanao Cultural Heritage Foundation, Inc., serving as its Chairman and
President from then onward.

PAGE 3
MEMBERSHIP AFFILIATIONS
Pangarungan's reach across civic and women's organizations in Lanao del Sur is extensive. She served as Regional
Governor of the National Council of Women in the Philippines for the Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao
from 1998 to 1999, and as President of the Girl Scouts of the Philippines, Marawi City and Lanao del Sur Chapter,
from 1995 to 1997. She has led the Philippine Women's University Alumni Association's Lanao del Sur and
Marawi City Chapter as President since 1994, and earlier served as Director of Kiwanis International's Valle Verde
Chapter in Pasig City from 1994 to 1995.
Her organizational leadership also extended to education and interfaith civic life. She was President of the League
of Filipino Muslim Educators from 1993 to 1999, and President of the Rotary Marawi City Chapter from 1991 to
1995. She chaired the Philippine National Red Cross's Marawi City and Lanao del Sur Chapter from 1990 to 1994,
served as President of the Lanao del Sur Mayor's Wives Association from 1990 to 1995, and was Director of the
Fatima Sorority's Marawi City and Lanao del Sur Chapter, also from 1990 to 1994.
TRAININGS AND STUDY GRANTS
Pangarungan's record includes a wide range of in-service trainings and seminars tied to her work in governance,
health, and regional planning. Through the Philippine National Red Cross, she attended the 2nd Strategic Planning
Workshop Seminar for Board of Governors in October 1998, a Regional Training Program for Community Health
and Nursing Service in February 1999, an Orientation Session for Board Members in February 2000, and a
Strategic Planning Workshop and Session on Governance and Management in June 2000.
Her legislative training included the Parliamentary Procedures, Resolutions, Bills and Laws Drafting Workshop
Seminar held at the Congressional Training and Research Center in Batasan Hills, Quezon City, in October 1994,
as well as a Strategic Planning and Workshop session organized by the ARMM's Regional Planning and
Development Office in November 1996. On the international stage, she took part in the EACAD High Level Inter-
Governmental Meeting to Review Regional Implementation of the Beijing Platform for Action in Bangkok,
Thailand, in October 1999, the ASEAN Export Workshop on Operationalizing the Work Program Activities II in
Bandar Seri Begawan, Brunei Darussalam, in October 2000, and the APEC Summit on the Role of Women in
Countrywide Development held at Malacanang in Manila in July 2000. She also completed her one year study
grant in Strategic Business and Economic Planning at the University of Asia and the Pacific from 1996 to 1997.
RECOGNITION
Pangarungan's decades of public and civic service earned her recognition at multiple levels. The Philippine
Women's University named her a CAPA Awardee and Most Outstanding Alumni for the entire Philippines in 1995
to 1996. The Marawi City and Lanao del Sur Sultanate League honored her as Most Outstanding Muslim Women
Leader in 1992, 1993, and 1995, and the Mayor's League Association of Lanao del Sur Province gave her an
Achievement Awardee distinction in 1992. She was also recognized in 1992 as a catalyst in the establishment of the
Lanao People's Park and Public Library, a project she had championed from the ground up.
LEGACY
Pangarungan's legacy sits at the intersection of governance and grassroots civic building. Where many legislators
are remembered mainly for the bills they passed, she is remembered just as much for the institutions she physically
built and kept running long after her term ended, the municipal plazas, the skills training center, the public library,

PAGE 4
and the cultural heritage foundation that continues to carry her name in Marawi City and Lanao del Sur today. Her
work also helped spearhead Senator Santanina Rasul's "Tayo Ay Magbasa" literacy project across Lanao del Sur
and Marawi City in 1994, extending her reach into the province's broader push for education and literacy.

Datu Omar M.T. Pangarungan
Datu Omar M.T. Pangarungan is a distinguished Filipino diplomat and humanitarian whose career spans nearly
three decades. A Maranao noble and former Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA) economic diplomat, he is
renowned for his pioneering work in Middle Eastern diplomatic relations and his legendary crisis management
efforts evacuating Filipinos from war zones, particularly during the Yemen conflict. His legacy bridges traditional
Bangsamoro leadership with modern international relations.
Lead
Datu Omar M.T. Pangarungan stands as one of the Philippines'
most accomplished yet understated diplomats. His three decades
of service are marked by two defining legacies: pioneering the
nation's economic and cultural presence in the Middle Eastern
mainstream market, and becoming the architect of countless
Filipino rescues from active war zones through sheer ingenuity
and determination. As a Maranao, one of the major Bangsamoro
ethnic groups, he embodies the modern incarnation of the Datu
tradition, translating ancestral leadership into contemporary
international diplomacy.
Early Life and Heritage
Maranao Identity
Datu Omar was born into the noble Pangarungan lineage of the
Islamic City of Marawi. The title "Datu," held by his family for
generations, signifies authority and prestige within the Maranao
socio-political hierarchy.
He is a direct descendant of Sultan Amai Manabilang, one of the
most revered Bangsamoro leaders of the 20th century and a
visionary advocate for Muslim Mindanao's autonomy. This
genealogical connection placed him within an intellectual and
diplomatic tradition that valued cultural preservation, Islamic
scholarship, and progressive governance.
The Marawi he grew up in, despite decades of conflict and
external pressures, maintained its standing as a center of Muslim
learning and culture in the Philippines. This heritage instilled in
him a deep sense of responsibility toward both his ethnic
community and the broader Islamic world.

PAGE 3
The Lake That Defines a People
The Maranao are known as the "People of the Lake," their identity inextricably tied to Lake Lanao. This
geographic and spiritual centeredness shaped Pangarungan's worldview: a sense of place, a commitment to
protecting one's own, and a pragmatic approach to cultural survival. That sensibility would animate his entire
career.
Education and Formative Years
While formal institutional credentials are secondary to his decades of field expertise, Datu Omar developed
mastery across three critical domains:
International Trade and Tourism
He emerged as a specialist in mainstream Arab markets, with the rare ability to move fluidly between Philippine
business interests and the intricate hierarchies of Gulf Cooperation Council economies. His understanding of trade
protocols, visa regimes, and cultural expectations became indispensable to government and private sector
delegations.
Islamic Diplomacy
His religious identity as a Muslim was not decorative; it was foundational. He could speak to Arab leaders not as an
external representative but as a coreligionist, lending credibility to bilateral negotiations and fostering trust at levels
unavailable to non-Muslim diplomats. This capacity proved invaluable in building relationships with royal courts
and government officials across the GCC.
Crisis Management
Through firsthand exposure to humanitarian emergencies, Pangarungan developed expertise in conflict-zone
evacuation, safe passage negotiation, and the logistical choreography required to move vulnerable populations
through active war areas. This skill set became his calling.
Diplomatic Career: 28 Years in the Middle East
Economic Representation in the GCC (1990s-2010s)
For nearly three decades, Datu Omar served as the Philippine government's official economic diplomacy
representative to the Gulf Cooperation Council countries, including Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates,
Kuwait, and Qatar.
During this period, he spearheaded a strategic reorientation of Philippine-Arab relations. Prior to his tenure, Middle
Eastern markets were largely untapped by mainstream Philippine tourism and trade interests. He identified an
opportunity: the Gulf's affluent Muslim-majority population represented an underutilized consumer base for
Philippine goods, services, and destinations.

PAGE 4
Tourism and Trade Breakthroughs
Working with government tourism boards and the Department of Trade and Industry, Pangarungan systematized
Philippine tourism marketing for Arab audiences. He attended trade exhibitions, organized cultural showcases, and
facilitated introductions between Philippine entrepreneurs and Gulf-based business leaders. The results were
measurable: Philippine tourism and remittance flows from the GCC region increased substantially, and Philippine
goods gained market presence in Saudi supermarkets and retail networks.
His "conquest of the Arab mainstream market," as it is described in diplomatic circles, was neither military nor
aggressive, but rather a patient, persistent campaign of relationship-building that yielded long-term commercial
partnerships.
Presidential Missions
Pangarungan's reputation for excellence extended to the highest levels of government. He orchestrated and
facilitated state visits by Philippine presidents Fidel V. Ramos (FVR), Joseph Estrada, and Gloria Macapagal-
Arroyo (GMA) to GCC nations. In each case, his role was critical: coordinating logistics, briefing delegations on
cultural protocol, and translating the nuanced diplomatic language required for such high-stakes engagements.
These visits yielded tangible outcomes, from trade agreements to bilateral aid packages, and Pangarungan's
meticulous preparation was instrumental in their success.
Humanitarian Valor: The Man of Action
The Yemen Crisis (2014-2016)
Datu Omar's true calling revealed itself during the Yemeni conflict, particularly during the 2015-2016 escalation
when Saudi-led airstrikes and Houthi ground forces made Yemen one of the world's most dangerous operating
environments.
Thousands of Overseas Filipino Workers (OFWs) were trapped in Sana'a, the capital, with limited government
evacuation capacity. The Philippine government faced a diplomatic nightmare: how to extract its citizens from an
active war zone where both sides viewed foreign nationals with suspicion.
Pangarungan arrived in Yemen with a simple mandate: bring the Filipinos home.
The Bus Mission
What followed became the stuff of diplomatic legend. With commercial flights grounded and military airlifts
unavailable, Pangarungan implemented a plan that required equal parts audacity and cultural sophistication.
He rented a brand-new intercity bus and assembled a manifest of evacuees. The challenge: the bus would have to
pass through 27 Houthi rebel checkpoints across Yemeni territory to reach the port of Aden.
Rather than attempt subterfuge, Pangarungan sought out a locally respected Houthi community leader known for
supporting humanitarian efforts. He explained his mission directly: these are Filipino Muslims seeking safe passage
home; they pose no threat to your struggle; allowing them passage honors Islamic principles of hospitality and
mercy.

PAGE 5
The Houthi leader agreed. At each checkpoint along the route, his personal endorsement protected the bus. The
convoy navigated minefields of conflict, passing through territory where foreign nationals had recently been
kidnapped or killed, and arrived safely in Aden. The evacuees boarded transport home.
This operation, unnamed and unsung in official histories, exemplified Pangarungan's operational philosophy:
understand the local context, appeal to shared values, and execute with precision.
The Scope of Repatriation
The Yemen operation was not isolated. Throughout his career, Pangarungan oversaw or personally executed
repatriation missions for Filipinos stranded in Malaysia, across Sub-Saharan Africa, and in other politically volatile
regions.
His methodology was consistent: rapid intelligence gathering, identification of local power brokers or
peacekeepers, negotiation of safe passage, and careful orchestration of transport. Colleagues in the diplomatic
service described him as "a man of action who knows no sleep," a phrase that captured both his work ethic and his
obsessive commitment to outcomes.
The number of lives he saved through these operations remains uncounted; many occurred in coordination with
other agencies and were never formally documented.
Institutional Leadership: Bridging Marawi and the World
Jameo Al Islamie
In recent years, Pangarungan has shifted his focus to institutional development within Marawi. He serves as Vice
President for External Affairs at Jameo Al Islamie (the Islamic Center), one of Marawi's foremost cultural and
religious institutions.
In this capacity, he functions as a bridge between the Bangsamoro community and the international stakeholders,
investors, and organizations interested in supporting Marawi's recovery and development. His diplomatic
experience and global network make him invaluable in attracting international attention and resources to the city's
post-conflict rebuilding efforts.
BARMM Advocacy
Pangarungan has become a vocal proponent for the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao
(BARMM) as a destination for international trade, investment, and tourism. He leverages his three decades of
Middle Eastern experience to position Bangsamoro not as a conflict zone, but as an emerging market with unique
cultural and spiritual value.
He has advocated, in interviews and public forums, for the Philippine government to retain experienced diplomats
like himself, Rafael Seguis, and Jesus I. Yabes in senior advisory roles on OFW protection and humanitarian
affairs, particularly regarding Filipinos in war-torn nations. His argument: institutional memory and established
relationships save lives.

PAGE 6
Philosophy and Approach
Optimism Tempered with Caution
Throughout interviews and public statements, Pangarungan's worldview blends pragmatic caution with stubborn
optimism. He does not believe that cultures are incompatible or that conflicts are inevitable; rather, he operates
from the premise that shared interests and mutual respect can overcome political divides.
Self-Sacrifice as Imperative
A recurring theme in accounts of his work is his willingness to sacrifice personal comfort, sleep, and safety for
operational success. He does not position himself as a desk officer issuing instructions from afar; he is present,
sometimes in the most dangerous locations, personally ensuring that operations succeed.
Cultural Authenticity as Diplomatic Tool
Pangarungan never exploits his Muslim identity or Maranao heritage instrumentally or performatively. Rather, it is
the authentic foundation of his diplomatic method. His ability to navigate Arab power structures stems from
genuine cultural fluency and shared religious conviction. This authenticity is perceptible and disarms skepticism.
Results Over Recognition
He is notably indifferent to media coverage or public accolades. Colleagues describe him as motivated by the
tangible outcome, "uplifting emotions upon the successful saving of lives." This orientation makes him unusual in
diplomatic circles, where reputation and recognition often drive behavior.
Legacy
The Modern Datu
Datu Omar M.T. Pangarungan represents a contemporary reimagining of the Datu tradition. Historically, a Datu
was a leader responsible for the welfare of his people, a warrior and statesman who defended territory and
negotiated treaties. In the modern era, territorial defense has been replaced by economic and diplomatic
advancement, yet the underlying principle remains: a Datu serves his people, even at personal cost.
Pangarungan's legacy is thus both traditional and modernist. He honors the Maranao commitment to family,
community, and Islamic principles while deploying the tools of 21st-century diplomacy, international law, and
humanitarian logistics.
Maranao Representation
He has elevated the international visibility of Maranao intellectual and professional capacity. In Arab capitals and
international forums, he has consistently demonstrated that Muslims from the Philippines are sophisticated,
educated, and trustworthy partners in commerce and governance, countering stereotypes that have historically
marginalized the Bangsamoro diaspora.

PAGE 7
The Cost of Conflict
Implicitly, his life's work serves as documentation of the human cost of the Moro conflict and subsequent regional
instability. Every repatriation mission, every evacuee rescued from a war zone, represents a failure of peace-
building efforts and a testament to the desperation that conflict creates for ordinary working people seeking
livelihoods abroad.
Personal Life
Limited biographical details regarding his immediate family have been made public. He maintains strong ties to
Marawi and the broader Pangarungan clan, and resides periodically in the Islamic City while maintaining
international engagement.
Recognition and Honors
While Pangarungan has not pursued public recognition, his contributions have been acknowledged within
diplomatic circles and by various Bangsamoro cultural and civic organizations. His work with OFWs in crisis
situations has been cited in legislative discussions regarding Philippine foreign service reform.

Sultan Salic Manalusug Amai Manabilang
Pangarungan
Sultan Salic Manalusug Amai Manabilang Pangarungan, known by his honorary title Sultan Dimasangcay Sa
Dansalan, was a distinguished political leader and institutional steward who shaped the governance and
educational landscape of Lanao del Sur for decades. His legacy lives on through his role as the longest-serving
Senior Provincial Board Member of Lanao del Sur, his institutional leadership of the Pangarungan Islamic College,
and the continued prominence of the Amai Manabilang-Pangarungan lineage in Maranao political and cultural life.
A trusted appointee of President Ferdinand Marcos Sr., Sultan Salic navigated the complexities of Martial Law-era
governance while maintaining his commitment to Maranao institutions and educational advancement. His
leadership bridged traditional sultanate authority with modern provincial governance, establishing a political
dynasty that continues to serve Lanao del Sur through his descendants.

Background
Sultan Salic Manalusug Amai Manabilang Pangarungan was born into the prominent Amai Manabilang family, one
of the most influential royal houses in Lanao del Sur. His father, Datu Pangarungan Desalongan, was a respected
traditional leader who founded and led the Pangarungan Islamic College (PIC) and the Jameo Mindanao Al-Islamie
Islamic Center, establishing a foundation for Islamic education in the region. The Amai Manabilang lineage carries
deep historical significance in Maranao society, with ties to the traditional governance structures of the sultanate
system that predated Philippine colonial rule.
Growing up in this environment of traditional authority and educational advocacy, Sultan Salic inherited both the
political acumen and the commitment to Islamic scholarship that defined his family's contributions to Lanao. The
Pangarungan name became synonymous with educational excellence and political leadership in the Islamic City of
Marawi and the broader province of Lanao del Sur.

Political Career
Municipal Leadership
Sultan Salic began his public service career as Vice Mayor of the
Islamic City of Marawi, the cultural and political heart of the
Maranao people. In this role, he worked to advance the interests
of Marawi's residents during a period of significant political
transition in the Philippines. His service at the municipal level
provided him with deep insights into the everyday governance
challenges facing Lanao's urban center.
Provincial Governance
Sultan Salic's most enduring political legacy came through his
service as a Provincial Board Member of Lanao del Sur, where he
became the longest-standing Senior Provincial Board Member in
the province's history. This remarkable tenure reflected both his
political skill and the trust placed in him by Lanao del Sur's
electorate.
During the Martial Law period under President Ferdinand Edralin
Marcos Sr., Sultan Salic was appointed to key executive positions
within the provincial government. He served as both Acting
Governor and Vice Governor of Lanao del Sur, navigating the
complex political landscape of authoritarian rule while
representing the interests of the Maranao people. These
appointments demonstrated the Marcos administration's
recognition of Sultan Salic's leadership capabilities and his
influence within Lanao's political circles.
His provincial board service spanned multiple administrations and
political eras, giving him a unique perspective on the evolution of
local governance in Lanao del Sur from the Martial Law period
through the restoration of democratic processes.
Institutional Leadership
Pangarungan Islamic College
Following the death of his father, Datu Pangarungan Desalongan,
Sultan Salic assumed the presidency of the Pangarungan Islamic
College (PIC), becoming its longest-serving president. Under his
leadership, PIC continued its mission of providing Islamic
education to students in Lanao del Sur, serving as a vital
institution for the preservation and transmission of Islamic
scholarship in the region.

PAGE 3
Ethnic
Affiliation
Maranao
His stewardship of PIC reflected his commitment to educational
advancement and his dedication to maintaining the institutional
legacy established by his father. The college became a cornerstone
of Islamic learning in Mindanao, producing generations of
scholars, religious leaders, and community servants.
Jameo Mindanao Al-Islamie Islamic Center
Sultan Salic also served as President of the Jameo Mindanao Al-Islamie Islamic Center, another institution founded
by his father. This center played a crucial role in coordinating Islamic educational efforts across Mindanao and
promoting cultural and religious understanding within the Muslim community. His leadership of both institutions
demonstrated his dual commitment to formal Islamic education and broader community religious development.
Legacy and Family Succession
The Pangarungan-Amai Manabilang Dynasty
Sultan Salic's passing did not diminish the political and cultural influence of the Pangarungan-Amai Manabilang
family. His favorite grandson, Saidamen Balt Pangarungan, emerged as a towering figure in Philippine politics
and Maranao leadership. Saidamen Balt served as Governor of Lanao del Sur, Secretary of the National
Commission on Muslim Filipinos (NCMF), and Chairman of the Commission on Elections (Comelec), one of the
most powerful constitutional bodies in the Philippines. Following his grandfather's legacy, Saidamen Balt assumed
leadership of the Pangarungan Clan and currently holds the title of Sultan of Madaya in the Islamic City of
Marawi.
Sultan Salic's youngest son, Cabugatan Sa Bacolod Anwar Tahir Malomalo Amai Manabilang, continues the
family's engagement with traditional governance structures as the current Chairman of the Marawi Sultanate
League, an organization that coordinates the activities of Marawi's various sultanates and preserves traditional
Maranao leadership systems.
Family Connections
Sultan Salic's family ties extended to other prominent Maranao political families. He was first cousin to Sultan
Mastura Amai Manabilang, who served as Mayor and holds the title of Sultan Sa Ranao. This familial connection
further solidified the Amai Manabilang family's central role in both traditional sultanate governance and modern
electoral politics in Lanao del Sur.
The continued prominence of Sultan Salic's descendants in provincial governance, national politics, and traditional
sultanate leadership demonstrates the enduring impact of his political and institutional work. His grandson
Saidamen Balt, highly respected by the family, represents the successful transition of leadership across generations
while maintaining the family's commitment to public service.
Recognition and Influence
Sultan Salic's honorary title, Sultan Dimasangcay Sa Dansalan, reflected his status within the traditional Maranao
sultanate system and his connection to the historical governance structures of Lanao. The title "Dansalan" refers to
the traditional name for what is now the Islamic City of Marawi, emphasizing his deep roots in the region's

PAGE 4
political and cultural heritage.
His dual role as both an elected official under the Philippine government structure and a sultan within the
traditional Maranao system exemplified the complex political landscape of Muslim Mindanao, where modern
democratic institutions coexist with centuries-old sultanate governance. Sultan Salic successfully navigated both
worlds, earning respect in the halls of provincial government and in the traditional councils of Maranao royalty.
Impact on Lanao del Sur
Sultan Salic Manalusug Amai Manabilang Pangarungan's decades of service left an indelible mark on Lanao del
Sur's political institutions and educational landscape. His record as the longest-serving Senior Provincial Board
Member established a standard of longevity and consistent leadership that few have matched. His stewardship of
the Pangarungan Islamic College and Jameo Mindanao Al-Islamie Islamic Center ensured the continuation of his
father's educational mission and provided opportunities for Islamic learning across generations.
The political dynasty he helped establish continues to influence Lanao del Sur's governance, with his descendants
holding positions of authority at the provincial, national, and traditional sultanate levels. His life exemplified the
unique character of Maranao political leadership: rooted in traditional royal lineage, committed to Islamic
scholarship, and engaged with the modern structures of Philippine democracy.

Haron A. Pangcoga
Haron A. Pangcoga (December 30, 1956 – February 16, 2019)
was a Filipino Islamic legal scholar, educator, and traditional
leader from Tugaya, Lanao del Sur who spent nearly four decades
shaping how the Bangsamoro community understood and
practiced Islamic law in the Philippines. He served as a professor
and administrator at the Mindanao State University (MSU), most
notably as Director of the Shari'ah Center and as the Director of
MADARIS under the Department of Education, Culture, and
Sports (DECS) of the Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao
(ARMM). Beyond the academy, Pangcoga was enthroned in 2018
as the Diamla Sa Tugaya, one of the four principal traditional
leaders of his home municipality, a title that recognized his
lifelong work as a custodian of Maranao culture and custom. His
crowning scholarly achievement, the Islamic Law Dictionary, was
published posthumously in 2023 by Xavier University Press and
stands as the first comprehensive reference of its kind in the
Philippines. For those who knew him, Pangcoga's life embodied a
rare kind of synthesis: the ability to hold tradition and modernity
together without letting either one break.

PAGE 2
Ancestral Lineage and Early Life
Pangcoga was born on December 30, 1956, in Tugaya, Lanao del Sur, a municipality known throughout the Lanao
region as the artisanal heart of the Maranao world. Tugaya is the place where the Taritib and Igma (the traditional
order and consensus system of the Maranao) governs social life with a force almost equivalent to written law.
Growing up there wasn't simply a matter of geography; it meant being raised within a living framework of custom,
rank, and responsibility.
His family background placed him squarely within the upper tier of Maranao traditional leadership. He was a
nephew of Dr. Salipada S. Tamano, a widely respected figure in the Bangsamoro educational sector who served as
Regional Secretary of the DECS in the ARMM. His kinship network also included Ayonan "Datu sa Palao"
Pangcoga, a former Vice Mayor of Tugaya, and his sister, Hadja Moshrifah "Iram" Pangcoga-Acop, who remained
an active figure in community affairs. These connections were never just personal. They represented a web of
influence that drew together modern administrative authority and traditional communal governance.
His marriage to Hadja Hafsah "Norhaya" Manugangcar Zacaria deepened those roots considerably. Norhaya
came from the Sultanate of Tugaya lineage: her father was Sheikh Zacaria Moka Disomnong, a prominent business
leader during the early years of Dansalan (now Marawi City), and her mother, Hadja Omensalam Tocalo
Manugangcar Zacaria, carried the prestigious title of Bae a Labi a Diamla Sa Tugaya.<ref
name="salsila">Salsila/Genealogical record of Sultan Mohammad Muid Zacaria of Tugaya. Tugaya Artefacts Blog.
Retrieved March 11, 2026, from https://tugayaartefactsblog.wordpress.com/2014/02/25/salsilageneological-record-
of-sultan-mohammad-muid-zacaria-of-tugaya/</ref> The Zacaria family belonged to the Nine Maruhoms of
Tugaya, the founding lineages that have held sultanate positions across centuries of Maranao history.<ref
name="salsila" /> Through this marriage, Pangcoga became formally anchored to the Salsila (genealogical records)
of the Sultanate of Tugaya and took on the custodianship of the Amito Clan, a responsibility that would eventually
lead to his enthronement.
Together, Pangcoga and Norhaya raised ten children: Mohammad (married to Mohairah Salbo Pamlian), Yusoph
(married to Jalfah Salong Farhan), Zeenal Abdul (married to Faizah Bacaraman Matanog), Walid (married to Nor-
Aisah Molan Lomodag), Rohaida (married to Abdul Mughnie Marohombsar Gunting), Mohammad Rasul (married
to Omaimah Calauto Abdulazis), Alihassan (married to Hanifah Tamano Latiph), Rohanisa (married to Aleem
Abdul Rauf Sampaco Mapunud), Omar (married to Jannairah Guinar Matanog), and Rohanifah Goldie. His son
Walid Zacaria Pangcoga has since carried forward the family's documentary work, maintaining digital archives of
the Salsila and the history of the Sultanate of Tugaya.<ref name="salsila" />
Education and Professional Formation
Pangcoga entered Mindanao State University (MSU) in the mid-1970s, a period of intense political and cultural
awakening among Muslim students in the country. He earned his Bachelor of Arts in Islamic Studies in 1977,
giving him a solid grounding in theology, Islamic history, and jurisprudence. But he wasn't content to stay in one
lane. Recognizing that the Bangsamoro community needed leaders who could move between religious authority
and state administration, he pursued a Master in Public Administration in 1981, followed by a Master of Arts in
Shari'ah in 1988, the latter being a program that was at the forefront of reconciling the Philippine legal system
with Shari'ah principles.
His academic formation didn't stop there. He completed 24 units toward a Doctor of Philosophy and three years of
a Bachelor of Laws (LL.B.) at the MSU College of Law. The range of his study was intentional. He was building
the capacity to speak fluently in the languages of both the Ulama (Islamic religious scholars) and the secular legal
community.

PAGE 3
On the professional certification front, his record was equally deliberate. He passed the Career Service Professional
examination in 1977, the Shari'ah Bar Examinations administered by the Supreme Court of the Philippines in 1992,
and the Board Examinations for Teachers under the Professional Regulation Commission (PRC) in 1998. This
combination of administrative, legal, and pedagogical licensure was rare, and it gave him an unusual range of
authority. At different points in his career, he could function as a government official, a Shari'ah counselor, and a
classroom teacher, all with formal credentials to back each role.
Career
Early Teaching and International Exposure
Pangcoga's career began on the ground. He started as a teacher at Dansalan College in 1977 and moved on to teach
at MSU-Tugaya in 1979. These years gave him a firsthand understanding of how education actually worked (and
didn't work) in the Lanao countryside. A brief stint as an Administrative Manager in Saudi Arabia in 1982
broadened his perspective considerably. Living and working at the center of the Islamic world shaped his sense of
what Shari'ah could look like when properly institutionalized, and that experience informed much of his reform
work back home.
Faculty Career at MSU
Returning to the Philippines, Pangcoga joined the faculty of MSU – King Faisal Center for Islamic, Arabic, and
Asian Studies (KFCIAAS), where he rose from Instructor to full Professor over the course of nearly four decades.
The progression was steady and hard-earned. He taught courses in Muslim Personal Law, Islamic jurisprudence,
and Shari'ah practice, becoming one of the institution's most recognized voices on the intersection of religion and
law.
Director of MADARIS, DECS-ARMM (1992)
One of the defining chapters of Pangcoga's career came when he served as Director of MADARIS for the DECS-
ARMM. At the time, the Madrasah (Islamic school) system in the Philippines was largely informal. It operated on
community goodwill, with Ustads (male religious teachers) and Ustadjas (female religious teachers) receiving little
to no compensation from the state and working without any recognized professional standing.
Pangcoga changed that. In 1992, he proposed and implemented a licensure examination system for Madrasah
teachers. The goal was straightforward: bring Islamic education into the formal structure of the Department of
Education so that religious teachers could receive funded positions, regular salaries, and the professional
recognition they had long been denied. This was a bold move at the time. It required convincing both the
government bureaucracy and the traditional religious community that professionalization was not a threat to faith
but a support for it.
The reform worked. Thousands of teachers across the ARMM gained formally recognized positions as a direct
result of this initiative, and it laid the institutional groundwork for what would eventually become the nationwide
ALIVE Program (Arabic Language and Islamic Values Education) of the Department of Education.<ref
name="pia">Philippine Information Agency. (n.d.). Muslims affirm PH's first Islamic law dictionary banners
justice and compassion. Retrieved from https://pia.gov.ph/news/muslims-affirm-phs-first-islamic-law-dictionary-
banners-justice-compassion/</ref>

PAGE 4
Director of the Shari'ah Center, MSU (2015–2017)
Pangcoga's most focused period of institutional reform at the university came during his tenure as Director of the
Shari'ah Center from 2015 to 2017. He became the primary architect of the review programs for the Shari'ah Bar
Examinations, a national examination administered by the Supreme Court of the Philippines. He understood clearly
that the scarcity of qualified Shari'ah counselors was a serious bottleneck in the delivery of justice for Muslims.
Too few people were passing the bar, too few law schools were preparing graduates to work within Presidential
Decree 1083 (the Code of Muslim Personal Laws of the Philippines), and the communities that needed legal
representation the most were being left without it.
His work at the Shari'ah Center addressed this directly. He developed structured review materials, coordinated legal
training programs, and mentored the next generation of Shari'ah practitioners who would go on to serve in Shari'ah
courts across the ARMM and later the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM).
Scholarly Contributions
Reconciling Adat and Shari'ah
If there is one intellectual question that anchored all of Pangcoga's scholarly work, it's this: how do you harmonize
the divine principles of Shari'ah with the ancient Adat (customary law) of the Maranao people and the statutory law
of the Philippines? He didn't treat these as competing forces. He treated them as layers of a single living legal
tradition that needed careful documentation and thoughtful reconciliation.
His 1992 paper, Some Un-Islamic Provisions of Code of Muslim Personal Laws of the Philippines, was a direct and
critical engagement with that tension. He argued that for Shari'ah to serve Muslims effectively in the Philippines,
the Code had to be honest about where it diverged from classical Islamic jurisprudence, and those gaps needed to
be addressed rather than papered over.
In 2015, he produced Survey of the Customary Law of the Bangsa Moro, an ethnographic and legal map of Adat as
practiced across Bangsamoro communities. The work explored the Maranao Taritib, the intricate system of
protocols and genealogical lineages that governs disputes, marriages, and communal alliances among the Maranao.
His unpublished manuscripts, A Reviewer in Islamic Criminal Law and Shari'ah and Shari'ah and the Local Adat:
A Comparative Study of Their Differences, remain significant resources for researchers working on legal pluralism
in the Philippines.
The Islamic Law Dictionary (Posthumous, 2023)
The most consequential single work Pangcoga left behind is the Islamic Law Dictionary, published by Xavier
University Press in 2023, four years after his death.<ref name="xu">Xavier University Press Catalogue, October
2023. Retrieved via Scribd, March 11, 2026, from https://www.scribd.com/document/705866468/XU-Press-
Catalogue-October-2023</ref> It is the first comprehensive reference of its kind in the Philippines, providing
standardized Arabic and English definitions for legal terms used in Shari'ah courts and in the study of Adat.<ref
name="xu2">XU Press – Published Titles 2018–2023. Retrieved via Scribd, March 11, 2026, from
https://www.scribd.com/document/705865917/XU-Press-Published-Titles-2018-2023</ref>
The Philippine Information Agency (PIA) and Muslim legal advocates described the dictionary as a milestone for
justice and compassion in the Philippines.<ref name="pia" /> The reasons aren't hard to see. In Shari'ah courts,
terminology matters enormously. When a judge, a counselor, and a litigant are working from different

PAGE 5
understandings of the same Arabic legal term, the result is confusion at best and injustice at worst. The dictionary
standardizes that language, giving practitioners a shared foundation to work from.<ref name="pia" />
"A milestone for justice and compassion," wrote advocates in the Philippine Muslim community upon
the dictionary's release, noting that it demystifies Shari'ah as a system built on benevolence and
humanity rather than the harsh interpretations often found in mainstream public discourse.
The book was launched in the context of post-Marawi Siege recovery, which gave it added resonance. Marawi City
was still rebuilding, and the dictionary was received not just as a legal tool but as a contribution to the broader
intellectual recovery of a community that had been through a devastating ordeal. It was Pangcoga's way of saying,
in print and for the record, that the laws and traditions of the Bangsamoro had a place in the national story of the
Philippines.<ref name="pia" />
Traditional Leadership: Diamla Sa Tugaya
On February 24, 2018, Professor Haron A. Pangcoga was formally enthroned as the Diamla Sa Tugaya.<ref
name="sultan">Mohammad Muid Zacaria enthroned as Sultan of Tugaya. Tugaya Artefacts Blog. Retrieved March
11, 2026, from https://tugayaartefactsblog.wordpress.com/2014/02/25/mohammad-muid-zacaria-enthroned-as-
sultan-of-tugaya/comment-page-1/</ref> In the Maranao Taritib, the Diamla is one of four principal traditional
pillars of the community, alongside the Sultan, the Cabugatan, and the Rajamuda. The title belongs specifically to
the AMITO Clan, making Pangcoga's enthronement both a recognition of personal achievement and a fulfillment
of genealogical responsibility.
As Diamla, his most visible public mission was to transform Tugaya into what he called the "Center for Muslim
Culture and the Arts." He was deeply concerned that the traditional crafts of Tugaya, including brass casting,
woodcarving (Okir), and silver smithing, were quietly disappearing as younger generations moved toward urban
employment and as international trade undercut local artisans economically. He devoted significant energy to
encouraging Tugaya craftspeople to raise the quality of their work and to find sustainable markets for their
products.
His advocacy found national reach through Senator Loren Legarda's cultural programs Dayaw and Buhay na
Buhay, where he appeared as a spokesperson for Maranao artistry.<ref name="dayaw">Legarda, L. (n.d.). Dayaw
Season 2: The Art of the Vessel – Maranao, Tugaya. Facebook video. Retrieved from
https://m.facebook.com/lorenlegarda/videos/dayaw-season-2-the-art-of-the-vessel-maranao-
tugaya/10154869275988891/</ref> On these platforms, he made a point that was both practical and philosophical:
preserving traditional crafts wasn't just about keeping old techniques alive. It was a form of economic
empowerment, a way to maintain the decency and security of the community, and a statement that the Maranao
identity was worth protecting on its own terms.
Mentorship and Community Work
Outside his formal roles, Pangcoga was the kind of person students and younger colleagues genuinely sought out.
He was a founding father of the first Muslim Toastmaster Club at MSU-Marawi, believing that public speaking
and leadership skills were essential tools for Muslim youth navigating both traditional community life and modern
professional environments. He was also an active member of the Beta Sigma fraternity of Marawi and served as
an advisor to the Olympiads Tugayanians, a group that encouraged youth from Tugaya to compete and excel
beyond their hometown.

PAGE 6
These initiatives reflected a conviction that ran throughout his career: the Bangsamoro community could only
thrive if its young people were equipped to engage confidently with the wider world, and that confidence had to be
built at home.
Legacy
Professor Pangcoga's legacy works on three levels that build on each other.
At the level of knowledge, he moved Shari'ah in the Philippines from the realm of oral tradition and scattered
manuscripts toward a codified, accessible academic discipline. The Islamic Law Dictionary is the clearest evidence
of this, but it's the culmination of decades of writing, teaching, and institutional work that made the dictionary
possible.
At the level of profession, his Madrasah licensure reform in the 1990s turned Islamic teaching from an informal
religious service into a recognized career. Thousands of Ustads and Ustadjas across the ARMM gained economic
security and professional standing because of that decision. The ALIVE Program now operating in public schools
nationwide carries that reform forward.
At the level of culture, his work as Diamla used the weight of traditional leadership to reframe Maranao
craftsmanship as a serious national heritage asset, not a regional curiosity. By taking that argument to national
television and into formal advocacy, he helped ensure that the arts of Tugaya would continue to be seen as part of
the Filipino story.
His own words, shared in his final speeches, expressed what he understood his life's work to be:
He wished to be "remembered in books," not out of personal vanity, but from a deep conviction that
for a marginalized culture, the written word is the most durable shield against erasure, and that the
intellectual contributions of the Bangsamoro deserved recognition as potent elements in transitioning
to a better society.
Recognition and Public Presence
Pangcoga's recognition came in different forms across his career. Within MSU-KFCIAAS, he was acknowledged
as one of the most authoritative voices on Muslim Personal Law and Shari'ah practice in the Philippines. His
appointment as Director of the Shari'ah Center reflected the university's confidence in his ability to shape the
professional formation of the next generation of Shari'ah practitioners.
On the national stage, his appearances on Senator Loren Legarda's cultural programs brought Tugaya's heritage and
his advocacy for Maranao arts to a broad Filipino audience. The posthumous reception of his Islamic Law
Dictionary by the Philippine Information Agency and Muslim legal advocates further cemented his standing as a
contributor to the country's legal and cultural heritage.<ref name="pia" />
His enthronement as Diamla Sa Tugaya in 2018 was itself a public recognition by his own community of
everything he had built over a lifetime.

PAGE 7
Death
Professor Haron A. Pangcoga died on February 16, 2019, in the Philippines. He was 62 years old. He passed away
with the manuscript of his Islamic Law Dictionary completed but not yet published, a reminder that some of the
most important work a person does outlives them. The book would appear four years later, in 2023, through Xavier
University Press, and the community he served would finally have the reference he had prepared for them.
His death came just under a year after his enthronement as Diamla Sa Tugaya, at a point when he had never been
more fully himself: scholar, traditional leader, cultural advocate, and teacher, all at once.

title: Panolong, Allan Gani
text:
PAGE 1
Allan Gani Panolong
Atty. Allan Gani Panolong is a Filipino lawyer from Lanao del Sur and a proud member of the Meranao people —
the indigenous Muslim community of the Lake Lanao basin in Mindanao.
On July 1, 2025, he was sworn in as the 28th National President of the Integrated Bar of the Philippines (IBP) and
Chairperson of its 27th Board of Governors for the term 2025 to 2027, making him the first Muslim and the first
Meranao ever to lead the organization in its more than five decades of existence.
That milestone is more than a personal achievement — it represents something the Bangsamoro legal community
had long been waiting for: a seat at the very top of the Philippine legal profession for one of their own.
His journey to the IBP's highest post was one he earned step by step: chapter president, regional governor, national
executive vice president, and finally, national president — a trajectory that colleagues and observers have called a
genuine "rose from the ranks" story.
Contents

2 Education
3 Career

8 See Also

Early Life and Family Roots
Panolong comes from the heart of Meranao country in Lanao del Sur, with family roots connecting him to places
like Malabang and Butig — communities known for their deep cultural traditions, historical resilience, and the
distinct identity of the Meranao people.
Growing up in Lanao del Sur shaped who he is.
The province carries the weight of centuries of Islamic tradition, the enduring values of maratabat (roughly
understood as personal and family honor), and a community culture that places high regard on education and public
service.

Details about his immediate family remain largely private, which is
fairly typical of many Mindanao professionals in public life who
prefer to keep personal matters separate from their public roles.
What comes through clearly in his public persona, though, is a man
firmly grounded in his Meranao identity while navigating and
contributing to a national professional arena.
Education
Panolong earned his degree in law from the Mindanao State
University (MSU) College of Law, an institution with a well-
established reputation for producing lawyers who understand both
national jurisprudence and the particular realities of life in Mindanao.
He passed the Philippine Bar Examinations in 2006.
MSU later recognized him with its Outstanding Rawaten Alumni
distinction, an honor that acknowledges not just academic
performance but the kind of practical service and professional
leadership that reflects the university's broader mission.
For someone who would go on to lead the national bar, the MSU
College of Law was a fitting starting point — an institution that
understands what it means to serve a region that has long felt the
distance between itself and the corridors of national power.
Career
Government Service
Early in his legal career, Panolong served as an Associate Graft
Investigation Officer at the Office of the Ombudsman, the
independent government body tasked with handling complaints of
corruption and misconduct by public officials.
The work demanded sharp legal reasoning, strong ethical grounding,
and the ability to handle sensitive cases with both rigor and fairness
— qualities that would continue to define his professional reputation
in the years that followed.
He later crossed into elective public office, serving as a Provincial
Board Member (Sangguniang Panlalawigan) of Lanao del Sur,
where he represented his constituents at the provincial legislative
level.

PAGE 3
Executive Vice
President
Atty. Randall C.
Tabayoyong
Bar Leadership
Within the Integrated Bar of the Philippines, Panolong's rise was
deliberate and thorough.
He first led the IBP Lanao del Sur Chapter as its president, building credibility at the grassroots level of the
organization.
From there, he moved up to serve as Governor for Western Mindanao, representing the region's lawyers at the
IBP's national governing board.
His next step was the National Executive Vice President position for the 2023 to 2025 term, a role he served
under 27th IBP National President Atty. Antonio C. Pido.
During his tenure as EVP, Panolong also served as a member of the 26th Board of Governors, giving him close
exposure to national bar administration and governance before he took the top seat himself.
IBP National Presidency (2025–2027)
Oath-Taking
On July 1, 2025, the Supreme Court of the Philippines held a special session at its Session Hall in Manila for the
oath-taking of the 27th Board of Governors of the IBP.
Supreme Court Associate Justice Ramon Paul L. Hernando administered the oath of office to Panolong as the IBP's
28th National President and Chairperson.
Chief Justice Alexander G. Gesmundo and several other associate justices were present at the ceremony.
Joining Panolong in the oath-taking was Executive Vice President Atty. Randall C. Tabayoyong, who also serves as
Governor for Bicolandia, along with governors representing all major regions of the country.
Inaugural Address
In his remarks at the ceremony, Panolong underscored the strong partnership between the Supreme Court and the
IBP, pointing to their shared commitment to judicial excellence and the rule of law.
He affirmed the IBP's full support for the Supreme Court's Strategic Plan for Judicial Innovations (SPJI) 2022 to
2027, especially in the areas of judicial reform and innovation.
The tone of his address was clear: he intends to lead the bar not as a ceremonial figure but as a working partner
with the judiciary in advancing meaningful justice for all Filipinos.
Priorities and Agenda
As National President, Panolong has consistently emphasized that being a lawyer is a privilege that carries serious
obligations — not just to clients, but to the broader public.

PAGE 4
His administration's agenda centers on several key areas: strengthening the integrity and ethical standards of the
legal profession; expanding access to justice, especially in underserved and geographically remote communities;
deepening the IBP's pro bono and legal aid programs, including its involvement in the Unified Legal Aid Service;
supporting anti-political dynasty measures; and reinforcing the IBP's institutional role in upholding constitutional
values.
For Panolong, legal professionalism and social responsibility are not separate concerns — they belong together.
Cultural and Symbolic Significance
Panolong's ascent to the IBP's highest post carries meaning that goes well beyond his personal record.
For more than fifty years since the IBP was formally organized, its national leadership was drawn almost entirely
from lawyers based in or connected to traditional centers of legal practice in Luzon and the Visayas.
The election and assumption of a Meranao Muslim from Lanao del Sur as the IBP's national president signals a
shift in that pattern.
For the Bangsamoro people and Muslim Filipinos more broadly, his leadership represents a form of institutional
validation — proof that excellence and credibility in the legal profession are not tied to a particular region, religion,
or cultural background.
Colleagues and community members across the Bangsamoro region have described his election as a "proud
moment" not only for the Meranao but for the whole of Mindanao.
His story carries a particular resonance for young Muslim Filipinos studying law or entering public service: a
Meranao professional who built his career quietly, earned trust at every level of the bar, and eventually led the
entire Philippine legal community.
Personal Values and Public Image
From his public statements and conduct in office, Panolong comes across as principled, measured, and deeply
committed to institutional integrity.
He speaks with the practicality of someone who has worked at local, regional, and national levels of both
government and the bar — someone who understands both the grassroots reality of legal practice in Mindanao and
the broader demands of national leadership.
Colleagues describe him as focused on service, respectful of due process, and firm in his belief that the legal
profession is — and must be — a force for genuine societal good.
His Meranao identity is not a backdrop to his professional life — it is part of how he understands his
responsibilities as a lawyer and as a public servant.

title: Papandayan, Mauyag Balt Jr
text:
PAGE 1
Mauyag Balt Papandayan Jr
Mauyag "Jun" Balt Papandayan Jr. (born October 14, 1964, in Marawi City, Lanao del Sur) is a Filipino
politician, local executive, and legislator whose career has been defined by two things: a deep commitment to his
Maranao roots, and a willingness to fight for his constituents at every level of government — from the barangay all
the way to Batasan Pambansa.
He served as the long-running Mayor of Tubaran, Lanao del Sur, and went on to represent Lanao del Sur's 2nd
Congressional District in the 17th Congress of the Philippines (2016–2019) under the PDP-Laban banner.
His name is permanently embedded in Philippine legal history through the Supreme Court case Papandayan, Jr. v.
Commission on Elections (G.R. No. 147909), a decision routinely cited in law schools across the country when
studying electoral residency and democratic mandates.
Contents
1 BACKGROUND
2 EDUCATION
3 CAREER
3.1 Local Governance: Mayor of Tubaran
3.2 Congress: Lanao del Sur's 2nd District (17th Congress)
4 INSTITUTIONAL CONTRIBUTIONS
4.1 Lake Lanao Development Authority
4.2 Marawi Siege Reparation
4.3 Bangsamoro Basic Law
4.4 Infrastructure and Connectivity
4.5 Social Welfare and Gender-Responsive Facilities
5 LEGACY
6 RECOGNITION
7 CHALLENGES
8 SEE ALSO
9 REFERENCES
10 EXTERNAL LINKS
BACKGROUND
Papandayan grew up in Marawi City, surrounded by the political rhythms and traditional social structures of the
Maranao people.
His early career was decidedly unglamorous: he started as a municipal employee with the local government unit of
Bayang, Lanao del Sur, learning the inner workings of rural governance from the ground up.
That foundational experience would later shape how he approached both local administration and legislative work
— always through the lens of someone who had sat on the other side of the bureaucratic counter.

PAGE 2

His family carries significant traditional standing in Tubaran and the
wider Lanao del Sur area, rooted in the Pat a Pangampong sa Ranao
(the Four Principalities of Lanao), the historic system of Maranao
clan governance that continues to inform local leadership to this day.
EDUCATION
Formal details of his tertiary education remain largely out of the
public record.
What is clear is that his education was substantially practical: years
in local government service, navigating Lanao del Sur's complex
political landscape, gave him a working knowledge of Philippine
law, rural development, and community leadership that few
academic programs could replicate.
CAREER
Local Governance: Mayor of Tubaran
Papandayan's political career took a defining turn in the May 2001
local elections, when he ran for Mayor of Tubaran, Lanao del Sur.
His opponent, Fahida P. Balt, filed a disqualification case before the
Commission on Elections (COMELEC), arguing that Papandayan
was not a legal resident of Tubaran.
COMELEC agreed and disqualified him, just days before election
day.
Tubaran voted for him anyway.
Despite the disqualification order, he received the highest number of
votes, and he took the matter directly to the Supreme Court of the
Philippines.
On April 16, 2002, the Supreme Court En Banc reversed
COMELEC's decision in Papandayan, Jr. v. Commission on
Elections (G.R. No. 147909).
The high court found that Papandayan had maintained lifelong ties
to Tubaran: he owned property there, registered to vote there, and
had genuine roots in the community.
The ruling ordered his immediate proclamation as Mayor,
reinforcing the legal principle that the will of the electorate must be
respected when a candidate can demonstrate bona fide residency.

PAGE 3

Notability

consequential local leaders, known for
winning a landmark Supreme Court case that
defined residency standards in Philippine
election law, championing the Bangsamoro
Basic Law, and authoring legislation to
protect and develop Lake Lanao.
Known For

Pull Quote
"Addressing historical injustices against the
Moro people is the only path to permanent
peace."
He subsequently served multiple terms as Tubaran's municipal chief
executive.
Congress: Lanao del Sur's 2nd District (17th Congress)
In May 2016, Papandayan won the congressional seat for Lanao del
Sur's 2nd Congressional District under PDP-Laban, transitioning
from local to national politics.
He served from June 30, 2016, to June 30, 2019.
His legislative work during the 17th Congress covered a wide range
of concerns, all of them tied directly to conditions on the ground in
his district and the broader Bangsamoro region.
INSTITUTIONAL CONTRIBUTIONS
Lake Lanao Development Authority
Papandayan authored House Bill No. 2318, which sought to
establish a dedicated regulatory authority for Lake Lanao, the
second-largest freshwater lake in the Philippines.
The bill aimed to protect the lake's ecology, regulate its use, and
develop it as an economic resource for the surrounding communities
— a long-overdue framework for one of Mindanao's most vital
natural assets.
Marawi Siege Reparation
When the 2017 Marawi Siege erupted, Papandayan's personal
residence in Marawi City was caught in the crossfire between
Philippine military forces and Islamic State-linked militants.
That firsthand experience informed his co-authorship of early
foundational bills aimed at securing monetary compensation for
residents whose properties were destroyed during the five-month
siege — legislation that laid the groundwork for what later became
more formal reparation frameworks.
Bangsamoro Basic Law
He was among the vocal congressional advocates for the passage of the Bangsamoro Basic Law (BBL), which
eventually created the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM).
His position was direct: that acknowledging and addressing historical injustices against the Moro people was not
just morally necessary, but the only realistic foundation for lasting peace in Mindanao.

PAGE 4
Infrastructure and Connectivity
Papandayan filed legislation to convert the provincial road linking Butig, Lanao del Sur, to Barira, Maguindanao
into a national road.
This seemingly technical bill carried real consequences: reclassifying the road unlocked national funding,
improved military access to a historically volatile corridor, and opened the path for trade in previously isolated
municipalities like Butig and Tubaran.
Social Welfare and Gender-Responsive Facilities
He also sponsored localized versions of safety-net programs, including support for the Bayang Historical Park and
Convention Center, and advocated for gender-responsive facilities for female inmates within his district.
LEGACY
Papandayan's impact on Lanao del Sur is tangible.
The communities he served — Tubaran, Butig, and the municipalities along the Lanao-Maguindanao corridor —
are more connected today in part because of his legislative groundwork.
His structural framework for Lake Lanao's conservation has continued to guide environmental policy discussions
within BARMM.
And beyond infrastructure: his Supreme Court victory in 2002 produced a precedent that has since been cited
across the Philippines in cases involving electoral residency disputes, making his legal fight a contribution not just
to Tubaran, but to Philippine jurisprudence broadly.
His son, Khaledyassin Dimaporo Papandayan, now serves as Mayor of Tubaran — carrying the family's public
service tradition forward into a new generation.
RECOGNITION
Legal Legacy: Papandayan, Jr. v. COMELEC (G.R. No. 147909) is a frequently cited Supreme Court
precedent on electoral residency and the primacy of democratic mandates.
Traditional Leadership: As a member of the Pat a Pangampong sa Ranao, Papandayan holds significant
standing as a mediator in traditional Maranao clan disputes (maratabat matters), a role that operates
alongside, and often enables, his formal political work.
CHALLENGES
The 2017 Marawi Siege was both a personal and professional crucible for Papandayan.
His own home in Marawi City was damaged during the conflict, giving him direct, lived knowledge of what his
constituents endured.
Turning that grief into policy was not straightforward: reparation legislation for Marawi Siege victims moved
slowly through a complex legislative process, and many affected families waited years for meaningful relief.

PAGE 5
His decades in Lanao del Sur's political landscape also meant navigating the province's historically intense clan
dynamics, COMELEC disputes, and the security challenges of representing a district that includes conflict-affected
areas like Butig.

title: Papandayan-Ampatua, Zenaida
text:
PAGE 1
Zenaida Papandayan-Ampatua
Bai Zenaida Papandayan-Ampatua is a retired Meranaw educator, school administrator, and royal title holder
from Lanao del Sur who spent more than four decades in the Philippine public school system.
She rose from classroom teacher to Schools Division Superintendent, passing the Superintendent's Examination as
a topnotcher at just 34 years old, and went on to lead the Division of Lanao Sur II through some of its most
formative years.
A daughter of the late Superintendent Mauyag C. Papandayan Sr., she followed her father's footsteps into public
service and carried that legacy well beyond it, earning recognition not just as an educator but as a community
leader and traditional ruler.
She holds the royal title Sulutan a Bae sa Biabi, a distinction conferred by her clan that reflects her lineage from
the panoroganan communities of Bayang, Biyabi, Tatarikun, Pagayawan, and Tubaran — all considered noble seats
of leadership in the Lake Lanao area.
In 2025, she became the first recipient of the Bae a Rawaten Award of the Division of Lanao Sur II, a
prestigious recognition given to educators who have made exceptional and lasting contributions to the educational
system while exemplifying strong character as a public servant and community figure.
Contents

2 Education
3 Career

3.2 Rising Through the Ranks

3.4 Regional Leadership

Background and Lineage
Bai Zenaida comes from one of the more storied families in the Ranao educational tradition.
Her father, the late Superintendent Mauyag C. Papandayan Sr., served as Schools Division Superintendent of Lanao
Sur II, and Zenaida herself worked under his administration as Planning Officer during the early years of her
career.
Her family roots trace back to the noble communities of Bayang, Biyabi, Tatarikun, Pagayawan, and Tubaran — all
recognized as panoroganan (traditional seats of governance and prestige) within the Paengampong a Ranao.

She is married to Hon. Abdillah Ampatua, who served as
Municipal Mayor of Bayang, and together they raised seven

the Bangsamoro region.
Education
Even while serving as a division superintendent, Bai Zenaida
continued her own studies, a commitment that speaks to the
seriousness with which she treated educational leadership.
She earned her Master's Degree from Mindanao State
University (MSU), and later completed her Doctorate in
Educational Management from Xavier University in Cagayan
de Oro.
Earning a doctorate while managing a large and complex school
division wasn't a small thing, and it underscored the kind of
discipline she was known for — balancing the demands of
leadership, family, and scholarship at the same time.
Career
Early Years
Bai Zenaida started her career as an Elementary Classroom
Teacher in the Division of Marawi City.
She later transferred to the Division of Lanao Sur II, where she
took on the role of Music Coordinator, developing a reputation for
administrative capability that opened further doors.
She then served as Planning Officer under the administration of
her father, the late Superintendent Mauyag C. Papandayan Sr.,
before being promoted to Science Supervisor.
Rising Through the Ranks
Her advancement through the division was steady.

in-Chief, KAPRANON
After her father's retirement, she was promoted to Assistant
Schools Division Superintendent — and then, in 1988, she was
elevated to Schools Division Superintendent of the Division of
Lanao Sur II, having passed the Superintendent's Examination as
the topnotcher at the remarkable age of 34.
That achievement made her one of the youngest and most highly
qualified school administrators in the region at the time.
Leadership of the Division
Under her watch, the Division of Lanao Sur II became a model
division in the ARMM (Autonomous Region in Muslim
Mindanao), recognized for its programs, leadership culture, and
physical development.
Among her most tangible accomplishments during this period
were the construction of the LSII Sports Complex and the three-
story Division Office — at the time, the most admired division
building in the entire ARMM.
Both projects were accomplished despite limited resources, a point
often highlighted by those who worked with her during that era.
Before the Division of Lanao Sur II was split into two sub-
divisions, Bai Zenaida had already managed the full scope of that
large organization.
She later led Division of Lanao Sur II-A and then returned to
head the original Division in 2008, this time under the rallying
slogan: "LSII at Its Best."
Regional Leadership
Her influence extended beyond her own division.
She was elected President of the ARMM Superintendents
Association, a role that placed her at the center of regional
education policy conversations and gave her a platform to
advocate for improved standards across all ARMM school divisions.
She also attended numerous seminars and conferences at the national and international levels, broadening her
perspective and bringing back knowledge and best practices to her teams.
Recognition and Awards
Bai Zenaida accumulated a number of awards over the course of her career, including:
Most Outstanding Public Service Award from the Association of Media
Outstanding Superintendent Award from the Association of SDS (Schools Division Superintendents)

The Bae a Rawaten Award is a distinction given to educators who have demonstrated exceptional contributions to
educational improvement and who embody strong character as both a professional and a community leader.
Royal Title and Community Role
Beyond her career in public education, Bai Zenaida holds a recognized place in Meranaw society as Sulutan a Bae
sa Biabi.
This title reflects both her noble lineage and the trust her community places in her as a leader.
Her family connections span several of the Lake Lanao area's most historically significant communities, including
Bayang, Biyabi, Tatarikun, Pagayawan, and Tubaran — all panoroganan within the Paengampong a Ranao.
Those who know her describe the title as fitting, pointing to her consistent record of service and her reputation for
caring deeply about the people around her.
Personal Life
Bai Zenaida is married to Hon. Abdillah Ampatua, who served as Municipal Mayor of Bayang.
They have seven children:
1. Pisigi, wife of Hon. Atty. Saadudin Alauya Jr., a former Regional Assemblyman currently working at the
MSU System
2. Mayor Saharodin Maya
3. Sandra, married to Alexie
4. Tohami, Protocol Officer, BARMM Parliament
5. Aliza, wife of Mayor Hon. Mohammad Aquil Mamaenti and currently serving as DTI Provincial Director
6. Fahad
7. Rajiv
In retirement, she continues to serve her community, spending time with her family while remaining active in local
and traditional leadership.
Legacy
Bai Zenaida's career is the kind that leaves a mark you can still see decades later.
The buildings she built are still standing. The division she shaped is still recognized as a model institution. The
educators she mentored have gone on to lead their own schools and offices.
She did all of this while raising seven children, pursuing graduate studies, and carrying the weight of a royal title
and community leadership that came with its own set of responsibilities.
Those who worked with her in the Division of Lanao Sur II remember her as firm but caring, principled but human
— and that combination, more than any award or infrastructure project, is probably the truest measure of her
legacy.

PAGE 5
The Bae a Rawaten Award, named for a woman of wisdom worthy of emulation, feels like the right recognition for
someone who spent her life being exactly that.
References

Papandayan-Ampatua. KAPRANON, Official Publication of the Division of Lanao Sur II.
