Princess Fatima Parahiman
Atty. Princess Fatima T. Parahiman is a Maranao lawyer from Masiu,
Lanao del Sur who made history by placing 2nd in the 2019 Philippine
Bar Examinations, earning a rating of 89.523%.
She is recognized as the second female Bangsamoro lawyer to break into
the Top 10 of the Philippine Bar Examinations, following the pioneering
achievement of Judge Mylene Amerol-Macumbal in 2008.<ref
name="bangsamoro_parliament">Bangsamoro Parliament Resolution
No. 71, formally commending Atty. Princess Fatima T. Parahiman for
her achievement in the 2019 Philippine Bar Examinations.</ref>
Her historic placement came at a defining moment: the Bangsamoro
Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM) was still in its
earliest years, and Parahiman's success gave the region something
tangible and undeniable to point to, a Maranao woman from Lanao del
Sur competing at the very top of the country's most demanding
professional examination and winning.
To the Bangsamoro people, she isn't just a topnotcher. She's proof.
Contents
1 Early Life and Background
2 Education
2.1 University of the Philippines Diliman
2.2 University of the East College of Law
3 The 2019 Philippine Bar Examinations
3.1 Results and National Standing
3.2 Historical Significance
3.3 Humility as a Public Statement
4 Recognition and Honors
4.1 Bangsamoro Parliament Resolution No. 71
4.2 Cultural Honors
5 Cultural and Social Significance
5.1 A Symbol for the BARMM
5.2 Representation for Muslim Filipino Women
6 Legacy
7 See Also
8 Further Reading

PAGE 2
Early Life and Background
Parahiman grew up in Masiu, Lanao del Sur, a municipality situated along the shores of Lake Lanao in the heart of
Maranao country.
The Maranao are one of the major Muslim ethno-linguistic groups in the Philippines, known for a deep cultural
code called Maratabat, which carries ideas of honor, dignity, and collective pride. Growing up within that tradition
meant that Parahiman's personal achievements were always understood to carry weight beyond herself, that what
she accomplished reflected on her family, her community, and her faith.
Lanao del Sur, for all its cultural richness, has lived through decades of conflict, displacement, and
underinvestment. Against that backdrop, pursuing higher education at the country's most competitive universities
was not a small decision. It was a deliberate, sustained act of faith in what was possible.
That combination of cultural rootedness and personal determination would follow her through every stage of her
academic and professional life.
Education
University of the Philippines Diliman
Parahiman took her undergraduate degree at the University of the Philippines Diliman, the country's national
university and one of its most academically rigorous institutions.
She graduated Cum Laude with a degree in Economics, a discipline that gave her a structured way to understand
the systemic forces shaping communities like her own.<ref name="ue_profile">University of the East College of
Law records and publications on Atty. Princess Fatima T. Parahiman's academic distinctions.</ref>
Economics isn't a typical pre-law path, and that choice reveals something important about how she thinks. She
came into law not just as an advocate for individuals, but as someone who'd already spent years examining how
institutions work, and fail, and can be made to work better.
University of the East College of Law
For her Juris Doctor, Parahiman enrolled at the University of the East College of Law in Manila.
She didn't just survive law school. She led it. She graduated as Class Valedictorian, finishing at the top of her class
in a program that demands everything from its students.<ref name="ue_profile"/>
Her peers knew her as someone with quiet strength, someone who carried the pressures of law school with
steadiness and was active in the law student government. That combination of academic excellence and genuine
engagement with her community would become characteristic of everything she did after graduation.

PAGE 3
The 2019 Philippine Bar Examinations
Results and National Standing
The results of the 2019 Philippine Bar Examinations were officially released in April 2020. Out of 7,685 examinees
who sat for the exams, Parahiman placed 2nd nationally with a rating of 89.523%.<ref
name="sc_results">Supreme Court of the Philippines, Official Results of the 2019 Bar Examinations, released
April 2020.</ref>
That's a remarkable number under any circumstances. The Philippine Bar is notoriously difficult, and the exam
tests candidates across multiple subjects over several Sundays. Placing in the Top 10 requires not just intelligence
but months of total commitment, and doing it while maintaining her cultural and religious identity as a Hijabi
Muslim woman from Mindanao added dimensions to her achievement that numbers alone can't fully capture.
Historical Significance
Parahiman's 2nd place finish made her the second female Bangsamoro bar topnotcher in Philippine history,
following Judge Mylene Amerol-Macumbal, who placed in the Top 10 of the 2008 Philippine Bar Examinations.
<ref name="bangsamoro_parliament"/>
More than a decade had passed between Amerol-Macumbal's milestone and Parahiman's. The gap itself is part of
the story: Muslim Filipino women had been largely invisible in national narratives of legal excellence, and
Parahiman's placement brought that conversation back, loudly.
In a field dominated by graduates of Manila-based law schools and examinees from Luzon, her success reframed
what the Philippine legal community looks like and where its talent comes from.
Humility as a Public Statement
What came after the results were announced was almost as significant as the results themselves.
Parahiman spoke publicly about her experience of Tawakkul, the Islamic concept of surrendering one's outcomes to
God after doing one's best. She shared that she had dreamed she failed the exams, and that her journey through that
fear, and the relief on the other side, was inseparable from her faith.
That moment of vulnerability connected her to thousands of bar examinees across the country who had
also sat in fear, also prayed, and also hoped. She wasn't performing humility; she was living it out
loud.
In a culture that often treats topnotchers as superhuman, Parahiman made herself relatable. And in doing so, she
became a more powerful symbol, not just of excellence, but of what it looks like to pursue excellence while
remaining fully yourself.

PAGE 4
Recognition and Honors
Bangsamoro Parliament Resolution No. 71
The Bangsamoro Parliament passed Resolution No. 71 formally commending Atty. Princess Fatima T. Parahiman
for her historic placement in the 2019 Bar Examinations.<ref name="bangsamoro_parliament"/>
The resolution described her success as a "beacon of hope" for the youth of the BARMM, and called on the
Bangsamoro community to take inspiration from her example.
It was a rare moment of formal institutional recognition for an individual achievement, and it underscored how
seriously the Bangsamoro government understood the symbolic weight of what she had accomplished.
Cultural Honors
Within Maranao communities, Parahiman has been honored with the title Bae a Labi, a designation for noble
women of distinction whose conduct and achievement bring honor to their lineage and their people.
The title isn't handed out lightly. It speaks to a communal recognition that she hasn't just done well for herself; she
has carried something forward for the community.
Cultural and Social Significance
A Symbol for the BARMM
Parahiman's achievement landed at a historically significant moment. The Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in
Muslim Mindanao was established in 2019 under the Bangsamoro Organic Law, replacing the Autonomous Region
in Muslim Mindanao (ARMM). The region was, in its truest sense, just beginning.
Her bar placement offered early evidence that the Bangsamoro's human capital was not just competitive at the
regional level, but at the national level. She became, without ever seeking the role, a kind of living argument for
what the region could produce when its people were given the chance to compete on equal footing.
Representation for Muslim Filipino Women
As a practicing Muslim who wore the hijab throughout her academic career and into her professional life,
Parahiman also represented something important for young Muslim Filipino women who often feel the pressure to
choose between their faith identity and their professional ambitions.
She didn't choose. She brought both with her, all the way to 2nd place on the national bar.
That visibility matters. Young women across Lanao del Sur, Maguindanao, Tawi-Tawi, and the wider Bangsamoro
region saw someone who looked like them, prayed like them, and dressed like them achieving something that the
whole country was talking about.

PAGE 5
Legacy
Parahiman's legacy is still being written.
She belongs to a lineage of Bangsamoro women who have pushed into spaces where they were not expected and
did not simply survive those spaces but reshaped them. She follows Judge Mylene Amerol-Macumbal and stands
now as a reference point herself, the person that future Bangsamoro lawyers will look back at when they need a
reason to believe the distance is crossable.
Her story carries a quiet insistence: that excellence and identity are not in conflict, that you can be Maranao,
Muslim, and a woman, and still stand at the top of Philippine legal achievement. Not despite those things, but as
those things.
The Bangsamoro region has a phrase that captures this well. Mastura a Ranao, the beautiful lake, has always
produced people of depth and resilience. Parahiman is one of them, and she's shown that depth has no ceiling.

title: Paudac, Amerhassan C. Sr.
text:
PAGE 1
Amerhassan C. Paudac Sr.
Amerhassan C. Paudac Sr. (born in Lanao del Sur; also spelled Amerhassan Paudac) is a retired Filipino career
prosecutor and a member of the Maranao community of Bangsamoro. He served for decades as the City
Prosecutor of Parañaque City under the National Prosecution Service of the Department of Justice, making him
one of the most senior Muslim prosecutors ever to lead a major metropolitan prosecution office in the National
Capital Region.
For much of his professional life, Atty. Paudac carried a quiet but unmistakable weight: he was a son of the lake
region of Mindanao sitting at the apex of one of Metro Manila's busiest legal institutions. That combination, a
deeply-rooted Maranao identity and a command of the most demanding corridors of Philippine criminal justice,
defines his legacy. Upon his retirement in December 2025, the Integrated Bar of the Philippines (IBP) Lanao del
Sur Chapter recognized his lifetime of service with the Emerald Pillar of Law Award, a fitting tribute to a man
who spent his career as a literal pillar of the justice system.
Contents
1 Early Life and Family Background
2 Education
3 Career
3.1 Entry into the National Prosecution Service
3.2 Office of the City Prosecutor, Parañaque City
3.3 The Okada Manila Estafa Cases (2018)
3.4 Leadership and Institutional Stewardship
4 Achievements and Recognition
4.1 Emerald Pillar of Law Award
4.2 Recognition as a Trailblazer
5 Personal Values and Cultural Significance
6 Legacy
7 See Also
8 Further Reading
Early Life and Family Background
Atty. Amerhassan C. Paudac Sr. traces his roots to the heartland of Lanao del Sur in Mindanao, the ancestral
domain of the Maranao, one of the major Muslim ethnolinguistic groups of the Bangsamoro region.
The Maranao, whose name is derived from the word ranao meaning "lake," have historically built their civilization
around Lake Lanao and are known for a rich artistic tradition, a strong oral legal code, and an enduring
commitment to community and faith. It is within this cultural setting that Atty. Paudac grew up, absorbing the
values that would later shape how he approached his decades in public service: a sense of duty rooted in communal
responsibility, a respect for process, and an abiding faith in Islam.
He is married to Norminah Diampuan Dimaporo-Paudac, and together they built a family that has become
something of a professional dynasty in the Philippines. Their six children have pursued distinguished careers across
medicine, law, finance, international advocacy, and business:

PAGE 2

Dr. Ehsan Paudac is a physician, married to Dra. Wedad
Zainoden-Paudac.
Atty. Mohammad Fayez Paudac serves as Acting Chief of the
Legal Division in San Juan City, married to Princess Habibah
Sarip-Paudac, the Salaam TV Channel Manager and first Filipina
hijabi news presenter on national television.
Johayfah Paudac, CPA serves as Vice President at Deutsche
Bank, married to Atty. Anshary Saud Cosain, Legal Counsel of the
Philippine Statistics Authority.
Atty. Hasminah Paudac is an international lawyer and climate
change advocate, married to Aleem and Hafidh Abdulrakim
Tawano, a Shariah counselor.
Amerhassan Paudac Jr. is an entrepreneur and accountant.
Amerhussien Paudac, CPA serves as Vice President of Fortune
Care Philippines.
That six children from one household went on to hold positions in
banking, international law, government service, medicine, and media is
not coincidence. It is the direct fruit of values that Atty. Paudac and his
wife modeled throughout their lives: education as a path, integrity as a
non-negotiable, and public service as a calling.
Education
Atty. Paudac completed his legal education in the Philippines, passing
the Philippine Bar Examinations to qualify for entry into the National
Prosecution Service. The specific institution where he obtained his law
degree has not been confirmed in public records, and this article does
not speculate on that detail.
Throughout his career, he continued to deepen his professional
competence. He participated in advanced training programs through the
Philippine Judicial Academy (PhilJA) and the Department of Justice,
with particular focus on criminal procedure, evidence, and the
prosecution of complex financial crimes. These continuing legal
education programs were instrumental in preparing him to handle the
increasingly sophisticated criminal complaints that landed on his desk as
Parañaque grew into one of Metro Manila's most commercially active
cities.

PAGE 3
Career
Entry into the National Prosecution Service
Atty. Paudac joined the National Prosecution Service (NPS) after passing the bar, beginning what would become a
multi-decade career as a career prosecutor. The NPS, operating under the Department of Justice, is responsible for
the preliminary investigation and prosecution of all criminal complaints filed before Philippine courts. As a Muslim
professional working in the NCR's legal infrastructure, Paudac's career placed him in a context where Maranao and
Bangsamoro representation in Metro Manila's prosecutorial ranks was rare.
Office of the City Prosecutor, Parañaque City
Atty. Paudac would eventually rise to lead the Office of the City Prosecutor (OCP) of Parañaque City, the
primary prosecutorial body responsible for all criminal complaints filed within the jurisdiction of one of Metro
Manila's fastest-growing cities. The OCP-Parañaque handled a massive and diverse caseload: local criminal
complaints from individual complainants, complex intracorporate disputes, and high-profile cases involving major
institutions. As City Prosecutor, Paudac was the approving authority for all resolutions issued by his office,
exercising the final call on whether cases would be filed in court or dismissed.
Official records confirm him as head of the OCP-Parañaque, with the office at the time located at the 3rd Floor of
the City Hall Building, San Antonio Valley I, Sucat, Parañaque City.<ref name="docshare">DocShare. (n.d.).
OCP-Parañaque City office profile. Retrieved from
http://docshare01.docshare.tips/files/12904/129041296.pdf</ref> The IBP-Philippine Plaza de La Marina list also
confirms his designation as City Prosecutor, Parañaque.<ref name="ibp-pplm">Integrated Bar of the Philippines,
Philippine Plaza La Marina Chapter. (n.d.). List of Judges and Prosecutors. Retrieved from https://ibp-
pplm.org/list-of-judges-and-prosecutors/</ref>
The Okada Manila Estafa Cases (2018)
The most nationally prominent chapter of Atty. Paudac's career came in 2018, when his office handled the estafa
complaints filed by Tiger Resort Leisure and Entertainment, Inc. (TRLEI), the operator of Okada Manila in
Entertainment City, Parañaque, against Japanese gaming tycoon Kazuo Okada and his co-respondents.
TRLEI accused Okada of embezzling more than USD 10 million in company funds during his tenure as chief
executive officer, filing two separate estafa complaints before the Parañaque City Prosecutor's Office. The first
alleged that Okada caused the disbursement of approximately USD 3.15 million in company funds for his
consultancy fees and salaries without board authorization. The second involved the supply of LED strip lights to
Okada Manila through Okada's affiliated company, Aruze Philippines Manufacturing Inc. (APMI), for a contract
price of approximately USD 7 million.<ref name="inquirer-estafa">Inquirer Business. (June 16, 2018). Estafa
cases against Okada dismissed. Retrieved from https://business.inquirer.net/252576/estafa-cases-okada-
dismissed</ref>
On May 11 and May 15, 2018, Atty. Paudac's office issued resolutions dismissing both complaints for lack of
probable cause. In the first resolution, Paudac noted that the legal controversies were civil in nature, arising from
intracorporate disputes, and that the OCP could only take cognizance of complaints that are criminal in nature.<ref
name="inquirer-estafa" />

PAGE 4
The dismissals, however, became the subject of sharp controversy. TRLEI accused Paudac of gross partiality and
bias after portions of the yet-to-be-officially-released resolutions appeared on May 18 on the social media accounts
of Chloe Kim, a known companion of Okada, even as TRLEI's own legal counsels had yet to receive official copies
as of May 21.<ref name="pna-inhibit">Philippine News Agency. (May 23, 2018). Parañaque fiscal asked to
inhibit from estafa raps vs. Okada. Retrieved from https://www.pna.gov.ph/articles/1036337</ref>
"As city prosecutor, [Paudac] is expected to manifest such degree of impartiality which should not be
tainted by scintilla of doubt." — Tiger Resort Leisure and Entertainment, Inc., Motion for Inhibition
(2018)<ref name="rappler-inhibit">Rappler. (May 23, 2018). Parañaque prosecutor asked to inhibit
from Okada estafa complaint. Retrieved from https://www.rappler.com/business/203210-paranaque-
prosecutor-kazuo-okada-manila-estafa-complaint/</ref>
Paudac inhibited himself from the case by resolution dated May 28, 2018.<ref name="pna-doj">Philippine News
Agency. (n.d.). DOJ asked to indict Okada on USD10-M estafa cases. Retrieved from
https://www.pna.gov.ph/articles/1038479</ref> The Department of Justice subsequently ordered the National
Bureau of Investigation to probe the circumstances surrounding the premature disclosure of the resolutions, with
Justice Secretary Menardo Guevarra stating that "premature disclosure of orders and resolutions prior to official
release is not allowed unless there are compelling reasons."<ref name="pna-doj-probe">Philippine News Agency.
(n.d.). DOJ to probe Parañaque fiscal handling estafa raps vs. Okada. Retrieved from
https://www.pna.gov.ph/articles/1036614</ref>
Notably, the DOJ ultimately affirmed the merits of Paudac's dismissals. In December 2018, the DOJ issued a
resolution affirming the May 15, 2018 dismissal of the LED-supply estafa case, finding that TRLEI "failed to prove
that there is conspiracy" among the respondents.<ref name="bworld">BusinessWorld. (January 20, 2019). DoJ
affirms dismissal of estafa case vs Okada, others. Retrieved from https://www.bworldonline.com/editors-
picks/2019/01/20/209827/doj-affirms-dismissal-of-estafa-case-vs-okada-others/</ref> The legal reasoning behind
Paudac's resolutions, notwithstanding the procedural controversy, was thus upheld by the department.
The Okada Manila episode illustrates the kind of high-pressure environment that defined Paudac's leadership of the
OCP-Parañaque: a jurisdiction where the city's role as home to major casino resorts and business interests
frequently placed his office at the center of nationally consequential disputes.
Leadership and Institutional Stewardship
Beyond the high-profile cases, Atty. Paudac's sustained contribution to the OCP-Parañaque was organizational. He
led an office responsible for one of the most demanding dockets in the NCR, with a team of assistant city
prosecutors handling hundreds of cases across criminal categories. He was known for working within the "Pillars
of Justice" framework that underpins the National Prosecution Service's philosophy of fairness, accountability, and
due process.
The OCP-Parañaque under his leadership maintained the institutional pledge that defined its public posture:
"We undertake to provide every person equal access to justice, to faithfully safeguard constitutional
rights and to ensure that no one is deprived of due process of law."<ref name="docshare" />
Under Paudac's watch, the office served this mandate across the full spectrum of Parañaque's population, from the
city's working-class barangays to its entertainment and commercial districts.

PAGE 5
Achievements and Recognition
Emerald Pillar of Law Award
In December 2025, upon his retirement from government service, Atty. Paudac was honored with the Emerald
Pillar of Law Award by the Integrated Bar of the Philippines (IBP), Lanao del Sur Chapter. The award
recognized his lifetime of dedication to the rule of law, his decades of service in the National Prosecution Service,
and his role in anchoring the institutional credibility of the Parañaque prosecution office.<ref name="source-
doc">Source document: Atty. Amerhassan C. Paudac. Biographical brief submitted for BangsamoroPedia. (2025).
</ref>
The "Pillar of Law" recognition is among the IBP's most meaningful tributes, reserved for senior members of the
bar who have demonstrated sustained fidelity to the ideals of the legal profession. That the recognition came from
the IBP's Lanao del Sur Chapter, the chapter rooted in his Maranao homeland, carries particular significance: it was
his own community acknowledging a son who carried their name with distinction into the highest offices of Metro
Manila's justice system.
Recognition as a Trailblazer
Atty. Paudac's significance extends beyond his own record. By reaching the position of City Prosecutor in the NCR
as a Muslim professional from Lanao del Sur, he became a visible example that the Bangsamoro community's
capacity for professional excellence was not limited by geography. At a time when Muslim Mindanaoans in Metro
Manila's legal institutions were few, his presence at the helm of the OCP-Parañaque carried a representational
weight that went beyond his individual performance.
His career demonstrated that the values of the Maranao, rooted in a tradition that prizes both learning (ilmu) and
honor (maratabat), translated powerfully into the demands of modern state institutions.
Personal Values and Cultural Significance
Atty. Paudac's public identity is inseparable from his faith and his ethnicity. As a practicing Muslim and a Maranao,
he navigated a predominantly Christian institution, the Philippine legal system, without abandoning either his
cultural grounding or his professional obligations. He is a living example of what Bangsamoro scholars and
advocates often describe as the capacity of Muslim Filipinos to contribute to national institutions while remaining
rooted in their own heritage.
His family's collective achievement reflects his personal conviction that education and integrity are not just
individual virtues but communal ones. Six children in six different professional fields, all at senior levels, is not an
accident of talent. It's the product of a household that treated learning as worship and service as obligation.
His children's careers also span the full arc of Bangsamoro professional aspiration: from Atty. Hasminah's work in
international law and climate advocacy, to Atty. Mohammad Fayez's government legal service, to Princess Habibah
Sarip-Paudac's pioneering presence as the first Filipina hijabi to appear as a news presenter on national television,
<ref name="barmm">Bangsamoro Information Office. (March 30, 2024). Breaking stereotypes as an empowered
Bangsamoro hijabi. Retrieved from https://bangsamoro.gov.ph/news/latest-news/breaking-stereotypes-as-an-
empowered-bangsamoro-hijabi/</ref> the Paudac family's story is, in many ways, a microcosm of the Bangsamoro
community's journey into the mainstream of Philippine professional life.

PAGE 6
Legacy
Atty. Amerhassan C. Paudac Sr. leaves behind a record defined by longevity, institutional commitment, and cultural
courage. For decades, he led one of Metro Manila's most active prosecution offices, navigating complex criminal
litigation, high-profile controversies, and the daily demands of a system where justice can be slow and the
pressures can be enormous.
His legacy is also familial and communal. The legal dynasty he and Norminah built is not just a point of family
pride: it is a public argument, made in the form of six distinguished careers, for the capacity of the Maranao people
and the broader Bangsamoro community to excel in every domain of Philippine society.
When the IBP-Lanao del Sur Chapter placed the Emerald Pillar of Law Award in his hands in December 2025, it
was recognizing more than years of service. It was acknowledging a man who, for decades, quietly held up a
portion of the edifice of Philippine justice, carrying the weight of his community's hopes alongside his docket.
He is, in the truest sense of the word, a pillar.

title: Pendatun, Salipada K.
text:
PAGE 1
Datu Salipada K. Pendatun
Born

Pikit, Cotabato, Moro Province
(present-day North Cotabato),
Philippines

Salipada K. Pendatun
Datu Salipada K. Pendatun (December 3, 1912 – January 27,
1985) was a Maguindanaoan lawyer, soldier, legislator, and one of
the most consequential figures in the political history of Muslim
Mindanao.
He was the first Filipino Muslim elected to the Philippine Senate,
and the first to hold the rank of Brigadier General in the Armed
Forces of the Philippines.
For close to five decades, Pendatun moved with ease between two
worlds: the traditional datu leadership of Mindanao, rooted in
Islamic law and sultanate lineage, and the modern republican state
centered in Manila.
He chose neither to romanticize the old order nor to abandon it.
Instead, he became a practitioner of what might be called
constitutional Moro politics, insisting that the Bangsamoro people's
best path forward was not through armed separation but through
mastery of the very institutions that had historically excluded them.
His career touched nearly every major chapter of 20th-century
Philippine history: American colonial transition, Japanese
occupation, postwar reconstruction, Cold War geopolitics, and the
turbulent years of martial law.

EARLY LIFE AND ETHNIC
AFFILIATION
Salipada K. Pendatun was born on December 3, 1912, in Pikit,
Cotabato, during the waning years of the American-administered
Moro Province.
It was a time of enormous flux: the old sultanate structures were
being systematically dismantled and replaced by a colonial
bureaucracy, and local datu families were navigating an uncertain
transition between two very different political orders.
Historical records also note family roots in Pagalungan, suggesting
the family maintained connections across several communities in
the Cotabato Basin.
Ethnic Identity and Royal Lineage
Pendatun was Maguindanaoan, belonging to one of the principal
Muslim ethnolinguistic communities of Mindanao and a people
with a documented history of statehood going back to the 16th
century.
He was not simply born into a prominent family. He was born into royalty.
His lineage traced directly to the royal houses of the Maguindanao Sultanate, and further still to Sharif
Kabungsuan, the Johor-born Arab-Malay Islamic missionary who arrived in Mindanao in the early 1500s,
converted the local population, married into the ruling Iranun aristocracy, and established the Sultanate of
Maguindanao.
This ancestry carried weight in the world Pendatun grew up in. Being a descendant of Sharif Kabungsuan was not a
mere genealogical detail; it conferred religious legitimacy, political authority, and community trust in ways that no
elected title could fully replicate.
That dual identity, as a traditional datu and as a citizen building a career within the Philippine state, became the
defining tension and the defining strength of his entire public life.

PAGE 3
FAMILY AND PERSONAL LIFE
Paternal Influence
Pendatun's father, Datu Pendatun, was a local leader of considerable influence who recognized early that the world
his son would inherit was going to be very different from his own.
On his deathbed, Datu Pendatun gave his son a piece of advice that would prove remarkably far-sighted: pursue a
Western, secular education alongside the traditional Islamic upbringing.
He did not frame this as a compromise of identity. He framed it as a tool of service, the most practical thing a
young Maguindanaoan datu could do to protect his people in the coming decades.
Salipada took that counsel to heart and ran with it.
Kinship Networks
Like most prominent datu families in Muslim Mindanao, the Pendatuns were woven into a web of matrimonial and
political alliances that connected them to other powerful clans across the region.
His family ties linked him to the Matalams and the Paglases, two of the most influential political dynasties in
Cotabato and Maguindanao.
That network did not simply benefit him. It also meant he carried responsibilities, expectations, and loyalties that
shaped every political decision he made.
His grandson, Ibrahim "Toto" Paglas III, later carried forward something of his grandfather's model, combining
traditional datu authority with modern corporate and political leadership in Maguindanao.
Interpersonal Style
To his peers and inner circle, Pendatun was simply "Sali."
He was described physically as stocky and solidly built, with a presence that commanded attention without
demanding it. He had the kind of natural charisma that worked equally well in a Maguindanaoan community
gathering and in the halls of the Manila Congress, which is rarer than it sounds.
EDUCATION
Following his father's counsel, Pendatun pursued formal education with unusual speed and focus.
He completed his elementary schooling in just three years rather than the standard course, a detail that speaks to
either exceptional ability or extraordinary determination, or both.
He finished his secondary education in Cotabato before relocating to Manila to attend the University of the
Philippines, the country's flagship state university.
He earned his Associate in Arts degree from UP in 1934, then continued to the UP College of Law, graduating with
a Bachelor of Laws in 1938.

PAGE 4
He passed the Philippine Bar Examination that same year.
While at UP, Pendatun also participated in the Reserve Officers' Training Corps (ROTC), laying the groundwork
for a military career that would define the most dramatic years of his life.
It is worth pausing on this combination of qualifications. By 1938, Pendatun was a licensed lawyer, a trained
reserve officer, a hereditary datu, and a descendant of the founder of the Maguindanao Sultanate. He was twenty-
five years old.
WORLD WAR II GUERRILLA LEADERSHIP
The Japanese invasion of the Philippines in December 1941 transformed Salipada Pendatun from a young
politician into a legend.
When Bataan fell in April 1942 and the remaining United States Army Forces in the Far East (USAFFE) in
Mindanao capitulated, many Filipino officers had little choice but to surrender or go into hiding.
Pendatun refused to surrender.
He took to the hills and began organizing what would become one of the most effective armed resistance networks
in wartime Mindanao.
Building the Resistance
He started with the Bolo Battalion, a local fighting unit named after the traditional Filipino bladed weapon,
drawing from Moro fighters in and around Pikit.
What distinguished Pendatun's approach from the outset was his determination to build a coalition, not a sectarian
force. He actively recruited both Muslim and Christian fighters, a significant undertaking in a region where
religious and cultural divisions ran deep.
The Bolo Battalion grew into the Muslim-Christian Guerrilla Movement, and that formation was eventually
formalized into the Bukidnon-Cotabato Force (BCF), a unified military unit integrated into the broader anti-
Japanese resistance across central and northern Mindanao.
This was not simply a military achievement. It was a political one. In a landscape where the Japanese occupation
was actively trying to exploit Muslim-Christian divisions to fracture the resistance, Pendatun was building a force
that crossed those lines deliberately.
Major Tactical Operations (1942–1943)
The BCF under Pendatun was operationally aggressive. His forces did not wait for liberation. They went looking
for the enemy.
In September 1942, he launched a direct assault on the Japanese garrison in Pikit.
In October 1942, his forces raided the Japanese base in Kabacan.
In December 1942, they eliminated the enemy garrison in Kitaotao, Bukidnon, and conducted a rescue operation
freeing Filipino prisoners of war held at Camp Casisang.

PAGE 5
Beginning in January 1943, Pendatun's forces began a sustained two-month siege of the Japanese garrison in
Malaybalay, Bukidnon, one of the more ambitious sustained operations carried out by any guerrilla force in
Mindanao during the occupation.
The Japanese occupation command took notice. They placed a price on his head.
Pendatun survived through a combination of tactical agility and the fierce loyalty of local civilian networks who
sheltered him and fed his forces intelligence. His ability to maintain that loyalty across religious and community
lines was, in many ways, his greatest operational asset.
His wartime performance earned him formal recognition by his peers: he was promoted to the rank of Brigadier
General in late 1942, becoming the first Filipino Muslim to reach general officer status in the national military.
POLITICAL CAREER
After liberation, Pendatun transitioned into civilian governance and built a legislative career that would span nearly
four decades and multiple presidential administrations.
Cotabato Provincial Board and Governorship (1938–1945)
Pendatun had actually entered politics before the war. He was appointed to the Cotabato Provincial Board in 1938
and was formally elected to that post in 1940.
In 1945, President Sergio Osmeña appointed him Provincial Governor of Cotabato to oversee the enormous task of
postwar rehabilitation across the undivided province.
It was a fitting first executive assignment for a man who had spent the occupation years fighting to keep the
province free.
Senate (1946–1949): A Historic First
In 1946, Pendatun made history.
He was elected to the Philippine Senate, becoming the first Filipino Muslim ever to win a seat in the upper house
of the national Congress.
The significance of this was not merely symbolic. The Senate was the most powerful legislative body in the
country, and Moro Filipinos had been effectively absent from it since the Philippine Commonwealth was
established. Pendatun's election signaled that Moro participation in national politics was not just possible. It was
real.
Presidential Adviser and Return to Congress (1950–1972)
After his Senate term, President Elpidio Quirino appointed Pendatun as Technical Adviser to the President from
1950 to 1953, with a specific focus on Mindanao affairs and the government's anti-communist strategy in the
region.
He returned to elective office in 1958 when he won a seat in the House of Representatives, representing Cotabato.
He would hold that congressional seat across multiple consecutive terms until 1972.

PAGE 6
During his time in the House, he served as Speaker Pro Tempore from 1962 to 1967, one of the most senior
leadership roles in the chamber.
Batasang Pambansa (1984–1985)
Even into his seventies, Pendatun remained politically active.
He returned to legislative service under the Kilusang Bagong Lipunan (KBL) party, winning a seat in the Regular
Batasang Pambansa representing Maguindanao in 1984.
He again served as Speaker Pro Tempore during this final term.
He was still serving as an assemblyman when he died on January 27, 1985.
MAJOR WORKS AND INSTITUTIONAL CONTRIBUTIONS
Legislative Legacy
Across his decades in Congress, Pendatun focused his legislative energy on practical, structural integration: new
municipalities, public schools, and road networks across the Cotabato Basin.
He sponsored bills that brought government presence, literally and physically, to communities that had been
historically peripheral to the national project.
He also worked on legislation that championed constitutional protections for cultural minorities and pushed for the
formal recognition of Muslim customary laws within the Philippine judicial system, an early and largely
unrecognized forerunner to the legal pluralism debates that would become central to Bangsamoro governance
negotiations decades later.
Global Diplomacy
Pendatun served as the first Muslim delegate representing the Philippines to the United Nations, attending key
assemblies in both New York and Paris.
In that role, he positioned the Philippines as a sympathetic voice for post-colonial states in Asia and the Middle
East.
His Islamic identity was not incidental to that diplomacy. It was an asset. He was able to open doors with Arab
nations that a non-Muslim Filipino diplomat might not have, and he used that access to build early diplomatic
relationships that served the country's broader foreign policy interests.
Islamic Preservation and Civil Society
Outside his government roles, Pendatun co-founded Ansar El Islam (Helpers of Islam) alongside other prominent
Muslim Filipino leaders including Domocao Alonto and Udtog Matalam.

PAGE 7
The organization focused on the preservation and development of Islamic faith, education, and cultural heritage in
the Philippines, functioning as a non-violent vehicle for Moro identity at a time when the Bangsamoro community
was navigating significant demographic and political pressure in Mindanao.
It was, in its own way, another expression of Pendatun's core belief: that the best defense of Moro identity was
organized, peaceful, civic engagement.
AWARDS AND RECOGNITION
Pendatun's wartime record and public service earned him several of the Philippines' most distinguished honors.
The Distinguished Conduct Star, the second-highest military decoration awarded to Armed Forces of the
Philippines personnel, was conferred on him for conspicuous gallantry and wartime leadership in Mindanao.
He received the Philippine Legion of Honor for his civic and statesmanlike service.
His promotion to Brigadier General, formally recognized in late 1942, made him the first Filipino Muslim to hold
general officer rank in the national military.
DEATH
On January 27, 1985, Salipada K. Pendatun died in Manila from injuries sustained in a severe automobile accident.
He was seventy-two years old, and he was still in office at the time of his death, serving as an assemblyman in the
Regular Batasang Pambansa.
The circumstances of his passing, dying in service, not in retirement, were in their own way consistent with the life
he had lived. He never really stopped working.
His death marked the close of a generation: the pioneer cohort of Moro legislators who had built their careers in the
immediate postwar republic, before the separatist movements, before martial law reshaped the political landscape,
before the Bangsamoro question became the protracted armed conflict it would become in the 1970s.
LEGACY, IMPACT, AND CULTURAL SIGNIFICANCE
Bridging the Center and Periphery
Pendatun's most enduring contribution was not any single law he passed or battle he won. It was the argument his
career embodied: that Moro Filipinos could engage the Philippine state on their own terms without surrendering
their identity.
When later movements like the Moro National Liberation Front (MNLF) chose armed revolution, Pendatun had
already spent decades making the opposite case. He believed the Bangsamoro people could achieve meaningful
self-determination, protect their faith, and correct historic injustices by mastering state institutions and reshaping
them from within.
Whether that path was ultimately sufficient is a question that historians and the Bangsamoro people themselves
continue to debate. But Pendatun pursued it with complete conviction and real results.

PAGE 8
Geopolitical Philosophy
Pendatun was a committed anti-communist throughout his political career.
He argued, with notable rhetorical force, that the Christian and Islamic worlds shared a fundamental theological
common ground in their belief in God, and that this shared monotheism could serve as a combined ideological
bulwark against communist expansion in Southeast Asia.
During the height of the Vietnam War, he went as far as offering to mobilize thousands of Filipino veterans and
reserve officers to assist South Vietnam against communist forces, a proposal that reflected both his anti-
communist convictions and his continuing sense of regional responsibility.
Toponym and Monuments
Few Filipino politicians of any era have had their name embedded into the physical landscape as thoroughly as
Pendatun.
A municipality in Maguindanao del Sur, General Salipada K. Pendatun, was established and named in his honor,
ensuring that his name is now literally part of the geography of the region he spent his life serving.
Camp Brigadier General Salipada K. Pendatun, located in Parang, Maguindanao, serves as the regional
headquarters of the Police Regional Office of the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region (PRO-BAR).
The National Historical Commission of the Philippines (NHCP) has installed a permanent bronze historical marker
at his birthplace, formally certifying his standing as a National Statesman.
These are not minor recognitions. They represent an institutional consensus that Salipada Pendatun belongs not
only to the history of Muslim Mindanao but to the history of the Philippine Republic itself.
REFERENCES
Source: Online deep research (https://tinyurl.com/32v7e3jh)

Philippine Engineering and Agro-Industrial College, Inc.
(PEACI) is a private, non-stock, non-profit higher education
institution based in Marawi City, Lanao del Sur, in the Bangsamoro
Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM). It primarily
serves local students with programs focused on engineering,
technology, education, health sciences, business, and Islamic studies.
Founded as one of the first private engineering schools in the Marawi
area, PEACI emphasizes practical education, character development,
and contributions to regional development amid the unique socio-
economic and cultural context of Mindanao. It operates basic
education (elementary, secondary, and senior high school) alongside
tertiary programs and has demonstrated resilience, notably
continuing operations and supporting student completion during and
after the 2017 Marawi Siege.
Contents
1 History and Founding
2 Institutional Development and Campus
3 Vision, Mission, and Philosophy
4 Academic Structure and Programs
5 Student Life, Organizations, and Traditions
6 Administration and Governance
7 Accreditation and Recognition
8 Significant Milestones

Community
11 Legacy and Impact
12 Research Assessment
History and Founding
A group of young engineers led by Dr. Rasid M. Paca (an associate
professor at Mindanao State University-Marawi) established PEACI
in 2007. It was duly registered with the Securities and Exchange
Commission as a non-stock, non-profit entity. The institution opened
its doors to students in 2008.
Founders and early leadership include: Dr. Rasid M. Paca
(founding president); Engr. Salem S. Usman; Engr. Basher U. Bula;
Engr. Hadji Nor Tingag M. Paca; Engr. Cosain P. Mambuay; Engr.

PAGE 2
Education, College of Nursing, College of
Arts and Sciences in Islamic Studies, plus
basic and technical-vocational education
Recognition
CHED-recognized private higher
education institution in the Bangsamoro
region
Notability
One of the first private engineering
schools established in Marawi City,
offering the region's earliest local access to
civil, mechanical, and electrical
engineering education
Known For
Sustaining educational operations and
producing licensed professionals despite
the disruption of the 2017 Marawi Siege
Pull Quote
"Educating Marawi's engineers, even
through siege and rebuilding."
Abdulzamad R. Mala-amama; Engr. Ansary Hadji Zaman; and Engr.
Khalid D. Ansano. Many held government or academic engineering
positions in Lanao del Sur and nearby areas.
Initial offerings in 2008 focused on Bachelor of Science in Civil
Engineering (BSCE), Mechanical Engineering (BSME), and
Electrical Engineering (BSEE), plus complete basic education
(kindergarten through secondary). It positioned itself as the premier
private engineering provider in Marawi City and Lanao del Sur. Over
time, it expanded into agro-industrial, business, education, health,
and Islamic studies programs.
Dr. Rasid M. Paca, a mechanical engineer with additional
qualifications in agricultural engineering, law, and public
administration, has been central to its leadership. He later served in
senior roles at MSU, including as Executive Vice President.
Institutional Development and Campus
PEACI began in modest facilities and has grown, with current
operations centered at Datu Gonsi Street (or similar nearby addresses like Datu Conding St.), Brgy. Lomidong
(Barrio Salam), Marawi City. It maintains a campus environment described as peaceful and conducive to
learning.
The institution navigated challenges like the Marawi Siege (2017), relocating or adapting to ensure educational
continuity and celebrating post-siege achievements, such as civil engineering licensure passers.
Vision, Mission, and Philosophy
Philosophy: Committed to the total development of honest, trustworthy, and God-fearing individuals in the
pursuit of truth, virtue, justice, equality, and the highest degree of academic excellence.
Vision: To become a modern world-class institution of the highest academic excellence in the region
(originally framed for the ARMM).
Mission: To introduce reforms contributing to peace, prosperity, equality, and sustainable development; lead
in science, technology, arts, and sports; serve as a catalyst for economic, cultural, socio-political, and agro-
industrial progress; and promote poverty alleviation, employment, and improved quality of life.
Academic Structure and Programs
PEACI organizes programs under several colleges:
College of Information Technology and Engineering: BS Civil Engineering, BS Electrical Engineering,
BS Information Technology.
College of Arts, Sciences and Education: BS Accountancy, BS Social Work, BS Criminology, BEEd
(General Education and Early Childhood Education), BSEd Mathematics, Certificate in Professional
Teaching.
College of Nursing: BS Nursing.

PAGE 3
College of Arts and Sciences in Islamic Studies: Kuliyato Shari'ah, Kuliyato Tarbiyah, Diploma in Arabic
Language, programs for Asatidh (educators), with influences from curricula like those of Al-Imam
University and Islamic University of Madinah.
It also offers basic education (elementary, secondary, senior high with strands like STEM, ABM, HUMSS, TVL-
CSS) and technical-vocational programs under TESDA (e.g., Computer Systems Servicing NC II, Agricultural
Crops Production).
Programs are CHED-recognized.
Student Life, Organizations, and Traditions
Student activities include the PEACI Supreme Student Government (PSSG), debate clubs (e.g., participating in
MSU debate championships), and various academic organizations. The institution promotes holistic development,
community engagement, and cultural relevance, including Islamic studies.
Administration and Governance
As a private non-stock corporation, governance follows its articles and by-laws, with a board and president
(founding leadership prominent). It operates under Philippine education laws, CHED, DepEd, and TESDA
regulations.
Accreditation and Recognition
PEACI appears in CHED lists of recognized private higher education institutions in the Bangsamoro region.
Specific program accreditations beyond CHED recognition (e.g., PAASCU or PTC-ACBET for engineering) are
not prominently detailed in public sources reviewed; engineering programs follow standard CHED policies.
Significant Milestones
2007: Founding.
2008: Opening of classes.
Post-2017 Marawi Siege: Continued operations and produced licensed professionals.
Expansion into diverse programs including nursing and Islamic studies.
Strong performance in certain licensure exams (e.g., Social Work pioneering batch).
Notable Alumni and Faculty
Public information on widely recognized notable alumni remains limited. Faculty include practicing engineers,
educators from state universities, and specialists in Islamic studies trained in Middle Eastern institutions. Founders
often hold concurrent government or academic roles.

PAGE 4
Contributions to Education, Society, and the Bangsamoro Community
PEACI provides accessible higher education options in a region with historical challenges, focusing on engineering
and technical skills relevant to infrastructure and agro-industrial needs. It supports peace and development goals
through its mission and community-oriented programs, contributing to local human capital in BARMM. Its
resilience during crises exemplifies commitment to educational continuity.
Legacy and Impact
As a relatively young institution, PEACI's legacy centers on pioneering private engineering education in
Marawi/Lanao del Sur and expanding access to diverse, culturally attuned programs. It aims to produce
professionals who contribute to regional progress, poverty alleviation, and sustainable development.
Research Assessment
This article draws primarily from the institution’s official historical page, CHED listings, public Facebook
communications, and cross-referenced secondary sources. Information is consistent across available references. No
major factual conflicts were identified; the school’s self-reported history aligns with its CHED recognition.
Verified Facts: Founding year and founders; initial programs; location in Marawi City; CHED recognition;
expansion of offerings; resilience post-Marawi Siege.
Information Not Yet Verified: Detailed current enrollment figures, comprehensive alumni lists with prominent
achievements, specific higher-level accreditations (beyond CHED recognition), audited financials, or exhaustive
facility inventories. In-depth academic outputs (research publications) were not prominently surfaced in general
searches.
Research Gaps: Limited independent third-party profiles or historical newspaper coverage (common for newer
regional institutions). Further primary sources, such as SEC filings for governance details or official CHED
program-specific authorizations, would strengthen the record. As of 2026, PEACI continues active enrollment and
operations.

title: Pimping, Mahadi M.
text:
PAGE 1
Mahadi M. Pimping
𝗛𝗼𝗻𝗼𝗿𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗟𝗲𝗴𝗮𝗰𝘆 𝗼𝗳 𝗝𝘂𝗱𝗴𝗲 𝗠𝗮𝗵𝗮𝗱𝗶 (𝗿𝗮𝗵𝗶𝗺𝗮𝗵𝘂𝗹𝗹𝗮𝗵) 𝘑𝘶𝘳𝘪𝘴𝘵, 𝘚𝘵𝘢𝘵𝘦𝘴𝘮𝘢𝘯, 𝘢𝘯𝘥 𝘗𝘦𝘢𝘤𝘦𝘮𝘢𝘬𝘦𝘳. 🕊️
He wore many hats across four decades of public service, and each one tells a piece of Mindanao’s story.
𝗞𝗲𝘆 𝗛𝗶𝗴𝗵𝗹𝗶𝗴𝗵𝘁𝘀:
📥 𝘽𝙪𝙧𝙚𝙖𝙪 𝙤𝙛 𝘾𝙪𝙨𝙩𝙤𝙢𝙨 Began his career in public service at the Bureau of Customs in Cagayan de Oro,
handling tariffs and trade at one of Northern Mindanao’s busiest ports.
🏛️ 𝙇𝙤𝙘𝙖𝙡 𝙂𝙤𝙫𝙚𝙧𝙣𝙢𝙚𝙣𝙩 𝙇𝙚𝙖𝙙𝙚𝙧𝙨𝙝𝙞𝙥 Entered local government service as 𝗩𝗶𝗰𝗲 𝗠𝗮𝘆𝗼𝗿 𝗼𝗳 𝗠𝗮𝗿𝗮𝘄𝗶 𝗖𝗶𝘁𝘆
following the 1980 local elections. During his tenure, he witnessed and became part of the city’s most significant
milestones, the official adoption of the title “Islamic City of Marawi” through City Council Resolution No. 19-A on
April 15, 1980. He also played a key leadership role during the city’s political transition, assuming the office of
Mayor in 1984 after the incumbent mayor was elected to the Batasang Pambansa.
Following his tenure as 𝗖𝗶𝘁𝘆 𝗠𝗮𝘆𝗼𝗿, he served as 𝗣𝗿𝗼𝘃𝗶𝗻𝗰𝗶𝗮𝗹 𝗔𝗱𝗺𝗶𝗻𝗶𝘀𝘁𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗼𝗿 of Lanao del Sur during the
administration of his grandson, 𝗚𝗼𝘃𝗲𝗿𝗻𝗼𝗿 𝗔𝘁𝘁𝘆. 𝗦𝗮𝗶𝗱𝗮𝗺𝗲𝗻 𝗣𝗮𝗻𝗴𝗮𝗿𝘂𝗻𝗴𝗮𝗻, in 1986.
🌾 𝘼𝙜𝙧𝙖𝙧𝙞𝙖𝙣 𝙅𝙪𝙨𝙩𝙞𝙘𝙚 Served as the 𝗣𝗿𝗼𝘃𝗶𝗻𝗰𝗶𝗮𝗹 𝗔𝗴𝗿𝗮𝗿𝗶𝗮𝗻 𝗥𝗲𝗳𝗼𝗿𝗺 𝗔𝗱𝗷𝘂𝗱𝗶𝗰𝗮𝘁𝗼𝗿 (𝗣𝗔𝗥𝗔𝗗) for (DAR) in Lanao
del Sur and Lanao del Norte, helping farmers to protect their rights to the land they cultivated and ensuring the fair
administration of agrarian laws. In this capacity, he became known for resolving complex agrarian disputes with
fairness and deep respect for the rule of law.
🏗️ 𝙂𝙤𝙫𝙚𝙧𝙣𝙢𝙚𝙣𝙩 𝙇𝙚𝙜𝙖𝙡 𝙎𝙚𝙧𝙫𝙞𝙘𝙚 Rose to become 𝗥𝗲𝗴𝗶𝗼𝗻𝗮𝗹 𝗟𝗲𝗴𝗮𝗹 𝗖𝗵𝗶𝗲𝗳 of the Department of Public Works
and Highways (DPWH), provided legal counsel involving major government infrastructure and public works
projects across Central Mindanao.
⚖️ 𝙅𝙪𝙙𝙞𝙘𝙞𝙖𝙧𝙮 Culminated his distinguished legal career as a 𝗠𝘂𝗻𝗶𝗰𝗶𝗽𝗮𝗹 𝗧𝗿𝗶𝗮𝗹 𝗖𝗼𝘂𝗿𝘁 (𝗠𝗧𝗖) 𝗝𝘂𝗱𝗴𝗲, dedicating
himself to the fair and impartial administration of justice.
In addition to his government service, he was active in civic leadership. He served as 𝗣𝗿𝗲𝘀𝗶𝗱𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗼𝗳 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗥𝗼𝘁𝗮𝗿𝘆
𝗖𝗹𝘂𝗯 𝗼𝗳 𝗠𝗮𝗿𝗮𝘄𝗶, where he championed humanitarian service, community development, and fellowship.
🏫 𝙁𝙖𝙢𝙞𝙡𝙮
Judge Pimping was married to 𝗕𝗮𝗲 𝗦𝗼𝗹𝗮𝗶𝗰𝗮 “𝗙𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗺𝗮 𝗭𝘂𝗵𝗿𝗮” 𝗧𝗮𝗵𝗶𝗿 𝗠𝗮𝗹𝗼𝗺𝗮𝗹𝗼 𝗔𝗺𝗮𝗶 𝗠𝗮𝗻𝗮𝗯𝗶𝗹𝗮𝗻𝗴
𝗣𝗮𝗻𝗴𝗮𝗿𝘂𝗻𝗴𝗮𝗻-𝗣𝗶𝗺𝗽𝗶𝗻𝗴, who bears the royal title 𝗕𝗮𝗲 𝗟𝗮𝗯𝗶 𝗮 𝗣𝗮𝗻𝗼𝗿𝗼𝗴𝗮𝗻𝗮𝗻 𝘀𝗮 𝗧𝗼𝗿𝗼𝘀. Together, they were
blessed with eight children.
𝘈𝘵𝘵𝘺. 𝘗𝘪𝘮𝘱𝘪𝘯𝘨’𝘴 𝘭𝘪𝘧𝘦 𝘸𝘢𝘴 𝘥𝘦𝘧𝘪𝘯𝘦𝘥 𝘣𝘺 𝘶𝘯𝘸𝘢𝘷𝘦𝘳𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘱𝘶𝘣𝘭𝘪𝘤 𝘴𝘦𝘳𝘷𝘪𝘤𝘦, 𝘧𝘳𝘰𝘮 𝘤𝘶𝘴𝘵𝘰𝘮𝘴 𝘢𝘥𝘮𝘪𝘯𝘪𝘴𝘵𝘳𝘢𝘵𝘪𝘰𝘯 𝘵𝘰 𝘭𝘰𝘤𝘢𝘭
𝘨𝘰𝘷𝘦𝘳𝘯𝘢𝘯𝘤𝘦, 𝘧𝘳𝘰𝘮 𝘭𝘦𝘨𝘢𝘭 𝘢𝘥𝘷𝘰𝘤𝘢𝘤𝘺 𝘵𝘰 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘫𝘶𝘥𝘪𝘤𝘪𝘢𝘳𝘺, 𝘢𝘯𝘥 𝘧𝘳𝘰𝘮 𝘨𝘰𝘷𝘦𝘳𝘯𝘮𝘦𝘯𝘵 𝘭𝘦𝘢𝘥𝘦𝘳𝘴𝘩𝘪𝘱 𝘵𝘰 𝘤𝘰𝘮𝘮𝘶𝘯𝘪𝘵𝘺
𝘱𝘦𝘢𝘤𝘦𝘮𝘢𝘬𝘪𝘯𝘨. 𝘏𝘪𝘴 𝘭𝘦𝘨𝘢𝘤𝘺 𝘰𝘧 𝘪𝘯𝘵𝘦𝘨𝘳𝘪𝘵𝘺, 𝘫𝘶𝘴𝘵𝘪𝘤𝘦, 𝘢𝘯𝘥 𝘤𝘰𝘮𝘱𝘢𝘴𝘴𝘪𝘰𝘯 𝘤𝘰𝘯𝘵𝘪𝘯𝘶𝘦𝘴 𝘵𝘰 𝘪𝘯𝘴𝘱𝘪𝘳𝘦 𝘧𝘶𝘵𝘶𝘳𝘦 𝘨𝘦𝘯𝘦𝘳𝘢𝘵𝘪𝘰𝘯𝘴.

title: Polog, Aminolah Datu-Ramos Jr
text:
PAGE 1
Aminolah Datu-Ramos Polog Jr
Aminolah "Rial" Datu-Ramos Polog Jr., widely known in competitive gaming circles as PBE Rial, is a Filipino
professional e-sports athlete, a two-time NBA 2K Asia Champion, and the Head Coach of the De La Salle
University (DLSU) NBA 2K Esports Team competing in the UAAP.
He's one of the most decorated NBA 2K players the Philippines has produced, and his legacy goes well beyond
trophies and prize money.
Rial made history as the first Bangsamoro and the first Filipino Muslim to represent the Philippines in an
international basketball e-sports competition, earning his spot on the national squad for the inaugural FIBA E-
Sports Open 2020.
That milestone alone puts him in a category of his own, because he didn't just compete for personal glory. He
carried a community that had long been underrepresented in the Philippine gaming scene, and he did it on the
biggest stages the sport had to offer.

Background
Aminolah Datu-Ramos Polog Jr., popularly called Rial, is a Filipino Muslim athlete of Bangsamoro heritage.
His identity as a member of the Bangsamoro community is a defining part of his story, particularly because of his
role in breaking through barriers in a competitive field where Bangsamoro representation has historically been
limited.

Specific details about his early life, birthplace, and upbringing are

updates.
Education
Details about Rial's formal educational background are not
currently documented in available public sources.
His current role as Head Coach of the DLSU NBA 2K Esports
Team places him within one of the Philippines' most prestigious
academic and athletic institutions, suggesting a meaningful
professional relationship with De La Salle University.
This section will be updated as additional biographical information
becomes available.
Career
Early Competitive Gaming
Rial built his reputation in competitive NBA 2K through years of
disciplined practice and consistent performance.
He developed his skills within the Philippine gaming community,
eventually earning the alias "PBE Rial," a handle that became
recognized across the competitive NBA 2K circuit in Asia.
His path to the top wasn't a sudden leap. It was a steady, deliberate
climb built on technical mastery of the NBA 2K franchise, an
understanding of opponent tendencies, and the kind of game-day
composure that separates good players from champions.
NBA 2K19 Asia Tournament Finals
One of the defining moments of Rial's competitive career came at
the NBA 2K19 Asia Tournament Finals, held at the Trinoma
Activity Center in Metro Manila and organized by Playbook
Esports.

PAGE 3
External Relations (NCMF-
BER)
The tournament brought together elite NBA 2K competitors from
across the region, including players from Hong Kong, South
Korea, Taiwan, and the Philippines.
Rial came out on top, claiming the championship and cementing his status as one of the best in Asia.
As the tournament champion, he received a championship trophy, a cash prize of ₱300,000 (approximately USD
6,000), and a coveted slot to compete in the United States for a grand prize worth USD 1 million.
His victory was more than a personal achievement. It was a statement about the quality and competitiveness of
Filipino talent in international e-sports.
Two-Time NBA 2K Asia Champion
Rial's win at the NBA 2K19 Asia Tournament Finals contributed to his distinction as a two-time NBA 2K Asia
Champion.
This back-to-back regional dominance placed him among the most accomplished NBA 2K competitors in
Philippine e-sports history and reinforced his reputation as a consistent performer under pressure.
FIBA E-Sports Open 2020
Rial made history in 2020 when he joined the Philippine national team for the inaugural FIBA E-Sports Open,
becoming the first Bangsamoro and the first Filipino Muslim to be selected for the country's e-sports national squad
in a FIBA-sanctioned competition.
As part of a seven-member Philippine delegation, he competed against 16 nations, including Australia, Russia,
Italy, Spain, Indonesia, and Saudi Arabia.
The tournament marked the first time FIBA organized an official e-sports competition under its global basketball
governance framework, making Rial's inclusion in the inaugural roster all the more historically significant.
Coaching Career
Following his success as a competitive player, Rial transitioned into coaching, taking on the role of Head Coach of
the DLSU NBA 2K Esports Team, which competes in the University Athletic Association of the Philippines
(UAAP) E-Sports tournament.
In this capacity, he mentors student-athletes, drawing from his international experience to guide the next generation
of Filipino NBA 2K competitors.
His move into coaching reflects a broader commitment to the growth of Philippine e-sports, extending his influence
beyond personal competition and into the development of young talent.

PAGE 4
Institutional Contributions
NCMF Bureau of External Relations
Rial serves under the National Commission on Muslim Filipinos Bureau of External Relations (NCMF-BER), a
government body mandated to promote the interests and welfare of Filipino Muslims in the Philippines and abroad.
His achievements in competitive gaming have brought recognition not just to himself but to the NCMF-BER,
where his colleagues and supporters take pride in his accomplishments as a representative of the Filipino Muslim
community.
His presence within a government institution underscores the dual role he plays: champion on the gaming floor,
advocate by association for Bangsamoro visibility in spaces where that community is rarely seen.
Advocacy for Bangsamoro Representation in E-Sports
Through his landmark inclusion in the 2020 FIBA E-Sports Open national roster, Rial became a living example that
Bangsamoro athletes belong at the highest levels of competitive gaming.
His trailblazing presence opened conversations about inclusivity and representation in Philippine e-sports
governance and national team selection.
Whether intentional or not, he helped make the case that talent knows no regional or religious boundaries.
Legacy
Rial's legacy in Philippine e-sports is tied closely to three things: championship performance, historic firsts, and the
quiet but powerful act of showing up where no Bangsamoro had gone before.
As a two-time NBA 2K Asia Champion, he proved that Filipino players can compete at the highest regional level.
As the first Bangsamoro in a FIBA e-sports competition, he opened a door for an entire community. And as a coach
at DLSU, he's making sure that door stays open.
His story is often cited in discussions about the growing diversity of Philippine e-sports, and it resonates especially
for young Filipino Muslim gamers who see in him both a champion and a pioneer.
The arc of his career, from competitive grinder to international champion to national coach, reflects a maturity of
purpose that extends well beyond the screen.

Champion, NBA 2K19 Asia Tournament Finals (Playbook Esports, Trinoma Activity Center)
Cash prize: ₱300,000 (approximately USD 6,000) and a US grand finals slot (prize pool: USD 1 million)

E-Sports Open 2020

nations)

PAGE 5
Recognition from the NCMF Bureau of External Relations for contributions to Filipino Muslim
representation in competitive gaming
Challenges
Rial's journey wasn't without its share of hurdles. Competing at the international level as a Filipino requires
overcoming logistical, financial, and competitive barriers that are common in the Philippine e-sports ecosystem.
As a Bangsamoro Muslim, he also navigated a competitive gaming landscape where his community had virtually
no visible representation, particularly in nationally organized and internationally recognized competitions.
His selection for the FIBA E-Sports Open 2020 wasn't just a personal milestone. It was, in many ways, a quiet
challenge to the structural gaps in how Philippine e-sports institutions had historically engaged with athletes from
Muslim Mindanao.
That Rial reached the top without the infrastructure of support that more established gaming communities often
enjoy makes his achievements more remarkable, not less.

title: Pundato, Dimasangkay A.
text:
PAGE 1
Dimasangkay Alangadi Pundato
Photo: To be uploaded
Born
c. 1948, Lanao del Sur, Philippines
Died
August 13, 2020 (aged approx. 72), Marawi
City, Philippines
Ethnicity
Maranao
Dimasangkay A. Pundato
Dimasangkay Alangadi Pundato (c. 1948 – August 13,
2020), widely known as Kumander Dimas, was a Maranao
revolutionary commander, reformist leader, and public
official whose life traced the full arc of the Bangsamoro
struggle across more than four decades. He rose from the hills
of Lanao as a founding-generation fighter of the Moro
National Liberation Front (MNLF), became one of its
highest-ranking leaders as Vice Chairman, broke with the
central command to found the MNLF Reformist Group, and
then, in a pivot that surprised many of his contemporaries,
crossed into formal government service, becoming Executive
Director of the Office on Muslim Affairs (OMA) and later
Undersecretary for Muslim Affairs under the Office of the
Presidential Adviser on the Peace Process (OPAPP). What
makes his story worth telling isn't just the titles he held, but
the thread that ran through all of it: a stubborn, lifelong
commitment to improving the condition of Bangsamoro
people, pursued through whatever tools the moment allowed.
He was, above everything else, a bridge.
