Early Life and Maranao Roots
Pundato grew up in Lanao del Sur during a period when
Muslim Mindanao was living through the slow erosion of its
traditional political structures. He was a son of Maranao
society in the fullest sense: shaped by its clan networks, its
sense of dignity and honor (maratabat), and its deep
historical awareness of being a people who had never fully
submitted to colonial rule.
By the time Pundato came of age in the 1960s, that history
was pressing hard on the present. National development
policies under the Philippine state had consistently privileged
Christian settler communities in Mindanao, while Muslim-
majority areas faced land dispossession, electoral
manipulation, and growing militarization. The political
avenues available to Muslim Filipinos were narrow and
frequently blocked.<ref name="context1">Historical
reconstruction based on conflict documentation and published
accounts of Bangsamoro political history, as compiled in the
Kumander Dimas research dossier (2024).</ref>
For many young Maranao men of that generation, these
conditions led either to resignation or to radicalization.
Pundato chose a third path: organized resistance.
The MNLF and Revolutionary
Formation
Training Abroad and the "Top 90"
By the late 1960s and early 1970s, a new political
imagination had taken hold in Muslim Mindanao: the idea of
a unified Bangsamoro people asserting a collective right to
self-determination. The Moro National Liberation Front,
founded under the leadership of Nur Misuari, became the
primary vehicle for that vision.<ref name="mnlf1">Moro
National Liberation Front organizational history, as
referenced in Bangsamoro Parliament Resolution on Pundato
(2020).</ref>

PAGE 3
Bangsamoro Parliament Resolution of
Sympathy and Condolences (2020)
Notability
One of the Bangsamoro struggle's founding-
generation commanders; former Vice
Chairman of the MNLF and founder of the
MNLF Reformist Group.
Among the first Moro leaders to transition
from armed revolutionary leadership into
civilian government, serving as Executive
Director of OMA and Undersecretary for
Muslim Affairs under OPAPP.
A member of the elite "Top 90," the first
organized cohort of foreign-trained MNLF
fighters.
Known For
Founding the MNLF Reformist Group on
principles of collective leadership and
organizational accountability.
Serving as Executive Director of the Office on
Muslim Affairs during its formative years,
including crisis response to the 1990 Mecca
incident affecting Filipino pilgrims.
Contributing to the institutionalization of
Bangsamoro peace negotiations within
OPAPP across multiple administrations.
Supporting the legislative efforts that
produced the Bangsamoro Organic Law and
the establishment of BARMM.
Pull Quote
"He did not abandon the dream of
Bangsamoro dignity. He pursued it through
evolving means."
The declaration of Martial Law in 1972 by President
Ferdinand Marcos pushed the situation past the point of no
return. What had been political protest became armed
rebellion across wide stretches of Mindanao. The MNLF
mobilized thousands of fighters and positioned itself
internationally as the representative of Bangsamoro
aspirations.
Pundato was part of this founding moment in the most literal
sense. Historical accounts identify him as a member of the
first organized batch of Moro fighters to undergo foreign
military and political training in the MNLF's early years, a
cohort that later became known by the honorific designation
of the "Top 90."<ref name="top90">Bangsamoro Parliament
Resolution recognizing Dimasangkay Pundato, 2020.</ref>
That name took on a meaning far beyond its number. Being
counted among the Top 90 meant you were part of the
movement's founding generation, a cadre that had
transformed scattered resistance into a coordinated liberation
front. These early trainees were sent back to Mindanao not
just as fighters but as organizers, instructors, and future
leaders.
Pundato's membership in this group explains, in large part,
how quickly he rose. In revolutionary organizations,
proximity to origins produces political capital, and he had that
capital from the start.
Rise to Vice Chairman
Pundato didn't just return home and wait for instructions. He
demonstrated a genuine aptitude for command and
coordination, and his standing grew steadily through the
1970s. His ethnic and clan ties in Central Mindanao and the
Lanao corridor gave him natural credibility among Maranao
fighters, but colleagues recall that his influence extended
beyond ethnic lines because of his seriousness and his Top 90
standing.
By the late 1970s, he had ascended to the position of Vice
Chairman of the MNLF, placing him directly beneath
Chairman Misuari in the movement's decision-making
hierarchy.<ref name="vcmnlf">Research dossier on
Dimasangkay Pundato; confirmed in Bangsamoro Parliament
Resolution, 2020.</ref> Simultaneously, he carried command
responsibilities for Central Mindanao, making him both a
political figure at the top and an operational field commander
on the ground. That combination, the conference room and
the jungle encampment, defined his early career.

PAGE 4
— BangsamoroPedia Editorial, citing the
Kumander Dimas research dossier (2024)
Those who knew him from this period describe him as
methodical rather than theatrical. He wasn't the kind of leader
who made speeches for the crowd. He listened carefully,
spoke when he had something concrete to say, and earned
loyalty through consistency rather than charisma.
Internal Dissent and the Reformist Break
Fault Lines Within the MNLF
Success brought its own complications. As the MNLF expanded through the 1970s into a vast, multi-regional
organization, unresolved questions about its internal life became harder to ignore.<ref name="internal1">Conflict-
history scholarship on MNLF internal dynamics, as synthesized in Kumander Dimas research dossier (2024).</ref>
Several tensions became increasingly open:
Centralization of power in the Chairman's office, which many commanders felt left their concerns unheard.
Debates over strategy, particularly the balance between military operations and diplomatic engagement.
Questions of accountability, particularly around how external aid and organizational resources were being
managed.
Pundato was among the senior figures who gave these concerns a voice. His criticisms were not ideological in the
usual sense. He wasn't arguing that the Bangsamoro struggle was wrong or misdirected. He was arguing that a
movement claiming to fight oppression had a responsibility to govern itself with transparency and collective
decision-making.
That put him on a collision course with the dominant leadership.
The MNLF Reformist Group
The formal break came in the early 1980s. Rather than walking away from the MNLF entirely or forming an
entirely new organization with a new name and ideology, Pundato framed his departure as a reformist
intervention. His faction became known as the MNLF Reformist Group (MNLF-RG), and the name was
deliberate: he wasn't rejecting the movement's goals, he was arguing that the movement had drifted from its
founding principles and needed correction from within.<ref name="mnlfrg">MNLF Reformist Group founding and
orientation, as documented in research dossier (2024).</ref>
This distinction carried real weight. Because he was a Top 90 founding member and a former Vice Chairman, he
couldn't be easily dismissed as an outsider or a latecomer with a grievance. He was a founder raising his hand in
dissent, and that gave the Reformist Group a credibility that similar factions from lower-ranking figures would not
have commanded.
The MNLF-RG drew its core strength from Lanao and Maranao areas, reflecting Pundato's networks and the
broader pattern of regional clustering that was reshaping the Moro movement landscape. The group positioned
itself around three core principles: collective leadership rather than concentrated authority; organizational
accountability over financial and logistical decisions; and strategic flexibility, treating armed struggle and political
engagement as complementary tools rather than mutually exclusive paths.

PAGE 5
He did not reject the legitimacy of Bangsamoro grievances. He argued that political context had
changed and that strategies must change accordingly. From this perspective, working inside the state
was not capitulation but repositioning.
From the perspective of the central MNLF leadership, the Reformist Group was a dangerous precedent. But from
the perspective of many field commanders, it validated what they had long felt. Pundato gave organized form to
frustrations that had previously been whispered.
Return to the Fold of Law
A New Political Opening
The collapse of the Marcos regime in 1986 and the installation of President Corazon Aquino's civilian government
reopened political space that had been sealed for over a decade. For Bangsamoro leaders outside the mainstream
MNLF, this was a moment of strategic reassessment.
Pundato had spent years watching an armed landscape that was growing more fragmented, not less. Internal
divisions across Moro factions were producing competing commands, competing claims, and diminishing returns
on the ground. At the same time, the new government was signaling a genuine willingness to engage Muslim-
Filipino concerns through civilian institutions rather than purely through the security apparatus.
His calculation was direct: meaningful gains for Bangsamoro people might now be achievable through institution-
building rather than perpetual warfare. This wasn't a conclusion he arrived at quickly or lightly. It was the product
of years of frustration with organizational dysfunction and a clear-eyed reading of the political moment.
Returning to the fold of law didn't mean abandoning the cause. For Pundato, it meant shifting the arena of struggle,
from the battlefield to the bureaucracy.
The Office on Muslim Affairs
In January 1987, the Aquino administration established the Office on Muslim Affairs (OMA) as an agency under
the Office of the President. Its mandate covered the coordination of government programs for Muslim Filipinos, the
promotion of Islamic cultural development, and the administration of specific functional areas including the annual
Hajj pilgrimage.<ref name="oma1">Executive Order establishing OMA, 1987; as referenced in Pundato research
dossier (2024).</ref>
This was a signal that Muslim affairs were no longer to be treated solely as a security problem. They were now a
domain of governance requiring permanent civilian structures. It was into this evolving institutional space that
Pundato entered.
Executive Director of OMA
Documentary records confirm that Pundato received a presidential appointment as Executive Director of OMA in
1988, with a subsequent reappointment in 1992.<ref name="oma2">Presidential appointment records, OMA, 1988
and 1992, as cited in research dossier (2024).</ref>
The appointment put him at the helm of the principal national institution for Muslim Filipino concerns during two
successive administrations. For a man who had spent years as an underground commander, it was a remarkable
transition, and one that made sense to those who understood the logic: Pundato brought genuine credibility among

PAGE 6
Maranao and broader Moro constituencies, direct experience navigating conflict-era politics, and the kind of
institutional trust that career civil servants typically don't carry into Muslim communities.
Colleagues who worked with him at OMA describe an administrator who brought the same discipline he had
practiced as a commander. He was patient and detail-oriented, focused on building systems and clarifying
responsibilities. He approached bureaucracy much as he had approached command: by creating clear chains of
accountability and insisting on follow-through.
His tenure coincided with OMA's own identity formation. The office was still developing its routines, its
procedures, and its institutional culture. Much of the work involved improvisation, building the airplane while
flying it. Pundato played a central role in establishing the early operational norms that would shape OMA's work
for years afterward.
Hajj Administration and Crisis Response
One of OMA's most visible functions was managing the annual Hajj pilgrimage, a responsibility with both deep
religious significance and real diplomatic weight in the Philippines' relations with Saudi Arabia and the wider
Muslim world.<ref name="hajj1">OMA pilgrimage administration records, as cited in research dossier (2024).
</ref>
Under Pundato's leadership, OMA coordinated passport processing, travel logistics, pilgrim orientation, and liaison
with Saudi authorities. The work required precision and political sensitivity in equal measure.
His role became sharply visible in 1990, when a catastrophic incident in Mecca caused the deaths of hundreds of
pilgrims from several countries, including Filipinos.<ref name="mecca1990">Reports of the 1990 Mecca incident
affecting Filipino pilgrims, OMA records, as cited in research dossier (2024).</ref> As Executive Director, Pundato
addressed the situation publicly, confirmed casualties, and urged Filipino pilgrims to strictly follow safety protocols
issued by Saudi authorities. It was one of those moments that illustrated how completely his role had transformed:
he was now acting as the face of the Philippine government in matters affecting Filipino Muslims abroad.
National Peacebuilding: OPAPP
From Sectoral Governance to the Peace Bureaucracy
By the mid-1990s, the Philippine state had begun consolidating peace work into a more formalized and permanent
institutional system. The creation of the Office of the Presidential Adviser on the Peace Process (OPAPP)
marked the government's decision to treat peace negotiations not as ad hoc political exercises but as a standing
state function with dedicated personnel, resources, and institutional memory.
Pundato's transition into this space was a natural progression. His profile was genuinely unusual: a former MNLF
Vice Chairman who had founded a reformist faction, served as a senior government administrator, and accumulated
years of experience working with both revolutionary actors and state institutions. Few people in the Philippines
held that combination.<ref name="opapp1">OPAPP institutional mandate and Pundato's appointment, as
documented in research dossier (2024).</ref>

PAGE 7
Undersecretary for Muslim Affairs
Under successive administrations, including those of President Gloria Macapagal Arroyo and President Benigno
Aquino III, Pundato served as Undersecretary for Muslim Affairs within OPAPP. The position placed him at a
strategic junction between government negotiating panels, Moro political organizations, conflict-affected
communities, and international partners and mediators.
His primary contribution was not technical. He functioned as a political bridge.
He understood the psychology of commanders who had spent decades in the hills, how they thought, what they
feared, and what they needed to hear to trust the process. He also understood the language of bureaucrats, lawyers,
and diplomats. That dual fluency, rare in any peace process, was his greatest asset.
He wasn't a headline-seeker. His work unfolded in quieter spaces: preparatory meetings, backchannel consultations,
internal strategy sessions, and confidence-building dialogues with actors who were not yet ready to appear at a
formal table. Colleagues consistently describe him as patient, precise, and unassuming. He preferred persuasion
over pressure and explanation over confrontation.
In long and difficult peace processes, such figures often matter more than the visible spokespersons. They stabilize
negotiations, reduce misunderstandings, and prevent small disputes from becoming deal-breaking crises.
Institutional Memory Across Administrations
One of the distinguishing features of Pundato's OPAPP career was its continuity across political administrations.
Peace work in the Bangsamoro context is cumulative. Each government inherits unfinished business from the
previous one. Institutional memory becomes invaluable, and Pundato became part of that memory.
He carried lessons from earlier negotiations, from failures and partial successes, from proposals that collapsed and
those that gained traction. This long view allowed him to temper unrealistic expectations and to warn against
repeating past mistakes. He also contributed to internal capacity-building efforts that aimed to professionalize
peace work, including programs on conflict analysis, negotiation skills, program management, and monitoring and
evaluation.
Support for the Bangsamoro Organic Law and BARMM
In his later years at OPAPP and beyond, Pundato was a consistent supporter of the legislative and political efforts
that culminated in the Bangsamoro Organic Law and the creation of the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in
Muslim Mindanao (BARMM).<ref name="barmm1">Bangsamoro Organic Law (Republic Act No. 11054);
BARMM establishment, 2019, as referenced in research dossier (2024).</ref>
He was clear-eyed about what BARMM was and wasn't. It wasn't the sovereign Bangsamoro state that the early
revolutionaries had imagined. It was a constitutionally recognized political space, imperfect, still contested in many
ways, but real. A concrete arena where Bangsamoro identity, self-governance, and development could be pursued
without armed confrontation.
For Pundato, that was a historic compromise worth accepting. Not with blind enthusiasm, but with a realistic
assessment of what the political terrain made possible.

PAGE 8
Leadership Style and Personal Character
Across every phase of his career, a consistent portrait of Pundato emerges. He was not flamboyant. He did not
cultivate a cult of personality. He didn't rely on theatrical speeches or dramatic gestures to build his standing.
Instead, he practiced a style of leadership grounded in restraint, discipline, and quiet authority. As a revolutionary
commander, this meant an emphasis on internal order and clear chains of responsibility. As an administrator, it
manifested in methodical attention to procedure and documentation. As a peace official, it took the form of patient
mediation and careful, sustained listening.
He was known among colleagues as austere in his personal lifestyle. He didn't display conspicuous wealth,
cultivate business interests alongside his official work, or leverage his positions for political dynasty-building.
These traits reinforced widespread perceptions of personal integrity and sat naturally alongside the revolutionary
ethic of sacrifice and service he had carried since the 1970s.
His preference throughout was for process over spectacle. He believed that durable change comes from institutions
rather than personalities, from procedures rather than proclamations, and from incremental gains rather than sudden
ruptures. That worldview explains both his reformist break inside the MNLF and his later embrace of bureaucratic
peacebuilding. They were, in his own logic, expressions of the same underlying commitment.
Legal Proceedings and Acquittal
During Pundato's tenure at OMA, allegations arose regarding irregularities in certain transactions from the late
1980s. These allegations eventually became the subject of criminal cases filed before the Sandiganbayan, the
Philippines' anti-graft court.<ref name="sandig1">Sandiganbayan case records involving OMA administration, as
referenced in research dossier (2024).</ref>
The existence of these cases reflects the post-Marcos state's effort to assert accountability over public officials,
including those who came from revolutionary backgrounds. No one in Philippine public life, regardless of their
history, was exempt from that process.
After years of litigation, the Sandiganbayan ruled that the evidence presented against Pundato was insufficient to
establish criminal liability. He was acquitted.<ref name="acquittal1">Sandiganbayan acquittal ruling on
Dimasangkay Pundato, as documented in research dossier (2024).</ref>
Any honest accounting of his record holds both facts simultaneously: allegations were made and investigated
through the proper legal process, and the court found no proof beyond reasonable doubt. An acquittal doesn't mean
a bureaucracy was perfect. But it does mean the state failed to demonstrate that its leader used his position for
criminal personal gain. Given what colleagues described of his personal austerity and institutional seriousness, the
outcome aligned with the broader picture that emerges from the historical record.
Final Years and Death
In his later years, Pundato gradually stepped back from the daily intensity of government work, though he
remained a quiet presence in discussions around peace, Muslim affairs, and Bangsamoro governance. Those who
sought him out in this period describe conversations marked by sobriety and realism. He didn't indulge in nostalgia
about the revolutionary past, and he didn't exaggerate the achievements of the present. He spoke, consistently, of
unfinished work.

PAGE 9
For him, peace was never a single event to be declared and celebrated. It was a generational process that required
constant tending.
Dimasangkay Alangadi Pundato passed away on August 13, 2020, in Marawi City, at the age of seventy-two.
<ref name="death1">Bangsamoro Parliament Resolution of Sympathy, 2020, confirming death of Dimasangkay
Pundato on August 13, 2020.</ref>
He died as BARMM was still in its infancy, the autonomous region he had helped make possible still navigating its
first years of operation. He didn't live to see its final shape. But he lived long enough to witness its formal birth,
and to know that the institutions he had spent decades building were, however imperfectly, standing.
Official Recognition
Following his death, the Bangsamoro Parliament adopted a resolution expressing condolences to his family and
formally recognizing his contributions to the Bangsamoro struggle and to Philippine governance.<ref
name="bpresolution">Bangsamoro Parliament Resolution of Sympathy and Condolences for Dimasangkay
Alangadi Pundato, 2020.</ref>
The resolution described him as a member of the first batch of foreign-trained Moro fighters (the "Top 90"), former
Vice Chairman of the MNLF, founder of the MNLF Reformist Group, former Executive Director of the Office on
Muslim Affairs, and former Undersecretary for Muslim Affairs under OPAPP.
That official acknowledgment by the Bangsamoro government carries historical weight. It places Pundato squarely
within the lineage of leaders whose work made Bangsamoro autonomy possible, even if his name rarely appeared
in the bigger headlines of the peace process.
Legacy
Dimasangkay Pundato belongs to the category of transitional figures that post-conflict societies frequently produce
but rarely fully honor. He is remembered neither solely as a warrior nor solely as a technocrat, but as someone who
moved deliberately between both worlds, carrying the legitimacy of one into the other.
Several contributions stand out in any honest historical assessment:
He belonged to the founding generation of organized Bangsamoro resistance. Without the cohort that built the
MNLF from the ground up, the later negotiations and political settlements that produced BARMM would not have
been conceivable.
He gave internal dissent an organized form. By founding the MNLF Reformist Group, he demonstrated that
revolutionary movements are not monolithic and that leaders of genuine stature can challenge their own
organizations from within, on principled grounds, without defecting to the enemy.
He helped build the first civilian bureaucratic structures devoted to Muslim Filipino governance. The work of the
OMA period was often invisible, underfunded, and unglamorous. But it laid the procedural and institutional
foundations that later became the National Commission on Muslim Filipinos (NCMF) and related bodies.
He professionalized peace work. At OPAPP, he contributed to the transformation of Bangsamoro peace
negotiations from a personality-driven exercise into a permanent state function with institutional memory and
accumulated expertise.

PAGE 10
He embodied strategic adaptation without self-betrayal. He changed his methods as political conditions changed,
but he never changed his purpose: the dignity, recognition, and self-governance of the Bangsamoro people.
His legacy is not a story of final triumph. The institutions he helped build continue to struggle with underfunding
and political interference. Many Bangsamoro communities remain poor and insecure. These realities remind us that
no individual, however committed, can single-handedly resolve structural problems rooted in centuries of
marginalization.
But what Pundato demonstrated, through a life lived across rebellion, reform, administration, and peacebuilding, is
that sustained effort across a lifetime is itself a form of courage. He pursued a necessary path, not a straight one.
And he pursued it, by every available account, with integrity.
He did not abandon the dream of Bangsamoro dignity. He pursued it through evolving means.

Arsenio A. Quibranza
Arsenio Arcelo Quibranza (1907 – February 28, 1986) was a Filipino
educator turned politician who served as the third Governor of Lanao del
Norte from 1965 until his term ended on February 28, 1986, making him
one of the longest-serving provincial executives in Mindanao's modern
history.
A Christian settler originally from Cebu, Quibranza built his career from
the ground up in a predominantly Muslim province, earning the trust of
communities across ethnic and religious lines through decades of
consistent public service.
He started as a classroom teacher, became the founding mayor of Tubod
following the municipality's formal creation in 1949, and eventually rose
to lead the entire province through some of its most turbulent decades,
including the Ilaga-Barracuda sectarian conflict of the early 1970s and
the years of Martial Law under President Ferdinand Marcos.
His name now lives on in three major public institutions in Lanao del
Norte: the provincial government center where the province conducts its
affairs, a national highway that passes through the heart of Tubod, and a
public high school that continues to serve the youth of the capital
municipality.
Through his daughter Imelda "Angging" Quibranza-Dimaporo and her
children with Governor Abdullah Dimaporo, the Quibranza political
legacy remains woven into the fabric of Lanao del Norte's governance to
this day.

Early Life and Background
Arsenio Arcelo Quibranza was born in 1907 in Cebu, the son of José Quibranza Sr.<ref name="geni">Geni.com.
"Arsenio Arcelo Quibranza (1907–1986)." Genealogy profile. Accessed 2025.
https://www.geni.com/people/Arsenio-Quibranza/6000000198484291822</ref>
Like many Christian Filipino migrants from the Visayas and Luzon in the early twentieth century, his family settled
in Mindanao, eventually making their home in what would become the municipality of Tubod in Lanao del Norte.
<ref name="tubodwiki">Wikipedia. "Tubod, Lanao del Norte."
https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tubod,_Lanao_del_Norte</ref>
He trained and worked as a teacher in his formative years, a background that shaped his lifelong emphasis on
education and community service.
The province he eventually came to lead, Lanao del Norte, was itself a young institution. Republic Act No. 2228
divided the old Province of Lanao into two separate provinces in 1959, giving birth to both Lanao del Norte and
Lanao del Sur.<ref name="ldnhistory">Provincial Government of Lanao del Norte. "History."
https://lanaodelnorte.gov.ph/history/</ref>
Before that division, the region had been a single administrative unit encompassing both the predominantly
Christian northern coastal areas and the predominantly Muslim communities around Lake Lanao to the south.
Quibranza grew up and built his career in this complex, multi-ethnic frontier landscape, and it defined him as a
politician who had to govern across cultural boundaries from the very beginning.
Early Political Career: Mayor of Tubod
Quibranza's formal entry into politics came through a combination of circumstance and community confidence.
On June 10, 1949, President Elpidio Quirino issued Executive Order No. 222, which created the Municipality of
Baroy out of a portion of the then-existing municipal territory. When that order took effect, virtually all of the
elected municipal officials in the area opted to transfer their service to the newly created Baroy, leaving the residual
municipality of Tubod without a functioning government. Quibranza, who had been serving as a municipal
councilor at the time, was the sole elected official who chose to remain.<ref name="tubodwiki"/>
As a result, he was appointed as Municipal Mayor of Tubod effective June 24, 1949, essentially taking charge of a
municipality that had just been emptied of its other leaders.<ref name="tubodwiki"/>
That early test of character set the tone for everything that followed. He stepped up when others stepped away.

PAGE 3
In the 1951 local elections, he was formally elected as Municipal Mayor of Tubod and subsequently re-elected in
both the 1955 and 1959 elections, giving him three consecutive elected terms in addition to his two-year appointed
tenure.<ref name="tubodwiki"/>
Over more than a decade as mayor, Quibranza built Tubod from a newly carved-out municipality into a stable local
government unit and a community that identified with him personally.
His tenure as mayor ended on March 8, 1962, when President Diosdado Macapagal appointed him as Vice
Governor of Lanao del Norte.<ref name="tubodwiki"/>
Vice Governor of Lanao del Norte (1962–1965)
Quibranza's appointment as Vice Governor under President Macapagal came as a recognition of his decade-long
track record in Tubod and his standing as a respected Christian political figure in a province whose Muslim-
majority areas were increasingly becoming an important part of national political calculations.
He served under Governor Mohammad Ali Dimaporo, a formidable Muslim politician who had risen to become the
second Governor of Lanao del Norte following the retirement of the province's first governor, Salvador T. Lluch.
<ref name="ldnhistory"/>
The relationship between Quibranza and Ali Dimaporo was, at best, a cautious coexistence between two men who
represented different communities, different political networks, and ultimately different ambitions for the province.
In September 1965, Governor Dimaporo ran for and won the congressional seat of Lanao del Norte, vacating the
governorship in the process. Under the law of succession, Vice Governor Arsenio Quibranza automatically became
the third Provincial Chief Executive of Lanao del Norte.<ref name="ldnhistory"/>
He had arrived at the governorship not through an election but through the workings of political succession, a detail
that would add meaning to the strong mandates he received at the ballot box in the years that followed.
Governor of Lanao del Norte (1965–1986)
First Years: Succession and Election
Quibranza took over the governorship in 1965 in the middle of a term, stepping into a role that had been shaped
largely by his predecessor's personality and patronage networks.
He had to establish his own authority quickly and demonstrate that he could govern the full breadth of a province
that stretched from Panguil Bay in the northwest to the Muslim communities along the periphery of Lanao del Sur
in the southeast.
By the mandate of his constituents, Quibranza was elected Governor in 1967 and was almost unanimously re-
elected in 1971 and again in 1980, a record of electoral endorsement that few provincial executives in Mindanao
could match.<ref name="ldnhistory"/>
The near-unanimous re-elections of 1971 and 1980 are perhaps the clearest measure of the kind of political trust he
built over time: a Christian politician winning overwhelming support in a province with a substantial Muslim
population, and doing so across multiple election cycles.

PAGE 4
The Ilaga-Barracuda Crisis and Political Confrontation
Prior to the declaration of Martial Law in 1972, Mindanao was engulfed in escalating sectarian violence between
the Ilaga, a predominantly Christian armed vigilante group, and the Barracuda, which was associated with Moro
communities.
In Lanao del Norte, the conflict was particularly intense.
Governor Quibranza and Iligan Mayor Cabili were among those who publicly accused former Governor
Mohammad Ali Dimaporo and his brother Naga of providing support to the Barracuda.<ref
name="ijijournal">IJRISS. "Between Security and Repressions: The Martial Law Years in Iligan City 1972–1981."
https://rsisinternational.org/journals/ijriss/articles/between-security-and-repressions-the-martial-law-years-in-
iligan-city-1972-1981/</ref>
The allegations added a layer of political rivalry to what was already a dangerous security situation, and they
deepened the already strained relationship between Quibranza and the Dimaporo clan, a tension that would define
Lanao del Norte politics for years.
Martial Law, Arrest, and the Actub Interlude
When President Marcos declared Martial Law on September 21, 1972, Quibranza was arrested by order of the
president.<ref name="ldnwiki">Wikipedia. "Lanao del Norte."
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lanao_del_Norte</ref>
The circumstances of his arrest have not been fully documented in the public record, but they were likely
connected to the volatile political environment in Lanao del Norte, the ongoing Ilaga-Barracuda violence, and the
Marcos administration's broader policy of consolidating control over regional political figures who had their own
independent bases of power.
While Quibranza was held in detention, Vice Governor Felix Z. "Toto" Actub succeeded him as Governor of Lanao
del Norte.<ref name="ldnwiki"/>
The period of Quibranza's imprisonment remains one of the less documented chapters of his political life. What is
clear is that he was eventually released and returned to active political life: he won re-election as Governor in the
1980 elections, resuming his position at the head of the provincial government.
His participation in the political activities surrounding the Interim Batasang Pambansa in 1978 reflects that he
navigated the political landscape of the Martial Law years carefully, finding a way to remain a relevant and
functioning political actor even in a heavily constrained environment.
Capital Relocation and the Government Center
In 1977, President Marcos signed Resolution No. 805 of the Sangguniang Panlalawigan of Lanao del Norte into
Presidential Decree 181, transferring the provincial capital from Iligan City to the municipality of Tubod.<ref
name="ldnhistory"/>
The resolution had been sponsored by Assemblyman Abdullah Dimaporo, Ali Dimaporo's son, in an irony of
political geography: the son of Quibranza's greatest rival helped engineer the transfer of the provincial capital to the
very municipality that Quibranza had built and governed for more than a decade.

PAGE 5
In October 1984, inaugural ceremonies were held to mark the transfer of the Provincial Capitol from Poblacion,
Tubod, to the Don Mariano Marcos Government Center at Pigcarangan, also in Tubod.<ref name="ldnhistory"/>
That building was later renamed the Governor Arsenio A. Quibranza Provincial Government Center, the name
by which it is still known today.<ref name="ldngovph">Provincial Government of Lanao del Norte. Official
website. https://lanaodelnorte.gov.ph/</ref>
End of Tenure
Quibranza's final year as governor coincided with the political earthquake of February 1986. By virtue of the
People Power Revolution at EDSA on February 25, 1986, the Aquino government took over, and local
governments across the Philippines were swept into sudden transition.<ref name="ldnhistory"/>
Quibranza's term formally ended on February 28, 1986. Three days later, on March 3, 1986, OIC Atty. Francisco L.
Abalos was installed as the appointed governor of Lanao del Norte.<ref name="ldnhistory"/>
Quibranza passed away on February 28, 1986, the same day his tenure officially closed. He did not live to see the
full political realignment that followed the restoration of democracy in the Philippines.<ref name="geni"/>
Family and the Quibranza-Dimaporo Political Alliance
Quibranza married Teofila dela Cruz, and together they had a daughter, Imelda, born on January 15, 1959, in
Tubod.<ref name="imeldawiki">Wikipedia. "Imelda Dimaporo."
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imelda_Dimaporo</ref>
In 1977, Imelda married Abdullah "Bobby" Dimaporo, the son of former Governor Mohammad Ali Dimaporo, in a
dual civil and Islamic ceremony.<ref name="imeldawiki"/>
The marriage was remarkable precisely because it united two families who had been political rivals. The Quibranza
and Dimaporo clans had spent years on opposite sides of provincial politics, with the elder Ali Dimaporo
representing the Muslim political establishment and Arsenio Quibranza representing the Christian settler
community. Imelda's marriage to Abdullah effectively created a cross-community political alliance that would
prove enormously durable.
The union produced five children. Two of them, Mohamad Khalid Quibranza Dimaporo and Sittie Aminah
Quibranza Dimaporo, went on to hold significant legislative and executive positions in Lanao del Norte, continuing
the family's governing role into the twenty-first century.<ref name="ldngovph"/>
Imelda Quibranza-Dimaporo
Imelda "Angging" Quibranza-Dimaporo studied Business Administration at the Philippine Women's University and
built a political career on the combined legacy of both her father and her husband's family.<ref
name="imeldawiki"/>
She was elected Governor of Lanao del Norte in the 1998 elections and served until 2007. She returned to the
governorship in 2016 and served until 2025, during which time the province received the Seal of Good Local
Governance from the Department of the Interior and Local Government.<ref name="sglg">Provincial Government
of Lanao del Norte. "Lanao del Norte Bags Seal of Good Local Governance Award."
https://lanaodelnorte.gov.ph/lanao-del-norte-bags-seal-of-good-local-governance-award/</ref>

PAGE 6
She also served as the Representative for Lanao del Norte's 1st District, from 2010 to 2016 and again from 2025
onward.<ref name="imeldawiki"/>
Legacy and Honors
The Arsenio Arcelo Quibranza Highway
In 2018, the Philippine Congress enacted Republic Act No. 11051, naming the Poblacion-Caniogan National Road,
which traverses Barangays Poblacion, San Antonio, Patudan, Pinpin, Mabngao, Licapao, Candis, Caniogan, and
Barakanas in the Municipality of Tubod, as the Arsenio Arcelo Quibranza Highway.<ref name="ra11051">The
Corpus Juris. "R.A. No. 11051: An Act Naming the Poblacion-Caniogan National Road Traversing Barangay
Poblacion and Barangay Barakanas in the Municipality of Tubod, Province of Lanao del Norte as the Arsenio
Arcelo Quibranza Highway." https://thecorpusjuris.com/legislative/republic-acts/ra-no-11051.php</ref>
The bill had passed the House of Representatives on May 29, 2017, and was approved by the Senate on March 12,
2018.<ref name="ra11051"/>
The highway naming was proposed with the support of the Dimaporo family's legislative bloc, a gesture that
underscored how thoroughly the political alliance forged through Imelda's marriage had redefined the old
Quibranza-Dimaporo rivalry into a shared political inheritance.
The Provincial Government Center
The Governor Arsenio A. Quibranza Provincial Government Center at Pigcarangan, Tubod, serves as the
official seat of the Lanao del Norte provincial government. The complex, originally opened in October 1984 as the
Don Mariano Marcos Government Center, was renamed in Quibranza's honor following his death, recognizing his
role as the longest-serving governor and the chief executive during whose administration the capital transfer was
completed.<ref name="ldnhistory"/>
Arsenio A. Quibranza National High School
The Arsenio A. Quibranza National High School in Tubod, Lanao del Norte, bears his name in recognition of his
background as an educator and his advocacy for access to public education during his years in office. The school
continues to serve secondary-level students in the provincial capital.
A Legacy Carried Forward
Quibranza's most enduring legacy may not be any single institution but the political dynasty he helped create: a
family network that bridged the Christian-Muslim divide in Lanao del Norte at a time when sectarian tensions
made that kind of bridge-building genuinely dangerous.
He was a Visayan Christian who earned the trust of a predominantly Muslim electorate, held his ground during
Martial Law even at the cost of his personal freedom, and left behind a family that continues to govern the province
he shaped.
"By the mandate of the inhabitants, Governor Quibranza was elected Governor in 1967 and almost
unanimously re-elected in 1971 and again in 1980." (Provincial Government of Lanao del Norte,
Official History)

PAGE 7
That near-unanimity across ethnically diverse communities says more about the man than any list of
accomplishments could.
Challenges and Controversies
Quibranza's tenure was not without its complexities. The accusations he leveled against the Dimaporo brothers
over alleged support for the Barracuda were politically charged and contributed to the climate of distrust that
preceded Martial Law in Lanao del Norte.<ref name="ijijournal"/>
His arrest under Marcos remains only partially documented, and the full circumstances behind it, including how
long he was held and under what conditions, are not part of any accessible official record.
The coexistence of his governorship with the operations of both Ilaga and Barracuda groups in the province also
raises questions about the limits of what he was able to accomplish in terms of protecting civilian communities
from sectarian violence, a challenge that confronted every provincial executive in Mindanao during the early
1970s.
Historians studying the Martial Law period in Iligan and the surrounding region note that the overall security
framework of the time relied heavily on military intervention, and that local civilian executives like Quibranza had
limited independent capacity to manage the conflict once the Armed Forces of the Philippines took a central role.
<ref name="ijijournal"/>
Death
Arsenio Arcelo Quibranza died on February 28, 1986, in Tubod, Lanao del Norte, the municipality he had served as
founding mayor and the capital of the province he governed for more than two decades.<ref name="geni"/>
His death came on the same day his gubernatorial tenure formally ended, as the People Power Revolution swept
local government leadership across the Philippines into transition.
He was survived by his wife Teofila dela Cruz Quibranza and their daughter Imelda "Angging" Quibranza-
Dimaporo, as well as his grandchildren and the extended family network that continued his political legacy in the
years that followed.

Sohayle M. Hadji Abdul Racman
Dr. Sohayle M. Hadji Abdul Racman, LPT is a Filipino academic scholar and faculty member of the College
of Social Sciences and Humanities at Mindanao State University in Marawi City. He stands as a leading
contemporary authority on Maranao cultural preservation and Islamic civilization studies, earning international
recognition for his ethnographic research on pre-colonial and early modern Lanao Sultanate political thought
and traditions. His scholarly mission centers on documenting and safeguarding the tangible and intangible
heritage of the Meranaw through rigorous academic inquiry, international research collaboration, and hands-on
museum curation. He is also the founder and owner of the Sohayle M. Hadji Abdul Racman's Maranao
Museum, dedicated to archiving Meranaw material culture and maintaining living connections to ancestral
knowledge systems.

Early Life and Roots
Sohayle M. Hadji Abdul Racman was born and raised in Lanao del Sur, a predominantly Muslim region of
Mindanao in the southern Philippines. His family background within Meranaw society and his deep cultural
rootedness shaped his lifelong commitment to scholarly preservation of Maranao traditions. Growing up in the
heart of historic Lanao, he developed intimate knowledge of local sultanate history, traditional governance
systems, and the spiritual dimensions of Meranaw Islam. This lived experience became the foundation for his
later academic work bridging indigenous knowledge systems with contemporary Islamic scholarship.
Education and Professional Credentials
Hadji Abdul Racman earned his Bachelor of Science in International Relations from Mindanao State University in 2002, followed by a Master of Arts in Islamic
Studies from the University of the Philippines at Diliman in 2006. During his graduate studies at UP Diliman, he pursued advanced coursework in Philippine
Studies, Sikolohiyang Pilipino (Filipino Psychology), physical anthropology, and world archaeology as applied research specializations.<ref
name="docbio">Extracted biographical data from official document, 2025</ref>
In 2020, he completed his PhD in Islamic Civilization and Contemporary Issues at the Sultan Omar Ali Saifuddien Centre for Islamic Studies (SOASCIS),
Universiti Brunei Darussalam. His doctoral dissertation, titled The Political Legitimacy of Lanao Sultanate in the 17th Century with Special Reference to the
Political Theory of al-Māwardī, represents the first comprehensive scholarly treatment of Lanao Sultanate governance through the lens of classical Islamic
political philosophy. He also earned professional credentials in teaching, completing 18 units of Professional Education coursework at St. Peter's College in
Iligan City and passing the national Licensure Examination for Teachers (LET) in Social Studies in 2020.<ref name="docbio" />
Academic Career
Teaching Experience
Hadji Abdul Racman's teaching career spans multiple institutions and academic disciplines. From 2010 to 2014, he served as faculty member at St. Peter's
College in Iligan City, where he taught social sciences subjects to secondary and higher education students. In 2014 and 2015, he held a position in the
International Relations Department of the Institute of Middle East and Asian Studies at University of Southern Mindanao in Kabacan, teaching courses in
international relations and regional geopolitics.

PAGE 2
Since joining Mindanao State University's College of Social Sciences and Humanities, he has taught courses spanning international relations, Islamic
civilization, cultural anthropology, Islamic studies, and Philippine history. His teaching approach integrates primary source analysis with fieldwork-based
ethnographic methods, encouraging students to ground theoretical knowledge in lived community experience.
Scholarly Research Focus
His research trajectory reflects a sustained commitment to understanding Meranaw cultural and political systems from both insider and rigorous academic
perspectives. His scholarly work addresses four interconnected domains:
The political legitimacy and Islamic governance structures of the Lanao Sultanate in the 17th century and their contemporary relevance
Ethnographic documentation of Meranaw tangible and intangible cultural heritage, including material culture, artistic traditions, and ceremonial practices
Comparative linguistic and cultural analysis examining shared elements between Maranao and Malaysian cultural vocabularies, suggesting historical
connections across maritime Southeast Asian trade networks
The preservation and interpretation of Meranaw cultural traditions through museum practice and digital archiving
His dissertation research challenging the underrepresentation of Lanao Sultanate history in Western and Filipino scholarship established him as the primary
contemporary scholar bridging Islamic political philosophy and Philippine regional history.<ref name="docbio" />
International Conference Presentations and Publications
Hadji Abdul Racman has presented at more than 10 major international conferences across Asia, Europe, and the Middle East, disseminating his research to
diverse academic audiences. Notable presentations include:
2025 Presentation: The Similarities Between Malaysia-Bahasa and Meranao Words: An Ethnographic Research Experience, delivered at the Pekan Budaya
Melayu Serumpun (Malay Cultural Exhibition) in Pekanbaru, Riau Province, Indonesia, August 8-9, 2025.<ref name="docbio" />
2022 Presentations: Two papers delivered at the National and International Academic Conference on Multidisciplinary Research Studies and Social Innovation
hosted by Fatoni University in Thailand: The Festivities and the Material Cultures Employed by the Mёranao During the Crowning Ceremonies of the Royalties
and The Islamicity of Mёranao Traditional Sports, Games, Entertainments and Pastimes: Its Importance to Cultural Preservation and Wellness.<ref
name="docbio" />
2022 Presentations: The Indian-Hinduism and Chinese-Buddhism Elements in the Mёranao Tangible and Intangible Archaic Cultures presented at the 3rd
International Conference on Development of Literature, Arts, Culture, Language, and Heritage (ICDETAH 3.0) at Universiti Pendidikan Sultan Idris, Perak,
Malaysia, October 26-27, 2022; and The Historical Narrative of Lanao Sultanate in the 17th Century until the 21st Century, and its Zakāt Practices from Sunni-
Islamic Perspectives presented at the 2nd International e-Conference of Ulul Albab (e-ICUA 2.0) organized by Universiti Pendidikan Sultan Idris, December 17,
2022.<ref name="docbio" />
2021 Presentations: The Islamicity of the Lanao Sultanate's Land Grant with Special Reference to the Political Thought of al-Mawardi on Land Grant
presented at the 1st International e-Conference of Ulul Albab (e-ICUA) at Universiti Pendidikan Sultan Idris, December 13, 2021; and The Lanao Sultanate
Leadership Legitimacy: Its Bases from Islamic Principles on Leadership, Mёranao Traditions, Salsilas, and Historical Claims presented at the International
Conference on Global Consequences of Islamophobia and the Muslim World organized by the University of Management and Technology in Lahore, Pakistan,
and the International Islamic University, Malaysia.<ref name="docbio" />
2018 Presentation: The Political Legitimacy of the Sultans of the Lanao Sultanate in the 17th Century with Special Reference to the Political Views of al-
Māwardī at the 1st International Conference and Workshop of the Institute of Islamic Studies at the University of the Philippines, Diliman, September 21, 2018.
<ref name="docbio" />
2017 Presentation: The Socio-Cultural Context of Lanao Sultanate in the 17th Century delivered at the Sultan Omar Ali Saifuddien Centre for Islamic Studies
Seminar, Universiti Brunei Darussalam, January 21, 2017.<ref name="docbio" />
2012 Presentation: The Epistemology of Islamic Political Governance: A Case Study of the Lanao Sultanate in the 17th Century Philippines presented at the
4th Annual Nottingham Postgraduate Conference in Politics and International Relations at the University of Nottingham, United Kingdom, June 10, 2012.<ref
name="docbio" />
The Lanao Sultanate Dissertation: Core Scholarly Contribution
His doctoral work, conducted under the supervision of scholars at Sultan Omar Ali Saifuddien Centre for Islamic Studies, directly addressed a critical gap in
Southeast Asian historical studies. As he articulated in his research objectives:
While the polities of the sultanates of Magindanao, Manila, and Sulu in the colonial era have been studied by numerous Western and Filipino
scholars, the Lanao Sultanate during the said era has been underrepresented in the literature. In addition, there is no research done on the Lanao
Sultanate as practical Islamic governance in the 17th century.
His dissertation argues that the Lanao Sultanate in the 17th century functioned as a sophisticated system of Islamic governance guided by principles derived
from classical Islamic political theory, particularly the writings of the medieval Islamic legal and political theorist al-Māwardī. The research demonstrates that
despite its indigenous character, the sultanate maintained formal structures and decision-making processes consistent with Islamic juridical principles.
Furthermore, he contends that understanding this historical precedent matters for contemporary policy:

PAGE 3
The scholars in the 21st century have not explored the various facets of Lanao Sultanate's governance within the spectrum of broad ranging theories
on Islamic politics by Muslim scholars. This attempts to draw the holistic construct of the Lanao Sultanate in the 17th century as a case study by
which it will highlight how its political structure functioned as well as how Islamic principles had guided its policies despite its indigenous nature.
His work establishes that the Lanao Sultanate successfully maintained Islamic governance while promoting the religious, social, cultural, and political welfare
of Meranaw communities across centuries, achievements that continue to shape Muslim Meranaw identity and socio-political consciousness into the present
day.<ref name="docbio" />
Museum Curation and Cultural Heritage Preservation
Hadji Abdul Racman founded and operates the Sohayle M. Hadji Abdul Racman's Maranao Museum (Business Registration No. 5917453), located in
Cormatan, Mulondo, Lanao del Sur, within the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM). The museum represents a hands-on
commitment to Meranaw cultural preservation beyond academic publication. Its mission centers on safeguarding tangible artifacts and intangible knowledge
systems that face erosion from globalization, urbanization, and cultural displacement.
The museum's collection includes traditional Meranaw crafted items, material culture from historical periods, ceremonial objects, and contemporary artisanal
works. Display practices emphasize living cultural context rather than static curation, linking objects to ongoing community practices and knowledge systems.
The museum serves as an educational resource for Meranaw youth, researchers, and international visitors seeking to understand Meranaw civilization.
To deepen his museum expertise, Hadji Abdul Racman undertook a comprehensive cultural research tour across Europe, the Middle East, North Africa, and
Southeast Asia, studying modern museum design architectures, artifact preservation methodologies, and interpretive practices at leading institutions. These
travels informed his approach to contemporary museum work while maintaining Meranaw cultural epistemology as the organizing framework.<ref
name="docbio" />
International Editorial and Peer Review Roles
Hadji Abdul Racman serves in leadership capacities across 21 academic journals spanning Islamic studies, education, law, Islamic jurisprudence, psychology,
cultural studies, and international relations. His roles range from international advisory board member to associate editor, international reviewer, and editorial
board member. These appointments reflect international recognition of his scholarly standing and commitment to advancing academic discourse on Islam,
Muslim societies, and cultural preservation.
Prominent journal positions include:
International Advisory Board, InVest Journal of Shariah and Economic Law (IAIN Ponorogo, Indonesia, 2020 to present)
Associate Editor, Ongangen Journal, College of Social Sciences and Humanities, Mindanao State University, 2025
Advisory Board, Al-Hameed Islamic Studies Research Journal (Jamia Siddique Akbar, Lahore, Pakistan)
International Advisory Board, Firdaus Journal (Universiti Pendidikan Sultan Idris, Malaysia)
Editorial Advisory Board, Islam in the Philippines Series (IIUM Press, International Islamic University Malaysia)
Additional reviewer appointments include TAFKIR: Interdisciplinary Journal of Islamic Education (Indonesia), Journal of Islamic Studies Abhath (Garrison
University, Pakistan), At-tadzkir: Islamic Education Journal (Indonesia), Journal of Noesantara Islamic Studies (West Sumatra, Indonesia), and multiple other
publications across Southeast Asia and the Islamic world.<ref name="docbio" />
International Travel and Cultural Exchange
His scholarly networks span across Europe, Middle East, North Africa, and Southeast Asia. He has conducted research and presented at universities in:
United Kingdom (University of Nottingham, Nottingham University)
Netherlands (Amsterdam)
France (Paris)
Belgium (Brussels)
Germany (Hamburg)
Spain (Málaga)
Italy (Milan)
Malaysia (Kuala Lumpur, Perak, Kota Belud)
Brunei (Bandar Seri Begawan)
Indonesia (Jakarta, Riau)
Pakistan (Lahore)
Thailand (Bangkok, surrounding provinces)
These international engagements position him as a transnational intellectual bridging Philippine Muslim scholarship with global Islamic studies discourse.<ref
name="docbio" />
Educational Approach and Teaching Philosophy
Hadji Abdul Racman's pedagogy integrates primary source analysis, ethnographic fieldwork, and community engagement. He encourages students to treat
academic knowledge not as abstraction detached from lived reality but as tools for understanding and serving their own communities. His research seminars
often involve field visits to Lanao historical sites, interviews with community elders, and collaborative documentation projects. This approach reflects his
conviction that scholarship on Meranaw culture should remain rooted in and accountable to Meranaw communities themselves.

PAGE 4
Legacy and Contemporary Significance
Hadji Abdul Racman's work arrives at a critical historical moment for Meranaw cultural and political identity. The establishment of the Bangsamoro
Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM) in 2019 created renewed institutional space for Muslim Filipinos to articulate self-governance
frameworks rooted in Islamic and indigenous traditions. His scholarly documentation of Lanao Sultanate political thought provides historical precedent and
intellectual resources for contemporary BARMM institutional design, educational policy, and cultural preservation initiatives.
Simultaneously, his research challenges Western academic narratives that have often marginalized Philippine Muslim polities or portrayed them primarily
through colonial or conflict frameworks. By centering Meranaw intellectual agency and Islamic civilization's sophisticated institutional achievements, he
repositions Meranaw history as a rich subject of scholarly attention rather than a peripheral footnote to Philippine history.
His museum work ensures that cultural preservation extends beyond academic circles to accessible community spaces where Meranaw youth can encounter their
heritage in embodied, meaningful ways. His editorial roles across international journals amplify voices from the Global South and from Muslim-majority
contexts, challenging the geographic and religious biases of global academic publishing.<ref name="docbio" />

Israel Ariraya Radiaganding
Dr. Israel Ariraya Radiaganding (born December 26, 1990) is
a Maranao Muslim Filipino engineer, educator, public servant,
and cultural leader from Angeles City, Pampanga.
He's widely recognized as one of the first Muslim Filipinos to
graduate in Railway Engineering and Management in the
Philippines, a distinction that places him at the forefront of both
the country's growing transportation sector and its broader
narrative of Bangsamoro representation in fields historically
dominated by others.
Today, he serves as Chief Transportation Development Officer at
the Philippine Railways Institute under the Department of
Transportation, where he leads the development of the country's
railway workforce.
Alongside his government role, he teaches at the Polytechnic
University of the Philippines Manila and carries the cultural title
of Sultan a Rumapunut in Pampanga, making him one of the rare
figures who holds meaningful standing in engineering,
academia, governance, and community leadership all at once.
Contents
1 Background
2 Education
3 Professional Career
4 Leadership in Railway, Education, and Culture
5 Institutional and National Impact
6 Recognition
7 Legacy
8 References
9 See Also
Background
Israel Ariraya Radiaganding was born on December 26, 1990, in
Angeles City, Pampanga, to Hadji Nasser Radiaganding and
Hadja Nasrifah Mauyag Ariraya Radiaganding.
His Maranao roots ground his identity as a proud Muslim
Filipino, even as he was raised in Pampanga, far from the
traditional heartland of the Maranao in Lanao del Sur.

PAGE 2
M.S. Management Engineering, Pamantasan ng
Lungsod ng Maynila Ph.D. Technology
Management, Technological University of the
Philippines

Chief Transportation Development Officer,
Philippine Railways Institute, Department of
Transportation
Other Role
Part-time Faculty, Polytechnic University of the
Philippines Manila
Cultural Title
Sultan a Rumapunut, Pampanga
Career Start
2012 (railway sector)
Notability
Pioneer Muslim Filipino graduate in Railway
Engineering and Management in the Philippines
Known For
Railway workforce development; academic
mentorship; cultural leadership as Sultan a
Rumapunut; CHED technical advisory on railway
engineering programs
Pull Quote
"From a pioneering railway engineering student
to a leader in national infrastructure and a
recognized cultural figure, his journey reflects
dedication, resilience, and faith-driven service."
His parents instilled in him the values that would define his path:
perseverance, discipline, and faith. Those aren't just words in his
biography. They're the through-line of a life built on hard work
and a genuine sense of purpose.
His journey from humble beginnings in Central Luzon to
national leadership in Manila is, in many ways, a quiet but
powerful story of what's possible for Muslim Filipinos who push
past the boundaries set by geography and circumstance.
Education
Dr. Radiaganding completed his early schooling in Angeles City
before pursuing higher education in Manila.
He earned his Bachelor of Science in Railway Engineering
and Management from the Polytechnic University of the
Philippines (PUP), graduating as a Shell Scholar, a distinction
that recognized both his academic merit and his potential.
That degree placed him among the first Muslim Filipinos to
specialize in railway engineering, a field that was still
establishing its academic footing in the Philippines during his
student years.
He went on to earn a Master of Science in Management
Engineering from Pamantasan ng Lungsod ng Maynila,
deepening his grounding in both technical and organizational
systems.
He completed his academic formation with a Doctor of
Philosophy in Technology Management from the
Technological University of the Philippines, equipping him with
the research and policy perspective needed for national-level
leadership.
Professional Career
Dr. Radiaganding stepped into the railway sector in 2012,
building his expertise in planning, project development, and corporate strategy during the country's early push to
modernize its rail infrastructure.
He served at the Department of Transportation and Communications (now the Department of Transportation) and at
the Light Rail Transit Authority (LRTA), where he gained hands-on exposure to the operational and planning
realities of urban rail systems.
He later rejoined the Department of Transportation, this time at the Philippine Railways Institute (PRI), where his
career advanced steadily from Supervising Transportation Development Officer to his current role as Chief
Transportation Development Officer.

PAGE 3
In that capacity, he now leads the institute's human resource development agenda, shaping how the country trains
and certifies its railway professionals.
His academic career runs parallel to his government service. He started teaching as early as 2015, serving as a
faculty member and research adviser, and continues to teach part-time at PUP Manila, mentoring students in
engineering, research methods, and railway systems.
Leadership in Railway, Education, and Culture
As Training Head of the Philippine Railways Institute, Dr. Radiaganding is directly responsible for building the
technical capacity of the country's railway workforce.
His work in that role includes designing competency-based training programs for railway professionals, aligning
academic curricula with both industry needs and international standards, mentoring learners in railway
transportation, and supporting broader capacity-building initiatives across the sector.
Beyond the technical side, he brings the same seriousness to his role as a resource person for the Commission on
Higher Education (CHED), where he contributes to the evaluation of railway engineering programs and helps
ensure that what students learn in Philippine universities is relevant, current, and globally competitive.
His role as Sultan a Rumapunut in Pampanga adds another dimension to his leadership. It's a cultural and
community responsibility, not just a title, and it speaks to his commitment to representing Muslim heritage and
identity in a region where the Muslim community is a minority.
Institutional and National Impact
Through his work at the Philippine Railways Institute, Dr. Radiaganding is helping to build something the country
genuinely needs: a skilled, professional, and sustainable railway workforce.
The Philippines is investing heavily in rail infrastructure, and the human capital behind that infrastructure matters
just as much as the tracks and trains. His work sits squarely at that intersection.
His involvement with CHED as a Technical Resource Person also ensures that railway engineering education keeps
pace with national and international standards, a contribution that shapes not just current professionals but the next
generation of railway engineers.
Recognition
Dr. Radiaganding has been recognized as one of the Faces of Inspiration of Angeles City National High School,
an acknowledgment of his journey from student to national leader and of the example he sets for young Filipinos,
especially those from the Muslim community.
His standing as Sultan a Rumapunut further affirms his role as a recognized figure not just in professional circles
but within his cultural community.

PAGE 4
Legacy
Dr. Israel Ariraya Radiaganding represents a new generation of Muslim Filipino leaders who are making their mark
far beyond the traditional boundaries drawn for them.
He's a pioneer in a technical field that barely had Muslim Filipino representation when he started out. He's a public
servant shaping national transportation policy. He's a teacher. He's a Sultan. And he's still, by most measures, early
in his career.
For young Muslim Filipinos looking for proof that they belong in engineering, in government, in the classroom,
and in spaces of cultural leadership, Dr. Radiaganding's story makes that case without needing to say a word. He
just lives it.

Roosevelt R. Radiaganding
Roosevelt R. Radiaganding is a retired Filipino law enforcement
officer, legislator, and traditional aristocrat from Mindanao. He
holds a unique stature in the Bangsamoro region for bridging the
modern security and political apparatus of the Philippine state with
the ancient cultural governance systems of the Maranao people.
He is a retired Police Brigadier General of the Philippine National
Police (PNP), a former elected member of the Sangguniang
Panlalawigan (Provincial Board) of Lanao del Sur, and the reigning
traditional Sultan sa Lumbatan.
Contents

2 Political Career
3 Traditional and Cultural Leadership
4 Conflict Resolution and Peace Advocacy

7 See Also
Law Enforcement Career
Radiaganding dedicated decades of public service to the Philippine
National Police (PNP), rising through the officer ranks to attain the
star-rank of Police Brigadier General (formerly designated as Police
Chief Superintendent).
His operational tenure was largely concentrated within the conflict-
vulnerable areas of Mindanao. Throughout his service, he managed
complex security dynamics including counter-terrorism efforts,
local insurgencies, communal clan feuds (locally known as rido),
and community-oriented policing. Within the force, he became a
strong proponent of using traditional cultural mechanisms to de-
escalate local tensions before they manifested into armed conflicts.
Political Career
Following his retirement from active police service, Radiaganding
transitioned into formal democratic governance to continue his
public service career:
Provincial Legislator: He successfully contested a seat in the
Sangguniang Panlalawigan of Lanao del Sur, serving as a
Provincial Board Member representing his district.

Policy and Civic Oversight: During his legislative tenure, he
collaborated extensively with municipal executives
throughout the province—including leadership in the Islamic
Municipality of Tamparan—to advance local programs
focused on public education, social welfare, and rural
developmental frameworks.
Traditional and Cultural Leadership
Parallel to his modern administrative titles, Radiaganding holds a
revered, hereditary seat within the Pat a Pangampong ko Ranao
(The Four Principalities of Lanao), which dictates the traditional
socio-political organization of the Maranao people.
As the enthroned Sultan sa Lumbatan, he functions as a formal
custodian of Maranao ancestral customs (Adat) and Islamic
jurisprudence. He frequently represents the Federation of the Royal
Sultanates of Lanao del Sur in high-level civic functions, multi-
agency assemblies, and traditional cultural events.
Conflict Resolution and Peace Advocacy
Due to his dual background as both a top-tier former police
commander and an active traditional royal leader, Radiaganding is
regularly sought after as an arbiter for local and regional stability:
Electoral Integrity: During volatile local election cycles, he
frequently partners with the Armed Forces of the Philippines
(AFP), the PNP, and grassroots networks like the
Kazalimbago Movement to lead political candidates in signing
multi-party peace covenants.
Inter-faith Dialogue: He represents traditional Islamic
leadership in collaborative dialogues with Christian prelates
and non-governmental organizations to foster peaceful, multi-
cultural coexistence in the province.
Personal Life
Radiaganding belongs to a prominent Maranao family native to the
Lanao region. As a member of the royal lineages of the
*Pangampong*, his upbringing was deeply grounded in both
Islamic principles and traditional Maranao nobility. He maintains a
close-knit family life, balancing regional leadership commitments
with his roles as a father and community elder. He is highly
regarded in local civic circles as a mentor to younger Maranao
public servants entering law enforcement and local government
units.

PAGE 3

Awards and Decorations
Throughout his long career in public safety, regional development,
and cultural peacekeeping, Radiaganding has received numerous
commendations, including:

Medalya ng Kagalingan (PNP Merit Medal) – Awarded for
heroic and exceptional performance of operational police
duties.
Gawad Kapayapaan Commendation – Received from local
government and non-governmental peace networks for his
successful interventions in settling rido (clan feuds) in Lanao
del Sur.
Traditional Leadership Excellence Plaque – Conferred by
the Council of Royal Sultanates of Lanao for his dedication to
preserving Maranao cultural heritage and managing
customary conflicts.

Salma Pir T. Rasul
Atty. Salma Pir T. Rasul is a Filipino lawyer, academic, and civic
leader whose career has been defined by one big, persistent mission:
making Islamic law comprehensible, accessible, and respected
within the Philippine legal system. As both a practitioner and
educator, she works at the intersection of civil law and Shari'ah,
translating between two legal worlds that too often talk past each
other. She serves as Programs Director of the Philippine Center
for Islam and Democracy (PCID) and as the designated Director
for Islamic Law Studies at the University of the Philippines Law
Center (UPLC), making her one of the most institutionally
grounded authorities on Muslim personal law in the country. She is
the daughter of the late Senator Santanina Tillah Rasul, the first
Muslim woman elected to the Philippine Senate, and the late
Ambassador Abraham A. Rasul Sr., and the sister of peace advocate
Amina Rasul-Bernardo, president of PCID.

EARLY LIFE AND FAMILY
BACKGROUND
Salma Pir Rasul comes from a family that has long been at the
center of Bangsamoro public life. Her mother, Senator Santanina
Tillah Rasul, made history in 1987 as the first Muslim woman
elected to the Philippine Senate, serving two terms until 1995 and
authoring landmark legislation on civil service reform, gender
