policymakers
equality, and women's rights before passing away in November
2024 at the age of 94. Her father, the late Ambassador Abraham A.
Rasul Sr., was a Tausug leader who served as Philippine
Ambassador to Saudi Arabia. Growing up in this household meant
growing up around diplomacy, legislation, and grassroots advocacy
as everyday realities rather than distant ideals.
Salma is the youngest of six children. Her siblings include her sister
Amina Rasul-Bernardo, a prominent peace advocate who serves as
president of PCID, and four brothers: Fatima, Amroussi, Abraham
Jr., and Yusuf. The family legacy, shaped by both public service and
a deep rootedness in Tausug culture, gave Salma an early and
grounded sense of what it meant to carry the concerns of the
Bangsamoro people forward.
ETHNIC AFFILIATION AND
CULTURAL HERITAGE
Atty. Rasul belongs to the Tausug people, the indigenous
community historically known as the "people of the current," rooted
in the Sulu Archipelago in Southwestern Mindanao. The Tausug
have long been known for their seafaring traditions, distinct legal
and cultural customs, and a strong sense of collective identity
shaped by centuries of resistance and self-governance.
Her Tausug heritage is not incidental to her legal career; it's
foundational. The traditional customs, or Adat, of the Sulu region
inform the way she approaches questions of Muslim personal law,
community rights, and the gaps between state legislation and lived
Islamic practice. For her, working with the Code of Muslim
Personal Laws isn't just a professional specialty; it's also a personal
responsibility.
EDUCATION
Atty. Rasul earned her undergraduate degree in Business Economics from the University of the Philippines School
of Economics in Diliman, a program known for its rigorous analytical training. She then pursued law at the
University of the Philippines College of Law, completing her Juris Doctor (formerly the Bachelor of Laws or
LLB), the country's most prestigious legal training ground.
What sets her apart globally is her additional bar admissions in the United States: she has passed the bar
examinations in both New York and Maryland, making her a dual-qualified lawyer cleared to practice in the
Philippines and in two major U.S. jurisdictions. This breadth of legal credentialing reflects the same orientation
that defines her career: an insistence on engaging the law not just locally but across systems and borders.

PAGE 3
CAREER AND PROFESSIONAL TRAJECTORY
Philippine Center for Islam and Democracy (PCID)
Atty. Rasul serves as Programs Director of PCID, a non-partisan, non-profit think tank established in 2002 and
formally incorporated as a center in 2010. PCID is dedicated to studying the relationship between Islamic and
democratic political thought, and to supporting peace, development, and human rights in Muslim communities. In
this role, she designs and manages programs that promote democratic participation, counter extremist narratives,
and build civic capacities within Muslim communities across the Philippines. Her work at PCID also includes
producing accessible educational materials that explain democratic principles through an Islamic framework, a
direct response to fringe voices that have long claimed Islam and democracy are incompatible.
University of the Philippines Law Center
At the UPLC, Atty. Rasul carries the designation of Director for Islamic Law Studies, where she oversees
institutional efforts around the administration of Muslim personal laws. She previously served as Programs
Development Consultant at the UPLC's Institute for the Administration of Justice. She also lectures for the
Mandatory Continuing Legal Education (MCLE) program of the UPLC, ensuring that practicing Filipino
lawyers get up to speed on the intersections of civil law and Shari'ah. Additionally, she has taught at Lyceum of the
Philippines College of Law.
Consulting and International Work
Her expertise has made her a sought-after consultant for international institutions. She has done consulting work
for UN Women on the Women, Peace and Security (WPS) agenda for Southeast Asia, and for the United Nations
Development Programme (UNDP) on preventing violent extremism (PVE), Shari'ah law, and peacebuilding. She
has also participated as a delegate and expert speaker at international forums, including the International Law and
Religion Symposium hosted by Brigham Young University.
MAJOR WORKS AND LEGAL ADVOCACY
Shari'ah Jurisprudence and P.D. 1083
Atty. Rasul has been a consistent voice for strengthening the implementation of Presidential Decree No. 1083, the
Code of Muslim Personal Laws of the Philippines. Enacted in 1977, the Code governs matters of family, marriage,
inheritance, and personal status for Filipino Muslims, but it has historically been underserved in terms of trained
practitioners, accessible interpretation, and coordination with civil courts. Her work has focused on training
Shari'ah court judges and lawyers to apply the Code competently and to protect the rights of individuals,
particularly women, navigating both the Shari'ah and civil court systems.
Women, Peace and Security
Atty. Rasul has authored field manuals and programmatic frameworks that place Muslim women at the center of
conflict prevention and peacebuilding work. Her perspective, that women approach conflict resolution with a
fundamentally collaborative and community-grounded orientation, shapes her contributions to PVE discourse in

PAGE 4
the Philippines and across Southeast Asia. This work is part of the broader Women, Peace and Security agenda that
she has helped develop through her UN consulting engagements.
Federalism and Legal Reform
She has also been part of the study group on Federalism organized by the Local Government Development
Foundation and the Konrad Adenauer Stiftung, contributing a Muslim Mindanao perspective to ongoing debates
about constitutional restructuring and regional self-governance.
INSTITUTIONAL AFFILIATIONS
Beyond her core roles at PCID and UPLC, Atty. Rasul is active in several significant institutions:
NAMFREL: She is a member of the National Council of the National Citizens' Movement for Free Elections, a
civil society organization that monitors elections and advocates for democratic integrity in the Philippines.
ASEAN Society Philippines: She serves as Vice President for Legal Affairs, contributing to diplomatic and
socio-cultural cooperation across Southeast Asia.
UP Women Lawyers Circle: She is a member of the board of trustees of this organization dedicated to women in
the legal profession.
LEGACY AND SIGNIFICANCE
Atty. Salma Pir Rasul's contribution to Philippine legal history can be summed up this way: she made Islamic law
legible to a legal establishment that had long treated it as peripheral. By institutionalizing Shari'ah legal education
at the University of the Philippines, the country's flagship state university, she ensured that Muslim personal law
would be studied, debated, and developed alongside civil law rather than apart from it.
Her family name carries enormous weight in Bangsamoro history, but Atty. Rasul has built her own standing
through decades of institutional work, academic writing, and field engagement. She represents a generation of
Muslim Filipino professionals who have moved between local community life, national institutions, and
international platforms without losing the thread that connects all three.
For the growing generation of Muslim women entering law and public service, her career is a working blueprint:
rigorous, principled, and deeply rooted in community.

title: Remo, Rosemawattee A.
text:
PAGE 1
Rosemawattee A. Remo
Brigadier General Rosemawattee A. Remo, PAF is a trailblazing military officer and aviator who made
Philippine history as the first female Muslim pilot in the Philippine Air Force (PAF).
She belongs to the Tausug people of Sulu in the southern Philippines, and her rise through the ranks of the PAF is
one of the most compelling stories of faith, grit, and quiet determination in contemporary Bangsamoro history.
In 1998, she earned her wings, breaking a ceiling that had never been broken before, not just for women, but for
Muslim Filipinas in uniform.
On May 8, 2026, she was promoted to the one-star rank of Brigadier General, and she currently serves as the
Wing Commander of the 410th Maintenance Wing (410MW) at Clark Air Base, where she leads the PAF's
depot-level aircraft maintenance and airworthiness operations.
Her legacy is simple but profound: she proved that a woman from Sulu, rooted in Islamic tradition, can fly fighter
missions, lead rescue operations, and command a wing, all while keeping her feet on the ground.

Early Life and Background
Rosemawattee Esmael Abbarani-Remo was born and raised in
Sulu, one of the southernmost provinces of the Philippines and
one of the heartlands of Tausug culture and identity.
She grew up in a traditional Muslim household. Her father was a
school principal, which meant that education was always part of
the family's foundation. But even with that background, choosing
the military was not an easy call. In her community, it was
considered unconventional, even unexpected, for a young woman
to pursue a career in the armed forces.
She pursued it anyway.
That decision, made against the grain of social expectations,
would eventually redefine what was possible for Muslim
Filipinas in public and national service.
Education
Remo's academic journey reflects both discipline and ambition.
She completed her secondary education at St. Scholastica's
Academy in Siasi, Sulu, graduating in 1991.
She went on to earn a Bachelor's degree in Airline
Management, a choice that already pointed toward her
fascination with aviation and flight.
Her entry into the military followed the passage of Republic Act
7192, the Women in Development and Nation Building Act,
which opened combat roles to Filipino women for the first time.
That law created the legal door. Remo walked through it.
She enrolled in the Officer Candidate School (OCS) and earned
her commission, completing the same grueling pipeline as her
male counterparts.
Later in her career, she advanced her professional education
further, earning a Master in National Security Administration
(MNSA), reinforcing her credentials as both a practitioner and a
strategic thinker.

PAGE 3
in National Security

Philippine Air Force (1998)

Military Career
Early Career and Commissioning
Remo was commissioned in 1994, becoming one of the first
women to enter the PAF as a combat-qualified officer. At that
time, the integration of women into combat roles was still new
territory for the Philippine military, and she was part of the
pioneering cohort that normalized it.
Aviation Milestone: The First Female Muslim Pilot in the PAF
In 1998, four years after her commissioning, Rosemawattee Remo earned her pilot's wings, becoming the first
female Muslim pilot in the history of the Philippine Air Force.
It was a milestone that carried both national and cultural weight. For the PAF, it signaled real progress in inclusion.
For the Bangsamoro community, it was something more personal: a young Tausug woman from Sulu, raised
Muslim, had broken through one of the most elite and demanding fields in the armed forces.
She went on to serve primarily as a helicopter pilot with the 505th Search and Rescue Group, logging over 2,000
flight hours in rotary-wing aircraft, a record that speaks not just to skill but to years of sustained, mission-critical
service.
Key Operations
Remo's career has not been confined to training sorties and administrative work. She has seen real operations in the
field.
One of her most significant operational contributions came during the aftermath of Typhoon Frank in 2008, when
she participated in relief operations that brought aid to communities devastated by one of the deadliest typhoons to
hit the Philippines in years.
She also took part in various search and rescue missions and rehabilitation operations across the archipelago,
bringing her skills as a helicopter pilot directly into service for Filipino communities in distress.
Leadership Roles
Before taking command of the 410th Maintenance Wing, Remo held several senior leadership positions within the
PAF:
She served as Chief of Office for the Air Force Adjutant, where she handled personnel and administrative
matters at the institutional level.
She also served as Deputy Assistant Chief of Air Staff for Personnel (A-1), a role that gave her broad oversight
of human resource management across the Air Force.
She served as Deputy Wing Commander of the 410MW before assuming full command of the wing, giving her
deep familiarity with its operations before leading them.

PAGE 4
Command of the 410th Maintenance Wing
As Wing Commander of the 410th Maintenance Wing at Clark Air Base, BGen Remo oversees the PAF's depot-
level maintenance, repair, and overhaul (MRO) operations. This is one of the most technically demanding
commands in the Air Force, responsible for keeping the PAF's fleet airworthy and mission-ready.
Her tenure has been marked by concrete, measurable results.
Institutional Contributions
In-Country MRO Expansion
One of BGen Remo's most significant achievements as Wing Commander has been the dramatic expansion of the
PAF's in-country maintenance capabilities.
Under her leadership, the 410MW has reduced the Air Force's reliance on foreign MRO facilities from over 80
percent to less than 20 percent. That is not a small shift. It represents a fundamental change in how the PAF
sustains its airpower, moving from external dependency to genuine self-reliance.
This shift has strategic implications that go beyond cost savings. A military that can maintain its own aircraft is
more operationally resilient, more flexible, and less vulnerable to supply chain disruptions.
Asset Regeneration and Airworthiness
The 410MW under Remo's command has successfully completed 3,000-hour inspections for primary trainer
aircraft including the SF-260FH, as well as four-year inspections for the C-295 cargo fleet, restoring multiple air
assets to full operational capability.
These are depot-level operations that require technical precision and careful coordination. Their successful
completion directly translates to mission readiness for the Air Force.
Infrastructure Modernization
BGen Remo's tenure has also included the modernization of MRO Hangar 1 at Clark Air Base, which has been
upgraded to accommodate wide-body cargo planes for complex depot-level inspections. This infrastructure
improvement positions the 410MW to handle increasingly sophisticated and larger aircraft as the PAF continues to
modernize its fleet.
Personnel and Workforce Development
Recognizing that technical capability is only as strong as the people who execute it, BGen Remo has championed
programs that bridge the gap between academic training and military employment.
Under her watch, the 410MW has expanded opportunities for civilian interns, building a pipeline of skilled
technicians who can support the wing's growing MRO operations into the future.

PAGE 5
Safety and Innovation Culture
BGen Remo has made Safety Excellence a core pillar of the 410MW's culture. She has integrated best practices in
maintenance operations with insights drawn from the PAF Innovation Challenge, encouraging her personnel to
think creatively about technical problems and airworthiness standards.
Cultural Significance
BGen Remo's story carries meaning that goes beyond her professional accomplishments.
She is widely regarded as a symbol of inclusion and progress in a country where the Muslim Filipino community
has long been underrepresented in national institutions. Her career demonstrates that faith and cultural identity are
not obstacles to national service. For her, being Tausug and Muslim has always been a source of strength, not a
limitation.
Her story resonates deeply in the Bangsamoro region, where young Muslim women are often navigating the same
kinds of pressures and expectations that she once did. She shows what becomes possible when those expectations
are refused.
She is also a living example of what RA 7192 was meant to achieve: not just formal policy change, but real,
sustained transformation in who gets to serve and lead.
Personal Values and Philosophy
BGen Remo's leadership philosophy is values-based and grounded in personal accountability.
She places a high premium on perseverance and humility, two qualities she returns to often when speaking about
her journey. Despite the historic nature of her achievements, she's known for keeping her "feet grounded," which in
her own words means staying focused on service rather than status.
She is married to a fellow PAF pilot, and she has spoken openly about the particular challenge of balancing the
demands of motherhood with the responsibilities of a rescue pilot. She doesn't frame it as a contradiction. She
frames it as one more thing she chose to navigate, and did.
Her leadership aligns with the AXEL PAF framework, which emphasizes accountability, good governance, and
force development. She sees her role as a pioneer not just in terms of gender or religion, but in terms of setting
standards that others can follow.
Recognition and Legacy
BGen Remo's promotion to Brigadier General on May 8, 2026 is itself a recognition of a career built on
consistent excellence, mission commitment, and leadership at every level.
Her historic firsts, the first female Muslim officer commissioned through OCS to flight training, the first female
Muslim pilot in the PAF, continue to serve as reference points for discussions about diversity and inclusion in the
Philippine military.
She is increasingly recognized not just as a senior officer, but as a figure whose story belongs to the broader history
of Muslim Filipino achievement in the modern era.

PAGE 6
Challenges
Remo's path was not an easy one. She entered the military at a time when women in combat roles were still a new
and contested idea, and she did so as a Muslim woman from a province that was often viewed through the lens of
conflict rather than contribution.
She faced cultural resistance from within her community early on, where her choice to join the military was seen
as unconventional for a woman. She navigated institutional challenges as one of the first women through the OCS
pipeline. And she built her flying career in an environment where she was, by definition, breaking new ground with
every step.
That she did all of this without abandoning her identity, her faith, or her family, is perhaps the most instructive part
of her story.

Yasser Nursam Salahuddin Rizal
Yasser Nursam Salahuddin Rizal is a Filipino pharmacist and Yakan
professional from Basilan who achieved national prominence by
ranking first in the April 2025 Pharmacist Licensure Examination
administered by the Professional Regulation Commission.
A product of Basilan's educational institutions and the Universidad de
Zamboanga, Rizal's top board performance immediately marked him
as a symbol of excellence for the Bangsamoro region and a
transformative figure for youth from conflict-affected areas of
Mindanao.
His success resonates far beyond pharmacy rankings—it challenges
long-standing stereotypes about intellectual capacity in marginalized
communities and demonstrates that geographic origin and
socioeconomic circumstance do not determine professional
achievement or excellence.
Throughout his journey, Rizal has consistently attributed his
accomplishment to persistent effort, family support, and spiritual
faith, making his narrative one of determined resilience rather than
effortless privilege.

PAGE 2
Early Life and Family
Rizal grew up in Basilan, specifically in the communities of Al-Barka and Tuburan, surrounded by educators and
healthcare professionals.
His mother, Nihma Salahuddin Rizal, serves as principal of Bangcuang Elementary School, while his father, Jun S.
Rizal, teaches at the same institution.
This household environment fostered a culture of academic achievement and professional aspiration from
childhood.
Healthcare was woven into his family's fabric—multiple relatives worked as nurses, establishing a tradition of
service in allied health professions.
However, it was a maternal aunt already practicing in pharmacy who inspired Rizal to pursue that specific field
rather than simply follow the family nursing trajectory.
His early schooling at Geras Integrated School demonstrated his natural aptitude; he graduated as valedictorian and
emerged as one of Basilan's promising young scholars.
Rizal himself has described his educational journey as neither a straight path nor an automatic ascent, but rather a
process of finding his academic footing and then sustaining momentum.
Education
Secondary Education
Rizal attended Basilan National High School, where he completed both junior and senior high school.
His performance in the Senior High School years earned him valedictorian honors for his batch.
In retrospect, Rizal has characterized his high school experience as a "roller-coaster ride"—a candid
acknowledgment that even top performers sometimes pass through periods of self-doubt and recalibration.
He noted that he initially felt like an "average student" before regaining academic momentum, a reflection that
humanizes his path to excellence and speaks to the psychological demands of competitive academics.
Higher Education
Rizal pursued pharmacy at the Universidad de Zamboanga (UZ), part of the institution's School of Allied Medicine.
During his college years, he concentrated on mastering pharmaceutical sciences, pharmacology, chemistry, and the
regulatory and clinical dimensions of the profession.
His undergraduate performance set a trajectory toward his eventual board exam success, though Rizal has
emphasized that preparation for the licensure examination required sustained discipline beyond classroom
performance.
He credits his success in part to focused study habits, peer support, and the mentorship of instructors who
recognized his potential.

PAGE 3
Career and Achievements
The April 2025 Pharmacist Licensure Examination
Rizal's defining professional moment came in April 2025, when the Professional Regulation Commission (PRC)
announced the results of the nationwide Pharmacist Licensure Examination.
Among thousands of examinees from across the Philippines, Rizal placed first nationally with a score of 93.50%.
This achievement made him not merely a board topnotcher but the nation's top-ranked pharmacy graduate of that
examination cycle.
The announcement generated immediate recognition from government agencies, educational institutions, and
community organizations.
The Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM) government formally hailed him as a
"shining example of excellence" for Bangsamoro youth, framing his achievement as a symbol of the region's
intellectual potential.
The National Commission on Muslim Filipinos (NCMF) recognized his accomplishment as an inspiring milestone
for Muslim Filipinos across the country.
The local government of Basilan province issued formal congratulations, acknowledging that his success brought
honor to the entire region.
Significance of the Achievement
For Bangsamoro communities, Rizal's top board ranking holds symbolic weight beyond pharmacology.
He represents proof that excellence in competitive professional fields is not the exclusive province of privileged
urban centers or historically advantaged populations.
His achievement directly challenges persistent stereotypes about intellectual capability in regions affected by
conflict and marginalization.
For young people in Mindanao considering careers in healthcare and allied professions, Rizal demonstrates that
geographic origin does not determine destiny or professional ceiling.
Personal Values and Cultural Significance
On Resilience and Overcoming Doubt
In interviews and public reflections following his April 2025 success, Rizal has been candid about the
psychological dimensions of his journey.
He has spoken openly about moments of self-doubt during his academic career, particularly during high school
when he questioned whether he could sustain excellence.

PAGE 4
It was not always easy. There were times when I doubted if I could even pass, but I kept pushing
because I knew I was carrying the dreams of my family and my community.
This reflection underscores a critical aspect of Rizal's narrative: his achievement was not the product of natural
talent alone, but of deliberate persistence even in moments of uncertainty.
He has repeatedly characterized his path as a "roller-coaster ride rather than a fairy tale," deliberately rejecting
romanticized narratives of effortless success.
Success is the result of persistent effort and not just luck.
Identity and Representation
Rizal identifies proudly as both Yakan and Bangsamoro, and he views his professional achievement as a collective
triumph for his communities rather than a purely individual accomplishment.
This isn't just my story or a story of a board topnotcher. This is a story of a son of Basilan. A proud
Yakan. A proud Bangsamoro.
His emphasis on geographic and ethnic identity is intentional—it positions his success as evidence that stereotypes
about Mindanao and its peoples contradict lived reality.
He has expressed a deliberate mission to challenge limiting narratives:
I want to show that where you come from does not limit what you can achieve. We in the Bangsamoro
are capable of excellence in any field.
Spiritual and Family Foundation
Throughout his reflections on success, Rizal frequently invokes faith as a central pillar of his resilience.
He regularly uses the phrase "Alhamdulillah" (Praise be to God in Arabic), attributing his achievement not solely to
personal effort but to divine guidance.
He has spoken about the significance of his parents' prayers and their belief in his potential, especially during
periods when he doubted himself.
This integration of spiritual faith and family support reflects values deeply rooted in Islam and in Bangsamoro
family culture, where collective prayer and intergenerational encouragement are central to community life.
Mentorship and Advice to Future Professionals
Rizal's messages to aspiring pharmacists and students generally emphasize mastery of fundamentals and
consistency over shortcuts.
He counsels students to "master the basics and stay consistent," recognizing that sustained discipline matters more
than intensity of last-minute effort.
He also frames the simple act of completing the pharmacy board examination as a genuine accomplishment,
reminding students that many who attempt the licensure test do not pass.

PAGE 5
For aspiring healthcare professionals from underrepresented communities, he models an approach grounded in
faith, family support, peer collaboration, and refusal to internalize limiting stereotypes.
Recognition and Impact
The Bangsamoro Youth Commission has cited Rizal as a "shining example of excellence" whose achievement will
"inspire positive change in the region and beyond."
Beyond formal commendations, his success has generated organic grassroots recognition within Bangsamoro
communities, where his story circulates as evidence of intellectual capacity and professional potential in
populations historically marginalized by national narratives.
Educational institutions in Basilan and across BARMM have referenced his achievement when recruiting students
and demonstrating pathways to professional success.
His top board ranking has also influenced discussions within pharmacy programs about curriculum effectiveness,
student support systems, and the responsibility of educational institutions to prepare pharmacists capable of serving
diverse populations.
Legacy
Yasser Nursam Salahuddin Rizal's significance extends well beyond a single examination score.
He embodies the intersection of personal resilience, family investment, spiritual faith, and regional identity,
creating a narrative that speaks to multiple audiences: students considering healthcare careers, Bangsamoro youth
navigating systems not designed with them in mind, and Filipino professionals demonstrating excellence in any
field.
His willingness to publicly acknowledge doubt and difficulty has proven as influential as his top ranking—it
normalizes struggle as a component of achievement rather than a marker of unworthiness.
For the Bangsamoro region specifically, Rizal represents a tangible counter-narrative to conflict-era discourse
about "development deficits" or "underdevelopment."
He is living evidence that excellence flourishes in communities with strong family structures, educational
institutions committed to student success, and cultural values centered on knowledge and service.
His achievement in pharmacy will likely inspire similar recognition and support for Bangsamoro professionals in
medicine, law, engineering, education, and other regulated professions.
As Basilan's first board topnotcher in pharmacy, Rizal has effectively reopened conversations about intellectual
representation and who gets positioned as an "achiever" in national professional narratives.

title: Romato, Rommel Ariman
text:
PAGE 1
Rommel Ariman Romato
Rommel Ariman Romato (born 1981) is a Meranaw diplomat from Marawi City and one of the most
consequential Philippine foreign service officers of his generation.
He currently serves as Consul General of the Republic of the Philippines in Jeddah, Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, a
post he assumed on February 14, 2025.
Before that, he held the entire Philippine diplomatic mission in Riyadh together as Chargé d'Affaires ad interim
from July 2022 to early 2025 — a tenure marked by landmark breakthroughs in Philippine-Saudi labor, trade, and
energy relations.
His story is a quiet but remarkable one: a Muslim scholar from Lanao del Sur who broke barriers at the country's
premier state university, earned a postgraduate degree at Oxford, and built a career that now places him at the
center of one of the Philippines' most strategically important bilateral relationships.

Background
Rommel Ariman Romato was born in 1981 in Marawi City, the heart of Meranaw civilization in Lanao del Sur,
Mindanao.

PAGE 2
Rommel Ariman Romato
Born
1981
Marawi City, Lanao del Sur, Philippines
Ethnicity
Meranaw
Nationality
Filipino
Spouse
Dr. Nizhreen Mapandi-Romato
Children
Four
Education
Marawi has produced generations of Muslim Filipino scholars,
jurists, and public servants, and Romato belongs squarely to that
tradition — educated, principled, and driven by a sense of duty
that extends well beyond his community.
Before entering government service, he worked as a legal
researcher at the Office of the Ombudsman from 2004 to 2009,
building a foundation in law and governance before pivoting to
diplomacy.
Education
Romato earned his Bachelor of Arts in Philosophy from the
University of the Philippines Diliman, where he didn't just study
— he led.
He became the first Muslim student ever elected chairperson of
the UP Diliman University Student Council, a distinction that
speaks to both his character and the confidence his peers placed in
him across lines of faith and background.<ref>Abdulwahid,
Shahana (27 April 2007). "Beating the Odds." The Manila Times,
p. D2.</ref>
He went on to earn a Master of Studies in Diplomatic Studies
from the University of Oxford, Linacre College, where he won the
Ralph Feltham Prize for his research on maritime piracy in the
Horn of Africa.<ref>Philippine Consulate General in Jeddah.
"Biography of Consul General Rommel A. Romato."
Template:Cite web</ref>
While at Oxford, he also co-founded the Oxford Philippines
Society, keeping a thread of Filipino community and identity alive
in one of the world's most storied academic institutions.
He further attended the The Hague Academy of International Law,
deepening his grounding in international legal frameworks that
would prove essential throughout his diplomatic career.
Career
Joining the Foreign Service
Romato joined the Department of Foreign Affairs in 2009,
formally beginning what would become a wide-ranging
diplomatic career touching London, the United Nations, Riyadh,
and Jeddah.

PAGE 3
University of the Philippines Diliman (BA,
Philosophy)
University of Oxford, Linacre College (MSt,
Diplomatic Studies)
The Hague Academy of International Law

Notability

Diliman University Student Council; career
diplomat who led the Philippine mission to
Saudi Arabia as Chargé d'Affaires ad interim
and currently serves as Consul General in
Jeddah

Saudi Arabia; MV Galaxy Leader hostage
negotiations; ASEAN-GCC Summit facilitation;
Hajj welfare advocacy; Philippine–Saudi energy
MOU; Oxford Ralph Feltham Prize
Pull Quote
"A diplomat from Marawi who went from
leading students at UP Diliman to leading a
country's mission in the heart of the Arab
world."
In 2012 to 2013, he was seconded to the International Maritime
Organization of the United Nations, a fitting assignment given his
Oxford prize-winning research on maritime security.
<ref>"Philippines acts on call for support to the International
Maritime Organization." Philippine Embassy in the United
Kingdom. Template:Cite web</ref>
Philippine Embassy in London (2013–2019)
From 2013 to 2019, Romato served at the Philippine Embassy in
London, where his contributions went beyond the usual consular
work.
He played a key role in establishing Philippine Studies at SOAS
University of London — an academic program that gave the
Filipino intellectual tradition a formal home in one of Europe's
leading institutions of Oriental and African studies.
<ref>Alcantara, Melissa (20 February 2018). "University of
London opens PH Studies forum after £75k grant from DFA."
Philippine Daily Inquirer.</ref>
It was the kind of cultural diplomacy that rarely makes headlines
but carries lasting significance for how the Philippines is seen and
understood abroad.
Philippine Embassy in Riyadh (2021–2025)
In 2021, Romato was assigned as Consul General at the Embassy
of the Philippines, Riyadh, stepping into one of the most complex
and high-stakes postings in the Philippine foreign service.
Saudi Arabia is home to nearly a million Overseas Filipino
Workers (OFWs), and managing that reality — their welfare, their
legal protections, their access to justice — is part of the daily work
of the mission.
In July 2022, with no resident Philippine Ambassador in place,
Romato stepped up as Chargé d'Affaires ad interim, effectively
leading the entire Philippine diplomatic mission in the Kingdom.
<ref>Saudi Press Agency. "Riyadh Region Mayor Attends
Embassy of Philippines National Day Ceremony." 18 July 2024.
Template:Cite web</ref>
Lifting the Deployment Ban
In September 2022, Secretary Susan Ople of the Department of Migrant Workers made an official visit to Riyadh.
Romato facilitated the meetings that followed, which resulted in the lifting of the Philippine government's
deployment ban for workers to Saudi Arabia and opened negotiations on improving the working conditions of
hundreds of thousands of OFWs in the Kingdom.<ref>Ople, Susan. "State of Saudi-Philippine labor cooperation is

PAGE 4
'all good'." Arab News. Template:Cite web</ref>
It was a concrete, consequential win for Filipino migrant workers that traced directly back to diplomatic
groundwork laid in Riyadh.
GCC Engagement
On February 26, 2023, Romato met with Gulf Cooperation Council Secretary-General Jassem Mohamed Albudaiwi
in Riyadh to explore avenues for stronger GCC-Philippines cooperation — covering security, migrant welfare,
trade, and tourism.<ref>Secretariat General of the Gulf Cooperation Council. "GCC Secretary General Discusses
Means to Strengthen GCC-Philippines Relations With the Chargé d'Affaires." Template:Cite web</ref>
ASEAN-GCC Summit
On October 19–20, 2023, Chargé d'Affaires Romato oversaw the official visit of President Bongbong Marcos to
Saudi Arabia for the inaugural ASEAN-GCC Summit in Riyadh, including the bilateral meeting between President
Marcos and Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman.<ref>Saudi Press Agency. "President of Philippines Arrives in
Riyadh to Participate in GCC-ASEAN Summit." 19 October 2023. Template:Cite web</ref>
Managing a presidential visit of that scale — with all its protocol, logistics, and political weight — falls squarely
on the shoulders of the mission chief, and Romato handled it.
MV Galaxy Leader Hostage Negotiations
In March 2024, Romato and embassy officials traveled to Aden, Yemen to meet with intermediaries and push for
the release of the crew of the MV Galaxy Leader, a vessel seized in the Red Sea that had 17 Filipino seafarers
among those held captive.
After 430 days in captivity, the crew was released on January 21, 2025 — a result that, while shaped by many
forces, involved direct diplomatic engagement that Romato was part of.<ref>Philippine News Agency. "17 Filipino
hostages in Yemen safe from Israeli strike: PBBM." Template:Cite web</ref>
Shari'ah Bar Access for OFWs
In May 2024, following a request initiated by the Philippine Embassy, the Supreme Court of the Philippines
allowed Filipino professionals in Saudi Arabia to participate online in the Shari'ah training seminar and take the
Shari'ah Bar examination from within the Kingdom.<ref>"2024 Shari'ah Bar Makes History." Supreme Court of
the Philippines. Template:Cite web</ref>
The move expanded access to professional advancement for Muslim Filipino lawyers based overseas — a
meaningful policy gain with lasting implications.
Trade Missions and the Philippine Trade and Investment Center
From 2024 to 2025, Romato facilitated DTI-led business missions to Saudi Arabia and spearheaded the
establishment of the Philippine Trade and Investment Center (PTIC) at the Embassy, along with the appointment of
the first Philippine commercial attaché in Riyadh on November 1, 2024.<ref>Aben, Ellie (14 February 2024).
"Philippines sends first business mission to Saudi Arabia since pandemic." Arab News.</ref>

PAGE 5
First Philippine-Saudi Energy MOU
In October 2024, Romato welcomed Secretary Raphael Lotilla of the Department of Energy to Riyadh, where
historic meetings with Saudi Energy Minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman and Minister of Investment Khalid al-
Falih resulted in the signing of the first-ever Memorandum of Understanding on energy cooperation between
the Philippines and Saudi Arabia.<ref>Hassan, Nadin (15 October 2024). "Saudi Arabia, Philippines ink first
energy cooperation agreement." Arab News.</ref>
Philippine Consulate General in Jeddah (2025–present)
On February 14, 2025, Romato assumed his current post as Consul General of the Philippine Consulate General in
Jeddah, succeeding Edgar Tomas Auxilian.
Three days later, on February 17, he presented his Letter of Commission to His Excellency Farid bin Saad Alshehri,
Director General of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Makkah al-Mukarramah Branch, during which both officials
discussed opportunities for boosting economic cooperation and cultural exchanges between the Philippines and
Saudi Arabia.<ref>Saudi Press Agency. "Foreign Ministry's Makkah Branch Director General Receives Consul
General of the Philippines." Template:Cite web</ref>
Hajj Site Inspection
In May 2025, Consul General Romato led the Philippine Consulate General's Hajj Team — together with National
Commission on Muslim Filipinos Hajj Attaché OIC Omar Mandia — on an on-site inspection of the Mina and
Arafat pilgrimage sites in Makkah.
It was the first such inspection led by a Philippine Consul General in Jeddah in recent years, signaling a more
hands-on, personal approach to ensuring the safety and comfort of Filipino pilgrims during Hajj.<ref>Department
of Foreign Affairs. "PH Consulate General in Jeddah Inspects Hajj Sites to Ensure Filipino Pilgrims' Safety." 16
May 2025. Template:Cite web</ref>
Later that month, Romato was also among those who welcomed the first batch of 376 Filipino pilgrims arriving in
Madinah for Hajj 2025, greeting them alongside Ambassador Raymond Balatbat and other Philippine government
officials.
Filipiniana Cultural Exchange
In November 2025, in celebration of Philippine Book Development Month, the Consulate partnered with King
Fahad Public Library and the National Commission for Culture and the Arts (NCCA) to mount Windows to the
Philippines: Stories, Culture, and Art Through Books — a Filipiniana book display at King Fahad Public
Library in Jeddah.
Romato personally turned over the curated collection from the Consulate's Sentro Rizal library to Dr. Abdullah
Alahmadi, CEO of the library, making Philippine literature, art, and culture accessible to Saudi and international
readers in both the male and female sections of the facility.
Legacy
Romell Ariman Romato's career is a study in what representation can look like when given room to grow.

PAGE 6
He entered the Philippine foreign service as a Meranaw from Marawi — already carrying the distinction of being
the first Muslim to lead the UP Diliman student government — and has since built a record of diplomatic
achievement that serves not just his community but the entire Filipino diaspora.
His years in Riyadh were defined by the kind of unglamorous, high-stakes work that rarely generates recognition:
negotiating deployment terms, managing labor disputes, coordinating presidential logistics, following hostage leads
to Yemen, and laying the groundwork for energy and trade agreements that will outlast his tenure.
In Jeddah, he's brought that same seriousness to the welfare of Filipino pilgrims and the broader cultural
relationship between the Philippines and the Kingdom.
He's also a living argument — made quietly, through a career, not through a speech — that Muslim Filipinos
belong not just in the margins of national life but at its center.
Personal Life
Romato is married to Dr. Nizhreen Mapandi-Romato, a physician.
They have four children.

title: Ronsing, Asnawil G.
text:
PAGE 1
Dr. Asnawil G. Ronsing
Asnawil G. Ronsing
Dr. Asnawil G. Ronsing is a distinguished Filipino academic, legal expert, and institutional leader whose name has
become synonymous with the advancement of Philippine Shari'ah Law. A respected voice in Islamic jurisprudence,
he currently serves as System President of the RC-Al Khwarizmi International College Foundation, Inc. (RC-
AKICFI), where he champions educational excellence rooted in Islamic values. Of Meranaw descent, Dr. Ronsing
has dedicated his career to bridging traditional Islamic law with the Philippine legal framework, particularly for the
Bangsamoro community. His signature contribution—authoring the seminal reference "Islamic Law on
Succession"—has shaped the training of countless Shari'ah practitioners and scholars across the nation.
Contents
1 Early Life and Background
2 Education
3 Professional Career
3.1 Academic Leadership
3.2 Legal Consultation and Speaking Engagements
4 Contributions to Shari'ah Law
4.1 Published Works
4.2 Institutional Development
4.3 Academic Mentorship
5 Cultural Significance
6 Personal Values and Community Service
7 Legacy and Recognition
8 External Links
Early Life and Background
Dr. Asnawil G. Ronsing hails from the Meranaw people, the
indigenous "people of the lake" who have inhabited the Lanao
provinces of Mindanao for centuries. Growing up within this rich
cultural tapestry, where Islamic traditions and Filipino heritage
interweave, Dr. Ronsing developed an early appreciation for the role of Shari'ah in community life. The Meranaw
are known for their deep Islamic faith and scholarly traditions, and these values clearly shaped his trajectory
toward becoming one of the Philippines' foremost authorities on Islamic law.
Education
Dr. Ronsing pursued his higher education at the International Islamic University Malaysia (IIUM), a premier
institution recognized globally for its excellence in Islamic studies and jurisprudence. At IIUM, he immersed
himself in the study of Shari'ah, gaining both theoretical knowledge and practical insights that would later define
his career. The rigorous academic environment at IIUM equipped him with the tools to navigate complex legal
questions at the intersection of Islamic and Philippine law, preparing him for a lifetime of service to his community
and country.

PAGE 2
Professional Career
Academic Leadership
Dr. Ronsing's career has been marked by significant leadership roles within the Mindanao State University (MSU)
system and beyond. He served as Dean of the King Faisal Center for Islamic, Arabic, and Asian Studies
(KFCIAAS) at MSU-Main Campus in Marawi City, where he oversaw programs that trained the next generation of
Shari'ah scholars and legal practitioners. His tenure at KFCIAAS saw the center flourish as a hub for Islamic
scholarship, drawing students not only from Mindanao but from across the Philippines and neighboring countries.
In his current role as System President of RC-Al Khwarizmi International College Foundation, Inc. (RC-AKICFI),
Dr. Ronsing provides strategic direction and policy formulation for the entire institution. Under his leadership, RC-
AKICFI has expanded its academic offerings, including the establishment of a Senior High School program and
specialized departments in Civil Engineering and Biology. His vision for RC-AKICFI goes beyond conventional
education—he seeks to create what he calls a "Generation of Unity," grounded in both academic excellence and
moral integrity.
Legal Consultation and Speaking Engagements
Beyond the walls of academia, Dr. Ronsing is a sought-after legal consultant and speaker on matters of Shari'ah
law. He is frequently invited by the Philippine Consulate General in Jeddah and other governmental and
international bodies to deliver lectures on Shari'ah Bar examinations, legal writing, and Bangsamoro affairs. His
expertise bridges the gap between traditional Islamic jurisprudence and contemporary legal practice, making him
an invaluable resource for policymakers, lawyers, and community leaders alike.
Contributions to Shari'ah Law
Published Works
Dr. Ronsing is the author of "Islamic Law on Succession," a critical reference that has become required reading for
Shari'ah law practitioners and students throughout the Philippines. The book addresses complex questions of
inheritance under Islamic law, providing clear guidance that honors both religious principles and Philippine legal
contexts. His ability to distill intricate legal concepts into accessible language has made this work indispensable for
anyone navigating succession matters in Muslim communities.
Institutional Development
Under Dr. Ronsing's presidency, RC-AKICFI has emerged as a model institution that balances modern educational
standards with Islamic values. He has spearheaded the expansion of academic programs, ensuring that students
receive comprehensive training in fields ranging from engineering to the biological sciences, all while maintaining
a strong foundation in Islamic ethics. The institution's growth reflects his belief that excellence in education is a
form of devotion—a principle he frequently emphasizes in his addresses to students and faculty.

PAGE 3
Academic Mentorship
Dr. Ronsing's impact extends through the many students he has mentored over the years. Numerous graduates
under his guidance have gone on to ace the Shari'ah Bar Examinations and achieve top honors at major universities.
His mentorship style emphasizes not only mastery of legal principles but also the cultivation of moral character and
community responsibility. Many of his former students now serve as lawyers, judges, and educators, carrying
forward his vision of Shari'ah as a living tradition that serves contemporary needs.
Cultural Significance
Dr. Ronsing's work holds deep cultural significance for the Bangsamoro community and the broader Filipino
Muslim population. As an expert in Shari'ah, he plays a critical role in preserving and institutionalizing Islamic
jurisprudence within the Philippine legal system. His efforts help ensure that Muslim Filipinos can navigate
personal and family matters—such as marriage, divorce, and inheritance—in accordance with their faith, while
remaining fully integrated into the national legal framework. He is often called upon as a resource person for
government missions and international delegations seeking to understand the nuances of Islamic law in the
Philippine context. This work is particularly important in the Bangsamoro region, where the implementation of
Shari'ah law is a key component of the broader peace and autonomy process.
Personal Values and Community Service
At the heart of Dr. Ronsing's philosophy is the conviction that excellence and moral governance are inseparable
pillars of development. He frequently advocates for the pursuit of excellence as a form of devotion, urging students
and colleagues alike to see their work as an act of worship. This principle animates his leadership at RC-AKICFI,
where he has fostered a culture of high academic standards coupled with strong ethical commitments. Dr. Ronsing
is also a strong proponent of community service. He actively supports initiatives such as the Ramadhan Donation
Drive and blood-letting activities organized in partnership with the Philippine Red Cross. These efforts reflect his
belief that education and scholarship must serve the broader good, addressing not only intellectual needs but also
the material and social welfare of the community.
Legacy and Recognition
Dr. Asnawil G. Ronsing's legacy is written in the institutions he has led, the students he has mentored, and the legal
frameworks he has helped shape. His work has ensured that Shari'ah law remains a vibrant and relevant part of
Filipino Muslim life, while also contributing to the broader national dialogue on religious freedom, cultural
diversity, and legal pluralism. As one of the foremost experts on Philippine Shari'ah Law, Dr. Ronsing has earned
the respect of colleagues, students, and policymakers alike. His contributions to Islamic legal scholarship,
combined with his dedication to education and community service, have made him a towering figure in Mindanao's
academic and legal landscapes. For the Meranaw people and the wider Bangsamoro community, he represents the
possibility of honoring tradition while embracing progress—a delicate balance that he has navigated with wisdom
and grace throughout his career.

title: Saaduddin A. Alauya, Sr.
text:
PAGE 1
Saaduddin A. Alauya, Sr.
Alim Atty. Saaduddin A. Alauya Sr. was a Filipino Islamic jurist, lawyer, educator, and statesman from Lanao del
Sur who spent his entire career building the institutional foundations of Shariah within the Philippine national legal
system. He served successively as a municipal judge, university professor, provincial vice-governor and acting
governor, chairman of the Code Commission on Muslim Laws in the ARMM, and — as the capstone of it all — as
the nation's first Jurisconsult in Islamic Law, appointed by President Fidel V. Ramos in 1996. That last post made
him the highest state-recognized authority on Islamic law in the country, essentially the Philippines' national Mufti.
Scholars, practitioners, and officials across the Bangsamoro know him simply as the "Father of Shariah" — a
title that reflects not just a career, but a lifelong mission to make the divine law a living, enforceable reality for
millions of Muslim Filipinos.<ref name="wiki">Wikipedia: "Saaduddin Alauya." Retrieved March 2026.
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saaduddin_Alauya</ref><ref name="amno">A.M. No. 11238-Ret. In Re: Expiration
of Fixed Term of Jurisconsult in Islamic Law Saaduddin A. Alauya, Sr. Supreme Court of the Philippines. 2015.
https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/60991</ref>
His books — on inheritance, personal law, jurisprudence, penal law, and procedure — are the reference texts for
the Special Shariah Bar Examinations and are cited daily in Shariah courts from Zamboanga to Lanao. His family
has continued his work across medicine, law, academia, and engineering, extending a legacy of excellence from the
shores of Lake Lanao to Harvard Medical School and New York University.

Early Life and Background
Saaduddin A. Alauya Sr. was born into the Maranao community of
Lanao del Sur, in the cultural and spiritual heartland of the
Bangsamoro people. The Maranao — whose name literally means
"People of the Lake" — have long prized both Islamic learning and
professional achievement, and it was within that tradition that Alauya
came of age.<ref name="wiki"/>
His early education followed two parallel tracks that would define his
entire career: the traditional Madrasah system, which gave him his
grounding in the Qur'an, Hadith, and classical Islamic scholarship;
and the Philippine secular education system, which opened the door
to the Philippine Bar and the formal legal profession. That
combination — Alim and lawyer — was extraordinarily rare at the
time, and it turned out to be exactly what the Bangsamoro needed.
He completed the academic preparation that would later take him to
the faculty of Mindanao State University (MSU), where he taught
Islamic studies and law.<ref name="wiki"/> His training in ijtihad —
the practice of independent legal reasoning — shaped how he would
later approach the codification of Muslim personal laws. He didn't
just study the law; he thought critically about how it could be made to
work inside a modern, predominantly secular state.<ref
name="scribd">Scribd. "Shariah in the Philippines: Status,
Challenges, and Prospects." ResearchGate.
https://www.researchgate.net/profile/Ating-
Diacat/publication/349945622</ref>
Judicial Career: A Decade in Bubong
(1971–1981)
Before becoming a national figure, Alauya spent ten formative years
as a Municipal Trial Court (MTC) judge in Bubong, Lanao del Sur,
serving from March 16, 1971 to April 29, 1981.<ref name="amno"/>
Those years turned out to be much more than a career starting point
— they were a first-hand research phase.
Day after day on the bench, he saw exactly where the Philippine Civil
Code fell short for Muslim communities. Marriage, divorce,
inheritance, child custody — all of these were governed by laws
rooted in Western and Catholic legal traditions that had little room for
Islamic practice. He watched the friction between state law and lived
religious experience play out in real cases involving real families, and
he kept mental notes.
By the time he left the bench, Alauya had the clearest possible picture
of why a separate, state-recognized Shariah court system wasn't just
desirable — it was overdue. His decade in Bubong gave his later

PAGE 3
advocacy a grounded, practical authority that purely academic scholars couldn't match.
Academic Career: Teaching Shariah at MSU (1983–1987)
After his judicial years, Alauya moved into academia, joining the faculty of Mindanao State University from March
1983 to November 1987.<ref name="wiki"/> He taught at both the MSU College of Law and the King Faisal
Center for Islamic, Arabic and Asian Studies (KFCIAAS), and his goal was bigger than just filling classes — he
was working to establish Shariah as a rigorous academic discipline on par with secular law.
His lectures during this period became the foundation for his textbooks. He standardized the curriculum for Shariah
studies at MSU and mentored the young lawyers and scholars who would eventually staff the Shariah Circuit and
District Courts across the Mindanao region. His courses laid out the theoretical framework for Muslim self-
determination within the Philippine state — not as a rejection of the republic, but as a constitutionally compatible
form of governance.<ref name="scribd2">Scribd. "Untitled — Moro Self-Determination." Document 639352565.
https://www.scribd.com/document/639352565/Untitled</ref>
He argued that a regional Islamic government could function effectively under Shariah without stepping outside the
sovereign bounds of the Philippine state.<ref name="scribd2"/> It was a position that required both religious
credibility and legal precision, and Alauya had both.
Political Leadership in Lanao del Sur (1988–1995)
The late 1980s brought Alauya into electoral politics. He won as Vice-Governor of Lanao del Sur in 1988, and
served in that capacity until 1992, after which he took on the role of Acting Governor until 1995.<ref
name="wiki"/>
His time in provincial leadership coincided with one of the most turbulent periods in southern Philippine history,
following the People Power Revolution and amid the ongoing Moro conflict. He managed the competing pressures
of a province that was central to the Bangsamoro struggle — underdeveloped infrastructure, an underperforming
education system, and deep-seated internal divisions that scholars have called the "triumvirate quandaries" of
Muslim Mindanao.<ref name="cids">UP-CIDS Discussion Paper 2020-01. "The Triumvirate Quandaries of
Muslims in the Philippines." https://cids.up.edu.ph/wp-content/uploads/2022/02/UP-CIDS-Discussion-Paper-2020-
01.pdf</ref> His approach to governance wove Islamic principles into practical public administration — a style
that was both culturally authentic and institutionally functional.
The most consequential appointment of this phase came in March 1994, when he was named Chairman of the Code
Commission on Muslim Laws in the ARMM.<ref name="wiki"/> In that role, he moved from advocating for a
Shariah court system to actually designing it. He envisioned the courts not as isolated religious tribunals but as
modern judicial institutions capable of delivering justice efficiently, with the procedural rigor that the Supreme
Court of the Philippines would respect.
The Office of the Jurisconsult (1996–2003)
The pinnacle of Alauya's service to the Philippine state came on August 12, 1996, when President Fidel V. Ramos
appointed him as Jurisconsult in Islamic Law — an office based in Zamboanga City and created under the Code of
Muslim Personal Laws (Presidential Decree No. 1083).<ref name="amno"/> The Jurisconsult is the highest
authority in the country for issuing legal opinions (fatwa) on Islamic law to the government and the judiciary.

PAGE 4
"The completeness and timelessness of Islam make Shariah applicable even to the most modern legal
challenges. For Muslims to live in peace and development, their legal system must be recognized as
part of the law of the land." — Alim Atty. Saaduddin A. Alauya Sr., as cited in "Shariah in the
Philippines: Status, Challenges, and Prospects"
He served his seven-year fixed term, ending in August 2003.<ref name="amno"/> As the Philippines' national
Mufti, he clarified how Shariah applied to modern scenarios — from inheritance disputes to Islamic contract law
— and issued the opinions that standardized practice across Mindanao. His influence was so central to the office
that when he retired, the Jurisconsult's post was effectively without a functioning successor for a period, because
finding someone with his level of dual religious-legal legitimacy proved genuinely difficult.<ref
name="shariah">ResearchGate. "Shariah in the Philippines: Status, Challenges, and Prospects." Diacat, Ating.
https://www.researchgate.net/profile/Ating-Diacat/publication/349945622</ref>
The Supreme Court Battle for Judicial Recognition
Alauya's retirement in 2003 set off a legal fight that became a landmark case in Philippine jurisprudence. After
more than 33 years of government service, he applied for retirement benefits under Republic Act No. 910 — the
law that governs pensions for justices and judges.<ref name="amno"/> The Office of the Court Administrator
initially denied the claim on the grounds that the Jurisconsult was not technically a judicial officer.<ref
name="amno"/>
Alauya challenged that ruling, arguing that the rank and privileges attached to his office were equivalent to those of
a regular court judge. The Supreme Court en banc eventually ruled in his favor, granting him the rank and
privileges of a Regional Trial Court judge effective October 1996, and awarding him a lifetime monthly pension
accordingly.<ref name="amno"/>
The decision was significant well beyond Alauya's personal case. The Court ruled that treating him differently from
other court officials would "perpetuate a wrong" — effectively creating a "compartmentalized justice" that
discriminated against Muslim legal practitioners.<ref name="amno"/> By formally recognizing the Jurisconsult's
work as the equivalent of judicial service, the Supreme Court put on record that Shariah and its practitioners belong
in the national judiciary — not on its margins.
Scholarly Works
Alauya's books are his most tangible and lasting contribution to the Bangsamoro. He understood early on that for
Shariah to survive in a Philippine legal environment, it had to be written down, standardized, and made accessible
to students sitting for the Special Shariah Bar Examinations. His works did exactly that.
Muslim Inheritance Law (Mirath)
First published in 1987, Muslim Inheritance Law remains the definitive Philippine text on Islamic succession.<ref
name="googlebks1">Google Books. "Muslim Inheritance Law — Saaduddin A. Alauya."
https://books.google.com/books/about/Muslim_Inheritance_Law.html?id=7km7AAAAIAAJ</ref> It bridges the
Quranic verses on inheritance with the specific provisions of Presidential Decree No. 1083, walking through the
fixed shares (fardh) and residuary portions (asaba) of Islamic succession law. His treatment of the "Al Gharawaini"
or Umariatān cases — classic scenarios involving the distribution of an estate among parents and a spouse —
became the standard reference for resolving these disputes in Shariah District Courts across the country.<ref
name="serialsjournals">Serialsjournals. "Al Gharawaini Cases in Islamic Inheritance."
https://serialsjournals.com/abstract/77253_10_jamel.pdf</ref>

PAGE 5
The Quizzer in Muslim Personal Law
To help candidates prepare for the Special Shariah Bar Examinations, Alauya authored the Quizzer in Muslim
Personal Law, structured in a question-and-answer format that breaks down complex Islamic concepts into
manageable, testable material.<ref name="googlebks2">Google Books. "Quizzer in Muslim Personal Law —
Saaduddin A. Alauya." https://books.google.com/books/about/Quizzer_in_Muslim_Personal_Law.html?
id=yU3AwAEACAAJ</ref> The book covers legal capacity, the restrictions imposed by age and mental condition,
the rules on maradhul-maut (death-illness), and the acquisition of civil personality under Islamic law. It's become a
standard study tool — practical, precise, and written by someone who had been on both sides of the bench.<ref
name="scribdmplaw">Scribd. "Muslim Personal Law." Document 317333796.
https://www.scribd.com/document/317333796/Muslim-Personal-Law</ref>
Fundamentals of Islamic Jurisprudence and Islamic Penal Law
His works on the Fundamentals of Islamic Jurisprudence and Islamic Penal Law (1999) pushed Philippine Shariah
scholarship into deeper theoretical territory.<ref name="wiki"/> These texts explore the Usul al-Fiqh (principles of
jurisprudence) and how concepts like Hudud (prescribed sanctions) and Tazir (discretionary punishment) can be
understood within the limits of the Philippine Constitution. Even where these provisions are not fully
operationalized under national law, Alauya documented them carefully — keeping the scholarly record intact for
future generations.
Islamic Procedure and Evidence
His final major contribution to the canon, Islamic Procedure and Evidence, formalized the rules for Shahada
(testimony) and Iqrar (confession) in Shariah court proceedings.<ref name="wiki"/> By documenting evidentiary
procedure at this level of detail, Alauya helped the Shariah courts earn the respect of the broader Philippine
judiciary. These aren't customary tribunals making decisions by feel — they're courts of record operating under
defined, written rules.
Legacy and the Alauya Family
The most eloquent proof of Alauya Sr.'s legacy isn't an award or a court ruling — it's the generation of
professionals he raised and inspired. His children and grandchildren have pursued careers in medicine, law,
engineering, business, and academia, carrying the Alauya name to some of the world's most prestigious institutions.
Dr. Aslama Alauya-Lamping
His daughter Dr. Aslama Alauya-Lamping is a specialist in pulmonary medicine and internal medicine who
completed the "Leadership in Medicine: Asia Pacific" program at Harvard Medical School.<ref
name="hms">Harvard Medical School. "From Mindanao to Harvard: A Pulmonologist's Journey in Medicine and
Leadership." https://learn.hms.harvard.edu/insights/learner-stories/mindanao-harvard-pulmonologists-journey-
medicine-and-leadership</ref> While there, she applied lean management principles to improve cardiopulmonary
resuscitation outcomes at Amai Pakpak Medical Center in Marawi City — work that earned her the Excellence
Award from Harvard faculty.<ref name="hms"/> At the 65th Araw ng Lanao del Sur, she received the "Pride of
Ranaw" award and attributed her drive directly to her identity as a Mëranaw woman and the example set by her
father.<ref name="pia">Philippine Information Agency. "65th Araw ng Lanao del Sur opening spotlights Meranaw
achievers." https://pia.gov.ph/news/65th-araw-ng-lanao-del-sur-opening-spotlights-meranaw-achievers/</ref>

PAGE 6
Atty. Saaduddin M. Alauya Jr. (Duds)
His son Atty. Saaduddin M. Alauya Jr., known as "Duds," is today the Vice Chancellor for Administration and
Finance at MSU-Marawi — the same center where his father once taught.<ref name="msumain">MSU Main
Campus — Marawi City. "Prof. Abdulcader M. Ayo, Ph.D." https://www.msumain.edu.ph/personnel/dodong/</ref>
He holds degrees in Mining Engineering, Laws, Islamic Studies, and a PhD in Philippine Studies, and he was a
topnotcher in the 1999 Special Shariah Bar Examinations.<ref name="msumain"/> He also served as an examiner
for the 2022 Shariah Bar Examinations in Islamic Law of Inheritance — ensuring that the Alauya family's authority
on Shariah succession continues into the next generation.<ref name="msumain"/>
Ameladim Alauya
Another family member, Ameladim Alauya, authored the Shari'a Remedial Law Compendium, an essential
procedural reference for practitioners in the Shariah courts.<ref name="nyu">GlobaLex / NYU Law. "Philippine
Legal Information Resources and Citations." https://www.nyulawglobal.org/globalex/philippines_part2.html</ref>
Other Alauya family members have pursued graduate education at New York University and Harvard Business
School, specializing in business administration and international finance.<ref name="hms"/> The family's
professional range — spanning pulmonology, jurisprudence, engineering, nursing, and business — reflects the
patriarch's belief that excellence in any field and fidelity to Islam are not in tension; they strengthen each other.
Significance for Bangsamoro Identity
The title "Father of Shariah" captures something real: Alauya didn't just practice Islamic law in the Philippines, he
made the Philippines practice it back. His career made the case — through teaching, legislating, adjudicating, and
writing — that Shariah is not a foreign imposition or a source of conflict, but a "necessity in a multi-cultural
country" that, when properly institutionalized, leads to greater understanding and tolerance.<ref name="shariah"/>
His argument was always that being a "real Muslim" and a Filipino citizen were not competing identities. Shariah,
as he framed it, was the "kernel of Islam" — and for the Bangsamoro to live with dignity and development within
the Republic, that kernel had to have a formal place in the law of the land.<ref name="shariah"/> His work
provided the institutional scaffolding for the ARMM and, by extension, the BARMM — not just as political
achievements, but as legal realities grounded in a codified, court-ready Shariah system.
He moved Shariah in the Philippines from oral tradition to published textbook, from community custom to formal
court procedure, from religious conviction to enforceable national law. That transformation — quiet, incremental,
and built book by book and ruling by ruling — is the measure of the man.
Death
For more on this office, see Jurisconsult in Islamic Law.
Alauya Sr. completed his term as Jurisconsult in August 2003 and retired after more than three decades of
government service. The exact date of his death is not confirmed in publicly available sources at the time of this
article's writing. His Supreme Court retirement case (A.M. No. 11238-Ret.), decided in 2015, documents the
conclusion of his official career and the legal recognition of his service by the Philippine judiciary.<ref
name="amno"/> His legacy continues through his family, his books, and the Shariah court system he spent his life
building.

PAGE 7

title: Saber, Mamitua D.
text:
PAGE 1
Mamitua D. Saber
Dr. Mamitua D. Saber (March 18, 1921 – January 31, 1992) was a Filipino sociologist, historian, cultural
advocate, and institution-builder whose life's work reshaped how the Bangsamoro people are seen, studied, and
understood.
Born into Maranao royalty in what is now Marawi City, Lanao del Sur, Saber spent decades building the academic
foundations of Muslim Mindanao, from co-founding Mindanao State University in 1961 to establishing the first
museum in Mindanao dedicated to Meranaw culture.
He's widely honored as the Patron of Mindanao's Arts and Culture, a title that speaks to his single-minded
dedication to preserving Maranao heritage at a time when it was at serious risk of being overlooked or absorbed
into a dominant national narrative.
What made Saber remarkable wasn't just his credentials; it was the combination of scholarly rigor and cultural
rootedness he brought to everything he did. He was the first Maranao, and the first Muslim in the Philippines, to
earn a doctorate in Sociology, and he used that platform not for personal prestige but to document, protect, and
celebrate the people he came from.
His enduring legacy lives on at the Mamitua Saber Institute of Research and Creation (MSIRC) at MSU
Marawi, an institution that continues his mission of grounding knowledge in the lived realities of Bangsamoro
communities.
Contents
1 Early Life and Ethnic Affiliation
2 Education
3 Career and Professional Life
3.1 Mindanao State University
3.2 The Aga Khan Museum
4 Major Works and Publications
5 Personal Values and Advocacy
6 Recognition and Honors
7 Death and Lasting Legacy
8 See Also
9 References
Early Life and Ethnic Affiliation
Mamitua Saber was born on March 18, 1921, in Barrio Dayawan, Dansalan, a lakeside town in Lanao del Sur that
would later be renamed Marawi City.
He came from the noble lineages of both Masiu and Marawi, two of the most prominent royal houses among the
Maranao people, giving him a cultural inheritance that would shape his scholarly orientation for the rest of his life.
His father, Datu Saber Sinal-Desarip Rapitan, was a recognized local figure who worked as a contractor for the
U.S. military installation at Camp Keithley. His mother, Bai Linggaonan Daurog, was a native of Masiu, and
through her, Mamitua was connected to one of the oldest aristocratic lines in the Lanao region.

PAGE 2
Dr. Mamitua D. Saber

As a boy, he went by the nickname Pitó, a name drawn from the
Maranao word mamitowa, meaning one who explains or
elucidates.
That name turned out to be almost prophetic. His entire adult life
was spent doing exactly that: explaining the Maranao world to
those outside it, and helping Maranaos understand themselves
more deeply through scholarship and institutional memory.
Education
Saber's educational path was anything but ordinary for a young
Maranao man of his generation, and each step he took was a first
in its own way.
He completed his undergraduate studies at the University of
Santo Tomas in Manila, earning a degree in Journalism. That
early training gave him the communication instincts that would
later make him an effective editor, writer, and public intellectual.
From there, he pursued graduate studies in the United States as a
Fulbright Scholar, enrolling at the University of Kansas where
he earned both his Master's degree and his Ph.D. in Sociology.
In 1967, he became the first Maranao to earn a doctorate in
Sociology, and by extension, the first Muslim sociologist in the
Philippines.
That milestone wasn't just personal. It was a signal to an entire
community that Maranao scholarship could reach the highest
rungs of global academia, and that their culture and history were
worthy subjects of serious scientific inquiry.
Career and Professional Life
Saber's professional career began at the national level, where he
worked as a translator-researcher for both the National Library
of the Philippines and the National Museum of the Philippines.
That grounding in archival and ethnographic work gave him a
keen sense of what it meant to document a people's identity, and
what could be lost if no one bothered to write it down.
His most consequential chapter, though, came with his
involvement in building the academic infrastructure of Muslim
Mindanao.

PAGE 3
Notable
works

Mindanao State University
In 1961, Saber was part of the founding cohort of Mindanao
State University (MSU), established by Republic Act 1387.
He served as the university's first Dean of Research, a role that
put him at the center of defining what knowledge production at
MSU would look like.
Over the years, he also served as the inaugural head of the Office
of the Vice Chancellor for Research and Extension (OVCRE),
an administrative position that allowed him to institutionalize
research as a core function of the university rather than an
afterthought.
He's also credited with establishing the departments of Sociology and Anthropology at MSU, laying the
disciplinary foundations that have since trained generations of scholars from the Bangsamoro region.
The Aga Khan Museum
On June 13, 1962, Saber founded the Aga Khan Museum at MSU Marawi, making it the first museum in
Mindanao specifically dedicated to Meranaw culture and heritage.
The museum's establishment was the result of both Saber's vision and his diplomatic skill. He successfully secured
funding for the building through a donation from Prince Karim Aga Khan IV, the 49th Imam of the Shia Imami
Ismaili Muslims, who was known for his patronage of cultural and educational institutions in Muslim-majority
communities worldwide.
The Aga Khan Museum became a living archive of Maranao artistic tradition, housing collections of traditional
weaving, metalwork, and other material culture that might otherwise have disappeared amid rapid social change.
Major Works and Publications
Saber was a prolific writer who believed that scholarship had a responsibility to speak to real communities, not just
academic journals.
His most significant publications include:
The Maranao (1975), co-edited with Dr. Antonio Isidro, which remains a foundational reference on Maranao
society, culture, and history.
Battle of Marawi, 1895 (1980), a historical account of Maranao resistance during the Spanish colonial
period, recovering a chapter of local heroism that had been largely absent from mainstream Philippine
historiography.
Comparative Notes on Museum Exhibits (1977), which drew on his international study of Southeast Asian
museums and informed how the Aga Khan Museum developed its curatorial approach.
He was also a founding editor of two flagship regional publications:

PAGE 4
The Mindanao Journal (1974), a peer-reviewed academic publication that gave Mindanao scholars a home
venue for their research.
Mindanao Art and Culture (1979), which documented the artistic and cultural traditions of the region for
broader public audiences.
These publications weren't just academic outputs. They were instruments of cultural self-determination, giving the
Bangsamoro people a documented, published record of who they are.
Personal Values and Advocacy
Those who knew Dr. Saber consistently describe him as humble and soft-spoken, qualities that stood in contrast to
the boldness of his institutional ambitions.
He was a strong advocate for what he called meaningful integration, a philosophy that rejected forced
assimilation while affirming the possibility of constructive dialogue between Bangsamoro communities and the
broader Philippine state.
For Saber, integration didn't mean erasure. It meant finding a way for Maranao identity, with all its royal traditions,
Islamic values, and artistic richness, to coexist within and contribute to a pluralist Philippine society.
This philosophy ran through everything he did, from the museum he built to the academic departments he founded
to the journals he edited. His life's work was, at its core, an argument for the dignity and distinctiveness of Maranao
culture in a country that didn't always make room for it.
His documentation of traditional weaving techniques and oral folklore was especially valuable during the late 20th
century, when rapid urbanization and political conflict in Mindanao threatened to sever communities from their
cultural roots.
Recognition and Honors
In recognition of his decades of service to MSU and to Maranao scholarship, Dr. Saber was in the process of being
designated Professor Emeritus at the time of his death, which would have made him the first recipient of that
honor in MSU's history.
He is remembered in the broader Mindanao community as the Patron of Mindanao's Arts and Culture, a title
that reflects the scope and lasting impact of his cultural contributions.
The most tangible institutional tribute came when the MSU University Research Center was renamed the
Mamitua Saber Institute of Research and Creation (MSIRC) in his honor, ensuring that his name remains
synonymous with research, cultural documentation, and community-centered scholarship at the university he
helped build.
Death and Lasting Legacy
Dr. Mamitua D. Saber passed away on January 31, 1992, in Marawi City, Lanao del Sur.
He left behind a university system he helped build from the ground up, a museum that gave Maranao material
culture a permanent public home, a body of scholarship that documented Bangsamoro history with rigor and love,
and a generation of students and colleagues who carry his approach forward.

PAGE 5
His legacy isn't just biographical. It's structural. The institutions he founded, the departments he established, the
journals he launched, and the museum he built continue to shape how Bangsamoro communities understand
themselves and how the rest of the world understands them.
In a region that has often had to fight for its own narrative, Mamitua Saber made sure the Maranao people had
scholars, texts, and institutions on their side.
