Saleha Pangarungan Sacar
Saleha Pangarungan Sacar is a Filipino Juris Doctor,
distinguished public servant, and development leader who
currently serves as Director IV of the Bureau of Muslim
Economic Affairs (BMEA) at the National Commission on
Muslim Filipinos (NCMF). Born in Saudi Arabia as a natural-born
Filipino citizen, Sacar has emerged as one of the country's most
influential voices in Islamic finance, halal industry development,
and inclusive economic policy—earning recognition as a key
architect of the Philippines' emerging Islamic economic
ecosystem. Her groundbreaking work in diplomacy, governance,
Islamic banking and finance, and halal industry development has
positioned her at the forefront of advancing inclusive, ethical, and
sustainable economic systems for Muslim Filipinos and the
broader national economy. With a career defined by bridging
policy, finance, and industry development, Sacar stands as a
trailblazer whose leadership in the 5th International Islamic
Finance Conference and sustained advocacy for the halal industry
demonstrate a cohesive strategy that integrates economic
development with cultural and religious values. A recipient of
numerous international accolades—including the Excellence in
Public Service and Humanitarian Award of the Year 2025, Most
Outstanding Woman in Public Service 2025, and multiple Global
Women Achiever awards—Sacar represents a new generation of
Filipino Muslim leaders whose work not only uplifts Muslim
Filipino communities but also contributes to a broader national
vision of a more inclusive, ethical, and globally competitive
Philippine economy.
Contents
1 Early Life and Background
2 Education
3 Career
3.1 Legal Practice and Early Government Service
3.2 Private Sector Leadership
3.3 Director IV, Bureau of Muslim Economic Affairs
4 Institutional Contributions and Advocacy
4.1 Islamic Finance and Banking Advocacy
4.2 Halal Industry Development

7 Legacy and Impact
8 External Links

PAGE 2
Early Life and Background
Saleha Pangarungan Sacar was born in Saudi Arabia to Filipino parents, making her a natural-born Filipino citizen
with deep cultural ties to both the Middle East and the Philippines. Growing up with exposure to Islamic
governance and finance systems in Saudi Arabia while maintaining strong connections to her Filipino heritage
shaped her unique perspective on economic development and public service. This bicultural upbringing would later
prove instrumental in her ability to bridge Western governance frameworks with Islamic economic principles,
positioning her as an effective advocate for Muslim Filipino communities within the Philippine government
system. Her early exposure to Islamic banking practices and halal industry standards in Saudi Arabia provided
foundational knowledge that would become central to her professional mission of establishing robust Islamic
economic infrastructure in the Philippines.
Education
Sacar's educational journey reflects a deliberate progression from public administration fundamentals to specialized
legal training and advanced governance studies. She began her tertiary education at Mindanao State University,
where she earned a Bachelor of Science in Public Administration from June 2000 to October 2005. This
foundational training in governance, policy analysis, and administrative systems provided her with essential
frameworks for understanding how government institutions serve diverse populations.
Recognizing the critical importance of legal expertise in policy advocacy and institutional reform, Sacar pursued
her Juris Doctor degree at the Philippine Law School from October 2006 to March 2012. This legal training
equipped her with the analytical skills and regulatory knowledge necessary to navigate complex legislative
environments and advocate for policy changes affecting Muslim Filipino communities. Her legal background has
proven particularly valuable in her work on Islamic banking regulations, halal certification frameworks, and
economic rights advocacy.
Building on her practical experience in government service, Sacar pursued a Master's in Public Administration at
the University of Perpetual Help System Dalta from November 2020 to May 2022. This advanced degree deepened
her understanding of public sector management, strategic planning, and policy implementation. Currently, she is
pursuing a Doctor of Public Administration at the same institution, demonstrating her commitment to continuous
learning and her aspiration to contribute scholarly research to the field of public governance and Islamic economic
development.
Her educational background is further strengthened by specialized training programs that have enhanced her
professional capabilities. She completed the 17th Shariah Training Course conducted by the Supreme Court of the
Philippines in partnership with NCMF, which deepened her understanding of Islamic jurisprudence and its
application in Philippine legal contexts. She also received Best Diplomat training in Diplomacy and Leadership
from UNITAR, participated in Islamic Banking and Finance training programs offered by the Bangko Sentral ng
Pilipinas (BSP), and completed various training courses on supervisory and managerial skills. Additionally, she has
developed technical competencies in graphics design and Microsoft Office applications, demonstrating versatility
that extends beyond traditional governance training.
Career
Sacar's career trajectory reflects a strategic progression from legal practice to executive leadership in Muslim
economic affairs, with each role building on previous experiences to culminate in her current influential position.

PAGE 3
Legal Practice and Early Government Service
Following her admission to the bar, Sacar served as Attorney 1 at the Bureau of Legal Affairs within the National
Commission on Muslim Filipinos from February 1, 2019, to January 30, 2020. In this capacity, she provided legal
counsel on matters affecting Muslim Filipino rights, reviewed legislative proposals, and contributed to the
development of legal frameworks supporting Islamic institutions in the Philippines. This role gave her firsthand
insight into the legal barriers facing Muslim Filipino communities and the regulatory gaps that needed to be
addressed to support Islamic economic activities.
Private Sector Leadership
Before joining NCMF in a legal capacity, Sacar gained valuable private sector experience as Chief Executive
Officer and President of Arphil International Corporation from May 30, 2012, to June 23, 2018. This six-year
tenure in corporate leadership provided her with practical insights into business operations, international
commerce, and private sector challenges that would later inform her public policy work. Her experience bridging
public service and private enterprise has proven valuable in her current role, where she works to create enabling
environments for Muslim Filipino businesses and halal industry entrepreneurs.
Director IV, Bureau of Muslim Economic Affairs
Since February 6, 2020, Sacar has served as Director IV of the Bureau of Muslim Economic Affairs at the National
Commission on Muslim Filipinos—a position that has allowed her to translate her vision for inclusive Islamic
economic development into concrete policies and programs. In this role, she leads strategic initiatives to advance
Islamic banking and finance, expand halal industry development, and create economic opportunities for Muslim
Filipino communities across the country.
Her leadership extends to her role as Chairman of the Regional Halal Programs Management Committee within
NCMF, where she coordinates efforts to strengthen halal certification systems, support halal entrepreneurs, and
position the Philippines as a competitive player in the global halal market. Under her guidance, NCMF has
strengthened partnerships with Islamic financial institutions, developed training programs for halal industry
stakeholders, and advocated for policy reforms that recognize and accommodate Islamic economic principles
within the Philippine regulatory framework.
Institutional Contributions and Advocacy
Sacar's most significant contributions lie in her strategic vision for building comprehensive Islamic economic
infrastructure that serves both Muslim Filipino communities and the broader Philippine economy. Her work
transcends traditional administrative functions to encompass policy advocacy, international diplomacy, industry
development, and grassroots capacity building.
Islamic Finance and Banking Advocacy
One of Sacar's primary advocacy areas is the expansion and institutionalization of Islamic banking and finance in
the Philippines. Recognizing that conventional banking systems often fail to meet the religious requirements of
Muslim Filipinos, she has worked tirelessly to promote Shariah-compliant financial products and services. Her
advocacy has focused on creating regulatory frameworks that accommodate Islamic banking principles while
ensuring compliance with Philippine banking standards—a delicate balance that requires both legal expertise and
cultural sensitivity.

PAGE 4
Through her work with the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas and collaboration with Islamic financial institutions, Sacar
has contributed to expanding access to halal financial services, promoting financial inclusion for Muslim
communities, and positioning the Philippines as an emerging hub for Islamic finance in Southeast Asia. Her efforts
align with broader regional trends toward Islamic financial integration while respecting local contexts and
regulatory requirements.
Halal Industry Development
Sacar has been a driving force behind efforts to develop and professionalize the Philippines' halal industry. She
recognizes that the global halal market represents a significant economic opportunity for Filipino Muslim
entrepreneurs and that establishing robust halal certification systems can open export markets while creating jobs in
Muslim-majority regions. Her work in this area has included developing training programs for halal certifiers,
strengthening quality assurance mechanisms, promoting halal entrepreneurship, and advocating for government
support for halal industry development.
Her leadership in organizing and participating in the 5th International Islamic Finance Conference demonstrates her
commitment to positioning the Philippines within global Islamic economic networks. By facilitating knowledge
exchange, attracting international investment, and showcasing Filipino Muslim economic initiatives, she has helped
elevate the country's profile in the Islamic economic sphere.
Policy Integration and Sustainable Development
What distinguishes Sacar's approach is her holistic vision that integrates Islamic economic principles with broader
goals of sustainable development, ethical business practices, and inclusive growth. Rather than treating Islamic
finance and halal industry development as niche sectors serving only Muslim communities, she frames these
initiatives as contributions to national economic competitiveness and alignment with global trends toward ethical
and values-based economic systems.
Her work demonstrates how culturally sensitive economic policies can serve both specific communities and
broader national interests—creating models for inclusive development that respect religious and cultural diversity
while advancing shared economic goals. This integrative approach positions her as a bridge-builder who can
navigate between different stakeholder groups and articulate shared interests across religious and cultural lines.
Leadership and Recognition
Sacar's contributions have garnered extensive recognition both domestically and internationally, establishing her as
one of the most decorated Filipino public servants of her generation.
Her awards and recognitions include the Excellence in Public Service and Humanitarian Award of the Year 2025
from the Global Excellence Leadership Award, Most Outstanding Woman in Public Service 2025 from the Rotary
Club of San Francisco Del Monte, and Upholder of Halal Excellence Award 2025 from the Prime Group of
Companies held in Dubai, UAE. She was named Premier Achiever Outstanding Public Servant of the Year 2024 by
the Southeast Asian Premier Business and Achiever Award, and received multiple Empowered Female Advocate
for Muslim and Humanitarian Affairs awards in 2024 and 2023 from various international organizations.
Additional honors include National Outstanding Women of Achievements in the Field of Public Service of the Year
2024 from the 2024 Greater Good Achievers Leadership Awards, Dynamic Female Leader Award 2024 from
PRIME GROUP held in Dubai, and Global Women Achiever recognition in 2024, 2023, and 2022 from the World

PAGE 5
Women Leadership Congress and Awards. She was recognized as Asia's Empowered Female Advocate for Muslim
and Humanitarian Affairs 2023 by Asia's Golden Icon Awards and the Kasosyo Summit Committee.
She has also received recognition as Heroes' Notable Female Leader and Advocate for Muslim Filipinos 2023 from
Asia's Modern Hero Awards, Asia's most distinguished female public servant for Muslim Filipinos from Asia's
Pinnacle Awards, and Asia's Woman Leader 2022 from the World Women Leadership Organization. The
Bangsamoro Transition Authority passed BTA Resolution No. 254 congratulating Sacar as a recipient of the 9th
World Woman Leadership Congress, and she was honored as Galing Pinas PEZA Investment and Promotion
Awardee 2021.
Beyond governmental awards, Sacar serves as Club President of the Rotary Club of Diliman International, Rotary
District 3780, Rotary International for Rotary Year 2024-2025—a role that reflects her commitment to community
service and humanitarian causes beyond her official government duties.
Personal Life and Interests
Outside her professional achievements, Sacar maintains active interests in athletics and endurance sports,
particularly marathon running and triathlon competitions. These pursuits reflect her disciplined approach to
personal development and her commitment to maintaining physical and mental resilience—qualities that serve her
well in the demanding environment of public service and advocacy.
Her athletic endeavors also symbolize her broader philosophy of pushing boundaries and demonstrating that
Muslim Filipino women can excel across multiple domains—from legal practice and government leadership to
competitive sports—challenging stereotypes and inspiring younger generations.
Legacy and Impact
Saleha Pangarungan Sacar's legacy lies in her role as a pioneering architect of the Philippines' Islamic economic
infrastructure and her demonstration of how culturally grounded public service can advance both community-
specific needs and broader national interests. Her work has fundamentally shifted how the Philippine government
approaches Muslim economic affairs—moving from symbolic representation to substantive policy development
and institutional capacity building.
By establishing frameworks for Islamic banking, professionalizing the halal industry, and positioning Filipino
Muslim economic initiatives within global networks, Sacar has created institutional foundations that will continue
to generate opportunities long after her tenure. Her leadership model—combining legal expertise, diplomatic skill,
private sector experience, and deep cultural understanding—provides a blueprint for effective advocacy in
multicultural democracies.
Perhaps most significantly, Sacar represents a visible counter-narrative to deficit-based portrayals of Muslim
Filipino communities. Her international recognition, professional excellence, and values-based leadership
demonstrate the contributions that Filipino Muslims make to national development and global Islamic economic
systems. For young Muslim Filipino women, her career trajectory offers proof that they can aspire to the highest
levels of professional achievement while maintaining strong religious and cultural identities.
As the Philippines continues to navigate questions of economic inclusion, religious accommodation, and cultural
diversity, Sacar's integrated approach to policy development offers valuable lessons. Her work demonstrates that
economic systems can be both culturally sensitive and globally competitive, that religious values can align with

PAGE 6
ethical business practices, and that serving specific communities can contribute to broader national progress. In this
sense, her legacy extends beyond specific policies or programs to encompass a vision of inclusive development that
the Philippines—and other diverse democracies—can build upon for generations to come.

title: Sadain, Mehol K.
text:
PAGE 1
Mehol K. Sadain
Mehol K. Sadain (born December 24, 1955) is a Filipino lawyer, Shari'ah counselor, educator, peace advocate, and
writer from Jolo, Sulu. A proud Tausug Muslim, he's spent decades building a career that bridges Islamic tradition
with Philippine legal and democratic life, making him one of the more distinctive public intellectuals to emerge
from Muslim Mindanao.
He's been at the center of some of the country's most important conversations: election integrity, Muslim Filipino
rights, the Mindanao peace process, and the role of Islamic jurisprudence within the Philippine legal framework. As
a writer, he's added a literary voice to those conversations, writing fiction, poetry, and essays that bring the Tausug
experience into the national cultural conversation.
Contents
1 Early Life and Family Background
2 Education
3 Career
3.1 Public Service
3.2 Academic Career
3.3 Civil Society and Other Roles
4 Literary Contributions
5 Legacy and Cultural Significance
6 Categories
Early Life and Family Background
Mehol Kiram Sadain was born on December 24, 1955, in San Raymundo, Jolo, Sulu, in the heartland of Tausug
society. He grew up in a household with genuine literary and intellectual life. His brother, Said K. Sadain Jr., made
his own mark as a pioneering Tausug poet, fictionist, and essayist, and that family environment clearly shaped
Mehol's instincts for both scholarship and storytelling.
His early schooling showed just how sharp he was. He finished elementary school at Notre Dame of Jolo in 1968
with special distinction honors. He then went to Ateneo de Zamboanga High School, where he didn't just excel
academically. He graduated as valedictorian in 1972 and took home both the Gerry Roxas Leadership Award and
the Insular Life Award, early signals of a young man who was already combining intellectual seriousness with a
sense of civic purpose.
Education
Sadain left Sulu for Quezon City on a scholarship to study at the University of the Philippines Diliman, where he
completed his Bachelor of Arts in Islamic Studies in 1978. He stayed on at UP and enrolled in the College of Law,
graduating 16th in his class in 1986. He passed the Philippine Bar examinations in 1987.

What sets his educational background apart is that he didn't stop
at civil law. In 1992, he completed a Shari'ah training course
sponsored by the Office of Muslim Affairs at UP Diliman. That
dual grounding in Philippine civil law and Islamic jurisprudence
became the defining feature of his professional identity, giving
him a kind of credibility and range that's genuinely rare.
Career
Public Service
Sadain has held some significant positions in the Philippine
government. He served as Commissioner of the Commission on
Elections (COMELEC), where he contributed to protecting the
integrity of Philippine elections at the national level.
He was later appointed Secretary of the National Commission on
Muslim Filipinos (NCMF), the government agency tasked with
promoting the rights and welfare of Muslim Filipinos. In that
role, he also sat as a member of the government peace panel in
negotiations with the Moro Islamic Liberation Front (MILF),
putting him at the table during one of the country's most
consequential peace processes.
Academic Career
His academic home has been the University of the Philippines
Institute of Islamic Studies (UP IIS), where he served as dean
and continues to work as a senior professorial lecturer. He's also
taught at the UP College of Law and lectures regularly at the
Philippine Judicial Academy of the Supreme Court of the
Philippines. He's chaired the Supreme Court's Special Shari'ah
Bar Examination Committee, a role that puts him at the
intersection of judicial institutions and Islamic legal standards.
Civil Society and Other Roles
Beyond government and the university, Sadain is a convenor of
the Philippine Center for Islam and Democracy (PCID), an
organization that works to reconcile Islamic values with
democratic governance. He also serves as a board member and
vice chairman of First Asia Financial and Productivity, Inc. In
that capacity, he drafted proposed legislation on securities
issuance for the regional autonomous government in Muslim
Mindanao in 2008.

PAGE 3
Sibling
Said K. Sadain Jr. (poet,
fictionist, essayist)
Literary Contributions
Sadain writes, and he does it across multiple forms. His short
fiction includes "The River Below," published in Philippine Graphic in 1991, and "Ocean" (1979), among others.
Several of his stories have been anthologized in The Many Ways of Being Muslim: Fiction by Muslim Filipinos, a
landmark collection of Muslim Filipino literary work. His poetry has appeared in Brown River, White Ocean and in
various protest anthologies.
He's also a serious essayist and has written monographs on Islamic fundamentalism from a Philippine perspective,
Shari'ah law, human rights, and governance in Muslim Mindanao. His written work is consistently reform-oriented:
grounded in faith, attentive to practical realities, and alert to the political stakes involved in how Islam is
understood and practiced in the Philippines.
Legacy and Cultural Significance
What makes Sadain's career worth examining is how consistently he's moved between worlds that don't always talk
to each other: Jolo and Manila, Islamic tradition and Philippine jurisprudence, literature and law, faith and
democratic governance. He's done it without losing his Tausug identity or softening his commitments.
He's been vocal about implementing Shari'ah effectively within the Philippine legal framework, building stronger
Muslim institutions, and pursuing genuine autonomy that actually respects pluralism. Those aren't safe or easy
positions to hold in Philippine public life, and he's held them for decades.
As a model for Muslim Filipino public intellectual life, Atty. Sadain shows that deep faith and serious engagement
with democratic institutions aren't in conflict. They can, and often do, reinforce each other.
He continues to teach, write, mentor, and take part in ongoing conversations about Islam, democracy, and
development in the Philippines.

Akmad Atlah Sakkam
Akmad Atlah Sakkam (June 6, 1946 – early 2023) was a Filipino
diplomat, lawyer, and public servant from Indanan, Sulu, widely
regarded as one of the most distinguished Tausug figures in the
history of Philippine foreign service. A proud son of the
Bangsamoro, he carried his Moro heritage with quiet confidence
through more than four decades of national and international
service. He served as Philippine Ambassador to Iraq (1986–1992),
Bahrain (1994–1999), Oman (1999–2003), and Jordan with
concurrent jurisdiction over Palestine (2018–2022), spanning the
administrations of six Philippine presidents. His most celebrated
act of service came during the first Gulf War, when he personally
led the safe evacuation of thousands of Filipino overseas workers
from Kuwait and Iraq under extraordinarily dangerous conditions,
an achievement for which President Corazon Aquino personally
awarded him the Special Presidential Award of Merit. Beyond
diplomacy, he contributed to the Bangsamoro peace process as a
member of the Bangsamoro Transition Commission (2014–2016)
under President Benigno Aquino III, helping shape the draft
Bangsamoro Basic Law. Ambassador Sakkam's life was a
testament to how one could be, at the same time, a proud son of
Sulu and a dedicated servant of the entire Filipino nation. He
passed away in Manila in early 2023, mourned by the Bangsamoro
community and honored by the Bangsamoro Transition Authority
Parliament, which adopted formal resolutions in his memory.
Contents
1 Early Life and Background
2 Education
3 Career

3.2 Labor Attaché in Saudi Arabia (1977–1982)
3.3 Private Sector Interlude
3.4 Ambassador to Iraq (1986–1992)
3.5 Ambassador to Bahrain (1994–1999)
3.6 Ambassador to Oman (1999–2003)

4.2 Ambassador to Jordan and Palestine (2018–2022)

8 Death and Tributes

PAGE 2
9 See Also
Early Life and Background
Akmad Atlah Sakkam was born on June 6, 1946, in Indanan, Sulu, a municipality long recognized as a heartland of
Tausug culture and heritage in the southern Philippines. He also had close ties to the neighboring community of
Patikul, another historically significant area in Sulu. Growing up in a region steeped in Islamic tradition and
Tausug identity, Sakkam came of age during a period when Moro professionals in national positions were still
relatively few, making his eventual rise through the ranks of Philippine diplomacy all the more meaningful. His
story is as much about community pride as it is about personal achievement; in the eyes of many Tausugs and
Bangsamoro Filipinos, he was proof that a son of Sulu could stand at the highest levels of government and
represent the entire nation with competence and grace.
Education
Sakkam began his formal education at Indanan Central Elementary School, where he graduated with honors, an
early sign of the dedication and intellectual ability that would define his career. He went on to complete his
secondary education at Sulu High School, finishing in 1963. Like many ambitious young men from Mindanao and
the Sulu Archipelago during that era, he made the journey north to Manila to pursue higher education. At Manuel
L. Quezon University, he earned degrees in AB Political Science and History, laying a strong foundation in law,
governance, and Philippine public affairs. He followed those with a Bachelor of Laws degree in 1971 from the
same university, and that same year, he passed the Philippine Bar examinations. His legal training gave him a sharp
analytical edge that would serve him well across every phase of his career, from labor arbitration to high-stakes
diplomatic negotiations.
Career
Early Career in Labor (1975–1977)
After completing his law degree and passing the bar, Sakkam spent some years before entering government service.
His public career formally began in 1975 when he joined the Department of Labor and Employment (DOLE) as a
legal consultant and med-arbiter. In this role, he handled labor disputes and mediation work, gaining early
experience in the practical realities of Filipino workers' rights and the legal frameworks that governed them. It was
hands-on work that connected him directly to the lives of ordinary laborers, a concern that would echo throughout
his diplomatic career.
Labor Attaché in Saudi Arabia (1977–1982)
In 1977, Sakkam was posted to Jeddah, Saudi Arabia, as a Philippine Labor Attaché, a posting that would prove to
be formative. He was part of the early wave of Philippine officials who helped establish a formal labor presence in
the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, contributing to the opening of one of the first Philippine labor offices there. The
posting put him at the intersection of two communities he cared deeply about: Filipino overseas workers seeking
better lives abroad, and the broader Muslim world in which he felt a natural sense of belonging. His five years in
Jeddah (1977–1982) gave him both the diplomatic experience and the credibility in the Middle East that would
later shape his ambassadorial assignments.

PAGE 3
Private Sector Interlude
Following his Saudi posting, Sakkam stepped briefly into the private sector, where he served as president of a
company. This period gave him exposure to business leadership and management, rounding out his profile beyond
government and legal work. He would eventually return to public service, this time at the level of ambassador.
Ambassador to Iraq (1986–1992)
President Corazon Aquino appointed Sakkam as Philippine Ambassador to Iraq in 1986, a posting that would
define the most dramatic chapter of his career. The Philippines had a substantial population of overseas workers in
the region, and maintaining their welfare required steady, capable representation. Then came the first Gulf War in
1990–1991. When Iraqi forces invaded Kuwait and the entire region descended into conflict, tens of thousands of
Filipino overseas workers in Kuwait and Iraq found themselves stranded in a war zone, uncertain, frightened, and
far from home. Ambassador Sakkam coordinated and led the safe evacuation of thousands of these workers under
extremely dangerous and logistically complex conditions. The operation required quick thinking, coordination with
multiple governments and agencies, and genuine personal courage. It was one of the most significant humanitarian
achievements in the history of Philippine overseas labor relations. For his work during the crisis, President Aquino
personally presented him with the Special Presidential Award of Merit, one of the most meaningful recognitions of
his long career.
Ambassador to Bahrain (1994–1999)
After the conclusion of his Iraq posting, Sakkam was appointed Ambassador to Bahrain in 1994 by President Fidel
V. Ramos. He served in Manama until 1999, continuing the work of protecting Filipino workers and strengthening
bilateral ties between the Philippines and the Gulf state. His track record in Iraq made him a trusted figure for
postings in the Middle East, where the Philippines had significant labor interests and a growing diaspora
community.
Ambassador to Oman (1999–2003)
President Joseph Estrada appointed Sakkam as Ambassador to Oman in 1999, and he served in Muscat until 2003.
By this point, he had accumulated well over a decade of ambassadorial experience across the Arab world. His
postings in Iraq, Bahrain, and Oman together represent an unbroken stretch of more than 15 years as a Philippine
ambassador, an extraordinary record of sustained diplomatic service in one of the most geopolitically complex
regions on earth.
Post-Retirement Public Service
Bangsamoro Transition Commission (2014–2016)
Even after concluding his ambassadorial career, Sakkam did not retreat from public life. Under President Benigno
Aquino III, he was appointed as one of the 15 members of the Bangsamoro Transition Commission (BTC), serving
from 2014 to 2016. The BTC was tasked with drafting the proposed Bangsamoro Basic Law, the foundational legal
framework for the new Bangsamoro political entity that would eventually lead to the creation of the Bangsamoro
Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM). At times, Sakkam served as deputy vice chair of the
commission. His colleagues on the commission, including prominent peace negotiator Mohagher Iqbal,

PAGE 4
remembered him as diligent, cooperative, and genuinely committed to the peace process. His participation in the
BTC showed that his sense of duty to the Bangsamoro people extended well beyond his formal diplomatic duties,
and that he was willing to roll up his sleeves for his community even in retirement.
Ambassador to Jordan and Palestine (2018–2022)
In 2018, President Rodrigo Duterte brought Sakkam out of retirement once more, appointing him Ambassador to
the Hashemite Kingdom of Jordan, with concurrent jurisdiction over Palestine. He presented his credentials not
only in Amman but also to Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas, reflecting the breadth of his diplomatic
responsibilities. During his tenure in Jordan, Sakkam looked after a Filipino community that at one point numbered
over 38,000 workers, a figure that spoke to Jordan's role as a significant destination for Philippine labor migrants.
He was known for calling Jordan a "second home" for many of these workers, and for making sure their welfare
remained at the center of his mission. His time in Amman included hosting President Duterte's official visit to
Jordan, a moment of bilateral diplomacy that demonstrated his continuing capacity for high-profile representational
work. He also extended consular outreach to the Gaza Strip, an unusual and significant dimension of his posting
that required both diplomatic sensitivity and logistical creativity. He served in Jordan until around 2022.

Personal Life
Sakkam was married to Ruby, affectionately known as Madam Ruby by those who knew the family. The couple
had three children. Their son, Judge Eric Ismael P. Sakkam, continued the family’s legal tradition through public
service and currently serves as Presiding Judge of Branch 197 of the Regional Trial Court in Las Piñas City, Metro
Manila. Their other children likewise established successful careers in the business sector, reflecting the family’s
tradition of excellence and public-minded leadership.
Outside of his professional life, Sakkam was known as a man of varied personal pursuits. He was a skilled debater,
winning the DFA debate championship three times, and a sports enthusiast who also won DFA golf championships.
Those who knew him personally recalled a warm and fatherly personality, someone who carried the gravitas of a
senior diplomat without losing the approachability of a man deeply rooted in the culture and values of the Tausug
people.

PAGE 5
Legacy
Ambassador Sakkam's legacy rests on more than the titles and appointments that marked his career. What made
him stand out to those who knew him, and to the communities he served, was a quality that's hard to manufacture:
quiet excellence rooted in genuine identity. He navigated the halls of Malacañang, the corridors of embassies across
the Middle East, and the conference rooms of peace negotiations without ever seeming to lose sight of where he
came from. He was, in the truest sense, a bridge-builder: between the Bangsamoro and the national government,
between Filipino workers and the foreign lands where they sought better futures, and between the Muslim world
and the Philippines. In an era when Moro professionals in prominent national roles were still a relative rarity,
Sakkam demonstrated through his own career that Tausug Filipinos belonged not just in their home communities
but in the highest expressions of Philippine public service. His participation in the Bangsamoro Transition
Commission in his retirement years also showed a man who saw his responsibilities to his people as lifelong, not
something that ended with a last posting or a pension. For Tausug communities in Sulu and across the diaspora, he
remains a figure of pride and inspiration, a reminder of what's possible when personal ambition is matched with
genuine service.
Death and Tributes
Ambassador Akmad Atlah Sakkam passed away in Manila in early 2023, marking the end of a life defined by
decades of dedicated service across multiple continents and administrations. News of his passing was received with
deep sadness across the Bangsamoro community. The Bangsamoro Transition Authority (BTA) Parliament formally
adopted resolutions mourning his loss, recognizing his invaluable contributions to the Bangsamoro people and
offering official condolences to his family. Tausug communities both in Sulu and online remembered him with
warmth, celebrating him as a kind, fatherly figure and a genuine source of community pride. His passing was
mourned not just as the loss of a former official but as the loss of a singular voice: one that had spoken for Tausug
and Bangsamoro Filipinos in the most important rooms of power, in the Philippines and abroad, for nearly five
decades. Allahyarhamu. May God have mercy on him.

Yasser Muti Salacop
Yasser Muti Salacop (born January 21, 1983) is a Filipino
administrative professional and public servant from Saguiaran,

Mindanao. He has worked in university finance administration, local

hospitality roles overseas. As of the most recent available records, he
serves as Administrative Aide VI in the Finance Department of
Mindanao State University (MSU) Main Campus in Marawi City.
Contents
1 Early Life and Family
2 Education
3 Career and Public Service
4 Achievements and Recognition
5 Personal Life and Legacy
6 References
Early Life and Family
Salacop was born on January 21, 1983, and grew up in Saguiaran,
Lanao del Sur. He is the second child of Sultan Nasser M. Salacop
and the late Prof. Norhaya Amauikurot Muti Salacop, CPA. He has
four sisters (Farinah, Sarahata, Rohana, and Sadjarah) and two
brothers (Nasser Jr. and Hassanor, the youngest).
His family has deep roots in local governance and university service.
His paternal grandfather, Mayor Hadji Ali Salacop Dimacaling (also
listed in some records as Hadji Salacop Dimacaling), served as
mayor of Saguiaran from 1965 to 1978. Other relatives, including
Atty. Kimal Salacop, later held the same mayoral post. An uncle on
his father's side served as an RTC judge in Agusan, Lanao del Sur,
and previously as mayor of Saguiaran as well. On his mother's side,
his grandfather held senior posts at MSU as Assistant Vice President
and Finance Director under President Ahmad Alonto Jr., while an
aunt has served as Vice President for Finance at MSU Marawi.
Education
Salacop completed his undergraduate studies at the King Faisal
Center for Islamic, Arabic and Asian Studies at Mindanao State
University, earning a Bachelor of Science in International Relations
in April 2005 and a Bachelor of Arts in Islamic Studies (major in
Shari'ah) in April 2010.

PAGE 2
"From a DFA internship in Pasay City to a
Fairmont hotel post at the Makkah Clock
Tower, and finally back home to MSU
Marawi: a career built quietly, one
institution at a time."
He later completed a Certificate in Governmental Management in
Organizational Management (CGM) from the College of Public
Affairs Graduate Studies at MSU in July 2019. His other credentials
include a post-baccalaureate intensive training program in English
communication skills at MSU's Student Resource Center (June to
August 2007), computer office applications training at Mas
Computer Learning Center in Marawi City during the same period, and a Food and Beverage Services NC II from
Western Philippine College Inc., completed in December 2019.
Earlier MSU profile materials referenced an ongoing Master in Human Resource Management at Iligan Medical
Center College (started 2022) and a Master in Public Administration, major in Organization and Management
(2019). These are not detailed in his curriculum vitae, so they are noted here for the record but not treated as
confirmed credentials.
Career and Public Service
Salacop's early professional exposure came through competitive internships. From April to May 2004, he interned
in the Office of Consular Affairs at the Department of Foreign Affairs in Pasay City, Manila, where he was
recognized as Most Outstanding Intern for that period. From August to November 2011, he interned with the
Committee on Foreign Affairs at the Philippine House of Representatives in Manila, as part of the USAID-GEM-
sponsored Congressional Internship Program for Young Mindanao Leaders.
From August 2011 to December 2012, he worked as a Birth Registration Clerk with the Department of Social
Welfare and Development in the Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (DSWD-ARMM).
Between August 2013 and March 2016, he lived and worked in the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia at the Makkah Clock
Tower, a Fairmont Hotel property. He served as a Data Processor from August 2013 to March 2016, and earlier as a
Server at the Saudi Restaurant within the same property from August 2013 to August 2015.
Since July 2016, he has worked as Administrative Aide VI in the Finance Department (University Business Office)
at Mindanao State University Main Campus in Marawi City.
In his student years, he organized an International Relations Conference at MSU's Academic Complex (College of
Law) on February 12 to 13, 2005, under the theme "Mindanao as a Foreign Policy Issue."
Achievements and Recognition
Most Outstanding Intern, Office of Consular Affairs, Department of Foreign Affairs (2004)
Organizer, MSU International Relations Conference on Mindanao as a foreign policy issue (2005)
Winner, Best Policy Recommendation on ASEAN Sub-Regional Configuration (BIMP-EAGA), awarded by
the Philippine Chamber of Commerce and Industry (PCCI) and USAID at an event in Surigao City (2012)
No independent record of published academic work or major institutional honors beyond these appears in the
available sources. His career instead reflects a steady climb through government internships, regional social
welfare service, overseas hospitality work, and long-term university administration.
Personal Life and Legacy
Available records offer little on Salacop's private life beyond his family background, already detailed above.

PAGE 3
Within the local context of Lanao del Sur and the wider Bangsamoro region, Salacop's path reflects a familiar
trajectory for educated professionals from established municipal families: university education at MSU, early
exposure to national institutions through competitive internships, service in ARMM agencies, a stretch of overseas
employment, and an eventual return to steady administrative work at the regional state university. His contributions
have remained largely institutional rather than public-facing or political.
References

Abdulghani "Gerry" Ajul Salapuddin
Abdulghani "Gerry" Ajul Salapuddin (born March 25, 1952) is a
Filipino statesman, institutional leader, and legislator from Basilan
Province whose life story traces the arc of modern Moro history:
from guerrilla commander in the hills of Basilan, to three-term
Governor, to Congressman and Deputy Speaker of the House of
Representatives, and now as the Administrator and Chief Executive
Officer of the Southern Philippines Development Authority
(SPDA).
He is Yakan, the predominant indigenous Muslim ethnolinguistic
group native to Basilan, and has spent his public life advocating for
the rights, development, and recognition of Moro communities
within the Philippine republic.
Contents
1 EARLY LIFE
2 REVOLUTIONARY YEARS: MNLF COMMANDER
3 EDUCATIONAL BACKGROUND
4 POLITICAL AND INSTITUTIONAL CAREER
4.1 Regional Autonomous Government (1984–1986)
4.2 Governor of Basilan (1988–1998)
4.3 House of Representatives (1998–2007)
4.4 Administrator and CEO, SPDA (2018–Present)
5 RECOGNITION AND AWARDS
6 LEGACY AND SIGNIFICANCE
7 SEE ALSO
8 REFERENCES
EARLY LIFE
Salapuddin was born on March 25, 1952, in Tuburan, Muhammad
Ajul Municipality, Basilan Province, a small coastal settlement on
Basilan Island in the Sulu Archipelago.
His early academic record was strong. He topped his class from
Grades 1 to 5 at Tuburan Elementary School and graduated as class
valedictorian in 1966.
For high school, he enrolled at Basilan City High School (BCHS),
transferred to Lamitan Barangay High School (LBHS) for his
second and third year (1968–1970), then returned to BCHS,
completing secondary education with honors in 1972.

PAGE 2
Administrator and CEO, Southern
Philippines Development Authority
(SPDA)
Appointed: February 2, 2018
Political Career
Executive Council Member, Regional
Autonomous Government (RAG) Region
IX (1984–1986)
Governor of Basilan (1988–1998)
Representative, Lone District of Basilan
(1998–2007)
Deputy Speaker, House of
Representatives, 12th and 13th Congress
(2002–2007)
Party Affiliation
Lakas–CMD; previously LAMMP (1998–
2001)
Notability
Former MNLF Provincial Commander
turned three-term Governor and three-
term Congressman from Basilan;
Founding Father of Basilan State
College; principal author of landmark
Bangsamoro legislation; current head of
SPDA.
Known For
Authoring RA 9054 (ARMM Organic
Act), RA 9023 (Isabela City), and RA
9393 (Lamitan City); founding Basilan
State College; leading post-conflict
economic development in southern
Mindanao through the SPDA.
Like many young Moro men coming of age in the 1960s and early
1970s, Salapuddin grew up amid escalating tension between Moro
communities and the Philippine state. When family circumstances
made college financially impossible, he joined the armed struggle
rather than set aside his aspirations entirely.
REVOLUTIONARY YEARS: MNLF
COMMANDER
In the early 1970s, Salapuddin joined the Moro National
Liberation Front (MNLF), the main armed movement fighting for
Moro self-determination under the leadership of Nur Misuari.
He served as an active combatant and commander in both land and
sea operations across Basilan and the Zamboanga Peninsula,
eventually rising to the rank of Provincial Revolutionary
Commander for Basilan. Within the MNLF, he was known by the
revolutionary alias "Faihk."
In 1984, after more than a decade in the field, Salapuddin returned
to mainstream civilian life. According to the official SPDA
biographical record, his first act upon reintegrating was to request
from then-President Ferdinand Marcos the establishment of a state
college in Basilan and a scholarship program, because he wanted to
give the youth of Basilan the very educational opportunity that
conflict had denied him.
EDUCATIONAL BACKGROUND
Salapuddin pursued higher education while simultaneously building
his political career, a reflection of the same persistence that defined
his earlier years.
He enrolled at Western Mindanao State University (WMSU) in
Zamboanga City, completing three years of college (1985–1988)
before transferring to Basilan State College (BaSC), where he
finished his Bachelor of Arts in Political Science in 1990.
He then completed his graduate and post-graduate studies entirely at
BaSC, earning a Master in Public Administration (MPA) and a
Doctor of Philosophy (Ph.D.).
He also attended international programs, including a 1989 Regional Development Management course at the Asian
Institute of Management (AIM) in Makati, and a 1992 fellowship on Local Autonomy in Berlin, Germany.

PAGE 3
POLITICAL AND INSTITUTIONAL CAREER
Regional Autonomous Government (1984–1986)
After returning from the field, Salapuddin served as a member of the Executive Council of the Regional
Autonomous Government (RAG) of Region IX in Zamboanga City from 1984 to 1986. This transitional body
was part of the government's effort to integrate returning MNLF commanders into formal governance structures.
Governor of Basilan (1988–1998)
In 1988, Salapuddin won the governorship of Basilan, unseating an incumbent in a close election. He served three
consecutive terms spanning a full decade (1988–1998).
His tenure coincided with some of the most difficult years for Basilan, a province contending with the remnants of
armed conflict, deep poverty, and limited infrastructure. He is credited with stabilizing local governance,
accelerating rural infrastructure construction, and negotiating local peace compacts that helped bring brief but
meaningful periods of economic activity to the island in the 1990s.
One of his signature accomplishments during this period was the founding of Basilan State College (BaSC),
which he established to provide accessible, affordable higher education to Basilan's youth. The college now
operates multiple campuses across the province, including in Isabela City, Lamitan City, Maluso, and Tipo-Tipo.
More than 5,000 scholarship grantees have passed through the institution.
House of Representatives (1998–2007)
After completing his gubernatorial terms, Salapuddin ran for and won the congressional seat for the Lone District
of Basilan, serving three consecutive terms from 1998 to 2007.
His colleagues elected him Deputy Speaker of the House of Representatives during the 12th and 13th
Congresses (2002–2007), a recognition of his standing among Mindanao's legislative bloc.
In Congress, he authored and championed several landmark laws that significantly shaped the legal and
institutional landscape of Muslim Mindanao:
Republic Act 9054 (2001): The amended Organic Act of the Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao
(ARMM), the foundational law expanding the region's autonomy.
Republic Act 9023: The law that converted Isabela into a city, creating Isabela City, now the most populous
urban center in Basilan.
Republic Act 9393: The law that created Lamitan City, the second city in the province.
National Commission for Muslim Filipinos (NCMF): Salapuddin is credited as the original author of the
law establishing this key national agency for Muslim Filipino affairs.
Basilan Circumferential Road (BCR): He authored the legislation that nationalized the BCR, placing
responsibility for the road under the national government.
His congressional career was not without controversy. A bitter political rivalry with the Akbar clan culminated
when Congressman Wahab Akbar (who had succeeded him as Governor of Basilan) was assassinated in a bombing
at the Batasan Pambansa complex in November 2007. Salapuddin was among those initially linked to the incident
but was subsequently cleared of involvement.

PAGE 4
Administrator and CEO, SPDA (2018–Present)
On February 2, 2018, President Rodrigo Duterte appointed Salapuddin as the 13th Administrator and CEO of
the Southern Philippines Development Authority (SPDA), a government-owned and controlled corporation
mandated to promote agro-industrial development in Mindanao and the Sulu Archipelago.
He assumed office on February 6, 2018.
Under his leadership, the SPDA has been repositioned as an active facilitator of agricultural investment and public-
private partnership. Key initiatives under his tenure include:
Developing a halal feed industry hub and strengthening food security infrastructure across the Bangsamoro
region.
Advocating for the rescue of Basilan's struggling rubber industry, including proposals for modern rubber
processing plants and financial assistance for agrarian cooperatives.
Facilitating joint-venture discussions with agro-industrial investors, including explorations of abaca and
palm oil development in SPDA landholdings in Lanao del Sur and Basilan.
Brokering inter-agency dialogues between the national government and the Bangsamoro Autonomous
Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM) to resolve land proclamation disputes and support the
establishment of economic zones.
Relocating and upgrading the SPDA's main office in Davao City to a larger, modernized facility in Catalunan
Pequeño in 2022.
Salapuddin has also championed SPDA's role as a peace dividend institution, framing agricultural development as
inseparable from the consolidation of peace in the Bangsamoro.
RECOGNITION AND AWARDS
Salapuddin's transition from armed combatant to institution builder has earned him recognition at the national
level.
Honorary Public Servant of the Year (2024): Awarded at the Nation Builders and Mosliv Awards held at
Okada Manila, for excellence in Peace and Nation Building.
Basilan Exemplary Leadership Recognition: Honored by the Provincial Government of Basilan for his
foundational contributions to the province's governance and geographic development, particularly the
conversion of Isabela and Lamitan into cities.
LEGACY AND SIGNIFICANCE
Gerry Salapuddin's place in Bangsamoro history is distinctive precisely because of the full arc he has lived. He was
not merely a witness to the Moro struggle but an active participant in its armed phase, then an architect of its
political and legislative phase, and now one of its economic managers.
His founding of Basilan State College alone represents a concrete, lasting contribution to Yakan and Moro
communities, providing a gateway to higher education on an island historically left behind in national
development.
In Congress, his legislative fingerprints are on some of the most consequential laws affecting Muslim Mindanao:
the expanded ARMM Organic Act, the creation of two Basilan cities, and the establishment of the NCMF. Each of
these changed the institutional terrain of the region in ways that outlast any single political term.

PAGE 5
More broadly, his career demonstrates what peace advocates often argue in the abstract: that former combatants can
become credible, effective builders of the very state they once contested. In Salapuddin's case, that argument is not
theoretical. It is a biography.

Dimszar M. Sali
Dimszar M. Sali is a Filipino politician serving as the representative
of the lone district of Tawi-Tawi in the House of Representatives of
the Philippines. He represents one of the southernmost provinces of
the country, bringing the concerns of island communities into
national legislative discussions.
His role reflects the importance of representation for geographically
isolated provinces within the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in
Muslim Mindanao (BARMM).
Background
Dimszar M. Sali hails from Tawi-Tawi, an island province located in
the Sulu Archipelago. The province is known for its maritime culture, diverse communities, and strong connections
to neighboring Southeast Asian regions.
His background is rooted in local governance and community leadership, shaped by the unique social and
economic conditions of island-based communities.
Education
Publicly available information on his formal education remains limited in widely accessible sources. His
experience in governance, however, reflects familiarity with administrative processes and legislative work.

PAGE 2
Political career
Local leadership
Before entering Congress, Sali held positions in local government in Tawi-Tawi. His involvement in local
governance helped build his political base and strengthened his ties with constituents across the province.
Member of the House of Representatives
Dimszar M. Sali serves as the representative of the lone district of Tawi-Tawi in the House of Representatives of
the Philippines.
As congressman, his responsibilities include:
representing the interests of Tawi-Tawi at the national level
participating in legislative processes
supporting development initiatives for island and coastal communities
His role highlights the need to connect remote provinces to national policymaking.
Contributions
Sali’s contributions are often associated with regional representation and development advocacy.
Island representation – bringing attention to the needs of geographically isolated communities
Legislative participation – involvement in national lawmaking
Development advocacy – supporting infrastructure and services for maritime provinces
His work emphasizes the importance of inclusive governance that considers the realities of island provinces.
Legacy
Dimszar M. Sali’s leadership reflects the ongoing participation of Tawi-Tawi in national governance.
He represents a continuing effort to ensure that the voices of the Sulu Archipelago are heard in national institutions,
particularly in discussions on development, connectivity, and regional equity.
Recognition
He is recognized within Tawi-Tawi as a key political figure and representative of the province in Congress.
His position in the national legislature places him among leaders responsible for articulating the concerns of island
communities.
Challenges
His role involves several challenges, including:

PAGE 3
addressing infrastructure gaps in island provinces
improving access to basic services
balancing national responsibilities with local needs
These challenges are part of the broader realities faced by leaders in geographically remote regions.
Death
As of available information, Dimszar M. Sali is alive and actively serving as representative of Tawi-Tawi.

Amin Manking Salomabao
Sultan Amin Manking Salomabao is a Maranao Muslim Filipino
leader, entrepreneur, and cultural icon from Lanao del Sur whose
life weaves together royal heritage, overseas work, intellectual
achievement, and homegrown business success.
He carries the title of Sultan of Tamparan, a traditional royal
designation rooted in one of Lanao del Sur's most historically
significant royal lines, and he has built on that legacy not just by
serving his community but also by making a real mark in
Philippine commerce.
As the founder and CEO of Goldmine Pearl and Jewelry, he built
a jewelry supply chain that reaches SM Supermalls across the
country, sourcing fine pieces from Japan, China, and the Middle
East.
His story spans decades and continents: from the classrooms of
Cebu and Manila, to the labor markets of Saudi Arabia, to the
competitive halls of a national Scrabble tournament, and finally
back home to the boardroom and the throne.
Sultan Amin belongs to the Maranao people of Mindanao, a
Muslim Filipino ethnolinguistic group known for their rich oral
traditions, intricate okir craft designs, and proud sultanate
traditions.
Contents
1 Background and Lineage
2 Education
3 Career
3.1 Overseas Work and Al Safi Company
3.2 The 1993 Scrabble Championship
3.3 Goldmine Pearl and Jewelry
4 Traditional Leadership
5 Personal Life
6 Legacy
7 Recognition
8 See Also
Background and Lineage
Sultan Amin's royal roots run deep in the history of Tamparan.

PAGE 2
He is a direct descendant of Sultan Manking Sugador, recognized as the first Sultan of Tamparan and the first
District President of Tamparan in Lanao del Sur.
On the maternal or ancestral side, one of his great-grandfathers was the late Datu a Cabugatan sa Masiu, Liawao
Mokamad, who came from the lineage of Dhulkarnain of Maruhom Jalalodin, placing Sultan Amin squarely
within one of the most venerable noble genealogies in Maranao political history.<ref>Professional biography of
Sultan Amin Manking Salomabao, source document on file with BangsamoroPedia, wiki.maranaw.com.</ref>
The Sultanate of Tamparan is a royal institution in the Lake Lanao region of Mindanao and is among the traditional
governing structures of the Maranao people whose authority predates the Philippine republic.
This heritage wasn't just a title Sultan Amin inherited. It's a responsibility he has carried through every chapter of
his life, whether in the corporate corridors of Riyadh or the trading floors of SM Supermalls.
Education
Sultan Amin's academic path reflects both ambition and a grounded sense of purpose.
He completed his Bachelor of Arts, major in Political Science, at Southwestern University in Cebu City, one of
the Philippines' established private universities in the Visayas region.<ref>Ibid.</ref>
Political Science gave him a framework for understanding power, governance, and law, the very foundations he
would later draw on both in business negotiations and in his role as a traditional ruler.
He followed that up by enrolling in the Bachelor of Laws program at Manuel L. Quezon University in Manila,
one of the country's long-standing law schools known for producing public servants and legal practitioners.
<ref>Ibid.</ref>
While the source record does not confirm whether he completed the law degree, his pursuit of legal education
alongside a liberal arts foundation speaks to a man who understood early on that leadership demands both moral
grounding and intellectual rigor.
Career
Overseas Work and Al Safi Company
Before building his business empire in the Philippines, Sultan Amin spent formative years working in the
Kingdom of Saudi Arabia as an Overseas Filipino Worker (OFW).
During his time there, he was closely involved in the day-to-day operations and promotion of Al Safi Company,
one of the most prominent milk and dairy brands in the Middle East.
Al Safi, which would later grow into a regional giant through a partnership with Danone, was already a household
name in the Gulf during Sultan Amin's tenure.
His work there wasn't just a job. It was an immersion in international business culture, supply chain operations, and
the kind of organizational thinking that would later shape his entrepreneurial vision back home.<ref>Ibid.</ref>

PAGE 3
The 1993 Scrabble Championship
One of the more unexpected chapters in Sultan Amin's story is his record as a competitive Scrabble player.
In 1993, he represented the Western Region of Saudi Arabia in a nationwide Scrabble competition held across the
kingdom, and he beat all his opponents to claim the championship.<ref>Ibid.</ref>
It's a detail that might seem like a footnote, but it actually tells you a lot about the man: strategic, patient, precise
with language, and comfortable competing on an unfamiliar stage.
Scrabble at a competitive level demands vocabulary depth, pattern recognition, and the ability to stay composed
under pressure. These are, not coincidentally, the same qualities that define his later work as a businessman and a
traditional leader.
Goldmine Pearl and Jewelry
Upon returning to the Philippines, Sultan Amin channeled his overseas experience and business instincts into
founding Goldmine Pearl and Jewelry, a company he leads as Chief Executive Officer (CEO).<ref>Ibid.</ref>
Under his leadership, the company built a supply chain that sources jewelry from Japan, China, and the Middle
East, then brings those pieces directly to the Philippine retail market.
Goldmine Pearl and Jewelry became a supplier to the majority of SM Supermalls across the country, giving it a
nationwide retail footprint that few Filipino jewelry entrepreneurs have managed to achieve.
Beyond the commercial success, the company has become a meaningful source of employment, providing stable
livelihoods to numerous Filipinos working across various SM branches throughout the archipelago.<ref>Ibid.
</ref>
His business model blends global sourcing with local distribution, a formula that takes advantage of his deep
familiarity with both Middle Eastern and East Asian markets, built during his years as an OFW.
Traditional Leadership
In recognition of his lineage and his continued service to his community, Sultan Amin was formally crowned
Sultan of Tamparan in Lanao del Sur.<ref>Ibid.</ref>
The Sultanate of Tamparan is one of the traditional governance structures of the Maranao people, and the sultan's
role carries both ceremonial and moral authority within the community.
As sultan, he serves as a guardian of Maranao cultural heritage and a voice for the people of Tamparan, navigating
the responsibilities of traditional leadership alongside the demands of modern entrepreneurship.
He has often been described as a Sultan-Entrepreneur, a figure who doesn't see a contradiction between honoring
ancestral custom and engaging fully with the global economy.
His approach to the sultanate reflects a broader truth about Maranao identity: that modernity and tradition aren't
opposites but partners, each giving the other meaning and direction.

PAGE 4
Personal Life
Sultan Amin is married to Hajja Bae Asliah Macalandong Tabao of Marawi City, and together they've built a
family that continues their shared commitment to education and public service.<ref>Ibid.</ref>
Their three children have each pursued distinct paths, all of them high-achieving:
A Certified Public Accountant (CPA), bringing financial expertise to the family's professional legacy.
A graduate of Medical Technology, extending the family's reach into the health sciences.
A Political Science student at the International Islamic University Malaysia (IIUM), carrying forward
the family's tradition of international academic engagement and governance-minded education.
The children's trajectories reflect both their parents' values and the broader aspirations of Muslim Filipino families
who see education as the most durable form of empowerment.
Legacy
Sultan Amin Manking Salomabao represents a generation of Maranao leaders who refused to choose between their
heritage and their ambitions.
He built a jewelry business that reaches every corner of the Philippine mall landscape. He served as a top-
performing OFW who brought home not just earnings but experience. He competed and won on an international
stage. And through it all, he remained connected to the sultanate, the community, and the cultural traditions that
shaped him.
His legacy is less about any single achievement and more about the coherence of his life: a Muslim Filipino man
who took the responsibilities of royal lineage seriously, treated his years abroad as an education, and used every
advantage he gained to create employment, preserve culture, and raise a family grounded in excellence.
For the Bangsamoro community and the broader Muslim Filipino world, his story offers a model of leadership
that's both rooted and forward-moving.
Recognition
1993 Scrabble Champion, Western Region of Saudi Arabia, defeating all opponents in a nationwide

title: Salomabao, Salimar M.
text:
PAGE 1
Salimar M. Salomabao
Salimar Manking Salomabao is a Maranao Muslim banking executive and community leader who has dedicated
over three decades to reshaping the financial future of Overseas Filipino Workers in the Middle East.
As Senior Assistant Vice President and Region Head of the Middle East at Philippine National Bank, he stands as
the primary architect of PNB's remittance and cross-border payment operations across one of the world's most
critical corridors for Filipino economic empowerment.
His signature legacy is rooted in a simple but transformative belief: that banking is not merely about moving
money, but about nation-building and personal liberation.

Lead
Salimar Manking Salomabao embodies the intersection of heritage and purpose. A proud Maranao Filipino Muslim
descended from Sultan Manking Sugador, the first Sultan of Tamparan, he carries a legacy of leadership that
manifests not in titles alone, but in direct impact on the lives of over 2.1 million Filipinos across the Gulf
Cooperation Council region.
His career trajectory from Saudi Arabia to the United Arab Emirates to his current position at Philippine National
Bank reveals a man shaped by the struggles of OFWs and determined to translate that empathy into financial
systems that work for ordinary Filipinos.
His most enduring achievement is not a transaction volume or an earnings report, but a movement: transforming
workers into investors through systematic financial literacy advocacy across the GCC, creating pathways for
hundreds of Filipinos to secure meaningful employment, and positioning PNB as the undisputed financial bridge
between diaspora and homeland.

Heritage and Family Legacy
Salimar Manking Salomabao hails from a lineage of considerable
historical and cultural weight in Lanao del Sur.
His roots span the municipalities of Tamparan, Lumba Bayabao,
and Taraka, grounded in the legacy of Sultan Manking Sugador,
who established the Sultanate of Tamparan and set the cultural
foundation for Maranao leadership.
He is the son of the late Salomabao Bano and Haja Raisah
Mamayamban Manking Liawao.
Through his paternal line, he descends directly from Sultan
Manking Sugador; through his maternal heritage, he connects to
Liawao Mokamad, the late Datu a Cabugatan of Masiu.
This dual lineage anchors his understanding of public service and
institutional responsibility, values that would define his
professional trajectory.
Education
Salimar Manking Salomabao began his formal education at
Malungun Taraka for elementary school before pursuing
secondary studies at Mindanao State University in Tamparan.
Recognizing the need to broaden his professional prospects, he
relocated to Manila and enrolled at Manuel L. Quezon University,
where he earned his Bachelor of Science in Commerce with a
major in Accountancy in 1993.
The rigorous foundation in accounting and financial analysis
provided the technical toolkit necessary for his subsequent ascent
into international banking.
Career in International Finance
Early Years in Saudi Arabia
Salimar Manking Salomabao's international banking career began
in Saudi Arabia, where he joined Al Rajhi Bank, one of the
world's largest Islamic banking institutions.
In his initial role as Senior Marketing Officer, he demonstrated an unusual gift for navigating complex financial
markets and understanding the distinct needs of expatriate workers.
This early exposure to Islamic banking principles and the mechanics of remittance flows would become the
foundation for his future work in cross-border finance.

PAGE 3
Arab National Bank Era
In 2001, Salomabao transitioned to Arab National Bank (ANB), where he spent sixteen formative years as
Remittance Manager.
This was the crucial period of his career, where specialized expertise in cross-border payments, regulatory
compliance, and the logistics of moving capital across continents became his professional identity.
During his tenure at ANB, he oversaw the seamless flow of capital for thousands of expatriates, ensuring that the
hard-earned money of overseas workers reached their families in the Philippines and across the Muslim world with
security and efficiency.
The work was not glamorous, but it was essential: every transaction represented a family's investment in a child's
education, a home, a business, or a dignified retirement.
Philippine National Bank and Current Role
In 2017, Salimar Manking Salomabao joined Philippine National Bank, assuming the position of Senior Assistant
Vice President.
His rapid ascent to Region Head and General Manager for the Middle East reflected both his track record and the
strategic importance PNB placed on the Middle Eastern market.
In this capacity, he oversees the bank's entire business footprint across one of the world's most dynamic economic
regions: from the financial hubs of Riyadh and Dubai to the emerging markets of Muscat and Manama.
His mandate is clear: ensure that PNB remains not just a financial intermediary, but the trusted bridge between the
Global Filipino and the homeland.
Financial Literacy Advocacy
Beyond boardrooms and balance sheets, Salimar Manking Salomabao built a parallel career as a crusader for
financial education.
He has dedicated a significant portion of his professional life to addressing a fundamental problem: most OFWs,
despite earning substantial incomes, lack the knowledge to build wealth systematically.
His advocacy operates on a deceptively simple principle: the transition from "spender" to "investor."
Through targeted financial literacy programs conducted across the GCC region, specifically in Saudi Arabia, the
United Arab Emirates, Qatar, Bahrain, Kuwait, and Oman, he has empowered thousands of individuals to move
beyond living paycheck to paycheck.
He emphasizes investment in real estate, educational assets, and small business ventures as pathways toward
sustainable wealth creation.
His approach combines the rigor of banking with the compassion of someone who understands the sacrifices that
OFWs endure.
I believe that banking is more than just a series of transactions; it is a tool for nation-building and
personal liberation.

PAGE 4
Community Leadership and Human Capital Development
Salimar Manking Salomabao's influence extends well beyond finance.
He has been instrumental in facilitating employment opportunities for hundreds of Filipinos across the GCC
region, leveraging his professional network and institutional knowledge to open doors that might otherwise remain
closed.
Whether in the bustling hubs of Dubai and Riyadh or the developing economic corridors of Muscat and Manama,
he has positioned himself as an active broker of opportunity.
His community leadership roles reflect this commitment:
He serves as President of the Tamparan Islamic Development Association in Riyadh, an organization focused on
preserving Maranao cultural identity while addressing the socio-economic needs of the diaspora community.
He holds a directorship position at Filicom in the United Arab Emirates, where he advocates for Filipino business
interests and cross-cultural commerce.
He serves as a trusted Adviser to the Maranao Community in the UAE, offering guidance on matters ranging from
family welfare to cultural preservation to economic empowerment.
Recognition and Awards
Salimar Manking Salomabao's contributions to the banking industry and the Filipino community have earned
recognition through multiple prestigious accolades:
The Pioneer Award for Excellence in Banking Leadership acknowledges his foundational work in establishing new
standards for remittance efficiency and customer care in the international banking sector.
Asia's Empowered International Leader Award recognizes his role in advancing not just his institution, but the
broader cause of Filipino economic dignity in Asia's most critical markets.
The Global Filipino Icon Award celebrates his embodiment of the values that define the diaspora at its best: hard
work, cultural pride, a commitment to community, and an unwavering belief in Filipino potential.
Legacy and Impact
Salimar Manking Salomabao occupies a singular position in the history of Filipino financial services.
He arrived in international banking at a time when OFWs were often treated as transactional entities, their
remittances managed by systems indifferent to their aspirations.
He leaves behind a legacy of institutional practice and personal example that treats each transaction as sacred, each
client as a builder of nations, each remittance as an act of hope.
His ongoing work at Philippine National Bank continues this mission: ensuring that the 2.1 million Filipinos in the
Middle East have access to financial systems that respect their dignity, protect their assets, and empower their
families.

title: Sampulna, Jim Oliveros
text:
PAGE 1
Jim Oliveros Sampulna
Jim Oliveros Sampulna, PhD, CESO I (June 2, 1957, Cotabato City, Mindanao, Philippines – May 31, 2025) was
a career government official of Maguindanaon descent who spent more than four decades in dedicated service to
the Philippine Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR).
He rose from tree marker to the highest levels of environmental governance, eventually becoming the 22nd Officer-
in-Charge (Acting) Secretary of the DENR in 2022, appointed by President Rodrigo Duterte.
Sampulna's career stands as one of the most compelling stories of merit-based advancement in Philippine public
service. He started from the most grounded vantage point possible: marking trees in the field. From there, he
methodically built a four-decade career that stretched from Mindanao to Luzon to the Visayas, giving him a
genuinely national understanding of the country's environmental challenges.
Colleagues and tributes consistently pointed to the same qualities: integrity, humility, and a deep, unwavering care
for both the environment and the communities that depended on it. His legacy as a Mindanaoan leader who rose on
merit to national prominence continues to inspire those who believe that genuine service and quiet dedication can
still take someone to the top.
Contents

2 Education
3 Career

Background
Jim Oliveros Sampulna was born on June 2, 1957, in Cotabato City, a city at the heart of Mindanao's rich natural
landscapes and its equally complex history.
He belongs to the Maguindanaon people, one of the major ethno-linguistic groups of the Bangsamoro region, a
community with deep cultural roots and a long history of navigating the tensions between tradition, governance,
and development.
Growing up in Cotabato City meant growing up in a place where forests were close and the pressures on those
forests were real. That early awareness of the land shaped who Sampulna would become.

He entered government service at just 20 years old, in 1977,
working as a tree marker for the then-Bureau of Forest
Development in Cotabato City. It was the kind of entry-level field
work that gave him a ground-level, hands-on understanding of
forestry realities that no classroom could fully replicate.
That foundation, gritty and practical as it was, became the bedrock
of everything that followed.
Education
Sampulna was a committed lifelong learner who pursued
advanced degrees even while managing the demands of a rising
government career.
He earned his Bachelor of Science in Commerce from Notre
Dame University in Cotabato City on a government scholarship,
and that degree earned him his first promotion from tree marker to
budget examiner.
He then completed his Bachelor of Laws, also from Notre Dame
University, in 1983, equipping him with the legal grounding that
would become essential in his later work on environmental law
enforcement and regulatory policy.
His graduate education continued steadily. He earned a Master of
Professional Studies, with a major in Public Affairs Management,
from the University of Southern Mindanao in 1994. He followed
that with a Master of Science in Business Administration from
Agusan Colleges in 2002.
He capped his academic journey with a Doctor of Philosophy in
Management, specializing in Human Resources Development,
from the University of the Visayas in 2012.
In 2021, he attained the rank of Career Executive Service Officer I
(CESO I), the highest level in the Philippine civil service
executive track, a recognition of his decades of exemplary
performance and leadership.
Colleagues frequently noted how Sampulna brought both
academic rigor and practical, street-level experience to policy
decisions. His education wasn't just credentials: it was a toolkit he
actively used to navigate complex issues like environmental law,
solid waste management, clean energy, and regional cooperation
frameworks such as BIMP-EAGA.

PAGE 3
Notable

(2022)

(multiple regions)
