Career
Early Career (1977–1995)
Sampulna began his government career in 1977 as a tree marker
with the Bureau of Forest Development in Cotabato City. This
early, boots-on-the-ground role gave him an understanding of
forestry and field environmental work that became a defining
feature of his leadership style throughout his life.
After earning his B.S. Commerce, he was promoted to budget examiner, combining field experience with
administrative and financial skills. That combination of practical fieldwork and office competence would set the
pattern for his entire career.
By 1988, he was serving as Chief Regional Development Specialist for DENR Region 12, and in 1989, he moved
into a Planning Officer V role. In 1996, he became a Provincial Environment and Natural Resources Officer
(PENRO).
Rising Through the Ranks (1996–2018)
Sampulna's career advanced steadily through a series of directorships and regional leadership positions. He became
Director III in 2001 and Director IV in 2004, and went on to serve as Regional Executive Director and Regional
Director across multiple DENR regions.
His regional postings were notably diverse. He served in Regions 11, 12, and 13 in Mindanao, Region 1 in Luzon,
and Region 6 in the Visayas, giving him a genuinely national perspective on the Philippines' environmental
landscape and the very different challenges that different parts of the country face.
This breadth of experience made him unusual among senior government officials: he had walked the terrain, not
just read the reports.
Undersecretary (2019–2021)
From 2019 to 2021, Sampulna served as Undersecretary of the DENR, taking on overlapping portfolios that
included enforcement, field operations, mining regulation, Muslim affairs, and oversight of attached agencies.
His Undersecretary roles placed him at the intersection of some of the most contentious and consequential
environmental governance questions in the country: balancing resource extraction with ecological protection,
managing a large and geographically dispersed bureaucracy, and navigating politically sensitive issues like
responsible mining.
OIC Secretary (2022)
On February 17 to 18, 2022, President Rodrigo Duterte appointed Jim Sampulna as Officer-in-Charge (Acting)
Secretary of the DENR, making him the 22nd person to lead the department.
His tenure as OIC Secretary, though brief, was active and purposeful. He pushed forward priorities including the
rehabilitation of Manila Bay, solid waste management enforcement, responsible mining governance, biodiversity
conservation efforts, and national greening programs.

PAGE 4
He was known during this period for conducting audits of mining operations, formally recognizing companies
demonstrating responsible practices, facilitating land title turnovers and donations (including to the Research
Institute for Tropical Medicine), and maintaining strong working relationships with regional offices and community
stakeholders.
His leadership style throughout this period mirrored what had always defined him: building genuine rapport with
rank-and-file employees because he had been one. He knew what field work looked like because he had done it.
Family and Personal Life
Jim Sampulna was married to Agnes Makilala Duruin Sampulna, a registered nurse and former Regional Director
of the Commission on Population in Region XI, based in Davao City.
Together, they raised four children.
Friends and colleagues who offered tributes after his passing consistently painted a picture of a man whose
devotion to his family was as genuine and deep as his commitment to public service. The values he embodied at
work, humility, care, steadiness, were the same ones he brought home.
Institutional Contributions
Throughout his career, Sampulna made lasting contributions to the systems and structures of Philippine
environmental governance.
He strengthened field operations across multiple DENR regional offices, building institutional muscle for
enforcement and monitoring that outlasted his individual postings.
His work on mining governance helped advance a more accountability-driven framework for resource extraction,
one that sought to recognize and incentivize responsible operators while maintaining regulatory pressure on those
who fell short.
He contributed to biodiversity conservation efforts, including support for projects like Rafflesia conservation, and
helped advance regional environmental cooperation through frameworks like BIMP-EAGA.
He also played a role in inter-agency coordination on environmental issues, working across government institutions
to align efforts on concerns like solid waste management, Manila Bay rehabilitation, and clean energy initiatives.
His decades of service across seven DENR regions left behind strengthened institutional capacity, better-networked
regional offices, and a generation of colleagues and subordinates who had been shaped by his example.
Legacy
Jim Oliveros Sampulna's legacy is inseparable from the story of where he started. He began his government career
marking trees. He ended it as the acting head of the very department responsible for managing the nation's forests,
watersheds, and natural resources.
That arc tells the story: principled, patient, merit-based public service can take someone from the most modest
starting point to the highest levels of leadership.

PAGE 5
His legacy lives on in the DENR's institutional systems, in the people he mentored and supported across four
decades, and in the quiet but powerful reminder that great service is built one honest day at a time. He didn't
manage resources from a distance; he knew the land, understood the people who depended on it, and served both
with his whole self.
As a Maguindanaon leader who rose to national prominence entirely through merit and dedication, Sampulna also
carries a broader symbolic significance for Mindanao and for the Bangsamoro community. He showed that the
provinces produce leaders of national consequence, and that a commitment to inclusive, honest public service can
bridge regions, cultures, and political divides.
His story continues to be an inspiration to anyone who serves the public, or hopes to.
Recognition
Sampulna's career brought him a range of formal recognitions that reflected both his professional accomplishments
and the esteem of his peers and institutions.
He attained the rank of Career Executive Service Officer I (CESO I) in 2021, the highest level in the Philippine
civil service executive track, a distinction reflecting decades of exemplary leadership and performance.
His appointment as OIC Secretary of the DENR in 2022 by President Duterte was itself a recognition of his stature
within the department and his trustworthiness as a steward of a critical national institution.
Upon his passing on May 31, 2025, tributes poured in from across the DENR family, the Career Executive Service
Board, and colleagues spanning multiple regions. These expressions of grief and gratitude were among the most
meaningful recognitions of a life devoted to service.
Challenges
Sampulna's career unfolded across some of the most demanding terrain in Philippine environmental governance.
Working in Mindanao meant operating in a region where development pressures, resource conflicts, and political
complexities intersected constantly. His ability to navigate those realities, while maintaining integrity and building
genuine relationships, was a defining feature of his leadership.
As Undersecretary and later OIC Secretary, he faced the inherent tensions of managing an agency whose mandate
often put environmental protection in direct conflict with economic interests, particularly in areas like mining.
Striking that balance, without abandoning either principle, required the kind of judgment that can only come from
decades of experience.
His brief tenure as OIC Secretary also meant operating under significant time and institutional constraints,
inheriting ongoing programs and challenges while working within the transition timeline of a presidential
administration.
That he left behind a reputation for fairness, integrity, and genuine commitment under those pressures speaks to the
quality of his character.

Ali B. Sangki
Datu Ali B. Sangki is a Maguindanaon statesman, traditional datu,
and Member of the Bangsamoro Parliament under the Bangsamoro
Transition Authority (BTA), the interim governing body of the
Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao
(BARMM).
His career stretches across more than five decades, touching nearly
every critical institution that shapes Muslim Mindanao: regional
development, local legislation, Islamic banking, national Muslim
affairs, and now Bangsamoro parliamentary governance.
He is widely regarded as an elder statesman whose personal
credibility transcends the political fractures that characterize the
region, and his family name, Sangki, is among the most politically
consequential in all of central Mindanao.

EARLY LIFE, ANCESTRY, AND
ETHNIC AFFILIATION
Datu Ali B. Sangki was born into the traditional aristocracy of
Mindanao, rooted in the lineage of the Maguindanao Sultanate,
one of the oldest and most influential Muslim polities in Southeast
Asian history.
He is Maguindanaon, a member of one of the largest and
historically most powerful Moro ethnolinguistic communities in the
Southern Philippines.
The Maguindanaon people are bound by a cultural and political
tradition that traces authority through hereditary datu lineages, and
Sangki's birth into this framework was not incidental; it set the
expectations and responsibilities that would follow him throughout
his public life.
Growing up during a period of intense socio-political turbulence in
Mindanao, when the Moro struggle for self-determination was
taking on its most organized and confrontational forms, Sangki
navigated that world with the weight of ancestral prestige behind
him and the practical realities of a nation in transition ahead of him.
His trajectory reflects the broader story of Maguindanaon leadership: deeply rooted in adat and customary
authority, yet compelled by historical circumstance to engage fully with the institutions of the modern Philippine
state.
FAMILY AND PERSONAL LIFE
The Sangki name carries enormous political weight in central Mindanao, particularly across the provinces of
Maguindanao del Sur and Sultan Kudarat.
Ali Sangki is the patriarch of a multigenerational political dynasty, and his family's reach across both provinces
represents one of the most formidable kinship networks in contemporary Moro governance.
His daughter, Bai Mariam Sangki-Mangudadatu, serves as the governor of Maguindanao, a position that keeps
the Sangki name at the center of the province's political landscape.
Through Bai Mariam's marriage to former Sultan Kudarat Governor Suharto "Teng" Mangudadatu, the
Sangki family forged an alliance with one of the most powerful clans in the adjacent province, creating a cross-
provincial political bloc that is nearly without parallel in the region.
Their son, Datu Pax Ali Sangki-Mangudadatu, made national headlines as one of the youngest elected officials in
Philippine history, first serving as mayor of the municipality named after their ancestor, Datu Abdullah Sangki,
before rising to the governorship of Sultan Kudarat.
This three-generation chain of public service is not merely a matter of family ambition; it reflects a deeply
embedded Maguindanaon tradition of hereditary stewardship, where responsibility for community welfare passes
down within a datu lineage as both a right and an obligation.

PAGE 3
EDUCATIONAL JOURNEY
Specific details about Sangki's formal academic credentials from his earlier years have not been extensively
documented in public records.
What his career makes unmistakably clear, however, is the breadth and depth of knowledge he accumulated across
multiple domains: public administration, development economics, Islamic finance and Sharia law, corporate
management, and statutory legislation.
To hold executive leadership positions at the Al-Amanah Islamic Bank, to serve as Undersecretary of the Office
on Muslim Affairs, and to navigate the technical terrain of Bangsamoro peace negotiations, a person needs more
than good instincts; they need rigorous institutional knowledge built across years of direct engagement.
Sangki's expertise is best understood as a fusion of two distinct traditions: the classical Islamic intellectual heritage
that informs Maguindanaon community authority, and the secular bureaucratic training that the Philippine state
demands of its senior administrators.
That combination, rare among public officials in any region, gave him the ability to speak credibly to conservative
religious communities and national-level technocrats in the same breath.
A CAREER ACROSS ERAS
Ali Sangki's professional biography is essentially a chronicle of how Bangsamoro governance itself evolved: from
colonial-era regional development frameworks, through the contested years of autonomy negotiations, and finally
into the parliamentary institutions that exist today.
THE FORMATIVE DECADES (1975–1992)
Sangki entered public service in the mid-1970s with the Southern Philippines Development Authority (SPDA), a
government agency tasked with driving economic recovery and infrastructure development in a region that had
been severely destabilized by armed conflict.
For seventeen years, he worked as a project and department manager, designing and implementing economic
initiatives aimed at uplifting communities in conflict-affected areas of Mindanao.
That era was not easy terrain. The Moro National Liberation Front (MNLF) insurgency was at its height during the
late 1970s and early 1980s, and the daily work of regional development was conducted against a backdrop of
military operations, displacement, and deep community distrust of government institutions.
His sustained engagement with the SPDA through that period gave him an unusually grounded understanding of
regional infrastructure, agricultural systems, resource distribution, and the human costs of prolonged conflict,
knowledge that would prove foundational to everything he did afterward.
LOCAL GOVERNANCE (1992–2002)
Moving into electoral politics, Sangki served for a decade as a Provincial Board Member representing the second
district of Maguindanao.

PAGE 4
This decade in local governance placed him squarely in the day-to-day work of provincial legislation: drafting
ordinances, mediating land disputes, deliberating over provincial budgets, and representing constituent concerns in
a territory where the line between political and clan-based authority was never entirely clean.
Provincial board service in Maguindanao during this period also meant operating in a post-ARMM context, when
the Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao had been formally established but its institutions were still fragile,
underfunded, and contested.
Sangki's decade at this level gave him a legislator's instinct for the practical mechanics of governance, a skill set
that would serve him well when he later returned to lawmaking at the Bangsamoro parliamentary level.
ISLAMIC BANKING LEADERSHIP (2005–2007)
One of the most distinctive chapters of Sangki's career came in 2005, when he was appointed Chief Executive
Officer of the Al-Amanah Investment Islamic Bank of the Philippines, the country's first and only Islamic
bank.
Al-Amanah was established precisely to serve the financial needs of Muslim Filipinos through Sharia-compliant
banking products, offering an alternative to conventional interest-based (riba) finance that many devout Muslims
are unable to participate in on religious grounds.
Leading Al-Amanah was a high-stakes assignment. Islamic banking requires not only sound corporate management
but also genuine fluency in Sharia finance principles, fiqh al-muamalat, and the realities of serving an
economically marginalized community with limited access to formal financial systems.
Under Sangki's leadership, Al-Amanah worked to expand its reach across Muslim Mindanao and push for greater
financial inclusion in a market that conventional banking had largely bypassed.
His tenure at Al-Amanah remains a signal moment in his biography: it established his credibility as a leader who
could operate at the intersection of Islamic law and modern institutional finance.
NATIONAL BUREAUCRACY (2007–2010)
From the banking sector, Sangki moved to one of the most politically sensitive positions in the Philippine national
government: Undersecretary and Executive Director of the Office on Muslim Affairs (OMA), the agency that
preceded the modern National Commission on Muslim Filipinos (NCMF).
The OMA served as the primary institutional bridge between Malacañang Palace and the approximately ten million
Filipino Muslims spread across the country.
Its mandate covered an unusually broad range of responsibilities: coordinating the logistics of the annual Hajj
pilgrimage for Filipino pilgrims, supporting cultural preservation efforts, overseeing halal certification, and
implementing economic development programs specifically designed for Muslim communities.
As Undersecretary, Sangki was the principal conduit between the national government and the Filipino Muslim
population, a role requiring both bureaucratic competence and the kind of community credibility that only a
recognized datu from a major Maguindanaon family could provide.
His time at the OMA deepened his national-level policy networks while reinforcing his standing as a trusted
interlocutor across the political and cultural divide between Manila and Muslim Mindanao.

PAGE 5
LEGISLATIVE CONTRIBUTIONS AND INSTITUTIONAL IMPACT
In January 2020, President Rodrigo Duterte appointed Ali Sangki as the 79th member of the Bangsamoro
Transition Authority, the interim parliament established under the Bangsamoro Organic Law (BOL) to guide
the region through its transition toward full autonomy.
The BTA was a historically significant body: a parliament composed largely of appointees drawn from the Moro
Islamic Liberation Front (MILF), civil society organizations, indigenous communities, and recognized community
leaders, all tasked with drafting the foundational laws of the new autonomous region.
Sangki's appointment was well-received across political lines, including among factions that might otherwise be
cautious about figures associated with the old ARMM-era establishment.
As a Member of Parliament (MP), he proved to be a substantive lawmaker rather than a ceremonial one.
THE LIGUASAN MARSH BILL
Among his most significant individual legislative contributions is a principal bill focused on the conservation and
integrated management of the Liguasan Marsh, the vast wetland complex straddling Maguindanao, Cotabato,
and Sultan Kudarat.
The Liguasan Marsh is one of the largest freshwater marshes in the Philippines and holds enormous ecological
value as a biodiversity hotspot and the primary water regulation system for the Mindanao River basin.
It also sits above substantial natural gas reserves, making it the subject of competing development and extraction
interests.
Sangki's legislative framework addresses this tension directly: ensuring that local communities, particularly the
Maguindanaon and Iranun peoples who have lived along the marsh for centuries, benefit equitably from any
resource extraction while establishing enforceable mechanisms for environmental protection.
The bill reflects a philosophy of development that takes both ecological integrity and community rights seriously, a
position not always easy to maintain in a region where resource competition has historically been a driver of
conflict.
DISPLACED PERSONS PROTECTION
Sangki authored comprehensive legislation protecting the rights of Internally Displaced Persons (IDPs) within
BARMM.
Internal displacement in Muslim Mindanao is not an abstract policy issue; it is a lived reality for hundreds of
thousands of families who have been forced from their homes by cycles of armed conflict, clan warfare (rido), and
natural disasters over generations.
The act he authored institutes state-backed mechanisms for resettlement, economic rehabilitation, trauma-informed
support, and safety guarantees for displaced families, creating a legal framework that obligates the Bangsamoro
government to treat IDP welfare as a core governance responsibility rather than an emergency afterthought.

PAGE 6
FOUNDATIONAL BANGSAMORO CODES
Beyond his individual-authored bills, Sangki co-authored and voted for two of the most foundational statutes of the
new autonomous region: the Bangsamoro Local Governance Code and the Bangsamoro Electoral Code.
The Local Governance Code established the operational guidelines, fiscal structures, and accountability
mechanisms for local government units operating within the BARMM framework.
The Electoral Code defined the rules, timelines, and procedures for future Bangsamoro elections, laying the
groundwork for the region's transition from an appointed interim parliament to a fully elected legislative body.
These are not glamorous legislative achievements in the way that high-profile individual bills tend to be, but they
are arguably more consequential: the plumbing laws that determine whether an autonomous region actually
functions.
PEACE PROCESS DIPLOMACY
Sangki's institutional contribution to the Bangsamoro peace process extends well beyond his parliamentary work.
He served on the Government Technical Working Group on Resources, a body that worked behind the scenes to
hammer out the complex wealth-sharing arrangements between the national government and the MILF that form a
core component of the Bangsamoro Organic Law.
Resource-sharing negotiations are among the most technically demanding and politically contentious aspects of
any peace agreement, and his participation in that process placed him at the table during some of the most
consequential discussions in the history of the Bangsamoro peace talks.
AWARDS, RECOGNITION, AND CULTURAL SIGNIFICANCE
Over a career spanning more than fifty years, Sangki has received numerous institutional commendations and
professional recognitions from the various government agencies and bodies he served.
His deepest and most enduring recognition, however, is cultural rather than bureaucratic.
The title of Datu he bears is not ceremonial in Maguindanaon society; it carries active obligations, expectations of
mediation, responsibility for community welfare, and the maintenance of the social fabric that adat and customary
tradition define.
What makes Sangki's cultural standing particularly significant in the contemporary context is his demonstrated
ability to command respect across factional lines.
In a region where rido (clan feuds) and political rivalries can paralyze governance and freeze legislative processes
for months or years, recognized elder statesmen who are trusted by multiple competing groups are genuinely rare
and genuinely valuable.
His appointment to the BTA was welcomed across political divides in part precisely because he represents a kind of
structural continuity: a traditional leader who is equally at home in a corporate boardroom, a peace-talk summit, a
provincial capitol session, or a legislative chamber.
That versatility, grounded in decades of genuine institutional experience rather than inherited prestige alone, is the
core of his cultural significance.

PAGE 7
LEGACY AND LASTING IMPACT
Datu Ali B. Sangki's legacy is one of institutional endurance and adaptive leadership.
He belongs to a generation of Moro leaders who came of age during the open-armed rebellion of the 1970s,
survived the prolonged and often frustrating years of the ARMM experiment, and lived to see the Bangsamoro
Organic Law translate the ideals of that struggle into actual parliamentary institutions.
His fingerprints are on the foundational structures of modern Muslim Mindanao in concrete ways: in the
frameworks of Islamic banking that Al-Amanah operates under, in the national Muslim welfare programs that the
NCMF continues to administer, in the wealth-sharing provisions of the Bangsamoro Organic Law that his technical
group helped draft, and in the parliamentary codes that govern how the BARMM's local governments function and
how its elections will be conducted.
His authored legislation on the Liguasan Marsh and on IDP protection speaks to a priorities framework that takes
the welfare of ordinary Bangsamoro citizens seriously: the fishermen and farmers who depend on the marsh, and
the displaced families who need something more than goodwill from their government.
As the region moves toward its first Bangsamoro elections, Sangki's role as a living institutional memory, a figure
who has navigated every major phase of Mindanao's political transformation since the 1970s, gives him a
significance that goes beyond the specific bills he has authored or the positions he has held.
He is, in the fullest sense, a builder of Bangsamoro institutions.

Alyssa Fathma Berowa Sani
Alyssa Fathma Berowa Sani is a Maranao student leader, youth
diplomat, and cultural advocate from Marawi City, Lanao del Sur, in
the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao
(BARMM), Philippines. A graduating Senior High School student at
the Mindanao State University – Integrated Laboratory School
(MSU-ILS) in 2026, she has built a remarkable record of academic
achievement, international exchange, cultural performance, and
community service while still in secondary school. Her
accomplishments — from placing in the top three of a competitive
university-level entrance examination to serving as a U.S.
Department of State-recognized youth ambassador — have drawn
attention to the capacity and potential of young Bangsamoro women
in national and global arenas.

Background and Family
Alyssa Fathma Berowa Sani was born and raised in Marawi City, the capital of Lanao del Sur and the seat of
Maranao intellectual and cultural life in the Bangsamoro. The city, perched above the shores of Lake Lanao and
long considered the heart of Maranao civilization, has produced generations of scholars, artists, and community

PAGE 2
leaders. Growing up in this environment shaped Alyssa's early orientation toward both academic achievement and
cultural preservation — two values that define her public profile as a young person.
Her full name reflects that layered identity: Fathma is a variant of Fatimah, the daughter of the Prophet
Muhammad (peace be upon him), signaling a faith-rooted naming tradition common among Maranao Muslim
families; Berowa is a prominent surname within the MSU academic community, linking her to a lineage associated
with learning and public service; and Sani grounds her firmly in Maranao heritage. Together, the name tells a story
about where she comes from and what her community expects of her.
Education
MSU-Integrated Laboratory School
Alyssa is an upcoming 2026 graduate of the Mindanao State University – Integrated Laboratory School (MSU-
ILS), one of the most respected pre-collegiate institutions in Muslim Mindanao. Established in 1964 on the MSU
Main Campus in Marawi City, MSU-ILS serves as a laboratory school for the university's College of Education,
enrolling students from kindergarten through Senior High School. It operates within the academic culture of MSU-
Marawi — a institution established in 1961 as a social laboratory for national integration and the first state
university in Mindanao. For Alyssa, studying within this ecosystem meant being immersed in an environment that
prizes both rigorous scholarship and multicultural engagement from an early age.
MSU Senior High School Entrance Examination (SHSEE) — Top 3
One of Alyssa's most concrete academic distinctions is her Top 3 placement in the Senior High School Entrance
Examination (SHSEE) administered by Mindanao State University. The SHSEE is a competitive and highly
selective examination that screens applicants for the Senior High School program within the MSU System — a
process that draws hundreds of applicants across the region each cycle. Placing in the top three puts Alyssa among
the highest-performing examinees, a distinction that reflects not just test-taking ability but the sustained academic
discipline that comes from years of preparation.
International Exchange — The Storm King School, New York
Perhaps the most internationally significant chapter of Alyssa's secondary education was her stint as an exchange
student at The Storm King School (SKS) in Cornwall-on-Hudson, New York, United States. Founded in 1867,
The Storm King School is a distinguished coeducational boarding and day school serving students in Grades 8
through 12 and postgraduate, with an enrollment drawn from the United States and more than twenty countries
worldwide. The school is known for its low student-to-faculty ratio and its global exchange program, which brings
international students into a rigorous academic environment alongside their American peers.
For a young Maranao woman from Marawi City — a city that only a few years prior had been the site of a
devastating five-month urban siege in 2017 — the opportunity to study in an elite New York boarding school
carries extraordinary weight. Her time at Storm King gave her firsthand exposure to American academic culture,
cross-cultural dialogue, and the kind of global learning environment that few students from the Bangsamoro region
have had the chance to access.

PAGE 3
Xavier University – Senior High School (XU SHS) Passer
Alyssa also passed the entrance examination for Senior High School at Xavier University – Ateneo de Cagayan
in Cagayan de Oro City. XU is a Filipino, Catholic, and Jesuit university known for its rigorous academic standards
and selective admissions process, and successfully passing its senior high school qualifying exam speaks to the
breadth of Alyssa's academic preparation — strong enough to open doors at competitive institutions across
different educational traditions.
Youth Leadership and Ambassadorial Roles
YA-EAP Ambassador
Alyssa served as an ambassador under the Youth Ambassadors – East Asia and Pacific (YA-EAP) Program, a
fully funded youth leadership exchange sponsored by the U.S. Department of State's Bureau of Educational and
Cultural Affairs (ECA). The YA-EAP program brings together young leaders aged 15 to 17 from across the East
Asia and Pacific region — including the Philippines, Burma, Papua New Guinea, Fiji, and other Pacific nations —
for leadership development, civic engagement, and community problem-solving workshops, typically held in the
United States. Participants stay with host families and engage in sessions on democracy, digital engagement,
conflict resolution, and inclusive leadership. The program is administered by PH International and recognized as
one of the U.S. government's premier people-to-people exchange initiatives.
Being named a YA-EAP Ambassador places Alyssa in a cohort selected from hundreds of applicants based on
criteria including academic achievement, leadership potential, community engagement, English proficiency, and
commitment to social inclusion. For a student from Marawi City — in a region often associated in the international
imagination with conflict rather than diplomacy — her selection signals a broader story about the Bangsamoro's
emerging generation of globally connected young people.
Model United Nations Korea Ambassador
Alyssa also participated as an ambassador in the Model United Nations (MUN) Korea circuit — a platform that
brings together youth delegates from across Asia to simulate UN deliberations and develop skills in diplomacy,
research, and international relations. MUN Korea events, including high-profile gatherings like the Asia World
Model United Nations (AWMUN) held in Seoul, regularly draw hundreds of young delegates from countries
including South Korea, the Philippines, Indonesia, the United States, and Mongolia. Participating as an ambassador
in such a forum requires mastery of position papers, formal debate procedures, and international issue analysis —
skills that go well beyond the typical secondary school curriculum.
Student Ambassador of the Year
Within her own school community, Alyssa was recognized as Student Ambassador of the Year — an
acknowledgment of her consistent role as a representative of her institution across multiple platforms, from
community service to international exchange. This kind of school-level recognition, layered on top of her external
accomplishments, paints the picture of a student who doesn't just compete in external arenas but brings that energy
back into her home institution.

PAGE 4
Cultural Advocacy
Rinayong Cultural Performer
Alyssa is a recognized Rinayong Cultural Performer, situating her within the tradition of Maranao cultural
expression and indigenous performing arts. Maranao performance culture is rich and historically significant —
encompassing dances like the Singkil, the Pagapir, and the Kappa Malong, accompanied by the kulintang and
agung, instruments central to the musical heritage of the "people of the lake." The Rinayong is a form of cultural
performance that celebrates Maranao identity through song, movement, and attire, and has long been a vehicle for
transmitting community values and artistic memory across generations.
In a generation that is often pulled between modernization and cultural continuity, Alyssa's active participation in
cultural performance is both a personal choice and a community statement. It reflects the Bangsamoro's ongoing
project of reclaiming and asserting their cultural identity — particularly in the aftermath of the 2017 Marawi siege,
which not only displaced thousands but also threatened the physical and symbolic spaces where Maranao culture
had been practiced and preserved for centuries.
Recognition and Awards

secondary education:

Cultural and Historical Significance
Alyssa Fathma Berowa Sani's story is inseparable from the story of Marawi City itself. The city that shaped her
early years was also the city that bore one of the most destructive conflicts in recent Philippine history — the 2017
Battle of Marawi, a five-month urban siege that displaced hundreds of thousands of residents, damaged or
destroyed much of the city's historic center, and left deep psychological and material wounds on the Maranao
community. Many of the young people who grew up in Marawi in the years after 2017 did so amid reconstruction,
displacement, and the slow, painful work of rebuilding not just buildings but community identity.

PAGE 5
Against that backdrop, the emergence of a young Maranao woman who has earned a top ranking in a university
entrance exam, studied in a New York boarding school, represented her country in youth diplomatic programs, and
performed her culture on public stages carries a significance that goes well beyond individual achievement. She is,
in a very real sense, a visible answer to the narrative of decline — proof that Marawi's next generation is not
defined by the siege, but by resilience, scholarship, and cultural pride.

title: Sani, Punduma Sumndad
text:
PAGE 1
Punduma Sumndad Sani
Punduma "Duma" Sumndad Sani (born September 15, 1946), widely known as Kaka Duma, is a Maranao
educator, martial arts grandmaster, traditional royalty, revolutionary figure, and legislator from Marawi City, Lanao
del Sur.
He is a professor at Mindanao State University (MSU) in Marawi, the founder and longtime head of the MSU
Karate Club (MSUKC), a former MNLF commander and peace process panelist, the Sultan of the Royal House of
Guimba of the United Sultanates of Marawi, and a former member of the first Bangsamoro Transition Authority
(BTA) Parliament representing the MNLF sector.
Across more than five decades of public life, Sani has moved between the classroom, the training mat, the peace
negotiating table, and the legislative chamber, building a reputation as one of the most multi-dimensional figures in
contemporary Bangsamoro and Maranao public life.
He's the kind of person you hear about in almost every corner of Marawi: from MSU alumni who trained under
him in karate, to MNLF veterans who fought alongside him, to BTA colleagues who co-authored landmark
legislation with him.

Background and Early Life
Punduma Sumndad Sani was born on September 15, 1946, in Buadi Sakayo, Marawi City, in the heart of the
Maranao homeland in Lanao del Sur.
He comes from the prominent Sani Clan, a family with deep royal and political roots across Ranao, Maguindanao,
and Sulu.
His father granted him the use of the maternal surname, a practical family decision that also reflects the fluid and
layered nature of Maranao kinship and identity.

In 1994, Sani was formally enthroned as Sultan of the Royal
House of Guimba, one of the United Sultanates of Marawi,
succeeding a distinguished lineage that includes former
legislators and municipal executives from the region.
He grew up attending grade school in Bangon, Marawi, before
proceeding to Dansalan Junior High School for his secondary
education.
Education
For college, Sani made his way to Manila and enrolled at Manuel
L. Quezon University, where he earned a Bachelor of Science in
Commerce, major in Business Administration, in 1968.
Returning to Mindanao, he pursued graduate studies at the
University of the East, completing the academic requirements for
a Master of Arts in Physical Education and passing his
comprehensive examinations in 1981.
He later added another postgraduate credential at Mindanao State
University itself, completing a Master of Arts in Public
Administration in 1997.
This combination of commerce, physical education, and public
administration training reflects the range of his professional
engagements throughout his career.
The Revolutionary Years
Like many Maranao men of his generation who came of age
during the turbulence of the late 1960s and the imposition of
Martial Law under the Marcos regime, Sani found himself drawn
into the Moro struggle for self-determination.
He underwent military training with the Moro National
Liberation Front's Top 90 in Pulau Pangkor, Malaysia, one of the
early elite formations of the MNLF's armed cadre.
During this period he was known in movement circles as
"Commander Juma," a name that carried weight among fellow
fighters and organizers in Mindanao.
What distinguished Sani during this chapter was that he never
entirely abandoned his civilian roles, continuing to teach and
engage with his community even while active in the resistance.
That combination of armed conviction and patient institution-
building would become a defining thread throughout his life.

9th Dan; addressed as Hanshi
and Kyoshi
Founded
MSU Karate Club (MSUKC),
1972; Bangsamoro Martial Arts
Academy
He maintained his loyalty to the MNLF's mainstream track
through the decades-long peace process that eventually led to the
1996 Final Peace Agreement with the Philippine government.
His involvement in the peace negotiations was significant: he
served as one of the few Maranao representatives among the
MNLF panelists at the 18th Islamic Conference of Foreign
Ministers held in Saudi Arabia in 1989, and participated in
critical exploratory talks between the Government of the
Republic of the Philippines (GRP) and the MNLF held in
Indonesia.
Those Indonesian consultations were among the substantive
preliminary discussions that paved the way for the 1996
agreement.
Career at Mindanao State University
Sani's connection with Mindanao State University in Marawi goes back to the early 1970s, when he started out as
an accounting clerk and part-time instructor.
He rose steadily through the academic ranks, eventually becoming a full professor, and was appointed Director of
the Sports Scholarship and Development Office, a position he held from 1971 to 1987.
In 1993, he was elected by his colleagues as Dean of the College of Sports, Physical Education, and Recreation
(CSPEAR), serving in that role until 1996.
His election as dean during a particularly tense period in Marawi's history is remembered as a meaningful show of
confidence: Christian faculty members reportedly voted for him alongside Muslim colleagues, a small but telling
sign of the trust and respect he had built across community lines.
Throughout his academic career, Sani was known as a professor who pushed students toward discipline, leadership,
and community service, not just technical skills.
After his term in the BTA Parliament, he returned to the university with evident enthusiasm, continuing to teach
and mentor the next generation.
The Martial Arts Legacy
Of all the chapters in Prof. Sani's life, his work in martial arts may be the most enduring in terms of institutional
impact.
In 1972, he founded the MSU Karate Club (MSUKC) on the Marawi campus, and has guided the organization for
more than five decades since.
He holds the rank of 9th Dan, the highest gradations in the Japanese karate tradition, and is addressed with the
honorifics Hanshi and Kyoshi, titles reserved for grandmasters of advanced rank and long experience.

PAGE 4
Under his guidance, the MSUKC has produced local, national, and international champions, run community
outreach programs, and served as a consistent space for Muslim-Christian camaraderie in a city that has seen its
share of tension and tragedy.
Three generations of martial artists have now trained under the club he built, including his own children: Revie,
Hanifi, and Maylanie, all of whom became accomplished competitors in their own right.
He also established and continues to oversee the Bangsamoro Martial Arts Academy, extending the club's mission
into a broader regional platform for developing youth through the discipline of martial arts.
For Sani, karate has never been just about sport or combat technique. He consistently frames it as a vehicle for
character development, resilience, and a quiet but meaningful expression of cultural pride.
Even while serving in the BTA Parliament, he remained hands-on in the club's activities, showing up on the mats
and staying connected to the athletes he has mentored.
In the Bangsamoro Transition Authority Parliament (2019-2022)
When the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM) was established following the
ratification of the Bangsamoro Organic Law (Republic Act No. 11054) in 2019, Sani was appointed as one of the
MNLF representatives to the inaugural BTA Parliament.
His legislative record during the BTA's three-year transitional period was notably wide-ranging.
He was a principal author or co-author of measures covering the Bangsamoro flag, emblem, and official hymn; the
creation of sports and youth development commissions; planning and development bodies for the region; education
reform initiatives; the establishment of women's and human rights commissions; the Bangsamoro budget and local
governance codes; and resolutions focused on the rehabilitation of Marawi City following the devastating 2017
siege.
He also co-authored practical legislation on public health, internally displaced persons (IDPs), the welfare of
Bangsamoro overseas workers, and the integration of former MNLF and MILF combatants into civilian life and the
BARMM's security forces.
Colleagues in the BTA Parliament and constituents who followed his work describe him as principled and
community-focused, someone who spoke with clarity on issues like Ranao development and the historical valor of
the Bangsamoro people.
He was also among those who advocated for commemorating significant milestones in the Bangsamoro people's
collective memory.
Family and Personal Values
Sani is married to Hadja Faizah Minerva Alicer Saber, daughter of the late Mamitua Saber, one of the founding
pillars of Mindanao State University and a towering intellectual figure in the Maranao community.
Together, they built a family where academics and martial arts have both been passed on as living traditions, with
their children carrying forward commitments to sport, discipline, and community service.

PAGE 5
His values come through consistently in how people who know him describe him: discipline, humility, a genuine
commitment to unity across ethnic and religious divides, and a deep sense of responsibility to the Bangsamoro
cause that never loses sight of faith and good governance.
He has long been seen as someone who bridges worlds without pretension: traditional royalty and elected public
servant, martial arts grandmaster and classroom teacher, MNLF veteran and institution-builder.
Legacy and Continuing Contributions
Now in his late seventies, Prof. Punduma B. Sani hasn't stepped back from public life in any meaningful way.
He remains active on the training mats, continues to mentor students and young community members, participates
in regional initiatives, and is still regarded as a respected and authoritative voice in Maranao and Bangsamoro
affairs.
His legacy rests on the breadth and consistency of what he built across more than five decades: a karate club that
became a community institution, a teaching career that shaped thousands of students, a legislative contribution that
helped lay the legal groundwork for the Bangsamoro government, and a life of principled engagement with some
of the most difficult questions facing Mindanao.
Whether people know him as Kaka Duma, as Sultan of Guimba, as Hanshi Sani, or simply as the man who founded
the MSUKC, the through-line is the same: a teacher, a fighter, a lawmaker, and a builder who led consistently by
example and always kept the next generation in view.
In the story of contemporary Mindanao and the long, difficult project of building peace and self-governance in the
Bangsamoro homeland, Prof. Punduma Sumndad Sani is one of the steady hands.

title: Sani, Shihan Revie Saber Sumndad
text:
PAGE 1
Shihan Revie Saber Sumndad Sani
Shihan Revie Saber Sumndad Sani is a Maranao martial arts master, sports administrator, and community leader
based in Marawi City, Lanao del Sur, in the heart of the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao
(BARMM).
He serves as the BARMM Regional Director for the Karate Pilipinas Sports Federation Inc. (KPSFI), the only
national governing body for karate officially recognized by the Philippine Olympic Committee and the World
Karate Federation.
As the Chief Master Instructor of the Mindanao State University Karate Club (MSUKC), widely known as the
"Warriors of the Lake," Sani carries forward one of the oldest and most culturally rooted martial arts institutions in
the southern Philippines.
His legacy is built on a simple but powerful idea: that martial arts, practiced with integrity and discipline, can serve
as a genuine force for peace.
Contents

Background
Revie Saber Sumndad Sani grew up in Marawi City, raised within a family that wove together Maranao royalty,
Islamic scholarship, and a deep devotion to athletic excellence.
He is the son of Hanshi Professor Punduma Sumndad Sani, one of the most celebrated figures in Philippine
martial arts history and a former statesman whose influence shaped the karate landscape across Mindanao.
Growing up on the main campus of Mindanao State University in Marawi, Revie was practically born into the
dojo.

PAGE 2

From early childhood, he trained directly under his father,
absorbing not just the physical mechanics of combat but also the
historical lineages of Okinawan karate, the deeper philosophical
traditions of Japanese Budo, and the ethical codes that define
Bangsamoro martial identity.
His wife, Sensei Sheryll Sani, has been a steady partner in
building their shared mission. She serves as the primary
administrative manager and logistics coordinator for their regional
athletic delegations, keeping operations running smoothly behind
the scenes.
Education and Martial Lineage
Sani completed his formal academic education at Mindanao State
University, an institution where his family carries a long and
distinguished legacy of academic leadership.
His deepest education, though, came through decades of rigorous
classical martial arts training under the tradition of Japanese and
Okinawan Karatedo.
The lineage that shaped him traces directly back to Okinawan
masters of the Shorin-ryu and Shotokan traditions.
Hanshi Punduma Sani, his father and lifelong mentor, brought
these structured systems to Mindanao in 1972, planting the roots of
what would become one of the region's most enduring martial arts
institutions.
Shihan Revie Sani now stands as the current standard-bearer of
that system, certified under both national and international
federations to license practitioners and award rank across the entire
Bangsamoro region.
That certification isn't just a credential. It's a responsibility he takes
seriously.
Career
Sani's career covers a wide range of roles: grassroots sports coach,
regional athletic administrator, community builder, and volunteer
program director.
Leadership of the MSUKC
When Sani took over the technical leadership of the Mindanao
State University Karate Club (MSUKC), he inherited an
institution with history, weight, and community trust behind it.

PAGE 3
Under his guidance, the MSUKC evolved from a university-based club into a structured, non-profit development
academy serving the broader Bangsamoro community.
He established localized training hubs, called dojos, across the region. One of the most notable outcomes of this
effort is the Sapadan Martial Arts Center, a development hub that reinforces the club's historical footprint while
expanding its reach to more communities.
BARMM Regional Directorate, KPSFI
As BARMM Regional Director for the Karate Pilipinas Sports Federation Inc., Sani took on the task of
modernizing local tournament structures and bringing them into alignment with global standards.
He synchronized BARMM athletic criteria with World Karate Federation rules, creating legitimate national ranking
pathways for athletes from conflict-vulnerable communities.
For many young athletes in the region, this wasn't a small thing. It meant that a karateka from Marawi City could
compete on equal footing with athletes from Manila or Cebu.
Summer Karate Outreach Program (SKOP)
One of Sani's most impactful contributions is his leadership of the Summer Karate Outreach Program (SKOP),
a regional youth development initiative he helped institutionalize under the Sani family's stewardship.
The program was originally conceptualized in the early 1990s and has since grown into one of the most recognized
youth diversion initiatives in the Bangsamoro region.
SKOP provides free martial arts, self-defense, and physical fitness training to thousands of Maranao children every
year.
The goal goes beyond athletics. By engaging young people in structured, discipline-driven activity, the program
actively steers youth away from violent extremism, drug abuse, and localized clan conflicts known locally as rido.
For Sani, SKOP isn't a charity project. It's a long-term investment in the social fabric of Maranao communities.
Institutional Contributions
Sani's contributions extend well beyond his roles as coach and administrator.
He has worked to re-engineer how karate functions as a community institution in the Bangsamoro, transforming it
from a sport practiced by a select few into a widely accessible discipline that anyone, regardless of background,
can participate in.
His dojo philosophy explicitly breaks cultural and religious barriers. Under his watch, Christian and Muslim
practitioners train side by side, under the same standards and the same expectations.
This inclusive approach has deep historical roots in the MSUKC. The club produced some of the region's earliest
female martial arts leaders, including the late Sensei Chona Documento-Cuizon, who set early precedents for
gender inclusivity in Bangsamoro sports.
Sani has continued and deepened that tradition, making it a defining characteristic of his leadership.

PAGE 4
Achievements and Recognition
5th Karate Pilipinas National Championship
At the 5th Karate Pilipinas National Championship held in Tagaytay City, Sani led the MSUKC delegation into
elite competition against a field of 1,231 athletes from across the country.
The MSUKC's performance at this national meet was significant enough that the Bangsamoro Parliament
formally recognized it by issuing Resolution No. 460, a legislative commendation honoring the club's contribution
to regional sports development.
WKF Karate 1-Youth League, Manila (2026)
In May 2026, Shihan Revie Sani served as head coach and national official at the WKF Karate 1-Youth League
held at the SM Mall of Asia Arena in Manila, one of the most prestigious global youth karate tournaments on the
international calendar.
He steered elite Maranao youth competitors into the highest tier of international sport karate, including Abdul
Rauf Macawadib, Muhammad Affan-Khan Carimbaran, and Muhammad Ajwad-Khan Carimbaran.
Their presence on that international stage was a direct result of Sani's years of patient, systematic development
work in the region.
Philosophy and Values
Shihan Revie Sani is known for a guiding principle he calls Martial Arts as Peacebuilding.
Rooted in his father's teachings and his own Islamic faith, Sani views karate not as an instrument of violence but as
a framework for inner development. He draws on the Islamic concepts of Jihad al-Asghar (the lesser struggle, or
physical discipline) and Jihad al-Akbar (the greater struggle, or mastery of the self) to frame what it means to truly
practice martial arts.
His instructions to students consistently emphasize two things above all else: egalitarianism and character over
title.
On egalitarianism, his position is direct. Everyone who steps onto the mat trains under the same rules and the same
expectations, regardless of religion, gender, or background.
On character, he's equally clear. He frequently reminds students that legitimate leadership isn't measured by ranks,
belts, or formal titles. It's measured by community care, personal restraint, and a willingness to serve from the
ground up.
These aren't just words. They're principles he's demonstrated consistently throughout his career.
Cultural Significance
Within Maranaw society, Shihan Revie Sani occupies a unique and meaningful space.

PAGE 5
He functions as a living bridge between the ancestral code of Maranao honor, known as Maratabat, and the
demands and opportunities of modern civic leadership.
Maratabat is one of the most distinctive cultural values of the Maranao people. It speaks to dignity, personal honor,
and the pride of one's lineage. Historically, it has sometimes fueled retributive conflicts between clans. Sani has
spent his career redirecting that same energy, channeling it into athletic excellence, mental discipline, and
international representation.
In a very real sense, he's taken one of the most complex cultural forces in Maranao life and turned it into a driver of
positive community development.
He is, in the truest sense, a guardian of modern Maranao physical culture.
Legacy
Shihan Revie Saber Sumndad Sani's legacy is still being written, and that's perhaps the most compelling thing
about it.
He's not a figure of the distant past. He's actively coaching, building programs, competing on international stages,
and shaping the next generation of Maranao athletes right now.
What he's built through the MSUKC, SKOP, and the KPSFI regional directorate represents something rare: a sports
institution that genuinely serves its community, that reflects the culture and values of the people it belongs to, and
that reaches beyond sport toward something larger.
The Warriors of the Lake don't just compete. They carry a legacy with them onto every mat and into every arena.
And at the center of that legacy, guiding it forward, is Shihan Revie Sani.

Ameroddin "Abu Mohammad" Sarangani
Ameroddin "Abu Mohammad" Sarangani is a distinguished Filipino Islamic scholar (Alim), religious leader, and
diplomat who served as the Philippine Special Envoy for Islamic Affairs. A prominent Maranao figure, he's
recognized for bridging the Philippine government and the global Muslim community while advocating for Islamic
banking and interfaith dialogue. His legacy centers on the integration of Islamic principles into national governance
and the empowerment of Bangsamoro communities through education and economic opportunity.

Early Life and Background
Ameroddin Sarangani was born and raised in Lanao del Sur, on the
island of Mindanao. He belongs to the Maranao ethnic group, known
as the "people of the lake" for their historical connection to Lake
Lanao and their rich cultural traditions deeply rooted in Islamic faith.
Growing up within the traditional social structures of the Lanao
sultanates, his early life was shaped by the ethical teachings of Islam
and family traditions of regional leadership. This dual heritage of
Maranao identity and Islamic scholarship became the foundation of
his life's work.

PAGE 2
Education
Sarangani's academic journey blended traditional Islamic learning with international university education. He
pursued advanced studies in Sharia (Islamic law) and theology, earning the respected title of *Alim*, a designation
reserved for Islamic scholars who have demonstrated mastery of Islamic jurisprudence and theology.
His international education took him to Kuwait University, where he gained fluency in Arabic and developed a
nuanced understanding of Middle Eastern geopolitics and Islamic scholarship traditions. This educational
foundation became the cornerstone of his later diplomatic work, allowing him to navigate complex international
conversations about Islam and Muslim affairs with both scholarly authority and cultural sensitivity. The
combination of traditional Islamic training and modern university education positioned him uniquely to serve as a
bridge between the Philippine government and the international Muslim community.
Career and Diplomatic Service
Special Envoy for Islamic Affairs
Sarangani's most significant professional contribution came through his service as the Philippine Special Envoy
for Islamic Affairs, a formal presidential designation empowering him to represent the President in matters of
religious and regional importance. This role recognized his standing as both a scholar and a diplomat capable of
engaging with complex questions of governance, faith, and international relations.
Hajj Coordination and Pilgrimage Leadership
One of his most notable achievements was his oversight of the Hajj pilgrimage process, particularly during 2011.
His work focused on streamlining the logistics for thousands of Filipino pilgrims traveling to Mecca. His
responsibilities included negotiating fair pilgrimage quotas with the Saudi Ministry of Hajj, improving
transportation and housing standards to meet international safety protocols, and serving as a diplomatic liaison to
resolve administrative challenges with Saudi authorities. These efforts ensured smoother visa processing and
documentation for Filipino Muslims undertaking this central Islamic obligation.
"Providing pilgrims with safe passage and dignified treatment is not merely an administrative task, but
a sacred trust. The Hajj is the spiritual journey of a lifetime, and our role is to ensure that every
Filipino Muslim can undertake it with peace of mind."
Liaison to the Organization of Islamic Cooperation (OIC)
As a primary point of contact between the Philippine government and the Organization of Islamic Cooperation
(OIC), which comprises 57 member states, Sarangani was tasked with explaining Philippine domestic policies to
the international Muslim community. He worked to ensure international understanding and support for regional
stability in Mindanao, effectively serving as a cultural and political translator between Manila and the Muslim
world.

PAGE 3
Educational Exchange Programs
Leveraging his ties to prestigious Middle Eastern academic institutions, Sarangani facilitated scholarship programs
for Filipino students to study at renowned centers such as Al-Azhar University in Egypt. These initiatives expanded
opportunities for young Bangsamoro Muslims to access world-class Islamic education and return to their
communities as leaders, educators, and advocates for social development.
Contributions to Islamic Banking
Sarangani has been a vocal advocate for integrating Islamic finance into the Philippine national economy.
Recognizing that many Muslim Filipinos avoid conventional banking for religious reasons, he argued that
providing interest-free banking options is essential for financial inclusion in Muslim-majority communities.
His work supported the evolution of the Al-Amanah Islamic Investment Bank of the Philippines (AAIIBP), the
country's first and only state-owned Islamic bank. He provided scholarly guidance emphasizing core Islamic
finance principles, particularly the prohibition of *riba* (usury) and the promotion of risk-sharing models like
*musharakah* (profit-sharing partnerships) and *murabahah* (cost-plus-profit arrangements). These models align
banking practice with Islamic values while serving the economic development of Mindanao and the BARMM.
By promoting Islamic banking as a tool for socioeconomic development, Sarangani connected spiritual principles
to tangible economic empowerment, demonstrating that faith and finance could work in harmony for community
benefit.
Institutional Leadership and Ulama Councils
Sarangani has held leadership positions in various councils of Islamic scholars (*Ulama*), advocating for their
active participation in civic life and ethical governance. Rather than viewing religious authority and public service
as separate domains, he championed the idea that Islamic scholars have a responsibility to contribute to the moral
and political life of the nation.
Interfaith Dialogue
He has been a consistent proponent of the Bishops-Ulama Conference, an organization dedicated to fostering
mutual respect and peaceful coexistence between Muslim and Christian communities in Mindanao. This work
reflects his belief that the diversity of Mindanao is a strength to be celebrated and protected, not an obstacle to be
overcome. Through dialogue and collaborative action, he worked to build bridges between faith communities and
reduce misunderstandings that could fuel conflict.
Personal Values and Philosophy
Sarangani's work is underpinned by three core values: **peace, moral integrity, and social justice**. He frequently
emphasizes that Islamic principles are compatible with modern democratic service and views education as the
primary tool for community empowerment.
His philosophical approach centers on the concept of the *Wasatiyyah* (the "Middle Way"), promoting moderation
and explicitly rejecting extremist interpretations of faith. This principle grounds his diplomatic work, his advocacy
for interfaith dialogue, and his vision of Islamic banking as a inclusive, ethical alternative to conventional finance.

PAGE 4
"The true measure of a scholar is not how loudly he speaks, but how effectively he serves his
community. Islam calls us to be bridges, not walls, between peoples."
Cultural Significance and Legacy
In the cultural landscape of Mindanao and the Bangsamoro region, Sarangani is regarded as a vital link between
traditional Maranao heritage and modern statecraft. As a scholar-diplomat, he embodies the possibility of
integrating Islamic identity and Maranao culture into broader national and international frameworks without loss of
authenticity or pride.
His work has demonstrated that religious authority and secular governance need not be in tension. Instead, when
guided by principles of integrity, scholarship, and dialogue, Islamic leadership can contribute meaningfully to
nation-building and regional stability. Sarangani has shown that the Bangsamoro people, and the Maranao in
particular, have much to offer the Philippines and the world, not as supplicants seeking recognition but as dignified
partners with wisdom and values to share.
Political Engagement and Community Leadership
Sarangani has remained engaged in provincial affairs beyond his diplomatic roles. He served as a former chairman
of the Lanao del Sur Electric Cooperative, demonstrating his commitment to practical community development.
His 2022 gubernatorial candidacy in Lanao del Sur, filed under the Ummah Party, reflected his willingness to
extend his advocacy for Islamic principles and good governance into the electoral arena, mobilizing imams and
religious leaders around a vision of ethical leadership.
Recognition and Influence
As a respected Islamic scholar with formal training in Islamic jurisprudence, international experience, and
diplomatic credentials, Sarangani has earned recognition among Muslim leaders, government officials, and
international observers. His contributions to Islamic banking policy, educational exchange, and interfaith relations
have shaped institutional development and public discourse around Islam in the Philippines.

Datumanong A. Sarangani
Datumanong A. Sarangani (September 17, 1946 – 2011) was a
Filipino educator, academic administrator, and scholar from Lanao
del Sur, Philippines. He is best remembered for his forty-five
years of service at Mindanao State University (MSU), where he
served in various capacities — from faculty member, to college
secretary, to dean, to chancellor of two MSU campuses, to
University Secretary, to Secretary to the Board of Regents, and
finally to Executive Vice President (EVP) of the entire MSU
System. He entered MSU in 1962 as one of its first 282 students
and graduated in 1966 as part of its pioneer batch of 63 graduates,
making his personal story almost a mirror image of the
university's own growth.
Within the MSU community, he is widely regarded as the "best
President MSU never had" — a phrase that captures how deeply
he was respected not for the title he held, but for the kind of
person and leader he was throughout his long career.<ref

Background and Early Life
Datumanong A. Sarangani was born on September 17, 1946, in
Lanao del Sur, a province in what is now the Bangsamoro
Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM). He grew
up in a Maranao Muslim community where Islamic tradition and
close-knit clan networks shaped everyday life. Not much has been
formally documented about his parents or siblings, but what is
clear is that he came from a generation of Muslims who had very
limited access to quality higher education in the Philippines.
When Mindanao State University was founded in 1961 through
Republic Act No. 1387, it was created specifically to address that
problem — to bring educational opportunity to Muslim Filipinos
and to test whether Muslim and Christian youth could genuinely
study and live together under one roof. Sarangani walked into that
experiment in June 1962, just a year after MSU opened its doors.
The campus he arrived at was rough by any standard. Electricity
was unreliable. Water supply was inconsistent. Infrastructure was
barely in place. He later described those early years at MSU as a
"no man's land," where students had to tough it out and lean on
each other to get through.<ref name="gcpe">Global Campaign
for Peace Education. (2018, September 5). Teaching peace in the

PAGE 3

President of the MSU System (longest-
serving in the role)

for Muslim-Christian integration and
peace-building
