PULL QUOTE
"MSU democratized education. Even the poor
now have access to it."
— Dr. Datumanong A. Sarangani
battleground: Mindanao State University celebrates 57th year.
https://www.peace-ed-campaign.org/teaching-peace-in-the-
battleground-mindanao-state-university-celebrates-57th-
year/</ref> Far from discouraging him, that environment seems to
have become the foundation for one of his most enduring beliefs
about education: that surviving difficulty together builds
something deeper than any classroom lesson alone can offer.
Education
Sarangani earned his undergraduate degree from Mindanao State
University, graduating in April 1966 as part of the institution's
first-ever graduating class of 63 students.<ref
name="msua">Mindanao State University. (n.d.-a). About us:
History of Mindanao State University.
https://www.msumain.edu.ph/about-us/</ref> That milestone was
no small thing — these 63 graduates were proof that MSU's
founding mission was not just a political idea but a reality.
He later pursued advanced studies and earned a Doctor of
Education (Ed.D.), making him one of the early Muslim Filipino
scholars who went through a full academic pipeline — from
pioneer student to doctoral degree holder — at MSU itself. This
put him among the first wave of Muslim Filipino academics
whose credentials were earned entirely within a Philippine state
university context, rather than through foreign scholarships or
metropolitan institutions in Manila.<ref name="msub">Mindanao State University. (n.d.-b). The MSU System
executive vice presidents. https://www.msumain.edu.ph/office-of-the-executive-vice-president/the-msu-system-
executive-vice-presidents/</ref>
Career Overview
Faculty Member and Early Academic Work
After graduation, Sarangani joined the MSU faculty in the College of Social Sciences and Humanities, teaching
sociology and related subjects.<ref name="msua"/> His early teaching years coincided with a turbulent period in
Mindanao — the 1970s and early 1980s saw political upheaval, the declaration of Martial Law, and the rise of the
Moro National Liberation Front (MNLF), all of which surrounded MSU even as the university tried to hold on to
its mission of integration.
Throughout this period, he chose to remain with MSU, building his reputation through consistent teaching and
early scholarly work rather than seeking positions elsewhere.
College Secretary and Dean
Before moving into system-wide positions, Sarangani served in middle-level administrative roles as college
secretary and later as dean within MSU.<ref name="msua"/> These roles introduced him to the practical realities
of running an academic unit — faculty evaluation, curriculum oversight, student discipline, and resource

PAGE 4
management. Colleagues noted that even at this stage, he showed a preference for documentation, proper
procedure, and doing things by the book — habits that would define his later career.
Chancellor, MSU–General Santos City (1988)
In 1988, Sarangani was appointed Chancellor of MSU–General Santos City,<ref name="msub"/> one of the
constituent campuses of the growing MSU System. The chancellorship gave him responsibility for campus-level
governance, and he used that platform to emphasize orderly administration, faculty morale, and academic programs
that served the community. His approach to leadership — calm, principled, and transparent — was already visible
at this stage.
Chancellor, MSU–Main Campus, Marawi (1990)
Two years later, in 1990, he moved to the most prominent campus in the system, becoming Chancellor of MSU–
Main Campus in Marawi City.<ref name="msub"/> Marawi was — and still is — the heart of the MSU System
and the symbolic center of Muslim Filipino higher education. As chancellor, he continued to prioritize campus
peace and order, support for social sciences and Islamic studies, and the kind of transparent administrative
processes that reduce room for favoritism or political interference.
University Secretary and Secretary to the Board of Regents (1990)
Also in August 1990, Sarangani took on the dual role of University Secretary and Secretary to the Board of
Regents,<ref name="msub"/> positions that placed him at the center of all official MSU governance. These roles
made him the custodian of MSU's official records, the person who authenticated board resolutions, and the
coordinator of communications across the university's growing number of campuses. In practice, this made him
MSU's institutional memory — the person who knew what had been decided, why, and on what basis.
Executive Vice President, MSU System (1990–2011)
Sarangani served as Executive Vice President of the MSU System from 1990 until his retirement on his sixty-
fifth birthday, September 17, 2011 — a continuous tenure of twenty-one years in the system's top operational role.
<ref name="msub"/> As EVP, he functioned as the chief operating officer of the entire MSU System, assisting the
president in strategic governance and overseeing day-to-day operations across what had grown into an eleven-
campus system — one of the largest state university systems in the Philippines.<ref name="msua"/>
What makes this tenure historically unusual is that he held the EVP position continuously across multiple
presidential administrations, a rare achievement in Philippine public higher education where political transitions
typically bring leadership reshuffles. Each successive MSU president chose to retain him — a reflection of the trust
and credibility he had built across decades.

PAGE 5
Scholarly Work and Intellectual Contributions
Context of Muslim Filipino Scholarship
When Sarangani started writing and doing research, Muslim Filipino scholars were a rare presence in Philippine
academic circles. For a long time, Muslims in Mindanao were more often written about than given the chance to
write for themselves. Sarangani belonged to the generation that began to change that.
His intellectual interests were grounded and practical. Rather than pursuing abstract theoretical work disconnected
from Mindanao's realities, he focused on history and sociology as tools for understanding Muslim communities on
their own terms.
"Islamic Penetration in Mindanao and Sulu" (1974)
His most cited scholarly contribution is the article Islamic Penetration in Mindanao and Sulu, published in 1974
in the Mindanao Journal of the MSU University Research Center.<ref name="sarangani">Sarangani, D. A. (1974).
Islamic penetration in Mindanao and Sulu. Mindanao Journal, 1(1).</ref> The study traces how Islam spread
through the southern Philippines across several centuries through trade, religious missions, and political alliances.
Three things stand out about this work:
1. It pushed back against simplistic histories. The article challenged colonial-era and Eurocentric accounts
that treated Islamic polities in Mindanao and Sulu as peripheral or backward. Instead, it demonstrated that
these societies had sophisticated political and religious institutions long before Spanish colonization arrived.
2. It centered local agency. Rather than portraying Islamization as something done to the people of Mindanao
and Sulu, it showed local rulers and communities actively choosing and shaping how Islam took root in their
societies.
3. It combined history and sociology. While the subject is historical, the article also examined how religious
change intersected with social organization and political authority — an interdisciplinary approach unusual
for its time in this field.<ref name="sarangani"/>
Broader Intellectual Themes
Across his scholarly and professional work, several consistent themes run through Sarangani's thinking:
Islam as a full civilization — He consistently treated Islam not just as a religion of rituals but as a complete
system covering law, governance, ethics, and culture.
Education as the road to dignity — He viewed education as the primary way marginalized communities
could reclaim their voice and place in society.<ref name="gcpe"/>
Integration without forced assimilation — He supported being part of the Philippine nation while insisting
that Muslim Filipino identity had to be respected and preserved, not quietly erased — a balance he saw as
central to MSU's founding purpose.<ref name="msua"/>

PAGE 6
Teaching Philosophy and Mentorship
The Classroom as More Than Instruction
By all accounts from alumni and colleagues, Sarangani was a demanding teacher who also genuinely cared for his
students. He expected intellectual seriousness, but he was also known for being approachable and willing to sit
with a student who needed guidance.<ref name="rnc"/> In his classrooms, sociological theory was tied to the
realities students already knew — clan relations, interfaith tensions, economic hardship, and political exclusion in
Mindanao. The result was that students' own experiences were treated as legitimate subjects of serious inquiry, not
just local color.
The "Survivor" Philosophy
One of his most frequently quoted sayings captures something essential about how he saw education:
"If you survive in MSU, you can survive everywhere."
He wasn't just being dramatic. Early MSU was genuinely difficult — limited electricity, scarce water, sparse
facilities. His point was that the hardships students shared built resilience and taught them how to rely on each
other across religious lines. In his view, the difficulties were not a failure of the institution; they were part of what
made the institution transformative.
Known as "Manong"
Even after becoming one of the most senior officials in the MSU System, Sarangani remained the kind of person
students felt comfortable approaching. Alumni remember visiting his office to talk about graduate school plans and
career paths.<ref name="rnc"/> He was widely known as Manong — a Filipino term of respect that roughly
translates as "respected elder brother" — a form of address that reflects the relational, not just formal, authority he
held.
Mentorship That Outlasted His Time at MSU
Graduates mentored by Sarangani went on to careers in academia, government, and civil society. During his
retirement tribute, many of them showed up to say so publicly.<ref name="rnc"/> That kind of showing-up is its
own kind of measurement — a sign that what he gave them went beyond what could be graded.
MSU and the Peace Education Mandate
MSU as a "Social Laboratory"
Sarangani consistently described MSU as a "social laboratory" — a place where peaceful coexistence between
Muslims and Christians wasn't just talked about but actually lived out in dormitories, classrooms, and campus life.
<ref name="gcpe"/> He was an ardent defender of MSU's practice of assigning Muslim and Christian students as
roommates, viewing daily interaction as one of the most powerful tools available for reducing prejudice and
building genuine understanding.<ref name="gcpe"/>

PAGE 7
From a sociological standpoint, this practice aligns closely with intergroup contact theory, which holds that
sustained, equal-status contact between groups reduces prejudice over time. Sarangani understood this intuitively
from his own student experience, even if he articulated it through the lens of lived experience rather than academic
theory.
Keeping Peace During Instability
His career unfolded against a backdrop of chronic conflict in Mindanao — the Moro insurgency, martial law, cycles
of peace talks and renewed hostilities, and eventually the Marawi Siege in the year following his death. Through it
all, he consistently worked to keep MSU's campus from becoming an extension of the conflict outside its gates.
As chancellor and later as EVP, he prioritized student safety, institutional neutrality, and procedural fairness during
periods of tension.<ref name="rnc"/> Colleagues described him as measured and calm in deliberations — a quality
that mattered enormously in environments where a poorly handled campus incident could have serious
consequences.
Peace Education in the Curriculum
During his EVP tenure, MSU strengthened its programs in peace and development studies and Islamic education.
<ref name="msua"/> Sarangani supported these not as peripheral additions but as expressions of MSU's core
purpose. He saw peace education not as a specialty for specialists but as something woven into the university's
entire reason for existing.<ref name="gcpe"/>
Institutional Growth Under His Watch
During Sarangani's two decades as EVP, the MSU System grew from a smaller network of campuses into a full
eleven-campus system — one of the largest in the country.<ref name="msua"/> From its first graduating class of
63 students in 1966, MSU had produced approximately 150,000 graduates by 2018, a substantial portion of whom
passed through the system during his watch.<ref name="gcpe"/>
The EVP's office under his leadership played a central role in harmonizing academic calendars and policies across
those campuses, ensuring that growth did not come at the cost of coherence or quality. Programs were expanded to
include medicine, law, education, engineering, and information technology, all while maintaining compliance with
national accreditation standards.<ref name="msua"/>
By the early 2000s, MSU was nationally recognized as:
A major producer of Muslim Filipino professionals across a wide range of fields
A regional research institution with its own scholarly tradition
A working model of peace-oriented higher education in a conflict-affected area<ref name="gcpe"/>
Governance Philosophy
Sarangani's approach to running things was built around a few consistent principles:
Rules over personalities. He believed that institutions survive when decisions are grounded in documented
policies rather than whoever happens to be in charge at the moment.
Quiet influence. He exercised authority through persuasion, documentation, and institutional consistency
rather than through spectacle or politics.<ref name="rnc"/>

PAGE 8
Mission first. He consistently framed MSU's purpose as service to marginalized communities — especially
Muslim Filipinos — and held that standard up as the measure against which any institutional decision should
be judged.<ref name="msua"/>
His governance style explains why multiple MSU presidents, across different administrations and different political
climates, chose to keep him in place. He was, in a very practical sense, the person who made continuity possible.
Honors and Recognition
MSU Rawaten (Model) Outstanding Alumnus Award (2011)
In 2011, the year of his retirement, Sarangani received the MSU Rawaten Outstanding Alumnus Award, which
recognizes graduates whose lives embody MSU's ideals of service, excellence, and integration.<ref name="rnc"/>
That a pioneer student and pioneer graduate of MSU received this recognition from the same institution was fitting
in a way that is hard to manufacture — it was genuinely circular, in the best sense of the word.
Board of Regents Retirement Tribute (September 17, 2011)
Upon his retirement on his sixty-fifth birthday, the MSU Board of Regents formally honored him for his forty-
five years of service.<ref name="rnc"/> During the tribute, he was publicly acknowledged for having served as
Chancellor of MSU–General Santos City, Chancellor of MSU–Main Campus, University Secretary, Secretary to
the Board of Regents, and Executive Vice President of the MSU System. He was described in official tributes as
"almost synonymous with Mindanao State University."<ref name="rnc"/>
The "Best President MSU Never Had"
Perhaps the most revealing recognition Sarangani received was informal and unplanned: peers and alumni across
generations consistently called him the "best President MSU never had".<ref name="rnc"/> The phrase is not a
complaint about an opportunity denied. It is a recognition that his influence, competence, and moral authority were
of presidential caliber — and that his choice to lead quietly from within was itself a form of leadership the
institution needed more than a title.
Challenges and Constraints
Structural Challenges
Sarangani built his career at an institution perpetually working under difficult conditions — chronic budget
limitations, infrastructure deficiencies, and security risks tied to regional conflict that never fully went away.<ref
name="gcpe"/> None of these were problems he created, and none of them derailed him. His response was to favor
steady, incremental improvement over risky expansionism, and to prioritize institutional stability as an end in itself,
not just as a means to something flashier.

PAGE 9
A Career Free of Public Controversy
A review of available institutional records and media accounts reveals no documented allegations of misconduct,
corruption, or abuse of authority throughout his forty-five years of service.<ref name="rnc"/><ref name="msub"/>
In Philippine public higher education, where administrative scandals are not uncommon, this record is itself a form
of distinction — a sign of consistent procedural integrity and ethical self-discipline.
The Trade-Off Between Administration and Research
One area where Sarangani's career reflects a common tension in higher education leadership is scholarly output.
The record of his publications is modest in volume. This is not unusual for someone who carried the kind of
administrative load he did for as long as he did — the work of institution-building tends to crowd out the time
needed for sustained research.<ref name="msub"/> What he gave to scholarship, he gave earlier; the second half of
his career, he gave to governance.
Legacy
An Institutional Type: The Steward
Within Philippine higher education history, Sarangani represents what might be called the institutional steward —
a kind of leader who is not always the one at the front of the room but without whom institutions do not hold
together across generations.<ref name="msub"/> These figures are often underrepresented in official histories,
because they rarely produce the dramatic moments that make for easy narrative. What they produce instead is
durability — the kind of thing you only fully appreciate when it is gone.
Contribution to Muslim Filipino Professional Class
MSU has been one of the main pipelines through which Muslim Filipinos entered the professional world in the
Philippines — as teachers, engineers, doctors, lawyers, administrators, and scholars.<ref name="gcpe"/>
Sarangani's life is a symbol of that transformation. He was not born into a world where that path was obvious or
easy, and he walked it anyway, and then spent the rest of his life holding the door open for others.
Memory as Institutional Standard
The persistence of tributes to him — phrases like "almost synonymous with MSU" and "best President MSU never
had" — are not just nostalgic remembrances.<ref name="rnc"/> They are ongoing statements about what MSU
values in its leaders. To remember him in this way is to say: this is the kind of person this institution should aspire
to produce and attract.
That is perhaps his most durable contribution — not any single policy or decision, but the standard his life sets for
those who come after.

PAGE 10
Death
Dr. Datumanong A. Sarangani retired on September 17, 2011, his sixty-fifth birthday, after forty-five years of
uninterrupted service to Mindanao State University. He passed away in 2011. The circumstances of his passing are
not detailed in available institutional records, but his retirement tribute — attended by colleagues, alumni, and
university officials — was itself a form of farewell that few people in any institution ever receive.

presidents/

barely in place. He later described those early years at MSU as a
"no man's land," where students had to tough it out and lean on
each other to get through.<ref name="gcpe">Global Campaign
for Peace Education. (2018, September 5). Teaching peace in the

PAGE 3
KNOWN FOR
21-year tenure as Executive Vice
President of the MSU System (longest-
serving in the role)
Pioneering scholarship on the history of
Islamic penetration in Mindanao and Sulu
Advocacy for MSU as a social laboratory
for Muslim-Christian integration and
peace-building
Championing the role of public higher
education in democratizing access for
poor Muslim Filipino communities
PULL QUOTE
"MSU democratized education. Even the poor
now have access to it."
— Dr. Datumanong A. Sarangani
battleground: Mindanao State University celebrates 57th year.
https://www.peace-ed-campaign.org/teaching-peace-in-the-
battleground-mindanao-state-university-celebrates-57th-
year/</ref> Far from discouraging him, that environment seems to
have become the foundation for one of his most enduring beliefs
about education: that surviving difficulty together builds
something deeper than any classroom lesson alone can offer.
Education
Sarangani earned his undergraduate degree from Mindanao State
University, graduating in April 1966 as part of the institution's
first-ever graduating class of 63 students.<ref
name="msua">Mindanao State University. (n.d.-a). About us:
History of Mindanao State University.
https://www.msumain.edu.ph/about-us/</ref> That milestone was
no small thing — these 63 graduates were proof that MSU's
founding mission was not just a political idea but a reality.
He later pursued advanced studies and earned a Doctor of
Education (Ed.D.), making him one of the early Muslim Filipino
scholars who went through a full academic pipeline — from
pioneer student to doctoral degree holder — at MSU itself. This
put him among the first wave of Muslim Filipino academics
whose credentials were earned entirely within a Philippine state
university context, rather than through foreign scholarships or
metropolitan institutions in Manila.<ref name="msub">Mindanao State University. (n.d.-b). The MSU System
executive vice presidents. https://www.msumain.edu.ph/office-of-the-executive-vice-president/the-msu-system-
executive-vice-presidents/</ref>
Career Overview
Faculty Member and Early Academic Work
After graduation, Sarangani joined the MSU faculty in the College of Social Sciences and Humanities, teaching
sociology and related subjects.<ref name="msua"/> His early teaching years coincided with a turbulent period in
Mindanao — the 1970s and early 1980s saw political upheaval, the declaration of Martial Law, and the rise of the
Moro National Liberation Front (MNLF), all of which surrounded MSU even as the university tried to hold on to
its mission of integration.
Throughout this period, he chose to remain with MSU, building his reputation through consistent teaching and
early scholarly work rather than seeking positions elsewhere.
College Secretary and Dean
Before moving into system-wide positions, Sarangani served in middle-level administrative roles as college
secretary and later as dean within MSU.<ref name="msua"/> These roles introduced him to the practical realities
of running an academic unit — faculty evaluation, curriculum oversight, student discipline, and resource

PAGE 4
management. Colleagues noted that even at this stage, he showed a preference for documentation, proper
procedure, and doing things by the book — habits that would define his later career.
Chancellor, MSU–General Santos City (1988)
In 1988, Sarangani was appointed Chancellor of MSU–General Santos City,<ref name="msub"/> one of the
constituent campuses of the growing MSU System. The chancellorship gave him responsibility for campus-level
governance, and he used that platform to emphasize orderly administration, faculty morale, and academic programs
that served the community. His approach to leadership — calm, principled, and transparent — was already visible
at this stage.
Chancellor, MSU–Main Campus, Marawi (1990)
Two years later, in 1990, he moved to the most prominent campus in the system, becoming Chancellor of MSU–
Main Campus in Marawi City.<ref name="msub"/> Marawi was — and still is — the heart of the MSU System
and the symbolic center of Muslim Filipino higher education. As chancellor, he continued to prioritize campus
peace and order, support for social sciences and Islamic studies, and the kind of transparent administrative
processes that reduce room for favoritism or political interference.
University Secretary and Secretary to the Board of Regents (1990)
Also in August 1990, Sarangani took on the dual role of University Secretary and Secretary to the Board of
Regents,<ref name="msub"/> positions that placed him at the center of all official MSU governance. These roles
made him the custodian of MSU's official records, the person who authenticated board resolutions, and the
coordinator of communications across the university's growing number of campuses. In practice, this made him
MSU's institutional memory — the person who knew what had been decided, why, and on what basis.
Executive Vice President, MSU System (1990–2011)
Sarangani served as Executive Vice President of the MSU System from 1990 until his retirement on his sixty-
fifth birthday, September 17, 2011 — a continuous tenure of twenty-one years in the system's top operational role.
<ref name="msub"/> As EVP, he functioned as the chief operating officer of the entire MSU System, assisting the
president in strategic governance and overseeing day-to-day operations across what had grown into an eleven-
campus system — one of the largest state university systems in the Philippines.<ref name="msua"/>
What makes this tenure historically unusual is that he held the EVP position continuously across multiple
presidential administrations, a rare achievement in Philippine public higher education where political transitions
typically bring leadership reshuffles. Each successive MSU president chose to retain him — a reflection of the trust
and credibility he had built across decades.

PAGE 5
Scholarly Work and Intellectual Contributions
Context of Muslim Filipino Scholarship
When Sarangani started writing and doing research, Muslim Filipino scholars were a rare presence in Philippine
academic circles. For a long time, Muslims in Mindanao were more often written about than given the chance to
write for themselves. Sarangani belonged to the generation that began to change that.
His intellectual interests were grounded and practical. Rather than pursuing abstract theoretical work disconnected
from Mindanao's realities, he focused on history and sociology as tools for understanding Muslim communities on
their own terms.
"Islamic Penetration in Mindanao and Sulu" (1974)
His most cited scholarly contribution is the article Islamic Penetration in Mindanao and Sulu, published in 1974
in the Mindanao Journal of the MSU University Research Center.<ref name="sarangani">Sarangani, D. A. (1974).
Islamic penetration in Mindanao and Sulu. Mindanao Journal, 1(1).</ref> The study traces how Islam spread
through the southern Philippines across several centuries through trade, religious missions, and political alliances.
Three things stand out about this work:
1. It pushed back against simplistic histories. The article challenged colonial-era and Eurocentric accounts
that treated Islamic polities in Mindanao and Sulu as peripheral or backward. Instead, it demonstrated that
these societies had sophisticated political and religious institutions long before Spanish colonization arrived.
2. It centered local agency. Rather than portraying Islamization as something done to the people of Mindanao
and Sulu, it showed local rulers and communities actively choosing and shaping how Islam took root in their
societies.
3. It combined history and sociology. While the subject is historical, the article also examined how religious
change intersected with social organization and political authority — an interdisciplinary approach unusual
for its time in this field.<ref name="sarangani"/>
Broader Intellectual Themes
Across his scholarly and professional work, several consistent themes run through Sarangani's thinking:
Islam as a full civilization — He consistently treated Islam not just as a religion of rituals but as a complete
system covering law, governance, ethics, and culture.
Education as the road to dignity — He viewed education as the primary way marginalized communities
could reclaim their voice and place in society.<ref name="gcpe"/>
Integration without forced assimilation — He supported being part of the Philippine nation while insisting
that Muslim Filipino identity had to be respected and preserved, not quietly erased — a balance he saw as
central to MSU's founding purpose.<ref name="msua"/>

PAGE 6
Teaching Philosophy and Mentorship
The Classroom as More Than Instruction
By all accounts from alumni and colleagues, Sarangani was a demanding teacher who also genuinely cared for his
students. He expected intellectual seriousness, but he was also known for being approachable and willing to sit
with a student who needed guidance.<ref name="rnc"/> In his classrooms, sociological theory was tied to the
realities students already knew — clan relations, interfaith tensions, economic hardship, and political exclusion in
Mindanao. The result was that students' own experiences were treated as legitimate subjects of serious inquiry, not
just local color.
The "Survivor" Philosophy
One of his most frequently quoted sayings captures something essential about how he saw education:
"If you survive in MSU, you can survive everywhere."
He wasn't just being dramatic. Early MSU was genuinely difficult — limited electricity, scarce water, sparse
facilities. His point was that the hardships students shared built resilience and taught them how to rely on each
other across religious lines. In his view, the difficulties were not a failure of the institution; they were part of what
made the institution transformative.
Known as "Manong"
Even after becoming one of the most senior officials in the MSU System, Sarangani remained the kind of person
students felt comfortable approaching. Alumni remember visiting his office to talk about graduate school plans and
career paths.<ref name="rnc"/> He was widely known as Manong — a Filipino term of respect that roughly
translates as "respected elder brother" — a form of address that reflects the relational, not just formal, authority he
held.
Mentorship That Outlasted His Time at MSU
Graduates mentored by Sarangani went on to careers in academia, government, and civil society. During his
retirement tribute, many of them showed up to say so publicly.<ref name="rnc"/> That kind of showing-up is its
own kind of measurement — a sign that what he gave them went beyond what could be graded.
MSU and the Peace Education Mandate
MSU as a "Social Laboratory"
Sarangani consistently described MSU as a "social laboratory" — a place where peaceful coexistence between
Muslims and Christians wasn't just talked about but actually lived out in dormitories, classrooms, and campus life.
<ref name="gcpe"/> He was an ardent defender of MSU's practice of assigning Muslim and Christian students as
roommates, viewing daily interaction as one of the most powerful tools available for reducing prejudice and
building genuine understanding.<ref name="gcpe"/>

PAGE 7
From a sociological standpoint, this practice aligns closely with intergroup contact theory, which holds that
sustained, equal-status contact between groups reduces prejudice over time. Sarangani understood this intuitively
from his own student experience, even if he articulated it through the lens of lived experience rather than academic
theory.
Keeping Peace During Instability
His career unfolded against a backdrop of chronic conflict in Mindanao — the Moro insurgency, martial law, cycles
of peace talks and renewed hostilities, and eventually the Marawi Siege in the year following his death. Through it
all, he consistently worked to keep MSU's campus from becoming an extension of the conflict outside its gates.
As chancellor and later as EVP, he prioritized student safety, institutional neutrality, and procedural fairness during
periods of tension.<ref name="rnc"/> Colleagues described him as measured and calm in deliberations — a quality
that mattered enormously in environments where a poorly handled campus incident could have serious
consequences.
Peace Education in the Curriculum
During his EVP tenure, MSU strengthened its programs in peace and development studies and Islamic education.
<ref name="msua"/> Sarangani supported these not as peripheral additions but as expressions of MSU's core
purpose. He saw peace education not as a specialty for specialists but as something woven into the university's
entire reason for existing.<ref name="gcpe"/>
Institutional Growth Under His Watch
During Sarangani's two decades as EVP, the MSU System grew from a smaller network of campuses into a full
eleven-campus system — one of the largest in the country.<ref name="msua"/> From its first graduating class of
63 students in 1966, MSU had produced approximately 150,000 graduates by 2018, a substantial portion of whom
passed through the system during his watch.<ref name="gcpe"/>
The EVP's office under his leadership played a central role in harmonizing academic calendars and policies across
those campuses, ensuring that growth did not come at the cost of coherence or quality. Programs were expanded to
include medicine, law, education, engineering, and information technology, all while maintaining compliance with
national accreditation standards.<ref name="msua"/>
By the early 2000s, MSU was nationally recognized as:
A major producer of Muslim Filipino professionals across a wide range of fields
A regional research institution with its own scholarly tradition
A working model of peace-oriented higher education in a conflict-affected area<ref name="gcpe"/>
Governance Philosophy
Sarangani's approach to running things was built around a few consistent principles:
Rules over personalities. He believed that institutions survive when decisions are grounded in documented
policies rather than whoever happens to be in charge at the moment.
Quiet influence. He exercised authority through persuasion, documentation, and institutional consistency
rather than through spectacle or politics.<ref name="rnc"/>

PAGE 8
Mission first. He consistently framed MSU's purpose as service to marginalized communities — especially
Muslim Filipinos — and held that standard up as the measure against which any institutional decision should
be judged.<ref name="msua"/>
His governance style explains why multiple MSU presidents, across different administrations and different political
climates, chose to keep him in place. He was, in a very practical sense, the person who made continuity possible.
Honors and Recognition
MSU Rawaten (Model) Outstanding Alumnus Award (2011)
In 2011, the year of his retirement, Sarangani received the MSU Rawaten Outstanding Alumnus Award, which
recognizes graduates whose lives embody MSU's ideals of service, excellence, and integration.<ref name="rnc"/>
That a pioneer student and pioneer graduate of MSU received this recognition from the same institution was fitting
in a way that is hard to manufacture — it was genuinely circular, in the best sense of the word.
Board of Regents Retirement Tribute (September 17, 2011)
Upon his retirement on his sixty-fifth birthday, the MSU Board of Regents formally honored him for his forty-
five years of service.<ref name="rnc"/> During the tribute, he was publicly acknowledged for having served as
Chancellor of MSU–General Santos City, Chancellor of MSU–Main Campus, University Secretary, Secretary to
the Board of Regents, and Executive Vice President of the MSU System. He was described in official tributes as
"almost synonymous with Mindanao State University."<ref name="rnc"/>
The "Best President MSU Never Had"
Perhaps the most revealing recognition Sarangani received was informal and unplanned: peers and alumni across
generations consistently called him the "best President MSU never had".<ref name="rnc"/> The phrase is not a
complaint about an opportunity denied. It is a recognition that his influence, competence, and moral authority were
of presidential caliber — and that his choice to lead quietly from within was itself a form of leadership the
institution needed more than a title.
Challenges and Constraints
Structural Challenges
Sarangani built his career at an institution perpetually working under difficult conditions — chronic budget
limitations, infrastructure deficiencies, and security risks tied to regional conflict that never fully went away.<ref
name="gcpe"/> None of these were problems he created, and none of them derailed him. His response was to favor
steady, incremental improvement over risky expansionism, and to prioritize institutional stability as an end in itself,
not just as a means to something flashier.

PAGE 9
A Career Free of Public Controversy
A review of available institutional records and media accounts reveals no documented allegations of misconduct,
corruption, or abuse of authority throughout his forty-five years of service.<ref name="rnc"/><ref name="msub"/>
In Philippine public higher education, where administrative scandals are not uncommon, this record is itself a form
of distinction — a sign of consistent procedural integrity and ethical self-discipline.
The Trade-Off Between Administration and Research
One area where Sarangani's career reflects a common tension in higher education leadership is scholarly output.
The record of his publications is modest in volume. This is not unusual for someone who carried the kind of
administrative load he did for as long as he did — the work of institution-building tends to crowd out the time
needed for sustained research.<ref name="msub"/> What he gave to scholarship, he gave earlier; the second half of
his career, he gave to governance.
Legacy
An Institutional Type: The Steward
Within Philippine higher education history, Sarangani represents what might be called the institutional steward —
a kind of leader who is not always the one at the front of the room but without whom institutions do not hold
together across generations.<ref name="msub"/> These figures are often underrepresented in official histories,
because they rarely produce the dramatic moments that make for easy narrative. What they produce instead is
durability — the kind of thing you only fully appreciate when it is gone.
Contribution to Muslim Filipino Professional Class
MSU has been one of the main pipelines through which Muslim Filipinos entered the professional world in the
Philippines — as teachers, engineers, doctors, lawyers, administrators, and scholars.<ref name="gcpe"/>
Sarangani's life is a symbol of that transformation. He was not born into a world where that path was obvious or
easy, and he walked it anyway, and then spent the rest of his life holding the door open for others.
Memory as Institutional Standard
The persistence of tributes to him — phrases like "almost synonymous with MSU" and "best President MSU never
had" — are not just nostalgic remembrances.<ref name="rnc"/> They are ongoing statements about what MSU
values in its leaders. To remember him in this way is to say: this is the kind of person this institution should aspire
to produce and attract.
That is perhaps his most durable contribution — not any single policy or decision, but the standard his life sets for
those who come after.

PAGE 10
Death
Dr. Datumanong A. Sarangani retired on September 17, 2011, his sixty-fifth birthday, after forty-five years of
uninterrupted service to Mindanao State University. He passed away in 2011. The circumstances of his passing are
not detailed in available institutional records, but his retirement tribute — attended by colleagues, alumni, and
university officials — was itself a form of farewell that few people in any institution ever receive.
Further Reading

presidents/

Sheikh Esmail Laut Sarip
Sheikh Esmail Laut Sarip, also known as Sultan Sheikh Ismail Laut Sarip, was a respected figure in the history
of Muslim communities in the Philippines, particularly among the Maranao people of Lanao del Sur.
He left a lasting mark through his efforts in Islamic education, community leadership, and land stewardship during
a time when Mindanao faced no small number of challenges. While detailed public records on his personal story
remain somewhat limited compared to other ulama of his era, what emerges from local histories, institutional
accounts, and family remembrances paints him as a sultan and sheikh who bridged traditional authority with
practical, on-the-ground support for religious and educational causes.
Contents

AND RECOGNITION
4 PERSONAL LIFE, LEGACY, AND IMPACT
5 CULTURAL SIGNIFICANCE
6 SEE ALSO
7 REFERENCES
EARLY LIFE, ETHNIC AFFILIATION,
AND FAMILY
Sheikh Esmail Laut Sarip belonged to the Maranao ethnic group,
one of the major Muslim Filipino communities centered around
Lake Lanao in Mindanao.
The Maranao have a rich tradition of sultanates, Islamic scholarship,
and intricate social structures tied to clans and titles.
His title "Laut Sarip" likely connects to lineage or a specific royal
house in the Poona Bayabao area of Lanao del Sur, where his
influence remains visible today.
Details about his exact birth date or childhood are not widely
documented in accessible sources, but he rose as a traditional leader,
or sultan, in a region where such roles often combined political,
judicial, and religious responsibilities.
Family connections appear strong in the area. One descendant has
referred to him publicly as a "late grandfather" on the foster
mother's side, pointing to a legacy that continues through relatives
in Poona Bayabao and Cadayunan.

PAGE 2
Notability
Maranao sultan and Islamic community
leader who helped secure the land for
Jamiatu Muslim Mindanao, one of the
oldest and largest madrasas in the
Philippines, through a direct appeal to
President Ferdinand E. Marcos resulting
in Proclamation No. 2223.
Known For
Facilitating the transfer of military
reservation land for Islamic education;
waqf stewardship; and the founding of
Masjid Sheikh Ismail Laut Sarip in
Poona Bayabao, Cadayunan, Lanao del
Sur.
EDUCATION AND CAREER
Like many Maranao leaders of his generation, Sheikh Esmail's
background would have included deep immersion in local Islamic
learning, though specifics on formal schooling abroad or advanced
degrees are not prominently recorded in accessible sources.
His career centered on community leadership rather than prolific
writing or international scholarship.
He worked closely with political figures, including Lanao del Sur
Governor Mohammad Ali Dimaporo (also known as Sultan sa
Masiu), and maintained ties that extended to the national level.
In the early 1970s, he played a key supportive role in a pivotal
moment for Islamic education in Mindanao.
When the Agama Islam Society, under Sheikh Ahmad Bashir, sought to expand its madrasa (Ma'had Mindanao Al-
Arabie Al-Islamie) to a new site in Darussalam, Matampay, Marawi City, the land was tied up as a military
reservation.
Sheikh Esmail Laut Sarip, alongside Governor Dimaporo, helped appeal directly to President Ferdinand E. Marcos.
This effort led to Proclamation No. 2223, which excluded the needed portion from the reservation, allowing the
institution to establish its main campus.
Part of the land also came through waqf (charitable endowment) donations.
This assistance proved crucial for what became Jamiatu Muslim Mindanao (JMM), one of the oldest and largest
madrasas in the Philippines, which grew to offer comprehensive Islamic and secular education with branches
across the country.
MAJOR WORKS, INSTITUTIONAL CONTRIBUTIONS, AND
RECOGNITION
Sheikh Esmail did not author widely known books, unlike some contemporaries in the ulama tradition. His
contributions were more hands-on: facilitating land security, supporting waqf arrangements, and bolstering
institutions that served the religious and educational needs of Muslim Filipinos during a period of significant
political and social pressure.
His institutional legacy shines most clearly in the mosque named after him, Masjid Sheikh Ismail Laut Sarip in
Poona Bayabao, Cadayunan, Lanao del Sur. Locals and family members still highlight it as a landmark of his
devotion and community standing.
Formal awards or recognitions beyond his sultan title and community respect are not extensively documented in
public records, but his role in high-level appeals and the enduring memorials he left behind speak to the quiet
influence he wielded.
His closeness to figures like Governor Dimaporo and President Marcos suggests a pragmatic engagement that
translated directly into concrete benefits for Islamic causes during the Marcos era.

PAGE 3
PERSONAL LIFE, LEGACY, AND IMPACT
Information on his immediate family, including his spouse or children, remains private in available sources,
consistent with cultural norms around personal matters in traditional Maranao families. His descendants continue to
honor his memory through the mosque and through local narratives passed down within the community.
Sheikh Esmail passed away before recent decades (referred to consistently as "late" by those who knew him or
know of him), but his impact endures in very tangible ways.
In a region where education and faith have long been lifelines amid conflict and change, his practical support for
the JMM helped sustain a vital center for learning that has since produced graduates serving in public life,
education, and beyond.
The mosque in Poona Bayabao stands as a tangible symbol of his commitment to worship and community
gathering, and it continues to serve the people of the area today.
CULTURAL SIGNIFICANCE
In Maranao and broader Bangsamoro society, figures like Sheikh Esmail Laut Sarip embody the fusion of sultanate
traditions with Islamic stewardship. They navigate the tensions between local customs (adat) and faith while
advancing education as a form of resistance to marginalization.
His story reflects how community leaders in Mindanao often worked behind the scenes, leveraging relationships
and personal credibility to protect and grow waqf lands and madrasas at critical historical junctures.
Today, the mosque in Poona Bayabao and the thriving JMM serve as living testaments to what that kind of quiet
advocacy can accomplish. They remind people that personal influence, when rooted in faith and local authority, can
shape institutions that outlast any single lifetime.
In the larger tapestry of Philippine Muslim history, Sheikh Esmail represents a generation that kept Islamic learning
alive and relevant, one parcel of land, one appeal, and one enduring structure at a time.
His legacy invites reflection on how personal influence and collective effort sustain cultural and religious identity
in challenging contexts, and how the leaders who work without fanfare often leave the most lasting marks.

title: Sarip-Paudac, Sittie Habiba
text:
PAGE 1
Sittie Habiba Sarip-Paudac
Sittie Habiba Sarip-Paudac, more widely known as Princess Habiba Sarip-Paudac or simply Princess Habiba,
is a Bangsamoro journalist, broadcaster, educator, and community advocate from Marawi City in the Bangsamoro
Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM).
She is of Maranao descent, one of the prominent Muslim ethnic groups of the Lanao region in Mindanao, and
carries that heritage into every platform she steps onto.
On August 8, 2012, she made history as the first Filipina news anchor to wear a hijab on national television,
breaking ground on PTV (People's Television Network) at a time when hijabi professionals in mainstream
Philippine media were virtually non-existent.
Her on-air debut wasn't just a career milestone; it was a quiet but powerful act of representation for the broader
Bangsamoro and Filipino Muslim community, a group that makes up roughly five to six percent of the Philippine
population but had long remained underrepresented in national broadcasting.
Beyond the newsroom, she has served as Channel Manager and host of Salaam TV and co-host of Salaam Radio on
Presidential Broadcast Services (PBS)/Radyo Pilipinas, platforms dedicated to showcasing Filipino Muslim stories,
culture, and faith to audiences across the country.
In 2025, she received the Bravo Woman for Media and Public Affairs award from Security Bank and Zonta Club
of Makati and Environs, one of only eight Filipinas honored that year.
Her signature legacy can be summed up in her own framing of the hijab: not a limitation, but the very thing that
opened doors.

Roots and Early Life
Sittie Habiba Sarip-Paudac was born into a Maranao family
rooted in Marawi City, the capital of Lanao del Sur and the heart
of Maranao cultural life in the Philippines.
Her family spent part of her childhood in Saudi Arabia, giving
her early exposure to a broader Muslim world while keeping her
deeply tied to her Maranao heritage and Filipino identity.
That cross-cultural upbringing likely shaped the worldview she'd
later bring into broadcasting: a person equally at home discussing
Islamic faith and navigating the dynamics of a largely Christian-
majority Philippine media landscape.
Maranao culture is one of the richest in the Philippines, marked
by intricate okir artistry, the epic oral tradition of the Darangen,
and a deep communal emphasis on family, faith, and honor.
These cultural roots are visible in how she carries herself
publicly, with dignity, confidence, and a clear sense of purpose.
Education
She pursued higher education at Mindanao State University
(MSU), where she earned a master's degree in English
Language and Literature/Letters.
She also pursued studies connected to the University of the
Philippines, with a focus on public policy and advocacy.
That combination of literary training and policy awareness gave
her a communication foundation that went well beyond reading
scripts. It prepared her to engage with complex issues in
nuanced, accessible ways, an ability that proved valuable in both
the classroom and the studio.
Pre-Media Career
Before stepping in front of a camera, she built her professional
foundation in education and community development.
She taught at the grade school level and later served as a college
professor, experiences that sharpened her ability to explain
complex ideas to diverse audiences.
She also worked with non-governmental organizations (NGOs)
focused on community development, deepening her
understanding of the real-world challenges facing communities
across Mindanao.

PAGE 3

She had no formal broadcast training before entering the
industry. What she brought instead was strong communication
skills, cultural fluency, and a willingness to learn on the job,
diving straight into the deep end.
Career Breakthrough and Milestones
Joining PTV and Making History
In 2012, PTV (People's Television Network) was looking for its
first hijab-wearing Muslim news anchor.
Princess Habiba auditioned in Manila, reportedly while en route to a Hong Kong trip, and landed the position.
On August 8, 2012, she made her on-air debut, becoming the first Filipina news anchor to appear on national
television wearing a hijab.
Communities back home in Mindanao tuned in with pride. She wasn't simply reading the news; she was
representing an entire segment of the Philippine population that had rarely seen itself reflected in the faces of
mainstream media.
Her presence immediately challenged prevailing assumptions. Colleagues were surprised by her fluency in both
English and Filipino (Tagalog), a reaction she turned into an opportunity to highlight the reality of educated, highly
capable Bangsamoro women, including lawyers, doctors, professors, and now, a national television anchor.
She often found herself informally educating the newsroom about Islam, Maranao culture, and the realities of life
in Mindanao, converting moments of unfamiliarity into conversations that built understanding.
Salaam TV and Salaam Radio
Under the Duterte administration, she took on expanded roles through the Presidential Communications Operations
Office (PCOO).
She became Channel Manager and host of Salaam TV, a Muslim-oriented television program that showcases
Filipino Muslim stories, culture, and faith for a national audience.
She also served as co-host of Salaam Radio on Presidential Broadcast Services (PBS)/Radyo Pilipinas, further
extending her reach beyond television.
These platforms serve a dual purpose: educating non-Muslim Filipinos about Islam as a religion of peace and
inclusivity, while also spotlighting the diverse Muslim ethnic groups across the Philippines and celebrating
Bangsamoro identity and heritage.
She has continued delivering national newscasts and hosting programming that bridges cultural and religious
divides within Philippine society.

PAGE 4
Institutional Contributions
Through her roles at PTV, Salaam TV, and Salaam Radio, she has helped institutionalize Muslim representation in
Philippine state broadcasting.
As Channel Manager of Salaam TV, she shaped editorial direction for a program with a national platform, ensuring
that Bangsamoro voices and perspectives were presented with accuracy, dignity, and depth rather than reduced to
stereotypes or crisis coverage.
Her work in both television and radio has contributed to a growing ecosystem of Bangsamoro media
representation, demonstrating to other broadcasters and media institutions that Muslim Filipino professionals not
only belong in national media but enrich it.
She has also participated in public events such as World Hijab Day, using those platforms to share her personal
story and encourage Muslim women to pursue professional ambitions without compromising their faith.
Recognition and Awards
Her contributions to media and public affairs have been formally recognized at the national level.
In 2025, she received the Bravo Woman for Media and Public Affairs award, conferred by Security Bank in
partnership with the Zonta Club of Makati and Environs. She was one of eight remarkable Filipinas honored
through the program that year.
She dedicated the award to her family and the wider Bangsamoro community, framing the recognition not as a
personal achievement alone but as a collective affirmation.
Her story has been featured in international and national media outlets, including Arab News and various
Philippine publications, positioning her as a recognized symbol of empowered Bangsamoro womanhood on a
global stage.
Cultural Significance
Princess Habiba's trailblazing role carries significant weight in the Philippine cultural and social context.
Filipino Muslims make up approximately five to six percent of the national population, concentrated primarily in
Mindanao and the Sulu Archipelago, and have historically faced stereotyping, discrimination, and
underrepresentation in mainstream media.
Her sustained visibility on national television since 2012 helped normalize the image of a hijabi professional in the
public imagination, actively challenging narratives that had long reduced Bangsamoro identity to conflict and
marginalization.
She embodies a form of cultural peacebuilding that works not through formal negotiations but through visibility:
by humanizing Muslim Filipinos on air, correcting misconceptions in real time, and showcasing the vibrancy and
richness of Bangsamoro culture, she has contributed to bridging one of the most historically complex divides in
Philippine society.
Her story resonates particularly with young Muslim women navigating the tension between professional ambition
and religious identity, demonstrating that the two are not in conflict but can, in fact, amplify each other.

PAGE 5
Challenges
Despite her accomplishments, Princess Habiba's path was not without friction.
Entering a Manila-based newsroom as a hijabi Maranao woman meant confronting assumptions that she would
need to set aside her religious expression to fit into the professional environment.
Colleagues' surprise at her fluency in English and Filipino underscored a deeper challenge: the persistent
underestimation of educated Bangsamoro women in professional spaces outside of Mindanao.
She has also navigated the broader challenge of representing a diverse and complex community to a national
audience that often lacks context. Being the lone visible Muslim face in a newsroom means carrying the informal
burden of cultural ambassador on top of the professional duties of broadcasting.
She has consistently turned those challenges into platforms for dialogue rather than sources of bitterness, using
them to create space for greater understanding and more accurate representation.
Personal Life, Values, and Family
She is married to a lawyer and is a proud mother of two sons. She has frequently credited her family as her greatest
source of strength throughout her broadcasting career.
Her personal values are deeply rooted in Islamic faith. She speaks openly about her hijab not as a constraint but as
a defining expression of her identity, the very thing that, in her words, took her to where she is today.
She is committed to da'wah in its most personal form: not through formal preaching but by living publicly as a
faithful, professional Muslim woman and allowing that lived example to speak for itself.
She emphasizes modesty, professional excellence, and trust in divine providence, and she regularly advises young
Muslim women to wear their hijabs with confidence, pursue their ambitions without apology, and trust that staying
true to one's faith and identity is a strength, not a disadvantage.
Legacy
Sittie Habiba Sarip-Paudac didn't set out to be a pioneer. She showed up as herself, hijab, Maranao pride,
professional drive, and all, and history met her there.
Her legacy is one of quiet but lasting impact: the visibility she created on a national stage in 2012 opened a
conversation about Bangsamoro representation that continues to ripple through Philippine media, education, and
public life.
She proved that authenticity is not a liability in professional spaces but a source of credibility and connection.
For the Bangsamoro community, she remains a living example that faith and ambition are powerful companions,
and that the daughters of Mindanao belong wherever excellence is gathered.

AbdulKhaliq Sharif Saripada
AbdulKhaliq Sharif Saripada (born 1955) is a Filipino Muslim scholar, translator, and author of Maranao
heritage from Marawi City. Over his career spanning multiple decades, he authored and translated more than
seventeen Islamic booklets in Tagalog and English, becoming one of the most prolific disseminators of Islamic
knowledge to Filipino Muslim communities worldwide. His works focus on fundamental Islamic teachings, moral
ethics, spiritual guidance, and comparative religious studies, reaching audiences across the Philippines and the
global Filipino diaspora.
Early Life and Maranao Heritage
AbdulKhaliq Sharif Saripada was born on 27 January 1955 in Barangay Bangon, Marawi City, in the heart of the
Bangsamoro homeland. He comes from a family deeply embedded in Maranao tradition and Islamic scholarship.
His father, Disomimba Saripada, hailed from Pualas in Lanao del Sur, while his mother, Bae Labe a Diamla sa
Marawi, held an honored traditional title within the community, reflecting their family's standing and influence.
On his maternal side, AbdulKhaliq descends from the lineage of Sharief Ismael of Buadi Sakayo in Marawi City, a
respected Sharief clan within Maranao society. This genealogical connection to Islamic nobility and traditional
leadership deeply shaped his intellectual and spiritual path. The Sharief heritage carries with it centuries of Islamic
learning and community stewardship, values that would become central to his life's work.<ref
name="lineage">AbdulKhaliq Sharif Saripada biographical document, lineage section</ref>
Education
AbdulKhaliq pursued diverse educational pathways in both secular and Islamic studies:
Bachelor of Science in Liberal Arts (A.B., majoring in Political Science)
Bachelor of Science in Education (BSE, serving as a prerequisite for graduate studies)
Bachelor of Science in Business Administration (BSBA, majoring in Accounting)
Arabic Language Studies, Institute of Language, Imam Muhammad Ibn Saud Islamic University, Riyadh,
Kingdom of Saudi Arabia

His studies at one of the Islamic world's premier institutions gave
him rigorous training in classical Arabic, Islamic jurisprudence,
and traditional scholarly methodology. This combination of
secular education and Islamic linguistic mastery equipped him
uniquely to bridge knowledge systems and make Islamic concepts
accessible to Tagalog-speaking audiences.
Da'wah Career and Service in Saudi
Arabia
From 1990 to 2006, AbdulKhaliq served in various capacities as a
da'ie (Islamic propagator) and translator in the Eastern Province
and Riyadh, Saudi Arabia:
Da'ie, Comparative Religion (1990–1992), Eastern
Province, KSA: Engaged in interfaith dialogue and
comparative religious studies, presenting Islamic
perspectives to diverse audiences.
Da'ie and Preacher (1993–1995), Al-Sulay Charity
Library, Riyadh, KSA: Delivered sermons and religious
instruction at one of Riyadh's significant Islamic centers.
Mutarjim (Translator-Propagator) (1996–2006),
Cooperative Office for Call and Guidance (Al-Sulay),
Riyadh, KSA: Coordinated translation and dissemination of
Islamic knowledge, working with institutional networks
focused on da'wah (Islamic propagation).
During these sixteen years abroad, AbdulKhaliq honed his craft as
both a speaker and translator, learning how to adapt Islamic
concepts for different cultural and linguistic contexts. His
experience in Saudi Arabia's diverse Islamic scholarly
environment, combined with his Maranao-Filipino roots, made
him exceptionally well-positioned to serve as a bridge between
global Islamic tradition and the Filipino Muslim community.
Literary Works and Publications
AbdulKhaliq's most enduring legacy lies in his prolific authorship and translation of Islamic educational materials.
He authored and translated more than seventeen Islamic booklets in Tagalog and English, designed for both
beginners and intermediate learners of Islamic faith and practice:
1. 40 Hadith Nawawiyyah (Tagalog translation)
2. Hisnul Muslim (Kutang-Tanggulan ng Muslim) (Islamic fortifications and supplications)
3. Talakayan sa pagitan ng Atheistang Propesor at Muslim na Estudyante (Dialogue between an atheist
professor and a Muslim student)
4. Ang mga Katangian ng Hajj at 'Umrah (Characteristics and rulings of pilgrimage)
5. Zad-ul-Hajj (Comprehensive guide for the pilgrimage)
6. Kayo ay Walang Karapatan... (Rights and duties in Islam)
7. Mga Piling Aral sa Islam (Selected lessons in Islam)
8. Aqeedah (Simplified Islamic creed and theology)

PAGE 3
9. Islamic Belief Fundamentals (Beginner's guide to Islamic doctrine)
10. Du'ā & Adhkar Collections (Tagalog compilations of supplications and remembrances)
11. Guide to Prayer (Salah) (Step-by-step instructions and spiritual dimensions)
12. Youth Islamic Guidance Booklets (Series addressing young Muslims)
13. Family in Islam (Ethics, responsibilities, and family law)
14. Islamic Morals and Manners (Akhlaq) (Character development and conduct)
15. Selected Qur'an Explanations (Tafsir excerpts in Tagalog)
16. Basic Fiqh (Islamic jurisprudence simplified for practitioners)
17. Da'wah Compilation Booklets (Various thematic collections)
These publications were distributed through Islamic networks including IslamHouse, Muslim-library.com, local
mosques (masjids), and Islamic educational centers throughout the Philippines and beyond. Their consistent focus
on Tagalog-language accessibility meant that Filipino Muslims with limited Arabic proficiency could deepen their
understanding of Islamic theology, law, ethics, and practice in their own language.<ref
name="works">AbdulKhaliq Sharif Saripada biographical document, achievements section</ref>
Legacy and Impact
AbdulKhaliq Sharif Saripada stands as one of the most prolific Tagalog-language Islamic scholars of the
contemporary era. His work addresses a critical gap in Islamic education for Filipinos: the scarcity of high-quality,
culturally-appropriate Islamic materials in the national language. By authoring and translating across diverse
topics, from fundamental theology to practical ritual guidance, he democratized access to Islamic knowledge for
millions of Tagalog speakers worldwide.
His publications have been circulated by major Islamic distribution networks and downloaded through digital
platforms, reaching Filipino Muslims in the Philippines, North America, the Middle East, and other diaspora
communities. The breadth of his output, from beginner-level guides to comparative religious studies, reflects a
teaching philosophy rooted in gradual enlightenment and intellectual inclusion.
As a Maranao Muslim scholar, AbdulKhaliq represents the scholarly tradition of Bangsamoro Islamic thought
while simultaneously serving as a translator and bridge-builder for the broader Muslim Filipino community. His
legacy is not marked by institutional positions or political prominence, but by the quiet, sustained contribution of
knowledge shared freely for the benefit of believers seeking to understand and practice their faith.

title: Saripada, Sacar
text:
PAGE 1
Sacar Saripada
Datu Sacar Saripada was a Maranao traditional leader, public administrator, and political figure from the
ancestral municipality of Ditsaan-Ramain in the historical province of Lanao, Philippines.
In 1958, he was appointed Deputy Governor of Lanao Province, making him one of the first Maranao nobles to
formally occupy a senior post within the Philippine Republic's provincial government.
His tenure coincided with one of the most consequential periods in the region's administrative history: the years
immediately preceding the bifurcation of Lanao into two separate provinces under Republic Act No. 2228.
Saripada is remembered not only as a competent administrator, but also as a cultural bridge-builder who carried the
weight of Maranao tradition into the formal structures of the modern state.
He belonged to the distinguished Saripada royal lineage (bangsa), a family group long associated with upholding
the three pillars of Maranao community governance: Adat, Agama, and Kawsa.
His legacy, preserved largely through oral genealogies and a now-iconic 1958 official portrait, continues to inspire
public servants from the Bangsamoro region.
Contents
1 Background
2 Education
3 Career in Public Service
3.1 Deputy Governorship of Lanao Province (1958)
3.2 Territorial Mediation and the Division of Lanao
4 Cultural Legacy and Visual Iconography
5 Later Life
6 Legacy and Recognition
7 References
8 See Also
Background
Ditsaan-Ramain, the municipality where Saripada was born and raised, sits east of Lake Lanao and carries deep
historical significance.
It was, and remains, one of the principal centers of Islamic scholarship, traditional leadership, and customary law
within the Bayabao principality of the broader Lanao Sultanate.
The Maranao people of this region have long been organized under the Pat a Pangampong sa Ranao, the four
confederated sovereign states around the lake, each with its own royal hierarchy, customary code, and territorial
jurisdiction.

PAGE 2
Datu Sacar Saripada
Personal Information
Born: Ditsaan-Ramain, Lanao Province,
Philippines
Ethnicity: Maranao
Lineage (Bangsa): Saripada Royal Family
Education
Not specified in available records
Public Office
Position: Deputy Governor, Lanao Province
Year Appointed: 1958
Saripada grew up within this layered world, where political
authority wasn't just inherited through bloodline, but also earned
through a demonstrated commitment to the community's three
foundational obligations:
Adat covered the ancestral laws and social customs that governed
everything from land rights to inter-clan diplomacy.
Agama referred to Islamic religious practice and jurisprudence,
the moral backbone of Maranao political life.
Kawsa was the civic duty: the expectation that those born into
leadership would give back, through direct service, to the welfare
of the people.
These weren't abstract ideals for families like the Saripadas. They
were lived responsibilities, passed down across generations.
Education
Detailed records of Saripada's formal education have not been
preserved in available archival sources.
What the historical record does suggest is that, by the mid-20th
century, educated Maranao youth from noble families were
increasingly navigating two educational worlds: traditional
Islamic instruction and the secular public school system
introduced under American colonial governance.
His appointment to a senior provincial post in 1958 implies a
level of civic literacy and administrative competence that was
remarkable for its time, particularly among indigenous leaders
from the lake communities.
Career in Public Service
Deputy Governorship of Lanao Province (1958)
Saripada's most documented public role came in 1958, when he
was officially designated as Deputy Governor of Lanao
Province.
At that point, the province was under the leadership of Governor
Salvador T. Lluch, who served from 1955 to 1959.
His appointment wasn't just a bureaucratic selection. It was a
deliberate effort by the national government to draw reform-
minded, educated Maranao leaders into the formal machinery of
provincial administration.

PAGE 3
Governor Served Under: Salvador T. Lluch
(1955–1959)
Regional Origin
Ditsaan-Ramain, Bayabao District, Lanao
Province
Traditional Governance Framework
Adat (Customary Law), Agama (Islamic
Jurisprudence), Kawsa (Public Service)
Known Association

Sultanates of Lanao)
Notability
One of the earliest Maranao traditional leaders
to formally serve in the Philippine Republic's
provincial bureaucracy, bridging centuries-old
indigenous governance with modern democratic
administration.
Known For
Deputy Governorship of Lanao Province
(1958); Mediation during the territorial
bifurcation that produced Lanao del Norte and
Lanao del Sur; Cultural iconography as a
"traditional modernist" statesman.
Pull Quote
The context mattered enormously. The late 1950s were tense and
transitional for Lanao. The postwar boom had brought new
settlers, new roads, and new political pressures from Manila, all
converging on a region that had its own centuries-old systems of
authority.
Saripada walked into that complexity and served as a stabilizing
presence.
Territorial Mediation and the Division of Lanao
The year of Saripada's appointment, 1958, was also the height of
legislative debate over the future of Lanao's territorial integrity.
On May 22, 1959, Republic Act No. 2228 formally divided the
unified province into Lanao del Norte and Lanao del Sur,
separating the largely Christian-majority coastal municipalities in
the north from the Muslim-majority lake communities in the
south.
As Deputy Governor, Saripada's work centered on managing the
friction that came with that transition.
He worked on sovereign mediation, finding workable balances
between Manila's centralizing directives and the customary
constitutions (Igma ago Taritib) that the traditional Datus and
Sultans still considered binding.
He was also involved in boundary negotiations, helping navigate
the complicated geographic and demographic divides between the
region's communities.
And he contributed to institutional integration, supporting the
handoff of regional authority to a new generation of political
figures including Mohammad Ali Dimaporo and Madki A. Alonto.
Cultural Legacy and Visual Iconography
One of the most enduring artifacts of Saripada's public life is an
official portrait taken in 1958.
The photograph shows him in what cultural researchers have
called "traditional modernist" attire, a style that was popular
among mid-century Filipino Muslim intellectuals and statesmen,
most notably Senator Salipada Pendatun.
The look combined a tailored, Western-style suit jacket with a
traditional Maranao headpiece (toao or pekes).

PAGE 4
"He wore both worlds with ease: a Maranao
datu's pride in one hand, a provincial
administrator's mandate in the other."
It's a small detail, but a meaningful one. That sartorial choice was
itself a political statement: pride in Maranao cultural identity,
paired with a clear readiness to engage with the modern
Philippine state on equal terms.
The image has become a touchpoint in discussions about Maranao
political heritage, particularly among historians and cultural advocates documenting the region's mid-century
leadership.
Photo credit: Bilangatao Guwani.
Later Life
Detailed records of Saripada's life and career after 1959 are scarce.
Mid-century municipal archives in Lanao were significantly disrupted by conflict, displacement, and institutional
turnover across the following decades, and many records from that era simply haven't survived in formal
repositories.
What has survived is memory: oral genealogies (salsila), family histories, and community accounts that continue to
place Saripada within the lineage of principled, service-oriented Maranao leaders.
Within Lanao del Sur, he's remembered as an early model of what indigenous public service could look like:
grounded in tradition, but fully capable of operating within the structures of a democratic republic.
Legacy and Recognition
Datu Sacar Saripada's legacy sits at the crossroads of two worlds he helped hold together.
He brought the moral weight of Maranao royal tradition into a government office at a moment when that office
desperately needed someone who could speak both languages: the language of the state, and the language of the
lake.
His brief but meaningful tenure as Deputy Governor helped pave the way for the institutional evolution that would
eventually lead to the creation of the Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao and, later, the Bangsamoro
Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM).
Among historians, genealogists, and civic advocates in the Bangsamoro region, he's counted among the pioneers
who proved that Maranao leadership and Philippine democratic governance didn't have to be in conflict.
They could, with the right person in the room, work together.

title: Saripada, Sheik Datu Ramos
text:
PAGE 1
Sheik Datu Ramos Saripada
Sheik Datu Ramos Saripada was an influential Maranao traditional ruler who made history as the first Municipal
President of the Municipal District of Watu — the seat of governance for a territory known today as the
Municipality of Balindong in Lanao del Sur, Mindanao.
He lived and led during one of the most complicated chapters of Philippine history: the American colonial period,
when foreign administrators were trying to bring the fiercely independent communities of the Lanao region under a
centralized government.
Saripada didn't simply accept that role — he shaped it. He served as a living bridge between two very different
systems of authority: the centuries-old customary law of the Maranao known as taritib, and the formal bureaucratic
structure the Americans were building across the archipelago. That balance defined his legacy.
His administration is most vividly documented through a letter he received from Theodore Roosevelt Jr. — then
Governor-General of the Philippines and eldest son of the 26th U.S. President — a document that his family
managed to preserve through war, occupation, and the upheaval of the mid-20th century.
Contents
1 Historical Context: Lanao Under American Rule
2 The Policy of Attraction
3 Administration of the Municipal District of Watu
4 The Theodore Roosevelt Jr. Letter
4.1 A Document That Survived the War
5 Legacy and the Birth of Balindong
6 Descendants and Continuing Legacy
7 Recognition
8 See Also
9 External Links
Historical Context: Lanao Under American Rule
When the Americans took hold of the Philippines in the early 1900s, they quickly realized that governing the Moro
Province — and Lanao in particular — wasn't going to work the same way it did elsewhere in the archipelago.
The Maranao had their own systems, their own rulers, and their own deeply rooted sense of how communities
should be run. The Americans weren't going to simply overlay a foreign structure on top of all that without
consequence.
So instead of forcing the issue head-on, colonial administrators tried a different approach. The major trade centers
of the region — places like Iligan and Dansalan (now Marawi City) — were organized as standard municipalities.
But most of the Lanao region was divided into 30 distinct Municipal Districts, each one meant to respect the local
character of the communities within it.

PAGE 2
Sheik Datu Ramos Saripada
Title / Position
Municipal President, Municipal District of Watu
Jurisdiction
Municipal District of Watu (now Balindong,
Lanao del Sur)

Ethnicity

Traditional Standing
