lineages of Lanao
Notable Archival Record
The Policy of Attraction
At the heart of this approach was what American administrators
called the "Policy of Attraction." The idea was straightforward:
rather than displacing traditional leaders, the colonial government
would bring them into the fold by giving them formal positions
within the new administrative system.
This meant reaching out to the most respected sultans and datus
in each area — the men whose authority their communities
already recognized — and appointing them to lead the newly
created municipal districts.
Saripada was one of those leaders. His appointment as Municipal
President of the District of Watu wasn't a coincidence or a
consolation prize — it was a deliberate choice by colonial
administrators who understood that stability in Lanao depended
on working with leaders the Maranao people already trusted.
The arrangement gave Saripada legal authority within the
colonial state. But he brought something to the role that no
appointment letter could confer: the customary legitimacy and
the personal standing he had earned among his own people.
Administration of the Municipal District
of Watu
The territory Saripada governed — the Municipal District of
Watu, also recorded historically as Uatu or Wato — was situated
in the undivided province of Lanao, in the heart of Maranao
country.
As Municipal President, Saripada held a dual mandate. On paper,
he was an officer of the colonial government, accountable to the
American administrative chain of command. In practice, he was
also the custodian of his community's traditions and the guarantor
of a way of life that long predated the American arrival.
Managing both of those roles at once, without letting one
swallow the other, was the real work of his administration. Under
Saripada's stewardship, Watu remained deeply rooted in Maranao
cultural identity — connected to the foundational royal lineages
known as the Pangampong of Lanao, the ancestral networks that
gave the region its social and political structure.

PAGE 3
Official correspondence from Governor-General
Theodore Roosevelt Jr., dated July 27, 1932
Notability
First Municipal President of the Municipal
District of Watu (now Balindong, Lanao del
Sur); one of the first formally appointed
Maranao traditional leaders under American
colonial governance
Known For
Bridging Maranao customary law (taritib) with
American colonial administration; preserving
ancestral governance during a period of deep
political change; recipient of a formal letter
from Governor-General Theodore Roosevelt Jr.
Pull Quote
"He held two worlds together — the ancestral
law of his people and the unfamiliar machinery
of a colonial state — and he did it without
abandoning either."
The Theodore Roosevelt Jr. Letter
The most significant piece of archival evidence that survives
from Saripada's time in office is a formal typed letter, dated July
27, 1932, issued directly from the Office of the Governor-
General in Manila.
The author was Theodore Roosevelt Jr. — the eldest son of U.S.
President Theodore Roosevelt, and at that time serving as
Governor-General of the Philippines.
The letter formally addressed Saripada as the Municipal
President of "Uatu" and extended the Governor-General's official
gratitude for the hospitality and reception that Saripada had
organized during Roosevelt Jr.'s official tour of the Lanao region.
It was, in the language of the era, a formal acknowledgment from
the highest colonial authority in the Philippines to a Maranao
datu — a moment that captured, in a single document, just how
central figures like Saripada were to the colonial government's
strategy in the region.
A Document That Survived the War
What makes the letter even more remarkable is what happened to it afterward.
The physical document carries a series of handwritten annotations marked "Noted," written at different points
between 1934 and 1948. One of those signatures, dated 1943, belongs to a Lieutenant Colonel of the 108th
Division.
That date is significant. 1943 was deep inside the Japanese occupation. The fact that the letter was being annotated
and preserved during that period tells a story of its own: Saripada's family chose to hold onto this record through
one of the most dangerous and disruptive periods in Philippine history, carrying it through war and into the early
years of postwar reconstruction.
That act of preservation speaks to how much the document meant — not just as a piece of paper, but as proof of a
man's standing and his community's place in a larger story.
Legacy and the Birth of Balindong
Saripada's time as Municipal President planted roots that lasted well beyond his own era. Watu continued as an
anchor of traditional Maranao culture through the American period and into the Commonwealth years, its
connection to the Pangampong lineages keeping its identity intact through the changes that came with each new
administration.
In 1956, that chapter closed and a new one opened. Under Republic Act No. 1424, the Municipal District of Watu
was formally elevated and renamed the Municipality of Balindong — a name honoring a prominent ancestral ruler
of the area and recognizing the community's deep historical roots.

PAGE 4
The transformation from colonial district to independent municipality was, in a sense, the completion of what
Saripada's administration had helped to protect: a community that navigated colonial rule without losing itself.
Descendants and Continuing Legacy
Saripada's legacy didn't stay frozen in the past. His modern descendants have remained active in Philippine history,
in law, and in local sports — people who carry forward a family story that stretches back to one of the Lanao
region's most consequential periods of political transition.
They also continued what their ancestor started: preserving the records. The Roosevelt Jr. letter and other archival
materials from Saripada's era have been kept across generations, making it possible to document and tell this story
today.
Recognition
Saripada's historical significance rests on several intersecting contributions:
His appointment as the first Municipal President of Watu made him a pioneer of Maranao participation in formal
governance structures during the colonial era. His ability to hold traditional authority and colonial responsibility in
balance offered a model for how indigenous leadership and outside administration could coexist — even if
imperfectly. And the survival of the Roosevelt Jr. letter, with its multi-decade trail of annotations, gives historians a
rare primary source that illuminates the texture of colonial-era governance in Lanao.
Together, these pieces of his life add up to a portrait of a man who led with both roots and reach.

Abdulazis Guroalim Saromantang
Sheikh Abdulazis Guroalim Saromantang (Rahimahullah) (also spelled Abdulaziz Guroalim Saromantang was a
pioneering Maranao Islamic scholar and the first Filipino Muslim to complete a full translation of the Qur'an into
the Maranao language. A native of Tugaya, Lanao del Sur, he bridged the spiritual and political spheres, serving as
the municipality's mayor while simultaneously undertaking one of the most significant religious scholarship
projects in Philippine Islamic history. His vernacular Qur'an translation, published by the King Fahd Complex in
Madinah, remains the definitive reference for over 1.3 million Maranao-speaking Muslims across Mindanao and
the diaspora.
Contents
1 Early Life and Heritage
2 Political and Civic Leadership
3 Path to the Qur'an Translation
4 The Translation Project
5 Publication and Title
6 Legacy and Cultural Impact
7 Orthographic Innovation
8 Scholarly Reception and Debate
8.1 Critical Perspectives
8.2 Scholarly Defenses
9 Death and Ongoing Legacy
10 See Also
11 Further Reading
Early Life and Heritage
Abdulazis Guroalim Saromantang was born into the Maranao
community of Tugaya, a municipality in Lanao del Sur long
regarded as a center of Islamic scholarship in Mindanao. The
Maranao, often described as "the people of the lake" for their
historical settlement around Lake Lanao, had developed a
sophisticated oral tradition of Islamic learning passed through
successive generations of Ulama.
Saromantang emerged from this cultural foundation as a "home-
grown" scholar, initially teaching in local madrasas (Islamic
schools) before gaining recognition for his exceptional mastery of
classical Arabic and Islamic jurisprudence. Unlike many of his
contemporaries who sought advanced training exclusively in the
Middle East, Saromantang's early education was rooted in the
Maranao scholarly tradition, where he developed an intimate
understanding of both Arabic linguistic nuances and the
vernacular idioms of his people.

PAGE 2
His family later became one of Tugaya's most prominent households, producing subsequent generations of Islamic
leaders and cultural advocates. His grandsons would later become vocal defenders of his scholarly legacy during
academic and theological debates.
Political and Civic Leadership
Before devoting himself fully to the monumental task of Qur'an translation, Saromantang served as Mayor of
Tugaya during the 1960s. This period in his life reflected a distinctive Maranao leadership model where religious
scholarship and civic governance were not seen as competing pursuits but as complementary responsibilities to the
community.
As mayor, he navigated the complex political landscape of post-independence Mindanao while maintaining his
reputation as a principled Islamic scholar. This dual role demonstrated his ability to operate effectively in both
traditional and modern institutional frameworks, a capacity that would later prove invaluable when engaging with
Saudi Arabian government officials and the international Islamic academic community.
Path to the Qur'an Translation
The idea of translating the Qur'an into Maranao did not originate with Saromantang alone. In the 1980s, the Saudi
Arabian government, through the King Fahd Complex for the Printing of the Holy Qur'an, launched an initiative to
support vernacular translations of the Qur'an in minority Muslim communities worldwide. Saromantang was
identified and officially commissioned as the first, and ultimately the only, Filipino Muslim scholar authorized to
undertake this task.
The decision to entrust this responsibility to Saromantang was not arbitrary. His reputation for linguistic precision,
theological grounding, and deep knowledge of Maranao cultural idioms made him the obvious choice. Unlike a
direct, word-for-word rendering, the translation required solving a unique challenge: how to convey the theological
depth and poetic beauty of classical Arabic within the grammatical and phonological constraints of Maranao, a
language that had never before been systematically used for complex religious discourse.
The Translation Project
What began in the early 1980s as an ambitious vision became a painstaking, methodical labor that would define
Saromantang's final decades. The project consumed 10 years of intense, focused translation work. During this
period, Saromantang did not work in isolation. He led a collaborative panel of respected Islamic and cultural
figures, including the late Senator Ahmad Domocao Alonto (a prominent Maranao political figure and Islamic
scholar) and Imam Nashrodeen Basman, to ensure the translation's theological accuracy and cultural
appropriateness.
The completed manuscript then entered a rigorous validation phase. For an additional 5 years, a committee of
Maranao Shariah scholars at the Islamic University of Madinah scrutinized every verse, cross-referencing
Saromantang's Maranao renderings against the original Arabic text and established interpretive traditions. This
dual-phase process, spanning 15 years total, meant that the translation was not merely a one-person achievement
but a validated scholarly work blessed by one of Islam's most prestigious academic institutions.

PAGE 3
Publication and Title
The translation was finally published in the 1990s by the King Fahd Complex in Madinah, with a standard edition
running approximately 1,088 pages. The full title in Maranao was So Qur'an al Karim ago so Kiya pema ana iron
Ko basa a iranon sa pilimpinas, which translates roughly as "The Noble Qur'an and Its Meaning in the Maranao
Language in the Philippines."
The publication marked a historic milestone. Notably, Saromantang's Maranao translation was completed before
the Tagalog translation of the Qur'an was finished, meaning that Maranao speakers gained access to their own
vernacular Qur'an before the larger Filipino Christian and Muslim populations received a comparable Tagalog
edition.
The standard edition was assigned ISBN 9960-847-34-9. Subsequent printings and digital editions followed,
including a widely cited 1422 AH edition (approximately 2001-2002) from the King Fahd National Library
catalog.
Legacy and Cultural Impact
Saromantang's translation achieved something more significant than a simple linguistic conversion. It affirmed that
the Maranao language, long marginalized in academic and religious contexts, was capable of expressing the full
theological complexity of Islamic revelation. This shift had profound implications for Maranao cultural identity.
The translation proved immediately valuable to Maranao Muslim communities. By making the Qur'an accessible in
the vernacular language spoken at home, in markets, and in mosques, Saromantang's work deepened the spiritual
engagement of ordinary believers who might struggle with Classical Arabic or reliance on Malay as an auxiliary
religious language.
His work has since been integrated into multiple modern formats. Maranao Muslims now access his translation
through dedicated mobile applications, including the Quran Maranao MP3 Translation app (updated around 2023),
and through YouTube playlists featuring his audio recitations. These digital distributions have extended the reach of
his work globally, allowing diaspora communities and new generations to encounter the Qur'an in their ancestral
language.
Academic archives, including the University of Hawaii and the Maisie van Vactor Collection at Brigham Young
University, now catalog his work as a significant contribution to Maranao linguistic and religious scholarship.
Orthographic Innovation
Beyond the translation itself, Saromantang made an enduring contribution to Maranao orthography. Working
alongside Ahmad Domocao Alonto and Aleem Abdulmajeed Ansano, he developed a standardized writing system
for Maranao that departed from earlier romanized conventions influenced by Filipino standards.
The most distinctive feature of his orthographic system is its explicit marking of "heavy" or aspirated consonants,
sounds that are phonologically contrastive in Maranao but are typically ignored in simplified modern scripts.
Where common standardized systems would write "p," "t," "k," and "s," Saromantang's system distinguishes these
from their aspirated counterparts through digraphs: "ph," "th," "kh," and "z" (or "sh").
For example:
phaphaag versus papaag (heavy p versus plain p)

PAGE 4
thatharo versus tataro (heavy t versus plain t)
khipanananggila versus kipanananggila (heavy k versus plain k)
This system reflects sophisticated phonological knowledge. Saromantang recognized that vowels undergo
predictable changes after heavy consonants, and his orthography accounts for this variation by allowing the heavy
consonant marker itself to signal the correct pronunciation without requiring additional diacritics.
His handling of vowels and the mid-central schwa (the neutral vowel sound) also reflected careful linguistic
observation. Where modern dictionaries might use complex digraphs, Saromantang's system keeps vowel letters
simple and lets the preceding heavy consonant context guide pronunciation.
Academic linguists have recognized this system for its phonological accuracy, particularly in representing Maranao
sounds that earlier Western linguistic studies had overlooked. While modern educational standards increasingly
align with national Komisyon sa Wikang Filipino recommendations (which favor spellings like "Maranaw" and
"tabangay" over his "Maranao" and "tabangai"), specialists in Maranao language acknowledge Saromantang's
system as uniquely suited for precise native recitation and preservation of linguistic subtleties.
Scholarly Reception and Debate
Saromantang's translation did not escape academic scrutiny. The process of rendering Classical Arabic into any
vernacular language inevitably involves interpretive choices, and his work became the subject of significant
scholarly debate within Islamic and linguistic circles.
Critical Perspectives
The most notable critiques emerged from scholars outside the Maranao community, particularly from
Maguindanaon Islamic figures like Ustaz Mohammad Sulaiman. Their arguments centered on three main points:
Literalism and Theological Interpretation: Critics argued that Saromantang's approach to certain passages
leaned too heavily toward literal word-for-word correspondence, potentially resulting in theological
meanings that, while etymologically accurate to the Arabic roots, diverged from established Islamic
exegetical traditions.
The "Cow" Controversy: A specific and widely discussed critique focused on a verse in Surah Al-Baqarah
(the second chapter of the Qur'an). Critics claimed that a literal rendering of certain divine attributes in
Maranao inadvertently used language associated with an animal, which they deemed a serious error in
Islamic exegesis and potentially offensive to believers. This critique, though specific, reflected broader
concerns about the challenges of conveying divine imagery across linguistic and cultural boundaries.
Dialectal Bias: Some observers noted that Saromantang's translation incorporated linguistic nuances so
deeply rooted in the Tugaya dialect of Maranao that scholars and speakers from other Maranao regions (or
from neighboring ethnolinguistic groups like the Maguindanaon) sometimes found the text difficult to
reconcile with their own regional pronunciation and theological understanding.
Scholarly Defenses
In response, Maranao scholars and Saromantang's family have mounted several compelling defenses grounded in
institutional validation and linguistic science:
Rigorous Review Process: Defenders, including his grandsons Rasol Abbas and Rashid Gurualim, stressed
that the translation underwent a full 5-year expert review by a committee of Maranao Shariah scholars at the

PAGE 5
Islamic University of Madinah before being cleared for publication by the King Fahd Complex. This
institutional endorsement from one of the Islamic world's most respected academic centers carries significant
weight.
Orthographic Precision: Saromantang is recognized in academic literature for developing the first writing
system capable of accurately representing the full phonological inventory of Maranao, including sounds that
had been overlooked by previous Western linguists. This precision, while sometimes creating a translation
that feels demanding to modern readers, reflects scholarly rigor.
Vernacular Empowerment: Studies on interlinear religious translations in Mindanao credit Saromantang
with shifting the region away from dependence on Malay as the default auxiliary language for complex
Islamic thought. His work established Maranao as a legitimate, sophisticated vehicle for theological
discourse, a contribution that transcends the translation itself.
Death and Ongoing Legacy
The exact date of Saromantang's death is not specified in available sources, though he is referred to in respectful
terms as "Rahimahullah" (may God have mercy upon him), a phrase used to honor deceased Muslims of standing
in the community.
What is certain is that his work continues to shape the spiritual lives of Maranao Muslims. Each time a believer
opens the Qur'an in their mother tongue and encounters Saromantang's carefully chosen words, they encounter not
merely a translation but a bridge between the sacred text and their own cultural identity.
His family, particularly his descendants, have become stewards of his legacy, defending his scholarly choices and
ensuring that his translation remains accessible to new generations through modern digital platforms. The ongoing
updates to Maranao Qur'an mobile applications and audio recordings represent an extension of his original vision:
making the word of God available in the language of the Maranao people.

title: Sawadjaan, Cassandra Karemaeh Bahjin
text:
PAGE 1
Cassandra Karemaeh Bahjin Sawadjaan
Cassandra Karemaeh Bahjin Sawadjaan (born c. 1980s) is a career diplomat from the Philippine Department of
Foreign Affairs (DFA) and currently serves as First Secretary and Consul General at the Philippine Embassy in the
State of Qatar, based in Doha. A proud Tausug from the Sulu Archipelago, she has built a reputation as a tireless
advocate for the Filipino diaspora in the Middle East, earning the informal title Magiting na Babae ng Mindanao
(Brave Woman of Mindanao) among her community. With more than 15 years of dedicated public service,
Sawadjaan has become a recognized figure in Philippine bilateral diplomacy, consular protection, and inter-agency
outreach, consistently bridging the gap between government services and the Filipino migrant community abroad.
In September 2025, she was conferred the DFA Loyalty Award, a formal recognition of her 15 years of continuous
service to the Philippine government.<ref>DBM Gov PH Facebook Post on Cassandra Sawadjaan (https://www.fac
ebook.com/DBMgovph/posts/icymi-embassy-of-the-philippines-in-the-state-of-qatar-first-secretary-and-consu/100
0194665600737/)</ref><ref>Instagram post featuring Cassandra Sawadjaan, Philippine Embassy Doha (https://ww
w.instagram.com/p/DWj7GV5Ckoz/)</ref>
Contents
1 Early Life and Heritage
2 Education and Entry into Diplomacy
3 Diplomatic Career
3.1 Tokyo, Japan (c. 2019)
3.2 Doha, Qatar (2022–Present)

Early Life and Heritage
Sawadjaan is of Tausug descent, with roots in the Sulu Archipelago in Mindanao. The Tausug, often called the
"People of the Current," are one of the major ethnolinguistic groups of the Bangsamoro region, known for a long
maritime tradition and a strong sense of community identity. Her Tausug heritage is not just a biographical footnote
for Sawadjaan; it's a thread that runs through how she approaches public service. She has spoken openly about her
cultural background in official settings, and it clearly shapes the community-focused, on-the-ground style of
diplomacy she has become known for. In many circles, particularly among Filipinos in the Gulf, she's recognized
as a symbol of what a Bangsamoro woman in senior government service looks like.

Education and Entry into Diplomacy
Sawadjaan entered the Philippine Foreign Service by passing the
highly competitive Foreign Service Officer (FSO) examinations
conducted by the DFA. The FSO exam is among the most rigorous
government examinations in the country, testing candidates on
international law, political science, economics, and the Philippine
constitution, among other subjects. Her academic and professional
preparation equipped her for the demanding work of consular
protection, bilateral negotiations, and multi-stakeholder
coordination that defines a career in the foreign service. Specific
details about her undergraduate studies and graduate-level training
have not been disclosed in available sources.
Diplomatic Career
Sawadjaan's diplomatic career spans more than 15 years with the
Department of Foreign Affairs. She has served in multiple posts,
including Tokyo and Doha, handling a range of responsibilities
from protocol and bilateral affairs to frontline consular work.
Tokyo, Japan (c. 2019)
One of her earlier assignments brought her to the Philippine
Embassy in Tokyo, where she served as First Secretary.<ref>DFA
Philippines Facebook Post, Philippine Embassy Tokyo (https://ww
w.facebook.com/dfaphl/posts/deputy-chief-of-mission-eduardo-mr
-me%C3%B1ez-and-first-secretary-cassandra-sawadjaan/1271304
803024351/)</ref> In this role, she was involved in managing
bilateral relations between the Philippines and Japan, one of the
country's most significant diplomatic partnerships. She also
provided strategic briefings and logistical support to visiting
Philippine local government delegations, giving local officials
direct engagement with Japanese counterparts and relevant
agencies.
Doha, Qatar (2022–Present)
Since 2022, Sawadjaan has been posted to the Philippine Embassy
in Doha, Qatar, serving as First Secretary and Consul General.
Qatar hosts one of the largest Filipino communities in the Middle East, with hundreds of thousands of Overseas
Filipino Workers (OFWs) employed across construction, hospitality, healthcare, and domestic work sectors. At a
critical point in the embassy's operations, during the transition before the appointment of the current ambassador,
Sawadjaan served as Chargé d'Affaires, a.i. (ad interim), effectively acting as the temporary head of the Philippine
mission in Qatar.<ref>Instagram post featuring Cassandra Sawadjaan, Philippine Embassy Doha (https://www.insta
gram.com/p/DWj7GV5Ckoz/)</ref> This appointment placed her in charge of the embassy's full operations and
diplomatic communications during a sensitive institutional period.

PAGE 3
Key Contributions and Achievements
Inter-Agency Outreach (June 2025)
In June 2025, Sawadjaan spearheaded a major multi-agency community outreach program held at the Philippine
International School Qatar. The event brought together several government agencies, including the Migrant
Workers Office (MWO), the Social Security System (SSS), and the Home Development Mutual Fund (Pag-IBIG),
to deliver services directly to the Filipino community in Doha. The initiative is a clear example of her "go to the
people" approach to consular work, reducing the need for OFWs to take time off work just to access government
services.
Economic Diplomacy (April 2025)
In April 2025, Sawadjaan held a consultative meeting with Budget Secretary Amenah F. Pangandaman to discuss
investment opportunities and the overall state of Philippines-Qatar bilateral relations.<ref>DBM Gov PH Facebook
Post on Cassandra Sawadjaan (https://www.facebook.com/DBMgovph/posts/icymi-embassy-of-the-philippines-in-t
he-state-of-qatar-first-secretary-and-consu/1000194665600737/)</ref> This engagement reflects the embassy's
active role in facilitating economic ties and keeping senior Philippine government officials updated on conditions
in the Gulf.
ASEAN Representation in Doha
Sawadjaan represents the Philippines in the ASEAN Committee in Doha (ACD), a grouping of ASEAN member-
state missions in Qatar that coordinates regional diplomatic initiatives in the Gulf. Her participation in the ACD
extends Philippine engagement beyond bilateral work, situating the country's interests within a broader Southeast
Asian diplomatic framework.
Cultural Advocacy and Personal Values
Beyond her technical diplomatic duties, Sawadjaan is a visible advocate for Filipino heritage and national values.
During the chartering ceremony of the Knights of Rizal Qatar Chapter in 2024, she graced the event as an official
embassy representative and called on the Filipino community to carry the "indomitable spirit" that Jose Rizal
embodied, encouraging them to find strength in identity and service even while living and working far from home.
<ref>Philippine Embassy Doha: Embassy Graces Chartering of Knights of Rizal Qatar Chapter (https://dohape.dfa.
gov.ph/newsroom/embassy-news/1086-ph-embassy-graces-chartering-of-knights-of-rizal-qatar-chapter.html)</ref>
This kind of engagement with civil society organizations in the diaspora is characteristic of how she views the
consular role: not just as a legal and administrative function, but as a form of community stewardship.
Recognition
In September 2025, Sawadjaan was officially conferred the DFA Loyalty Award in recognition of her 15 years of
continuous and dedicated service to the Republic of the Philippines through the Department of Foreign Affairs.
This award is one of the formal honors given to career foreign service officers who have maintained active and
uninterrupted service to the government. The conferment was a recognition not just of longevity, but of consistent,
high-quality performance across multiple diplomatic assignments.

PAGE 4
Legacy
Cassandra Karemaeh Bahjin Sawadjaan represents something worth noting in Philippine diplomatic history: a
Tausug woman from Mindanao who climbed through the ranks of a highly competitive foreign service to handle
one of the country's busiest diplomatic missions in the Middle East. Her career offers a concrete example of
Bangsamoro women taking their place in the national government not on the periphery, but in roles that matter,
managing thousands of OFWs, representing the country in multilateral settings, and holding the mission together as
acting head during critical transitions. She's often described as a diplomat who gets things done without losing
sight of the people she's supposed to serve. That combination of institutional competence and ground-level
empathy is what those who've worked with her and the Filipino community in Qatar tend to remember most.

Wisdom Islamic School
Wisdom Islamic School, Davao City Inc. (often referred to as WIS
or Wisdom Islamic School) is a private, non-stock, non-profit
Islamic educational institution located in Davao City, Philippines.
The school integrates the Philippine Department of Education
(DepEd) K-12 curriculum with a comprehensive Islamic studies
program grounded in the Qur'an and Sunnah, following the
understanding of the Righteous Predecessors (Salaf).
WIS serves Muslim learners from kindergarten through senior high
school, with a mission to prepare students for success both in this
world and the Hereafter. It runs both face-to-face classes and Online
Distance Learning (ODL), always keeping authentic Islamic
teachings, academic excellence, and character development front and
center.
Contents
1 Founding and Establishment
2 Location and Facilities
3 Purpose and Curriculum
4 Programs and Activities
5 Contributions and Current Status
6 See Also
7 References
Founding and Establishment
The story of WIS traces back to the Wisdom International School for
Higher Education Studies (WISHES), founded by Dr. Mamarinta
Omar Mababaya, who served as President, and Dr. Norlain Dindang
Mababaya, Chairman of the Board of Trustees. WISHES earned its
DepEd recognition in May 2010 for pre-school and elementary levels
in Davao City.
By 2012, the institution had grown enough to offer high school
education, taking on the name Wisdom Islamic School, Davao City,
Inc. The high school department opened its doors in the 2012-2013
school year, and by 2014-2015, the school had also secured
government recognition for its pre-school and elementary levels.
Today, WIS is registered with the Securities and Exchange
Commission (SEC) and holds proper DepEd permits and
recognitions, including Elementary Government Recognition (R-XI)
No. 006 s. 2014 and Secondary Government Recognition (R-XI) No.

PAGE 2
Blending national K-12 education with an
authentic Islamic upbringing grounded in
the understanding of the Salaf
014 s. 2015. Its roots also reach back to an earlier accreditation for
higher Islamic studies through the Commission on Higher Education-
Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (CHED-ARMM) in 2005.
Location and Facilities
WIS sits at Wisdom Compound, Abinsay Street, Dumanlas, Buhangin, Davao City, Davao del Sur. The campus is
built to serve both regular and online learners, with classrooms and a masjid, Masjid Al-Hikmah, at its heart.
Over the years, the community has stepped up to support the school's growth. Recent projects funded through
parental and donor involvement include electrical upgrades and masjid renovations such as ceiling repairs, fresh
paint, comfort rooms, and wudoo areas.
Purpose and Curriculum
At its core, WIS is built around a simple but powerful vision: raising a learned, prosperous society that holds fast to
authentic Islamic teachings. The goal is for students to grow into individuals who please Allah, live by pure Islamic
principles, and work toward success in the Hereafter, all while getting a solid, well-rounded education.
To make that happen, the school blends DepEd-mandated subjects like English, Math, and Science with Arabic,
Qur'an studies, and Islamic Studies covering Aqeedah, Fiqh, Hadith, and Seerah, along with character education
woven throughout.
WIS follows the Salafi methodology in its approach to Islamic education and embraces blended learning to reach
students both on campus and online. Its teaching staff includes graduates from respected institutions, among them
Madinah University, and leadership includes members of the founding family, such as Ahmad D. Mababaya, who
serves as CEO, President, and School Head, and Abdurrahman D. Mababaya, who serves as COO and Head
Supervisor.
Programs and Activities
WIS keeps a full calendar of academic and community life going. On the academic side, the school runs the
complete K-12 program with added Islamic components, plus support for students learning online.
Outside the classroom, students take part in inter-madrasah competitions, including the WISers Inter-Madrasah
Invitational Cup, along with sports and other student-led activities.
The school also anchors a lot of community life. Weekly halaqah, or study circles, are held at the masjid for both
adults and children, alongside Jumu'ah khutbahs, guest lectures, and fundraising drives for facility improvements.
Throughout the year, WIS holds general assemblies, orientations, and semestral breaks that follow both the
academic and Hijri calendars, and the school takes part in local events like Eid bazaars.
The institution keeps its DepEd recognition current and takes part in teacher licensure efforts, counting LET
passers among its faculty.

PAGE 3
Contributions and Current Status
As one of only a handful of DepEd-recognized private Islamic schools in Davao City, WIS fills an important gap:
giving Muslim students a way to hold onto their religious identity while still meeting national education standards,
in a country where Muslims are a minority.
The school's approach has drawn academic attention too. A case study by Ahmad Dindang Mababaya looked into
how WIS provides integrated education that parents see as balanced and effective.
As of 2026, WIS continues active enrollment for School Year 2026-2027, runs its ongoing classes, and keeps
pursuing facility upgrades through community support. It remains a small-to-medium institution that has chosen to
focus on quality over scale, and it holds a dedicated following within the local Muslim community.

Omar Yasser Sema
Omar Yasser Sema is a Filipino Moro politician and public servant from Sulu. He currently serves as a Member of
the Bangsamoro Parliament under the Bangsamoro Transition Authority (BTA). He is affiliated with the Moro
National Liberation Front (MNLF) and is part of a prominent political family in Sulu, being the son of former
Cotabato City mayor Muslimin Sema.<ref name="barmm2023">Bangsamoro Government. Profiles of
Bangsamoro Parliament Members. Official BARMM Website, 2023.</ref><ref name="pia2022">Philippine
Information Agency. MNLF leaders in Bangsamoro governance. 2022.</ref>
---
Early Life and Background
Omar Yasser Sema hails from Sulu, a historical and political center of the Sultanate of Sulu and Moro
resistance movements.
He is the son of Muslimin Sema, a senior leader of the Moro National Liberation Front (MNLF) and former
mayor of Cotabato City.
His upbringing in a politically active family influenced his involvement in governance and public service.
<ref name="pia2022" />
---
Political Career
Moro National Liberation Front
Omar Yasser Sema is affiliated with the Moro National Liberation Front (MNLF), contributing to its political
engagement within the Bangsamoro peace process.
He represents the continuation of MNLF leadership participation in formal governance structures.

PAGE 2
Bangsamoro Parliament
He was appointed as a Member of the Bangsamoro Transition Authority Parliament, representing MNLF
constituencies.
As a parliament member, he participates in legislative deliberations, policymaking, and institutional
development within BARMM.<ref name="barmm2023" />
---
Contributions to Bangsamoro Governance
Advocates for inclusive governance by ensuring representation of MNLF-aligned communities.
Supports peace-building initiatives and the political normalization process in the Bangsamoro region.
Promotes development programs for Sulu and other underserved areas in BARMM.
---
Legacy and Significance
Omar Yasser Sema represents the younger generation of Moro leaders engaged in formal political
institutions.
His role highlights the continued integration of revolutionary movements into democratic governance under
BARMM.
He contributes to strengthening political inclusivity and long-term stability in the Bangsamoro region.
---

title: Sharief, Bae Okile Mangondato
text:
PAGE 1
Bae Okile Mangondato Sharief
Bae Okile Mangondato Sharief, PhD (Alhadja), is a Filipino educator, philanthropist, and community leader who
founded Lanao Central College, Inc. (LCCI) in Marawi City—famously known as "The Home of Free Tuition
Fee." A member of the Maranao ethnic group, she holds the traditional title of Bae (noblewoman) and has
dedicated her life to providing accessible education in post-conflict Mindanao. Her humanitarian work earned her
the Mother Teresa Award and appointment as a World Peace Ambassador, making her one of the most influential
Bangsamoro women in contemporary Philippines.
Contents
1 Early Life and Family
2 Ethnic Affiliation and Cultural Significance
3 Education
4 Career and Institutional Leadership
4.1 Lanao Central College, Inc. (LCCI)
4.2 PMTC Laboratory School Inc.
5 Humanitarian Work and Peace-Building
5.1 Post-Marawi Siege Response
5.2 Community Outreach Programs
6 Awards and Recognition

6.2 National Awards
7 Personal Values and Philosophy
8 Legacy and Impact
9 Cultural and Regional Significance
10 See also
11 External links
Early Life and Family
Dr. Sharief was born into one of Lanao del Sur's most prominent families of educators and traditional leaders. She
is the youngest daughter of Hadji Ali Alimatar Sawasa Sharief and Dr. Norma Mangondato Sharief, the latter
widely recognized as the "Mother of Education" in Lanao del Sur. Her family lineage traces back to the First
Sultan of Cabugatan sa Poona Masiu, connecting her to centuries of Maranao royal heritage.
Her late brother, Agakhan "Bin Laden" Sharief, became a local hero during the 2017 Marawi Siege when he
brokered critical ceasefires to rescue trapped civilians. His death deeply influenced Dr. Sharief's commitment to
peace-building and humanitarian service in the region.
Ethnic Affiliation and Cultural Significance
As a member of the Maranao people, Dr. Sharief represents one of the Philippines' major Muslim indigenous
groups. The Maranao, also spelled Meranaw, are primarily based around Lake Lanao in Mindanao and maintain
distinct cultural practices, including a matrilineal nobility system.

PAGE 2

The title Bae designates her status as a traditional noblewoman in
Maranao society, carrying both cultural authority and social
responsibility. This position allows her to bridge traditional
leadership structures with modern institutional frameworks,
particularly in advocating for women's empowerment in Muslim-
majority regions. Her work is deeply rooted in Bangsamoro cultural
and religious values, making her a role model for young Maranao
women pursuing education and public service.
Education
Dr. Sharief holds multiple advanced degrees that reflect her
commitment to lifelong learning:
Doctor of Philosophy (PhD)
Doctor of Education (Ed.D.)
Doctor of Humane Letters (D.Hum.) – Honorary degree
conferred by Ganka International Awards (Gawad Agila ng
Kadakilaan) in 2024 in recognition of her humanitarian
excellence
Her academic credentials complement her traditional cultural
authority, positioning her as both a modern educator and a respected
traditional leader.
Career and Institutional Leadership
Lanao Central College, Inc. (LCCI)
In 2012, Dr. Sharief founded Lanao Central College, Inc. (LCCI)
in Marawi City, establishing what would become known as "The
Home of Free Tuition Fee." The institution revolutionized higher
education accessibility in conflict-affected Lanao del Sur by offering
completely free first-year tuition across multiple degree programs.
LCCI provides undergraduate programs in Criminology, Civil
Engineering, Computer Science, Social Work, Agriculture,
Elementary Education, and Islamic Studies (Major in Shari'ah), along
with graduate programs including Master in Public Administration
and Master of Arts in Education. The college specifically targets
marginalized students, offering specialized support for orphans (Wata
a Ilo), children of mujahideen, persons with disabilities (PWDs), and
the economically disadvantaged (miskeen).
The institution's impact is measurable: in 2026 alone, LCCI produced
58 new Criminology board passers, demonstrating the quality of
education alongside its accessibility.

PAGE 3
PMTC Laboratory School Inc.
Dr. Sharief also serves as President of PMTC Laboratory School Inc., extending her educational mission to
primary and secondary education levels.
Humanitarian Work and Peace-Building
Post-Marawi Siege Response
Following the devastating 2017 Marawi Siege, Dr. Sharief mobilized LCCI and personal resources to provide
critical humanitarian assistance. She organized medical aid, distributed relief goods, and offered community legal
services to internally displaced persons (IDPs). Her efforts helped stabilize education in the region when many
institutions had been destroyed.
Continuing her late brother's legacy of mediation and peace advocacy, she supported government peace initiatives
and created educational opportunities as a form of community healing. Her work embodies the principle that
education is essential infrastructure for post-conflict recovery.
Community Outreach Programs
Beyond classroom education, Dr. Sharief regularly hosts massive community events distributing ayuda (aid) such
as grocery packs and water to hundreds of participants. These initiatives reinforce community resilience and
demonstrate her commitment to holistic social welfare.
Awards and Recognition
Dr. Sharief has received extensive international and national recognition for her dual contributions to education and
humanitarian service.
International Awards
World Peace Prize (2024) – Conferred alongside ambassadors from various countries for dedicated
humanitarian efforts
World Peace Ambassador – Appointed by the World Peace Committee (WPC) for pursuit of regional
stability and social healing
Mother Teresa Award – Distinctive worldwide recognition for lifetime philanthropic work
Asian Sterling Awards (2022) – "Most Outstanding Individual Achievement as Humanitarian Ambassador"
Global Educator's Award – Recognized for innovative approach to accessible higher education
National Awards
Honorary Public Servant of the Year (2025) – Excellence in Foreign Relations and Foreign Affairs (Nation
Builders & Mosliv Awards)
Honorary Public Servant of the Year (2024) – Excellence in Foreign Relations and Diplomatic Affairs,
ceremony at Okada Manila
Honorary Public Servant of the Year (2023) – Excellence in Peace and Nation Building, contributions
toward UN Sustainable Development Goals

PAGE 4
Philippines Choice Awards (2024) – National Outstanding Humanitarian and Community Service
Outstanding Philanthropist of the Year – Gawad Filipino Awards as social-civic icon
Noble Woman of Influence & Empowered Business Leader of the Year
Personal Values and Philosophy
Dr. Sharief's life work is guided by the philosophy of "selfless contribution" to the Sustainable Development Goals
(SDGs), particularly focusing on quality education (SDG 4), poverty reduction (SDG 1), and peace (SDG 16). Her
frequent use of Alhamdulillah (praise be to God) reflects her deep Islamic faith, which informs her humanitarian
approach.
As an Alhadja (one who has completed the Hajj pilgrimage), she integrates Islamic principles of charity (zakat)
and community service (sadaqah) into her institutional mission. She participates regularly in Umrah (lesser
pilgrimage) and views education as a form of worship and service to humanity.
Legacy and Impact
Dr. Sharief's significance lies in her ability to merge traditional Maranao leadership with modern educational
administration. By leveraging her cultural authority as a Bae and her international diplomatic standing as a World
Peace Ambassador, she created a scalable blueprint for educational philanthropy in post-conflict zones.
The LCCI "Free Tuition" model demonstrates that accessible higher education can function sustainably while
maintaining academic quality. Her work challenges conventional assumptions about the relationship between
educational quality and cost, proving that institutions can prioritize social mission without compromising
standards.
Her leadership provides a template for women in Muslim-majority regions of Southeast Asia, showing how
traditional cultural roles can be vehicles for progressive social change rather than barriers to it. By maintaining her
titles as Bae and Alhadja while simultaneously holding doctoral degrees and international awards, she embodies a
synthesis of tradition and modernity.
Cultural and Regional Significance
As one of the most visible Bangsamoro women leaders in contemporary Philippines, Dr. Sharief plays a crucial
role in representing Maranao perspectives in national discourse. Her work in Marawi City—a symbolic center of
Islamic culture in the Philippines—carries particular weight in the context of ongoing peace processes between the
Philippine government and Moro groups.
Her institutional presence in Marawi also serves as a counter-narrative to extremism, demonstrating that Islamic
values and modern education are complementary rather than contradictory. The survival and growth of LCCI
despite the 2017 siege symbolizes the resilience of Maranao civil society.

title: Sinsuat, Datu Mama
text:
PAGE 1
Datu Mama Sinsuat
Commissioner Datu Mama Sinsuat (The Elder) was a Maguindanaon statesman, attorney, and traditional royal
leader who played a pivotal role in bridging Muslim Mindanao with the Philippine national government during the
turbulent mid-to-late 20th century.
He's best remembered for heading the Commission on National Integration (CNI) and serving as Presidential
Adviser on Muslim Affairs under President Ferdinand Marcos Sr.
Throughout his career, Sinsuat championed the idea that regional identity and national unity weren't in conflict
with each other, that a Muslim Filipino could be fully Maguindanaon and fully Filipino at the same time.
He was a son of the legendary Datu Sinsuat Balabaran, the first Muslim Senator of the Philippines, and he carried
that legacy forward through law, institution-building, and a lifelong commitment to the welfare of his people.
Contents
1 Background and Royal Lineage
2 Education and Legal Formation
3 Career and Institutional Contributions
3.1 Commission on National Integration (CNI)
3.2 Presidential Adviser on Muslim Affairs
4 Personal Values and Cultural Advocacy
5 Legacy
6 See Also
7 References
8 Categories
Background and Royal Lineage
Datu Mama Sinsuat was born into the Sinsuat royal clan of the Sultanate of Maguindanao, centered in what is now
Cotabato City.
His father, Datu Sinsuat Balabaran, wasn't just a family elder. He was a political titan, the first Muslim to serve in
the Philippine Senate in 1935, and one of the most recognizable names in Maguindanaon history.
Growing up surrounded by leaders shaped Datu Mama Sinsuat in profound ways.
His brothers were all figures of consequence: Datu Blah Sinsuat served as a delegate to the 1935 Constitutional
Convention and later as a Congressman; Datu Odin Sinsuat became such a respected figure that a municipality in
Maguindanao del Norte now bears his name; and Datu Duma Sinsuat and Datu Mando Sinsuat each carried the
family's tradition of public service.
From childhood onward, Datu Mama Sinsuat understood that being a Maguindanaon Datu wasn't just about
ancestral title. It was a responsibility to govern, advocate, and protect.

PAGE 2

Education and Legal Formation
What set Datu Mama Sinsuat apart from many traditional leaders of
his generation was his decision to pursue formal legal education.
He graduated as an attorney, giving him a skill set that few
traditional leaders in Muslim Mindanao possessed at the time.
That legal training was never just personal ambition. It was a tool. He
understood that the rights of Muslim Filipinos could only be
defended if someone from within their community could argue those
rights in the language of Philippine law and governance.
His legal background equipped him to navigate the bureaucratic
corridors of Manila, to read and challenge policy, and to author
institutional programs that reached thousands of people who would
never set foot in a courtroom.
Career and Institutional Contributions
Commission on National Integration (CNI)
In the 1960s and 1970s, Datu Mama Sinsuat was appointed
Commissioner of the Commission on National Integration (CNI),
a cabinet-level body established under Republic Act No. 1888 to
uplift the economic, social, moral, and political standing of the
country's non-Christian communities.
Under his leadership, the CNI became far more than an
administrative office.
The Scholarship Program: Sinsuat personally oversaw the
expansion of the CNI's flagship national scholarship initiative,
securing funding and placements for thousands of young Muslim,
Moro, and indigenous students in top Manila universities.
This wasn't a minor program. It was the first time an institution had
systematically channeled Mindanao youth into higher education at
scale, and the graduates of that initiative became the first massive
wave of modern, college-educated professionals from the region.
Beyond scholarships, Sinsuat used the CNI platform to roll out
agricultural assistance programs, local infrastructure projects, and
land homesteading initiatives designed to prevent the displacement of
indigenous and Muslim communities from their ancestral lands.

PAGE 3
expansion, Moro refugee
relief, cultural pluralism
advocacy
Presidential Adviser on Muslim Affairs
As the Moro rebellion intensified in the 1970s, President Ferdinand
Marcos Sr. appointed Datu Mama Sinsuat as his Presidential
Adviser on Muslim Affairs.
It was one of the most sensitive political roles of that era, and Sinsuat took it seriously.
Refugee Relief: At the height of the conflict, he coordinated large-scale government relief operations for hundreds
of thousands of Mindanao residents displaced by the fighting. His on-the-ground familiarity with Muslim
communities made him an effective mediator between military priorities and civilian needs.
Diplomatic Work: In 1971, Sinsuat joined a group of prominent Muslim leaders, including Senator Mamintal
Tamano, Congressman Ali Dimaporo, and Congressman Salipada Pendatun, to co-found the Islamic Directorate
of the Philippines (IDP).
The IDP went on to negotiate directly with international figures, including Libyan leader Muammar Gaddafi, and
secured funding for significant community assets, among them the land for the Grand Mosque in Tandang Sora,
Quezon City.
That negotiation was a quiet but consequential act: it demonstrated that Muslim Filipinos could engage
international Islamic solidarity networks on their own terms, bringing resources home without surrendering local
leadership.
Personal Values and Cultural Advocacy
At the core of everything Datu Mama Sinsuat did was a philosophy of cultural pluralism.
During a period when national policy frequently pressured minorities to assimilate fully into a Christian-majority
mainstream, Sinsuat pushed back with conviction.
He argued publicly and consistently that Filipino Muslims didn't need to abandon their religion, their customary
laws, or their cultural identity to be genuine citizens of the Philippine republic.
He viewed education as the most powerful tool for equality, more durable than political appointments, more far-
reaching than any single legislation.
By using his institutional access to open doors for students from Muslim and indigenous communities, he didn't
just fill classrooms. He changed the leadership landscape of an entire region for generations.
Legacy
Datu Mama Sinsuat's dedication to public service didn't end with him.
His daughter, Bai Moihra Sinsuat, married into the prominent Baraguir royal lineage, extending the Sinsuat
family's ties to Maguindanaon leadership traditions.
His son, Datu Mama Sinsuat Jr., carried his father's work forward over decades of service as a long-time
Regional Director of the National Commission on Muslim Filipinos (NCMF), the direct successor agency to the
old CNI that his father once led.

PAGE 4
That continuity is one of the clearest signs of a meaningful legacy: the institutions he helped build are still running,
and the family that shaped them is still engaged.
Through his legal acumen, his institutional leadership, and his fierce insistence on the dignity of Muslim Filipinos,
Commissioner Datu Mama Sinsuat (The Elder) is remembered not simply as a royal heir to a historic sultanate, but
as one of the principal architects of Muslim-Christian integration in the modern Philippines.

title: Sinsuat, Fatima Palileo
text:
PAGE 1
Fatima Palileo Sinsuat
Bai Fatima Palileo Sinsuat (c. 1939/1940 – February 4, 2022) was a Maguindanaon royal, humanitarian leader,
local government official, and academic regent who spent more than five decades quietly rewriting the rules of
what a Moro woman could be in Philippine public life.
She's best remembered as the first Muslim woman in at least 30 years to be elected to the National Board of
Governors of the Philippine National Red Cross (PNRC), a milestone that cracked open a multi-decade glass
ceiling in one of the country's most prominent civic institutions.
But she was a lot more than that one historic moment. She was a union organizer who fought for dockworkers'
rights in Cotabato City, a mayor who governed with a soft touch, a labor advocate, a regent who helped steer the
University of the Philippines, and a 47-year volunteer of the Red Cross.
When she passed on February 4, 2022, at the age of 82, the Bangsamoro Transition Authority Parliament formally
honored her as a "princess for her people," in language that captured exactly who she was: someone who took the
weight of a royal name and used it to carry others.
Contents
1 Background
2 Education
3 Career
3.1 Local Governance
3.2 Labor Advocacy
3.3 Economic Development
4 Institutional Contributions
4.1 Philippine National Red Cross
4.2 PRC Cotabato Chapter
4.3 International Humanitarian Law
5 Recognition
6 Legacy
7 See Also
8 References
Background
Bai Fatima was born into the Sinsuat family, one of the most powerful political dynasties in Maguindanao and a
family whose name is inseparable from the modern history of Muslim Mindanao.
Her father was Datu Blah Sinsuat, a commanding figure in regional politics, often described as a strongman in the
tradition of Maguindanao governance. Growing up as a genuine Bai, or princess, meant she was immersed in the
realities of leadership from an early age.

PAGE 2
Bai Fatima Palileo Sinsuat
Born
c. 1939 or 1940
Died
February 4, 2022 (aged 82)
Ethnicity
Maguindanaon
Religion
Islam
Royal Title
Bai (Princess), Maguindanao Royal Family
Father
Datu Blah Sinsuat
Political Office
Municipal Mayor of Upi, Maguindanao (1980-
1986)
Academic Appointment
Rather than living a sheltered aristocratic life, she worked
alongside her father, absorbing the rhythms of grassroots
organizing and community advocacy. That early exposure to
real-world governance would shape everything that came after.
She was Maguindanaon, Muslim, and royal. In the political
landscape of Mindanao, those identities came loaded with
expectations. What made Bai Fatima remarkable was how
consistently she turned those expectations into something
broader and more universal than her family's traditional sphere
of influence.
Education
Detailed records of her earliest schooling remain within private
family archives, but her intellectual and administrative
capabilities eventually placed her at the center of national
academic governance.
President Joseph Estrada appointed her to the Board of Regents
of the University of the Philippines, the highest governing
body of the country's premier state university. The UP Board of
Regents oversees everything from institutional policy to the
appointment of the UP president, and being asked to serve on it
represents a significant expression of national trust.
What stood out even more was her staying power: she served
three consecutive terms as a UP Regent. That kind of
continuity is rare, and it gave her a meaningful window to
champion the academic representation of Muslim Mindanao at
the very top of Philippine higher education.
Career
Local Governance
Bai Fatima entered electoral politics and served as the
Municipal Mayor of Upi, Maguindanao from 1980 to 1986.
Locals who remember her tenure describe a leader with an
approachable, soft-spoken style that distinguished her from the
harder-edged political culture of the region. She governed at a
time of considerable tension in Mindanao, and her quiet but firm
approach left a lasting impression on the communities she
served.

PAGE 3
Member, Board of Regents, University of the
Philippines (3 consecutive terms)
Other Positions
Chairperson, Board of Investments, ARMM;
Chairperson, PRC Cotabato Chapter Board
Awards
National Outstanding Volunteer Award (NOVA),
2003; Gold Humanitarian Service Cross, 2005
NOTABILITY
First Muslim woman in 30 years elected to the
National Board of Governors of the Philippine
National Red Cross; 47-year Red Cross volunteer
leader; Maguindanao royal who converted
heritage into a lifetime of public service
KNOWN FOR
Breaking a multi-decade glass ceiling at the
PNRC; founding the Progressive Labor Union at
Cotabato City's port; serving three consecutive
terms on the UP Board of Regents; championing
humanitarian law in Mindanao conflict zones
PULL QUOTE
"A princess for her people, who converted a
royal heritage into a lifetime of community
service."
Labor Advocacy
One of her lesser-known but significant contributions was in the
field of labor rights.
In 1986, working independently of her family's traditional
political domain, she organized and established the Progressive
Labor Union (PLU). Her campaign was thorough: under her
leadership, every single dockworker at the Cotabato City port
became a protected union member, ensuring safer working
conditions and fair wages for one of the region's most vulnerable
labor sectors.
That kind of ground-level organizing, often unglamorous and
always demanding, said something important about her values.
She didn't limit her advocacy to the corridors of power where her
family name carried weight. She went to the docks.
Economic Development
Recognizing her executive capabilities, she was later appointed
as Chairperson of the Board of Investments for the
Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (ARMM).
The role placed her at the center of efforts to attract economic
investment to conflict-affected areas of Mindanao, a task that
required both political acumen and the ability to project stability
and confidence to potential investors.
Institutional Contributions
Philippine National Red Cross
The defining chapter of Bai Fatima's public life was her 47-year relationship with the Philippine National Red
Cross.
Her election to the National Board of Governors of the PNRC stands as a formally verified historic milestone.
Official records, including BTA Parliament Resolution No. 214, explicitly confirmed that she was the first
Muslim woman in 30 years to be elected to that body.<ref>Bangsamoro Transition Authority Parliament. (2022).
Resolution No. 214: Honoring the Late Bai Fatima Palileo Sinsuat. Retrieved from
https://parliament.bangsamoro.gov.ph/wp-content/uploads/2022/06/AR-214-Honoring-the-late-Bai-Fatma-Palileo-
Sinsuat-for-the-Iate-BAI-FATIMA-PALILEO-SINSUAT.pdf</ref>
Her election ensured that the unique humanitarian needs of Muslim Mindanao, including communities living in or
near armed conflict, had direct representation at the highest level of national disaster response and medical policy.

PAGE 4
PRC Cotabato Chapter
Following her national stint, she served as the long-time Chairperson of the Board for the PRC Cotabato
Chapter, where she became the region's foremost authority on volunteer coordination and blood donation
programs.
Her leadership of blood program expansion efforts was so effective that it earned her national recognition from the
Office of the President in 2003.
International Humanitarian Law
She also initiated and led the IHL Core Group of the PRC, an essential body within the Red Cross framework
tasked with protecting civilian populations caught in armed conflict zones across Mindanao.
This work placed her at the intersection of humanitarian law and the lived reality of communities affected by
decades of conflict, a role few others were both willing and qualified to take on.
Recognition
Bai Fatima's decades of service drew formal recognition from both national and international humanitarian
institutions.
National Outstanding Volunteer Award (NOVA) (2003): Conferred at Malacañang Palace by the President
of the Philippines, specifically recognizing her exceptional blood program expansion under the Philippine
Red Cross.
Gold Humanitarian Service Cross (2005): One of the highest honors the Philippine Red Cross can award
to an individual, given in recognition of sustained life-saving service.
BTA Parliament Resolution No. 214 (2022): Posthumous formal recognition by the Bangsamoro
Parliament, honoring her life and legacy as a "princess for her people."
Legacy
Bai Fatima Palileo Sinsuat's legacy matters most not just as a record of offices held or awards received, but as a
model of how cultural identity and civic duty can reinforce each other.
She navigated one of the most politically complex regions in the Philippines at a time of genuine conflict and
uncertainty. She was Maguindanaon royalty in an era when that title came with both privilege and limitation. And
instead of leaning into regional divisions, she chose the politically neutral ground of humanitarianism, making
herself a trusted figure across Muslim and Christian communities alike.
Her work with the Red Cross spanning 47 years is the clearest measure of where her deepest commitments lay. Not
in the offices she was appointed to, not in the family dynasty she was born into, but in the blood donation drives,
the volunteer coordination sessions, and the quiet work of keeping humanitarian infrastructure alive in a region that
needed it desperately.
She's an enduring blueprint for what indigenous representation in civic institutions can look like: principled,
sustained, and rooted in community rather than personal ambition.
As the Bangsamoro Parliament put it in its formal resolution honoring her: she was a princess who chose to serve.
That choice, made consistently over more than half a century, is the truest measure of who she was.

PAGE 5

title: Sultan Hadji Malic Romapunut Dimakuta
text:
PAGE 1
Sultan Hadji Malic Romapunut Dimakuta

PAGE 2
The Sultan Who Chose Service Over Power A Legacy of Peace –
He Died on the Night of Power (Lailatul Qadr) And Lived Forever
in the Hearts of Marawi and the 12 IB Also known as Sapolo Ago
Dowa Ka Agama/Ingud
Sultan Hadji Malic Romapunut Dimakuta "Amai Kurot" – former
Sultan Panoroganan of Sapolo Ago Dowa Ka Ingud, Pisugodan a
Mala a Bayabao, Islamic City of Marawi.
The Sultan belonged to the noble and prominent clans of Lanao – the Romapunut and
Dimakuta families.
Known as the Sultan a Maongangun (Sultan of Wisdom), Sultan Hadji Malic Romapunut
Dimakuta was not just a leader but a true servant of peace. As a former undefeated City
Councilor of Marawi, he was a pillar of his community – a religious advisor, a mediator of
conflicts, and a public servant willing to work even in the darkest hours of the night just to
ensure peace and provide for the needs of his fellow citizens.
He also served as a Consultant to the former Governor of the Undivided Lanao, Sheikh
Hadji Alawi Mandangan Dimakuta – his cousin and closest friend.
During his term, he became an instrument of reconciliation, especially in settling rido (clan
feuds) that plagued Marawi and the whole of Lanao. His dedication was not only for his 17
barangays in Sapolo Ago Dowa Ka Agama, where he was Sultan, but for all Muslim. His
life was an offering – a sacrifice for peace.
The Great Departure – A Great Faith
On June 19, 2017, while the battle in Marawi was raging, Sultan Hadji Malic passed away
in Kayontor, Kauswagan, Lanao del Norte. But his death was not ordinary – he died on the
holiest night of Ramadan, Lailatul Qadr (the Night of Power). According to Islamic belief,
whoever dies on this night is guaranteed entry into Paradise. His family and followers
believe he was blessed with such a death – a miracle that proved his pure heart and
sincere service to God (Allah s.w.) and to his fellowmen.
His last wish was to rest beside his closest friend and cousin, Governor Sheikh Hadji Alawi
Mandangan Dimakuta, who lies in Wato Balindong. But because of the war, he was buried
beside another beloved cousin, Hadji Musa Dimakuta.
The Legacy of a True Leader

PAGE 3
Though Sultan Hadji Malic Dimakuta has passed, his legacy of peace, service, and
devotion remains alive. His children and grandchildren continue to serve the people, just
like his daughter, who became an undefeated City Councilor of Marawi, Senior Board
Member, Vice Governor, and OIC Governor of Lanao del Sur – Bae Monera Dimakuta
Macabangon (Bae a Labi sa Panoroganan o Sapolo Ago Dowa Ingud).
His life is a testament to the true meaning of being a Muslim and a leader not for power,
but for love of fellowmen and commitment to justice.
A true leader never dies he becomes a memory, a lesson, and an inspiration in every heart
of the people he served.
A tribute to a great leader of Marawi and all of Lanao del Sur. Sultan Hadji Malic
Romapunut Dimakuta "Amai Kurot"

Monadato A. Sumagayan
Engr. Monadato A. Sumagayan is a Filipino Maranao civil
engineer known for his long-standing career in international
construction and infrastructure development, particularly in Saudi
Arabia.
With more than four decades of experience in engineering, project
management, and construction supervision, his work reflects a life
shaped by discipline, sacrifice, and technical expertise.
A native of Taraka, Lanao del Sur, Sumagayan represents a
generation of Bangsamoro professionals who built careers abroad
while maintaining strong ties to their community, contributing both
technical knowledge and mentorship to fellow overseas workers.
Contents
1 Early Life and Background
2 Education
3 Professional Career
4 Major Projects
5 Institutional Affiliations

7 Current Role
8 Legacy
9 Challenges
10 See Also
Early Life and Background
Monadato A. Sumagayan was born in the municipality of Taraka,
Lanao del Sur into a modest Maranao Muslim family.
His early life was marked by simplicity and self-reliance. From a
young age, he pursued both Arabic and English education, reflecting
a balance between religious grounding and formal academic
development.
During his formative years, he supported his own education through
small income-generating efforts, demonstrating independence and determination that would later define his
professional journey.
Education
Sumagayan completed his first degree in Bachelor of Arts in Islamic (Arabic) Studies at Mindanao State
University in Marawi City in 1979.

PAGE 2
He later pursued a second degree in engineering, earning his Bachelor of Science in Civil Engineering from the
Cebu Institute of Technology in 1983.
This dual academic background, combining Islamic studies and technical training, shaped both his personal values
and professional discipline.
Professional Career
Sumagayan’s professional career spans over 40 years in the construction industry, primarily in the Kingdom of
Saudi Arabia, beginning in 1984 and continuing until 2024. :contentReference[oaicite:0]{index=0}
He held multiple roles across various construction firms, including: - Project Site Engineer and Project Manager -
Civil Inspector and Quantity Surveyor - Maintenance Supervisor - Procurement Officer and Sales Administrator -
Consultant Project Manager
His work covered both vertical and horizontal construction, ranging from residential buildings to large-scale
infrastructure projects.
He also briefly served as a Temporary Manager for a construction company in Malaysia, expanding his
international experience beyond the Middle East.
Major Projects
Throughout his career, Sumagayan contributed to numerous construction and infrastructure projects, including:
- Renovation of private villas in Jeddah - Ministry of Housing construction projects and supervision of large-scale
precast housing developments - Land development projects in Al-Khumra - Commercial developments such as
Danube Mall along Madinah Road - Palace construction and renovation projects, including works associated with
the Saudi royal family - Water and sewerage infrastructure projects in Mecca and Jeddah - High-rise buildings and
hotel construction in Mecca - Coastal and tourism infrastructure at Jeddah Touristic City (Durat Al Arous) - Road
construction, asphalt works, and camp infrastructure maintenance in Muzdalifa
These projects reflect a broad range of engineering responsibilities, from site supervision to full project
management.
Institutional Affiliations
Sumagayan is affiliated with several professional and civic organizations, including:
- Saudi Council of Engineers - American Military Engineers Association - Board of Directors, INSAN Group
(Islamia Assembly, Inc.), Lanao Chapter
He was also associated with leadership structures connected to the Moro Islamic Liberation Front (MILF) during
the time of Sheikh Salamat Hashim.

PAGE 3
Community Engagement and Advocacy
Beyond technical work, Sumagayan became known for assisting fellow Overseas Filipino Workers (OFWs),
particularly those facing unstable employment or legal difficulties.
He extended guidance and support to individuals seeking work opportunities or assistance, reflecting a personal
commitment to community welfare among Filipinos abroad.
His experience as an overseas worker informed his understanding of the challenges faced by migrant laborers,
shaping his approach to mentorship and assistance.
Current Role
Following his decades-long career abroad, Sumagayan returned to his home municipality of Taraka, where he
currently serves as a Municipal Consultant Engineer.
In this role, he contributes to local infrastructure planning and development, with a focus on improving public
works and ensuring that projects are properly managed and implemented.
His ongoing work reflects a continued commitment to applying his international experience to local development
in Lanao del Sur.
Legacy
Engr. Monadato A. Sumagayan’s career reflects a life of sustained effort in both professional and personal spheres.
His journey, from a self-supporting student to an experienced international engineer, highlights the role of
perseverance and adaptability in achieving long-term success.
His contributions lie not only in the structures he helped build, but also in the example he set for future generations
of Bangsamoro engineers and overseas professionals, emphasizing discipline, integrity, and service to community.
Challenges
Like many overseas professionals, Sumagayan’s career involved extended periods away from family, demanding
work environments, and the uncertainties of working abroad.
These challenges shaped his perspective on labor, resilience, and responsibility, reinforcing his belief in hard work
and personal integrity as foundations for success.

title: Sumndad-Usman-ss, Rohaniza
text:
PAGE 1
Rohaniza Sumndad-Usman
Bai Rohaniza Sumndad-Usman (born c. 1984), widely known and beloved as "Ate Honey," is a Filipino peace
advocate, community leader, and social entrepreneur whose life's work is rooted in a simple but powerful
conviction: that peace is something you teach, not just something you hope for.
She is the Founder and Chief Peace Mission Keeper of the Teach Peace Build Peace Movement (TPBPM) (htt
ps://tpbpm.org/), a non-profit organization dedicated to raising a generation of Filipino children and youth who
don't just know the word "peace" but actually live it.
A Maranao on her father's side, Sumndad-Usman carries the blood of traditional Nobel custodians of peace and
mediators in Mindanao. That heritage, combined with her own experience of war as a child and a lifetime spent
bridging Muslim and Christian communities, makes her one of the most authentic voices for peacebuilding in the
country today.
She has been called the "Peace Princess of the Philippines" and for good reason: from conflict zones in
Mamasapano and Marawi to digital classrooms and interfaith forums around the world, Bai Rohaniza has spent
decades turning the idea of peace into something children can hold in their hands.
Contents
1 Early Life and Background
2 Education
3 Career
3.1 Early Professional Work
3.2 Founding the Teach Peace Build Peace Movement
4 Institutional Contributions and Key Initiatives
4.1 The Peaceable Classroom Toolkit
4.2 Cyberpeace Campaign
4.3 Conflict Zone Interventions
5 Legacy
6 Recognition
7 Challenges
8 See Also
9 External Links
Early Life and Background
Bai Rohaniza Sumndad-Usman grew up at the intersection of two worlds that the Philippines often struggles to
reconcile.
Her father comes from a Maranao Muslim family with a long lineage as traditional Nobel custodians of peace and
mediators in Mindanao. That's not just a title. In Maranao society, these are the families entrusted with resolving
conflict, maintaining harmony, and carrying the community's moral weight through generations of tension and
change.

PAGE 2
Bai Rohaniza Sumndad-Usman
Born
c. 1984
Also Known
As
"Ate Honey"; "Peace
Princess"
