Award
Her mother, on the other hand, is a Catholic-born musician from
Bulacan who converted to Islam after marriage. Growing up in a
household where the Quran and hymns, the azan and the sound of a
piano, could all exist in the same space, Bai Rohaniza learned early
that difference doesn't have to mean division.
That lesson came into sharper focus during her childhood years in
Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, where her family had relocated. She was
around seven years old when the Gulf War broke out. She
remembers the sirens. She remembers the fear. And she remembers
what it felt like to be a child with no control over the violence
happening around her.
That experience didn't leave her. It shaped her. Everything she
would go on to build professionally traces back to that little girl in
Riyadh who decided, even then, that children shouldn't have to grow
up like that.
Education
Sumndad-Usman completed her secondary education in Saudi
Arabia before returning to the Philippines for college. She graduated
from Assumption College in Manila, an institution known for its
Catholic tradition and commitment to social responsibility.
For her senior thesis, she chose to write a comparative study
between Assumption (Christian) and Madrasa (Muslim)
education. Her conclusion was direct: prejudice, more often than
not, is a product of ignorance. People fear what they don't
understand.
That academic insight wasn't just theoretical for her. It confirmed
what she'd already felt growing up in a home where faith was both
diverse and unifying. And it gave her a framework she'd carry into
every peacebuilding initiative she would later create.
Career
Early Professional Work
Before founding her own movement, Sumndad-Usman cut her teeth
in public service and civil society work. She started her career at the
Office of the Presidential Assistant for Youth Affairs, where she
got her first real exposure to policy-level thinking about young
Filipinos.
She later moved into the international arena as the Philippine
Country Director for the Asia America Initiative (AAI), a US-
based organization focused on people-to-people diplomacy and

PAGE 3
post-conflict recovery in the Philippines. In that role, she established the "Catalysts for Peace" children's arm,
which became an early proof-of-concept for her belief that peace education works best when it reaches children
directly and in ways they actually enjoy.
Founding the Teach Peace Build Peace Movement
In 2013, she took the leap and founded the Teach Peace Build Peace Movement (TPBPM).
The organization's mission is as straightforward as it is ambitious: "Make Every Filipino Child and Youth a
Peace Hero."
The TPBPM doesn't teach peace by lecturing at children. Instead, it uses what Bai Rohaniza calls the Peace Heroes
Formation Program, a methodology built on music, arts, games, and sports to bring concepts like conflict
resolution, empathy, and mindfulness to life in classrooms and communities.
The idea is that peace isn't abstract. It's a skill. And like any skill, it's best learned through practice.
Institutional Contributions and Key Initiatives
The Peaceable Classroom Toolkit
One of TPBPM's most practical contributions is the development of the Peaceable Classroom Toolkit, a structured
resource designed to help teachers integrate peace education into their daily lessons. Rather than adding a separate
"peace subject" to an already crowded curriculum, the toolkit gives educators the tools to weave peacebuilding into
what they're already teaching.
Cyberpeace Campaign
Recognizing that today's children live as much online as they do offline, Sumndad-Usman partnered with Google
Philippines on a Cyberpeace Campaign focused on digital citizenship and online kindness. The campaign
acknowledged that the same skills needed to resolve conflicts in a classroom, listening, empathy, restraint, are the
same skills needed to navigate social media without causing harm.
Conflict Zone Interventions
Perhaps the most emotionally significant dimension of TPBPM's work is its direct presence in conflict-affected
areas. The movement has brought psychosocial support and peace education to communities in Mamasapano
and Marawi, two places that carry deep wounds from violence and displacement. In these settings, the work isn't
just educational. It's healing.
Legacy
Bai Rohaniza Sumndad-Usman has built something genuinely rare: a peacebuilding movement that operates at the
level of the individual child while aspiring to reshape an entire nation's culture.

PAGE 4
What makes her work sustainable is that it doesn't depend on political goodwill or government budgets. It's planted
inside schools, inside communities, inside the habits of teachers and students who have internalized its principles.
The TPBPM has reached children across the Philippines, including in some of the country's most fractured
communities, and its methodology has gained international recognition as a model worth studying.
Beyond the programs and the awards, her legacy is also deeply personal. She is a Maranao woman who grew up
between cultures, survived the psychological weight of wartime as a child, and chose to spend her adult life making
sure other children don't carry that same weight. That's not a career. That's a calling.
Recognition
Bai Rohaniza's work has been recognized by both national and international bodies across her career:
Ashoka Fellow (2018): One of the most prestigious honors in the social entrepreneurship world. She was
inducted into Ashoka's global network, which recognizes individuals with innovative solutions to social
problems.
N-Peace Award (2013): Awarded by the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP), which named
her an "Emerging Peace Champion" in the region.
Doha International Center for Interfaith Dialogue (DICID) Award: She was the first Filipino to be
recognized by this Qatar-based institution for her contributions to interfaith tolerance and understanding.
Tatler Asia's Gen.T (https://www.tatlerasia.com/people/bai-rohaniza-sumndad-usman) (2020): Listed
among the "Leaders of Tomorrow" in the categories of philanthropy and public service.
TOWNS Awardee: Honored by The Outstanding Women in the Nation's Service for her contributions to
education and community development.
Challenges
Working for peace in the Philippines, particularly in Mindanao, has never been a clean or comfortable undertaking.
Bai Rohaniza has had to carry her programs into communities still raw from conflict, navigate the skepticism of
those who see peacebuilding as naive, and sustain a non-profit movement in a funding environment that doesn't
always reward long-term, values-based work.
Her background as a Muslim woman working across religious and ethnic lines has also meant operating in spaces
where she is simultaneously an insider and an outsider. That position carries its own kind of weight, but it's also,
arguably, what makes her a credible bridge builder in both directions.

Aliah Badio Sumpingan
Aliah Badio Sumpingan, LPT, MAFIL(CAR) is a Filipino educator, published author, and public servant from
Taraka, Lanao del Sur, known for her dedication to education, youth empowerment, and community development
in Muslim Mindanao. A licensed professional teacher and emerging scholar in Filipino language and literature, she
represents a generation of Meranaw educators who bridge traditional values with modern pedagogy, shaping
learners while advancing social welfare initiatives across government and civic sectors.
Contents
1 Early Life and Background
2 Education and Professional Qualifications
3 Literary and Editorial Contributions
4 Teaching Career

Early Life and Background
Aliah Badio Sumpingan was born and raised in Taraka, a
municipality in Lanao del Sur, within the Bangsamoro
Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao. Growing up in a region
deeply rooted in Islamic traditions and Meranaw culture, she
developed an early appreciation for language, education, and
community service. Her formative years in Taraka exposed her to
both the challenges and richness of life in Muslim Mindanao,
shaping her commitment to educational access and youth
empowerment in underserved communities.
Her upbringing in Lanao del Sur instilled in her a strong sense of
cultural identity and social responsibility, values that would later
define her career as an educator and public servant. The linguistic
diversity of the region—where Maguindanaon, Meranaw, and
Filipino languages intersect—sparked her passion for Filipino
language education and literary expression.

PAGE 2
Education and Professional Qualifications
Sumpingan earned her Bachelor of Arts in Filipino from Mindanao State University (MSU), one of the premier
institutions in Mindanao for language and cultural studies. Her undergraduate education provided a solid
foundation in Filipino linguistics, literature, and pedagogy, equipping her with the academic rigor necessary for a
career in teaching and scholarship.
Building on her undergraduate achievements, she is currently pursuing a Master of Arts in Filipino at MSU,
demonstrating her commitment to continuous learning and professional growth. Her graduate studies focus on
advancing her expertise in language education, literary analysis, and curriculum development, positioning her as an
emerging scholar in Filipino studies.
Beyond her academic degrees, Sumpingan holds several professional qualifications that enhance her teaching
practice and public service capacity. She successfully passed the Licensure Examination for Professional
Teachers (LET), earning her LPT credential and affirming her status as a qualified professional educator in the
Philippines. Additionally, she is a licensed and duly registered National Publisher, a distinction that recognizes
her contributions to the publishing industry.
Her professional development also includes specialized training in Technical Education and Skills Development
under the Ministry of Basic, Higher, and Technical Education (MBHTE), along with basic computer literacy
training. These certifications have equipped her with practical skills in educational technology and technical
instruction, essential competencies for modern teaching and public administration.
Literary and Editorial Contributions
Sumpingan is a published author and active member of the literary community. Her book, Echos of Expression,
showcases her creative writing and reflects her engagement with contemporary Filipino literature. The work
demonstrates her ability to articulate experiences and perspectives rooted in Mindanao's cultural landscape,
contributing to the broader discourse on regional literature in the Philippines.
She also serves as a member of the Editorial Board of Lakbay Diwa Publishing, a role that involves curating and
shaping literary content, mentoring emerging writers, and promoting Filipino-language publications. Her editorial
work bridges her academic expertise in Filipino literature with practical contributions to the publishing industry,
supporting the dissemination of culturally relevant educational and literary materials.
Through her dual roles as author and editor, Sumpingan actively participates in the production and circulation of
Filipino literary works, particularly those that center Mindanao voices and narratives often underrepresented in
mainstream Philippine literature.
Teaching Career
Sumpingan's primary professional identity is that of an educator. She currently serves as a full-time teacher at Bae
Cacasi Macasalong Al-Islamiyah Inc., an Islamic educational institution where she actively shapes the academic
and moral development of learners. Her role in a faith-based school reflects her commitment to culturally
responsive pedagogy that integrates Islamic values with national curriculum standards.
Her teaching philosophy emphasizes student-centered learning, critical thinking, and the preservation of cultural
heritage through language education. She has taught students across various grade levels, adapting her instructional
strategies to meet diverse learning needs while maintaining high academic standards.

PAGE 3
Beyond her full-time position, Sumpingan has held multiple teaching roles throughout her career. She previously
worked as a college instructor at Tamparan Pupolace Islamic Inc., where she taught Filipino language courses
and contributed to higher education in the region. She also served as a substitute teacher at Aba Al-Khail
Computer College Foundation, demonstrating her versatility across different educational contexts and her
willingness to support institutions in need of qualified instructors.
Her combined experience in secondary, tertiary, and technical education institutions has given her a comprehensive
understanding of the Philippine educational landscape, particularly within Islamic and community-based schools
that serve Bangsamoro learners.
Public Service and Government Work
Sumpingan's commitment to public service extends beyond the classroom into active participation in government
programs aimed at social welfare and national development. She has worked with multiple government agencies,
contributing her skills to data collection, social assistance validation, and community welfare initiatives.
She served as a PhilSys Operator and Field Enumerator for the Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA), playing
a crucial role in the implementation of the Philippine Identification System (PhilSys), the country's national ID
program. As a field enumerator, she facilitated the registration process for community members, ensuring accurate
data collection and proper documentation—work that directly supports national statistics and evidence-based
policymaking.
Additionally, Sumpingan worked as a Validator for the Department of Social Welfare and Development
(DSWD), a position that required her to verify the eligibility of beneficiaries for social assistance programs. Her
role as a validator involved conducting home visits, assessing household conditions, and ensuring that government
aid reached the most vulnerable populations. This work demanded both administrative precision and compassionate
community engagement, skills Sumpingan brought to the task with dedication.
She also volunteered at the Provincial Social Welfare and Development Office (PSWDO), contributing her time
and expertise to support welfare programs at the provincial level. Her volunteer work demonstrated her genuine
commitment to community service beyond professional obligations, reinforcing her role as a civic-minded public
servant.
Her government service reflects a practical engagement with social development challenges in Mindanao, where
poverty, displacement, and limited access to services remain pressing issues. Through her work with PSA, DSWD,
and PSWDO, Sumpingan contributed to programs designed to strengthen social safety nets and improve the lives
of marginalized communities.
Youth Leadership and Civic Engagement
Sumpingan is an active participant in youth empowerment and civic organizations, channeling her leadership skills
into movements that advance social change and community development. Her affiliations with multiple youth-
focused groups highlight her belief in the transformative potential of organized collective action.
She is a member of the Coalition Moro Youth Movement, an organization that advocates for the rights, interests,
and development of Moro youth across Mindanao. The coalition works to amplify youth voices in political
discourse, promote educational opportunities, and address issues affecting young Muslims in the Philippines.

PAGE 4
Sumpingan is also affiliated with the Youth Leadership Summit Lanao del Sur Chapter, a platform for
leadership training, capacity-building, and civic engagement among young people in the province. Through this
organization, she participates in programs that develop leadership competencies, foster civic consciousness, and
prepare youth for active participation in democratic processes.
Additionally, she is a member of Salianti Maguing Youth Changemakers, a group dedicated to empowering
young people in Lanao del Sur to become agents of positive change in their communities. The organization focuses
on social entrepreneurship, community organizing, and youth-led development initiatives, areas where Sumpingan
contributes both as a participant and mentor.
Her involvement in these organizations reflects a deep commitment to youth empowerment as a pathway to broader
social transformation. By engaging with youth movements, Sumpingan not only contributes her own skills and
perspectives but also helps build the next generation of leaders in Muslim Mindanao.
Corporate and Administrative Experience
Beyond education and government service, Sumpingan has also gained experience in the private sector. She served
as Secretary of Best-Fam Marketing Corporation in Cebu City, a role that required administrative competence,
organizational skills, and the ability to manage corporate documentation and communications.
Her work in the corporate sector provided her with a different perspective on professional practice, exposing her to
business operations, client relations, and organizational management. This experience complements her public
service and educational work, giving her a well-rounded skill set applicable across multiple sectors.
Legacy and Continuing Impact
Aliah Badio Sumpingan represents a model of multi-dimensional public service rooted in education, civic
engagement, and community empowerment. Her career trajectory reflects a conscious choice to invest her talents
in institutions and initiatives that serve the most vulnerable and underserved populations in Muslim Mindanao.
As an educator, she contributes to the intellectual and moral formation of young learners in Islamic schools,
ensuring that education remains culturally relevant and academically rigorous. As a government worker, she
supports social welfare programs that address poverty and inequality. As a youth advocate, she mentors emerging
leaders and participates in movements for social change.
Her literary contributions through Echos of Expression and her editorial work with Lakbay Diwa Publishing add
another dimension to her impact, ensuring that Meranaw and Bangsamoro perspectives are represented in Filipino
literature. Her ongoing graduate studies at MSU signal her commitment to lifelong learning and her aspiration to
contribute to Filipino language scholarship at the highest levels.
Sumpingan's work is particularly significant in the context of Muslim Mindanao, where education and public
service are often challenged by limited resources, conflict, and historical marginalization. Her ability to navigate
multiple sectors—education, government, civil society, and publishing—demonstrates resilience, adaptability, and
a profound sense of mission.

PAGE 5
Recognition and Professional Standing
While Sumpingan's work is characterized more by grassroots impact than by formal accolades, her professional
credentials and affiliations speak to her standing in the fields of education and public service. Her licensure as a
professional teacher, registration as a national publisher, and active membership in editorial and civic organizations
establish her as a credible and respected figure in her communities of practice.
Her participation in youth summits, civic coalitions, and educational institutions positions her within networks of
educators and advocates working to advance the Bangsamoro cause and improve social conditions in Mindanao.
These affiliations, while not formal awards, represent meaningful recognition of her leadership and contributions
by peers and communities.
Challenges and Future Directions
Like many educators and public servants in Mindanao, Sumpingan faces challenges inherent to working in
conflict-affected and resource-constrained environments. The educational institutions she serves often operate with
limited budgets, infrastructure gaps, and competing demands. Government agencies in the region contend with
bureaucratic constraints and implementation challenges that can hinder the effectiveness of social programs.
Despite these obstacles, Sumpingan continues to pursue her work with dedication and optimism. Her enrollment in
graduate studies suggests a trajectory toward greater academic and professional leadership, potentially expanding
her impact through research, policy advocacy, or advanced educational administration.
Her future contributions may include more formal scholarly publications in Filipino studies, leadership roles in
educational institutions, or deeper engagement with policy initiatives related to Bangsamoro education and social
development. Whatever path she chooses, her track record suggests a continued commitment to service,
scholarship, and social transformation.

text:

Ali Macapado Tabao

Maranao

Ali Macapado Tabao
Engr. Ali M. Tabao is a name that quietly carries a lot of weight in
Marawi City's public service circles, and once you look at his record,
it's easy to see why. He has spent more than four decades working
inside the government agencies devoted to Muslim Filipino affairs,
and in 2026 that long climb reached its peak when President
Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr. appointed him Regional Director of the
National Commission on Muslim Filipinos (NCMF) Marawi
Regional Office. That kind of tenure is rare anywhere, and it says
something about a man who built his entire working life around one
mission: serving his own community from the inside.
Contents
1 Early Life and Family
2 Education
3 Civil Engineering License
4 Career in Public Service
5 Civic and Professional Involvement
6 Training and Continuing Development
7 Personal Standing
8 References
Early Life and Family
Ali Macapado Tabao was born on October 2, 1963, in Marawi City,
and he has never really left. His residential and permanent address
both trace back to the same neighborhood in Marawi, a detail that fits
a man who has stayed rooted in the place where he grew up. He is
Maranao, a Filipino citizen, and married to Farnaida Tanggol Tabao
(rahimahallah), who runs her own business out of Saduc, Marawi
City. Together they raised five children, several of whom are now
adults building their own paths: Tasneem, Ameer Fahad,
Mohammad Ali, Taheema Najmus Sahar, and Neezam, all
carrying the Tanggol Tabao name. His parents were Mustapha Karic
Tabao and Zainab Macapado Tabao, and it's worth noting that Ali's
own record traces cleanly back to a Marawi household that valued
both faith and hard work.
Education
Ali's schooling followed a path familiar to many Maranao
professionals of his generation: local roots first, then Manila for the
technical training. He attended Camp Keitly Elementary School from
1969 to 1974, then moved on to Lanao National College of Arts and

PAGE 2
Tasneem; Ameer Fahad, Mohammad Ali;
Taheema Najmus Sahar; Neezam.
Parents
Mustapha Karic Tabao (father)
Zainab Macapado Tabao (mother)
Affiliations
Philippine Institute of Civil Engineers
Marawi Tennis Club
Marawi Association of Motorists Group
Achievers Badminton Club
Notability
One of the longest-serving career officers
in the National Commission on Muslim
Filipinos, having risen from casual
Engineer Aide to Regional Director over
four decades, an appointment made by
President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr. in 2026
that capped a career spent almost entirely
within the agency tasked with Muslim
Filipino affairs.
Known For
Steering technical and community
programs out of the NCMF Marawi
Regional Office, including Hajj
coordination, Halal awareness, cooperative
development, and Islamic finance training,
while keeping his civil engineering license
active and in good standing throughout his
public service career.
Pull Quote
"Forty years in the same house of service,
one engineer who never stopped showing
up for Marawi."
Trade for his secondary education, finishing in 1979. From there he
headed to Manuel L. Quezon University, where he earned his
Bachelor of Science in Civil Engineering, graduating in 1985. No
honors or scholarships are noted for either stage of his schooling, but
the degree itself set the stage for everything that came after.
Civil Engineering License
The same year he graduated, Ali sat for the Civil Engineering Board
Examination, passing it on May 1, 1985, at Far Eastern University
with a rating of 70.50 percent. He holds Professional Regulation
Commission license number 042953-96, and he has kept that license
active for decades, a detail that matters because it shows he never let
go of his engineering identity even as his government career pulled
him deeper into administrative and community work.
Career in Public Service
Ali's government career began in 1984 as a casual Engineer Aide at
the Department of Public Works and Highways, earning a modest
990 pesos a month. By August 1986 he had moved to the Office on
Muslim Affairs, taking on the role of Development Management
Officer II under a temporary appointment. He was promoted to
Senior Development Management Officer in 1987, and by July 1989
he had settled into the position he would hold, in one form or
another, for the rest of his career: Development Management Officer
III.
That position carried him through the agency's transformation from
the old Office on Muslim Affairs into the National Commission on
Muslim Filipinos, and his salary records trace a steady, uninterrupted
climb from 5,670 pesos a month in 1989 to over 55,000 pesos a
month by 2025, all under Salary Grade 18. What stands out isn't just the length of service but the consistency of it:
no gaps, no resignations, no breaks in the record, just one continuous thread of public service stretching back to the
mid-1980s.
That thread reached a new milestone in 2026, when President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr. appointed him Regional
Director of the NCMF Marawi Regional Office, elevating him from the Development Management Officer III
post he had held since 1989. In this expanded role, his work continues to touch programs that matter deeply to the
Maranao and broader Muslim Filipino community, from Hajj coordination to Halal certification awareness to
cooperative development, now carried out under his direct regional leadership.
Civic and Professional Involvement
Outside his government post, Ali has stayed active in a handful of organizations that reflect both his professional
identity and his personal interests. He has been a member of the Philippine Institute of Civil Engineers since June
8, 1985, keeping that connection alive for essentially his entire career. He also belongs to the Marawi Tennis Club
(since 1996), the Marawi Association of Motorists Group (since 2001), and the Achievers Badminton Club (since

PAGE 3
2008), memberships that hint at a man who balances desk work with an active lifestyle. His hobbies, by his own
account, include tennis, badminton, and basketball, alongside basic computer literacy, a useful skill for a civil
servant navigating decades of shifting office technology.
Training and Continuing Development
Few civil servants can point to a training record as dense as Ali's. Across the past two decades alone, his Personal
Data Sheet lists dozens of seminars, workshops, and conventions, ranging from technical civil engineering
conferences with PICE to NCMF-run programs on Islamic finance, Halal awareness, cooperative fundamentals,
disaster preparedness, and peacebuilding. Recent entries include the 2025 Hajj Awareness Program in January 2025
and the 50th Philippine Institute of Civil Engineers National Convention in October 2024, both attended just
months before his Personal Data Sheet was signed. Earlier entries stretch back through pandemic-era webinars on
CSC rules and mental health support, community legal education programs, and sessions on preventing and
countering violent extremism, a training history that reads almost like a timeline of what mattered most to Muslim
Filipino communities over the past several years.
Personal Standing
According to his own disclosures, Ali has never faced an administrative case, a criminal charge, or a conviction of
any kind, and he has never been separated from government service through resignation, dismissal, or similar
means. He has also never run for national or local elective office outside of barangay-level contests, keeping his
record squarely on the civil service side of Philippine public life.
Taken together, the record paints a picture of a Maranao professional who chose one lane early in life, civil
engineering in service of Muslim Filipino affairs, and stayed in it for more than forty years without wavering, a
patience that was rewarded in 2026 with his appointment as Regional Director. That kind of quiet, sustained
commitment doesn't always make headlines, but it's exactly the sort of career that keeps institutions like NCMF
running in places like Marawi.

2025.

President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr., 2026 (editorial update, supplementary to the 2025 Personal Data Sheet).

Abdul Hannan M. Tago
Abdul Hannan Magarang Tago (also referred to as Dr. Abdul
Hannan M. Tago) is a Filipino journalist, diplomat, government
official, and religious scholar from Muslim Mindanao whose career
has stretched across more than three decades and three continents. He
is best known for his twenty-five years as a senior correspondent and
bureau chief at Arab News, the leading English-language daily in
Saudi Arabia, where he covered everything from oil markets and
diplomatic summits to the grinding legal struggles of Filipino migrant
workers far from home. For many in the Filipino diaspora in the
Gulf, he was the journalist who actually showed up, who could write
in Arabic and speak to Saudi officials in their own idiom, and who
used that access to fight for people who had no other advocate. That
is probably the most accurate single-sentence summary of his legacy:
a Filipino from Muslim Mindanao who earned a seat at every table
that mattered, and then used it.

Early Life and Formation
The biographical record does not provide a specific birthdate for Abdul Hannan Tago in any publicly available
source, but his educational timeline places his birth in the late 1950s or early 1960s, likely in Mindanao. What is
clear is that his formation was deeply shaped by the southern Philippine Muslim world, and that he chose, at a
young age, to pursue his intellectual development not in Manila but in Cairo, the gravitational center of Sunni
scholarship for over a millennium.<ref name="bfbci">Bangsa Moro Federal Business Council, Inc. — Officer
Profile: Dr. Abdul Hannan M. Tago. Accessed March 11, 2026. http://bfbci.com/338-2/</ref>
Education
Al-Azhar University, Cairo
Tago spent eight years in Egypt, completing his undergraduate studies at Al-Azhar University, the oldest
continuously operating institution of higher learning in the Islamic world.<ref name="azhar">Eccel, A. C. (1984).
Egypt, Islam and Social Change: Al-Azhar in Conflict and Accommodation. Klaus Schwarz Verlag. See also: Al-
Azhar University official website, https://www.azhar.eg/en/</ref> Al-Azhar was not simply a place to study
theology. It was an immersive environment where students were expected to develop a working command of
Fusha, the classical literary Arabic of the Quran and of formal public life, and Tago's command of that idiom was
thorough enough that he would later publish original opinion pieces in major pan-Arab newspapers without a
translator. That was an achievement virtually unmatched among Filipino professionals anywhere in the Arab world.
<ref name="bfbci" />
Al-Azhar also transmitted a philosophical orientation that would characterize Tago's entire public career. The
university has long been the institutional home of Wasatiyyah, usually translated as the "Middle Way" or "Way of
Moderation," which frames Islamic practice as inherently balanced, rejecting extremism and embracing tolerance,
gradualism, and honest engagement with the world as it actually is.<ref name="mwl">Remarks by Dr. Abdul
Hannan Magarang Tago at the Global Conference for Building Bridges between Islamic Schools of Thought and
Sects, Makkah, March 2024. Muslim World League. https://themwl.org/en/node/40141</ref> That framework
appears repeatedly in Tago's speeches, writings, and public positions, from labor disputes in the Gulf to land reform
debates in Mindanao.
Arab League Institution: Political Science
Alongside his theological training, Tago pursued a Master of Arts in Political Science at the Arab League
Institution in Cairo.<ref name="ofwempowerment">OFW Empowerment, author profile page. Accessed March 11,
2026. https://ofwempowerment.wordpress.com/author/ofwempowerment/page/27/</ref> The combination was
deliberate. He wanted to understand the Arab world not only through faith but through the hard mechanics of
governance, diplomatic protocol, and geopolitical calculation. Studying in Cairo during the aftermath of the Camp

PAGE 3
David Accords and the reverberations of the Iranian Revolution meant he was receiving a live education in how
ideology and statecraft interact in the Middle East. Years later, when he was reporting on multilateral summits or
negotiating with Saudi ministry officials over the fate of detained Filipino workers, that dual formation would
cease to be mere background and become, as one account described it, "professional infrastructure."
Career
Arab News: Twenty-Five Years at the Heart of the Kingdom
Tago joined Arab News, the flagship English-language daily of the Saudi Research and Marketing Group (SRMG),
in 1992 and remained with the organization for twenty-five years, eventually rising to Riyadh Bureau Chief.<ref
name="bfbci" /> His tenure there bracketed an era of enormous change in Saudi Arabia: the aftermath of the Gulf
War, the Kingdom's gradual opening to foreign investment, the early emergence of social media, and the first
articulations of what would become Vision 2030. He covered all of it, and he covered it from a vantage point no
other Filipino journalist in the Kingdom was positioned to occupy.
Economic and Financial Reporting
A substantial portion of Tago's journalism concerned the economic machinery that drives Saudi Arabia. He
provided coverage of the landmark merger between Vela International Marine, the shipping arm of Saudi Aramco,
and the National Shipping Company of Saudi Arabia (Bahri), a consolidation that created one of the world's largest
shipping companies.<ref name="aramco">Energy to the World: The Story of Aramco (History Book, English
Edition). Aramco Life Publications. https://www.aramcolife.com/-/media/aramco-life/publications/history-
books/history-book-english-v-2.pdf</ref> He also held a concurrent posting with the Saudi Capital Market
Authority's Media and Investment Awareness Department, which required him to translate complex financial
regulations for a general readership and deepened his expertise in Islamic finance.<ref name="bfbci" />
The ASPA Summit and Diplomatic Reporting
One of the more consequential assignments of his journalistic career was his coverage of the Arab-South American
Countries (ASPA) summit in Riyadh, which brought together heads of state and ministers from two continents to
advance a framework of South-South economic cooperation.<ref name="arabnews_aspa">Arab News. "Draft
Declaration Calls for an Arab Defense Force." Riyadh, November 2015.
https://www.arabnews.com/featured/news/833271</ref> His reporting on the summit, including coverage of
proposals for a collective Arab defense posture and the sharp rise in inter-regional trade, demonstrated a grasp of
multilateral diplomacy that went well beyond standard foreign correspondence. For many Filipino readers of Arab
News, his analysis of these events was their primary window onto the geopolitics shaping the world around them.
Social Policy and Legal Reporting
Tago was equally attentive to the domestic social landscape of Saudi Arabia. He reported on the codification of
penalties for online defamation under Saudi cybercrime law,<ref name="arabnews_defam">Arab News.
"SR500,000 Fine, One-Year Jail for Defamation on Social Media." October 2015.
https://www.arabnews.com/node/823871/</ref> and produced nuanced accounts of social practices such as Misyar,
a legally recognized marriage arrangement in which certain conventional cohabitation obligations are waived,
interviewing scholars and practitioners to keep his reporting both accurate and contextually grounded.<ref
name="arabnews_misyar">Arab News. "Misyar Now a Widespread Reality." Riyadh.

PAGE 4
https://www.arabnews.com/node/642991/</ref> This kind of journalism required someone who could move
comfortably between the world of classical Islamic jurisprudence and the realities of contemporary Saudi social
life. His Cairo formation made him unusually well-suited for it.
Advocating for Overseas Filipino Workers
The dimension of Tago's work that earned him the most enduring recognition within the Filipino community was
not his coverage of summits or stock markets. It was his sustained advocacy for Overseas Filipino Workers
(OFWs) caught in the Kingdom's legal system. The label "journalistic hero," applied to him in the Filipino
community press, captures something genuine about the role he played during moments when formal diplomatic
channels were either slow to respond or had exhausted their options.<ref name="illustrado">Illustrado Life. "Most
Influential Filipinos in the Gulf: Dr. Abdul Hannan Tago — Thoughtleader." November 9, 2015.
http://illustradolife.com/most-influential-filipinos-gulf-dr-abdul-hannan-tago-thoughtleader/</ref>
The Rodelio Lanuza Case
The most widely cited instance of his OFW advocacy was his persistent coverage of the case of Rodelio Celestino
"Dondon" Lanuza, a Filipino worker who had been imprisoned in a Dammam jail since 2000, convicted of killing a
Saudi national and sentenced to death by beheading.<ref name="arabnews_lanuza">Arab News. "Death Row
Filipino Pleads for Release." https://www.arabnews.com/node/452474/amp</ref> By the time Tago's Arab News
reporting reached its most intensive phase, Lanuza had already spent roughly thirteen years on death row.
The aggrieved Saudi family had, after years of negotiation, agreed to accept diya (blood money) as the basis for
granting forgiveness. A portion of the required amount, SR 3 million in total, had been raised through Filipino
community fundraising and diplomatic pressure; the remainder was ultimately covered by a directive from the late
King King Abdullah.<ref name="arabnews_bloodmoney">Arab News. "Part Blood Money Paid by KSA Spares
Filipino from Death." https://www.arabnews.com/saudi-arabia/part-blood-money-paid-ksa-spares-filipino-
death</ref> But even after those financial arrangements were in place, Lanuza remained in custody because the
Dammam High Court had not yet scheduled the hearing required to formalize his release.
It was during this standstill that Tago's reporting proved most valuable. By keeping the case before the public,
quoting Lanuza's own words from his prison cell, documenting the embassy's repeated follow-ups with the Saudi
Reconciliation Committee, and naming the specific court responsible for the delay, he created a record that
functioned simultaneously as a news report, a human document, and a form of measured institutional pressure.<ref
name="arabnews_lanuza" /> Lanuza was ultimately released in September 2013 and arrived in Manila to a
community reception that reflected how deeply his case had resonated.<ref name="gma">GMA News Online.
"From Saudi Death Row to Home: Pardoned OFW Lanuza Back in PHL After 13 Years." September 19, 2013.
https://www.gmanetwork.com/news/pinoyabroad/dispatch/327199</ref> His written thanks to Arab News upon his
release acknowledged, implicitly, the role that sustained press attention had played in his eventual freedom.
Labor Standards and Systemic Advocacy
Beyond individual cases, Tago consistently used his platform to advocate for systemic improvements in the
conditions governing Filipino and other migrant workers in Saudi Arabia. He publicized the Saudi Ministry of
Labor's directive prohibiting outdoor work between noon and 3 p.m. during summer months, a regulation with
direct life-safety implications for the hundreds of thousands of laborers working on construction sites across the
Kingdom.<ref name="arabnews_sun">Arab News. "Laborers Shielded from Sun; Ministry to Enforce Reduced
Ramadan Hours." https://www.arabnews.com/featured/news/762211</ref>

PAGE 5
As a representative of Migrant Middle East, he also made formal representations to the Council of Saudi Chambers
opposing a proposed two-year re-entry ban on expatriate workers who had departed the Kingdom on final-exit
visas, arguing with considerable economic logic that such restrictions would ultimately undermine Saudi Arabia's
own interest in maintaining a flexible and skilled labor supply.<ref name="carpediem">CARPE DIEM — Seize
the Moment. Blog of Abdul Hannan M. Tago. Accessed March 11, 2026. https://dars0357.wordpress.com/</ref>
This advocacy was characteristically Tago: framed not as confrontation but as an appeal to shared interest, and
grounded in a detailed understanding of the regulatory architecture he was asking authorities to reconsider.
Return to Government Service
Tago's return to the Philippines marked a transition from journalism to policy, but the concerns that had animated
his Saudi career remained precisely the concerns that shaped his government work.
Philippine Economic Zone Authority
In April 2017, he was appointed Special Adviser to the Director General of the Philippine Economic Zone
Authority (PEZA) for the Middle East, tasked with promoting Philippine economic zones to investors in the Gulf
Cooperation Council.<ref name="bfbci" /> His existing network of business and government contacts in Saudi
Arabia, built over two and a half decades, made him effective in this role from the outset. He understood not only
the formal mechanisms of Saudi investment but the informal relational dimensions: the importance of trust,
personal endorsement, and framing the Philippine investment environment in language that resonated with Gulf
entrepreneurs.
National Commission on Muslim Filipinos
As Executive Assistant IV at the National Commission on Muslim Filipinos (NCMF), Tago served as a key liaison
between the Philippine government and Saudi authorities on matters involving the Filipino Muslim community.
<ref name="arabnews_ofw">Arab News. "Saudi Arabia, Philippines Agree to Resume Deployment of Filipino
Workers." 2022. https://www.arabnews.com/node/2161686/saudi-arabia</ref> His most practically important
responsibility in this role was coordinating the annual Hajj pilgrimage for thousands of Filipino Muslims traveling
to Makkah and Madinah, a logistically demanding task that required ongoing negotiation with the Saudi Ministry
of Hajj and Umrah over quotas, accommodation, and welfare services.
In 2022, when Saudi Arabia and the Philippines moved to resume the deployment of Filipino workers following a
period of restrictions, Tago provided public commentary that helped frame the resumption within its proper
historical context. He noted that the bilateral labor relationship was already five decades old, and that the Filipino
workforce in the Kingdom, including skilled professionals in medicine, engineering, and technology, represented
far more than a source of domestic help.<ref name="arabnews_ofw" />
Department of Agrarian Reform
As a former Undersecretary of the Department of Agrarian Reform (DAR), Tago brought to that agency an unusual
sensitivity to the intersection between land rights and Muslim customary law in Mindanao. He advocated
consistently for an approach to agrarian reform that looked beyond simple land redistribution to address the deeper
structural drivers of rural poverty, including the land displacement caused by large-scale extractive industries.<ref
name="carpediem" /> He was particularly attentive to the rights of women smallholders and to the need to ensure
that adjudication processes respected the parallel legal frameworks governing land use in Muslim communities.
<ref name="carpediem" /> His conviction was that genuine agrarian reform in the Bangsamoro could only succeed
if it was culturally literate, and if it understood that land in Mindanao carries meanings and obligations that do not

PAGE 6
always translate cleanly into the categories of the Comprehensive Agrarian Reform Program.<ref
name="pmt">Philippine Muslim Today, Vol. III, No. 44. Issuu. https://issuu.com/philippinemuslimtoday/docs/pmt-
iii-44</ref>
Bangsamoro Economic Development
Bangsa Moro Federal Business Council, Inc.
As Executive Director of the Bangsa Moro Federal Business Council, Inc. (BFBCI), Tago has been the primary
architect of the region's international economic outreach strategy.<ref name="bfbci" /> The BFBCI functions as a
bridge between Moro entrepreneurs and the broader Islamic investment world, particularly the capital-rich Gulf
states. He was instrumental in organizing events designed to showcase the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in
Muslim Mindanao (BARMM) as a credible investment destination, including the first Bangsamoro Global
Economic Summit, and in making the case that the region's agricultural resources, renewable energy potential, and
Halal services sector represent a seriously underexplored opportunity for Gulf capital.
The logic underlying his BFBCI strategy is straightforward: the Bangsamoro region possesses natural endowments
and a young population that could support a thriving economy, but it requires the connective tissue of institutional
infrastructure — business councils, regulatory frameworks, financial services — to translate those endowments
into productive activity. He has spent the better part of two decades trying to build that connective tissue.
Al-Amanah Islamic Investment Bank
Tago's most direct contribution to financial infrastructure in the Bangsamoro was his service as a Member and Vice
Chairman of the Board of Directors of Al-Amanah Islamic Investment Bank of the Philippines.<ref name="bfbci"
/> Al-Amanah holds a unique position in Philippine financial history: it is the only bank in the country authorized
to offer Islamic banking products, and its geographic footprint is centered on the Muslim communities of
Mindanao where conventional interest-based banking conflicts with religious practice.<ref name="amanah">Al-
Amanah Islamic Investment Bank of the Philippines — Overview. Scribd Presentation.
https://www.scribd.com/presentation/452710933/Phil-amanah-Bank-pptx</ref>
His experience with the Saudi Capital Market Authority gave him a working knowledge of how Islamic financial
products are structured and regulated in a context where they represent the mainstream, not the exception.<ref
name="bfbci" /> Bringing that experience to Al-Amanah's board meant advocating for product designs and
governance standards that could make the bank a genuinely functional partner for Bangsamoro entrepreneurs,
capable of providing Sharia-compliant financing that would allow small and medium businesses to access capital
without compromising their religious principles.
Religious and Interfaith Leadership
Ulama Supreme Council of the Philippines
As President of the Ulama Supreme Council of the Philippines for Peace and Development, Tago has positioned
religious scholarship as an active participant in, rather than a passive observer of, the Bangsamoro region's
transformation.<ref name="mwl" />

PAGE 7
Makkah Conference, 2024
In March 2024, he represented the Philippines at the Global Conference for Building Bridges between Islamic
Schools of Thought and Sects, held in Makkah under the auspices of the Muslim World League.<ref name="mwl"
/> His remarks centered on what he described as the divine intentionality of human diversity, grounding in Quranic
hermeneutics the argument that differences of interpretation and practice among Muslims are features rather than
flaws of the tradition. They should be navigated with curiosity and respect, not suppressed through enforced
uniformity.
The practical relevance of this argument to the Philippine context is direct. Mindanao is a region where sectarian
boundaries, between Muslims and Christians but also among different Muslim communities, have historically been
sites of friction. Tago's philosophical position on diversity, worked out through decades of engagement with both
the classical Islamic tradition and the lived realities of Philippine pluralism, offers a framework for navigating
those boundaries that draws on the religious tradition itself rather than asking communities to set it aside.
Interfaith Dialogue
The practical dimension of his religious diplomacy has involved sustained engagement with Christian and
indigenous community leaders in Mindanao.<ref name="pmt" /> His guiding text in this work has been the
Quranic injunction to invite others with wisdom and beautiful discourse, an approach that prioritizes the
relationship over the argument. This orientation has enabled him to build personal credibility across sectarian
divides that have, at other moments in Mindanao's history, translated into armed conflict.
Private Ventures and Civil Society
PHILSACO
As the CEO and Founder of Philippine-Saudi Business Consultancy Services and Trade Inc. (PHILSACO), Tago
built a private-sector vehicle for translating his personal networks and knowledge into concrete commercial
outcomes for both Filipino exporters and Saudi investors.<ref name="bfbci" /> PHILSACO functions essentially as
a bridge firm that identifies credible counterparts on both sides of the Saudi-Philippine trade relationship, facilitates
introductions, interprets regulatory requirements, and provides the kind of ground-level guidance that is invaluable
in any cross-border commercial venture but particularly important where cultural distance and language barriers
can derail promising negotiations.
SPMUDA International
His involvement with SPMUDA International, a non-governmental organization recognized by the United Nations
and focused on peace, unity, and development in the southern Philippines, reflects the consistency of his conviction
that civil society organizations have a role to play in building the Bangsamoro future alongside government and the
private sector.<ref name="bfbci" /> He serves as Vice-Chairman and Senior Vice-President for International
Relations and Cooperation with SPMUDA, with the concurrent title of Goodwill Ambassador to Saudi Arabia, a
designation that formalizes the informal bridging role he has occupied for most of his professional life.
Recognition and Awards

PAGE 8
Year
Award
Awarding Body
2012
Doctor of Humanities and Ambassador of Goodwill and Peace for
Saudi Arabia
Academy of Universal Global Peace
2015
Most Influential Filipinos in the Gulf (Thoughtleader category)
Illustrado Life
2016
Filipino Media Icon
Global Officials of Dignity Awards (We Care for
Humanity)
2017
Management Man of 2017
Philippine Council of Management
The recognition that has attached itself to Tago's career does not appear to have been actively pursued. It arrived,
rather, as a side effect of work done for other reasons. In 2012, the Academy of Universal Global Peace conferred
on him the designation of Doctor of Humanities and Ambassador of Goodwill and Peace for Saudi Arabia,
recognizing a career of humanitarian advocacy that by that point already spanned two decades.<ref name="bfbci"
/> In 2016, he was named Filipino Media Icon at the fourth Global Officials of Dignity Awards.<ref name="bfbci"
/> A year later, the Philippine Council of Management recognized him as its Management Man for 2017,
acknowledging a record of organizational leadership that cut across the public and private sectors.<ref
name="bfbci" />
He has been consistently featured among the Most Influential Filipinos in the Gulf, categorized specifically as a
"Thoughtleader," a designation reserved for Filipinos whose primary contribution to the diaspora experience is
intellectual rather than economic.<ref name="illustrado" />
Philosophy
Tago has articulated his personal philosophy in a number of interviews and public statements, and it is organized
around the conviction that transformation begins within the individual before it can manifest in institutions or
societies. The formulation he has returned to most often is direct:
Every change must come first within yourself.
That conviction runs through his entire career: that the quality of one's preparation, one's character, and one's
relationships determines the range of what is possible, and that no institutional position, however senior, can
substitute for the foundation those qualities provide.<ref name="illustrado" /> His other guiding principle, drawn
from Quranic teaching, frames the aspiration of his broader public work: to invite all, with wisdom and beautiful
discourse, to the way of peace.<ref name="pmt" />
Legacy
Dr. Tago's career offers, above all, a demonstration that a Filipino from Muslim Mindanao could engage with the
Arab world not as a supplicant or a laborer but as an intellectual equal, someone who had mastered the language,
absorbed the scholarship, understood the politics, and earned the trust of the community he was covering and
serving. That demonstration matters beyond the individual. It established a model of engagement that a new
generation of Bangsamoro professionals can build on, and it contributed, in concrete and traceable ways, to the
improved conditions of hundreds of thousands of Filipino workers in the Gulf.
For the Bangsamoro region specifically, his legacy is one of institutional investment. The BFBCI, the Islamic
banking framework he helped develop, the interfaith networks he cultivated, and the advocacy infrastructure he
built during his years in Riyadh are not achievements that evaporate when their architect leaves the room. They are

PAGE 9
structures that remain, available to whoever comes next. In a region that has seen too much of its human capital
depart for cities elsewhere or abroad, the work of building institutions that outlast their founders is not a small
thing.
Further Reading
Tamano, Ashary S. "From Cairo to the Capitals: The Diplomatic, Journalistic, and Peacebuilding Legacy of
Dr. Abdul Hannan M. Tago." Bangsamoro Digital Ecosystem Journal Series. Quezon City, 2026.
Illustrado Life. "Most Influential Filipinos in the Gulf." November 2015. http://illustradolife.com/most-
influential-filipinos-gulf-dr-abdul-hannan-tago-thoughtleader/

title: Tago, Ezzedin
text:
PAGE 1
Ambassador Ezzedin Tago
Personal Information
Born: Cairo, Egypt
Nationality: Filipino
Heritage: Maranao (paternal),
Egyptian (maternal)
Education
University of California, Davis (UC
Davis)

Ezzedin Tago
Ezzedin Tago is one of the Philippines' most accomplished career
diplomats, and arguably the most effective Philippine envoy the
Arab world has ever seen. His story is unusual from the very
beginning: born in Cairo to a Maranao father from Lanao del Sur
and an Egyptian mother, he grew up speaking Arabic the way most
people speak their mother tongue, because for him, it literally is.
That linguistic and cultural inheritance turned out to be one of the
most consequential assets the Philippine foreign service ever had.
Tago joined the Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA) in 1995 and
spent the better part of three decades navigating some of the most
volatile corners of the globe. He is not the kind of diplomat who
manages crises from a comfortable embassy office. He is the kind
who shows up at the border, at the airport, at the labor center,
wherever Filipinos are stuck and scared, and works the problem
from the inside. His career is a sustained argument for what it
means to represent your country not just in name, but in body.
Contents

2 CAREER PATH AND FIELD-FIRST DIPLOMACY

2.2 The Lebanon Crisis (2006)
2.3 Consul General in Jeddah (2007–2010)
2.4 Ambassador to Saudi Arabia (2011–2016)

6 SEE ALSO
7 EXTERNAL LINKS
EARLY LIFE AND HERITAGE
Tago's background is what diplomats and academics might call a
"natural bridge," though the phrase doesn't quite capture how
organically it all fits together. His father, a Filipino from Lanao del
Sur, belongs to the Maranao people, one of the major Muslim
communities of Mindanao and a group with a long, proud tradition
of engagement with the broader Islamic world. His mother is

PAGE 2
Consul General, Sydney (2019–
2021)
Ambassador to Egypt (2021–
2025)
Awards and Honors
Gawad Mabini, Grand Cross
(Dakilang Kamanong), 2024
Gawad Mabini, Commander,
2007

Order of Sikatuna (Dakilang
Kasugo)
Presidential Citations (2005,
2006)
Notability

Ambassador; native Arabic speaker of
Maranao-Egyptian heritage; led the
2023 Sudan crisis evacuation
Known For
Crisis diplomacy in the Middle East;
protection of Overseas Filipino Workers
(OFWs); field-first leadership under
combat and emergency conditions
Egyptian. He was born in Cairo, the Arabic-speaking heart of the
Arab world, and he finished high school at the Philippine School in
Jeddah, which means the region that would later become the site of
his most consequential diplomatic work was also the region where
he came of age.
This "third culture" upbringing gave him something that cannot
really be taught in any diplomatic training program. He understands
the Arab world not as an outsider studying it, but as someone who
grew up inside its rhythms, its language, its everyday texture. When
he walks into a negotiation or a crisis coordination meeting in
Egypt, Sudan, or Saudi Arabia, he is not relying on an interpreter or
a cultural briefing. He already knows.
His formal academic training came from the University of
California, Davis, where he earned a degree in Political Science.
The combination of that Western academic framework with his
lived experience in the Middle East gave him an analytical toolkit
that is, in the truest sense, bicultural: he can read power dynamics
through a structural lens and through a cultural one at the same
time.
CAREER PATH AND FIELD-FIRST
DIPLOMACY
Tago entered the DFA in 1995 and built his career almost entirely
around the Middle East, with a handful of other critical assignments along the way. His postings trace some of the
most demanding chapters in Philippine foreign service history.
The Baghdad Detail (2004–2005)
Early in his career, Tago was sent to Baghdad, Iraq, for a ten-month assignment during one of the most dangerous
periods in the country's modern history. This was the year after the 2003 invasion, when Iraq was still in a state of
near-total volatility. His role there involved, among other things, the Angelo Dela Cruz hostage case and the Robert
Tarongoy hostage case, two high-profile crises involving Filipino workers trapped in a war zone. His handling of
these situations earned him presidential citations in both 2005 and 2006, and more importantly, it established his
reputation as someone who does not flinch when the situation gets dangerous.
The Lebanon Crisis (2006)
In 2006, when the Israel-Hezbollah conflict erupted and thousands of Overseas Filipino Workers found themselves
stranded in Lebanon, Tago was again in the thick of it. He played a key role in the repatriation effort, helping bring
Filipinos home under conditions that were anything but routine. This was one of his first large-scale crisis
evacuations, and it set a pattern that would define his career: go to where the Filipinos are, use every tool available,
and get the job done.

PAGE 3
Consul General in Jeddah (2007–2010)
The Jeddah post is one of the most consequential in the entire Philippine foreign service, simply because of the
sheer volume of Filipinos living and working in the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia. Managing their welfare, their labor
disputes, their legal cases, and their documentation needs is an enormous operation, and Tago ran it during a
critical three-year stretch. His familiarity with the language and the culture made him effective in ways that a
typical diplomat posted there might not be.
Ambassador to Saudi Arabia (2011–2016)
His promotion to Ambassador in Riyadh was a natural progression. During his five-year tenure, he oversaw large-
scale labor regularizations and repatriation operations, managing the kind of complex, multi-stakeholder processes
that require both diplomatic finesse and administrative command. The Saudi post demands both, and Tago handled
it across one of the busiest periods for Filipino labor migration to the Gulf.
Home Office Leadership
Not all of Tago's career was spent abroad. He also held significant administrative positions in Manila that shaped
the DFA's direction on issues he knows from the inside out. As Assistant Secretary for Human Resources, he
oversaw the welfare and management of the DFA's own personnel. As Director for Gulf States, he had a hand in
shaping the Philippines' broader policy toward the region he knows better than almost anyone else in the service.
He also served as Deputy Chief of Presidential Protocol, managing the high-level logistics of state visits and the
formal mechanics of international diplomatic interaction.
Consul General in Sydney (2019–2021)
Sydney was a brief detour from the Middle East, though no less demanding a post for the significant Filipino
community in Australia. It gave Tago a different kind of consular experience, one less defined by crisis and more
by the steady, daily work of serving a diaspora community in a stable country.
Ambassador to Egypt (2021–2025)
His final major assignment brought him full circle, literally and figuratively. Egypt is the country of his birth, and
his appointment as Philippine Ambassador there meant he was representing the Philippines in a country where he
already had deep roots. His jurisdiction covered not just Egypt but also Sudan, Djibouti, and Eritrea, a portfolio
that would soon test him in ways that even his Baghdad experience had not quite prepared him for.
THE 2023 SUDAN CRISIS
In April 2023, Sudan descended into armed conflict between rival military factions, and Filipino workers and
residents in the country found themselves in immediate danger. The evacuation that followed became one of the
most operationally demanding repatriations in recent Philippine diplomatic history, and it became the defining
chapter of Tago's career.
What set Tago apart was not just his coordination of the evacuation from the safety of the embassy. He physically
went toward the crisis. Along with Vice Consul Bojer Capati, he drove toward the Sudanese border to assist
evacuees directly, and on the way, their vehicle rolled over twice in a serious road accident in the Egyptian desert.

PAGE 4
He reportedly treated the crash as a delay rather than a reason to stop. They continued.
His native Arabic proved to be operationally critical. Navigating Egyptian border bureaucracy in a moment of
regional chaos, coordinating crossings at the Argeen and Qustul border points, communicating directly with local
officials without the filter of a translator: all of this required exactly the kind of linguistic and cultural fluency that
Tago carries as a birthright. Hundreds of Filipinos crossed those borders safely because of the work he and his team
did on the ground during those chaotic days.
In 2024, President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. awarded him the Gawad Mabini at the Grand Cross level, the rank of
Dakilang Kamanong, in recognition of his exceptional leadership during the Sudan crisis and his overall service as
Ambassador to Egypt. It is one of the highest honors a Philippine civil servant can receive.
AWARDS AND RECOGNITION
Tago's career is marked by a consistent record of recognition at the highest levels of the Philippine government. His
awards reflect not just individual acts of service but a sustained pattern of performance under pressure.

CULTURAL AND PROFESSIONAL SIGNIFICANCE
Tago represents something specific and important in the history of Bangsamoro participation in Philippine
statecraft. The Maranao people have long contributed to the Philippines' diplomatic engagement with the Islamic
world, and Tago's career is one of the most visible expressions of that tradition in the contemporary era. His father's
roots in Lanao del Sur connect him to a community with its own deep traditions of leadership, scholarship, and
cross-cultural engagement.
What makes him distinctive, though, is not heritage alone. It is how completely he has synthesized his Maranao
roots, his Egyptian upbringing, his Western education, and his decades of field experience into a coherent
diplomatic identity. He is not performing cultural fluency. It is simply who he is.
His approach to the work is also worth noting because it represents a philosophy, not just a practice. He is known
for being directly present in the spaces where OFWs deal with their most pressing concerns: passport releases,
labor case handlings, welfare assessments. He does not only delegate from a distance. He shows up. The 2023 car
accident in the Egyptian desert, where he kept going after the vehicle rolled over twice, is not an anomaly in his
record. It is consistent with everything else he has done.

PAGE 5
His political science background from UC Davis gives him a structural framework for understanding the power
dynamics of the regions where he works. His native Arabic gives him direct access to those regions without the
mediation of translators or cultural brokers. Together, these two things make him one of the most genuinely
effective Philippine envoys of his generation.

title: Tago, Paisalin Pangandaman
text:
PAGE 1
Paisalin Pangandaman Tago
Atty. Paisalin Pangandaman Tago, CPA (born October 25, 1967) is a Filipino lawyer, certified public accountant,
and the 9th Regular President of the Mindanao State University (MSU) System, appointed on June 27, 2025, by
President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr.<ref name="appointment">MSU Main Campus, "Mindanao State University
Welcomes the 9th Regular President of the System, MP Atty. Paisalin P. Tago," accessed March 10, 2026,
https://www.msumain.edu.ph/the-9th-regular-president-of-the-msu-system/</ref> A native of Marawi City and a
Maranao by birth and by formation, Tago brings to the MSU presidency more than three decades of government
work spanning finance, law, regional legislation, and executive administration. He is widely credited as one of the
architects of the fiscal foundation of the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM), most
notably for his central role in securing the block grant provision of the Bangsamoro Organic Law and for filing the
proposed Bangsamoro Revenue Code. His investiture at MSU on August 13, 2025, introduced a Nine-Point
Agenda built around the Latin maxim he has adopted as both personal and institutional standard: Acta non verba,
or Actions, not words.<ref name="profile">MSU Main Campus, "The System President," accessed March 10,
2026, https://www.msumain.edu.ph/the-system-president/</ref> At its core, Tago's presidency represents an
argument that has defined his entire career: that durable peace in the Philippine South depends less on declarations
than on institutions that actually work.
