His introduction to technology began at approximately age seven,
when his uncle gifted him his first computer and taught him basic
DOS commands to run simple games. What started as youthful
curiosity about operating systems evolved into genuine fascination
with how systems worked and what made them function. This
technical curiosity was complemented by an intuitive inclination
toward building and problem-solving. Throughout his childhood,
Tolentino spent considerable time assembling and experimenting
with Legos and puzzles, activities that nurtured a natural tendency
to construct, deconstruct, and understand complex systems.
This early combination of technical exposure and hands-on
problem-solving became foundational to his later approach to
software engineering and systems architecture. Rather than
viewing technology as merely academic or abstract, he developed
a pragmatic, builder-first mindset that would characterize his entire
professional career.
Education
Tolentino earned his Bachelor of Science in Computer Science
from Capitol University in Cagayan de Oro. His academic training
provided the theoretical foundation and technical depth necessary
for a career that would ultimately synthesize engineering rigor,
architectural thinking, and strategic product vision.
Career
Early Technical Foundation
Tolentino began his professional journey in hands-on technical
roles that exposed him to technology across multiple layers. He worked as an IT specialist, troubleshooting
hardware, networks, and peripheral systems while simultaneously contributing to software development projects.
During this period, he held roles as a technical analyst, graphic artist, software engineer, and SAP engineer, giving
him exposure to both infrastructure-level work and enterprise business systems.
This deliberate range of early experience shaped a fundamental philosophy: that effective technology solutions
must be grounded in real-world problems and operational constraints, not theoretical elegance alone.
Understanding how systems actually failed and how end-users experienced technology became central to his
design approach.

PAGE 3
Cloud Architecture and Early Leadership
Tolentino became part of the pioneering wave of Philippine software engineers adopting and designing with cloud
technologies such as Amazon Web Services and Microsoft Azure. During a period when cloud adoption in the
country was still nascent, his work contributed to designing scalable, cloud-native architectures that enabled
organizations to modernize legacy systems and operate more efficiently across distributed environments.
This expertise in cloud infrastructure and microservices architecture positioned him as a technical authority during
a critical transformation phase in the Philippine technology industry.
Head of Systems Engineering at QuadX
At a relatively young age, Tolentino became Head of Systems Engineering at QuadX, a logistics and e-commerce
technology company focused on addressing the Philippines' last-mile delivery challenges. In this role, he led the
architecture and scaling of platforms that orchestrated logistics operations, managed fulfillment workflows, and
coordinated delivery services across the country.
His work directly addressed critical inefficiencies in the Philippine logistics sector by building systems that
improved delivery coordination, visibility, and operational scalability. The experience taught him how technology
could solve infrastructure gaps while supporting rapid growth in digital commerce, a lesson he carried forward into
subsequent leadership roles.
Chief Software Architect and Data Privacy Officer at Olelo
Following his tenure at QuadX, Tolentino took on dual responsibilities as Chief Software Architect and Data
Privacy Officer at Olelo, an analytics company helping brands understand audience behavior and optimize
communication strategies.
In this role, he designed systems enabling data-driven insights for brands, public figures, and organizations seeking
to analyze social media engagement and audience dynamics. Simultaneously, he stewarded data privacy
compliance, ensuring that innovative systems adhered to emerging standards and protected user information. This
dual responsibility deepened his understanding of building technology that balanced innovation with
accountability, a principle he would emphasize throughout his career.
Founder of Zest Technology
Tolentino founded Zest Technology, a consultancy through which he worked closely with startups and enterprises
to design systems, launch digital products, and support digital transformation initiatives. The venture reflected his
philosophy of bridging the gap between business strategy and technical execution.
Through Zest, he helped founders and organizations avoid unnecessary technical complexity while ensuring that
architecture decisions remained aligned with business objectives. His focus was on sustainable, pragmatic solutions
that could evolve as organizations scaled.
Chief Technology Officer at Singlife Philippines
Tolentino's most visible and impactful leadership role came when he became Chief Technology Officer of Singlife
Philippines, a mobile-first digital life insurer disrupting the traditional insurance industry. He assumed this position
at age 31, making him one of the youngest CTOs in the Philippine financial services sector at that time.

PAGE 4
In this role, Tolentino built Singlife Philippines' entire digital platform from inception. He led the design and
development of a fully integrated life insurance ecosystem that unified distribution, underwriting, policy
management, and customer engagement into a single digital experience accessible via smartphone. The platform
supported both B2B2C partnerships (notably through GCash and the Mynt ecosystem) and direct-to-consumer
engagement through the Singlife Plan and Protect mobile application.
His technical leadership enabled multiple key innovations: dramatically simplified onboarding processes,
automated underwriting workflows, and transparent customer experiences that demystified insurance for everyday
Filipinos. The platform reached tens of thousands of customers in its first year and demonstrated that digital-first
financial services could serve underserved populations excluded from traditional insurance channels.
"This level of convenience coupled with affordability and reliability are what today's middle-class
Filipinos are looking for in a life insurer, and what we aim to deliver."
Tolentino's work at Singlife became a case study in fintech innovation, demonstrating how strategic technology
architecture could expand financial inclusion while maintaining operational efficiency and security.
Co-Founder and Chief Technology Officer at Workbean
During his fintech career, Tolentino also co-founded Workbean, a culture technology platform focused on
organizational and talent matching based on work persona and company culture alignment. As Chief Technology
Officer, he translated insights from leading teams and organizations into structured models and algorithms that
power the platform.
Workbean reflected his conviction that technology could solve not only system-level technical challenges but also
the human dimensions of organizational success. The platform addressed a persistent gap: the misalignment
between talented individuals and organizational cultures, a problem that transcends traditional skills-based
matching.
Chief Technology Officer at Stratpoint Technologies
In June 2024, Tolentino was appointed Chief Technology Officer of Stratpoint Technologies, a leading Philippine
software and digital transformation company. In this role, he leads the organization's technology strategy and
transformation, with responsibility for advanced technology development, solution delivery, and innovation.
A central focus of his tenure is developing Filipino technology talent to compete globally. He has introduced
structured practices across architecture, engineering, product, and security, enabling the company to deliver higher-
quality outcomes while strengthening internal capabilities. His leadership emphasizes that the Philippines'
competitive advantage in technology rests on investing in people, processes, and long-term capability building.
Vice President of Technology at Pickup Coffee
Tolentino currently serves as Vice President of Technology at Pickup Coffee, the Philippines' fast-growing
premium coffee franchise. He oversees product engineering, enterprise technology, Technology Delivery
Management, Enterprise Solutions, Engineering and Security, Data, and IT Experience (ITX).
His mandate is establishing scalable, sustainable technology foundations that integrate operations, customer
platforms, and data systems to improve efficiency and decision-making. This role demonstrates his versatility in
applying digital transformation across industries beyond fintech, extending his impact to consumer-facing retail
technology.

PAGE 5
Advocacy, Values, and Community Impact
Beyond his corporate roles, Tolentino is committed to expanding the Philippine technology ecosystem and creating
pathways for underrepresented communities. He is a co-founder of WeHackPH, a community initiative bringing
together developers, product builders, and founders to collaborate, learn, and innovate collectively.
A project particularly close to his heart involves supporting technology education and exposure in Muslim
communities. He has been involved in initiatives designed to introduce young students, particularly young women,
to technology and career opportunities in software engineering. Through these efforts, he seeks to inspire more
young Muslims, especially women, to pursue and advance in technology careers.
His advocacy is rooted in a conviction that technology sectors thrive when they include talent and perspectives
from all communities. The underrepresentation of Muslim professionals in Philippine technology, despite the
country's growing tech economy, is a gap he actively works to address through mentorship, visibility, and
community engagement.
Vision and Legacy
Tolentino's long-term vision extends beyond corporate leadership to institutional transformation. He envisions
establishing a fully digital Islamic bank in the Philippines, a project that would synthesize his fintech expertise,
commitment to financial inclusion, and dedication to serving Muslim communities.
This vision exemplifies his broader philosophy: technology should be purposeful, grounded in solving real
problems, and directed toward expanding access and opportunity for those currently underserved by existing
systems.
His career trajectory represents a broader shift in the Philippine technology landscape, where builders from diverse
ethnic, religious, and geographic backgrounds are shaping the future of digital systems and services. As a Filipino
Muslim occupying senior technology leadership roles, Tolentino contributes to expanding visibility and creating
role models for future generations of Muslim technologists.
Recognition and Industry Engagement
Tolentino has been featured in industry publications and podcasts discussing fintech innovation, technology
leadership, and career development in Philippine technology. His insights on microservices architecture, cloud
strategy, and building high-performing engineering teams have contributed to professional discourse around digital
transformation.
His career demonstrates that technology leadership in the Philippines can be built not through imported
frameworks alone, but through deep understanding of local problems, commitment to sustainable solutions, and
deliberate investment in people and capability.

text:

Acmad M. Tomawis
Acmad Maruhom Tomawis is a Maranao politician, government
administrator, and businessman from Lanao del Sur, Philippines. He
currently serves as Administrator and Chief Executive Officer of the
Southern Philippines Development Authority (SPDA), and
previously represented the ALIF (Ang Laban ng Indiginong Filipino)
party-list in the House of Representatives for three consecutive
terms. He also served as Executive Director of the Office on Muslim
Affairs (OMA) and, earlier in his career, owned and operated a
private bus transport company serving Northern and Central
Mindanao.
Contents
1 Overview
2 Early Life & Family
3 Career, Public Service & Leadership Roles
3.1 ARMM Regional Legislative Assembly
3.2 Domestic Transport Business (1990s)
3.3 Executive Director, Office on Muslim Affairs (OMA)
3.4 Founder, ALIF Party-list
3.5 Member, House of Representatives (ALIF Party-list)
3.6 Administrator and CEO, Southern Philippines
Development Authority
4 Major Works, Achievements, Awards & Recognition
5 Personal Life, Legacy, Impact & Historical Significance
6 Research Assessment
Overview
Tomawis has moved between elected office, appointive government
posts, and private enterprise across nearly five decades of public life
in Lanao del Sur and the wider Bangsamoro region. He founded the
ALIF party-list group in Marawi City in February 2003 and
represented it in Congress from 2004 to 2013.<ref>Template:Cite
web</ref><ref>Mindanews, "Mindanawons in Congress: 67 in the
House, two in the Senate," 2013.</ref> He was appointed
Administrator and CEO of SPDA around June 2026, succeeding
Abdulghani "Gerry" Ajul Salapuddin.<ref>Template:Cite web</ref>
Early Life & Family
Verified information on Tomawis's exact date of birth, early
schooling, and formal education has not been located in government
records, news archives, or academic sources as of this writing.

PAGE 2
Occupation
Government administrator,
politician, businessman
Secondary sources describe him as originating from Marawi City,
Lanao del Sur, and beginning public life there, though the earliest
specific dates in circulation (a councilorship starting in 1976, a
mayoralty from 1978, and an ARMM assembly seat "from 1982 to
1996") do not align with the historical record, since the ARMM itself was not established until 1989 and its first
Regional Legislative Assembly only convened in 1990.<ref>Template:Cite web</ref> These earlier claims are
flagged here as unverified pending a primary source.
His brother is Sultan Yahya "Jerry" Tomawis, who administered SPDA during the 2000s, the same agency Acmad
now leads.<ref>Template:Cite web</ref> His sons Abdul Tomawis and Agakhan Tomawis have both served as
ALIF party-list nominees.<ref>Template:Cite web</ref> A 2010 party-list nominee list also names Jamela M.
Tomawis as ALIF's fourth nominee, though her exact relationship to Acmad has not been independently confirmed.
<ref>Template:Cite web</ref>
Research gap: Date of birth, place of birth details beyond city, parents' names, and formal educational history are
not yet documented in citable sources.
Career, Public Service & Leadership Roles
ARMM Regional Legislative Assembly
Tomawis sat in the 1st ARMM Regional Legislative Assembly (1990–1993), representing Lanao del Sur's first
district, and returned briefly to the 2nd Assembly from May 28 to September 30, 1996, under the Laban ng
Demokratikong Pilipino (LDP) banner.<ref>Template:Cite web</ref><ref>Template:Cite web</ref>
Domestic Transport Business (1990s)
Before entering Congress, Tomawis owned and operated Tomawis Super Transport (known in its early operations
as AMT Express), a bus and transport line serving Northern and Central Mindanao. City-route operations began in
1993 using former Metro Manila Transit Corporation (MMTC) units, expanding to regional routes by 1994.
Primary routes included Cagayan de Oro–Marawi (via Iligan), Cagayan de Oro–Butuan, and Cagayan de Oro–Wao
(via Valencia and Maramag), operated using Nissan Diesel units and surplus Japanese coaches.<ref>Community
transport-history archive, Iligan City 1990s bus operations, Facebook.</ref> This business is the basis for his
continuing local reputation as a transport-sector businessman.
Executive Director, Office on Muslim Affairs (OMA)
Tomawis served as Executive Director of the Office on Muslim Affairs (OMA) from June 1998 to January 2001,
appointed under the administration of President Joseph Estrada.<ref>Firsthand account, former OMA Planning
Director under Tomawis's term.</ref> A Philippine Supreme Court decision independently places him in the post
by mid-1998: in G.R. No. 166547, the Court's narration of facts states that on July 3, 1998, then-OMA Executive
Director Acmad Tomawis removed a regional director from post and appointed a replacement.<ref>Template:Cite
web</ref>
As Executive Director, Tomawis headed an agency created under Executive Order No. 122-A (1987), which
established OMA with a mandate to ensure the rights and well-being of Muslim Filipinos, organized around
bureaus covering pilgrimage and endowment, cultural affairs, cooperatives development, and settlements.
<ref>Template:Cite web</ref> His tenure centered on three areas:

PAGE 3
Bureau of Pilgrimage and Endowment. Tomawis oversaw the agency's annual Hajj operations, a function EO
122-A assigns to the Bureau of Pilgrimage and Endowment, covering the administration of the annual Muslim
pilgrimage to Mecca, Saudi Arabia, and the management of Awqaf (endowment) properties and institutions.
<ref>Template:Cite web</ref> By firsthand account, this included coordinating logistics, medical assistance, and
travel processing for Muslim Filipino pilgrims, and administering properties and endowments designated for the
welfare of the Muslim community.<ref>Firsthand account, former OMA Planning Director under Tomawis's term.
</ref>
The 2000 Mindanao conflict. Tomawis's term coincided with President Estrada's "all-out war" campaign against
the Moro Islamic Liberation Front (MILF), declared on March 21, 2000, a military campaign that independent
sources describe as displacing hundreds of thousands of civilians before the MILF's main camp fell in July 2000.
<ref>Template:Cite web</ref><ref>Template:Cite web</ref> By firsthand account, Tomawis pivoted OMA's
operations toward socio-economic relief for internally displaced Moro civilians during the conflict, and advised the
Office of the President on the cultural and political implications of the fighting, advocating non-military
interventions and multi-faith dialogue.<ref>Firsthand account, former OMA Planning Director under Tomawis's
term.</ref>
Shariah and institutional development. By firsthand account, Tomawis backed the institutionalization of Madaris
(Islamic schools) and provided legal and logistical support to the country's Shariah court system during his term.
<ref>Firsthand account, former OMA Planning Director under Tomawis's term.</ref> The agency he led was later
abolished under Republic Act No. 9997 (February 18, 2010), which created the National Commission on Muslim
Filipinos (NCMF) and transferred OMA's functions to it.<ref>Template:Cite web</ref>
Founder, ALIF Party-list
Organized ALIF (Ang Laban ng Indiginong Filipino) in Marawi City in February 2003 following consultations
with indigenous cultural community leaders, including Muslim Filipinos.<ref>Template:Cite web</ref>
Member, House of Representatives (ALIF Party-list)
Won a House seat in the 2004 elections; ALIF topped the party-list vote in several ARMM provinces, though
discrepancies in the Lanao del Sur count led rival group Cibac to formally question the results.<ref>Template:Cite
web</ref> He served three consecutive terms, through the 15th Congress (2010–2013).<ref>Mindanews,
"Mindanawons in Congress: 67 in the House, two in the Senate," 2013.</ref> In 2007, he joined other party-list
representatives in signing a "Covenant of Common Purpose and United Action" bringing several party-list groups
into the Lakas-CMD coalition under then-Speaker Jose de Venecia.<ref>Template:Cite web</ref>
A 2004 accreditation petition by Kilosbayan argued that Tomawis's business background, described as overseas
trucking, particularly in Iraq, undercut ALIF's claim to represent a marginalized sector.<ref>Template:Cite
web</ref><ref>Template:Cite web</ref>
As a sitting representative, Senate records list him as principal author of several bills, including a tuition fee
discount measure for students from indigenous cultural communities, a bill establishing the Sultan Labay Technical
Institute in Masiu, Lanao del Sur, and a bill exempting overseas Filipino workers from taxes and customs duties on
vehicles brought into the country.<ref>Template:Cite web</ref>

PAGE 4
Administrator and CEO, Southern Philippines Development Authority
Appointed Administrator and CEO of SPDA around June 2026. Shortly after assuming office, he ordered a 30-day
fast-track reopening of the Sulop Poultry Farm in Davao del Sur, personally conducting a site visitation with
SPDA's management team on June 20, 2026.<ref>Template:Cite web</ref> SPDA also credited his leadership with
a June 17, 2026 donation of relief goods to earthquake-affected Sarangani province.<ref>Template:Cite web</ref>
Research gap: SPDA's published "Personal Profile" page had not been updated to reflect Tomawis's appointment
as of this writing, so the exact appointment date and appointing order are not yet available from a primary source.
Major Works, Achievements, Awards & Recognition
Founded and operated Tomawis Super Transport (AMT Express), a bus line serving Northern and Central
Mindanao routes through the 1990s.
Founded ALIF, sustaining it as a functioning party-list group that won House seats across three consecutive
congressional elections.
Principal author of legislation covering indigenous student tuition discounts, technical education in Lanao
del Sur, and tax relief for returning overseas Filipino workers.
As SPDA Administrator, initiated an early operational push to revive the Sulop Poultry Farm as an income-
generating project, alongside directives to resolve environmental compliance issues with the local
government unit.
No independently verified awards, honors, or formal citations have been located as of this writing.
Personal Life, Legacy, Impact & Historical Significance
Tomawis's career reflects a political and business family with sustained influence across Lanao del Sur and the
wider ARMM/BARMM region. His brother Jerry Tomawis administered SPDA during the Arroyo era, working on
infrastructure and livelihood projects such as the Koronadal Business Center.<ref>Template:Cite web</ref>
Decades later, Acmad now holds the same administratorship. His sons' continued involvement in ALIF, together
with the family's footprint across SPDA, the ARMM legislative assembly, and Congress, places the Tomawis
family among a small set of Maranao political families whose influence spans multiple government institutions
over several decades.
A 2012 report on a pyramiding-scam bust noted that the scheme's operator was married to a daughter of then-SPDA
chairman Jerry Tomawis, identified in that article as Acmad's brother.<ref>Template:Cite web</ref> Acmad is not
named as a party to that case in available sources; this is included here strictly as family-background context.
Research Assessment
Verified facts: ALIF founding (February 2003); OMA Executive Director tenure, June 1998 to January 2001, per
firsthand account from a former OMA Planning Director who served under him, with the mid-1998 portion
independently corroborated by a Supreme Court decision; three consecutive House terms (2004–2013); 1st ARMM
Regional Legislative Assembly seat (1990–1993) and brief 2nd Assembly service (1996); current SPDA
Administrator/CEO role (2026); declared net worth of ₱18.56 million per 2012 SALN; ownership of Tomawis
Super Transport/AMT Express, corroborated by an independent period photograph of a "Tomawis"-branded bus on
the Cagayan de Oro–Iligan route and by firsthand recollection from a former OMA colleague. The structural
mandate and historical context of his OMA tenure (EO 122-A's bureau functions, the 2000 Estrada-MILF conflict,
and OMA's 2010 abolition under RA 9997) are each independently documented in law and historical record; the

PAGE 5
specific claim that Tomawis personally carried out relief coordination, peace advocacy, and Shariah/Madaris
institutional support during that period rests on firsthand testimony rather than independent documentary sources,
and is presented here on that basis.
Unverified information: Claimed 1976 councilorship and 1978 mayoralty; claimed ARMM assembly tenure
"1982–1996" (inconsistent with ARMM's actual founding date); undated OIC Mayor of Marawi role; exact family
relationship of ALIF nominee Jamela M. Tomawis.
Research gaps: Date and place of birth; parents' names and pre-political family background; formal educational
history; exact SPDA appointment date and order; a government, SEC, or news-archive citation for Tomawis Super
Transport/AMT Express; awards and honors.

Sitti Djalia Turabin-Hataman
Sitti Djalia Turabin-Hataman (born November 26, 1977),
widely known as Mayor Dadah, is a Filipina politician, peace
advocate, and human rights activist from Basilan who has built a
career out of a single, steady conviction: that good governance
and genuine peace can coexist, even in the country's most
complex conflict zones.
She currently serves as the Mayor of Isabela City, Basilan, a
city she's led since 2019 and was re-elected to serve in 2025
under the banner of the #HAPIsabela (Happy Isabela) platform.
Before entering electoral politics, she spent years doing the kind
of unglamorous, ground-level work that rarely makes headlines:
running human rights centers, organizing Moro women in
conflict-affected communities, and pushing for spaces where
displaced families could feel safe.
Her administration has racked up over 147 awards in six years,
earned Isabela City a place among the 2025 Green Destinations
Top 100, and won the city the 2025 Open and Transparent
Local Governance Award, a recognition that reflects her
personal insistence on transparency and accountability.
Turabin-Hataman represents the new face of Bangsamoro
leadership: educated, rooted in activism, and deeply committed
to bridging the religious and cultural divides that have long
shaped Basilan's political landscape.
Contents
1 Early Life and Background
2 Education
3 Career
3.1 Grassroots Advocacy
3.2 Executive Director, NCMF
3.3 House of Representatives (2013–2017)
3.4 Mayor of Isabela City (2019–Present)
4 Institutional Contributions
5 Legacy
6 Awards and Recognition
7 Challenges
8 Personal Life
9 See Also
10 External Links

PAGE 2
Early Life and Background
Sitti Djalia Turabin-Hataman was born on November 26, 1977, in Basilan, an island province that sits at the
crossroads of Muslim and Christian Mindanao and has historically been one of the more tension-prone areas of the
southern Philippines.
Growing up in Basilan shaped her understanding of what governance failures look like up close: communities
caught in cycles of conflict, women bearing the heaviest burdens of displacement, and institutions that too often
felt absent or inadequate.
That lived experience would become the foundation of everything she did after, from her academic choices to her
career trajectory to the kind of mayor she chose to become.
Education
Turabin-Hataman started her university studies at Western Mindanao State University (WMSU), where she
pursued a degree in Biology.
She later shifted direction toward the social sciences, completing a Bachelor of Science in Business Economics at
the University of the Philippines Diliman.
She followed that with a Master of Arts in Economics, also from UP Diliman, giving her both the analytical
grounding to understand development policy and the academic credibility to engage with it at a national level.
Career
Grassroots Advocacy
Before she ever ran for office, Turabin-Hataman spent years in the trenches of civil society work.
She served as director of the Moro Human Rights Center, an organization focused on documenting abuses and
protecting the rights of communities caught in Mindanao's long-running conflict.
She also served as president of Pinay Kilos (PINK), a women's organization dedicated to empowering Moro
women in conflict-affected areas of Mindanao. The work wasn't glamorous, but it was formative, and it built the
networks and credibility she'd rely on throughout her public life.
Executive Director, NCMF
In 2010, she made her first formal entry into government when she was appointed as the Executive Director of the
National Commission on Muslim Filipinos (NCMF).
The role placed her at the center of national policy conversations around Muslim Filipino identity, rights, and
welfare, and it marked a clear transition from community-based organizing to institutional leadership.

PAGE 3
House of Representatives (2013–2017)
From 2013 to 2017, she served as a party-list representative for Anak Mindanao (AMIN) in the House of
Representatives.
During her tenure in Congress, she was a consistent advocate for women's rights, children's welfare, and the
broader interests of the Bangsamoro people. She pushed for legislation on child-friendly evacuation spaces, an
issue that speaks directly to the experience of displaced families in conflict zones.
In October 2017, she made the unusual decision to resign from her congressional seat to return to community-
based work, a move that reinforced her reputation as someone more interested in impact than in holding office for
its own sake.
Mayor of Isabela City (2019–Present)
She was elected Mayor of Isabela City in 2019 and re-elected in the May 2025 elections for what is her final term.
Her administration operates under the #HAPIsabela platform, a governance vision centered on happiness,
accountability, and progress for all communities in the city.
Isabela City is a religiously and culturally diverse place, with a predominantly Christian population alongside
significant Muslim and Indigenous communities. Turabin-Hataman has made inclusive leadership central to how
she governs, consistently working to bridge divides rather than exploit them.
Under her watch, the city institutionalized Freedom of Information (FOI) at the local level, a significant
governance reform that reflects her administration's commitment to transparency.
Institutional Contributions
Turabin-Hataman's contributions go well beyond her formal roles in government.
Her years leading the Moro Human Rights Center helped establish a more systematic approach to documenting and
addressing human rights concerns in Basilan and the broader Bangsamoro region.
Her work with Pinay Kilos (PINK) helped formalize structures for women's organizing in conflict-affected
communities, building a model for civil society engagement that others could follow.
At the national level, her time with the NCMF allowed her to help shape how the Philippine government engages
with Muslim Filipinos on matters of identity, faith, and welfare.
As mayor, she's helped position Isabela City as a model for transparent, accountable local governance, particularly
through the institutionalization of FOI, which earned the city the 2025 Open and Transparent Local Governance
Award from the national government.
Legacy
It's still early to write a final verdict on Sitti Djalia Turabin-Hataman's legacy, but the contours are already clear.
She represents a generation of Bangsamoro leaders who came up through civil society, who understand conflict
from the inside, and who've chosen governance as a tool for peace rather than a platform for personal advancement.

PAGE 4
Her signature contribution may well be proving that a city like Isabela, with all its demographic complexity and
historical tension, can be governed with transparency, cultural sensitivity, and genuine care for all its residents.
The #HAPIsabela vision isn't just a tagline. It's a governance philosophy rooted in the belief that happiness, in the
most practical sense, comes from institutions that work, communities that feel safe, and leaders who show up.
The over 147 awards her administration has earned are not just trophies. They're evidence that what she's been
trying to build in Isabela City is real.
Awards and Recognition
The Outstanding Women in the Nation's Service (TOWNS) awardee, October 2025, recognized for
transformative work in peacebuilding and socio-economic development
2025 Open and Transparent Local Governance Award, for institutionalizing Freedom of Information at
the local level
2025 Green Destinations Top 100 Stories, for sustainable tourism initiatives involving Indigenous Sama
Bajau women
Multiple Seal of Good Local Governance (SGLG) citations
Over 147 awards across six years of mayoral service
Challenges
Governing Isabela City has never been a simple task.
Basilan has long been associated with armed conflict, and the city's demographic diversity, while a source of
strength in the right hands, can also be a source of tension if not managed carefully.
Turabin-Hataman has had to navigate the complex religious and cultural dynamics between the city's Christian
majority and its Muslim and Indigenous communities, all while keeping the peace process on track and delivering
basic services.
Her decision to resign from Congress in 2017 was itself a signal that she understood the limits of what national-
level work could accomplish, and that real change in places like Basilan has to be built from the ground up.
Personal Life
Sitti Djalia Turabin-Hataman is married to Mujiv Hataman, the former governor of the Autonomous Region in
Muslim Mindanao (ARMM) and currently a Representative of Basilan.
They have children, including Ahmed Djaliv Amin Hataman, who serves as a Board Member and is active in
local governance in Basilan.

1.6.1 A. Appointment and Institutional Context When Dr. Umpa returned to the Philippines in 1977, he joined
the MSU system in an administrative capacity, serving initially as Assistant Dean of the College of Arts
and Social Sciences and as Senior Technical Assistant to the Vice President for Academic Affairs.3 His
administrative aptitude was evident from the outset. By 1988, the MSU Board of Regents elected him to
lead the Iligan Institute of Technology, making him the first Chancellor of MSU-IIT following Professor
Manaros B. Boransing, who had served as Vice President and Acting head of the unit during its
formative autonomy period.2 That distinction — first Chancellor — was not a technicality. It meant
Umpa was charged with defining what the role of Chancellor would mean for this institution going
forward.

Scholar, Builder, Maranao Statesman
The Life and Institutional Legacy of Dr. Camar Ampaso Umpa
A Contribution to the Bangsamoro Digital Ecosystem Journal Series
Introduction
There are figures in any nation's history whose importance is best understood not at the moment of their prominence, but decades after the institutions they shaped have
matured into something larger than themselves. Dr. Camar Ampaso Umpa belongs to that rare category. In the Mindanao-Sulu-Palawan corridor, where the project of state-
building has long been tangled with questions of cultural identity and political grievance, Umpa carved a particular path — one that insisted education was the surest and
most dignified route through the tensions his community faced. He did not carry a weapon or hold elected office. He carried academic credentials and an administrator's
conviction, and those proved sufficient to change the trajectory of a major Philippine university system.
This article draws on primary source documents — including resolutions of the Bangsamoro Transition Authority Parliament, the official institutional history of the
Mindanao State University-Iligan Institute of Technology, published research presented to the National Academy of Science and Technology Philippines, and biographical
testimonies — to trace the arc of Dr. Umpa's life and work. It situates his leadership within the broader history of the Mindanao State University (MSU) System and the
social challenges the system was created to address. The result is a portrait not of a saint or a myth, but of a deeply serious man who understood that institutions outlast
individuals, and who spent the better part of five decades making certain that the institutions he touched would outlast him well.
I. A University Born from Conflict: The MSU Mandate
The Mindanao State University was not founded in the ordinary sense of the word — it was constructed as a political intervention. When President Carlos P. Garcia signed
Republic Act No. 1387 on September 1, 1961, establishing MSU in Marawi City, the legislation was a direct acknowledgment that the Philippine state had failed to integrate
the Muslim and indigenous peoples of its southern regions into its larger national narrative.1 The university's founding charter gave it a mandate that no other Philippine
institution of higher learning carried: to serve as a social laboratory where students of different religious and ethnic backgrounds — Muslim, Christian, and Lumad — would
study together, thereby building the kind of mutual understanding that political arrangements alone could not produce.1
The late Senator Domocao Alonto is widely credited as the driving intellectual force behind this vision.1 The institution was deliberately planted in Marawi City, the heart of
Maranao country in Lanao del Sur, to demonstrate that the nation's commitment to its Muslim minority was real and permanent. Its first president, Dr. Antonio Isidro, was
charged with translating this idealism into operating curricula and academic programs.1 As the system grew, it expanded into specialized campuses, with the Iligan Institute
of Technology — later redesignated MSU-IIT — emerging as the system's center for science and engineering education.2
It was into this charged institutional environment that Camar Ampaso Umpa was born, educated, and would eventually return as the institution's most consequential leader
since its founding generation.

PAGE 2
II. Roots in Ranao: Early Life and Formation
Camar Ampaso Umpa was born on November 3, 1949, in Uyaan, Madamba, in the province of Lanao del Sur.3 His parents were Datu Montila "Oti" Umpa and Bae
Macasimpan Ampaso — names that locate him within the Maranao nobility, in a society where lineage carries not merely social prestige but a lived ethical code.3 That code,
encapsulated by the concept of maratabat — a nuanced Maranao framework of honor, dignity, and reciprocal respect — would prove formative in shaping his leadership
philosophy.3
His formal schooling began in the public schools of Lanao del Norte. He attended the Lanao del Norte National Comprehensive High School in Baroy, where his academic
gifts became quickly apparent. He completed his secondary education in 1965, at the age of fifteen, graduating with high honors.3 That early finish — years ahead of most of
his peers — foreshadowed a pattern that would define the first decade of his adult life.
Entering the Mindanao State University on a full academic scholarship, Umpa enrolled in the Bachelor of Arts program in Political Science. He was captivated by the
discipline's core questions: how power is organized, how institutions are built or dismantled, and how governance either serves or fails the communities under its authority.
He completed the standard four-year degree in three years, graduating Cum Laude on April 21, 1968, when he was just eighteen years old.4 In doing so, he made history: he
became the first member of a cultural minority group to graduate with Latin honors from the Mindanao State University.4 The significance of that distinction was not
ceremonial. It was proof, delivered from within the very institution designed to promote national integration, that the local population it served was capable of meeting and
exceeding the highest academic standards it could set.
III. Graduate Training in Hawaii: Becoming the Scholar
The path that followed undergraduate graduation took Umpa to the University of Hawaii at Manoa, an institution long regarded as a gateway for scholars from Asia and the
Pacific navigating American academic culture.5 His performance there exceeded any reasonable expectation. In 1973, he completed his Master of Arts in Political Science in
a remarkable eleven months — a pace that required not merely intelligence but a capacity for sustained, focused effort that those who knew him would later describe as
characteristic.3
He remained at Hawaii for his doctoral studies, earning his PhD in Political Science in 1977.5 His performance left such an impression on his faculty that Dr. Harry
Friedman, a distinguished international educator with more than two decades of teaching behind him, went on record with an assessment that his colleagues apparently
considered unprecedented: he called Umpa the best student he had encountered across his entire twenty-one-year career.3 Such a commendation from a seasoned academic
carries weight precisely because it was not given lightly.
The discipline of political science, as Umpa absorbed it at Hawaii, provided him with more than theoretical frameworks. It gave him tools for analyzing institutional design
— how governance structures shape behavior, and how the deliberate restructuring of an institution's priorities can redirect its trajectory over time. He would put every one
of those tools to work upon his return to Mindanao.
IV. The Chancellorship of MSU-IIT: Charting the Research Path (1988–1999)
A. Appointment and Institutional Context When Dr. Umpa returned to the Philippines in 1977, he joined the MSU system in an
administrative capacity, serving initially as Assistant Dean of the College of Arts and Social Sciences and as Senior Technical Assistant to
the Vice President for Academic Affairs.3 His administrative aptitude was evident from the outset. By 1988, the MSU Board of Regents
elected him to lead the Iligan Institute of Technology, making him the first Chancellor of MSU-IIT following Professor Manaros B.
Boransing, who had served as Vice President and Acting head of the unit during its formative autonomy period.2 That distinction — first
Chancellor — was not a technicality. It meant Umpa was charged with defining what the role of Chancellor would mean for this institution
going forward.
MSU-IIT at that point had strong technical roots — its predecessor institutions included the Lanao Technical School and the Northern Mindanao Institute of Technology, and
the campus carried a well-earned reputation for producing competent engineers and technologists.2 What it lacked was the kind of research culture and international standing
that distinguished a university from a higher-level vocational institution. Dr. Umpa identified that gap on his first day and spent the next eleven years closing it.
B. The Research University Transformation
The phrase "research university status" appears repeatedly in institutional accounts of Umpa's chancellorship, and it represents a deliberate strategic decision rather than a
casual aspiration.2 Under his leadership, MSU-IIT shifted its institutional emphasis from training and teaching alone to the systematic production of new knowledge through
research. This required investment in laboratory facilities and equipment, a sustained drive to recruit faculty who held doctoral degrees and published in peer-reviewed
journals, and a structural reorganization of how the university's internal offices related to one another.
That last element — organizational architecture — was where Umpa's political science training proved most directly applicable. He moved the institution away from a
hierarchical, top-down model where direction flowed exclusively from the president's office, and toward what contemporaries described as a more distributed administrative
arrangement: one that empowered academic units, departments, and individual researchers to take initiative, attract grants, and contribute to the institution's collective
standing.2 He brought, in the words of those who worked under him, "bracing moral support" to researchers pursuing original work.2
Physical infrastructure followed strategic reorientation. The construction of the College of Education building, initiated under his predecessor, was completed under Umpa's
watch — a tangible marker of institutional growth.6 Faculty recruitment accelerated, and the standards governing academic hiring rose correspondingly. By the time Umpa
completed his tenure in 1999, MSU-IIT had developed the institutional muscle it needed to compete with universities well beyond the Mindanao region.
The long-term fruits of that decade of effort are not difficult to trace. MSU-IIT is today ranked among Asia's top universities by Quacquarelli Symonds (QS), holds ISO
9001:2015 certification, and is recognized as a regional leader in sustainable materials research and resilient engineering.2 That institutional standing did not emerge from
nothing; it grew from the soil that Umpa prepared between 1988 and 1999.

PAGE 3
V. The MSU System Presidency (1999–2005)
A. Assumption of Office
In 1999, Dr. Umpa was appointed as the fifth President of the Mindanao State University System, succeeding Dr. Emily Marohombsar.7 The appointment placed him at the
head of a complex constellation of autonomous campuses spanning the Mindanao-Sulu-Palawan corridor — a system whose constituent units ranged from the
technologically advanced IIT in Iligan to campuses embedded in among the most conflict-affected communities in the Philippines. Managing the system required Umpa to
hold two things simultaneously: a coherent institutional vision for the whole and sensitivity to the distinct political and social realities of each part.
B. Science and Technology as National Strategy
Among the most intellectually substantive contributions of Umpa's presidency was his sustained argument that science and technology investment was not merely an
educational preference but a national economic imperative. In 2001, he presented a paper at the National Academy of Science and Technology Philippines — titled "Gearing
National S&T Capability for Global Competitiveness in the 21st Century: Theoretical and Empirical Considerations" — that laid this case out with considerable analytical
rigor.8
The paper drew on evidence from the Industrial Revolution and the more recent industrialization of Singapore, Taiwan, and South Korea — economies then grouped under
the label "Newly Industrializing Economies" — to argue that the wealth of nations tracks closely with their investment in research and development personnel and
expenditure.8 Umpa developed an empirical model using per capita gross national product as the outcome variable and the density of R&D scientists and engineers per
million population as a primary predictor.8 His conclusion was direct: the Philippines' persistent failure to industrialize was inseparable from its chronically low investment
in technical human capital.
His policy prescription was proportionally bold. He argued that at least 75% of tertiary enrollees and graduates in the Philippines should be concentrated in science,
technology, engineering, and mathematics fields.8 As MSU System President, he made the reorientation of the system's programs toward S&T a defining institutional
priority — not as an abstract aspiration but as a concrete allocation of resources, faculty hiring, and curriculum development.
C. Socioeconomic Empowerment and the Bangsamoro Transition
Umpa's presidency coincided with a significant period in Bangsamoro political history, encompassing the consolidation of the Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao and
the ongoing peace negotiations that would eventually lead to the Bangsamoro Organic Law.9 He understood — and publicly articulated — that political arrangements alone
could not produce lasting peace without accompanying economic development and educational access. He actively supported research into trade and investment conditions
in Muslim areas of Mindanao, recognizing that economic agency was a prerequisite for genuine self-determination.10
He also participated in high-level consultations on the quality of basic education for Muslim learners, joining regional academics and policy practitioners — including
figures like Michael Mastura and Dr. Eddie Alih — in pressing for systemic improvements to Muslim basic education in the south.11 These consultations reflected a
conviction that ran throughout Umpa's career: that the MSU System's mandate was not fulfilled by producing university graduates alone, but by contributing to the
conditions under which every child in the region could receive an education worth having.
VI. Cultural Stewardship: The Pagana Maranao and the Defense of Heritage
It would be a distortion to treat Dr. Umpa purely as an administrator of science and technology programs. One of the more distinctive aspects of his presidency was his
insistence that the MSU System should be as committed to preserving Maranao cultural heritage as it was to building engineering laboratories.
Under his presidency, the Pagana Maranao — the traditional royal feast of the Maranao people — was formalized as an institutional practice within the university system.12
The Pagana Maranao is not a simple ceremony; it is a highly structured event that communicates the Maranao social order, acknowledges the authority of traditional leaders
including Sultans and Bai-a Labis, and demonstrates the hospitality and cultural refinement that the Maranao hold as core values.12 By making this feast a formal part of
how the university welcomed distinguished visitors, Umpa was doing something quietly significant: he was asserting that the state's premier academic institution in the south
was not indifferent to, or embarrassed by, the traditions of the people it was supposed to serve.
That assertion carried weight on multiple levels. For the Maranao community, it signaled institutional respect. For international foundations and national government
partners visiting the campus, it provided an authoritative introduction to a culture they might otherwise have encountered only through the lens of conflict. And for the
researchers who eventually studied and published on the Pagana as an institution, it contributed to a growing body of scholarly literature on Maranao cultural practices that
might otherwise have remained undocumented.12
VII. The Private Man: Marriage, Family, and Character
In an age of loud pronouncements and relentless self-promotion, there is something profoundly compelling about the private man. His story is not written in press releases or
splashed across social media, but etched quietly into the lives he has touched, the family he has built, and the quiet, deliberate choices of his daily existence. Dr. Umpa was
such a man. To understand his character is not to look for a single monumental achievement, but to appreciate the intricate mosaic formed by a life of love, discipline, quiet
industry, and a deeply personal pursuit of wholeness. His legacy is a testament to the power of a life lived with intention, away from the spotlight, yet radiating an influence
that shaped generations.
The cornerstone of Dr. Umpa’s private world was his marriage. He was happily wed to Hadja Prof. Sapia Malawad Alango Dangcal Ali, a woman of immense stature in her
own right. Hailed and raised in the historic city of Dansalan, now Marawi, she was not only a revered retired professor from the College of Education at MSU Main Campus
but also held the esteemed traditional title of Bae-a-Labi sa Dansalan. This was a union of two powerful currents: his quiet, administrative drive and her public roles as an
educator and a guardian of cultural heritage. Their home was not merely a house, but a confluence of academic rigor and Maranao tradition, a foundation of mutual respect
that would prove sturdy enough to support a large and flourishing family. In her, he found an equal, a partner whose own public service complemented his private dedication,
creating a partnership that was the very bedrock of their world.
From this solid foundation sprang their greatest legacy: eleven children. To raise eleven children in today’s world is an act of profound faith and resilience. But to raise them
to become a distinguished cohort of doctors, engineers, nurses, an accountant, psychologists, a diplomat, and a mathematician is nothing short of extraordinary. This
remarkable outcome offers the clearest window into Dr. Umpa’s character. He is remembered as a disciplined father, a term that in his hands meant far more than mere

PAGE 4
rigidity. His discipline was the discipline of the gardener—patient, consistent, and deeply invested in providing the right environment for each unique seed to thrive. He
understood that discipline, when rooted in love, is not about restriction, but about channeling potential. His children’s success is not a story of luck; it is a direct reflection of
his character, a living testament to a father who modeled the values of hard work, perseverance, and the relentless pursuit of excellence, not just through words, but through
the unwavering example of his own life.
This inclination toward cultivation was not merely metaphorical. When he was a boy, Dr. Umpa loved to farm, and this love was a current that ran, undimmed, beneath the
surface of his entire life. No matter how packed his schedule as an administrator, he always returned to the soil. He found his sanctuary not in an office, but in his garden, a
verdant kingdom where he tended to his orchids, his aloe vera, and a host of other medicinal plants. This was not a performance of rustic simplicity; it was a core part of his
being. The patience required to nurture a delicate orchid, the practical knowledge needed to harness the healing properties of aloe—these were the same qualities he brought
to nurturing his family and solving complex problems. And, in a gesture that speaks volumes about his generous spirit, he would eagerly share cuttings and seedlings with
friends and relatives who visited. His garden was not a private retreat but a source of connection, a living expression of his belief that the best things in life—beauty, health,
knowledge—are meant to be shared.
His character was also marked by a forward-looking pragmatism. He was not only a cultivator of plants and people but also of ideas. He ventured into business, his
entrepreneurial spirit finding expression in ventures as thoughtful as his gardening. His retailing of chia seeds and vitamins was a natural extension of his core values. It
wasn't just about commerce; it was a mission to share the tools for a better life. He was, at his heart, a health-conscious man, a student of vitality. He studied and
experimented with methods to delay aging and maintain his well-being, embracing a holistic approach that combined exercise, a balanced diet, and vitamin supplements.
This was not a vanity project, but a profound act of stewardship—a belief that the body, like the mind and the family, required diligent care and informed attention. He
sought not just a long life, but a life lived with full, vibrant capacity, so he could continue to be present for the people and pursuits he loved.
In the end, the life of Dr. Umpa reveals a powerful truth: character is not a single act, but a collection of habits. It is found in the enduring love for a life partner, the quiet
discipline that shapes successful children, the calloused hands of a man who still loves the soil, the generosity that shares the fruits of one’s labor, and the personal discipline
that seeks a healthy and vibrant life. He was a private man, yes, but his legacy is a public square where his values—love, discipline, generosity, and a holistic view of well-
being—stand as monuments. He teaches us that greatness is not always a matter of public acclaim, but can be found in the quiet, steadfast cultivation of a life well-lived, a
garden well-tended, and a family well-loved.
VIII. After the Presidency: Al-Khwarizmi and Continued Engagement
When Dr. Umpa's term as MSU System President concluded in 2005, he did not ease into retirement. In 2008, he led the Ranao Council in establishing the Al-Khwarizmi
International College in Marawi City — a private institution named after the medieval Muslim mathematician whose work laid the foundations of algebra and algorithmic
thinking.5 Serving as the college's founding president, Umpa extended to the private sector the same standards of academic rigor he had pursued within the state system,
ensuring that Lanao del Sur's youth had access to quality higher education beyond what MSU could directly accommodate.
He also remained active in the national social science community, serving as a regional vice president for Mindanao in relevant professional organizations and continuing to
contribute to scholarly discourse on peace, governance, and the Bangsamoro situation.9 In his later public writings and engagements, his concerns grew more explicitly
toward the foundational questions of justice: land rights, cultural recognition, and the protection of the basic human rights of the Bangsamoro people.15 The administrator
had always carried the advocate within him; in his later years, the advocate moved more openly to the surface.
IX. Death and the Resonance of a Life
Dr. Camar Ampaso Umpa passed away on March 7, 2022, in Marawi City.5 His death drew expressions of grief from across the Philippine academic establishment and from
the Bangsamoro community at large. The Bangsamoro Transition Authority Parliament, in formal session, passed multiple resolutions acknowledging his passing and
recording for the legislative record the extent of his contributions.5
Those resolutions described him with terms that the BTA Parliament reserved for those who had genuinely shaped the region's possibilities: an "academic icon," a figure of
dedication to "educational and research excellence," and someone whose life had been an example to those who "endeavor for the best in their personal and community
lives."4 The parliamentary record is a formal document, not given to sentiment, which makes those phrases all the more worth noting.
The institution he did most to build, MSU-IIT, stands today as a monument to the wisdom of his choices. A university that in the 1980s was primarily known for technical
training now holds rankings among the top universities in Asia, carries international research certifications, and sends graduates into scientific and professional careers that
Umpa's own generation could barely imagine for people from Lanao del Sur.2 The path from Uyaan, Madamba, to a QS-ranked research university runs through the
decisions that one man made, term by term, over more than two decades of institutional leadership.
X. An Assessment
Any honest reckoning with the legacy of Dr. Camar A. Umpa must acknowledge what made his leadership unusual rather than merely successful. He operated in an
environment where academic institutions in Muslim Mindanao faced chronic underfunding, political interference, security pressures, and the weight of a historical grievance
that the broader Philippine state had never fully addressed. Within those constraints, he chose a strategy of institutional depth over political visibility: build the research
capacity first, earn the rankings second, and let the demonstrated excellence of the institution make the argument for the community it serves.
That strategy required patience of a kind that is genuinely difficult to sustain in political environments where short-term results command most of the attention. Umpa
sustained it because he had a reasonably clear theory of change: that technological capability, properly measured and systematically cultivated, determines national
prosperity, and that a university system serving a marginalized region has no more important task than proving that the people of that region can produce world-class
scientists and thinkers.8
He was also, it bears emphasizing, a man who held his personal integrity intact across decades in positions where the opportunities for corruption or the abuse of influence
were real. His peers remembered him not for wealth or political connections but for a quality harder to fake and harder to maintain: the quiet authority of someone who had
never been purchased.14
The Bangsamoro community has produced remarkable leaders across many fields. Among those who chose education as their terrain, Dr. Camar Ampaso Umpa left a mark
that will take generations to measure fully. The universities he shaped are still teaching, still researching, still ranking. The students they produce carry forward something he
put in motion long before many of them were born.

Edd K. Usman
Edmund "Edd" K. Usman is a veteran Filipino Muslim journalist
whose career spans several decades of award-winning reporting in
science, technology, and Muslim affairs.
He is best known nationally as a longtime senior correspondent for the
Manila Bulletin (https://mb.com.ph), one of the Philippines' oldest and
most widely read broadsheets, where he covered the Department of
Science and Technology (https://dost.gov.ph) (DOST), the Philippine
Charity Sweepstakes Office (https://pcso.gov.ph) (PCSO), and Muslim
community affairs, among other beats.
His journalism has always aimed at bridging worlds that might
otherwise seem far apart: the world of rockets and microsatellites, and
the world of faith, peace, and Bangsamoro identity.
In 2018, Usman made history as the first-ever winner of the Best
Science Feature Story for Print and Online award at the inaugural UP
Science Journalism Awards, held at the University of the Philippines
Diliman (https://upda.edu.ph).<ref name="UP2018">University of the
Philippines. (2018, February 19). "UP honors top science journalists."
Retrieved from https://up.edu.ph/up-honors-top-science-
journalists/</ref>
The winning entry, published through Rappler, explored the engineering
improvements of the Philippines' second microsatellite, Diwata-2, over
its predecessor, Diwata-1.<ref name="Rappler2018">Rappler. (2018,
February 18). "Rappler wins best science feature story at 1st UP Science
Journalism Awards." Retrieved from
https://www.rappler.com/about/196309-rappler-up-science-journalism-
awards-best-science-feature-story/</ref>
That recognition cemented his reputation not just as a beat reporter, but
as someone who genuinely cared about helping ordinary Filipinos
understand why science matters to their daily lives.
Today, he continues his work as the founder and publisher of SDN
SciTech and Digital News (scitechanddigital.news), an independent digital outlet that covers science, technology,
and Muslim Filipino community affairs.

Background
Usman's full given name is Edmund, though he has gone by "Edd" throughout his professional life, a pen name
that became as familiar in newsrooms as it was on bylines.
His journalism reflects a dual identity that is deeply personal: he is both a seasoned national reporter with access to
science ministries and satellite engineers, and a Muslim Filipino deeply attuned to the concerns of communities in
Mindanao, Metro Manila's Muslim quarters, and the broader Bangsamoro diaspora.
While detailed public records about his early life, hometown, and family background are not extensively
documented in available sources, his reporting consistently reflects a journalist shaped by both secular professional
training and a lived understanding of Islam as practiced in the Philippine context.
His range of covered topics, from the mechanics of microsatellite orbits to the annual logistics of the Hajj
pilgrimage for Filipino Muslims, suggests a reporter who moves naturally between the worlds of science and faith,
and who sees no contradiction between the two.
Education
Specific details of Usman's formal academic education have not been extensively documented in publicly available
records.
What is on record, however, is a consistent pattern of professional development through international training that
shaped his capacity as a science and technology journalist.
In 2002, he participated in the Executive Seminar for Information Technology Journalists in South Korea, an
early indicator of his specialization in technology reporting at a time when the internet was only beginning to
reshape Philippine newsrooms.<ref name="WorldNgayon">WorldNgayon. "Edd K. Usman - Author Profile."
Retrieved from https://worldngayon.com/author/edd-uzman/</ref>
In 2008, he was accepted as a fellow to the prestigious East-West Center Senior Journalists Seminar in the
United States, a program run by the East-West Center in Honolulu, Hawaii, which brings together senior journalists
from across Asia and the Pacific to deepen regional understanding and journalistic practice.<ref
name="WorldNgayon"/>
These two international fellowships, separated by six years, trace the arc of a journalist who treated learning as an
ongoing professional obligation, not a credential to collect and shelve.

PAGE 3
Professional Career
Manila Bulletin Years
The anchor of Usman's professional career was his long tenure as a senior journalist at the Manila Bulletin (http
s://mb.com.ph), a publication founded in 1900 and widely regarded as one of the country's most trusted
broadsheets.<ref name="MBHistory">Manila Bulletin. "Our Company." Retrieved from https://mb.com.ph/our-
company</ref>
He served the Bulletin for many years, covering a remarkably broad set of beats that ranged from police and crime
to health, governance, and science policy.
His core institutional beats included the DOST, the PCSO, the TESDA, and Muslim affairs, a combination that
placed him at intersections most reporters rarely occupied.<ref name="Rappler2016">Rappler. (2016, December
2). "DOST researchers win P1.3 million in total prizes for published studies." Retrieved from
https://www.rappler.com/technology/154296-dost-researchers-published-studies-awards/</ref>
His tenure at the Bulletin ended on April 15, 2016, after which he transitioned fully into freelance and independent
journalism.
Freelance and Contributor Work
After leaving the Bulletin, Usman remained prolific. He contributed work to several major and niche platforms,
including Rappler, Newsbytes.ph, Claire Delfin Online Magazine, Malaya Business Insight, the Agriculture
Magazine (a Manila Bulletin publication), and the U.S.-based Philippine News.<ref name="WorldNgayon"/>
He also contributed exclusive reports to the BusinessMirror, including coverage of the Palestinian diplomatic
community in Manila in the context of the 2023 Gaza conflict and its impact on Filipino workers in Israel.<ref
name="BizMirror2023">BusinessMirror. (2023, November 6). "Our hearts bleed for them: Palestinian envoy
mourns Filipino victims in Gaza." Retrieved from https://businessmirror.com.ph/2023/11/06/our-hearts-bleed-for-
them-palestinian-envoy-mourns-filipino-victims-in-gaza/</ref>
This kind of story, connecting Muslim Filipino concerns to global events through direct diplomatic sourcing, is
very much Usman at his most characteristic: grounding international stories in local human stakes.
SDN SciTech and Digital News
Perhaps his most entrepreneurial step was launching his own independent digital news outlet, SDN SciTech and
Digital News (scitechanddigital.news).
The platform covers science and technology news, BARMM governance, Muslim Filipino community affairs,
national policy, and international stories relevant to Filipino Muslims.
His byline at SDN carries his social media handles: Twitter at @edd1819 and Instagram at @bluestar0910,
reflecting a journalist who embraced digital distribution as comfortably as he once filed broadsheet copy.
Through SDN, Usman has reported on the BARMM, the NCMF, Metro Manila Muslim traders, and the recurring
controversies surrounding the annual Hajj operations for Filipino pilgrims, stories that sit squarely at the
intersection of governance and faith.<ref name="SDN2024">SDN SciTech and Digital News. (2024, March 8).

PAGE 4
"DILG Secretary Benhur Abalos Designates Com. Michael Mamukid as NCMF Officer-in-Charge." Retrieved
from https://scitechanddigital.news/2024/03/08/dilg-secretary-benhur-abalos-designates-com-michael-mamukid-as-
ncmf-officer-in-charge/</ref>
Contributions to Science Journalism
The Diwata Satellite Coverage
If there is one body of work that defines Usman's legacy in Philippine science journalism, it's his sustained
coverage of the Phil-Microsat program and, in particular, the Diwata satellite series.
His article for Rappler, published in June 2017, titled "How Diwata-2 is better than PH's first satellite, Diwata-1,"
brought readers inside the engineering decisions behind the country's second microsatellite with a clarity that few
journalists achieved.<ref name="RapplerDiwata">Rappler. (2017, June 5). "How Diwata-2 is better than PH's first
satellite, Diwata-1." Retrieved from https://www.rappler.com/technology/features/171988-diwata-1-diwata-2-
improvements-up-tech-fair/</ref>
The article explained improvements such as the addition of a radio for better communication, a sun-synchronous
orbit placed 213 kilometers higher than Diwata-1's, and the satellite's enhanced camera payload, all written in the
kind of plain language that invited general readers in rather than shutting them out.
It was this article, submitted under his Rappler contributor byline, that won the inaugural UP Science Journalism
Award in 2018.
It's also worth noting that Usman coined the collective nickname "Magnificent 9" for the nine pioneering Filipino
engineers who designed and assembled Diwata-1, a moniker that stuck in Philippine science reporting and became
part of how that milestone was remembered.<ref name="WorldNgayon2">WorldNgayon. "Diwata-2 Launched:
DOST intensifies space program." Retrieved from https://worldngayon.com/diwata-2-launched-dost-intensifies-
space-program/</ref>
That's the kind of contribution that goes beyond a single article. It shapes how a nation tells its own scientific story.
Bridging Faith and Technology
Beyond satellites, Usman has long explored the intersection of Islamic life and modern technology, asking
questions like: How does the internet change the way Filipino Muslims practice their faith? How do digital systems
reshape the Hajj experience for pilgrims from the Philippines?
These stories don't fit neatly into any single beat. They require a journalist with one foot in the science ministry and
another in the mosque, and Usman has occupied that rare position throughout his career.
Advocacy for Science Communication
Usman has been a consistent voice for raising the standard of science reporting in the Philippines.
His win at the UP Science Journalism Awards, which were themselves created specifically to reward accuracy and
accessibility in science reporting, placed him at the center of an emerging national conversation about what good
science journalism looks like.<ref name="UP2018"/>

PAGE 5
"Very often, science is perceived to be something that is not understandable, something that exists in
laboratories. Our program aims to highlight the fact that developments in science benefit everything
we do and use." — Dr. Elena Pernia, UP CoST Program Leader, on the purpose of the UP Science
Journalism Awards where Usman was first honored.<ref name="UPhonors">University of the
Philippines. (2018, February 19). "UP honors top science journalists." Retrieved from
https://up.edu.ph/up-honors-top-science-journalists/</ref>
The sentiment captures exactly what Usman has practiced throughout his career: the belief that science journalism
is a public service, not just a technical exercise.
Awards and Recognition
Usman's awards track the specific commitments that have defined his career.
In 2014, he won the Print Media category of the Kabalikat Award, part of the PCIEERD-DOST Science
Journalism Awards given by the Philippine Council for Industry, Energy and Emerging Technology Research and
Development (PCIEERD) under the DOST, in recognition of his contribution to promoting science and technology
journalism in the Philippines.<ref name="WorldNgayon"/>
In 2018, he became the first-ever winner of the Best Science Feature Story for Print and Online at the
inaugural UP Science Journalism Awards, organized by the University of the Philippines College of Mass
Communication and held at UP Diliman on February 17.<ref name="UP2018"/><ref name="Rappler2018"/>
The awards jury at UP included journalists, academicians, scientists, and an economist, reflecting the
multidisciplinary standard against which his Diwata-2 feature was measured and found exemplary.<ref
name="UPhonors"/>
These two awards, separated by four years, confirm a journalist who consistently performed at the highest level of
a specialized field.
Cultural Significance
In the landscape of Philippine journalism, Usman represents something that's genuinely rare: a Muslim Filipino
journalist working at a national broadsheet level, covering both hard science and Muslim community affairs with
equal fluency.
His reporting on the ARMM and later the BARMM, on the Hajj, and on Muslim traders and community leaders in
Metro Manila gives voice to a constituency that is too often absent from mainstream Philippine media, or present
only in the context of conflict.
Through SDN, he continues to provide a platform where Bangsamoro governance, Muslim Filipino identity, and
science and digital news coexist in a single editorial space, which is itself a statement about how broad and
interconnected those concerns actually are.
His career models a form of journalism that sees no contradiction between faith and empirical inquiry, between
community accountability and national science coverage.

PAGE 6
Personal Values
Usman's body of work reflects a journalist driven by a few clear values.
The first is a commitment to accuracy, particularly in science reporting, where the gap between what researchers
know and what the public understands can be wide enough to do real harm. His sustained focus on DOST and the
Phil-Microsat program was never just about filing stories. It was about building public literacy.
The second is a commitment to the Muslim Filipino perspective, covering the Bangsamoro community not as an
object of national policy but as a subject with its own voice, its own governance debates, and its own relationship
to modernity and faith.
The third is independence. In founding SDN SciTech and Digital News, Usman chose the harder road of building
his own platform rather than depending entirely on established outlets. For a veteran journalist of his standing,
that's a choice that says something about where he thinks the work needs to happen.

Charisma Samparani Ututalum
Prof. Charisma Samparani Ututalum, CESE is a Muslimah nurse-educator, academic administrator, and public
servant who has served as President of Sulu State University (SSU) — formerly Sulu State College (SSC) —
continuously since her election in June 2018. A proud Tausug woman from the province of Sulu, she is widely
recognized for steering her institution through a period of dramatic growth, quality assurance reform, and its
historic elevation to full university status under Republic Act No. 12296 in 2025. As the first president of Sulu
State University, she stands as one of the most consequential higher education leaders in the Bangsamoro region.
Contents
