Background
Prof. Charisma S. Ututalum was born and raised in Sulu, a
province situated at the southwestern tip of the Philippine
archipelago and one of the constituent provinces of the
Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao
(BARMM). She belongs to the Tausug people — whose name
translates roughly as "people of the current" — a maritime
Muslim ethnic group known for their seafaring heritage, rich oral
traditions, and a deeply ingrained culture of Islamic faith and
communal solidarity.
Her full name often appears with the middle name or family
identifier "Samparani," a naming practice common in Tausug
society that reflects matrilineal or extended family heritage. Public
records note that Engr. Firash Zhed S. Ututalum, known
informally as "Dong" and serving as Dean of Student Affairs at
Sulu State University, shares the Ututalum surname — pointing to
a close-knit family network with meaningful institutional
involvement.

PAGE 2
Details of her early childhood remain relatively private, consistent with many Filipino public leaders whose careers
and contributions speak more prominently than personal biographical accounts. What emerges clearly from the
record is her formation as a Tausug woman who internalized values of magsabil (resilience), educational
aspiration, and community accountability — values that would define her later leadership style.
Education
Ututalum trained formally as a nurse and built her foundational credentials within the nursing profession. She
subsequently pursued advanced academic qualifications, earning doctoral-level credentials that allowed her to be
addressed as both Professor and Doctor in various institutional contexts. Her landmark professional qualification is
the Career Executive Service Eligibility (CESE), a rigorous certification administered by the Career Executive
Service Board of the Philippines that marks readiness for senior leadership roles in the national government and
public sector.
Her academic research engagements have spanned nursing education during the COVID-19 pandemic, the
integration of generative artificial intelligence in teaching practice, virtues-based approaches in psychiatric nursing
education, and broader issues in higher education management within conflict-affected or underserved
communities. She has also contributed to open educational resource development through collaborative work with
institutions such as the University of the Philippines Open University.
Career
Clinical and Academic Nursing
Before ascending to institutional leadership, Ututalum served as a clinical instructor and faculty member, gaining
direct experience in health education delivery. Her nursing background gave her a practical lens through which to
understand the intersection of community health, educational access, and public service — particularly relevant in
Sulu's complex socio-political environment.
Election as President of Sulu State College
She was elected President of Sulu State College (SSC) on June 21, 2018, and has served continuously since, with
her term subsequently extended. Her ascension marked a significant moment for the institution and for Sulu's
higher education landscape. Taking the helm of a regional state college in a province historically affected by armed
conflict and economic marginalization, she embarked on a multi-pronged agenda of institutional development.
Institutional Development and Quality Assurance
Under her leadership, SSC underwent substantial expansion across enrollment, programs, infrastructure, and
institutional systems. Enrollment grew significantly during her tenure, and new academic programs were
introduced across disciplines including tourism, public administration, early childhood education, advanced
nursing, and information technology. Physical infrastructure improvements included the construction and upgrade
of nursing laboratories, administrative buildings, library facilities, and campus-wide Wi-Fi connectivity.
In the area of quality management, the college achieved ISO 9001:2015 certification — a globally recognized
standard for quality management systems — and pursued program accreditations through relevant Philippine
accrediting bodies. SSC also attained PRIME-HRM Maturity Level 2 recognition from the Civil Service

PAGE 3
Commission, affirming the college's human resource management capabilities. Ututalum was re-elected to the
Board of Trustees of the Accrediting Agency of Chartered Colleges and Universities in the Philippines (AACCUP),
underscoring her recognized standing in national quality assurance governance.
Pandemic Response
When the COVID-19 pandemic reached the Philippines, Ututalum spearheaded the college's community response
under the banner of "Pagpahgang ha Covid 19" — a Bayanihan-style initiative that mobilized institutional
resources for health and welfare support. She prioritized ensuring that no student was left behind academically,
implementing flexible learning modalities, achieving high campus vaccination rates, and maintaining continuity of
instruction under extraordinary conditions.
Technology Integration and Community Programs
She championed a SMART campus program that expanded digital infrastructure, along with the adoption of an
online library and administrative automation systems. Community-facing programs launched under her watch
included organic farming partnerships, scholarship expansions for students from disadvantaged backgrounds, and
free bus rides for commuting students — a practical welfare intervention that lowered the daily cost burden of
attending college in a resource-constrained province.
Transition to Sulu State University
The capstone achievement of Ututalum's leadership is the successful conversion of Sulu State College into a full
state university. Republic Act No. 12296 authorized this transformation, with the law lapsing into effect in
September 2025 and the formal institutional transition marked in 2026. As the president who shepherded this
process, she became the inaugural president of Sulu State University (SSU).
The conversion fulfilled long-held aspirations within the province and the broader Bangsamoro region for a
flagship state university anchored in Sulu. SSU is positioned with a mandate toward technological, professional,
and vocational excellence, while also advancing research, cultural preservation, and regional development. The
milestone is regarded as a significant contribution to peace-building and socio-economic progress in BARMM,
expanding access to quality higher education for Tausug youth closer to home.
International Engagement
Ututalum has represented SSC/SSU at international academic events in Japan (notably the International Network
for Quality Assurance Agencies in Higher Education, or INQAAHE), Turkey, and New York, where she engaged
with Filipino educators abroad. She has served as a keynote speaker at international conferences, and has engaged
in global partnerships aimed at enriching the university's academic profile and research visibility.
Recognition
Among the recognitions she has received:
Most Outstanding Governance and Leadership Award in the Academe — a distinction recognizing
exceptional institutional leadership

PAGE 4
Re-election to the AACCUP Board of Trustees — affirming national-level trust in her quality assurance
expertise
Gawad Sulo ng Pamumuno — a local honor recognizing distinguished leadership in the Sulu context
Various institutional and community recognitions tied to her pandemic response initiatives and higher
education contributions
Personal Values and Cultural Significance
Those familiar with her leadership describe a figure who combines approachability with vision — a leader whose
commencement messages and community programs consistently reflect what colleagues characterize as a genuine
"heart for service." She balances professional ambition with cultural sensitivity, actively promoting Tausug identity
within the institution while embracing contemporary imperatives around innovation, sustainability, and inclusivity.
Her research and programmatic interests in Halal-aligned development, Sustainable Development Goals (SDG)
integration, and organic agriculture reflect a leadership philosophy that seeks to root the university's development
within the cultural and ecological context of Sulu.
As a contemporary Tausug woman in a high-profile public institutional role, Ututalum has become a source of
inspiration for young people across Mindanao — particularly young women and girls — who see in her a model of
how local identity, professional excellence, and community commitment can converge into transformative
leadership. Her trajectory also illustrates the expanding role of women in governance and academic administration
within the Bangsamoro region.
Legacy
Prof. Charisma S. Ututalum's legacy is still actively being written. As the founding president of Sulu State
University, she inherits the twin mandates of consolidating hard-won institutional gains and charting new directions
for a province whose youth have long deserved world-class educational infrastructure. Her tenure has demonstrated
that even in regions marked by historical conflict and resource constraints, committed institutional leadership
rooted in cultural pride and genuine service can produce measurable, lasting transformation.
Her story is significant not only for what she has built but for what she represents: a Tausug woman who turned
educational access into a form of peacebuilding, and who led her community's university from a state college to a
full university one milestone at a time.

title: Velez, Patrick Abdulmalik Marban
text:
PAGE 1
Patrick Abdulmalik Marban Velez
Atty. Patrick Abdulmalik Marban Velez (Muslim name: Abdulmalik) is a Filipino lawyer, legal scholar,
national security specialist, and bar association executive whose career cuts across three distinct worlds: the
Philippine defense establishment, Islamic jurisprudence, and bar governance.
A multifaceted jurist, he is one of a rare few Filipino lawyers who holds credentials in both the regular Philippine
court system and the Shari'ah courts, while simultaneously carrying a military commission as a Lieutenant
Colonel in the Philippine Marines.
Born into a family where the law was a way of life, Velez grew up as the son of the late Atty. Puro Velez of the
celebrated UP Law Batch 1958.
That legal inheritance shaped everything that followed: a Juris Doctor from the country's premier law school, a
master's degree in national security, and a postgraduate qualification in Islamic Studies, all from the University of
the Philippines system.
Since October 2025, he has served as the National Executive Director of the Integrated Bar of the Philippines
(IBP), the country's mandatory organization for all licensed attorneys and the central institution of Philippine bar
governance.
Beyond his administrative and government work, Velez is a committed advocate for the Bangsamoro community
and Muslim Filipinos, championing the integration of Islamic legal perspectives into national legislation and
pushing for the adoption of Artificial Intelligence in modernizing the Philippine legal profession.
His legacy phrase, drawn from his own philosophy, says it plainly: "Excellence is a ladder, and service to the
Ummah and the country must go hand in hand."

Background
Patrick Abdulmalik Marban Velez did not stumble into law.
He was born into it.
His father, the late Atty. Puro Velez, was a member of the
University of the Philippines College of Law, Batch 1958, one
of the most distinguished graduating classes in Philippine legal
history.
Growing up in a household where legal reasoning, public service,
and respect for the rule of law were everyday conversations,
Patrick developed a deep appreciation for the profession long
before he ever stepped into a courtroom.
That upbringing set the stage for a journey that would eventually
take him from the halls of the UP College of Law to the corridors
of the Department of National Defense, from the United Nations
to the executive offices of the Integrated Bar of the Philippines.
He joined the UP Sigma Rho Fraternity (Batch '87), a
prestigious law fraternity known for shaping many of the
country's most distinguished legal careers.
That fraternal formation, steeped in discipline, intellectual rigor,
and peer excellence, would remain a cornerstone of his
professional identity throughout his career.
As a Muslim Filipino, Velez also carries a cultural and spiritual
identity that sets him apart in Philippine legal circles: the embrace
of his Islamic faith as an active, professional asset rather than a
private matter, expressed most tangibly in his decision to pursue
formal Shari'ah qualifications alongside his mainstream legal
career.
Education
Velez didn't settle for one credential when three were possible.

PAGE 3

His academic profile is a trilogy: law, defense, and Islamic
scholarship, each building on the last, and each from one of the
Philippines' most respected institutions.
Juris Doctor, University of the Philippines College of
Law (1998)
The foundation of everything came from the University of the
Philippines College of Law, where Velez earned his Juris Doctor
(JD) in 1998.
He went on to pass the Philippine Bar Examinations in 1999,
joining the rolls of the country's licensed attorneys.
The UP College of Law is widely regarded as the Philippines' most rigorous and prestigious law school, and
graduating from it marked Velez as part of an elite tier of Filipino legal practitioners from the very beginning.
Master in National Security Administration (MNSA), National Defense College of the
Philippines (2009)
In 2009, Velez completed his Master in National Security Administration (MNSA) at the National Defense
College of the Philippines (NDCP).
The NDCP program is designed for senior civilian officials and military officers, and it covers the full spectrum of
national security policy, strategic analysis, and defense management.
Completing it earned Velez a commission as a Lieutenant Colonel in the Philippine Marines, a remarkable
distinction for a civilian lawyer and a credential that few attorneys in the country can claim.
Master of Arts in Islamic Studies (MAIS), University of the Philippines Diliman
Perhaps the most distinctive credential in his portfolio, Velez completed a Master of Arts in Islamic Studies
(MAIS) at the University of the Philippines Diliman.
He finished the program with a General Weighted Average (GWA) of 1.08, an exceptional academic mark in the
Philippine grading scale, where 1.0 represents the highest possible achievement.
This degree gave Velez deep formal training in Islamic theology, jurisprudence, and Shari'ah law, opening a
dimension of legal practice that very few Filipino lawyers have ever pursued at the graduate level.
Career
Velez's career moves in three clear chapters, each with its own stage and its own demands.
Department of National Defense (2010 to 2015)
From 2010 to 2015, Velez served as the Assistant Secretary for Acquisitions, Installations, and Logistics at the
Department of National Defense (DND).

PAGE 4
In that role, he was the point person for the AFP Modernization Program, a flagship national initiative to upgrade
the weapons systems, infrastructure, and logistics of the Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP).
Managing large-scale defense acquisitions requires a sharp combination of legal, regulatory, and administrative
expertise.
Velez brought all of that to the DND, overseeing programs that directly shaped the military's operational
capabilities during a period of significant security challenges in the country.
International Consultancy: United Nations Food and Agriculture Organization
Alongside his domestic government work, Velez also contributed on the international stage as a consultant to the
United Nations Food and Agriculture Organization (UN FAO).
His consultancy covered parliamentary expertise and food security, two areas that require a sophisticated
understanding of legislative frameworks and international policy processes.
This international engagement added a multilateral dimension to a career that had already spanned defense, law,
and academia.
Co-Founding of Marcoleta Julian Reyes and Velez (MJRV) Law Offices (2015)
In 2015, Velez co-founded Marcoleta Julian Reyes and Velez (MJRV) Law Offices, bringing his extensive
government, policy, and national security experience into private legal practice.
The firm allowed him to channel his specialized competencies into client service while maintaining his engagement
with bar governance and legal education.
Professor of Laws, Philippine Law School
Running parallel to his government and private practice work, Velez has also served as a Professor of Laws at the
Philippine Law School, shaping the legal thinking of the next generation of Filipino attorneys.
His lectures draw from an unusually broad experiential base: national defense, Islamic jurisprudence, bar
discipline, and international policy.
National Executive Director, Integrated Bar of the Philippines (October 2025 to present)
Since October 2025, Velez has held the post of National Executive Director of the Integrated Bar of the
Philippines (IBP).
The IBP is the mandatory organization for all licensed lawyers in the Philippines, and its National Executive
Director carries responsibility for the institution's day-to-day operations, governance, and delivery of services to
tens of thousands of legal practitioners nationwide.
The appointment brings together every strand of Velez's career: his legal expertise, his administrative experience at
the DND, his decade-long service as a Bar Discipline Commissioner, and his broader vision for a modern,
technology-forward legal profession.

PAGE 5
Institutional Contributions
Velez's contributions to Philippine law extend well beyond his official titles.
Passage of the Shari'ah Bar Examinations (2024)
In 2024, Velez passed the Shari'ah Bar Examinations, a specialized exam that formally qualifies lawyers to
practice in the Philippines' Shari'ah court system.
This placed him among a very small number of Filipino lawyers certified to practice in both the civil court system
and Shari'ah courts simultaneously.
The significance of this cannot be overstated: the Philippines has a substantial Muslim population concentrated in
the Bangsamoro region, and having lawyers who can operate fluently within both legal systems is essential for
meaningful access to justice in Muslim communities.
Commissioner for Bar Discipline
For close to two decades, Velez has served as a Commissioner for Bar Discipline within the IBP's professional
responsibility framework.
The role involves overseeing disciplinary proceedings against lawyers who violate ethical standards, a function that
is central to maintaining the integrity of the Philippine bar.
His sustained service in this capacity reflects a level of institutional trust that is earned only through consistency,
fairness, and deep familiarity with bar regulations.
Advocacy for Artificial Intelligence in Legal Practice
Velez has been an outspoken advocate for integrating Artificial Intelligence (AI) into the Philippine legal
profession.
In an institution known for its traditional rhythms and conservative culture, his push for technology adoption
positions him as a reform-minded voice within bar leadership.
His advocacy covers using AI to improve legal research, streamline case management, and expand access to legal
services, particularly for underserved communities who cannot afford traditional legal representation.
Bangsamoro and Muslim Community Advocacy
By embracing his Muslim identity as a professional asset and qualifying as a Shari'ah Counselor, Velez has
established himself as a meaningful advocate for the Bangsamoro community and Muslim Filipinos more broadly.
He works to ensure that Islamic legal perspectives are reflected in national legislation and policy discussions,
pushing for an inclusive legal framework that recognizes the rights and traditions of Muslim communities within
the Philippine constitutional order.

PAGE 6
Personal Values and Cultural Significance
At his core, Velez is a bridge-builder.
He operates comfortably at the intersection of worlds that don't always speak to each other: national defense,
Islamic scholarship, bar governance, international policy, and legal education.
His personal philosophy is disarmingly simple but demanding in practice: excellence is a ladder, and service to the
Ummah (community) and the country should go hand in hand.
That philosophy shapes how he moves through every role he occupies.
Whether he's lecturing on national security strategy, advising on policy matters, or guiding the IBP's institutional
priorities, Velez carries the identity of a "Sigma Rhoan" throughout: driven by discipline, grounded in peer
excellence, and deeply committed to the law as a tool for genuine public service.
His Muslim identity is not peripheral to his legal career; it is integral to it.
As a Shari'ah-qualified attorney, an Islamic studies graduate with honors, and a community advocate for
Bangsamoro Filipinos, Velez has shown that a Filipino Muslim lawyer doesn't have to choose between professional
ambition and cultural identity.
He can carry both to the highest levels of the nation's legal institutions, and his career is proof of exactly that.
Legacy
The title "The Renaissance Jurist" was not handed to Patrick Abdulmalik Marban Velez.
He earned it, credential by credential, role by role, and community by community.
Few Filipino lawyers can claim a combination remotely similar to his: a Juris Doctor from UP, a master's degree in
national security, a master's in Islamic studies with a near-perfect GWA, a Philippine Marine commission, dual bar
qualifications in civil and Shari'ah law, an international consultancy record with the UN, and a top executive
appointment at the country's bar association.
Each piece connects to the others.
His national security training informs how he understands institutional governance.
His Islamic scholarship grounds his advocacy for Bangsamoro communities.
His decades of bar discipline service underpins his credibility as IBP Executive Director.
His push for AI adoption reflects a lawyer who has watched the law evolve across three decades and wants to keep
it moving forward.
Velez represents a new model of Filipino legal professional: deeply rooted in tradition while genuinely oriented
toward the future.
His work as a bridge between Islamic jurisprudence and Philippine civil law may prove to be his most enduring
contribution, especially as the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao continues to develop and
refine its own legal and governance frameworks.

PAGE 7
For Muslim Filipinos who want to pursue careers in the law without setting aside who they are, Velez's story is
both a precedent and an aspiration.
Recognition
Commission as Lieutenant Colonel, Philippine Marines, earned upon completion of the MNSA at the
National Defense College of the Philippines (2009)
Completion of a Master of Arts in Islamic Studies at UP Diliman with a General Weighted Average of
1.08 (among the highest in the Philippine academic grading scale)
Appointment as National Executive Director of the Integrated Bar of the Philippines (October 2025)
Certification as a Shari'ah Bar lawyer, qualifying him to practice before Shari'ah courts (2024)
Nearly two decades of continuous service as a Commissioner for Bar Discipline within the IBP
International consultancy recognition through engagement with the United Nations Food and Agriculture
Organization (UN FAO)
Challenges
Building a career that spans multiple disciplines is never without friction.
Velez's path has required navigating institutional environments that are not always designed to accommodate
someone who moves fluently between national defense, Islamic law, and bar governance.
Being a Muslim Filipino lawyer within institutions predominantly shaped by civil law traditions and non-Muslim
cultural norms means consistently having to assert the legitimacy and relevance of Islamic legal perspectives, not
just as a cultural matter but as a legal and policy imperative.
Advocating for the integration of Shari'ah principles into national legislation is a long-term project that requires
scholarly credibility, diplomatic patience, and sustained engagement with lawmakers, legal academics, and civil
society, all of which Velez has worked to build over the course of his career.
His push for AI adoption in the legal profession also places him in the position of a reformer within a traditionally
conservative institution.
Driving meaningful technological change in the IBP means persuading a large and diverse membership of the value
of tools and practices that many practitioners have never used, a task that calls for the same combination of vision
and pragmatism that has defined Velez's career from the start.

title: Wadi, Julkipli M.
text:
PAGE 1
Julkipli M. Wadi
Prof. Julkipli M. Wadi is a Filipino Muslim scholar, educator, political analyst, and one of the most respected
voices on Islam, governance, and the Bangsamoro question in the Philippines today. A Tausug intellectual from
Jolo, Sulu, he has spent more than two decades at the University of the Philippines Institute of Islamic Studies
(UP IIS) in Diliman, where he has served as dean across four terms, including his most recent appointment
covering 2025 to 2028. Wadi's signature legacy is the bridge he's spent a career building: between classical Islamic
learning and modern political analysis, between Muslim and non-Muslim Filipino communities, and between the
ivory tower and the urgent, lived realities of Mindanao and the broader Muslim world. He edits the Pangadjian
Journal of Islamic Studies and writes the widely-read "Crucible" column for MindaNews, making him one of the
few Muslim Filipino academics who consistently reaches both scholarly and public audiences.
Early Life and Background
Julkipli M. Wadi was born and raised in Jolo, Sulu, in the heart of Tausug country in the southern Philippines.
Growing up in that environment shaped him in fundamental ways: Jolo has always been a place where Islam,
culture, history, and politics are not separate subjects but a single, lived reality. He absorbed Bahasa Sug, the
Tausug language, alongside Jawi script as a child, giving him a linguistic and cultural grounding that has informed
his scholarship throughout his career. His early years exposed him to the complex history of the Bangsamoro
people, including the long struggle for recognition, autonomy, and justice that would later become a central
concern in his academic and public work.
Education
Wadi's educational journey is itself a story of two worlds weaving together. In the late 1970s and early 1980s, he
studied at the Yahya Radjaie Memorial Islamic School in Jolo, a madrasa where he received a classical Islamic
formation under teachers including Ustadh Abduraqib Azhari and Tuan Sharif Mudar. The curriculum covered the
full range of traditional Islamic sciences: Quran and its recitation, Hadith, Seerah (prophetic biography), Shariah,
Fiqh (Islamic jurisprudence), and Arabic grammar, among others. At the same time, he attended Notre Dame of
Jolo for Boys for his conventional secondary education, graduating as the Batch '86 valedictorian, a distinction
that speaks to his early intellectual seriousness.
After passing the UP College Admission Test (UPCAT) in 1986, family priorities kept him from enrolling
immediately at the national university. He passed through UST and Mapua before eventually settling at the
University of the East (UE), where he completed his Bachelor of Arts in Political Science. That detour turned
out to be formative: political science gave him a systematic framework for analyzing power, governance, and social
movements, which he would later apply directly to Muslim Filipino experience.
He finally arrived at UP in 1990, completing his Master of Arts in Islamic Studies at the Institute in 1993. His
MA thesis examined Islamic diplomacy and the role of the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation (OIC) in the
Bangsamoro question, a topic that sat squarely at the intersection of his two disciplines. He also undertook doctoral
coursework in Political Science at UP, though he did not complete a PhD. That dual foundation in political science
and Islamic studies became his distinctive analytical lens.

PAGE 2

Academic Career
Wadi's career at UP IIS unfolded gradually and organically. He
began as a part-time researcher and research associate before
moving into a full faculty role, then college secretary, and
eventually the deanship. He first became dean around 2009, and
has since served through a second term beginning in 2012, a third
term approved in 2022, and a fourth term covering 2025 to 2028,
reappointed in early 2025. The sustained trust placed in him by the
university reflects both his institutional knowledge and his steady,
principled leadership style.
In the classroom, Wadi covers a rich and demanding curriculum. His
courses include Islamic Revivalism and Contemporary Movements,
Kalam and Islamic Philosophy, Islamic Political Thought, Tafsir
(Quranic commentary), Islamic History, Arabic Historiography,
Islamic Civilization, Islamic Economics, and Islam in Southeast
Asia. He has mentored graduate students at UP across many years,
and has lectured at institutions including the National Defense
College of the Philippines and the University of Santo Tomas.
His research agenda is consistent and coherent: Philippine Muslim
history, the Bangsamoro struggle, the Mindanao conflict, Islamic
political thought, and interfaith dialogue. He approaches these
subjects not as separate fields but as interconnected dimensions of a
single, ongoing story.
Scholarly Work and Publications
Wadi's published output reflects the same dual commitment that has
defined his career: rigorous scholarship and accessible public
writing. His 1993 MA thesis on Islamic diplomacy and the OIC's
relationship to the Bangsamoro question remains an important early
contribution to the field. He has written on Philippine political
Islam, Moro political dynasties, the phenomenon of multiple
colonialism in Moroland, and contributed chapters and essays to
edited volumes on Mindanao narratives. His 2005 piece «Braving
Muslim–Christian Dialogue in the Philippines» stands as one of
his more widely cited contributions to the interfaith literature.
As editor of the Pangadjian Journal of Islamic Studies, he has
helped shape the direction of Islamic scholarship in the Philippine
academic context. His «Crucible» column in MindaNews reaches
a broader readership, offering analysis on regional security, the
Mindanao peace process, global Muslim issues, and moral
dimensions of contemporary politics. The column is notable for its
combination of scholarly grounding and clear, accessible prose, and
it has established him as one of the most consistent public
intellectuals on Bangsamoro and Islamic affairs in the country.

He has built academic linkages across Southeast Asia, the Middle
East, Japan, Europe, and North America, and has co-organized
research consortia spanning multiple institutions.
Public Engagement and Media
Wadi has never been the kind of academic who stays locked in the
university. He appears regularly in media as a political analyst,
offering commentary on Islam and Philippine politics, the Mindanao
peace process, and broader developments in the Muslim world. He
has spoken at national and international conferences and has been a
consistent voice in public discourse on issues that many analysts
treat superficially. His approach to media is measured and principled: he explains, contextualizes, and challenges
stereotypes rather than simply confirming them.
He has spoken and written movingly on Palestine, Gaza, and global calls for solidarity and empathy, framing these
issues within a broader ethical and humanist framework rather than as narrowly political talking points.
Community, Interfaith, and Advisory Work
Beyond academia and media, Wadi is also a man of practice. He serves as imam and khatib at the institute and at
other venues, a role that keeps him anchored in the spiritual and communal dimensions of Islam rather than just its
theoretical study.
His ties to the Silsilah Dialogue Institute in Zamboanga are long-standing, reflecting a sustained personal
commitment to Muslim–Christian dialogue as a practical peacebuilding tool, not just an academic subject.
On the community development side, he was involved in a peace, development, and microfinance pilot project
in Barangay Siunugan, Indanan, Sulu. The project integrated conflict resolution, women's empowerment, and
environmental rehabilitation, demonstrating his interest in connecting Islamic values to grassroots development
work.
On the institutional advisory side, he has sat on the advisory group for the Philippine Stock Exchange's Islamic
finance initiatives, and chairs or serves on Shari'ah compliance boards for microfinance and takaful (Islamic
insurance) organizations. These roles reflect a rare versatility: few Filipino Islamic scholars have moved
comfortably across the university, the mosque, civil society, and the financial sector.
Institutional Contributions
As dean of UP IIS across four terms, Wadi has shaped the institute's academic direction, faculty development, and
public profile over more than a decade. He has worked to position UP IIS as the leading academic center for
Islamic Studies in the Philippines, strengthening its curriculum, research output, and connections to both local
Muslim communities and international academic networks. His editorship of the Pangadjian Journal has raised the
institute's scholarly profile, and his own prolific writing has kept the institute visible in national public discourse.
He has championed the importance of understanding Islam and the Bangsamoro experience not as peripheral or
specialized concerns but as central to any serious engagement with Philippine history, identity, and governance.

PAGE 4
Personal Life and Values
Details about Wadi's immediate family remain largely private, in keeping with his reserved personal style. He is
married, and occasional glimpses in his writing reveal a man with warmth, humor, and a deeply relational sense of
the world. In one column, he recounted a visit to a Palestinian art event where he and his wife noticed another
"Wadi" (the artist Ala Wadi) among the exhibitors, prompting a lighthearted exchange about possible Palestinian
family connections. Small moments like these show the human texture behind the scholar.
His values come through consistently across everything he does: a commitment to dialogue across religious and
cultural divides, ethical seriousness in his engagement with politics and power, advocacy for justice and peace in
Mindanao, and a humanist insistence on shared humanity in the face of global conflicts.
Legacy
In the wider landscape of Philippine intellectual and public life, Julkipli M. Wadi occupies a distinctive and
important place. He is one of the few Filipino scholars who can move fluently between the madrasa tradition and
the national university, between the mosque and the boardroom, between the academic journal and the newspaper
column. As a Tausug intellectual who made his mark at the national university while staying rooted in the culture,
language, and concerns of his home community, he models a form of engagement that is both authentically Muslim
and fully Filipino.
His ongoing leadership at UP IIS ensures that future generations of students will inherit a balanced, historically
informed, and ethically grounded perspective on Islam, the Bangsamoro, and Philippine society. In an era of quick
soundbites and easy polarizations, Wadi's career is a quiet but powerful argument for depth, patience, and dialogue.
Challenges
Wadi's career has unfolded in a context that presents its own structural difficulties. The academic study of Islam
and Muslim Filipino communities has long occupied a marginal position within Philippine higher education,
underfunded and undervalued relative to its importance for national cohesion and peacebuilding. Advocating for
the Bangsamoro cause within mainstream Philippine academia, navigating the sensitivities of Muslim–Christian
relations, and sustaining rigorous scholarship on politically charged topics have all required not just intellectual
skill but also personal resilience. His consistent re-appointment as dean across four terms suggests that he has
managed these pressures with considerable grace, but the structural challenges facing UP IIS and Bangsamoro
studies more broadly remain ongoing.

Sali Wali
Sali "Sal" Wali was a pioneering Moro revolutionary who stood
among the co-founders of the Moro National Liberation Front
(MNLF) and served as one of the key architects of the early
Bangsamoro self-determination movement.
As a prominent member of the historic "Top 90" cadre, Wali made
the leap from elite student activist to feared guerrilla strategist,
commanding the Zamboanga Peninsula with a combination of
tactical genius and cross-ethnic political skill.
His life traces the full arc of the Moro conflict: clandestine military
training in Malaysia, fierce battlefield command under Martial Law,
and a controversial but pragmatic shift into civilian governance
under the Philippine state's early autonomy frameworks.
Contents

EARLY LIFE AND ETHNIC
AFFILIATION
Sali Wali was born into a prominent Muslim family in the southern
Philippines, belonging to the Tausug ethno-linguistic group.
The Tausug are a maritime people native to the Sulu Archipelago,
long known for their complex social structures and an unbroken
tradition of fierce resistance against foreign colonization.
Growing up, Wali came of age during a period defined by shifting
demographics, severe land disputes, and the systematic political
marginalization of the Moro people by the central Manila
government.

PAGE 2
Alicia, Zamboanga Sibugay (historically
part of Zamboanga del Sur)
Post-conflict Role
Regional administrator, LTP (Lupong
Tagapagpaganap ng Pook) Region 9
Notability
Tausug co-founder of the MNLF; one of
the original "Top 90" cadres; guerrilla
commander of the Zamboanga
Revolutionary Command during the
Martial Law era
Known For
Cross-ethnic military leadership in the
Zamboanga Peninsula; establishing the
Alicia stronghold as an MNLF logistics
hub; transitioning from revolutionary
commander to regional civilian
administrator under early Bangsamoro
autonomy frameworks
By the late 1960s, state-sanctioned land pressures and a string of
localized massacres, culminating in the infamous 1968 Corregidor
(Jabidah) Massacre, had galvanized a generation of young Moro
intellectuals.
Like many of his contemporaries, Wali was driven by a deepening
political consciousness centered on defending Bangsamoro identity
and territorial sovereignty.
EDUCATION AND CLANDESTINE
BEGINNINGS
Before taking up arms, Wali belonged to a select generation of
educated Moro youth who studied at major universities in the
Philippines.
That academic environment exposed him to secular political
theories, anti-colonial frameworks, and the radical student activism
of the era.
When regional leaders and early secessionist networks began looking for capable young men to form a physical
defense force, Wali volunteered.
In 1969, he was selected for a highly secretive mission: he became a member of the "Top 90" (also known as the
Freedom Fighters 90, or FF90), a foundational batch of young Moro men who were quietly smuggled out of the
Philippines to Pangkor Island (Pulau Pangkor), Malaysia.
There, they underwent grueling, specialized guerrilla warfare training conducted by international instructors, away
from the reach of Philippine intelligence.
FOUNDATION OF THE MNLF AND INSTITUTIONAL
CONTRIBUTIONS
Upon completing their training on Pangkor Island, the "Top 90" recognized that raw military capability had to be
matched with a coherent political structure.
While still abroad, the core trainees organized themselves, held elections, and formed a central leadership circle.
Wali emerged as a primary institutional pillar of this new apparatus.
He was elected as an original member of the MNLF Central Committee, serving directly alongside founding
Chairman Nur Misuari (a fellow Tausug), Vice-Chairman Abul Khayr Alonto, and pioneer revolutionaries
including Hashim Salamat, Jimmy Lucman, and Caloy Bundaying.
It was this committee that officially adopted the name Moro National Liberation Front, a decision that would
permanently alter the geopolitical landscape of Mindanao.
Within the early military structure, Wali's organizational alignment was with the AB Group (denoting the Alonto-
Basilan operational network), a faction that was instrumental in weapon distribution and in setting up the earliest
tactical units of the Bangsamoro Army.

PAGE 3
CROSS-ETHNIC LEADERSHIP IN THE ZAMBOANGA
PENINSULA
One of the most defining aspects of Wali's revolutionary career was the intersection of his Tausug heritage with his
command over a highly diverse, multi-ethnic force.
The MNLF leadership deliberately distributed its "Top 90" founders across specific geographic sectors to maximize
regional mobilization, and Wali was designated to build and head the front in the Zamboanga sector (Zone III of
the Zamboanga Revolutionary Command).
This was no small challenge.
The Zamboanga Peninsula mainland was a complex ethnic tapestry, home to the Sama, Yakan, and indigenous
Subanen communities, and for a Tausug commander to operate effectively there, Wali had to transcend deeply
embedded tribal distinctions.
His alignment with the AB Group became a natural bridge between the Yakan populations of Basilan and the
diverse Muslim communities of the mainland.
By consistently promoting a unified Bangsamoro identity that cut across individual tribal affiliations, Wali
successfully consolidated these distinct groups into a singular, highly disciplined military force.
REVOLUTIONARY CAREER AND MAJOR ACTIONS
When the structural war erupted in full force following Ferdinand Marcos's declaration of Martial Law in 1972,
Commander Sal Wali proved to be a formidable field tactician.
He established his primary military stronghold in Alicia, Zamboanga Sibugay (which was historically part of
Zamboanga del Sur), turning it into a vital sanctuary and logistics hub for the MNLF in the region.
Operating across the dense terrain of the Zamboanga Peninsula, Wali commanded a crucial maritime and terrestrial
corridor that kept his forces supplied and mobile.
During the heavy Philippine military counter-offensives of 1974, Wali's sector coordinated closely with
neighboring commands to blunt the government's advances.
Historical accounts from fellow fighters recall the punishing conditions of those years: evading Philippine Navy
bombardments in Sibuco, surviving major skirmishes on Sacol Island, and orchestrating the historic "long march"
across the Zamboanga Peninsula to link up with Wali's well-fortified pumpboat network in Alicia.
TRANSITION TO GOVERNANCE AND PERSONAL LIFE
The peak of the military conflict eventually gave way to a diplomatic standstill, marked by the signing of the 1976
Tripoli Agreement.
But the deep structural rifts over how the Philippine government implemented autonomy caused serious fractures
within the MNLF leadership in the years that followed.
During this period of fragmentation, the government pursued a "policy of attraction," offering local leadership roles
to battlefield commanders who agreed to lay down their arms.

PAGE 4
Wali made the pragmatic, and for many of his comrades, highly controversial decision to return to the fold of the
law, entering into a truce ahead of the 1996 Final Peace Agreement.
He transitioned from jungle commander to civilian administrator under the LTP (Lupong Tagapagpaganap ng
Pook) Region 9 framework, the Philippine state's earliest formal experimentation with Moro regional autonomy.
His post-war years were characterized by fierce political maneuvering and an unyielding refusal to accept
marginalization even in a civilian setting.
A particularly striking episode occurred during the post-Martial Law transition in 1986, when the Corazon Aquino
administration appointed Zacaria Candao to restructure the regional offices.
While other commanders vacated their posts peacefully, Sali Wali barricaded his Region 9 office and openly
challenged government officials to a shootout to defend his jurisdiction.
The standoff was serious enough that it forced national cabinet secretaries to temporarily delay their regional
merger plans, a moment that encapsulated his personality perfectly: fierce, unyielding, and absolutely unwilling to
back down.
LEGACY, IMPACT, AND CULTURAL SIGNIFICANCE
Sali "Sal" Wali's legacy is layered and not without its contradictions.
Within the official history of the Bangsamoro, he is revered as a member of the vanguard: one of the foundational
few who sacrificed comfort, safety, and certainty to build a revolutionary movement from nothing.
He is celebrated for his physical bravery and operational genius during the darkest years of the Martial Law era,
and for his rare ability to unite fighters from different ethnic communities under a single Bangsamoro banner.
Though no physical bronze monuments bear his name, Moro historians point to something more durable: his true
monument, they argue, is enshrined within the hard-fought institutional autonomy that modern Bangsamoro
generations now enjoy in Mindanao.
He remains a symbol of the raw, unyielding spirit of the original "Top 90" cadres who proved that an organized
guerrilla force, drawn from a politically marginalized people, could compel a sovereign state to come to the
negotiating table.

title: Wikipedia, Pangalian Balindong -
text:
PAGE 1
Pangalian Balindong
Ali Pangalian Macaorao Balindong[3] (January 1, 1940 – October 2, 2025) was a Filipino lawyer and
politician. He was the speaker of the Bangsamoro Parliament from 2019 until his death in 2025.
Balindong was also a deputy speaker of the Philippine House of Representatives and a member of
the 1971 Philippine Constitutional Convention.
Early life and education
Pangalian Balindong was born on January 1, 1940, in Lanao (modern-day Dapao in Pualas, Lanao del
Sur) to an influential clan.[3][4] He was the eldest son of Sultan Amer Macaorao Balindong, a former
mayor of Malabang, and Maimona Marohom.[5]
Balingdong finished his primary education at the Malabang Central Elementary School in 1954 and
finished his secondary education at the Our Lady of Peace High School in 1958.[6]
He attended the Manuel L. Quezon University in Manila graduating with a political science degree in
1962 and a law degree in 1966. He passed the bar examinations in the following year. He took some
master's units in public administration at the Mindanao State University.[6][4]
Career
Balindong engaged in private legal practice and served as legal counsel for the Moro National
Liberation Front (MNLF) which works for peace initiatives with the government. In 1971, he joined
the Philippine Constitutional Convention representing the Lone District of Lanao del Sur.[7]
ARMM assemblyman
Balindong started his political career when he held the post of Assemblyman from 1990 to 1993
representing the 2nd District of Lanao del Sur and was elected as Speaker of the Regional Legislative
Assemblyman of the Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (ARMM) between 1991 and 1993.[7]
House of Representatives
Balindong was a member of the House of Representatives with Lanao del Sur's 2nd district as his
constituency. He ran in the 1987 elections but lost to Mohammad Ali Dimaporo.[8]
He was elected as Lanao del Sur 2nd district representative in the 1995 election for the 10th
Congress. He ran again in 2007 and became a representative during the 14th, 15th, and 16th

PAGE 2
Congresses. In 2013, he rose to the deputy
speaker post of the House of Representatives
until 2016.[9][10][7]
Balindong authored the law (Republic Act No.
9997) which created the National Commission on
Muslim Filipinos in 2009. Balindong also authored
Integrated History Act of 2016 (Republic Act No.
10908) which mandates the inclusion of Moro and
indigenous people's history in the national history
curriculum. He also proposed House Bill 144
which bans the use of "Muslim" and "Christian" in
describing suspects of a crime in news reporting
to discourage harmful stereotypes.[11]
He also authored and an advocate of the
Bangsamoro Basic Law during his tenure as a
congressman. A similar measure which proposed
the creation of a Bangsamoro autonomous region
became law in 2018 which is now known as the
Bangsamoro Organic Law.[11]
Consultative Committee
In 2018, under Executive Order No. 10, Balindong
was appointed by President Rodrigo Duterte as a
member of the 25-member Consultative
Committee to Review the 1987 Philippine
Constitution, a committee composed of former
government officials, veteran lawyers, and
academicians tasked by Duterte to craft a federal
constitution.[12]
Bangsamoro Parliament
Balindong became part of the Bangsamoro
Transition Authority, which forms part of the
interim Bangsamoro Parliament, in 2019. On
March 29, 2025, Balindong was elected as
parliament speaker having been nominated by

Personal life and death
Balindong was a Maranao.[5] He married Jamela

After six years in office, Balindong died at age 85
on October 2, 2025, while at the St. Luke's
Medical Center in Quezon City for an undisclosed
illness.[4]

title: Wikipedia, Yusop Alano -
text:
PAGE 1
Yusop Alano
Yusop Tanduh Alano[1] (born June 9, 1976) is a Filipino politician who has served as the
representative for Basilan's lone district since 2025. A member of the Partido Federal ng Pilipinas, he
previously served as the vice governor of Basilan from 2016 to 2025.
Vice Governor
First term
In the 2016 Philippine gubernatorial elections, he ran for Vice Governor under the Nationalist
People's Coalition. He won with 77,709 votes, defeating three other candidates.[2] In 2017, he gave
out special medals for Basilan graduates.[3] Alano attended the opening of the Agro-Industrial Trade
Fair for the 44th founding anniversary of Basilan, stating that the fair "showcases not only the
development but to include the potentials of the province."[4]
Second term
In the 2019 Philippine gubernatorial elections, he ran for Vice Governor under Partido Demokratiko
Pilipino. He won with 100,357 votes, beating two other candidates.[5] A "School of Living Tradition"
or Lumah Yakan was created on November 25, 2020, in Isabela, Basilan, as a project by Alano.[6] He
contributed to providing aid to Overseas Filipino Workers during the COVID-19 pandemic.[7]
Third term
In the 2022 Philippine gubernatorial elections, he ran for his third and final term asVice Governor
under Partido Demokratiko Pilipino. He won with 140,399 votes, 78.44 percent of the votes, beating
three other candidates.[8] On August 7, 2023, he joined the Taguima Youth Congress. In the
congress, he had an address and a Q&A session.[9] During his term, he supported a revenue code in
the Bangsamoro Parliament to increase revenue-raising capacity.[10]
House of Representatives
In the 2025 Philippine House of Representatives elections, he ran for Basilan's lone district under the
Partido Federal ng Pilipinas. He won with 119,696 votes, 37.93 percent of the votes, beating one
other candidate by a margin of 10 percent.[11]

Mohammad Shuaib Yacob
Mohammad Shuaib Yacob, Ph.D. (born 30 April 1970) is a
Maguindanaon politician, academic, and development professional
who currently serves as the Speaker of the Bangsamoro
Parliament.
As one of the senior architects of the Bangsamoro Autonomous
Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM), Yacob embodies the
intersection of grassroots development work and democratic
institution building.
His rise from conflict-affected community organizer to
parliamentary leader represents a distinctive model of leadership:
one grounded in lived experience of post-conflict reconstruction
and committed to what he calls "moral governance" rooted in the
rule of law.
Contents
1 Early Life and Formation
2 Education and Intellectual Formation
3 The Bangsamoro Development Agency Years
4 Political Career: Building Democratic Institutions
4.1 Minister of Agriculture
4.2 Senior Minister and Bureaucratic Coordination
4.3 Speaker of the Bangsamoro Parliament
5 Legacy and Institutional Contribution
6 Challenges and Ongoing Work
7 Recognition
8 See Also
9 Further Reading
Early Life and Formation
Yacob grew up in Maganoy, a town in the heart of Maguindanao
province.
His parents, Maslamama Yacob and Salama Omar, ensured he
received education spanning both Islamic and secular traditions.
He attended Al-Islaah Elementary School and Ma'had Kutawato Al
Islamic for his early schooling, absorbing the intellectual currents of his community while maintaining connection
to broader educational horizons.
This dual formation would later define his approach to governance: one that honors Islamic principles while
engaging secular institutional frameworks.

PAGE 2
Education and Intellectual Formation
Yacob pursued advanced study with deliberate purpose.
He earned a Bachelor of Science in Shariah Law from the International Islamic University in Madinah, Saudi
Arabia, positioning himself within Islamic jurisprudential traditions.<ref name="speaker_profile">Speaker of
Parliament Profile, Bangsamoro Parliament Official Website (2026).</ref>
Upon returning to the Philippines, he shifted toward public administration, completing a Master's degree at
Cotabato City State Polytechnic College.
In 2013, Cotabato State University conferred upon him a Doctor of Philosophy in Public Administration, granting
him the academic credentials to match his growing practical experience in institutional development.<ref
name="phd_conferred">Mohammad Yacob elected new Bangsamoro Parliament speaker, BTA Media (Oct 21,
2025).</ref>
The Bangsamoro Development Agency Years
Before entering formal government, Yacob spent nine years (2010-2019) as Executive Director of the Bangsamoro
Development Agency (BDA), the development arm of the Moro Islamic Liberation Front.
Established under the 2001 GPH-MILF Tripoli Agreement, the BDA was tasked with delivering relief,
rehabilitation, and socio-economic programs to conflict-affected communities across Mindanao.
Under Yacob's leadership, the agency became more than a relief mechanism.
He championed modernized approaches to food security, rural livelihoods, and infrastructure rehabilitation in some
of Mindanao's most marginalized municipalities.
His work bridged a critical gap: it demonstrated that development and peace-building are not separate tracks but
deeply intertwined.
Communities recovering from conflict needed not just security, but dignified pathways to economic participation
and institutional trust.
Alongside his development work, Yacob served as a visiting professor in graduate studies and as a Shariah Advisor
for Al Amanah Investment Islamic Bank, maintaining intellectual engagement even while managing operational
responsibilities.
Political Career: Building Democratic Institutions
Minister of Agriculture
When the Bangsamoro Organic Law was ratified and the Bangsamoro Transition Authority (BTA) was established
in 2019, President Rodrigo Duterte appointed Yacob as the inaugural Minister of Agriculture, Fisheries, and
Agrarian Reform (MAFAR).

PAGE 3
In this portfolio, he focused on modernizing irrigation systems in conflict-affected municipalities, establishing food
security frameworks for the newly formed region, and creating linkages between smallholder farmers and regional
markets.
His tenure emphasized practical institutional building rather than grand proclamations.
Senior Minister and Bureaucratic Coordination
In April 2025, Yacob was elevated to Senior Minister of the BARMM, succeeding Abunawas Maslamama.<ref
name="senior_min">Dr. Mohammad Yacob Appointed as BARMM Senior Minister, Ministry of Agriculture,
Fisheries, and Agrarian Reform (April 8, 2025).</ref>
As Senior Minister, he served as the primary coordinator of the regional bureaucracy under Chief Minister Ahod
"Al-haj Murad" Ebrahim, managing cross-ministry collaboration and ensuring policy coherence across the
emerging institution.
Speaker of the Bangsamoro Parliament
On 21 October 2025, the 80-member Bangsamoro Parliament unanimously elected Yacob as its Speaker, filling
the vacancy left by the passing of Atty. Ali Pangalian Balindong.
His election underscored rare consensus among competing BARMM political blocs, a testament to his reputation
for institutional neutrality and procedural rigor.
Upon taking his oath, Yacob articulated a leadership philosophy centered on what he termed "moral governance": a
commitment to transparent deliberation, equitable representation of all BARMM communities, and institutional
strength grounded in constitutional fidelity rather than factional advantage.<ref name="pna_speaker">Bangsamoro
Parliament elects new speaker, key officers, Philippine News Agency (Oct 22, 2025).</ref>
As Speaker, he presides over parliament during a critical transitional moment.
The deliberative body is moving toward the first regular parliamentary elections, and Yacob's role is to ensure that
the institution matures with credible procedures and public confidence.
He also serves as Vice President for Southern Mindanao of the United Bangsamoro Justice Party (UBJP).
Legacy and Institutional Contribution
Yacob's trajectory traces a quiet revolution in Bangsamoro governance.
He did not build his authority through patronage networks or rhetorical flourish, but through demonstrated
competence in translating policy into livelihood, and institutions into trust.
His signature contribution is the model he embodies: development practitioner turned parliamentary leader, one
who carries conflict-affected communities into the chambers of power not as abstractions but as lived experience.
In an autonomous region still negotiating its place within the Philippine state and its own internal political ecology,
Yacob represents something rare: a senior leader whose authority derives equally from grassroots credibility and
institutional legitimacy.

PAGE 4
His emphasis on moral governance acknowledges that institutions in post-conflict contexts cannot survive on
procedure alone; they require leaders willing to subordinate partisan advantage to constitutional principle.
Challenges and Ongoing Work
The Bangsamoro Parliament faces structural challenges: resource constraints, coordination with the national
government, and the need to deliver tangible benefits to diverse Muslim communities while maintaining political
cohesion ahead of 2025 elections.
As Speaker, Yacob navigates these constraints without the resources of mature legislatures, yet with heightened
scrutiny from both BARMM constituents and national observers.
His responsibility is to demonstrate that the autonomous region's parliamentary system can function with integrity
and responsiveness.
Recognition
Yacob has been recognized by civil society organizations focused on peace-building, good governance, and
development effectiveness for his work in bridging development and democratic institution building.
His elevation to Speaker was widely interpreted as affirmation of his commitment to procedural neutrality in a
region where deliberative bodies have historically been instruments of factional power.

Corazon Yap-Bahjin
Ma. Corazon Yap-Bahjin is a pioneering Filipino diplomat of Tausug
descent whose career rewrote what was possible for Muslim women in
Philippine public service. Born in Jolo, Sulu, she climbed the ranks of
the Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA) over three decades, becoming
the first Muslim Filipina to pass the career Foreign Service Officers'
Examination and, in 2009, the first Muslim woman to head a Philippine
diplomatic mission when she was appointed Ambassador to the
Kingdom of Bahrain.
Her story isn't just about personal achievement. It's about what
representation looks like in practice: a woman from a Muslim minority
community sitting at the table of international relations, negotiating
trade agreements, protecting overseas workers, and showing the world a
more complete picture of who Filipinos are. Among the Bangsamoro
people, she stands as one of the clearest proofs that the corridors of
Philippine governance have always had room for Muslim excellence.
The challenge was never about ability but access.

PAGE 2

Early Life and Family Background
Corazon Yap-Bahjin grew up in Jolo, the historic heart of the Sulu Archipelago, surrounded by a culture of deep
Islamic faith, oral tradition, and an enduring sense of place. She is the eldest of two siblings born into a family
where scholarship and public service were not optional but expected.<ref name="illustrado2011">Template:Cite
web</ref>

PAGE 3
Her father was a lawyer. Her mother was a trailblazer in her own right: the first Regional Director of the
Commission on National Integration (CNI), the defunct government office tasked with addressing the needs of
indigenous peoples, and a college professor who shaped young minds long after her government service. Both
parents impressed upon their children a set of values that Yap-Bahjin has carried throughout her career.<ref
name="illustrado2011"/>
"The pursuit of excellence and hard work has always been a tradition in our family, with both my
mother and my father. We were taught to be honest and dedicated, and to be loyal to our service."
Growing up in a region defined by political complexity and intermittent conflict, she developed early what would
become her professional signature: a calm, principled resilience in the face of difficult circumstances.
Education
Yap-Bahjin pursued her undergraduate studies at the University of Santo Tomas (UST) in Manila, one of the oldest
universities in Asia. She earned her Bachelor of Science in Education in 1967, graduating cum laude with a co-
major in English and Theology. The academic distinction was a signal of things to come.<ref
name="illustrado2011"/>
She went on to earn a Master of Arts degree with a major in Social Studies from the University of the Philippines
(UP) in 1974, the same institution that has produced a disproportionate number of the country's diplomats,
legislators, and senior civil servants.<ref name="illustrado2011"/>
This combination of humanistic formation at UST and rigorous academic engagement at UP gave her the
intellectual foundation to navigate both the deeply human dimensions of diplomacy and its formal, policy-driven
demands.
Career
Teaching (1967-1979)
Before she ever set foot in a foreign service office, Yap-Bahjin was an educator. She spent more than a decade
teaching from 1967 to 1979, a period that sharpened her communication skills and gave her something many
diplomats lack: genuine experience explaining complex things to people who aren't already experts.<ref
name="illustrado2011"/>
Entering the Foreign Service (1979)
In 1979, she made the transition to government service, joining the DFA and starting as Acting Director of the
Cultural Division of the Office of Islamic Affairs (now the Office on Muslim Affairs).<ref
name="illustrado2011"/> It was a role perfectly suited to someone of her background, and she used it as a
launchpad.
The milestone that defined her early career, however, came when she passed the grueling career Foreign Service
Officers' Examination (FSO Exam), one of the most demanding professional licensure tests in the Philippine civil
service, requiring mastery of international law, economics, history, and diplomacy. She became the first Muslim
Filipina to pass it.<ref name="dfafb">Template:Cite web</ref>

PAGE 4
Overseas Postings
Her diplomatic career took her across the Middle East, Southeast Asia, and East Asia, often to postings where her
Tausug identity and Islamic background gave her a strategic and human advantage.
Jeddah (1986)
Her first overseas assignment was as Vice Consul in Jeddah, Saudi Arabia, one of the most significant postings in
the Philippine foreign service given the large Filipino worker population in the Kingdom. It was her first direct
exposure to the realities of overseas Filipino workers (OFWs), an issue that would define much of her later career.
<ref name="illustrado2011"/>
Amman (1990)
Posted to Jordan as Second Secretary and Consul at the Philippine Embassy in Amman, she found herself in the
middle of a regional crisis. When Iraq invaded Kuwait in 1990 and triggered the Gulf War, thousands of Filipino
workers were suddenly stranded and in danger. Yap-Bahjin was part of the team that coordinated the emergency
repatriation of Filipinos from Kuwait, a high-pressure operation that demanded both logistical precision and human
sensitivity.<ref name="illustrado2011"/>
Cairo
From Jordan, she moved to Egypt as Second Secretary and Consul at the Philippine Embassy in Cairo, deepening
her expertise in Middle Eastern affairs and expanding her network in the Arab world.<ref name="illustrado2011"/>
Bangkok (1992)
She was posted to Thailand in 1992 as part of the Philippine Embassy in Bangkok, initially in the same Second
Secretary and Consul role. She was later promoted to First Secretary, taking charge of the Political Division and
serving concurrently as Consul and Deputy Representative to the United Nations Economic and Social
Commission for Asia and the Pacific (ESCAP), a significant multilateral responsibility.<ref
name="illustrado2011"/>
Xiamen (1995-2001)
Her longest pre-ambassadorial posting was in Xiamen, China, where she served as Consul General for six years
active tour of duty. A six-year stint in one posting speaks to both her effectiveness in the role and the DFA's
confidence in her ability to manage a complex bilateral relationship.<ref name="illustrado2011"/>
Home Office Assignments
Between and alongside her overseas postings, Yap-Bahjin held several senior positions at the DFA's central office
in Manila:
She served as Acting Assistant Secretary of the Office of Consular Affairs in 1999, then as Assistant Secretary of
the Office of Strategic Planning and Policy Coordination from 2006 to 2007, and subsequently as Assistant
Secretary of the Office of Personnel and Administration Services from 2007 to July 2009.<ref
name="illustrado2011"/>

PAGE 5
Ambassador to the Kingdom of Bahrain (2009-2012)
In 2009, President Gloria Macapagal-Arroyo appointed Yap-Bahjin as the Philippine Ambassador to the Kingdom
of Bahrain, making her the first Muslim woman in Philippine history to lead a diplomatic mission abroad.<ref
name="illustrado2011"/><ref name="illustradolegacy">Template:Cite web</ref> She was the fourth female
ambassador the Philippines had sent to that kingdom.<ref name="illustradolegacy"/>
During her tenure in Manama, she oversaw the welfare of approximately 45,000 Filipinos in Bahrain, the majority
of them household service workers and skilled laborers.<ref name="illustrado2011"/> Her open door approach at
the embassy was widely noted: she prioritized access, listened to workers' grievances directly, and worked with
labor agencies and employers to strengthen protections for domestic workers in particular.<ref
name="ogembassy">Template:Cite web</ref>
She also kept her eye on economic diplomacy. In 2012, she met with Mahmood Al Kooheji, then-CEO of
Mumtalakat, Bahrain's sovereign wealth fund, to urge the kingdom to consider investing in Philippine
infrastructure and socio-economic projects under the government's Public-Private Partnership (PPP) program.<ref
name="ppp">Template:Cite web</ref>
Beyond trade, she brought entrepreneurship directly to the Filipino community. She facilitated the expansion of the
Go Negosyo advocacy to Bahrain, bringing business development seminars to OFWs to help them build the skills
and the mindset needed to eventually return home and create their own livelihoods rather than remain in precarious
domestic employment.<ref name="philstar">Template:Cite web</ref>
During the 2011 Bahraini uprising, when civil unrest threatened the safety of Filipino workers, she quickly secured
assurances from Bahraini Prime Minister Prince Khalifa bin Salman Al Khalifa, who met with her alongside
ambassadors from India, Bangladesh, Pakistan, and Thailand to affirm the government's commitment to protecting
foreign workers.<ref name="ogbahrain">Template:Cite web</ref>
Personal Values and Philosophy
Yap-Bahjin has never framed her career as a feminist project, and she's clear about why. In an interview with
Illustrado Magazine, she described herself as "feminine but not a feminist," explaining that women don't need
special treatment because they're already capable of performing at the highest level alongside anyone else.
"Forget that you are a woman; because dignity and humanity has no gender. Women do not need any
special treatment, because we can do it just like everyone else can."
What drives her isn't competition with others but with herself. As she put it:
"I was never competitive. I only competed with myself. At the end of the day, if you want to set your
target on 80 percent, or 100 percent, or even 120 percent, it is all up to you."
Her views on OFW welfare are equally direct. While she supports Filipinos' right to work abroad, she's never been
shy about the social cost of mass labor migration, particularly the vulnerability of domestic workers:
"It would be better if our women did not put themselves at such a vulnerable situation, for meager
salaries, especially considering the social cost of such employment. If they really want to work abroad,
it is better for them to acquire some skills that will allow them to work in other fields, instead of
having to take care of other people's children. Then at least, they will have the freedom to move and
they will be treated better."

PAGE 6
Her Islamic faith is inseparable from her identity, but she's always insisted that her output speaks for itself
regardless of religion or gender:
"In the long run, when it comes to my work, it is really not about me being a Muslim, or me being a
woman. It is the work and the service that I am focused on. My output and work do not depend on my
religion or gender."
Advocacy and Continuing Public Service
Even after her formal diplomatic service, Yap-Bahjin has stayed engaged with the public. In December 2025, she
participated in career development seminars for Political Science and Legal Management students, sharing insights
drawn from her decades of experience in the foreign service.<ref name="sscr">Template:Cite web</ref>
Her accessibility to young people, especially those from Muslim-Filipino communities, reflects the same
commitment that animated her entire career: making space for others so that the path she broke open doesn't close
behind her.
Cultural and Historical Significance
For the Bangsamoro people, Corazon Yap-Bahjin is more than a diplomat. She's a proof of concept. At a time when
Muslims in the Philippines were, and continue to be, systemically underrepresented in the national bureaucracy, she
didn't just enter the system. She rose to its highest diplomatic tier.
Her significance plays out in at least three dimensions. First, she expanded the visible face of Philippine diplomacy.
In Gulf states where her Muslim identity created instant rapport and credibility, she modeled what genuine cross-
cultural representation looks like and demonstrated that the Philippines is a plural nation, not a monolithic
Christian one. Second, she created a template for Bangsamoro women with professional ambitions in government,
proving that meritocracy, if genuinely applied, has no ethnic or religious ceiling. Third, her advocacy for OFW
dignity kept the human cost of migration at the center of policy conversations, particularly for the most vulnerable
segment: domestic workers far from home with limited legal recourse.
Her Tausug heritage, drawn from the same culture that produced the Sultan of Sulu's storied maritime tradition of
resilience and negotiation, resonates through her diplomatic career as something more than biographical backdrop.
It's a living argument for the richness that the Bangsamoro brings to the Philippine national story.
Recognition and Awards
In 2013, Ambassador Yap-Bahjin, along with other AEPs, was awarded outstanding service conferred by the
Philippine government on its foreign service officers. The award recognizes exceptional and distinguished service
to the country through diplomacy.<ref name="gmanet">Template:Cite web</ref>
She was also featured as a "Woman of Substance" by Illustrado Magazine, a publication covering prominent
Filipinos in the Gulf, and has been cited in retrospectives on the legacy of Filipino diplomats in the Middle East.
<ref name="illustrado2011"/>

PAGE 7
Challenges and Barriers
Her career was not without friction. She navigated a professional environment where Muslim Filipinos were a
statistical rarity, and where being both Muslim and a woman in a senior role was still, for some, a novelty that
required justification.
She has spoken candidly about having to prove herself on multiple axes simultaneously: not just as a new entrant in
a competitive service, but as a representative of a minority community facing persistent negative stereotypes, and
as a woman in a field still dominated by men at its upper levels.
"I have to prove that we also have what it takes to succeed and that we can be as good, if not better, as
everybody else."
Her response to these pressures was not to make noise about them but to outperform. Her stint as Consul General in
Xiamen and her three-year ambassadorship in Bahrain suggest she did exactly that.

title: Yusop, Abdulgani L.
text:
PAGE 1
Grand Mufti Abdulgani L. Yusop
Al-Haj
Full Name
Al-Ustadz AbdulGhani L. Yusop Al-Haj Al-
Azhari
Abdulgani L. Yusop
Al-Ustadz AbdulGhani L. Yusop Al-Haj Al-Azhari (rahimahullah), widely known as Grand Mufti Abdulgani
L. Yusop, was one of the most distinguished Islamic scholars and religious leaders in the history of the Philippines.
Born on Sacol Island, Zamboanga City, he rose from humble beginnings to become the highest Islamic religious
authority across the Zamboanga Peninsula, Palawan, and much of the Bangsamoro homeland in Southern
Philippines. A graduate of Al-Azhar University in Cairo, he was elected by a Mindanao-wide assembly of Ulama in
1989 as the first Grand Mufti of the Darul Ifta' Region IX and Palawan, an institution he founded and led until
1997. He is remembered as a man of profound learning, rare humility, and extraordinary courage: a scholar who
stepped into conflict zones not with weapons but with wisdom, and who made the Islamic tradition a force for
healing rather than division.
Contents

2 EDUCATION
3 CAREER

4.2 Zambasul Ulama Center for Arabic and Islamic
Studies

BACKGROUND
Abdulgani L. Yusop was born on Sacol Island, Zamboanga City,
into a family that carried both noble lineage and deep religious
purpose. On his father's side, his family held a position of strong
religious leadership within the Banuwa Bangingih Tribal
Hierarchy. His maternal lineage traced back to Indonesia, to the
generation thirty years after the death of the Prophet Muhammad
(peace be upon him), connecting him directly to the earliest
missionaries who brought Islam to the Philippine archipelago.
His household was modest in material terms but rich in faith,
learning, and a sense of sacred responsibility. That dual
inheritance, of tribal leadership and missionary piety, would
shape the entire arc of his life's work.

PAGE 2
Also Known As
AbdulGhani Yusuf Al-Azhari
(rahimahullah)
Born
Sacol Island, Zamboanga City, Philippines
Creed and School
Sunni Ash'ari ('Aqeedah); Shafi'i
(Madh'hab); Scholar of Tasawwuf and
Ilmul Kamaasan
Office

Education
